sections.title: Defining Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)
sections.content: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED), also known as Graves’ Orbitopathy, is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammation and swelling of the extraocular muscles (EOMs) and orbital fat. It is the most common cause of both unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults.

sections.title: Scenario 1: Interpreting Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs)
content: Scenario: A 45-year-old female presents with eyelid retraction. Labs: Suppressed TSH and elevated Free T4.
Definition: Hyperthyroidism (Thyrotoxicosis) – excessive secretion of thyroid hormones.
Examiner's Pick: Suppressed TSH with high T4/T3 is classic for Graves' disease.
High Yield: Severity of TED often does not parallel serum levels of T3 or T4.
Red Flag: TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) or Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI) are specific markers for Graves' and correlate with eye disease activity.

sections.title: Scenario 2: The Medical Emergency – Thyrotoxic Storm
content: Clinical Picture: Hyperpyrexia (>41°C), dehydration, tachycardia (>140 bpm), heart failure, and coma.
Scenario: Patient with known Graves’ presenting for surgery with Temp 41°C, HR 150 bpm, and extreme agitation.
TREATMENT DOSES:
Beta-blockers: Propranolol (40 mg PO or 1 mg slow IV) to control heart rate.
Antithyroid Drugs: Carbimazole (15–25 mg Q6H PO) or Propylthiouracil.
Iodine: Lugol’s solution (0.3 mL PO Q8H) to block hormone release.
Corticosteroids: Hydrocortisone (100 mg Q6H IV) to block T4-to-T3 conversion.

sections.title: Scenario 3: The Hypothyroid Emergency – Myxoedema Coma
content: Clinical Picture: Hypothermia (34°C), bradycardia (45 bpm), hypotension, seizures, and 'myxoedema madness'.
Management Step 1: Thyroid replacement with T3 (5–20 µg IV Q12H) or Levothyroxine.
Management Step 2: Steroids – Hydrocortisone (100 mg Q8H IV) if pituitary involvement is suspected.
Pitfall: Avoid rapid rewarming; treat infections and hypoglycemia concurrently.

sections.title: Scenario 4: Sight-Threatening TED (CON)
content: Diagnosis: Compressive Optic Neuropathy (CON).
Clinical Scenario: 'Washed out' colors, reduced vision, and positive RAPD.
Mechanism: Crowding of the orbital apex by enlarged EOMs.
Treatment: Pulse Steroids – IV Methylprednisolone (500 mg–1 g daily for 3 days).
Emergency Surgery: Urgent orbital decompression if steroids fail within 48–72 hours.

rows: Tachycardia, Tremor, Heat intolerance, Weight loss, Goiter
Bradycardia, Cold intolerance, Weight gain, Dry skin, Constipation

sections.title: Scenario 5: Exposure Keratopathy in TED
content: Clinical Picture: Incomplete blink (lagophthalmos), inferior punctate erosions, and possible bacterial keratitis.
Scenario: 26 mm proptosis with central corneal infiltrate.
Management: Intensive lubricants, nocturnal eyelid taping, or Moisture goggles.
Hazard: Permanent vision loss from corneal perforation.

sections.title: Smoking Key Points
sections.content: Smoking is the single most important modifiable risk factor for TED progression. Smokers are 7–10 times more likely to develop TED and have a longer active phase (2–3 years vs. 1 year in non-smokers).

rows: Parinaud syndrome (Collier sign), 3rd nerve misdirection, Myasthenia Gravis (Hering’s law), or orbital mass.
Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) - Rule out with Platelet count and ESR.

content.explanation: Order of Muscle Involvement: Inferior Rectus > Medial Rectus > Superior Rectus > Lateral Rectus > Obliques.

sections.title: Scenario 9 & 10: Signs & Management
content: Restrictive Myopathy: Persistent 20-prism diopter hypotropia in TED.
Strabismus Management: Recession only (avoid resection due to fibrosis). Delay until 6 months of stability.
Eyelid Signs: Dalrymple sign (retraction at rest), von Graefe sign (lid lag on downgaze).

branches: Diagnosis (2 of 3): Immune dysfunction, Ocular signs (Proptosis/CON), Imaging (Tendon-sparing EOM)
Assessment: CAS Score (Pain, redness, swelling). Score ≥ 3/7 = Active
Tiered Rx: Mild (Lubes, Selenium 100µg BD), Mod/Severe (Steroids), Sight-Threat (CON)

sections.title: Clinical Phases: Active vs. Quiescent (Rundle’s Curve)
content: Active Phase: Congestive stage, red/painful eyes, lasts 6–18 months. Requires immunosuppression.
Quiescent Phase: 'Burned-out' phase, white eyes but persistent fibrosis/motility defects.
Examiner's Pick: Clinical Activity Score (CAS) ≥ 3/7 indicates active disease.

sections.title: Systemic Hazards & Precautions
content: Radioactive Iodine (RAI): Can exacerbate/trigger TED. Precaution: Co-administer oral steroids (Prednisone).
Myasthenia Gravis (MG): Occurs in 5% of TED. Suspect MG if PTOSIS is present instead of lid retraction.
Timolol Glaucoma Meds: Can mask hyperthyroid tachycardia. Abrupt withdrawal can precipitate thyroid storm.
Surgical Pitfall: Do not perform strabismus or lid surgery until euthyroid and stable for 6–9 months.

rows: Best for bony resolution, planning decompression, and identifying 'apical crowding' in CON.
Best for identifying active muscle inflammation via increased water content.
Tendons are characteristically SPARED in TED (unlike orbital pseudotumor).

sections.title: Management Pearls & New Horizons
content: Pearl: Apraclonidine 0.5% acts as 'chemical sympathectomy' for temporary relief of lid retraction.
Highlight: Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor) is a new FDA-approved biologic that effectively reduces proptosis in active disease.
Pediatric Fact: TED is rare in children; symptoms are milder and vision loss is exceptional.
Order of Rehab: Decompression changes orbital volume and must be done first as it alters muscle/lid position.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Neuro-Ophthalmic Headaches: Clinical Scenarios & Management Masterclass ---
sections.content: An exhaustive clinical guide for identifying, triaging, and managing headaches in ophthalmic practice. From benign primary syndromes to life-threatening neuro-surgical emergencies, this poster covers 15 critical scenarios, workup protocols, and clinical pearls.

sections.title: The Neuro-Ophthalmic Headache Landscape
sections.content: Headache is one of the most common complaints in ophthalmic practice [32, 785]. While many cases are benign primary syndromes, the ophthalmologist must identify secondary causes that are life- or vision-threatening, such as Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), intracranial mass lesions, and aneurysms [30, 567].

sections.title: Scenario 1: The Ophthalmic Emergency (GCA)
content: Scenario: 75-year-old female, 3-day history of severe right-sided temporal headache, malaise, and a 'shade' coming down over her vision for several minutes.
Diagnosis: Suspected Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) with amaurosis fugax [85, 760].
Red Flags: Scalp tenderness (pain when combing hair), jaw claudication (pain while chewing), and sudden visual loss [36, 85, 754].
Investigations: Immediate ESR, CRP, and Platelet count (Platelets are a strong predictor) [36, 757].
Gold standard: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) (specimen >2 cm to avoid skip lesions) [5, 586, 762].
Management: Do not wait for biopsy results. Immediate IV Methylprednisolone (g/day for 3 days) followed by oral Prednisone ( mg/kg/day) [5, 89, 762].

sections.title: Scenario 2: The Obese Young Patient (IIH)
content: 1. Identify: 28-year-old obese female, constant global headache (worse in morning/coughing), 'greying out' (TVOs) when standing.
2. Clinical Picture: Papilledema (bilateral disc swelling), transient visual obscurations (TVOs), pulsatile tinnitus, and possible CN VI palsy [38, 40, 182].
3. Workup: Blood pressure check (exclude malignant HTN) [183]. Emergent MRI and MRV (rule out mass/venous thrombosis) [39, 183, 769].
4. LP: Lumbar puncture (LP) showing opening pressure ≥ 250 mm H2O with normal CSF composition [4, 184, 770].
5. Management: Weight loss primary [185, 554]. Acetazolamide (250 mg QID to g BID). Surgery: Optic nerve sheath fenestration (vision) or CSF shunting (headache) [44, 45, 554].

sections.title: Scenario 3: 'Worst Headache of My Life'
content: Scenario: 50-year-old male, sudden explosive headache, 'droopy' eyelid, double vision, large non-reactive pupil.
Diagnosis: Ruptured intracranial aneurysm (typically PCoA) causing Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) [38, 199, 343].
Key Finding: Pupil-involving Third Nerve Palsy (fixed, dilated pupil) [0, 174, 198].
Action: Neurosurgical emergency. Urgent CTA preferred over MRA [202, 200, 346].
Treatment: Referral for endovascular coiling or surgical clipping [016, 346].

content.explanation: C: Conjunctival injection; L: Lacrimation; U: Unilateral (stabbing pain); S: Smoking history (35y male); T: Time-locked (2:00 AM); E: Eye/Ear autonomic signs (Rhinorrhea/Horner); R: Relief with 100% Oxygen (10–15 L/min) or Sumatriptan (6 mg SC). Prophylaxis: Verapamil or Lithium [157, 801, 1195].

sections.title: Scenario 5 & 6: Migraine & ICA Dissection
content: Scenario 5 (Migraine): 24-year-old female, 20-min shimmering zig-zag aura, followed by unilateral throbbing headache/nausea. Aura: 5–60 mins. Mgmt: Aspirin, Ibuprofen, Triptans. Avoid triggers [41, 795, 791].
Scenario 6 (ICA Dissection): 45-year-old male, acute temple/neck pain after car accident, small right pupil, 1 mm ptosis. Diagnosis: Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) Dissection [24, 180, 783].
Red Flag: A painful Horner syndrome is an ICA dissection until proven otherwise; high stroke risk. Mgmt: Urgent MRA/CTA head and neck; antiplatelet/anticoagulation [515, 784].

sections.title: Scenario 7 & 8: Pituitary & Trigeminal Pain
content: Scenario 7 (Pituitary Apoplexy): 40-year-old female, sudden severe headache, bilateral vision loss, total ophthalmoplegia. Red Flags: Bitemporal hemianopia, multiple CN palsies (III, IV, VI). Mgmt: Urgent MRI, immediate steroids to prevent Addisonian crisis [138, 802, 1532].

Scenario 8 (Trigeminal Neuralgia): 60-year-old male, 'electric shock-like' stabs in cheek triggered by shaving. Mgmt: Carbamazepine (100 mg BID up to 1200 mg/day) or Baclofen. Image to rule out MS or vascular compression [362, 805, 1197].

sections.title: Scenario 9: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
content: 1. Presentation: 65-year-old hyperope, sudden severe headache, eye pain, vomiting, hazy cornea.
2. Exam: IOP 50–80 mmHg, rock-hard eye, fixed mid-dilated vertically oval pupil, shallow anterior chamber [487, 681, 1235].
3. Acute Mgmt: Lie supine. Systemic Acetazolamide (500 mg IV) + topical suppressants.
4. Definitive: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (PI) in BOTH eyes [488, 686, 1236].

sections.title: Scenario 10, 11, & 12: Inflammation, Meds, & Ischemia
content: Scenario 10 (Tolosa-Hunt): 50-year-old, intense boring orbital pain, CN III, IV, VI palsies. MRI shows apex enhancement. DX of exclusion (rule out lymphoma/aneurysm). Rx: Systemic steroids [962, 1800].
Scenario 11 (Medication Overuse): Chronic migraineur, headache ≥15 days/month, daily paracetamol/triptans. Mgmt: Abruptly stop offending drug (withdrawal lasts ~3 weeks) [838, 1012].

Scenario 12 (Ocular Ischemic Syndrome): 70-year-old, carotid disease, dull aching 'ocular angina', vision improves in dark. Mid-peripheral dot-blot hemorrhages, iris neovascularization. Mgmt: Carotid endarterectomy; manage IOP/PRP [81, 1597].

sections.title: Scenario 13, 14, & 15: Tension, Meningitis, & Raeder
content: Scenario 13 (Tension): 30-year-old student, 'viselike' band, worse end of day. Bilateral, pressing, no physical aggravation. Rx: NSAIDs, Amitriptyline [153, 798].

Scenario 14 (Meningitis): 20-year-old, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia. Pearl: Pain on eye movement is common; normal ocular exam. Mgmt: LP (after CT if focal) + IV antibiotics [139, 1568].
Scenario 15 (Raeder Paratrigeminal): Middle-aged man, Horner syndrome + daily unilateral periorbital headaches (V1). Mgmt: Exclude parasellar/cavernous sinus pathology with MRI [126, 807].

branches: Life-Threatening Screening: Sudden (Aneurysm), Fever (Meningitis), Age >55 (GCA), High BP (Crisis)
Detailed History: Timing (Morning=ICP, Night=Cluster), Triggers (Touch=CN V, Food=Migraine)
Special Tests: Hertel (Proptosis), Corneal Sensation (CN V), LP (if imaging normal)
Labs: ESR/CRP/FBC for all patients >50 years

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination
content: Pupils: Check for RAPD (Optic nerve) and Anisocoria (Horner/CN III).
Fundus: Look for Disc edema (Papilledema/GCA) and Hemorrhages (HTN/CRVO).
IOP/Gonio: Crucial to exclude Acute Glaucoma.
Motility: Identify CN III, IV, or VI palsies indicating compressive lesions.

content.explanation: Pearl: SVP absence is common in papilledema, but presence strongly suggests normal ICP [1572]. Pitfall: Never LP before neuroimaging if mass suspected (herniation risk). Examiner's Pick: Headache + Adie-like pupil? Check for CN III aberrant regeneration. Precaution: Beta-blockers for glaucoma can mask migraine/systemic signs. High Yield: Pregnant + Headache + Vision Loss? Consider Preeclampsia/Eclampsia & PRES.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: The SNOOP Mnemonic
content: S: Systemic signs/symptoms (Fever, Weight Loss, Pregnancy)
N: Neurologic signs (Palsies, Papilledema, RAPD)
O: Onset (Sudden, Thunderbolt, Explosive)
O: Older age of onset (>50 years, GCA risk)
P: Progression or Pattern change (New type of headache)

Scenario: A patient has a "staring look" but normal thyroid tests.

DDx: Parinaud syndrome (Collier sign), 3rd nerve misdirection, Myasthenia Gravis (Hering’s law), or orbital mass.
Scenario 11: Active vs. Quiescent TED (Rundle’s Curve)
Scenario: Describe the clinical course of TED.
Active Phase: Congestive stage, red/painful eyes, lasts 6–18 months.
Quiescent Phase: "Burned-out" phase, white eyes but persistent fibrosis/motility defects.
Examiner's Pick: Clinical Activity Score (CAS) ≥ 3/7 indicates active disease requiring immunosuppression.
Scenario 12: Systemic Associations (Autoimmune)
Scenario: What other diseases should you screen for in a TED patient?
Answer: Myasthenia Gravis (MG) (occurs in up to 5% of TED patients).
Clinical Pearl: Suspect MG if the patient has ptosis instead of lid retraction.
Scenario 13: Order of Surgical Rehabilitation
Scenario: A patient needs several surgeries for TED. What is the correct sequence?
Sequence: 1. Orbital Decompression → 2. Strabismus Surgery → 3. Eyelid Surgery.
Rationale: Decompression changes orbital volume and can alter muscle alignment and lid position.
Scenario 14: Orbital Imaging in TED (CT vs. MRI)
Scenario: Which imaging modality is preferred for TED and why?
CT: Best for bony resolution and planning decompression.
MRI (T2/STIR): Best for identifying active muscle inflammation (water content).
Key Point: Tendons are characteristically spared in TED (unlike orbital pseudotumor).
Scenario 15: Complications of Glaucoma Meds in Thyroid Disease
Scenario: You prescribe Timolol for a patient with TED and hyperthyroidism.
Hazard: Topical beta-blockers can mask symptoms of hyperthyroidism (e.g., tachycardia).
Precaution: Abrupt withdrawal of beta-blockers can precipitate a thyroid storm.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Comparison: Hyperthyroidism vs. Hypothyroidism
Feature
Hyperthyroidism (Graves)
Hypothyroidism (Hashimoto)
TSH Level
Suppressed (Low)
Elevated (High)
Systemic Signs
Tachycardia, Tremor, Heat intolerance, Weight loss, Goiter
Bradycardia, Cold intolerance, Weight gain, Dry skin, Constipation
Ocular Relation

Associated with 5-10% of TED
Red Flag

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Workup & Approach Mind Map (The "TED Algorithm")
Diagnosis (2 of 3 signs):
Immune thyroid dysfunction (Graves/Hashimoto).
Ocular signs (Lid retraction, proptosis, CON).
Imaging findings (Tendon-sparing EOM enlargement).
Assessment of Activity:
CAS Score: Pain, redness, swelling (Score ≥ 3/7 = Active).
Tiered Management:
Mild: Lubricants, smoking cessation, Selenium (100 µg BD).
Moderate/Severe: Oral Prednisone or pulsed IV Methylprednisolone.
Sight-Threatening (CON): Urgent IV Steroids → Orbital Decompression.
Rehabilitation Sequence:
Decompress → Squint → Lids.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Management Pearls & Pitfalls
Pearl: Apraclonidine 0.5% can be used as a "chemical sympathectomy" for temporary relief of lid retraction while waiting for stabilization.
Pitfall: Do not perform strabismus or lid surgery until the patient has been euthyroid and measurements stable for 6–9 months.
Examiner's Pick: In CON, the orbital apex is the site of maximal compression; CT scans will show "apical crowding".
Highlight: Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor) is a new FDA-approved biologic that effectively reduces proptosis in active disease.
High Yield: Platelet count and ESR are important to rule out Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) in elderly patients presenting with AION-like vision loss.

sections.title: Definition & Core Concept
sections.content: Accommodative Esotropia is a convergent deviation associated with the activation of the accommodation reflex. It is rooted in Donders' theory, which posits that hyperopes must accommodate to clear their vision, even at distance, thereby triggering the neurologically linked accommodative convergence (AC).

rows: Aligned with full plus correction at all distances.
ET at near significantly greater than distance (>10 PD diff).
Requires full plus AND bifocal add for alignment.
Remains esotropic even with full hyperopic correction.

sections.title: The AC/A Ratio: Calculation Methods
content: 1. Gradient Method: Change in deviation (PD) / Change in lens power (D). Normal is 3-5:1.
2. Heterophoria Method: AC/A = IPD(cm) + [ (Dn - Df) / Acc_Demand ].
3. Clinical Rule: Difference of >10 PD between distance and near suggests High AC/A.

sections.title: Mandatory Ocular Examination
content: Cycloplegic Refraction: Mandatory. Use 1% Atropine (BID x 3 days) or 1% Cyclopentolate.
Cover Test: Prisms and alternate cover at 6m and 33cm using accommodative targets.
Sensory Testing: Titmus/Randot stereoacuity and Worth 4-Dot.
Fundus Exam: Rule out sensory causes of ET (e.g., Retinoblastoma, Macular Scar).
Dilation: Check for optic nerve hypoplasia or morning glory disc.

rows: Onset <6 months, large stable angle, latent nystagmus.
Poor VA in one eye (cataract, retinal disease).
Incomitant deviation, worsens on abduction, often traumatic/viral.
Regular 24-48 hour clockwork cycles of ET and orthophoria.
ET greater at distance, common in older adults/neuro cases.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Full Cycloplegic Hyperopic Correction. Do NOT cut the plus.
Step 2: Amblyopia Treatment. Patching or Atropine penalization of the sound eye.
Step 3: Evaluate High AC/A. If ET remains at near with distance glasses, add +2.50 to +3.00D bifocals.
Step 4: Surgical Intervention. Indicated only for the non-accommodative component (Partial ET).

sections.title: Bifocal Management in High AC/A
content: Prescribe: Flat-top 35 or Executive (bisecting the pupil) to ensure child uses it.
Strength: Lowest plus that aligns the eyes at near (usually +2.50 or +3.00).
Tapering: Consider 'weaning' plus after age 8-10 as the AC/A ratio naturally improves.

sections.title: Surgical Protocols
content: Goal: Correct the 'residual' manifest deviation with full glasses on.
Procedure: Bilateral Medial Rectus Recession (BMR).
Dosing: Use the 'Parks' table or similar for the manifest residual angle.
Caution: Overcorrection leads to consecutive Exotropia (XT), especially in kids with high hyperopia.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Amblyopia: 35-50% risk if treatment is delayed.
Consecutive XT: Risk increases if surgery is too aggressive or hyperopia regresses.
Sensory Outcome: Excellent prognosis for stereopsis if aligned early.
Loss of Binocularity: If 'Partial ET' is not addressed, permanent suppression scotoma develops.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Incomitant Deviation (suggests palsy or restrictive process)
Abnormal Optic Nerve Appearance
Associated Neurological Signs (Ataxia, Papilledema)
Sudden Onset in an older child without refractive error

content.explanation: Refractive (Total correction), Non-Refractive (High AC/A), Mixed (Both), Partial (Surgery needed for residual).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: NEVER cut the plus in accommodative ET; the brain needs the full correction to relax convergence.
Bifocal lines must be high (mid-pupil) in children, unlike adults.
Always check for a 'small angle' residual ET which can cause monofixation syndrome.
Repeat cycloplegia every 6 months as hyperopia may increase in early childhood.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The PEDIG (Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group) studies have solidified the role of Atropine penalization as equal to patching for moderate amblyopia. Recent studies on the 'Natural History of Accommodative ET' suggest that many children can be successfully weaned off bifocals as they enter teenage years due to a physiological decrease in the AC/A ratio.

sections.content: Accommodative Esotropia is the most common form of childhood strabismus, occurring when the effort to focus (accommodation) triggers excessive inward turning (convergence). This guide covers the nuanced classification, physiological mechanisms, and evidence-based management protocols required for board-level mastery.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Accommodative Esotropia (ET) is a convergent deviation of the eyes associated with the activation of the accommodative reflex. It is rooted in Donders' theory (1864), which describes the physiological link between accommodation and convergence. When a hyperopic child accommodates to clear a blurred image, the linked accommodative convergence (AC) causes the eyes to cross. If the fusional divergence amplitudes are insufficient to overcome this inward pull, an manifest esotropia develops.

branches: Refractive: Normal AC/A ratio, High Hyperopia (+2.0D to +7.0D)
Non-Refractive: High AC/A ratio, Variable Hyperopia
Mixed: High Hyperopia AND High AC/A ratio
Decompensated: Chronic ET leading to secondary muscle changes
Partially Accommodative: Residual ET despite full correction

rows: Change in deviation / Diopters of lens (use -2.00D or +3.00D)
IPD (cm) + (Near Dev - Dist Dev) / Lens Power at Near

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings

Variable angle of deviation (worse when tired or focusing)
Full Cycloplegic Refraction (1% Atropine or 1% Cyclopentolate)
Cover/Uncover Test: Manifest ET at dist/near
Stereopsis assessment (Titmus/Randot): Crucial for prognosis
Assess for V-pattern ET (often due to inferior oblique overaction)

rows: Limited Abduction, globe retraction on adduction

sections.title: Management Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Full Cycloplegic Refraction. Prescribe FULL hyperopic correction (no 'cutting' plus in kids).
Step 2: Adaptation Period. Wear glasses full-time for 4-6 weeks.
Step 3: Evaluate for Amblyopia. Start patching or Atropine penalization if VA is asymmetric.
Step 4: Check Near Deviation. If ET persists at near despite straight at distance, check AC/A.
Step 5: Add Bifocals (Flat-top D-segment) for High AC/A. Bisect the pupil with the line.
Step 6: Surgical Intervention. Indicated ONLY for the non-accommodative (residual) component.

sections.title: Surgical Protocols & Criteria
content: Target: The 'Residual' ET (the crossing that remains while wearing full correction).
Procedure: Bilateral Medial Rectus Recession (BMR) or R&R (Recess/Resect).
Calculation: Base surgery on the 'At-Distance' residual deviation.
Instruments: Jameson or Green muscle hooks, Westcott scissors, 6-0 Vicryl sutures.
Augmented BMR: Consider if the near deviation remains significantly higher (Fells procedure).

sections.title: NEURO RED FLAGS
content: Sudden onset ET in an older child (>6 years) without hyperopia
Associated Papilledema or Optic Nerve Pallor
Abduction deficits or Nystagmus
Associated Ataxia, Headache, or Cranial Nerve Palsies
Incomitant deviation (angle changes significantly in different gazes)

content.explanation: 1. CYCLOPLEGIA (Full refraction is mandatory), 2. CORRECTION (Full plus power), 3. COMPLIANCE (Full-time wear is essential for fusion).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: The 'Plus Build-up' Technique: If a child won't tolerate glasses, use Atropine to relax accommodation.
Bifocals in kids MUST be high (Flat-top 35) to ensure they actually look through them.
Pseudo-esotropia: Wide epicanthal folds can mimic ET; check Hirschberg/Brückner reflex.
Sensory Fusion: Patients with refractive ET have better potential for 40 sec/arc stereo than infantile ET.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The ETDRS & ATS Impact
sections.content: Recent evidence from the Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group (PEDIG) reinforces that patching (2 hours/day) is as effective as Atropine penalization for moderate amblyopia associated with Accommodative ET. The 'Convergence Insufficiency Treatment Trial' (CITT) concepts are also being applied to those who develop secondary exotropia after over-correction.

sections.title: Surgical Complications

Lost or Slipped Muscle
Suture Granuloma or Conjunctival Inclusion Cyst

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Etiology
sections.content: Ocular toxoplasmosis is a retinochoroiditis caused by Toxoplasma gondii. Humans are accidental intermediate hosts. The parasite exists in three forms: Oocysts (excreted by cats), Tachyzoites (active, proliferative form causing tissue damage), and Bradyzoites (inactive, encysted form in chronic infection).

content.explanation: Chorioretinitis (often bilateral/macular), Convulsions (CNS involvement), and Cerebral Calcifications.

rows: Responsible for acute inflammation and tissue destruction.
Latent stage; rupture causes recurrent retinochoroiditis.
Product of sexual cycle in cat gut
Environmental contaminant; highly resistant to disinfection.

sections.title: Primary Ocular Findings
content: Focus of fluffy white retinitis (satellite lesion) adjacent to a pigmented scar.
Moderate to severe vitritis ('Headlight in the Fog').
Kyrieleis Arteritis (periarterial immune deposits).
Anterior uveitis (Granulomatous or non-granulomatous).
Elevated Intraocular Pressure (secondary inflammatory glaucoma).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Clinical Examination: Dilated fundoscopy to identify active vs scarred lesions.
2. Serology: Serum IgG (exposure) and IgM (acute infection).
3. Multimodal Imaging: OCT (identifies focal thickening), FFA (early hypofluorescence, late leakage).
4. Anterior Chamber Tap: PCR for T. gondii DNA or Goldmann-Witmer Coefficient (GWC) for local antibody production.
5. Systemic Screening: Evaluate for immunosuppression (HIV/AIDS).

rows: Typically unilateral, peripheral/macular granuloma with tractional bands.
Rapidly progressing peripheral necrosis, significant vitritis, viral etiology (HSV/VZV).

sections.title: Indications for Systemic Treatment
content: Lesion within 1 disc diameter of Fovea or Optic Nerve.
Lesion threatening a major retinal vessel.
Significant vitritis causing 2+ drop in visual acuity.
Immunocompromised patients (MANDATORY treatment).
Congenital toxoplasmosis in the first year of life.
Only seeing eye or bilateral involvement.

sections.title: Classic 'Triple Therapy' Regimen
content: 1. Pyrimethamine: 50-100mg loading dose, then 25-50mg daily.
2. Sulfadiazine: 1g four times daily.
3. Folinic Acid (Leucovorin): 5-15mg 3x weekly (prevents bone marrow suppression).
4. Systemic Prednisone: 0.5-1.0mg/kg daily (start 48h AFTER antibiotics).

sections.title: Alternative Treatment Options
content: Bactrim DS (Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole): 160/800mg BID. Increasingly popular due to cost and safety.
Clindamycin: 300mg QID (Risk of Pseudomembranous colitis).
Azithromycin: 500mg daily (Used in pregnancy or sulfa allergy).
Intravitreal Injection: Clindamycin (1mg/0.1ml) + Dexamethasone (400µg/0.1ml).

content.explanation: Pyrimethamine can cause thrombocytopenia and leukopenia. Check Weekly Complete Blood Count (CBC)!

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: NEVER give systemic steroids without antibiotic coverage (risk of fulminant retinal necrosis).
The 'satellite lesion' is the most characteristic finding.
Toxoplasmosis is the most common cause of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent patients.
Recurrence risk is highest in the first year after an active episode.
In HIV patients, lesions may be large, multifocal, and lack pigmentary scarring.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: A landmark study by Silveira et al. demonstrated that prophylactic treatment with Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole (one tablet every other day) significantly reduced the rate of recurrent retinochoroiditis in high-risk patients. Recent trends show a shift toward intravitreal therapy to minimize systemic side effects, especially in pregnant patients or those with contraindications to systemic sulfa drugs.

sections.content: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular protozoan and the most common identifiable cause of focal retinitis worldwide. This comprehensive guide covers the lifecycle, clinical manifestations, and the 'classic' vs. modern management protocols for ocular toxoplasmosis.

sections.title: The Pathogen & Global Burden
content: Causative Agent: Toxoplasma gondii (obligate intracellular protozoan).
Northern Temperate Countries: Estimated 10% adult infestation.
Mediterranean & Tropical Countries: Over 50% adult infestation.
Brazil: Responsible for up to 85% of posterior uveitis cases.
Global Posterior Uveitis: Accounts for 20–60% of all cases.
Primary Ocular Presentation: Average age of 29 years (likely due to decreasing immunity).

branches: Definitive Host: Cats (Oocysts excreted in faeces)
Intermediate Hosts: Humans, livestock, birds, rodents
Inactive Stage: Bradyzoite (Dormant in tissue cysts: eye, brain, skeletal muscle)
Active Form: Tachyzoite (Proliferating form released upon cyst rupture)
Transmission: Ingestion of contaminated water/soil, cat litter disposal, undercooked meat/eggs
Medical Transmission: Organ transplantation, Blood transfusion, Transplacental spread

rows: Often subclinical; 10% result in fetal death. 75%+ have retinochoroiditis. Severity depends on gestation duration (worse in early pregnancy).
Accounts for >50% of childhood cases. Usually subclinical. Ocular lesions may develop years later.
80–90% subclinical. Symptomatic: Cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise, pharyngitis. Retinitis in up to 20%.
Reactivation or acquired. Risks: Meningoencephalitis, pneumonitis, fulminant retinochoroiditis.

sections.title: Ocular Presentation & Symptoms
content: Symptoms: Unilateral acute/subacute floaters, blurring, and photophobia.
Spill-over Anterior Uveitis: Common; can be granulomatous or resemble FUS. Elevated IOP may occur.
Typical Lesion: Fluffy white retinitis associated with a pigmented 'satellite' scar.
Vitritis: Often severe. 'Headlight in the fog' appearance (inflammatory nidus viewed through vitreous haze).
Vasculitis: More commonly venous than arterial.
Optic Disc: Oedema is common.
Punctate Outer Retinal Toxoplasmosis: Small (25–75 μm) grey-white lesions in younger patients.
Neuroretinitis: Rare; marker of acutely acquired infection (mimics cat-scratch).

rows: More rapid progression, peripheral location, lack of adjacent pigmented scars (usually).
Can mimic any uveitis; 'ground glass' vitritis, positive treponemal serology.
Neuroretinitis with macular star; history of cat scratch/bite; negative Toxo serology.
Granulomatous uveitis, but usually lacks the focal necrotizing retinitis and satellite scar.
Multifocal 'fluff-balls' in vitreous; history of IV access/candidemia.

sections.title: Complications Leading to Vision Loss
content: Overall Risk: Permanent vision reduction in 25% of eyes.
Macular Pathology: Inflammatory lesions, oedema, and late secondary neovascularization.
Vascular: Retinal vascular occlusion (periarteritis).
Structural: Serous, rhegmatogenous, or tractional retinal detachment.
Optic Nerve: Involvement leading to atrophy.
Healing: Spontaneous resolution in 6–8 weeks (immunocompetent); vitreous takes longer.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: 1. Clinical Exam: Primary method of diagnosis.
2. Serology (IgG): Indicates past exposure; 1/3 community seroprevalence.
3. Serology (IgM): Indicates infection within 1 year; critical in pregnancy.
4. Goldmann–Witmer Coefficient: Ratio of specific IgG in aqueous vs. serum (48–90% sensitivity).
5. PCR Testing: Intraocular fluid; highly specific, variable sensitivity (16–67%).
6. Imaging (OCT/B-Scan): Monitor macular oedema or exclude RD in severe vitritis.
7. Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): Facilitates monitoring of inflammatory activity.

sections.title: Treatment Indications & Duration
content: General: Treatment is not always needed as spontaneous resolution occurs.
Sight-Threatening Lesion: Involving macula, papillomacular bundle, optic nerve, or major vessel.
Severe vitritis: Clear indication for therapy.
Immunocompromised Status: Always requires treatment.
Duration: Typically 4–6 weeks for antibiotics.
Healing Time: Active lesions take 4–6 months to heal completely.

content.explanation: Pyrimethamine (75-100mg load, then 25-50mg daily) + Sulfadiazine (1g QID) + Prednisolone (1mg/kg). ALWAYS add Folinic Acid (5mg 3x/week) to prevent marrow toxicity.

rows: Clindamycin (1mg) + Dexamethasone (400µg). 2-3 injections 2 weeks apart. Effective as triple therapy.
Trimethoprim 160mg / Sulfamethoxazole 800mg BID. Low cost, better tolerated.
250–500 mg daily. Shows promise in reducing recurrence rates.
300 mg QID. Risk of pseudomembranous colitis.
750 mg 2–4 times daily. Attacks encysted bradyzoites (theoretically).

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNINGS & CONTRAINDICATIONS
content: NEVER use depot steroids (e.g., triamcinolone) intra- or periocularly (uncontrolled progression reported).
Systemic steroids should be used with extreme caution in immunocompromised patients.
Pyrimethamine: Perform weekly blood counts (risk of thrombocytopenia/leukopenia).
Sulfonamides: Risk of Stevens–Johnson syndrome and renal stones.
AIDS Patients: Avoid or reduce pyrimethamine due to marrow suppression and zidovudine antagonism.
Pregnancy: Avoid pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine (fetal harm). Use Spiramycin or Intravitreal therapy.

sections.title: Recurrence & Long-term Management
content: Average Recurrences: 2.7 attacks per patient.
2-Year Risk: 12–15% recurrence rate.
5-Year Risk: Over 50% experience a further episode.
Prophylaxis Regimen: Co-trimoxazole (160/800) three times daily for 12 months.
Prophylaxis Benefit: Reduces recurrence from 22% to 3% for up to 3 years.
Neonatal Care: 1 year of antimicrobials in congenital cases may reduce future scarring.

content.explanation: Start steroids 24–48 hours AFTER starting antimicrobial therapy to ensure parasitic cover before dampening the immune response.

Healing results in a sharply demarcated atrophic scar with a pigmented border (Fig 12.33). Children should undergo varicella zoster vaccination if they have not had chickenpox before starting steroids.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Foster Kennedy Syndrome (FKS) is a constellation of neuro-ophthalmic findings caused by a mass lesion (typically a meningioma) in the anterior cranial fossa. The syndrome was first formally described by Robert Foster Kennedy in 1911. It highlights the dual effect of a single lesion: direct mechanical compression of one optic nerve and the systemic effect of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) on the other.

sections.title: Etiology: Primary Culprits
content: Olfactory Groove Meningioma (Most Common)
Sphenoid Wing Meningioma
Frontal Lobe Glioma / Astrocytoma
Craniopharyngioma
Esthesioneuroblastoma (Olfactory Neuroblastoma)
Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (Extension into cranium)
Large Aneurysms (Internal Carotid Artery)

sections.title: Pathophysiology: Dual Mechanisms
content: 1. Expanding mass in the anterior cranial fossa.
2. Direct pressure on the ipsilateral Optic Nerve (CN II) causes axonal death and atrophy.
3. Compression of the Olfactory Nerve (CN I) leads to loss of smell.
4. Large mass increases Intracranial Pressure (ICP).
5. Elevated ICP transmitted through subarachnoid space to the contralateral (uncompressed) optic nerve, causing papilledema.

content.explanation: Frontal lobe tumor, Optic atrophy (ipsilateral), Smelling loss (anosmia), Tumor-induced, Edema (contralateral papilledema), Raised ICP symptoms.

rows: Usually normal (early) or enlarged blind spot
New acute AION in fellow eye

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: 1. Comprehensive History: Inquire about headaches, personality changes, and smell.
2. Smell Testing: Use coffee/citrus (UPSIT test) to confirm anosmia.
3. Visual Field Testing: Automated Perimetry (HVF 24-2) and Goldmann.
4. OCT: Measure RNFL thickness and GCL (Ganglion Cell Layer) loss.
5. Emergent Neuroimaging: MRI Brain with/without Gadolinium (Gold Standard).
6. MRA/MRV: If vascular etiology or dural venous sinus involvement is suspected.
7. Neurology/Neurosurgery Consult: Immediate referral for surgical planning.

sections.title: Red Flags: Urgent Indicators
content: Sudden progressive vision loss in the 'good' eye.
Projectile vomiting (sign of severely raised ICP).
Altered mental status or coma.
Cushing Triad: Hypertension, Bradycardia, Irregular Respiration.
New onset seizures or focal neurological deficits.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Surgical Resection: Primary treatment for meningiomas or gliomas.
Corticosteroids: Dexamethasone (Decadron) to reduce peri-tumoral edema.
ICP Management: Acetazolamide or CSF shunting if papilledema is severe.
Radiation Therapy: Adjuvant therapy for malignant gliomas or subtotal resections.
Follow-up: Serial OCT, HVF, and MRI every 3-6 months post-op.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check smell! Anosmia is the 'forgotten' third sign of the triad.
Pseudo-FKS is far more common than true FKS in clinical practice.
The atrophic eye may develop secondary optic nerve head cupping, mimicking glaucoma.
Frontal lobe signs: Personality changes (apathy/disinhibition) are often missed.
The papilledema side is usually the side with BETTER visual function.

branches: Primary: No preceding edema (Compression in FKS)

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
sections.content: Prognosis is highly dependent on the tumor type and the duration of compression. The atrophic eye rarely recovers significant vision due to axonal death. However, the eye with papilledema usually has an excellent visual prognosis if ICP is lowered promptly before chronic changes (atrophy) occur in that eye. Survival rates for benign meningiomas are high (>90% at 5 years), whereas high-grade gliomas carry a poor survival prognosis.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Olfactory Groove Meningioma & Foster Kennedy Syndrome ---
sections.content: A comprehensive guide to the neuro-ophthalmic manifestations of Olfactory Groove Meningiomas (OGMs), specifically detailing the classic Foster Kennedy Syndrome (FKS) triad of ipsilateral optic atrophy, contralateral papilledema, and anosmia.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Olfactory groove meningiomas (OGMs) arise from the arachnoid cap cells of the cribriform plate and planum sphenoidale. They represent approximately 10% of all intracranial meningiomas. Because of their slow growth and the spaciousness of the subfrontal area, they often reach massive sizes before detection. Foster Kennedy Syndrome is the classic but rare ophthalmic presentation resulting from these tumors' mass effect and intracranial pressure elevation.

rows: Low mitotic rate; Meningothelial, Fibrous, Psammomatous.
4-19 mitoses/10HPF; Brain invasion; High N:C ratio.

sections.title: The Foster Kennedy Syndrome Triad
content: 1. Ipsilateral Optic Atrophy: Direct compression of the optic nerve by the tumor leads to primary axonal death.
2. Contralateral Papilledema: Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) from the mass causes axonal transport stasis in the unaffected nerve.
3. Anosmia: Destruction or compression of the olfactory bulbs/tracts (earliest clinical sign, often missed).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Visual Acuity: Unilateral or bilateral decline (central scotoma).
Color Vision: Dyschromatopsia out of proportion to VA loss.
Pupils: Ipsilateral Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD).
Fundus: Pale disc (Ipsi) vs. Hyperemic/Blurred margins (Contra).
Visual Fields: Central/paracentral scotoma or junctional scotoma.
Motility: Occasional 6th nerve palsy due to raised ICP (False localizing sign).

rows: Isointense to gray matter; marked homogenous enhancement with Gadolinium.
Hyperintense (suggests soft consistency) or Hypointense (suggests calcification).
Hyperostosis of the planum sphenoidale; tumor calcification (20%).
Sunburst pattern of vascularity (Internal Carotid & Ophthalmic artery supply).

content.explanation: Pseudo-FKS is much more common than true FKS. It is caused by sequential Non-Arteritic Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (NAION). The first eye has old atrophy, and the second eye presents with acute disc edema.

sections.title: Surgical Management Strategies
content: Step 1: Bifrontal Craniotomy (Standard for large tumors).
Step 2: Pterional Approach (Used for smaller, lateralized tumors).
Step 3: Endoscopic Endonasal Transcribriform Approach (Minimal access).
Step 4: Tumor Debulking and devascularization of the ethmoidal supply.
Step 5: Optic Canal Decompression (if vision is threatened).

rows: Total removal including dura and bone
Total removal + coagulation of dural attachment

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Considerations
content: Rapidly progressive vision loss (Emergency decompression needed)
CSF Rhinorrhea (Risk of meningitis)
New onset seizures (Frontal lobe irritation)
Mental status changes (Personality changes, apathy, or 'Frontal Lobe Syndrome')

sections.title: Surgical Complications
content: Anosmia: Permanent in almost all OGM surgical cases.
CSF Leak: High risk due to ethmoid bone manipulation.
Injury to ACoA: Anterior Communicating Artery complex is often draped over the tumor.
Venous Infarction: Damage to the Superior Sagittal Sinus.
Post-operative Diabetes Insipidus.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Anosmia is the 'silent' symptom—always test sense of smell in patients with unexplained optic atrophy.
The 'Dural Tail Sign' on MRI is characteristic but not pathognomonic for meningioma.
Frontal lobe syndrome (indifference, inappropriate behavior) can mimic depression or early dementia.
Meningiomas are hormone-sensitive; they may grow rapidly during pregnancy.
Stereotactic Radiosurgery (SRS) is a viable primary option for small tumors or as adjuvant for WHO Grade II/III.

content.explanation: F: Frontal Lobe tumor; O: Optic Atrophy (Ipsi); S: Swelling/Papilledema (Contra); T: Total Smell Loss (Anosmia).

sections.title: Pathophysiology Process
content: Tumor originates from arachnoid cells.
Expansile growth in subfrontal space.
Direct compression of Olfactory Nerve (CN I).
Encroachment on the Optic Canal/Intracranial Optic Nerve.
Increase in global ICP via mass effect or venous obstruction.

data.title: The Watery Eye: Clinical Assessment & Management
data.summary: A comprehensive guide to managing epiphora, ranging from transient irritants to permanent disabling conditions. This poster outlines the rigorous diagnostic approach and surgical interventions required for elderly and symptomatic populations.

sections.title: Clinical Overview
sections.content: This is a common complaint, particularly in the elderly population. It ranges from the transient and trivial (e.g. associated with a local irritant) to the permanent and disabling. objective quantification is difficult, but the main issue is how much of a problem it is for the patient (see Tables 5.1 and 5.2).

sections.title: Initial Diagnostic Tests
content: Fluorescein dye disappearance test (FDT): Assess Tear film height, symmetry, and dilution.
Perform nasendoscopy, where possible.
CT DCG: Indicated if previous trauma, destructive disease, or suspected tumour.
Lacrimal scintigraphy: More useful than DCG, as it simulates physiologic tear drainage conditions.

sections.title: Table 5.1: Clinical Assessment - History & Vital Signs

rows: episodic/permanent, frequency of wiping eyes, exacerbating factors (in/outside, cold/warm), site where tears spill over (laterally/medially)
previous surgery/trauma; concurrent eye disease; herpes simplex blepharoconjunctivitis
previous ENT problems (e.g. sinusitis, surgery/nasal fracture, granulomatous disease), VIIth palsy

sections.title: Table 5.1: Clinical Assessment - Physical Examination
content: Facies: Scars (previous trauma/surgery), asymmetry, prominent nasal bridge, mid-face hypoplasia, or age-related sag.
Lacrimal sac: Swelling, any punctal regurgitation on palpation.
Lids: MG disease, lash malposition, lid position, molluscum contagiosum (ectropion/entropion/low lateral canthus), laxity (lid/canthal tendons).
Puncta: position, scarring, concretions, patency.
Conjunctiva: Irritation (e.g. chronic conjunctivitis).
Cornea: Inflammation, chronic corneal disease.
Tear film: Meniscus high/low, TBUT, dry eye (Schirmer’s test).

sections.title: Assessment: Advanced Drainage Evaluation
content: Dye recovery (Jones I): Physiological—without syringing.
Dye recovery (Jones II): Nonphysiological—after syringing. Retrieve dye with cotton bud under inferior turbinate or ideally visualize with nasendoscope.
Cannulation: Check patency of puncta.
Syringing Step 1: Do gently with lateral distraction of lid to avoid false passage.
Syringing Step 2: Do not advance through an obstruction.
Syringing Step 3: Careful assessment will indicate site of obstruction—assess flow, regurgitation through upper or lower punctum, and presence of fluorescein or mucus in the fluid.

sections.title: Table 5.2: Causes of the Watery Eye (Common in BOLD)

branches: Increased Production (Basal): Autonomic disturbance, pro-secretory drugs.

Increased Production (Reflex): Chronic lid disease (blepharitis), Local irritant (FB, trichiasis), Systemic disease (TED), Chronic conjunctival disease (OCMMP), Chronic corneal disease (KCS), Aberrant regeneration after VIIth palsy (crocodile tears).
Lacrimal Pump Failure: Lid tone (Lid laxity), Orbicularis weakness (VIIth palsy), Lid position (Ectropion).
Punctal Obstruction: Congenital atresia/accessory punctum, Idiopathic stenosis (elderly), 2° to punctal eversion, HSV infection, post-irradiation, Trachoma, Cicatricial conjunctivitis.
Canalicular Obstruction: Idiopathic fibrosis, HSV infection, Actinomyces, Chronic dacrocystitis, Cicatricial conjunctivitis, 5-FU administration (systemic).
Lacrimal Sac Obstruction: Granuloma, sarcoidosis, syphilis, fungi, papillomas, epithelial papillary (squamous and transitional cell) carcinomas, Lymphoma, Invasive pharyngeal or sinus carcinoma.

Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction: Congenital (delayed canalization), Idiopathic stenosis, Trauma (nasal/orbital fracture), nasal pathology (chronic inflammation/polyps), post-irradiation, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), Tumours (nasopharyngeal carcinoma).

sections.title: Treatment: Increased Production & Pump Failure
content: Reflex Tearing: Control disease process (e.g., ocular lubricants for KCS). Note: Explain to patient that using drops for a watery eye may seem counterintuitive.
MG Disease: Hot compresses, massage, lid cleaning ± lubricants/topical steroid/antibiotic/oral doxycycline.
Crocodile Tears: Botulinum toxin injection into lacrimal gland (Caution: ptosis complication).
Pump Failure: Usually due to lid laxity/ectropion causing punctal eversion and 2° stenosis. Treatment: Restore lid and punctum position via lid shortening procedures.

sections.title: Treatment: Decreased Drainage
sections.content: Obstruction may arise at the level of the punctum, the canaliculi, the sac, or the nasolacrimal duct. The extent of surgery required will depend on the level of blockage, but most cases arising distal to the puncta require a dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).

sections.title: Table 5.3: Operations to Improve Nasolacrimal Drainage

rows: Cauterize tissue 5mm inferior to punctum: causes scarring/inversion
Diamond of tarsoconjunctiva excised just inferior to punctum + inverting suture
Lid shortened laterally and tightened + elevated at lateral canthus
Vertical and small medial cut in punctal ampulla enlarges opening
Canaliculi intubated with silastic tube secured at nasal end; left for 6mo. May require opening by trephination
DCR + carunculectomy with a Jones (pyrex) tube from sac to medial canthus
The lacrimal sac is opened directly to nasal mucosa by a rhinostomy + membranectomy if there is a membrane over the common canalicular opening

sections.title: Important Considerations
content: Botulinum toxin for crocodile tears can cause ptosis.
Avoid advancing through an obstruction during syringing to prevent false passages.
Ensure lateral distraction of the lid during syringing.
Distal blockages (distal to puncta) usually require DCR.

sections.title: Pleomorphic Adenoma (Benign Mixed Cell Tumour)
content: Commonest lacrimal neoplasm: Accounts for up to 20% of all lacrimal fossa lesions.
Origin: Derived from epithelial and mesenchymal tissue.
Lobe Involvement: May arise from either lobe, most commonly the orbital lobe.
Demographics: Occurs in middle age; slight ♂ bias (♂:♀ 1.5:1).
Malignant Transformation: Occurs in <3% in 10y and 10–20% in 20y.
Clinical Features: Gradual painless proptosis (inferonasal), upper lid swelling, diplopia, palpable mass (orbital lobe tumours may not be palpable).
Globe Effects: Indentation may cause choroidal folds ± hypermetropic shift.

rows: Round, lobulated lesion, typically medium/high reflectivity.
Expansion of lacrimal fossa, indentation of globe, well-circumscribed and slightly nodular tumour, calcification in 3%.
Surgical removal of whole tumour with intact pseudocapsule by anterior (palpebral lobe) or lateral (orbital lobe) orbitotomy.
Excellent with complete excision; needs prolonged follow-up for malignant transformation even if clearance is complete.

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNING: Pleomorphic Adenoma
content: DO NOT PERFORM PRIOR BIOPSY: Risk of seeding.
Patient must be warned regarding subsequent KCS (Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca).

sections.title: Lacrimal Carcinomas
content: Commonest malignant lacrimal tumour: Adenoid cystic carcinoma.
Other types: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma and pleomorphic adenocarcinoma.
Clinical: Rapid proptosis, ophthalmoparesis, and orbital pain.
Spread: Sensory disturbance from perineural spread is common.
Imaging: Irregular poorly defined lesion; bony destruction and calcification (20–30%).
Treatment: Seldom curative; exenteration ± radiotherapy.
Prognosis: Very poor with high mortality.

branches: Slow-growing tumour of glial tissue (Children focus)
Presentation: Gradual dVA (often stabilizes), disc swelling/atrophy, proptosis
Imaging: Fusiform enlargement of optic nerve ± chiasmal mass
Management: Observation (good vision), MRI monitoring, Surgery (reduced vision/pain/chiasm threat), Chemo/Radio (chiasmal/midbrain involvement)

sections.title: Optic Nerve Sheath Meningioma
content: Rare benign tumour of meningothelial cells; middle age focus.
Gender: Slight ♀ bias (♀:♂ 1.5:1).
Association: Neurofibromatosis-2.
Presentation: Gradual dVA, disc swelling/atrophy, optic disc collateral vessels (30%), proptosis, ophthalmoparesis.
Imaging Hallmark: Tubular enlargement with ‘tram-track’ enhancement of the sheath ± calcification.
Management: Observation if VA is good. Surgery for blind eyes, severe proptosis, or chiasm threat.
Prognosis: Good for life.

rows: Childhood; NF-1; ‘bag-of-worms’ mass; S-shaped lid deformity; Poorly defined/unencapsulated; Hard to excise (debulking needed).
Adulthood; Gradual proptosis; Well circumscribed; Straightforward surgical excision.
Slow-growing/Benign (rarely malignant); NF association; Adulthood; Superior orbit; Cystic non-tender mass; Good prognosis with excision.

sections.title: Vascular Tumours: Cavernous Haemangioma
content: Commonest benign orbital neoplasm in adults.
Pathology: Hamartoma of dilated large vascular spaces lined by endothelial cells.
Presentation: Young adulthood; accelerated growth during pregnancy.
Location: 80% Intraconal.
Features: Axial proptosis, restricted motility, globe indentation (choroidal folds/hypermetropic shift), dVA.
Rare Sign: Gaze-evoked amaurosis (apical retrobulbar lesions).
US: Well-defined, round intraconal lesion with high internal reflectivity.
CT/MRI: Well-circumscribed intraconal lesion; mild/moderate enhancement; possible thrombosis.
Treatment: Observation (most); excision (symptomatic).

rows: Hamartoma; Kasabach–Merritt syndrome (dplatelets, dHb, dclotting factors) or cardiac failure in large tumours. Treatment: Corticosteroids (topical/intralesional/systemic), Propranolol, Surgery.
‘Strawberry naevus’ (dermis); appears <2mo, full size at 1y, involutes by 6y. Risk: Amblyopia/astigmatism.
Posterior to septum; proptosis worsens with Valsalva/crying; partial involution.

Rare hamartoma (childhood); size increases with Valsalva/head-down posture. Superficial: Transilluminable cystic lid/conjunctival spaces. Deep: 'Chocolate cyst' (haemorrhage). Treatment: Observation, sclerosing agents, Bleomycin, Onyx®, drainage, or surgery (difficult/friable).

sections.title: Lymphoproliferative Disorders
content: Spectrum: Benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas (85% B-lymphocytes). Classified by WHO system.
Benign Reactive Lymphoid Hyperplasia: Polyclonal; superolateral orbit/lacrimal gland; firm rubbery mass. 25% progress to lymphoma by 5y. Rx: Steroids, Radio, Rituximab.
Atypical Lymphoid Hyperplasia: Intermediate; homogeneous pattern with larger nuclei.
Malignant Orbital Lymphoma: Low-grade B-cell (Non-Hodgkin); commonest is Marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of MALT (40–70%).
Lymphoma Stats: 50% are primary tumours; 25% bilateral; up to 60% systemic involvement within 5y. Rx: Systemic work-up mandatory; Radio/Chemo/Antibody.

sections.title: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis
content: Rare proliferative disorder of childhood.
Spectrum: Eosinophilic granuloma (benign/unifocal) to Letterer–Siwe form (disseminated).
Presentation: Rapid proptosis with superotemporal swelling.
Bilateral involvement occurs in disseminated forms.
Treatment: Surgical excision is usually curative.

sections.title: Rhabdomyosarcoma: The Pediatric Emergency
content: Commonest primary orbital malignancy in children; 87% present <15y.
Types: Embryonal (commonest), Alveolar, Pleomorphic.
Clinical: Acute/subacute proptosis, ptosis, and inflammation (mimics orbital cellulitis).
Investigations: US (high internal flow on Doppler); CT/MRI (mass ± bony erosion).
Mandatory: Biopsy + Systemic work-up.
Rx: Surgery (localized) or Combined Radio/Chemo (extensive).

rows: Commonest adult mesenchymal tumour; superonasal location; benign or malignant.
Complete surgical excision; recurrences common; metastases rare.
Aggressive; rapid proptosis, restricted motility, CN involvement. Scirrhous (Breast/Gastric) may cause enophthalmos.
Half of cases precede primary tumour diagnosis.

sections.title: Vascular Lesions: Varices & AV Fistulae
content: Orbital Varices: Congenital; intermittent proptosis (worse with Valsalva/coughing); phleboliths on imaging. Rx: Surgery (difficult) or sclerosant/coil.

Carotid–Cavernous Fistula (Direct): High-flow; Trauma/Spontaneous; Pulsatile proptosis + audible bruit, chemosis, iIOP, ophthalmoparesis, RAPD, disc swelling. Rx: Catheter embolization (>85% success).
Dural Shunt (Indirect CCF): Low-flow; Spontaneous (Hypertension); Episcleral venous arterialization, chemosis. Rx: 40% spontaneously thrombose; intervention for glaucoma/pain/dVA.
AV Fistula Investigations: US/CT/MRI show dilated superior ophthalmic vein and thick EOMs.

sections.title: Prognosis Summary
content: Pleomorphic Adenoma: Excellent with complete excision.
Lacrimal Carcinoma: Very poor; high mortality.
Optic Nerve Glioma: Good for life (if restricted to nerve).
Schwannoma: Good with excision.
Langerhans (Eosinophilic): Curative with excision.
Dural Shunt: 40% Spontaneous resolution.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Orbital Tumours & Vascular Lesions: The Complete Clinical Compendium ---
sections.content: An exhaustive clinical guide detailing the epidemiology, clinical features, investigations, and management of orbital neoplasms and vascular anomalies including lacrimal, neural, lymphoproliferative, and metastatic conditions.

sections.title: Lacrimal Gland: Pleomorphic Adenoma (Benign Mixed Cell Tumour)

branches: Epidemiology: Commonest lacrimal neoplasm (up to 20% of fossa lesions). Middle age, slight male bias (♂:♀ 1.5:1).
Origin: Derived from epithelial and mesenchymal tissue. Arises from either lobe, most commonly the orbital lobe.

Clinical Features: Gradual painless inferonasal proptosis, upper lid swelling, diplopia, palpable mass (orbital lobe tumours may not be palpable). Globe indentation: choroidal folds ± hypermetropic shift.

rows: Round, lobulated lesion, typically medium/high reflectivity.
Expansion of lacrimal fossa, globe indentation, well-circumscribed/nodular, calcification (3%).
Removal of whole tumour with intact pseudocapsule without prior biopsy (risk of seeding). Anterior (palpebral) or lateral (orbital) orbitotomy.
Excellent with complete excision. Warn regarding KCS. Prolonged follow-up needed for malignant transformation.

sections.title: Lacrimal Carcinomas: High Alert
content: Commonest malignant: Adenoid cystic carcinoma, followed by mucoepidermoid and pleomorphic adenocarcinoma.
Clinical: Rapid proptosis, ophthalmoparesis, orbital pain, or sensory disturbance from perineural spread.
Imaging: Irregular poorly defined lesion, bony destruction, calcification (20–30%).
Treatment: Seldom curative; exenteration ± radiotherapy.
Prognosis: Very poor with high mortality.

sections.title: Neural Tumours: Optic Nerve Glioma
content: Uncommon slow-growing glial tissue tumour; usually occurs in children.
Strong association with Neurofibromatosis-1 (NF-1).
Presentation: Gradual dVA (often stabilizes), disc swelling or atrophy, and proptosis.
Distribution: Isolated nerve (22%), Chiasm (72%), often involves midbrain/hypothalamus.
Imaging: Fusiform enlargement of optic nerve ± chiasmal mass.
Observation: For isolated nerve tumours distant from chiasm, good vision, non-disfiguring proptosis. Monitor with serial MRI.
Surgical Excision: For reduced vision, pain, severe proptosis, or posterior spread threatening chiasm.
Other Tx: Chemotherapy or radiotherapy for chiasmal/midbrain involvement.
Prognosis: Good for nerve-restricted; worsens with posterior involvement.

rows: Gradual dVA, disc swelling/atrophy, disc collateral vessels (30%), proptosis, ophthalmoparesis.
Adulthood. Superior orbit. Non-tender mass (often cystic), proptosis, dVA, restricted motility.
Observation if VA good. Excision for blind eyes, severe proptosis, or chiasm threat.

sections.title: Neurofibroma Variants
content: Plexiform Neurofibroma: Childhood onset, strongly associated with NF-1. 'Bag-of-worms' mass with S-shaped lid deformity. Poorly defined, not encapsulated. Surgery: difficult, may need repeated debulking.
Isolated Neurofibroma: Adulthood onset, gradual proptosis. Well-circumscribed. Surgery: usually straightforward.

branches: Type: Commonest benign orbital neoplasm in adults. Hamartoma of large vascular spaces.
Presentation: Young adulthood, accelerated in pregnancy. Usually intraconal (80%).
Clinical: Axial proptosis, restricted motility, globe indentation (choroidal folds/hypermetropic shift), dVA. Rare: amaurosis.
Investigations: US (well-defined, high internal reflectivity). CT/MRI (intraconal, mild/mod enhancement, possible thrombosis).
Treatment: Observation for asymptomatic; excision for symptomatic.

sections.title: Vascular: Capillary Haemangioma
content: Definition: Hamartoma. Massive tumours may cause Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (dplatelets, dhb, dclotting factors) or high-output cardiac failure.
Superficial ('Strawberry Naevus'): Confined to dermis. Bright red, appears <2mo, full size by 1y, involutes by 6y. May cause amblyopia/astigmatism.
Deep Lesions: Posterior to septum. Variable proptosis (worsens with Valsalva/crying). Partial involution with time.
Treatment: Topical/intralesional/systemic corticosteroids, Systemic propranolol, Surgical excision.

sections.title: Vascular: Lymphangioma
sections.content: A rare hamartoma of lymph vessels presenting in childhood. Size increases with head-down posture or Valsalva. Superficial: transilluminable cystic spaces (lid/conjunctiva) ± blood. Deep: gradual proptosis or acute pain/dVA due to haemorrhage (‘chocolate cyst’). CT shows low-density cyst-like mass and orbital enlargement. Treatment: Observation, sclerosing agents, bleomycin, Onyx® (ethylene-vinyl-alcohol co-polymer), surgery, or drainage of sight-threatening bleeds. Surgery is difficult (large/friable).

sections.title: Lymphoproliferative Diseases
content: Range: Benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphoma (85% B-lymphocytes). Classified by WHO system.
Benign Reactive Lymphoid Hyperplasia: Polyclonal, superolateral orbit (lacrimal gland). Gradual proptosis, ptosis, firm mass. Tx: Steroids, radiotherapy, rituximab. 25% progress to lymphoma in 5y.
Atypical Lymphoid Hyperplasia: Intermediate. Homogeneous pattern with larger nuclei.

Malignant Orbital Lymphoma: Low-grade B-cell (Non-Hodgkin’s). Commonest: Marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of MALT (40–70%). Bilateral in 25%. Systemic involvement in 40% (diagnosis) to 60% (5y). Tx: Radiotherapy, chemo, monoclonal antibodies.

sections.title: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis
content: Rare childhood proliferative disorder.
Spectrum: Benign unifocal 'Eosinophilic Granuloma' to disseminated 'Letterer–Siwe'.
Eosinophilic Granuloma: Orbital involvement common; rapid proptosis with superotemporal swelling.
Letterer-Siwe: May cause bilateral proptosis.
Treatment: Surgical excision is usually curative.

sections.title: Rhabdomyosarcoma: Pediatric Emergency
content: Commonest 1° orbital malignancy in children; 87% present before 15y (♂ bias 1.6:1).
Histology: Embryonal (commonest), Alveolar, Pleomorphic. Pluripotent mesenchymal origin.
Location: Intraconal (50%) or superior orbit (25%).
Clinical: Acute/subacute proptosis, ptosis, inflammation (mimics orbital cellulitis).
Imaging: US (irregular, well-defined, low/med reflectivity, high Doppler flow); CT/MRI (irregular mass ± bony erosion).
Management: Biopsy + Systemic work-up mandatory. Surgery for localized; Combined Radio+Chemo for extensive.

rows: Commonest adult mesenchymal orbital tumour. Middle-aged or children post-radiotherapy. Benign or malignant. Located superonasally. Gradual proptosis, pain, dVA, restricted motility. Tx: Complete excision. Recurrence common.
Uncommon. In 50% cases, precede diagnosis of primary tumour. Aggressive: rapid proptosis, restricted motility, CN involvement, inflammation.
Breast, Lung, Prostate, GI. Scirrhous (Breast/Gastric) may cause enophthalmos.

sections.title: Vascular Lesions: Orbital Varices
content: Definition: Uncommon congenital venous enlargements (medial orbit, usually unilateral).
Clinical: Intermittent proptosis/visible varix (worsens with Valsalva/coughing/head-down). Possible thrombosis/haemorrhage.
Investigations: CT/MRI show multiple masses, orbital wall expansion, and phleboliths.
Treatment: Surgery (difficult) if painful/disfiguring/sight-threatening. Radiological endovascular sclerosant/coil possible.

rows: High-flow: Direct ICA to Cavernous Sinus.
Low-flow: Dural arteries to Cavernous Sinus.
dVA, diplopia, audible bruit, pulsatile proptosis, orbital oedema, chemosis, iIOP, ophthalmoparesis (III/VI), vein engorgement, RAPD, disc swelling, ischemia.
Often asymptomatic; pain, cosmesis, chemosis, episcleral engorgement/arterialization, iIOP.
B-scan/Doppler US, CT, MRI: Dilated superior ophthalmic vein + thickened EOMs.
Embolization (success >85%). Visual loss occurs in 50% without Tx.
40% thrombose spontaneously. Tx reserved for glaucoma, dVA, diplopia, or severe pain.

sections.title: AION: Epidemiology & Vascular Supply
sections.content: Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is a significant cause of acute visual loss in the elderly population, affecting up to 10/ 100,000/ y of those over 50y. In 5– 10%, the aetiology is arteritic, in which the majority of these are caused by GCA, and in 90– 95%, the aetiology is non- arteritic (see Table 16.5). The vascular supply to the anterior optic nerve is from the short posterior ciliary artery and the choroidal circulation.

rows: Major: GCA. Minor: Churg– Strauss, PAN, GPA, RA, Relapsing polychondritis, Other connective tissue disorders (e.g. SLE)

Major: Hypertension, Diabetes, Disc morphology ‘disc at risk’. Minor: Smoking, Hyperlipidaemia, Acute hypotension, Anaemia, Obstructive sleep apnoea, Optic disc drusen, Cataract surgery, Non- ocular surgery (e.g. cardiac, spinal), Drugs (e.g. amiodarone, erectile dysfunction drugs), Radiation- induced optic neuropathy
Sudden d, Usually >6/ 60, Often altitudinal field loss
Swollen (often sectoral), Commonly hyperaemic, Predisposed (small + crowded)

sections.title: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) Essentials
content: GCA or temporal arteritis is an ophthalmic emergency.
Requires immediate assessment and systemic corticosteroid treatment.
Mean onset is 70y; rare before 50y.
Commonly occurs in Caucasians; 3x more likely in ♀.
Pathology: Short posterior ciliary artery vasculitis leads to ischaemic necrosis of the optic nerve head.
Clinical judgement is required due to disease heterogeneity.

sections.title: GCA Clinical Features
content: Sudden dVA (<6/ 60 in 76%).
New- onset headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, weight loss, night sweats, myalgia (association with PMR).
Warning episode: Transient dVA (short obscurations or longer amaurosis fugax- like episodes).
Signs: RAPD, swollen disc (typically pale; rarely segmental) ± peripapillary haemorrhages and CWS.
Abnormal temporal arteries: Thickened, tender, non- pulsatile.
Associations: CRAO, BRAO, cilioretinal artery occlusion; III, IV, VIn palsy.

content.explanation: 3+ criteria = 93.5% sensitivity/91.2% specificity: 1. Age ≥50y. 2. New onset localized headache. 3. Temporal artery tenderness or dpulse. 4. ESR ≥50mm/ h (Westerngren). 5. Arterial biopsy showing necrotizing arteritis with mononuclear cell infiltrates or granulomatous process with multinuclear giant cells.

sections.title: Investigations Strategy
content: 1. Immediate Bloods: ESR, CRP, FBC (iESR, iCRP, and iPlt support GCA).
2. Prompt TAB: Recommended length ≥2cm, no <1cm. Aim within 1wk (positive up to 2– 6wk post-treatment).
3. Additional: U+E, LFTs, CXR, and urinalysis.
4. Long term: 2- yearly CXR for aneurysm detection (suspected large-vessel GCA).

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging & Specialized Tests
content: Duplex US: Hypoechoic ‘halo’ (vessel wall oedema) + stenosis/occlusion. User-dependent; positive >2wk post-steroids.
Fluoro- deoxyglucose PET: Assessing disease activity/extent, especially in large-vessel vasculitis.
High- resolution MRI: Superficial cranial/extracranial arteries (not routinely performed).

sections.title: Emergency Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Immediate systemic corticosteroids: e.g. 1g IVMP 1×/ d for 1– 3d.
2. Oral Follow-up: PO prednisolone 1– 2mg/ kg 1×/ d.
3. Patient Counseling: Mandatory explanation of side effects (gastric/bone protection required).
4. Titration: Once controlled, titrate by symptoms and markers (CRP responds faster than ESR).
5. Specialist Referral: Seek rheumatologist if comorbidities complicate therapy.
6. Emerging Agents: Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) inducing sustained remission at 1yr. Leflunomide under investigation.

sections.title: Management of Negative TAB
sections.content: If there is a typical clinical/laboratory picture and positive steroid response despite negative TAB, manage as GCA. If history and markers are atypical with negative TAB, consider alternative diagnoses and specialist referral. Steroids can be rapidly tapered within 2wk.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis of GCA
content: GPA
PAN
SLE
RA
Takayasu arteritis

sections.title: Prognosis & Systemic Risks
content: Risk to fellow eye: 10% if treated; up to 95% if untreated.
TIA and Stroke
Myocardial infarcts
Neuropathies
Mesenteric artery occlusion
Thoracic artery aneurysms
Death

sections.title: Surgical Approach: Superficial TAB (Box 16.3)
content: Preoperative: Choose side of visual loss/abnormality. Map artery by palpation or US Doppler. Mark skin. Hair removal.
Procedure - Cleaning & LA: Clean skin. Infiltrate LA (27G). Adrenaline optional (helps haemostasis/visualization).
Procedure - Incision: Parallel to Langer's lines. Blunt dissection (do not breach superficial temporalis fascia).
Procedure - Ligation: Tie 4- 0 silk/Vicryl twice at distal/proximal ends. Pass needle backwards or double suture without needle. Ligate local tributaries.
Procedure - Specimen Care: Do not crush by regrasping specimen. Maximize biopsy length.
Procedure - Closure: Subcutaneous (5- 0 interrupted Vicryl). Skin (running 6- 0 Vicryl subcuticular).
Post-operative: Compression bandage for 24h. Optional antibiotic ointment for 3– 4d.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA): The Ophthalmic Emergency + Temporal Artery Biopsy... ---
sections.content: Giant Cell Arteritis (Horton's Disease) is a systemic granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large-sized arteries. In ophthalmology, it represents a 'code red' emergency due to its propensity for sudden, irreversible bilateral vision loss via Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (A-AION). An exhaustive guide to the diagnostic accuracy of temporal artery biopsy (TAB) and ultrasound in Giant Cell Arteritis, featuring findings from the landmark TABUL study. This layout details sensitivity, specificity, clinical indications, and the essential risks required for informed patient consent. Anterior Ischaemic Optic Neuropathy (AION) is a major cause of acute vision loss in patients over 50. This guide provides an exhaustive breakdown of diagnostic criteria, emergency management for Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), and the surgical approach for temporal artery biopsy. A-AION is an ophthalmic emergency secondary to Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), characterized by acute, painless, altitudinal visual field loss. Rapid recognition is essential to prevent bilateral blindness and systemic complications.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) is a chronic vasculitis of large and medium-sized vessels, primarily involving the extracranial branches of the carotid artery. It is the most common primary systemic vasculitis in adults over 50. The ophthalmic hallmark is Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (A-AION), caused by occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries (SPCAs).

branches: Activation of adventitial dendritic cells via Toll-like receptors
Recruitment of CD4+ T-cells (Th1 and Th17 pathways)
Macrophage fusion into Multinucleated Giant Cells
Destruction of the Internal Elastic Lamina

rows: New onset or new type of localized pain in the head
Tenderness to palpation or decreased pulsation
Vasculitis with mononuclear cell infiltration or granulomatous inflammation

sections.title: Systemic Clinical Features
content: New-onset localized headache (often temporal)
Jaw Claudication (High specificity for GCA)
Scalp tenderness (pain when brushing hair)
Polymyalgia Rheumatica (stiffness in hips/shoulders)
Constitutional: Fever, weight loss, anorexia, malaise
Carotidynia or limb claudication

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations
content: Amaurosis Fugax: Transient vision loss (Warning sign!)
A-AION: Sudden, profound, painless vision loss
CRAO: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion
Cilio-retinal Artery Occlusion (Pathognomonic if combined with A-AION)
Diplopia: Due to cranial nerve palsies or EOM ischemia
Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (rare)

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Red Flags
content: Sudden vision loss in a patient >50 years old
New-onset headache with jaw claudication
Chalky-white disc edema on fundoscopy
Diplopia in an elderly patient with constitutional symptoms
Delayed choroidal filling on Fluorescein Angiography

sections.title: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) Protocol
content: Step 1: Perform within 1-2 weeks of starting steroids
Step 2: Obtain 2-3 cm length to minimize 'skip lesion' errors
Step 3: Incise skin over the frontal branch of the temporal artery
Step 4: Careful dissection to preserve facial nerve branches
Step 5: Ligation and excision of the segment
Step 6: Histopathological exam for Giant Cells and Intimal thickening

sections.title: The 'Halo Sign' on Ultrasound
sections.content: Color Doppler Ultrasound of the temporal arteries is an increasingly used non-invasive tool. A positive 'Halo Sign'—a hypoechoic area around the arterial lumen representing vessel wall edema—has high specificity. If bilateral halos are seen, sensitivity approaches 85%.

sections.title: Acute Management Protocol
content: 1. Immediate Start: DO NOT wait for biopsy if suspicion is high.
2. Vision Loss Present: IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day) for 3 days.
3. Oral Bridge: Transition to Oral Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (Max 60-80mg).
4. Tapering: Very slow taper (over 12-18 months) based on CRP/ESR and symptoms.
5. Steroid Sparing: Consider Tocilizumab (Actemra) - IL-6 Receptor Antagonist.
6. Protection: Add PPI, Calcium/Vitamin D, and Bisphosphonates for bone health.

content.explanation: S: Scalp tenderness, T: Temporal headache, A: Amaurosis fugax, I: Ischemic optic neuropathy, R: Rheumatism (PMR symptoms)

sections.title: Recent Advances: GiACTA Trial
content: Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6) is FDA approved for GCA.
Proven to increase sustained remission rates.
Significantly reduces cumulative steroid dose.
Administered as weekly or bi-weekly subcutaneous injections.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Bilateral blindness: Risk is highest in the first 24-48 hours without treatment.
Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm: Late complication (occur in up to 18%).
Stroke: From vertebrobasilar involvement.
Steroid-induced: Diabetes, Osteoporosis, Glaucoma, Cataract.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: Normal ESR does NOT rule out GCA (Occurs in ~15-20% of biopsy-proven cases).
Always check CRP; the combination of ESR and CRP has 97% sensitivity.
If vision is lost in one eye, there is a 50-90% chance of the second eye being affected within days.
Biopsy remains the gold standard but should never delay treatment.

sections.title: The TABUL Study Findings
content: The TABUL study found that for diagnosing GCA, clinical judgement (clinician’s assessment at 2wk) combined with a TAB showed sensitivity and specificity of 91% and 81%, respectively.
Clinical judgement combined with duplex US showed sensitivity and specificity of 93% and 77%, respectively.
The cost-effectiveness was found in favour of US.
Reference: See Table 16.6 and Box 16.4.

rows: US compared with the ACR criteria‡

sections.title: Indication & Clinical Context
sections.content: Superficial TAB remains highly specific for the diagnosis of GCA (see E Arteritic AION and giant cell arteritis, pp. 744–6). Temporal artery biopsy 749.

sections.title: Consent: Procedure & Rationale
content: Discuss what the procedure involves
Discuss the rationale for the biopsy
Discuss possible complications

sections.title: Surgical Risks & Complications
content: Visible scarring (particularly if incision is pretrichial and not parallel to Langer’s lines).
Haematoma.
Wound infection.
Scalp or skin necrosis.
Facial nerve injury, with variable recovery (particularly if pretrichial incision).
Biopsy does not include the temporal artery (up to 1.25% of specimens in one report were vein or peripheral nerve).
Cerebral infarction (rare; possibly related to collateral blood flow to the brain from the superficial temporal artery).

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: A-AION is an ischemic infarction of the optic nerve head due to occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries (PCAs), typically caused by Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA). It is rare under age 50; incidence increases sharply with age, peaking between 70–80. Prevalence is approximately 15–25 per 100,000 in those over 50 years old.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: The Classic 5-Point Check
content: Sudden, painless loss of vision
Altitudinal visual field defect (most common)
Afferent pupillary defect (APD) present
Chalky-white, swollen optic disc
Peripapillary splinter hemorrhages

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Referral Criteria
content: Jaw claudication
Scalp tenderness
New-onset temporal headache
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) symptoms
Unilateral vision loss in patient > 60y

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: Step 1: Immediate ESR (>50-100 mm/hr) and CRP (>10 mg/L) labs.
Step 2: Start high-dose systemic steroids (e.g., IV Methylprednisolone 1g daily for 3 days) BEFORE biopsy.
Step 3: Perform Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) within 1-2 weeks; minimum 2cm length to avoid skip lesions.
Step 4: Ultrasound (USG) of temporal arteries (Halo sign).

rows: Usually associated with disc-at-risk, DM, HTN; no systemic GCA signs
Cherry-red spot, pale retina, no optic disc swelling
High IOP, cup-disc ratio changes, classic arcuate defects
Pain on eye movement, young age, central scotoma

content.explanation: Temporal headache, Jaw claudication, Altered ESR/CRP, Polymyalgia rheumatica, Scalp tenderness.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Normal ESR does not rule out GCA (up to 20% of biopsy-proven cases). CRP is often more sensitive.
Temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard; continue steroids regardless of initial biopsy results if clinical suspicion remains high.
Always inquire about constitutional symptoms: weight loss, night sweats, fatigue.
The 'Halo sign' on temporal artery ultrasound has high specificity but operator-dependent sensitivity.

data.summary: An exhaustive clinical guide to lens-related, open-angle, and closed-angle secondary glaucomas. This poster details the mechanisms, clinical presentations, and multi-modal treatment strategies for these complex ocular conditions.
