rows: The enlarging lens causes pupillary block and anterior bowing of the iris, with 2° angle closure. In an eye of normal axial length, this occurs 2° to an intumescent cataractous lens; in a short eye, this may result simply from the normal increase in lens size with age.

iIOP, shallow AC, fixed semi-dilated pupil, swollen cataractous lens. Ipsilateral closed angle (appositional; sigma sign may be seen on indentation gonioscopy). Contralateral angle may be open with deep AC (in contrast to PACG); however, this helpful sign may not be present if the contralateral eye also has significant cataract.
Medical (topical and systemic): as for PACG. Nd-yAG PI to reverse pupillary block component. early cataract extraction is the definitive treatment—needs an experienced surgeon.

sections.title: Phacolytic Glaucoma
content: Mechanism: the hypermature cataract loses soluble lens proteins through the anterior capsule, causing trabecular obstruction and subsequent 2° open-angle glaucoma.
Clinical features: iIOP, lens protein in a deep AC (may form a pseudohypopyon), hypermature/mature cataract, open angle (with lens protein); AC tap reveals lens protein and foamy macrophages.
Treatment Medical: topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents, as required; consider topical steroids for associated inflammation.
Surgical: early cataract extraction—needs experienced surgeon.

sections.title: Phacoanaphylactic Uveitis
content: Mechanism: Inflammatory reaction to lens protein post-trauma or surgery (must distinguish from endophthalmitis). May cause sensitization in contralateral eye.
Clinical Features: recent trauma/surgery, exposed lens protein, AC flare + cells ± hypopyon, KPs, synechiae (PS + PAS), angle usually open (but ± PAS); IOP may be high, normal, or low.
Treatment Of inflammatory process: topical steroid (e.g. dexamethasone 0.1% hourly) and surgical removal of any retained lens fragments.
Treatment of iIOP: medical—topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents, as required.
For contralateral cataract: consider removal by intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCe) to reduce lens protein exposure.

sections.title: Glaucoma 2° to Lens Subluxation/Dislocation
content: Mechanism: pupillary block by anterior lens subluxation or complete dislocation into the AC; there may also be a coincident angle abnormality (e.g. Marfan’s syndrome).
Clinical features: iIOP, subluxed/dislocated lens ± corneal oedema (if acute or lenticulocorneal touch); lenticular astigmatism and variable refraction.

Treatment Positional: dilate and lie patient supine (to encourage posterior movement of lens), and constrict (to keep lens safely behind pupil); long-term miotic therapy may be needed, unless the lens dislocates safely into the vitreous.
Early lens extraction: if positional measures fail, if complete dislocation into the AC, if cataract, or if recurrent problem. Often best dealt with by a vitreoretinal approach.

sections.title: Steroid-Induced: Mechanism & Treatment
sections.content: Exogenous, and occasionally endogenous, steroids may decrease outflow facility, leading to iIOP after a few days or weeks. POAG patients are often particularly sensitive. Possible mechanisms include prostaglandin inhibition (e.g. PGF2A) and structural changes in the eCM (glycosaminoglycans) and trabecular meshwork (cross-linking of actins). History: specifically ask for steroid-containing anabolics, skin/haemorrhoid creams, inhaled steroids, or oral steroids (asthma/COPD). Treatment: Decrease frequency/potency or stop steroid (± steroid-sparing agent)—liaise with physician. If corticosteroids essential, treat as POAG. SLt may be helpful.

sections.title: Red Cell Glaucoma
content: Hyphaema (usually traumatic) leads to TM blockage.
10% risk of rebleed usually at ~5d post-injury.
Sickle-cell disease/trait patients do worse and are harder to treat (acidosis from CAIs worsens sickling).

sections.title: Red Cell Glaucoma Management
content: Of hyphaema: strict bed rest, topical steroid (e.g. dexamethasone 0.1% 6×/d), mydriatic/cycloplegic (e.g. atropine 1% 2×/d).
Of IOP: topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, CAI) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents.
Surgical: AC paracentesis ± AC washout. In rare refractory cases, trabeculectomy.

sections.title: Ghost Cell Glaucoma
content: Mechanism: Vitreous haemorrhage leads to blockage of TM by degenerate red blood cells, usually 2–4wk after haemorrhage.
Appearance: Cells are tan-coloured (lost haemoglobin) and seen in AC and angle.
Treatment: Medical (as for POAG) is usually sufficient. If failure: AC washout + vitrectomy.

content.explanation: Traumatic Recession = 10% risk of glaucoma at 10 years. Risk increases with extent of recession.

sections.title: Angle Recession: Clinical & Screening
content: Mechanism: Blunt trauma causes angle recession and trabecular damage.
Observation: Best seen by simultaneous gonioscopy. Look for asymmetry of AC depth, pupil, and angle.
Screening: Periodic IOP check (e.g. 3mo, 6mo, yearly) if known angle recession.
Treatment: As for POAG.

sections.title: Raised Episcleral Venous Pressure
sections.content: Aqueous drainage reduced as pressure increases. Causes: Vascular abnormalities in orbit (Sturge–Weber syndrome, orbital varices), cavernous sinus (AV fistulae), or SVC obstruction. Manifestations: Unilateral/bilateral engorged episcleral veins, chemosis, proptosis, with blood in Schlemm’s canal on gonioscopy. Treatment: Directed at underlying pathology; medical/surgical IOP lowering if necessary. Surgical warning: extremely hazardous with refractory uveal effusion.

rows: Open-angle (clogging/infiltration) or Closed-angle (rubeosis/displacement). 20% of malignant melanoma associated with iIOP.
Directed by tumour; B-scan US essential if poor posterior view. iIOP suggests poor prognosis.
Uncommon association of mild AC inflammation and iIOP (open angle) from RRD. Photoreceptor outer segments obstruct TM.
IOP/uveitis treated medically in interim; resolves rapidly with surgical repair of retinal detachment.

sections.title: Other Secondary Closed-Angle: Iridoschisis
content: Bilateral splitting/atrophy of anterior iris leaf.
Associated with nanophthalmos; usually in elderly.
Angle-closure type: treat with Nd-YAG PI.
Open-angle type: treat as POAG (due to debris blocking TM).

branches: Iris naevus (Cogan–Reese) syndrome (protrusions of iris stroma)

sections.title: ICE Syndrome Details
content: Unilateral (rarely bilateral) condition; abnormal endothelium migrates across angle, TM, and iris. Usually 20-40y old female. HSV proposed as causative.
Clinical features: Unilateral pain, blurred vision. Fine corneal guttata ('beaten metal'), corneal oedema, iris atrophy, corectopia (displaced pupil), pseudopolycoria (accessory pupil).
Gonioscopy: Broad-based PAS that may insert anterior to Schwalbe’s line.
Investigations: Consider specular microscopy for endothelial changes.
Treatment: Medical (β-blocker, α2-agonist, CAI, PGA), surgery (trabeculectomy ± augmented or tube), or cyclodestruction.

rows: Bilateral, dominantly inherited, detectable in childhood. Abnormal endothelium forms extensive adhesions with angle closure. 15% risk of glaucoma.
Trauma/surgery allows epithelium to proliferate across corneal endothelium and angle. Similar to ICE syndrome but unchecked proliferation.
Very difficult; lower IOP as for POAG; intracameral antifibrotics (e.g. 5-FU), surgical excision. Prognosis for vision is poor.
Oedema of the peripheral cornea may cause 2° angle closure.
Risk is highest in eyes with pre-existing shallow ACs.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Comprehensive Guide to Secondary Glaucomas ---
sections.content: An exhaustive clinical reference covering lens-related, open-angle, closed-angle, and iatrogenic glaucomas. This guide details mechanisms, clinical features, and multi-modal treatment strategies for secondary intraocular pressure elevations.

sections.title: Lens-Related Glaucoma Overview
sections.content: Lens-related glaucoma may result from abnormalities of lens size, lens position, release of lens protein (mature cataract/trauma/surgery), and/or the consequent inflammatory response.

branches: Normal eye: 2° to intumescent cataractous lens
Short eye: 2° to normal increase in lens size with age

sections.title: Phacomorphic: Clinical & Treatment
content: Clinical Features: iIOP, shallow AC, fixed semi-dilated pupil, swollen cataractous lens.
Ipsilateral: Closed angle (appositional; sigma sign may be seen on indentation gonioscopy).
Contralateral: Angle may be open with deep AC (contrast to PACG); sign may be absent if contralateral eye has significant cataract.
Treatment Medical: Topical and systemic (as for PACG).
Treatment Laser: Nd-yAG PI to reverse pupillary block component.
Definitive Treatment: Early cataract extraction (needs an experienced surgeon).

rows: Hypermature cataract loses soluble lens proteins through the anterior capsule, causing trabecular obstruction and subsequent 2° open-angle glaucoma.
iIOP, lens protein in a deep AC (may form a pseudohypopyon), hypermature/mature cataract, open angle (with lens protein); AC tap reveals lens protein and foamy macrophages.
Topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents; consider topical steroids for associated inflammation.

sections.title: Phacoanaphylactic Uveitis
sections.content: Mechanism: This is an inflammatory reaction to lens protein, usually following traumatic capsular rupture or post-operative retention of lens material (when it must be distinguished from endophthalmitis). This insult may also cause sensitization such that lens protein exposure in the contralateral eye (surgery, hyper-/mature cataract) may be associated with an aggressive response.

sections.title: Phacoanaphylactic Clinical & Management
content: Clinical Features: Recent trauma/surgery, exposed lens protein, AC flare + cells ± hypopyon, KPs, synechiae (PS + PAS), angle usually open (but ± PAS); IOP may be high, normal, or low.
Treatment of Inflammatory Process: Topical steroid (e.g. dexamethasone 0.1% hourly) and surgical removal of any retained lens fragments.
Treatment of iIOP: Medical—topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents, as required.
Contralateral Eye: Consider removal by intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCe) to reduce lens protein exposure.

sections.title: Lens Subluxation / Dislocation
content: Mechanism: Pupillary block by anterior lens subluxation or complete dislocation into the AC; possible coincident angle abnormality (e.g. Marfan’s syndrome).
Clinical: iIOP, subluxed/dislocated lens ± corneal oedema (if acute or lenticulocorneal touch); lenticular astigmatism and variable refraction.
Positional Management: Dilate and lie patient supine (encourage posterior movement), then constrict (keep lens behind pupil).
Surgical: Early lens extraction if positional measures fail, complete dislocation to AC, cataract, or recurrence. Often requires vitreoretinal approach.

sections.title: Steroid-Induced: Mechanisms & Rx
sections.content: Exogenous/endogenous steroids decrease outflow facility. POAG patients are particularly sensitive. Mechanisms include prostaglandin inhibition (e.g. PGF2A) and structural changes in ECM (glycosaminoglycans) and trabecular meshwork (cross-linking of actins). Always check for steroid use (anabolics, skin/hemorrhoid creams, inhaled, oral courses for asthma/COPD). Treatment: Decrease frequency/potency or stop steroid (± steroid-sparing agent); if essential, treat as POAG. SLT may be helpful.

rows: Hyphaema (traumatic) blocks TM. Rebleed 10% risk at ~5d. Sickle-cell patients harder to treat (acidosis from CAIs worsens sickling).
Strict bed rest, topical steroid, mydriatic/cycloplegic, topical/systemic IOP agents. Surgical: AC paracentesis ± washout. Refractory: Trabeculectomy.
Vitreous hemorrhage leads to TM blockage by degenerate RBCs (tan-colored) usually 2–4wk post-hemorrhage.
Medical treatment (as for POAG) usually sufficient. If failure: AC washout + vitrectomy.

sections.title: Other Open-Angle Varieties
content: Angle Recession: Blunt trauma risk; 10% glaucoma risk at 10y. Look for asymmetry of AC depth, pupil, and angle. Screen 3mo, 6mo, yearly. Treat as POAG.

Raised Episcleral Venous Pressure: From vascular abnormalities (Sturge–Weber, orbital varices, AV fistulae, SVC obstruction). Signs: Engorged veins, chemosis, proptosis, blood in Schlemm's canal. Surgery is hazardous (refractory uveal effusion).

Tumours: iIOP via TM clogging/infiltration, rubeosis, or 2° angle closure. 20% of malignant melanoma associated with iIOP. Suspect in atypical unilateral glaucoma. B-scan essential if posterior view poor.
Schwartz–Matsuo Syndrome: Mild AC inflammation + iIOP from RRD. Photoreceptor outer segments obstruct TM. Resolves rapidly with retinal detachment surgical repair.

sections.title: Iridocorneal Endothelial (ICE) Syndrome
content: General: Unilateral condition; abnormal endothelium migrates across angle/TM/iris. Rare, typically 20–40y old females. 50% glaucoma risk. HSV possible cause.
Variants: Chandler syndrome (corneal focus), Essential iris atrophy (iris focus), Iris naevus (Cogan–Reese) syndrome (pigmented nodules).
Clinical: Unilateral pain, blurred vision, fine corneal guttata ('beaten metal'), corneal oedema, corectopia, pseudopolycoria.
Gonioscopy: Broad-based PAS inserting anterior to Schwalbe’s line.
Management: Specular microscopy for diagnosis. Treatment: Medical (β-blocker, α2-agonist, CAI, PGA), Surgery (trabeculectomy ± augmented/tube), or cyclodestruction.

rows: Bilateral splitting/atrophy of anterior iris leaf. Elderly. Associated with nanophthalmos.
Angle-closure: Nd-YAG PI. Open-angle: As for POAG.
Bilateral, dominantly inherited, childhood detection. Iridocorneal adhesions. 15% glaucoma risk.
Trauma/surgery allows epithelium to proliferate on endothelium/angle. Poor prognosis.
Difficult. Lower IOP (POAG style), intracameral 5-FU, extensive surgical excision.
Peripheral corneal oedema causes 2° angle closure, especially in at-risk eyes with shallow AC.
Refer to primary corneal dystrophy management.

content.explanation: Mechanism: Posterior misdirection of aqueous into vitreous causing anterior displacement of vitreous, ciliary processes, and lens/PCIOL.

sections.title: Aqueous Misdirection Management
content: Risk Factors: Short axial length, chronic angle closure, previous acute closure, nanophthalmos, uveal effusion, surgery (trab, tube, cataract), laser PI, miotics.
Diagnosis: Acute iIOP, shallow/flat AC, patent PI present (no pupillary block/bombé), no choroidal detachment/hemorrhage.

Initial Medical: Patent PI check (repeat if needed), Dilate (Atropine 1% 3x/d + Phenylephrine 2.5% 4x/d), Systemic (Acetazolamide IV stat then PO + mannitol/glycerol), Topical (β-blocker + Apraclonidine).
Laser Intervention: YAG anterior vitreous disruption (capsulotomy/hyaloidotomy); Argon laser to ciliary processes; Trans-scleral cyclodiode photocoagulation.
Surgery (Goal: Uni-chamber eye): Peripheral zonulo-hyaloidectomy is key.
Phakic Surgery: VPV procedure (vitrectomy–phacoemulsification–vitrectomy) or phaco/ECCE + capsulotomy + vitrectomy.
Aphakic/Pseudophakic Surgery: Pars plana vitrectomy and posterior capsulotomy.

sections.title: Post-Cataract & VR Surgery
content: Post-Cataract Spike: Retained viscoelastic, lens fragments, or inflammation. Prophylaxis: Acetazolamide SR 250mg stat.
Post-Cataract Rare Causes: Suprachoroidal hemorrhage, phacolysis, phacoanaphylaxis, Amsler hemorrhage (Fuchs’ heterochromic), epithelial downgrowth, aqueous misdirection, UGH syndrome.
Intraocular Gas (SF6, C3F8): iIOP from expansion/overfill. Rx: Short-term medical (Acetazolamide SR 250mg 2x/d for 5d) or gas removal.
Scleral Buckles: 2° angle closure from ciliary body swelling/choroidal detachment. Usually resolves; medical treatment interim.
Silicone Oil: Oil in AC blocks TM. Rx: Medical; cyclodestruction if persistent. Early removal (<6mo) helps; late removal (>6mo) less effective due to macrophage incorporation.
Vitrectomy: Increases risk of rubeosis in PDR and ghost cell glaucoma.

title: Merged: (Not oxford) Keratoconus: Navigating the Conical Curve
summary: Keratoconus is a progressive, non-inflammatory eye condition where the normally round cornea thins and begins to bulge into a cone-like shape. This structural change deflects light as it enters the eye, causing significant visual distortion and sensitivity.

sections.title: Common Symptoms
content: Blurred or distorted vision
Increased sensitivity to light and glare
Frequent changes in eyeglass prescriptions
Clouding or sudden worsening of vision
Monocular polyopia (ghosting/multiple images)

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNING: EYE RUBBING
content: Vigorous eye rubbing is strongly linked to disease progression.
Mechanical trauma can accelerate corneal thinning.
Chronic rubbing is often associated with atopic (allergic) eye disease.
Stopping the 'rubbing habit' is the first step in management.

rows: Iron deposits in the basal epithelium at the base of the cone.
Fine, vertical stress lines in the deep stroma/Descemet’s membrane.
V-shaped indentation of the lower lid on down-gaze.
A conical reflection on the nasal cornea when light is shone from the temporal side.
Sudden swelling caused by a rupture in Descemet’s membrane.

sections.title: The Treatment Ladder
content: Step 1: Spectacles or Soft Contact Lenses (Early stages)
Step 2: Rigid Gas Permeable (RGP) or Scleral Lenses
Step 3: Corneal Collagen Cross-linking (CXL) to halt progression
Step 4: Intracorneal Ring Segments (Intacs) to flatten the cone
Step 5: Topography-guided Laser (Partial/Combined treatments)
Step 6: Corneal Transplant (DALK or PKP for advanced cases)

content.explanation: T: Topography is gold standard, H: Hydrops (acute risk), I: Irregular astigmatism, N: Non-inflammatory, C: Cross-linking (CXL), O: Optical correction (Lenses), N: Nasal light reflex (Rizutti), E: Eye rubbing avoidance.

sections.title: Diagnostic Gold Standards
content: Corneal Topography/Tomography: Essential for mapping curvature.
Pachymetry: Measures corneal thickness (thinning at the apex).
Slit-lamp Biomicroscopy: Visualizing striae and rings.
Retinoscopy: Detection of the 'Scissor Reflex'.

sections.title: Disease Definition
sections.content: Keratoconus is characterized by the biomechanical failure of the corneal stroma. As the collagen matrix weakens, intraocular pressure causes the cornea to distend forward, usually beginning in puberty and progressing until the third or fourth decade of life. It is the most common primary ectasia.

sections.title: Orbital Geometry & Anatomy (1)
content: The orbit forms a pyramid: lateral and medial walls are at 45° to each other.
Central axis is at 22.5° (approximated to 23°).
The four rectus muscles originate from the annulus of Zinn.
The SO (like the LPS) originates from the orbital apex outside the annulus.
The IO arises from the nasal orbital floor.
Obliques lie inferior to their corresponding rectus: SO lies inferior to the SR; IO lies inferior to the IR.
The SO tendon and sheath uniquely pass through a cartilaginous rigid pulley attached to the superonasal orbital wall.

sections.title: Spiral of Tillaux & Innervation
content: The spiral of Tillaux: recti insert increasingly posterior to the limbus (MR, IR, LR, then SR).
Innervation: IIIn for SR, MR, IR, IO.
Innervation: IVn for SO.
Innervation: VIn for LR.
Blood Supply: Each rectus muscle carries two anterior ciliary arteries, except the lateral which carries only one (vital for anterior segment perfusion).

sections.title: Fascial Layers & High-Resolution Imaging
sections.content:
Tenon’s capsule is a diffuse fascial layer between the conjunctiva and globe which envelops the EOMs. Condensations of this layer form: 
1. Check ligaments: spanning radially from the globe to the lateral and medial orbital walls and between muscles.
2. Lockwood’s ligament: slung below and supporting the globe.
3. Intermuscular septum: concentrically surrounding the anterior globe between muscles.

MRI shows EOMs do not pass in a straight line from origin to insertion; pulleys and associated passive and active sling structures control the muscle paths. (Ref 1: Demer JL. Pivotal role of orbital connective tissues in binocular alignment and strabismus. 2004).

sections.title: Detailed Taxonomy of Eye Movements
content: Axes of Fick: Rotations around horizontal (x), anteroposterior (y), and vertical (z) axes.
Ductions: Abduction (outward), Adduction (inward), Supraduction (upward), Infraduction (downward), Intorsion (superior limbus moves inward), Extorsion (superior limbus moves outward).

Versions: Dextroversion (right gaze), Laevoversion (left gaze), Supraversion (upgaze), Infraversion (downgaze), Dextrocycloversion (superior limbus moves right), Laevocycloversion (superior limbus moves left).
Vergences: Convergence (inward), Divergence (outward).

content.explanation: Sherrington’s law: i innervation of the agonist is accompanied by d innervation of its antagonist (ipsilateral). Hering’s law: During conjugate movement, yoke muscles (contralateral) receive equal and simultaneous innervation.

sections.title: Muscle Compartmentalization
sections.content: There is compartmentalization within the EOMs. Compartments are characterized by distinct innervation, function, and central control. (Ref 2: Demer JL. Compartmentalization of extraocular muscle function. Eye (Lond). 2014;29:157– 162.)

sections.title: Binocular Single Vision (BSV) Essentials
sections.content:
BSV is the ability to view the world with two eyes, form two separate images, and fuse them centrally into a single percept. Prerequisites: correct alignment and similar image clarity from the neonatal period. 

Key Concepts:
- Normal Retinal Correspondence: Image stimulates anatomically corresponding points on each retina.
- Horopter: An imaginary plane where points in space project to corresponding retinal points.
- Panum’s fusional area: The narrow region around the horopter where points are seen as single despite disparity.

sections.title: Levels of BSV & Fusion
content: 1. Simultaneous perception: Perception of a single image due to simultaneous formation of an image on each retina.
2. Fusion: Stimulation of corresponding points in each retina allows central fusion of image.
3. Stereopsis: Disparity in fused images gives a perception of depth.

sections.title: Fusion Components & Reserves
content: Sensory fusion: Generates a single image from corresponding points.
Motor fusion: Adjusts eye position to maintain sensory fusion.
Fusional reserves: The level beyond which mechanisms break down, usually resulting in diplopia.

sections.title: Abnormalities: Confusion & Diplopia
content: Confusion: Stimulation of corresponding points by dissimilar images (images appear on top of each other).
Diplopia: Stimulation of non-​corresponding points by the same image (double vision).

sections.title: Adaptive Mechanisms
content: Suppression: Cortical mechanism to extinguish images (central/foveal or peripheral). Monocular foveal suppression leads to amblyopia.
Sbiza filter bar: Successively denser filters used to measure suppression density until fixation switch occurs.
Abnormal retinal correspondence (ARC): Cortical remapping of non-corresponding points to produce single perception despite deviation.
Abnormal head posture: Behavioral mechanism to move the field of single vision to a useful location.

sections.title: The Phenomenon of Microtropia
sections.content:
Microtropia is a small manifest deviation with a degree of BSV created by ARC, eccentric fixation, and a central suppression scotoma.

- Microtropia with identity: No movement on cover test due to absolute eccentric fixation.
- Microtropia without identity: Movement occurs on cover test because eccentric fixation is not absolute.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Extraocular Anatomy & Binocular Single Vision: The Complete Clinical Map ---
sections.content: An exhaustive anatomical and physiological guide to the extraocular muscles, the complex mechanics of ocular motility, and the sensory frameworks of binocular single vision and its adaptive mechanisms.

sections.title: Orbital Geometry & Rectus Origins
content: The orbit forms a pyramid structure.
Lateral and medial walls are at 45° to each other.
The central axis is at 22.5° (approximated to 23°).
The four rectus muscles (MR, LR, SR, IR) originate from the annulus of Zinn.

branches: SO: Orbital apex outside the annulus (like LPS)

sections.title: Specialized Structures of the EOMs
sections.content: The SO tendon and sheath uniquely pass through a cartilaginous rigid pulley attached to the superonasal orbital wall. The spiral of Tillaux describes the way the recti insert increasingly posterior to the limbus (MR, IR, LR, then SR). Each rectus muscle carries two anterior ciliary arteries, except the lateral which carries only one. These are important for anterior segment perfusion.

sections.title: Fascial Layers & Orbital Connective Tissue
content: Tenon’s capsule: Diffuse fascial layer between conjunctiva and globe envelops EOMs.
Check ligaments: Spanning radially from globe to lateral/medial walls and between muscles.
Lockwood’s ligament: Slung below and supporting the globe.
Intermuscular septum: Concentrically surrounding the anterior globe between muscles.

sections.title: Modern Imaging Insights (Demer)
content: MRI shows EOMs do not pass in a straight line from origin to insertion.
Pulleys and associated passive and active sling structures control muscle paths (Demer JL, 2004).
Compartmentalization: EOMs have compartments with distinct innervation, function, and central control (Demer JL, 2014).

sections.title: Axes of Fick
content: Horizontal axis: (x)
Anteroposterior axis: (y)
Vertical axis: (z)

sections.title: Definitions: Ductions
content: Abduction: Outward
Adduction: Inward
Supraduction: Upward
Infraduction: Downward
Intorsion: Superior limbus moves inward
Extorsion: Superior limbus moves outward

sections.title: Definitions: Versions & Vergences
content: Dextroversion: Right gaze
Laevoversion: Left gaze
Supraversion: Upgaze
Infraversion: Downgaze
Dextrocycloversion: Superior limbus moves right
Laevocycloversion: Superior limbus moves left
Convergence: Inward vergence
Divergence: Outward vergence

content.explanation: Sherrington’s Law: Increased innervation of the agonist (e.g., LR) is accompanied by decreased innervation of its antagonist (ipsilateral MR). Hering’s Law: During conjugate movement, yoke muscles (e.g., LR of one eye and MR of the other) receive equal and simultaneous innervation.

sections.title: Binocular Single Vision (BSV) Fundamentals
sections.content: BSV is the ability to view the world with two eyes, form two separate images, and fuse them centrally to create a single percept. Development depends on correct alignment and similar image clarity from the neonatal period. Prerequisite: Normal retinal correspondence where images stimulate anatomically corresponding points on each retina, stimulating functionally corresponding points in the occipital cortex. The Horopter is the imaginary plane of points in space projecting to these retinal points. Panum’s fusional area is the narrow region around the horopter where points are seen as single despite disparity.

sections.title: Levels of Binocularity
content: 1. Simultaneous perception: Perception of a single image due to formation on each retina.
2. Fusion: Central fusion allowed by stimulation of corresponding retinal points.
3. Stereopsis: Perception of depth resulting from disparity in fused images.

sections.title: Fusion Components
content: Sensory Fusion: Generates a single image from corresponding points.
Motor Fusion: Adjusts eye position to maintain sensory fusion.
Fusional Reserves: The level beyond which mechanisms break down, usually resulting in diplopia.

sections.title: Abnormalities of Simultaneous Perception
content: Confusion: Stimulation of corresponding points by dissimilar images (images appear on top of each other).
Diplopia: Stimulation of non-corresponding points by the same image (double vision).

sections.title: Adaptive Mechanisms
content: Suppression: Cortical mechanism to extinguish one image. Central (fovea) for confusion, Peripheral for diplopia.
Abnormal Retinal Correspondence (ARC): Cortical remapping of non-corresponding points to produce a single perception despite deviation.
Abnormal Head Posture: Behavioral mechanism to move the field of single vision to a useful location.

sections.title: Detail: Suppression & Amblyopia
sections.content: Monocular foveal suppression, if not treated, leads to amblyopia; equal alternation between eyes does not. Suppression scotoma size and density are variable. Density is measured with a Sbiza filter bar, using successively denser filters in front of the better eye until a fixation switch occurs.

sections.title: Microtropia
sections.content: A small manifest deviation with a degree of BSV created by ARC, eccentric fixation, and a central suppression scotoma. Microtropia with identity: No movement on cover test. Microtropia without identity: Movement occurs because eccentric fixation is not absolute.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: RP is a primary dystrophy of the retinal photoreceptors (rods > cones) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Pathophysiology typically involves mutations in genes responsible for the phototransduction cascade, structural integrity (e.g., Rhodopsin, peripherin-2), or RPE metabolism. Common outcomes include apoptosis of rods followed by secondary cone death due to oxidative stress, nutrient deprivation, and toxic byproduct accumulation.

sections.title: Classic Clinical Triad
content: 1. Bone-spicule intraretinal pigmentary changes
2. Attenuation of retinal arterioles
3. Waxy pallor of the optic disc

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Full clinical history (including systemic syndromes like Usher or Bassen-Kornzweig).
Step 2: Goldmann Visual Fields (typically show mid-peripheral scotomas progressing to ring scotomas).
Step 3: Full-field ERG (scotopic b-wave reduction is the hallmark, often preceding visible fundus changes).
Step 4: SD-OCT (measures ellipsoid zone loss and central retinal thickness).
Step 5: Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF) to assess RPE integrity/hyperautofluorescent rings.
Step 6: Genetic Testing (Next-Generation Sequencing/Panel testing).

rows: Rapid onset, associated with systemic malignancy

sections.title: Red Flags: When to refer urgently
content: Sudden, unilateral vision loss (consider macular edema or rhegmatogenous RD).
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) not responsive to topical dorzolamide.
Signs of associated systemic vasculitis or malignancy.
New-onset nyctalopia that progresses rapidly in childhood (consider syndromic association).

content.explanation: Bone-spicules (pigmentation), Arteriolar attenuation, Waxy optic disc.

sections.title: Management Framework
content: Vitamin A Palmitate (15,000 IU/day) - Controversial, monitor liver function.
DHA/Omega-3 supplements (modest benefits in some cohorts).
Topical CAIs (Dorzolamide 2%) for CME treatment.
Low vision aids and vocational rehabilitation.
Voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna) for RPE65 mutation-associated disease.
Retinal prostheses (Argus II) for late-stage patients.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Ring Scotoma' on visual field testing is the classic deficit pattern.
ERG testing remains the gold standard for early diagnosis before symptomatic onset.
Always inquire about hearing loss; Usher syndrome is the most common syndromic cause (RP + sensorineural hearing loss).
Ellipsoid zone (EZ) integrity on OCT is the strongest predictor of visual potential.
The disease is 'progressive'; counseling patients regarding driving status and legal blindness is essential early on.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Retinitis Pigmentosa: Comprehensive Clinical Roadmap ---
sections.content: Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) represents a genetically heterogeneous group of progressive rod-cone dystrophies characterized by the primary degeneration of photoreceptor cells and the retinal pigment epithelium. This masterclass poster details the pathophysiology, diagnostic gold standards, and the current landscape of gene-based therapeutics.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) is the most common hereditary retinal dystrophy, affecting approximately 1 in 4,000 individuals worldwide. It is defined by the progressive loss of rod photoreceptor function, followed by cone degeneration. The condition may be isolated (nonsyndromic) or part of a multi-system syndrome. Pathologically, it involves apoptosis of photoreceptors and the migration of RPE cells into the inner retina, forming the classic bone-spicule patterns.

sections.title: The Classic Diagnostic Triad
content: 1. Arteriolar Attenuation: Significant narrowing of retinal vessels.
2. Bone-Spicule Pigmentation: Perivascular pigment migration in the mid-periphery.
3. Waxy Disc Pallor: Reactive gliosis covering the optic nerve head.

sections.title: Progression of Symptoms
content: 1. Nyctalopia: Difficulty adapting to darkness (Rod dysfunction).
2. Peripheral Field Loss: Development of mid-peripheral scotomas.
3. Tunnel Vision: Constriction of visual fields to <20 degrees.
4. Central Loss: Eventual cone involvement or CME development.
5. Total Blindness: Often occurs in later decades, depending on genotype.

rows: Rapid onset, recoverin antibodies (+), normal fundus early
Central vision lost first, photophobia, bull's eye maculopathy

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for Cystoid Macular Edema (CME); occurs in 10-50% of patients.
Posterior Subcapsular Cataracts (PSC) are highly prevalent in RP.
High myopia is frequently associated with XLRP.
FAF 'Ring of Fire' correlates with the edge of the functional visual field.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Considerations
content: Sudden vision loss (Rule out CME or Macular Hole)
Systemic weakness or cardiac issues (Think Kearns-Sayre Syndrome)
Polydactyly or obesity in a child (Think Bardet-Biedl)
Hearing loss (Screen for Usher Syndrome immediately)

branches: Refsum Disease (Phytanic acid buildup, Ataxia, Anosmia)

sections.title: Evidence-Based Management Protocol
content: 1. Baseline Testing: Complete ERG, VF, OCT, and Genetic Testing.
2. Systemic Screening: Pediatric patients must have hearing tests and metabolic screens.
3. Pharmacotherapy: Consider Vitamin A Palmitate (15,000 IU/day) for adults (Berson Study).
4. Monitor Complications: Treat CME with topical/oral Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs).
5. Surgical Intervention: Cataract surgery (careful with zonular laxity) or Luxturna if RPE65 positive.
6. Low Vision Rehabilitation: Prisms, magnifiers, and mobility training.

content.explanation: U: Ultrasound/Imaging (OCT/FAF), S: Systematic family history, H: Hearing test (audiometry), E: ERG (Full-field), R: Refraction/Review for syndromes.

sections.title: The Genetic Revolution: Luxturna (voretigene neparvovec-rzyl)
content: Mechanism: Adeno-associated virus (AAV2) vector delivering a functional RPE65 gene.
Eligibility: Confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutations and sufficient viable retinal cells.
Delivery: Subretinal injection via pars plana vitrectomy.
Significance: First FDA-approved gene therapy for an inherited disease.

sections.title: Surgical Complications in RP Patients
content: Zonular Weakness: High risk of phacodonesis or late IOL dislocation.
CME Flare-up: Post-operative inflammation can worsen macular edema.
Epiretinal Membranes: Increased incidence in RP cases.
Capsular Opacification: Accelerated PCO formation is common.

sections.title: Future Frontiers & Research
content: Optogenetics: Turning remaining retinal cells into photoreceptors.
CRISPR/Cas9: In-vivo gene editing for specific mutations (e.g., CEP290).
Stem Cell Therapy: RPE and photoreceptor replacement.
Artificial Vision: Advanced retinal implants and cortical stimulators.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Anaphylaxis is an acute, systemic IgE-mediated (or non-IgE-mediated) reaction involving mast cell and basophil activation. Pathophysiology involves the rapid release of mediators: Histamine, Tryptase, Prostaglandin D2, and Leukotrienes, leading to vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and bronchoconstriction.

sections.title: Emergency Treatment Algorithm
content: 1. Remove inciting agent immediately.
2. Administer IM Epinephrine (1mg/mL): 0.01 mg/kg (Max 0.5mg in adults) into mid-outer thigh.
3. Position patient supine with legs elevated.
4. High-flow Oxygen (10-15 L/min).
5. Volume expansion with Crystalloids (1-2L isotonic saline).
6. Adjuncts: Albuterol, H1-antagonists (Diphenhydramine 50mg), H2-antagonists (Famotidine), Corticosteroids (Methylprednisolone 125mg).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Do not wait for cutaneous signs (skin symptoms absent in 20% of anaphylaxis).
IM injection in the thigh is superior to SC or subcutaneous injection for rapid absorption.
Biphasic reactions occur in 1-20% of cases; keep patients observed for 4-6 hours.
Beta-blockers can render epinephrine ineffective; consider Glucagon (1-5mg IV) in such patients.
Serum tryptase levels (peak at 60-90 min post-onset) can confirm the diagnosis retrospectively.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Anaphylactic Shock: Ophthalmic Emergency Protocol ---
sections.content: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic Type I hypersensitivity reaction. In the ophthalmic setting, it is most commonly triggered by intravenous dyes (FFA/ICG), local anesthetics, or latex, requiring immediate recognition and IM Epinephrine administration.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Anaphylaxis is a rapidly developing, multi-systemic immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. It results from the sudden systemic release of mediators (histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes) from mast cells and basophils. In ophthalmology, it represents the most critical office-based emergency, often occurring within minutes of diagnostic dye injection or anesthetic block.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Type I Cascade
content: 1. Sensitization: Initial exposure leads to IgE production by B-cells.
2. Priming: IgE binds to FcεRI receptors on Mast cells and Basophils.
3. Re-exposure: Allergen cross-links IgE on cell surfaces.
4. Degranulation: Massive release of Histamine, Prostaglandin D2, and Leukotrienes.
5. Systemic Effect: Vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and smooth muscle contraction.

rows: Generalized urticaria, pruritus, flushing, angioedema (lips, tongue, uvula).
Hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmia, chest pain, cardiac arrest.
Anxiety, 'sense of impending doom', altered mental status, syncope.

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations
content: Severe conjunctival chemosis (often immediate).
Periorbital edema and erythema.
Profuse lacrimation and conjunctival injection.
Sudden vision blurring (due to corneal edema or hypotension).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Threats
content: Stridor or hoarseness (Laryngeal edema)
Silent chest on auscultation (Severe bronchospasm)
Systolic BP < 90 mmHg
Rapidly spreading urticaria after IV dye injection
Cyanosis or SpO2 < 92%

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup (Post-Stabilization)
content: 1. Serum Tryptase: Drawn 0.5–3 hours after onset (peak at 1hr).
2. Repeat Tryptase: At 24 hours to establish baseline.
3. Allergy Referral: For skin prick or IgE testing (after 4-6 weeks).
4. Review FFA/ICG logs for lot numbers and dosages.

rows: Bradycardia, pallor, no urticaria, rapid recovery when supine.
Normal BP/O2, tachypnea, carpopedal spasm, no angioedema.
Chest pain, ECG changes, elevated troponins.
No skin changes, history of triggers, slow onset.

sections.title: Management Step-by-Step
content: 1. STOP the offending agent (Disconnect FFA infusion immediately).
2. CALL for help / Activate Emergency Medical Services (EMS).
3. POSITION: Supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress predominates).
4. ADRENALINE (Epinephrine): 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1:1000) in the mid-outer thigh.
5. AIRWAY: High-flow Oxygen (15L/min via non-rebreather mask).
6. FLUIDS: Rapid IV bolus of Normal Saline (1-2 Liters).
7. ADJUNCTS: Antihistamines (H1/H2 blockers) and Corticosteroids.

content.explanation: A: Airway, D: Dye Stop, R: Recline/Raise legs, E: Epinephrine IM, N: Normal Saline, A: Antihistamines, L: Lungs (Oxygen/Albuterol), I: IV Access, N: Next dose of Epi if needed.

rows: Skin & subcutaneous tissues only (generalized erythema, urticaria).
Respiratory, cardiovascular, or GI involvement (dyspnea, stridor, nausea).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Ophthalmologist
content: IM Epinephrine is safer and easier than IV Epinephrine for non-coding patients; use the mid-thigh (Vastus Lateralis).
Patients on Beta-blockers may be resistant to Epinephrine; consider Glucagon (1-5mg IV over 5 mins).
Biphasic reactions occur in up to 20% of cases; observe patients for at least 4-12 hours post-event.
Always have a 'Crash Cart' in the FFA suite with up-to-date medications and a portable oxygen tank.
ICG contains Iodine; check for shellfish or iodine allergy before administration.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Consensus
sections.content: The 2020 World Allergy Organization (WAO) Anaphylaxis Guidance emphasizes that there are no absolute contraindications to Epinephrine in anaphylaxis. Recent studies in 'Ophthalmology' (AAO) suggest that pre-filled auto-injectors (EpiPens) should be accessible in every retina clinic due to their ease of use during high-stress FFA reactions.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (due to prolonged shock).
Myocardial Ischemia / Stress-induced Cardiomyopathy.
Biphasic Reaction (recurrence of symptoms without re-exposure).
Prognosis is excellent if Epinephrine is administered early.

Circumferential tear along ora serrata; usually from blunt trauma. Large peripheral break with rolled edge (Fig. 16.17D).
Vitreous gel remains attached to the posterior margin.
Variant of U-tear involving 90° or more of retinal circumference (Fig. 16.17E and F). Located in immediate post-oral retina or equator.
Vitreous gel remains attached to the anterior margin.

sections.title: Management Philosophy & Risk Management
content: Management remains imperfectly defined; approaches differ between subspecialists.
Trend: Less aggressive prophylactic treatment for asymptomatic/operculated breaks; focus on observation and education.
Patient Education: Instruct on symptoms of vitreous detachment and RD; provide written information; urge urgent review for new symptoms.
Prophylaxis Risks: Small risk of new break formation or epiretinal membrane formation. Severe complications are rare.

sections.title: Risk Factors for Progression to Detachment

branches: Miscellaneous: Fellow eye RD, Prior cataract surgery (vitreous loss), Myopia, Family history, Marfan/Stickler/Ehlers–Danlos
Symptoms: Acute PVD symptomatic breaks are higher risk than routine asymptomatic ones
Persistent Traction: U-tears (high) vs. Operculated/Round holes (low)
Shape: U-tears higher risk than round holes
Location: Superior breaks (gravity effect), Superotemporal (threatens macula), Equatorial (higher risk than oral/vitreous base)
Stability Signs: Pigmentation around break indicates chronicity
Lens Status: Aphakia (now rare) confers higher risk

rows: Observation safe. Review: 2-4 wks, 1-3 mos, 6-12 mos, then annually. Treat if bridging vessel is present.
Observation safe as per operculated tears unless other high-risk factors present.
Can sometimes be followed; surgery if RD present.
Case-by-case (e.g., treat large superotemporal; observe small inferior). Informed consent/regular review vital.
No prophylactic treatment; review every 1-2 years.
Consider prophylaxis for asymptomatic breaks (inc. atrophic) prior to cataract surgery, laser capsulotomy, or intravitreal injection.

sections.title: Critical Clinical Tip
content: TIP: A patient with a symptomatic retinal break associated with an acute PVD is at risk of RD and needs rapid treatment.

rows: Most cases; precise; less collateral damage; lower ERM risk.
Multiple contiguous tears; extensive lesions; hazy media; small pupils.
Slit lamp or BIO; indentation needed for very peripheral lesions.
Requires BIO visualization and indentation; may need conjunctival incision for post-equatorial access.
Freeze until whitening; single row of applications (Fig 16.19).

sections.title: Laser Retinopexy Protocol
content: Duration: 0.1 second
Spot Size: 200–300 μm (3-mirror) or 100–200 μm (wide-field)
Power: Starting at 200 mW (adjust for moderate blanching)
BIO Delivery: Adjust spot via condensing lens (usually 20 D)
Pattern: 2-3 rows of confluent burns
Caution: Identify landmarks to avoid macular damage

sections.title: Cryoretinopexy Procedure Steps
content: Step 1: Instrument Purge (10 sec @ -25 °C, repeat after 1 min)
Step 2: Set Treatment Temperature (typically -85 °C)
Step 3: Verification (check ice ball in sterile water; 5-mm ball in 10 sec)
Step 4: Indentation and Activation until visible whitening
Step 5: Thawing (2-3 seconds) before moving tip
Step 6: Maintain probe orientation; surround lesion with 1 row

sections.title: Post-Treatment Care & Follow-Up
content: Post-Cryo: Eye is usually padded; oral analgesia prescribed.
Activity: Avoid strenuous physical exertion for about 1 week until adhesion forms.
Review Schedule: Typically 1–2 weeks after treatment.
Visual Evidence: Pigmentation and chorioretinal atrophy indicate healing (Fig. 16.19).

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Posterior Vitreous Detachment & Retinal Breaks: The Clinical Compendium ---
sections.content: An exhaustive clinical guide covering the pathogenesis, symptoms, signs, and management of Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD) and the associated risks and treatments for retinal breaks.

sections.title: POSTERIOR VITREOUS DETACHMENT: Introduction & Pathogenesis
sections.content: PVD refers to separation of the cortical vitreous, along with the delineating posterior hyaloid membrane (PHM), from the neurosensory retina posterior to the vitreous base. PVD occurs due to vitreous gel liquefaction with age (synchysis) to form fluid-filled cavities (Fig. 16.15A) and subsequently condensation (syneresis), with access to the preretinal space allowed by a dehiscence in the cortical gel and/or PHM. Perifoveal 674. Posterior Vitreous Detachment. A B C Fig. 16.12 Retinoschisis. (A) Early changes (arrow); (B) inner and outer layer breaks; (C) large outer layer break. TIP Degenerative retinoschisis has a convex, smooth, thin and relatively immobile appearance and should be distinguished from a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, which is slightly opaque and has a corrugated appearance. A B C Fig. 16.13 (A) White with pressure; (B) white without pressure showing retinal tear (arrow) and adjacent pseudo-break (arrowheads); (C) strong attachment of condensed vitreous gel to an area of ‘white without pressure’. (Courtesy of NE Byer, from The Peripheral Retina in Profile, A Stereoscopic Atlas, Criterion Press, Torrance, CA 1982 – fig. A; S Chen – fig. B; CL Schepens, ME Hartnett and T Hirose, from Schepens’ Retinal Detachment and Allied Diseases, ButterworthHeinemann 2000 – fig. C.) CHAPTER Retinal Detachment 16 675. Fig. 16.14 Myopic choroidal atrophy. (Courtesy of S Chen.)

sections.title: Inducing Events & Triggers
content: Spontaneous event (most common)
Cataract surgery
Trauma
Uveitis
Panretinal photocoagulation

sections.title: The Progression of PVD
content: Step 1: Perifoveal hyaloid detachment
Step 2: Foveal separation
Step 3: Detachment from the posterior retina as far as the equator (attachment initially retained at optic disc)
Step 4: Complete detachment of cortical vitreous as far anteriorly as the vitreous base takes place (Fig. 16.15B)
Note: This process can occur in stages over many months. Except for the vitreous base, physiological attachments are disengaged in a normal PVD.

sections.title: Clinical Features: Symptoms (Myodesopsia & Photopsia)
content: Symptoms are usually, though not invariably, present.

Flashing lights (photopsia): Often described as a lightning-like arc induced by eye or head movement; more noticeable in dim illumination. Almost always seen in the temporal periphery. Mechanism: Traction on optic disc and sites of vitreoretinal adhesion/tears.
Floaters (myodesopsia): Mobile vitreous opacities evident against bright pale backgrounds. Described as spots, cobwebs, or flies (muscae volitantes). Common in myopes without PVD.
Weiss ring (Fig. 16.15C and D): Detached former attachment to the optic disc margin; seen as a circle or large solitary lesion. Presence ≠ total PVD; absence ≠ no PVD.
Vitreous blood floaters: Can appear as floaters.
Blurred vision: Diffuse haze due to dispersed hemorrhage (reduced VA). Bleeding arises from torn vessels or retinal breaks. Also caused by visually significant PHM or floaters in the visual axis.

sections.title: Clinical Features: Objective Signs
content: Detached PHM: Seen on slit lamp as a crumpled translucent membrane in mid-vitreous with an optically clear cavity behind it (Fig. 16.16A).
Hemorrhage: Red blood cells in anterior vitreous, focal intragel collections, or preretinal crescent shapes. Prompt search for retinal break (40–90% risk). Larger amounts suggest posterior breaks.
Pigment granules (Shafer sign / 'tobacco dust'): Larger, darker, less reflective than RBCs (Fig. 16.21). Sensitivity for retinal break is up to 95%. Indicates RPE communication with vitreous.
Vitreous cells: If numerous, may signify a break.
Retinal breaks: Detailed below.

content.explanation: B-scan ultrasound (Fig. 16.16B) demonstrates extent of PVD. OCT (Fig. 16.16C) shows separation of posterior vitreous face and retina. TIP: A retinal break is usually present if pigment granules ('tobacco dust') are seen.

sections.title: URGENT Management & Examination
content: Examine acute symptoms within 24–48 hours.
Greater urgency for: Myopia, history of RD, Stickler syndrome, pseudophakia, visual field defects, reduced vision, prominent floaters.
Check for predisposing VH conditions (e.g., Diabetes Mellitus).
Single small floater + no photopsia: Risk is insignificantly higher than asymptomatic eye; assessment may not be urgent.

sections.title: Examination & Review Protocol
content: Anterior vitreous: Assess for blood and pigment.
Retinal Exam: 360° visualization of ora serrata via binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy (BIO) or contact lens scleral indentation.
Fellow Eye: Always examine. If ≥10 vitreous cells (1mm field) are present, fellow eye break risk is >30%.
Routine Review: Not necessary if no suspicious findings (blood) or risk factors.
High Risk Review: Interval of 1–6 weeks depending on characteristics. Some recommend 6–12 months.
Multiple floaters/hazy vision: Mandatory review due to higher break risk.
Discharge Instructions: Urgent re-attendance for new symptoms; provide written info. Floatars usually resolve, though vitrectomy is rarely needed.

Obscured fundus (Blood): Weekly review. Diffuse fundus-obscuring VH (without diabetes) = 60-90% break risk and 40% RD risk. Exclude RAPD; perform regular B-scans. Low threshold for vitrectomy if RD history in fellow eye.

sections.title: RETINAL BREAKS: Introduction
sections.content: Retinal breaks develop in most cases as a result of traction at sites of vitreoretinal adhesion and occur in up to about 1 in 5 eyes with symptomatic PVD. In the presence of a break, retrohyaloid fluid has access to the subretinal space. Asymptomatic retinal breaks of some sort are present in about 8% of the general population. CHAPTER Retinal Detachment 16 677. Fig. 16.16 Posterior vitreous detachment. (A) Biomicroscopy showing detached and collapsed gel; (B) ultrasound B-scan; (C) OCT of posterior pole.

rows: Usually at/soon after symptoms; 5% delayed by several weeks.
Usually upper retina; Temporal > Nasal. Macular breaks (rare) are usually round/myopic.
Flap apex pulled anteriorly by vitreous, base attached to retina (Fig. 16.17A).
Flap completely torn away; leaves round/oval break. Operculum suspended in vitreous (Fig. 16.17B).
Round/oval, smaller, lower RD risk. Commonly found in lattice degeneration or young female myopes.
Circumferential tear along ora serrata; usually blunt trauma. Vitreous remains attached to posterior margin (Fig. 16.17D).
Variant of U-tear involving ≥90° of circumference. Vitreous attached to anterior margin (Fig. 16.17E/F).

sections.title: Risk Factors for Progression to Detachment
content: History: RD in fellow eye, prior cataract surgery (especially with vitreous loss), myopia, family history, systemic syndromes (Marfan, Stickler, Ehlers–Danlos).
Symptoms: Symptomatic breaks (acute PVD) > Asymptomatic breaks.
Size & Shape: Larger breaks and U-tears carry higher risk than round holes.
Traction: Persistent traction (U-tears) > Detached traction (Operculated). Complete PVD (no residual attachment) is favorable.
Location: Superior breaks (gravity effect) and Equatorial breaks (outside vitreous base) are higher risk. Superotemporal tears threaten the macula early.
Pigmentation: Indicates chronicity and stability (protective).
Aphakia: Confers higher risk (though now rare).
Special Case: Symptomatic U-tears lead to RD in up to 90% of cases (reduced to 5% with treatment).

rows: Observation. Review: 2–4 wks, 1–3 mos, 6–12 mos, then annually. Treat if bridging vessel present.
5% risk of RD. Observation is generally safe unless high-risk factors exist.
Follow without treatment OR surgery if RD is present.
10% become symptomatic (2-3 yrs). Case-by-case (e.g., treat large superotemporal, observe small inferior).
No prophylactic treatment; review every 1–2 years.
Consider for asymptomatic/atrophic holes before cataract surgery, laser capsulotomy, or IVI.

sections.title: Treatment Technique: Laser Retinopexy
content: Method: Slit lamp or BIO delivery. Slit lamp is more precise, less collateral damage.
Settings: 0.1s duration, 200–300μm (3-mirror) or 100–200μm (wide-field).
Power: Start at 200 mW, adjust for moderate blanching.
Application: Surround lesion with 2–3 rows of confluent burns (Fig. 16.18).
Caution: Identify landmarks to avoid macular damage.

sections.title: Treatment Technique: Cryoretinopexy
content: Indications: Multiple contiguous tears, hazy media, small pupils, or very peripheral lesions.
Preparation: Purge probe (10s @ -25°C). Set to -85°C. Check for 5mm ice ball in sterile water.
Procedure: Indent under BIO visualization until retinal whitening. Do not remove until thawing (2–3s).
Application: Surround with single row (1–2 applications for a tear).
Post-Op: Eye padding and oral analgesia often prescribed.

sections.title: Post-Treatment Care & Figures
sections.content: After treatment the patient should avoid strenuous physical exertion for about a week until an adequate adhesion has formed (Fig. 16.19). Review should usually take place after 1–2 weeks. Fig. 16.15 Vitreous degenerative changes. (A) Synchysis and syneresis; (B) complete posterior vitreous detachment; (C) Weiss ring on retroillumination; (D) Weiss ring on slit lamp biomicroscopy. Fig. 16.18 Laser retinopexy after treatment. (A) U-tear; (B) retinal hole; (C) recent penetrating injury. Fig. 16.19 Pigmentation and chorioretinal atrophy following prophylactic cryotherapy to several retinal breaks. TIP A patient with a symptomatic retinal break associated with an acute PVD is at risk of RD and needs rapid treatment.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: DME is defined as retinal thickening or hard exudate accumulation within 1 disc diameter of the center of the macula. It results from the breakdown of the inner Blood-Retinal Barrier (BRB), leading to the leakage of fluid and plasma constituents into the intraretinal layers, specifically the Outer Plexiform Layer (Henle's layer) and Inner Nuclear Layer.

branches: VEGF Pathway: Upregulation due to hypoxia
Angiopoietin-2: Competes with Ang-1 for Tie2 receptor
Leukostasis: Neutrophil adhesion to capillary endothelium
Oxidative Stress: PKC pathway & Polyol pathway activation
Pericyte Loss: Leading to microaneurysm formation

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Microaneurysms (MAs): Earliest sign, focal leakage points.
Hard Exudates (HE): Lipid deposits, often in circinate patterns.
Retinal Edema: Thickening/clouding of the macula.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Fluid pockets in a petaloid pattern.
Ischemic Maculopathy: Enlarged Foveal Avascular Zone (FAZ).
Vitreomacular Interface issues: Epiretinal membranes (ERM).

rows: Hard Exudates within 500µm of center + thickening
Thickening ≥ 1 disc area within 1 DD of center

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: BCVA & Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (90D lens) for baseline.
Step 2: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) to measure CST and identify IRF/SRF.
Step 3: Fluorescein Angiography (FA) to differentiate Focal vs. Diffuse leakage.
Step 4: OCT-Angiography (OCT-A) to assess FAZ and capillary non-perfusion.
Step 5: Fundus Photography for longitudinal tracking of hard exudates.

rows: Post-cataract surgery, classic petaloid leakage on FA.
Widespread flame hemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins.
White dots, vitreous cells, younger demographic.
Visible VMT or ERM on OCT causing mechanical pull.

sections.title: Medical Management: The Systemic 'Big Three'
content: Glycemic Control: Target HbA1c < 7.0% (DCCT/UKPDS).
Blood Pressure Control: Target < 130/80 mmHg.
Lipid Management: Statins to reduce hard exudate accumulation (FIELD study).
Renal Function: Monitoring GFR and albuminuria.

rows: 2mg (VIVID/VISTA) - VEGF Trap, binds VEGF-A, B, PlGF

sections.title: Corticosteroid Implants
content: Ozurdex (Dexamethasone 0.7mg): 3-6 month duration, biodegradable.
Iluvien (Fluocinolone 0.19mg): 36 month duration, non-biodegradable.
Indications: Chronic DME, pseudophakic patients, anti-VEGF non-responders.
Side Effects: Cataract progression (near 100%), IOP elevation (approx 30%).

sections.title: Laser & Surgery
content: Focal Laser: Target MAs 50-100µm size, 0.1s duration, 'light gray' burn.
Grid Laser: Applied to areas of diffuse thickening.
Subthreshold Micropulse: Minimizes collateral RPE damage.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): Reserved for tractional DME (VMT/ERM) or refractory cases.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Endophthalmitis: Post-injection pain, redness, hypopyon.
IOP Spike: Post-steroid injection glaucoma.
Retinal Detachment: Floaters/flashes post-injection or surgery.
Ischemic Maculopathy: BCVA < 20/200 with normal CST on OCT.
Pregnancy: Caution with anti-VEGF (potential systemic absorption).

content.explanation: If vision is 20/50 or worse, Aflibercept was superior to Bevacizumab/Ranibizumab at 1 year. If 20/40 or better, all drugs performed similarly.

rows: Focal laser reduced risk of moderate vision loss by 50%.
Ranibizumab significantly improved VA vs Sham.
Observation is viable for DME with 20/25 or better vision.
Aflibercept can improve DR severity scale (DRSS) score.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for 'Disorganization of Retinal Inner Layers' (DRIL) on OCT as a prognostic marker.
DME can be 'Tractional' or 'Non-tractional'—vitrectomy only helps the former.
Hard exudates at the fovea often leave permanent scarring/subfoveal fibrosis.
NSAID drops (e.g., Nepafenac) may be an adjunct in mild, non-CI DME.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Future Trends
sections.content: Port Delivery Systems (PDS) for continuous ranibizumab release and Gene Therapy (RGX-314) aiming for 'one-and-done' treatment are currently in advanced clinical trials. Dual inhibition of Ang-2 and VEGF-A (Faricimab) represents the new standard for extending treatment intervals up to Q16 weeks.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Diabetic Macular Edema (DME): The Master Clinician's Guide ---
sections.content: DME is the leading cause of vision loss in the working-age population. This comprehensive guide covers the intricate pathophysiology, evolving classification systems, and the evidence-based management protocols established by landmark clinical trials.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Diabetic Macular Edema (DME) is defined as the accumulation of fluid in the intraretinal layers (outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers) and/or subretinal space within the macular region. It results from a breakdown of the inner and outer blood-retinal barriers (BRB), primarily triggered by chronic hyperglycemia-induced microvascular damage. It can occur at any stage of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR).

sections.title: ETDRS Criteria: Clinically Significant Macular Edema (CSME)

rows: Thickening at or within 500 µm of the center of the fovea.
HE at or within 500 µm with adjacent retinal thickening.
Retinal thickening ≥ 1 disc area in size, any part of which is within 1 disc diameter of the foveal center.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Painless, gradual blurriness of central vision.
Metamorphopsia (distorted lines).
Micropsia / Macropsia.
Reduced contrast sensitivity.
Central or paracentral scotoma.
Hard exudates in a circinate pattern.
Microaneurysms (MA) and dot-blot hemorrhages.

rows: Post-cataract surgery; classic petaloid leakage on FFA.
Right-angle vessels; temporal foveal atrophy; no lipid.
History of head/neck radiation; sluggish capillary refill.

sections.title: Evidence-Based Management (DRCR.net Protocols)
content: Step 1: Systemic Optimization (HbA1c < 7.0%, Blood Pressure < 130/80, Lipids).
Step 2: Center-Involved (CI-DME) with VA 20/25 or better: Observation (Protocol V).
Step 3: CI-DME with VA 20/30 or worse: First-line Anti-VEGF (Protocol T).
Step 4: Non-Center Involved DME: Focal/Grid Laser (ETDRS Guidelines).
Step 5: Refractory to Anti-VEGF: Switch agents or add Intravitreal Steroids (Ozurdex/Iluvien).
Step 6: VMT-associated DME: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV).

rows: VEGF-Trap; superior in VA < 20/50 baseline (Protocol T).
Fab fragment; highly effective in all VA ranges.
Non-erodible implant; lasts up to 36 months.

sections.title: Red Flags: Steroid Precautions
content: Pre-existing Glaucoma (High risk of IOP spike).
Advanced Cup-to-Disc ratio (> 0.8).
Phakic Status (Steroids accelerate cataract formation).
History of Herpetic Keratitis/Endophthalmitis.
Active Ocular Infection.

content.explanation: A: A1c (Poor glycemic control); B: Blood Pressure (Hypertension); C: Cholesterol (Dyslipidemia); D: Duration (Years since diagnosis).

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Trials Summary
content: ETDRS: Focal/Grid laser reduces risk of moderate vision loss by 50%.
Protocol T: Aflibercept performed better than Bevacizumab/Ranibizumab in patients with VA 20/50 or worse at 1 year.
Protocol I: Anti-VEGF + prompt or deferred laser is superior to laser alone.
Protocol V: Patients with 20/25 vision can be observed safely if monitored closely.
PANORAMA: Aflibercept can improve DR severity scales and prevent DME.
YOSEMITE/RHINE: Faricimab (Ang-2/VEGF) shows non-inferiority with potential for Q16 dosing.

sections.title: Surgical Technique: PPV for DME
content: 1. Core Vitrectomy with posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) induction.
2. Removal of the Internal Limiting Membrane (ILM) using ICG or Brilliant Blue G.
3. Release of any tangential traction or epiretinal membranes.
4. Consideration of steroid injection or endolaser if needed.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & High-Yield Facts
content: DRIL (Disorganization of Retinal Inner Layers) is a strong biomarker for poor visual prognosis.
Hard exudates in the fovea can lead to permanent photoreceptor loss and subfoveal fibrosis.
Anemia and Renal Disease (high Creatinine) are strong systemic drivers of DME severity.
In pregnancy, DME may worsen significantly but often regresses postpartum.

sections.title: Epidemiology & Histology
content: Choroidal melanomas account for 65% of all uveal melanomas.
Presentation: Usually at about 50–60y of age.
Histological Types: Spindle cells (types A and B), epithelioid cells, or a mixture (commonest type).
Necrosis: May prevent cell typing in 5% of cases.

branches: ‘Ball of light’ slowly moving across vision
Occasional: Vitreous haemorrhage, iIOp, cataract, uveitis

sections.title: Box 15.2: Suspicious Features
content: Symptomatic
Juxtapapillary location
SRF/retinal detachment
Lipofuscin on the surface
Large size (e.g. >2mm thickness)
Significant growth

sections.title: Diagnostic Dilemma Note
sections.content: NB: The key diagnostic dilemma is to distinguish a malignant melanoma from a benign naevus (see E Choroidal naevus, p. 706). Suspicious features are listed in Box 15.2.

sections.title: Investigations
content: US (Ultrasound): Solid, acoustically hollow, low internal reflectivity, with choroidal excavation.
CT and MRI: May detect extraglobar extension; cannot reliably differentiate between types of tumour.
Biopsy: Diagnostic incisional biopsy or FNa may be performed in selected cases.
Prognostic Biopsy: Using genetic analysis; may be offered to patients undergoing radiotherapy. (Controversial: confers no survival advantage, small risk of extraocular seeding).
Systemic Assessment: FBC, LFTs, liver/abdominal US (or CT, MRI).
Metastasis Status: At presentation, most (98%) do not have detectable metastatic disease.

sections.title: Treatment: Observation & Radiotherapy
content: Specialist advice should be sought for all options.
Observation: For small asymptomatic lesions without suspicious features. Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study (COMS) showed growth in only 31% of small melanomas by 5y.
Radiotherapy - Plaques: 3mm larger in diameter than lesion; deliver 80–100Gy to tumour apex.
Radiotherapy - Proton Beam: Usually 50–70Gy in 4–5 fractions.
Stereotactic Radiosurgery: Used in selected patients (e.g., where GA is contraindicated).
Plaque vs Proton: Plaque has fewer local side effects; as effective as enucleation for medium-sized melanomas (COMS).
Radiotherapy Side Effects: Dry eyes, radiation retinopathy (treatable with anti-VEGF), cataracts, and NVG.

sections.title: Surgical & Other Treatment Modalities
content: Local Resection: For smaller anterior tumours; preserves vision/cosmesis. Risks: Vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment, cataract. Requires hypotensive anaesthesia (unsuitable for CV comorbidities). Adjuvant brachytherapy if margins contaminated.
Enucleation: For large tumours (>15mm diameter, 10mm thickness), optic nerve involvement, or painful blind eyes. No benefit for pre-enucleation radiotherapy.
Orbital Exenteration: For extrascleral/orbital extension or recurrence after enucleation.
PDT (Photodynamic Therapy): Can be used for small tumours.
Transpupillary Thermotherapy (TTT): Largely abandoned as 1° treatment due to high local recurrence; still used as an adjunct.

content.explanation: Older patient, large tumour size, extrascleral extension, epithelioid cell type, high mitotic count, and specific genetic mutations.

sections.title: Genetic Stratification
content: Most important genetic predictors of mortality: Chr 3 loss (monosomy 3) and duplication (partial or total) of Chr 8q.
Microarray Analysis: Stratifies metastatic risk based on the pattern of expression of multiple genes.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: CHOROIDAL TUMOURS: A Clinical Masterclass ---
sections.content: An exhaustive guide to the diagnosis, differential diagnosis, investigation, and multi-modal treatment of choroidal melanoma and simulating lesions. This poster details clinical signs, histopathological features, and modern genetic prognostic indicators.

sections.title: Diagnosis and Initial Presentation
content: Symptoms are often absent, with a tumour detected by chance on routine fundus examination.
A range of visual disturbance can occur depending on tumour characteristics.
Signs: A solitary elevated subretinal grey-brown (Fig. 20.26A) or rarely amelanotic (Fig. 20.26B) dome-shaped mass.
Diffuse infiltration is uncommon.
About 60% are located within 3 mm of the optic disc (Fig. 20.26C) or fovea.
Clumps of overlying orange pigment are common (Fig. 20.26D).

sections.title: Advanced Clinical Signs
content: Breakthrough: If the tumour breaks through Bruch membrane it acquires a ‘collar stud’ appearance (see Fig. 20.25C and Fig. 20.28C).
Associated haemorrhage and subretinal fluid (Fig. 20.26E) are common.
Exudative retinal detachment (Fig. 20.26F) may result from subretinal fluid, which can mask the underlying lesion.
Other signs: Sentinel vessels (Fig. 20.27), choroidal folds, inflammation, rubeosis iridis, secondary glaucoma and cataract.

rows: Usually exhibits numerous surface drusen, without serous retinal detachment and little if any orange pigment.
Deeply pigmented and usually located at the optic disc.
Flat, often grey-black; has a well-defined margin with lacunae.
In subretinal or suprachoroidal space (e.g., from choroidal neovascularization or retinal artery macroaneurysm).
Smooth surface, light brown colour, indistinct margins, extensive retinal detachment; often a past history of malignancy.
Typically posterior, pink, dome-shaped with a smooth surface.
Often associated with exudative retinal detachment.
Presents with large elevated lesion; unlike melanoma, pain is a common feature.
Eccentrically located (temporal pre-equatorial), associated with exudate and fresh haemorrhage (rare in melanoma).
Small, smooth, brown, dome-shaped lesion that disappears with pressure on the eye.
Tightly arranged fusiform cells with indistinct cell membranes and slender or plump oval nuclei.
Large pleomorphic cells with distinct cell membranes, large vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations (Imaging)
content: Examination: Sufficient for diagnosis in the majority of cases.

Fluorescein Angiography (FA): Limited diagnostic value; no pathognomonic pattern. Shows intrinsic ‘dual’ circulation (Fig. 20.28A), mottled fluorescence (arteriovenous phase), late diffuse leakage and staining.

Ultrasound: Measures dimensions and detects tumours through opaque media/exudative detachment. Shows internal homogeneity, low to medium reflectivity, choroidal excavation (Fig. 20.28B), and orbital shadowing.
Acoustic Hollowing: A basal acoustically quiet zone due to greater tissue homogeneity in this region.
Collar Stud (US): Configuration (Fig. 20.28C) is almost pathognomonic when present.
FAF: Intense diffuse or confluent hyperautofluorescence is a useful indicator of melanoma.
OCT: Measures dimensions and demonstrates subretinal fluid/secondary retinal changes overlying the lesion.
ICGA: Usually shows hypofluorescence throughout; provides more information than FA about tumour extent due to lower RPE interference.
MRI: Useful for extraocular extension (Fig. 20.28D) and differential diagnosis.

sections.title: Biopsy and Advanced Pathology
content: Biopsy: Used when diagnosis is not established by non-invasive methods. Performed via fine needle or 25-gauge vitrectomy system (larger sample).
Immunocytochemistry (PAX8): Distinguishes tumours. Melanoma and melanocytoma are PAX8-negative; pigmented adenocarcinomas are PAX8-positive.

content.explanation: Loss of one copy of chromosome 3 (M3) and changes in chromosome 8 (i8q) strongly correlate with poor outcome, especially when occurring together. Metastasis occurs almost exclusively with certain genetic profiles.

sections.title: Prognostic Resources
content: The Liverpool Uveal Melanoma Prognosticator is an online resource combining anatomic, genetic, and histopathological data to determine prognosis for life.
Reduced surveillance can be adopted for patients with a low-risk genetic profile.

sections.title: Systemic Investigation Protocol
content: Step 1: Detect metastatic spread (primary focus on liver).
Step 2: Liver function testing and ultrasonography (mainstays).
Step 3: Chest radiography (rarely shows lung secondaries without liver disease).
Step 4: Consider whole-body PET/CT (Greater sensitivity for extrahepatic lesions, but high ionizing radiation dose).

sections.title: Treatment Principles
content: Objective: Avoid a painful/unsightly eye while conserving useful vision.
Survival: Influence of ocular treatment on survival is not yet defined, though smaller earlier tumours may have lower risk of metastasis.
Management: Individualized based on tumour characteristics (apical height, basal diameter) and patient factors (health, age, preferences, fellow eye).

rows: Tumours < 20mm basal diameter and < 10mm thick. Plaque sutured to sclera for several days. Regression starts 1–2 months post-treatment.
Cataract, papillopathy, disc neovascularization, radiation retinopathy, 'toxic tumour syndrome'.
Used for large or posterior tumours unsuitable for brachytherapy. Targeting aided by tantalum markers. Survival comparable to brachytherapy.
Lashes loss, eyelid depigmentation, keratitis, and intraocular complications similar to brachytherapy.
Multiple collimated beams (concurrent or sequential) delivering high dose only to the tumour.
Effective, but may have a comparatively high complication rate.

sections.title: Laser and Surgical Therapies
content: Transpupillary thermotherapy (TTT): Uses infrared laser for hyperthermia (not coagulation). For small tumours when radiotherapy is inappropriate or for vision-threatening exudation. Tumour disappears to leave bare sclera.
TTT Complications: Retinal traction, tears, rhegmatogenous detachment, vascular occlusion, neovascularization. Local recurrence common in thick, amelanotic, or disc-margin tumours.
Trans-scleral choroidectomy: Technically difficult. For tumours > 16mm in diameter too thick for radiotherapy. Complications: Detachment, hypotony, wound dehiscence, recurrence.
Light-activated AU-011: Novel treatment for small melanomas (2–3.4 mm). Nano-particles from HPV + infrared dye injected into vitreous; activated by infrared light to cause necrosis.

sections.title: Enucleation: Removal of the Eye
content: Large tumour size
Optic disc invasion
Extensive involvement of ciliary body or angle
Irreversible loss of useful vision
Poor motivation to keep the eye
Critical: Must perform ophthalmoscopy after surgical draping to ensure correct eye is removed.

sections.title: Metastatic Disease Management
content: No standard treatment for metastatic disease exists.
Tebentafusc: Immunotherapy drug that can modestly increase survival in some patients.
Note: Cutaneous melanoma checkpoint inhibitors are NOT effective against uveal melanoma.
Systemic chemotherapy has NOT been shown to benefit cases without evidence of metastatic spread.
