sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Brown Syndrome is a restrictive ocular motility disorder where the eyeball is mechanically prevented from moving upward when it is turned toward the nose (adduction). It is primarily caused by an abnormality of the Superior Oblique (SO) tendon-trochlea complex, preventing the smooth passage of the tendon through the trochlear pulley.

branches: Acquired: Iatrogenic (Following SO tuck or scleral buckling)

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Deficient elevation in adduction (Primary Sign).
Normal or near-normal elevation in abduction.
Down-shoot of the eye in adduction.
V-pattern exotropia (divergence in up-gaze).
Compensatory head posture (Chin-up and contralateral head tilt).
Positive 'click' or 'snap' felt by the patient in intermittent cases.
Widening of the palpebral fissure on adduction.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Brown vs. IO Palsy
Forced Duction Test (FDT) Protocol
content: Step 1: Instill topical proparacaine or perform under general anesthesia.
Step 2: Grasp the globe at the limbus (usually 6 o'clock and 12 o'clock).
Step 3: Attempt to move the globe into elevation while in the adducted position.
Step 4: Assess for mechanical resistance. In Brown, there is a hard stop.
Step 5: Compare resistance in abduction (should be free).

sections.title: Wright's Grading System
content: Mild: Restricted elevation in adduction; no hypotropia or downshoot in primary position.
Moderate: Restricted elevation in adduction + downshoot in adduction; no hypotropia in primary.
Severe: Marked restriction in elevation in adduction + marked downshoot + hypotropia in primary position.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Hess Chart/Lees Screen: Shows constricted field of elevation in adduction.
High-Resolution MRI (Orbits): To visualize SO tendon thickening or trochlear inflammation.
Blood Work: ESR, CRP, RF, and Anti-CCP if inflammatory etiology is suspected.
Prism Cover Test: In 9 cardinal positions of gaze.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Diagnosis: Confirm mechanical restriction via FDT.
Conservative: Observation if no primary position deviation or abnormal head posture.
Medical: Local corticosteroid injection to the trochlear area (for acquired inflammatory cases).
Medical: Systemic NSAIDs for painful 'clicking' cases.
Surgery: Indicated for significant hypotropia in primary position or severe head tilt.
Post-Op: Immediate aggressive duction exercises to prevent adhesion.

rows: Risk of creating SO palsy; unpredictable.
Maintains tendon direction; reduces SO palsy risk; may extrude or cause granuloma.
Adjustable but can lead to scarring/adhesion.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Considerations
content: Rapid onset of painful motility restriction (Suspect Orbital Myositis).
New onset head tilt in adults (Rule out underlying systemic disease).
Associated Proptosis or Vision Loss (Suspect Neoplasm/Apex Syndrome).
Failure of FDT to show restriction (Re-evaluate for IO Palsy or CN III palsy).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Prep
content: Brown syndrome is 'elevation deficiency in adduction' - remember the SO tendon is too short to allow the eye to go up and in.
The 'True' Brown syndrome is ALWAYS restrictive on FDT.
Simulated Brown Syndrome: Can occur after a scleral buckle or orbital roof fracture.
Surgical overcorrection is common; patients may end up with a Superior Oblique Palsy.

content.explanation: B: Below (Hypotropia in adduction), R: Restrictive FDT, O: Oblique (SO) tendon issue, W: Widening of fissure on adduction, N: Normal elevation in abduction.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Landmark Insights
sections.content: Recent studies using high-resolution dynamic MRI have shown that some cases of 'congenital' Brown are actually associated with SO tendon hypoplasia or abnormal pulleys. Additionally, the use of non-absorbable 'Chicken-beak' silicone expanders (Wright's technique) remains the gold standard for reducing the high rate of iatrogenic SO palsy seen with simple tenotomy.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Mastering Brown Syndrome: The Superior Oblique Tendon Restriction ---
sections.content: Brown syndrome is a restrictive motility disorder characterized by the inability to elevate the eye in adduction. This comprehensive guide covers the mechanical pathophysiology of the trochlear-tendon complex, diagnostic pearls, and the surgical nuances of tendon lengthening.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Brown syndrome (Superior Oblique Tendon Sheath Syndrome) is a mechanical restriction of the superior oblique (SO) tendon's movement through the trochlea. Pathophysiology involves a short or inelastic SO tendon, or an inflammatory thickening (nodule) that prevents the tendon from sliding through the pulley mechanism when the eye attempts to elevate in an adducted position.

sections.title: Clinical Hallmarks: The Diagnostic Triad
content: Severe limitation of elevation in ADDUCTION.
Minimal or no limitation of elevation in ABDUCTION.
Minimal or no Superior Oblique Overaction (SOOA) — helps distinguish from IO Palsy.
Positive Forced Duction Test (FDT) on attempt to elevate the eye in adduction.
V-pattern strabismus (divergence in upgaze).
Downshoot in adduction (pseudo-overaction of the SO).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Brown vs. IO Palsy

rows: Limited elevation in adduction; No downshoot; Ortho in primary.
Limited elevation in adduction; Downshoot in adduction; Ortho in primary.
Severe limitation in adduction; Marked downshoot; Hypotropia in primary.

sections.title: The Forced Duction Test (FDT) Protocol
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic (proparacaine) or perform under general anesthesia.
Step 2: Grasp the limbus at 3 and 9 o'clock with toothed forceps.
Step 3: Move the globe into an adducted position.
Step 4: Attempt to rotate the globe upward (elevation).
Step 5: Feel for mechanical resistance (positive result if eye cannot be elevated).

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Observation for asymptomatic patients with good binocular vision/no head tilt.
Step 2: Treat underlying inflammation (Steroids/NSAIDS) for acquired/inflammatory cases.
Step 3: Steroid injection (Triamcinolone 40mg) near the trochlea for 'Click Syndrome'.
Step 4: Surgical Intervention if there is hypotropia in primary position or significant abnormal head tilt.
Step 5: Post-operative monitoring for Inferior Oblique Overaction (consecutive palsy).

sections.title: Surgical Techniques & Options
content: SO Tenotomy or Tenectomy: Simple but high risk of SO palsy.
SO Tendon Lengthening: Using a silicone spacer (Wright's technique).
SO Tendon Suture Spacers (Non-absorbable): Graduated lengthening.
Split-Tendon Lengthening: Z-plasty of the tendon.
Superior Oblique Recession: Less effective due to anatomical constraints.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Acquired Brown
content: Sudden onset in adulthood
Pain upon eye movement or palpation of the trochlea
History of Rheumatoid Arthritis or Autoimmune disease
Recent orbital trauma or sinus surgery
Intermittent 'locking' and 'unlocking' with an audible click

content.explanation: B: Below (Hypotropia in primary if severe); R: Restriction on FDT; O: Outward (V-pattern divergence); W: Worse in adduction; N: No SO overaction.

sections.title: Canine Tooth Syndrome
sections.content: A specific subset of traumatic Brown syndrome caused by penetrating injury to the trochlea (classically a dog bite to the superior medial orbit). It results in a combined Brown syndrome and Superior Oblique palsy due to damage to both the trochlea and the nerve/muscle fibers.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Acquired Brown syndrome is more likely to resolve spontaneously than congenital.
The 'Click' in intermittent Brown syndrome represents the nodule snapping through the trochlea.
A compensatory chin-up and contralateral head tilt are common to maintain binocularity.
In surgical spacers, the standard length of silicone used is 6mm to 7mm.
Always check for IO palsy in the DDx using the Parks 3-step test (though 3-step is for paretic, not restrictive).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
content: The Wright Silicone Spacer Study: Established the use of medical-grade silicone for controlled tendon lengthening to prevent consecutive SO palsy.
MRI Studies: Demonstrated that in some 'True' Brown cases, the SO muscle belly is actually hypoplastic.
Bupivacaine Injection: Emerging research into chemodenervation/activation, though not yet standard of care.
Botulinum Toxin: Limited utility in Brown, but occasionally used in the SO for acute inflammatory phases.

sections.title: Complications of Surgery
content: Consecutive Superior Oblique Palsy (Most common)
Extrusion of the silicone spacer (Foreign body reaction)
Persistence of restriction (Under-correction)
Fat Adherence Syndrome
Post-operative scarring/Adhesions

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging Workup
content: Thin-cut MRI of the Orbits (Coronal & Sagittal views).
Focus on the trochlea and SO tendon complex.
Look for: Tendon thickening, enhancement (inflammatory), or trochlear masses.
Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM): Can sometimes visualize the anterior tendon dynamics.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Esotropia (ET) is a form of strabismus where the visual axes intersect in front of the object of regard. It is categorized by onset (congenital vs. acquired), frequency (constant vs. intermittent), and mechanism (accommodative vs. non-accommodative). Precise diagnosis is critical as it may be the presenting sign of life-threatening pathology such as retinoblastoma or intracranial tumors.

sections.title: Infantile Esotropia Syndrome (IES)
content: Onset: Within the first 6 months of life.
Angle: Usually large (>30 Prism Diopters) and stable.
Refraction: Usually normal for age (approx +1.50D).
Cross-fixation: Patient looks left with right eye and right with left eye.
Latent Nystagmus: Jerk nystagmus appearing when one eye is covered.
Dissociated Vertical Deviation (DVD): Upward drift of the non-fixing eye (found in 50-90%).
Inferior Oblique Overaction (IOOA): Frequent late finding.

rows: ET greater at near than distance
Significant ET at both, worse at near
Residual ET remains after full correction

sections.title: Ocular Examination Protocol
content: Step 1: History (Onset, frequency, family history).
Step 2: Visual Acuity (Fix and Follow, CSM, or Snellen/LEA).
Step 3: Cover/Uncover and Alternate Cover Test (Prism neutralization).
Step 4: Ocular Motility (Versions/Ductions, look for IOOA or A/V patterns).
Step 5: Cycloplegic Refraction (1% Atropine or 1% Cyclopentolate mandatory).
Step 6: Dilated Fundus Exam (Rule out sensory causes like Retinoblastoma).

sections.title: Sensory Esotropia Red Flags
content: Leukocoria (White pupillary reflex)
Optic Atrophy or Hypoplasia
Macular Scars (e.g., Toxoplasmosis)
Retinoblastoma (Must exclude in ALL new cases)
Dense Cataract

rows: Prominent epicanthal folds; symmetrical Hirschberg reflex.
Limited abduction, globe retraction/narrowing of palpebral fissure on adduction.
Recent onset, limited abduction, diplopia (if old enough), head turn.
Large angle ET with limited abduction and jerk nystagmus.

content.explanation: AC/A = (Δ1 - Δ2) / D. Where Δ1 is original deviation, Δ2 is deviation with lens, and D is power of lens used.

sections.title: Surgical Management: Infantile ET
content: 1. Stabilization: Ensure amblyopia is treated first.
2. Procedure Selection: Bilateral Medial Rectus (BMR) Recession is gold standard.
3. Dosing: 5mm for 20-25PD; 6mm for 30-35PD; 7mm for 45-50PD.
4. Associated Patterns: Address Inferior Oblique (Myectomy) if OAIO is present.
5. Timing: Ideally before 2 years of age to maximize binocular potential.

sections.title: Post-Operative Complications
content: Slipped or Lost Muscle (Surgical emergency)
Consecutive Exotropia (Overcorrection)
Globe Perforation
Anterior Segment Ischemia (Risk if >2 muscles/eye)
Suture Granuloma or Tenon's Prolapse

sections.title: Special Form: Acute Acquired Comitant ET
content: Swan Type: Following occlusion/loss of vision.
Burian-Franceschetti Type: Idiopathic, large angle, no refractive error.
Bielschowsky Type: Found in uncorrected myopes due to near work.
NEURO ALERT: Acute ET can be a sign of cerebellar tumor (Chiari Malformation).

sections.title: The ELIS Trial & Timing of Surgery
sections.content: The Early vs. Late Infantile Strabismus (ELIS) study suggests that surgery performed before age 2, specifically between 6 months and 2 years, results in better stereopsis and gross binocularity compared to delayed surgery, though re-operation rates may be higher.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Board Exam
content: Always check for a 'V' or 'A' pattern; 'V' is often IOOA, 'A' is often SOOA.
Prism Adaptation Test (PAT): Used to identify patients who 'eat' prism before surgery.
Monofixation Syndrome: A common 'success' state after ET surgery (small angle, central scotoma, peripheral fusion).
Sensory ET in adults: If sudden onset, think intracranial pressure.

content.explanation: D: Diminished Abduction, U: Up/Down shoots, A: Adduction causes globe retraction, N: Narrowing of fissure, E: Esotropia in primary position.

sections.title: Investigations: Ancillary Testing
content: Worth 4-Dot Test: Assess for suppression or diplopia.
Stereopsis Testing: Titmus Fly or Randot (IES usually has no stereopsis).
Hess Screen / Lancaster Red-Green: Useful for paralytic ET.
Neuroimaging (MRI/CT): Mandatory if ET is associated with neurological signs, ataxia, or papilledema.

sections.title: Summary of Success Criteria
content: Primary Success: Orthotropia within 10 PD of central alignment.
Functional Success: Restoration of gross stereopsis (e.g., 200-400 arc sec).
Cosmetic Success: Deviation not noticeable by casual observers.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Concomitant Strabismus: The Esotropia Compendium ---
sections.content: An exhaustive clinical guide to Esotropia, a manifest inward deviation of the visual axes and the most common form of childhood strabismus in the UK. This poster covers the classification, assessment, and management of accommodative, non-accommodative, and secondary esodeviations.

sections.title: Core Definitions & Classification
content: Definition: Esotropia is a manifest inward deviation of the visual axes.
Prevalence: It is the commonest form of childhood strabismus in the UK.
Primary (1°): Classified as accommodative or non-accommodative.
Secondary (2°): Most commonly due to poor vision (sensory deprivation).
Consecutive: Occurs after surgery for an exodeviation.

sections.title: Essential Clinical Assessment
content: Step 1: Perform full refraction.
Step 2: Conduct a full ophthalmic examination.
Step 3: Address amblyopic risk if appropriate (consider patient age).
Step 4: Rule out underlying pathology at the outset.

sections.title: Pathology Alert: Rule Out At Outset
content: Intraocular tumour (e.g., Retinoblastoma)
Cataract
Other underlying organic pathology

branches: Neurological Link: Accommodation and convergence are neurologically linked.
AC:A Ratio: Measure of accommodative convergence per unit of accommodation; varies between individuals.
Mechanism: Young, uncorrected hypermetropes accommodate to see clearly, triggering convergent drive.
High AC:A Ratio: Particularly likely to develop esotropia at near vision.
Presentation: Usually presents between 1 and 5 years of age.
Types: May be refractive or non-refractive (abnormally high AC:A), often with overlap.

rows: Fully corrected for distance and near by hypermetropic correction (+2 to +7D).
Only partially corrected by full hypermetropic correction.
Normal Binocular Single Vision (BSV) if corrected.
BSV absent or limited with ARC (Abnormal Retinal Correspondence).
Often intermittent initially (e.g. with fatigue, illness).
Full hypermetropic correction; allow 12wk for spectacle adaptation; treat amblyopia.
Full hypermetropic correction; treat amblyopia; consider surgery for BSV potential or cosmesis.

sections.title: Non-Refractive: Convergence Excess
content: Mechanism: Esotropia for near due to high AC:A ratio.
Distance Status: Ortho- or esophoric for distance.
BSV: dBSV for near, normal BSV for distance.
Refraction: Usually hypermetropic.
Treatment 1: Treat any associated hypermetropia or amblyopia.
Treatment 2: Consider orthoptic exercises or executive bifocal glasses.
Treatment 3: Surgery (bilateral MR recession and/or posterior fixation sutures) or miotics.

sections.title: Infantile Esotropia (Congenital)
content: Definition: Commonest non-accommodative esotropia; presents before 6 months of age.
Clinical Signs: Large angle (>30Δ) and alternating fixation (low risk of amblyopia).
Potential: Poor Binocular Single Vision (BSV) potential.
DVD: Dissociated Vertical Deviation - incomitant tendency for occluded eye to elevate and extort, resolving on uncovering.
LN: Latent Nystagmus - horizontal, conjugate jerk nystagmus on occluding one eye, fast phase away from covered eye (ACE).
IOOA: Inferior Oblique Overaction - hyperdeviation in adduction, greatest in field of IO.

sections.title: Management of Infantile Esotropia
content: Treat associated amblyopia (e.g., occlusion of better eye if not freely alternating).
Correct hypermetropia if >2D.
Surgery: Aims for ocular alignment.
Additional Surgery: May be required for significant IOOA or DVD.

rows: Increased chance of BSV (Simonsz et al. 2005; Birch et al. 2000).
Less accurate preoperative measurements (Prism Cover Test - PCT).
BSV from early Sx is poor quality/functionally not important.
Proceeding without stable PCT does not affect outcome (Lueder et al. 2008).
BSV can be achieved even after late surgery (Murray et al. 2007).

sections.title: Other Non-Accommodative Types
content: Basic Esotropia: Constant ET for near and distance; treat surgically.
Near Esotropia (Non-accommodative convergence excess): ET for near, ortho-/esophoria for distance; normal AC:A ratio. Treatment: Surgical (MR > LR).
Distance Esotropia (Divergence insufficiency): Esophoria/small ET for near, larger ET for distance; poor fusional divergence. NB: Exclude bilateral VI palsy. Treat with orthoptic exercises initially.
Cyclic Esotropia: Rare, periodic (e.g., alternate days); may proceed to constant esotropia.
Nystagmus Blockage & Cianca Syndrome: Large angle infantile ET, nystagmus increases on abduction, head turn towards fixing eye.

sections.title: Secondary Esotropias & Pseudoesotropia
content: Sensory Deprivation: Secondary to unilateral/bilateral decreased Visual Acuity (dVA).
Divergence Paralysis: Secondary to tumour, trauma, or stroke. Deviation remains constant or decreases on lateral gaze (unlike VI palsy).

Convergence Spasm: Intermittent, associated with blurred vision (pseudomyopia) and pupillary miosis. Ductions normal without miosis. Exclude upper midbrain pathology; often non-organic. Treat with cycloplegia.
Pseudoesotropia: Various conditions mimicking esotropia (see Table 17.6).

sections.title: Footnotes & Academic References
sections.content:
4. Simonsz HJ et al. Final report of the early vs. late infantile strabismus surgery study (ELISSS). Strabismus. 2005;13:169–99. 
5. Birch EE et al. Why does early surgical alignment improve stereoacuity outcomes in infantile esotropia? J AAPOS. 2000;4:10–14. 
6. Lueder GT et al. Effect of preoperative stability of alignment on outcome of strabismus surgery for infantile esotropia. J AAPOS. 2008;12:66–8. 
7. Murray AD et al. Changes in the functional binocular status of older children and adults with previously untreated infantile esotropia. J AAPOS. 2007;11:125–30.

summary: Mastering the physics and clinical applications of visual field testing is essential for detecting glaucomatous progression and neuro-ophthalmological defects. This guide contrasts traditional kinetic perimetry with modern automated static threshold techniques.

data.title: Clinical Perimetry: Kinetic vs. Static Strategies
data.summary: Mastering the physics and clinical applications of visual field testing is essential for detecting glaucomatous progression and neuro-ophthalmological defects. This guide contrasts traditional kinetic perimetry with modern automated static threshold techniques.

sections.title: Definition & Foundations
sections.content: Perimetry measures the differential light sensitivity across the visual field. Kinetic perimetry (Goldmann) involves moving a stimulus of constant intensity toward the fixation point until detection (isopters). Static perimetry measures the threshold sensitivity at fixed locations by varying stimulus intensity (decibels, dB).

sections.title: Clinical Indications
content: Kinetic: Detecting peripheral contractions (e.g., Retinitis Pigmentosa, advanced Glaucoma).
Kinetic: Pediatric/Low-cognition patients (less demanding).
Static: Early detection of glaucomatous damage (RNFL thinning).
Static: Neuro-ophthalmology (Chiasmal/Retrochiasmal lesions).
Static: Longitudinal monitoring of VF index progression.

sections.title: Red Flags in Testing
content: High Fixation Losses (>20%): Invalidates reliability.
False Positives (>15%): Suggests 'trigger-happy' patient; elevates sensitivity.
False Negatives (>20%): Suggests inattention or advanced field loss.
Gaze Tracking Errors: Significant misalignment during testing.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: Step 1: Patient education and lens correction (near addition calculated per age).
Step 2: Trial frame alignment (check for rim artifacts).
Step 3: Fixation monitoring (Heijl-Krakau method for blind spot).
Step 4: Threshold strategy selection (SITA Fast vs. SITA Standard).
Step 5: Analysis of Global Indices (Mean Deviation, Pattern SD).

content.explanation: Fixation losses (check blind spot), False-positives (trigger-happy), False-negatives (inattention).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always adjust for age: Thresholds naturally decline with aging due to miosis and media opacities.
The 'Hill of Vision': Imagine the central fovea as the peak; sensitivity drops rapidly toward the periphery.
SITA (Swedish Interactive Threshold Algorithm) reduces test time by 50% compared to traditional Full Threshold.
Look for 'biconcave' patterns in bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal pathology).
Artifacts: Eyelid ptosis or trial lens rims can create 'pseudoscotomas' in superior fields.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Mastering Perimetry: Static, Kinetic, & SITA Strategies ---
sections.content: An essential clinical guide to visual field assessment, covering the physics of threshold perimetry, kinetic mapping, and the evolution of modern SITA testing algorithms.

sections.title: Definition & Purpose
sections.content: Perimetry measures the sensitivity of the retina to light stimuli across the visual field. It maps the 'island of vision in a sea of darkness'. Static perimetry (automated) assesses threshold at fixed locations, while kinetic perimetry moves stimuli from non-seeing to seeing areas.

sections.title: The SITA Revolution
content: SITA (Swedish Interactive Thresholding Algorithm): Uses mathematical models to predict thresholds.
SITA Standard: Traditional 24-2 or 30-2 protocols.
SITA Fast: Reduces testing time by ~50% with minimal loss in sensitivity.
SITA Faster: Further reduces time, removes blind spot monitoring to optimize fixation.
SITA Faster 24-2C: Adds 10 peripheral points specifically to detect glaucomatous damage in the central 10 degrees.

sections.title: Red Flags in Reliability
content: False Positives > 15%: Suggests 'trigger happy' patient (invalid).
False Negatives > 20%: Suggests fatigue or inattention.
Fixation Losses > 20%: Unreliable gaze tracking.
Gaze Tracking Graph: Look for spikes, indicating frequent ocular movements.

sections.title: Clinical Workflow: The Perimetry Process
content: Step 1: Proper refraction for age and testing distance (add +3.25D for near for 30cm).
Step 2: Trial frame or bowl-mounted lens correction (prevent rim artifacts).
Step 3: Patient instruction and practice 'dummy' run.
Step 4: Real-time gaze monitoring during testing.
Step 5: Analysis of Global Indices (MD, PSD, VFI).

content.explanation: G (Global Indices: MD/PSD), L (Losses/Fixation), A (Artifacts: Rim/Ptosis), D (Defect morphology: Arcuate/Nasal Step).

sections.title: Landmark Studies
content: OHTS (Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study): Utilized SAP (Standard Automated Perimetry) to define conversion to glaucoma.
EMGT (Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial): Established the 'Mean Deviation' (MD) as a primary metric for progression.
Comparison Studies: Confirmed that SITA-Faster provides comparable clinical utility to SITA-Standard while increasing patient satisfaction.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: A Full-Thickness Macular Hole (FTMH) is a foveal dehiscence involving all retinal layers from the internal limiting membrane (ILM) to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). It typically results from tangential and anteroposterior vitreous traction at the macula.

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Metamorphopsia (Amsler grid distortion)
Central scotoma expansion
Sudden drop in BCVA
Associated Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD)

content.explanation: Metamorphopsia (wavy lines), Amsler grid distortion, Central vision loss, Unilateral symptoms, Loss of contrast sensitivity, Aching (minimal/none).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Step 1: BCVA - Usually 20/70 to 20/200.
Step 2: Amsler Grid testing - Reveal central metamorphopsia.
Step 3: Slit-Lamp Biomicroscopy - Watzke-Allen test (positive).
Step 4: SD-OCT - Gold standard to confirm hole diameter and integrity of EZ (Ellipsoid Zone).

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) - 23/25/27 Gauge.
Step 2: Induction of PVD - Vital for releasing traction.
Step 3: Internal Limiting Membrane (ILM) Peeling - Use of Brilliant Blue G or Indocyanine Green (ICG).
Step 4: Fluid-Air Exchange.
Step 5: Tamponade - C3F8 (14%) or SF6 (20%) gas.
Step 6: Face-down positioning - Essential for 3-5 days.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Closure rates exceed 90-95% for most primary macular holes.
Inverted ILM flap technique is preferred for chronic or large (>400um) holes.
Post-operative BCVA improvement is highly dependent on the integrity of the Ellipsoid Zone (EZ) on OCT.
Risk of cataract progression is nearly 100% following gas tamponade.

sections.title: Recent Advances
sections.content: Recent landmark trends emphasize the use of autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) or amniotic membrane grafts for refractory macular holes. Additionally, studies on micro-incision vitrectomy (MIVS) demonstrate faster recovery times and reduced inflammation.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Mastering the Macular Hole: From Pathogenesis to Post-Op ---
sections.content: A comprehensive clinical deep-dive into Full-Thickness Macular Holes (FTMH), covering the evolution of staging from Gass to IVTS, gold-standard diagnostic maneuvers, and the nuances of vitreoretinal surgical management.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A Full-Thickness Macular Hole (FTMH) is a primary neurosensory retinal defect involving all layers from the internal limiting membrane (ILM) to the outer segments of the photoreceptors. It typically occurs at the fovea centralis, leading to a significant loss of central visual acuity and metamorphopsia. While most are idiopathic and related to age-related vitreoretinal interface changes, they can also be secondary to trauma or high myopia.

sections.title: The Gass Staging System (Historical Gold Standard)

rows: Central yellow spot; loss of foveal reflex.
Central yellow ring; further elevation of the foveola.
Small eccentric break in the foveal floor; 'can-opener' tear.
Large hole with cuff of subretinal fluid; No Weiss Ring.
Large hole; Weiss ring present on biomicroscopy.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Gass Theory
content: 1. Perifoveal Vitreous Detachment begins.
2. Focal tangential traction at the fovea by the posterior hyaloid.
3. Cystic changes occur in the foveolar layers (Stage 1).
4. Centrifugal migration of photoreceptors.
5. Full-thickness dehiscence and centripetal retraction of retinal edges.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Progressive decrease in central vision (usually 20/80 to 20/400).
Metamorphopsia: Distorted lines on Amsler Grid.
Central Scotoma: A 'hole' in the center of vision.
Micropsia: Objects appearing smaller.
Typically painless and unilateral onset.

sections.title: Diagnostic Ocular Examination
content: Watzke-Allen Sign: Slit beam over hole is perceived as thinned or broken.
Laser Beam Test: 50um spot disappears into the hole.
Biomicroscopy: Round, red lesion with yellow-white deposits (drusen-like) at the base.
Cuff of Subretinal Fluid: Surrounding the hole edges.
Pseudo-operculum: Suspended tissue over the hole (condensed vitreous).

rows: Verticalized foveal edges; no tissue loss.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Spectral Domain OCT (SD-OCT): The gold standard for sizing and staging.
2. Amsler Grid: To document the area of metamorphopsia.
3. Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Shows 'window defect' early, but rarely necessary.
4. Microperimetry: Maps the depth and extent of the central scotoma.
5. Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): Increased autofluorescence in the hole due to RPE unmasking.

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol
content: 1. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (23G, 25G, or 27G).
2. Induction of Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD) if not present.
3. ILM Peeling: Often aided by Brilliant Blue G (BBG) or Indocyanine Green (ICG).
4. Fluid-Air Exchange (FAX).
5. Gas Tamponade: Long-acting (C3F8) or short-acting (SF6).
6. Post-operative positioning: Face-down for 3-7 days (surgeon dependent).

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Considerations
content: Acute vision drop in the fellow eye (15% risk).
Signs of Endophthalmitis post-op (pain, hypopyon).
Iatrogenic retinal breaks during surgery.
Rapidly progressive cataract (common after vitrectomy).
Elevated Intraocular Pressure (IOP) from gas expansion.

content.explanation: Beam broken = Macular hole; Ray is bent = Pseudohole; Entirely normal = Malingering/Functional; All light seen = Lamellar hole; Kinked beam = Epiretinal membrane.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Cataract formation (occurs in >75% within 2 years).
Retinal Detachment (1-2% risk).
Visual field defects (often related to air-fluid exchange).
RPE Toxicity (if ICG dye is used for ILM peeling).
Success Rate: >90% closure for Stage 2 holes.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Small holes (<250μm) have a higher chance of spontaneous closure (rare but documented).
Inverted ILM flap technique is superior for large holes (>400μm) and high myopia.
The presence of a Weiss ring confirms Stage 4 and reduces risk to the fellow eye.
OCT 'Base Diameter' is always larger than 'Minimum Linear Diameter' (MLD).

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: MIVS (Micro-Incision Vitrectomy Surgery): Reducing surgical trauma and recovery time.
Ocrplasmin (Jetrea): Pharmacologic vitreolysis for VMT, though use has declined due to limited efficacy in FTMH.
Autologous Retinal Flaps: For refractory or ultra-large holes.
Valved Cannulas: Maintaining stable IOP during ILM peeling.
Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) adjuvants: Exploring biological 'glue' for closure.

sections.title: Long-Term Monitoring Protocol
content: 1. Week 1: Check IOP and wound integrity.
2. Month 1: Monitor gas bubble resolution and OCT for closure.
3. Month 3: Assess visual acuity and metamorphopsia improvement.
4. Ongoing: Annual Amsler Grid monitoring of the fellow eye.

summary: The most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, originating from melanocytes within the uveal tract. Early detection is critical to preventing systemic metastasis and preserving vision.

data.summary: The most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, originating from melanocytes within the uveal tract. Early detection is critical to preventing systemic metastasis and preserving vision.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Choroidal melanoma arises from uveal melanocytes. Incidence is approximately 5-7 per million per year in Caucasians. Peak incidence occurs between 50-70 years of age. It is rare in individuals with darker pigmentation (African/Asian descent). Major risk factors include light iris color, fair skin, BAP1 mutation (hereditary), and choroidal nevus transformation.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Often asymptomatic in early stages.
Blurred vision or visual field defects.
Photopsias (flashes of light).
Metamorphopsia (distorted vision).
Secondary glaucoma (if angle involvement).
Retinal detachment (exudative).

sections.title: The TFSOM-UHHD Criteria (Risk of Growth)
content: Thickness > 2mm
Fluid (subretinal)
Symptoms
Orange pigment (lipofuscin)
Margin near optic disc
Ultrasound Hollowness
Halo absent
Diameter > 5mm

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy & Indirect ophthalmoscopy.
Step 2: Fundus Photography (document size/pigment).
Step 3: B-scan Ultrasonography (low internal reflectivity).
Step 4: SD-OCT (detect subretinal fluid, RPE changes).
Step 5: Fundus Autofluorescence (detect orange pigment).
Step 6: Systemic staging: Liver LFTs, Abdominal Ultrasound/MRI/CT.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: Presence of subretinal fluid is the strongest clinical indicator of malignancy.
Growth documented on serial examinations is an absolute indication for treatment.
Liver metastases are the most common site of spread (up to 90% of systemic disease).
Do not mistake a choroidal metastasis for a primary melanoma (metastases are usually bilateral/multifocal).

content.explanation: Use the acronym (TFSOM) to determine if a lesion requires immediate treatment vs observation.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: COMS Study: No survival difference between I-125 brachytherapy and enucleation for medium tumors.
Genetic Testing: Monosomy 3 and BAP1 mutation correlate with high metastatic risk.
Prognosis: Depends on tumor size, ciliary body involvement, and extra-scleral extension.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Choroidal Melanoma: A Comprehensive Clinical Guide ---
sections.content: Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, arising from melanocytes within the uveal tract. Early detection via clinical markers is essential for systemic prognosis and vision preservation.

sections.title: Disease Overview
sections.content: Choroidal melanoma is a malignant tumor arising from the melanocytes of the uveal tract. It represents approximately 80% of all uveal melanomas and is recognized as the most common primary intraocular cancer found in the adult population.

sections.title: Predisposing Risk Factors
content: Fair skin and light eye color (Blue/Green)
Oculodermal melanocytosis (Nevus of Ota)
Presence of pre-existing uveal nevi
BRCA1-associated protein 1 (BAP1) mutation
Congenital ocular melanocytosis

content.explanation: T: Thickness > 2 mm; F: Fluid (subretinal); S: Symptoms (blurred vision/flashes); O: Orange pigment (lipofuscin); M: Margin within 3 mm of optic disc; U: Ultrasound (acoustic hollowness); HH: Halo absence; D: Drusen absence.

rows: Acoustic hollowness, choroidal excavation, and 'collar-button' (mushroom) shape.
Double circulation pattern (simultaneous retinal and tumor vessel filling).
Documentation of pigmentation (melanotic vs. amelanotic) and borders.

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNING SIGNS
content: Rapid growth of a documented pre-existing nevus
Presence of Sentinel Vessels (dilated episcleral vessels)
Extraocular extension through the scleral emissary channels
Diffuse growth pattern (higher risk of delayed diagnosis)

sections.title: Management Pathway
content: Step 1: Observation for small, low-risk, dormant lesions.
Step 2: Radiation Therapy (Plaque Brachytherapy or Proton Beam).
Step 3: Surgical Enucleation for large tumors or blind/painful eyes.
Step 4: Systemic Surveillance for hepatic metastasis.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect LHON
content: Painless, subacute sequential vision loss in one eye followed by the other within weeks/months.
Profound dyschromatopsia (red-green deficiency) out of proportion to acuity.
Absence of pain on eye movement (differentiates from Optic Neuritis).
Family history of sudden blindness in maternal relatives.
Young male presenting with cecocentral scotoma.

rows: Optic nerve head pallor, RNF loss

sections.title: Diagnostic Protocol
content: Step 1: Careful history (maternal lineage) and clinical exam.
Step 2: Fundoscopy (look for characteristic telangiectatic microangiopathy).
Step 3: OCT (RNFL thickness analysis - note initial swelling followed by thinning).
Step 4: Visual Field (Humphrey 30-2: typically dense cecocentral scotoma).
Step 5: Genetic testing (Mitochondrial DNA blood panel for the 3 primary mutations).

sections.title: Management & Therapeutic Advances
content: Idebenone (Short-chain Coenzyme Q10 analogue): Improves mitochondrial ATP production. Approved at 900mg/day (divided dose).
Gene Therapy: Lumevoq (Lenadogene nolparvovec) - viral vector delivery of wild-type ND4 gene via intravitreal injection.
Avoidance of toxic factors: Strict cessation of tobacco and ethanol consumption.
Neuro-ophthalmological monitoring: Frequent follow-up for the fellow eye.

content.explanation: L: Loss (Subacute), H: Hereditary (Maternal), O: Optic Nerve (Pseudo-edema), N: ND4/ND1/ND6 mutations.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Pseudo-disc edema does not leak on Fluorescein Angiography.
The '14484' mutation has a significantly better prognosis for spontaneous visual recovery.
Mitochondrial genes are not affected by Mendelian inheritance laws (maternal only).
LHON-Plus syndrome: consider if patient exhibits dystonia, tremor, or cardiac conduction defects.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: LHON: The Mitochondrial Silent Thief of Sight ---
sections.content: Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON) is the most common primary mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) disorder, characterized by subacute, painless, bilateral central vision loss primarily affecting young males. It represents a paradigm of mitochondrial genetics and selective retinal ganglion cell (RGC) vulnerability.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: LHON is a maternally inherited mitochondrial disease resulting from mutations in the ND genes (encoding subunits of Complex I of the respiratory chain). It causes selective apoptosis of Retinal Ganglion Cells (RGCs), specifically the parvocellular pathway, leading to severe optic atrophy and permanent central scotoma.

sections.title: Clinical Progression Stages
content: Step 1: Asymptomatic Carrier (Normal acuity, subclinical RNFL thickening)
Step 2: Subacute Phase (Weeks 0-6): Rapid painless vision loss, dyschromatopsia
Step 3: Dynamic Phase (Months 1-6): Fellow eye involved (sequential > simultaneous)
Step 4: Chronic Phase (>6-12 Months): Progressive RNFL loss, optic atrophy

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Peripapillary telangiectatic microangiopathy
Pseudo-edema: Swelling of the nerve fiber layer (NFL) without leakage
Absence of Optic Disc Cupping (unlike glaucoma)
Tortuosity of retinal arterioles
Centrocecal scotoma on Visual Field testing
Pupillary light reflex is often DISPROPORTIONATELY spared

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: Genetic Testing: Targeted screening for the 3 primary mutations
OCT RNFL/GCL: Shows temporal thinning followed by global atrophy
Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): CRITICAL to show NO disc leakage
Visual Field (Goldmann or HVF): Demonstrates central/centrocecal scotomas
Neuroimaging (MRI): To rule out compressive or demyelinating lesions

sections.title: Red Flags & Contraindications
content: Smoking: Strongest environmental trigger for conversion
Excessive Alcohol: Synergistic effect with tobacco
Ethambutol/Linezolid: Avoid mitochondrial toxins
Rapid, Painful loss: Consider inflammatory etiology instead
Extraocular Signs: 'LHON Plus' (Dystonia, tremors, MS-like symptoms)

content.explanation: S: SYMMETRIC (eventually), S: SUBACUTE (painless), S: SMOKING (must stop!)

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Lifestyle Modification: Immediate cessation of smoking and limited alcohol consumption.
Step 2: Idebenone (Raxone): 900mg/day (300mg TID). Start early for best results, continue for at least 1 year.
Step 3: Gene Therapy (Lumevoq/GS010): Intravitreal injection of rAAV2/2-ND4. Recent studies show bilateral benefit after unilateral injection.
Step 4: Supportive Care: Low vision aids and genetic counseling for maternal relatives.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: LHON is often misdiagnosed as 'Retrobulbar Optic Neuritis' in the early phase.
Fenestration of the optic nerve sheath is CONTRAINDICATED.
The pseudo-edema corresponds to stasis of axoplasmic transport, NOT fluid.
Melanopsin-containing RGCs are spared, explaining the preserved pupillary reflex.
Wait at least 12-18 months before declaring no chance of spontaneous recovery.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
content: RESCUE & REVERSE Trials: Evaluated Lumevoq gene therapy for ND4 mutations.
REFLECT Trial: Confirmed the efficacy of bilateral IVT gene therapy injections.
RHODOS Trial: Provided the evidence base for high-dose Idebenone (900mg/day).
The 'Bilateral Benefit' Phenomenon: Discovery of viral vector transfer via the optic chiasm.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Microbial Keratitis (MK) is an infectious process involving the corneal epithelium and stroma. A 'corneal abscess' specifically refers to a localized collection of white blood cells (neutrophils), necrotic tissue, and pathogens within the stroma, often presenting as a dense, yellowish-white opacity with an overlying epithelial defect.

rows: Chronic lid disease, post-op, bullous keratopathy.
Rapidly spreading, soup-like melting, greenish discharge.
Serpiginous ulcer, deep stromal abscess, hypopyon.
Indolent, often in the inferior cornea.
Feathery margins, satellite lesions, immune ring.

sections.title: The Four Stages of Pathogenesis
content: 1. Stage of Infiltration: PMN migration from limbus/tears into the stroma.
2. Stage of Active Ulceration: Necrosis and sloughing of epithelium and stroma.
3. Stage of Regression: Immune response limits the infection; lines of demarcation form.
4. Stage of Cicatrization: Healing via fibroblast activity, resulting in permanent nebula, macula, or leucoma.

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Red Flags for Perforation
content: Descemetocele formation (clear bubble in the floor of the ulcer)
Sudden decrease in IOP (intraocular pressure)
Seidel's test positive (aqueous leak)
Shallow or flat anterior chamber
Iris prolapse into the corneal defect
Rapidly progressive stromal thinning ('melting')

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: The Scrape Protocol
content: 1. Stop antibiotics 24-48h if possible (unless severe).
2. Instill topical anesthetic (Proparacaine preferred over Tetracaine).
3. Scrape the base and the active margins using a Kimura spatula or 25G needle.
4. Inoculate onto Blood Agar, Chocolate Agar, and Sabouraud Dextrose Agar.
5. Prepare slides for Gram and Giemsa stains (and KOH/Calcofluor white if fungal suspected).

sections.title: Initial Management: Medical Protocol
content: Monotherapy (Non-central, <2mm): Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin 0.5% or Gatifloxacin 0.5%) q1h.
Duotherapy (Severe/Central): Fortified Tobramycin (15mg/mL) + Fortified Vancomycin (50mg/mL) q1h around the clock.
Cycloplegia: Atropine 1% BID or Cyclopentolate 1% TID to reduce pain and prevent synechiae.
Oral Doxycycline: 100mg BID to inhibit collagenase and prevent melting.
Steroid Timing: Wait at least 48-72h of effective antibiotic cover (SCUT trial recommendations).

sections.title: Fortified Antibiotic Preparation (Pearls)
sections.content: Vancomycin (50mg/mL): Add 10mL of sterile water or BSS to 500mg Vancomycin powder. Stable for 14 days refrigerated. Tobramycin (15mg/mL): Add 2mL of injectable Tobramycin (40mg/mL) to a 5mL bottle of 0.3% Tobramycin ophthalmic solution.

content.explanation: P: Painful (Severe), S: Soup-like melt, E: Extended wear CL risk, U: Ulceration rapid, D: Discharge (Greenish/Purulent), O: Odor (often associated with Pseudomonas cultures).

branches: Amniotic Membrane Graft (for persistent epithelial defects)
Bandage Contact Lens (only after infection is sterilized)

sections.title: Landmark Study: The SCUT Trial
content: Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT).
Finding: No significant difference in visual outcome at 3 months for the whole group.
Subgroup benefit: Patients with very poor baseline vision and central/deep ulcers showed better outcomes with early steroids (after 48h of antibiotics).
Key Rule: Never start steroids until the organism is identified and fungal/acanthamoeba are ruled out.

sections.title: Complications and Prognosis
content: Endophthalmitis (Infection spread to the vitreous/aqueous).
Secondary Glaucoma (Inflammatory debris blocking the trabecular meshwork).
Anterior Polychromatic Cataract.
Corneal Leucoma (Permanent opaque scar).
Phthisis Bulbi (Shrinkage of the eye following severe infection).

sections.title: Pathogens that can Penetrate Intact Epithelium

content.explanation: N: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, H: Haemophilus influenzae, L: Listeria monocytogenes, C: Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Lid Flip': Always evert the eyelid to look for retained foreign bodies (e.g., a lost contact lens) which can be the nidus for infection.
Acanthamoeba Hint: Pain out of proportion to clinical signs and radial keratoneuritis.
Moraxella: Classically occurs in patients with pre-existing ocular surface disease and malnutrition.
Toxicity vs. Infection: If the ulcer is not improving, consider if the 1-hour drops are causing 'medicamentosa' or toxic epithelial toxicity.
Hypopyon: In bacterial ulcers, the hypopyon is usually sterile (inflammatory); in fungal ulcers, it may contain active fungal elements.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Microbial Keratitis: The Suppurative Storm ---
sections.content: Bacterial keratitis is a sight-threatening ocular emergency characterized by rapid corneal destruction and stromal suppuration. Management requires immediate identification of risk factors, grading of severity, and aggressive, broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy to prevent perforation and permanent scarring.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Microbial (bacterial) keratitis is a serious infection of the corneal stroma. Unlike viral or sterile keratitis, it often presents with an epithelial defect overlying a dense, necrotic stromal infiltrate, often accompanied by significant anterior chamber inflammation (hypopyon). Most bacteria (except N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis, C. diphtheriae, and H. influenzae) require a breach in the corneal epithelium to initiate infection.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Cascade of Destruction
content: 1. Epithelial Breach: Trauma or contact lens-induced hypoxia creates an entry point.
2. Adherence: Bacteria utilize fimbriae or pili to bind to the exposed corneal stroma/extracellular matrix.
3. Invasion & Multiplication: Organisms replicate and release exotoxins (e.g., Exotoxin A in Pseudomonas).
4. Host Response: Neutrophil infiltration (chemotaxis) releases matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).
5. Stromal Melting: Combination of bacterial toxins and host enzymes leads to keratomalacia (liquefactive necrosis).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Scraping Protocol
content: 1. Topical Anesthesia: Proparacaine is preferred (Benoxinate may be more bacteriostatic).
2. Sample Collection: Use a Kimura spatula, 25G needle, or sterile blade to scrape the leading edge and base.
3. C-Streaks: Transfer directly to agar plates using 'C-streaks' for semi-quantitative assessment.
4. Slide Prep: Gram and Giemsa/Diff-Quik stains for immediate visualization.
5. Culture: Blood Agar (aerobes), Chocolate Agar (fastidious), Sabouraud (fungi), Thioglycollate (anaerobes).

sections.title: Primary Medical Management
content: Loading Dose: 1 drop every 5–15 minutes for the first hour, then every 30–60 minutes around the clock.
Monotherapy (Mild/Mod): 4th Generation Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin 0.5%, Gatifloxacin 0.5%, Besifloxacin 0.6%).
Duo-therapy (Severe/Central): Fortified Tobramycin (14 mg/mL) AND Fortified Vancomycin (25-50 mg/mL).
Cycloplegia: Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1% TID to reduce ciliary spasm and prevent synechiae.
Systemic Rx: Consider if scleral involvement (e.g., Ciprofloxacin 500mg BID) or N. gonorrhoeae (Ceftriaxone 1g IM/IV).

sections.title: Steroid Use: The SCUT Trial (2011)
sections.content: The Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT) found no significant difference in 3-month visual outcomes between topical corticosteroids and placebo. However, a subgroup analysis showed benefit in vision for central, deep, and severe ulcers (excluding Nocardia). RULE: Start steroids only AFTER 48-72 hours of clinical improvement and negative cultures, and NEVER if fungus or Acanthamoeba is suspected.

branches: Marginal Keratitis (Sterile, lucid interval at limbus)

sections.title: CRITICAL: Red Flags for Worsening
content: Enlarging Infiltrate or Epithelial Defect despite 48h therapy.
Progressive Stromal Thinning (Descemetocele or Perforation).
Scleral involvement (Scleritis/Scleral melting).
Rise in Intraocular Pressure (Secondary Glaucoma).
Signs of Endophthalmitis (hypopyon increase, vitreous cells, loss of red reflex).

content.explanation: P: Pain (is it increasing?); E: Epithelial defect size; D: Discharge (purulent?); A: Anterior chamber reaction/hypopyon; L: Location and Size of infiltrate.

sections.title: Surgical Interventions
content: Cyanoacrylate Tissue Adhesive: For small perforations (<2mm) or impending perforation.
Tectonic Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): For large perforations or uncontrolled infection.
Amniotic Membrane Graft (AMG): Promotes re-epithelialization in neurotrophic cases.
PACK-CXL: Photoactivated Chromophore for Keratitis (Cross-linking) as adjuvant therapy for resistant organisms.

rows: Enriched with Factor V and X
Low pH, contains antibiotics to inhibit bacteria

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: Contact lens wearers with ulcers have Pseudomonas until proven otherwise.
Wessely Ring: An immune ring (antigen-antibody complex) often seen in Gram-negative infections.
Fortified drops are generally stable for 7-14 days if refrigerated.
Never use a 'taper' on antibiotics until the infection is sterilized; maintain 'therapeutic' levels.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Corneal Scarring/Leucoma (Permanent vision loss if central).
Irregular Astigmatism (Secondary to scarring).
Anterior Synechiae and Secondary Glaucoma.
Infectious Endophthalmitis (Rare unless perforation occurs).
Phthisis Bulbi (In severe, untreated cases).

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Microbial Keratitis: The Sight-Threatening Emergency ---
sections.content: An urgent, sight-threatening infection of the corneal stroma characterized by epithelial defect, infiltrate, and associated inflammation. Rapid diagnosis and targeted antimicrobial therapy are mandatory to prevent stromal melting and permanent vision loss.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Microbial keratitis is an infection involving the corneal stroma, often secondary to contact lens wear, ocular surface disease, or trauma. Globally, bacterial keratitis is the most common form, with Pseudomonas aeruginosa being the most frequent pathogen in contact lens wearers. Incidence is estimated at 2.5–799 per 100,000 person-years depending on geography and risk factor prevalence.

sections.title: Red Flags: Urgent Intervention Required
content: Corneal thinning or impending perforation (Seidel positive)
Involvement of the visual axis (central location)
Hypopyon exceeding 2mm
Scleral involvement (Sclerokeratitis)
Lack of response to initial therapy at 24-48 hours

rows: Peripheral, smaller, less pain, no hypopyon
Radial perineuritis, severe pain out of proportion to exam
Feathery edges, satellite lesions, slow progression

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Visual Acuity & Slit-lamp exam (map infiltrate size).
Step 2: Corneal scrapings using Kimura spatula or platinum blade.
Step 3: Inoculate onto Blood Agar, Chocolate Agar, Sabouraud Agar, and Thioglycolate broth.
Step 4: Perform Gram stain and initiate empiric fortified antibiotics.
Step 5: Perform in-vivo confocal microscopy if Acanthamoeba/Fungal suspected.

sections.title: Treatment Protocol: Fortified Antibiotics
content: Fortified Tobramycin (15mg/ml) q1h
Fortified Cefazolin (50mg/ml) q1h
Monotherapy: Gatifloxacin or Moxifloxacin 0.5% (for smaller lesions)
Cycloplegics (Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1%) for pain
Topical steroids: Only after epithelialization and reduced organism load

content.explanation: S: Staining (Fluorescein), T: Tincture (Stains like Gram), A: Acanthamoeba check, M: Microscopy (Confocal), P: Pathogen identification

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always evaluate for contact lens case contamination.
Avoid eye patching; it creates a warm, hypoxic environment for bacterial growth.
The 'SCUT trial' provided evidence that adjunctive topical corticosteroids do not improve visual outcomes at 3 months for bacterial ulcers.
If the patient is monocular, hospitalize for intensive monitoring.

title: Merged: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (AACG): The Ophthalmic Emergency
summary: AACG is a vision-threatening emergency characterized by a rapid, symptomatic rise in intraocular pressure (IOP) due to the sudden occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris. Timely diagnosis and management are critical to prevent permanent optic nerve damage and vision loss.

data.summary: AACG is a vision-threatening emergency characterized by a rapid, symptomatic rise in intraocular pressure (IOP) due to the sudden occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris. Timely diagnosis and management are critical to prevent permanent optic nerve damage and vision loss.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: AACG is a clinical syndrome resulting from the rapid closure of a pre-existing narrow anterior chamber angle. This leads to a total or near-total obstruction of aqueous outflow, resulting in a dramatic spike in IOP (often 40-80 mmHg). It is a surgical emergency requiring immediate medical and procedural intervention.

branches: Pupillary Block: Most common. High pressure in PC pushes iris forward.
Plateau Iris: Anteriorly positioned ciliary processes.
Malignant Glaucoma: Ciliary block; aqueous misdirection.
Anatomical: Short axial length, thick lens, small corneal diameter.

rows: ITC > 270°; Normal IOP, Disc, and Field.
ITC > 270° with raised IOP or PAS; Normal Disc/Field.
PAC with Glaucomatous Optic Neuropathy (GON) and Field loss.
Sudden symptomatic IOP spike with corneal edema.

sections.title: Patient Presentation: Symptoms
content: Severe Ocular Pain: Often described as a deep, boring ache.
Nausea and Vomiting: Often misdiagnosed as a GI issue.
Blurred Vision with Halos: Due to corneal epithelial edema (Sattler’s veil).
Frontal Headache: Radiating from the affected eye.
Photophobia and Lacrimation.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: IOP: Typically 40-80 mmHg; eye feels 'stony hard'.
Conjunctiva: Ciliary flush/injected.
Cornea: 'Steamy' or hazy epithelial edema.
AC: Extremely shallow; peripheral iris-corneal contact.
Pupil: Mid-dilated, vertically oval, and fixed (non-reactive).
Fundus: Edematous/hyperemic disc (acute) vs. cupping (chronic).

sections.title: Red Flags: The Do-Not-Miss Signs
content: The 'Hard' Globe on palpation: Immediate sign of severely elevated IOP.
Systemic misdiagnosis: Acute nausea/vomiting leads patients to ER, not Eye Clinic.
Contralateral Eye: High risk of synchronous or future attack (Must check!).
Ischemic Pupil: Failure to respond to pilocarpine suggests iris sphincter ischemia (>50-60 mmHg).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Gonioscopy: Gold standard (Goldmann or Sussman 4-mirror). Use indentation to differentiate appositional vs. synechial closure.
2. Van Herick Grading: Slit-lamp estimate (AC depth < 1/4 corneal thickness = narrow).
3. AS-OCT: Non-contact objective measurement of AOD and TISA.
4. UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy): Visualizes ciliary body and posterior chamber anatomy.

rows: Mild pain, high IOP, open angle, small KPs.
Miotic; pulls iris from angle. Only works if IOP < 40.

sections.title: Surgical & Laser Interventions
content: 1. Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI): Definitive treatment for pupillary block. Equalizes pressure between PC and AC.
2. Argon Laser Peripheral Iridoplasty (ALPI): Used if LPI is impossible due to corneal edema or for Plateau Iris.
3. Lens Extraction: Removing the lens (cataract surgery) significantly deepens the AC and lowers IOP.
4. Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: Immediate mechanical lowering of IOP in refractory cases.
5. Trabeculectomy/GDD: Reserved for cases where medical/laser therapy fails and PAS is extensive.

content.explanation: P: Pilocarpine (once IOP <40); R: Reduce Aqueous (Timolol/Brimonidine); E: Examine contralateral eye; S: Systemic Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors; S: Supine position (avoid); U: Urea/Mannitol; R: Relieve block (LPI); E: Evaluate optic nerve.

sections.title: Post-Attack Complications
content: Glaucomflecken: Small grey-white anterior subcapsular lens opacities (lens epithelial necrosis).
Iris Atrophy: Typically sectoral atrophy due to ischemia.
Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS): Permanent adhesion of iris to meshwork.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Post-acute inflammation.
Chronic Angle-Closure Glaucoma.

sections.title: Landmark Study: The EAGLE Trial
sections.content: The EAGLE Study (Effectiveness in Angle-closure Glaucoma of Lens Extraction) demonstrated that clear-lens extraction showed greater efficacy and was more cost-effective than LPI as a first-line treatment for patients with PAC and IOP >30 mmHg or PACG. It suggests moving towards earlier surgical lens intervention.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Practice Points
content: Never dilate a patient with a shallow chamber before performing gonioscopy.
Prophylactic LPI in the fellow eye is mandatory as the risk of an attack is ~50% within 5 years.
Avoid systemic anticholinergics and adrenergics in patients with narrow angles.
If the cornea is too cloudy for LPI, use topical glycerin to clear edema or perform ALPI to pull the iris away from the angle mechanically.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (AACG): The Ophthalmological Emergency ---
sections.content: AACG represents a true ocular emergency characterized by a rapid, sustained elevation of intraocular pressure due to mechanical obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris. Immediate recognition and intervention are critical to prevent permanent optic nerve damage and blindness.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: AACG is defined by the sudden apposition of the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork (TM), causing acute outflow obstruction. The primary mechanism is pupillary block (relative resistance to aqueous flow between the lens and iris), leading to iris bombe and angle closure. Secondary causes include plateau iris, phacomorphic glaucoma, or tractional mechanisms.

sections.title: Clinical Features (The 5 'P's)
content: Pain: Severe, boring ocular/periorbital pain.
Pupil: Mid-dilated, non-reactive.
Pressure: Often > 50 mmHg.
Prostration: Nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis.
Perception: Blurred vision with halos around lights.

sections.title: Red Flags (Emergency Signs)
content: Corneal Edema (hazy view)
Fixed mid-dilated pupil
Shallow anterior chamber (Van Herick Grade 1)
Glaukomflecken (anterior subcapsular lens opacities)
Nausea/Vomiting (often misdiagnosed as GI event)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (Assess AC depth, corneal edema, iris position).
Step 2: Tonometry (Goldmann Applanation or Tono-Pen).
Step 3: Gonioscopy (The Gold Standard - assess TM pigmentation and synechiae).
Step 4: Fundoscopy (Evaluate C/D ratio if view allows; check for disc edema).
Step 5: UBM or Anterior Segment OCT (Assess angle anatomy).

sections.title: Management Protocol
content: Immediate: Topical Beta-blockers, Alpha-agonists, Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors.
Systemic: Oral or IV Acetazolamide (500mg), Hyperosmotic agents (Mannitol/Glycerol).
Miotics: Pilocarpine 1-2% (once pressure < 40 mmHg).
Definitive: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) or surgical peripheral iridectomy.

content.explanation: C: Corneal edema, A: A-chamber shallow, M: Mid-dilated pupil, P: Pressure high.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never perform LPI on a hazy cornea; use topical glycerin to clear it.
Always examine the fellow eye; 50% risk of closure in 5 years.
Avoid pilocarpine in high pressure as it is ineffective due to iris ischemia.

branches: Early Postoperative (<1 week: TASS, Endophthalmitis, High IOP)
Late Postoperative (>1 month: PCO, CME, IOL Malposition, RD)

sections.title: Intraoperative Red Flags: The 'Big Three'
content: Sudden deepening of the AC (Posterior Capsule Rupture)
Hard eye + Loss of red reflex (Expulsive Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage)
Asymmetric 'Argentinian Flag' sign (Intumescent tear risk)
Loss of followability or vitreous in the port

sections.title: Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR) Management
content: Step 1: Freeze! Do not pull the phaco tip out; maintain AC stability with OVD through the sideport.
Step 2: Inject dispersive OVD beneath the nuclear fragments to prevent posterior migration.
Step 3: Lower bottle height/aspiration settings and remove phaco tip carefully.
Step 4: Perform Bimanual Anterior Vitrectomy (cut/suck mode) using high cut rate (2500+ CPM).
Step 5: Assess residual capsular support; implant IOL in sulcus with optic capture or ACIOL if needed.

sections.title: The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS) Protocol
content: Visual Acuity 'Light Perception' (LP) only: Immediate PPV is indicated.
Visual Acuity 'Hand Motion' (HM) or better: Tap & Inject is sufficient.
Antibiotics: Vancomycin (1mg/0.1ml) + Ceftazidime (2.25mg/0.1ml).
Amikacin is an alternative for Ceftazidime but carries risk of macular toxicity.

content.explanation: R: Retained fragment; A: Acute Endophthalmitis; P: Pressure (IOP) spike; I: Iritis/TASS; D: Detachment of Retina.

branches: First-line: Topical NSAIDs (Nepafenac 0.3% or Bromfenac) + Steroids
Second-line: Sub-tenon Triamcinolone or Intravitreal Anti-VEGF
Risk Factors: Diabetes, ERM, Vein Occlusions, Prostaglandin use

sections.title: UGH Syndrome (Uveitis-Glaucoma-Hyphema)
content: Etiology: Mechanical chafing of the iris/ciliary body by IOL (often ACIOL or sulcus IOL).
Signs: Micro-hyphema, pigment dispersion, elevated IOP, chronic low-grade inflammation.
Management: Topical IOP lowering and steroids; often requires IOL exchange or repositioning.
High-yield: Use Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM) to visualize IOL-haptic-iris contact.

sections.title: Late Complication: PCO
sections.content: Posterior Capsule Opacification (PCO) is the most common late complication. It results from the migration and proliferation of residual lens epithelial cells (LECs). Types include Fibrotic (metaplastic LECs) and Elschnig Pearls (swollen LECs). Management is YAG Laser Capsulotomy. Note: Perform only after 3 months post-op to allow IOL stability and prevent CME risk.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: ESCRS Antibiotic Prophylaxis
content: Study showed a 5-fold decrease in endophthalmitis with intracameral Cefuroxime (1mg in 0.1ml).
Current Trends: Use of intracameral Moxifloxacin (Vigamox off-label) is increasing in the US.
Povidone-iodine (5%) in the conjunctival sac for 3 minutes is the single most important aseptic step.

sections.title: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage Management
content: 1. Immediate recognition: AC shallows, IOP rises, loss of red reflex.
2. Rapid wound closure: Use 10-0 Nylon immediately to secure the eye.
3. Stop the surgery: Do not attempt to drain blood in the primary setting.
4. Post-op: Systemic steroids and IOP control. Delayed drainage (7-14 days) if choroidals are kissing.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Nearly 100% PCO rate: Primary Posterior Capsulotomy + Anterior Vitrectomy (PPC+AV) is mandatory.
Higher inflammatory response: Require aggressive topical/systemic steroids.
Risk of Glaucoma: Lifetime risk of 'Aphakic Glaucoma' even after successful IOL placement.

rows: Poor dilation (use Malyugin rings), phacodonesis assessment.
Zonular dialysis; use Capsular Tension Ring (CTR) or CTS.
Late IOL-Capsular bag complex dislocation (Sunset Syndrome).
High risk of post-op IOP spikes and corneal decompensation.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: The 'Seidel Test' should be performed on every clear corneal wound if a leak is suspected.
Don't chase a dropped nucleus: If a large fragment goes south, perform vitrectomy and refer to a vitreoretinal surgeon.
Descemet's Detachment: Usually occurs at the incision; inject air or 20% SF6 to 're-bubble' the membrane.
IOL Power Error: Rule out wrong biometry or transcription error before considering IOL exchange or piggyback IOL.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Post-Cataract Surgery Complications: The Master Clinical Roadmap ---
sections.content: An exhaustive guide to identifying and managing post-cataract surgical complications, ranging from posterior capsule rupture to endophthalmitis. This poster integrates incidence statistics, intraoperative management protocols, and clinical pearls for the anterior segment surgeon.

sections.title: Signs of Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR)
content: Sudden deepening or shallowing of the Anterior Chamber (AC)
Momentary pupillary dilation
Nucleus falls away and cannot be approached by phaco tip
Marked slowing of aspiration due to clogged vitreous in phaco tip
Torn capsule may be directly visible
Vitreous gel may be directly visible

sections.title: Sequelae of Vitreous Loss after PCR
PCR Management: Core Principles
content: Management depends on the magnitude of the tear
Depends on the size and type of any residual lens material
Depends on the presence or absence of vitreous prolapse
CRITICAL: Do NOT pull out the phaco probe immediately (maintains AC pressure)

sections.title: PCR Surgical Protocol
content: Step 1: Inject dispersive viscoelastic before removing phaco probe
Step 2: If a complete or nearly complete nucleus remains, convert to ECCE
Step 3: If residual nuclear fragments, remove by phaco using low bottle height and low aspiration flow rate
Step 4: If large fragments, use visco-expression after extending the main wound
Step 5: Once remnants are removed, replug the tear with dispersive OVD
Step 6: Gently fill the AC with cohesive viscoelastic
Step 7: Use manual aspiration cannula with irrigation OFF to aspirate residual cortex
Step 8: Remove all vitreous from AC, wound, and capsular tear with a vitrector
Step 9: Infusion cannula of vitrector remains HIGH; Cutter remains LOW
Step 10: Visualize vitreous using 0.1 ml of 40mg/ml Triamcinolone

rows: Constrict pupil following PC IOL or prior to AC IOL

sections.title: Clinical Complications: Continuous List
sections.content: Additional complications noted include: Corneal decompensation, chronic endophthalmitis, and specific post-operative inflammation rates ranging from 2% to 6%. PCO remains a primary late complication at 10% within 2 years.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Acute Post-Op Vision Loss

rows: Immediate onset (12-24h), no pain, limbus-to-limbus edema
Elevated IOP, corneal edema, mid-dilated pupil
Loss of red reflex, sudden pain, AC shallowing

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Endophthalmitis (0.1%): Immediate referral if pain/hypopyon present
Choroidal Haemorrhage (0.1%): Intraoperative disaster requiring immediate wound closure
Loss of nuclear fragment posteriorly (0.3%): Requires vitreoretinal consultation
Wound leak (1%): Risk for hypotony and endophthalmitis
Iris Prolapse (0.7%): Requires surgical repair to prevent infection

content.explanation: D: Deepening/shallowing of AC. R: Red reflex change/loss. O: Out of reach nucleus (falls away). P: Pupil dilation (momentary).

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Vitreous Visualization
content: Always use preservative-free Triamcinolone (0.1ml of 40mg/ml) to stain vitreous strands.
Stained vitreous appears as white specks trapped in the gel, making clean-up far more precise.
Ensure AC is stable with OVD before starting the vitrectomy cutter.

sections.title: Acute GI Bleeding Management
content: 1. INITIAL ACTIONS: Protect airway, Nothing Per Oral (NPO), insert two large bore cannulae.
2. URGENT BLOODS: FBC, U&E, LFT, glucose, clotting screen, cross match 4-6 units.
3. RESUSCITATION: Rapid IV crystalloid infusion up to 1L.
4. SHOCK PROTOCOL: If signs of shock, give group specific or group O Rh -ve until crossmatch is done.
5. TRANSFUSION: Continue IV fluids to maintain BP; transfuse if HB < 7.
6. COAGULOPATHY: Correct clotting abnormalities using Vit K, FFP, and platelet concentration.
7. VARICEAL RISK: Give Terlipressin IV 1-2mg/6h and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
8. ICU & MONITORING: ICU referral, CVP insertion to guide fluid replacement (aim >5cm H2O).
9. RENAL/OUTPUT: Catheterize and monitor output (aim >30ml/h).
10. VITALS: Monitor every 15min until stable, then hourly. Notify surgeons of all severe bleeds.
11. DEFINITIVE CARE: Urgent endoscopy for diagnosis +/- control of bleeding at earliest point after resuscitation.

rows: Rate Control: Metoprolol (1-10mg IV), Verapamil (5-10mg IV), Digoxin (HF: 500mcg PO, then 500mcg/8h, then 250mcg/8h). Rhythm: Amiodarone.
Anticoagulation: Warfarin or NOAC. Cardioversion: DC under sedation if onset <48h or anticoagulated >3wks.
Aspirin 300mg or Ticagrelor 180mg. Morphine 5-10mg IV + Metoclopramide 10mg IV. PCI or Fibrinolysis.
12-lead ECG, bloods (FBC, U&E, Glu, Lipid, Troponin). Check pulse (both arms), JVP, murmurs, CHF signs, CXR.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Ophthalmic Regional Anesthesia Complications

rows: Conjunctival chemosis, subconjunctival hemorrhage, vortex vein injury, raised IOP, globe trauma, EOM damage.
Retrobulbar hemorrhage, Suprachoroidal block, block failure.
Globe perforation, oculocardiac reflex (OCR), expulsive retrobulbar hemorrhage, globe explosion.
Anaphylaxis, cardiorespiratory complications, neurological complications, Optic nerve injuries (AION), Amaurosis fugax.
Higher risk of optic nerve sheath penetration and brainstem anesthesia compared to Sub-tenon.

content.explanation: C: Coloboma; H: Heart defect; A: Atresia choanae; R: Retarded growth; G: Genital anomalies; E: Ear abnormality syndrome.

sections.title: Miller Fisher Syndrome (MFS)
content: Variant of Guillain-Barré Syndrome triggered by viral/bacterial infection.
TRIAD: Ophthalmoplegia, Ataxia, Areflexia.
Diagnostic Marker: Anti-GQ1b antibody.
Treatment: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG).
Prognosis: Self-limited; usually resolves within weeks to months.

sections.title: Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
content: Step 1: ABCs and 2 large bore cannulae.
Step 2: FLUIDS: 0.9% Saline over 1h. If Systolic BP <90, give 500ml bolus over 15min. If no improvement, ICU admission.
Step 3: INVESTIGATIONS: VBG (pH, Bicarb), Glucose (bedside/lab), U&E, FBC, CRP, CXR, ECG.
Step 4: INSULIN: 50 units Soluble Insulin in 50ml 0.9% Saline at 0.1 unit/kg/h. Continue long-acting insulin.
Step 5: TARGETS: Fall in ketones (0.5 mmol/L/h), raise bicarb (3 mmol/L/h), fall in glucose (3 mmol/L/h). Increase insulin by 1U/h if targets not met.
Step 6: MONITORING: Ketones hourly. VBG (pH, HCO3, K+) at 2, 4, 8, 12, 24 hours.
Step 7: POTASSIUM: Continue fluids and assess K+. Catheterize if no urine by 1h (aim 0.5ml/kg/h).
Step 8: COMPLICATIONS: NG tube if vomiting/drowsy. Start LMWH for all patients.
Step 9: HYPO PREVENTION: When glucose <14 mmol/L, start 10% Glucose at 125ml/h alongside Saline.
Step 10: DISCONTINUATION: Continue fixed-rate insulin until Ketones <0.6, pH >7.3, and Bicarb >15. Treat underlying infection.

branches: DKA Symptoms: Fruity breath, Nausea, Vomiting, Confusion
Hypoglycemia Symptoms: Shaking, Sweating, Tachycardia, Confusion, Irritability
HHS Management: LMWH, Slow rehydration (0.9% saline over 48h), Replace K+ when urine flows
HHS Targets: Glucose 10-15 mmol/L (first 24h) to avoid Cerebral Edema
HHS Insulin: Only if glucose not falling by 5mmol/L with hydration or if ketonaemia exists

sections.title: Hypoglycemia Management Protocol
content: CONSCIOUS/ORIENTED: 15-20g quick acting carbohydrate snack (200ml orange juice). Recheck glucose after 15m (repeat up to 3 times).
CONSCIOUS/UNCOOPERATIVE: Squirt glucose gel between teeth and gums.
UNCONSCIOUS/NON-RESPONDING: IV Glucose 10% at 200ml/15min OR Glucagon 1mg IV/IM.
STABILIZATION: Give long-acting carbohydrate when glucose > 4.0 mmol/L.

sections.title: Seizure Management Steps
content: 1. Secure airway, remove false teeth, 100% Oxygen + suction.
2. IV access: U&E, LFT, FBC, Glucose, Ca+2, Toxicology.
3. Lorazepam 4mg IV (2nd dose if no response in 10-20 min).
4. Thiamine 250mg IV (if alcohol/malnourishment) + Glucose 50ml (50%).
5. Correct Acidosis and Hypotension (fluids).
6. Phenytoin 15-18mg/kg (rate 50mg/min) with ECG/BP monitoring. Maint: 100mg 6-8 hourly.
7. Refractory: GA (Propofol) and Ventilation with continuous EEG in ICU.

branches: Goldmann Perimetry: Spiralling isopters (regress toward fixation)
VA Tests: Normal Stereoacuity = Normal VA; Reading vision normal despite poor Snellen
Color Vision: Normal Ishihara plate response = VA at least 6/24
Cross Cylinder: +6D fog in trial frame, rotate +3D/-3D cylinders to negate and encourage reading
Management: Reassurance, counseling, follow-up, Clinical Psychologist referral
Diagnostics: Normal VEP, MRI (contrast) of visual pathway, PET in exceptional cases

sections.title: Systemic Manifestations of Thyrotoxicosis
content: 1. Increased Temperature
2. Agitation / Psychosis / Panic
3. Confusion / Coma
4. Tachycardia / Palpitations
5. Atrial Fibrillation
6. Goitre / Thyroid Bruit
7. Acute Abdomen / Diarrhoea
8. Heart Failure
9. Weight Loss with Increased Appetite
10. Sweating / Heat Intolerance
11. Oligomenorrhoea / Infertility
12. Chorea / Itch / Urticaria

sections.title: Clinical Red Flags & Reminders
content: GI BLEEDING: Maintain CVP > 5cm H2O and Urine Output > 30ml/h.
DKA: Avoid hypoglycemia when glucose < 14 mmol/L; start 10% glucose.
HHS: Rehydrate slowly over 48 hours to prevent cerebral edema.
ANESTHESIA: Monitor for Oculocardiac Reflex (Bradycardia) during blocks.
THYROID: Be alert for 'Thyroid Storm' in patients with acute abdomen and tachycardia.
