sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Marfan syndrome is a systemic connective tissue disorder due to mutations in the FBN1 gene (15q21.1) encoding fibrillin-1. Pathophysiology involves defective microfibril formation, leading to TGF-beta dysregulation, causing weakened elastic fibers in the zonules, aortic media, and joint capsules.

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations
content: Ectopia Lentis (Superotemporal displacement in 60-80%)
Increased axial length (High Myopia)
Flat corneas (Cornea Plana)
Hypoplastic iris dilator muscle
Increased risk of Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment
Early-onset Glaucoma (Open or Closed angle)

sections.title: Red Flags: Life-Threatening
content: Aortic Root Dilatation (Z-score > 2.0)
Aortic Dissection (Type A)
Spontaneous Pneumothorax
Dural Ectasia (Lumbosacral pain)

content.explanation: M: Mitral valve prolapse, A: Aortic root dilation, R: Retinal detachment, F: Fibrillin, A: Arachnodactyly, N: Negative lens displacement (inferior in homocystinuria), S: Striae

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Step 1: Annual ophthalmic exam (Refraction, slit-lamp, fundus).
Step 2: Beta-blockers or ARBs (Losartan) to slow aortic root growth.
Step 3: Surgical intervention (Lens extraction if visual axis is obscured).
Step 4: Prophylactic laser retinopexy for high-risk peripheral retinal degeneration.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Ectopia lentis in Marfan usually displaces superotemporally due to weak superior zonules.
Homocystinuria presents with downward lens subluxation and should be ruled out via metabolic screening (urinary cyanide-nitroprusside test).
Avoid pilocarpine in lens subluxation as it induces miosis and potentially pupillary block if the lens is mobile.
Marfan patients undergoing cataract surgery are at high risk for zonular dialysis; consider capsular tension rings (CTR) or iris-claw intraocular lenses.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Marfan Syndrome: A Visual Guide to Connective Tissue Pathology ---
sections.content: Marfan syndrome is a systemic, autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene. It is characterized by specific ocular, cardiovascular, and skeletal manifestations that require lifelong monitoring.

sections.title: Ocular Hallmarks
content: Ectopia Lentis: Classic Upward and Superotemporal subluxation of the crystalline lens.
Zonular Integrity: Stretched or broken zonules (fibrillin-rich fibers).
Cornea Plana: Characteristically flat corneal curvature.
Increased Axial Length: Leading to high axial myopia.
Iris Hypoplasia: Resulting in transillumination defects and poor pupillary dilation.
Ciliary Body Hypoplasia: Often observed on ultrasound biomicroscopy.
Vitreous Liquefaction: Premature vitreous syneresis.

sections.title: Major Systemic Involvement
content: Cardiovascular: Aortic root aneurysm, Aortic dissection, Mitral valve prolapse (MVP).
Skeletal: Arachnodactyly (spider fingers), Pectus excavatum or carinatum, Scoliosis.
Integumentary: Striae atrophicae (stretch marks) without weight change.
Pulmonary: Spontaneous pneumothorax, apical blebs.
Dural Ectasia: Widening of the dural sac in the lumbosacral spine.

sections.title: Red Flag Complications
content: Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (High Risk due to axial length and vitreous changes)
Aortic Dissection (Life-threatening emergency)
Secondary Glaucoma (Angle-closure due to lens subluxation or pupillary block)
Presenile Cataracts (Nuclear sclerosis)
Endophthalmitis (Increased risk if lens surgery is required)

content.explanation: M: Mitral valve prolapse; A: Aortic Aneurysm; R: Retinal detachment; F: Fibrillin-1 mutation; A: Arachnodactyly; N: Near-sightedness (Myopia); S: Subluxated lens.

sections.title: Diagnostic Pathway: Ghent Criteria
content: Step 1: Clinical Evaluation of Systemic Score (>7 points).
Step 2: Slit-lamp exam to confirm Ectopia Lentis.
Step 3: Echocardiography to measure Aortic Root Z-score.
Step 4: Molecular Genetic Testing for FBN1 mutation.
Step 5: Review Family History of Marfan Syndrome.

sections.title: Exhaustive Overview of Marfan
sections.content: Marfan syndrome (MFS) is a pervasive multi-system genetic disorder. In the eye, the classic finding of ectopia lentis occurs because the zonular fibers, composed of fibrillin-1, are weak or absent. This leads to the lens being pulled toward the strongest remaining zonules, typically in a superior-temporal direction. Beyond the eye, the cardiovascular implications are the most life-threatening, particularly aortic root dilation which can lead to rupture. Skeletal features like a high-arched palate and joint hypermobility are common. Management requires a multidisciplinary team including ophthalmologists, cardiologists, and geneticists. Regular dilated fundus exams are mandatory to monitor for retinal tears and detachments, which occur at a higher frequency in this population due to increased axial length and collagen defects.

sections.title: Introduction to Angle Grading
sections.content: Gonioscopy remains the clinical gold standard for evaluating the iridocorneal angle. Accurate grading is crucial for differentiating between open-angle and angle-closure glaucomas, identifying risk factors for primary angle closure (PAC), and determining the necessity of laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI). While Shaffer's system is widely used for its simplicity, Spaeth's system provides a more granular anatomical description.

rows: Only Schwalbe's Line (+/- top of TM)

sections.title: The Spaeth System: (A) Iris Insertion
content: A (Anterior): Iris inserts anterior to Schwalbe's line.
B (Behind): Iris inserts posterior to Schwalbe's line but anterior to the Scleral Spur.
C (Scleral Spur): Iris inserts at the Scleral Spur.
D (Deep): Iris inserts into the Ciliary Body Band.
E (Extremely Deep): Iris inserts into the Scleral Wall/deep Ciliary Body.
Note: Parentheses (e.g., (D)) indicate the insertion seen upon indentation gonioscopy.

sections.title: The Spaeth System: (B) Angular Width
sections.content: This is the angle formed by a line tangential to the inner surface of the trabecular meshwork and a line tangential to the iris surface about one-third of the way from the periphery. It is recorded in degrees (e.g., 10°, 20°, 30°, 40°).

rows: Steep rise from insertion (often in high insertions)
Iris follows a straight plane from insertion

content.explanation: From Posterior to Anterior (Deep to Superficial): I (Iris), C (Ciliary Body Band), S (Scleral Spur), T (Trabecular Meshwork), S (Schwalbe's Line).

sections.title: Gonioscopy Red Flags
content: Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS) bridging the angle
Neovascularization of the Angle (NVA) crossing Scleral Spur
Sampaolesi Line (pigment on or anterior to Schwalbe's Line)
Double Hump Sign on indentation (Plateau Iris)
Blood in Schlemm's Canal (Elevated EVP/Sturge-Weber)

sections.title: The Dynamic Gonioscopy Process
content: Step 1: Patient Selection - Ensure topical anesthesia and no recent surgery/trauma.
Step 2: Lens Choice - Use a Zeiss/Sussman four-mirror lens for indentation (no coupling gel) or Goldmann lens for stability.
Step 3: Dim the Lights - Minimize miosis; use a short, narrow slit beam avoiding the pupil to prevent false opening.
Step 4: Primary View - Identify the most posterior structure visible without manipulation.
Step 5: Indentation - Apply gentle pressure to the cornea to force aqueous into the angle, distinguishing appositional from synechial closure.
Step 6: Documentation - Record Grade (Shaffer or Spaeth), Pigment (0-4+), and abnormalities (NVA/PAS).

branches: Scleral Spur: Attachment for Ciliary Muscle
Ciliary Body Band: Dull gray/brown band
Iris Processes: Fine extensions from iris to TM
Pupillary Block: Most common; aqueous trapped behind iris
Plateau Iris: Anteriorly positioned ciliary processes
Lens-Induced: Phacomorphic (large lens) or Ectopia Lentis
Posterior Pushing: Suprachoroidal hemorrhage or Effusion
Anterior Pulling: PAS from inflammation or NVA

sections.title: Surgical/Laser Decision Algorithm
content: 1. Perform Gonioscopy: Identify Grade 0-2 or ITC (Iridotrabecular Contact).
2. Dynamic Gonioscopy: Is it appositional? (Opens with pressure).
3. Assess Risk: High IOP, PAS, or symptomatic?
4. Intervention: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) for pupillary block.
5. Post-LPI Gonioscopy: If angle remains narrow, consider Plateau Iris or Phacomorphic components.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: Always check the 'worst' quadrant (usually superior) as it is typically the narrowest.
Use the '10 o'clock/2 o'clock' rule for PAS: they are usually broader and higher than iris processes.
In Spaeth's system, 'D40f' describes a wide, deep, flat angle—the 'ideal' open angle.
Plateau iris is suggested when the angle is narrow but the central AC is deep.

sections.title: Recent Advances: AS-OCT vs. Gonioscopy
sections.content: While Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT) provides objective, reproducible measurements of the Angle Opening Distance (AOD) and Trabecular Iris Space Area (TISA), it cannot distinguish between appositional and synechial closure as effectively as dynamic gonioscopy. AS-OCT is an excellent screening tool but does not replace the expert clinical assessment of the Spaeth system.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Mastering the Anterior Chamber Angle: Clinical Evaluation & Gonioscopy ---
sections.content: The definitive guide to anterior chamber angle assessment, transitioning from clinical suspicion to precise, evidence-based gonioscopic grading for glaucoma management.

sections.title: Anatomy: The Angle Landmarks (Schwalbe to Ciliary Body)
content: 1. Schwalbe's Line: Termination of Descemet's membrane.
2. Non-pigmented Trabecular Meshwork: Posterior to Schwalbe's.
3. Pigmented Trabecular Meshwork: Primary site of aqueous outflow.
4. Scleral Spur: The most anterior projection of the sclera; attachment site of the ciliary muscle.
5. Ciliary Body Band: The vascularized, darker, most posterior structure visible.

sections.title: Gonioscopy Red Flags
content: Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS)
Iris processes masking the angle
Neovascularization of the angle (NVA)
Blood in Schlemm's Canal (high episcleral venous pressure)
Exfoliation material on the trabecular meshwork

content.mnemonic: I Can See The Scleral Spur
content.explanation: I (Iris) - C (Ciliary Body) - S (Scleral Spur) - T (Trabecular Meshwork) - S (Schwalbe's Line). Posterior to Anterior.

sections.title: Technique: Dynamic Gonioscopy
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic; ensure patient is upright or supine.
Step 2: Apply gonioscopy lens (e.g., Goldmann 3-mirror or Posner 4-mirror) with viscoelastic coupling agent.
Step 3: Keep the beam narrow and vertical (1-2mm width) to avoid light-induced pupil constriction.
Step 4: Use indentation (compression) gonioscopy to differentiate appositional from synechial closure.
Step 5: If angle opens under compression, the closure is appositional (potential for LPI).

sections.title: Recent Advances: Imaging vs. Gonioscopy
content: AS-OCT (Anterior Segment OCT): Non-contact, high resolution (5-10 microns). Useful for objectively measuring AOD500 (Angle Opening Distance at 500 microns).
UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy): 35-50 MHz frequency. The gold standard for visualizing structures behind the iris (e.g., ciliary cysts, ciliary body position).
Note: Gonioscopy remains the clinical gold standard as it allows for direct observation of pigment and PAS that OCT may miss.

summary: Mastering the gold standards of axial length measurement is fundamental to modern refractive surgery and intraocular lens power calculations. sections.title: The IOL Power Formula Imperative
content: Axial Length (AL) error of 1mm = ~2.5 to 3.0 D of IOL power error.
Optical biometry is the gold standard for modern formulas (Barrett Universal II, Hill-RBF, Kane).
Ultrasound remains the fallback for dense cataracts where laser light cannot reach the RPE.

branches: Optical: Routine phaco, Refractive lens exchange, Post-LASIK (if topography available)
Contact US: Dense PSC/Nuclear cataracts, Corneal opacity, Vitreous hemorrhage
Immersion US: Superior to contact (avoids compression artifact)

sections.title: Red Flags: Avoiding 'IOL Surprise'
content: Corneal compression during contact A-scan (leads to falsely short AL).
Poor fixation during optical biometry (leads to decentered measurement).
Failure to account for silicone oil (requires specialized velocity settings in US).
Inaccurate velocity settings (standard: 1550m/s for phakic eyes, 1532m/s for aphakic).
Anisometropia > 0.3mm difference between eyes without clinical explanation.

sections.title: Diagnostic Protocol: Ultrasound
content: Step 1: Topical anesthesia (Proparacaine).
Step 2: Ensure perpendicular probe alignment (maximize echo spikes).
Step 3: Immersion shell placement (Prager shell) to prevent compression.
Step 4: Capture 5-10 readings; discard outliers.
Step 5: Verify standard deviation < 0.1mm.

sections.title: Diagnostic Protocol: Optical
content: Step 1: Patient alignment (chin rest, fixation light).
Step 2: Automated signal peak acquisition.
Step 3: Check SNR (Signal-to-Noise Ratio) > 2.0.
Step 4: If poor signal due to cataract, repeat 3-5 times.
Step 5: Compare K-readings with manual keratometry if discrepant.

content.explanation: O: Optical (Laser); P: Precise (micron-level); T: Tissue (RPE target); I: Interferometry; C: Cataract-limited (requires optical clarity).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always measure the fellow eye to confirm symmetry.
In staphylomatous eyes, optical biometry may target the fovea rather than the absolute posterior pole.
Immersion ultrasound is significantly more accurate than contact ultrasound because it eliminates indentation.
Post-refractive surgery: Use Barrett True-K or Hill-RBF with clinical history method as a check.
Always verify the IOL formula constants (A-constant) are optimized for the specific biometer used.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Precision Ocular Biometry: IOL Master vs. Ultrasound ---
sections.content: Mastering the shift from acoustic to optical biometry is fundamental for modern refractive cataract surgery. This guide compares gold-standard optical coherence interferometry with immersion A-scan ultrasound to optimize IOL power calculations.

sections.title: Indications for A-Scan Ultrasound
content: Dense mature cataracts (White/Black/Brown cataracts)
Advanced posterior subcapsular cataracts
Vitreous hemorrhage or dense asteroid hyalosis
Corneal scarring preventing light penetration
Phthisis bulbi or microphthalmos
Fixation difficulties or nystagmus

sections.title: The IOL Master Process
content: Step 1: Patient alignment to the chinrest; fixate on the internal target.
Step 2: Dual-beam emission to measure axial length (AL) from tear film to RPE.
Step 3: Automated keratometry using 6 spots in a hexagonal pattern.
Step 4: White-to-White (WTW) measurement for anterior segment evaluation.
Step 5: Automated calculation using SRK/T, Holladay 2, or Barrett Universal II formulas.

sections.title: Gold Standard: Immersion vs. Contact
content: Immersion Technique: Use a Prager shell filled with BSS; avoids direct pressure on the globe, decreasing error by ~0.15mm.
Contact Technique: Risk of corneal indentation leading to artifactual shortening of the AL by up to 0.5mm, causing hyperopic shift.
Standardized Velocity: Always confirm 1550 m/s in phakic eyes. Use 1532 m/s for aphakic and 1532 m/s for pseudophakic eyes.
Signal Quality: Ensure clear retinal spike with 80-100% gain.

content.explanation: O: Optical is best (IOL Master); I: Immersion is second; L: Least precise is contact (Log/Applanation).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A 1mm error in AL measurement results in a ~2.5D error in IOL power calculation.
Always compare eyes: AL difference between two eyes should typically be <0.3mm.
Refractive Surprise: Always re-verify biometry if the calculated IOL power differs by >1.0D from the predicted emmetropic power.
Modern Formula Evolution: Shift from regression formulas (SRK II) to vergence-based formulas (Barrett, Hill-RBF, Haigis) to account for effective lens position (ELP).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is a true vascular emergency of the eye, analogous to a cerebral stroke. It occurs when the main artery supplying the inner retina is obstructed, leading to acute ischemia. The foveola remains red (the 'Cherry-Red Spot') because it is thin and receives oxygen from the underlying choriocapillaris, while the surrounding infarcted retinal nerve fiber layer becomes opaque and white.

branches: Calcific: Heart valves, white/dull, more obstructive

sections.title: Pathophysiological Mechanisms
content: Intracellular edema of the inner 2/3 of the retina (Ganglion Cell Layer).
Pyknosis of nuclei and eventual necrosis of retinal elements.
Survival window: In primates, irreversible damage occurs after 90–240 minutes of total occlusion.
Cilioretinal artery presence (15–30% of population) may preserve the foveal region.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD): Rapidly present, often profound.
Cherry-Red Spot: Macular center remains red against white retina.
Box-carring: Segmentation of the blood column in retinal veins.
Cattle-tracking: Interrupted flow in retinal arterioles.
Narrowed Arterioles: Severe attenuation and straightening.
Optic Disc Edema: More common in the Arteritic (GCA) variety.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Strategy
content: 1. Immediate Clinical Exam & VA testing.
2. STAT ESR, CRP, and Platelets (Rule out GCA).
3. Multi-modal Imaging: OCT and FFA.
4. Systemic Workup: Carotid Doppler, Echocardiography (TEE preferred).
5. Neurology Referral: Evaluation for acute stroke (MRI/MRA).

rows: Marked delay in arm-to-retina & filling time

sections.title: Emergency Management Protocol
content: 1. Digital Ocular Massage: Firm pressure for 10-15s, then release (dislodge embolus).
2. Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: 0.1-0.2ml removal using 30G needle at limbus.
3. IOP Reduction: Acetazolamide 500mg IV/PO + topical Beta-blockers/Alpha-agonists.
4. Vasodilation: Breathe into a paper bag (increase CO2) or Carbogen therapy.
5. Systemic: Aspirin 325mg and urgent Stroke Center transfer.

branches: Commotio Retinae: History of trauma (Berlin's edema)
BRAO: Focal whitening in a vascular distribution
Tay-Sachs / Storage Diseases: Bilateral, chronic, pediatric
Quinine Toxicity: Rapid onset, history of ingestion

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS: GCA Warning
content: Scalp tenderness or Jaw Claudication
New-onset headache in elderly patients
Proximal muscle aches (Polymyalgia Rheumatica)
Bilateral vision loss (indicates imminent disaster)
Elevated ESR (>50) or CRP (>10)

content.explanation: C: Cilioretinal sparing (sometimes), H: Hollenhorst plaques, E: Emergency workup needed, R: Red spot (macula), R: Reduced VA (acute/painless), Y: Yield (High stroke risk).

sections.title: Complications & Long-term Monitoring
content: Neovascularization of the Iris (NVI): Occurs in ~18% of cases (Rubeosis Iridis).
Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG): Onset typically 4-12 weeks (the '100-day' window).
Neovascularization of the Disc (NVD): Less common than in CRVO.
Retinal Atrophy: Chronic inner retinal thinning on OCT.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The EAGLE Study investigated Intra-arterial Fibrinolysis (tPA). It found no significant visual benefit compared to conservative management and noted a higher risk of adverse events. Current consensus favors rapid stroke center evaluation. Newer studies are exploring Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) within 8 hours as a potentially effective adjunct.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: CRAO is an Ocular Stroke until proven otherwise—check the carotids and the heart.
In a patient under 50, consider thrombophilia workup, trauma, or vasospastic triggers (Migraine/Cocaine).
Digital massage should be done with a Goldman lens or finger to fluctuate IOP and 'flush' the clot.
If the cherry-red spot is missing but VA is NLP, suspect Ophthalmic Artery Occlusion (no choroidal flow).

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Ocular Stroke: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) ---
sections.content: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is a true ocular emergency characterized by sudden, painless monocular vision loss. It represents the ocular equivalent of a cerebral stroke and requires immediate neuro-ophthalmic triage.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: CRAO is an infarction of the inner retinal layers due to blockage of the central retinal artery. The central retinal artery is an end-artery, meaning there is no collateral circulation. Retinal viability is lost after approximately 90-100 minutes of total occlusion.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Fundoscopy
content: Sudden, profound painless loss of vision (typically 'counting fingers' or 'hand motion').
Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD) — often profound.
Fundoscopy: 'Cherry-red spot' at the fovea (due to choroidal blood supply).
Retinal whitening: Edematous, necrotic inner retina.
Cattle-trucking (segmentation of blood flow in arterioles).

rows: Scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, ESR/CRP elevation

sections.title: Emergency Protocols
content: Rule out Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) with STAT ESR, CRP, and Platelet count.
Immediate stroke workup (Carotid Doppler, EKG, Echo, MRI Brain) is mandatory.
Irreversible retinal damage occurs after 90-100 minutes of occlusion.
Rule out hypercoagulable states in patients under 50 years of age.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Ocular massage (digital pressure to induce movement of embolus).
Step 2: Lower Intraocular Pressure (Topical timolol, acetazolamide 500mg IV).
Step 3: Paracentesis (if within 2-4 hours, though efficacy is debated).
Step 4: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (if available within 8-24 hours).
Step 5: Systemic anticoagulation/thrombolytics (if indicated by neuro-consult).

content.explanation: S: Sudden vision loss, T: Thinning of vessels, O: Ocular massage, K: Kidney function check (for contrast), E: ESR/CRP for GCA.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Cilioretinal artery sparing: Occurs in 15-30% of eyes, preserving central visual acuity.
Always listen for carotid bruits.
Follow-up for NVI/NVA (Neovascularization) at 4-6 weeks.
Prognosis is generally poor; no randomized trial has proven superiority of a single treatment.

title: Merged: VIP:::FRCS:DKA: Systemic Emergency & Ophthalmic Implications
summary: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening triad of hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. While primarily systemic, it presents critical ophthalmic risks including acute refractive shifts, snowflake cataracts, and the vision-threatening emergency of Rhino-orbital-cerebral Mucormycosis.

branches: Ketosis: Presence of Acetoacetate/β-hydroxybutyrate in blood or urine
Metabolic Acidosis: Arterial pH <7.30 or Bicarbonate <18 mEq/L

rows: Osmotic swelling of the lens and changes in aqueous refractive index.
Subcapsular opacities due to sudden osmotic stress; may be reversible with slow control.
Severe dehydration leading to decreased aqueous production by ciliary body.
Can occur due to cranial nerve palsies or secondary Mucormycosis.
Secondary to invasive fungal infections (Mucor/Rhizopus) in acidotic states.
Creamy white appearance of retinal vessels when serum triglycerides >2500 mg/dL.

sections.title: CRITICAL EMERGENCY: Mucormycosis
content: Rhino-orbital-cerebral Mucormycosis is a fatal fungal infection triggered by DKA.
Red Flag: Black necrotic eschar on the palate or turbinates.
Red Flag: Orbital Apex Syndrome (CN III, IV, VI, V1 involvement) + Vision Loss.
Mechanism: Acidosis releases iron from sequestering proteins, feeding fungal growth (Rhizopus/Mucor).
Treatment: URGENT surgical debridement + IV Amphotericin B + Reversal of Acidosis.

sections.title: Systemic Pathophysiology
content: 1. Absolute Insulin Deficiency + Counter-regulatory Hormone Excess (Glucagon, Cortisol).
2. Increased Lipolysis → Increased Free Fatty Acids.
3. Hepatic Ketogenesis → Production of Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate.
4. Ketoacidosis → Bicarbonate buffering exhaustion.
5. Osmotic Diuresis → Profound dehydration and electrolyte depletion (K+, Na+).

sections.title: Stepwise Management Protocol
content: 1. Fluid Resuscitation: 1L 0.9% NaCl over 1 hour, then adjust based on Na+ status.
2. Potassium Replacement: If K+ <5.2 mEq/L, start replacement BEFORE or with insulin. If K+ <3.3, hold insulin.
3. Insulin Therapy: 0.1 Unit/kg bolus followed by 0.1 U/kg/hr infusion. Goal: Reduce glucose by 50-75 mg/dL/hr.
4. Glucose Switch: When blood glucose reaches 200 mg/dL, add 5% Dextrose (D5NS) to prevent hypoglycemia.
5. Bicarbonate: Only if pH <6.9. Rarely used due to risk of paradoxical CSF acidosis.

content.explanation: D: Dehydration (Isotonic Saline); K: Potassium (Replace even if normal due to total body depletion); A: Anion Gap (Target the gap, not just the glucose).

rows: History of binge, lower glucose levels

sections.title: Ocular Investigation & Imaging
content: Dilated Fundus Exam: Monitor for progression of DR after rapid glycemic control (Early Worsening Phenomenon).
CT/MRI Orbit & Sinuses: Indicated if any ptosis, proptosis, or ophthalmoplegia (Rule out Mucor).
A-Scan/B-Scan: Evaluate lens thickness and vitreous status if view is obscured.
IOP Measurement: High importance as hypotony reflects systemic hydration status.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Pseudohyponatremia: Measured Na+ drops 1.6 mEq/L for every 100 mg/dL glucose elevation.
Paradoxical DR Worsening: Aggressive insulin therapy can temporarily exacerbate Diabetic Retinopathy.
Euglycemic DKA: Seen in patients on SGLT2 inhibitors (Canagliflozin); pH is low but glucose is <250.
Cerebral Edema: Most common cause of death in pediatric DKA patients; monitor for headache and bradycardia.

sections.title: Recent Landmark Studies
sections.content: The DCCT (Diabetic Control and Complications Trial) and EDIC follow-up studies established the 'Metabolic Memory' concept. While intensive control prevents long-term DR, rapid correction in the setting of DKA/severe hyperglycemia can lead to transient worsening of soft exudates and macular edema. The CLOVER trial and various ADA guidelines emphasize that managing DKA requires focusing on the anion gap closure rather than just normalization of blood glucose.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Hemodynamics
sections.content: Carotid-cavernous fistulae (CCF) represent an arteriovenous shunt where blood flows directly or indirectly from the internal or external carotid arteries into the cavernous sinus. This reverses the normal pressure gradient, leading to venous hypertension in the ophthalmic veins, causing 'arterialization' of the conjunctival vessels and orbital congestion.

rows: Mild features, often spontaneous in post-menopausal women.
Slow onset, localized to orbital congestion.
Meningeal branches of both ICA and ECA
Most common 'indirect' type; can mimic chronic conjunctivitis.

sections.title: The Dandy's Triad of Direct CCF
EMERGENCY: Vision-Threatening Red Flags
content: Rapidly declining Visual Acuity (Compressive Optic Neuropathy)
IOP > 40 mmHg (Secondary Glaucoma risk)
Pulsatile Exophthalmos with Cornea Exposure
Severe Intracranial Hemorrhage signs
Abrupt worsening of Proptosis (Venous Thrombosis risk)

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Corkscrew epibulbar vessels: Dilated, tortuous vessels reaching the limbus.
Ophthalmoplegia: CN VI is most common (intracavernous), followed by III and IV.
Raised IOP: Due to increased episcleral venous pressure and choroidal effusions.
Fundus: Dilated retinal veins, intraretinal hemorrhages, disc edema (Venous Stasis Retinopathy).
RAPD: Positive if there is significant optic nerve compression or ischemic neuropathy.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: 1. Bedside Auscultation: Listen for bruit over the globe or temple.
2. Non-Invasive Imaging: CTA or MRA to look for 'flow voids' and SOV enlargement.
3. B-Scan Ultrasound: Identify dilated Superior Ophthalmic Vein (SOV).
4. Formal Gold Standard: Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) for definitive mapping.
5. Tonometry/Gonioscopy: Assess IOP and angle neovascularization.

rows: Confirms the exact site of the fistula.

content.explanation: A: Artery (ICA direct), B: Branches of ICA, C: Carotid (External) branches, D: Dual (Both ICA/ECA branches).

sections.title: Management Hierarchy
content: Step 1: Observation - Indicated for low-flow (Type B,C,D) as 50-70% may spontaneously thrombose.
Step 2: Carotid Massage - Digital compression of the carotid artery to induce thrombosis (only for low-flow).
Step 3: Endovascular Intervention - First-line for Direct CCF. Transarterial or transvenous coiling.
Step 4: Embolic Agents - Use of detachable coils, Onyx, or N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA).
Step 5: Surgical Ligation - Historically significant, but rarely used in the modern endovascular era.

sections.title: Surgical & Endovascular Techniques
content: Transvenous route: Often accessed via the Inferior Petrosal Sinus.
SOV Cutdown: Surgical exposure of the Superior Ophthalmic Vein for coil delivery if other routes fail.
Flow-Diverting Stents: Emerging technology for complex ICA wall defects.
Balloon Occlusion: Detachable balloons (though less common now than coils).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'White-Eyed CCF': Indirect fistulae can present very subtly, mimicking chronic conjunctivitis that doesn't respond to drops.
Trauma + Bruit: Post-head injury patient with a pulse-synchronous sound is Type A until proven otherwise.
Paradoxical Worsening: Symptoms may worsen immediately after successful treatment due to temporary thrombosis-related inflammation.
The 6th Nerve: CN VI is the most vulnerable as it sits freely within the cavernous sinus.

rows: Cortical venous reflux from the shunt.

sections.title: Landmark Study: Barrow et al. (1985)
sections.content: The seminal paper 'Vascular malformations of the cavernous sinus' established the A-D classification system. It remains the clinical foundation for determining whether a fistula requires urgent endovascular intervention (High-flow Type A) or can be managed conservatively (Low-flow Types B-D).

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Carotid-Cavernous Fistula (CCF): The Vascular Shunt Spectrum ---
sections.content: A Carotid-Cavernous Fistula is an abnormal communication between the carotid arterial system and the cavernous sinus. It represents a complex neuro-ophthalmic emergency that requires precise classification and multi-disciplinary management to prevent permanent vision loss or intracranial catastrophe.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: A Carotid-Cavernous Fistula (CCF) is a high- or low-flow communication between the internal or external carotid arteries (or their branches) and the cavernous sinus. This results in high-pressure arterial blood entering the low-pressure venous cavernous sinus, leading to venous engorgement of the orbit and globe. It is a potentially sight-threatening and life-threatening condition depending on the flow dynamics and venous drainage patterns.

rows: Direct shunt between ICA and Cavernous Sinus
Dural shunt: Meningeal branches of ICA
Dural shunt: Meningeal branches of ECA
Dural shunt: Meningeal branches of ICA + ECA

content.explanation: P: Pulsatile Proptosis (with thrill). C: Conjunctival Chemosis (corkscrew vessels). B: Bruit (heard over the globe or temple).

sections.title: Red Flags: Impending Danger
content: Cortical Venous Reflux (High risk of ICH/Stroke)
Rapidly Progressive Visual Loss (AION or Glaucoma)
Massive Epistaxis (Rupture into Sphenoid Sinus)
New-onset 3rd, 4th, or 6th Nerve Palsy

sections.title: Comprehensive Clinical Features
content: Corkscrew Vessels: Dilated, tortuous epibulbar veins reaching the limbus.
Increased Intraocular Pressure (IOP): Due to elevated episcleral venous pressure and choroidal effusions.
Ophthalmoplegia: Usually CN VI (intracavernous) first, followed by III and IV.
Pulsatile Proptosis: Best seen by observing the patient's profile or with an exophthalmometer.
Fundus Findings: Venous dilation, disc edema, intraretinal hemorrhages (Central Retinal Vein Occlusion-like).
Anterior Segment: Ischemia, corneal edema, iris neovascularization (rare).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Hierarchy
content: 1. Clinical Auscultation: Listening for a bruit with a stethoscope diaphragm over the globe.
2. Non-Invasive Imaging: CTA or MRA to identify enlarged Superior Ophthalmic Veins (SOV).
3. Ultrasound: B-scan/Color Doppler showing reversed (arterialized) flow in the SOV.
4. Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): The GOLD STANDARD to identify the shunt site and venous drainage.
5. Tonometry: High-amplitude ocular pulsations on Goldmann Tonometry.

rows: Bilateral usually, EOM enlargement (tendon sparing), no bruit.
Fever, leukocytosis, pain on eye movement, no pulsation.
Acute onset pain, dramatic response to steroids.
Systemic illness, rapid progression, usually secondary to infection.

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: IOP Control: Beta-blockers, Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (avoid miotics).
Lubrication: Management of exposure keratopathy.
Observation: Appropriate for low-flow dural CCFs (Type B-D) as 50% may spontaneously close.
Carotid Massage: 10 mins/hour in selected low-flow cases (contraindicated in carotid stenosis).

content.explanation: O: Oculomotor (III), T: Trochlear (IV), O: Ophthalmic (V1), M: Maxillary (V2). C: Carotid (ICA), A: Abducens (VI), T: T (Structural mnemonic).

sections.title: Ocular Complications & Prognosis
content: Secondary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (Choroidal effusion).
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME).
Proliferative Retinopathy (Hypoxia induced).
Permanent Cranial Nerve Palsy.
Post-treatment transient increase in symptoms (Normal).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: Dural CCFs are often misdiagnosed as 'chronic conjunctivitis' due to the red eye.
If IOP is high and the eye is pulsing, think CCF first.
The 6th nerve is the most common palsy because it sits freely within the cavernous sinus next to the ICA.
Venous drainage to the contralateral cavernous sinus can cause 'bilateral' symptoms from a 'unilateral' fistula.
Superior Ophthalmic Vein (SOV) diameter > 2mm on CT is highly suggestive of CCF.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Evidence
sections.content: Recent studies emphasize the use of Onyx (ethylene vinyl alcohol copolymer) for more durable dural fistula closure compared to coils alone. The trans-inferior petrosal sinus (IPS) remains the preferred transvenous route; however, when the IPS is thrombosed, direct orbital access to the SOV via lid crease incision is a highly successful secondary technique used by combined neuro-interventional and ophthalmic plastic surgery teams.

sections.title: Stroke: Definition & Clinical Manifestation
sections.content: Definition: ischemic infarction (or bleeding into) any part of the brain. It manifests by rapid onset (over minutes) of focal CNS signs and symptoms (contralateral hemiplegia & sensory loss + homonymous hemianopia).

branches: CNS bleed (hypertension, trauma and aneurysm rupture)

sections.title: Risk Factors
content: Hypertension
Hypercholesterolemia
Smoking
DM
Heart disease (AF, valvular, ischaemic)

sections.title: Immediate Management Protocol
content: 1. Call for help.
2. A → Adequate ventilation.
3. B → Oxygenation.
4. C → Circulation → IV line.
5. Document Level of consciousness.
6. Vital sign monitoring: For hypertension, admit and control over days not hours.
7. Admission to stroke units for nursing/physio (saves lives and provides motivation).

rows: Within a few days to differentiate hemorrhagic from ischemic if considering anticoagulation.
Meningism, severe headache, and coma within hours.
Carotid bruit, AF, and past TIA.

content.explanation: NB1. TIA: sudden onset of focal CNS signs (resolve within few minutes) due to temporary occlusion, usually by emboli, of part of cerebral circulation. NB2: carotid bruit may signify stenosis (>30%), often near internal carotid origin. Best heard behind the angle of the jaw.

sections.title: Comprehensive Investigations List
content: FBC
CXR
ECG
ESR
U&E
Lipids
Blood glucose
Clotting tests
Echo
Carotid doppler
Carotid angiography

sections.title: Stroke Treatment Strategy
content: Aspirin: 300mg/24h PO (unless strong suspicion of CNS bleeding).
Nil by mouth if swallowing is a problem.
Maintain hydration: Do not over-hydrate (cerebral edema).
Monitor and treat ↑ BP.
Immediate evacuation: Refer if cerebellar hemorrhage is possible.
Nursing care: Turn regularly and keep dry (consider catheterization) to stop bed sores.
DVT Prophylaxis: Passive limb movements, subcutaneous heparin, and compressing stockings.
Support: Emotional support and rehabilitation.

sections.title: Thrombolysis & Prevention
content: NB Thrombolysis: Alteplase within 3h of onset may decrease adverse outcomes (trials). Requires dedicated 24h CNS thrombolysis teams. Note: Not yet recommended in the UK in 2016.
Prevention 1: Control risk factors.
Prevention 2: Exercise (↑ HDL).
Prevention 3: Life long anticoagulants for rheumatic/prosthetic heart valves on left side.
Prevention 4: Aspirin 75 mg/day for life.

sections.title: Increased Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
content: Normal ICT: 0-10 mmHg.
Causes: Tumours (1ry or metastatic), Head injury, Brain haemorrhage (any type).
Causes: Infection (meningitis, encephalitis, brain abscess), Hydrocephalus, Cerebral oedema, Status epilepticus.

sections.title: Signs & Symptoms of ICP
content: Headache, vomiting ± nausea.
Deterioration of consciousness: drowsiness, irritability, seizures, coma.
Cushing’s response: ↓ pulse, ↑ BP & Cheyne-Stokes respiration.
Ophthalmic: ↓ VA & peripheral visual field loss.
Ophthalmic: Pupil changes (constriction 1st, later dilatation). DON’T DILATE.
Papilloedema: Loss of previous spontaneous venous pulsation. (If preserved, exclude papilloedema).

sections.title: ICP Management
content: 1. ABC (Intubate if needed).
2. Correct hypotension & treat seizures.
3. Brief history & examination.
4. Elevate head of bed 30º- 40º.
5. Mannitol 20%: 1-2g/kg IV over 10-20 min (5mL/kg). Clinical effect after 20 min, lasts 2-6h. Aim for serum osmolarity 300 mosmol/kg.
6. Dexamethasone: 10 mg IV then 4 mg/6h IV/PO (if cerebral oedema).
7. Fluid restriction to < 1.5L/d.
8. Close monitoring of ICP & vitals.
9. Search for cause & treat factors like hyperglycaemia, hyponatraemia.
10. Refer to neurosurgeon for definitive treatment.

sections.title: Hypoglycemia Treatment
content: Give 200–300 mL of 10% dextrose IV (20-30g).
OR Glucagon 1mg IM (if no IV access; will not work in drunk patients).
Once conscious: give sugary drinks & a meal.
Thiamine 1-2 mg/kg IV: if malnutrition or alcohol suspicion.
If oral hypoglycemic history: Admission for 10% glucose over 1-2 hours.

sections.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
sections.content: DKA coma only occurs in type I D.M (IDDM); it may be the mode of presentation. Diagnosis requires: hyperglycaemia + ketosis + metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.3).

sections.title: DKA: Signs & Precipitants
content: Signs: Gradual drowsiness, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, polydipsia, lethargy, anorexia, polyuria, ketotic breath, coma.
Precipitants: Infection, surgery, MI, chemotherapy, non-compliance, or wrong insulin dose.

sections.title: DKA Fluid Replacement Protocol
content: 1. IV 0.9% saline immediately (Dehydration correction is priority).
2. 1L stat.
3. 1L over next 1 hour.
4. 1L over next 2 hours.
5. 1L over next 4 hours.
6. 1L over next 6 hours.
7. Use Dextrose 5% when blood glucose is < 10 mmol/L.
8. Caution in elderly/heart failure; monitor CVP.

sections.title: DKA Insulin & Potassium Management
content: Insulin Pump: 50U soluble insulin in 50ml saline (1U/ml). Give 4-8 U/h if glucose > 20mmol/L. Aim for fall of 5 mmol/L per h.
If No Pump: Load 20U IM, then 4-6 U/h IM while glucose > 10mmol/L.
K+ Replacement: Add 20-40mmol/L to IV fluid (Normal K+: 3.5-5).
K+ Shifting: Serum K+ is high in DKA due to lack of insulin, but total body K+ is low. Insulin shifts K+ into cells; must monitor to prevent hypokalaemia/arrhythmias.
K+ Timing: Don't add to 1st bag. Start when urine flow > 30ml/h.

rows: Longer history (1 wk), glucose > 35 mmol/L, marked dehydration.
Focal CNS signs, DIC, DVT (fully heparinize).
Rehydration with 0.9% saline (1/2 DKA rate) over 48h. Heparinize.

sections.title: Hyperthyroid Crisis (Thyrotoxic Storm)
content: Signs: Hyperpyrexia (>41°C), Tachycardia (>140bpm), AF, CHF, Diarrhea, Vomiting, Agitation, Coma.
Precipitated by: Infection, trauma, MI, stroke, stopping antithyroid meds, surgery, radioiodine.
Propranolol: 40 mg/8h PO or 1 mg IV over 1min (unless asthma/heart failure).
Carbimazole: 15-25 mg/6h PO; followed by Lugol’s solution 0.3 mL/8h after 4h.
Hydrocortisone: 100 mg/6h IV or Dexamethasone 4 mg/6h PO (blocks T4 to T3 conversion).
Aspirin Warning: Avoid Aspirin as it can ↑ T4.

sections.title: Myxoedema Coma
content: Signs: Hypothyroid, >65yrs, hypothermia, hyporeflexia, ↓ glucose, bradycardia, goitre, cyanosis.
Management: High flow O2, Correct hypoglycaemia.
T3: 5-20 ug/12h IV slowly (Caution: may precipitate ischaemia).
Hydrocortisone: 100 mg/8h IV if pituitary cause suspected.
Avoid precipitating LVF with saline.

sections.title: Addisonian & Hypopituitary Crisis
content: Addisonian: Endocrinal shock, hypoglycemia. Treat with Hydrocortisone 100mg/6h IV and IV fluids.
Hypopituitary: Refractory hypotension, short stature, loss of axillary/pubic hair, hypoglycaemia.
Hypopituitary Management: Hydrocortisone IV first, then Liothyronine (T3) 10 ug/12h PO. Surgery if pituitary apoplexy.

sections.title: Pheochromocytoma
content: Definition: Rare catecholamine-producing tumour of adrenal medulla.
Signs: Pallor, pulsating headache, malignant hypertension, VT, cardiogenic shock.
Emergency Management: Phentolamine 2-5 mg IV (repeat to maintain safe BP).
Follow-up: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg/24h PO (titrate up to 30 mg).
Elective surgery usually performed after 4-6 weeks.

title: Lateral Dermoid Cyst: The Classic Pediatric Orbital Choristoma
summary: Lateral dermoid cysts are the most common pediatric orbital tumors, representing benign choristomatous sequestrations of ectoderm at the zygomaticofrontal suture. While slow-growing, they require surgical excision with an intact capsule to prevent severe granulomatous inflammation.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A dermoid cyst is a choristoma—normal histological tissue located in an abnormal anatomical site. In ophthalmology, the lateral dermoid is the most frequent subtype, typically occurring at the zygomaticofrontal suture. These cysts are lined by keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium and contain dermal appendages like hair follicles and sebaceous glands.

rows: Not easily palpable; may be firm

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Painless, slow-growing mass at the lateral brow.
Smooth, rubbery, or firm consistency on palpation.
Non-pulsatile and non-reducible (unlike cephaloceles).
Usually mobile under skin but fixed to underlying periosteum.
Minimal effect on visual acuity unless large enough to induce astigmatism.
Rarely causes motility restriction or diplopia.

sections.title: Imaging Findings (CT/MRI/USG)
content: CT: Well-circumscribed, round/oval mass with fat-density center (-30 to -100 HU).
CT Bone Windows: Focal thinning or 'scalloping' of the zygomatic bone.
MRI T1: High intensity (hyperintense) signal due to lipid content.
MRI T2: Variable signal; often hypointense compared to T1.
B-Scan USG: Well-demarcated with low internal reflectivity and internal echoes (keratin).

rows: Similar but lacks dermal appendages (no hair/sebum).
Older adults, slower growth, posterior location.
Translucent cyst of lacrimal ductule, fluctuating size.
Plexiform 'bag of worms' feel, associated with NF1.

sections.title: Red Flags & Emergency Signs
content: Sudden Onset Pain/Erythema: Indicates cyst rupture and granulomatous reaction.
Dumbbell Configuration: Posterior extension through the zygomatic bone into the temporal fossa.
Rapid Increase in Size: Raises suspicion for malignancy or acute hemorrhage.
Significant Proptosis or Optic Nerve Compression: Rare in superficial cysts.
Bony Destruction: Rather than simple scalloping, suggests aggressive lesions.

sections.title: Histopathology: Textbook Findings
content: Cyst wall: Keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium.
Lumen content: Desquamated keratin, sebum, and sometimes hair shafts.
Dermal Appendages: Sebaceous glands, sweat glands, and hair follicles in the wall.
If ruptured: Intense chronic granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells (Foreign body reaction to keratin).

content.explanation: Suture (usually Zygomaticofrontal), Smooth (regular borders), Scalloping (bone remodeling on CT).

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Incision choice - Lateral brow (within hair) or lid crease (better scar cosmesis).
Step 2: Blunt dissection through orbicularis muscle and septum to reach the cyst capsule.
Step 3: Careful dissection around the cyst, maintaining an intact capsule to prevent rupture.
Step 4: Separation from the periosteum at the suture line (often the most adherent point).
Step 5: Removal of the cyst and inspection for bone defects (dumbbell extension).
Step 6: Irrigation of the cavity and meticulous closure of layers.

rows: Risk of recurrence and chronic fistula.
Rare; occurs in medial dermoids or deep orbital extensions.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always rule out 'dumbbell' extension with imaging if the cyst is not clearly superficial.
A 'tail' extending toward the bone suture is a classic intraoperative finding.
If a dermoid ruptures during surgery, wash the area thoroughly with saline to prevent 'lipogranulomatous' inflammation.
In children, surgery is often deferred until 6-12 months of age unless growth is rapid.
Unlike a mucocele, a dermoid cyst is NOT connected to the paranasal sinuses.

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-up
sections.content: The prognosis for lateral dermoid cysts is excellent following complete surgical excision. Recurrence is extremely rare if the capsule remains intact. Long-term follow-up is primarily for cosmetic monitoring and to ensure no late-onset inflammatory response occurs if a micro-rupture happened during surgery.

summary: An abnormal communication between the carotid arterial system and the cavernous sinus, resulting in high-pressure arterial blood entering the low-pressure venous system. This Ophthalmic emergency requires rapid diagnosis to prevent permanent vision loss from glaucoma or optic neuropathy.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Hemodynamics
sections.content: Carotid-cavernous fistulae (CCF) represent an arteriovenous shunt where blood flows directly or indirectly from the internal or external carotid arteries into the cavernous sinus. This reverses the normal pressure gradient, leading to venous hypertension in the ophthalmic veins, causing 'arterialization' of the conjunctival vessels and orbital congestion.

rows: Mild features, often spontaneous in post-menopausal women.
Slow onset, localized to orbital congestion.
Meningeal branches of both ICA and ECA
Most common 'indirect' type; can mimic chronic conjunctivitis.

sections.title: The Dandy's Triad of Direct CCF
EMERGENCY: Vision-Threatening Red Flags
content: Rapidly declining Visual Acuity (Compressive Optic Neuropathy)
IOP > 40 mmHg (Secondary Glaucoma risk)
Pulsatile Exophthalmos with Cornea Exposure
Severe Intracranial Hemorrhage signs
Abrupt worsening of Proptosis (Venous Thrombosis risk)

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Corkscrew epibulbar vessels: Dilated, tortuous vessels reaching the limbus.
Ophthalmoplegia: CN VI is most common (intracavernous), followed by III and IV.
Raised IOP: Due to increased episcleral venous pressure and choroidal effusions.
Fundus: Dilated retinal veins, intraretinal hemorrhages, disc edema (Venous Stasis Retinopathy).
RAPD: Positive if there is significant optic nerve compression or ischemic neuropathy.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: 1. Bedside Auscultation: Listen for bruit over the globe or temple.
2. Non-Invasive Imaging: CTA or MRA to look for 'flow voids' and SOV enlargement.
3. B-Scan Ultrasound: Identify dilated Superior Ophthalmic Vein (SOV).
4. Formal Gold Standard: Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) for definitive mapping.
5. Tonometry/Gonioscopy: Assess IOP and angle neovascularization.

rows: Confirms the exact site of the fistula.

content.explanation: A: Artery (ICA direct), B: Branches of ICA, C: Carotid (External) branches, D: Dual (Both ICA/ECA branches).

sections.title: Management Hierarchy
content: Step 1: Observation - Indicated for low-flow (Type B,C,D) as 50-70% may spontaneously thrombose.
Step 2: Carotid Massage - Digital compression of the carotid artery to induce thrombosis (only for low-flow).
Step 3: Endovascular Intervention - First-line for Direct CCF. Transarterial or transvenous coiling.
Step 4: Embolic Agents - Use of detachable coils, Onyx, or N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA).
Step 5: Surgical Ligation - Historically significant, but rarely used in the modern endovascular era.

sections.title: Surgical & Endovascular Techniques
content: Transvenous route: Often accessed via the Inferior Petrosal Sinus.
SOV Cutdown: Surgical exposure of the Superior Ophthalmic Vein for coil delivery if other routes fail.
Flow-Diverting Stents: Emerging technology for complex ICA wall defects.
Balloon Occlusion: Detachable balloons (though less common now than coils).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'White-Eyed CCF': Indirect fistulae can present very subtly, mimicking chronic conjunctivitis that doesn't respond to drops.
Trauma + Bruit: Post-head injury patient with a pulse-synchronous sound is Type A until proven otherwise.
Paradoxical Worsening: Symptoms may worsen immediately after successful treatment due to temporary thrombosis-related inflammation.
The 6th Nerve: CN VI is the most vulnerable as it sits freely within the cavernous sinus.

rows: Cortical venous reflux from the shunt.

sections.title: Landmark Study: Barrow et al. (1985)
sections.content: The seminal paper 'Vascular malformations of the cavernous sinus' established the A-D classification system. It remains the clinical foundation for determining whether a fistula requires urgent endovascular intervention (High-flow Type A) or can be managed conservatively (Low-flow Types B-D).

sections.title: Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
sections.content: A crucial sign indicating asymmetric damage to the afferent visual pathway anterior to the optic chiasm. It signifies reduced input to the pretectal nucleus from one eye, leading to a diminished pupillary light reflex in that eye compared to the fellow eye. Often referred to as a 'Marcus Gunn Pupil'.

branches: Optic Nerve Lesions (e.g., Optic Neuritis, AION, Compressive Neuropathy, Trauma)
Severe Retinal Disease (e.g., Extensive Retinal Detachment, CRAO, CRVO, Macular Degeneration with extensive RPE atrophy, Glaucoma (severe asymmetric))

sections.title: RAPD: Clinical Detection (Swinging Flashlight Test)
content: **Step 1:** Dim room illumination. Patient fixes on a distant object.
**Step 2:** Shine a bright, narrow-beam light into one eye (e.g., right eye) for 3-5 seconds, observing pupillary constriction.
**Step 3:** Rapidly swing the light to the other eye (left eye) and immediately observe its initial reaction.

**Step 4:** In an eye with RAPD, when the light is swung to it, the pupil will *dilate* or show less constriction than the initial constriction of the first eye, because the direct response is weaker than the consensual response received from the healthier eye.
**Step 5:** The process is repeated, swinging back and forth, to confirm the relative defect.

rows: Pupil dilates on direct illumination after consensual constriction
Severe Unilateral Efferent Defect (e.g., CN III Palsy)
Pupil is fixed and dilated in the affected eye, no direct or consensual response *from* that eye. Consensual response *to* that eye is absent.
Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, often pain. The good eye will still show direct response and consensual response to light shown in the good eye. No RAPD.
Pupils remain constricted or show transient escape on swinging light, but no dilation
Symmetric responses, no pathologic pupillary escape

sections.title: RAPD: Red Flags & Urgent Evaluation
content: **Sudden, Painful Vision Loss with RAPD:** Suspect optic neuritis (especially in young adults, potential MS link).
**Sudden, Painless Vision Loss with RAPD (Elderly):** Rule out Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION), especially Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA). **ESR/CRP stat!**
**Proptosis/Orbital Mass with RAPD:** Urgent imaging (MRI orbit) to rule out compressive optic neuropathy.
**Acute Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)/Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) with RAPD:** Risk of vision loss, neovascularization (CRVO).

sections.title: Duane Retraction Syndrome (DRS) Type 1
sections.content: A congenital ocular motility disorder characterized by paradoxical innervation of the extraocular muscles. It involves limited abduction of the affected eye, co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on attempted adduction, leading to globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure. Type 1 is the most common subtype.

branches: **Abnormal Innervation:** Absence or hypoplasia of the abducens nucleus (CN VI) and nerve.
**Aberrant CN III Innervation:** Medial Rectus (MR) and Lateral Rectus (LR) muscles are both aberrantly innervated by branches of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
**Co-contraction:** On attempted adduction, both MR and LR contract simultaneously, causing globe retraction and palpebral fissure narrowing.
**Limited Abduction:** Due to absent/defective CN VI innervation and mechanical restriction from co-contracting LR.
**Genetic Link:** Mutations in *SALL4* gene (e.g., in Okihiro syndrome/Acro-renal-ocular syndrome) are associated with some cases, suggesting a developmental origin.

sections.title: DRS Type 1: Clinical Features
content: **Limited Abduction:** The hallmark feature. Eye cannot move outwards past the midline.
**Globe Retraction:** On attempted adduction, the eye pulls back into the orbit.
**Palpebral Fissure Narrowing:** Concomitant with globe retraction on adduction.
**Esotropia in Primary Gaze:** Common, but patients often adopt a compensatory head turn to maintain binocular single vision (BSV).
**Up- or Downshoot in Adduction:** Due to slippage of tight rectus muscles over the globe.
**Compensatory Head Turn:** Towards the affected side to use the field of BSV.
**Vision:** Usually good, amblyopia is uncommon unless severe esotropia and anisometropia are present.

rows: Globe retraction, palpebral fissure narrowing on adduction
Globe retraction, palpebral fissure narrowing on adduction
Globe retraction, palpebral fissure narrowing on adduction

sections.title: DRS Type 1: Management & Surgical Goals
content: **Observation:** For patients with minimal or no primary gaze deviation, no compensatory head posture, and maintaining good binocular vision.
**Surgical Indication:** Significant esotropia in primary gaze (>10-15 PD), cosmetically unacceptable compensatory head posture, or marked up/downshoot.
**Surgical Goals:** Improve primary gaze alignment, reduce compensatory head posture, minimize globe retraction and up/downshoots.
**Common Surgical Techniques:**

*   **Medial Rectus Recession (ipsilateral):** Most common procedure, typically 4-7mm recession to weaken the MR and reduce esotropia and globe retraction. Can be bilateral for large angles or if bilateral DRS.
*   **Lateral Rectus Recession (ipsilateral):** Used rarely, sometimes in combination with MR recession, if significant co-contraction and tight LR.

*   **Vertical Rectus Transposition (e.g., Knapp procedure):** Superior and inferior rectus muscles are disinserted and reattached near the lateral rectus insertion. This provides adducting power to aid abduction, but carries risks of anterior segment ischemia.
*   **Y-splitting of the Lateral Rectus:** May help reduce up/downshoot but does not improve abduction or primary gaze deviation.
**Post-Op Considerations:** Residual deviation is common. May require further surgery. Amblyopia treatment if necessary.

sections.title: Brown Syndrome (Superior Oblique Tendon Sheath Syndrome)
sections.content: A restrictive strabismus characterized by an inability or difficulty to elevate the eye in adduction, due to mechanical restriction of the superior oblique (SO) tendon or its trochlear pulley system. The restriction is more pronounced in adduction, giving the appearance of an inferior oblique muscle palsy, but forced duction testing differentiates it.

rows: Short/inelastic SO tendon, abnormal trochlea, tight SO sheath, anomalous fibrous attachments
Most common type. Present from birth. Usually unilateral (right eye>left). Often mild, non-progressive.
Tenosynovitis (e.g., JIA, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus), sinusitis, trauma, orbital inflammation
Acute onset, often painful, intermittent. May respond to steroid injections.
Trochlear fracture, iatrogenic after SO surgery or orbital trauma
Trochlear cysts, tumors, scleral buckle encroachment
Progressive restriction, imaging may reveal underlying mass.

sections.title: Brown Syndrome: Clinical Features
content: **Limited Elevation in Adduction:** The cardinal sign. Eye cannot elevate normally when looking nasally.
**Hypotropia in Primary Gaze:** May be present, especially if severe, often with a compensatory chin-up head position.
**V-pattern Exotropia:** The eyes diverge on upgaze, often associated with Brown syndrome.
**Normal Elevation in Abduction:** Important differentiating feature from IO palsy.
**Positive Forced Duction Test:** When attempting to elevate the eye in adduction, mechanical resistance is felt.
**Click Sensation:** Rarely, a 'click' may be felt on forced duction or heard on eye movement, due to the tendon snapping through the trochlea.
**Diplopia:** May be present in upgaze, especially in acquired cases.

rows: Limited depression in adduction (primary action of IO), no restriction in elevation in adduction (often overaction of SO)
Limited elevation in all fields of gaze, often ptosis
Inferior rectus restriction, often proptosis, lid retraction, other systemic signs
Trauma history, enophthalmos, infraorbital hypoesthesia, restriction of elevation *and* depression

sections.title: Brown Syndrome: Management & Surgical Approaches
content: **Observation (Congenital):** Many mild cases resolve spontaneously or cause no significant symptoms. Amblyopia management if present.
**Medical Management (Acquired Inflammatory):** Local steroid injections (e.g., triamcinolone acetonide 20-40mg near trochlea) for inflammatory cases. Systemic anti-inflammatory drugs.
**Surgical Indication:** Significant hypotropia in primary gaze, bothersome compensatory head posture, significant diplopia, or development of amblyopia.
**Surgical Goals:** Release the superior oblique tendon restriction, improve elevation in adduction, achieve ocular alignment in primary gaze.
**Common Surgical Techniques:**
*   **Superior Oblique Tenotomy/Tenectomy:** Cutting (tenotomy) or excising a segment (tenectomy) of the SO tendon. Effective but carries risk of iatrogenic superior oblique palsy (overcorrection).
*   **Superior Oblique Silicone Expander:** A silicone sleeve placed around the SO tendon to lengthen it. Reduces risk of overcorrection but may have residual restriction or require re-operation.
*   **Trochlectomy/Trochleotomy:** Rarely performed, involves removing or incising the trochlea, typically for cases with a mass or adhesion in the trochlear area.
*   **Recession of Inferior Oblique/Medial Rectus:** Sometimes performed as an adjunct to correct secondary deviations.
**Post-Op Considerations:** Risk of overcorrection (superior oblique palsy-like picture) leading to vertical diplopia. Undercorrection is also possible. Requires careful follow-up.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls for Ocular Motility & Pupil Exam
content: **Always perform forced duction test** in restrictive strabismus to differentiate paralytic from mechanical causes.
**RAPD indicates an afferent pathway problem**; a fixed dilated pupil with ophthalmoplegia suggests an efferent (CN III) problem.
**Duane's Type 1 is the most common:** Think limited abduction, retraction on adduction.
**Brown Syndrome:** Limited elevation in adduction, *not* full elevation in abduction (differentiates from IO palsy).
**Compensatory Head Posture:** A critical sign in both Duane's and Brown's, indicating the patient is trying to achieve binocular single vision.

content.mnemonic: MR SAD (for Superior Oblique and Superior Rectus actions)
content.explanation: **M**edial **R**ectus, **S**uperior **A**dduction, **D**epression.  This reminds you that for the superior muscles (Superior Oblique and Superior Rectus), their *primary* vertical action (depression for SO, elevation for SR) occurs when the eye is in **Adduction**. In abduction, their secondary actions (intorsion for SO, extorsion for SR) are more prominent, and the inferior oblique/rectus take over vertical actions. Useful for understanding oblique muscle actions and testing.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Genetics of DRS:** Continued research identifies more genetic loci, expanding understanding beyond *SALL4* and confirming developmental dysinnervation.

**Imaging for DRS/Brown's:** High-resolution MRI (HR-MRI) can visualize cranial nerves (e.g., absent CN VI in DRS) and extraocular muscles/tendons, aiding in confirming etiology, especially in atypical cases or for surgical planning in acquired Brown Syndrome.

**Surgical Techniques:** Refinement of adjustable suture techniques in strabismus surgery, and the use of silicone expanders for Brown syndrome, aim to improve outcomes and minimize over/undercorrection.

sections.title: Pediatric & Special Population Considerations
content: **Amblyopia Risk:** While rare in pure Duane's and Brown's, significant constant strabismus (especially esotropia in DRS or hypotropia in Brown's) can lead to amblyopia. Early detection and treatment are crucial.

**Associated Anomalies:** Duane's syndrome can be associated with systemic conditions (e.g., Goldenhar syndrome, Klippel-Feil anomaly, spinal defects, otologic abnormalities). Always perform a thorough systemic evaluation.
**Developmental Impact:** Children with significant compensatory head posture can develop musculoskeletal issues (e.g., torticollis). Early intervention is important.
**Acquired Brown Syndrome in Children:** Think about Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) as a potential underlying inflammatory cause.

title: DKA: Systemic Emergency & Ophthalmic Implications
summary: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening triad of hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. While primarily systemic, it presents critical ophthalmic risks including acute refractive shifts, snowflake cataracts, and the vision-threatening emergency of Rhino-orbital-cerebral Mucormycosis.

branches: Ketosis: Presence of Acetoacetate/β-hydroxybutyrate in blood or urine
Metabolic Acidosis: Arterial pH <7.30 or Bicarbonate <18 mEq/L

rows: Osmotic swelling of the lens and changes in aqueous refractive index.
Subcapsular opacities due to sudden osmotic stress; may be reversible with slow control.
Severe dehydration leading to decreased aqueous production by ciliary body.
Can occur due to cranial nerve palsies or secondary Mucormycosis.
Secondary to invasive fungal infections (Mucor/Rhizopus) in acidotic states.
Creamy white appearance of retinal vessels when serum triglycerides >2500 mg/dL.

sections.title: CRITICAL EMERGENCY: Mucormycosis
content: Rhino-orbital-cerebral Mucormycosis is a fatal fungal infection triggered by DKA.
Red Flag: Black necrotic eschar on the palate or turbinates.
Red Flag: Orbital Apex Syndrome (CN III, IV, VI, V1 involvement) + Vision Loss.
Mechanism: Acidosis releases iron from sequestering proteins, feeding fungal growth (Rhizopus/Mucor).
Treatment: URGENT surgical debridement + IV Amphotericin B + Reversal of Acidosis.

sections.title: Systemic Pathophysiology
content: 1. Absolute Insulin Deficiency + Counter-regulatory Hormone Excess (Glucagon, Cortisol).
2. Increased Lipolysis → Increased Free Fatty Acids.
3. Hepatic Ketogenesis → Production of Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate.
4. Ketoacidosis → Bicarbonate buffering exhaustion.
5. Osmotic Diuresis → Profound dehydration and electrolyte depletion (K+, Na+).

sections.title: Stepwise Management Protocol
content: 1. Fluid Resuscitation: 1L 0.9% NaCl over 1 hour, then adjust based on Na+ status.
2. Potassium Replacement: If K+ <5.2 mEq/L, start replacement BEFORE or with insulin. If K+ <3.3, hold insulin.
3. Insulin Therapy: 0.1 Unit/kg bolus followed by 0.1 U/kg/hr infusion. Goal: Reduce glucose by 50-75 mg/dL/hr.
4. Glucose Switch: When blood glucose reaches 200 mg/dL, add 5% Dextrose (D5NS) to prevent hypoglycemia.
5. Bicarbonate: Only if pH <6.9. Rarely used due to risk of paradoxical CSF acidosis.

content.explanation: D: Dehydration (Isotonic Saline); K: Potassium (Replace even if normal due to total body depletion); A: Anion Gap (Target the gap, not just the glucose).

rows: History of binge, lower glucose levels

sections.title: Ocular Investigation & Imaging
content: Dilated Fundus Exam: Monitor for progression of DR after rapid glycemic control (Early Worsening Phenomenon).
CT/MRI Orbit & Sinuses: Indicated if any ptosis, proptosis, or ophthalmoplegia (Rule out Mucor).
A-Scan/B-Scan: Evaluate lens thickness and vitreous status if view is obscured.
IOP Measurement: High importance as hypotony reflects systemic hydration status.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Pseudohyponatremia: Measured Na+ drops 1.6 mEq/L for every 100 mg/dL glucose elevation.
Paradoxical DR Worsening: Aggressive insulin therapy can temporarily exacerbate Diabetic Retinopathy.
Euglycemic DKA: Seen in patients on SGLT2 inhibitors (Canagliflozin); pH is low but glucose is <250.
Cerebral Edema: Most common cause of death in pediatric DKA patients; monitor for headache and bradycardia.

sections.title: Recent Landmark Studies
sections.content: The DCCT (Diabetic Control and Complications Trial) and EDIC follow-up studies established the 'Metabolic Memory' concept. While intensive control prevents long-term DR, rapid correction in the setting of DKA/severe hyperglycemia can lead to transient worsening of soft exudates and macular edema. The CLOVER trial and various ADA guidelines emphasize that managing DKA requires focusing on the anion gap closure rather than just normalization of blood glucose.

title: CHRPE: The Definitive Clinical Guide
summary: Congenital Hypertrophy of the Retinal Pigment Epithelium (CHRPE) is a benign but clinically significant pigmented fundus lesion. While usually solitary and harmless, specific phenotypic variations serve as a critical 'red flag' for life-threatening systemic malignancies like Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Core Concepts
sections.content: CHRPE is a congenital hamartoma characterized by a localized increase in the size of RPE cells (hypertrophy) rather than an increase in the number of cells (hyperplasia). These cells are packed with large, spherical melanin granules known as macromelanosomes. Clinically, it presents as a flat, sharply demarcated, hyperpigmented lesion often containing characteristic depigmented lacunae.

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Color: Slate-gray to jet-black
Shape: Round or oval with crisp, sharp margins
Lacunae: Well-circumscribed areas of depigmentation (enlarge over time)
Halo: Hypopigmented rim often surrounds the lesion
Elevation: Always FLAT (cannot be detected by B-scan ultrasound)
Location: Usually mid-periphery or periphery

rows: RPE thickening, overlying photoreceptor loss, posterior shadowing
Flat; No internal reflectivity; No thickness

sections.title: RED FLAG: Gardner Syndrome & FAP
content: Atypical CHRPE is often the FIRST sign of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP).
Lesions are typically bilateral, multiple (>3), and spindle-shaped (Pisciform).
Associated with APC gene mutation on Chromosome 5q21.
100% risk of colon cancer by age 50 if untreated.
Gardner Syndrome Triad: FAP, Osteomas (mandible/skull), and Soft tissue tumors (Desmoid).

sections.title: Symptomatology & Functional Deficits
content: Usually asymptomatic (discovered on routine exam)
Absolute Scotoma corresponds exactly to the lesion area
Reduced contrast sensitivity (rarely noticed by patient)
No effect on visual acuity unless the lesion involves the fovea (extremely rare)

sections.title: Management & Follow-up Protocol
content: Step 1: Perform dilated fundus exam and baseline photography.
Step 2: Assess for 'Atypical' features (bilaterality, pisciform shape).
Step 3: If solitary/grouped: Annual monitoring for growth/change.
Step 4: If atypical: Immediate referral to Gastroenterology for Colonoscopy.
Step 5: Genetic counseling for APC gene mutations if FAP suspected.

content.explanation: F: Flat (no elevation on USG); L: Lacunae (depigmented windows); A: APC Gene (association with FAP); T: Tall RPE cells (hypertrophy).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Lacunae tend to enlarge and coalesce over many years.
CHRPE is 'silent' on FFA except for the lacunae which show window defects.
Unlike nevi, CHRPE does not typically have overlying drusen.
Bear tracks (Grouped CHRPE) are NEVER associated with Gardner Syndrome.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
sections.content: Prognosis for vision is excellent. While slow growth occurs in up to 25% of cases over decades, malignant transformation into an RPE Adenocarcinoma is extremely rare but documented. Such transformation presents as a nodular growth with associated exudation or hemorrhage.

sections.title: Recent Landmark Insights
content: Enhanced Depth Imaging (EDI-OCT) confirms CHRPE is confined to the RPE layer.
Studies show that even a single pisciform lesion should prompt FAP screening in the right clinical context.
FAP-associated lesions are found in approximately 70-90% of patients with the condition.

sections.title: Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR) Management
content: Signs: Sudden deepening/shallowing of AC, momentary pupillary dilation, nucleus falls away, marked slowing of phaco aspiration, visible torn capsule/vitreous gel.
Step 1: DON’T get out with phaco probe.
Step 2: Inject dispersive viscoelastic.
Step 3: If complete nucleus remains, convert to ECCE.
Step 4: If small residual fragments, phaco with low bottle height/low aspiration.
Step 5: If large fragments, visco-expression after extending main wound.
Step 6: Replug tear with dispersive OVD; fill AC with cohesive OVD; manual aspiration of residual cortex (irrigation off).
Step 7: Remove all vitreous from AC, wound, and tear using vitrector.
Step 8: Vitrector infusion high, cutter low.
Step 9: Visualize vitreous using 0.1ml of 40mg/ml Triamcinolone.
Step 10: PC IOL if small tear; 3-piece sulcus IOL if large (0.5D less if optic capture, 0.5-1D less if no optic capture).
Step 11: Pilocarpine to constrict pupil post-PC IOL or prior to AC IOL.
Step 12: AC IOL with iridectomy if insufficient capsular support.

content.explanation: Risks: Advanced age, Glaucoma, High Axial Length, Systemic CVS, Vitreous loss, Phaco-to-ECCE conversion. Signs: AC shallowing, Increased IOP, Iris prolapse, Vitreous excursion, Loss of Red Reflex, Dark mound behind pupil.

sections.title: Management of Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage
content: 1. Immediate suture closure of incision.
2. Acetazolamide for pressure spike.
3. Topical/Systemic steroids.
4. Standard post-op antibiotics (Avoid NSAIDs/Antiplatelets).
5. Drainage of large unresolved hemorrhage after 7-14 days.
6. Completion of surgery after 1-2 weeks.

sections.title: PACG: Classification & Elevation DDx
content: PACS: ITC >= 3 quadrants, NO PAS, Normal IOP/Disc.
PAC: ITC >= 3 quadrants + High IOP/PAS, Normal Disc.
PACG: ITC >= 3 quadrants + Glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
Lens Vault: Dist. between ant. lens pole and line joining scleral spurs.
Acute IOP DDx: Lens-induced, Malignant Glaucoma, NVG, Hypertensive Uveitis (Herpetic/Posner-Schlossman), Scleritis, Pigment Dispersion, PXS, Orbital lesions (Hge/CCF).

sections.title: Medical Emergencies & Systemic Reviews
content: ANAPHYLAXIS: Secure airway, Adrenaline 0.5mg IM repeat q5m, Hydrocortisone 200mg IV.
DKA: 0.9% Saline, Insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h, K+ monitoring, Ketone checks hourly.
GI BLEED: Two large bore cannulae, FBC/Cross-match, Terlipressin 1-2mg/6h (if variceal).
STEMI: Aspirin 300mg, Ticagrelor 180mg, Morphine, immediate PCI/Fibrinolysis.
DVT RISKS: Immobilization, Cancer, Estrogen, Obesity. Rx: LMWH + Warfarin (Target INR 2-3).

sections.title: The Faden (Posterior Fixation) Operation
sections.content: Introduced by Cüppers, the Faden procedure involves suturing the muscle to the sclera posterior to the anatomic insertion without disinserting the muscle. This mechanically creates a new functional insertion, weakening the muscle specifically in its field of action while preserving primary position alignment.

sections.title: Adjustable Sutures: The Gold Standard for Precision
sections.content: Adjustable sutures allow for postoperative modification of muscle tension within the first 24-48 hours. This technique significantly reduces the risk of over- or under-correction, particularly in complex cases like adult strabismus, thyroid eye disease, and re-operations.

rows: Weakens action in field of gaze

sections.title: Indications & Contraindications
content: Faden: Scleral thinning/staphyloma (Risk of perforation)
Faden: Avoid in extremely thin sclera (e.g., high myopia)
Adjustable: Pediatric patients (Usually requires GA, limiting adjustability)
Adjustable: Poor patient cooperation/anxiety

sections.title: The Adjustable Suture Process
content: Step 1: Perform routine muscle recession/resection with hang-back suture.
Step 2: Place adjustable bow-tie knot using non-absorbable/monofilament suture.
Step 3: Close conjunctiva, ensuring clear access to suture.
Step 4: Assess alignment in office (topical anesthesia).
Step 5: Adjust tension, lock suture, and trim.

content.explanation: Fixation At Distance: Eliminates Near-Distance incomitance. Remember: Faden does not change Primary Position, it restricts the muscle's pull in its maximal field.

sections.title: Surgical Pearl: Faden Technique
content: Suturing site: Usually 12-14mm behind insertion for medial rectus.
Bite depth: Must be partial-thickness scleral bites to avoid perforation.
Avoid vortex veins: Careful visualization is required to prevent hemorrhage.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Use of 'Hang-back' adjustable techniques simplifies postoperative titration.
Endoscopic or minimally invasive muscle visualization in re-operation cases.
Long-term studies show high success in diplopia reduction for Graves' patients using adjustable sutures.

sections.title: Definitions: Primary vs. Secondary Deviation
sections.content: Primary Deviation is the angle of strabismus measured when the non-paretic (fixating) eye is used for fixation. Secondary Deviation is the angle of strabismus measured when the paretic (affected) eye is forced to fixate. By Hering’s Law of equal innervation, the increased innervation required to move the paretic eye results in an excessive impulse to the yoke muscle in the non-paretic eye, causing the secondary deviation to be larger than the primary deviation in paralytic strabismus.

sections.title: The Diagnostic Process: Deviation Measurement
content: Step 1: Patient fixates with the non-paretic eye; measure angle with prism and cover test (Primary Deviation).
Step 2: Patient fixates with the paretic eye (often requiring occlusion of the good eye to force fixation); measure angle (Secondary Deviation).
Step 3: Compare values: If Secondary > Primary, this indicates a paralytic etiology.
Step 4: If Secondary = Primary, this indicates a mechanical restriction (e.g., Brown syndrome, restrictive thyroid eye disease).

sections.title: Key Red Flags
content: Sudden onset diplopia in adults: Rule out cranial nerve palsies (CN III, IV, VI).
History of trauma: Rule out orbital floor blowout (entrapment).
Pupil involvement with CN III palsy: Surgical emergency (aneurysm until proven otherwise).
Positive Forced Duction Test (FDT): Confirms mechanical restriction over paralysis.

content.explanation: Paretic Secondary Increases (Paretic = Secondary > Primary). If the secondary is equal, suspect it's 'mechanical' or 'non-paretic'.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Evidence
content: Recent studies in 3D-MRI orbital imaging show precise volumetric analysis of rectus muscle cross-sections in patients with restrictive vs paretic deviations.
Development of adjustable suture techniques in strabismus surgery allows for immediate post-op adjustment of the angle, specifically targeting secondary deviations.
Implementation of computerized orthoptic protocols has improved the consistency of angle measurement in non-communicative pediatric cohorts.

sections.title: The Gold Standard: Prism Cover Test (PCT)
content: Step 1: Ensure patient has adequate visual acuity for fixation (ideally 6/60 or better).
Step 2: Perform Cover-Uncover test to differentiate Tropia (manifest) from Phoria (latent).
Step 3: Perform Alternate Cover Test (ACT) to dissociate the eyes and reveal total deviation.
Step 4: Introduce prisms over one eye (usually non-fixing) until all movement is neutralized.
Step 5: Over-correct slightly and then reduce to find the exact neutralization point.
