sections.title: Maddox Rod: Subjective Dissociation
content: Optical Principle: High-powered cylinders convert a point source of light into a streak.
Orientation: The streak is perceived 90 degrees to the axis of the cylinders.
Horizontal Deviation: Rods horizontal -> Vertical streak (measures Esophoria/Exophoria).
Vertical Deviation: Rods vertical -> Horizontal streak (measures Hyperphoria).
Cyclodeviation: Use two Maddox rods (Double Maddox Rod test) to measure degrees of torsion.

sections.title: Maddox Wing: Near Measurement
content: Fixed Distance: Measured specifically at 33 cm (near).
Dissociation: Septum separates the two eyes visually.
Right Eye Sees: White arrow (horizontal) and Red arrow (vertical).
Left Eye Sees: Horizontal scale (numbers) and Vertical scale (numbers).
Measurement: Patient reports where the arrow points on the numbered scale.
Torsion: Includes a small adjustable lever for measuring cyclodeviation.

sections.title: Head-to-Head: Maddox Rod vs. Maddox Wing
Critical Prism Rules & Orientation
content: Prism Orientation: Glass prisms MUST be held in the position of minimum deviation.
Plastic/Fresnel Prisms: Must be held in the Frontal Plane (Preston's position).
Apex vs. Base: Prisms always shift the image towards the APEX; Base goes opposite to the deviation.
Stacking Prisms: Do not stack two prisms of the same direction in one eye; additive error occurs.
Oblique Deviations: Do not tilt the prism; use two separate prisms for vertical and horizontal.

content.explanation: Maddox Rod: Horizontal cylinders = Vertical streak (Horizontal dev). Vertical cylinders = Horizontal streak (Vertical dev).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Hirschberg (Screening for gross deviation)
2. Cover-Uncover (Determine manifest vs latent)
3. Alternate Cover Test (Measure total deviation with PCT)
4. Extraocular Motility (Check for underactions/overactions)
5. Sensory Testing (Worth 4-Dot, Bagolini, Stereoacuity)
6. Cycloplegic Refraction (Essential for Accommodative Esotropia)

sections.title: Landmark Concept: Prism Adaptation Test (PAT)
sections.content: The Prism Adaptation Test (PAT) involves wearing prisms for hours or days to evaluate for 'prism adaptation' or 'eating the prism.' In the landmark PAT study, patients with acquired esotropia who responded to prisms with further deviation required larger surgical dosages for successful outcomes.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Pitfalls
content: Bielschowsky Head Tilt Test: Mandatory for identifying the paretic muscle in vertical deviations (Superior Oblique palsy).
Monocular vs. Binocular: PCT is a binocular test; Hirschberg/Krimsky are technically binocular but used when binocularity is disrupted.
Prism Diopter (PD) vs. Degrees: 1 Degree ≈ 2 Prism Diopters.
Suppression: If a patient suppresses, Maddox Rod will only show one image; the test becomes invalid.
Latent Nystagmus: Use a high plus lens (e.g., +10.00D) instead of an opaque occluder to prevent inducing nystagmus during PCT.

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Sudden Onset Diplopia: Rule out 3rd, 4th, or 6th Nerve Palsy.
Varying Deviation: Rule out Myasthenia Gravis (check for ptosis/fatigue).
New Onset Esotropia: Rule out intracranial pressure elevation (CN VI palsy).
Strabismus with Leukocoria: MUST rule out Retinoblastoma via dilated fundus exam.
Pupil Involving 3rd Nerve Palsy: Emergency! Neuro-imaging for Aneurysm.

title: Mapping the Dark: Retrochiasmal & Chiasmal Visual Field Defects
summary: A comprehensive neuro-ophthalmic guide to localizing lesions posterior to the optic tract, featuring the nuances of congruity, macular sparing, and the differential diagnosis of chiasmal syndromes.

data.title: Mapping the Dark: Retrochiasmal & Chiasmal Visual Field Defects
data.summary: A comprehensive neuro-ophthalmic guide to localizing lesions posterior to the optic tract, featuring the nuances of congruity, macular sparing, and the differential diagnosis of chiasmal syndromes.

sections.title: Overview of Retrochiasmal Pathways
sections.content: Retrochiasmal lesions involve the optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), optic radiations, and the visual cortex. Unlike pre-chiasmal lesions, these produce contralateral homonymous visual field defects. A fundamental rule in neuro-ophthalmology states: the more posterior the lesion, the more 'congruous' (symmetric) the field defect between both eyes.

rows: Macular sparing (if PCA stroke), Riddoch Phenomenon

sections.title: Optic Tract Syndrome: The Trinity
content: 1. Contralateral Incongruous Homonymous Hemianopia.
2. Wernicke's Hemianopic Pupil: RAPD in the eye with the greater field loss (the eye with the temporal field defect contralateral to the lesion).
3. Bow-tie Atrophy: Primary optic atrophy in the contralateral eye and temporal/nasal pallor ipsilaterally.

content.explanation: PITS: Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior. PARE: Parietal (decreased) Pursuit, Angular Gyrus (Gerstmann), Reading (Alexia), Extinction (Neglect).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls: Occipital Cortex
content: Congruity: If the defects match perfectly, look at the occipital pole.
Temporal Crescent Sparing: The most peripheral 30 degrees of the nasal field is represented monocularly in the anterior visual cortex.
Riddoch Phenomenon: Perception of motion in a blind hemifield (statokinetic dissociation).
Anton Syndrome: Cortical blindness with denial of vision (anosognosia).

sections.title: The Binasal 'Differential' Mindset
content: Glaucoma: Most common cause; usually respects horizontal, not vertical.
Atherosclerosis: Calcified ICAs compressing the lateral chiasm fibers.
Congenital: Optic Nerve Head Drusen or Tilted Discs.
Neurological: Chiari malformation or hydrocephalus causing 3rd ventricle expansion.

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Sudden Bitemporal Hemianopia + Headache + Ophthalmoplegia: Suspect Pituitary Apoplexy.
Homonymous Hemianopia + Sudden Neurological Deficit: Rule out CVA (Stroke) immediately.
Progressive Field Loss + Optic Atrophy: Suspect intracranial compressive neoplasm.
Bilateral Blindness with Normal Pupillary Reflexes: Suspect Cortical Blindness (V1 lesion).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Automated Static Perimetry (HVF 24-2 or 30-2) for pattern detection.
2. Goldmann Kinetic Perimetry for far peripheral mapping (Temporal Crescent).
3. Pupil Exam: Check for RAPD (Optic tract vs Radiation).
4. DFE/OCT: Check for Bow-tie pallor or RNFL loss.
5. Neuroimaging: MRI Brain & Orbits with/without Gadolinium (Sagittal/Coronal cuts).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Pseudohomonynous Defects
content: Tilted Discs: Can mimic bitemporal hemianopia but usually crosses the vertical midline.
Functional Visual Loss: Cloverleaf or tubular fields.
Severe Glaucoma: Mimicking hemianopias (check RNFL and Cupping).

sections.title: Surgical & Management Principles
content: Compressive Lesions: Transsphenoidal resection of Pituitary adenomas.
Vascular: Stroke management (antiplatelets, risk factor control).
Rehabilitation: Prisms (Frensel) to shift images into the seeing field.
Training: Saccadic exploration therapy for hemianopia.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearl: Traquair's Junctional Scotoma
sections.content: A junctional scotoma occurs at the junction of the optic nerve and the chiasm. It is characterized by a central scotoma in the ipsilateral eye (optic nerve involvement) and a superior temporal defect in the contralateral eye (compression of the inferior nasal fibers, or 'Willebrand’s knee'). This is a localization 'holy grail' for neuro-ophthalmologists.

For the ophthalmologist, it presents a relentless challenge of managing recurrent ocular surface neoplasia and progressive adnexal destruction.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) is a heterogeneous group of DNA repair disorders. The primary defect lies in the Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) pathway, which is responsible for removing pyrimidine dimers (cyclobutane dimers and 6-4 photoproducts) caused by UV radiation. This leads to a 10,000-fold increase in the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer and a 2,000-fold increase in melanoma before age 20.

rows: Severe, early onset, neurological symptoms (De Sanctis-Cacchione).
Classic skin findings; usually no neurological signs.
Associated with Trichothiodystrophy (TTD) and Cockayne Syndrome.
Milder phenotype; later onset of symptoms.
Mild skin features; associated with late-onset neurological decline.
Extremely severe; overlap with Cockayne Syndrome.
Variant form; defect in DNA polymerase eta; normal NER, high cancer risk.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The DNA Repair Failure
content: Step 1: UV-B (290-320nm) radiation causes DNA cross-linking (Thymine Dimers).
Step 2: Defective NER proteins fail to recognize or excise the damaged segment.
Step 3: DNA polymerase bypasses damage during replication, inducing mutations (C to T transitions).
Step 4: Accumulation of mutations in P53 and RAS oncogenes leads to uncontrolled apoptosis or carcinogenesis.

sections.title: Dermatologic Triad
content: Acute Sun Sensitivity: Severe sunburn/erythema with minimal exposure in infancy.
Cutaneous Poikiloderma: Diffuse pigmentation, telangiectasia, and atrophy (freckle-like lentigines).
Neoplasia: Early onset Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC), and Malignant Melanoma (MM).

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations: Eyelids & Adnexa
content: Eyelid Lentigines: Multiple dark brown pigmented macules.
Atrophy & Cicatrization: Leads to Ectropion (eversion) or Entropion (inversion).
Madarosis: Complete loss of eyelashes due to chronic inflammation or tumor.
Neoplasms: Frequent BCC and SCC of the lid margins; high risk of orbital invasion.

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations: Anterior Segment
content: Conjunctival Hyperemia: Chronic 'red eye' from UV-induced inflammation.
Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN): High frequency of carcinoma in situ.
Corneal Xerosis: Severe dry eye due to tear film instability and lid malposition.
Corneal Scarring & Vascularization: Progressive opacification/pannus (pterygium-like).
Corneal Perforation: Resulting from thinning or aggressive neoplasia.

rows: Dwarfism, 'bird-like' facies, retinal pigmentary degeneration; NO skin cancer.
Poikiloderma, juvenile cataracts, radial limb defects.
Telangiectatic erythema, growth retardation, high risk of leukemia.
Brittle sulfur-deficient hair, ichthyosis, intellectual disability; variable UV sensitivity.
Pellagra-like rash, aminoaciduria, triggered by diet/stress.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Clinical Examination: Family history (consanguinity) and skin/eye findings.
2. Functional Assays: UDS (Unscheduled DNA Synthesis) in cultured skin fibroblasts.
3. Comet Assay: Measures DNA strand breaks.
4. Molecular Genetic Testing: Multi-gene panels for XPA-XPG and POLH.
5. Histopathology: Biopsy of any suspicious ocular surface or eyelid lesions.

sections.title: Management: The Protective Protocol
content: Phase 1: Total UV Avoidance: UV-blocking films on windows, 100% UV-wrap sunglasses, wide-brimmed hats, and face shields.
Phase 2: Medical Prevention: Oral Isotretinoin (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/day) to reduce skin cancer frequency; Topical T4N5 liposome lotion.
Phase 3: Ocular Care: Frequent preservative-free lubricants, bandage contact lenses for exposure, and moisture chambers.
Phase 4: Neoplasia Surveillance: Full ophthalmic and dermatologic exams every 3 months for life.
Phase 5: Early Excision: Wide surgical excision of tumors with margin control (Mohs for lids).

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Referral
content: New enlarging pigmented lesion on conjunctiva (Possible Melanoma).
Chronic non-healing lid ulcer (Suspect SCC/BCC).
Rapidly progressive corneal thinning or white plaque (OSSN).
Sudden loss of vision or severe pain (Corneal Perforation).

content.explanation: UV sensitivity, Vascularization of cornea, Recessive inheritance, Eyelid tumors, Pigmentary changes, Ataxia/Neurology, IRrepairable DNA damage.

sections.title: Surgical Pearls for the Ophthalmologist
content: Cryotherapy: Useful for conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) adjunct.
No-Touch Technique: Vital during excision of OSSN to prevent seeding.
Amniotic Membrane Grafting: For reconstruction after large ocular surface excisions.
Lid Reconstruction: Prioritize protecting the globe; avoid tension that worsens ectropion.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: Most common ocular tumor in XP: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC).
Avoidance of UV must include artificial sources: Certain fluorescent lights and halogen lamps emit UV.
XP-Variant (XP-V): Patients have normal NER but a defect in translesion synthesis; they present later in life.
The cornea in XP often mimics 'severe chronic actinic keratitis'.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Core Concepts
sections.content: Cluster Headache (CH) is a primary headache disorder classified as a Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia (TAC), characterized by excruciating unilateral periorbital pain and ipsilateral cranial autonomic features. Hemifacial Spasm (HFS) is a peripherally mediated movement disorder characterized by involuntary, paroxysmal, intermittent tonic or clonic contractions of muscles innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), typically beginning in the orbicularis oculi.

sections.title: CH: ICHD-3 Diagnostic Criteria
content: At least 5 attacks fulfilling criteria.
Severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain.
Ipsilateral conjunctival injection or lacrimation.
Ipsilateral nasal congestion or rhinorrhea.
Ipsilateral eyelid edema or forehead/facial sweating.
Ipsilateral miosis or ptosis (Horner-like).
Sense of restlessness or agitation during attack.
Attacks occur from 1 every other day to 8 per day.

rows: Mild, noticeable twitching; no functional disability
Severe, disfiguring spasm; functional blindness during event

sections.title: The Cluster Headache 'Red Flags'
content: New onset 'Cluster-like' pain in patients >50 (Rule out GCA)
Abnormal Neurological Exam between attacks (Suggests secondary cause)
Horner Syndrome that persists after the headache resolves (Carotid dissection)
Resistance to standard therapy (Consider pituitary imaging)
Atypical location (strictly occipital or lower face)

sections.title: Imaging & Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Clinical History focusing on periodicity and autonomic signs.
Step 2: MRI Brain with/without Gadolinium for all new Cluster cases (Rule out Pituitary/Sinus pathology).
Step 3: MRI/MRA with CISS/FIESTA sequences for HFS (Identify Neurovascular Conflict).
Step 4: EMG/Nerve Conduction (Identify synkinesis and 'after-discharges' in HFS).
Step 5: MRA Neck if Carotid Dissection is suspected in persistent Horner's.

content.explanation: P: Ptosis/Miosis (Sympathetic paresis), L: Lacrimation (Parasympathetic excess), U: Upper Eyelid Edema, N: Nasal Congestion, G: Gushing (Rhinorrhea).

sections.title: Management of Cluster Headache
content: Abortive: 100% Oxygen (12-15 L/min for 15 mins) via non-rebreather mask.
Abortive: Sumatriptan 6mg SC or 20mg Intranasal.
Transitional: Oral Steroids (Prednisone 60-100mg/day taper) or Greater Occipital Nerve Block.
Prophylaxis: Verapamil (First line) 240-960mg daily (Requires baseline ECG).
Prophylaxis: Lithium Carbonate (Target level 0.6-1.2 mEq/L).
Recent Advance: Galcanezumab (Emgality) 300mg SC monthly.

sections.title: Management of Hemifacial Spasm
content: First Line: Botulinum Toxin Type A (OnabotulinumtoxinA).
Injection Sites: Orbicularis oculi, corrugator, procerus, zygomaticus major.
Dosage: Typically 10-40 Units total; repeated every 3-4 months.
Pharmacotherapy: Carbamazepine or Baclofen (limited efficacy).
Definitive: Microvascular Decompression (MVD).

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Microvascular Decompression (MVD)
content: Step 1: Suboccipital craniectomy/craniotomy in the park-bench position.
Step 2: Microsurgical dissection of the cerebellopontine angle (CPA).
Step 3: Identification of the offending vessel (usually PICA or AICA) at the Root Exit Zone (REZ) of CN VII.
Step 4: Transposition of the vessel away from the nerve.
Step 5: Interposition of a non-absorbable 'cushion' (e.g., Teflon felt) between the vessel and the nerve.
Step 6: Intraoperative monitoring of 'lateral spread response' (LSR) to confirm decompression.

branches: HFS: Facial Myokymia (Continuous 'bag of worms' contraction)
HFS: Post-paralytic Synkinesis (History of Bell's Palsy)

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Other' Babinski Sign: In HFS, the brow elevates during eye closure (contradictory to normal physiology).
Cluster Periodicity: Attacks often occur at the same time each day ('Alarm clock' headache).
Verapamil Safety: Always obtain an ECG to monitor for PR interval prolongation (Heart block risk).
MVD Success: Approximately 85-95% long-term cure rate for HFS.
Botox Duration: Tends to be shorter in HFS than in Blepharospasm due to muscle hyper-excitability.

rows: Chronic CH (no remission), Depression/Suicide risk, Verapamil-induced bradycardia
80% maintain episodic pattern; good response to medical prophylaxis
Facial weakness (post-Botox or MVD), Hearing loss (MVD risk), Corneal exposure
Excellent with MVD; requires lifelong Botox if surgery is declined

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Horner syndrome, or oculosympathetic paresis, results from a lesion anywhere along the three-neuron sympathetic pathway supplying the eye and adnexa. It is classically characterized by the triad of miosis, partial ptosis, and facial anhidrosis. The severity of symptoms often depends on the chronicity and completeness of the sympathetic interruption.

branches: 1st Order (Central): Hypothalamus → Brainstem → Ciliospinal Center of Budge (C8-T2)
2nd Order (Preganglionic): C8-T2 → Over Lung Apex → Superior Cervical Ganglion (C2)
3rd Order (Postganglionic): SCG → Internal Carotid Artery → Cavernous Sinus → Orbit

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Miosis: Anisocoria is greater in dim light (failure to dilate).
Ptosis: 1-2mm due to paralysis of Müller’s muscle (Superior tarsal).
Inverse Ptosis: Elevation of the lower lid ('upside-down ptosis').
Dilation Lag: Sluggish pupillary redilation after light removal (pathognomonic).
Anhidrosis: Reduced sweating; location depends on lesion level.
Iris Heterochromia: Affected iris is lighter (if congenital/longstanding).

rows: Gliomas of the brainstem or spinal cord
CN III, IV, VI palsies often coexist

sections.title: Pharmacological Testing Protocol
content: Step 1: Confirm Horner with Apraclonidine 0.5% (Reversal of anisocoria) or Cocaine 4-10% (No dilation). Wait 30-45 mins.
Step 2: Allow 48-72 hours for washout before localization testing.
Step 3: Localize with Hydroxyamphetamine 1% (Paredrine). Dilation = 1st or 2nd Order; No Dilation = 3rd Order.
Step 4: Alternative Localization: Phenylephrine 1%. Dilation of Horner pupil only = 3rd Order (Denervation supersensitivity).

branches: 1st Order: Entire ipsilateral half of body
3rd Order: Absent or very localized (brow only)

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Emergency Workup
content: ACUTE PAINFUL HORNER: Suspect Internal Carotid Artery Dissection until proven otherwise.
Associated CN VI Palsy: Localization to the Cavernous Sinus (Parkinson’s Sign).
Hand Wasting / Weakness: Lower brachial plexus involvement (Klumpke's / Pancoast).
Thunderclap Headache: Possible SAH or vascular catastrophe.
New onset in Pediatrics: High risk for Neuroblastoma (Check urine VMA/HVA).

content.explanation: M: Mediastinum/Lung Apex (2nd Order). A: Artery/Carotid (3rd Order). P: Posterior Fossa/Brainstem (1st Order).

rows: Carotid Artery, Cavernous Sinus, Skull Base

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Neuroblastoma is the primary concern in non-traumatic pediatric Horner.
Workup includes MRI of entire sympathetic chain.
Urine catecholamines (VMA/HVA) have limited sensitivity but are part of the classic workup.
Congenital Horner often associated with birth trauma (brachial plexus injury).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Harlequin' sign (unilateral facial flushing) may occur in first-order lesions.
Hydroxyamphetamine (Paredrine) testing is only valid if the 3rd order neuron is mature (wait >24 hours after injury).
Apraclonidine can produce a 'false negative' in acute cases (first 36-48 hours) before alpha-1 receptors upregulate.
In Horner syndrome, the anisocoria is most prominent in the first 5 seconds of darkness due to dilation lag.

sections.title: Infantile Nystagmus Syndrome (INS)
content: Onset: Birth to 6 months.
Waveform: Typically horizontal, conjugate, and stays horizontal in up/down gaze.
Accelerating Slow Phase: Pathognomonic feature on electronystagmography (ENG).
Null Point: Position of least intensity where VA is best; often leads to compensatory head turn.
Inverted OKN: Paradoxical response where the fast phase is in the same direction as the drum rotation.
Absence of Oscillopsia: Due to neural adaptation/suppression.

content.explanation: D: Damping with convergence and Decreased during sleep; W: Waveform (accelerating slow phase); A: Abolished/Attenuated during sleep; R: Reverse (Inverted) OKN; F: Fixation effort worsens intensity.

sections.title: Latent & Manifest Latent Nystagmus (LN/MLN)
content: Definition: Nystagmus that appears only when one eye is occluded (Latent) or when both eyes are open but one is suppressed (Manifest Latent).
Direction: Fast phase beats TOWARD the fixing (uncovered) eye.
Waveform: Decelerating slow phase (unlike INS).
Associations: Strongly linked with Infantile Esotropia and the Ciancia Syndrome (large angle ET, cross-fixation, latent nystagmus).
Alexander's Law: Intensity increases when looking in the direction of the fast phase.

sections.title: Periodic Alternating Nystagmus (PAN)
content: 1. Active Phase (90s): Horizontal jerk nystagmus in one direction.
2. Neutral Phase (5-10s): Brief period of relative quiet or transition.
3. Reversal Phase (90s): Nystagmus beats in the opposite direction.
4. Etiology: Cerebellar nodulus/uvula lesions or idiopathic (congenital).
5. Treatment: Baclofen (GABA-B agonist) is often highly effective.

sections.title: Downbeat Nystagmus (DBN)
content: Localization: Cervicomedullary junction (Foramen Magnum).
Top Causes: Chiari Malformation Type 1, Cerebellar Degeneration, Lithium toxicity, Magnesium deficiency, B12 deficiency.
Clinical Tip: Worsens on down-gaze and lateral-gaze.
Management: Check MRI Brain/Posterior Fossa; consider 4-aminopyridine.

sections.title: Upbeat Nystagmus (UBN)
content: Localization: Medulla (large lesions) or Pontomesencephalic junction (anterior vermis).
Primary Position: Nystagmus beats upward in primary gaze.
Causes: Wernicke encephalopathy, MS, Brainstem stroke, Medullary tumors.
Observation: Can change to downbeat nystagmus over time in some degenerative conditions.

sections.title: Ataxic Nystagmus & INO
content: Step 1: Identify Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) via adduction deficit on the side of the MLF lesion.
Step 2: Observe the contralateral eye during abduction.
Step 3: Note 'Ataxic' horizontal jerk nystagmus in the abducting eye.

Mechanism: Interruption of the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) preventing excitatory signal to the contralateral medial rectus, with compensatory 'over-firing' to the lateral rectus (Hering's Law).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Comprehensive History: Age of onset, oscillopsia, family history, drug/toxin exposure.
2. Clinical Exam: VA (monocular vs binocular), head posture, waveform direction, presence of null point.
3. Sensorimotor: Check for strabismus (LN association), convergence effect.
4. Neuro-Imaging: MRI Brain + Orbit (Mandatory for DBN, UBN, PAN, or any new-onset acquired nystagmus).
5. Ancillary: Electroretinography (ERG) if sensory INS suspected (e.g., LCA, Albinism), VEP for optic nerve hypoplasia.

sections.title: Surgical Management Strategies
content: Anderson-Kestenbaum: Recession/Resection of EOMs to shift the null point to primary position to eliminate head turn.
Large 4-Muscle Recessions: Decreases the 'gain' of the nystagmus, improving foveation time and visual acuity even without a null point.
Artificial Divergence: Inducing convergence (using base-out prisms or surgery) to utilize the convergence damping effect.
Tenotomy and Reattachment: Proposed by Dell'Osso to disrupt the proprioceptive feedback loop.

sections.title: Neurological Red Flags
content: Acquired nystagmus in an adult (Always pathological until proven otherwise).
Associated Papilledema or focal neurological deficits.
Monocular nystagmus in a child (Rule out Glioma or Spasmus Nutans).
See-Saw Nystagmus (Chiasmal/Parasellar lesions).
Sudden onset Oscillopsia.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: In albinism, the nystagmus is usually INS-type and is sensory-defect related.
Nutational movements (head nodding) in Spasmus Nutans are often compensatory but don't always match the frequency of the eye movements.
Always measure monocular VA in INS patients using high-plus lenses to blur the other eye rather than an occluder, to avoid triggering latent nystagmus.

title: Brainstem Localization: CN Palsies & Long Tract Syndromes
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to localizing brainstem lesions by integrating cranial nerve deficits with motor and sensory 'long tract' signs. Essential for diagnosing strokes, tumors, and demyelinating lesions of the midbrain, pons, and medulla.

data.title: Brainstem Localization: CN Palsies & Long Tract Syndromes
data.summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to localizing brainstem lesions by integrating cranial nerve deficits with motor and sensory 'long tract' signs. Essential for diagnosing strokes, tumors, and demyelinating lesions of the midbrain, pons, and medulla.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Long tract signs refer to neurological deficits resulting from damage to the major pathways traversing the brainstem: the Corticospinal (motor), Medial Lemniscus (fine touch/vibration), and Spinothalamic (pain/temp) tracts. When combined with ipsilateral Cranial Nerve (CN) palsies, they provide 'crossed signs'—the hallmark of brainstem localization.

branches: Weber (Ventral): Ipsilateral CN III + Contralateral Hemiparesis
Benedikt (Tegetum): Ipsilateral CN III + Contralateral Tremor/Chorea
Claude (Dorsal): Ipsilateral CN III + Contralateral Ataxia
Nothnagel: Ipsilateral CN III + Cerebellar Ataxia (Superior Cerebellar Peduncle)
Parinaud (Dorsal Midbrain): Vertical gaze palsy + Convergence-retraction nystagmus

sections.title: Weber Syndrome: The Classic Ventral Lesion
content: Etiology: Occlusion of paramedian branches of PCA or top-of-basilar artery.
Ipsilateral Finding: Complete CN III palsy (ptosis, 'down and out' eye, dilated pupil).
Contralateral Finding: Hemiparesis of face, arm, and leg (Corticospinal/Corticobulbar tracts).
Localization: Cerebral peduncle of the midbrain.

sections.title: The Rule of 4s for Brainstem Anatomy

content.explanation: 4 CNs above pons (1,2,3,4); 4 CNs in pons (5,6,7,8); 4 CNs in medulla (9,10,11,12). 4 Medial structures (Motor nuclei, Motor tract/Corticospinal, MLF, Medial Lemniscus). 4 Lateral structures (Spinocerebellar, Spinothalamic, Sensory nucleus of CN 5, Sympathetic pathway).

branches: Foville (Dorsal): CN VI + VII + PPRF + Hemiparesis
Raymond: CN VI + Hemiparesis (spares CN VII)
Locked-In: Bilateral Ventral Pons (Bilateral paralysis except vertical gaze)

sections.title: Red Flags: Pupil Involvement & Emergencies
content: Sudden 'Worst Headache of Life' + CN III: Suspect PCom Aneurysm.
CN III + Long Tract Signs: Suspect acute Midbrain Infarct (Stroke).
Bilateral CN III involvement: High risk for dorsal midbrain compression/herniation.
Rapidly progressing vertical gaze palsy: Parinaud syndrome (Pinealoma).

rows: Vascular risk factors, discrete neurological deficits.
Dissemination in time and space; INO is common.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Clinical localization (Is the lesion in the Midbrain, Pons, or Medulla?).
Step 2: Emergency Non-Contrast CT to rule out hemorrhage.
Step 3: MRI Brain with DWI/ADC and gadolinium (Gold standard for infarct/tumor/demyelination).
Step 4: MRA or CTA of the head and neck to evaluate the vertebrobasilar system.
Step 5: Ancillary labs (Glucose, Lipids, HbA1c) and Cardiac echo/Holter if stroke is suspected.

sections.title: Medullary Syndromes (Wallenberg)
content: Classic Lateral Medullary Syndrome (PICA occlusion).
Nerve Signs: Ipsilateral CN IX, X (hoarseness, dysphagia), CN V (facial numbness), Horner Syndrome.
Long Tract Signs: Contralateral Spinothalamic (pain/temp loss) + Ipsilateral Cerebellar Ataxia.
Note: Does NOT involve CN III, IV, or VI, but crucial for 'long tract' differential.

sections.title: Surgical & Medical Management
content: Acute Stroke: Consider IV Thrombolytics (Alteplase/Tenecteplase) within 4.5 hours or Endovascular Thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion.
Secondary Prevention: Antiplatelets (Aspirin/Clopidogrel), Statins, and Blood Pressure control.
Tumor: Neurosurgical consultation for biopsy or resection; Radiation/Chemotherapy as indicated.
Demyelination (MS): IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day for 3-5 days) for acute flares.
Diplopia Management: Patching, Prisms (Fresnel), or Strabismus surgery after 6-12 months of stability.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: If the pupil is involved in CN III palsy, imaging for aneurysm is mandatory, even if long tract signs are absent.
Weber syndrome involves the cerebral peduncle; if the lesion moves dorsally, it becomes Benedikt.
Pontine lesions involving the PPRF will cause an 'ipsilateral gaze palsy'—the patient looks AWAY from the lesion.
Skilled localization can often predict the specific artery involved (e.g., PICA vs. AICA vs. Basilar).

sections.title: Landmark Study: TOPAS
sections.content: The 'Top of the Basilar' Artery Syndrome (Caplan, 1980) remains a sentinel study, describing how distal basilar occlusion causes multi-level brainstem and thalamic ischemia, presenting with complex ocular motility disorders and behavioral changes.

sections.title: Definition & Foundations
sections.content: Perimetry measures the differential light sensitivity across the visual field. Kinetic perimetry (Goldmann) involves moving a stimulus of constant intensity toward the fixation point until detection (isopters). Static perimetry measures the threshold sensitivity at fixed locations by varying stimulus intensity (decibels, dB).

sections.title: Clinical Indications
content: Kinetic: Detecting peripheral contractions (e.g., Retinitis Pigmentosa, advanced Glaucoma).
Kinetic: Pediatric/Low-cognition patients (less demanding).
Static: Early detection of glaucomatous damage (RNFL thinning).
Static: Neuro-ophthalmology (Chiasmal/Retrochiasmal lesions).
Static: Longitudinal monitoring of VF index progression.

sections.title: Red Flags in Testing
content: High Fixation Losses (>20%): Invalidates reliability.
False Positives (>15%): Suggests 'trigger-happy' patient; elevates sensitivity.
False Negatives (>20%): Suggests inattention or advanced field loss.
Gaze Tracking Errors: Significant misalignment during testing.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: Step 1: Patient education and lens correction (near addition calculated per age).
Step 2: Trial frame alignment (check for rim artifacts).
Step 3: Fixation monitoring (Heijl-Krakau method for blind spot).
Step 4: Threshold strategy selection (SITA Fast vs. SITA Standard).
Step 5: Analysis of Global Indices (Mean Deviation, Pattern SD).

content.explanation: Fixation losses (check blind spot), False-positives (trigger-happy), False-negatives (inattention).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always adjust for age: Thresholds naturally decline with aging due to miosis and media opacities.
The 'Hill of Vision': Imagine the central fovea as the peak; sensitivity drops rapidly toward the periphery.
SITA (Swedish Interactive Threshold Algorithm) reduces test time by 50% compared to traditional Full Threshold.
Look for 'biconcave' patterns in bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal pathology).
Artifacts: Eyelid ptosis or trial lens rims can create 'pseudoscotomas' in superior fields.

sections.title: ffERG: The ISCEV Standard
content: Dark-Adapted (Scotopic): Measures rod-mediated responses (0.01 and 3.0 ERG).
Light-Adapted (Photopic): Measures cone-mediated responses (3.0 and 30Hz flicker).
a-wave: Hyperpolarization of photoreceptors.
b-wave: Depolarization of ON-bipolar cells.
Oscillatory Potentials: Inner retinal/amacrine cell activity.

sections.title: PERG: Ganglion Cell Integrity
content: P50: Reflects macular/ganglion cell function.
N95: Highly specific marker for ganglion cell dysfunction (e.g., glaucoma, optic neuropathy).
Does not require diffuse retinal health, but requires stable fixation.
Amplitude correlates with the number of functioning RGCs.

sections.title: mfERG: Localized Macular Mapping
content: Produces a 3D topographic map of cone-driven activity in the central 40-50 degrees.
Crucial for diagnosing hydroxychloroquine toxicity (pre-perimetric phase).
Useful in occult macular dystrophies, cone-rod dystrophies, and toxic maculopathies.
N1 (negative deflection) and P1 (positive peak) represent retinal response.

sections.title: Red Flags for Testing
content: Stable fixation is MANDATORY for PERG and mfERG; inaccurate results in nystagmus or poor visual acuity.
Severe media opacities (dense cataract/vitreous hemorrhage) attenuate ffERG results significantly.
Corneal scarring or surface disease alters electrode impedance.
Uncalibrated monitors or non-ISCEV standard protocols lead to misdiagnosis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Patient dark adaptation (20 mins for scotopic ffERG).
Step 2: Electrode placement (DTL fiber or Gold cup) with thorough corneal anesthesia.
Step 3: Impedance check (ensure low resistance <5kΩ).
Step 4: Stimulus delivery (ISCEV standardized intensity).
Step 5: Waveform analysis comparing patient trace to age-matched laboratory normative data.

content.explanation: P (Photoreceptors = a-wave), B (Bipolar cells = b-wave), O (Others/Amacrine = Oscillatory Potentials).

sections.title: Recent Advances

Portable handheld ERG devices are improving utility in pediatric and non-clinic environments.
Studies confirm mfERG is superior to standard visual fields for detecting early toxicity.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Core Logic
sections.content: SITA (Standard Interactive Thresholding Algorithm) is the gold-standard software used in the Humphrey Field Analyzer (HFA) to estimate visual field thresholds. Developed by Bengtsson and Heijl, it utilizes complex Bayesian mathematical models to predict threshold values based on real-time patient responses and a large database of normal and glaucomatous visual fields. Unlike the old 'staircase' method (Full Threshold), SITA continuously recalculates the probability of a point's threshold, significantly reducing test time without sacrificing clinical accuracy.

rows: Cross-references neighbor points; very high precision.
Gold standard; Baseline testing; Research (EMGT Study).
Larger error tolerance; terminates earlier than SS.
Screening; Patients with fatigue; Elderly; Advanced loss.
Eliminates False Negative tests & blind spot checks.

sections.title: Crucial Reliability Indices
content: Fixation Losses (FL): >20% suggests poor fixation (Heijl-Krakau method or Eye Tracking).
False Positives (FP): The 'Trigger Happy' patient. Rates >15% significantly invalidate the Mean Deviation (MD).
False Negatives (FN): Failure to respond to a brighter stimulus. In SITA, high FN in glaucoma is often a sign of disease (short-term variability) rather than poor effort.
Gaze Tracking: Upward spikes indicate saccades; downward spikes indicate blinks.

sections.title: The SITA Bayesian Process
content: Step 1: Start with Age-Corrected Normative data for the first four primary seed points.
Step 2: Present stimulus at expected threshold. Update 'Probability Map' based on hit/miss.
Step 3: Information from neighboring points informs the prior probability of the current point.
Step 4: Algorithm calculates the 'likelihood' of the true threshold after every response.
Step 5: Termination: Test stops once the measurement error (standard deviation) falls below a pre-set limit.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Visual Field Artifacts
content: Cloverleaf Pattern: Patient stops responding after initial points (malingering/fatigue).
Rim Artifact: High plus lens too far from eye; creates peripheral ring scotoma.
Learning Effect: First test is often 'worse' than subsequent; always repeat a suspicious field.
Trigger Happy (FP > 20%): Can 'mask' real defects by creating super-normal thresholds (white scotomas).

content.explanation: R: Reliability Indices (FP, FN, FL). P: Pattern Deviation (filters out cataracts). G: Global Indices (MD, PSD, VFI).

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: VFI (Visual Field Index) is less affected by media opacities than MD.
PSD (Pattern Standard Deviation) is the most sensitive marker for early localized glaucomatous damage.
SITA Faster does NOT measure False Negatives. It uses Saccadic Eye Tracking for fixation instead of blind-spot re-testing.
Always use the same SITA strategy for GPA (Guided Progression Analysis) to ensure longitudinal validity.

rows: Often asymmetric across horizontal midline (Nasal Step).

sections.title: Guided Progression Analysis (GPA)
sections.content: GPA is the software tool within HFA that tracks change over time. It compares follow-up fields to a 2-test baseline. 'Possible Progression' is defined as 3 or more points showing significant decline (p < 0.05) in two consecutive tests. 'Likely Progression' requires three consecutive tests showing the same decline. The VFI Rate of Progression (RoP) slope helps predict the functional lifespan of the patient's vision.

sections.title: Special Populations: Pediatric & Geriatric
content: Pediatrics: Use SITA Fast to reduce boredom/fatigue; 10-2 may be easier to perform than 24-2.
Geriatrics: Beware of 'miotic' effect on MD; ensure proper pupil dilation (>3mm) if possible or maintain consistency.
Advanced Glaucoma: Switch to Size V (Goldmann 5) stimuli or SITA Fast to decrease test duration and increase dynamic range.

sections.title: Landmark Study: EMGT (Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial)
sections.content: The EMGT was instrumental in validating SITA Standard. It demonstrated that SITA Standard 24-2 was as sensitive as the Full Threshold 24-2 strategy in detecting progression while cutting test time by half. The study solidified the use of SITA in both clinical trials and routine practice, proving that Bayesian models could provide high-quality data for long-term management of intraocular pressure reduction therapy.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Choroidal melanoma arises from uveal melanocytes. Incidence: 5-7 per million per year in Caucasians. Peak incidence occurs in the 6th decade of life. Major risk factors include light iris color, fair skin, inability to tan, and presence of ocular/oculodermal melanocytosis.

F: Fluid (Subretinal)
S: Symptoms (Photopsia/Blur)
O: Orange pigment (Lipofuscin)
M: Margin (Disc proximity)
U: Ultrasonographic hollowness
H: Halo (Absence of)

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Malignancy
content: Presence of subretinal fluid (not associated with other pathologies)
Documentation of growth on serial exam
Orange pigment on tumor surface
Acoustic hollowness on B-scan ultrasonography
Tumor thickness exceeding 2mm

sections.title: Treatment Modalities (COMS Protocols)
content: Step 1: Plaque Brachytherapy (I-125, Ru-106, Pd-103) - Gold standard for medium-sized tumors.
Step 2: Proton Beam Irradiation - Indicated for large tumors or juxtapapillary locations.
Step 3: Transpupillary Thermotherapy (TTT) - Adjunctive therapy for thin tumors.
Step 4: Enucleation - Indicated for massive tumors with no visual potential or significant extraocular extension.
Step 5: Anti-VEGF therapy - Used post-radiation to manage radiation maculopathy/retinopathy.

content.explanation: To Find Small Ocular Melanoma: Thickness, Fluid, Symptoms, Orange pigment, Margin, Ultra-sound, Halo absence.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Genetic Prognostication
content: Gene Expression Profiling (GEP): Class 1A/1B (low risk), Class 2 (high metastatic risk).
Chromosome 3 Monosomy: Strong correlation with metastatic disease.
BAP1 mutation: Frequently associated with Class 2 tumors and poor systemic prognosis.
Liquid Biopsy: Investigational use of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in aqueous humor.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Retinoblastoma (Rb) arises from the malignant transformation of primitive retinal neuroectodermal cells. It is caused by biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene (13q14). Hereditary cases (40%) involve germline mutations, predisposing to bilateral/multifocal disease and secondary cancers (e.g., osteosarcoma). Sporadic cases (60%) are typically unilateral and unifocal.

rows: Local subretinal fluid or isolated seeds
Diffuse subretinal fluid or massive/diffuse seeds
Neovascular glaucoma, hemorrhage, or tumor at lens

sections.title: Clinical Presentation
content: Leukocoria (most common: 60%)
Strabismus (secondary to macular involvement)
Hyphema / Vitreous hemorrhage
Pseudohypopyon
Buphthalmos (advanced cases)
Orbital cellulitis-like presentation (necrosis)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Exam under anesthesia (EUA) with wide-field fundus imaging.
Step 2: B-scan ultrasonography (to assess calcification and extent).
Step 3: MRI Orbit/Brain (with/without contrast) to rule out trilateral Rb.
Step 4: Systemic staging (Bone marrow/CSF) for high-risk extraocular features.
Step 5: Genetic counseling and RB1 mutation analysis.

sections.title: Emergency Warning Signs
content: Rubeosis iridis (neovascularization) indicating ischemia/advanced tumor.
Rapid onset proptosis or orbital mass.
Any pupil asymmetry or fixed dilated pupil.
Family history of Rb (immediate screening required).

content.explanation: C: Chemotherapy (Systemic/IAC), C: Cryotherapy, C: Chemoreduction-Laser (TTT), P: Plaque radiotherapy.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Calcification is the hallmark of Rb on imaging (CT/USG).
Always screen the fellow eye; unilateral Rb in a child under 1 is highly suspicious for germline mutation.
Trilateral Rb: Bilateral ocular Rb + midline intracranial primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET).
Intra-arterial chemotherapy (IAC) is now the standard for eye salvage in groups B-D.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Retinoblastoma (RB) is a malignant tumor of the neurosensory retina arising from primitive multipotential photoreceptor precursors (retinoblasts). It is driven by the biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13q14. It is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, with 95% of cases diagnosed before age 5.

sections.title: Molecular Pathogenesis: Knudson's Two-Hit Hypothesis
content: 1. Germline/First Hit: Inherited mutation in one allele of RB1 gene (all cells).
2. Somatic/Second Hit: Spontaneous mutation in the remaining allele within a retinal cell.
3. Loss of Heterozygosity (LOH): Complete loss of pRB protein function.
4. Unregulated Cell Cycle: E2F transcription factors remain active, driving S-phase entry.
5. Malignant Transformation: Formation of retinoblastoma tumor clones.

rows: Lumen surrounded by columnar cells; nuclei at base.
Pathognomonic for RB; represents retinal differentiation.
Fibrillar material in center (no true lumen).
Less specific; also seen in neuroblastoma/medulloblastoma.
Flower-like groupings of neoplastic cells with bulbous processes.

sections.title: Low Penetrance Retinoblastoma
content: Phenotype where mutation carriers do not develop tumors or develop benign retinomas.
Often associated with specific RB1 mutations (e.g., promoter mutations or missense).
Risk to offspring remains high even if parent is clinically normal.
Requires careful molecular testing of 'unaffected' family members.

rows: Focal seeds (subretinal or vitreous) within 3mm of tumor
Diffuse seeds (> 3mm from tumor) or 'snowball' vitreous seeding
Neovascular glaucoma, phthisis, tumor touching lens, anterior segment involvement

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. EUA (Examination Under Anesthesia): Scleral depression and 360° fundus drawing.
2. B-Scan Ultrasonography: Detect high-reflectivity calcium peaks.
3. Wide-field Digital Imaging (RetCam): For documentation and staging.
4. MRI Orbits & Brain: Rule out trilateral RB (pineoblastoma) and optic nerve invasion.
5. Genetic Testing: Mandatory for both somatic (tumor) and germline (blood) DNA.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Indicators for Enucleation
content: Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG)
Tumor invasion of the Anterior Chamber
Phthisis Bulbi or Pre-phthisical state
Opaque media preventing monitoring
Suspected Optic Nerve involvement on MRI

sections.title: Modern Management Paradigms
content: Intravenous Chemotherapy (IVC): Carboplatin, Vincristine, Etoposide (VEC).
Intra-arterial Chemotherapy (IAC): Melphalan/Topotecan via ophthalmic artery.
Intravitreal Chemotherapy: For recalcitrant vitreous seeds.
Local Therapy: Cryotherapy (anterior) or Laser Photocoagulation/TTP (posterior).
Plaque Brachytherapy: For localized salvage.

content.explanation: Calcification (High spike), Conical Shape (Solid mass), and shadowing (Choroidal excavation/attenuation).

sections.title: Trilateral Retinoblastoma
sections.content: A rare association of bilateral RB (germline) with a midline intracranial neuroectodermal tumor (usually in the pineal gland). Requires routine neuroimaging (MRI) every 6 months until age 5 in germline-positive patients.

sections.title: Second Malignant Neoplasms
content: Lifetime risk for germline patients: ~30-50%.
Most common: Osteosarcoma, Soft tissue sarcoma, Melanoma.
Risk is significantly increased by external beam radiation therapy (EBRT).
Strict UV protection and lifelong surveillance are mandatory.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls for Boards
content: RB is the most common cause of leukocoria in children.
Avoid FNA/Biopsy: High risk of extraocular tumor seeding.
Endophytic Growth: Tumor grows into the vitreous (white seeds).
Exophytic Growth: Tumor grows toward subretinal space (serous detachment).
Regression Patterns: Type 1 (Cottage cheese/calcified), Type 2 (Fish-flesh/non-calcified), Type 3 (Mixed), Type 4 (Atrophic/Chorioretinal scar).

content: Leukocoria (white pupil) in any child < 5 years old.
Sudden onset strabismus in a child.
Unexplained vision loss + elevated pigmented choroidal mass.
Painful red eye with secondary glaucoma in a phthisical or atrophic eye.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Pathway
content: Step 1: Dilated Indirect Fundoscopy & B-Scan Ultrasound.
Step 2: RB: Orbital MRI (check optic nerve). CM: Liver LFTs & PET/CT.
Step 3: RB: Lumbar Puncture (if high risk). CM: Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) if unsure.
Step 4: Genetic testing for familial counseling (RB1 germline testing).

sections.title: Management Framework
content: Retinoblastoma: Goal is eye preservation and vision. Treatment includes systemic chemoreduction (VEC protocol: Vincristine, Etoposide, Carboplatin), intra-arterial chemotherapy (Melphalan), intravitreal chemotherapy, and focal laser/cryotherapy.

Choroidal Melanoma: COMS (Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study) criteria. Small tumors: TTT or plaque brachytherapy (I-125). Medium: Plaque brachytherapy. Large: Enucleation vs. Proton Beam Radiotherapy.
Recent Advances: Intravitreal Topotecan for RB vitreous seeds; Tebentafusp for metastatic Uveal Melanoma.

content.explanation: To differentiate suspicious nevi from Melanoma: Thickness >2mm, Fluid (subretinal), Symptoms (photopsia), Orange pigment, Margin near disc, Ultrasonographic Hollowness, Absence of Halo, Absence of Drusen.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Landmark Studies
content: RB Landmark Study: Children's Oncology Group (COG) protocols have improved 5-year survival rates to >95%.
CM Landmark Study: COMS study proved that plaque brachytherapy is equivalent to enucleation for medium-sized choroidal melanomas regarding mortality.
Always evaluate the fellow eye in RB; bilateral disease occurs in ~30% of cases.
A pigmented lesion with orange pigment (lipofuscin) is highly suggestive of malignant melanoma.

sections.title: Glaucoma Hemifield Test (GHT)
sections.content: The GHT compares 5 zones in the superior hemifield to corresponding zones in the inferior hemifield. It is the most sensitive HFA test for early glaucomatous damage. Results: 'Outside Normal Limits' (highly specific for glaucoma), 'Borderline' (warrants follow-up), or 'Within Normal Limits'. 'General Reduction in Sensitivity' may occur if the entire field is depressed.

rows: Global index representing remaining visual function; 100% = normal, 0% = perimetrically blind.
Measures localized field loss (irregularity); high PSD indicates localized scotoma/glaucoma.
Average departure from age-matched norms; reflects overall field depression (cataract vs. glaucoma).

sections.title: Pattern Analysis: Temporal Wedge vs. Nasal Step

branches: Temporal Wedge: Often indicates early nerve fiber bundle defects or chiasmal lesions
Nasal Step: Classic early glaucoma indicator; asymmetrical loss across the horizontal meridian
Paracentral Scotoma: Often the earliest manifestation of glaucomatous optic neuropathy

sections.title: Red Flags in Perimetry
content: False Positive Rate > 15% (Unreliable, 'trigger happy')
False Negative Rate > 20% (Inattention or advanced disease)
Fixation Loss > 20% (Poor compliance)
Gaze tracking 'spikes' exceeding 10 degrees

content.explanation: Reliability (Fixation/False Positives), Indices (MD/PSD), GHT, Interpretation (Pattern of loss), Diagnosis correlation.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: Step 1: Check Reliability Indices (Fixation losses, false +/-).
Step 2: Inspect Global Indices (MD and PSD).
Step 3: Analyze Pattern Deviation plots (not just Total Deviation) to remove cataract bias.
Step 4: Check GHT status.
Step 5: Correlate field defect location with Disc/RNFL (e.g., inferotemporal rim thinning correlates with superior field loss).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Pattern Deviation is the 'Gold Standard' for identifying glaucomatous localized loss, as it filters out generalized depression.
A 'Nasal Step' is often the first reproducible sign of early glaucoma, occurring due to the anatomical distribution of retinal nerve fibers.
Always repeat the first visual field test; the 'Learning Effect' often artificially inflates severity on the first attempt.
Temporal wedge defects can mimic glaucoma but should trigger a search for chiasmal pathology (e.g., pituitary adenoma) via MRI.

sections.title: Clinical Overview & Pharmacology
sections.content: Amiodarone is an iodine-rich benzofuran derivative used for refractory ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias. Due to its cationic amphiphilic nature, it binds to polar lipids and accumulates in lysosomes, forming complexed intralysosomal inclusions. Its half-life ranges from 20 to 100 days, meaning ocular side effects can persist or even appear months after drug cessation.

branches: Axoplasmic flow stasis in Optic Nerve

sections.title: Cornea Verticillata (Vortex Keratopathy)
content: Bilateral, golden-brown/grey deposits in the basal corneal epithelium.
Pattern starts at the junction of the middle and lower thirds of the cornea.
Dose-dependent: Rarely seen at doses <100mg/day; almost universal >400mg/day.
Visual acuity is usually unaffected, though halos/glare can occur.
Reversible over 3–20 months following discontinuation.

rows: Fine horizontal line in lower third of cornea.
Early arborization (branching) from the main line.
Irregular clumps of pigment with visual disturbances.

sections.title: AAON vs. NAION: The Critical Distinction
Diagnostic Workup & Examination
content: Step 1: Baseline Slit-Lamp Exam & Fundoscopy prior to treatment.
Step 2: Annual surveillance for asymptomatic patients.
Step 3: Immediate BCVA, Color Vision (Ishihara), and VF if symptoms arise.
Step 4: OCT RNFL to document disc edema thickness.
Step 5: Coordination with Cardiology for medication review.

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Red Flags
content: Sudden decrease in visual acuity or blurred vision.
New onset arcuate or altitudinal visual field defects.
Acquired color vision deficiency (Dyschromatopsia).
Asymptomatic bilateral optic disc swelling.
Persistent halos that interfere with driving.

content.explanation: F: Fabry Disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency); A: Amiodarone; B: Baytan (triadimenol); R: Rhopressa/Rocklatan (Netarsudil); Y: Yielding to Chloroquine/Hydroxychloroquine; C: Chlorpromazine / Clofazimine / Cyclophosphamide.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Resident Exams
content: Amiodarone is 37% iodine by weight.
Unlike NAION, AAON does not have a 'disc at risk' (small C/D ratio) prerequisite.
Vortex keratopathy is NOT a reason to stop the drug.
Anterior subcapsular lens deposits occur in 50% of patients on >600mg/day for 6+ months.
Pseudotumor cerebri has been rarely reported in association with amiodarone.

sections.title: Management & Legal Protection
content: Inform Cardiology immediately if AAON is suspected.
Do NOT stop the drug unilaterally (risk of fatal arrhythmia).
If AAON confirmed, discontinuation is usually required to save vision.
Document 'Risk-Benefit Discussion' in the medical record.
Perform serial VF and OCT to monitor resolution after cessation.

sections.title: Recent Evidence: Meta-Analysis Data
sections.content: Recent systematic reviews indicate that while amiodarone users have a 2x increased risk of developing optic neuropathy compared to the general population, the absolute risk remains low (~0.1% per year). Distinguishing drug-induced neuropathy from idiopathic NAION remains a clinical challenge, often relying on the duration of disc edema (prolonged in AAON).

content.explanation: 1. Photosensitivity (Skin/Lids); 2. Pigment (Vortex Keratopathy); 3. Pulmonary Fibrosis (Most serious systemic); 4. Peripheral Neuropathy; 5. Pro-arrhythmic (QT prolongation); 6. Papilledema/Papillopathy (AAON).

sections.title: Prognosis
content: Keratopathy: 100% reversible, no permanent sequelae.
Lens Deposits: Usually stable, rarely affects vision.
AAON: Variable; some regain vision post-cessation, others have permanent field loss.
Systemic: Pulmonary and hepatic toxicities are the primary drivers of mortality.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Visual Field (VF) testing is the quantitative assessment of the 'island of vision in a sea of blindness' (Traquair). It measures differential light sensitivity across the retina. In clinical practice, Automated Static Perimetry (SAP), primarily using the Humphrey Field Analyzer (HFA) or Octopus, is the gold standard for monitoring glaucoma and neurological vision loss.

rows: Heijl-Krakau method: stimuli in blind spot. High FL suggests poor gaze tracking.
'Trigger happy' patient. Increases sensitivity abnormally; produces 'white scotomas'.
Patient fails to respond to brighter stimuli where they previously saw dimmer ones. Common in advanced glaucoma.

branches: Mean Deviation (MD): Overall depression or elevation compared to age-matched normals.
Pattern Standard Deviation (PSD): Measures focal loss; highlights 'hills and valleys' in the island of vision.
Visual Field Index (VFI): Percentage of normal age-corrected sensitivity; weighted toward the center.
Glaucoma Hemifield Test (GHT): Compares 5 mirror-image clusters in upper vs lower halves.

sections.title: Total vs. Pattern Deviation Maps
content: Total Deviation (TD): Highlights all points deviating from the norm. Includes media opacities (cataracts) and refractive errors.
Pattern Deviation (PD): Filters out generalized depression (like cataract) to reveal localized defects (like glaucoma).
Clinical Rule: If TD is worse than PD, consider cataract. If they look identical, the loss is likely purely focal.

branches: Nasal Step: Respects the horizontal raphe.
Arcuate (Bjerrum) Scotoma: Connects blind spot to nasal raphe, arching over fixation.
Paracentral Scotoma: Small focal island within 10 degrees of fixation.
Temporal Wedge: Rare; signifies damage to nasal fibers.
Altitudinal Defect: Loss of an entire upper or lower hemifield.

rows: Usually monocular; respects horizontal midline if vascular.
Respects the vertical midline; 'Crossing fibers' damaged.
Worse symmetry as you move posteriorly; Wernicke's pupil.
'Pie in the Sky'; Meyer's Loop involvement.
'Pie on the Floor'; Baum's Loop involvement.
High symmetry; may have Macular Sparing (dual blood supply).

sections.title: Step-by-Step Interpretation Protocol
content: Step 1: Verify Patient Data (Name, Age, Refractive correction - use +3.00D trial lens for presbyopes).
Step 2: Check Reliability (FL <20%, FP <15%, FN <20%).
Step 3: Analyze Global Indices (Look at MD for severity and VFI for rate of change).
Step 4: Examine the GHT (Normal, Borderline, or Outside Normal Limits).
Step 5: Review Deviation Maps (Identify patterns: Arcuate, Nasal Step, Hemianopia).
Step 6: Correlate with Clinical Findings (Disc cupping, IOP, neuro-imaging).

content.explanation: Parietal = Inferior defect | Temporal = Superior defect.

sections.title: Red Flags: When the Field is Unreliable
content: Cloverleaf Pattern: Patient stops responding mid-test (Fatigue or Malingering).
High False Positives: 'White scotomas' on the grayscale; patient is over-eager.
Learning Effect: Significant improvement between the first and second test.
Rim Artifact: A ring of depression caused by the trial lens frame being too far from the eye.

branches: Optic Disc Drusen: Can mimic arcuate scotomas.
Retinal Branch Artery Occlusion: Sudden altitudinal loss.

sections.title: Recent Advances in Perimetry
content: 10-2 Testing in Glaucoma: Essential for 'Central Island' monitoring in advanced cases or early macular involvement.
SITA-Faster: Reduces test time by 50% compared to SITA-Standard without significant loss of data quality.
VR-Based Perimetry: Portable headsets (e.g., Olleyes, Heru) allowing for home-based monitoring.
AI/Deep Learning: Algorithms now predicting progression faster than traditional GPA (Guided Progression Analysis).

rows: VF conversion often occurs before disc changes in some, but vice versa in most.
Treat ocular hypertension if risk factors are high.
Lowering IOP by 25% reduced progression from 62% to 45%.
Every 1 mmHg drop reduces progression risk by 10%.
Initial surgery vs. medicine had similar long-term VF outcomes for most.
Surgery may be better for advanced baseline VF loss.
Low IOP (consistent <18mmHg) halted VF progression in advanced glaucoma.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the 'Blind Spot' on the grayscale to ensure it's in the correct hemifield (Left vs Right eye).
A 'Nasal Step' of 10 degrees or more is highly suspicious for early glaucoma.
In neurological cases, 'Respecting the Vertical' is the most important feature.
Never diagnose based on one field; look for reproducibility across at least two sessions.

sections.title: Monitoring Progression (GPA)
sections.content: Guided Progression Analysis (GPA) uses a 'baseline' of two tests. It looks for consistent decreases at specific points (Probability symbols). Three triangles (filled) indicate 'Likely Progression,' while two open triangles indicate 'Possible Progression.' Always correlate the VFI slope to estimate the 'Rate of Loss' over time.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology of Regression
sections.content: Regression in PDR is defined by the involution of neovascularization (NV) following a reduction in intraocular VEGF levels. Mechanistically, this involves the collapse of immature vascular channels, apoptosis of endothelial cells, and replacement of leaky, fragile vessels with fibrous glial tissue (fibrotic transformation).

sections.title: Clinical Signs of Regression
content: Blanching of neovascular fronds (loss of central perfusion)
Reduction in caliber and tortuosity of NVD/NVE
Conversion from 'active/leaky' to 'fibrotic/ghost' vessels
Reduction in associated intraretinal or preretinal hemorrhages
Resolution of hard exudates and lipid deposition
Decreased vascular permeability on Fluorescein Angiography

sections.title: Stages of NV Involution
content: Step 1: Early Response (Days 1-7): Reduction in vessel permeability/leakage.
Step 2: Active Regression (Weeks 2-8): Fragile vessels collapse and lose caliber.
Step 3: Fibrosis (Months 3+): Replacement by acellular fibrous white cords.
Step 4: Stabilization: Maintenance of quiescent state without new NV growth.

rows: Absence of late-phase leakage from previously active NVs.
Demonstration of absent flow signal in neovascular complexes.
Monitoring for tractional retinal detachment despite regression.

sections.title: Red Flags: Non-Regression & Progression
content: Continued leakage on FFA despite full PRP
New onset of vitreous hemorrhage (VH)
Growth of new neovascularization elsewhere (NVE)
Development of tractional retinal detachment (TRD)
Iris neovascularization (NVI) or secondary neovascular glaucoma

content.explanation: F: Fibrosis replacing vessels; A: Abatement of leakage; D: Decreased caliber/size; E: Empty/ghost vessels visible on exam.

rows: Stable scar tissue, no leakage on FFA.
Chorioretinal atrophy from laser burns vs. fibrous NV.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
content: DRCR.net Protocol S: Demonstrated that anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab) is non-inferior to PRP for PDR management.
CLARITY Study: Aflibercept vs. PRP; showed superior regression rates for anti-VEGF in PDR.
OCT-A advancements allow for quantification of vessel density and flow, providing objective metrics for regression beyond clinical observation.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Congenital Stationary Night Blindness (CSNB) is a group of rare, genetically determined, non-progressive retinal disorders. While patients present with impaired night vision (nyctalopia) from birth, the condition is 'stationary,' meaning it does not lead to total blindness. It is primarily categorized into those with a normal fundus (Schubert-Bornschein and Riggs types) and those with an abnormal fundus (Oguchi disease and Fundus Albipunctatus). The hallmark is a defect in the transmission of signals from the photoreceptors to the second-order neurons (ON-bipolar cells).

branches: Autosomal Dominant (RHO, PDE6B, GNAT1 - Riggs type)

rows: Both ON- and OFF-pathways partially affected

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Signal Block
content: 1. Photoreceptor captures photon and hyperpolarizes.
2. Reduced Glutamate release into the synaptic cleft.
3. cCSNB: Defect in mGluR6 receptor or TRPM1 channel prevents ON-bipolar depolarization.
4. iCSNB: Defect in Ca2+ channels (CACNA1F) impairs neurotransmitter release from both rods/cones.
5. Result: Interruption of signal transmission despite normal photoreceptor structure.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Nyctalopia (Difficulty in dark or dim light)
Decreased Visual Acuity (20/30 to 20/200)
Nystagmus (Often horizontal, present from infancy)
Strabismus (Exotropia or Esotropia)
Paradoxical Pupillary Response (Constriction in darkness)
Myopia (Usually high in X-linked variants)
Normal Fundus appearance (in Schubert-Bornschein and Riggs)

sections.title: The Diagnostic Gold Standard: ERG
content: Scotopic 0.01 (Rod Response): Non-recordable in Complete; profoundly reduced in Incomplete.
Scotopic 3.0 (Maximal Response): 'Negative ERG' (Large a-wave, but b-wave amplitude is smaller than a-wave).
Photopic 3.0 (Cone Response): Normal in Complete; reduced amplitude and square-wave appearance in Incomplete.
30 Hz Flicker: Normal timing in Complete; markedly delayed and bifid appearance in Incomplete.
Dark Adaptation: Elevated rod threshold (stays at cone level in Complete; slow descent in Incomplete).

rows: Progressive field loss, family history of blindness
Bitot spots, dry eye, history of malabsorption
Absent Photopic ERG; Normal Scotopic ERG

branches: Fundus: Metallic golden-yellow sheen in light
Adaptation: Sheen disappears after 2-12 hours of dark adaptation
ERG: Riggs-type; slow b-wave recovery after prolonged dark

sections.title: Specific Variant: Fundus Albipunctatus
content: Mutation: RDH5 gene (impaired 11-cis retinal regeneration)
Fundus: Multiple, small, uniform white-yellow dots (sparing fovea)
Symptoms: Stationary night blindness; slow recovery of vision after bright light
ERG: Initially reduced amplitudes; normalize after ultra-prolonged dark adaptation (hours)
Differentiate from: Retinitis Punctata Albescens (which is progressive)

sections.title: Management & Patient Care
content: 1. Accurate Diagnosis: Confirm 'stationary' nature to provide prognosis (reassurance to family).
2. Refraction: Early and accurate correction of myopia to prevent refractive amblyopia.
3. Strabismus/Nystagmus: Monitor and treat surgically if a significant compensatory head turn is present.
4. Low Vision Aids: Refer for bioptics or specialized dim-light mobility training if required.
5. Genetic Counseling: Determine inheritance pattern for family planning.
6. Career Guidance: Advise against professions requiring night driving or dark-room activities.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Doubt CSNB
content: Progressive narrowing of visual fields (suggests RP)
Bone-spicule pigmentation or vessel attenuation (suggests RP)
Absence of 'negative' ERG configuration (b-wave > a-wave)
History of nyctalopia starting in adolescence (not congenital)
Rapidly declining visual acuity

content.explanation: N: Night blindness, E: Early onset, G: Genetic, B: B-wave is Bottomed out (Negative ERG: b-wave amplitude < a-wave amplitude).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Paradoxical Pupil' (constriction when lights go out) is a classic sign of CSNB and Achromatopsia.
Mizuo-Nakamura Phenomenon is pathognomonic for Oguchi disease but can rarely be seen in X-linked Retinoschisis.
X-linked CSNB is the most common cause of a negative ERG in a child with a normal fundus.
Unlike RP, the a-wave in CSNB remains normal because the primary defect is post-photoreceptoral.
High myopia is so prevalent in cCSNB that its absence should prompt re-evaluation of the diagnosis.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Research
sections.content: Recent research focuses on gene therapy for CACNA1F and TRPM1 mutations using AAV vectors. Studies in animal models (e.g., the noble's rat) have shown restoration of b-wave function and signal transmission. Advanced imaging with Adaptive Optics (AO) has confirmed that while signal transmission is blocked, the photoreceptor mosaic remains structurally intact, making CSNB an ideal candidate for future gene replacement therapies.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) is a microscopic surgical procedure involving the removal of the vitreous gel from the posterior segment of the eye. This allows direct access to the retina and underlying structures for the treatment of various vitreoretinal pathologies. It is a critical intervention for complications of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) and complex Retinal Detachments (RD). Diabetic Retinopathy is a microvascular complication of diabetes, leading to retinal ischemia, neovascularization, and potentially severe vision loss. Retinal Detachment is the separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), a sight-threatening emergency.

sections.title: Risk Factors for DR & RD
content: **For Diabetic Retinopathy:** Duration of diabetes (most significant), poor glycemic control (HbA1c > 7%), hypertension, dyslipidemia, nephropathy, pregnancy.

**For Retinal Detachment:** Myopia (high axial length), previous cataract surgery (pseudophakia/aphakia), trauma, family history of RD, lattice degeneration, inflammation, Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR).

branches: Increased VEGF, IGF-1, other Growth Factors

rows: More than mild, less than severe
Microaneurysms, hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading
4 quadrants of severe hemorrhages/MA, 2 quadrants of venous beading, 1 quadrant of prominent IRMA (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities)
Neovascularization (NVD, NVE, NVI/NVA) without vitreous hemorrhage (VH) or tractional RD
NVD > 1/4-1/3 disc area, or NVD with VH, or NVE > 1/2 disc area with VH
Dense vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment (TRD), combined TRD/RRD, neovascular glaucoma

branches: Rhegmatogenous RD (RRD): Caused by a full-thickness retinal break (hole/tear), allowing vitreous fluid into subretinal space.
Tractional RD (TRD): Caused by vitreoretinal membranes pulling on the retina, lifting it off the RPE (common in PDR).
Exudative (Serous) RD: Caused by subretinal fluid accumulation from RPE/choroidal pathology (e.g., inflammation, tumor), without a break or traction.

sections.title: 6. Clinical Features & Symptoms (DR & RD)
content: **Diabetic Retinopathy:** Often asymptomatic in early stages. Symptoms include blurred vision, vision fluctuation, metamorphopsia (from macular edema), floaters (from vitreous hemorrhage), sudden painless vision loss (VH or TRD involving macula).

**Retinal Detachment:** Acute onset of 'flashes' (photopsia) and 'floaters' (new PVD/hemorrhage), progressive 'curtain' or 'shadow' in peripheral vision, decreased central vision (if macula involved), metamorphopsia, sensation of 'cobwebs'.

sections.title: 7. Ocular Examination Findings (DR & RD)
content: **Findings in DR:** Microaneurysms, dot/blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, IRMA, venous beading, neovascularization (NVD, NVE, NVI/NVA), pre-retinal hemorrhage, vitreous hemorrhage, fibrovascular membranes, macular edema (CME), tractional retinal detachment.

**Findings in RD:** Reduced visual acuity, afferent pupillary defect (if severe/macula-off), reduced IOP (may be normal or high in chronic cases), loss of red reflex, Shafer's sign (tobacco dust in anterior vitreous - pathognomonic for RRD), undulating/bullous detached retina, pigment demarcation lines (chronic RD), retinal breaks (holes, tears, dialysis), PVR (proliferative vitreoretinopathy - fixed folds, starfolds), specific for TRD: concave retinal surface, fixed folds, vitreous membranes, often no associated breaks in primary TRD.

rows: Prevents fundus view for PRP, persistent vision loss. Typically >3 months wait for spontaneous clear.
To relieve vitreoretinal traction, prevent/repair macula-off RD, restore retinal anatomy.
To relieve traction and close retinal breaks simultaneously.
Severe Proliferative DR unresponsive to PRP/Anti-VEGF
Persistent neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, or progressive traction.
Complex RRD (PVR C, inferior breaks, giant tears)
Unsuitable for scleral buckle or pneumatic retinopexy; extensive PVR requires membrane peeling.
Macular Hole (MH), Epiretinal Membrane (ERM), Vitreomacular Traction (VMT)
To release traction and improve/restore macular anatomy and function.
Vitreous biopsy, intravitreal antibiotic delivery, clearing inflammatory debris.
Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB), traumatic VH, retained lens fragments
Removal of foreign bodies, clearing hemorrhage, managing associated RD.
Retained lens fragments/dropped nucleus post-cataract surgery
Removal of fragments to prevent inflammation/glaucoma.

sections.title: 9. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content:
**Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic Examination**
   - Visual acuity, IOP measurement, Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (anterior segment, NVI/NVA).
   - Dilated fundus examination with indirect ophthalmoscopy and scleral depression (for full peripheral view, identifying breaks, extent of RD, traction).

**Step 2: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**
   - High-resolution cross-sectional imaging of the retina.
   - Essential for diagnosing macular edema, ERM, VMT, subtle TRD, and assessing retinal attachment.

**Step 3: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA)**
   - Identifies areas of capillary non-perfusion, microaneurysms, neovascularization (leakage), macular edema, and IRMA.
   - Crucial for guiding PRP treatment.

**Step 4: B-scan Ultrasonography**
   - Indispensable when media opacities (dense VH, mature cataract) preclude direct visualization of the fundus.
   - Differentiates VH from RD, identifies choroidal detachment, IOFB, and assesses retinal configuration.

**Step 5: Systemic Workup (for DR patients)**
   - HbA1c, fasting blood glucose, blood pressure, renal function tests (serum creatinine, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio), lipid profile.
   - Optimizing systemic health is paramount for surgical success and long-term prognosis.

rows: Splitting of neurosensory layers (not full separation). Immobile, typically smooth and dome-shaped. Absence of Shafer's sign. May be bilateral. Absolute scotoma corresponding to the schisis.
Smooth, bullous, dark brown-orange elevations. Usually posterior to ora serrata. Associated with hypotony. 'Kissing choroidals' configuration. Does not undulate with eye movement.
Smooth, shifting subretinal fluid. No retinal breaks or traction. Associated with inflammatory conditions (e.g., Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada), tumors, severe hypertension, choroidal effusions.
Sudden vision loss/floaters. No 'curtain' unless settling. B-scan shows mobile echoes in vitreous, but retina attached. Red reflex may be dimmed/absent.
Usually stable, congenital or post-surgical. Retinal tissue is attached. OCT confirms folds without detachment.
Subretinal fluid/schisis in macula associated with congenital optic disc pit. Distinct fundus appearance of the optic nerve head.

sections.title: 11. Principles of Vitrectomy for Diabetic TRD
content:
**Step 1: Anesthesia & Trocar Placement**
   - Peribulbar or general anesthesia. 23G, 25G, or 27G trocar-cannula system placed through pars plana (3.5-4mm posterior to limbus), creating self-sealing sclerotomies.

**Step 2: Core Vitrectomy**
   - Removal of central clear vitreous with high-speed vitrectomy probe to gain access to posterior pole and release anterior traction.

**Step 3: Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD) Induction (if absent)**
   - May use active aspiration (suction) with the vitrectomy probe or Tano-diamond dusted membrane scraper to induce PVD, if safely possible.

**Step 4: Membrane Segmentation & Delamination**
   - **Segmentation:** Cutting fibrotic membranes into smaller pieces to reduce tangential traction, often using micro-scissors or cutter.
   - **Delamination:** Peeling fibrovascular membranes off the retinal surface using intraocular forceps (e.g., Eckardt, serrated), picks, or MVR blades. Often requires bimanual technique (one hand for illumination, one for instruments) for counter-traction and stability. This is the most critical and challenging step.

**Step 5: Hemostasis**
   - Control bleeding from fibrovascular tissue using intraocular diathermy, increased infusion pressure, or temporary application of perfluorocarbon liquid (PFCL).

**Step 6: Epiretinal Membrane (ERM) Peeling (if indicated)**
   - Peeling of residual ERM or internal limiting membrane (ILM) for macular holes or severe macular edema using diamond-dusted membrane peel forceps, often aided by vital dyes (e.g., brilliant blue G, indocyanine green).

**Step 7: Endolaser Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP)**
   - Application of 532nm green laser to the entire retina (excluding macula) to ablate ischemic areas and suppress neovascularization. Critical for preventing recurrence.

**Step 8: Fluid-Air Exchange (FAE) & Drainage of Subretinal Fluid (SRF)**
   - If a combined TRD/RRD or iatrogenic break occurs, FAE is performed to flatten the retina. SRF is drained through a retinal break (pre-existing or iatrogenic) using a soft-tipped cannula.

**Step 9: Vitreous Tamponade**
   - Injection of a vitreous substitute (air, gas, or silicone oil) to provide internal tamponade, support the retina, and facilitate fluid absorption/scarring. Choice depends on retinal pathology and surgeon preference.

**Step 10: Sclerotomy Closure**
    - Self-sealing sclerotomies with smaller gauges (23G, 25G, 27G) often require no sutures. 20G incisions always require suturing (e.g., 8-0 Vicryl).

sections.title: 12. Surgical Instruments & Techniques in PPV
content: **Vitrectomy Systems:** Modern high-speed systems (e.g., Alcon Constellation, Bausch & Lomb Stellaris Elite) with cutter speeds >10,000 cuts/minute and integrated laser/fluidics.
**Trocar-Cannula Systems:** 23-gauge (0.64mm), 25-gauge (0.50mm), 27-gauge (0.40mm) for micro-incisional vitrectomy (MIVS).
**Vitreous Cutters:** High-speed, dual-port cutters minimize vitreoretinal traction.
**Endo-illuminators:** Fiber optic light sources (standard, wide-angle, chandelier) for retinal visualization.
**Endo-laser Probes:** 532nm (green) diode lasers for PRP and focal photocoagulation.
**Membrane Forceps:** Delamination forceps (e.g., Eckardt, serrated), grasping forceps, micro-scissors for membrane dissection.
**Picks/Spatulas:** MVR blades, diamond-dusted scrapers, retinal picks for initiating membrane dissection or creating retinotomies.
**Visco-Dissection:** Use of viscoelastic agents (e.g., Healon, Viscoat) to hydro-dissect membranes off the retinal surface.
**Bimanual Surgery:** Using an instrument in each hand (e.g., light pipe in one, forceps in other) for optimal traction and dissection.
