sections.title: 14. Complications of PPV & Prognosis
content: **Intra-operative Complications:** Iatrogenic retinal breaks (most common, 5-10%), choroidal hemorrhage, suprachoroidal hemorrhage, lens touch/damage, dropped nucleus, subretinal hemorrhage.
**Early Post-operative Complications:** Acute endophthalmitis (rare, <0.1%), vitreous hemorrhage (recurrent or new), hypotony/hypertony, choroidal detachment, fibrin reaction.

**Late Post-operative Complications:** Nuclear sclerotic cataract (universal with gas/oil), glaucoma (neovascular, steroid-induced, silicone oil-induced), redetachment (due to PVR, missed breaks), silicone oil emulsification/migration, corneal decompensation, epiretinal membrane formation, cystoid macular edema.

sections.title: Prognosis after PPV for TRD
content: **Retinal Reattachment Rates:** Generally high (80-90%) for TRDs with macula-on. Lower for macula-off or combined TRD/RRD with extensive PVR.

**Visual Outcomes:** Highly variable. Dependent on preoperative VA, duration of macula-off RD, extent of retinal damage, control of systemic diabetes, development of post-operative complications (especially cataract and glaucoma). Many patients achieve functional vision, but pre-existing damage may limit best-corrected vision.

sections.title: 15. Red Flags / Emergency Signs in DR/RD
content: **Acute onset of severe floaters and/or flashes:** Suggests acute PVD or new retinal break, potentially leading to RRD.
**Sudden, profound, painless vision loss:** May indicate dense vitreous hemorrhage (e.g., from PDR), macula-off retinal detachment, or central retinal artery occlusion.
**A 'curtain' or 'shadow' obscuring vision:** Classic symptom of progressive retinal detachment.
**Severe eye pain with vision loss in a diabetic patient:** Consider acute angle closure glaucoma (especially neovascular glaucoma in advanced DR) or endophthalmitis post-op.
**Persistent blurred vision or pain post-PPV:** Requires urgent evaluation for endophthalmitis, high IOP, or redetachment.

content.explanation: At least one of the following: 4 quadrants of severe intraretinal hemorrhages/microaneurysms; 2 quadrants of venous beading; 1 quadrant of prominent IRMA (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities). Crucial for determining progression to PDR.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Systemic Control is Key:** Tight glycemic control, blood pressure, and lipid management significantly impact DR progression and surgical outcomes.
**Pre-op Anti-VEGF:** Can reduce intraoperative bleeding and improve surgical planes in PDR/TRD by regressing fragile neovascularization.
**Always Examine Peripheral Retina:** After membrane peeling, always re-examine the peripheral retina thoroughly for iatrogenic breaks, especially near sclerotomy sites.
**Patient Positioning Post-op:** Crucial for gas tamponade (e.g., face down for macular hole, specific head position for superior breaks). Contraindicated for air travel with gas.
**Silicone Oil Removal:** Generally advised (typically 3-6 months post-op) due to potential long-term complications, unless a life-long tamponade is indicated.

**Pediatric Considerations:** While this infographic focuses on DR, PPV indications in children (e.g., ROP, FEVR, trauma) require specialized instruments, techniques, and anesthetic considerations due to smaller eyes and different vitreoretinal anatomy.

sections.title: 17. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content:
**Micro-Incisional Vitrectomy Systems (MIVS):** Transition from 20-gauge to 23G, 25G, and 27G has revolutionized PPV, offering smaller incisions, reduced conjunctival scarring, less post-op astigmatism, faster visual recovery, and typically sutureless closure. 

**Anti-VEGF Therapy:** DRCR.net studies (e.g., Protocol S, T) have solidified the role of anti-VEGF agents (e.g., Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, Bevacizumab) not only for diabetic macular edema but also as an adjuvant therapy in PDR, both pre-operatively to reduce active neovascularization and intra-operatively to minimize bleeding and facilitate membrane peeling. 

**3D Heads-Up Display Surgery:** Systems like Ngenuity (Alcon) and Artevo (Zeiss) project magnified, high-resolution 3D images onto a large screen, improving surgeon ergonomics, depth perception, and allowing the entire surgical team to view the operative field simultaneously. 

**Intraoperative OCT (iOCT):** Provides real-time, cross-sectional imaging during surgery, aiding in delicate membrane peeling, identifying subtle macular pathology, and ensuring complete retinal reattachment.

sections.title: Clinical Overview & Taxonomy
sections.content: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) is the cornerstone of posterior segment surgery. While 23G, 25G, and 27G micro-incisional vitrectomy surgery (MIVS) has reduced trauma, complications remain significant. They are categorized by timing: Intraoperative (related to instrumentation and technique), Early Postoperative (<2 weeks), and Late Postoperative (>2 weeks).

branches: Scleral/Trocar: Subconjunctival gas, poor wound seal, uveal incarceration
Lens: Iatrogenic cataract (lens touch), phacofragmentation drop
Cornea: Epithelial edema (DM fold), Descemet's detachment
Vascular: Suprachoroidal hemorrhage (SCH), Retinal artery occlusion
Retina: Iatrogenic breaks (at trocar site or during traction relief)

rows: Severe pain, hypopyon, loss of Red Reflex
Aqueous suppressants (Timolol, Brimonidine); check gas volume
Intensive topical Pred Forte 1% or subconjunctival steroids
Suture leaky trocars, check for cyclodialysis cleft

sections.title: Late Complications: The Long-Term Burden
content: Cataract Progression: 80-100% of phakic patients require surgery within 2 years.
Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR): The leading cause of RD repair failure.
Epiretinal Membrane (ERM): Secondary to surgical trauma or residual hyaloid.
Neovascular Glaucoma: Especially in diabetic patients post-PPV.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Persistent inflammation or Irvine-Gass.
Silicone Oil Emulsification: 'Inverse hypopyon' and secondary glaucoma.

rows: Moderate: Inner retinal wrinkling, rolled edges of break
Severe: Full-thickness fixed retinal folds (CP: posterior, CA: anterior)

sections.title: The Endophthalmitis Protocol
content: Step 1: Clinical Suspicion (Pain out of proportion, AC cells/hypopyon).
Step 2: Immediate Vitreous/AC Tap (Gram stain, Culture & Sensitivity).
Step 3: Intravitreal Antibiotics (Vancomycin 1mg/0.1ml and Ceftazidime 2.25mg/0.1ml).
Step 4: Intensive Topical Antibiotics/Corticosteroids.
Step 5: Immediate Vitrectomy (EVS Trial: recommended if vision is Light Perception (LP)).

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Sudden loss of Light Perception (LP) - rule out Central Retinal Artery Occlusion.
Increasing pain after post-op Day 1 - suspect Endophthalmitis.
Progressive vision loss with 'curtain' - suspect recurrent Detachment or PVR.
Hard eye on palpation - Acute Post-vitrectomy IOP spike (Gas expansion).

content.explanation: P: Pressure (IOP spike); O: Oil/Gas (Overfill or migration); P: PVR/Peeling trauma; S: Sepsis (Endophthalmitis).

sections.title: Landmark Studies in Vitreoretinal Complications
content: Silicone Study: Compared Silicone Oil vs. Sulfur Hexafluoride (SF6) for PVR. Oil was superior to SF6 for retinal reattachment.
EVS (Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study): Confirmed immediate PPV is beneficial for patients presenting with Light Perception (LP) vision or worse.
DRCR.net Protocol N: Evaluated PPV for DME; found it may be beneficial when vitreoretinal traction is present.

sections.title: Surgical Pearl: Avoiding Iatrogenic Breaks
content: 1. Angle Trocar Entry: 30-45 degree tunnel for better self-sealing.
2. Clear the Base: Use Chandelier lighting or indentation to view and clear the vitreous base.
3. Trim the Wound: Ensure no vitreous incarceration before removing trocars.
4. Check for 'Whisps': Use Triamcinolone Acetonide (Kenalog) to visualize residual hyaloid.
5. Low-Vacuum Entry: Approach the retina with caution using high-cut rate, low-vacuum settings.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a 360° depressed fundus exam at the conclusion of every vitrectomy.
If IOP is high post-op with gas, check for pupillary block or expansion issues.
Pre-op prophylactic Aspirin usually doesn't need to be stopped for PPV, but Warfarin/DOACs require individual risk assessment.
Triamcinolone staining is your best friend for ensuring a complete posterior vitreous detachment (PVD).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Nyctalopia, or night blindness, is not a disease in itself but a symptom of rod-photoreceptor or Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) dysfunction. It manifests as a significantly delayed or absent adaptation to low-light environments. While often hereditary (e.g., Retinitis Pigmentosa), it can also be acquired through nutritional deficiencies or toxicities.

sections.title: Classic Retinitis Pigmentosa: The 'Diagnostic Triad'
content: 1. Bone-spicule pigmentation (mid-periphery)
2. Arteriolar attenuation (narrowed vessels)
3. Waxy pallor of the optic disc
Secondary features: Posterior Subcapsular Cataract (PSC)
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) in 10-20% of cases
Epiretinal Membranes (ERM)

sections.title: Advanced Ocular Imaging Findings
content: FAF: Hyperautofluorescent Ring (Robson-Holder ring) — represents the edge of active degeneration.
OCT: Loss of Ellipsoid Zone (EZ) line, thinning of Outer Nuclear Layer (ONL).
OCT: 'Central Island' of preserved photoreceptors in advanced cases.
Visual Fields: Mid-peripheral ring scotoma progressing to tunnel vision.

sections.title: Management Strategy & Protocols
content: Step 1: Baseline documentation (Visual Fields, ERG, FAF, OCT).
Step 2: Genetic Testing (Crucial for clinical trial eligibility).
Step 3: Medical Management (Vitamin A Palmitate 15,000 IU/day - monitor liver/lipids).
Step 4: Treat complications (CME: Topical CAIs like Dorzolamide; Cataract: Phacoemulsification).
Step 5: Low Vision Rehabilitation and mobility training.
Step 6: Gene Therapy Screening (RPE65-mediated disease only).

sections.title: Gene Therapy: The Luxturna (voretigene neparvovec) Era
content: Indication: Biallelic RPE65-mediated inherited retinal disease.
Requirement: Must have sufficient viable retinal cells (determined by OCT).
Delivery: Subretinal injection in a specialized surgical setting.
Mechanism: Delivers functional RPE65 cDNA via AAV2 vector.
Outcome: Significant improvement in multi-luminance mobility testing (MLMT).

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Sudden onset nyctalopia in an adult (Suspect CAR/MAR).
Bitot's Spots on conjunctiva (Severe Vit A deficiency - Emergency).
High doses of Vitamin E (May accelerate RP progression).
Smoking in RP patients (Accelerates vascular attenuation).
Nyctalopia with neurological symptoms (Suspect Refsum's - requires diet).

content.explanation: CSNB (Congenital Stationary Night Blindness) = Clear Fundus (usually) + Negative ERG + Stationary course. RP = Pigmented Fundus + Extinguished ERG + Progressive course.

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: Fundus Albipunctatus: A form of CSNB characterized by white dots and a delayed 'slow' regeneration of rhodopsin. ERG normalizes after prolonged dark adaptation.
Oguchi Disease: Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon (golden-yellow fundus that disappears after prolonged dark adaptation).
Refsum Disease: Triad of RP, peripheral neuropathy, and ataxia. Management is low-phytanic acid diet.
Usher Syndrome: Most common cause of combined blindness and deafness.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Trials
sections.content: Current research is focusing on Optogenetics (turning remaining bipolar or ganglion cells into photosensitive cells) and CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing for Pro23His RHO mutations. The Argus II Retinal Prosthesis System, while providing 'artificial vision,' has largely been supplanted by advancements in gene and cell-based therapies. Landmark studies like the Berson trials (Vitamin A supplementation) remain the foundation for current antioxidant recommendations.

sections.title: Epidemiology & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Gyrate atrophy is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the OAT gene (10q26.13). The metabolic hallmark is a 10-20 fold increase in plasma ornithine levels. Deficiency in OAT prevents the conversion of ornithine to pyrroline-5-carboxylate, leading to Ornithine accumulation, which is toxic to the RPE and choriocapillaris, causing the characteristic peripheral scalloped atrophy.

sections.title: Key Clinical Features
content: Nyctalopia (Night blindness) in childhood
Progressive visual field constriction
Myopia (High, often 6-10D)
Posterior subcapsular cataracts
Macular edema (Cystoid type)
Progressive peripheral chorioretinal atrophy

rows: Bone spicule pigmentation, classic ERG findings

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Plasma amino acid chromatography (Elevated Ornithine 400-1000 µmol/L).
Step 2: Fundus Examination (Peripheral scalloped RPE atrophy progressing to macula).
Step 3: Electroretinography (ERG) (Progressive reduction in scotopic and photopic responses).
Step 4: OCT (Evaluation for secondary macular edema).
Step 5: Genetic testing (Confirmation of OAT gene mutation).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to act
content: Rapid onset of central vision loss (CME)
Rapidly progressive myopia in pediatric patients
Hyperornithinemia detected in neonatal screening
Family history of early cataract development

content.explanation: O for Ornithine buildup, A for Atrophy (scalloped), T for Treatment (Vitamin B6/Pyridoxine or Diet).

sections.title: Management & Treatment
content: Dietary Modification: Low arginine, low protein diet (Ornithine is a metabolite of Arginine).
Supplementation: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) 100-500mg/day for B6-responsive patients.
Cataract Surgery: Consider early if vision is limited, but be aware of higher risk of macular edema.
CME Management: Topical NSAIDs or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
Monitoring: Annual ERG, Goldmann visual fields, and plasma amino acid levels.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Not all patients are Pyridoxine responsive; metabolic monitoring is mandatory.
Early dietary intervention significantly delays visual field loss.
The scalloped edges of the atrophy are pathognomonic—it starts mid-periphery and expands.
Maintain low plasma ornithine levels < 200 µmol/L for optimal neuroprotection.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Choroideremia (CHM) is a relentless, progressive X-linked recessive disorder leading to the pan-retinal atrophy of the choroid, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and neurosensory retina. Unlike Retinitis Pigmentosa, the hallmark is the early and profound loss of the choriocapillaris, leaving the underlying white sclera visible in a characteristic scalloped pattern.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Rab Prenylation Trap
content: 1. CHM Mutation leads to deficient Rab Escort Protein-1 (REP-1).
2. Failed geranylgeranylation (prenylation) of Rab GTPases.
3. Rabs cannot anchor to intracellular organelle membranes.
4. Failure of vesicular transport and protein trafficking.
5. Progressive RPE cell death followed by Choriocapillaris and Photoreceptor loss.

rows: Severe field loss; Central island of vision remains.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Early: Mid-peripheral pigmentary mottling resembling RP.
Mid-stage: Scalloped areas of chorioretinal atrophy expanding from periphery to center.
Late: Exposure of large choroidal vessels and white sclera; Macular sparing until the very end.
Optic Nerve: Generally preserved color (unlike the waxy pallor of RP).
Retinal Vessels: Minimal attenuation compared to Retinitis Pigmentosa.
Female Carriers: 'Moth-eaten' RPE appearance or peripheral pigmentary changes (Lyonization).

rows: Bone-spicule pigmentation, waxy disc pallor, severe vessel attenuation, primary PR loss.
Autosomal Recessive, associated with High Myopia, markedly HIGH serum Ornithine levels.
Refractile crystals in cornea/retina, different atrophy pattern (CYP4V2 mutation).
Tilted disc, peripapillary atrophy, posterior staphyloma, lack of X-linked history.
Sensorineural hearing loss accompanying retinal degeneration.

sections.title: Multimodal Imaging Gold Standards
content: FAF: Markedly hypoautofluorescent areas (atrophy) with hyperautofluorescent borders of active stress.
OCT: Loss of Outer Plexiform, Ellipsoid Zone, and RPE; Presence of Outer Retinal Tubulations (ORTs).
EDI-OCT: Shows extreme thinning of the choroid and choriocapillaris.
FFA: 'Swiss-cheese' appearance early; late visualization of large choroidal vessels and sclera.
Goldmann Perimetry: Concentric constriction with central island preservation.

rows: Focal areas of peripheral RPE loss; scalloped edges.
Confluent areas of atrophy; peripheral choriocapillaris loss.
Extensive atrophy sparing only the macula/fovea.
Total chorioretinal atrophy including the fovea.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Considerations
content: Sudden central vision drop: Rule out Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV), though rare in CHM.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Can occur and significantly reduce quality of life.
Misdiagnosis: Always check Serum Ornithine to rule out Gyrate Atrophy (which is treatable via diet).
Pediatric Presentation: Early nyctalopia in boys requires immediate genetic screening.

content.explanation: C: Chorioretinal scalloped atrophy; H: Hereditary X-linked; M: Mutations in REP-1/CHM gene.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: Unlike RP, retinal vessels are often relatively spared until very late stages.
Outer Retinal Tubulations (ORTs) on OCT are a classic sign of slow RPE degeneration in CHM.
Female carriers may show peripheral pigmentary changes due to random X-inactivation.
Genetic testing is MANDATORY for clinical trial eligibility.

sections.title: Management & Future Frontiers
content: 1. Diagnosis Confirmation: Genetic testing (CHM gene) and Genetic Counseling for families.
2. Supportive Care: UV-protecting sunglasses and Low Vision Rehabilitation.
3. Complication Management: Topical/Oral Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs) for CME.
4. Gene Therapy: AAV2-REP1 subretinal injections (Clinical trials like STAR/NIGHT studies).
5. Future Tech: Optogenetics and Retinal Prosthetics for end-stage disease.

sections.title: Recent Landmark Studies
sections.content: The Phase 3 STAR trial investigated the efficacy of voretigene-like gene therapy for CHM. While some early trials (MacLaren et al.) showed significant gain in BCVA in a subset of patients, later larger trials faced challenges meeting primary endpoints, highlighting the complexity of timing intervention before irreversible choriocapillaris loss.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Capsular phimosis is the fibrotic contraction of the anterior capsulorhexis opening (ACO) following Phacoemulsification. It results from the metaplasia and proliferation of residual lens epithelial cells (LECs) into myofibroblasts, which exert centripetal contractile forces on the capsular bag. While mild contraction is common, severe phimosis can lead to IOL decentration, zonular dialysis, and significant visual impairment.

sections.title: Etiology & Risk Factors
content: Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (PEX): Weak zonules fail to counteract contractile forces.
Small Capsulorhexis: Openings <5.0mm are significantly more prone to phimosis.
IOL Material: Silicone lenses (especially 3-piece) show higher rates than hydrophobic acrylic.
Chronic Inflammation: Uveitis increases cytokine release (TGF-beta).
Myotonic Dystrophy & Retinitis Pigmentosa: Associated with early and severe contraction.
Inadequate Cortical Cleanup: Residual LECs are the primary engine of fibrosis.

sections.title: The Pathophysiological Cascade
content: Step 1: Surgical trauma triggers cytokine release (TGF-β, IL-1, IL-6) into the aqueous humor.
Step 2: Residual A-cells (Lens Epithelial Cells) migrate from the equatorial region to the anterior capsule margin.
Step 3: Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) converts LECs into myofibroblasts.
Step 4: Expression of α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) within myofibroblasts.
Step 5: Coordinated centripetal contraction of the fibrotic membrane, reducing the ACO diameter.

rows: Significant visual loss, zonular stress, RD risk.
Aphakia-like vision, high risk of IOL dislocation.
Opacity of the posterior capsule, not the rhexis edge.
Surface deposits on the IOL optic, often hydrophilic acrylic.
Peripheral lens material sequestration, doesn't constrict ACO.
Lens tilt without obvious rhexis fibrosis.

branches: Zonular elongation or dialysis (visible on gonioscopy)

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS
content: Progressive IOL Decentration: Indicates asymmetric zonular failure.
Sunset Syndrome: Inferior subluxation of the IOL/capsular bag complex.
Anterior Displacement of IOL: Causes a 'myopic shift' and shallowing of the anterior chamber.
Vitreous in the Anterior Chamber: Sign of frank zonular dialysis.
Peripheral Retinal Tears: Resulting from excessive centripetal traction on the vitreous base.

sections.title: Neodymium:YAG Laser Management
content: 1. Dilate the pupil fully to visualize the fibrotic edge.
2. Apply topical anesthesia (e.g., Proparacaine).
3. Use a YAG-laser offset of 0 to +100μm.
4. Energy: 1.2 – 2.5 mJ per pulse.
5. Create 4 to 6 radial relaxing incisions (Cruciate pattern).
6. Post-op: Topical NSAIDs or Steroids for 3-5 days; monitor IOP.

content.explanation: R-adial incisions (4-6), A-void IOL pits, D-iameter expansion goal, I-ncremental energy, A-ssess zonules, L-ower IOP monitoring.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention (Advanced Cases)
content: Manual Capsulectomy: Use micro-scissors (Vannas) to excise the fibrotic ring.
Plasma Blade (Fugo Blade): High-frequency cutting to reopen the ACO.
IOL Exchange: Required if the IOL is severely damaged or permanently decentered.
Scleral Fixation: If zonular loss is >4 clock hours, the bag-IOL complex may require sutured fixation (Gore-Tex or Yamane).

sections.title: Intraoperative Prevention Strategies
content: Optimal Rhexis Size: Aim for 5.5mm to 6.0mm (never <5.0mm).
Capsular Polishing: Thoroughly polish the underside of the anterior capsule to remove A-cells.
IOL Selection: Choose hydrophobic acrylic with sharp square edges.
Capsular Tension Ring (CTR): Distributes contractile forces; essential in PEX patients.
Large Optic IOLs: 6.0mm optics provide more mechanical resistance to contraction than 5.0mm optics.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Early intervention is easier: YAG is much more effective before the fibrosis becomes 'woody'.
Zonular check: If you see the IOL 'shaking' during YAG, the zonules are already compromised.
The 'Aqueous Outflow' theory: Chronic inflammation leads to higher levels of TGF-beta in the aqueous, fueling the myofibroblasts.
In RP patients, perform prophylactic YAG relaxing incisions 1-month post-op if contraction is seen.

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
sections.content: With timely YAG laser anterior capsulotomy, the visual prognosis is excellent. The ACO usually remains stable after radial incisions are made. However, if zonular dialysis has already occurred, the patient may face long-term risks of IOL subluxation requiring complex vitreoretinal intervention.

content.explanation: S-ilicone IOLs, M-yopia/Myotonic Dystrophy, A-dvanced PEX, L-ow zonular integrity, L-imited (Small) Rhexis.

title: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage: The Ophthalmic Surgeon's Nightmare
summary: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage (SCH) is a devastating ocular emergency characterized by the accumulation of blood in the suprachoroidal space between the choroid and the sclera, often triggered by sudden hypotony during intraocular surgery.

data.title: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage: The Ophthalmic Surgeon's Nightmare
data.summary: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage (SCH) is a devastating ocular emergency characterized by the accumulation of blood in the suprachoroidal space between the choroid and the sclera, often triggered by sudden hypotony during intraocular surgery.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Suprachoroidal hemorrhage (SCH) involves the rupture of the long or short posterior ciliary arteries, leading to rapid blood accumulation in the potential space between the choroid and the sclera. It is categorized into 'limited' (localized) or 'expulsive' (massive hemorrhage with extrusion of intraocular contents). While rare (incidence <0.2% in modern phacoemulsification), it remains one of the most vision-threatening complications in ophthalmic surgery.

sections.title: The Pathophysiological Cascade
content: 1. Sudden Hypotony: Opening the globe or rapid drop in IOP.
2. Vascular Dilation: Choroidal vessels expand due to pressure gradient.
3. Serous Effusion: Fluid moves into suprachoroidal space.
4. Vessel Rupture: Stretch on ciliary arteries leads to shearing and rupture.
5. Massive Hemorrhage: High-pressure arterial blood fills the space.

rows: Localized, often in one or two quadrants; may resolve with medical therapy.
Involves 360 degrees; high IOP; 'kissing choroidals' on B-scan.
Ejection of vitreous, lens, or retina through surgical wound.
Occurs days after surgery, often associated with a cough or Valsalva.

sections.title: INTRAOPERATIVE RED FLAGS
content: Sudden shallowing of the anterior chamber (AC)
Rapid increase in Intraocular Pressure (IOP)
Loss of the Red Reflex (replaced by dark mass)
Hardening of the globe (stony-hard)
Prolapse of the iris, vitreous, or lens material
Severe, acute ocular pain (if patient is under local anesthesia)

branches: Slit Lamp: Shallow AC, high IOP

rows: Clear fluid, transilluminates well, low/normal IOP
Undulating membrane, no dome shape, 'tobacco dust'
Intrinsic vascularity, sentinel vessels, slow onset

sections.title: Immediate Intraoperative Management
content: Step 1: Immediate closure of all surgical incisions (Suture everything).
Step 2: Restore Intraocular Pressure using OVD (Viscoelastic) or saline.
Step 3: Administer IV Acetazolamide or Mannitol to lower IOP.
Step 4: Do NOT attempt to drain the blood immediately (arterial pressure will just refill it).
Step 5: Administer subconjunctival steroids and end the case.

content.explanation: P: Pain (Severe, boring), A: AC Shallowing, I: IOP Elevation, N: No Red Reflex, S: Sudden Vision Loss.

sections.title: Postoperative Medical Therapy
content: Intensive topical steroids (e.g., Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h)
Systemic steroids (Prednisone 60-80mg daily) to reduce inflammation
Aggressive IOP control (Topical Beta-blockers, CAIs, Alpha-agonists)
Cycloplegics (Atropine 1%) to stabilize blood-aqueous barrier
Pain management with systemic analgesics

sections.title: Surgical Drainage Protocol
content: 1. Observation Period: Wait 7 to 14 days for clot liquefaction (Gold Standard).
2. Imaging Check: Repeat B-scan to confirm liquefaction (decreasing echogenicity).
3. Sclerotomies: Perform radial or circumferential sclerotomies in affected quadrants (usually 6-8mm from limbus).
4. AC/Vitreous Maintenance: Use an infusion cannula to maintain IOP during drainage.
5. Vitrectomy: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) often required to manage vitreous incarceration or associated RD.
6. Perfluorocarbon Liquid (PFCL): Use 'heavy water' to flatten the choroid and push blood out through sclerotomies.

sections.title: Landmark Study: AREDS and SCH
sections.content: While AREDS is for ARMD, various retrospective series (e.g., the Beaver Dam Eye Study and smaller surgical cohorts) have established that the highest risk for SCH occurs in patients with axial lengths >26mm and those undergoing combined Glaucoma-Cataract procedures. The timing of drainage was significantly influenced by the 'liquefaction study' (Hoffman et al.), advocating for the 10-14 day delay.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Phthisis Bulbi: Chronic hypotony and globe atrophy (high risk in expulsive SCH).
Tractional or Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment.
Corneal Decompensation: Due to prolonged high IOP or AC shallowing.
Chronic Secondary Glaucoma.
Prognosis: Poor if macula-involving or if expulsive; 50% achieve <20/200.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Pre-op: Always ask about Aspirin, Warfarin, or Clopidogrel. Control BP before surgery.
Intra-op: If you suspect SCH, CLOSE THE WOUND IMMEDIATELY. A single suture can save the eye.
Imaging: B-scan is the most critical tool for monitoring; serial scans show when the clot is ready for drainage.
Management: Do not rush to the OR for drainage on Day 1. Patient outcomes are better when blood has liquefied.
Differential: If the IOP is low, think Serous Effusion. If the IOP is high, think Hemorrhage.

title: Ocular Surface Reconstruction: AMG vs. MMG
summary: A comprehensive comparative guide for Ophthalmic surgeons on biological scaffolds. While Amniotic Membrane Grafting (AMG) provides temporary anti-inflammatory and pro-healing support, Mucous Membrane Grafting (MMG) offers permanent structural reconstruction for end-stage ocular surface disease.

data.summary: A comprehensive comparative guide for Ophthalmic surgeons on biological scaffolds. rows: Innermost layer of human placenta (Fetal tissue)
Autologous (Patient's own buccal, labial, or tarsal mucosa)
Avascular basement membrane + thick avascular stroma

sections.title: AMG: The Biological Swiss Army Knife
Indications for AMG (Exhaustive)
content: Persistent Epithelial Defects (PED) unresponsive to medical therapy
Acute Chemical/Thermal Burns (to suppress immediate inflammation)
Acute Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS/TEN) - Grade 1-3
Pterygium surgery (Primary or Recurrent) to reduce recurrence risk
Bullous Keratopathy (Symptomatic pain relief in poor visual potential)
Partial Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency (LSCD)
Filtering Bleb leaks (Glaucoma surgery rescue)
Mooren's Ulcer and peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK)
Neurotrophic Keratopathy
Conjunctival Chalasis and symblepharon prevention

sections.title: Indications for MMG (Structural)
content: Chronic Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (Late cicatricial stage)
Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid (OCP) - End stage reconstruction
Lid Margin Keratinization (Grafting the posterior lid margin)
Severe Symblepharon or Anophthalmic Socket contraction
Fornix Reconstruction (Restoring depth for motility or prosthetics)
Superior Limbic Keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) - Refractory cases
Severe Trichiasis/Distichiasis causing corneal trauma
Lagophthalmos secondary to cicatricial eyelid shortening

rows: Sutured or glued within the defect edges
Permanent integration, scaffold for epithelial crawl
Combination of Inlay and Overlay layers
Filling deep stromal craters while protecting surface
Sutureless AM held by a polycarbonate ring

sections.title: Harvesting Buccal MMG: Process
content: Step 1: Identify donor site (Buccal mucosa or lower labial mucosa)
Step 2: Local infiltration with Xylocaine 2% + Epinephrine 1:100,000
Step 3: Mark graft size (usually 20% larger to account for shrinkage)
Step 4: Dissect Split-thickness or Full-thickness graft (avoid Stensen's duct!)
Step 5: Defat the graft meticulously using Westcott scissors
Step 6: Secure to ocular surface with 8-0 or 9-0 Vicryl/Silk sutures

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: When to use which?

rows: Persistent inflammation if basement membrane is lost
Donor site morbidity (pain, scarring, restricted jaw opening)
Keratinization of the graft if ocular surface is extremely dry

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Never use AMG in active infection (Fungal/Bacterial) without antimicrobial coverage.
Avoid harvesting MMG near Stensen's duct (opposite the upper 2nd molar).
MMG will keratinize if the patient has zero tear production (Schirmer 0).
AMG 'epithelium-up' vs 'epithelium-down' matters for integration (Inlay vs Overlay).

content.explanation: Anti-inflammatory, Anti-fibrotic, Anti-angiogenic, Anti-microbial.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Cryopreserved AM (AmnioGraft) retains heavy-chain hyaluronic acid/PTX3 complex, making it superior for anti-inflammation compared to dehydrated AM.
In MMG harvesting, a 'thin' graft is preferred for the lid margin to prevent a bulky look, while a 'thicker' graft is better for deep fornix reconstruction.
Glue (Fibrin/Tisseel) can be used to secure AMG, significantly reducing surgical time and post-op irritation compared to sutures.
The 'Lid Margin Rotation' combined with MMG is the gold standard for treating corneal-chafing keratinized lids in OCP.
For PED, if the AMG melts within 7 days, it suggests a highly proteolytically active ocular surface—consider systemic collagenase inhibitors (Tetracyclines).

sections.title: Landmark Evidence: SJS/TEN
sections.content: The landmark study by Gregory (2011) and later Kim et al. established that AMG applied within the first 72-96 hours of SJS onset significantly reduces long-term visual morbidity from 70% down to less than 10%. MMG remains the secondary choice for rehabilitating those who missed the early AMG window.

title: Sunset & Sunrise IOL Syndromes: Navigating Post-Operative Decentration
summary: Sunset and Sunrise syndromes represent distinct patterns of Intraocular Lens (IOL) decentration resulting from zonular instability, asymmetric haptic placement, or capsular bag contraction. This guide details the clinical recognition and surgical management of these malpositioned lenses.

branches: Sunset Syndrome: Inferior decentration of the IOL where the superior edge of the optic is visible in the pupillary axis.
Sunrise Syndrome: Superior decentration of the IOL where the inferior edge of the optic is visible in the pupillary axis.
Windshield Wiper: Lateral oscillating movement of a sulcus-placed IOL due to inadequate haptic-to-haptic diameter.
Lost Lens: Complete dislocation into the vitreous cavity.

sections.title: Sunset vs. Sunrise: The Comparative Anatomy

rows: Superior zonular dialysis or gravity (one haptic in bag, one in sulcus)
Asymmetric haptic placement (superior haptic in sulcus, inferior haptic in bag) + fibrosis

sections.title: Etiology & Risk Factors
content: Zonular Laxity: PXF, Marfan syndrome, Homocystinuria, Weill-Marchesani.
Trauma: Blunt ocular trauma causing zonular dialysis.
Surgical Factors: Asymmetrical haptic placement (one haptic out/one in).
Capsular Factors: Progressive capsular phimosis and bag contraction.
High Myopia: Longer axial lengths (≥26.5mm) correlate with larger capsular bags and weaker zonules.
Previous Vitrectomy: Reduced vitreous support for the lens capsule.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Sudden decrease in visual acuity with new monocular diplopia.
Uveitis-Glaucoma-Hyphema (UGH) Syndrome: Haptic rubbing against the posterior iris.
Vitreous in the anterior chamber (sign of zonular/capsular rupture).
Retinal detachment associated with posterior IOL migration.
Phacodonesis or IOL-donesis on slit-lamp examination.

sections.title: The Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Dilated Slit Lamp Exam: Assess IOL centration, haptic position, and zonular integrity.
2. Retroillumination Photography: Essential to document the optic-pupil relationship.
3. Gonioscopy: Check for haptic erosion or iris tucking.
4. Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM): The gold standard for identifying haptic location (In-the-bag vs. Sulcus).
5. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Assess for Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) secondary to inflammation.

rows: Induces high astigmatism but optic center remains in axis
Occurs in phakic patients; phacodonesis present
Vision loss without diplopia or edge glare
Obscured red reflex; different clinical history

sections.title: Grading of Decentration (AAO/Guyton)
content: Grade 1: <1mm decentration (Usually asymptomatic).
Grade 2: 1-2mm decentration (Edge of optic visible in pupil).
Grade 3: 2-3mm decentration (Visual axis near edge of optic).
Grade 4: >3mm decentration (Visual axis outside of the optic).

sections.title: Surgical Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Observation if asymptomatic and stable.
Step 2: Miotics (Pilocarpine) for mild cases with edge-glare.
Step 3: Surgical Repositioning (McCannel or Siepser Suture).
Step 4: Scleral Fixation (Yamane Technique or Gore-Tex Suture).
Step 5: IOL Exchange (AC-IOL or Scleral-Fixated PCIOL).

rows: Mild to moderate decentration with intact iris
Total lack of capsular support; 3-piece IOL
Scleral suture fixation without conjunctival peritomy
Scleral-fixated PCIOL with Gore-Tex or Prolene

content.explanation: S: Superior haptic in Sulcus; U: Under-bag inferior haptic; N: Noted Sunrise; U: Upward shift; P: Phimosis/Fibrosis often contributes.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & High-Yield Facts
content: 1-Piece Acrylic IOLs should NEVER be placed in the sulcus (high risk of UGH).
3-Piece IOLs are the 'workhorse' for repositioning due to thin, flexible PMMA haptics.
If the IOL is sunsetting, check the superior zonules first.
YAG capsulotomy can sometimes worsen decentration if the bag is already unstable.
Wait at least 3-6 months post-op before deciding on surgery if the vision is functional.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Retinal Detachment: Higher risk during IOL manipulation/exchange.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Common after secondary IOL procedures.
Corneal Decompensation: Risk of endothelial cell loss during AC-IOL insertion.
Secondary Glaucoma: Pigment dispersion or UGH syndrome.
Endophthalmitis: Rare risk with any intraocular re-entry.

sections.title: Recent Advances: The Yamane Influence
sections.content: The Flanged Intrascleral Haptic Fixation (Yamane Technique) has revolutionized the management of Sunrise/Sunset syndromes. By using 30-gauge needles to create scleral tunnels and cautery to create haptic 'bulbs,' surgeons can securely fixate a 3-piece IOL without sutures. This has significantly reduced the operative time and long-term risk of suture degradation (e.g., 10-0 Prolene snapping).

title: Eales Disease: The Enigmatic Peripheral Perivasculitis
summary: A primary idiopathic inflammatory venous occlusive disease of the peripheral retina, predominantly affecting young healthy males. It is characterized by three distinct stages: perivascular inflammation, peripheral ischemia, and retinal neovascularization.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Eales disease is an idiopathic, inflammatory, peripheral retinal venulitis characterized by stages of inflammation (sheathing), non-perfusion (ischemia), and neovascularization. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and primarily affects the peripheral retina, often leading to recurrent vitreous hemorrhages.

branches: High prevalence of HLA-B5, DR1, DR4

rows: Neovascularization elsewhere (NVE) or on the Disc (NVD)
Complications: Rubeosis Iridis, NVG, Phthisis Bulbi

sections.title: 5. Ocular Examination Findings
content: Vascular Sheathing: Peripheral venous 'cuffing' (exudative white lines).
Venous Tortuosity: Dilated, beaded peripheral veins.
Peripheral Hemorrhages: Flame-shaped or dot-blot in the periphery.
Neovascularization: Classic 'Sea-fan' pattern at the junction of perfused/non-perfused retina.
Macular Edema: Cystoid changes due to chronic inflammation.
Vitreous: Cells (1+ to 3+), haze, or frank hemorrhage.

rows: Massive exudation; Telangiectatic vessels; usually unilateral
Sectoral; follows anatomy of vein crossing

sections.title: 7. Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Step 1: Ultra-Widefield FFA — Identify peripheral capillary non-perfusion (CNP) and NVE.
Step 2: Mantoux Test / QuantiFERON-TB Gold — Screen for TB hypersensitivity/exposure.
Step 3: Chest X-Ray — Rule out active TB or Sarcoidosis.
Step 4: Blood Panel — CBC, ESR, ESR, ANA, ACE, VDRL/RPR to exclude other vasculitides.
Step 5: B-Scan Ultrasonography — Essential when Vitreous Hemorrhage obscures view to rule out TRD.
Step 6: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) — Assess for Macular Edema or VMT.

sections.title: 8. Medical Management Protocols
content: Corticosteroids: Mainstay for active perivasculitis (Oral Prednisolone 1mg/kg tapered).
Periocular Injections: Sub-Tenon's Triamcinolone for localized inflammation or CME.
Anti-TB Therapy (ATT): Considered if Mantoux is strongly positive (though controversial).
Anti-VEGF: Intravitreal Ranibizumab or Bevacizumab for NVE regression or pre-op.
Antioxidants: Vitamin C and E supplements often used based on oxidative stress theory.

sections.title: 9. Laser & Surgical Intervention
content: Step 1: Sectoral PRP — Target areas of non-perfusion identified on FFA.
Step 2: 360-degree Peripheral Laser — If widespread ischemia is present.
Step 3: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) — Indicated for non-clearing VH (>1-3 months).
Step 4: Membrane Peeling — For TRD or epiretinal membranes.
Step 5: Endolaser — During PPV to ensure all ischemic areas are treated.

sections.title: 10. Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Sudden 'Shower of floaters' or 'black curtain' (Vitreous Hemorrhage).
Fixed shadow in vision (Tractional Retinal Detachment).
Severe eye pain and redness (Neovascular Glaucoma).
Rapid vision loss in a previously 'quiet' eye.
Strongly positive Mantoux (>20mm) or abnormal CXR (suggests active TB).

content.explanation: E: Early adulthood (Young males); A: Areas of non-perfusion (Peripheral); L: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis/Inflammation; E: Exclude other causes; S: Sea-fan neovascularization.

sections.title: 12. Key Clinical Pearls
content: The hallmark of Eales is peripheral venous sheathing; arterial involvement is rare.
Always check the 'good' eye; Eales is often bilateral but asymmetric.
Ultra-widefield FFA is the gold standard for management decisions.
Wait at least 48 hours after Anti-VEGF before Vitrectomy to reduce 'crunch' syndrome (though less common in Eales than DM).

sections.title: 13. Complications & Prognosis
sections.content: Visual prognosis is generally good if treated before Stage IIIb. Complications include recurrent Vitreous Hemorrhage, Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD), Macular ERM, and Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG). Chronic macular edema is the leading cause of persistent visual morbidity.

sections.title: 14. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: PCR for M. Tuberculosis: Nested PCR on aqueous/vitreous samples shows TB DNA in many Eales patients.
Proteomics: Identification of unique inflammatory markers (IL-6, MCP-1) in vitreous.
UWF-Imaging: Ultra-widefield fundus photography has revolutionized staging and laser targeting.

title: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA): The Ocular Perspective
summary: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (formerly Wegener’s) is a systemic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis primarily affecting small-to-medium vessels. Ocular involvement occurs in up to 50% of patients and is often the presenting sign, necessitating a multidisciplinary approach.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: GPA is a systemic pauci-immune vasculitis associated with anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA). It manifests as necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, typically involving the upper and lower respiratory tracts and kidneys. Ocular pathology stems from direct vasculitis or contiguous spread from orbital granulomatous tissue.

sections.title: Red Flags: Ocular Emergencies
content: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK) - high risk of globe perforation
Rapidly progressive orbital mass causing compressive optic neuropathy
Sudden vision loss from retinal artery or vein occlusion
Acute scleritis unresponsive to topical steroids

rows: Upper/lower respiratory tract, eye involvement, no systemic signs
Renal failure (Cr > 5.6 mg/dL) or other end-organ failure

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Serology (c-ANCA / PR3-ANCA)
Step 2: Biopsy (Gold Standard: Tissue biopsy from lung/sinus/sclera)
Step 3: Imaging (CT Orbit/Sinus for bony erosion; MRI for soft tissue)
Step 4: Chest X-ray/CT Chest to assess pulmonary nodules
Step 5: Urinalysis & Creatinine to assess renal involvement

content.explanation: W: Wegener's (GPA), E: Eyes/Ears, G: Granulomas, E: Entrapment (nasal/sinus), N: Necrotizing, E: Elevated PR3, R: Renal

sections.title: Treatment Protocol
content: Induction: Cyclophosphamide (oral or IV pulse) + High dose IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day x 3 days) followed by tapered oral Prednisone.
Biologics: Rituximab is non-inferior to Cyclophosphamide for induction, especially in relapsing disease.
Maintenance: Methotrexate or Azathioprine.
Ocular Surgery: Defer surgery if possible; perform only once inflammation is controlled due to poor wound healing (scleral patch grafts for PUK).
Recent Advances: Landmark RAVE (Rituximab in ANCA-Associated Vasculitis) trial established Rituximab as the preferred agent for induction in severe cases.

title: PUK vs. Mooren’s Ulcer: The Peripheral Melt Masterclass
summary: A high-stakes clinical distinction between life-threatening systemic vasculitis (PUK) and a relentless, idiopathic autoimmune keratitis (Mooren’s). This guide provides a textbook-level breakdown of diagnosis, systemic workup, and aggressive management strategies.

data.summary: A high-stakes clinical distinction between life-threatening systemic vasculitis (PUK) and a relentless, idiopathic autoimmune keratitis (Mooren’s). This guide provides a textbook-level breakdown of diagnosis, systemic workup, and aggressive management strategies.

rows: Peripheral corneal thinning with an overlying epithelial defect, associated with stromal infiltration and systemic autoimmune disease.
A rare, idiopathic, relentlessly progressive peripherally-located ulcerative keratitis that occurs in the absence of any detectable systemic disease.
Strictly limited to the cornea; Sclera is characteristically spared.

sections.title: Epidemiology & Demographics
content: PUK: Most common in 5th-7th decades; No gender predilection.
Mooren's Type 1: Typically elderly patients, usually unilateral, responds well to treatment.
Mooren's Type 2: Younger patients (20s-30s), often bilateral, aggressive, poor prognosis.
Mooren's Type 2 is more prevalent in parts of Africa and India.
PUK incidence is tied to the prevalence of systemic RA (approx 3/million/year).

sections.title: Clinical Features Checklist
content: Crescent-shaped peripheral stromal ulceration.
Undermining 'overhanging' leading edge (Pathognomonic for Mooren's).
Epithelial defect over the area of thinning.
Vascularization up to the base of the ulcer.
Severe pain, photophobia, and lacrimation.
Progresses circumferentially and then centrally.
Stromal loss can lead to descemetocele or perforation.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Ocular Emergencies
content: Presence of PUK may indicate active, life-threatening systemic vasculitis (Mortality up to 40% if untreated).
Sudden decrease in pain (may indicate impending perforation).
Positive Seidel test in the area of thinning.
Co-existing Scleritis: Signifies a much more aggressive systemic process.
Rapid circumferential progression (Full 360-degree 'Stage-Coach Wheel' melt).

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Detailed review of systems (joints, skin, respiratory, renal).
Step 2: Serology (RF, anti-CCP, ANA, ANCA, ESR, CRP).
Step 3: Infectious screen (Syphilis, Hep B/C, HIV, Quantiferon Gold).
Step 4: Chest X-ray (GPA, Sarcoidosis, TB).
Step 5: Urinalysis (to look for RBC casts/hematuria in Vasculitis).
Step 6: Corneal scraping (to rule out infectious keratitis).

branches: Catarrhal Keratitis (Staph Hypersensitivity, Clear space to limbus)

sections.title: Management Strategy: Step-Ladder Approach
content: 1. Aggressive Lubrication & Prophylactic Antibiotics (Moxifloxacin).
2. Topical Steroids (Pred Forte 1%) - Use with caution in PUK, more useful in Mooren's.
3. Systemic Corticosteroids (Prednisone 1mg/kg/day) for immediate control.
4. Steroid-Sparing Immunomodulatory Therapy (IMT): Methotrexate, Mycophenolate, or Azathioprine.
5. Cytotoxic Agents: Cyclophosphamide (Gold Standard for GPA/PAN related PUK).
6. Biologics: Rituximab (anti-CD20) or Infliximab (anti-TNFα) for refractory cases.
7. Surgical Intervention if perforation is imminent or medical therapy fails.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques & Interventions
content: Conjunctival Resection/Recession: Removes source of inflammatory cytokines/MMPs (Primarily for Mooren's).
Cyanoacrylate Tissue Adhesive: For small perforations (<2mm) or extreme thinning.
Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT): Multi-layered to provide a biological scaffold.
Lamellar Patch Graft: To restore tectonic integrity.
Tarsorrhaphy: To reduce evaporative stress and promote epithelial healing.

content.explanation: M: Mooren's is Marginal and Mostly Idiopathic. O: Overhanging edge is key. O: Only Cornea (Sclera spared). R: Resect Conjunctiva. P: PUK is Painful and Perilous (Systemic). U: Underlying Vasculitis. K: Keep checking the ANCA/RF.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: The use of Rituximab has shown superior results in GPA-related PUK compared to Cyclophosphamide in recent trials.
Topical Ciclosporin (1% or 2%) and Tacrolimus (0.03%) are increasingly used as adjuncts to reduce systemic steroid load.
Identification of Calgranulin C as a potential autoantigen in Mooren's Ulcer may lead to targeted biological therapies.
The importance of 'early hit' therapy: Initiating IMT within weeks of diagnosis improves 5-year survival rates in PUK patients.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: Never diagnose Mooren's Ulcer without a negative systemic workup.
In PUK, the ocular inflammation is often a barometer for systemic disease activity.
If a patient with RA develops PUK, their 5-year mortality risk increases significantly without systemic immunosuppression.
Avoid topical steroids in Mooren's if the stroma is extremely thin, as they can inhibit collagen synthesis and accelerate melting.
Oral Doxycycline (100mg BID) is a useful adjunct for its anti-collagenolytic (MMP-inhibitor) properties.

title: Navigating the 'Narrow Funnel': Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR) in Retinal Detachment
summary: This poster provides a comprehensive, expert-level overview of narrow funnel retinal detachment with Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR). It delves into the complex pathophysiology, detailed classification, advanced diagnostic techniques, and intricate surgical management strategies essential for ophthalmology residents and fellows.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: A 'Narrow Funnel Retinal Detachment' (RD) describes a severe form of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) complicated by advanced Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR). In this stage, the retina is contracted into a funnel-like configuration, often immobile, significantly shortened, and typically involving the macula. PVR is characterized by the proliferation, migration, and contraction of various cells (RPE, glial cells, fibroblasts, macrophages) within the vitreous and on both surfaces of the retina, leading to fixed retinal folds, subretinal bands, and eventual tractional RD. It is the leading cause of surgical failure in RRD repair.

sections.title: PVR Risk Factors
content: Giant retinal tears (>90 degrees)
Choroidal detachment
Vitreous hemorrhage
Long-standing RRD (>2 weeks)
Previous failed RD repair
Aphakia/Pseudophakia
Intraocular inflammation/trauma
Large or multiple retinal breaks
Poor visualization during surgery

branches: Retinal Break & RPE Detachment → RPE Cells Migrate
Inflammatory Cascade → Cytokine Release (PDGF, TGF-β, IL-6, IL-8)
Cellular Contraction → Fixed Retinal Folds, Traction

rows: Vitreous haze, pigment clumps (RPE cells), vitreous cells.
Wrinkling of inner retinal surface, rolled edge of retinal break, vascular sheathing, tortuosity, stiffness of retina, localized subretinal pigment dots.
Full-thickness retinal folds, often involving the macula. Retinal shortening with starfolds. Subretinal strands. Fixed folds (starfolds) on posterior retina.
Quantifies the extent of posterior fixed folds in clock hours (C1 = 1 clock hour, C12 = 12 clock hours). Further subdivided by location (Anterior, Posterior, Subretinal).
Total retinal detachment with fixed folds (often a narrow funnel shape). Anterior or posterior contraction.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Decreased vision (progressive, severe)
Visual field defect (non-resolving, often central)
Metamorphopsia (due to traction)
Photopsia/floaters (may be initial RD symptoms)
Pain (rare, suggests inflammation or secondary glaucoma)
Diplopia (if associated with ocular motility issues)

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: Reduced visual acuity
Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
Vitreous cells/hemorrhage
Retinal detachment (often bullous initially, then fixed)
Fixed retinal folds (starfolds, linear folds)
Rolled/elevated edges of retinal breaks
Subretinal membranes/bands
Vitreous traction bands (often pigmented)
Narrowed or stiffened retinal vasculature
Retinal shortening, leading to a 'funnel' configuration
Hypotony (common in severe PVR with ciliary body detachment)

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: **Detailed Ophthalmic Examination** (VA, IOP, RAPD, Slit-lamp, Fundoscopy with indirect ophthalmoscopy and scleral depression). Assess extent of RD and PVR.

Step 2: **B-scan Ultrasonography** (Required for opaque media e.g., vitreous hemorrhage). Characterizes RD configuration (funnel, open), PVR membranes, choroidal detachment, and ciliary body detachment.

Step 3: **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)** (If media allows). High-resolution imaging to identify epiretinal/subretinal membranes, vitreomacular traction, and assess macular integrity pre/post-op.
Step 4: **Anterior Segment OCT/Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM)** (To assess angle closure, anterior PVR, cyclitic membranes, ciliary body detachment/rotation).

rows: No retinal breaks, shifting fluid, often serous choroidal detachment, underlying systemic disease.
Caused by non-PVR vitreoretinal traction (e.g., severe diabetic retinopathy). No fixed folds from cellular proliferation.
Smooth, dome-shaped elevations, often bilobed (kissing choroidals), usually solid on B-scan (unless hemorrhagic). Retinal contour intact or minimally affected.
Inner and outer layers of retina split, typically stable, non-progressive. Immobile, no subretinal fluid shifting, absolute scotoma.
History of trauma, often visible IOFB on imaging (X-ray, CT), associated inflammation, localized RD or vitreous hemorrhage.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Strategy
content: Step 1: **Preoperative Optimization**: Control inflammation (topical/systemic steroids), manage IOP, consider prophylactic antibiotics.
Step 2: **Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV)**: Core vitrectomy, peripheral vitrectomy to relieve vitreous traction.

Step 3: **Membranectomy**: Meticulous removal of epiretinal and subretinal membranes using micro-forceps (e.g., 23/25/27G end-grasping forceps, Grieshaber), vitreoretinal picks (e.g., Finesse), and sometimes diamond-dusted scrapers. This is crucial for relaxing the retina.

Step 4: **Retinectomy/Relaxing Retinotomy**: If membranes are too adherent or retina is severely shortened (Grade C/D funnel), a peripheral retinectomy (full-thickness removal of a segment of retina) or relaxing retinotomy may be performed to release traction and allow the retina to flatten. Often combined with endolaser around the edges.
Step 5: **Fluid-Air Exchange**: Complete removal of subretinal fluid through a peripheral retinotomy or retinal break.
Step 6: **Endolaser Photocoagulation**: Barricade treatment around all retinal breaks and the edges of any retinectomy/retinotomy to create a chorioretinal adhesion.

Step 7: **Tamponade**: Long-acting tamponading agent (Silicone Oil or C3F8/SF6 gas). Silicone oil is preferred for severe PVR and narrow funnel RDs due to its prolonged tamponade effect, especially in inferior detachments.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: PPV for PVR
content: **Instrumentation**: 23/25/27-gauge micro-incisional vitrectomy system (MIVS) with wide-angle viewing (e.g., BIOM, RESIGHT). High-speed vitrectome.
**Core Vitrectomy**: Carefully remove central vitreous gel. Use triamcinolone acetonide for vitreous staining.

**Membrane Peeling**: Identify and delaminate epiretinal membranes (ERM) and subretinal membranes (SRM). Use bimanual technique with chandelier illumination for difficult cases. Utilize curved or angled micro-forceps. For SRMs, create a retinotomy if necessary to access, then gently peel.

**Relaxing Retinotomy**: Incise the peripheral retina circumferentially using a vitreous cutter or scissors. This is a complex maneuver requiring careful planning to avoid vital structures. Ensure sufficient healthy retina remains for reattachment.

**Perfluorocarbon Liquid (PFCL)**: Often used to flatten the retina intraoperatively after membrane peeling and before fluid-air exchange, especially in giant tears or highly mobile funnels. Slowly inject over the optic nerve, letting it push fluid out of breaks.
**Laser Retinopexy**: Apply 2-3 rows of confluent laser spots (e.g., 532nm green laser) around all breaks and retinotomy edges. Power typically 150-300mW, 100-200ms duration.

**Silicone Oil Injection**: Replace PFCL or air with silicone oil (e.g., 1000 cSt or 5000 cSt) using a pump, ensuring complete fill and no bubbles trapped under the retina. Ensure proper exchange with active aspiration of fluid from the periphery.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: Recurrent Retinal Detachment (most common failure)
Silicone Oil Complications (emulsification, migration, glaucoma, keratopathy)
Hypotony (due to cyclitic membrane, ciliary body detachment)
Secondary Glaucoma (e.g., pupillary block, angle closure, steroid-induced)
Cataract formation/progression (nearly universal post-vitrectomy)
Corneal decompensation (especially with silicone oil in aphakic eyes)
Macular pucker/edema
Phthisis Bulbi (end-stage, irreversible)

sections.title: Prognosis
sections.content: Anatomic success rates for PVR-RD repair range from 60-80% (often requiring multiple surgeries). Visual prognosis is guarded, with only 30-50% achieving functional vision (≥20/200). Factors influencing prognosis include initial PVR grade, macular status, duration of RD, and presence of hypotony.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Sudden, severe decrease in vision post-op (suspect re-detachment or hemorrhage).
New floaters, photopsias, or worsening field defect in operated eye.
Unremitting ocular pain (could indicate acute glaucoma, inflammation, or endophthalmitis).
Increasing redness, discharge, or lid swelling (suggests infection).
Persistent or severe hypotony (<6 mmHg), especially with vision loss.
Evidence of silicone oil migration into the anterior chamber with corneal contact.

content.explanation: **P**eel membranes. **V**itrectomy thorough. **R**etinectomy/Relaxing if needed. **F**luid-air exchange. **U**nderfill with PFCL. **N**arrow funnel needs oil. **N**one left behind (breaks). **E**ndolaser. **L**ong-term tamponade.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: The hallmark of PVR is fixed retinal folds, not mobile RD.
Early diagnosis and intervention for RRD are critical to prevent PVR.
Silicone oil is the tamponade of choice for most PVR-related RDs.
Bimanual surgery and wide-angle viewing systems significantly improve PVR management.
Retinectomy is a powerful, but aggressive, tool to achieve retinal flattening in severe cases.
Post-op hypotony is a strong predictor of poor outcome in PVR.
Visual recovery can be slow and often limited despite anatomic success.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Silicone Study**: Landmark trials (I and II) established silicone oil as superior to long-acting gases for complicated RDs with PVR, demonstrating better anatomic and visual outcomes.
**Micro-incisional Vitrectomy (MIVS)**: 23/25/27G systems reduce surgical trauma, faster recovery, comparable outcomes to 20G for PVR.

**Pharmacologic Adjuncts**: Ongoing research into anti-proliferative agents (e.g., 5-fluorouracil, methotrexate, corticosteroids) used as intraocular injections or in silicone oil to prevent PVR recurrence, though none are standard yet.
**Surgical Instrumentation**: Advances in wide-angle viewing, improved illumination, high-speed cutters, and precision micro-forceps have enhanced surgical capabilities.
**Heavy Silicone Oils/Tamponades**: Development of denser tamponade agents (e.g., Oxane HD) for complex inferior PVR, though not widely adopted due to challenges.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP)**: PVR-like changes are integral to severe ROP (Stage 4 & 5). Management involves lens-sparing vitrectomy, membrane peeling, and laser.
**Pediatric Trauma**: Higher incidence of PVR post-trauma in children due to increased inflammatory response and regenerative capacity. Early intervention is crucial.
**Marfan Syndrome/Stickler Syndrome**: These syndromes have a higher predisposition to RRD and PVR due to vitreoretinal degeneration. Prognosis often worse.
**Aphakic PVR**: High incidence in aphakic eyes, often requiring complex anterior and posterior segment management.
**Anatomic Differences**: Smaller eyes, denser vitreous, and often more robust inflammatory responses in children pose unique surgical challenges.

title: Sturge-Weber Syndrome: The Ocular Nexus
summary: Sturge-Weber Syndrome (SWS), or encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis, is a phakomatosis characterized by a facial port-wine stain and associated vascular malformations in the brain and eyes, most notably diffuse choroidal hemangioma.

sections.title: Definition & Etiology
sections.content: SWS is a sporadic neurocutaneous disorder. Etiology is linked to a somatic mosaic mutation in the GNAQ gene (c.548G>A) on chromosome 9q21. This results in constitutive activation of the MAPK/ERK pathway, leading to capillary/venous malformations.

sections.title: Clinical Features: The Triad
content: 1. Port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) typically involving the V1/V2 trigeminal distribution.
2. Leptomeningeal angioma (ipsilateral to facial stain), causing seizures, hemiparesis, and intellectual impairment.
3. Ocular involvement: Diffuse choroidal hemangioma (DCH) and Glaucoma.

sections.title: The 'Tomato Ketchup' Fundus
content: Diffuse choroidal hemangioma presents as a thickened, deep red-orange choroid.
Loss of the normal choroidal tessellation.
Secondary exudative retinal detachment (often bullous).
Cystoid macular edema (CME) as a chronic sequela.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to refer
content: Ipsilateral V1 port-wine stain (high risk for ocular involvement).
Acute onset of bullous exudative retinal detachment.
Refractory glaucoma unresponsive to topical medical therapy.
New-onset seizures or focal neurological deficits.

sections.title: Diagnostic Protocol
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with goniometry to assess for angle anomalies.
Step 2: Indirect ophthalmoscopy for the 'tomato ketchup' fundus appearance.
Step 3: B-scan Ultrasonography (crucial for verifying posterior segment thickening).
Step 4: Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) to show patchy hyperfluorescence/staining.
Step 5: OCT (EDI-OCT) to quantify choroidal thickness and subretinal fluid.

sections.title: Management of DCH
content: Observation for asymptomatic cases.
Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) with Verteporfin: Standard for symptomatic fluid.
Anti-VEGF intravitreal injections (adjunctive).
External beam radiotherapy (reserved for severe/refractory cases).

content.explanation: S: Seizures, T: Trigeminal distribution stain, U: Unilateral glaucoma, R: Retardation (intellectual), G: GNAQ mutation, E: Exudative detachment

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Avoid filtering surgery in SWS glaucoma if possible due to high risk of massive choroidal effusion/hemorrhage from low intraocular pressure.
Consider goniotomy or trabeculotomy for early-onset cases.
The choroidal hemangioma is benign, but its exudative nature threatens vision; treat the fluid, not just the lesion.
Monitor episcleral hemangioma as a clinical marker for glaucoma severity.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Overview
sections.content: Hypotony is typically defined as IOP ≤ 6 mmHg. A BLEB LEAK involves a physical breach in the conjunctival barrier (positive Seidel test), whereas OVERFILTRATION refers to excessive aqueous flow through the scleral flap into the subconjunctival space despite an intact conjunctiva (negative Seidel test). Both lead to a shallow anterior chamber and potential vision loss.

branches: Bleb Leak: Conjunctival tear, wound dehiscence, Mitomycin-C induced necrosis
Overfiltration: Loose scleral sutures, oversized flap, excessive MMC use
Internal: Ciliary body detachment, Cyclodialysis cleft, Ciliary shutdown (uveitis)

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: IOP measurement (Goldmann or Tonopen)
Seidel Test: Use 10% fluorescein (undiluted) for better visualization
Corneal Signs: Vogt's striae (Descemet folds)
Iris: Anterior bowing, iridocorneal contact
Fundus: Choroidal effusions ('kissing' choroidals if severe)
Macula: Chorioretinal folds (Hypotony Maculopathy)

sections.title: The Seidel Test Protocol
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic (Proparacaine).
Step 2: Apply a 2% or 10% Fluorescein strip directly to the suspected leak site.
Step 3: Examine under the Slit Lamp using a Cobalt Blue filter.
Step 4: Look for 'dilution' or 'streaming' of dark orange/yellow dye by clear aqueous.
Step 5: Apply gentle digital pressure on the globe (Provocative Seidel) if initially negative.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Surgical Consultation
content: Endophthalmitis: Purulent discharge, severe pain, hypopyon, vitreous cells.
Flat Anterior Chamber (Grade 3): Iridocorneal contact from center to periphery; risk of PAS and corneal decompensation.
Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage: Sudden pain, loss of red reflex, high IOP (switches from low to high).
Kissing Choroidals: Apposition of choroidal elevations in the posterior pole.

sections.title: Management of Early Bleb Leak
content: 1. Aqueous Suppressants: Paradoxically used to reduce flow through leak to allow healing.
2. Large Diameter Bandage Contact Lens (BCL): 16-20mm lens to compress leak.
3. Cyanoacrylate or Fibrin Glue: For small focal defects.
4. Pressure Patching: For 24-48 hours (less common now).
5. Surgical Repair: Resuturing of conjunctiva with 10-0 Nylon (tapered needle).

sections.title: Management of Overfiltration
content: 1. Conservative: Observation + Topical Atropine (deepen AC) + Steroids (induce scarring).
2. Simmons Shell / Pressure Patch: External compression to limit flow.
3. Autologous Blood Injection: Into the bleb to induce fibrin clot and scarring.
4. Transconjunctival Compression Sutures: (e.g., 'Cushing' or 'X' sutures) to tighten flap.
5. Surgical Revision: Return to OR to add scleral flap sutures.

content.explanation: S: Scleral flap overfiltration; H: Hemorrhage (Suprachoroidal); A: Aqueous suppression (Ciliary shutdown); D: Detachment (Ciliary body/Choroidal); E: External leak (Bleb leak).

sections.title: Agrawal & Agrawal Grading of Hypotony Maculopathy

rows: Chorioretinal folds limited to the periphery
Folds extending to the posterior pole but not fovea
Folds involving the fovea, significant vision drop

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Differentiate a 'sweating' bleb from a 'leaking' bleb: Sweating is diffuse oozing through intact tissue; leaking is a focal stream.
Always perform a Seidel test before dilating a post-op trabeculectomy patient.
Atropine 1% BID is vital in overfiltration to prevent ciliary muscle spasm and further AC shallowing.
In late-onset leaks, risk of blebitis/endophthalmitis is high; use fortified antibiotics if suspicious.
Don't wait too long to fix a flat AC; 48 hours of lens-cornea touch leads to permanent damage.

sections.title: Advanced Surgical Techniques
content: Tenon's Advancement: For late MMC-induced leaks, sliding healthy posterior Tenon's tissue over the defect.
Wisdom of Wise: Using a 4-mirror lens to perform Laser Suture Lysis (not applicable here, but relevant to *preventing* overfiltration).
Tisseel Fibrin Sealant: For 'sweating' avascular blebs.
Cross-linked Hyaluronic Acid: Emerging injectable to bulk up thin bleb walls.
