sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content:
**Bleb Leak**: An epithelial defect in the conjunctival bleb allowing aqueous humor to escape from the anterior chamber. This leads to hypotony, increases the risk of infection (blebitis/endophthalmitis), and can result in vision loss. The Seidel test is positive.

**Bleb Overfiltration**: Excessive aqueous humor outflow through a patent filtration bleb, leading to severe and prolonged hypotony, often without an overt leak (Seidel test negative). This can result in characteristic findings like choroidal detachment and hypotonous maculopathy, potentially causing irreversible vision loss if not managed promptly.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Risk Factors
content: **Bleb Leaks**: Early (first 3 months): 1.7-8.0%; Late (after 3 months): 2.7-10.0%.
**Risk Factors for Leaks**: Anti-metabolites (MMC/5-FU), superior blebs, thin-walled/avascular blebs, older age, post-operative inflammation, scleral flap ischemia, history of trauma/eye rubbing.
**Bleb Overfiltration**: Incidence of severe hypotony ranges from 1-10% post-trabeculectomy.

**Risk Factors for Overfiltration**: Younger age, high myopia, history of uveitis, extensive anti-metabolite use, very low pre-operative IOP, thin scleral flap, tightly secured limbal sutures (preventing peripheral leakage).

branches: Scleral flap incompetence (too loose, inadequate closure)

rows: Often suture-related or wound dehiscence, exposed scleral flap, visible defect.
Microcyst rupture in thin-walled, avascular blebs; ischemic necrosis area.
IOP 4-8 mmHg, often asymptomatic or mild vision changes, sometimes choroidal folds.
IOP < 6 mmHg, choroidal folds, retinal striae, disc edema, significant vision loss (myopic shift).
Serous fluid accumulation in suprachoroidal space (visible mounds), with or without severe hypotony. Can lead to 'kissing choroidals'.

sections.title: 6. Clinical Features & Symptoms: Bleb Leak
content: Watering / Epiphora
Foreign body sensation / Gritty feeling
Blurred vision (due to hypotony or corneal edema)
Reduced visual acuity
Bleb tenderness to touch
Flat or shallow anterior chamber
History of recent trauma or eye rubbing

sections.title: 7. Clinical Features & Symptoms: Overfiltration
content: Blurred vision (most common, often gradual)
Reduced visual acuity (especially with hypotonous maculopathy)
Headache (ocular hypotony)
Eye pain or discomfort (dull ache)
Photophobia
Shallow anterior chamber (variable, can be deep if choroidals push iris forward)
Myopic shift (due to choroidal detachment or lens-iris diaphragm pushing forward)

sections.title: 8. Ocular Examination Findings: Bleb Leak
content: **Seidel Test**: Positive (gold standard; fluorescein dilution under cobalt blue light).
**IOP**: Often low (<6 mmHg).
**Bleb Morphology**: Flat, diffuse, thin-walled, avascular; discrete epithelial defect or microcyst.
**Anterior Chamber**: Shallow, potentially flat (lens-cornea touch).
**Conjunctiva**: Localized injection/inflammation around the leak.
**Fundus**: Disc edema, choroidal folds (if significant hypotony).

sections.title: 9. Ocular Examination Findings: Overfiltration
content: **IOP**: Consistently very low (<6 mmHg, often 0-4 mmHg).
**Bleb Morphology**: Large, diffuse, cystic, often healthy-appearing or very elevated; usually no overt leak.
**Anterior Chamber**: Shallow to flat; peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) if chronic.
**Cornea**: Striae, edema (with very low IOP).
**Fundus (Hypotonous Maculopathy)**: Choroidal folds (Paton's lines), retinal striae, optic disc edema, macular edema.
**Fundus (Choroidal Detachment)**: Serous elevation of the choroid, visible as smooth, dark brown mounds, typically peripheral. Kissing choroidals in severe cases.

sections.title: 10. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. **Detailed History & Symptoms**: Surgical details, post-op course, current medications, specific symptoms.
2. **Visual Acuity & Refraction**: Baseline and changes (e.g., myopic shift).
3. **IOP Measurement**: Crucial for diagnosing hypotony. Multiple readings often helpful.
4. **Slit-lamp Biomicroscopy**: Assess AC depth, bleb morphology, corneal status, presence of PAS, inflammation.
5. **Seidel Test**: Mandatory for suspected bleb leak (2% fluorescein strip, cobalt blue filter).
6. **Gonioscopy**: Assess angle, look for cyclodialysis cleft, PAS, other bleb internal features.
7. **Fundus Examination**: Direct/indirect ophthalmoscopy to evaluate for choroidal folds, disc edema, choroidal detachment, hypotonous maculopathy.
8. **Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT)**: Gold standard for visualizing bleb wall integrity, confirming leak pathway, assessing AC depth, irido-corneal touch.
9. **Posterior Segment OCT**: Confirm hypotonous maculopathy (retinal folds, subretinal fluid, choroidal thickening).
10. **B-scan Ultrasonography**: If media opacities (corneal edema, hyphema) obscure view, to visualize choroidal detachment or suprachoroidal hemorrhage.

rows: Acute pain, redness, severe vision loss, hypopyon, vitreous cells, purulent bleb. **(EMERGENCY! Culture and prompt treatment)**
History of trauma/surgery, deep AC (often), direct visualization with gonioscopy/AS-OCT, resistant hypotony.
Vitreous cells, specific fundus appearance (undulating retina, not smooth choroidal detachments).
Evidence of active inflammation, often associated with posterior synechiae, keratic precipitates.
Patient's baseline IOP may naturally be low, no other signs of complication.
Pupillary block, aqueous misdirection syndrome (malignant glaucoma - typically high IOP).

sections.title: 12. Staging / Grading (Hypotony & Complications)
sections.content:
While no single universal staging system exists, hypotony and its complications are clinically graded by severity:

*   **Hypotony**: 
    *   **Mild**: IOP 6-8 mmHg, often asymptomatic.
    *   **Moderate**: IOP 3-5 mmHg, may cause mild vision blur, choroidal folds.
    *   **Severe**: IOP < 3 mmHg, usually symptomatic with hypotonous maculopathy, significant choroidal detachment, or shallow/flat AC.
*   **Choroidal Detachment**: Graded by extent (e.g., quadrant involvement, touching choroidals).
*   **Hypotonous Maculopathy**: Graded by visual acuity and OCT findings (presence/severity of folds, striae, subretinal fluid).

sections.title: 13. Management & Treatment: Bleb Leak
content: **Conservative (First-line)**:

1.  **Aqueous Suppressants**: Topical beta-blockers (e.g., Timolol 0.5% BID), alpha-agonists (e.g., Brimonidine 0.2% BID), oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., Acetazolamide 250 mg QID). Reduces aqueous flow through the leak.
2.  **Pressure Patch/Shield**: Apply for 24-48 hours to promote self-closure and splint the conjunctiva.
3.  **Bandage Contact Lens (BCL)**: Acts as a physical barrier, protects the healing epithelium, stabilizes the bleb.
4.  **Autologous Blood Injection**: Inject 0.1-0.2 mL of patient's own blood into the subconjunctival space adjacent to the leak (induces fibrosis).
5.  **Topical Antibiotics**: Prophylactic (e.g., Moxifloxacin 0.5% QID) if leak is chronic, exposed, or high-risk for infection.

6.  **Atropine 1% BID**: Cycloplegia stabilizes AC, reduces inflammation, pushes lens-iris diaphragm posteriorly.

**Surgical Repair (If conservative fails or severe)**:
1.  **Conjunctival Advancement**: Mobilize healthy conjunctiva from adjacent areas to cover and resuture over the leaking area (e.g., 8-0 Vicryl/Nylon).
2.  **Bleb Revision/Excision**: Excision of the thin, avascular bleb wall and reconstruction with more robust tissue, often combined with a conjunctival advancement.
3.  **Scleral Flap Re-suturing**: If the leak is due to dehiscence of the original scleral flap.
4.  **Tissue Adhesives**: Cyanoacrylate glue over small, persistent leaks (often with a BCL).

sections.title: 14. Management & Treatment: Bleb Overfiltration
content: **Conservative (First-line)**:
1.  **STOP Aqueous Suppressants & Steroids**: This is crucial to allow IOP to rise and facilitate scar formation, unless active inflammation mandates steroid use.
2.  **Head-down Positioning / Pressure Patching**: Increases episcleral venous pressure.
3.  **Viscoelastic Injection**: Into the anterior chamber (e.g., Healon, Viscoat) to temporarily tamponade inflow and raise IOP, deepening the AC.
4.  **Atropine 1% BID**: Cycloplegia to push the lens-iris diaphragm back, deepen the AC, and reduce ciliary body inflammation/fluid production.

5.  **Subconjunctival Injection of Autologous Blood**: Similar to leaks, can induce fibrosis to reduce outflow.

**Surgical Intervention (If severe hypotony, flat AC, or progressive maculopathy)**:
1.  **Scleral Flap Resuturing/Tightening**: Placement of additional 10-0 Nylon or Prolene sutures (adjustable or releasable) to the scleral flap to increase outflow resistance.
2.  **Bleb Revision/Reconstruction**: Excision of a large, overfiltering bleb and reconstruction with more robust tissue (e.g., scleral patch graft, conjunctival advancement).

3.  **Choroidal Drainage**: If 'kissing' choroidals are present and threatening vision/cornea. Requires creating sclerotomies (e.g., 2.5mm posterior to limbus) to drain suprachoroidal fluid, often combined with AC reformation.
4.  **AC Reformation with Air/Viscoelastic**: If flat AC with imminent lens-cornea touch.

sections.title: 15. Surgical Techniques (Bleb & Flap Repair)
content: **Conjunctival Advancement**: Dissection of healthy conjunctiva from fornix, mobilization, and re-suturing (e.g., 8-0 Vicryl) to cover the bleb defect.
**Bleb Excision & Reconstruction**: Excision of dysfunctional bleb tissue, often followed by scleral patch graft (donor sclera, pericardium) covered by a conjunctival flap.

**Scleral Flap Resuturing**: Identification of original scleral flap margins, placement of 10-0 Nylon or Prolene sutures (fixed or adjustable) to increase outflow resistance. Topical steroids and anti-VEGF agents may be used adjunctively.
**Choroidal Drainage**: Typically involves radial sclerotomies (e.g., 2.5 mm posterior to limbus, 1/2 thickness) followed by drainage of suprachoroidal fluid and AC reformation with air/viscoelastic.

sections.title: 16. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Bleb Leak Complications**: Blebitis, endophthalmitis (high risk!), persistent hypotony, flat anterior chamber, peripheral anterior synechiae, cataract.

**Overfiltration Complications**: Persistent hypotonous maculopathy (irreversible vision loss is possible), suprachoroidal hemorrhage, chronic choroidal detachment, secondary angle-closure glaucoma, persistent hypotony, cataract, corneal decompensation (if flat AC).

**Prognosis**: Good for both if managed early and effectively. Poor if infection occurs (endophthalmitis) or chronic hypotony leads to irreversible maculopathy. Visual recovery from hypotonous maculopathy is variable and may be incomplete.

sections.title: 17. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Acute onset of severe pain, redness, and vision loss post-trabeculectomy**: Immediate suspicion for blebitis or endophthalmitis. Culture and prompt empiric broad-spectrum intravitreal antibiotics are critical.

**Flat anterior chamber with lens-cornea touch**: Risk of irreversible corneal decompensation (endothelial damage, bullous keratopathy) and cataract formation. Requires emergency AC reformation (e.g., viscoelastic/air injection).
**Progressive vision loss with severe hypotony and/or hypotonous maculopathy**: Indicates potential for irreversible visual impairment; urgent intervention is needed.
**Sudden, excruciating pain with profound vision loss during hypotony**: Suspect suprachoroidal hemorrhage (requires urgent B-scan and potential surgical drainage).

content.mnemonic: FLAT AC Management (for shallow/flat anterior chamber)
content.explanation:
**F**luids (IV to rehydrate cautiously, or AC **F**ormation with air/viscoelastic)
**L**aser (YAG capsulotomy if pupillary block)
**A**tropine (cycloplegia)
**T**amponade (Pressure patch, Bandage Contact Lens, Viscoelastic)

sections.title: 19. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a Seidel test for any suspected bleb issue – even if the bleb looks fine, a microleak can be present.
Hypotonous maculopathy symptoms (blurred vision, myopic shift) can precede clear fundus signs; be vigilant with low IOP.
Early intervention for flat AC is crucial to prevent permanent corneal damage and cataract progression.
A large, 'healthy-looking' cystic bleb can still be severely overfiltering.
Anti-metabolite use significantly increases the risk of both early and late bleb leaks and overfiltration.
Patient education on avoiding eye rubbing, proper eye drop technique, and signs of complications is paramount post-op.
Differentiate blebitis from sterile inflammation; culture is mandatory for any suspected infection.

sections.title: 20. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content:
**Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT)**: Revolutionized diagnosis of bleb morphology, leak identification, and early detection of subclinical choroidal detachments or hypotonous maculopathy. Allows for precise localization of leaks and objective assessment of bleb health.

**Novel Surgical Glues**: Bio-compatible surgical glues (e.g., Tisseel, ReSure Sealant) offer less invasive options for small bleb leaks, providing temporary closure and reducing the need for sutures, particularly for avascular blebs.

**Minimally Invasive Glaucoma Surgeries (MIGS)**: While not directly managing bleb complications, the increasing adoption of MIGS aims to reduce the incidence of bleb-related complications altogether by avoiding traditional external filtration pathways.

**The Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (TVT) Study**: Provided crucial evidence comparing the efficacy and safety profiles of trabeculectomy with adjunctive mitomycin C versus aqueous shunts in refractory glaucoma, influencing surgical decision-making and complication anticipation.

sections.title: 21. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
sections.content:
**Pediatric Glaucoma**: Bleb complications are more common in children due to enhanced wound healing (leading to bleb failure/scarring) and often more robust inflammatory responses. Hypotony is a significant concern, potentially leading to amblyopia.

**High Myopia**: Increased risk of hypotony and hypotonous maculopathy due to thinner sclera and increased axial length. Extreme caution with anti-metabolites is warranted.

**Uveitic Glaucoma**: Challenging due to underlying inflammation, increasing the risk of bleb failure, but also susceptible to hypotony from cyclitic membrane formation or ciliary body shutdown. Meticulous anti-inflammatory management is crucial.

title: Trachoma: The Global Fight Against Blinding Keratoconjunctivitis
summary: Trachoma is the leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide, caused by recurrent infection with Chlamydia trachomatis. It progresses from childhood follicular conjunctivitis to adult cicatricial entropion and corneal opacification, managed via the WHO-endorsed SAFE strategy.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Microbiology
sections.content: Trachoma is a chronic keratoconjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, an obligate intracellular bacterium. Specifically, it is caused by serotypes A, B, Ba, and C. It is characterized by recurrent episodes of infection leading to progressive conjunctival scarring.

branches: Age: Children (Ages 1-9) are the primary reservoir

rows: 5 or more follicles (>0.5mm) on the upper tarsal conjunctiva
Inflammatory thickening obscuring >50% of deep tarsal vessels
Visible white bands/sheets of fibrosis in the tarsal conjunctiva
At least one eyelash rubbing on the eyeball
Easily visible corneal opacity over the pupil
Incipient: Immature follicles on upper tarsus
Papillary: Intense papillary hypertrophy masking follicles

sections.title: Pathophysiology Cascade
content: 1. Repeated C. trachomatis infection triggers cell-mediated immune response.
2. Chronic follicular & papillary conjunctivitis (T-cell mediated).
3. Secondary scarring (Cicatrization) due to cytokine release (TGF-β).
4. Tarsal plate shortening and conjunctival shrinkage.
5. Entropion and Trichiasis development.
6. Mechanical trauma from lashes + Dry Eye → Corneal ulceration → Blindness.

sections.title: Classic Ocular Findings
content: Upper Tarsal Follicles: Pale, round, 0.5-2.0mm elevated lesions.
Arlt's Line: Horizontal linear scar in the upper tarsal conjunctiva near the lid margin.
Herbert’s Pits: Excavated scars at the limbus (pathognomonic) after resolution of limbal follicles.
Trachomatous Pannus: Vascularization at the superior limbus, usually <2mm.
Symblepharon & Fornix Shortening: Due to severe cicatrization.
Xerophthalmia: Secondary to destruction of goblet cells and accessory lacrimal glands.

sections.title: Diagnosis & Laboratory Workup
content: Clinical Diagnosis: Standard in endemic areas (WHO Grading).
NAAT (Nucleic Acid Amplification Test): Gold standard for detecting C. trachomatis DNA (PCR).
Giemsa Stain: Shows Halberstaedter-Prowazek (HP) inclusion bodies (low sensitivity).
DFA (Direct Fluorescent Antibody): Detects elementary bodies.
Enzyme Immunoassay (EIA): Detects chlamydial antigens.
Culture: Difficult; McCoy or HeLa cell lines.

sections.title: The SAFE Strategy (WHO)
content: S - Surgery: Correcting trichiasis (TT) to prevent corneal blindness.
A - Antibiotics: Mass Drug Administration (MDA) to clear the community reservoir.
F - Facial Cleanliness: Hygiene education to reduce transmission via flies and fingers.
E - Environmental Improvement: Better access to water, sanitation, and waste management.

sections.title: Medical Management (Antibiotics)
content: Azithromycin: Single oral dose (20 mg/kg, max 1g). Preferred for MDA.
Tetracycline Ointment (1%): Twice daily for 6 weeks (used if Azithromycin contraindicated).
MDA Threshold: If TF prevalence >5% in children aged 1-9 years, treat the entire district.
Contraindications: Azithromycin avoided in infants <6 months (use Tetracycline eye ointment).

sections.title: Surgical Techniques for Trichiasis
content: 1. Goal: Evert the lid margin and eyelashes away from the cornea.
2. Bilamellar Tarsal Rotation (BTRP): Full-thickness incision through tarsus, 3mm from margin.
3. Posterior Tarsal Rotation (Trabut Procedure): Preferred for severe scarring.
4. Suture Placement: Everting sutures (usually 4-0 or 5-0 silk/vicryl) to rotate the distal fragment.
5. Post-op: Tetracycline ointment and follow-up at 1 week.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Referral
content: Corneal Ulceration (Central or Paracentral)
Sudden Drop in Visual Acuity
Severe Ocular Pain (suggests secondary bacterial keratitis)
Hypopyon in a patient with CO/TT
Lid margin infection (Cellulitis risk)

content.explanation: SAFE: Surgery, Antibiotics, Face, Environment. Arlt's line: ALWAYS on the Apex (upper tarsus). Serotypes A, B, C: Causes Blindness (Trachoma).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Trachoma is primarily an upper lid disease; follicles on the lower lid are rarely trachomatous.
The presence of Herbert’s Pits is pathognomonic for past trachomatous inflammation.
Post-surgical trichiasis recurrence is high; long-term follow-up is mandatory.
Active infection (TF/TI) is common in children; scarring (TT/CO) is common in adults.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Secondary Bacterial Keratitis (Staph aureus, Strep pneumo).
Dacryocystitis (Nasolacrimal duct scarring).
Severe Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca (Dry Eye Syndrome).
Ankyloblepharon (severe cases).
Prognosis: Excellent with early SAFE intervention; poor once CO occurs without access to keratoplasty.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: GET2020: WHO initiative for the Global Elimination of Trachoma by the year 2020 (transitioning to 2030 targets).
Azithromycin vs. Tetracycline: Studies (like the GAT study) showed single-dose Azithromycin is non-inferior and has better compliance.
Smartphone-based Grading: AI and tele-ophthalmology are being used to grade TF in remote areas.
Vaccine Research: Currently in early phases; targeting the Major Outer Membrane Protein (MOMP).

title: Precision Astigmatism Management: LRIs vs. Arcuate Keratotomy
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to corneal relaxing incisions for the correction of astigmatism. This poster contrasts the biomechanics, techniques, and outcomes of Limbal Relaxing Incisions (LRI) and traditional Arcuate Keratotomy (AK) for ophthalmologists and surgical fellows.

branches: LRIs: Incisions at the peripheral limbus (90% depth)
AK: Incisions within the clear cornea (more central)
Goal: Flatten the steep meridian and steepen the flat meridian

sections.title: LRI vs. AK: The Core Comparison

rows: Inside the clear cornea (7-8mm optical zone)
Slower; risk of foreign body sensation

sections.title: Biomechanics: The Coupling Rule
sections.content: The 'Coupling Ratio' in incisional surgery is ideally 1.0. This means for every 1.0 Diopter of flattening in the incised meridian (steep axis), there is an equal 1.0 Diopter of steepening 90 degrees away (flat axis). Consequently, the Spherical Equivalent (SE) remains unchanged. If the coupling ratio is >1, the SE moves toward hyperopia; if <1, it moves toward myopia.

sections.title: Etiology & Indications
content: Pre-existing corneal astigmatism in cataract patients
Residual astigmatism after Toric IOL placement
Post-penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) astigmatism (primarily AK)
Patients desiring spectacle independence but ineligible for Laser Vision Correction (LVC)
Low to moderate astigmatism (0.75D to 2.50D)

sections.title: Red Flags: Absolute Contraindications
content: Keratoconus or Forme Fruste Keratoconus (FFKC)
Pellucid Marginal Degeneration (PMD)
Significant Corneal Thinning or Ectatic Disorders
Prior Radial Keratotomy (RK) - Risk of 'Starfish' wound dehiscence
Active Ocular Surface Disease or Severe Dry Eye Syndrome
Active Infectious Keratitis
Connective Tissue Diseases (Rheumatoid Arthritis, SLE) due to risk of melt

sections.title: Pre-operative Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Manifest Refraction (Verify cylinder axis and power)
Step 2: Corneal Topography/Tomography (Rule out ectasia; identify steep axis)
Step 3: Manual Keratometry (To confirm steep axis regularity)
Step 4: Ultrasonic Pachymetry (Measure thickness at the intended incision site)
Step 5: Apply Nomogram (e.g., Donnenfeld or Nichamin) to calculate arc length

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Manual Diamond Knife
content: Step 1: Reference Marking (Mark 0-180 axis while patient is upright to avoid cyclotorsion)
Step 2: Intra-operative Marking (Mark the steep axis and the arc length degrees)
Step 3: Knife Depth Setting (Set diamond blade to 600μm or 90% of thinnest pachymetry)
Step 4: Fixation (Stabilize globe with Fine-Thornton ring)
Step 5: Incision (Steady, perpendicular stroke along the marked arc)

content.explanation: Steep Axis: Always incise the STEEP meridian. Arc Length: Longer arc = more correction. Location: Limbal (LRI) or Arcuate (AK). Thinnest: Check pachymetry before cutting.

sections.title: Femtosecond Laser Arcuate Keratotomy (FLAK)
content: Precision: Micron-level accuracy in depth (typically 80-90%)
Geometry: Ability to create truly vertical or angled side-cuts
Intrastromal AK: Incisions that do not break Bowman's or Epithelium (reduces infection risk)
Repeatability: Lower surgeon variability compared to manual diamond knives
Integration: Often performed as part of Femtosecond Laser-Assisted Cataract Surgery (FLACS)

sections.title: Instrumentation Checklist
content: Mendez Degree Gauge (for 360° orientation)
Fine-Thornton Swivel Fixation Ring
Preset Diamond Knife (600 micron standard for LRI)
Calibrated Micrometer Diamond Knife (for AK)
Gentian Violet or Sinskey hook for marking

rows: Wait for healing; suture if persistent

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always measure pachymetry at the limbus; it is significantly thicker than the center.
For 'Against-the-rule' (ATR) astigmatism, remember that incisions are placed horizontally (3 and 9 o'clock).
If the patient is over 70, consider reducing the arc length by 10% due to increased corneal rigidity.
Intrastromal incisions (FLAK) provide less correction than penetrating incisions but have a superior safety profile.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent studies (e.g., by the American Academy of Ophthalmology Ophthalmic Technology Assessment Committee) suggest that while FLAK is more precise in depth than manual LRI, the visual outcomes at 6 months are often comparable. Modern nomograms now incorporate Posterior Corneal Astigmatism (PCA), which typically adds ~0.5D of 'Against-the-rule' astigmatism, necessitating a slight over-correction of 'With-the-rule' steepness.

title: Mastering the Jones Tube: Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR)
summary: The definitive surgical bypass procedure for proximal lacrimal system failure. CDCR utilizes a Pyrex Jones tube to create a direct conduit from the lacrimal lake to the middle meatus when canalicular function is irrecoverable.

data.summary: The definitive surgical bypass procedure for proximal lacrimal system failure. CDCR utilizes a Pyrex Jones tube to create a direct conduit from the lacrimal lake to the middle meatus when canalicular function is irrecoverable.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) is a bypass surgery of the upper lacrimal drainage system. It involves the permanent placement of a prosthetic tube (usually a Pyrex glass Jones tube) extending from the medial canthus (lacrimal lake) directly into the nasal cavity. It is indicated when the natural canalicular system is absent, obliterated, or severely dysfunctional (<8mm of patent canaliculus remaining).

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Dye Disappearance Test (DDT): Assess functional tear clearance.
2. Lacrimal Probing: Determine the exact site and length of canalicular obstruction.
3. Diagnostic Irrigation: Confirm total vs. partial block (Hard vs. Soft stop).
4. Nasal Endoscopy: Rule out septal deviation or turbinate hypertrophy that may obstruct tube exit.
5. Schirmer Test: Ensure adequate tear production (Dry eye patients tolerate tubes poorly).

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Standard DCR approach (External or Endoscopic) to create an osteotomy (approx 15mm diameter).
Step 2: Excision of the caruncle to create a raw bed for the tube collar.
Step 3: Insertion of a 22-gauge MVR blade or 14-gauge needle from the caruncle bed towards the osteotomy, angled 45° inferiorly and medially.
Step 4: Dilation of the tract using a Bowman probe or specialized trephine.
Step 5: Tube Sizing: Measure the distance from the caruncle to the nasal cavity. Ensure the distal end is 2-3mm away from the nasal septum.
Step 6: Tube Insertion: Slide the Pyrex tube over a guide wire (usually a Supramid suture or Bowman probe).
Step 7: Fixation: A 6-0 Prolene suture is passed around the tube neck and secured to the medial canthal tendon.
Step 8: Closure: Standard closure of DCR flaps and skin if external approach was used.

branches: Functional Obstruction (Delayed DDT with patent system)

sections.title: Contraindications & Red Flags
content: Severe Dry Eye Disease (Tube increases evaporation and irritates ocular surface)
Active Dacryocystitis or Sinusitis
Psychiatric conditions/Dementia (Risk of self-mutilation or poor hygiene)
Nasal Cocaine Abuse (Septal necrosis/poor healing)
Bleeding Diathesis (high vascularity of nasal mucosa)

sections.title: Post-Operative Maintenance
content: Frequent 'Sniffing' of saline drops to clear mucus plugs.
Valsalva maneuver (with eyes closed) to clear debris.
Nasal steroid sprays if granulation tissue forms.
Annual professional cleaning (tube removal and ultrasound bath if calcified).
Teach patient to keep eyes closed when sneezing to prevent 'Tube Projectile'.

content.explanation: S: Saline drops frequently; N: Nose blowing (careful!); I: Inspection for migration; F: Follow-up for life; F: Fluid passage check (DDT).

rows: Replace with STOP-loss or longer tube

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Golden Rule': The distal end of the tube must be visible in the middle meatus and 2mm clear of the septum.
If the tube is too short, it will migrate into the ethmoid air cells.
A 'Sniff Test' in the office: If the patient can draw saline from the medial canthus into the throat, the tube is patent.
Canalicular reconstructive surgery should always be attempted before CDCR if >8mm of canaliculus is healthy.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Insights
sections.content: The original Lester Jones paper (1962) emphasized the use of Pyrex due to its high 'wettability' and capillary action. Modern series (e.g., Rose et al.) show that while initial success is high (>90%), long-term maintenance is required for life, with up to 50% of patients requiring at least one tube replacement or repositioning over 10 years.

sections.title: Pediatric CDCR Considerations
content: Rarely indicated; reserved for severe congenital agenesis.
General anesthesia required for all revisions/cleaning.
Growth of the midface may necessitate tube length changes over time.
Higher risk of accidental extrusion during play.

title: Carotid-Cavernous Fistula (CCF): The Vascular Shunt Spectrum
summary: A Carotid-Cavernous Fistula is an abnormal communication between the carotid arterial system and the cavernous sinus. It represents a complex neuro-ophthalmic emergency that requires precise classification and multi-disciplinary management to prevent permanent vision loss or intracranial catastrophe.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: A Carotid-Cavernous Fistula (CCF) is a high- or low-flow communication between the internal or external carotid arteries (or their branches) and the cavernous sinus. This results in high-pressure arterial blood entering the low-pressure venous cavernous sinus, leading to venous engorgement of the orbit and globe. It is a potentially sight-threatening and life-threatening condition depending on the flow dynamics and venous drainage patterns.

rows: Direct shunt between ICA and Cavernous Sinus
Dural shunt: Meningeal branches of ICA
Dural shunt: Meningeal branches of ECA
Dural shunt: Meningeal branches of ICA + ECA

content.explanation: P: Pulsatile Proptosis (with thrill). C: Conjunctival Chemosis (corkscrew vessels). B: Bruit (heard over the globe or temple).

sections.title: Red Flags: Impending Danger
content: Cortical Venous Reflux (High risk of ICH/Stroke)
Rapidly Progressive Visual Loss (AION or Glaucoma)
Massive Epistaxis (Rupture into Sphenoid Sinus)
New-onset 3rd, 4th, or 6th Nerve Palsy

sections.title: Comprehensive Clinical Features
content: Corkscrew Vessels: Dilated, tortuous epibulbar veins reaching the limbus.
Increased Intraocular Pressure (IOP): Due to elevated episcleral venous pressure and choroidal effusions.
Ophthalmoplegia: Usually CN VI (intracavernous) first, followed by III and IV.
Pulsatile Proptosis: Best seen by observing the patient's profile or with an exophthalmometer.
Fundus Findings: Venous dilation, disc edema, intraretinal hemorrhages (Central Retinal Vein Occlusion-like).
Anterior Segment: Ischemia, corneal edema, iris neovascularization (rare).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Hierarchy
content: 1. Clinical Auscultation: Listening for a bruit with a stethoscope diaphragm over the globe.
2. Non-Invasive Imaging: CTA or MRA to identify enlarged Superior Ophthalmic Veins (SOV).
3. Ultrasound: B-scan/Color Doppler showing reversed (arterialized) flow in the SOV.
4. Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): The GOLD STANDARD to identify the shunt site and venous drainage.
5. Tonometry: High-amplitude ocular pulsations on Goldmann Tonometry.

rows: Bilateral usually, EOM enlargement (tendon sparing), no bruit.
Fever, leukocytosis, pain on eye movement, no pulsation.
Acute onset pain, dramatic response to steroids.
Systemic illness, rapid progression, usually secondary to infection.

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: IOP Control: Beta-blockers, Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (avoid miotics).
Lubrication: Management of exposure keratopathy.
Observation: Appropriate for low-flow dural CCFs (Type B-D) as 50% may spontaneously close.
Carotid Massage: 10 mins/hour in selected low-flow cases (contraindicated in carotid stenosis).

content.explanation: O: Oculomotor (III), T: Trochlear (IV), O: Ophthalmic (V1), M: Maxillary (V2). C: Carotid (ICA), A: Abducens (VI), T: T (Structural mnemonic).

sections.title: Ocular Complications & Prognosis
content: Secondary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (Choroidal effusion).
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME).
Proliferative Retinopathy (Hypoxia induced).
Permanent Cranial Nerve Palsy.
Post-treatment transient increase in symptoms (Normal).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: Dural CCFs are often misdiagnosed as 'chronic conjunctivitis' due to the red eye.
If IOP is high and the eye is pulsing, think CCF first.
The 6th nerve is the most common palsy because it sits freely within the cavernous sinus next to the ICA.
Venous drainage to the contralateral cavernous sinus can cause 'bilateral' symptoms from a 'unilateral' fistula.
Superior Ophthalmic Vein (SOV) diameter > 2mm on CT is highly suggestive of CCF.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Evidence
sections.content: Recent studies emphasize the use of Onyx (ethylene vinyl alcohol copolymer) for more durable dural fistula closure compared to coils alone. The trans-inferior petrosal sinus (IPS) remains the preferred transvenous route; however, when the IPS is thrombosed, direct orbital access to the SOV via lid crease incision is a highly successful secondary technique used by combined neuro-interventional and ophthalmic plastic surgery teams.

title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (AACG): The Ophthalmic Emergency
summary: AACG is a vision-threatening emergency characterized by a rapid, symptomatic rise in intraocular pressure (IOP) due to the sudden occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris. Timely diagnosis and management are critical to prevent permanent optic nerve damage and vision loss.

data.summary: AACG is a vision-threatening emergency characterized by a rapid, symptomatic rise in intraocular pressure (IOP) due to the sudden occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris. sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: AACG is a clinical syndrome resulting from the rapid closure of a pre-existing narrow anterior chamber angle. This leads to a total or near-total obstruction of aqueous outflow, resulting in a dramatic spike in IOP (often 40-80 mmHg). It is a surgical emergency requiring immediate medical and procedural intervention.

branches: Pupillary Block: Most common. High pressure in PC pushes iris forward.
Plateau Iris: Anteriorly positioned ciliary processes.
Malignant Glaucoma: Ciliary block; aqueous misdirection.
Anatomical: Short axial length, thick lens, small corneal diameter.

rows: ITC > 270°; Normal IOP, Disc, and Field.
ITC > 270° with raised IOP or PAS; Normal Disc/Field.
PAC with Glaucomatous Optic Neuropathy (GON) and Field loss.
Sudden symptomatic IOP spike with corneal edema.

sections.title: Patient Presentation: Symptoms
content: Severe Ocular Pain: Often described as a deep, boring ache.
Nausea and Vomiting: Often misdiagnosed as a GI issue.
Blurred Vision with Halos: Due to corneal epithelial edema (Sattler’s veil).
Frontal Headache: Radiating from the affected eye.
Photophobia and Lacrimation.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: IOP: Typically 40-80 mmHg; eye feels 'stony hard'.
Conjunctiva: Ciliary flush/injected.
Cornea: 'Steamy' or hazy epithelial edema.
AC: Extremely shallow; peripheral iris-corneal contact.
Pupil: Mid-dilated, vertically oval, and fixed (non-reactive).
Fundus: Edematous/hyperemic disc (acute) vs. cupping (chronic).

sections.title: Red Flags: The Do-Not-Miss Signs
content: The 'Hard' Globe on palpation: Immediate sign of severely elevated IOP.
Systemic misdiagnosis: Acute nausea/vomiting leads patients to ER, not Eye Clinic.
Contralateral Eye: High risk of synchronous or future attack (Must check!).
Ischemic Pupil: Failure to respond to pilocarpine suggests iris sphincter ischemia (>50-60 mmHg).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Gonioscopy: Gold standard (Goldmann or Sussman 4-mirror). Use indentation to differentiate appositional vs. synechial closure.
2. Van Herick Grading: Slit-lamp estimate (AC depth < 1/4 corneal thickness = narrow).
3. AS-OCT: Non-contact objective measurement of AOD and TISA.
4. UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy): Visualizes ciliary body and posterior chamber anatomy.

rows: Mild pain, high IOP, open angle, small KPs.
Miotic; pulls iris from angle. Only works if IOP < 40.

sections.title: Surgical & Laser Interventions
content: 1. Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI): Definitive treatment for pupillary block. Equalizes pressure between PC and AC.
2. Argon Laser Peripheral Iridoplasty (ALPI): Used if LPI is impossible due to corneal edema or for Plateau Iris.
3. Lens Extraction: Removing the lens (cataract surgery) significantly deepens the AC and lowers IOP.
4. Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: Immediate mechanical lowering of IOP in refractory cases.
5. Trabeculectomy/GDD: Reserved for cases where medical/laser therapy fails and PAS is extensive.

content.explanation: P: Pilocarpine (once IOP <40); R: Reduce Aqueous (Timolol/Brimonidine); E: Examine contralateral eye; S: Systemic Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors; S: Supine position (avoid); U: Urea/Mannitol; R: Relieve block (LPI); E: Evaluate optic nerve.

sections.title: Post-Attack Complications
content: Glaucomflecken: Small grey-white anterior subcapsular lens opacities (lens epithelial necrosis).
Iris Atrophy: Typically sectoral atrophy due to ischemia.
Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS): Permanent adhesion of iris to meshwork.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Post-acute inflammation.
Chronic Angle-Closure Glaucoma.

sections.title: Landmark Study: The EAGLE Trial
sections.content: The EAGLE Study (Effectiveness in Angle-closure Glaucoma of Lens Extraction) demonstrated that clear-lens extraction showed greater efficacy and was more cost-effective than LPI as a first-line treatment for patients with PAC and IOP >30 mmHg or PACG. It suggests moving towards earlier surgical lens intervention.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Practice Points
content: Never dilate a patient with a shallow chamber before performing gonioscopy.
Prophylactic LPI in the fellow eye is mandatory as the risk of an attack is ~50% within 5 years.
Avoid systemic anticholinergics and adrenergics in patients with narrow angles.
If the cornea is too cloudy for LPI, use topical glycerin to clear edema or perform ALPI to pull the iris away from the angle mechanically.

title: Peripheral Retinal Neovascularization: An FFA Masterclass
summary: Peripheral retinal neovascularization (NVE) is a pathological response to chronic retinal ischemia, driven by the upregulation of VEGF. Fluorescein Fundus Angiography (FFA), particularly Ultra-Widefield (UWF), remains the gold standard for identifying capillary non-perfusion and the characteristic 'smoke-stack' or 'sea-fan' leakage of new vessels.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Peripheral Neovascularization (NVE) refers to the proliferation of new, fragile blood vessels arising from the retinal circulation, located at least 1 disc diameter away from the optic nerve head. These vessels lack a functional blood-retinal barrier, leading to the hallmark 'profuse leakage' seen on FFA. NVE is the hallmark of proliferative retinopathies and is a direct consequence of retinal capillary non-perfusion (CNP).

sections.title: Pathophysiological Cascade
content: 1. Chronic Retinal Capillary Non-Perfusion (Ischemia)
2. Upregulation of Hypoxia-Inducible Factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α)
3. Massive release of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF)
4. Endothelial cell proliferation and migration through the ILM
5. Formation of immature, leaky vascular tufts (NVE)
6. Fibrovascular scaffolding and vitreoretinal traction

branches: Vascular: PDR, BRVO, CRVO (Hemicentral), Ocular Ischemic Syndrome
Hematologic: Sickle Cell (SC, S-Thal), Hyperviscosity Syndromes
Inflammatory: Sarcoidosis, Eales Disease, Pars Planitis, Behcet's
Congenital/Genetic: FEVR, Coats Disease, ROP, Norrie Disease
Traumatic: Radiation Retinopathy, Scleral Buckle-induced ischemia

sections.title: FFA Imaging Protocol (Ultra-Widefield)
content: 1. Baseline red-free and autofluorescence photos.
2. Bolus injection (5ml of 10% Sodium Fluorescein).
3. Early Phase (0-30s): Identify transit time and early NVE filling.
4. Mid Phase (1-3 min): Map areas of Capillary Non-Perfusion (CNP).
5. Late Phase (5-10 min): Evaluate NVE leakage intensity and disc staining.

sections.title: Specific Entity: Sickle Cell Retinopathy
content: Stage 1: Peripheral arteriolar silver-wiring.
Stage 2: Peripheral arteriolar-venular anastomoses.
Stage 3: 'Sea-fan' neovascularization (Goldberg Class III).
Stage 4: Vitreous hemorrhage.
Stage 5: Tractional Retinal Detachment.
FFA Hallmark: Circumferential peripheral ischemia with 'Sea-fan' NV at the border of perfused and non-perfused retina.

content.explanation: S: Sickle Cell, O: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome, S: Sarcoidosis, D: Diabetes (PDR), E: Eales Disease, F: FEVR.

sections.title: Critical FFA Red Flags
content: NVD (Disc NV): High risk of rapid vision loss; requires immediate PRP.
Peripheral non-perfusion > 10 disc areas: High risk for neovascular glaucoma.
Enlarged Foveal Avascular Zone (FAZ): Signifies macular ischemia; poor visual prognosis.
Vitreous hemorrhage obscuring view: FFA may be limited; consider B-scan USG.

rows: Intravitreal injection; rapid regression of NV; 1-month intervals initially
1200-1500 burns; 200-500um size; creates 'controlled atrophy' to reduce VEGF demand
Laser only the ischemic segment identified on UWF-FFA
Removal of vitreous scaffold; endolaser; membrane peeling

sections.title: Surgical Pearl: Laser Settings
content: Laser Spot Size: 200–500 µm.
Duration: 0.1s (Standard) or 0.02s (Pattern/Pascal).
Power: Titrate to a 'creamy white' burn.
Spacing: One burn-width apart.
UWF-FFA Guidance: Use UWF images to ensure laser covers the extreme periphery and all CNP zones.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Trials
content: DRS (Diabetic Retinopathy Study): Established PRP as standard for high-risk PDR.
ETDRS: Defined NVE and the benefit of early PRP in certain cases.
Protocol S (DRCR.net): Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab) was non-inferior to PRP for PDR at 2 years.
PANORAMA: Aflibercept can prevent progression to PDR in severe NPDR cases.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD): Due to contraction of the fibrovascular stalk.
Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG): Migration of VEGF to the anterior segment; 'Rubeosis Iridis'.
Ghost Cell Glaucoma: Secondary to long-standing Vitreous Hemorrhage.
Macular Epiretinal Membrane: Post-inflammatory or post-ischemic fibrocellular proliferation.
Prognosis: Excellent if treated early; poor if NVG or foveal-involving TRD develops.

rows: Demarcation line / Ridge in Zone I/II

content.explanation: NVE leaks into the vitreous like smoke (fluorescein plumes). If it doesn't leak, it's 'mirroring' a vessel (IRMA).

sections.title: Recent Advances: OCT-A
sections.content: Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCT-A) now allows for non-invasive visualization of NVE. While limited in the far periphery compared to UWF-FFA, OCT-A can visualize the 'medusa-head' morphology of NVE tufts without dye injection, though it lacks the ability to demonstrate active 'leakage'.

title: Inferior Visual Field Defects: A Clinical Diagnostic Atlas
summary: Inferior visual field loss is a critical localizing sign in neuro-ophthalmology, often pointing to superior retinal or post-chiasmal pathway pathology. This guide navigates the topographic mapping of the visual system to localize lesions based on perimetric findings.

branches: Parietal Lobe (e.g., Inferior Optic Radiation/Meyer's Loop sparing)

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Emergent Causes
content: Sudden onset altitudinal defect: Rule out Arteritic AION (GCA) with ESR/CRP/PLT.
Transient loss: Rule out amaurosis fugax or impending central retinal artery occlusion.
Bilateral inferior defects: Evaluate for pituitary mass causing superior chiasmal compression.
Progressive defects with headache: Mandatory neuroimaging (MRI Brain/Orbits with contrast).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: Step 1: Confrontation field testing to confirm defect pattern.
Step 2: Automated Perimetry (Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2) to quantify density/scotoma depth.
Step 3: Slit-lamp exam with 90D/78D lens to inspect superior retina and optic nerve head.
Step 4: OCT (RNFL) to detect nerve fiber layer thinning corresponding to the defect.
Step 5: Neuroimaging (MRI) if post-chiasmal lesion is suspected (homonymous pattern).

content.explanation: Parietal = Inferior (field defect); Temporal = Superior (field defect).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Altitudinal defects that respect the horizontal meridian are typically pre-chiasmal (optic nerve).
Homonymous defects that respect the vertical meridian are post-chiasmal (chiasm/tracts/radiation/cortex).
In a pituitary adenoma, the compression is from below, causing a SUPERIOR field defect first; however, anatomical variations can present as inferior.
Always perform gonioscopy in glaucoma patients with inferior defects to rule out angle-closure history.

title: Endogenous Endophthalmitis: The Ocular Emergency from Within
summary: Endogenous endophthalmitis (EE) is a vision-threatening intraocular infection resulting from the hematogenous seeding of the eye from a distant primary source. Unlike exogenous forms, EE requires a multidisciplinary approach to identify the systemic origin while managing aggressive ocular inflammation.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Endogenous Endophthalmitis (EE) occurs when microorganisms cross the blood-ocular barrier and proliferate within the vitreous or aqueous humor. It accounts for 2-8% of all endophthalmitis cases. It is often a harbinger of occult systemic disease and carries a significantly worse visual prognosis compared to exogenous endophthalmitis due to the virulence of the pathogens and the compromised health of the host.

branches: Gram (+) : Staph. aureus, Strep. pneumoniae, Group B Strep

sections.title: Risk Factors & Predisposing Conditions
content: Diabetes Mellitus (Most common systemic association)
Intravenous Drug Use (IVDU) - often associated with fungal/Bacillus
Indwelling catheters (Port-a-cath, Hemodialysis)
Immunosuppression (Chemotherapy, AIDS, Organ transplant)
Recent major surgery (Abdominal/Cardiac)
Endocarditis and Valvular heart disease
Liver abscess (Highly associated with Klebsiella)
Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) or Meningitis

sections.title: The Klebsiella Syndrome
content: Emerging hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (K1/K2 serotypes)
Classic Triad: Liver abscess, Meningitis, and Endophthalmitis
Hypermucoviscosity phenotype allows escape from phagocytosis
Requires immediate Abdominal Imaging (CT/US) if EE is suspected without source

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: The 'Seek the Source' Protocol
content: Step 1: Immediate Ocular Tap (Aqueous and Vitreous) for Gram/GMS/PAS stain and Culture
Step 2: Obtain Blood Cultures (Aerobic/Anaerobic) from two different sites
Step 3: Collect Urine Culture and Throat/Sputum culture if symptomatic
Step 4: Systematic Imaging: Chest X-ray (Pneumonia/Abscess), Abdominal US/CT (Liver/Renal Abscess)
Step 5: Transthoracic (TTE) or Transesophageal Echocardiogram (TEE) to rule out Endocarditis
Step 6: PCR for 16S/18S rRNA if cultures are negative but clinical suspicion remains high

rows: Lacks systemic septic foci; steroid response
History of trauma to the other eye

sections.title: Systemic Antimicrobial Selection
content: Bacterial: Third-generation cephalosporins (Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h) or Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin 400mg) for high vitreous penetration.
Fungal (Candida): Loading dose Fluconazole (400-800mg) or Voriconazole (6mg/kg IV q12h).
Fungal (Aspergillus): Voriconazole is the gold standard due to superior penetration and survival benefits.
Duration: Usually 4-6 weeks depending on clearing of systemic focus.
Coordination: Infectious Disease (ID) consult is mandatory for all EE patients.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention: Pars Plana Vitrectomy
content: Indication: Severe vitritis preventing visualization, failure of IVT, or rapid progression.
Objective 1: Reduce microbial load and inflammatory cytokines.
Objective 2: Obtain large undiluted vitreous sample for diagnostics.
Objective 3: Clear media for better follow-up and monitoring.
Technique: 23/25G small-gauge PPV, core vitrectomy usually sufficient; avoid aggressive peripheral shave if retina is necrotic.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Phthisis Bulbi (high risk in Gram-negative cases)
Tractional or Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment
Secondary Glaucoma (neovascular or inflammatory)
Evisceration/Enucleation required in 25% of Klebsiella cases
Poor Visual Outcomes: < 20/200 in ~60% of bacterial EE
Mortality: Significant risk due to underlying sepsis or endocarditis

content.explanation: P: Primary Source (Find it!), U: Unilateral/Bilateral? (Bilateral favors EE), M: Microbiology (Blood + Vitreous), P: Penetration (Systemic drugs must cross blood-eye barrier)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & High-Yield Facts
content: Blood cultures are positive in up to 75% of EE, often higher than vitreous cultures.
In IVDU, think Bacillus cereus (explosive) or Candida (string of pearls).
Candida EE usually starts in the choroid and breaks into the vitreous.
Aspergillus EE often presents with a large subretinal abscess in the macula.
EVS (Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study) criteria DO NOT strictly apply to endogenous cases.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent literature highlights the increasing role of Intravitreal Voriconazole as a first-line agent for fungal EE due to its safety profile and broad coverage. Genomic sequencing (mNGS) is proving superior to traditional culture in culture-negative cases. Furthermore, early PPV (within 24-48 hours) is increasingly advocated for endogenous Klebsiella cases to save the globe, even if vision remains poor.

title: Drug-Induced Uveitis: The Clinical Masterclass
summary: Drug-induced uveitis (DIU) is a rare but critical diagnostic challenge where medications trigger intraocular inflammation. Recognition is vital to prevent irreversible ocular damage and differentiate from infectious or idiopathic causes.

data.title: Drug-Induced Uveitis: The Clinical Masterclass

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Drug-induced uveitis refers to intraocular inflammation caused by systemic, topical, or intraocular administration of pharmacological agents. It often mimics idiopathic anterior uveitis but may present with unique features like hypopyon or retinal vasculitis depending on the agent. Incidence is low but rising due to new biologics and checkpoint inhibitors.

branches: Direct Toxic Effect (e.g., Cidofovir on ciliary body)

rows: Previous conclusive reports on this reaction?
Did ADR appear after drug was administered?
Did ADR improve when drug was discontinued?
Did ADR reappear when drug was readministered?
Are there alternative causes for the reaction?
Associated with doses >300mg/day or Clarithromycin co-admin.
Reduced risk with oral Probenecid; acts on ciliary body.
Usually occurs within 48-72 hours of IV infusion.
Often associated with a systemic hypersensitivity rash.
Can continue drug if uveitis is manageable with topical steroids.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors (ICI)
content: Agents: Nivolumab, Ipilimumab, Pembrolizumab.
Mechanism: Disinhibition of T-cells leads to 'off-target' autoimmune ocular inflammation.
Presentation: Often bilateral anterior uveitis; can cause Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH)-like syndrome.
Timing: Median onset is 6-12 weeks after starting therapy.
Management: Topical or systemic steroids; drug cessation usually not required unless Grade 3+ toxicity.

sections.title: Topical & Intraocular Culprits
content: Brimonidine: Granulomatous follicular conjunctivitis and chronic anterior uveitis.
Prostaglandin Analogs: Reactivation of HSV or CME; subtle anterior chamber cell.
Metipranolol: High incidence of granulomatous AU (largely withdrawn from market).
Intravitreal Brolucizumab: High risk of Occlusive Retinal Vasculitis (4.6% IOI rate).
Intravitreal Vancomycin: Hemorrhagic Occlusive Retinal Vasculitis (HORV) - Type III hypersensitivity.

content.explanation: R: Rare if dose <300mg. I: Increased by protease inhibitors. F: Frequent Hypopyon (Pseudo-endophthalmitis). A: Always check for Clarithromycin use. BUT: But manageable with steroids. IN: Inflammation is usually bilateral.

sections.title: RED FLAG: Brolucizumab (Beovu) Warning
content: Sudden vision loss post-injection
Retinal Vasculitis (Arteritis focus)
Retinal Vascular Occlusion
Delayed onset (weeks after injection)
Avoid re-challenge if inflammation occurs

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Slit Lamp: AC cells/flare, 'Plastic' hypopyon (Rifabutin), Stellate KPs.
IOP: Hypotony (Cidofovir) or Elevation (Corticosteroids/Brimonidine).
Fundoscopy: Retinal vasculitis, Disk edema, Serous retinal detachments (ICIs).
Gonioscopy: Peripheral anterior synechiae in chronic cases.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Detailed Medication History (Including OTC and Supplements).
Step 2: Establish Temporal Relationship (Drug start vs. Symptom onset).
Step 3: Clinical Examination & Exclusion of Infection/Sarcoid/HLA-B27.
Step 4: Trial of De-challenge (Stopping the drug).
Step 5: Apply Naranjo Algorithm for Causality.

rows: Unilateral/Alternating, intense fibrin, positive family history.
Pain, severe vitreous involvement, post-surgical history.
Granulomatous KPs, Busacca/Berlin nodules, hilar lymphadenopathy.
Older age, vitreous clumps, poor response to steroids.
Diffuse stellate KPs, iris heterochromia, no synechiae.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Identify and Discontinue: The primary treatment is stopping the offending agent if medically permissible.
2. Topical Corticosteroids: Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h to qid depending on severity.
3. Cycloplegia: Cyclopentolate 1% or Atropine 1% for comfort and synechiae prevention.
4. Systemic Steroids: Required for ICI-induced VKH-like syndromes or severe vasculitis.
5. Collaboration: Consult with the prescribing physician (Oncologist/ID specialist) before stopping critical systemic meds.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: Always ask about 'bone strengthening' drugs (Bisphosphonates) in acute AU.
Cidofovir uveitis is often associated with profound hypotony due to ciliary body toxicity.
DIU is a diagnosis of exclusion; do not miss Syphilis or TB while blaming a drug.
Drug-induced hypopyon is often 'cold' (less pain than infectious hypopyon).

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
sections.content: Generally excellent if the drug is stopped early. Chronic use of offending agents can lead to secondary glaucoma, cataract formation, and in the case of Cidofovir, permanent hypotony and phthisis bulbi. Brolucizumab/Vancomycin vasculitis carries a guarded prognosis with potential for severe permanent vision loss.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: HAWK & HARRIER
content: Post-hoc analysis revealed the 4.6% rate of IOI for Brolucizumab.
Led to the formation of the SRC (Safety Review Committee).
Highlight the importance of aggressive monitoring for DIU in new drug launches.

summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the sterile accumulation of leukocytes in the anterior chamber. Differentiating non-infectious inflammatory responses from infectious endophthalmitis is critical for vision-saving management.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A sterile hypopyon is the gravitational settling of inflammatory cells (predominantly polymorphonuclear leukocytes) in the inferior angle of the anterior chamber in the absence of an active microbial infection. It represents a severe breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier and is a hallmark of intense intraocular inflammation, often associated with specific systemic HLA-B27 syndromes or toxic insults.

sections.title: The Great Divide: Sterile vs. Infectious
Ocular Examination Findings
content: Inferior layering of white cells (level measured in mm)
Ciliary flush / Circumcorneal injection
Fibrinous exudate in the pupil area
Posterior synechiae (PS) formation (Common in HLA-B27)
Corneal edema (Limbus-to-limbus in TASS)
Variable IOP (Low due to ciliary body shutdown or High due to trabeculitis)
Shifting hypopyon (Classic for Behçet's Disease)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Step 1: Rule out infection via Vitreous/AC tap if post-op or post-injection.
Step 2: HLA-B27 genetic testing for systemic association.
Step 3: Chest X-ray or CT for Sarcoidosis (Bilateral hilar adenopathy).
Step 4: Syphilis serology (RPR/VDRL) and FTA-ABS.
Step 5: B-Scan ultrasound to assess posterior segment/vitritis.
Step 6: Serum ACE levels and Lysozyme.

sections.title: Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS)
content: Acute sterile inflammation following intraocular surgery.
Causes: Denatured OVDs, detergents on instruments, contaminated solutions.
Onset: Characteristically 12–24 hours post-surgery.
Sign: Diffuse limbus-to-limbus corneal edema.
Treatment: Intensive topical steroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Infection
content: Pain out of proportion to clinical signs.
Rapidly progressive vitritis / loss of red reflex.
Hypopyon appearing >48 hours post-cataract surgery.
History of recent trauma with organic matter.
Lack of response to hourly topical steroids within 24 hours.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Aggressive Topical Steroids: Prednisolone Acetate 1% or Dexamethasone 0.1% every 1-2 hours initially.
2. Cycloplegia: Atropine 1% BID or Homatropine 5% TID to prevent posterior synechiae and reduce pain.
3. Subconjunctival Injections: Dexamethasone 4mg/1ml for severe cases.
4. Systemic Therapy: Oral Prednisone (1mg/kg/day) for bilateral or refractory cases.
5. Immunomodulators: Anti-TNF-alpha (Infliximab) specifically for Behçet disease.
6. Tapering: Slow taper over 4-6 weeks to prevent rebound inflammation.

content.explanation: B: Behçet's; A: Ankylosing Spondylitis; S: Sarcoidosis; H: HLA-B27 Associated (Psoriatic arthritis, IBD, Reactive arthritis).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The hypopyon of Behçet is 'cold' and 'mobile' (shifts with head tilt).
Always check for a hidden IOL haptic or lens fragment in chronic hypopyon.
Pseudo-hypopyon from Retinoblastoma is composed of tumor cells, not WBCs.
Intravitreal Triamcinolone can mimic a hypopyon (pseudohypopyon).

rows: CMV Retinitis treatment; often needs Probenecid.

sections.title: The HAWK & HARRIER Studies (Clinical context)
sections.content: Recent landmark studies identified an increased incidence of sterile intraocular inflammation (4.6%) and retinal vasculitis following Brolucizumab (Beovu) injections for nAMD. Clinicians must distinguish this from endophthalmitis to avoid unnecessary intravitreal antibiotics and focus on steroid therapy.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) - most common cause of vision loss.
Secondary Glaucoma due to peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).
Complicated Cataract (Posterior subcapsular).
Phthisis Bulbi (in chronic/recurrent Behçet's).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Core Concept
sections.content: Ocular Adnexal Lymphoma (OAL) refers to a heterogeneous group of malignancies arising in the conjunctiva, lacrimal gland, orbit, or eyelids. MALT lymphoma (Extranodal Marginal Zone B-cell Lymphoma) is the most frequent subtype, accounting for 50-80% of all OAL cases. It is characterized by an indolent course, localized disease at presentation, and exquisite radiosensitivity.

rows: Fleshy, 'Salmon-pink' mobile patch in the fornix; usually non-tender.
Molding of the mass to the globe; displacement of globe; restricted motility.
S-shaped eyelid contour; firm mass in the superotemporal orbit.
Lateral upper lid swelling, dry eye.

sections.title: The Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Incisional/Excisional Biopsy (Essential). Avoid FNA due to lack of architectural detail.
Step 2: Immunohistochemistry (CD20+, CD5-, CD10-, Cyclin D1-).
Step 3: Molecular Testing: Flow cytometry (Light chain restriction) and FISH for translocations.
Step 4: Local Imaging: MRI with gadolinium (look for 'molding' around the globe).
Step 5: Systemic Staging: PET/CT scan, CBC, LDH, SPEP, and Bone Marrow Biopsy (if systemic suspected).

sections.title: AJCC 8th Edition TNM Staging
content: T1: Limited to Conjunctiva (T1a: Isolate, T1b: Multi-focal, T1c: Bilateral)
T2: Orbit involved without bone invasion
T3: Involvement of Lacrimal gland or bone
T4: Extension to Sinus, Brain, or beyond adnexa
N: Lymph node status (N1: Parotid/Submandibular)
M: Distant metastasis (M1a: Skin, M1b: Other extranodal sites)

rows: Flow cytometry shows no light chain restriction.
Acute pain; Chemosis; EOM involvement involving the tendon.
Bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement; systemic involvement.
Elevated Serum IgG4; Storiform fibrosis on biopsy.
Highly aggressive; CD5+; Cyclin D1+; t(11;14).

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocols
content: 1. Radiotherapy (Gold Standard): Involved-Site Radiation Therapy (ISRT). Standard Dose: 24–25.2 Gy in 1.5–1.8 Gy fractions.
2. Antibiotics: Doxycycline 100mg BID for 3 weeks (specifically for C. psittaci associated MALT).
3. Immunotherapy: Rituximab (Anti-CD20) as monotherapy or in combination with chemotherapy for systemic disease.
4. Chemotherapy: Chlorambucil or CVP/CHOP regimens reserved for Grade 3 or systemic spread.
5. Observation: 'Watch and Wait' may be appropriate for elderly, asymptomatic patients with localized disease.

sections.title: Radiotherapy Considerations
content: Highly Radiosensitive: >95% local control rates.
Lens Shielding: Essential to prevent radiation cataracts.
Late Side Effects: Dry eye (Xerophthalmia), Retinopathy (rare at 24Gy), Neovascular Glaucoma (very rare).

sections.title: Red Flags: High-Risk Features
content: Rapidly progressive proptosis (Suggests high-grade transformation)
B-symptoms (Fever, night sweats, weight loss)
Bone destruction on imaging (Suggests T3/T4 or aggressive subtype)
Presence of LDH elevation (Marker of tumor burden/aggression)

content.explanation: MALT is positive for CD20. It's 'Small and Lazy' (Small cells, Indolent course) and 'Stays Local' (usually Stage 1E).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Boards
content: MALT lymphoma 'molds' to the globe rather than invading it (unlike SCC).
Flow cytometry is the fastest way to confirm B-cell clonality.
Always check for H. pylori or C. psittaci association depending on local prevalence.
The most common site is the orbit (40%), followed by conjunctiva (35-40%).

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent research into the IOLA (International Ocular Lymphoma Study Group) database has validated the AJCC 8th edition staging. Studies are now focusing on 'Ultra-low-dose' RT (4 Gy in 2 fractions) for MALT, showing high response rates with minimal side effects in select cases. Additionally, the use of targeted BTK inhibitors (e.g., Ibrutinib) is being explored for refractory extranodal marginal zone lymphomas.

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-up
content: Overall 10-year survival exceeds 90% for MALT.
Recurrence: 20-30% may recur locally or at distant sites.
Follow-up: Every 3-6 months for the first 2 years with clinical exams and MRI/CT as needed.

title: Morning Glory Disc Anomaly (MGDA): The Comprehensive Clinical Guide
summary: Morning Glory Disc Anomaly is a rare, unilateral, congenital excavation of the optic nerve head characterized by a funnel-shaped peripapillary configuration. This poster provides a fellowship-level deep dive into its pathophysiology, ocular associations, and management.

data.title: Morning Glory Disc Anomaly (MGDA): The Comprehensive Clinical Guide
data.summary: Morning Glory Disc Anomaly is a rare, unilateral, congenital excavation of the optic nerve head characterized by a funnel-shaped peripapillary configuration. This poster provides a fellowship-level deep dive into its pathophysiology, ocular associations, and management.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: MGDA is a congenital excavation of the optic nerve head, typically unilateral. Pathophysiology involves incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure or a defect in the primitive epithelial papilla. It is associated with a scleral defect allowing the peripapillary retina and pigment epithelium to herniate backward into the subarachnoid space.

sections.title: Key Clinical Features (The 5 Signs)
content: 1. Enlarged, excavated, funnel-shaped optic disc
2. Central glial tuft overlying the disc
3. Annulus of chorioretinal pigmentary disturbance
4. Radial arrangement of retinal vessels
5. Deep peripapillary scleral staphyloma

rows: General scleral thinning, not just peripapillary
Situs inversus of vessels, myopic astigmatism

sections.title: Red Flags: High Risk Associations
content: Transsphenoidal basal encephalocele (high risk of meningitis)
Moebius syndrome or PHACE syndrome
Severe Serous Retinal Detachment (occurs in ~30% of cases)
Risk of intracranial vascular abnormalities (Moyamoya)

content.explanation: F-unnel disc; L-eft or right (unilateral); O-utward vessels; W-hite glial tuft; E-xcavation; R-etinal detachment risk

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Dilated Fundoscopy & OCT (assess macular schisis/detachment)
Step 2: B-Scan Ultrasound (confirm excavation/staphyloma)
Step 3: MRI Brain/Orbit (Mandatory to rule out encephalocele)
Step 4: MRA (rule out intracranial vascular anomalies)

sections.title: Management Guidelines
content: Observation for stable, asymptomatic eyes.
Refractive management for amblyopia (common in MGDA).
Pars Plana Vitrectomy with ILM peeling + gas tamponade for associated peripapillary detachments.
Multidisciplinary consult: Neurosurgery (if encephalocele present) and Geneticists.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Visual acuity ranges from 20/20 to hand motions, heavily dependent on foveal involvement.
The vessel pattern is distinct: they exit the periphery of the excavation, not the center.
Always investigate the contralateral eye for subtle disc changes.
Avoid lumbar puncture if basal encephalocele is suspected.

sections.title: The Big Three Dyes: Comparative Utility
Red Flags for Cornea Specialists
content: Dendritic/Map-like staining: Consider Herpes Simplex Keratitis (HSV).
Punctate Epithelial Erosions (PEE) in 'catarrhal' configuration: Consider Staphylococcal hypersensitivity.
Rapid dye clearing: Possible aqueous leak (Seidel positive).
Confluent staining with stromal thinning: Impending corneal melt.

sections.title: Procedural Protocol
content: Step 1: Instill dye (use dry impregnated strips; avoid liquid solutions for infection control).
Step 2: Ensure adequate blinking to distribute the dye.
Step 3: Wait 60-90 seconds before evaluation.
Step 4: Use Cobalt Blue filter (for Fluorescein) or White/Yellow filter (for Lissamine).
Step 5: Document size, density, and location using the NEI/Industry workshop grid.

content.explanation: S: Superior (SLK), T: Tear film (DES), A: Assessment (Systematic), I: Inferior (Exposure), N: Nature (Epithelial vs. Stromal).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Lissamine Green is the preferred dye for dry eye exams as it does not sting.
Always evaluate staining BEFORE tonometry to avoid false-positive abrasions.
Rose Bengal may mask underlying HSV; verify presence of dendrites first.
Staining patterns are dynamic; timing of assessment is critical.

data.summary: Filamentary Keratitis is a chronic, often recalcitrant ocular surface disorder characterized by the presence of mobile, mucus-rich filaments attached to the corneal epithelium. It represents a hallmark sign of underlying tear film instability and severe dry eye disease.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: FK is defined by the formation of strands (filaments) composed of degenerated epithelial cells and mucus, anchored to the corneal basement membrane. Pathophysiology: The inciting factor is usually a localized epithelial defect or chronic ocular surface irritation. The 'three-hit hypothesis' involves 1) Decreased tear production/mucin deficiency, 2) Epithelial basement membrane instability, and 3) Excessive eyelid movement (mechanical tugging) causing the mucus to coalesce into a stalk.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation & Symptoms
content: Foreign body sensation (often severe)
Photophobia and reflex lacrimation
Blepharospasm
Fluctuating visual acuity due to filament movement
Mucoid discharge
Intense ocular burning/pain

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup (Process)
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (white light).
Step 2: Instill Fluorescein/Rose Bengal/Lissamine Green.
Step 3: Identify comma-shaped filaments staining brightly.
Step 4: Assess tear break-up time (TBUT) and Schirmer I/II.
Step 5: Evert lids to rule out concretions or SLK.

rows: History of trauma, often no filaments

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: 1. Immediate: Mechanical removal of filaments using fine jewelers forceps.
2. Topical: Preservative-free artificial tears (qid to hourly).
3. Mucolytic: N-acetylcysteine 5-10% drops (dissolves mucus).
4. Stabilization: Punctal occlusion (plugs) to increase reservoir.
5. Anti-inflammatory: Topical cyclosporine 0.05% or Lifitegrast.
6. Severe: Bandage contact lens (extended wear) or autologous serum.

sections.title: Red Flags (Emergency Signs)
content: Ulceration at base of filament (Infectious keratitis risk)
Melting of the underlying stroma
Severe thinning or impending perforation
Associated hypopyon

content.explanation: M-Mucolytic (N-acetylcysteine), U-Underlying (Dry eye workup), C-Cleaning (Manual removal), U-Uncover (SLK/Toxicity), S-Stabilization (Punctal plugs/Serum).

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Recent focus on 'Ocular Surface Microbiome' in patients with persistent filaments.
Utilization of Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT) for recalcitrant cases to promote epithelial healing.
Emerging data on Scleral Lenses (e.g., PROSE treatment) as the gold standard for severe underlying neurotrophic/dry eye states.

title: Secondary Sjögren Syndrome (sSS) in Rheumatoid Arthritis
summary: Secondary Sjögren syndrome is a common, often under-diagnosed autoimmune epithelitis occurring in the context of Rheumatoid Arthritis. It manifests as a keratoconjunctivitis sicca driven by lymphocytic infiltration of the lacrimal glands, requiring a precise multidisciplinary management approach.

data.title: Secondary Sjögren Syndrome (sSS) in Rheumatoid Arthritis
data.summary: Secondary Sjögren syndrome is a common, often under-diagnosed autoimmune epithelitis occurring in the context of Rheumatoid Arthritis. It manifests as a keratoconjunctivitis sicca driven by lymphocytic infiltration of the lacrimal glands, requiring a precise multidisciplinary management approach.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Secondary Sjögren Syndrome (sSS) is defined as the development of autoimmune exocrinopathy (dry eye, dry mouth) in patients with a pre-existing connective tissue disease, most commonly Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). Prevalence of sSS in RA patients is estimated between 10-30%, significantly impacting quality of life and ocular surface health.

sections.title: Clinical Features
content: Ocular: Chronic burning, grittiness, foreign body sensation.
Oral: Xerostomia, dysphagia to dry foods.
Systemic: Fatigue, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy.
Ocular Surface: Reflex tearing depletion.

sections.title: Red Flags: Severe Complications
content: Corneal melts or perforations due to extreme keratomalacia.
Development of B-cell MALT Lymphoma (increased risk in SS).
Severe filamentary keratitis impeding visual axis.
Secondary bacterial superinfection (e.g., Staph aureus).

sections.title: Management Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Patient education & environmental modification (humidifiers, eyelid hygiene).
Step 2: Preservative-free artificial tears (qid to hourly) and lubricating gels at night.
Step 3: Anti-inflammatory agents (Topical Cyclosporine 0.05% or Lifitegrast 5%).
Step 4: Punctal occlusion (collagen plugs for trial, then silicon).
Step 5: Systemic management of RA (DMARDs/Biologics) by Rheumatology.

content.explanation: S - Schirmer Test; T - Tear break-up time (TBUT); O - Ocular Surface Staining (Lissamine Green); R - Rose Bengal (optional); M - Mucin/Meibomian status.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always evaluate Meibomian Gland Dysfunction (MGD) concurrently.
RA patients on Plaquenil (Hydroxychloroquine) require baseline and annual fundus screening.
SS increases risk of corneal graft failure if transplant is indicated.
Don't rely solely on Schirmer's—OSS (staining) is a better functional marker.

title: Clinical Mastery: Resolving CRVO vs. Diabetic Retinopathy
summary: A high-yield comparative analysis between a resolving Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) and Diabetic Retinopathy (DR). Distinguishing these entities is critical for management, as CRVO requires ruling out underlying systemic vascular risk, while DR mandates glycemic control and metabolic optimization.

Resolving CRVO: Venous tortuosity improves, collaterals form, disc edema regresses

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: NVI/NVA (Iris/Angle neovascularization) - 90-day glaucoma risk
RAPD in CRVO (indicates >10 disc area of ischemia)
Sudden drop in BCVA
Tractional Retinal Detachment in DR
Vitreous Hemorrhage precluding fundus exam

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Dilated Fundus Exam with 90D lens
Step 2: SD-OCT (Measure central subfield thickness)
Step 3: Fluorescein Angiography (Map non-perfusion areas)
Step 4: Systemic workup (BP, CBC, HbA1c, ESR/CRP for CRVO)

content.explanation: C: Check Pressure (IOP), R: Rule out systemic disease (BP/DM), V: VEGF inhibitors, O: Observe for collaterals.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Resolving CRVO often exhibits optociliary shunts; these are distinct from neovascularization.
DR never presents as a sudden '4-quadrant' explosive change unless vitreal hemorrhage occurs.
Always perform gonioscopy in ischemic CRVO before Anti-VEGF injection.
HbA1c optimization is the most potent long-term treatment for DR.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect LHON
content: Painless, subacute sequential vision loss in one eye followed by the other within weeks/months.
Profound dyschromatopsia (red-green deficiency) out of proportion to acuity.
Absence of pain on eye movement (differentiates from Optic Neuritis).
Family history of sudden blindness in maternal relatives.
Young male presenting with cecocentral scotoma.

rows: Optic nerve head pallor, RNF loss

sections.title: Diagnostic Protocol
content: Step 1: Careful history (maternal lineage) and clinical exam.
Step 2: Fundoscopy (look for characteristic telangiectatic microangiopathy).
Step 3: OCT (RNFL thickness analysis - note initial swelling followed by thinning).
Step 4: Visual Field (Humphrey 30-2: typically dense cecocentral scotoma).
Step 5: Genetic testing (Mitochondrial DNA blood panel for the 3 primary mutations).

sections.title: Management & Therapeutic Advances
content: Idebenone (Short-chain Coenzyme Q10 analogue): Improves mitochondrial ATP production. Approved at 900mg/day (divided dose).
Gene Therapy: Lumevoq (Lenadogene nolparvovec) - viral vector delivery of wild-type ND4 gene via intravitreal injection.
Avoidance of toxic factors: Strict cessation of tobacco and ethanol consumption.
Neuro-ophthalmological monitoring: Frequent follow-up for the fellow eye.

content.explanation: L: Loss (Subacute), H: Hereditary (Maternal), O: Optic Nerve (Pseudo-edema), N: ND4/ND1/ND6 mutations.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Pseudo-disc edema does not leak on Fluorescein Angiography.
The '14484' mutation has a significantly better prognosis for spontaneous visual recovery.
Mitochondrial genes are not affected by Mendelian inheritance laws (maternal only).
LHON-Plus syndrome: consider if patient exhibits dystonia, tremor, or cardiac conduction defects.
