sections.title: Definition & Anatomy
sections.content: An orbital floor fracture, often termed a 'blowout fracture', occurs from blunt trauma to the orbit. The sudden increase in intraorbital pressure is transmitted to the weakest part of the bony orbit: the thin maxillary bone medial to the infraorbital groove. This often results in herniation of orbital fat and sometimes the inferior rectus muscle into the maxillary sinus.

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Oculocardiac Reflex: Bradycardia/nausea during manipulation (pediatric emergency!)
Traumatic Optic Neuropathy (Afferent Pupillary Defect)
Open Globe Injury (must be ruled out first)
Infraorbital nerve anesthesia (suggests significant nerve impingement)
Globe rupture or retrobulbar hemorrhage

sections.title: Clinical Features
content: Periorbital ecchymosis and edema
Enophthalmos (often masked by swelling initially)
Diplopia, specifically in vertical gaze
Infraorbital nerve paresthesia (cheek/upper lip)
Restriction of globe motility (forced duction test positive)

branches: Pure Blowout: Orbital rim remains intact

rows: Acute tension, proptosis, loss of vision
Fever, elevated WBC, pain on movement

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Visual acuity, pupils, and slit-lamp exam (rule out globe rupture).
Step 2: Hertel exophthalmometry to measure enophthalmos.
Step 3: Forced duction test to differentiate restriction vs. muscle weakness.
Step 4: Non-contrast CT Orbit (Axial/Coronal) - Coronal view is gold standard.

sections.title: Management Protocol
content: Conservative: Oral antibiotics (Augmentin), nasal decongestants, avoid nose blowing.
Surgical Threshold: Diplopia within 30 degrees of primary gaze.
Surgical Threshold: Enophthalmos > 2mm.
Surgical Threshold: Large fractures (>50% floor surface area).
Timing: Urgent for pediatric trapdoor (within 24-48hrs), elective for others (1-2 weeks).

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: Approach: Subciliary, transconjunctival (preseptal or retroseptal), or transcaruncular.
Release: Careful dissection of herniated contents back into the orbit.
Reconstruction: Use of porous polyethylene, titanium mesh, or absorbable implants.
Assessment: Post-placement forced duction test must be negative before closure.

content.explanation: D: Diplopia (persistent), E: Enophthalmos (>2mm), E: Eye muscle restriction (positive forced duction), P: Piece of bone/fat (large defect/Trapdoor).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the globe: 10-15% of blowout fractures have associated ocular injury.
Pediatric trapdoor fractures often show no external signs (white-eyed).
Avoid late surgery if possible: scarring leads to poor motility recovery.
The infraorbital nerve runs in the floor; numbness is a classic finding.

data.summary: The Tensilon test is a diagnostic procedure historically used to confirm Myasthenia Gravis (MG) by temporarily improving neuromuscular transmission. While largely superseded by serological and electrodiagnostic testing, understanding its execution and interpretation remains essential for every ophthalmologist.

sections.title: Definition & Mechanism
sections.content: Edrophonium chloride is a rapid-acting, short-lived acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. It prevents the degradation of acetylcholine (ACh) in the synaptic cleft, increasing the probability of binding to postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors. In patients with MG, this transiently overcomes the blockade caused by autoantibodies, resulting in objective improvement of ptosis or extraocular muscle (EOM) function.

sections.title: Safety Protocols (RED FLAGS)
content: Atropine sulfate (0.5–1.0 mg) MUST be at the bedside in a syringe to counteract cholinergic crisis/bradycardia.
Cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry are mandatory during the procedure.
Contraindicated in patients with asthma, COPD, and high-degree AV block.
The test is considered 'positive' only if an objective, quantifiable improvement (e.g., ptosis reversal) is observed.

sections.title: Procedure Protocol
content: Step 1: Baseline measurement of ptosis (palpebral fissure height) and EOM motility.
Step 2: Administer 2 mg IV over 15-30 seconds as a test dose.
Step 3: Wait 60 seconds. Monitor for side effects (fasciculations, bradycardia).
Step 4: If no side effects, administer the remaining 8 mg IV.
Step 5: Observe and record maximal improvement within 2-5 minutes of injection.

content.explanation: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, Gastric upset, Emesis (Muscarinic effects of cholinergic excess).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: The test is highly sensitive for ocular MG but has low specificity (false positives in ALS, Eaton-Lambert, and brainstem lesions).
Place a cold pack over the ptotic eyelid for 2 minutes (Ice Pack Test) as a safe, non-pharmacological alternative.
Always document the objective measurement (e.g., 'Ptosis improved from 2mm to 7mm').
Sensitivity decreases as the duration of MG increases.

summary: Anisocoria represents a critical junction in neuro-ophthalmology where physiological variants meet life-threatening pathologies. Mastery requires systematic differentiation between sympathetic and parasympathetic dysregulation.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiologic Framework
sections.content: Anisocoria is a pupillary size inequality >0.4mm. Clinically, it is categorized by the pupil that is 'abnormal' in light vs. dark conditions. A pupil that fails to constrict implies a parasympathetic (sphincter) defect (abnormal in light), while a pupil that fails to dilate implies a sympathetic (dilator) defect (abnormal in dark).

sections.title: The Anisocoria Diagnostic Algorithm
content: Step 1: Check pupillary reactions in bright and dim light.
Step 2: If anisocoria is greater in dim light, the smaller pupil is abnormal (Sympathetic/Horner's).
Step 3: If anisocoria is greater in bright light, the larger pupil is abnormal (Parasympathetic/CN III/Adie's).
Step 4: If equal in all lights, consider physiological anisocoria (up to 20% of population).

sections.title: Life-Threatening Horner's Syndrome Etiology
content: Carotid Artery Dissection (Painful Horner's + Neck/Head pain)
Pancoast Tumor (Apical lung mass compressing sympathetic chain)
Aortic Aneurysm (Disruption of thoracic sympathetic chain)
Brainstem Stroke (Wallenberg Syndrome - Lateral Medullary Infarction)
Cavernous Sinus Pathology (Mass effect or carotid-cavernous fistula)

content.explanation: P for Ptosis (Muller's muscle weakness), A for Anhidrosis (facial sweating loss), M for Miosis (sympathetic failure).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Large Pupil (Mydriasis)
content: Adie's Tonic Pupil (light-near dissociation)
Pharmacological Mydriasis (Anticholinergics/Sympathomimetics)
Third Nerve Palsy (Look for EOM involvement/Ptosis)
Traumatic Iridoplegia (Sphincter tear)
Iris Sphincter Ischemia

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always compare old photographs to rule out physiological anisocoria.
Painful Horner's syndrome is a medical emergency until carotid dissection is ruled out by CTA or MRA.
Light-near dissociation is pathognomonic for tonic pupil or Parinaud's syndrome.
Pharmacological miosis from pilocarpine can be identified by the 'pilocarpine test'—if the pupil doesn't constrict, it's likely fixed by iris synechiae or structural damage.

branches: 2nd Order: Lung Apex/Pleura to Superior Cervical Ganglion
3rd Order: Internal Carotid Plexus to Iris Dilator

data.title: Superotemporal Retinal Tears: Risk, Laser & Prophylaxis
data.summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis and management of superior retinal breaks. Focused on high-risk features like myopia, lattice degeneration, and trauma, with evidence-based protocols for laser retinopexy to prevent rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='80' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M100 20 A80 80 0 0 1 180 100' fill='none' stroke='hsl(0, 80%, 50%)' stroke-width='8' stroke-dasharray='10,5'/><path d='M130 50 L150 70 M150 50 L130 70' stroke='hsl(0, 80%, 50%)' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='140' cy='60' r='15' fill='hsla(0, 80%, 50%, 0.2)'/><path d='M100 100 L140 60' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='2,2'/><text x='100' y='115' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)'>SUPEROTEMPORAL RISK</text></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: A retinal tear is a full-thickness break in the neurosensory retina, typically resulting from vitreoretinal traction during a Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD). Superotemporal tears are clinically critical because gravity facilitates the rapid downward spread of subretinal fluid, leading to macula-threatening rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) faster than inferior breaks.

rows: Plug of retina pulled completely free

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: Symptoms
content: Photopsia: Flashing lights in periphery (dynamic traction)
Floaters: Sudden onset 'cobwebs' or 'flies'
Weiss Ring: Circular floater signifying complete PVD
Tobacco Dust: Shafer's sign (RPE cells in vitreous)
Curtain Sign: Progressive visual field loss (indicates RD evolution)

sections.title: The Ocular Examination Protocol
content: 1. Wide Dilation: Phenylephrine 2.5% + Tropicamide 1%.
2. Slit-Lamp Bio: Search for Shafer's sign in anterior vitreous.
3. Indirect Ophthalmoscopy: 20D/28D lens 360-degree sweep.
4. Scleral Depression: Mandatory to visualize the Ora and flap base.
5. Three-Mirror Gonioscopy: Detailed view of suspicious lesions.

sections.title: Shafer's Sign (Tobacco Dust)
content: Presence of pigment cells in the anterior vitreous.
90% predictive value for a retinal break in the setting of acute PVD.
Must perform exhaustive scleral depression to find the break.

rows: Inner wall elevation, no tobacco dust, absolute scotoma
Flat, milky appearance, common in blacks/myopes
Yellow-white atrophic patches, prominent choroidal vessels

sections.title: AAO PPP Indications for Laser
content: Symptomatic Horseshoe Tears: Treat urgently (high risk of RD).
Acute Symptomatic Operculated Tears: Usually safe to observe unless high risk (e.g. fellow eye RD).
Traumatic Dialysis: Treat promptly even if asymptomatic.
Lattice with Symptomatic Tear: Treat the tear and the lattice.
Asymptomatic Lattice: Observation generally recommended, except in high-risk eyes (Aphakia, Fellow eye RD).
Asymptomatic Horseshoe Tears: Controversial; many treat if large or superior.

sections.title: Laser Retinopexy Technique
content: 1. Anesthesia: Topical Proparacaine (Sub-tenon's if scleral depression needed).
2. Wavelength: 532nm (Green) or 810nm (Diode).
3. Spot Size: 200-500 microns (depends on contact lens).
4. Duration: 0.1 to 0.2 seconds.
5. Application: 3 rows of nearly confluent burns (Grade II-III white) surrounding the break.
6. Coverage: Ensure burns extend to the Ora Serrata for U-tears.

content.explanation: Factors making a break high risk: S: Symptoms (acute), A: Aphakia/Pseudophakia, L: Lattice (extensive), T: Trauma or Top (Superior) location.

sections.title: Complications of Laser Prophylaxis
content: Epiretinal Membrane (ERM) formation (~3-5%).
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) - rare with peripheral laser.
Inadvertent foveal burn (ensure orientation).
Iatrogenic retinal breaks.
Failure: Progression to RD despite laser (usually due to inadequate treatment of the anterior horn).

sections.title: Emergency Signs: Failed Prophylaxis
content: Increasing photopsia/floaters post-laser.
Subretinal fluid extending beyond the laser barricade.
Visual field defect ('Shadow' or 'Curtain').
Decreased visual acuity (Macular involvement).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Fellows
content: Always treat the 'horns' (anterior edges) of a horseshoe tear all the way to the Ora.
In cases of Vitreous Hemorrhage where the retina isn't visible, B-scan is mandatory to rule out RD.
Laser takes 7-14 days to reach maximum chorioretinal adhesion strength.
Advise patients: No heavy lifting or jarring exercise for 2 weeks post-laser.

sections.title: Evidence & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The AAO Preferred Practice Patterns (PPP) and several retrospective series (e.g., Byer et al.) emphasize that while 10% of the population has retinal breaks, only 1 in 10,000 develops RD annually. This underscores the importance of treating only 'high-risk' symptomatic breaks. The PIVOT trial and other surgical studies focus on RD repair, but the consensus remains that laser retinopexy is the gold standard for symptomatic tear prophylaxis with a >95% success rate.

data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='20' fill='black'/><path d='M30,30 L42,42 M70,30 L58,42 M30,70 L42,58 M70,70 L58,58' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M35,50 L45,50 M65,50 L55,50 M50,35 L50,45 M50,65 L50,55' stroke='hsl(20, 90%, 50%)' stroke-width='2'/></svg>

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A 'fixed dilated pupil with posterior synechiae (PS)' in a child is a complex clinical scenario where the iris is adhered to the anterior lens capsule in a mid-dilated or dilated state. Unlike the typical miotic pupil of acute uveitis, this presentation often suggests chronic inflammation that was either treated with long-acting cycloplegics (Atropine) during the fibrin-exudative phase or is secondary to blunt trauma with sphincter tear and subsequent inflammation. It carries a high risk of pupillary block glaucoma and amblyopia.

rows: Highest predictor of uveitis risk in JIA (1:160+ titer)
Evaluates for hilar lymphadenopathy or Blau Syndrome
Required if the view is obscured by cataract or PS
Tono-Pen or Icare essential in non-compliant children

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Band Keratopathy**: Calcium deposits at 3 and 9 o'clock in chronic JIA.
**Posterior Synechiae**: 360° adhesion leads to 'Seclusion Pupillae'.
**Iris Bombé**: Forward bowing of iris due to aqueous entrapment.
**Koeppe/Busacca Nodules**: Suggest granulomatous etiology (Sarcoid).
**Complicated Cataract**: Polychromatic luster at the posterior pole.
**Cystoid Macular Edema (CME)**: Most common cause of vision loss.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Pediatric Emergency Signs
content: Sudden ocular pain + nausea (Acute Pupillary Block)
Corneal epithelial edema (High IOP)
Total Seclusion Pupillae (360-degree PS)
Hypopyon (Behcet's or HLA-B27 associated)
White reflex (Leukocoria) in a young child
Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) in trauma

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Intensive Topical Steroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h).
Step 2: Aggressive Mydriasis (Atropine 1% or Phenylephrine 10% to break PS).
Step 3: IOP Control (Aqueous suppressants: Timolol 0.5% or Dorzolamide).
Step 4: Oral Corticosteroids (1mg/kg/day) for severe bilateral cases.
Step 5: Immunomodulatory Therapy (MTX or Adalimumab) for steroid-sparing.

content.explanation: B: Biologics (Adalimumab); R: Refraction (prevent amblyopia); E: Examination under anesthesia (EUA); A: Atropine (break synechiae); K: Keratopathy check (Calcium).

sections.title: Surgical Techniques: Synechiolysis
content: Step 1: Paracentesis and injection of Cohesive OVD.
Step 2: Viscosynechiolysis (using OVD to hydraulically separate iris).
Step 3: Mechanical synechiolysis with cyclodialysis spatula.
Step 4: Peripheral Iridectomy (LPI or Surgical) to prevent recurrence.
Step 5: Pupil expansion devices (Malyugin ring) if phaco is required.

sections.title: Surgical Complications & Prognosis
content: Fibrinous Membrane formation (higher in kids).
Secondary Glaucoma (15-30% of chronic cases).
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) post-op.
Phthisis Bulbi in end-stage JIA-Uveitis.
Prognosis is generally GOOD if quiescence is achieved for 3 months pre-op.

rows: Adalimumab + MTX is superior to MTX alone in JIA-Uveitis
Standard of care for refractory JIA-uveitis
Long-term safety of MTX, Mycophenolate, and Azathioprine
Validation of safety for steroid-sparing agents
Universal grading for AC cells and flare

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never dilate a child with 360° PS (Seclusion) without a patent peripheral iridectomy; it can trigger acute pupillary block.
The 'Quiet Eye' Rule: Ensure zero AC cells for at least 3 months before elective intraocular surgery.
Traumatic mydriasis without PS often requires only observation or pupillary cerclage later; PS indicates an inflammatory overlay.
In JIA, the eye is often WHITE and PAINLESS despite severe inflammation—regular screening is mandatory.
Phenylephrine 10% should be used with caution in infants due to systemic hypertensive risks.

data.title: Ocular Lymphoma: Mastering the Great Masquerader
data.summary: A comprehensive guide to Ocular Lymphoma, spanning Primary Vitreoretinal Lymphoma (PVRL) and Ocular Adnexal Lymphoma (OAL). Essential for identifying this lethal 'masquerader' and managing both intraocular and adnexal manifestations.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular lymphoma is a heterogeneous group of malignancies. Primary Vitreoretinal Lymphoma (PVRL) is the most common intraocular form, typically a high-grade Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL). It is considered a subset of Primary CNS Lymphoma (PCNSL), with 60-80% of PVRL patients eventually developing CNS involvement. Ocular Adnexal Lymphoma (OAL) involves the orbit, lacrimal gland, or conjunctiva and is usually a low-grade B-cell MALT lymphoma.

sections.title: The 'Masquerader' Warning
content: Vitreous cells that are non-responsive to topical or systemic steroids.
Painless vitritis in an elderly patient without sign of infection.
Presence of creamy yellow-white sub-retinal infiltrates.
Rapid recurrence of 'uveitis' after tapering therapy.
New-onset neurological deficits or unexplained cognitive changes.

branches: MYD88 L265P Mutation (90% of PVRL cases)

sections.title: Clinical Features of PVRL
content: Vitreous: 'Aurora Borealis' effect (cells aligned along vitreous fibrils).
Vitreous clumps, sheets, or large grey-white debris.
Retina: Multifocal, sub-retinal yellow-white infiltrates.
Leopard Skinning: Reticular pigmentary changes over resolving infiltrates.
Minimal aqueous cell despite significant vitritis.
Usually painless with progressive floaters and blurred vision.

sections.title: Ocular Adnexal Lymphoma (OAL) Signs
content: Salmon-patch: Fleshy, pink, forniceal conjunctival mass.
Orbital: Painless proptosis or globe displacement.
Motility: Mechanical restriction and diplopia.
Lacrimal Gland: S-shaped ptosis and temporal mass.
Rubber-like consistency on palpation.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Protocol
content: Step 1: Clinical Suspicion - Elderly patient with persistent vitritis.
Step 2: Neuroimaging - Contrast-enhanced MRI Brain & Orbits to rule out PCNSL.
Step 3: Tissue Diagnosis - Diagnostic Pars Plana Vitrectomy (25G/27G). Ensure 'dry' tap 1st.
Step 4: Specimen Handling - Immediate processing in CytoLyt; cells are fragile.
Step 5: Cytology & Flow - Look for high N:C ratio, pleomorphism, and B-cell markers.
Step 6: Biomarkers - Analyze IL-10 vs IL-6 levels (Ratio > 1.0 is highly suggestive).
Step 7: Molecular Testing - PCR for MYD88 L265P mutation and IGH rearrangement.
Step 8: Staging - Lumbar Puncture (Cytology) and PET-CT scan for systemic spread.

branches: White Dot Syndromes: APMPPE, Serpiginous Choroiditis

sections.title: Management: PVRL Treatment
content: Induction: Intravitreal Methotrexate (400µg/0.1mL) 2x weekly for 4 weeks.
Consolidation: Intravitreal Methotrexate 1x weekly for 8 weeks.
Maintenance: Intravitreal Methotrexate 1x monthly for 9 months.
Adjunct: Intravitreal Rituximab (1mg/0.1mL) for resistant cases.
Radiation: External Beam Radiation (EBRT) 30-40 Gy if systemic chemo not possible.
Systemic: High-dose Methotrexate (HD-MTX) + Rituximab if CNS/Systemic positive.

content.explanation: IL-10 is the key biomarker. IL-10 levels > IL-6 levels (Ratio >1) is the 'ten-ten' rule for identifying Ocular Lymphoma.

sections.title: Management: Adnexal Lymphoma (OAL)
content: Gold Standard: Involved-field Radiation Therapy (24-30 Gy).
Antibiotics: Doxycycline (100mg BID x 3 weeks) if Chlamydia psittaci suspected (MALT).
Monoclonal Antibodies: Intralesional or systemic Rituximab.
Observation: 'Watch and Wait' for very slow-growing asymptomatic MALT.
Surgical: Excision for small localized conjunctival lesions.

rows: Radiation Cataract, Radiation Retinopathy, Neovascular Glaucoma
High rate in PVRL; requires lifelong monitoring

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always stop steroids 2 weeks before a diagnostic vitrectomy to avoid 'vanishing tumor' phenomenon (lympholysis).
Cytopathology is often negative due to sample degradation; MYD88 mutation analysis significantly increases sensitivity.
In OAL, if you see a 'Salmon Patch', biopsying the conjunctiva is often more diagnostic and less invasive than orbital imaging.
Rituximab is increasingly used as an alternative to radiation for OAL to avoid ocular surface toxicity.
Landmark Study: IELSG (International Extranodal Lymphoma Study Group) guidelines suggest intensive systemic therapy for combined ocular-CNS disease.

summary: An in-depth guide to the immune-mediated rejection of corneal donor tissue, covering the pathophysiological mechanisms, clinical classifications, and evidence-based management protocols for the ophthalmic surgeon and resident.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Corneal graft rejection is an immunological response of the host against the donor corneal tissue. It is a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction and remains the most common cause of corneal graft failure. Unlike 'Primary Graft Failure' (which occurs within 24-48h due to poor donor quality), rejection requires a prior sensitization period of at least 2 weeks.

sections.title: Pathophysiological Mechanisms
content: Step 1: Afferent Path - Host APCs (dendritic cells) recognize donor MHC Class I and II antigens.
Step 2: Sensitization - APCs migrate to regional lymph nodes to activate T-helper (CD4+) and Cytotoxic T-cells (CD8+).
Step 3: Effector Path - Activated T-cells return to the graft via the limbal vasculature.
Step 4: Target Destruction - T-cells release cytokines (IFN-gamma, IL-2) and directly attack donor endothelium/epithelium/stroma.
Step 5: Angiogenic Switch - Pre-existing corneal vascularization breaks the 'immune privilege' by providing a direct route for T-cell infiltration.

rows: Elevated line of irregular epithelium (rejection line).
Often asymptomatic; may precede more severe forms.
Indicates stromal involvement; resembles EKC infiltrates.
Localized peripheral haze/edema starting at the graft-host junction.
Khodadoust line (keratic precipitates in a line), diffuse AC cells, corneal edema.
MOST CRITICAL. Causes irreversible loss of donor cells.

content.explanation: S: Sudden Redness; T: Terrible Pain (or aching); O: Obstruction of Vision (Blurring); P: Photophobia.

sections.title: Emergency 'Red Flags'
content: Sudden drop in BCVA in a previously clear graft
New onset limbal injection/ciliary flush
The presence of a Khodadoust line (linear KPs)
New onset of stromal thickening (>10% increase)
Broken or loose sutures with associated infiltration

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Slit Lamp Exam: Essential for KPs, Khodadoust line, and AC cell/flare grading.
AS-OCT: To quantify corneal thickness (pachymetry) and detect retrocorneal membranes.
Specular Microscopy: To monitor donor endothelial cell density (ECD) loss.
In Vivo Confocal Microscopy (IVCM): Visualizes activated keratocytes and inflammatory cell infiltration at the cellular level.
Intraocular Pressure (IOP): Crucial as steroid-response glaucoma is a common confounder.

rows: Usually bilateral, no specific graft-host junction focus.
High IOP, corneal edema but NO KPs/rejection line.

branches: Stromal: Lattice (High recurrence), Granular, Macular (Least risk)
Posterior: Fuchs (Low rejection in DMEK), PPCD
Ectatic: Keratoconus (Lowest rejection risk - 'Low Risk' eyes)

sections.title: Standard Management Protocol
content: 1. Intensive Topical Steroids: Prednisolone Acetate 1% or Dexamethasone 0.1% every hour (day and night).
2. Pulse Therapy: If severe, consider Methylprednisolone 500mg - 1g IV daily for 3 days.
3. Sub-conjunctival Injection: Betamethasone or Dexamethasone 4mg/1ml for sustained local levels.
4. Systemic Immunosuppression: Cyclosporine A (3-5mg/kg/day), Tacrolimus (0.05-0.1mg/kg/day), or Mycophenolate Mofetil (1g BID) for high-risk grafts.
5. Cycloplegia: Homatropine 5% or Atropine 1% for comfort and stabilization of blood-aqueous barrier.

sections.title: Surgical Nuances: PKP vs. EK
content: PKP: Highest risk due to full-thickness antigen load and sutures.
DSAEK: Moderate risk; rejection often presents as localized swelling without classic line.
DMEK: Lowest rejection risk (approx. 1%) due to minimal stromal/antigenic tissue transfer.
DALK: Avoids endothelial rejection entirely; only epithelial/stromal rejection possible.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Landmark Studies
content: CCTS Study: HLA matching did NOT significantly reduce rejection in high-risk grafts, but ABO compatibility might.
Steroid Taper: Never taper steroids faster than 1 drop/month once the rejection has resolved.
High Risk Factors: >2 quadrants of neovascularization, previous graft failure, active inflammation.
Epithelial rejection is a 'warning shot'—intensify topical steroids immediately.

title: The Kestenbaum Procedure: Surgical Management of Nystagmus & Null Points
summary: The Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure is a definitive surgical intervention for patients with congenital nystagmus and a compensatory head posture (CHP). By shifting the extraocular muscles, surgeons move the 'null point' from a peripheral position to the primary position, improving both cosmesis and visual acuity.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Core Concept
sections.content: The Kestenbaum procedure is a multi-muscle strabismus surgery designed to eliminate a compensatory head turn (CHT) by rotating the eyes in the direction of the head turn. This effectively shifts the nystagmus 'null point' (the position of gaze where nystagmus intensity is minimal and visual acuity is maximal) into the primary position.

sections.title: Indications for Surgery
content: Stable compensatory head posture (CHP) > 15-20 degrees.
Nystagmus with a clearly identifiable null point.
Documented improvement in visual acuity at the null point.
Good binocular potential (to avoid post-operative diplopia).
Patient/parental concern regarding neck pain or cosmesis.

branches: Decreased Foveation Time: Nystagmus velocity is highest outside the null zone.
Visual Acuity: Optimal foveal engagement occurs only at the null point.
CHP Development: The patient turns their head to use the peripheral null point while looking straight ahead.
Alexander's Law: Nystagmus intensity increases when looking away from the null point.

content.explanation: To correct a head turn, move the EYES in the SAME direction as the HEAD TURN. (e.g., If the face is turned RIGHT, the eyes are currently looking LEFT at the null point. Move both eyes to the RIGHT surgically.)

sections.title: Mandatory Red Flags: When NOT to Operate
content: Acquired Nystagmus (requires neuro-imaging/workup for CNS pathology).
Periodic Alternating Nystagmus (PAN) - Surgery may worsen this.
Unstable or shifting null points.
Associated Vestibular dysfunction without thorough evaluation.
Oscillopsia in an adult (suggests acquired etiology).

headers: Action for Left Head Turn (Eyes look Right)

sections.title: Pre-Operative Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Quantify Head Turn: Use a goniometer or orthopedic protractor.
2. Prism Trial: Place prisms base-out over the 'null' eye to see if it reduces head turn.
3. Sensory Testing: Assess for Worth 4-Dot and Stereoacuity.
4. Video-Oculography (VOG): Map the null zone and foveation time.
5. Rule out PAN: Observe the patient for at least 15-20 minutes for a shift in nystagmus direction.

rows: Horizontal deviation change in vertical gaze

sections.title: Surgical Step-by-Step (The Procedure)
content: 1. Exposure: Limbic or conjunctival fornix incision to expose the target rectus muscles.
2. Isolation: Isolate muscles using Stevens and Jameson hooks; ensure all check ligaments are freed.
3. Recessions: Perform measured recessions of the 'leash' muscles (e.g., LMR and RLR for a Right Head Turn) using 6-0 Vicryl sutures.
4. Resections: Perform measured resections of the antagonistic muscles (e.g., RMR and LLR) to reinforce the eye rotation.
5. Hemostasis: Careful cautery to avoid postoperative subconjunctival scarring.
6. Closure: Re-approximate conjunctiva with 8-0 Vicryl or 7-0 plain gut sutures.

branches: Anderson: Recessions only (less invasive, for smaller turns).
Tenotomy/Reattachment: For nystagmus without null point (improves waveform).
Large Recessions: To induce artificial divergence (dampens nystagmus by convergence).

sections.title: Potential Complications
content: Under-correction (Most common): Return of head turn over time.
Over-correction: Development of head turn in the opposite direction.
Induced Strabismus: New-onset diplopia in primary position.
Scleral Perforation: Risk during suture pass, especially in thin sclera.
Anterior Segment Ischemia: Risk when operating on >2 muscles per eye (rare in Kestenbaum).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Board Exam

content.explanation: Remember the augmented dosages: For a 30-degree turn, think 7-8-9-10 mm instead of the classic 5-6-7-8 mm. Always prioritize the recession of the medial rectus as it has the strongest effect on adduction.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The Evidence Base
content: Anderson (1953): First to propose recession of the rectus muscles for nystagmus.
Kestenbaum (1953): Proposed the combination of recession and resection.
Parks (1973): Standardized the 5-6-7-8 mm measurements.
Calhoun & Nelson (1983): Introduced augmented Kestenbaum (40% increase).
Hertle et al.: Recent work on Tenotomy & Reattachment (the 'Hertle Procedure') for dampening.

summary: A clinical roadmap for the evaluation and management of ocular oscillations. This poster synthesizes the complexity of congenital waveforms and the localization of acquired neurological patterns for the ophthalmic specialist.

sections.title: Definition & The Neural Integrator
sections.content: Nystagmus is a repetitive, involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of the eyes initiated by a slow phase drift. It results from a failure in the systems that maintain steady gaze: the Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR), the Optokinetic System, and the Neural Integrator (NI). The NI—comprising the Nucleus Prepositus Hypoglossi and Medial Vestibular Nucleus (NPH-MVN) for horizontal gaze and the Interstitial Nucleus of Cajal (INC) for vertical gaze—is responsible for converting velocity signals into position signals ('leaky integrator' leads to nystagmus).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: New onset oscillopsia (suggests acquired nystagmus)
Vertical nystagmus (Downbeat/Upbeat) - high risk of CNS pathology
Associated papilledema or focal neurological deficits
Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD) or significant optic atrophy
Nystagmus in a child with 'Spasmus Nutans' like features (Rule out Chiasmal Glioma)

branches: Infantile (INS): Accelerated slow phase, horizontal, dampened by convergence
Fusion Maladaptation (FMAS): Latent nystagmus, seen with monocular occlusion
Acquired: Decelerating or constant velocity slow phase, often vertical/torsional
Vestibular: Jerk nystagmus, follows Alexander's Law

sections.title: Clinical Examination Protocol
content: Step 1: History - Age of onset, oscillopsia, family history, medications.
Step 2: Waveform - Determine if Pendular (equal velocity) or Jerk (slow drift, fast reset).
Step 3: Direction - Note horizontal, vertical, torsional, or mixed components.
Step 4: Fixation & Convergence - Does it dampen with convergence (typical of INS)?
Step 5: Search for Null Point - Find the head position where nystagmus is minimized and VA is best.
Step 6: Monocular vs. Binocular - Check for Latent Nystagmus (FMAS) by covering one eye.
Step 7: Associated Signs - Check for head nodding, torticollis, and full neuro-ophthalmic exam.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis of Acquired Jerk Nystagmus

rows: Chiari Malformation, Cerebellar degeneration, Lithium toxicity, Vit B12 def.
Cerebellar atrophy, MS, Chiari, or Congenital.

sections.title: Infantile Nystagmus Syndrome (INS) Features
content: Onset: Birth to 6 months.
Waveform: Increasing velocity slow phase (pathognomonic).
Direction: Usually horizontal and conjugate; stays horizontal on upgaze.
No Oscillopsia: Patient does not perceive the world moving.
Null Point: Preferred head turn to optimize vision.
Convergence: Paradoxically dampens the nystagmus.
Inverted OKN: Fast phase goes with the drum direction (atypical).

content.explanation: 1. Fine, rapid, shimmering nystagmus (often asymmetric/monocular). 2. Head nodding. 3. Torticollis. IMPORTANT: Must image to rule out Chiasmal Glioma mimicking this triad.

sections.title: Surgical Strategies
content: Kestenbaum-Anderson Procedure: Moving the eyes toward the head turn (moving the null point to primary position).
Augmented Classic Rule: 5-6-7-8 mm (MR-LR-MR-LR) recess/resect adjustments.
Large 4-Muscle Recession: To dampen the nystagmus amplitude by weakening the 'rotors' of the globe.
Tenotomy and Reattachment: Proposed to disrupt the peripheral feedback loop of the EOM enthesis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Essentials
content: 1. High-Resolution MRI: Focus on posterior fossa, craniocervical junction, and chiasm.
2. Video-Nystagmography (VNG): For precise waveform and slow-phase velocity analysis.
3. ERG/VEP: Essential in infants to rule out LCA, Achromatopsia, or Albinism.
4. Genetic Testing: FRMD7 (X-linked) and other INS-related panels.
5. Lab Tests: Vit B12, Magnesium, and toxicology screen (Lithium/Anticonvulsants).

rows: Present (Greater in direction of fast phase)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: The 'Maddox' See-saw: One eye elevates and intorts, while the other eye depresses and extorts (Di-encephalic/Thalamic lesions).
Latent Nystagmus: Occurs only when one eye is covered; the fast phase beats toward the fixating (uncovered) eye.
Brun's Nystagmus: A 'Double-Whammy' sign of a large CPA tumor. Low-frequency large-amplitude (Cerebellar) looking one way, high-frequency small-amplitude (Vestibular) looking the other.
Oscillopsia Check: If a patient has nystagmus but no oscillopsia, it likely started in childhood.

sections.title: Optical Management
content: 1. Optimal Refraction: Contact lenses are superior to glasses as they move with the eye, keeping the optical center aligned.
2. Prism Trial: Use Base-Out prisms to induce convergence (dampens INS).
3. Null Point Shifting: Use prisms (Base toward the head turn) to shift images toward the null point.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Eye Tracking & Gene Therapy
content: Gaze-contingent displays: Using high-speed trackers to stabilize images on the retina for patients with severe oscillopsia.
Gene Therapy: Successful RPE65 and ongoing GUCY2D trials for retinal dystrophies can secondary improve associated nystagmus.
Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS): Investigational for severe, refractory acquired pendular nystagmus in MS.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Localization
sections.content: The combination of a wide-based (ataxic) gait and jerky nystagmus primarily localizes to the Midline Cerebellum (Vermis) and the Vestibulocerebellum (Flocculonodular lobe). While the hemispheres control appendicular coordination, the midline structures regulate axial stability and ocular motor control via connections with the vestibular nuclei and the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF).

branches: Vermis (Midline): Truncal ataxia, Wide-based gait, Titubation (head tremor)
Flocculonodular Lobe: Downbeat Nystagmus, Impaired VOR suppression

sections.title: Neuro-Ophthalmic Signs
content: Jerky Nystagmus: Typically gaze-evoked or primary position (Downbeat/Upbeat).
Saccadic Dysmetria: Overshooting (hypermetria) or undershooting (hypometria) of targets.
Impaired Smooth Pursuit: Pursuit becomes 'saccadic' or broken.
Dysfunctional VOR Suppression: Patient cannot maintain fixation while the head is rotated.
Square Wave Jerks: Small, involuntary saccades that take the eye away from and back to the target.

sections.title: Gait Characteristics (Ataxia)
content: Broad Base: Feet placed wide apart to compensate for instability.
Irregular Step Length: Inconsistent distance between steps.
Truncal Instability: Swaying of the torso even when seated (if vermis is heavily involved).
Tandem Gait Failure: Inability to walk heel-to-toe (most sensitive early test).
Veering: Tendency to deviate toward the side of the lesion (if hemispheric).

rows: Multiple Sclerosis (Charcot's Triad: Nystagmus, Intention Tremor, Scanning Speech).
Chronic Alcoholism (Vermis atrophy), Phenytoin toxicity, Vitamin B1/B12 deficiency.
Friedreich’s Ataxia (FXN gene), Spinocerebellar Ataxias (SCA 1-48), Episodic Ataxia (EA2).
Anti-Yo (Ovarian/Breast), Anti-Hu (SCLC) antibodies causing Purkinje cell loss.

sections.title: Downbeat Nystagmus (DBN) Localization
sections.content: DBN is a classic localization sign for the Craniocervical Junction (e.g., Arnold-Chiari Malformation Type 1) or the Flocculus. It is characterized by a slow upward drift followed by a fast downward corrective phase. It typically worsens on down-and-out gaze.

sections.title: Red Flags: Acute Cerebellar Syndrome
content: Sudden onset 'Thunderclap' headache with ataxia (Cerebellar Hemorrhage).
Progressive obtundation or coma (Obstructive Hydrocephalus due to 4th ventricle compression).
Papilledema (Raised Intracranial Pressure).
New-onset vertigo with 'Skew Deviation' (HINTS exam positive for stroke).
Rapidly progressive symptoms over weeks (Paraneoplastic Cerebellar Degeneration).

content.explanation: D: Dysmetria, A: Ataxia (Gait/Truncal), N: Nystagmus (Jerky), I: Intention Tremor, S: Slurred Speech (Scanning), H: Hypotonia.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Protocol
content: Step 1: Assess primary position for nystagmus (DBN/UBN).
Step 2: Check 9 cardinal positions for Gaze-Evoked Nystagmus.
Step 3: Test Smooth Pursuit with a slow-moving target (look for 'cogwheeling').
Step 4: Test Saccades (check for overshooting/hypermetria).
Step 5: Test VOR Suppression (rotate patient on a chair while they fixate on their own thumb).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Neuroimaging: MRI Brain with thin cuts through the Posterior Fossa (Gold Standard).
Laboratory: Vitamin B1, B12, Vitamin E levels, Thyroid function (TPO antibodies).
Serology: Paraneoplastic panel (Anti-Yo, Hu, Ri, Tr, CV2, PCA-2).
Genetic Testing: SCA panel (CAG repeat expansions) or Friedreich Ataxia testing (GAA repeats).
Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF): Oligoclonal bands (if MS suspected) or cytology (if neoplastic).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Lesions in the cerebellar hemispheres cause IPSILATERAL signs.
Episodic Ataxia Type 2 (EA2) is associated with CACNA1A mutations and responds to Acetazolamide.
The 'Gaze-Holding' mechanism (Neural Integrator) involves the Flocculus and NPH; failure leads to jerky nystagmus.
In children, consider Medulloblastoma or Ependymoma if gait/nystagmus is new and progressive.

sections.title: Management Strategies
content: Pharmacology: 4-Aminopyridine (4-AP) for Downbeat Nystagmus.
Hereditary: Idebenone (limited evidence) for Friedreich's Ataxia cardiomyopathy.
Surgical: Posterior fossa decompression for Chiari Malformations.
Rehabilitation: Physical therapy focused on core stability and vestibular habituation.
Prisms: Base-out prisms can sometimes dampen certain types of nystagmus.

data.generationPrompt: Wide based gait with jerky nystagmus (+localise the lesion)

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Aponeurotic ptosis (also known as involutional or senile ptosis) is an acquired drooping of the upper eyelid caused by the failure of the levator palpebrae superioris aponeurosis to transmit force to the tarsal plate. While usually age-related, it can be triggered by chronic inflammation, trauma, or intraocular surgery. Characteristically, the levator muscle function remains excellent, but the 'linkage' (the aponeurosis) is stretched or detached.

sections.title: The 'Classic' Clinical Tetrad
content: Variable Ptosis (often worse at the end of the day)
High or Absent Upper Eyelid Crease (Disinsertion point moves superiorly)
Good Levator Function (>12mm to 15mm excursions)
Thinning of the Upper Lid (Iris color may be visible through the skin)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Ruling Out the Dangerous
Hering's Law of Equal Innervation
content: Always lift the more ptotic lid manually in clinic to check for 'drop' in the contralateral lid.
Ewald Hering's law: Bilateral levator muscles receive equal innervation.
Failure to identify subclinical ptosis results in post-operative 'asymmetry surprise'.

sections.title: The Phenylephrine Test
content: 1. Measure baseline MRD1 and Palpebral Fissure.
2. Instill 1 drop of 2.5% Phenylephrine into the superior fornix.
3. Wait 5-10 minutes for Müller muscle contraction.
4. Re-measure: If MRD1 normalizes, patient is a candidate for posterior-approach surgery (MMCR).

rows: Any ptosis, especially with excess skin (Dermatochalasis)
NOT for aponeurotic; only for poor LF (<4mm)

sections.title: Step-by-Step: External Levator Advancement
content: 1. Skin incision at the desired lid crease height.
2. Dissection through orbicularis to expose the orbital septum.
3. Opening the septum to identify pre-aponeurotic fat pads (the landmark for the aponeurosis).
4. Identification of the white, fibrous aponeurosis (often dehisced or thinned).
5. Advancing and suturing the aponeurosis to the mid-tarsal plate using 6-0 Silk or Vicryl.
6. Intraoperative adjustment: Patient sits up to confirm height and contour symmetry.
7. Skin closure with creation of a new lid crease (lid crease formed by skin-aponeurosis-skin sutures).

sections.title: Surgical Red Flags
content: Poor Bell's Phenomenon: High risk of exposure keratopathy.
Reduced Corneal Sensitivity: Post-op ulcer risk.
Dry Eye Syndrome: Ptosis repair can worsen symptoms.
Lagophthalmos: Avoid over-resection.

content.explanation: H: High lid crease, I: Involutional (Age), G: Good levator function, H: History of intraocular surgery/rubbing.

sections.title: Post-Operative Complications
content: Under-correction: The most common complication (approx 10-15%).
Over-correction: Leads to lagophthalmos and dry eye.
Eyelid Contour Peaking: Usually due to improper suture placement.
Eyelid Crease Asymmetry.
Retrobulbar Hemorrhage: Rare but vision-threatening emergency.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: The 'Iris Show' sign: If you see the iris through the skin, the aponeurosis is paper-thin or gone.
Always check for concurrent dermatochalasis; removing skin without fixing the ptosis makes the ptosis look worse.
In MMCR surgery, never include the tarsus in the clamp unless doing a Fasanella-Servat.
Warn patients with Hering's law drop that they may need bilateral surgery even if only one side looks bad initially.

title: Filamentary Keratitis: The Sticky Truth of Mucoid Traction
summary: A chronic, painful corneal condition characterized by the formation of mucoid threads attached to the corneal surface. It stems from a vicious cycle of ocular surface instability, mucin excess, and mechanical friction, predominantly seen in severe dry eye and post-surgical patients.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Filamentary Keratitis (FK) is a chronic inflammatory condition where small, comma-shaped mucoid strands (filaments) adhere to the corneal epithelium. Each filament consists of a central core of mucin and desquamated epithelial cells, firmly anchored to the basement membrane. It represents a hallmark of ocular surface decompensation, most frequently associated with Aqueous Tear Deficiency (ATD).

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Vicious Cycle
content: 1. Ocular Surface Stress: Mucin/Aqueous imbalance leads to hyperviscous mucus.
2. Epithelial Instability: Focal areas of epithelial cell death or basement membrane damage occur.
3. Anchor Formation: Mucin strands anchor to denuded areas or necrotic cells.
4. Mechanical Traction: Blinking pulls on the filament, lifting the sensitive epithelium.
5. Chronic Inflammation: Recurring epithelial trauma maintains the cycle.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Patient Symptoms
content: Severe Foreign Body Sensation (FBS)
Pain exacerbated by blinking (Traction pain)
Photophobia and Blepharospasm
Redness and epiphora (reflex tearing)
Diurnal variation: Often worse in the morning upon waking

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Slit-Lamp: Small, grey-white, gelatinous strands (usually 0.5mm to 2mm long).
Distribution: Often found in the superior cornea in SLK; inferiorly in dry eye.
Staining: Filaments stain intensely with Rose Bengal or Lissamine Green.
Fluorescein: Stains the base where the filament is attached (epithelial defect).
Reduced Schirmer values and low Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT).

rows: Larger, flatter, immobile, associated with papillae
Diffuse punctate erosions, history of drug use
>10 filaments, central corneal involvement, visual drop

sections.title: Emergency Signs: Red Flags
content: Overlying Corneal Infiltrate (Rule out microbial keratitis)
Rapid Visual Loss (Potential melting/perforation)
Severe Neurotrophic Hypesthesia (Risk of painless melt)
Persistent epithelial defect despite BCL

sections.title: The Management Ladder
content: Step 1: Mechanical Debridement - Remove filaments with fine-tipped forceps or cellulose sponge at the slit lamp.
Step 2: Mucolytics - Topical N-acetylcysteine (5% or 10%) QID to dissolve existing mucus strands.
Step 3: Lubrication - Preservative-free artificial tears, ointments, and Secretagogues (Diquafosol/Rebamipide).
Step 4: Surface Protection - Bandage Soft Contact Lens (BCL) to reduce blink-related traction.
Step 5: Biological Therapy - Autologous Serum Tears (20%-100%) or Amniotic Membrane Grafts (Prokera).
Step 6: Inflammation Control - Pulse topical Steroids (Loteprednol) or Cyclosporine A 0.05%.

content.explanation: M: Mucin-core structure; U: Underlying Sjogren's/Dry Eye; C: Chronic friction; U: Unstable epithelium; S: Superior Limbic Keratoconjunctivitis.

sections.title: Surgical & Interventional Approaches
content: Punctal Occlusion: Collagen plugs or permanent cautery to increase tear lake.
Botulinum Toxin: Induced ptosis to reduce mechanical blinking friction in refractive cases.
Lateral Tarsorrhaphy: For neurotrophic or exposure-related cases.
Scleral Lenses: PROSE or ScCL to provide a constant fluid reservoir.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Recurrence: High recurrence rate if underlying dry eye is not managed.
Secondary Infection: BCL use in dry eyes increases risk of bacterial keratitis.
Corneal Scarring: Chronic debridement or traction can lead to subepithelial haze.
Prognosis: Excellent for visual recovery if surface is stabilized.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Points
sections.content: Recent studies highlight the efficacy of Autologous Serum Tears in refractive FK, showing a 90% resolution rate. The use of Lacrisert (hydroxypropyl cellulose insert) provides sustained lubrication. Emerging evidence also suggests that neuropathic pain modulation (e.g., Gabapentin) may be necessary for patients with chronic pain post-resolution of physical filaments.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the superior conjunctiva; if SLK is present, treat the thyroid status.
Filaments are NOT just mucus; they are anchored to the basement membrane—pulling them out creates a micro-defect.
Acetylcysteine 10% smells like rotten eggs; warn patients to improve compliance.
In post-op cases, suspect toxicity from preservatives in antibiotic/steroid drops (BAK) as the primary trigger.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Overview
sections.content: Stargardt Disease (STGD1) is the most common autosomal recessive macular dystrophy, characterized by subretinal lipofuscin accumulation and progressive RPE atrophy. Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy (BVMD) is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in the BEST1 gene, leading to the accumulation of yellowish lipofuscin-like material (egg-yolk lesion) in the sub-retinal space.

sections.title: The 5 Stages of Best Disease (BVMD)
content: Stage 1: Pre-vitelliform - Normal fundus; Abnormal EOG (Arden Ratio < 1.55).
Stage 2: Vitelliform - Classic 'Egg-Yolk' lesion (3-5mm) in the macula.
Stage 3: Pseudohypopyon - Partial resorption of yellowish material; fluid-level appears.
Stage 4: Vitelliruptive - 'Scrambled Egg' appearance; material breaks up, vision drops.
Stage 5: Atrophic/Cicatricial - RPE atrophy or fibrous scarring; potential CNV development.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Ocular Signs
content: STGD: 'Pisciform' flecks (fish-tail shaped) at the level of RPE.
STGD: Bull's eye maculopathy or beaten-bronze appearance.
STGD: Peripapillary sparing (highly characteristic).
BVMD: Solitary, well-circumscribed yellow subfoveal lesion.
BVMD: Usually bilateral, though can be asymmetric.
BVMD: Retinal periphery is typically normal.

branches: FFA: 'Dark Choroid' in 80% of STGD (blocked background fluorescence)
FAF: Hyper-autofluorescent flecks in STGD; Intense Hyper-AF in Vitelliform stage of BVMD
OCT: STGD - Loss of EZ zone, RPE thinning; BVMD - Subretinal hyper-reflective material
OCT-A: Monitoring for Type 2 CNV in late stages of both diseases

sections.title: STGD Classification (Fishman)
content: Stage 1: Pigmentary changes in fovea, no flecks within 1DD.
Stage 2: Flecks beyond 1DD, may extend to arcades.
Stage 3: Diffuse flecks, resorbing flecks with RPE atrophy.
Stage 4: Diffuse RPE atrophy; extensive choriocapillaris loss.

sections.title: Red Flags: Potential Complications
content: Sudden metamorphopsia (sign of CNV)
Subretinal hemorrhage in BVMD Stage 5
Rapidly progressive vision loss in STGD1
High sensitivity to Vitamin A in Stargardt

rows: Smaller lesion, Normal EOG, onset > 40 years
History of Hydroxychloroquine or Thioridazine use
Profound early photophobia, severely abnormal ERG early
Variant of STGD1; flecks without early macular atrophy

sections.title: Clinical Management & Protocol
content: Step 1: Genetic Counseling and Testing (ABCA4/BEST1).
Step 2: Low vision assessment and tinted lenses (UV protection).
Step 3: STGD Avoidance: Stop Vitamin A supplements (accelerates A2E).
Step 4: CNV Surveillance: Amsler grid and periodic OCT-A.
Step 5: Treatment of CNV: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab/Aflibercept).

content.explanation: BEST disease involves the BEST1 gene, chromosome 11, and usually starts with 1 central lesion. EOG is the #1 diagnostic electrophysiology test.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: ProgStar Study: Longitudinal data on STGD progression using FAF and microperimetry.
TEGSET Clinical Trial: Exploring gene therapy (lentiviral vectors) for ABCA4 replacement.
Emixustat: A visual cycle modulator aimed at reducing A2E accumulation in Stargardt (Phase 3).
ALKEUS Study (Gildeuretinpa): Deuterated Vitamin A to slow lipofuscin formation.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A 'Dark Choroid' on FFA is diagnostic for Stargardt but absent in 20% of cases.
Best disease patients often maintain surprisingly good vision despite the 'Egg-yolk' appearance.
If EOG is normal, it is NOT Best disease.
UV-blocking sunglasses are mandatory for all Stargardt patients.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Best disease may be found incidentally during school screenings.
Stargardt may present as 'oculocutaneous albinism' mimic due to foveal hypoplasia-like appearance.
Psychosocial support and IEP (Individualized Education Program) are vital for school-age children.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Nanophthalmos is a specific subtype of 'simple microphthalmos' characterized by a small eye (Axial Length <20mm) with a structurally normal, though crowded, appearance. In contrast, Microphthalmos describes a small eye that often possesses internal structural anomalies (colobomas, persistent fetal vasculature, etc.).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Small corneal diameter (<10mm white-to-white)
Shallow anterior chamber (ACD <1.5mm common)
Relatively large lens (high lens-to-eye volume ratio)
Narrow or closed angles (high risk of ACG)
Fundus: Macular folds, crowded optic disc, tortuous vessels
Thick sclera (often >2.0 mm on ultrasound)

sections.title: RED FLAGS: The Surgical Nightmare
content: High risk of Spontaneous or Post-op Uveal Effusion
Expulsive Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage during intraocular surgery
Malignant Glaucoma (Ciliary Block) post-op
Non-rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Avoid sudden intraocular pressure drops during surgery

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Comprehensive Refraction: Confirm high hyperopia
2. A-Scan Biometry: Measure Axial Length (Gold Standard)
3. B-Scan Ultrasonography: Assess scleral thickness/choroidal status
4. Gonioscopy: Evaluate for angle closure or PAS
5. UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy): Measure ACD and Ciliary Body anatomy
6. Fundus OCT: Check for foveal hypoplasia or macular folds

branches: Posterior Microphthalmos (Normal ant. seg, short AL)
High Hyperopia (Normal size eye, flat cornea/lens)

sections.title: Pre-Surgical Management Strategy
content: 1. Aggressive medical management of Glaucoma
2. Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) early if angle is narrow
3. Consider prophylactic Lamellar Sclerotomies (4 quadrants)
4. Pre-op systemics: Acetazolamide + Mannitol to soften eye
5. General anesthesia to ensure absolute control of venous pressure

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Phacoemulsification
content: Prefer micro-incisional approach (MICS)
Use OVD with high cohesive properties (Healon GV/5)
Perform small, centered capsulorhexis (risk of run-out)
Maintain deep AC: use automated infusion if possible
Consider IOL power: often requires 'piggyback' IOLs (e.g., +30 and +10)

content.explanation: N: Narrow angles/Near-sightedness (extreme hyperopia); A: Axial length (<20mm); N: No other malformations; O: Outflow issues (Uveal Effusion).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (Kanski Level)
content: The Lens-to-Eye Volume Ratio is 4-8x higher than normal in Nanophthalmos.
Uveal effusion syndrome occurs because the thick sclera acts like a 'noose' on vortex veins.
In Complex Microphthalmos, always check for systemic syndromes (e.g., Lenz, CHARGE, Walker-Warburg).
IOL calculation formulas: Haigis or Hoffer Q are generally more accurate for very short eyes.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Femtosecond laser-assisted sclerostomy (FLAS) for effusion management
AS-OCT guided angle assessment for surgical planning
Genetic counseling for MFRP-associated retinal dystrophies
Use of intrascleral IOL fixation (Yamane) in cases of zonular instability

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
sections.content: Amblyopia management is paramount. Early full cycloplegic refraction and patching are required. Monitor for early-onset angle-closure glaucoma, which can occur as early as the second decade of life in nanophthalmic patients.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Superior Oblique Palsy (SOP) results from dysfunction of the 4th Cranial (Trochlear) Nerve. It is the most common cause of isolated vertical strabismus in both children and adults. The trochlear nerve is unique: it is the longest CN, the only one to exit dorsally, and the only one to cross the midline completely before exiting the brainstem, making it highly susceptible to trauma.

rows: Reversing HT (RHT in L-gaze, LHT in R-gaze)

sections.title: Clinical Features (Unilateral)
content: Ipsilateral Hypertropia (HT) - worse in contralateral gaze.
Abnormal Head Position: Tilt to contralateral shoulder.
Excyclotorsion (subjective and objective).
Diplopia: Vertical and torsional, worse in downgaze.
Facial Asymmetry: Often seen in congenital cases (ipsilateral cheek fullness).

sections.title: The 'Masked' Bilateral SOP Red Flags
content: Traumatic origin (even mild head injury).
Excyclotorsion > 10 degrees on Double Maddox Rod.
Reversing Hypertropia on side-to-side gaze.
Significant V-pattern esotropia in downgaze.
Minimal Hypertropia in primary position despite large tilt test results.

sections.title: Diagnostics: Parks-Bielschowsky 3-Step Test
content: Step 1: Determine which eye is higher in primary position (e.g., Right Hypertropia).
Step 2: Determine if HT increases in Right or Left gaze (e.g., RHT increases in Left Gaze).
Step 3: Determine if HT increases on Right or Left head tilt (e.g., RHT increases on Right Tilt).
Conclusion: If all three correlate, positive for isolated cyclovertical muscle palsy (Right SO in this example).

rows: Weakening of ipsilateral IO AND contralateral IR
SO tuck + IO weakening + contra IR recession
Harada-Ito or Bilateral SO tuck/IO weakening
Exploration of the SO and tendon

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Slit-lamp: Usually normal.
Gonioscopy: Not routinely indicated unless trauma/glaucoma suspected.
Fundoscopy: Look for excyclotorsion (fovea below the base of optic nerve).
Lancaster Red-Green: Shows the torsional and vertical deviation profile.
Prism Under Cover Test: Measurement in 9 cardinal positions.

sections.title: Advanced Imaging & Workup
content: MRI Brain/Orbits: Thin-cut T1 images to look for SO muscle belly atrophy (congenital).
MRA/CTA: Indicated if associated with other CN palsies (rule out aneurysm).
Blood Work: HBA1c, Blood Pressure (if microvascular suspected in patients >50).
Tensilon/Ice Test: Only if Myasthenia Gravis is a differential.

content.explanation: Superior muscles are IN-torsionists; Recti muscles are AD-ductors. (Helps determine muscle action during tilt and gaze steps).

sections.title: Management: The Harada-Ito Procedure
content: Indication: Primarily for symptomatic excyclotorsion (Bilateral or Unilateral) without significant vertical deviation.
Step 1: Identify the Superior Oblique tendon.
Step 2: Split the tendon longitudinally, isolating the anterior fibers (responsible for torsion).
Step 3: Displace the anterior fibers anteriorly and laterally (Fells modification).
Step 4: Secure with non-absorbable suture (e.g., 6-0 Mersilene) to the sclera.
Effect: Increases the mechanical advantage of the SO for incyclotorsion.

sections.title: Surgical Hierarchy (Unilateral)
content: Small Deviation (<15PD): Weakening of the ipsilateral IO.
Medium Deviation (15-25PD): IO weakening + Contralateral IR recession.
Large Deviation (>25PD): 3-muscle surgery (SO tuck + IO weakening + Contra IR recession).
SO Laxity: Superior Oblique Tuck (be wary of inducing iatrogenic Brown Syndrome).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Clinical Pearls
content: PEDIG Studies: Highlight the effectiveness of prisms for small deviations.
The 'Over-Correction' Rule: In traumatic SOP, wait 6-12 months for spontaneous recovery.
Congenital SOP Pearl: Patients often have large vertical fusion amplitudes (>10-15PD), whereas acquired cases have normal amplitudes (1-3PD).
Bilateral Pearl: If you fix one side and a large HT appears on the other, you've 'unmasked' the bilateral palsy.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Iatrogenic Brown Syndrome: Following SO tuck, look for restricted elevation in adduction.
Overcorrection: Resulting in 'reverse' 3-step test positivity.
Undercorrection: Residual diplopia in downgaze (reading position).
Recurrence: Rare in congenital cases after surgery; more common in traumatic cases due to progressive atrophy.
Prognosis: Excellent with surgery; 80-90% success rate in achieving single binocular vision in primary position.

sections.title: Definition & Unique Anatomy
sections.content: The 4th cranial nerve (Trochlear) is the longest and thinnest cranial nerve, and the only one to exit the brainstem dorsally and decussate before exiting. It innervates the Superior Oblique (SO) muscle. Its unique course makes it highly susceptible to trauma, particularly at the point of decussation in the anterior medullary velum.

sections.title: Epidemiological Distribution of Acquired IV Nerve Palsy

rows: Early childhood, often subclinical until decompensation
Often absent due to suppression or large fusion
Present (hypoplasia on the side of tilt)

sections.title: The Park-Bielschowsky Three-Step Test
content: Step 1: Identify which eye is hypertropic in primary position (e.g., Right Hypertropia).
Step 2: Determine if the hypertropia is worse in Right or Left gaze (e.g., worse in Left gaze).
Step 3: Determine if the hypertropia is worse on Right or Left head tilt (e.g., worse on Right tilt).
Conclusion: If RHT is worse in L-gaze and R-tilt, it confirms a Right Superior Oblique (CN IV) palsy.

sections.title: Signs of Bilateral CN IV Palsy
content: Excyclotorsion > 10 degrees (measured by Double Maddox Rod)
Reversing Hypertropia (RHT on L-tilt, LHT on R-tilt)
V-pattern Esotropia > 15 PD difference between up/down gaze
Underaction of both Superior Obliques / Overaction of both Inferior Obliques
Small hypertropia in primary position despite large symptoms

content.explanation: Superiors are IN-torsionists. (Superior Oblique and Superior Rectus both intort the eye).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Ipsilateral Hypertropia (worsens in adduction)
Excyclotorsion (subjective and objective fundus torsion)
Abnormal Head Position: Tilt to the contralateral shoulder
V-pattern esotropia (due to loss of SO abducting effect in depression)
Pseudo-overaction of the Inferior Oblique

rows: Restrictive pattern, lid lag, positive forced ductions
Associated with brainstem signs, torsion follows tilt (donkey ear)
Restriction in elevation in adduction, positive traction test
Associated ptosis, pupil involvement, horizontal component

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Orthoptic Assessment (Prism Cover Test in 9 positions).
2. Double Maddox Rod (Measure subjective torsion).
3. FAT Test (Family Album Tomography) for congenital signs.
4. Forced Duction Test (Differentiate palsy from restriction).
5. Neuroimaging (MRI Brain/Orbit) if non-vasculopathic/traumatic or progression.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Observation: 6-12 months for acquired/ischemic cases (spontaneous recovery common).
Prisms: Base-down prism (ipsilateral) or Base-up (contralateral) for small deviations.
Botulinum Toxin: Injection into the IO to reduce overaction temporarily.
Surgery: Indicated for stable, large deviations or significant torticollis.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: Inferior Oblique Weakening (Recession, Myectomy, Anteriorization): Primary choice for IO overaction.
Superior Oblique Tuck: Indicated for SO laxity/underaction, especially in congenital cases.
Harada-Ito Procedure: Splitting the SO tendon and anteriorizing the lateral half to treat excyclotorsion.
Contralateral Inferior Rectus Recession: Effective for limiting deviation in the primary and down-gaze fields.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (BCSC Level)
content: In bilateral cases, the hypertropia may be 'masked'. Always check torsion and V-pattern.
A large vertical fusion amplitude (>6 PD) is pathognomonic for a long-standing (congenital) palsy.
In traumatic cases, CN IV is often damaged because the nerve decussates at the thin anterior medullary velum.
The 'FAT Test' refers to looking at old photos for a head tilt to prove chronicity.
Excyclotorsion > 10-15 degrees is the strongest indicator of bilateral involvement.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Traumatic cataract is the opacification of the crystalline lens resulting from blunt or penetrating ocular injury. It is a leading cause of unilateral visual impairment in children and young adults. Pathogenesis involves direct mechanical rupture of the lens capsule, osmotic swelling of lens fibers, or metabolic disruption (in the case of radiation or electric shock).

rows: Petal-shaped opacities along posterior lens sutures
Imprinted iris pigment on the anterior lens capsule
Rapid hydration of the entire lens cortex
Absorption of lens proteins leaving collapsed capsule

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination
content: Visual Acuity: Assessment of light projection (PR) if cataract is mature.
Pupils: Check for RAPD (indicates optic nerve or severe retinal damage).
Slit-lamp: Assess capsule integrity, phacodonesis, and iridodonesis.
Gonioscopy: Look for angle recession, cyclodialysis, or IOFB in the angle.
Tonometry: Rule out phacolytic, phacomorphic, or traumatic glaucoma.
Fundoscopy: B-scan required if view of the posterior pole is obscured.

sections.title: Diagnostic & Imaging Workup
content: Step 1: B-scan Ultrasonography to rule out Retinal Detachment (RD) or Vitreous Hemorrhage.
Step 2: Non-Contrast CT Orbits (1mm cuts) for suspected Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB).
Step 3: UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy) for visualizing zonular loss or sulcus anatomy.
Step 4: Biometry (IOL Master/A-scan) using the fellow eye for comparison if necessary.

rows: Often bilateral, no history of trauma, stable
History of metal injury, ERG changes (decreased b-wave)

sections.title: Emergency Surgical Indications
content: Phacomorphic Glaucoma (Intractable IOP elevation from lens swelling)
Phacolytic/Lens Protein Uveitis (Uncontrolled inflammation)
Ruptured Lens Capsule with cortical material in the anterior chamber
Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB) requiring immediate removal
Total Lens Subluxation into the Vitreous Cavity or Anterior Chamber

sections.title: Surgical Management Strategy
content: 1. Preoperative Control: Stabilize inflammation with topical/systemic steroids.
2. Incision: Consider sclerocorneal or small-gauge pars plana lensectomy if zonules are <180° stable.
3. Capsulorhexis: Use trypan blue; manual or femtosecond laser (if stable) to visualize the capsule.
4. Lens Removal: Low-parameter phacoemulsification or manual ECCE to minimize zonular stress.
5. Vitrectomy: Perform anterior vitrectomy if vitreous prolapse is present.
6. IOL Selection: In-the-bag (with CTR), Sulcus (if capsule allows), or Scleral-Fixated (Yamane/Gore-Tex).

sections.title: Surgical Tools for Zonular Instability
content: Capsular Tension Ring (CTR): For <4 hours of zonular dialysis.
Cionni Modified CTR: Scleral suturing for >4 hours of dialysis.
Capsular Tension Segments (CTS): Ahmed segments for focal support.
Iris Hooks / Capsule Hooks: Temporary intraoperative support.
Trypan Blue Dye: Critical for identifying capsular tears.

content.explanation: T: Tension (Zonular loss/IOP); R: Rosette (Cataract morphology); A: Angle (Recession/Hyphema); U: Uveitis (Lens-induced); M: Mechanism (Blunt vs Penetrating); A: Adnexa (Lid/Canalicular involvement).

sections.title: Postoperative Complications
content: Secondary Glaucoma (Steroid-induced or Angle-recession)
Retinal Detachment (Highest risk in penetrating trauma)
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME)
IOL Decentration or Dislocation
Endophthalmitis (Especially if IOFB involved)
Sympathetic Ophthalmia (Rare but devastating bilat. uveitis)

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Amblyopia: Rapid visual rehabilitation is critical for patients <7 years old.
IOL Power: Tendency toward under-correction to account for axial growth.
Inflammation: Children exhibit a more robust inflammatory response (Corticosteroid burst required).
PCO: Primary posterior capsulotomy and anterior vitrectomy are standard in young children.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Recent Advances
content: Pearls: Always perform an indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression (if safe) to rule out peripheral retinal breaks.
Pearls: Avoid MRI if there is even a 1% suspicion of a metallic IOFB; use CT instead.
Advances: Flanged intrascleral IOL fixation (Yamane technique) provides excellent stability in the absence of capsular support.
Advances: Use of pupillary expansion devices (Malyugin ring) in cases of traumatic miosis or iris sphincter damage.

rows: Vitrectomy beneficial only if presenting vision is LP (Light Perception).
Immediate TAP/BI (Intravitreal Antibiotics) for HM or better.
Intensive glucose control reduces risk/progression of DR.
Tube shunt (Baerveldt 350) more successful than MMC-Trab in patients with prior surgery.
Favors tubes for failed trabeculectomy or prior CE/IOL.
Equivalent visual acuity outcomes at 1 and 2 years.
Treatment for Type 1 ROP (Zone I any stage with plus, Zone I stage 3, Zone II stage 2/3 with plus).

branches: NF1: Lisch nodules, Optic pathway glioma, Sphenoid wing dysplasia
VHL: Retinal hemangioblastoma, Renal cell carcinoma, Pheochromocytoma
Sturge-Weber: Port-wine stain (V1/V2), Choroidal hemangioma, Glaucoma
Tuberous Sclerosis: Astrocytic hamartoma, Ash-leaf spots, Adenoma sebaceum

rows: Acute Anterior Uveitis (AS, IBD, Psoriatic, Reactive)

sections.title: Red Flags: Ocular Emergencies
content: CRAO with Giant Cell Arteritis suspicion (check ESR/CRP/PV/Plt)
Endophthalmitis (Hypopyon, pain, decreasing vision post-op)
Orbital Cellulitis (Proptosis, painful motility, RAPD)
Third Nerve Palsy (Pupil-involving - suspect P-Com Aneurysm)
Chemical Burn (Immediate irrigation until pH 7.0-7.2)

content.explanation: Lateral Rectus = CN VI; Superior Oblique = CN IV; All others = CN III.

sections.title: Management of Acute Angle Closure (AACG)
content: 1. Immediate pressure lowering: IV Acetazolamide 500mg.
2. Topical therapy: Beta-blocker, Alpha-agonist, Steroid.
3. Pilocarpine 2% (only once IOP < 40 mmHg and ischemia resolved).
4. Definitive: YAG Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) - both eyes.
5. Alternative: Lens extraction if cataract-induced (phacomorphic).

sections.title: FFA Phases: Timing and Pathology
content: 1. Choroidal (Pre-arterial): 10-12s - Cilioretinal art. fills.
2. Arterial: 13s - Complete filling of retinal arteries.
3. Arteriovenous (Capillary): Laminar flow in veins.
4. Venous: 15-20s - Complete filling of veins.
5. Recirculation/Late: 5-10m - Disc staining/leaks visible.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The most common cause of a spontaneous vitreous hemorrhage in a non-diabetic is a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) with a retinal tear.
Shafer's Sign (Tobacco Dust) indicates RPE cells in the vitreous - 90% risk of a retinal break.
Argyll Robertson Pupil: Small, irregular, accommodates but doesn't react (Neurosyphilis - Midbrain lesion).
Fuchs Heterochromic Iridocyclitis: Chronic low-grade uveitis, no posterior synechiae, diffuse fine KPs, risk of cataract/glaucoma.
Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (PXF): Associated with LOXL1 gene; risk of zonular dehiscence during phacoemulsification.

branches: Presence of 1 = Severe; Presence of 2 = Very Severe

sections.title: Surgical Instruments & Steps: Phacoemulsification
content: 1. Paracentesis & OVD (Viscoelastic) injection.
2. Clear corneal incision (CCI) - Keratome.
3. Continuous Curvilinear Capsulorhexis (CCC) - Cystotome/Utrata.
4. Hydrodissection & Hydrodelineation.
5. Nucleus Emulsification (Divide & Conquer or Stop & Chop).
6. Cortical aspiration (I&A) and IOL Implantation.

sections.title: Pediatric Cataract: Timing and Critical Periods
content: Congenital Unilateral: Surgery within 4-6 weeks to prevent amblyopia.
Congenital Bilateral: Surgery within 8-10 weeks.
Post-op: Aggressive aphakic contact lens fitting or primary IOL (if >6-12 months old).
Risk: High incidence of secondary glaucoma (30%) in aphakic infants.

rows: Grade I + Focal constriction and AV nicking
Grade II + Cotton wool spots, flame hemorrhages, hard exudates
Grade III + Optic disc swelling (Malignant Hypertension)

sections.title: Recent Advances: Gene Therapy & Biosimilars
sections.content: Voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna) is now the standard for RPE65-mediated inherited retinal dystrophy (LCA). Biosimilars for Ranibizumab (Byooviz) and Aflibercept are entering clinical practice to reduce costs. Port Delivery Systems (PDS) and longer-acting agents like Faricimab (dual VEGF/Ang-2 inhibitor) are reshaping management of nAMD and DME.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A retinal break is a full-thickness continuity defect in the neurosensory retina. Prophylaxis aims to create a chorioretinal adhesion around the break using laser photocoagulation or cryopexy, preventing liquefied vitreous from entering the subretinal space and causing a Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD). The decision to treat is a risk-benefit calculation based on symptoms, morphology, and systemic risk factors.

rows: Round plug of retina pulled off

sections.title: Treatment Indications: Symptomatic Lesions
content: Symptomatic Horseshoe Tears (HST): Mandatory treatment.
Symptomatic Dialysis: Mandatory treatment.
Symptomatic Operculated Tears: Treat if traction persists or large.
Symptomatic Lattice with Breaks: Treat holes/tears within lattice.
New Flashes/Floaters with Pigmented Cells (Shafer's Sign): Urgent intervention.

sections.title: Treatment Indications: Asymptomatic Lesions
content: HST in Fellow Eye of RD: Highly recommended.
Large Atrophic Holes in Myopes: Consider if >2DD.
Lattice Degeneration in Fellow Eye of RD: Strong consideration.
Subclinical RD (localized fluid >1DD): Usually treat.
Pre-Cataract/Refractive Surgery: Treat visible HST/high-risk lattice.

sections.title: Red Flags: Impending RD
content: Shafer's Sign (Tobacco Dust in anterior vitreous)
Vitreous Hemorrhage (70% risk of associated tear)
New onset 'curtain' or 'veil' in vision
Macular involving subretinal fluid

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Laser Photocoagulation
content: 1. Topical anesthesia and Goldmann 3-Mirror or wide-field lens.
2. Argon/532nm Green Laser: 200-500 micron spot size.
3. Exposure: 0.1 to 0.2 seconds.
4. Power: Titrate to obtain 'grey-white' uptake.
5. Pattern: 3 concentric rows of confluent burns around the break.
6. Extension: Ensure the 'horns' of the HST are well-surrounded.

sections.title: Cryopexy: When to Use?
content: Indications: Extreme periphery (Ora), hazy media (cataract/hemorrhage).
Mechanism: Freeze-thaw-freeze cycle to create adhesion.
Disadvantage: Increased risk of PVR due to RPE dispersion.
Procedure: Direct visualization with indirect ophthalmoscopy.

rows: Small risk of HST at posterior end
Asymptomatic lattice has very low progression to RD (~1%).
Symptomatic HST carry a 50% risk of RD without treatment.
Recommends against treating asymptomatic holes/lattice in low-risk eyes.
Fellow eyes of RD patients have a 10-15% cumulative risk of RD.

content.explanation: 3 rows of burns, 200-500 micron size, 1 (one) goal: prevent fluid entry.

sections.title: Complications of Prophylaxis
content: Epiretinal Membrane (ERM) formation (most common).
Iatrogenic retinal breaks.
Vitreous hemorrhage.
Subretinal neovascularization (rare).
Failure of prophylaxis: RD occurs despite laser.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Exam
content: Always perform scleral depression to rule out additional breaks before lasering.
Pigmented breaks are 'old' and usually stable, but symptoms override pigmentation.
If you find one break, look 180 degrees away; multiple breaks are common.
Wait 10-14 days for the laser scar to achieve maximal tensile strength.
Educate patients on the 'RD Warning Signs' even after successful laser.

sections.title: Definition & Overview of Regression
sections.content: Regression refers to the involutional stage of retinal vascular diseases following treatment (PRP, Anti-VEGF) or natural progression into a 'burned-out' phase. While active signs like hemorrhage subside, permanent structural changes and 'ghost' features remain as diagnostic footprints of past ischemia.

sections.title: Key Signs of Regressed PDR
content: Vascular 'Ghosting': White, thread-like vessels (atrophied NVD/NVE).
Fibrotic Stalks: Opaque, white/grey membranes on the disc or along arcades.
PRP Laser Scars: Pigmented or atrophic circular burns in the mid-periphery.
Tractional Changes: Fixed retinal folds or 'dragged' macula/vessels.
Venous Beading (VB) & Duplication: Residual evidence of severe NPDR prior to PDR conversion.
Arteriolar Narrowing: Significant attenuation of the arterial tree.
Vitreous Condensation: Remnants of old vitreous hemorrhage (Schaffer's sign or 'tobacco dust' is different, but look for old clots).

sections.title: Signs of Old CRVO / BRVO
content: Optociliary Shunt Vessels: Large, tortuous vessels on the disc (CRVO) connecting the retinal and choroidal circulations.
Venous Sheathing: White 'cuffing' around formerly engorged veins.
Collateral Vessels: Tortuous vessels crossing the horizontal raphe (BRVO) or disc (CRVO).
Macular Pigmentary Changes: Mottled RPE from chronic cystoid macular edema (CME).
Secondary ERM: Epiretinal membrane formation over the area of old occlusion.
Segmental Sclerosis: If BRVO, sheathing and narrowing are limited to the affected quadrant.

sections.title: The Great Mimicker: Collaterals vs. NV
Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: 1. Multi-modal Imaging: Start with color fundus photography (CFP).
2. FFA: Identify 'Silent' areas of non-perfusion vs. active leakage.
3. OCT-Angiography: Visualize the Deep Capillary Plexus (DCP) for remodeling.
4. Structural OCT: Look for DRIL (Disorganization of Retinal Inner Layers) and thinning.
5. Gonioscopy: MANDATORY to rule out NVA/NVG even if the fundus looks quiet.

sections.title: Red Flags: Reactivation Signs
content: New 'fuzziness' or blurring of previously sharp fibrotic vessels.
Sudden increase in IOP (check for NVI/NVA).
Recurrent vitreous hemorrhage (could be 'crunch' syndrome or new NV).
New onset of microaneurysms at the edge of old laser scars.

content.explanation: T: Tractional folds, H: Heme (old/hemosiderin), E: Ensheathment, G: Ghost vessels, O: Optociliary shunts, S: Scars (PRP), T: Thinning (Retinal), S: Sclerosis.

sections.title: Landmark Studies Impact
content: ETDRS: Defined PDR regression criteria after PRP.
CVOS/BRAVO: Established the natural history of vein occlusions and the role of grid laser.
Protocol S: Compared Anti-VEGF vs. PRP for PDR, highlighting the 'regression-reactivation' cycle.
SCORE: Defined the prognosis of chronic CME in RVO.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Resident Exams
content: If you see optociliary shunts but no diabetes, think CRVO or Optic Nerve Sheath Meningioma.
Collaterals never leak on FFA; Neovascularization always leaks.
PRP scars 'creep' or enlarge over time (atrophic creep).
The presence of DRIL on OCT is a strong predictor of poor visual recovery even after regression.

data.title: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO): The Ocular Stroke
data.summary: A critical ophthalmic emergency characterized by sudden, painless, profound vision loss. CRAO is a sentinel event for systemic cardiovascular disease and stroke, requiring immediate diagnosis, ocular pressure reduction, and a comprehensive systemic workup.
