sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Vitreous hemorrhage (VH) refers to the presence of blood within the vitreous cavity, anterior to the retina. It is a significant cause of sudden, painless decrease in visual acuity. The extent of vision loss depends on the density and location of the hemorrhage. Clearing can take weeks to months, and persistent hemorrhage can lead to complications such as ghost cell glaucoma or retinal detachment.

branches: Post-Surgical Complications (e.g., Anti-VEGF injection, YAG capsulotomy)

sections.title: Pathophysiology
sections.content: Blood enters the vitreous cavity due to rupture of retinal vessels or neovascular membranes (e.g., in PDR), or direct injury. The blood cells obstruct the light pathway, causing vision loss. Hemolysis and breakdown products can lead to complications like ghost cell glaucoma. Chronic iron deposition can cause hemosiderosis bulbi, damaging retinal cells.

rows: Few red blood cells, subtle opacities.
Minimal to no impact, usually 20/25 or better.
Diffuse haze, partial obscuration of fine fundus details.
Significant obscuration of major retinal vessels and optic disc.
Complete obscuration of fundus details, absent red reflex.
Severe reduction, often Hand Motions (HM) or Light Perception (LP).

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Sudden, painless decrease in visual acuity (most common).
New onset of floaters ('cobwebs', 'spiders', 'shower of black dots').
Perception of a 'red haze' or 'smoky vision'.
Photopsias (flashes of light) – less common, suggests associated PVD/tear.
Metamorphopsia (distorted vision) – rare, if macula involved or underlying cause.
Visual field defects (due to dense clots).

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: Visual Acuity: Ranging from 20/20 to no light perception (NLP).
Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD): May be present if significant retinal pathology.
Slit-lamp biomicroscopy: Red blood cells in the anterior vitreous; obscured view of the fundus.
Indirect Ophthalmoscopy: Hazy or absent red reflex (dense VH); difficulty or inability to visualize fundus details.
Gonioscopy: May reveal red blood cells in the angle or associated neovascularization (NVA).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: History & Ocular Examination** (VA, IOP, anterior segment, dilated fundus exam if possible).

**Step 2: B-scan Ultrasonography** (MANDATORY if fundus view is obscured). Essential to rule out retinal detachment, posterior vitreous detachment, intraocular foreign body, or intraocular tumor. Can assess vitreous clarity and mobility.
**Step 3: Systemic Workup** (as indicated): Blood pressure, fasting blood glucose/HbA1c (for diabetes), complete blood count, coagulation profile (INR/PTT) if coagulopathy suspected.

**Step 4: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) / Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**: Performed *after* significant clearing of the hemorrhage to identify and characterize the source of bleeding (e.g., neovascularization, macroaneurysm). Not useful in acute dense VH.

rows: Usually accompanied by more photopsia/floaters before vision loss; often associated with PVD. VH can mask view of detachment.
B-scan ultrasonography (essential if VH obscures view).
Sudden floaters, but vision loss not as severe unless subtle hemorrhage. Weiss ring visible.
Dilated fundus exam; B-scan (if view hazy).
Extensive retinal hemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins, disc edema, cotton wool spots. VH can occur secondary to neovascularization.
Pain, red eye, hypopyon, severe inflammation, possibly purulent vitreous.
Vitreous tap for culture and sensitivity.
Pain, photophobia, cells/flare in anterior chamber, inflammatory cells in vitreous but no frank blood.
Slit-lamp exam, rule out infectious causes.
Progressive vision loss, specific lesion on fundus exam. VH can occur if tumor bleeds.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Grading
sections.content: While there isn't a formal staging system like TNM, vitreous hemorrhage is typically graded by density and clinical impact (as described in Classification by Severity). The duration of hemorrhage (acute vs. chronic) is also clinically important, as chronic hemorrhages (e.g., >3 months) are less likely to clear spontaneously and carry a higher risk of complications like ghost cell glaucoma and epiretinal membrane formation, often warranting surgical intervention.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment
content: **Step 1: Initial Conservative Management**
•  Head elevation (30-45 degrees to help blood settle inferiorly).
•  Bed rest and avoidance of strenuous activity (to prevent re-bleed).
•  Bilateral patching (controversial, aims to reduce eye movements).
•  Manage systemic conditions (e.g., blood pressure, glucose control, anti-coagulation review).
**Step 2: Observation & Monitoring**
•  Small hemorrhages due to PVD or trauma often clear spontaneously within weeks-months.
•  Regular follow-up (e.g., weekly to monthly B-scans for dense VH) to monitor clearing and rule out complications like RD.
**Step 3: Medical Treatment (for underlying cause)**

•  Anti-VEGF injections (e.g., Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, Bevacizumab) for proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) to regress neovascularization and prevent further bleeding. May also hasten clearing.
**Step 4: Surgical Intervention (Pars Plana Vitrectomy - PPV)**
•  **Indications for Early PPV:** Retinal detachment, non-clearing VH (>3 months or 1-2 months in diabetics), ghost cell glaucoma, suspected penetrating trauma, significant epiretinal membrane.
•  **Urgent PPV:** Suspected giant retinal tear, endophthalmitis with VH, specific cases of Terson's syndrome, suspected intraocular foreign body.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV)
content: **Step 1: Anesthesia** (Local or general).
**Step 2: Sclerotomies** (23-gauge, 25-gauge, or 27-gauge for smaller incisions) made through the pars plana.
**Step 3: Infusion Cannula Placement** (maintains IOP).

**Step 4: Vitrectomy** (using a high-speed vitrector) to aspirate the hemorrhagic vitreous. Intraocular pressure is carefully controlled. Direct visualization through the microscope (or endoscope if view is completely obscured).

**Step 5: Identify & Treat Bleeding Source** After clearing blood, the retina is meticulously inspected for tears, detachments, or bleeding neovascularization. Endolaser photocoagulation or cryopexy is applied as needed.
**Step 6: Tamponade** Fluid-air exchange followed by gas (SF6, C2F6, C3F8) or silicone oil tamponade if retinal tears, detachment, or extensive neovascularization require prolonged internal support.
**Step 7: Sclerotomy Closure** (often sutureless with small gauge vitrectomy).

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: Ghost Cell Glaucoma: Hemolyzed red blood cells block trabecular meshwork.
Hemosiderotic Glaucoma: Iron deposition damages trabecular meshwork.
Pigmentary Glaucoma: Pigment dispersion from vitreous.
Recurrent Vitreous Hemorrhage.
Retinal Detachment (especially if initial cause was a tear).
Epiretinal Membrane (ERM) and Macular Pucker.
Optic Atrophy.
Amblyopia (in children).
Cataract formation (especially after PPV).
Corneal blood staining (rare, with very high IOP and hyphema).

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Sudden, profound vision loss with LP/NLP: Rule out Retinal Detachment.
Severe ocular pain: Suggests associated conditions (e.g., acute angle-closure glaucoma, endophthalmitis, trauma).
Hyphema (blood in anterior chamber): Indicates possible trauma or underlying anterior segment pathology.
Increasing Intraocular Pressure (IOP): Risk of ghost cell glaucoma.
Signs of posterior segment infection (Endophthalmitis): Pain, redness, hypopyon, severe inflammation.
Suspected penetrating ocular trauma: Risk of intraocular foreign body, endophthalmitis.

content.explanation:
•  **V**ascular: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy, RVO, Sickle Cell Retinopathy.
•  **I**njury: Ocular Trauma (blunt/penetrating), Shaken Baby Syndrome.
•  **P**VD: Posterior Vitreous Detachment (especially with retinal tear).
•  **E**tc: Retinal Macroaneurysm, Terson's Syndrome, ROP, AMD (rare).
•  **R**etinal Detachment: Often occurs secondary to PVD/tear.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a B-scan ultrasonography if the fundus view is obscured by dense VH to rule out retinal detachment.
Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) is the most common cause of spontaneous VH in adults.
Consider non-accidental trauma (Shaken Baby Syndrome) in pediatric VH cases without clear etiology.
Non-clearing VH in a diabetic patient for 1-3 months typically warrants vitrectomy due to higher risk of complications and potential for occult retinal detachment.
The presence of an ochre membrane and ghost cells suggests chronic VH.
Systemic review is crucial, especially for diabetes, hypertension, and coagulopathies.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent advances include the widespread use of anti-VEGF agents (e.g., ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab) for treating underlying proliferative retinopathies like PDR. Studies from the DRCR.net (Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research Network) have informed optimal timing and protocols for anti-VEGF use, which has significantly reduced the incidence of severe VH and the need for vitrectomy in some cases. The ETDRS (Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study) criteria for PDR still guide management decisions for laser photocoagulation. Innovations in small-gauge vitrectomy (23, 25, 27 gauge) have made surgical intervention safer with faster recovery and less inflammation.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Pediatric Population:**

•  **Non-Accidental Trauma (NAT) / Shaken Baby Syndrome:** Always consider in infants with VH, especially if bilateral or associated with retinal hemorrhages, subdural hematoma, or other systemic injuries.
•  **Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP):** Proliferative ROP can lead to VH.
•  **Juvenile X-linked Retinoschisis:** Can present with VH due to bleeding from retinal vessels in schisis cavities.
•  **Amblyopia Risk:** Dense, persistent VH in children can lead to severe amblyopia, necessitating prompt intervention.
**Special Populations:**
•  **Sickle Cell Disease:** Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy is a significant cause of recurrent VH.
•  **Coagulopathies:** Patients on anticoagulants (warfarin, NOACs) or with bleeding disorders (hemophilia) are at higher risk. Careful medication review is essential.
•  **Terson's Syndrome:** Associated with subarachnoid or subdural hemorrhage; can be bilateral and dense, usually clears spontaneously but may require vitrectomy.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Diabetic Macular Edema (DME) is defined as the accumulation of fluid in the intraretinal layers (outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers) and/or subretinal space within the macular region. It results from a breakdown of the inner and outer blood-retinal barriers (BRB), primarily triggered by chronic hyperglycemia-induced microvascular damage. It can occur at any stage of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR).

sections.title: ETDRS Criteria: Clinically Significant Macular Edema (CSME)

rows: Thickening at or within 500 µm of the center of the fovea.
HE at or within 500 µm with adjacent retinal thickening.
Retinal thickening ≥ 1 disc area in size, any part of which is within 1 disc diameter of the foveal center.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Painless, gradual blurriness of central vision.
Metamorphopsia (distorted lines).
Micropsia / Macropsia.
Reduced contrast sensitivity.
Central or paracentral scotoma.
Hard exudates in a circinate pattern.
Microaneurysms (MA) and dot-blot hemorrhages.

rows: Post-cataract surgery; classic petaloid leakage on FFA.
Right-angle vessels; temporal foveal atrophy; no lipid.
History of head/neck radiation; sluggish capillary refill.

sections.title: Evidence-Based Management (DRCR.net Protocols)
content: Step 1: Systemic Optimization (HbA1c < 7.0%, Blood Pressure < 130/80, Lipids).
Step 2: Center-Involved (CI-DME) with VA 20/25 or better: Observation (Protocol V).
Step 3: CI-DME with VA 20/30 or worse: First-line Anti-VEGF (Protocol T).
Step 4: Non-Center Involved DME: Focal/Grid Laser (ETDRS Guidelines).
Step 5: Refractory to Anti-VEGF: Switch agents or add Intravitreal Steroids (Ozurdex/Iluvien).
Step 6: VMT-associated DME: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV).

rows: VEGF-Trap; superior in VA < 20/50 baseline (Protocol T).
Fab fragment; highly effective in all VA ranges.
Non-erodible implant; lasts up to 36 months.

sections.title: Red Flags: Steroid Precautions
content: Pre-existing Glaucoma (High risk of IOP spike).
Advanced Cup-to-Disc ratio (> 0.8).
Phakic Status (Steroids accelerate cataract formation).
History of Herpetic Keratitis/Endophthalmitis.
Active Ocular Infection.

content.explanation: A: A1c (Poor glycemic control); B: Blood Pressure (Hypertension); C: Cholesterol (Dyslipidemia); D: Duration (Years since diagnosis).

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Trials Summary
content: ETDRS: Focal/Grid laser reduces risk of moderate vision loss by 50%.
Protocol T: Aflibercept performed better than Bevacizumab/Ranibizumab in patients with VA 20/50 or worse at 1 year.
Protocol I: Anti-VEGF + prompt or deferred laser is superior to laser alone.
Protocol V: Patients with 20/25 vision can be observed safely if monitored closely.
PANORAMA: Aflibercept can improve DR severity scales and prevent DME.
YOSEMITE/RHINE: Faricimab (Ang-2/VEGF) shows non-inferiority with potential for Q16 dosing.

sections.title: Surgical Technique: PPV for DME
content: 1. Core Vitrectomy with posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) induction.
2. Removal of the Internal Limiting Membrane (ILM) using ICG or Brilliant Blue G.
3. Release of any tangential traction or epiretinal membranes.
4. Consideration of steroid injection or endolaser if needed.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & High-Yield Facts
content: DRIL (Disorganization of Retinal Inner Layers) is a strong biomarker for poor visual prognosis.
Hard exudates in the fovea can lead to permanent photoreceptor loss and subfoveal fibrosis.
Anemia and Renal Disease (high Creatinine) are strong systemic drivers of DME severity.
In pregnancy, DME may worsen significantly but often regresses postpartum.

title: Anterior Vitrectomy: Mastering the Anterior Segment's Deep Cleanup
summary: Anterior vitrectomy is a crucial surgical procedure in ophthalmology, involving the removal of vitreous gel from the anterior chamber or pupillary plane. Essential for managing vitreous prolapse during cataract surgery, trauma, or to clear vitreous opacities, it safeguards against complications like cystoid macular edema and retinal detachment, preserving ocular integrity and visual function.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Anterior vitrectomy refers to the surgical excision and removal of vitreous gel located anterior to the posterior capsule or through the pupil, typically involving the anterior third of the vitreous cavity. It is distinct from pars plana vitrectomy, which primarily targets the posterior vitreous. Its primary purpose is to clear vitreous from the anterior segment, prevent its incarceration in wounds, and manage complications that arise from vitreous presentation.

rows: Vitreous prolapse into AC, Dropped nuclear fragments/IOL haptics, Posterior Capsular Rupture (PCR)
Vitreous wick syndrome, Vitreous incarceration in wounds, Aphakic/pseudophakic pupillary block glaucoma, Cystoid Macular Edema (Irvine-Gass syndrome)
Vitreous hemorrhage in AC, Vitreous prolapse into corneal/scleral lacerations
Vitreous prolapse during penetrating keratoplasty, trabeculectomy, or tube shunt insertion
Management of dislocated IOLs (anterior chamber or sulcus fixed) with vitreous involvement

sections.title: 4. Fundamental Principles of Vitrectomy
content: **Infusion**: Maintains globe stability, AC depth, replaces removed vitreous. Typically via side port or limbal cannula (BSS, 60-80cm H2O).
**Cutting**: High-speed vitrector (600-5000+ cpm) minimizes traction by cutting vitreous before aspiration. Essential for safe removal.
**Aspiration**: Controlled vacuum (80-150 mmHg) removes cut vitreous and BSS, preventing excessive retinal traction.
**Port Size**: Commonly 20G, 23G, 25G. Smaller gauges often for limbal approach, larger for pars plana if needed.

sections.title: 6. Preoperative Assessment & Planning
content: **Comprehensive History**: Prior ocular surgeries, trauma, systemic conditions (e.g., Marfan's, pseudoexfoliation).
**Slit-Lamp Exam**: Assess anterior chamber depth, iris-lens diaphragm stability, signs of zonular weakness.
**Dilated Fundus Exam**: Rule out pre-existing retinal pathology (tears, detachments), especially in high-risk eyes.
**IOL Calculations**: If cataract surgery is primary procedure, determine appropriate IOL power and potential placement (bag vs. sulcus).
**Patient Counseling**: Discuss risks like CME, RD, endophthalmitis, and possibility of alternative IOL placement or secondary procedure.

sections.title: 7. Anesthesia Considerations
sections.content: Anesthesia choice depends on patient cooperation and complexity. **Topical/Intracameral** may suffice for straightforward vitreous prolapse during phacoemulsification. **Peribulbar/Retrobulbar** block is preferred for more complex or prolonged cases due to superior akinesia and analgesia. **General Anesthesia** is indicated for pediatric patients, highly anxious individuals, or extensive trauma cases requiring maximum globe control and patient immobility.

sections.title: 8. Surgical Technique: Limbal Approach (Post-PCR)
content: **1. Confirm Vitreous Prolapse**: Observe peaked pupil (after miotic), vitreous strands on instruments/wounds, difficulty with IOL rotation. Perform Seidel test on wounds if suspicious.
**2. Tamponade & Stabilize**: Inject high molecular weight dispersive viscoelastic (e.g., Viscoat) into the anterior chamber to push vitreous posteriorly and maintain AC depth.
**3. Create Ports & Infusion**: Establish 1-2 paracentesis ports (1mm). Place a 23G infusion cannula via a separate port or utilize an irrigating vitrector handpiece. BSS bottle height: 60-80 cm.
**4. Visualize Vitreous (Optional but Recommended)**: Inject ~0.1-0.2 mL dilute Triamcinolone Acetonide (TA, 4mg/0.1mL) into the anterior vitreous cavity to stain and highlight vitreous fibrils.

**5. Perform Vitrectomy**: Introduce vitrector (23G/25G) through a separate port. Set parameters: high cut rate (2500-5000+ cpm), low vacuum (80-150 mmHg). Always direct the vitrector port towards vitreous, away from retina, iris, and cornea.

**6. Thorough Vitreous Removal**: Sweep the anterior chamber, pupillary plane, and behind the iris/IOL (if implanted). Ensure all vitreous incarcerated in the main wound is freed using bimanual technique with a cyclodialysis spatula from the inside, while the vitrector is active.

**7. Verification**: Inject intracameral acetylcholine (Miochol-E) to constrict the pupil. A perfectly round pupil indicates a vitreous-free anterior segment. Gently dab all wounds with a non-fenestrated cellulose sponge; no vitreous should adhere. Elevate IOP transiently to check for vitreous prolapse.
**8. IOL Placement**: If primary cataract surgery, implant IOL in the sulcus or utilize an AC-IOL, often avoiding in-the-bag placement due to capsular compromise.
**9. Wound Closure**: Hydrate clear corneal wounds; suture if necessary to ensure watertight seal.

sections.title: 9. Surgical Techniques: Pars Plana Approach (AV Context)
sections.content: While anterior vitrectomy primarily uses a limbal approach, a pars plana approach may be necessary for complex anterior segment issues or posterior segment involvement (e.g., dropped nucleus, extensive vitreous hemorrhage, severe trauma). This involves creating scleral ports 3.5mm (phakic) or 3.0mm (aphakic/pseudophakic) posterior to the limbus. It offers superior access and control for deep vitreous removal and vitreous base dissection, but typically requires a vitreoretinal surgeon. Infusion, high cut rates, and controlled aspiration remain key principles.

sections.title: 10. Intraoperative Pearls & Pitfalls
content: **PEARLS**: High cut rate & low vacuum are paramount to minimize traction. Always use TA for visualization. Adequate infusion is critical for globe stability. Meticulous wound sweeping prevents incarceration. A perfectly round pupil after miotic confirms successful vitrectomy. Have a plan B (e.g., pars plana setup).

**PITFALLS**: Insufficient vitrectomy leads to CME/pupillary block. Excessive traction risks retinal tears/detachment. Incorrect vitrector port orientation can damage intraocular structures. Inadequate infusion causes hypotony. Proceeding with phaco after vitreous prolapse significantly worsens outcomes.

rows: During vitreous removal around IOL, insufficient support
Inflammation, vitreous traction on macula (Irvine-Gass syndrome)
Delayed traction, missed tear, insufficient vitrectomy
Vitreous incarceration in wound, chronic leak/inflammation

sections.title: 12. Postoperative Management
content: **Topical Steroids**: Potent corticosteroids (e.g., Pred Forte 1% qid-qid x 4 weeks, then taper) to mitigate inflammation and reduce CME risk.
**Topical NSAIDs**: (e.g., Bromday qd, Ilevro qd) significantly reduce post-operative inflammation and CME incidence. Continue for 3-6 months.
**Topical Antibiotics**: (e.g., Moxifloxacin qid x 1 week) for infection prophylaxis as per standard cataract surgery protocols.
**Cycloplegics**: (e.g., Cyclopentolate 1% bid-tid) indicated if significant inflammation, pain, or ciliary spasm is present.
**IOP Monitoring**: Close monitoring for early post-operative IOP spikes (e.g., from retained viscoelastic) or hypotony (e.g., wound leak).
**Fundus Examination**: Dilated fundus exam at 1-2 weeks, then periodically, to screen for delayed retinal tears or detachment, especially in high-risk patients.
**OCT Imaging**: If vision remains poor, consider OCT of the macula to diagnose and monitor CME.

sections.title: 13. RED FLAGS: Post-Op Emergency Signs
content: **Sudden, severe decrease in vision**
**Intense, unremitting eye pain (unresponsive to analgesics)**
**Marked photophobia or severe headache**
**Progressive redness with ocular discharge (suggestive of endophthalmitis)**
**New onset of floaters or flashes of light (potential retinal tear/detachment)**
**Persistent pupillary distortion or peaking**
**Signs of hypotony (e.g., very low IOP, choroidal folds on examination)**

content.explanation:
**V**iscoelastic (Dispersive)
**I**nfusion (BSS via side port)
**T**riamcinolone (for visualization)
**R**emove vitreous (high cut, low vacuum)
**E**levate IOP (transiently to sweep wounds)
**O**cular integrity (check wounds, IOL position)
**U**se acetylcholine (Miochol-E for pupil)
**S**weep wounds (with spatula/repositor)

sections.title: 15. Special Considerations: Pediatric Cases
sections.content: Anterior vitrectomy in pediatric patients (e.g., for congenital cataracts, Persistent Fetal Vasculature, aphakic glaucoma) presents unique challenges. Eyes are smaller, sclera is more elastic, and the vitreous is often more formed and adherent. Combined primary posterior capsulotomy and anterior vitrectomy are common during congenital cataract surgery to prevent posterior capsular opacification. A pars plana approach is often favored by pediatric ophthalmologists or vitreoretinal surgeons due to better control and reduced risk of peripheral retinal traction in these delicate eyes. Decisions regarding primary IOL implantation vs. aphakia are complex and age-dependent.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Future Directions
content: **Smaller Gauge Systems**: Evolution to 25G and 27G vitrectomy for anterior segment surgeons, allowing for smaller incisions, faster healing, and improved ergonomics.
**Ultra-High Cut Rates**: Vitrectors now operate at 10,000+ cpm, further minimizing vitreous traction and enhancing safety, particularly near the retina.
**Integrated Surgical Platforms**: Advanced fluidics, intelligent pressure control, and 3D heads-up display visualization systems are improving precision and safety.

**Pharmacologic Vitreolysis**: Ongoing research into agents that can chemically detach or liquefy vitreous, potentially offering non-surgical alternatives for conditions like vitreomacular traction or some vitreous opacities.

sections.title: 17. Differential Diagnosis: Post-Op Pain/Redness after AV

rows: Severe pain, marked vision loss, hypopyon, vitritis, poor red reflex. Rapid onset (1-7 days).
Sterile inflammation, severe corneal edema (limbus-to-limbus), fibrinous reaction. Onset 12-48 hrs. Minimal pain usually.
Inflammation, elevated IOP, visible fragments (may be difficult).
Chronic inflammation, hypotony, visible vitreous strand to wound, irregular pupil.
Surgical excision of vitreous to wound, wound repair
Pain, headache, nausea, corneal edema, firm globe. No significant inflammation or discharge.
Mild pain/irritation, expected AC reaction, responsive to standard steroids.

sections.title: 18. Prognosis & Key Clinical Pearls for Practice
content: **Prognosis**: Generally good, especially when performed for acute vitreous prolapse during cataract surgery. Visual outcome largely depends on the underlying cause and prompt, thorough intervention. Risk of CME is significant but often manageable.
**Prevention > Cure**: Meticulous surgical technique during cataract surgery minimizes PCR and subsequent vitreous prolapse.
**Don't Fear the Stain**: Always use dilute Triamcinolone Acetonide to visualize vitreous – it dramatically improves safety and completeness of removal.
**High Cut, Low Vac - The Mantra**: This fluidics setting minimizes vitreous traction, crucial for preventing iatrogenic retinal tears.
**Verify Vitreous-Free AC**: Utilize both intracameral acetylcholine (Miochol-E) to round the pupil and a cellulose sponge test on wounds to confirm no residual vitreous.
**Strategic IOL Placement**: If posterior capsular support is compromised, prioritize sulcus or anterior chamber IOL placement over in-the-bag to avoid complications.
**Aggressive Post-Op Anti-Inflammatories**: Prophylactic topical steroids and NSAIDs are critical to reduce the risk and severity of post-operative Cystoid Macular Edema (Irvine-Gass syndrome).
**Vitreous in the AC is NEVER Benign**: Always remove it completely to prevent long-term complications like CME, chronic inflammation, and glaucoma.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: A congenital cataract is any opacity of the crystalline lens that is present at birth or develops shortly thereafter. It is a significant cause of visual impairment and treatable blindness in children, requiring prompt diagnosis and management to prevent severe amblyopia. The visual outcome critically depends on the size, density, location of the opacity, laterality, and the timing of surgical intervention.

sections.title: Epidemiology: Key Data
content: **Incidence:** Approximately 1-6 per 10,000 live births globally.
**Laterality:** Bilateral (approx. 60-70%) vs. Unilateral (approx. 30-40%). Bilateral cases are more often associated with systemic or genetic conditions.
**Etiology:** About 50-60% are idiopathic, 25-33% genetic, 10-15% metabolic/syndromic, <5% infectious.
**Risk Factors:** Prematurity, low birth weight, maternal infections during pregnancy (e.g., Rubella), maternal drug exposure, family history of congenital cataract.

branches.label: Genetic (25-33%)
sub_branches: Gene mutations: Crystallins (CRYAA, CRYBB1, CRYGC, CRYGD), Connexins (GJA8, GJA3), Lens-specific transcription factors (MAFA, PAX6), Aquaporins (AQP0)

branches.label: Infectious (TORCH <5%)
sub_branches: Rubella (classic triad: cataract, heart defects, sensorineural hearing loss)

branches.label: Idiopathic (50-60%)
sub_branches: No identifiable cause after thorough workup

branches.label: Other/Drug-induced
sub_branches: Maternal drug use (e.g., corticosteroids - rare for congenital)

sections.title: Pathophysiology: Mechanism of Opacification
sections.content: The lens is primarily composed of water and crystallin proteins. Any disruption to the precise organization of lens fibers or the delicate balance of lens protein solubility can lead to opacity. Genetic mutations often affect crystallin proteins, gap junction proteins (connexins), or lens structural proteins, leading to protein aggregation. Metabolic disorders can cause accumulation of toxic byproducts (e.g., galactitol in galactosemia), leading to osmotic changes and fiber swelling. Infectious agents can directly damage lens cells or disrupt developmental processes.

rows: Opacity affecting specific lamellae or layers, sparing the nucleus and cortex.
Often genetic or metabolic (e.g., hypocalcemia). Most common morphology.
Opacity confined to the embryonic or fetal nucleus.
Small, non-progressive, central anterior capsular/subcapsular opacity.
Often sporadic, can be associated with anterior segment dysgenesis.
Opacity at the posterior pole, often pyramidal, associated with posterior lenticonus/lentiglobus.
Often genetic (e.g., PITX3 mutations), can be familial.
Multiple small, bluish opacities in the peripheral cortex, non-progressive.
Opacity along the Y-sutures of the fetal nucleus.
Club-shaped opacities in the deep cortex, typically adolescent onset but can be congenital.
Entire lens is opaque; often shrunken, fibrotic with calcification.
Severe cases, often secondary to intrauterine inflammation, trauma, or severe metabolic insult. Requires lensectomy.
Fine, dusty opacities, usually within a lamellar or nuclear pattern.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Leukocoria (White Pupillary Reflex):** The most common and critical presenting sign. May be subtle or dense.
**Nystagmus:** Rhythmic, involuntary eye movements. Typically develops if the cataract is bilateral, dense, and prolonged, indicating severe visual deprivation.
**Strabismus:** Misalignment of the eyes, often exotropia in unilateral cases due to poor vision in the affected eye.
**Poor Visual Tracking/Fixation:** Infants may not make eye contact or follow objects.
**Photophobia:** Less common, but can occur.
**Microphthalmia:** Associated with some etiologies (e.g., persistent fetal vasculature, congenital rubella).
**Failure to Thrive/Systemic Signs:** Suggestive of underlying metabolic or syndromic conditions (e.g., poor feeding, vomiting in galactosemia; developmental delay).

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Step 1: Red Reflex Test (Bruckner Test):** Crucial screening. Absent, dim, asymmetric, or distorted red reflex indicates an abnormality and requires urgent referral. Performed with a direct ophthalmoscope at arm's length (about 1 meter).

**Step 2: Slit-Lamp Biomicroscopy (or handheld slit-lamp/portable microscope):** Detailed assessment of cataract morphology (size, density, location, laterality) and other anterior segment anomalies (e.g., microcornea, Peters anomaly, persistent pupillary membrane).

**Step 3: Fundoscopy (Dilated):** If the lens opacity allows, examine the optic nerve, macula, and peripheral retina for associated anomalies (e.g., Persistent Fetal Vasculature (PFV), coloboma, retinochoroiditis from TORCH infections, retinal detachment).

**Step 4: B-scan Ultrasonography:** Mandatory if the cataract is too dense to allow a view of the fundus. Rules out posterior segment pathology such as PFV, retinal detachment, or intraocular tumors (e.g., retinoblastoma).
**Step 5: Gonioscopy:** In selected cases (e.g., suspicion of glaucoma, anterior segment dysgenesis), to evaluate the angle structure.
**Step 6: Keratometry/Biometry:** For IOL power calculation if surgery is planned. Requires specialized pediatric biometers (e.g., IOLMaster, Lenstar) due to smaller eye size.

rows: Detailed prenatal, birth, and family history; complete systemic exam.
Maternal infections, drug use, consanguinity, developmental milestones, syndromic features.
Urine for reducing substances, blood tests.
Urgent screen for Galactosemia (GALT enzyme levels, erythrocyte G-1-PUT activity); blood glucose, calcium, phosphorus, amino acid chromatography.
TORCH panel: Toxoplasma IgG/IgM, Rubella IgG/IgM, CMV IgG/IgM, HSV IgG/IgM, VDRL/RPR for Syphilis.
Genetic Workup (Bilateral cases, Unilateral with other anomalies)
Karyotyping, specific gene panels, whole exome sequencing (WES).
Karyotype for chromosomal anomalies (e.g., Trisomy 21); panel for known cataract genes (CRYAA, GJA8); WES for idiopathic cases.
CT/MRI if neurological signs or suspicion of intracranial abnormality (e.g., TORCH, Lowe syndrome). Skeletal survey for syndromes (e.g., Conradi-Hünermann).
ERG if retinal disease is suspected (e.g., Norrie disease); VEP for objective assessment of visual pathway function, especially in pre-verbal children.

sub_branches: Persistent Fetal Vasculature (PFV)/Persistent Hyperplastic Primary Vitreous (PHPV)

branches.label: Corneal Opacities

sections.title: 9. Staging / Grading
sections.content: Unlike adult cataracts, a formal staging system like LOCS III or ETDRS isn't used for congenital cataracts. Severity is assessed based on amblyogenic potential, which considers: **1. Size:** Opacity >3mm in diameter affecting the visual axis. **2. Density:** Degree of opacity affecting light transmission. **3. Location:** Central opacities are more amblyogenic. **4. Laterality:** Unilateral cataracts carry a higher risk of severe amblyopia due to interocular competition. **5. Associated Ocular Anomalies:** Presence of microphthalmia, nystagmus, strabismus, or retinal disease.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Algorithm
content: **Step 1: Urgent Diagnosis & Etiology Workup:** Confirm cataract, rule out retinoblastoma, identify underlying systemic causes (see Section 7).
**Step 2: Surgical Decision & Timing:** Critical for visual outcome.
- **Unilateral Dense Cataract:** Surgery ideally by 4-6 weeks of age (absolute maximum 8 weeks).
- **Bilateral Dense Cataracts:** Surgery ideally by 8-10 weeks of age (absolute maximum 12 weeks), often staggered 1-2 weeks apart.

- **Partial/Small Cataracts:** Monitor visual acuity and amblyogenic potential. May require optical correction (cycloplegic refraction) or trial of penalization (e.g., atropine). Surgery if progressive or amblyogenic.
**Step 3: Surgical Intervention (Lensectomy/Aspiration):** Clear the visual axis.

- **Primary Posterior Capsulotomy (PPC) with Anterior Vitrectomy (AV):** Recommended for all infants <1 year to prevent posterior capsular opacification (PCO), which rapidly forms and is highly amblyogenic.
- **Intraocular Lens (IOL) Implantation:**
- **Infants <1 year:** Generally left aphakic; high risk of complications (glaucoma, IOL power errors) with primary IOL.
- **Children 1-2 years:** Primary IOL considered, but with careful power calculation and awareness of hyperopic shift with growth.
- **Children >2 years:** Primary IOL implantation is the standard approach.
**Step 4: Post-operative Refractive Management:** Essential for visual rehabilitation.
- **Aphakic:** Aphakic spectacles (high plus lenses + add for near) or contact lenses (RGPs, extended wear soft lenses) immediately post-op.
- **Pseudophakic:** Spectacles for residual refractive error and often an add for near (monofocal IOLs).
**Step 5: Amblyopia Management:** Lifelong commitment.
- **Occlusion Therapy (Patching):** Crucial, especially for unilateral cases. Patching schedule individualized based on age, compliance, and visual acuity.
- **Atropine Penalization:** Alternative for milder amblyopia or when patching compliance is an issue.
**Step 6: Long-term Follow-up:** Regular monitoring for complications (especially glaucoma) and refractive changes. Typically until early adulthood.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Lensectomy
content: **Anesthesia:** General anesthesia is mandatory. Often includes laryngeal mask airway (LMA) or endotracheal tube (ETT), regional block (peribulbar/retrobulbar) for post-op analgesia.

**Approach:** Limbal incision (anterior approach) or Pars Plana incision (posterior approach, especially for rigid lenses or cases with PFV). Limbal for simple aspiration, pars plana for vitrectomy-assisted lensectomy.
**Incisions:** 1-2 limbal paracenteses (e.g., 20-25G) for infusion/instrumentation. Main incision (e.g., 1.8-2.5mm clear corneal or scleral tunnel).
**Viscoelastics:** Ophthalmic Viscosurgical Devices (OVDs) like Healon (sodium hyaluronate) or OcuCoat (hydroxypropyl methylcellulose) to maintain anterior chamber depth and protect endothelium.
**Anterior Capsulotomy:** Manual continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis (CCC) is preferred, but vitrector-assisted capsulotomy can be used. Size typically 4.5-5.0mm.

**Lens Aspiration:** Using an automated irrigation/aspiration (I/A) handpiece with a vitrector (e.g., 23/25G high-speed vitrector via pars plana, or 20G/I/A via limbal) to emulsify and aspirate the soft lens material. High cut rates, low aspiration.
**Primary Posterior Capsulotomy (PPC):** Essential in infants <1 year. Performed through the anterior approach with a vitrector or via a small posterior CCC with micro-forceps.

**Anterior Vitrectomy (AV):** Following PPC, a limited anterior vitrectomy (1-2mm behind the capsule) is performed to remove the anterior vitreous face, preventing re-opacification and vitreous prolapse. Use high cut rates and low aspiration.

**IOL Implantation (if indicated):** Foldable IOLs (e.g., AcrySof IQ SN6WF, Tecnis ZCB00) are inserted via the main incision. Power calculation is challenging due to rapid eye growth (target slight hyperopia, e.g., +2.0 to +3.0 D for young children to compensate for growth).
**Wound Closure:** Hydration, suture (e.g., 10-0 Nylon) for limbal/corneal incisions to ensure watertight closure. Subconjunctival steroid/antibiotic injection.
**Post-op Medications:** Topical antibiotics (e.g., Moxifloxacin) and steroids (e.g., Prednisolone acetate 1%) for several weeks, cycloplegics (e.g., Atropine 1%).

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Amblyopia:** The most common and devastating complication, even with timely surgery. Requires aggressive and prolonged amblyopia treatment.
**Aphakic / Pseudophakic Glaucoma:** Major late complication. Incidence up to 20-30% in aphakic children. Can develop years after surgery. Requires lifelong monitoring (IOP, optic nerve).

**Posterior Capsular Opacification (PCO):** Very common without PPC/AV, especially in infants. If present, requires Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy (older children) or surgical capsulotomy (younger children).
**Retinal Detachment:** Increased risk in aphakic eyes, particularly with pars plana lensectomy or aggressive vitrectomy.
**IOL Decentration/Dislocation:** Can occur due to poor capsular support or inadequate fixation.
**Chronic Inflammation:** Particularly in cases with underlying inflammation (e.g., juvenile idiopathic arthritis, some infectious etiologies).
**Refractive Errors:** Significant hyperopia in aphakic eyes, often requiring complex contact lens fitting. Pseudophakic eyes can have refractive surprises and require spectacle correction.
**Strabismus & Nystagmus:** May persist despite excellent surgical and amblyopia management.

**Prognosis:** Highly variable. Unilateral cataracts generally have worse visual outcomes than bilateral. Early intervention, consistent amblyopia management, and meticulous follow-up are key. Even with optimal management, visual acuity is often lower than in eyes without congenital cataract.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **LEUKOCORIA (White Pupillary Reflex):** ALWAYS requires urgent ophthalmologic evaluation to rule out life-threatening conditions like retinoblastoma or severe amblyogenic conditions like dense cataract.
**Nystagmus:** Indicates chronic, severe visual deprivation. Sign of poor prognosis for visual rehabilitation and requires immediate intervention.
**Microphthalmia:** Suggests complex ocular or systemic anomalies, higher risk of complications.
**Systemic Signs (e.g., poor feeding, lethargy, developmental delay):** Point to underlying metabolic or syndromic etiology, requiring multidisciplinary approach.
**Acute Red Eye/Pain/Photophobia post-op:** Signs of endophthalmitis or severe inflammation, requiring immediate re-evaluation.

content.explanation:
**T** - Toxoplasmosis
**O** - Other (Syphilis, Varicella-zoster, HIV)
**R** - Rubella
**C** - Cytomegalovirus
**H** - Herpes Simplex Virus

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Time is Vision:** The amblyogenic period in infants is very short. Delay in surgery (especially for unilateral dense cataracts) leads to irreversible vision loss.
**Rule Out Retinoblastoma:** Leukocoria is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise. Urgent workup is critical.
**Aphakic Glaucoma is a Silent Thief:** High incidence, often late onset. Requires meticulous, lifelong monitoring of IOP and optic nerve status.
**Amblyopia Therapy is NOT an Option, It's Part of the Surgery:** Without rigorous post-operative patching/penalization, surgical success is meaningless.
**Primary PPC/AV in Infants:** Mandatory for prevention of aggressive PCO in infants <1 year.
**Systemic Workup for All Bilateral Cases:** Often reveals underlying genetic or metabolic conditions.
**Pediatric IOL Power Calculation:** Challenges due to eye growth. Target slight post-op hyperopia to compensate for myopic shift.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Infant Aphakia Treatment Study (IATS):** Multicenter, randomized trial comparing primary IOL vs. aphakic contact lens in infants (<7 months) with unilateral congenital cataract. At 10 years, no significant difference in visual acuity, but IOL group had more adverse events and reoperations (especially glaucoma). Supports aphakia management for very young infants.
**Genetic Discoveries:** Ongoing identification of new genes and mutations responsible for congenital cataracts, offering potential for future gene-based therapies or improved prognostication.

**IOL Technology:** Development of smaller, more biocompatible IOLs. Research into extended depth of focus (EDOF) IOLs and accommodating IOLs for pediatric use to reduce spectacle dependence, though challenges remain.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Anesthesia:** Requires specialized pediatric anesthesiology; considerations for airway, fluid management, thermoregulation.

**IOL Power Calculation:** More complex due to rapid axial length growth and unpredictable refractive development. Target hyperopia (+2 to +3 D) to become emmetropic in early childhood. Newer formulas (e.g., Baylor Nomogram, specific pediatric IOL formulae) aim to improve accuracy.
**Compliance:** Significant challenge for parents and children with post-operative regimen (contact lenses, patching). Requires robust education and support.
**Glaucoma:** Higher incidence and often more refractory to treatment. Regular IOP checks (often under sedation/anesthesia) and optic nerve evaluations are critical.
**Associated Systemic Anomalies:** Many children with congenital cataracts have other medical conditions requiring multidisciplinary care (pediatrician, geneticist, neurologist).
**Risk of Retinal Detachment:** Increased, requiring careful intraoperative technique and long-term monitoring.

title: Dragged Disc: Macular Heterotopia & Vitreoretinal Traction
summary: The 'dragged disc' appearance is a classic clinical sign of chronic peripheral vitreoretinal traction, characterized by the temporal displacement of the optic nerve head's vascular arcades and the macula. It is most commonly associated with Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP), FEVR, and Ocular Toxocariasis.

sections.title: Clinical Definition
sections.content: A 'dragged disc' refers to the physical displacement of the optic disc's vascular exit points and the macula (macular heterotopia) due to centripetal traction from peripheral fibrovascular membranes. This typically results in temporal straightening of the retinal vessels and an abnormally large positive Angle Kappa.

sections.title: Common Clinical Features
content: Pseudo-exotropia: Large positive Angle Kappa due to temporal macular displacement.
Temporal straightening of the superior and inferior vascular arcades.
Ectopic Macula: Often displaced temporally and sometimes superiorly.
Peripheral 'Shagreen' or white-without-pressure in ROP/FEVR.
Stretched retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) on the nasal side.
Falciform retinal folds: Often extending from the disc to the peripheral mass.

rows: Prematurity history, peripheral avascular zone, ridge.
Peripheral granuloma with tractional band to disc.
X-linked dominant (IKBKG gene), lethal in males.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Sudden decrease in vision (Threatens macular detachment or vitreous hemorrhage).
New onset of Leukocoria (White pupillary reflex).
Presence of 'Plus Disease' (Dilated/tortuous vessels) in ROP cases.
Progression of falciform folds toward the foveal center.
Total Rhegmatogenous or Tractional Retinal Detachment (Stage 4/5 ROP/FEVR).

content.explanation: FEVR, Eales disease, Toxocariasis, Coats disease, Hemoglobinopathies (Sickle Cell), Congenital Retinoschisis, Angiomatosis Retinae, K (Incontinentia Pigmenti), ET (ROP).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: Wide-field Fundus Photography (RetCam or Optos) to document the extent of dragging.
Step 2: Fluorescein Angiography (FA) - Look for peripheral non-perfusion and 'pruning' of vessels.
Step 3: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) - Assess macular anatomy, dragging, and foveal schisis.
Step 4: B-Scan Ultrasonography - Rule out total RD or mass lesions (Retinoblastoma) in hazy media.
Step 5: Genetic Testing - Crucial for FEVR (LRP5/FZD4) and IP (IKBKG).

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Laser Photocoagulation: Ablation of the peripheral avascular zone to reduce VEGF production.
Anti-VEGF Injections: Intravitreal Ranibizumab/Aflibercept/Bevacizumab as an adjunct or primary in ROP.
Scleral Buckling: To relieve circumferential traction in certain detachment patterns.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): Required for Stage 4/5 ROP or FEVR to peel membranes and flatten the retina.
Amblyopia Management: Aggressive patching/glasses for the pseudo-strabismus and visual deprivation.

sections.title: Surgical Technique: PPV for Dragged Disc
content: 1. Lens-sparing Vitrectomy (LSV) if possible in pediatric patients.
2. Induction of Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD) using Triescence.
3. Segmentation and Delamination of fibrovascular membranes.
4. Relieving 'Bridge Traction' between the disc and the periphery.
5. Endolaser to the ischemic peripheral retina.
6. Air/Gas/Oil Tamponade depending on retinal stability.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: Angle Kappa Pearl: The light reflex is nasal, giving an appearance of exotropia (pseudo-XT), because the fovea is pulled temporally.
Asymmetry: FEVR is often highly asymmetric; always check the 'normal' eye with FA for peripheral non-perfusion.
The 'Drag' Force: Traction is usually in the direction of the greatest peripheral ischemia.
The 'Macular Displacement' distance: In severe ROP survivors, the fovea can be dragged more than 2 disc diameters temporally.
Post-Surgical Prognosis: Visual recovery is often limited by structural foveal changes and amblyopia.

rows: Anterior displacement of the lens-iris diaphragm (ROP).
End-stage hypotony from ciliary body detachment.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Artificial Intelligence (AI): Deep learning models (e.g., i-ROP) to quantify vascular tortuosity and disc dragging.
Handheld OCT: Allowing high-resolution imaging of the infant fovea in the NICU or OR.
Anti-VEGF vs. Laser: The RAINBOW and BEAT-ROP studies provide evidence for anti-VEGF efficacy in Zone 1 disease.
Gene Therapy: Emerging research for FEVR to restore the Norrin/Wnt signaling pathway.

This comprehensive guide, structured around the 'STUMPED' mnemonic, provides an in-depth look into the etiology, diagnosis, and treatment of this complex ophthalmic presentation.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Bilateral corneal haze in an infant refers to any opacification or cloudiness affecting both corneas, present at birth or developing shortly thereafter. This condition is an ophthalmic emergency due to the critical period of visual development in infants. Any significant obstruction of the visual axis can lead to severe and irreversible amblyopia (lazy eye), making early diagnosis and prompt management paramount. The appearance can range from subtle stromal edema to dense, porcelain-white opacification, necessitating a systematic diagnostic approach to determine the underlying etiology.

content.explanation: A powerful mnemonic to systematically consider the broad differential diagnosis for bilateral corneal haze in infants, ensuring no critical etiology is missed. This framework guides the clinical workup, directing investigations and management strategies.

sections.title: 3. S - Sclerocornea
content: **Definition:** Congenital malformation where the cornea is opaque and vascularized, resembling sclera. Often associated with other anterior segment dysgenesis.
**Etiology:** Non-hereditary or AD/AR inheritance, associated with chromosomal anomalies (e.g., Trisomy 18, 13). Disruption of neural crest cell migration.
**Features:** Flat cornea, indistinguishable from sclera, obscure limbus. Often microphthalmic, can be associated with coloboma, aniridia, cataract, glaucoma.
**Prognosis:** Severely limited visual potential, PKP is technically challenging with poor visual outcomes.

sections.title: 4. T - Trauma / Tears in Descemet's
content: **Definition:** Corneal edema due to breaks in Descemet's membrane.

**Etiology:** *Birth Trauma:* Forceps delivery (usually unilateral, central/paracentral, vertical/oblique tears). *Congenital Glaucoma:* Elevated IOP causes circumferential, horizontal tears (Haab's striae).
**Features:** Localized or diffuse corneal haze (edema), photophobia, epiphora. Haab's striae appear as fine, curvilinear refractile lines.
**Management:** Birth trauma: usually clears spontaneously over weeks/months. Glaucoma: IOP control (medical/surgical) is paramount. Amblyopia management is crucial.

sections.title: 5. U - Ulcers / Infections
content: **Definition:** Corneal inflammation and opacification due to infectious agents.

**Etiology:** *Congenital Rubella Syndrome:* Salt-and-pepper retinopathy, microphthalmia, cataract, glaucoma, corneal haze. *Congenital Syphilis:* Interstitial keratitis (IK), often bilateral, presents later (2-3 months). *HSV/CMV:* Usually unilateral, can be bilateral. *Bacterial/Fungal:* Rare congenitally, more likely postnatal from conjunctivitis or exposure.
**Features:** Keratouveitis, stromal edema, vascularization, scarring. Often associated with systemic signs of infection.

**Management:** Specific antimicrobial therapy (e.g., penicillin for syphilis, antivirals for HSV), corticosteroids for non-infectious inflammation (e.g., old IK). Requires aggressive amblyopia treatment.

sections.title: 6. M - Metabolic / Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS)
content: **Definition:** Corneal stromal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) due to lysosomal enzyme deficiencies.
**Etiology:** Inherited (AR/XR) lysosomal storage disorders. E.g., MPS I (Hurler, Hurler-Scheie, Scheie), MPS IV (Morquio), MPS VI (Maroteaux-Lamy).

**Features:** Diffuse, finely punctate, grayish-white stromal haze. Often progressive. Associated systemic features: coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal dysplasia, cardiac defects, developmental delay.
**Diagnosis:** Urine GAGs analysis, specific enzyme assays, genetic testing.
**Management:** Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT). PKP for visual rehabilitation, but recurrence in graft possible.

sections.title: 7. P - Peter's Anomaly / Posterior Polymorphous Dystrophy (PPMD)
content: **Peter's Anomaly:** *Definition:* Central corneal opacification with iridocorneal or lenticulocorneal adhesions. Usually unilateral, but can be bilateral (10-20%). *Etiology:* Developmental failure of anterior chamber cleavage. Associated with glaucoma in 50-70%. *Features:* Central leukoma, iris strands to leukoma, lens adhesion/cataract. *Management:* PKP for visual axis clearance, glaucoma surgery.

**Posterior Polymorphous Dystrophy (PPMD):** *Definition:* Disorder of endothelial and Descemet's membrane, often AD. Can present congenitally with corneal edema. *Etiology:* COL8A2, ZEB1, VSX1 genes. *Features:* Vesicles, bands, geographic lesions on posterior cornea, often leading to corneal edema and glaucoma. *Management:* Hypertonic saline, PKP/DMEK if severe edema.

sections.title: 8. E - Endothelial Dystrophies (CHED)
content: **Definition:** Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED) is a rare disorder causing bilateral corneal edema and opacification due to primary endothelial dysfunction.

**Etiology:** Two main types: CHED1 (Autosomal Dominant, onset later, milder phenotype) and CHED2 (Autosomal Recessive, congenital onset, more severe). Both associated with mutations in the *SLC4A11* gene.

**Features:** Diffuse, ground-glass corneal haze, significant corneal thickening (pachymetry >1000 µm), usually no photophobia/epiphora unless severe edema. No Haab's striae, normal IOP. Nystagmus due to poor vision.
**Management:** Corneal transplantation (PKP for young infants, DSEK/DMEK in older, cooperative children). Early intervention is crucial to prevent profound amblyopia. Genetic counseling.

sections.title: 9. D - Dysgenesis / Glaucoma
content: **Primary Congenital Glaucoma (PCG):** *Definition:* Developmental anomaly of the anterior chamber angle leading to elevated IOP, buphthalmos, corneal edema, and optic neuropathy. *Etiology:* Often sporadic, some familial cases (AR, CYP1B1 gene). *Features:* The classic triad: epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm. Buphthalmos (corneal diameter >12mm in first year), corneal haze (epithelial/stromal edema), Haab's striae, deep anterior chamber, optic disc cupping. *Management:* Surgical (goniotomy, trabeculotomy, trabeculectomy). Medical (beta-blockers, topical/oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) as adjuncts or temporizing measures. **URGENT SURGERY.**

**Iridocorneal Dysgenesis (Axenfeld-Rieger Anomaly):** *Definition:* Developmental abnormalities of the iris and anterior chamber angle, often associated with glaucoma. *Features:* Posterior embryotoxon (prominent Schwalbe's line), iris stromal hypoplasia, corectopia, polycoria. Corneal haze is usually mild, typically due to associated glaucoma rather than primary corneal pathology. *Management:* Glaucoma management (medical/surgical).

content.description: Relative Incidence of Key Causes (Approximation: 1 unit represents 1:10,000 live births for PCG, others are rarer. Precise comparative data for 'bilateral corneal haze' overall is scarce. PCG is the most common *treatable* cause of congenital corneal opacity requiring urgent surgical intervention, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 10,000 to 18,000 live births globally. CHED2 is much rarer, estimated at 1:25,000 to 1:100,000 live births.

sections.title: 11. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Cloudy Corneas:** Bilateral, diffuse or focal, present at birth or noted shortly after.
**Photophobia:** Sensitivity to light (common in glaucoma, less so in CHED).
**Epiphora:** Excessive tearing (prominent in glaucoma).
**Blepharospasm:** Eyelid squeezing (classic for glaucoma).
**Buphthalmos:** Enlarged globe and corneal diameter (>12mm in infancy, >11mm at birth). Pathognomonic for congenital glaucoma.
**Nystagmus:** Often develops due to poor visual input, indicative of significant visual deprivation.
**Lack of Fixation/Following:** Poor visual behaviors.
**Systemic Signs:** Coarse facies, skeletal abnormalities, developmental delay, hepatosplenomegaly (MPS); rash, cardiac defects (Rubella); dysmorphic features (chromosomal anomalies).

Assesses glaucomatous damage and posterior segment causes. Obscured view necessitates B-scan ultrasound.

sections.title: 16. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Rapid Increase in Corneal Diameter (Buphthalmos):** Strongly indicative of congenital glaucoma and requires immediate intervention.
**Photophobia, Epiphora, Blepharospasm Triad:** Highly suggestive of congenital glaucoma.
**Increasing Density of Corneal Haze:** Worsening edema or scarring, threatening visual development.
**Associated Systemic Signs:** Suggests a syndromic or metabolic etiology requiring multidisciplinary management.
**Asymmetric Haze that is Rapidly Worsening:** Can be traumatic or infectious, requires prompt investigation.
**Infant with Nystagmus:** Indicates severe, chronic visual deprivation, emphasizing the urgency of diagnosis and treatment.

sections.title: 17. Management & Treatment Principles
content: **Early Diagnosis:** Paramount to prevent irreversible amblyopia.

**IOP Control:** Crucial for congenital glaucoma via surgical means (goniotomy, trabeculotomy). Medical therapy (timolol 0.25-0.5% q12h, dorzolamide 2% q8h) can be used as temporizing agents or adjuncts. Oral acetazolamide (5-10 mg/kg q6-8h) for short term.
**Visual Axis Clearance:** Surgical intervention (PKP, DSEK, DMEK, or cataract extraction) if corneal opacification or cataract is visually significant.
**Amblyopia Management:** Lifelong commitment essential, involving patching, spectacles, and close follow-up. Even with clear media, amblyopia can be profound due to early deprivation.
**Systemic Management:** For metabolic disorders (ERT, HSCT for MPS), infectious diseases (antimicrobials), or syndromic associations.
**Regular Follow-up:** Frequent monitoring of visual acuity, IOP, corneal status, and refraction is critical due to the dynamic nature of these conditions in infants.

sections.title: 18. Surgical Techniques for Corneal Haze
content: **Goniotomy (for PCG):** Incising the trabecular meshwork from within the anterior chamber. A goniolens is used to visualize the angle. Incisions are made circumferentially (e.g., 360-degree).

**Trabeculotomy (for PCG):** Creating an opening into Schlemm's canal and trabecular meshwork from external approach (ab externo) or internal approach (ab interno, e.g., Kahook Dual Blade). A trabeculotome is threaded into Schlemm's canal and rotated to break the trabecular meshwork.

**Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP):** Full-thickness corneal replacement. Indicated for dense, visually significant opacities (e.g., severe CHED2, Peter's Anomaly, Sclerocornea). Challenges include small eye size, anesthetic risk, high rates of graft rejection and glaucoma.

**Descemet's Stripping Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSEK) / Descemet's Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty (DMEK):** Endothelial cell transplantation. May be considered in older, cooperative children with endothelial dysfunction (e.g., CHED) once the globe has grown sufficiently, offering faster visual recovery and lower rejection rates compared to PKP.

**Lamellar Keratoplasty (ALK/DALK):** Partial thickness corneal replacement, preserving the host endothelium. Not typically used for primary endothelial diseases but can be considered for stromal opacities if the endothelium is healthy.

sections.title: 19. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Amblyopia:** The most common and severe long-term complication, even after successful surgical clearance of the visual axis. Requires aggressive and prolonged treatment.
**Glaucoma Progression/Recurrence:** Even after initial surgical success in PCG, recurrence is possible, requiring re-intervention.
**Corneal Graft Failure:** High rates in infants due to small eye size, inflammation, and rejection.
**Refractive Error:** High myopia and astigmatism are common, requiring optical correction.
**Systemic Progression:** For metabolic and syndromic conditions, the systemic disease may progress despite ocular treatment.

**Prognosis:** Highly variable depending on the underlying cause, severity, timing of intervention, and compliance with amblyopia treatment. Earlier intervention generally leads to better visual outcomes.

sections.title: 20. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **STUMPED** is your diagnostic roadmap for bilateral corneal haze in infants.
**EUA is indispensable:** Allows for accurate IOP measurement, detailed corneal assessment, and fundus examination.
**Think Glaucoma First:** Congenital Glaucoma is the most common treatable cause of congenital corneal opacity and requires urgent surgical intervention.
**Systemic Workup:** Don't miss the systemic associations; evaluate for metabolic, infectious, and syndromic conditions.
**Amblyopia is the ultimate enemy:** Even with perfect surgery, visual outcomes hinge on aggressive amblyopia management.
**Genetic counseling:** Offer to families for inherited conditions like CHED and some forms of PCG/MPS.

sections.title: 21. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Genetic Therapies:** Gene therapy (e.g., for certain forms of MPS, CHED) is an area of active research and early clinical trials, offering potential disease modification rather than just symptomatic treatment.
**Enhanced Corneal Transplant Techniques:** Refinements in DSEK/DMEK techniques are being explored for older children, potentially improving outcomes and reducing rejection compared to PKP.

**Improved Understanding of Amblyopia:** Advances in neuroplasticity research are exploring novel therapeutic approaches for amblyopia beyond traditional patching, including pharmaceutical interventions or perceptual learning strategies.

**Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT):** Increasingly used in pediatric ophthalmology for non-invasive, high-resolution imaging of the anterior segment, aiding in diagnosis of Peter's anomaly, iridocorneal dysgenesis, and monitoring corneal edema, often possible without sedation in cooperative infants.

**LiGHT trial (Laser in Glaucoma and Ocular Hypertension Treatment):** While for adults, the growing evidence for Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT) as primary therapy may influence future pediatric glaucoma management, although it's not yet standard for congenital glaucoma. Trabeculotomy/Goniotomy remain primary for PCG.

sections.title: 22. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Anesthetic Risk:** Infants, especially neonates, have higher anesthetic risks. A skilled pediatric anesthesiologist is crucial for EUA and surgery.
**Examination Challenges:** Limited cooperation necessitates EUA for detailed examination and accurate measurements (IOP, corneal diameter, fundus).
**Growth and Development:** Considerations for long-term prognosis, impact of systemic disease on overall development, and globe growth post-surgery.

**Amblyopia Sensitivity:** Infants have a highly plastic visual system but are extremely vulnerable to amblyopia. The younger the onset and longer the duration of visual deprivation, the worse the prognosis.
**Compliance:** Adherence to post-operative medications and amblyopia therapy (patching, glasses) can be challenging and requires strong parental involvement and support.
**Long-term Follow-up:** These children require lifelong follow-up for glaucoma, refractive error, amblyopia, and potential graft complications.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Primary Congenital Glaucoma (PCG) is defined as a form of developmental glaucoma characterized by an isolated developmental defect of the trabecular meshwork and anterior chamber angle (trabeculodysgenesis) that is not associated with other ocular or systemic anomalies. It results in obstructed aqueous outflow and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), leading to characteristic ocular stretching (buphthalmos) in the elastic infant eye.

rows: Flat or concave iris insertion; most common type.
Anterior iris stromal hypoplasia or structural iris defects.
Associations with Axenfeld-Rieger or Peters Anomaly (Secondary).

sections.title: The Pathognomonic Triad
content: 1. Epiphora (Excessive tearing)
2. Photophobia (Light sensitivity)
3. Blepharospasm (Involuntary eyelid squeezing)

sections.title: Clinical Signs & Ocular Exam
content: Buphthalmos: Corneal diameter >12mm in the first year.
Haab Striae: Horizontal or concentric ruptures in Descemet's membrane.
Corneal Edema: Ground-glass appearance from high IOP.
Optic Disc Cupping: Rapidly progressive but uniquely reversible if IOP is lowered.
Axial Length: Significant elongation measured by A-scan.

sections.title: EUA Protocol: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Immediate IOP measurement (Perkins or Tonopen) upon induction; avoid Halothane/Sevoflurane if possible as they lower IOP (Ketamine raises it).
Step 2: Measurement of Horizontal Corneal Diameter (White-to-White) using calipers.
Step 3: Gonioscopy using a Koeppe or Swan-Jacob lens to identify iris insertion level.
Step 4: Pachymetry to assess corneal thickness and edema state.
Step 5: Dilated Fundoscopy to assess C:D ratio and exclude retinal pathology.
Step 6: A-scan Ultrasonography for axial length measurement (tracking progression).

sections.title: Management & Surgical Algorithm
content: 1. Medical Temporization: Topical BB (caution with asthma) or CAI (Diamox 10-15 mg/kg/day).
2. Clear Cornea present? -> Perform Goniotomy (internal approach, 120-180 degrees).
3. Cloudy Cornea present? -> Perform Trabeculotomy (external approach with Harms trabeculotome).
4. Failure of Primary Surgery? -> Repeat Angle Surgery or 360-degree Trabeculotomy (illuminated microcatheter).
5. Refractory Cases? -> Mitomycin-C Trabeculectomy or Glaucoma Drainage Device (Ahmed/Baerveldt).
6. Last Resort? -> Diode Laser Cyclophotocoagulation.

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Sudden increase in corneal clouding (Acute Hydrops)
Rapidly increasing C:D ratio in an infant
Asymmetric corneal diameters (even 0.5mm)
Systemic BB side effects (Bradycardia, Apnea)
Loss of red reflex due to corneal opacity

content.explanation: DDx for Cloudy Cornea: Sclerocornea, Trauma, Ulcer, Metabolic (Mucopolysaccharidosis), Peters Anomaly, Edema (PCG), Dystrophy (CHED).

sections.title: Surgical Key Points
content: Goniotomy: Requires 100% visualization through a clear cornea.
Trabeculotomy: Gold standard when cornea is too cloudy to see angle.
Microcatheter-assisted 360-degree Trabeculotomy: Shows higher success rates than traditional methods.
Post-op Care: Prophylactic antibiotics and corticosteroids for 4 weeks.

sections.title: Complications & Long-term Prognosis
content: Amblyopia: Most common cause of vision loss (refractive/anisometropic).
High Myopia: Due to permanent axial elongation.
Lens Subluxation: In extreme cases of buphthalmos.
Lifelong Monitoring: 50% of successfully treated patients may require further surgery later in life.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Evidence
sections.content: Recent studies focus on 360-degree trabeculotomy using the iTrack microcatheter, which has demonstrated superior IOP lowering compared to standard 120-degree procedures. The BIG (British Infantile Glaucoma) study highlights that primary surgical intervention is significantly more effective than primary medical management. Genetic screening for CYP1B1 is now recommended for siblings in consanguineous families.

sections.title: Stroke: Definition & Clinical Manifestation
sections.content: Definition: ischemic infarction (or bleeding into) any part of the brain. It manifests by rapid onset (over minutes) of focal CNS signs and symptoms (contralateral hemiplegia & sensory loss + homonymous hemianopia).

branches: CNS bleed (hypertension, trauma and aneurysm rupture)

sections.title: Risk Factors
content: Hypertension
Hypercholesterolemia
Smoking
DM
Heart disease (AF, valvular, ischaemic)

sections.title: Immediate Management Protocol
content: 1. Call for help.
2. A → Adequate ventilation.
3. B → Oxygenation.
4. C → Circulation → IV line.
5. Document Level of consciousness.
6. Vital sign monitoring: For hypertension, admit and control over days not hours.
7. Admission to stroke units for nursing/physio (saves lives and provides motivation).

rows: Within a few days to differentiate hemorrhagic from ischemic if considering anticoagulation.
Meningism, severe headache, and coma within hours.
Carotid bruit, AF, and past TIA.

content.explanation: NB1. TIA: sudden onset of focal CNS signs (resolve within few minutes) due to temporary occlusion, usually by emboli, of part of cerebral circulation. NB2: carotid bruit may signify stenosis (>30%), often near internal carotid origin. Best heard behind the angle of the jaw.

sections.title: Comprehensive Investigations List
content: FBC
CXR
ECG
ESR
U&E
Lipids
Blood glucose
Clotting tests
Echo
Carotid doppler
Carotid angiography

sections.title: Stroke Treatment Strategy
content: Aspirin: 300mg/24h PO (unless strong suspicion of CNS bleeding).
Nil by mouth if swallowing is a problem.
Maintain hydration: Do not over-hydrate (cerebral edema).
Monitor and treat ↑ BP.
Immediate evacuation: Refer if cerebellar hemorrhage is possible.
Nursing care: Turn regularly and keep dry (consider catheterization) to stop bed sores.
DVT Prophylaxis: Passive limb movements, subcutaneous heparin, and compressing stockings.
Support: Emotional support and rehabilitation.

sections.title: Thrombolysis & Prevention
content: NB Thrombolysis: Alteplase within 3h of onset may decrease adverse outcomes (trials). Requires dedicated 24h CNS thrombolysis teams. Note: Not yet recommended in the UK in 2016.
Prevention 1: Control risk factors.
Prevention 2: Exercise (↑ HDL).
Prevention 3: Life long anticoagulants for rheumatic/prosthetic heart valves on left side.
Prevention 4: Aspirin 75 mg/day for life.

sections.title: Increased Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
content: Normal ICT: 0-10 mmHg.
Causes: Tumours (1ry or metastatic), Head injury, Brain haemorrhage (any type).
Causes: Infection (meningitis, encephalitis, brain abscess), Hydrocephalus, Cerebral oedema, Status epilepticus.

sections.title: Signs & Symptoms of ICP
content: Headache, vomiting ± nausea.
Deterioration of consciousness: drowsiness, irritability, seizures, coma.
Cushing’s response: ↓ pulse, ↑ BP & Cheyne-Stokes respiration.
Ophthalmic: ↓ VA & peripheral visual field loss.
Ophthalmic: Pupil changes (constriction 1st, later dilatation). DON’T DILATE.
Papilloedema: Loss of previous spontaneous venous pulsation. (If preserved, exclude papilloedema).

sections.title: ICP Management
content: 1. ABC (Intubate if needed).
2. Correct hypotension & treat seizures.
3. Brief history & examination.
4. Elevate head of bed 30º- 40º.
5. Mannitol 20%: 1-2g/kg IV over 10-20 min (5mL/kg). Clinical effect after 20 min, lasts 2-6h. Aim for serum osmolarity 300 mosmol/kg.
6. Dexamethasone: 10 mg IV then 4 mg/6h IV/PO (if cerebral oedema).
7. Fluid restriction to < 1.5L/d.
8. Close monitoring of ICP & vitals.
9. Search for cause & treat factors like hyperglycaemia, hyponatraemia.
10. Refer to neurosurgeon for definitive treatment.

sections.title: Hypoglycemia Treatment
content: Give 200–300 mL of 10% dextrose IV (20-30g).
OR Glucagon 1mg IM (if no IV access; will not work in drunk patients).
Once conscious: give sugary drinks & a meal.
Thiamine 1-2 mg/kg IV: if malnutrition or alcohol suspicion.
If oral hypoglycemic history: Admission for 10% glucose over 1-2 hours.

sections.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
sections.content: DKA coma only occurs in type I D.M (IDDM); it may be the mode of presentation. Diagnosis requires: hyperglycaemia + ketosis + metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.3).

sections.title: DKA: Signs & Precipitants
content: Signs: Gradual drowsiness, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, polydipsia, lethargy, anorexia, polyuria, ketotic breath, coma.
Precipitants: Infection, surgery, MI, chemotherapy, non-compliance, or wrong insulin dose.

sections.title: DKA Fluid Replacement Protocol
content: 1. IV 0.9% saline immediately (Dehydration correction is priority).
2. 1L stat.
3. 1L over next 1 hour.
4. 1L over next 2 hours.
5. 1L over next 4 hours.
6. 1L over next 6 hours.
7. Use Dextrose 5% when blood glucose is < 10 mmol/L.
8. Caution in elderly/heart failure; monitor CVP.

sections.title: DKA Insulin & Potassium Management
content: Insulin Pump: 50U soluble insulin in 50ml saline (1U/ml). Give 4-8 U/h if glucose > 20mmol/L. Aim for fall of 5 mmol/L per h.
If No Pump: Load 20U IM, then 4-6 U/h IM while glucose > 10mmol/L.
K+ Replacement: Add 20-40mmol/L to IV fluid (Normal K+: 3.5-5).
K+ Shifting: Serum K+ is high in DKA due to lack of insulin, but total body K+ is low. Insulin shifts K+ into cells; must monitor to prevent hypokalaemia/arrhythmias.
K+ Timing: Don't add to 1st bag. Start when urine flow > 30ml/h.

rows: Longer history (1 wk), glucose > 35 mmol/L, marked dehydration.
Focal CNS signs, DIC, DVT (fully heparinize).
Rehydration with 0.9% saline (1/2 DKA rate) over 48h. Heparinize.

sections.title: Hyperthyroid Crisis (Thyrotoxic Storm)
content: Signs: Hyperpyrexia (>41°C), Tachycardia (>140bpm), AF, CHF, Diarrhea, Vomiting, Agitation, Coma.
Precipitated by: Infection, trauma, MI, stroke, stopping antithyroid meds, surgery, radioiodine.
Propranolol: 40 mg/8h PO or 1 mg IV over 1min (unless asthma/heart failure).
Carbimazole: 15-25 mg/6h PO; followed by Lugol’s solution 0.3 mL/8h after 4h.
Hydrocortisone: 100 mg/6h IV or Dexamethasone 4 mg/6h PO (blocks T4 to T3 conversion).
Aspirin Warning: Avoid Aspirin as it can ↑ T4.

sections.title: Myxoedema Coma
content: Signs: Hypothyroid, >65yrs, hypothermia, hyporeflexia, ↓ glucose, bradycardia, goitre, cyanosis.
Management: High flow O2, Correct hypoglycaemia.
T3: 5-20 ug/12h IV slowly (Caution: may precipitate ischaemia).
Hydrocortisone: 100 mg/8h IV if pituitary cause suspected.
Avoid precipitating LVF with saline.

sections.title: Addisonian & Hypopituitary Crisis
content: Addisonian: Endocrinal shock, hypoglycemia. Treat with Hydrocortisone 100mg/6h IV and IV fluids.
Hypopituitary: Refractory hypotension, short stature, loss of axillary/pubic hair, hypoglycaemia.
Hypopituitary Management: Hydrocortisone IV first, then Liothyronine (T3) 10 ug/12h PO. Surgery if pituitary apoplexy.

sections.title: Pheochromocytoma
content: Definition: Rare catecholamine-producing tumour of adrenal medulla.
Signs: Pallor, pulsating headache, malignant hypertension, VT, cardiogenic shock.
Emergency Management: Phentolamine 2-5 mg IV (repeat to maintain safe BP).
Follow-up: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg/24h PO (titrate up to 30 mg).
Elective surgery usually performed after 4-6 weeks.

summary: Differential diagnosis of vertical strabismus in primary gaze is a classic board challenge. This guide delineates the mechanical restriction of Brown Syndrome from the neurogenic deficit of IO palsy.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Brown Syndrome is a restrictive ocular motility disorder characterized by a limited ability to elevate the adducted eye. Inferior Oblique (IO) Palsy is a cyclovertical muscle paresis leading to primary gaze hypertropia and limited elevation in adduction due to innervation failure.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Perform Cover-Uncover Test to confirm vertical deviation.
Step 2: Assess Ductions and Versions specifically in adduction.
Step 3: Perform Forced Duction Test (FDT) under topical anesthesia to rule out mechanical restriction.
Step 4: Execute Three-Step (Park-Bielschowsky) Test to confirm paretic muscle.
Step 5: Imaging (CT/MRI) if suspected orbital pathology or restrictive trauma.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Sudden onset in adulthood (Rule out tumor/myasthenia)
Evidence of orbital floor blowout fracture
Associated ptosis or pupillary involvement
Painful restriction (suggests inflammatory etiology)

content.explanation: H (Hyper in which eye?), I (In which gaze is it worse?), R/L (Right/Left head tilt test: Head tilt to the same side increases hyper in superior oblique palsy, opposite in IO).

sections.title: Treatment Protocols
content: Brown Syndrome: Observation for mild cases. Surgical management (SO tenectomy/lengthening) only for significant chin-up posture or severe orthotropic limitation.
IO Palsy: Treat underlying cause if paretic. Surgical recession of the contralateral superior rectus or ipsilateral inferior oblique myectomy if persistent binocular diplopia.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Brown Syndrome is characterized by a 'click' on forced duction if it is the clicking type (congenital).
Inferior oblique palsy is rarely isolated; always rule out ipsilateral SO overaction or contralateral SR palsy.
The FDT is the gold standard for distinguishing restrictive versus paretic etiologies.

summary: Differentiating a benign choroidal nevus from a life-threatening uveal melanoma is a critical skill for the ophthalmologist. This poster explores the epidemiology, multimodal imaging features, and the 'TFSOM-UHHD' risk assessment used to guide management.
