sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Choroidal nevus is a common, benign intraocular melanocytic tumor (prevalence 5-10%). Uveal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, arising from melanocytes within the uveal tract (choroid 85%, ciliary body 10%, iris 5%). Proper identification is vital to prevent systemic metastasis, primarily to the liver.

content.mnemonic: To Find Small Ocular Melanoma Using Helpful Hints Daily
content.explanation: T: Thickness >2mm; F: Fluid (subretinal); S: Symptoms (flashes/floaters/vision loss); O: Orange pigment (lipofuscin); M: Margin touching optic disc (<3mm); U: Ultrasonographic Hollowness; H: Halo Absence; H: Drusen Absence (Drusen suggest chronicity/benignity).

sections.title: Etiology & Genetics
content: GNAQ/GNA11 Mutations: Found in 85% of both nevi and melanomas (early event).
BAP1 Mutation: Associated with high metastatic risk (Monosomy 3).
SF3B1/EIF1AX: Associated with intermediate/low metastatic risk.
Risk Factors: Fair skin, light iris color, ocular melanocytosis (Nevus of Ota), BAP1-TPDS.

sections.title: Multimodal Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy & Indirect Ophthalmoscopy (Identify lesion location/color).
Step 2: Fundus Photography & Autofluorescence (FAF) to detect orange pigment.
Step 3: Enhanced Depth Imaging (EDI-OCT) to measure thickness and detect subretinal fluid/shaggy photoreceptors.
Step 4: B-scan/A-scan Ultrasonography (Assess reflectivity and dimensions).
Step 5: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) to rule out CNVM or confirm 'double circulation'.
Step 6: Fine Needle Aspiration Biopsy (FNAB) for prognostic GEP (Gene Expression Profiling) if treatment is planned.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Suspicious Nevus: Observation every 3-6 months with serial imaging.
Small Melanoma: Plaque brachytherapy (I-125) or Thermotherapy (TTT) or continued observation if dormant.
Medium Melanoma: Plaque brachytherapy (COMS showed no survival difference vs Enucleation).
Large Melanoma: Enucleation is standard; Brachytherapy if feasible.
Systemic Monitoring: Semi-annual Liver USG, MRI, or CT for metastatic surveillance.

sections.title: Emergency 'Red Flags'
content: Documented growth on serial photography
Presence of sentinel vessels (episcleral congestion)
Extrascleral extension on B-scan
Ciliary body involvement (worse prognosis)
Diffuse 'flat' growth pattern

sections.title: Surgical Techniques: Plaque Brachytherapy
content: Isotopes: Iodine-125 (common), Ruthenium-106, Palladium-103.
Procedure: Peritomy, muscle isolation/tagging, localization with transillumination.
Dose: Usually 85 Gy to the tumor apex.
Plaque stays in place for 4-7 days depending on activity level.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (High Yield)
content: Drusen are your friend; they indicate the lesion has likely been there for years.
Lipofuscin (orange pigment) is the 'hottest' indicator of malignancy.
If a lesion is <2mm but has 3+ risk factors, treat it as a melanoma.
Always check the other eye; uveal melanoma is almost always unilateral.

sections.title: Landmark Study: COMS Trial
sections.content: The Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study (COMS) established that: 1) There is no survival difference between enucleation and Iodine-125 brachytherapy for medium-sized tumors. 2) Pre-enucleation radiation for large tumors does not improve survival. 3) Small tumors can often be observed safely until growth is documented.

title: Optic Disc Drusen (ODD): The Great Mimicker
summary: Optic Disc Drusen are acellular, calcified hyaline-like deposits located within the prelaminar optic nerve head. They are a primary cause of pseudopapilledema and require rigorous multimodal imaging to differentiate from life-threatening optic disc edema.

data.summary: Optic Disc Drusen are acellular, calcified hyaline-like deposits located within the prelaminar optic nerve head. They are a primary cause of pseudopapilledema and require rigorous multimodal imaging to differentiate from life-threatening optic disc edema.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Optic Disc Drusen (ODD) are globular, often calcified collections of hyaline material located in the prelaminar portion of the optic nerve head. They are distinct from 'drusen' associated with AMD (which are located between RPE and Bruch's membrane). ODD are progressive, often starting as 'buried' in childhood and becoming 'visible' on the surface by the second decade of life.

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: Step 1: Inherited Anatomical Predisposition — Small scleral canal (crowded disc).
Step 2: Axoplasmic Stasis — Crowding leads to mechanical obstruction of orthograde axoplasmic transport in the optic nerve fibers.
Step 3: Mitochondrial Extrusion — Degenerating axons release mitochondria into the extracellular space.
Step 4: Calcium Deposition — Calcium salts (hydroxyapatite) deposit on the mitochondrial remnants and acellular matrix.
Step 5: Confluence & Growth — Small micro-drusen coalesce into larger, calcified lobulated masses.
Step 6: Progressive Atrophy — Chronic compression leads to RNFL thinning and visual field defects.

rows: Highly reflective at low gain with shadowing
Sub-surface signal void with hyper-reflective cap

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Lumpy-bumpy optic disc margin (Surface ODD).
Absence of physiological cup (Small scleral canal).
Anomalous vascular branching (Trifurcations, early branching).
Peripapillary pigmentary changes (Greyish-yellow circumpapillary halo).
Absence of Paton's folds (Helps distinguish from papilledema).
Visible Spontaneous Venous Pulsations (SVP) in 80% (Often absent in papilledema).

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: 1. Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): The first-line test for visible drusen. ODD are naturally autofluorescent due to calcium/porphyrins.
2. B-Scan Ultrasonography: Gold standard for calcified drusen. Look for high reflectivity at low gain (-15dB) with posterior acoustic shadowing.
3. EDI-OCT (Enhanced Depth Imaging): Gold standard for buried ODD. Shows signal-void core with hyper-reflective margins.
4. Automated Perimetry (SITA-Standard): Essential to monitor for arcuate scotomas or enlarged blind spots (75% of patients).
5. Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Used if diagnosis is uncertain; shows late staining without the leakage seen in papilledema.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Sudden vision loss (Rule out NAION or CNVM).
Headache/Nausea/Tinnitus (Evaluate for high ICP/Papilledema).
New onset Flame Hemorrhages (Usually suggests acute edema or AION).
Absence of ODD on B-scan in an elevated disc (Check MRI/MRV).
Bilateral elevation in an obese female of childbearing age (IIH suspect).

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Baseline Assessment — Document with FAF, EDI-OCT, and HVF 24-2.
Step 2: Observation — Most cases require only annual monitoring.
Step 3: IOP Control — Consider ocular hypotensives if progressive field loss occurs (though controversial, reduces total nerve stress).
Step 4: Treat Complications — Anti-VEGF (e.g., Ranibizumab 0.5mg or Aflibercept 2mg) for peripapillary CNVM.
Step 5: Genetic Counseling — Mention AD inheritance pattern to family members.

content.explanation: B: B-scan (Shadowing at low gain); A: Autofluorescence (Hyper-AF); S: Signal-void on EDI-OCT; E: Early vascular branching.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Non-Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (NAION) — Higher risk due to 'Disc at Risk' anatomy.
Peripapillary Choroidal Neovascularization (pCNVM) — Can cause sudden subretinal hemorrhage.
Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) — Rare, but secondary to mechanical compression.
Progressive Visual Field Constriction — Slow but irreversible.
Prognosis: Usually good for central acuity; guarded for peripheral fields.

sections.title: Recent Advances: ODDS Consortium
sections.content: The Optic Disc Drusen Studies (ODDS) Consortium recently standardized the diagnosis. A key finding is that 'Peripapillary Hyper-reflective Ovoid Mass-like Structures' (PHOMS) are NOT drusen, but rather herniated axons. True ODD on EDI-OCT must have a hyporeflective core and should be located internal to the peripapillary RNFL. This has revolutionized how we differentiate ODD from other forms of pseudopapilledema.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: ODD can cause a 'Pseudo-blind spot enlargement' on VF due to the physical size of the nerve.
If you see drusen and the patient has a large cup, rethink the diagnosis.
In children, the disc looks full and 'pinkish' rather than 'waxy' because the drusen are buried deep.
Always perform a B-scan at low gain; high gain can give false positives due to gain-related artifacts.
ODD are often found in patients with Retinitis Pigmentosa and Angioid Streaks.

branches: Second most common retinal vascular disease
Primary cause of vision loss: Macular Edema (ME)

sections.title: Systemic & Ocular Risk Factors
content: Age (most significant factor)
Systemic Hypertension (present in 60-70% of cases)
Hyperlipidemia and Obesity
Diabetes Mellitus (though more linked to DR)
Cigarette Smoking
Glaucoma or elevated Intraocular Pressure (IOP)
Hypercoagulable states (Protein C/S deficiency, Factor V Leiden) - especially in patients <50

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: Step 1: Artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath at crossing points.
Step 2: Thickened arterial wall (atherosclerosis) compresses the vein.
Step 3: Turbulence and endothelial damage lead to thrombus formation.
Step 4: Venous pressure rises, leading to fluid leakage (Edema) and hemorrhage.
Step 5: Capillary non-perfusion leads to ischemia and VEGF release.
Step 6: High VEGF levels drive Macular Edema and Neovascularization.

rows: Involvement of superior or inferior half

sections.title: Clinical Presentation Checklist
content: Sudden, painless unilateral vision loss
Metamorphopsia (due to macular edema)
Relative visual field defect (scotoma)
Sectoral flame-shaped hemorrhages
Dilated, tortuous venous system distal to crossing
Cotton wool spots in ischemic zones
Macular thickening and hard exudates

rows: Intraretinal fluid, SRF, CME, Hyperreflective foci
Delayed filling, capillary dropout, late leakage
Assess perfusion; define Ischemic vs Non-Ischemic
BP, CBC, Gluc, Lipids, PT/PTT, (Thrombophilia screen in young)

data.label: Risk of NV in Ischemic BRVO

rows: Bilateral, generalized narrowing, Grade IV = Papilledema
History of radiation, similar to DR appearance
Hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, optic disc swelling

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: 1. Baseline Evaluation: VA, OCT, and systemic BP check.
2. Treat Macular Edema: First-line Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, or Bevacizumab).
3. Re-evaluate monthly: Follow 'Pro Re Nata' (PRN) or 'Treat and Extend' protocols.
4. Second-line for ME: Intravitreal Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) - monitor IOP.
5. Manage Ischemia: If >5 disc areas of non-perfusion, monitor closely for NV.
6. Sectoral PRP: Perform if NVE or NVD develops (based on BVOS guidelines).
7. Vitrectomy: For non-clearing Vitreous Hemorrhage or TRD.

rows: GENEVA Trial (effective but higher IOP risk)

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Trials (High Yield)
content: BVOS (1984): Established Grid Laser for ME (VA 20/40 or worse) and Scatter Laser for NV.
BRAVO (2010): Ranibizumab 0.5mg is highly effective for BRVO-ME.
VIBRANT (2014): Aflibercept 2mg monthly showed 53% gained 15+ letters vs 27% with laser.
GENEVA: Ozurdex implant provides rapid improvement, though duration is 3-4 months.
SCORE: Triamcinolone was not superior to laser for BRVO, but effective for CRVO.

content.explanation: Grid Laser: Wait 3-6 months for hemorrhage to clear; VA < 20/40. Scatter Laser: Only after NV develops, NOT prophylactically.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Sudden 'spider-web' floaters (Vitreous Hemorrhage)
Neovascularization of the Iris (NVI) - rare in BRVO but possible in HRVO
Rising IOP after Steroid Implant (Steroid Response)
Endophthalmitis signs: Pain, worsening redness, hypopyon post-injection

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: BRVO at the disc margin is usually HRVO (Hemi-Retinal Vein Occlusion).
Always check for a 'cherry red spot' if vision loss is hand-motions or worse (suspect combined occlusion).
Collateral vessels (large, loopy vessels crossing the horizontal raphe) are a sign of chronicity and should NOT be lasered.
Young patients (<50 years) with BRVO need a thorough workup for thrombophilia and inflammatory vasculitis (Sarcoid, Lupus).
Anti-VEGF is now first-line; Grid laser is reserved for cases resistant to medical therapy or where injections are contraindicated.

title: Giant Retinal Tear (GRT): Mastery & Management
summary: A Giant Retinal Tear (GRT) is a full-thickness circumferential break extending ≥ 90° (3 clock hours) in the presence of a posterior vitreous detachment. It represents one of the most challenging vitreoretinal surgical frontiers due to the high risk of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) and the tendency for the posterior flap to invert.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: A Giant Retinal Tear is defined as a circumferential retinal break involving 90 degrees (three clock hours) or more of the retina. Unlike a retinal dialysis, a GRT occurs at the posterior border of the vitreous base and is associated with a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), leading to the characteristic 'inverted' posterior flap.

branches: High Myopia (Increased axial length & lattice degeneration)

sections.title: The Pathophysiological Mechanism
content: 1. Syneresis and liquefaction of the central vitreous gel.
2. Dynamic traction at the posterior edge of the vitreous base.
3. Rapid circumferential extension of the retinal break.
4. Vitreous enters the subretinal space via the large opening.
5. Gravitational forces and eye movements cause the posterior flap to fold over ('Inversion').

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Sudden onset of persistent Photopsia (flashing lights).
Shower of 'Tobacco Dust' floaters (Shafer's sign / RPE cells).
Peripheral field defect 'Curtain' or 'Shadow'.
Rapid, profound drop in Central Visual Acuity if Macula-off.
Hypotony (Lowered IOP) due to uveoscleral outflow through the tear.

sections.title: The 5 Red Flags of GRT
content: Shafer's Sign (Pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous).
Presence of 'White-Without-Pressure' in the fellow eye.
A flap that crosses the midline (folded over optic nerve).
Rapidly progressive Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR).
History of Stickler Syndrome (Mid-facial hypoplasia/cleft palate).

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Exam Findings
content: Scleral Depression: Mandatory to identify the ends of the tear.
Gonioscopy: To check for RPE cells in the angle and trabecular trauma.
B-Scan Ultrasonography: Essential if media is opaque; shows 'thickened' retina and flap.
Indirect Ophthalmoscopy: 'Inverted' flap showing the RPE side (pale appearance).
Vitreous Base: Look for condensation and 'heavy' traction at the edges.

sections.title: Surgical Management Algorithm
content: 1. Pre-op: Careful assessment of the fellow eye (360° laser prophylaxis if needed).
2. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): 23g, 25g, or 27g small-gauge approach.
3. Induce PVD & Shave the Vitreous Base: Crucial to remove all traction from the edges.
4. PFCL Injection: Use Perfluorocarbon Liquid to flatten the posterior flap and express subretinal fluid.
5. Endolaser: Apply 3-4 rows of laser to the edge of the tear and 360° to the periphery.
6. Tamponade: Direct PFCL-to-Gas (SF6/C3F8) or PFCL-to-Silicone Oil exchange.
7. Post-operative Positioning: Critical for 1-2 weeks to ensure adhesion.

rows: Wrinkling of inner retinal surface; rolled edges.

content.explanation: S: Stickler Syndrome, T: Trauma, O: Other eye involvement, R: Refractive (High Myopia), M: Male sex, M: Marfan Syndrome.

sections.title: Surgical Pearls & Technical Nuances
content: Lensectomy: Consider lensectomy to allow aggressive vitreous base shaving and prevent future cataract/oil issues.
PFCL Level: Do not overfill; leave space to work on the retinal edges.
Scleral Buckle: Controversial in GRT; most surgeons avoid unless there is significant anterior PVR.
Edge Trimming: If the flap is very fibrotic or stiff, consider judicious peripheral retinectomy.
Fellow Eye: Up to 50% risk of retinal break/RD in fellow eye in idiopathic cases; 360° laser is standard.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: Valved Cannulas: Reduced IOP fluctuations during surgery minimize 'flap flap'.
Heavier-than-water Silicone Oil (Densiron): Useful for inferior GRTs to provide better support.
EVRS Study: Suggested that for GRT without PVR, PPV alone has higher success than buckle/PPV combo.
Digital Visualization (Ngenuity/Artevo): Enhanced depth of field for base shaving.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: PVR (40-50%): The most common cause of surgical failure.
Retinal Slippage: Flap moves during fluid-air exchange (minimised by PFCL-Oil exchange).
Raised IOP: Secondary to silicone oil emulsification or steroid response.
Prognosis: Anatomical success 80-90% with modern techniques, but functional vision varies by macula status.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Core Rationale
sections.content: Adjustable suture surgery is a specialized technique where the final tension and position of a recessed or resected extraocular muscle (EOM) are modified in the immediate post-operative period (usually within 24 hours). This allows the surgeon to account for the 'unpredictable' brain-eye interface, including sensory fusion and muscle-contracture factors that static measurements cannot fully capture.

sections.title: Absolute & Relative Contraindications
content: Uncooperative patients (children or those with high anxiety/needle phobia)
Cognitive impairment (inability to follow instructions during adjustment)
Severe conjunctival scarring (precluding a clean sliding noose)
General anesthesia required for adjustment (rarely, unless propofol-assisted)
Extremely small-angle deviations where risks outweigh benefits
History of Malignant Hyperthermia or Suture Hypersensitivity

sections.title: Essential Surgical Instrumentation
content: 6-0 Polyglactin 910 (Vicryl) on an S-29 or S-24 spatula needle
Fine-toothed forceps (0.12 or 0.3 Castroviejo)
Jameson or Green Muscle Hook
Suture-tying forceps (smooth)
Westcott scissors and Bishop-Harmon forceps
Caliper for precise limbal distance measurement
Silicone bolster or 'suture bridge' (optional)

sections.title: Surgical Technique: The 'Hang-back' Method
content: Step 1: Perform a limbal-based peritomy or fornix incision to expose the EOM.
Step 2: Secure the muscle with two locking 6-0 Vicryl sutures at the insertion.
Step 3: Disinsert the muscle from the globe.
Step 4: Pass the sutures through the original insertion or scleral tunnels (Hang-back technique).
Step 5: Create a 'Sliding Noose' using a separate short piece of 6-0 Vicryl around the long ends.
Step 6: Tie the muscle sutures in a temporary 'bow-tie' or pull them through the conjunctiva if utilizing a trans-conjunctival approach.

sections.title: The Post-Operative Adjustment Protocol
content: 1. Timing: Perform adjustment 4-24 hours post-op (once patient is alert).
2. Preparation: Instill 0.5% Proparacaine (topical anesthesia). Use Phenylephrine 2.5% for blanching if necessary.
3. Sensory Testing: Perform Cover-Uncover and Prism tests at distance and near.
4. Motor Testing: Assess ocular rotations and ensure no 'slipped muscle' sign.
5. Manipulation: If over-corrected, pull the long ends to advance the muscle. If under-corrected, use a hook to allow the muscle to recess further.
6. Final Tie-off: Once alignment is optimal, secure the permanent knot and trim the excess suture.

rows: Friction-based noose over long suture ends
Risk of the noose sliding prematurely if too loose
Traditional bow-knot at the scleral insertion
Difficult to undo with wet/bloody sutures post-op
A single loop through the sclera

content.explanation: A: Abrasion (Corneal); L: Lost Muscle (Sutures snap); A: Arrhythmia (Oculocardiac reflex); R: Redness (Granuloma); M: Malalignment (Late drift).

sections.title: Oculocardiac Reflex During Adjustment
content: Sudden Bradycardia (<60 bpm) during suture manipulation
Nausea/Vomiting/Syncope
Risk is higher with Medial Rectus tension
MANAGEMENT: Cease pulling immediately; monitor HR; apply cold compress to face if needed.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Aim for a slight overcorrection in Exotropia (Exo-drift is common).
Aim for orthophoria or trace esophoria in Esotropia.
In Thyroid Eye Disease, under-adjust slightly due to post-op inflammation increasing restriction.
Always perform a 'tug-test' before the patient leaves the OR to ensure the noose holds.
Use 'no-sting' lubricants post-adjustment to prevent suture-related discomfort.

sections.title: Potential Surgical Complications
content: Suture breakage during adjustment (Major Disaster)
Slipped muscle (Pseudo-palsy post-op)
Infection / Endophthalmitis (very rare, <1:1000)
Scleral perforation during tunnel creation
Chronic suture granuloma
Conjunctival scarring (Dellen formation)

rows: Alignment looks good, patient sees double

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The Evidence Base
sections.content: The PRISM (Prospective Randomized In-office Strabismus Management) Trial and works by Jampolsky (1970s) popularized this. Recent Cochrane reviews suggest that while it is highly effective in complex cases, it may not be necessary for routine primary horizontal strabismus in adults.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Innovations
content: Semi-adjustable techniques: Small adjustments via 'short-tag' sutures.
Minimally Invasive Strabismus Surgery (MISS) with adjustable loops.
Delayed adjustment (up to 7 days) using non-absorbable sutures and local lidocaine.
Use of Fibrin glue to secure conjunctiva over the adjustable site.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Overview
sections.content: Congenital Fibrosis of the Extraocular Muscles (CFEOM) is a group of rare, non-progressive primary restrictive strabismus disorders characterized by the replacement of muscle tissue with fibrous tissue, now classified under Congenital Cranial Dysinnervation Disorders (CCDDs). Monocular Elevation Deficiency (MED), historically known as 'Double Elevator Palsy,' refers to a unilateral limitation of elevation in all positions of gaze, which can be paretic, restrictive, or supranuclear in origin.

rows: Dysgenesis of the oculomotor (CN III) or trochlear (CN IV) nuclei/nerves leading to secondary muscle fibrosis.
Heterogeneous: Can be restrictive (IR fibrosis), paretic (SR/IO weakness), or supranuclear (pretectal lesion).
Typically sporadic; rarely associated with syndromes.
Abnormal 'misfiring' or absence of cranial nerve subnuclei.
Deficient neural drive to the Superior Rectus and Inferior Oblique.

branches: CFEOM 1: KIF21A mutation, AD, classic phenotype, bilateral.
CFEOM 2: PHOX2A mutation, AR, ptosis, exotropic/fixed gaze.
CFEOM 3: TUBB3 mutation, AD, variable severity, can be unilateral.
Tukel Syndrome: CFEOM features + postaxial oligodactyly.

sections.title: Hallmark Clinical Features
content: CFEOM: Severe ptosis (bilateral), eyes fixed in infraduction (usually <10 degrees above midline).
CFEOM: Compensatory chin-up head position to maintain fusion or see.
MED: Unilateral elevation deficit in abduction, adduction, and primary gaze.
MED: Marcus Gunn Jaw-winking (found in ~25% of cases).
MED: True ptosis or Pseudoptosis (due to hypotropic eye).

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Forced Duction Test (FDT) - Essential to differentiate restriction (positive) from palsy (negative).
Step 2: Force Generation Test (FGT) - Assesses active muscle strength.
Step 3: Saccadic Velocity - Slowed up-saccades suggest paresis; abrupt stop suggests restriction.
Step 4: Bell's Phenomenon - Absent in CFEOM and Type 1/2 MED; preserved in supranuclear MED.
Step 5: High-Resolution MRI - Visualize CN III, IV, and VI; look for muscle atrophy/hypoplasia.

rows: Restriction ONLY in adduction; V-pattern divergence in upgaze.
Acquired, proptosis, eyelid retraction, lid lag.
History of trauma, diplopia, infraorbital anesthesia.

sections.title: Surgical Management: CFEOM
content: Goal: Move eyes to primary position and address head tilt.
Large Recessions: Bilateral Inferior Rectus recessions (often 8-12mm or more).
Adjuncts: Use of hang-back sutures or adjustable sutures.
Ptosis: Frontalis suspension is standard. Caution: Risk of exposure keratopathy due to poor Bell's phenomenon.

sections.title: Surgical Management: MED
content: Step 1: Perform FDT in OR. If positive IR restriction -> Recess Inferior Rectus.
Step 2: If FDT is negative (Paretic Type) -> Knapp Procedure.
Step 3: Knapp Procedure involves transposing MR and LR to the insertion of the SR.
Step 4: Address Ptosis ONLY after the hypotropia is corrected (to avoid worsening pseudoptosis).

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Exposure Keratopathy: Post-ptosis surgery risk is extremely high in CFEOM due to absent Bell's and restricted downgaze.
Malignant Hyperthermia: Increased risk in some congenital myopathies/fibrosis syndromes.
Corneal Anesthesia: Associated with CFEOM2 (PHOX2A) due to CN V involvement.
Amblyopia: Rapid development in unilateral MED or CFEOM3; requires aggressive patching.

content.explanation: P: Paretic (SR/IO palsy), R: Restrictive (IR fibrosis), S: Supranuclear (Pretectal).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Prep
content: Knapp Procedure: Full tendon transposition of MR and LR to SR insertion. Expect ~20-30 PD correction.
Pseudo-ptosis: In MED, the upper lid follows the hypotropic eye down. Occlude the 'good' eye; if the lid lifts as the eye takes up fixation, it is pseudoptosis.
CFEOM1: Always bilateral, symmetrical, and involves the Superior Division of CN III.
In CFEOM, horizontal deviations (Exotropia/Esotropia) are common and should be corrected simultaneously with vertical deviations.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Research
sections.content: The 'CCDD' paradigm shift has moved our understanding from primary muscle pathology to primary neurogenic dysgenesis. Recent studies using 3T and 7T MRI have confirmed the absence of the abducens or oculomotor nerves in specific CFEOM phenotypes. Landmark studies by Elizabeth Engle have mapped the genetic loci (KIF21A), proving that these disorders result from kinesin motor protein defects affecting axonal guidance.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pigmentary retinopathy refers to a group of hereditary and acquired disorders characterized by the migration of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) into the neurosensory retina. The most common form is Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP), a diffuse rod-cone dystrophy. While primarily an ocular disease, it frequently serves as a sentinel sign for systemic ciliopathies and metabolic disorders.

content.explanation: B: Bone-Spicule Pigmentation (perivascular); W: Waxy Disc Pallor (secondary to gliosis); A: Arteriolar Attenuation (vascular remodeling).

sections.title: Pathophysiology Workflow
content: Step 1: Genetic mutation (e.g., RHO, USH2A, RPGR) leads to rod photoreceptor dysfunction.
Step 2: Progressive shortening of rod outer segments and eventual apoptosis.
Step 3: Loss of rods leads to secondary oxidative stress and loss of trophic factors (like RdCVF), causing cone death.
Step 4: RPE cells migrate into the retina, clustering around vessels in a 'bone-spicule' pattern.
Step 5: Optic nerve gliosis occurs, resulting in the characteristic waxy pallor appearance.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Nyctalopia (Night Blindness): Often the first symptom in childhood.
Peripheral Field Loss: Starting as a mid-peripheral ring scotoma, progressing to tunnel vision.
Photopsia: Tiny shimmering lights in the peripheral field.
Central Vision Loss: Occurs late due to CME, ERM, or foveal atrophy.
Dyschromatopsia: Late-stage loss of color discrimination.

rows: Loss of Ellipsoid Zone (EZ) and External Limiting Membrane
Mid-peripheral ring scotoma to 5-degree central island

branches: Metabolic: Vitamin A deficiency, Refsum Disease

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Sudden vision drop: Suggestive of Cystoid Macular Edema (CME).
Unilateral presentation: Highly suspicious for Pseudo-RP (RP is bilateral).
History of high-dose Vitamin E: Can accelerate disease progression in some forms.
Presence of hearing loss: Must rule out Usher Syndrome immediately.

sections.title: Management & Treatment
content: Vitamin A Palmitate: 15,000 IU/day (controversial, monitor liver enzymes).
Omega-3 Fatty Acids: 1200mg/day may slow ERG decline.
CME Treatment: Topical or oral Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (Acetazolamide/Dorzolamide).
UV Protection: Dark amber wrap-around sunglasses to reduce phototoxicity.
Low Vision Aids: Bioptics, magnifiers, and mobility training.

sections.title: Gene Therapy: Luxturna (Voretigene Neparvovec)
content: 1. Confirm Biallelic RPE65 mutation via genetic testing.
2. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) performed by vitreoretinal surgeon.
3. Subretinal injection of AAV2 vector carrying RPE65 cDNA.
4. Restoration of the visual cycle and rod function.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Mizuo-Nakamura' phenomenon: Characteristic of Oguri disease, not classic RP.
Preserved peripapillary RPE: Often a sign of CRB1 mutations.
Bone spicules follow the vessels: Because the vessels provide the scaffold for RPE migration.
XL-RP: Check female carriers for a 'tapetal-like' retinal sheen.

sections.title: Surgical Complications
content: Posterior Subcapsular Cataract (PSC): Extremely common; manage with surgery.
Zonular Weakness: Higher risk of lens subluxation during phacoemulsification.
Vitreous Syneresis: Increased risk of retinal tears and detachment.
Epiretinal Membrane: Can cause significant tractional macular distortion.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The Berson Study (1993) established the role of Vitamin A Palmitate. Recent focus has shifted to Optogenetics (using viral vectors to make surviving cells light-sensitive) and Stem Cell therapy to replace the RPE layer. The ARGUS II Retinal Prosthesis, while now discontinued commercially, proved the feasibility of electronic retinal bypass in end-stage disease.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Leber Congenital Amaurosis (LCA): The severe, infantile-onset form of pigmentary retinopathy.
Oculodigital Reflex: Frequent eye poking (Franceschetti's sign) to induce phosphenes.
Nystagmus: Develops early in severe pediatric cases due to poor fixation.
Genetic Counseling: Essential for families to understand recurrence risk.

content.explanation: B: Big (Obesity); A: Atrial/Heart (less common); R: Renal; D: Digits (Polydactyly); E: Eyes (RP); T: Testes (Hypogonadism).

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) is characterized by slow, progressive, bilateral, non-fatigable ptosis followed by symmetrical restriction of all extraocular movements. When CPEO is associated with multisystem involvement including pigmentary retinopathy, onset before age 20, and cardiac conduction defects, it is classified as Kearns-Sayre Syndrome (KSS).

branches: Single large-scale mtDNA deletions (most common in KSS)
Nuclear DNA mutations affecting mtDNA maintenance (POLG1, PEO1, SLC25A4)
Heteroplasmy: Ratio of mutant to wild-type mtDNA determines severity
High metabolic demand tissues (Extraocular muscles, Retina, Heart) affected first

content.explanation: MUST have all three: 1. Onset < 20 years old. 2. CPEO (Ptosis + Ophthalmoplegia). 3. Pigmentary Retinopathy (Salt-and-pepper). PLUS at least one of: Cardiac conduction block, CSF protein >100mg/dL, or Cerebellar Ataxia.

rows: Slowly progressive, bilateral, symmetrical. Often the first sign.
Severe, early onset. Significant levator function loss.
Symmetrical restriction in all gazes. No diplopia (usually).
Spared, though retinopathy may affect visual fields.
Reduced Bell's phenomenon; risk of neurotrophic keratitis.
Fatigability, variability, diurnal fluctuation, Cogan's lid twitch, Ice test (+).
Autosomal Dominant, onset in 5th-6th decade, dysphagia, limb-girdle weakness.
Lid retraction (vs ptosis), proptosis, restrictive strabismus on forced duction.
Acute onset, ataxia, areflexia, post-viral, GQ1b antibodies (+).
Present from birth, lid lag on downgaze, poor levator function.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Clinical History & Exam (Evaluate for ptosis symmetry and diplopia presence).
Step 2: Cardiology Referral (MANDATORY EKG/Holter to rule out heart block).
Step 3: Blood/Urine Testing (Lactate, Pyruvate, Creatine Kinase levels).
Step 4: Genetic Testing (Targeted mtDNA deletion/point mutation analysis via blood/saliva).
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture (If KSS suspected: evaluate for CSF protein > 100 mg/dL).
Step 6: Muscle Biopsy (Gold standard if genetics inconclusive: Gomori Trichrome staining for 'Ragged Red Fibers').

sections.title: Lethal Warning Signs
content: Syncope or Dizziness (Potential Mobitz II or 3rd-degree heart block)
Sudden cardiac death risk in KSS (requires pacemaker)
Severe Dysphagia (Aspiration risk in CPEO+ syndromes)
Acute corneal ulceration post-ptosis surgery (Absent Bell's)

sections.title: Histopathology & Microscopy
content: Ragged Red Fibers (RRF): Subsarcolemmal accumulation of abnormal mitochondria (Gomori Trichrome).
COX-Negative Fibers: Cytochrome c oxidase deficiency in specific muscle fibers.
Electron Microscopy: 'Parking lot' crystalline inclusions (paracrystalline).
Succinate Dehydrogenase (SDH) staining: Hyper-reactive 'blue' fibers.

sections.title: Management Strategies
content: Conservative: Ptosis crutches on glasses, prisms (rarely needed).
Ptosis Surgery: Frontalis suspension (Sling) is preferred over levator resection.
Surgical Caution: Under-correct ptosis to prevent exposure keratopathy.
Medical: Coenzyme Q10 (120-160mg/day) and L-Carnitine (limited evidence).
Cardiac: Prophylactic pacemaker placement for KSS with any conduction delay.

content.explanation: S: Sling (Frontalis), T: Tension-free, A: Avoid overcorrection, Y: Yield to poor Bell's, S: Silicone rods (reversible), A: Artificial tears, F: Frequent follow-up, E: Exposure check.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy (MRT): 'Three-parent baby' techniques for prevention.
Gene Editing: Zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs) to shift heteroplasmy in vitro.
Study: Zeviani et al. (1988) first established the link between mtDNA deletions and KSS/CPEO.
Nadir et al. (2023): Investigating Elamipretide for mitochondrial stabilization.

sections.title: Epidemiology at a Glance
content: Prevalence: ~1.6 per 100,000 for all mitochondrial diseases.
Gender: No predilection; affects males and females equally.
Onset CPEO: Typically 18-40 years.
Onset KSS: Strictly < 20 years (usually first decade).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Because EOM restriction is symmetrical, patients rarely complain of diplopia; they simply turn their heads.
CPEO is the most common manifestation of mitochondrial disease in adults.
Always check for orbicularis weakness (often present in CPEO, mimicking MG).
The pigmentary retinopathy of KSS is often asymptomatic and doesn't usually cause significant vision loss, unlike Retinitis Pigmentosa.
A negative muscle biopsy does NOT rule out CPEO if only one muscle group was sampled (mosaic distribution).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Classification
sections.content: Unilateral Exotropia in the elderly refers to a constant or intermittent outward deviation of one eye. Unlike childhood strabismus, adult-onset XT is frequently secondary. It is classified into Sensory XT (vision loss in one eye), Consecutive XT (post-esotropia surgery), and Paralytic XT (nerve palsy).

sections.title: Sensory Exotropia: The Most Common Cause
content: Defined as XT resulting from unilateral visual impairment.
Mechanism: Loss of fusion reflexes leads to the eye seeking a position of rest (usually abduction in adults).
Common triggers: Dense nuclear sclerotic cataract.
Advanced Age-Related Macular Degeneration (wet or dry).
Chronic Retinal Detachment or Vitreous Hemorrhage.
Unilateral Glaucoma with severe field loss.
Corneal scarring (e.g., post-Herpetic).

sections.title: Emergency Warning Signs (Red Flags)
content: Sudden onset XT with an enlarged, non-reactive pupil (Aneurysm risk).
New onset XT accompanied by severe 'Thunderclap' headache.
XT with associated proptosis or chemosis (Carotid-Cavernous Fistula).
Variability of XT throughout the day with ptosis (Myasthenia Gravis crisis).
Bilateral involvement or 'Crossed' signs (Brainstem stroke).

sections.title: Neuromuscular: Ocular Myasthenia Gravis
content: The 'Great Mimicker': Can present as any pattern of strabismus.
Diurnal Variation: XT worse in the evening or with fatigue.
Cogan's Lid Twitch: Overshoot of the eyelid on upgaze.
Fatigability: XT increases during prolonged upgaze or reading.
Ice Test: Improvement of ptosis/alignment with cold application.

sections.title: The 'Sagging Eye' Syndrome
sections.content: A mechanical cause of strabismus in the elderly due to involutional degeneration of the Lateral Rectus-Superior Rectus (LR-SR) band. While it typically causes divergence insufficiency (Esotropia), it can manifest as a cyclovertical deviation or 'Heavy Eye' XT in high myopes, where the globe herniates through the muscle cone.

sections.title: Essential Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Visual Acuity & Refraction (Rule out sensory cause/anisometropia).
Step 2: Prism Cover Test (Measure at distance, near, and in 9 cardinal positions).
Step 3: Ductions & Versions (Check for limitation suggestive of palsy or restriction).
Step 4: Slit Lamp & Fundoscopy (Identify cataract, AMD, or optic nerve pathology).
Step 5: Pupil Assessment (Crucial for CN III palsy differentiation).
Step 6: Specialized Tests (Ice test for MG, Forced Duction for mechanical restriction).
Step 7: Imaging (MRI Brain/Orbits if neurogenic or orbital etiology suspected).

rows: Pain with eye movement, muscle swelling on CT

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol
content: 1. Establish Sensory Potential: Determine if the patient has fusion or if they will suppress.
2. Prism Adaptation: Trial prisms pre-operatively to assess risk of post-op diplopia.
3. Muscle Selection: Usually Lateral Rectus Recession + Medial Rectus Resection (R&R) on the non-dominant/blind eye.
4. Adjustable Sutures: Highly recommended in elderly to fine-tune alignment on Day 1.
5. Post-Operative Monitoring: Watch for consecutive esotropia in the early weeks.

rows: Base-In prisms; limited by weight/blur if >10PD
Acute CN III palsy or temporary relief
Injected into Lateral Rectus; temporary (3 mos)
Aligning the eyes often requires surgery even after cataract removal
Primary goal: Cosmetic for sensory; Functional for others

content.explanation: S: Secondary to cataract; E: Exotropia (Consecutive); N: Nerve Palsy (CN III); S: Sagging Eye; O: Ocular Myasthenia; R: Retinal disease (AMD); Y: Young-at-heart (Decompensated childhood XT).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for a 'Reverse' Binocularity (Horror Fusionis) before surgery in adults.
Vasculopathic CN III palsies usually resolve spontaneously within 90 days.
In sensory XT, the eye with poorer vision usually deviates outward in adults, whereas children may develop esotropia.
Adjustable sutures are the gold standard for adult strabismus surgery to account for variable muscle tone.

summary: A comprehensive guide to the complex interplay between lens pathology and optic nerve dysfunction. Understanding when a cataract masks a sick nerve and how the lens itself can trigger sight-threatening glaucoma.

sections.title: The RAPD Paradox in Cataract
sections.content: A fundamental rule in clinical ophthalmology: Cataract alone—no matter how dense—does NOT cause a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD). Because light is scattered rather than blocked from reaching the retina, the total amount of light reaching the photoreceptors remains sufficient to drive the pupillary reflex. If an RAPD is present in a cataractous eye, you MUST investigate for concurrent optic nerve or extensive retinal disease.

sections.title: Etiology of RAPD in Cataractous Patients
The 'Inverse' RAPD Trick
content: Used when one pupil is fixed (miotic, traumatic, or surgical) but the other is reactive.
Observe the reactive pupil only.
Shine light in the reactive eye: it constricts (direct).
Shine light in the non-reactive/opaque eye: if the reactive pupil dilates, an RAPD is present in the opaque eye.
Critical for pre-operative assessment in dense cataracts with suspected nerve damage.

rows: Secondary Angle Closure; intumescent lens pushes iris forward.
Sudden pain, high IOP, shallow AC, white lens.
Open Angle; HMW lens proteins leak through intact capsule, clogging TM.
Heavy flare, iridescent particles in AC, mature cataract.
Granulomatous uveitis; immune response to lens protein post-trauma/surgery.
KP on endothelium, mutton-fat appearance, cell & flare.
Pupillary block due to lens subluxation (Marfan's, Trauma).
Iridodonesis, asymmetric AC depth, visible lens equator.

sections.title: Glaucoma Leading to Cataract
content: Glaukomflecken: Minute white subcapsular opacities from lens epithelial necrosis post-acute angle closure.
Miotics: Long-term Pilocarpine use is associated with anterior subcapsular opacification.
Metabolic: Severe chronic IOP elevation disrupts lens fiber nutrition.
Iatrogenic: Post-Trabeculectomy/Tube surgery (mechanical contact or metabolic change).

sections.title: Red Flags: The Urgent Cataract
content: RAPD in an eye with simple nuclear sclerosis.
IOP > 40 mmHg with an intumescent (swollen) cataract.
Iridescent/polychromatic 'crystals' in the aqueous humor.
Sudden vision loss better than light perception in a mature white cataract.
Asymmetric AC depth between the two eyes.

rows: High C:D ratio, Notch in RIM, arcuate defects.
Pallor out of proportion to cupping.

sections.title: Pre-Op Evaluation of Opaque Media
content: 1. B-Scan Ultrasonography: Rule out RD, tumors, or posterior staphyloma.
2. Potential Acuity Meter (PAM): Estimate post-op VA if media allows.
3. Flash VEP: Assess optic nerve pathway integrity.
4. Entoptic Phenomenon: Patient visualizes retinal vasculature via trans-scleral light.
5. Two-Point Discrimination: Gross test of macular function.

content.explanation: Phacomorphic (Big lens), Phacolytic (Leaky lens), Phacoantigenic (Allergy to lens), Phacotopic (Displaced lens).

sections.title: Surgical Pearls for Phacomorphic Cases
content: Pre-op Hyperosmotics: IV Mannitol 20% (1-2g/kg) to dehydrate the vitreous and deepen the AC.
Trypan Blue: Essential for visualizing the capsule in white cataracts.
Argentinian Flag Sign Prevention: Decompress the lens with a needle aspiration before completing the capsulorhexis.
Healon 5 / OVD: Use high-viscosity cohesives to maintain the chamber and push the iris back.
Large incision ECCE: Consider if the cornea is too edematous for safe Phaco.

sections.title: Recent Advances: The EAGLE Study
sections.content: The Landmark EAGLE Trial (Effectiveness in Angle-closure Glaucoma of Lens Extraction) demonstrated that clear lens extraction showed greater efficacy and was more cost-effective than laser peripheral iridotomy as a first-line treatment for primary angle-closure glaucoma with IOP > 30 mmHg or primary angle-closure. This has shifted the management paradigm toward earlier lens removal in patients with narrow angles and glaucoma risk.

sections.title: Phacolytic Management Protocol
content: 1. Rapid IOP Reduction: Topical Beta-blockers, Alpha-agonists, and Oral Acetazolamide.
2. Inflammation Control: Intensive topical steroids (Pred Forte q1h).
3. Urgent Surgery: Usually within 24-48 hours. The goal is to remove the protein source.
4. Copious AC Washout: Ensure all lens proteins and macrophages are removed from the angle.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A dense cataract does not cause RAPD, but a RAPD can be caused by the advanced glaucoma the cataract itself triggered.
In phacolytic glaucoma, the angle is OPEN, distinguishing it from phacomorphic.
Pseudoexfoliation (PXF) is the 'Great Masquerader'—causing both weak zonules (cataract surgery risk) and secondary open-angle glaucoma.
Always check the fellow eye: Disc-at-risk suggests NAION; narrow angles suggest Phacomorphic risk.

summary: Angioid streaks are jagged, radiating cracks in a calcified and brittle Bruch’s membrane. While often asymptomatic, they are a harbinger of potential vision loss from choroidal neovascularization and serve as a crucial diagnostic clue for systemic elastic tissue disorders.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Angioid streaks are irregular, jagged, tapering lines that radiate from the peripapillary area into the peripheral fundus. They represent dehiscences (cracks) in a thickened, calcified, and abnormally brittle Bruch's membrane. Primarily involving the elastic lamina, these cracks allow for potential ingrowth of choroidal fibrovascular tissue, leading to vision-threatening complications. The condition is often bilateral and progressive.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Mechanism of Brittleness
content: Step 1: Abnormal mineralization (calcification) of the elastic lamina of Bruch’s membrane.
Step 2: Increase in fragility and brittleness of the Bruch's-RPE complex.
Step 3: Mechanical stress (ocular muscle traction or minor trauma) causes linear ruptures.
Step 4: Atrophy of overlying Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE).
Step 5: Access provided for Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV) to enter sub-retinal space.

content.explanation: P: Pseudoxanthoma Elasticum (PXE / Grönblad–Strandberg syndrome) | E: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (Type VI) | P: Paget’s Disease of Bone | S: Sickle Cell Disease (and other hemoglobinopathies like Thalassemia) | I: Idiopathic.

rows: Plucked-chicken skin (neck/axilla), mitral valve prolapse, GI bleeds
Skin biopsy (Von Kossa stain), ABCC6 genetic testing
Enlarged skull, bone pain, hearing loss
Serum Alkaline Phosphatase (elevated), Bone Scan, X-ray

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Peripapillary Configuration: Streaks radiate from a circular ring around the optic disc.
Color: Vary from red, brown, to grey depending on the background pigmentation.
Peau d'orange: Mottled RPE appearance (orange peel) temporal to the macula; often precedes streaks.
Optic Disc Drusen: Highly associated with PXE cases.
Salmon Spots: Small, yellowish peripheral chorioretinal scars (peripheral focal atrophies).
Crystalline Bodies: Small, subretinal white-yellow spots in the mid-periphery.

branches: FFA: Early hyperfluorescence (window defect) with late staining; leakage if CNV present
ICGA: Better detection; usually shows more streaks than clinical exam (hypofluorescent)
FAF: Usually hypo-autofluorescent streaks due to RPE atrophy; may show hyper-AF margins
OCT: Irregularity/breaks in the RPE-Bruch's complex; 'saw-tooth' configuration

rows: Associated with high myopia, usually more linear/yellow, lack peripapillary ring.
Concentric to the optic disc, history of trauma, usually white (exposed sclera).
Linear scars can mimic, but usually have pigmented borders and no peripapillary origin.
Can coexist with PXE, but pigment distribution is more central and symmetric.

sections.title: The Threat of CNV: Management Protocol
content: 1. Baseline Assessment: Multimodal imaging (OCT, FFA) to rule out occult CNV.
2. Home Monitoring: Daily Amsler Grid is mandatory for all patients.
3. First-line Treatment: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab 0.5mg, Aflibercept 2mg, or Bevacizumab 1.25mg).
4. Dosing Schedule: Usually Pro-re-nata (PRN) or Treat-and-Extend (T&E) based on fluid.
5. Laser: Only for extrafoveal CNV (rarely used now due to risk of streak expansion).

sections.title: Critical Complications
content: Subretinal Hemorrhage: Can occur from MINOR blunt trauma without CNV (fragile Bruch's).
Type 2 Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV): Most common cause of disciform scarring.
Geographic Atrophy: Progressive RPE loss leads to poor visual prognosis even without CNV.
Foveal Involvement: Direct extension of a streak through the fovea.

sections.title: Emergency Patient Education
content: MANDATORY: Polycarbonate safety glasses for all contact sports/high-risk activities.
Urgent reporting of metamorphopsia (wavy lines).
Avoidance of heavy lifting or Valsalva maneuvers (risk of subretinal bleed).
Smoking cessation (accelerates RPE degeneration and CNV risk).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & High-Yield Facts
content: Most common systemic association is PXE (up to 85%).
Streaks are 'angioid' because they resemble blood vessels, not because they contain blood.
Vision loss is rarely due to the streaks themselves, but rather secondary CNV or trauma.
Angioid streaks in Sickle Cell are usually found in patients >25 years old.
The 'peau d'orange' sign is highly specific for PXE.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent studies have highlighted the long-term efficacy of Anti-VEGF therapy in Angioid Streak-associated CNV, though the frequency of injections required may be higher than in AMD. Genetic research into the ABCC6 gene (PXE) has opened doors for potential enzyme replacement therapies or systemic pyrophosphate supplementation, which may one day prevent the mineralization of Bruch's membrane entirely. Landmark case series emphasize that early detection of CNV via OCT-Angiography (OCTA) leads to significantly better visual outcomes compared to waiting for symptomatic hemorrhage.

sections.title: Classification of Streak Progression
content: Stage 1: Peau d'orange (mottling) without visible streaks.
Stage 2: Discrete, fine streaks radiating from the disc.
Stage 3: Widening of streaks and focal RPE atrophy.
Stage 4: Development of CNV or subretinal fibrosis.
Stage 5: Extensive disciform scarring and macular atrophy.

title: Chorioretinal Scars: The Clinical Atlas & Diagnostic Roadmap
summary: Fundus scars represent the end-stage morphological footprint of prior inflammatory, infectious, traumatic, or degenerative insults. This comprehensive guide details the classification, multimodal imaging, and critical management of quiescent vs. active lesions.

data.summary: Fundus scars represent the end-stage morphological footprint of prior inflammatory, infectious, traumatic, or degenerative insults. This comprehensive guide details the classification, multimodal imaging, and critical management of quiescent vs. active lesions.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: A fundus scar is a permanent alteration of the chorioretinal architecture. It typically involves RPE hyperplasia (pigmentation), RPE atrophy, or subretinal fibrosis. Pathophysiologically, it follows the 'wound healing' response of the retina where glial cells (Müller cells) and RPE cells proliferate to replace damaged neurosensory tissue, often resulting in a loss of the blood-retinal barrier in the acute phase and dense scarring in the chronic phase.

rows: Black clumps of RPE migration, 'salt and pepper'
White, elevated, subretinal or epiretinal membranes
Linear, yellowish-white streaks at the level of Bruch's

branches: Inflammatory (Sarcoid, VKH, Sympathetic Ophthalmia, White Dot Syndromes)

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Scar Reactivation
content: New onset 'Metamorphopsia' (suggests CNVM)
'Headlight in the fog' appearance (active Toxo adjacent to old scar)
Subretinal fluid or hemorrhage around a pre-existing scar
Vitreous haze or cells (Inflammatory/Infectious flare)
Rapid expansion of atrophic borders (Geographic Atrophy progression)

content.explanation: P: Peripapillary atrophy (PPA); O: Old 'punched-out' chorioretinal spots; H: Hemorrhage (Subretinal CNVM); S: Sparing of the vitreous (No vitritis).

sections.title: Multimodal Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Color Fundus Photography: Baseline documentation of size and location.
Step 2: Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): Scars are characteristically 'Hypoautofluorescent' due to RPE death.
Step 3: OCT Macula: Assess for 'Sink-hole' effect, Outer Retinal Tubulations (ORT), or subretinal fibrosis.
Step 4: FFA/ICGA: Identify 'Window defects' in atrophy vs. 'Staining' in fibrosis vs. 'Leakage' in CNVM.
Step 5: OCT-Angiography (OCTA): Non-invasive detection of Choroidal Neovascularization within or adjacent to scars.

sections.title: Classic Scar Patterns
content: Toxoplasmosis: Heavily pigmented borders with central atrophy; often at the macula.
Choroidal Rupture: Crescent-shaped scars concentric to the optic nerve.
Laser Scars: Post-PRP; early are yellow/white, late are 'punched out' with pigment clumps.
Angioid Streaks: Peripapillary radiating 'jagged' lines (Peau d'orange appearance).
Fuchs Spot: Pigmented circular scar in the macula of high myopes.

sections.title: Management of Quiescent Scars
content: 1. Documentation with wide-field imaging.
2. Patient education on Amsler Grid monitoring.
3. Refraction (especially in myopic scars) for best corrected visual acuity.
4. Monitoring for secondary CNVM development (highest risk in POHS/Myopia).

sections.title: Management: When CNVM Complicates Scars
content: Anti-VEGF Therapy: Intravitreal Ranibizumab (0.5mg), Aflibercept (2.0mg), or Bevacizumab (1.25mg).
Dosing: Often follows a 'Pro Re Nata' (PRN) or Treat-and-Extend protocol.
Photodynamic Therapy (PDT): Historically used for myopic CNV; now largely secondary to anti-VEGF.
Steroids: If the scar is from an active inflammatory process (e.g., Sarcoidosis).

sections.title: Surgical Considerations
sections.content: Surgical intervention is rarely for the scar itself but for its complications. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) may be required for Epiretinal Membranes (ERM) secondary to scarring, or for submacular hemorrhage drainage in the setting of traumatic choroidal rupture. Subretinal surgery to remove fibrotic 'plaques' is largely obsolete due to high risk of RPE damage.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Pseudo-retinitis pigmentosa: Diffuse scarring from old trauma or syphilis can mimic RP; look for 'bone spicules' that don't respect the mid-periphery.
The 'Halos' of Histoplasmosis: Atrophic spots often have a thin rim of RPE changes; these are 'Histo spots'.
Laser scar creep: Photocoagulation scars (especially from CNV treatment or PRP) can enlarge over years, a phenomenon known as 'atrophic creep'.
Visual Field: Scars cause absolute scotomas. A macular scar = central scotoma; PRP = peripheral field constriction.

sections.title: Recent Advances: AI & Imaging
content: AI Algorithms: Deep learning models can now predict the 'expansion rate' of geographic atrophy scars.
Adaptive Optics (AO): Visualization of individual photoreceptor loss at the margins of scars.
Home-based OCT: Monitoring for fluid around scars to detect CNVM earlier than Amsler Grid.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
sections.content: Congenital fundus scars (e.g., from TORCH infections like CMV or Toxo) require aggressive amblyopia management. A central macular scar does not mean 'no vision'; these children often develop eccentric fixation and can have functional navigation vision.

content.explanation: Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study established the standard for focal/grid laser scars. It proved that macular edema could be reduced, even though the treatment itself created iatrogenic scars.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Visual Impairment: Depends on foveal involvement.
Retinal Detachment: Atrophic scars (especially in myopia or lattice) can lead to atrophic holes and rhegmatogenous RD.
Recurrence: Infectious scars (Toxo) have a lifetime risk of reactivation.
Epiretinal Membrane: Tractional forces common over areas of prior inflammation.

title: Mastering Zonular Dehiscence: Diagnosis, Mechanics, and Management
summary: Zonular dehiscence involves the focal or diffuse loss of the suspensory ligaments of the lens, leading to subluxation or dislocation. This critical complication demands precise surgical planning to avoid intraoperative catastrophes.

data.title: Mastering Zonular Dehiscence: Diagnosis, Mechanics, and Management
data.summary: Zonular dehiscence involves the focal or diffuse loss of the suspensory ligaments of the lens, leading to subluxation or dislocation. This critical complication demands precise surgical planning to avoid intraoperative catastrophes.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='30' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M50 20 L50 80 M20 50 L80 50' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='4'/><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='10' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Zonular dehiscence is the rupture or lysis of the ciliary zonules (Zinn's zonules), which connect the lens capsule to the ciliary body. A loss of <90 degrees is often focal; >180 degrees typically results in significant lens subluxation or phacodonesis. Failure to recognize preoperative dehiscence during phacoemulsification significantly increases the risk of vitreous loss and capsular bag drop.

sections.title: Clinical Examination Findings
content: Phacodonesis: Lens wobble on rapid eye movement
Iridodonesis: Tremulous iris indicating loss of lens support
Vitreous in Anterior Chamber: Direct sign of zonular gap
Asymmetric Anterior Chamber Depth: Deepening in the area of dehiscence
Lens Subluxation: Visible lens edge or equatorial notch

sections.title: Red Flags: Impending Complications
content: Preoperative identification of vitreous prolapse through the zonular defect.
Deep chamber and tremulous iris suggesting >6 clock hours of zonular loss.
Intraoperative 'shallow' chamber during phaco—sign of posterior pressure/vitreous force.
Sudden radial capsular tear progression during rhexis.
Significant lens tilt post-implant.

sections.title: Surgical Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Mydriasis and stabilization with heavy OVDs (e.g., Healon5).
Step 2: Utilization of Capsular Tension Rings (CTR) for <3-4 clock hours.
Step 3: If >4 clock hours, utilize Cionni modified CTR or Ahmed Segment.
Step 4: Consider scleral fixation of the CTR/segment using Gore-Tex or Prolene.
Step 5: Minimal flow/vacuum parameters during phaco to minimize zonular stress.
Step 6: Pars Plana Vitrectomy if vitreous is present or suspected.

content.explanation: Z: Zero/Mild (Standard IOL); O: Observed (CTR); N: Needs fixation (Cionni/Segment); S: Severe/Aphakia (AC IOL/Scleral Fixated IOL/Yamane).

sections.title: Recent Advances: The Yamane Technique
content: Double-needle intrascleral haptic fixation (Yamane technique).
Eliminates need for large incisions or scleral flaps.
Reduces incidence of endophthalmitis and suture-related erosions.
Current gold standard for severe zonulopathy or aphakia.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Always stain the capsule with Trypan Blue; zonular dehiscence makes the capsule difficult to visualize.
Do not over-fill with OVD in suspected PXE—can push the lens further posteriorly.
If the rhexis pulls toward the dehiscence, stop immediately—use capsule hooks to stabilize.
In Marfan patients, consider early surgery due to high risk of glaucoma secondary to pupillary block.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Scleral buckling is an extra-ocular surgical procedure for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD). It involves the application of a buckle (silicone explant) to the sclera, creating an indentation to relieve vitreous traction and seal the retinal break by closing the gap between the RPE and neurosensory retina.

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Step-by-Step
content: 1. Peritomy: 360-degree conjunctival peritomy.
2. Muscle Isolation: Secure 4 recti muscles with 2-0 silk sutures.
3. Localization: Indirect ophthalmoscopy to mark retinal break.
4. Cryotherapy: Apply trans-scleral cryopexy around the break to create chorioretinal adhesion.
5. Explant Placement: Suture silicone sponge or solid element to the sclera.
6. Drainage: Optional external subretinal fluid drainage via sclerotomy (if bullous).
7. Closure: Secure buckle, tighten encircling band (usually #40 or #240).

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Post-op endophthalmitis (pain, vitritis)
Ischemia from excessive buckle height (CRAO)
Extreme IOP spikes post-drainage
Signs of orbital cellulitis post-explant

content.explanation: C: Check the break localization; R: Relief of traction; Y: Yielding high attachment (cryo); O: Observe for post-op IOP spikes.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Goldmann three-mirror exam for peripheral break localization.
Indirect Ophthalmoscopy with 20D lens is the gold standard.
Scleral indentation reveals the break-buckle relationship.
Pre-op B-scan USG is mandatory in dense cataract to assess detachment extent.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the buckle height: it should be at least 2 disc diameters wide to cover the break.
Avoid over-tightening the encircling element to prevent anterior segment ischemia.
Prophylactic drainage of subretinal fluid is controversial; reserve for bullous detachments.
Post-operative myopic shift is expected; warn patients of change in refraction.

sections.title: Indications for Vitrectomy in PDR
content: Non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage (lasting > 1-3 months).
Tractional retinal detachment (TRD) involving or threatening the macula.
Combined tractional/rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
Progressive fibrovascular proliferation despite panretinal photocoagulation (PRP).
Dense premacular subhyaloid hemorrhage.
Iris neovascularization (NVI) or neovascular glaucoma with media opacity.

sections.title: Surgical Step-by-Step: The Core Procedure
content: Step 1: Port placement (usually 3.5-4.0mm from the limbus).
Step 2: Core vitrectomy to clear central hemorrhage.
Step 3: Posterior hyaloid separation (often using triamcinolone for visualization).
Step 4: Membrane delamination vs. segmentation using vertical scissors or pick.
Step 5: Endolaser photocoagulation (the 'new' PRP).
Step 6: Fluid-air/gas exchange or silicone oil tamponade if indicated.

sections.title: Red Flags: Intraoperative Risk Factors
content: Iatrogenic retinal breaks due to over-zealous membrane peeling.
Uncontrolled hemorrhage from fibrovascular stalks.
Unrecognized choroidal effusion.
Damage to the crystalline lens (cataractogenesis).

content.explanation: P: Peripheral clear (vitreous removal), R: Release traction (membrane peeling), E: Endolaser (ablation of ischemic retina), P: Pressure/Tamponade (gas/oil).

sections.title: Preoperative Workup Checklist
content: B-Scan Ultrasonography (to rule out RD).
Gonioscopy (check for NVI/NVA).
OCT (assess macular involvement).
HbA1c optimization (perioperative glycemic control).
Anti-VEGF injection 3-5 days pre-op (to induce regression of neovascularization).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The use of anti-VEGF prior to surgery significantly decreases intraoperative bleeding but may worsen pre-existing TRD through 'contraction effect'.
Internal limiting membrane (ILM) peeling is often required if macular edema persists.
Always check the status of the lens; combine vitrectomy with phacoemulsification if cataract is significant, especially in older patients.
Endolaser should reach the ora serrata to ensure maximum ablation of ischemic retina.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Context
sections.content: Posterior Capsule Opacification (PCO), often called 'secondary cataract,' results from the proliferation, migration, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) of lens epithelial cells (LECs) remaining in the capsular bag after cataract surgery. This forms Elschnig pearls (regenerative) or fibrotic membranes (fibrotic type) on the posterior capsule.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The LEC Cascade
content: 1. Surgical trauma activates dormant LECs.
2. LECs migrate to the posterior capsule equator.
3. Proliferation triggers Elschnig pearl formation (equatorial migration).
4. EMT leads to collagen deposition (fibrotic migration).
5. Capsular contraction ensues, causing IOL decentration.

rows: LEC growth in the capsular fornix

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Consult
content: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) post-Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy.
IOL damage (pitting/cracking) during laser energy delivery.
Significant Intraocular Pressure (IOP) spike > 25 mmHg post-procedure.
Retinal detachment following Nd:YAG laser (High risk in high myopes).
Endophthalmitis (Delayed onset/late-stage).

sections.title: Management Protocol: Nd:YAG Capsulotomy
content: Step 1: Dilate pupil and confirm visual deficit correlates with PCO severity.
Step 2: Topical anesthesia + Apraclonidine 0.5% (to prevent IOP spike).
Step 3: Abraham/Mainster lens placement with coupling gel.
Step 4: Nd:YAG (1064nm) laser; energy 0.8–2.0 mJ; focus slightly posterior to capsule.
Step 5: Create cruciate opening; avoid damage to the central IOL optic.
Step 6: Post-procedure topical steroid/NSAID for 5-7 days.

content.explanation: P: Proliferation of LECs, O: Opacification of Capsule, S: Surgical prevention (polishing), T: Treatment via YAG (or surgical discission).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Square-edged IOL designs significantly reduce PCO by creating a 'barrier' effect.
Hydrodissection and cortical cleanup (the 'polishing' technique) reduce LEC load.
Check for optic capture if performing YAG in sulcus-fixated IOLs.
Always document the specific location of the PCO (e.g., visual axis vs. peripheral).

sections.title: Recent Advances & Studies
sections.content: The 'PCO Study Group' research confirms that hydrophilic IOLs demonstrate higher rates of PCO compared to hydrophobic acrylic IOLs due to lower surface biocompatibility. Recent interest focuses on 'anti-proliferative' IOL coatings (e.g., pharmacologically-active IOLs) to inhibit LEC migration.

sections.title: Risk Stratification: The Collaborative Corneal Transplantation Studies (CCTS)
Red Flags for Impending Failure
content: Khodadoust line (endothelial rejection)
Persistent epithelial defect (PED)
Acute rise in IOP (steroid-induced or synechial)
Wedge-shaped stromal edema
Presence of retrocorneal membrane

content.explanation: Keratic precipitates, Hazy cornea (edema), Overlying epithelial line (Khodadoust), Decreased vision, Anterior chamber cells/flare.

sections.title: Pre-operative Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (assess vascularization intensity).
Step 2: AS-OCT to evaluate retrocorneal membranes and iris-cornea adhesion.
Step 3: Specular microscopy on the donor button (if feasible) to assess endothelial reserve.
Step 4: B-Scan Ultrasound to rule out posterior segment pathology (retinal detachment, endophthalmitis).
Step 5: Infectious workup (culture/PCR) if etiology of primary failure is suspected to be microbial.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Systemic immunosuppression (e.g., Mycophenolate Mofetil 1g BID) is mandatory for patients with >2 prior graft failures.
Always perform a thorough gonioscopy to identify hidden peripheral anterior synechiae that contribute to secondary glaucoma.
For high-risk eyes, consider the use of prophylactic anti-VEGF (Bevacizumab) subconjunctival injections to regress neovascularization prior to surgery.
Post-op steroid tapering in redo cases must be significantly slower than in primary grafts, often spanning 6-12 months.
Monitor for 'Stellate Endotheliopathy' as a subtle, early sign of chronic rejection.

sections.title: Recent Advances
sections.content: Recent landmark studies highlight the role of rho-kinase (ROCK) inhibitors (e.g., Netarsudil 0.02%) in promoting endothelial cell survival and migration post-DMEK. Additionally, emerging evidence suggests that topical immunomodulators (Cyclosporine 0.05% or Tacrolimus 0.03%) significantly decrease late endothelial rejection rates in redo settings. The integration of intraoperative digital overlays for graft trephination has improved the precision of button sizing, reducing post-operative astigmatism in complex cases.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: PESS is characterized by a specific triad of signs: superior sulcus deepening, upper eyelid ptosis, and lower eyelid laxity with enophthalmos. Pathophysiology is rooted in the loss of orbital volume (the globe, plus the surgical removal of surrounding fascia and potential atrophy of fat), leading to a mechanical retraction of the superior levator complex and lack of support for the ocular prosthesis.

sections.title: Key Clinical Features
content: Deepening of the superior conjunctival sulcus
Blepharoptosis (upper lid droop due to loss of prosthesis support)
Enophthalmos (posterior displacement of the prosthesis)
Lower lid ectropion or laxity
'Puffy' or redundant upper eyelid skin
Discharge or poor motility of the implant/prosthesis

sections.title: Etiology: Factors Leading to Volume Loss

rows: Usually proptosis, but can present with asymmetric ptosis

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Evaluation of implant motility and size (Imaging/USG)
Step 2: Replacement of orbital implant (secondary orbital implant exchange)
Step 3: Volume augmentation via dermis-fat graft or porous hydroxyapatite sphere
Step 4: Ptosis surgery (Levator advancement/resection)
Step 5: Lower lid tightening (lateral tarsal strip procedure)

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Investigate
content: Sudden increase in discharge (suspect giant papillary conjunctivitis or infection)
Implant exposure (urgent risk of extrusions)
Recurrent pain in the socket
Unexplained decrease in implant motility

content.explanation: D: Deep Superior Sulcus; P: Ptosis (Upper lid); L: Lower lid laxity/ectropion.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Primary prevention: Use the largest spherical implant that allows for conjunctival closure without tension.
Porous implants (e.g., Medpor, Hydroxyapatite) reduce long-term migration.
Always assess the status of the fornices before planning volume correction.
Consider fat grafting if the deep superior sulcus is the primary complaint.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: SWS is a non-hereditary neurocutaneous disorder caused by a somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene (c.548G>A; p.Arg183Gln). This leads to abnormal capillary venous malformations in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve (V1/V2) and the ipsilateral leptomeninges, resulting in impaired venous drainage, cortical ischemia, and elevated episcleral venous pressure.

sections.title: Clinical Features Checklist
content: Port-wine stain (Nevus flammeus) involving V1 distribution
Leptomeningeal angiomatosis (tram-track calcification)
Early-onset or adult-onset glaucoma
Choroidal hemangioma (tomato-ketchup fundus)
Ipsilateral cerebral atrophy
Contralateral hemiparesis/hemisensory loss
Intellectual disability

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergencies
content: Buphthalmos in infants (emergency IOP control)
Refractory glaucoma unresponsive to timolol/latanoprost
Acute neurological decline (status epilepticus)
Retinal detachment associated with choroidal effusion

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Step 1: Topical anti-glaucoma medication (Prostaglandin analogues, CAIs, Beta-blockers)
Step 2: Goniotomy or Trabeculotomy (if angle dysgenesis is present)
Step 3: Trabeculectomy with Mitomycin-C or Aqueous Shunt devices
Step 4: Cyclophotocoagulation for refractory cases

content.explanation: G: GNAQ mutation; N: Neurocutaneous; A: Angiomatosis (Leptomeningeal); Q: Query IOP early.

sections.title: Key Practice Pearls
content: Monitor for 'tomato-ketchup' fundus (diffuse red-orange choroidal hemangioma)
Risk of choroidal effusion post-trabeculectomy is significantly higher in SWS
Glaucoma is often bimodal: infancy or early adulthood
Always perform gonioscopy to differentiate primary dysgenesis from secondary causes
