sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Endophthalmitis is a severe intraocular inflammation of the vitreous cavity and/or aqueous humor, usually caused by microbial infection. It is a rare but devastating complication, primarily occurring after intraocular surgery (e.g., cataract extraction, intravitreal injection) or penetrating ocular trauma, leading to significant vision loss or even globe atrophy if not promptly and effectively managed. Prevention is paramount due to its severe prognosis.

sections.title: 2.1 Epidemiological Notes
content: Incidence varies by procedure: ~0.05-0.1% for cataract surgery (lower with intracameral antibiotics), 0.01-0.05% for intravitreal injections, up to 0.2% for glaucoma filtration surgery.
Post-traumatic endophthalmitis carries the highest incidence (4-30%), especially with retained intraocular foreign bodies.
Higher incidence reported in developing countries due to varied surgical standards and limited resources.

sections.title: 4. Pillars of Prevention: The Multi-Modal Approach
5. Pre-Operative Strategies
content: Patient Education: Emphasize hygiene, avoiding eye rubbing, and recognizing warning signs.
Risk Factor Identification: Control diabetes, manage blepharitis (topical azithromycin, tea tree oil, lid scrubs), dry eye, lacrimal system issues (dacryocystitis).

Topical Antibiotics: Pre-treatment with broad-spectrum topical antibiotics (e.g., moxifloxacin 0.5%, gatifloxacin 0.5%) 2-3 days prior to surgery, 4x/day. Evidence for routine use is debated but often practiced.
Povidone-Iodine (PVI) Prep: Essential. 5% PVI to periocular skin and eyelashes; 10% PVI diluted to 0.5-1% for conjunctival cul-de-sac. Apply 3-5 minutes before incision, then rinse.

sections.title: 6. Intra-Operative Asepsis & Technique: The Surgical Shield
content: Step 1: Strict Aseptic Technique — Proper hand scrubbing (alcohol-based rubs or iodophor/chlorhexidine scrub), sterile gowning, gloving, draping.
Step 2: Periocular Antisepsis — Application of 5-10% Povidone-Iodine to periocular skin, extending to forehead and malar regions. Allow to dry.
Step 3: Conjunctival Sac Antisepsis — Irrigation of conjunctival sac with 0.5-1% Povidone-Iodine solution for at least 30-60 seconds, then partially rinse.
Step 4: Eyelid Speculum & Draping — Use a sterile speculum to isolate lashes from the surgical field. Apply sterile drape with a sticky aperture to minimize contamination.
Step 5: Incision Construction — Create a self-sealing clear corneal incision or scleral tunnel incision to prevent external microbial ingress. Avoid excessive manipulation.
Step 6: Minimize Contact — Avoid instruments contacting lid margins or lashes. Use single-use instruments where possible.
Step 7: Intracameral Antibiotics — Inject at the conclusion of surgery. This is the SINGLE MOST EFFECTIVE intervention for preventing post-cataract endophthalmitis.

rows: 1 mg in 0.1 mL (prepared from 50 mg/5 mL vial, then diluted)
2nd gen Cephalosporin, cell wall synthesis inhibitor. Broad Gram-positive coverage.
Strong evidence (ESCRS study) for efficacy; low cost.
Risk of allergic reaction (cephalosporin), requires dilution in pharmacy/OR, not effective against MRSA or some Gram-negatives.

4th gen Fluoroquinolone, inhibits DNA gyrase. Broad spectrum (Gram-positive, Gram-negative, atypical).
Ready-to-use (preservative-free topical formulation), excellent ocular penetration, good Gram-positive and Gram-negative coverage.
Higher cost, off-label use (topical solution injected), potential for resistance development, no large-scale randomized trials like ESCRS for intracameral use.
Glycopeptide, inhibits cell wall synthesis. Excellent Gram-positive coverage, including MRSA.
Risk of hemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis (HORV) – **RED FLAG**, increasing resistance, nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity with systemic use (not relevant for intracameral).

sections.title: 8. Post-Operative Care & Vigilance
content: Topical Antibiotics: Continue for 1-2 weeks post-surgery (e.g., moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin). Reduces bacterial load on ocular surface during wound healing. (Debate exists, but commonly practiced).
Topical Steroids: Control inflammation (e.g., prednisolone acetate 1%, difluprednate 0.05%, dexamethasone 0.1%). Reduces inflammatory response but does not protect against infection.
Wound Integrity Check: Ensure adequate wound hydration and self-sealing. Consider suture if wound leak detected.
Patient Education: Reinforce instructions on medication use, hand hygiene, avoiding eye rubbing, and immediate reporting of any 'red flag' symptoms (pain, vision loss, redness).

branches: - Systemic: Diabetes Mellitus, Immunosuppression (HIV, chemotherapy), Atopy/Psoriasis, Systemic infections (septicemia)
- Ocular: Blepharitis, Meibomian Gland Dysfunction, Conjunctivitis, Chronic Dacryocystitis, Pterygium, Prior Ocular Surgery, Compromised Corneal Surface
- Behavior: Poor Hygiene, Non-compliance with medications
- Incision Type: Clear corneal (compared to scleral tunnel), non-self-sealing wounds, wound dehiscence
- Surgical Complexity: Prolonged surgery, Posterior capsular rupture, Vitreous loss, use of multiple instruments
- IOL Type/Position: Atypical IOLs (e.g., sulcus-fixated), Suture fixation
- Surgical Environment: Breach in sterile technique, contaminated solutions/instruments
- Post-operative topical steroid overuse (unlikely if antibiotics used)

sections.title: 10. Red Flags / Emergency Signs Post-Surgery
content: Progressive DECREASE IN VISION (out of proportion to expected post-op course)
SEVERE OCULAR PAIN (disproportionate to typical post-op discomfort), often worsening over time
Marked REDNESS of the eye (circumcorneal injection, chemosis)
Hypopyon (pus level in the anterior chamber)
Lid edema and periorbital swelling
Corneal edema and infiltrates (less common but severe)
Vitreous haze or white exudates (on slit-lamp or fundoscopy)
Loss of red reflex or poor view of fundus
IOL deposits or inflammatory membranes on IOL/capsule

P: Povidone-Iodine (periocular & intracameral)
A: Aseptic Technique (strict, meticulous)
C: Cefuroxime/Moxifloxacin (intracameral antibiotic)

S: Self-Sealing Incision (secure wound closure)

sections.title: 13. Key Clinical Pearls for Prevention
content: Povidone-iodine is the single most important and cost-effective antiseptic measure. Do not skip it!
Intracameral antibiotics (Cefuroxime 1mg or Moxifloxacin 100-200µg) are the strongest evidence-based prophylactic measure for post-cataract endophthalmitis.
Meticulous wound construction and hydration are critical for preventing external bacterial ingress.
Aggressively treat pre-existing blepharitis or dry eye before elective intraocular surgery.
Prompt recognition and referral of 'red flag' symptoms can differentiate endophthalmitis from sterile inflammation and save vision.

sections.title: 14. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: ESCRS Endophthalmitis Study (2007): Landmark randomized clinical trial demonstrating 5-fold reduction in endophthalmitis with intracameral cefuroxime (1mg in 0.1ml) at the conclusion of cataract surgery. No significant benefit from pre-operative topical levofloxacin.
AAO Preferred Practice Patterns: Strongly recommend perioperative Povidone-Iodine application and consider intracameral antibiotics for cataract surgery.

Moxifloxacin vs. Cefuroxime: Growing adoption of intracameral moxifloxacin (100-200µg) due to its broad spectrum, ready-to-use formulation (from preservative-free topical drops), and excellent intraocular penetration, despite lacking a large-scale RCT like the ESCRS study.

HORV and Vancomycin: The association of hemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis (HORV) with intracameral vancomycin (especially in bilateral simultaneous surgery) has led to recommendations against its routine use.

Role of Post-Op Topical Antibiotics: Current evidence suggests minimal additional benefit of post-operative topical antibiotics when intracameral antibiotics are used, but practice patterns vary. Some studies indicate they may prolong resistance development.

sections.title: 15. Special Population Considerations
content: Diabetic Patients: Higher risk of endophthalmitis. Emphasize stringent glycemic control pre-operatively and meticulous attention to all prophylactic measures.

Immunocompromised Patients (HIV, transplant, systemic chemotherapy): Increased risk, often with atypical organisms (fungal, less common bacteria). May warrant broader-spectrum or longer duration antibiotic prophylaxis, and lower threshold for aggressive management.

Pediatric Patients: Often undergo surgery under general anesthesia, which may mask early symptoms. Compliance with post-op medications can be challenging. Higher incidence of post-traumatic endophthalmitis.
Patients with Blepharitis/MGD: Requires aggressive pre-operative treatment (e.g., topical azithromycin, hypochlorous acid, lid scrubs) to reduce bacterial load on lid margin and lashes.

sections.title: 16. Surgical Management of a Suspected Case (Briefly, for Context)
content: Step 1: Immediate Referral to Retina/Endophthalmitis Specialist.
Step 2: Aqueous/Vitreous Tap for Microscopy (Gram stain, KOH) & Culture (aerobic, anaerobic, fungal).
Step 3: Intravitreal Antibiotics Injection (e.g., Vancomycin 1mg/0.1mL + Ceftazidime 2.25mg/0.1mL or Amikacin 0.4mg/0.1mL).
Step 4: Consider Vitrectomy if severe vision loss (hand motion or worse), non-responsive to injections, or fungal etiology suspected (EVRS study criteria).
Step 5: Topical and Systemic Antibiotics (adjunctive).

sections.title: 17. Future Directions in Prevention
sections.content: Research continues into novel preventative strategies, including sustained-release antibiotic implants, antimicrobial coatings for intraocular lenses, and advanced diagnostic techniques for rapid pathogen identification to guide targeted prophylaxis. The goal is to further reduce the already low, but still significant, incidence of this vision-threatening condition.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Secondary Sjögren Syndrome (sSS) is defined as the presence of keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS) and xerostomia in patients with a pre-existing systemic autoimmune disease, most commonly Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). Unlike Primary Sjögren, sSS occurs later in the disease course and is driven by the underlying connective tissue disease's inflammatory milieu, leading to progressive lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands.

branches: Acinar Apoptosis: Loss of secretory function
Neural Signaling Interference: Lacrimal gland fatigue

rows: ≤ 5 mm / 5 minutes in at least one eye

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Exam Findings
content: Reduced Tear Meniscus Height: < 0.2mm is highly suggestive.
Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT): < 10 seconds (instability); < 5 seconds (severe).
Filamentary Keratitis: Muco-epithelial strands attached to corneal surface.
Mucus Plaquing: Large grey-white opacities in severe KCS.
Lid Margin Disease: Concurrent Meibomian Gland Dysfunction (MGD).
Corneal Neovascularization: Peripheral pannus from chronic inflammation.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Sight-Threatening RA Complications
content: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK): Juxtalimbal thinning/ulceration with epithelial loss.
Necrotizing Scleritis: Severe pain, 'porcelain' white sclera (vasculitis-associated).
Corneal Melting: Sterile 'keratolysis' leading to rapid perforation.
Scleromalacia Perforans: Asymptomatic scleral thinning in long-standing RA.

sections.title: Stepped Management Protocol (TFOS DEWS II)
content: Step 1: Patient education, environmental modification, Preservative-Free (PF) artificial tears, lid hygiene.
Step 2: Punctal plugs, Topical Cyclosporine 0.05% or 0.1%, Lifitegrast 5%, Corticosteroid pulses, Oral secretagogues (Pilocarpine).
Step 3: Oral macrolides (for MGD), Autologous Serum Tears (20% or 50% concentration), Scleral lenses (PROSE).
Step 4: Long-term topical steroids, Amniotic membrane grafting, Surgical punctal occlusion, Tarsorrhaphy.

sections.title: Systemic Investigation Workup
content: Rheumatoid Factor (RF): Elevated in 70-80% of RA.
Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (Anti-CCP): More specific than RF (95%).
ANA: Often positive in sSS/RA overlap.
Anti-Ro (SS-A) and Anti-La (SS-B): Hallmarks of Sjögren's.
ESR/CRP: Markers of systemic inflammatory activity.
Salivary Gland Biopsy: If serology is equivocal but clinical suspicion is high.

content.explanation: S: Surface staining (Oxford/SICCA), I: Infiltration (Minor salivary gland biopsy), C: CCP/RF antibodies positive, C: Clinical dry mouth/eye symptoms, A: Anti-SSA/SSB positive.

sections.title: Surgical & Interventional Approaches
content: Punctal Cautery: For definitive occlusion in recalcitrant sSS.
Lateral Tarsorrhaphy: Reduces evaporative surface area in severe exposure/melting.
Amniotic Membrane (ProKera/Cryopreserved): Promotes healing in persistent epithelial defects (PED).
Cyanoacrylate Glue: Emergency management of corneal microperforations in RA melts.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Evidence
sections.content: The TFOS DEWS II (2017) report revolutionized the definition of dry eye to include the role of neurosensory abnormalities. The DREAM Study (2018) questioned the efficacy of Omega-3 fatty acids over placebo for dry eye, highlighting the importance of the tear film's aqueous and lipid components in systemic diseases like RA.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: Never treat PUK with topical steroids alone; it usually signals active systemic necrotizing vasculitis and requires urgent systemic immunosuppression.
Secondary Sjögren patients often have more severe ocular surface disease than Primary Sjögren due to the additive effects of RA-related inflammation.
Always check for dental caries and oral health; xerostomia in sSS leads to rapid periodontal decline.
Filamentary keratitis is best treated by manual removal followed by 5% NaCl or topical N-acetylcysteine (10%).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with Fluorescein staining to delineate epithelial defect.
Step 2: Measure lagophthalmos distance in mm using a ruler.
Step 3: Schirmer's test/TBUT to assess total tear film insufficiency.
Step 4: Corneal sensation testing (CN V integrity).
Step 5: If ulceration is present: Corneal scraping for culture and sensitivity.

content.explanation: A: Artificial tears (frequent), B: Barrier (lubricating ointment), C: Closure (taping/suture), D: Dew (humidity chamber), E: Eyelid surgery (tarsorrhaphy).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis
content: Neurotrophic Keratitis (diminished corneal sensation)
Severe Dry Eye Disease (SS, MGD)
Infectious Keratitis (Bacterial, Fungal, Viral)
Traumatic Abrasions
Drug Toxicity (preservative-induced)

sections.title: Step-by-Step Management Ladder
content: Level 1: Preservative-free artificial tears Q1H and viscous gels QHS.
Level 2: Moisture chamber goggles or taping the eyelid closed at night.
Level 3: Therapeutic Scleral Contact Lens or Amniotic Membrane Transplantation.
Level 4: Temporary tarsorrhaphy (suture or adhesive).
Level 5: Surgical reconstruction (Gold weight, ectropion repair, or permanent tarsorrhaphy).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Always evaluate for concurrent Bell's Palsy or structural lid malposition.
Overnight protection is paramount; the blink reflex is absent during sleep.
If a patient is in an ICU setting, prophylactic lubrication is mandatory to prevent 'ICU-related exposure keratopathy'.
Corneal melting can occur rapidly; monitor thickness via anterior segment OCT if suspicion is high.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Choroidal folds (striate choroidopathy) involve physical buckling of the inner choroid and RPE. Pathophysiology is usually mechanical (hypotony, posterior scleritis) or infiltrative (tumors, inflammation). The folds typically appear as alternating light and dark lines, often horizontal in the posterior pole.

content.explanation: H: Hypotony (Post-surgical), I: Inflammation (Scleritis), S: Scleral buckling/masses, T: Tumors (Choroidal hemangioma/melanoma), O: Orbital processes (Pseudotumor), R: Retinochoroidal scarring, R: Retrobulbar mass, Y: Young patients (Idiopathic).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Pain on EOMs (suggests Scleritis)
Proptosis or eyelid fullness (suggests Orbital Mass)
Vision loss < 20/40 (suggests maculopathy)
Associated RAPD (suggests Optic Nerve pathology)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: 1. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (+90D) to identify alternating striae.
2. B-Scan Ultrasonography (Look for T-sign/Scleral thickening).
3. OCT Macula (Cross-sections showing RPE undulation).
4. CT Orbit/MRI (If orbital mass is suspected).
5. FA/ICGA (To rule out choroidal neovascularization or inflammatory activity).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Boards
content: Choroidal folds usually preserve vision unless they involve the fovea.
They are commonly mistaken for papilledema; however, the vessel caliber in choroidal folds is usually normal.
Fluorescein Angiography reveals alternating hyper/hypofluorescent lines corresponding to the peaks and valleys of the folds.
If associated with disc edema, prioritize ruling out posterior scleritis and orbital masses first.

summary: An altitudinal visual field defect is a semi-circular loss of the superior or inferior visual field, typically indicating pathology along the visual pathway from the optic nerve to the chiasm. sections.title: Definition & Topography
sections.content: An altitudinal defect is a visual field loss that respects the horizontal meridian. Superior altitudinal defects are classically associated with inferior optic nerve/retinal pathology, while inferior altitudinal defects result from superior involvement. Unlike hemianopias, these defects are primarily pre-chiasmal in origin.

title: Trabeculectomy: The Gold Standard in Glaucoma Surgery
summary: Trabeculectomy is a filtering surgical procedure creating a new drainage pathway for aqueous humor, forming a subconjunctival bleb to lower intraocular pressure. It remains the most effective surgical option for medically uncontrolled or advanced glaucoma, often augmented with antimetabolites to enhance success rates and prevent scarring.

data.title: Trabeculectomy: The Gold Standard in Glaucoma Surgery
data.summary: Trabeculectomy is a filtering surgical procedure creating a new drainage pathway for aqueous humor, forming a subconjunctival bleb to lower intraocular pressure. It remains the most effective surgical option for medically uncontrolled or advanced glaucoma, often augmented with antimetabolites to enhance success rates and prevent scarring.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Trabeculectomy is a filtering surgical procedure that creates a new drainage pathway for aqueous humor from the anterior chamber to the subconjunctival space, forming a bleb. This bypasses the conventional outflow pathway, lowering intraocular pressure (IOP). It is considered the gold standard for surgically managing glaucoma when medical therapy, laser treatment, or less invasive procedures fail to achieve target IOP or halt disease progression.

sections.title: 2.1. Risk Factors for Surgical Failure
content: Young age (<40 years)
African/African-American ethnicity
Secondary glaucomas (e.g., neovascular, uveitic, aphakic)
Previous ocular surgery (e.g., vitrectomy, multiple laser procedures)
Extensive conjunctival scarring or inflammation
Poor compliance with post-operative medications

branches: 1. Scleral Flap: Creation of a partial-thickness scleral flap.
2. Trabeculectomy/Sclerectomy: Excision of a deep scleral block to create an ostium into the anterior chamber.
3. Peripheral Iridectomy: Creation of an opening in the iris to prevent pupillary block.
4. Aqueous Outflow: Aqueous humor flows from AC → ostium → under scleral flap → into subconjunctival space.
5. Bleb Formation: Formation of a subconjunctival filtering bleb for aqueous absorption by local vessels and lymphatics.
6. Antimetabolites (MMC/5-FU): Applied to modulate wound healing, inhibiting fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition, thereby preventing bleb scarring and failure.

rows: Older technique, less common due to higher failure rates.
Most common, significantly improved long-term success rates, but increased risk of thin bleb and leaks.
Convenience of a single surgery for cataract and glaucoma, but often results in less predictable or lower IOP reduction than trabeculectomy alone.
Offers broader surgical exposure, but potentially higher risk of early bleb leak and hypotony.
Conjunctival incision 2-3mm posterior to the limbus
Considered more technically challenging to dissect, but associated with lower rates of early bleb leak and better bleb integrity.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Indications
content: **Progressive optic neuropathy / visual field loss** despite Maximal Tolerated Medical Therapy (MTMT).
**Intolerable side effects** or documented poor adherence to glaucoma medications.
**Target IOP not achieved** with MTMT, laser procedures (e.g., SLT), or less invasive MIGS procedures.
**Advanced glaucoma** with high baseline IOP and significant risk of rapid progression and vision loss.
**Certain types of glaucoma** with poor response to conventional treatment: Neovascular glaucoma, Uveitic glaucoma, some congenital glaucomas, aphakic/pseudophakic glaucoma, trauma-induced glaucoma.

sections.title: 6. Pre-operative Ocular Examination
content: **Best-Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA)** and Refraction.
**IOP measurement** (Goldmann applanation tonometry is standard).

**Slit-lamp examination**: Assess cornea (edema, scarring), anterior chamber (depth, cells/flare), iris (PAS, neovascularization), lens (cataract), and conjunctiva (scarring, inflammation, blepharitis – crucial for surgical planning).
**Gonioscopy**: Evaluate angle anatomy, presence of Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS), blood, or pigment.
**Dilated Fundus Examination**: Detailed assessment of optic nerve head (C/D ratio, rim tissue, hemorrhages, RNFL), and macula.
**Pachymetry**: Central Corneal Thickness (CCT).

sections.title: 6.1. Post-operative Ocular Examination
content: **Bleb morphology**: Evaluate location (typically superior-nasal/temporal), area, height, vascularity (avascular is ideal), transparency (thin and translucent is ideal). Use Moorfields Bleb Grading System.
**Seidel test**: To identify any conjunctival wound leak.
**Anterior Chamber (AC) depth & clarity**: Note depth (shallow indicates over-filtration/wound leak) and presence of cells/flare (inflammation or infection).
**Scleral flap**: Position, integrity, and any signs of dehiscence or overlying congestion.
**Peripheral iridectomy**: Confirm patency to rule out pupillary block.
**IOP**: Measured cautiously to avoid bleb rupture or further hypotony.
**Fundus**: Check for choroidal detachments, hypotony maculopathy (optic disc edema, retinal striae).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. **Detailed Ophthalmic History**: Glaucoma type, duration, previous medical/laser/surgical treatments, compliance, systemic comorbidities.
2. **Baseline Ophthalmic Examination**: BCVA, IOP, Slit-lamp, Gonioscopy, Dilated Fundus Exam (Optic Nerve).
3. **Visual Field Testing**: Humphrey Visual Field Analysis (HVFA 24-2 or 30-2) to document baseline functional damage and progression.
4. **Optic Nerve & RNFL Imaging**: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) of optic nerve head and Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL) for structural assessment.
5. **Pachymetry**: Central Corneal Thickness (CCT) measurement.
6. **Biometry**: If combined with cataract surgery, for Intraocular Lens (IOL) power calculation.
7. **B-scan Ultrasonography**: Indicated if media opacities (e.g., dense cataract, vitreous hemorrhage) prevent fundus view.
8. **Systemic Workup**: Pre-anesthetic evaluation, routine blood tests (CBC, electrolytes, coagulation profile, especially if on anticoagulants).

sections.title: 9. Glaucoma Severity & Bleb Grading
sections.content: Trabeculectomy is typically considered for moderate to severe glaucoma, or in cases demonstrating significant progression despite aggressive medical and laser therapies. Glaucoma severity is often classified using criteria like Hodapp-Parrish-Anderson, based on optic nerve damage and visual field loss (Mild, Moderate, Severe).

rows: Extent of the bleb. Large, diffuse blebs are generally better.
Vertical elevation of the bleb. Elevated is generally better.
Presence of vessels. Avascular or minimally vascularized is ideal.
Clarity of the bleb wall. Clear or translucent is ideal (indicates thinness).
Seidel test result. Negative is ideal.
Morphology (e.g., diffuse, cystic, encapsulated). Diffuse blebs are generally associated with better outcomes.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment: Peri-operative Protocols
content: **Pre-operative**: Discontinue prostaglandin analogs 1-2 weeks prior to reduce inflammation. If safe, discontinue systemic anti-coagulants/antiplatelets (consult with PCP). Initiate topical antibiotics (e.g., Gatifloxacin 0.5% q.i.d.) 1-2 days before surgery.
**Intra-operative**: Use Balanced Salt Solution (BSS) for irrigation. Viscoelastics (e.g., Healon, Viscoat) may be used to maintain anterior chamber depth and prevent collapse.

**Post-operative Medications**: Topical steroids (e.g., Prednisolone Acetate 1% or Dexamethasone 0.1%) frequently (e.g., q1-2h) then tapered over 6-12 weeks, depending on inflammation and bleb appearance. Topical antibiotics (e.g., Moxifloxacin 0.5% q.i.d.) for 1-2 weeks. Cycloplegics (e.g., Atropine 1% b.i.d. or Cyclopentolate 1% t.i.d.) to prevent pupillary block, minimize inflammation, and deepen the anterior chamber.

rows: Laser suture lysis (e.g., using Argon laser) or transconjunctival suture cutting with a needle. Anterior chamber reformation with viscoelastic. Oral Acetazolamide (Diamox) if urgently needed.
Bleb needling with 5-FU/MMC for early signs of bleb failure.
Transconjunctival scleral flap compression. Suture placement/tightening if wound leak. Viscoelastic injection into AC. Blood injection into AC/bleb. Bed rest, head elevation, cycloplegics.
Urgent identification and repair of conjunctival wound leak (Seidel+).

Aggressive cycloplegics (Atropine 1%), topical/oral steroids, hyperosmotic agents (Mannitol). YAG laser posterior capsulotomy or hyaloidotomy (if pseudophakic/aphakic). Vitrectomy +/- lensectomy if refractory.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Step-by-Step Trabeculectomy
content: 1. **Anesthesia**: Local (peribulbar block e.g., 2% Lidocaine with Bupivacaine) or General Anesthesia.

2. **Conjunctival Flap**: Create a limbal-based (preferred) or fornix-based conjunctival flap. (Limbal-based: 2-3mm posterior limbal incision, dissect anteriorly to limbus. Fornix-based: Limbal incision, dissect posteriorly).
3. **Hemostasis**: Gentle wet-field cautery of episcleral vessels to ensure a bloodless field.
4. **Scleral Flap**: Create a partial-thickness, trapezoidal or rectangular (e.g., 3.5mm base, 3mm length) scleral flap, approximately 1/2 scleral thickness, hinge at the limbus.

5. **Antimetabolite Application**: Apply sponges soaked in Mitomycin C (0.02-0.04% concentration, for 1-3 minutes depending on risk factors) or 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) under the scleral and conjunctival flaps. Thoroughly irrigate the area with copious Balanced Salt Solution (BSS) (e.g., 200ml).
6. **Scleral Flap Sutures**: Place 2-3 releasable or adjustable 10-0 nylon sutures at the corners of the scleral flap. The tension of these sutures is critical for controlled aqueous outflow.
7. **Paracentesis**: Create a side-port entry with a 15-degree blade into the anterior chamber for post-operative IOP control and AC manipulation.

8. **Trabeculectomy/Sclerectomy**: Elevate the scleral flap. Using a Kelly punch or Vannas scissors, excise a block of deep sclera and trabecular meshwork (approx. 1x2mm) to create the ostium into the anterior chamber.
9. **Peripheral Iridectomy (PI)**: Grasp the peripheral iris and excise a small piece (e.g., using Vannas scissors or vitrector) to prevent post-operative pupillary block.
10. **Scleral Flap Closure**: Tie the previously placed scleral flap sutures. Assess intraoperative flow; the target IOP at this stage is typically 5-10 mmHg. Adjust suture tension if needed.
11. **Conjunctival Closure**: Close the conjunctiva meticulously with 10-0 nylon or 8-0 Vicryl sutures to achieve a watertight seal. Perform a Seidel test to ensure no leaks.
12. **Subconjunctival Injection**: Administer subconjunctival steroids (e.g., Dexamethasone 4mg) and/or antibiotics (e.g., Gentamicin 20mg).
13. **Eye Shield/Patch**: Apply a protective eye shield or patch.

sections.title: 12. Complications: Early (First Weeks Post-Op)
content: **Hypotony**: IOP < 6mmHg. Caused by over-filtration or wound leak. Can lead to choroidal detachment and hypotony maculopathy (optic disc edema, retinal striae, decreased vision).
**Flat Anterior Chamber (AC)**: Due to hypotony, wound leak, or pupillary block. Graded I-III based on extent of iris/lens contact with cornea.
**Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage**: Rare but devastating. Characterized by sudden severe pain, rapid vision loss, and a firm eye. Requires urgent surgical intervention.
**Conjunctival Wound Leak**: Positive Seidel test, usually at the conjunctival incision. Increases risk of infection and hypotony.
**Aqueous Misdirection (Malignant Glaucoma)**: Shallow AC with normal or high IOP despite a patent peripheral iridectomy. Requires aggressive medical and/or surgical management.
**Hyphema**: Intraoperative or early post-operative bleeding into the anterior chamber.
**Blebitis/Endophthalmitis**: Infection of the bleb or intraocular contents. Presents with acute pain, redness, vision loss, hypopyon, and vitreous inflammation. Urgent referral for tap and inject.
**Diplopia**: May result from hypotony or direct trauma to extraocular muscles during surgery.

sections.title: 12.1. Complications: Late (Months to Years Post-Op)
content: **Bleb Failure**: The most common late complication, typically due to excessive subconjunctival fibrosis and scarring leading to a gradual increase in IOP. Can manifest as an encapsulated bleb.
**Chronic Bleb Leak**: Persistent conjunctival dehiscence or thinning over the bleb. Significantly increases the long-term risk of late-onset blebitis/endophthalmitis.
**Cataract**: Accelerated progression of lens opacities, particularly posterior subcapsular cataracts, due to altered aqueous dynamics and inflammation.
**Late-onset Blebitis/Endophthalmitis**: Infection occurring months or years after surgery, often associated with thin, avascular blebs or chronic bleb leaks.
**Bleb Dysesthesia**: Patient discomfort or irritation from a prominent, typically superior, filtering bleb.
**Surgically Induced Astigmatism**: Changes in corneal curvature due to surgical manipulation.
**Chronic Choroidal Detachment**: Persistent hypotony can lead to chronic choroidal effusions, potentially requiring drainage.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs Post-Trabeculectomy
content: **Sudden severe eye pain and precipitous vision loss**: HIGH SUSPICION for Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage or Acute Endophthalmitis. Requires immediate emergency evaluation.

**Flat anterior chamber (especially Grade II/III)**: Poses immediate risk of permanent corneal decompensation, peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS), and irreversible vision loss. Urgent intervention is required.
**Positive Seidel test with low IOP**: Indicates a conjunctival wound leak, carrying a high risk for intraocular infection. Requires urgent repair or pressure patching.

**Signs of infection (Blebitis/Endophthalmitis)**: Any purulent discharge from the bleb, bleb congestion/whitening, hypopyon, significant vision drop, or vitreous cells. Requires urgent ophthalmology consultation and typically vitreous tap and inject.

**Uncontrolled high IOP (>25-30 mmHg)**: May indicate pupillary block, aqueous misdirection, or early bleb failure requiring urgent intervention (e.g., suture lysis, bleb needling, medical management).

content.mnemonic: To systematically assess a filtering bleb post-trabeculectomy, remember **B.L.E.T.S.**
content.explanation:
• **B**ody: Size, shape, and extent (e.g., diffuse, cystic, localized).
• **L**ocation: Position of the bleb (e.g., superior, superior-nasal).
• **E**levation: Height of the bleb (e.g., flat, moderate, high).
• **T**ransparency: Clarity and thickness of the bleb wall (e.g., clear, translucent, opaque/scarred).
• **S**eidel Test: To check for active aqueous leakage from the bleb or conjunctival wound.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Individualize Antimetabolite Use**: Higher concentrations (e.g., 0.04% MMC) or longer application times (e.g., 3 mins) are generally reserved for high-risk eyes (young patients, secondary glaucomas, previous failed surgery).

**Suture Lysis/Removal is Key**: Do not hesitate to perform laser suture lysis or transconjunctival suture removal if post-operative IOP is elevated and the bleb appears restricted. This is a critical tool for early IOP control.
**Watertight Conjunctival Closure**: This is paramount to prevent early wound leaks, reduce the risk of hypotony, and minimize the risk of infection.
**Early Bleb Failure Management**: Initial bleb failure due to fibrosis is often amenable to bleb needling with adjunctive antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU or MMC injection) to re-establish filtration.

**Aggressive Steroid Regimen**: An individualized, often intense, post-operative topical steroid taper is essential to modulate wound healing and prevent excessive fibrosis, which is the primary cause of bleb failure.

**Patient Education is Vital**: Thoroughly educate patients on symptoms of complications (especially infection) and the importance of strict compliance with post-operative medication and follow-up schedules.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (TVT) Study**: This landmark comparative study evaluated outcomes of trabeculectomy with MMC vs. Baerveldt glaucoma implant for refractory glaucoma. It found similar IOP control but different complication profiles (trabeculectomy had more early complications, tube had more late complications like diplopia).

**Micro-Invasive Glaucoma Surgery (MIGS) Devices**: Devices like the XEN Gel Stent (Allergan) and Preserflo Microshunt (Kahook Dual Blade) aim to create subconjunctival drainage, offering a filtering surgery with potentially lower complication rates than traditional trabeculectomy. They are often considered for earlier-stage or less severe glaucoma, bridging the gap between trabeculectomy and less invasive MIGS.

**Optimized Antifibrotic Delivery**: Ongoing research explores novel antifibrotic agents and sustained-release drug delivery systems to improve bleb longevity and reduce the need for repeat antimetabolite applications or needling procedures.

rows: Higher failure rates due to vigorous wound healing. Mitomycin C (MMC) is almost always used. Often a secondary procedure after failed goniotomy/trabeculotomy. Challenges with IOP measurement and post-operative compliance.
Increased risk of bleb failure. Antimetabolites are essential. Careful consideration of vitreous prolapse through the ostium if the posterior capsule is absent.

Requires meticulous control of inflammation pre- and post-operatively. Higher risk of failure due to inflammatory mediators and synechiae formation. Intensive topical and/or systemic steroids are standard.

Crucial to achieve regression of neovascularization with pre-operative Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) and anti-VEGF injections (e.g., intravitreal bevacizumab 1.25mg/0.05ml). Very high risk of bleb failure if not adequately managed.
Increased risk of hypotony maculopathy due to a pre-existing stretched retina and thinner sclera, making IOP reduction more delicate.

sections.title: Indications for Surgery
content: Progression of glaucomatous optic neuropathy despite maximum tolerated medical therapy.
Inability to tolerate topical anti-glaucoma medications (e.g., ocular surface disease).
Target IOP not achieved despite selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT).
Poor patient compliance with chronic drop regimen.
Need for low target IOP (e.g., advanced disease with narrow rim).

sections.title: Absolute & Relative Contraindications
content: Active external ocular infection (Blepharitis, Conjunctivitis).
Neovascular glaucoma (relative, often requires MIGS/tube first).
Severe conjunctival scarring (precludes successful bleb formation).
Patient unable to remain supine/cooperate during surgery.
Risk of profound hypotony (e.g., high myopia, underlying scleral pathology).

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Conjunctival peritomy (limbal-based or fornix-based).
Step 2: Mitomycin-C application (usually 0.2–0.4 mg/ml for 1–3 mins).
Step 3: Scleral flap creation (approx. 3x3 mm partial thickness).
Step 4: Paracentesis entry.
Step 5: Sclerostomy (punching the block) & peripheral iridectomy (PI).
Step 6: Scleral flap closure with releasable 10-0 nylon sutures.
Step 7: Water-tight conjunctival closure (running or interrupted sutures).

content.explanation: S: Steroids (frequent topical), T: Topical Antibiotics, A: Avoid pressure/rubbing, M: Monitor IOP/Seidel, P: Pupil dilation (if synechiae).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Success
content: A well-functioning bleb is diffuse, vascular, and non-cystic.
Always assess the bleb morphology using the 'Indiana Bleb Appearance Grading Scale'.
Early post-op: Use laser suture lysis if IOP remains elevated at 1-2 weeks.
If Seidel is positive, consider pressure patching or bandage contact lens.
Prophylactic antibiotic use should continue until the conjunctival wound is fully epithelized.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Trabeculectomy is a guarded filtration procedure. It involves the creation of a partial-thickness scleral flap, an excision of a block of trabecular meshwork and peripheral iris (peripheral iridectomy), and re-suturing the flap to allow aqueous humor to flow from the anterior chamber into a sub-conjunctival space (bleb).

sections.title: Surgical Technique Workflow
content: 1. Conjunctival peritomy: Limbal-based or Fornix-based incision.
2. Hemostasis: Cautery application to sclera to ensure a dry field.
3. Mitomycin-C (MMC) application: 0.2-0.4 mg/ml for 1-3 minutes under conjunctiva.
4. Scleral flap creation: 4x4mm partial thickness trapezoid or triangular flap.
5. Sclerostomy: Excision of the block containing trabecular meshwork.
6. Peripheral Iridectomy (PI): Prevention of iris plugging the sclerostomy.
7. Scleral flap closure: Titratable 10-0 nylon sutures to regulate aqueous flow.
8. Water-tight conjunctival closure.

content.explanation: Fibrosis (subconjunctival), Infection (late blebitis), Leaks (seidel positive), Tenon's cyst (encapsulation), Epiretinal membrane/maculopathy (hypotony), Retinal detachment.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Follow-up
content: Slit-lamp examination: Assess Seidel's test (Fluorescein dilution), bleb morphology (Height, Vascularity, Area).
Gonioscopy: Verify patency of the internal sclerostomy.
Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT): Visualize internal filtration pathway and fluid flow.
Visual Field testing: Monitor progression post-IOP stabilization.
IOP Monitoring: Diurnal curves in the first week post-op.

sections.title: Red Flag Warnings
content: Seidel positive test: Immediate patch or suturing required to prevent endophthalmitis.
Flat Anterior Chamber (AC): Risk of corneal endothelial decompensation and peripheral anterior synechiae.
Late-onset purulent discharge: Rule out bleb-associated endophthalmitis immediately (Ocular emergency).
Extreme hypotony (IOP < 5 mmHg): Risk of suprachoroidal hemorrhage.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: MMC usage significantly improves surgical success but increases the risk of thin, avascular 'cystic' blebs.
For fornix-based flaps, ensure the Tenon's capsule is well-anchored to the limbus to prevent retraction.
Adjustable sutures are preferred for post-operative titration of aqueous outflow.
Laser Suture Lysis (LSL): Use argon laser (typically 500-1000mW) 1-2 weeks post-op to increase flow if IOP is elevated.
The 'Needling' procedure: Effective intervention for encapsulated (Tenon's) cysts appearing 4-8 weeks post-op.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Examination
content: Always auscultate the globe if the eye is quiet to rule out low-flow carotid-cavernous fistulas.
A 'quiet' eye with proptosis is a hallmark of low-grade, slow-growing tumors (e.g., cavernous hemangioma).
Fat suppression is mandatory on MRI to distinguish orbital fat from infiltrative masses.
Inferior displacement suggests a superior orbital mass (e.g., lacrimal gland tumor).
Always evaluate for eyelid retraction, which strongly points towards thyroid eye disease even in unilateral presentation.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Transient Visual Loss (TVL), or amaurosis fugax, is defined as a monocular or binocular visual deficit lasting seconds to hours with full spontaneous recovery. Incidence increases significantly with age, particularly in patients >60, mirroring the prevalence of carotid artery disease and giant cell arteritis (GCA).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Age >50 with new onset headaches or scalp tenderness (Consider GCA)
Altitudinal or 'curtain coming down' sensation (Suggests carotid source)
Associated motor or sensory deficits (Suggests TIA/Stroke)
Pulse asymmetry or carotid bruits
Lasting >1 hour without clear migrainous features

sections.title: Clinical Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: History (Duration, laterality, associated symptoms, provoking factors).
Step 2: Full Ophthalmic Exam (Slit lamp, IOP, Funduscopy - look for Hollenhorst plaques).
Step 3: Labs (ESR, CRP, CBC, Platelets, Fasting Glucose, Lipid Panel).
Step 4: Imaging (Carotid Doppler, Echo, CTA/MRA head/neck).
Step 5: Cardiology referral (Holter monitor for occult AFib).

content.explanation: A: Artery (Carotid), B: Blood (Hypercoaguable), C: Cardiac (AFib/Valvular), D: Diabetes/Dyslipidemia, E: ESR/CRP (GCA)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Hollenhorst plaques are cholesterol emboli (bright, refractive) usually from the ipsilateral carotid artery.
Transient vision loss triggered by postural changes or bright light is pathognomonic for Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (OIS).
Papilledema-associated TVL results from transient elevation of intracranial pressure exceeding perfusion pressure at the optic nerve head.
Always check blood pressure in both arms; asymmetry may indicate subclavian steal syndrome.

data.summary: A comprehensive guide to Normal-Tension Glaucoma, a subtype of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma where progressive optic neuropathy occurs despite statistically normal intraocular pressure. Often considered a disease of ocular perfusion and structural susceptibility.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='none' stroke='#1e40af' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M30 50 Q 50 30 70 50' fill='none' stroke='#1e40af' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='10' fill='#1e40af'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: NTG is defined as progressive glaucomatous optic neuropathy with characteristic visual field defects and disc changes, occurring in patients with an intraocular pressure (IOP) consistently measured at or below 21 mmHg on diurnal testing. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

sections.title: Red Flags: Non-Glaucomatous Causes
content: Unilateral visual field loss (strongly suggests space-occupying lesion)
Pallor of the neuroretinal rim out of proportion to cupping
Visual acuity loss (typically spared in early NTG)
Color vision defects disproportionate to field loss
Presence of vertical visual field defects (neurological until proven otherwise)

sections.title: Clinical Examination & Findings
content: Splinter (Drance) hemorrhages on the optic nerve head
Peripapillary atrophy (Beta-zone/Alpha-zone)
Deeper, more focal neuroretinal rim notches
Higher prevalence of disc drusen
Greater susceptibility to progressive loss at low pressures

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Multiple diurnal IOP measurements (to rule out spikes).
Step 2: Pachymetry (Correct for CCT).
Step 3: Gonioscopy (Verify open angle).
Step 4: Humphrey Visual Field (HVF 24-2).
Step 5: OCT Disc/RNFL Analysis.
Step 6: MRI/CT (If suspicious for neurological etiology).

sections.title: Treatment Protocol (Collaborative Normal Tension Glaucoma Study)
content: Goal: Lower baseline IOP by at least 30%.
Step 1: Topical Monotherapy (Prostaglandin Analogs - Latanoprost/Bimatoprost).
Step 2: Add Second Agent (Beta-blockers or Alpha-agonists).
Step 3: Consider Laser Trabeculoplasty (ALT/SLT) for adjunctive support.
Step 4: Surgical intervention (Trabeculectomy/MIGS) if progression persists.

content.explanation: V: Vasospastic (Raynaud's), A: Apnea (Sleep), S: Systemic Hypotension, C: Cardiovascular diseases/Coagulation issues.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: NTG disc changes often appear more 'focal' compared to 'diffuse' damage in High-Tension Glaucoma.
Always evaluate for nocturnal systemic hypotension in patients with rapid progression.
Patients with NTG have a significantly higher prevalence of migraine and cold-induced peripheral vasospasm.
Treatment is indicated even if IOP is 'normal' if the optic nerve shows signs of structural or functional progression.

title: Clinical Appraisal of Darkly Pigmented Fundus Lesions
summary: A comprehensive diagnostic framework for evaluating pigmented fundus lesions, ranging from benign choroidal nevi to sight-threatening uveal melanoma and choroidal metastasis. Precise differentiation requires a synthesis of clinical examination, multimodal imaging, and rigorous monitoring protocols.

content.explanation: To Find Small Ocular Melanoma Using Helpful Hints: Thickness > 2mm, Fluid (subretinal), Symptoms (blurred vision/flashes), Orange pigment (lipofuscin), Margin (near optic disc), Acoustic Hollowness (on B-scan), Halo absence.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Biopsy or Refer
content: Documented growth on serial imaging
Presence of subretinal fluid (SRF)
Visual symptoms (scotoma, metamorphopsia)
Thickness > 2mm measured on EDI-OCT or B-scan
Orange pigment (Lipofuscin) accumulation
Presence of symptoms related to the lesion site

sections.title: Pathophysiology & Histology
sections.content: Pigmented fundus lesions arise from melanocytes (nevi, melanoma) or RPE cells (CHRPE). Uveal melanoma originates from uveal melanocytes and often undergoes GNAQ/GNA11 mutations. Pathologically, it exhibits spindle cells (A/B) or epithelioid cells, the latter carrying a higher metastatic potential. Invasion through Bruch's membrane results in the classic 'collar-button' configuration.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Clinical Slit-lamp Biomicroscopy with Indirect Ophthalmoscopy (90D/20D lens).
Step 2: Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF) to detect lipofuscin (hyper-autofluorescence).
Step 3: Enhanced Depth Imaging OCT (EDI-OCT) to measure lesion thickness and detect SRF.
Step 4: Ultrasonography (A/B-scan) for internal reflectivity and thickness measurement.
Step 5: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) to evaluate vascularity and 'double circulation'.
Step 6: Systemic evaluation (Liver function tests, abdominal ultrasound/CT/MRI) if malignancy is suspected.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Most choroidal nevi are dormant; do not biopsy unless suspicious.
Always document lesion location in relation to the optic disc in disc diameters (DD).
A halo around a nevus is a benign feature indicating stable/regressing margins.
B-scan ultrasonography is gold standard for measuring thickness of elevated lesions.
Genetic testing (BAP1, SF3B1, EIF1AX) is crucial for prognostication in melanoma.

title: Clinical Mastery: Ocular Toxocariasis (OT)
summary: Ocular toxocariasis is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the roundworm Toxocara canis or cati, typically resulting in unilateral granulomatous inflammation. This guide covers the spectrum from subclinical peripheral granulomas to severe endophthalmitis.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Ocular toxocariasis is the ocular manifestation of visceral larva migrans. It is caused by accidental ingestion of embryonated T. canis (most common) or T. cati eggs. Incidence is highest in children aged 5-10 years. Prevalence studies suggest up to 10-20% of the healthy population may be seropositive, though clinical disease is rare.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect
content: Unilateral leukocoria in a child
Unexplained unilateral uveitis
History of pica or contact with puppies
Peripheral retinal traction bands leading to drag of the macula
Evidence of subretinal abscess

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Detailed history (puppy exposure/pica).
Step 2: Slit-lamp exam (check for anterior chamber cells).
Step 3: Indirect ophthalmoscopy (peripheral granuloma).
Step 4: Serology (ELISA for anti-Toxocara IgG).
Step 5: B-scan USG (r/o vitritis/traction).

content.explanation: P: Peripheral Granuloma, U: Unilateral, P: Pica history, P: Parasitic etiology, Y: Young age (children).

sections.title: Treatment Protocol
content: Systemic corticosteroids (mainstay to control inflammation).
Anti-helminthics (Albendazole 400mg BID for 5-14 days) - Controversial, may cause inflammation if larva dies in situ.
Pars plana vitrectomy for severe vitreous traction/epiretinal membrane.
Laser photocoagulation for localized peripheral granulomas.

sections.title: Complications
content: Tractional retinal detachment (TRD) due to fibrous bands.
Permanent vision loss due to macular heterotopia/drag.
Chronic glaucoma from anterior segment inflammation.
Cataract formation from chronic uveitis.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Peripheral granulomas are often misdiagnosed as 'pars planitis'.
Serology may be negative in Ocular Toxocariasis because the parasite burden is low; serum IgG titers are less sensitive than in Visceral Larva Migrans.
Always perform a baseline B-scan in patients with unilateral vitritis of unknown origin in children.
Avoid aggressive anti-parasitic treatment without concomitant corticosteroids.

title: Phlyctenular Keratoconjunctivitis (PKC): A Comprehensive Clinical Guide
summary: A localized Type IV hypersensitivity reaction of the ocular surface to microbial antigens, characterized by the formation of inflammatory nodules (phlyctenules). Historically linked to Tuberculosis, it is now most commonly associated with Staphylococcus aureus-induced blepharitis in developed nations.

data.title: Phlyctenular Keratoconjunctivitis (PKC): A Comprehensive Clinical Guide
data.summary: A localized Type IV hypersensitivity reaction of the ocular surface to microbial antigens, characterized by the formation of inflammatory nodules (phlyctenules). Historically linked to Tuberculosis, it is now most commonly associated with Staphylococcus aureus-induced blepharitis in developed nations.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Phlyctenular Keratoconjunctivitis (PKC) is a non-infectious, inflammatory nodular affection of the cornea and conjunctiva. It represents a delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) response to a previously sensitized endogenous microbial antigen. The hallmark is the 'phlyctenule'—a small, greyish-white nodule surrounded by a localized zone of hyperaemia, which progresses to ulceration and eventual scarring.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The 3-Step Mechanism
content: Step 1: Sensitization — Initial exposure to microbial proteins (e.g., Staph cell wall or Tuberculoprotein) primes the T-lymphocytes.
Step 2: Re-exposure — Secondary exposure to the same antigen triggers a localized Type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
Step 3: Infiltration — Accumulation of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (early) and macrophages/lymphocytes (late) leads to subepithelial nodule formation and eventual necrosis/ulceration.

rows: Small nodule at the limbus or bulbar conjunctiva; moves with conjunctiva.
Nodule straddling the limbus; often triangular with apex towards cornea.
May leave a triangular sector-shaped scar.
Starts at limbus, migrates centrally dragging a leash of vessels (Fascicular Ulcer).

sections.title: Clinical Features & Patient Symptoms
content: Mild to severe irritation and foreign body sensation.
Intense lacrimation (tearing).
Severe Photophobia: Pathognomonic for corneal involvement; children often hide from light.
Blepharospasm: Involuntary eyelid closure.
Mucoid discharge (if secondary infection is present).
Itching (more common in Staph-related cases).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Phlyctenule: 1-3mm hard, greyish-white elevation.
Hyperemic Zone: Fan-shaped injection pointing towards the limbus.
Fascicular Ulcer: Serpiginous-like progression across the cornea with a 'leash' of vessels.
Marginal Phlycten: Can lead to peripheral thinning and gutter formation.
Chronic Blepharitis: Scurf, collarettes, and meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD).
Salzmann Nodular Degeneration: May occur secondary to long-standing PKC.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Slit-Lamp Biomicroscopy: Detailed assessment of nodule morphology and corneal depth.
2. Eyelid Margin Culture: Identify Staphylococcus aureus colonization.
3. Mantoux Test (PPD) / IGRA (QuantiFERON): Essential to rule out occult TB, especially in endemic areas.
4. Chest X-Ray: Screen for pulmonary tuberculosis.
5. Sputum Analysis: If CXR is suggestive of active TB.
6. Stool Examination: Check for ova/cysts of intestinal parasites in recalcitrant pediatric cases.

rows: Inflamed pre-existing pinguecula; nasal/temporal; no migration.
Deeper purple hue; nodule does not ulcerate; less photophobia.
Dendritic edge; decreased corneal sensation; recurrent.
Associated facial telangiectasia/flushing; bilateral; inferior thinning.
Trantas dots; giant papillae on tarsus; intense itching; stringy discharge.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Topical Steroids — Loteprednol 0.5% or Fluorometholone QID (tapered slowly) to reduce inflammation.
Step 2: Antibiotic Cover — Topical Erythromycin or Bacitracin ointment for lid margins.
Step 3: Lid Hygiene — Warm compresses and lid scrubs to manage underlying Staph blepharitis.
Step 4: Systemic Treatment — Oral Doxycycline (100mg BID) or Tetracycline for adults; Oral Erythromycin for children (Rosacea-related).
Step 5: Address Underlying Cause — Anti-TB therapy (RIPE regimen) if Mantoux/CXR is positive.
Step 6: Lubrication — Preservative-free artificial tears for symptomatic relief.

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Concerns
content: Progressive corneal thinning or impending perforation.
Significant reduction in visual acuity.
Presence of systemic symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, chronic cough).
Steroid-induced Intraocular Pressure (IOP) spikes.
Secondary bacterial superinfection of the phlyctenular ulcer.

sections.title: Remember the Path of the Phlycten

content.explanation: S: Staph/TB (Main triggers), T: Type IV Hypersensitivity, A: Apex towards cornea, R: Rosacea association, S: Steroids (Primary treatment).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: Photophobia in a child with a red eye should always raise suspicion for PKC or Keratitis.
The fascicular ulcer 'drags' its blood supply behind it; this leash of vessels is diagnostic.
Never start steroids without ruling out active Corneal Herpes Simplex (dendrite check).
If the phlyctenule is bilateral and recurrent, a systemic workup for TB is mandatory regardless of geographic location.
Salzmann nodules are often a long-term 'ghost' sign of previous phlyctenular disease.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Corneal Scarring: Leads to irregular astigmatism and vision loss.
Perforation: Rare, but possible in extreme thinning.
Recurrence: High if the underlying blepharitis or TB is not treated.
Secondary Infection: Bacterial keratitis can graft onto the ulcer site.
Amblyopia: In young children with central corneal scarring.

sections.title: Surgical & Advanced Interventions
content: PTK (Phototherapeutic Keratectomy): To clear superficial scars after the eye is quiet.
Lamellar Keratoplasty: Required for deep scars or significant thinning.
Penetrating Keratoplasty: Reserved for full-thickness central scars or perforation.
Gundersen Flap: In rare, non-healing recalcitrant cases.

summary: Ocular candidiasis is a sight-threatening intraocular infection, typically arising from hematogenous dissemination. This guide provides a deep-dive into the pathophysiology, diagnostic 'string-of-pearls' findings, and the latest evidence-based management protocols for residents and vitreoretinal fellows.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular candidiasis refers to intraocular infection caused by Candida species. It presents in two primary forms: Candida Chorioretinitis (infection confined to the retina and choroid) and Candida Endophthalmitis (infection involving the vitreous humor). It is most commonly a manifestation of disseminated candidemia, often requiring a multidisciplinary approach involving ophthalmology, infectious disease, and internal medicine.

sections.title: Pathophysiology Flow
content: Step 1: Primary infection or colonization (Gut, Skin, or IV site).
Step 2: Breakdown of mucosal barriers leads to Candidemia.
Step 3: Hematogenous seeding of the highly vascularized Choroid.
Step 4: Breakthrough of the Blood-Retinal Barrier into the Subretinal space.
Step 5: Invasion of the Neurosensory Retina.
Step 6: Vitreous seeding and inflammatory cascade (Endophthalmitis).

rows: Significant blur, floaters, and decreased vision.

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Findings
content: Early: Small, round, creamy-white 'fluffy' chorioretinal lesions (<1mm).
Evolution: Lesions enlarge and extend into the vitreous.
Vitreous: 'Cotton ball' opacities or 'string of pearls' (pseudohyphae colonies).
Anterior Segment: Mild cell/flare; occasionally large hypopyon in severe cases.
Vascular: Perivasculitis and retinal hemorrhages (Roth spots).
Late Stage: Tractional retinal detachment or epiretinal membrane formation.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Dilated Fundus Exam: Gold standard for screening.
2. Blood Cultures: Minimum 2 sets (yield is only 50-60% in chronic cases).
3. Vitreous Tap/Biopsy: For culture, Gram/GMS stain, and PCR (Higher yield than aqueous).
4. OCT: Identify depth of lesions and monitoring subretinal fluid.
5. B-Scan Ultrasound: If media is opaque to rule out RD and assess vitreous membranes.
6. Systemic Search: Echocardiogram (Vegetations) and Renal US (Abscesses).

rows: Usually unifocal, associated with old pigmented scar, more intense vitritis ('Headlight in fog').
More necrotic, granular appearance, minimal vitritis, often follows vessels.
Great masquerader; check RPR/FTA-ABS. Can have placoid lesions.
Bilateral, 'candle-wax drippings', granulomatous KPs, hilar adenopathy.
Much more rapid onset, painful, significant chemosis and lid edema.
Excellent intraocular penetration (~70% of serum). First-line for sensitive C. albicans.
Superior penetration and broader spectrum (covers C. krusei). Watch for visual disturbances/hallucinations.
Gold standard for resistant strains or critically ill. Poor ocular penetration; nephrotoxic.
Poor ocular penetration. Not recommended for primary ocular treatment.

sections.title: Intravitreal Pharmacotherapy
content: Indication: Mandatory for all cases with vitreous involvement (Endophthalmitis).
Amphotericin B Deoxycholate: 5-10 µg in 0.1 mL (Note: Highly toxic to retina if dose exceeds this).
Voriconazole: 100 µg in 0.1 mL (Safe and well-tolerated).
Frequency: May repeat every 48-72 hours based on clinical response.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV)
content: 1. Indication: Significant vitreous opacification or failure of medical therapy.
2. Core Vitrectomy: Removal of fungal load and inflammatory debris.
3. Targeted Sampling: Obtain undiluted vitreous for microbiology.
4. Induction of PVD: Careful management as hyaloid is often very adherent.
5. Intraoperative Intravitreal: Inject antifungal at the end of the case.

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Rapidly progressive vision loss despite systemic fluconazole.
Macular involving chorioretinal lesions (Threatens central vision).
Development of 'String of Pearls' in a patient previously on systemic meds only.
Signs of orbital cellulitis (Suspect Mucor or aggressive Aspergillus in immunocompromised).
Painful eye in the setting of fungemia (Suggests panophthalmitis).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Duration of treatment: Minimum 4-6 weeks total; continue for 2 weeks after resolution of lesions.
Screening Guidelines: AAO now suggests screening ONLY if patient has symptoms or is unable to communicate.
Resistance: Candida glabrata and krusei are often resistant to azoles; use Voriconazole or Ampho B.
The 'Lawn-Mower' Effect: Lesions heal from the periphery inward, leaving behind atrophic scars.

content.explanation: P: Peripheral fluffy lesions; E: Exudates in Vitreous; A: Aqueous cell/flare; R: Retinal involvement (Deep); L: Long-term IV access (Risk); S: String of pearls appearance.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Evidence
sections.content: Recent IDSA and AAO statements emphasize that the incidence of ocular involvement in candidemia has dropped significantly (~1-2%) due to earlier initiation of systemic therapy. This has led to a shift away from mandatory universal screening of all candidemic patients, focusing instead on those with visual symptoms or high-risk systemic factors (e.g., persistent candidemia despite treatment).

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Prognosis: Generally good for C. albicans if caught early.
Tractional Retinal Detachment: Secondary to vitreous membranes.
Epiretinal Membrane: Very common sequela of macular lesions.
Cataract: Due to inflammation or prolonged steroid use post-op.
Phthisis Bulbi: Rare, but possible in end-stage/untreated cases.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Acute dacryocystitis is an infection of the lacrimal sac, usually secondary to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD). Stasis of tears leads to bacterial overgrowth and subsequent inflammation, which can progress to abscess formation or orbital cellulitis.

rows: Staph. aureus, Strep. pneumoniae, H. influenzae
Strep. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Staph. aureus

sections.title: Clinical Signs & Symptoms
content: Painful, erythematous swelling over the medial canthal area (lacrimal sac region).
Epiphora (overflow tearing) due to NLD obstruction.
Purulent discharge expressed through the punctum (diagnostic maneuver).
Tenderness, warmth, and induration of the surrounding periocular tissues.
Potential for pre-septal cellulitis or frank abscess formation.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Warm compresses to localize infection.
Step 2: Systemic antibiotics (e.g., Augmentin 875/125mg BID or Cephalexin).
Step 3: Incision and Drainage (I&D) IF fluctuation/abscess is present.
Step 4: Irrigation of the lacrimal system is CONTRAINDICATED during acute phase.
Step 5: Definitive Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) performed after inflammation resolves.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Admit
content: Signs of Orbital Cellulitis: Ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, vision loss, or relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD).
Systemic sepsis: Fever > 38.5°C, altered mental status, tachycardia.
Extension of inflammation beyond the medial canthal area.
Failure to respond to outpatient oral antibiotics within 48 hours.

content.explanation: L: Lacrimal sac swelling, A: Acute pain, C: Chronic epiphora, R: Redness, I: Infection (purulence), M: Medial location, A: Antibiotics needed, L: Likely NLD obstruction.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Do NOT probe or syringe the system during the acute phase (risk of sepsis spreading).
If recurrence occurs, suspect lacrimal sac malignancy (biopsy mandatory).
Always evaluate for concomitant sinusitis on clinical exam.
Augmentin is the drug of choice due to high beta-lactamase resistance.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A corneal abscess (Infectious Keratitis) is a sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency characterized by suppurative inflammation of the corneal stroma. It involves the migration of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) into the stroma in response to invading pathogens (bacteria, fungi, protozoa, or viruses), often accompanied by epithelial breakdown and necrosis.

content.explanation: P: Pain (Severe in infectious); E: Epithelial defect (Usually overlying the infiltrate); D: Discharge (Mucopurulent); A: Anterior chamber reaction (Hypopyon); L: Location (Central is more likely infectious).

branches: Gram-Positive: S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, Coag-neg Staph

sections.title: The Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Stop all antibiotics for 24-48h if possible (unless severe).
Step 2: Proparacaine anesthesia (avoid preservative-heavy drops).
Step 3: Scrape leading edge and base of ulcer with Kimura spatula or 25G needle.
Step 4: Direct inoculation onto Blood, Chocolate, and Sabouraud agar.
Step 5: Prepare slides for Gram, Giemsa, and Calcofluor White stains.
Step 6: PCR for fastidious organisms or viruses if suspected.

sections.title: Management Algorithm: Bacterial
content: Loading Dose: 1 drop every 5-15 mins for 1 hour.
Maintenance: 1 drop every hour around the clock (24/7).
Cycloplegia: Atropine 1% BID or Cyclopentolate 1% TID to prevent synechiae and reduce pain.
Tapering: Only after clear signs of clinical improvement (e.g., blunting of edges, decreased AC reaction).
Steroids: SCUT Trial suggests waiting 48-72h of effective antibiotics; avoid in fungal/Nocardia.

sections.title: Surgical Interventions
content: PACK-CXL: Photoactivated Chromophore for Infectious Keratitis (Emerging adjunctive).
Tissue Adhesive (Cyanoacrylate): For impending or small (<2mm) perforations.
Tectonic Lamellar Keratoplasty: For severe thinning.
Therapeutic Penetrating Keratoplasty (TPKP): For large perforations or uncontrolled infection (high risk of graft failure).

sections.title: Red Flags: Impending Perforation
content: Descemetocele formation (clear central area in an opaque ulcer).
Sudden flattening of the anterior chamber.
Positive Seidel test (aqueous leak).
Significant stromal thinning (>90%).
Severe 'melting' (keratolysis) out of proportion to infiltration.

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: Pseudomonas ulcers can progress to perforation in <24-48 hours due to proteases.
Feathery borders and satellite lesions suggest Fungal Keratitis.
Ring infiltrates are classic for Acanthamoeba but can also seen in Pseudomonas and chronic fungal infections.
Never use a 'tapering' dose of antibiotics for a culture-positive active abscess; keep it at least QID until healed.

sections.title: Landmark Study: MUTT Trials
sections.content: The Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trials (MUTT I & II) established that topical Natamycin 5% is superior to Voriconazole 1% for filamentous fungal keratitis, particularly Fusarium. Furthermore, oral Voriconazole did not show significant benefit in typical cases and might worsen outcomes in Fusarium infections.

sections.title: Acanthamoeba Specifics
content: Symptoms: Pain out of proportion to signs.
Signs: Radial keratoneuritis (early), Ring infiltrate (late).
Treatment: Brolene (Propamidine) + Biguanides (PHMB 0.02% or Chlorhexidine 0.02%).
Note: Standard antibiotics will NOT work.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Corneal Scarring (Leucoma) requiring future optical PKP/DALK.
Secondary Glaucoma (Inflammatory/Synechial).
Endophthalmitis (Rare unless perforation occurs).
Cataract formation (Toxic/Inflammatory).
Phthisis Bulbi (In severe, uncontrolled cases).

title: Microbial Keratitis: The Corneal Abscess Masterclass
summary: Corneal abscess (Microbial Keratitis) is a sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency characterized by suppurative inflammation of the corneal stroma. Rapid identification of pathogens and aggressive antimicrobial therapy are mandatory to prevent perforation and permanent vision loss.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Microbial Keratitis (MK) is an infectious process involving the corneal epithelium and stroma. A 'corneal abscess' specifically refers to a localized collection of white blood cells (neutrophils), necrotic tissue, and pathogens within the stroma, often presenting as a dense, yellowish-white opacity with an overlying epithelial defect.

rows: Chronic lid disease, post-op, bullous keratopathy.
Rapidly spreading, soup-like melting, greenish discharge.
Serpiginous ulcer, deep stromal abscess, hypopyon.
Indolent, often in the inferior cornea.
Feathery margins, satellite lesions, immune ring.

sections.title: The Four Stages of Pathogenesis
content: 1. Stage of Infiltration: PMN migration from limbus/tears into the stroma.
2. Stage of Active Ulceration: Necrosis and sloughing of epithelium and stroma.
3. Stage of Regression: Immune response limits the infection; lines of demarcation form.
4. Stage of Cicatrization: Healing via fibroblast activity, resulting in permanent nebula, macula, or leucoma.

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Red Flags for Perforation
content: Descemetocele formation (clear bubble in the floor of the ulcer)
Sudden decrease in IOP (intraocular pressure)
Seidel's test positive (aqueous leak)
Shallow or flat anterior chamber
Iris prolapse into the corneal defect
Rapidly progressive stromal thinning ('melting')

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: The Scrape Protocol
content: 1. Stop antibiotics 24-48h if possible (unless severe).
2. Instill topical anesthetic (Proparacaine preferred over Tetracaine).
3. Scrape the base and the active margins using a Kimura spatula or 25G needle.
4. Inoculate onto Blood Agar, Chocolate Agar, and Sabouraud Dextrose Agar.
5. Prepare slides for Gram and Giemsa stains (and KOH/Calcofluor white if fungal suspected).

sections.title: Initial Management: Medical Protocol
content: Monotherapy (Non-central, <2mm): Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin 0.5% or Gatifloxacin 0.5%) q1h.
Duotherapy (Severe/Central): Fortified Tobramycin (15mg/mL) + Fortified Vancomycin (50mg/mL) q1h around the clock.
Cycloplegia: Atropine 1% BID or Cyclopentolate 1% TID to reduce pain and prevent synechiae.
Oral Doxycycline: 100mg BID to inhibit collagenase and prevent melting.
Steroid Timing: Wait at least 48-72h of effective antibiotic cover (SCUT trial recommendations).

sections.title: Fortified Antibiotic Preparation (Pearls)
sections.content: Vancomycin (50mg/mL): Add 10mL of sterile water or BSS to 500mg Vancomycin powder. Stable for 14 days refrigerated. Tobramycin (15mg/mL): Add 2mL of injectable Tobramycin (40mg/mL) to a 5mL bottle of 0.3% Tobramycin ophthalmic solution.

content.explanation: P: Painful (Severe), S: Soup-like melt, E: Extended wear CL risk, U: Ulceration rapid, D: Discharge (Greenish/Purulent), O: Odor (often associated with Pseudomonas cultures).

branches: Amniotic Membrane Graft (for persistent epithelial defects)
Bandage Contact Lens (only after infection is sterilized)

sections.title: Landmark Study: The SCUT Trial
content: Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT).
Finding: No significant difference in visual outcome at 3 months for the whole group.
Subgroup benefit: Patients with very poor baseline vision and central/deep ulcers showed better outcomes with early steroids (after 48h of antibiotics).
Key Rule: Never start steroids until the organism is identified and fungal/acanthamoeba are ruled out.

sections.title: Complications and Prognosis
content: Endophthalmitis (Infection spread to the vitreous/aqueous).
Secondary Glaucoma (Inflammatory debris blocking the trabecular meshwork).
Anterior Polychromatic Cataract.
Corneal Leucoma (Permanent opaque scar).
Phthisis Bulbi (Shrinkage of the eye following severe infection).

sections.title: Pathogens that can Penetrate Intact Epithelium

content.explanation: N: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, H: Haemophilus influenzae, L: Listeria monocytogenes, C: Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Lid Flip': Always evert the eyelid to look for retained foreign bodies (e.g., a lost contact lens) which can be the nidus for infection.
Acanthamoeba Hint: Pain out of proportion to clinical signs and radial keratoneuritis.
Moraxella: Classically occurs in patients with pre-existing ocular surface disease and malnutrition.
Toxicity vs. Infection: If the ulcer is not improving, consider if the 1-hour drops are causing 'medicamentosa' or toxic epithelial toxicity.
Hypopyon: In bacterial ulcers, the hypopyon is usually sterile (inflammatory); in fungal ulcers, it may contain active fungal elements.

title: Sympathetic Ophthalmia: The Ocular Duel
summary: A rare, sight-threatening bilateral granulomatous panuveitis occurring after penetrating ocular trauma or intraocular surgery. It represents a delayed T-cell mediated autoimmune response against uveoretinal self-antigens, leading to devastating inflammation in both the 'exciting' and 'sympathizing' eye.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Sympathetic Ophthalmia (SO) is a rare, bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that follows accidental or surgical penetrating trauma to one eye (the 'exciting' eye). The non-injured eye (the 'sympathizing' eye) subsequently develops inflammation. Historically associated with battlefield trauma, modern cases are frequently associated with multiple intraocular surgeries, particularly vitreoretinal procedures.

sections.title: Etiology: The Trigger Events
content: Accidental Penetrating Trauma: Historically the most common cause (60-70%).
Intraocular Surgery: Now accounts for ~30% of cases; Vitrectomy is the leading surgical cause.
Cataract extraction, evisceration (rarely), and even Nd:YAG cyclophotocoagulation.
Interval: Usually occurs within 3 months of injury (80%), but can range from days to decades.

branches: Sensitization: Uveoretinal antigens (S-antigen, Rhodopsin) released into lymphatics
Type IV Hypersensitivity: Delayed T-cell mediated response
MHC Class II Association: HLA-DR4, HLA-DRB1*04, and HLA-DQA1*03
Granulomatous Reaction: Non-necrotizing infiltration of uveal tract

rows: Diffuse, 'non-necrotizing' granulomatous infiltration of choroid with lymphocytes & epithelioid cells.
Relative sparing of the choriocapillaris (distinguishes from VKH).
Clusters of epithelioid cells, macrophages, and RPE cells located between RPE and Bruch's membrane.
Usually spared except for perivascular cuffing and edema.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: Symptoms
content: Sympathizing Eye: Earliest sign is often 'blurring at near' (loss of accommodation).
Photophobia and mild redness.
Floating spots and decreased visual acuity.
Exciting Eye: Sudden worsening of chronic low-grade inflammation.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Anterior Segment: 'Mutton-fat' Keratic Precipitates (KPs), Koeppe/Busacca nodules, and posterior synechiae.
Vitreous: Significant vitritis (cells and haze).
Posterior Segment: Diffuse choroidal thickening, exudative retinal detachment.
Dalen-Fuchs Nodules: Multiple yellow-white mid-peripheral lesions.

rows: Multiple fluorescent 'pinpoint' leaks at the RPE level (starry sky appearance).
Late pooling of dye in areas of exudative RD; staining of the optic disc.
Multiple hypofluorescent spots (more sensitive for choroidal involvement than FFA).
Significant choroidal thickening; subretinal fluid; bacillary layer detachment.
Diffuse thickening of the choroid without extrascleral extension.
No history of trauma; associated with exudative RD, hearing loss, and vitiligo; Choriocapillaris involved.
Systemic involvement (lungs, hilar nodes); positive ACE/Lysozyme levels.
Bilateral, but has no traumatic trigger.
Acute onset, intense pain, hypopyon, often bacterial/fungal markers present.
Smaller lesions, typically seen in myopic females.

sections.title: Surgical Prevention & Timing
content: Step 1: Primary repair of the penetrating injury (maintain globe integrity).
Step 2: Assess visual potential. If the eye is blind (NPL), consider enucleation.
Step 3: The 'Golden Period' — Enucleation within 10-14 days of trauma is historically considered protective.
Step 4: Once inflammation starts in the sympathizing eye, enucleation of the exciting eye is controversial and may not help.

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Initial Pulse: IV Methylprednisolone 1g/day for 3 days if severe.
High Dose Steroids: Oral Prednisolone 1.0–1.5 mg/kg/day, tapered slowly over 6-12 months.
Steroid Sparing: Early introduction of IMT (Immunomodulatory Therapy) if steroids fail or for long-term control.
Maintenance: Maintain on lowest effective dose to prevent relapse.

sections.title: Immunomodulatory Therapy (IMT)
content: Antimetabolites: Azathioprine (2mg/kg) or Mycophenolate Mofetil (1g BD).
Calcineurin Inhibitors: Cyclosporine A or Tacrolimus.
Biologics: Infliximab or Adalimumab (Anti-TNF alpha) for refractory cases.
Alkylating Agents: Chlorambucil or Cyclophosphamide (reserved for severe, resistant cases).

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS
content: Sudden loss of accommodation in a patient with history of ocular trauma.
New onset 'floaters' in the healthy eye post-surgery.
Non-compliance with steroid taper (leading to rebound inflammation).
Signs of Enucleation Delay beyond the 2-week window in a non-salvageable eye.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Complications: Complicated Cataract, Secondary Glaucoma, Macular Edema, Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV).
Prognosis: Historically poor, but with modern IMT, >75% of patients achieve 20/40 or better vision.
Recurrence: Relapses are common if steroids are tapered too rapidly.

sections.title: The Enucleation vs. Evisceration Debate
sections.content: Traditionally, enucleation was mandatory to prevent SO, as evisceration might leave residual uveal antigens. However, modern studies (including meta-analyses) suggest that the risk of SO after evisceration is extremely low (comparable to enucleation), leading many surgeons to prefer evisceration for better cosmetic outcomes in NPL eyes.

content.explanation: P: Pinpoint leaks on FFA; E: Exciting eye was the injured one; A: Antigens (uveoretinal) are the cause; R: Rare since modern microsurgery; L: Long-term steroids/IMT required; S: Sparing of Choriocapillaris.

title: VKH Syndrome: The Comprehensive Clinical Masterguide
summary: A multisystemic, T-cell mediated autoimmune attack on melanocyte-containing tissues, primarily affecting the eyes, ears, meninges, and skin. This guide covers the evolution from the prodromal phase to chronic recurrent granulomatous inflammation.
