sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is a bilateral, granulomatous panuveitis associated with extraocular manifestations involving the auditory, neurological, and integumentary systems. It is driven by a T-cell mediated autoimmune response against tyrosinase-related proteins in melanocytes.

rows: Viral-like illness, headache, meningismus, tinnitus, CSF pleocytosis.
Bilateral exudative RD, thickened choroid, optic disc hyperemia.
Sunset glow fundus, Sugiura sign (perilimbic vitiligo), skin changes.
Smouldering granulomatous anterior uveitis, mutton-fat KPs, Busacca nodules.
Bilateral Ocular + EITHER Neuro/Auditory OR Integumentary signs.
Bilateral Ocular signs ONLY (Isolated Ocular VKH).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Posterior Segment: Multifocal serous RDs, 'clover-leaf' fluid patterns.
Optic Nerve: Hyperemia and edema (Acute phase).
Fundus: 'Sunset Glow' (depigmentation revealing orange-red choroid).
Anterior Segment: Mutton-fat KPs, Koeppe/Busacca nodules.
Dalén-Fuchs Nodules: Small yellow-white granulomatous lesions (less common than SO).

sections.title: Essential Diagnostic Imaging
content: 1. OCT: Shows subretinal fluid, bacillary layer detachment, and choroidal thickening.
2. FFA: Pinpoint leaks ('Starry Sky') in early phase; pooling in late phase.
3. ICG: Early/mid-phase hypofluorescent spots (HDDs), fuzzy choroidal vessels.
4. B-Scan: Diffuse low-to-medium reflective choroidal thickening; no posterior scleritis 'T-sign'.

rows: History of penetrating trauma or surgery in the 'exciting' eye.
Pain with eye movement, T-sign on USG, usually unilateral.
Hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR, elevated ACE/Lysozyme.
Placoid lesions, rapid resolution, minimal vitreous reaction.

sections.title: Acute Phase Management Protocol
content: Step 1: IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day) for 3 days for severe cases.
Step 2: Transition to Oral Prednisolone (1-1.5 mg/kg/day).
Step 3: Ultra-slow taper (minimum 6-12 months total duration).
Step 4: Cycloplegics and topical steroids for anterior segment activity.

content.explanation: S: Sugiura Sign (Perilimbic vitiligo); U: Uveitis (Bilateral/Granulomatous); N: Neurological (Meningismus); S: Subretinal fluid; E: Ears (Tinnitus); T: Tegumentary (Vitiligo/Poliosis).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Treatment Pitfalls
content: Rapid steroid taper: High risk of transitioning to chronic-recurrent stage.
Under-recognizing 'smouldering' activity: Persistent choroidal thickening on EDI-OCT.
Steroid-induced Glaucoma/Cataract: Must monitor IOP and lens status at every visit.
Neurological deficits: May require neurology co-management and MRI.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: Early IMT initiation is now preferred (as per MUST trial principles) to prevent 'sunset glow' fundus.
The Sugiura Sign is the earliest integumentary sign (appears ~1 month).
EDI-OCT is the most sensitive non-invasive tool to monitor disease activity.
Avoid intravitreal steroid implants in the acute phase before systemic control is achieved.

sections.title: Prognostic Indicators
sections.content: Good visual prognosis (20/40 or better) is achievable in >70% of patients if treated aggressively within the first 2 weeks of symptoms. Poorer outcomes are linked to older age, more frequent recurrences, and delayed start of immunosuppression.

sections.title: Recent Landmark Insights
content: Bacillary Layer Detachment (BLD): Recognized on OCT as a split at the inner segment myoid, distinct from subretinal fluid.
The Role of IL-17: Newer studies suggest Th17 cells are pivotal in the chronic phase, suggesting potential for Secukinumab in refractory cases.
First-line IMT: Growing evidence supports starting Mycophenolate Mofetil concurrently with steroids in the acute phase.

title: Ocular Sarcoidosis: The Great Masquerader
summary: A systemic, idiopathic granulomatous disease characterized by non-caseating granulomas. Ocular involvement occurs in 25–50% of patients and can affect every structure of the eye, often serving as the sentinel sign of systemic disease.

rows: Positive tissue biopsy (conjunctiva, skin, lacrimal gland, or lung) AND compatible uveitis.
Bilateral Hilar Lymphadenopathy (BHL) on CXR/CT AND compatible uveitis.
No BHL, but biopsy-proven systemic sarcoidosis AND 3+ clinical ocular signs.
Lungs negative, but 4+ clinical ocular signs AND 2+ positive investigative tests.

sections.title: Clinical Signs: Anterior Segment
content: Mutton-fat Keratic Precipitates (Large, greasy, inferior)
Iris Nodules: Koeppe (pupillary margin) and Busacca (iris stroma)
Berlin Nodules (in the iridocorneal angle)
Tent-shaped Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS)
Lacrimal Gland Enlargement (S-shaped ptosis)
Conjunctival Granulomas (Small, pale, translucent nodules)

sections.title: Clinical Signs: Posterior Segment
content: Vitreous 'Snowballs' or 'String of Pearls' opacities
Perivenous Sheathing / Candle-wax Drippings (Exudative periphlebitis)
Multiple Chorioretinal Granulomas (Dalen-Fuchs-like)
Optic Nerve Head Granulomas
Cystoid Macular Edema (Most common cause of vision loss)
Preretinal Granulomas (Lander's signs)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Laboratory Screening: Serum ACE (elevated in 60-80%), Serum Lysozyme (more sensitive in kids), Serum Calcium.
Step 2: Imaging: Chest X-Ray (BHL screening) followed by High-Resolution CT Chest (Gold standard for lymphadenopathy).
Step 3: Tissue Diagnosis: Biopsy of visible lesions (Conjunctiva, Lacrimal gland, Skin) or Transbronchial biopsy (high yield).
Step 4: Ocular Imaging: OCT Macula (CME), FFA (Peripheral ischemia/vasculitis), ICGA (Choroidal granulomas).
Step 5: Multidisciplinary Referral: Pulmonology, Rheumatology, and Cardiology (to rule out heart block).

rows: Caseating granulomas; positive IGRA/Quantiferon; necrotic choroiditis.
Positive RPR/FTA-ABS; 'Salt and pepper' fundus; roseola of iris.
Bilateral exudative RD; sunset glow fundus; integumentary changes.
History of penetrating trauma or surgery in the fellow eye.
Older patients; 'sub-RPE' creamy infiltrates; vitreous sheet cells.

branches: Lofgren Syndrome: BHL, Erythema Nodosum, Arthralgia
Heerfordt Syndrome: Uveitis, Parotitis, Fever, Facial Nerve Palsy
Blau Syndrome: Pediatric, NOD2 mutation, Rash, Arthritis, Uveitis

sections.title: Management Hierarchy
content: Tier 1: Topical Steroids (Pred Forte 1% q1h-qid) + Cycloplegics (Atropine 1%).
Tier 2: Regional Steroids (Sub-tenon Triamcinolone 40mg or Intravitreal Dexamethasone implant).
Tier 3: Systemic Corticosteroids (Prednisone 1mg/kg/day with slow taper).
Tier 4: Steroid-Sparing Agents (Methotrexate 7.5-25mg/week, Mycophenolate Mofetil 1g BID).
Tier 5: Biologics (Infliximab or Adalimumab 40mg q2weeks).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Action Needed
content: Cardiac Sarcoidosis: Unexplained syncope or palpitations (High risk of sudden death).
Neurosarcoidosis: New onset cranial nerve palsies, seizures, or meningitis symptoms.
Ocular Hypertension: Rapid steroid-induced IOP spike or secondary glaucoma.
Retinal Neovascularization: 'Sea-fan' configuration (risk of vitreous hemorrhage).
Macular Ischemia: Sudden vision loss not explained by CME.

content.explanation: Spirals (Vitreous), Snowballs (Vitritis), Sheathing (Veins), Skin (Erythema Nodosum), Stones (Hypercalcemia), S-shaped Ptosis (Lacrimal), Synechiae (Iris).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: ACE levels are naturally high in children; use Lysozyme for screening.
A negative CXR does NOT rule out sarcoid; request high-res CT.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) can occur even in 'quiet' eyes.
Blind conjunctival biopsy has high yield even if the tissue looks normal.
Sarcoid is a 'thromboembolic' vasculitis risk factor; monitor for BRVO.

sections.title: Surgical Considerations
content: Cataract Surgery: Must be 'quiet' for 3 months prior; use prophylactic systemic steroids.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy: Indicated for non-clearing VH, ERM, or refractory CME.
Glaucoma Drainage Devices: Often preferred over trabeculectomy due to high inflammation/failure risk.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The ADVISE Study and VISUAL trials have solidified the role of Adalimumab (Humira) as a first-line biologic for non-infectious uveitis. Recent genomic studies suggest associations with HLA-DRB1*03, further refining our understanding of genetic susceptibility in different ethnic groups.

title: Viral Retinitis: ARN vs. PORN Masterclass
summary: A high-stakes comparison of Acute Retinal Necrosis (ARN) and Progressive Outer Retinal Necrosis (PORN), two devastating necrotizing herpetic retinopathies requiring rapid identification to prevent permanent visual loss.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: ARN is a necrotizing retinitis typically seen in immunocompetent patients, usually caused by VZV, HSV-1, or HSV-2. PORN is a rapidly progressive, fulminant necrotizing retinitis characterized by extensive outer retinal necrosis, occurring almost exclusively in severely immunocompromised individuals (CD4+ < 50 cells/µL), primarily due to VZV.

sections.title: Clinical Features Checklist
content: Peripheral retinal whitening (necrotic patches)
Rapid confluence of lesions
Arteritis (ARN hallmark)
Granulomatous anterior uveitis
Retinal detachment (Rhegmatogenous)
Optic disc edema

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergencies
content: Rapid loss of vision in immunocompromised patient
Dense peripheral whitening with minimal vitritis (PORN suspicion)
Symptoms of retinal detachment (floaters/flashes)
High risk of bilateral involvement

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Clinical Examination (Slit lamp & Dilated fundoscopy).
Step 2: Anterior Chamber (AC) or Vitreous Tap for PCR (HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, CMV).
Step 3: Serology for HIV/Systemic health assessment.
Step 4: Systemic workup for underlying autoimmune conditions if indicated.
Step 5: Imaging (B-scan USG to rule out RD, OCT to track macular involvement).

content.explanation: A: Arteritis (Occlusive), R: Retinal Necrosis (Peripheral), N: Necrosis (Necrotizing Uveitis). Always check for retinal detachment!

sections.title: Treatment Protocol (ARN)
content: 1. IV Acyclovir (10mg/kg TID) for 7-10 days.
2. Followed by Oral Valacyclovir (1g TID) for 6+ weeks.
3. Consider prophylactic laser photocoagulation (barrage).
4. Topical steroids and cycloplegics for anterior inflammation.
5. Intravitreal Foscarnet if resistant.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: PORN is not an inflammatory disease; the lack of vitritis makes the clear view deceptive.
The vitreous tap in PORN is essential for rapid diagnosis as serology is often useless.
Prophylactic laser barrage in ARN does not guarantee against RD due to vitreous base contraction.
Always treat the fellow eye with antivirals in ARN cases, as bilateral conversion is a high risk.

title: CMV Retinitis: Clinical Mastery & Management Protocol
summary: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis remains the most common and sight-threatening opportunistic ocular infection in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS. This guide covers the pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, and aggressive management strategies required to prevent permanent visual loss.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: CMV retinitis is a necrotizing retinitis caused by Human Herpesvirus 5 (HHV-5). Historically, it affected 30-40% of AIDS patients with CD4+ counts < 50 cells/µL. While HAART has drastically reduced incidence, it remains a critical diagnosis in patients with poor treatment adherence or undiagnosed immunocompromise.

rows: Dense white retinal infiltrates, 'pizza-pie' appearance, hemorrhages
Peripheral granular, fine white dots, minimal hemorrhage
Severe perivascular sheathing mimicking frost on vessels
Very rapid, associated with high viral load

sections.title: Red Flags: Sight-Threatening Indicators
content: Involvement of the posterior pole (macula/optic nerve head)
Retinal detachment (Rhegmatogenous) due to retinal necrosis
Decreased visual acuity (VA < 20/40)
Any signs of optic nerve edema or infarction
New onset 'floaters' in a high-risk patient

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: Step 1: Dilated indirect fundoscopy (gold standard).
Step 2: CBC with differential and CD4+ count.
Step 3: Aqueous humor sampling (PCR) if diagnosis is ambiguous.
Step 4: Systemic screening for CMV (PCR, shell vial culture).
Step 5: Regular monitoring via color fundus photography (ETDRS protocol).

content.explanation: P: Perivascular infiltration; I: Intraretinal hemorrhage; Z: Zone of necrosis; Z: Zenith of viral replication (CD4 <50); A: Atrophic retinal scarring.

sections.title: Treatment Protocol
content: Induction Therapy: IV Ganciclovir (5 mg/kg BID for 14-21 days) or IV Foscarnet (60 mg/kg TID).
Maintenance Therapy: Valganciclovir (900 mg daily).
Intravitreal Options: Ganciclovir (2 mg/0.05 mL) or Foscarnet (2.4 mg/0.1 mL) for sight-threatening lesions.
HAART Initiation: Crucial to restore immune function (wait 2-4 weeks post-induction to avoid Immune Recovery Uveitis - IRU).
Retinal Detachment: Surgical intervention via pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: CMV retinitis is NOT associated with significant anterior chamber inflammation; if the eye is 'quiet', think CMV.
Immune Recovery Uveitis (IRU) occurs when CD4 counts rise; it manifests as vitritis and cystoid macular edema.
Always perform a baseline and serial CD4 testing to monitor immune status.
Valganciclovir is associated with neutropenia; monitor absolute neutrophil count (ANC) weekly.
Once a retinal scar forms, it is permanent; the goal is to prevent progression to the macula.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Syphilis is a chronic, multi-systemic infection caused by the spirochete *Treponema pallidum*. Known as 'The Great Mimicker,' ocular syphilis can present at any stage of the disease (primary, secondary, or tertiary) and can affect almost any ocular structure. It is increasingly common in the setting of HIV co-infection. Any ocular inflammation with an uncertain etiology should prompt testing for syphilis.

sections.title: Anterior Segment Manifestations
content: Interstitial Keratitis (IK): Chronic, 'ground-glass' cornea with ghost vessels (typically late/congenital).
Iris Roseolae: Transient capillary dilatations on the iris surface.
Anterior Uveitis: Can be granulomatous or non-granulomatous; often resistant to steroids alone.
Iris Nodules: Fleshy yellowish-red masses (Gummas) can occur on the iris or ciliary body.
Dislocated Lens: Rare complication of chronic inflammation.

sections.title: Posterior Segment Findings
content: ASPPC: Acute Syphilitic Posterior Placoid Chorioretinitis (Large, yellowish-white subretinal lesions).
Vitreitis: Significant 'headlight in the fog' appearance (often more intense than toxoplasmosis).
Vasculitis: Typically an arteritis, often with perivascular sheathing/cuffing.
Neuroretinitis: Optic disc edema with a macular star pattern.
Necrotizing Retinitis: Can mimic Acute Retinal Necrosis (ARN) in immunocompromised patients.

sections.title: The 'Signature' Lesion: ASPPC
sections.content: Acute Syphilitic Posterior Placoid Chorioretinitis (ASPPC) is a highly suggestive finding. It presents as large, pale, yellowish-grey placoid lesions at the level of the RPE/choriocapillaris, typically in the macula or peripapillary area. OCT shows characteristic 'inner segment/outer segment' (IS/OS) junction disruption and punctate hyperreflectivity in the outer retina.

rows: Small, irregular pupils; accommodate but don't react to light
Sudden vision loss, disc edema, APD present
III, IV, or VI nerve involvement
Bilateral disc swelling with increased ICP
Reflects disease activity; can be false-negative in late stages (Prozone effect).
Remains positive for life; used to confirm previous or current infection.

sections.title: Mandatory CSF Analysis
content: Step 1: Lumbar Puncture (LP) is MANDATORY for all cases of Ocular Syphilis.
Step 2: Check CSF VDRL (High specificity, low sensitivity).
Step 3: Check CSF Protein (>45 mg/dL) and WBC count (>5 cells/mm³).
Step 4: CSF FTA-ABS (High sensitivity, low specificity; helpful if negative to rule out).

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Hospitalization for IV Therapy (Ocular = Neurosyphilis).
Step 2: Aqueous Crystalline Penicillin G: 18–24 million units per day (3–4 million units IV every 4 hours) for 10–14 days.
Step 3: Alternative (if PCN allergy): Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily OR Penicillin desensitization.
Step 4: Adjunctive Therapy: Topical steroids and cycloplegics for anterior uveitis; systemic steroids (after 24-48h of antibiotics) for severe posterior inflammation.
Step 5: Follow-up: Repeat RPR at 3, 6, and 12 months (expect a 4-fold drop in titer).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Emergency Signs
content: Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction: Acute febrile response within 24h of starting PCN; can worsen uveitis.
Rapidly Progressive Vision Loss: Potential optic nerve infarction or necrotizing retinitis.
HIV Co-infection: Higher risk of treatment failure and rapid progression to tertiary neurosyphilis.
Negative RPR with High Clinical Suspicion: Check for the 'Prozone Effect' (request dilution).

content.explanation: A-R-P: Argyll Robertson Pupil (Accommodates, Reflex to light absent, Prostitutes' pupil). I-K: Interstitial Keratitis (the classic triad of Hutchinson: notched incisors, deafness, and IK).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Ocular syphilis is ALWAYS treated as neurosyphilis, regardless of CSF results.
The 'Prozone Effect' occurs when very high antibody titers interfere with the formation of the antigen-antibody lattice, causing a false negative RPR.
Interstitial Keratitis in syphilis is usually an immune-mediated reaction, not an active infection of the cornea.
Bilateral involvement is the rule, not the exception (60-70% of cases).

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
sections.content: Prognosis is generally excellent if treated early. However, delays can lead to permanent vision loss from optic atrophy, macular scarring (post-ASPPC), or secondary glaucoma. Chronic vitreitis can lead to tractional retinal detachment or epiretinal membrane formation. Recurrence is rare unless re-infection or inadequate initial treatment occurs.

title: Ocular Tuberculosis: The Great Masquerader
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis, classification, and management of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections affecting the visual system. This resource integrates the latest COTS (Collaborative Ocular Tuberculosis Study) guidelines with gold-standard anatomical and pharmacological protocols.

sections.title: 1. Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb) that can affect any part of the eye, its adnexa, or the optic nerve. It is often a manifestation of extra-pulmonary TB (EPTB) and can occur in the absence of active systemic or pulmonary disease. It presents either through direct tissue invasion by the bacilli or as a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction (Type IV) to mycobacterial antigens.

sections.title: 4. Pathophysiology Mechanisms
content: 1. Inhalation of droplet nuclei containing M. tuberculosis.
2. Primary pulmonary infection and Ghon complex formation.
3. Hematogenous dissemination via alveolar capillaries to the uveal tract (highly vascular).
4. Latency within the RPE or uveal macrophages.
5. Reactivation: Direct bacterial multiplication vs. Immune-mediated inflammation (Delayed Hypersensitivity).

sections.title: 5. Ocular Examination Findings
content: Anterior: 'Mutton-fat' Keratic Precipitates (KPs), Koeppe/Busacca nodules.
Sclera: Necrotizing or non-necrotizing anterior scleritis.
Choroid: Unifocal/Multifocal tubercles (yellowish-white lesions).
Retina: Perivasculitis (predominantly venulitis) and Eales Disease.
Vitreous: 'Snowball' opacities or dense vitritis in endophthalmitis cases.

rows: Yellow-gray nodules (0.5 - 3mm) usually at the posterior pole.
Multifocal, amoeboid, non-contiguous lesions. Start in periphery.
Unlike classic Serpiginous, SLC often spares the peripapillary area initially.
Large solitary subretinal mass (up to 10mm) with exudative detachment.
Peripheral retinal perivasculitis, non-perfusion, and neovascularization.
Primarily affects young healthy males in India/Middle East.

sections.title: 7. Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Detailed History (Systemic symptoms, exposure, travel).
Step 2: TST (Mantoux) >10mm (endemic) or >5mm (high risk/HIV).
Step 3: IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) for higher specificity.
Step 4: Imaging: Chest X-ray and HRCT Chest (Hilar lymphadenopathy).
Step 5: Ocular Fluids: PCR for IS6110 sequence or mpb64.
Step 6: Gold Standard (Rarely possible): Culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium.

rows: Bilateral, serous detachments, diffuse uveal thickening, sunset-glow fundus.
Focal retinochoroiditis adjacent to a pigmented scar.

sections.title: 9. COTS Diagnostic Criteria
content: Definite Ocular TB: M. tb found in ocular fluids/tissues via culture or PCR.
Probable Ocular TB: Ocular signs + positive TST/IGRA + systemic TB evidence (Chest HRCT).
Possible Ocular TB: Ocular signs + positive TST/IGRA, but no systemic evidence on imaging.

rows: Monthly Visual Acuity, Color Vision (Ishihara), Humphrey Visual Field (HVF 10-2)

sections.title: 11. Treatment Regimen & Duration
content: Intensive Phase (2 Months): HRPE (Four drugs daily).
Continuation Phase (4-7 Months): HR (Two drugs daily).
Note: Total duration usually 6-9 months; extended to 12 months in CNS involvement or slow responders.

sections.title: 12. Corticosteroid Adjunct Protocol
content: Mandatory to control 'Paradoxical Reaction' (worsening after starting ATT).
Oral Prednisolone: 1 mg/kg/day started 48-72 hours after initiating ATT.
Slow Taper: Reduce over 6-12 weeks depending on clinical response.
Topical: Prednisolone Acetate 1% for anterior segment inflammation.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags & Critical Warnings
content: Ethambutol Toxicity: Progressive, painless bilateral vision loss and red-green color deficiency. Discontinue drug immediately if suspected.
Paradoxical Reaction (Jarisch-Herxheimer-like): Rapid worsening of uveitis/vitritis shortly after ATT initiation. Increase steroid dose.
Multidrug-Resistant (MDR-TB): Failure to respond to ATT after 2 months of compliant therapy.
Adrenal Crisis: If steroids are tapered too rapidly after long-term use.

content.explanation: Standard ATT: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol.
Choroidal tubercles, Creeping (Serpiginous), Conglomerate (Tuberculoma), Caseous (Necrosis), Chronic, Contiguous.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: COTS-1 Study: Confirmed that starting ATT in confirmed/probable TB reduces recurrence of uveitis by >50%.
Ultra-sensitive PCR: Targetting repetitive elements like IS6110 improves diagnostic yield in aqueous samples.
Interferon-Gamma Release Assays (IGRA): Now preferred over Mantoux in BCG-vaccinated populations due to higher specificity.

sections.title: 17. Complications & Prognosis
content: Complicated Cataract (due to chronic inflammation or steroids).
Secondary Glaucoma (Trabeculitis or Pupillary Block).
Tractional Retinal Detachment (Eales Disease).
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) - most common cause of vision loss.
Optic Atrophy (Ethambutol or chronic papillitis).

sections.title: 18. High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: TB can mimic any intraocular inflammation; always test for TB in granulomatous or refractory uveitis.
Negative Chest X-ray does NOT rule out Ocular TB; perform HRCT Chest if suspicion is high.
Eales Disease is a diagnosis of exclusion: think TB first in a young man with peripheral retinal perivasculitis.
Always check baseline visual fields and color vision BEFORE starting Ethambutol.
ATT without steroids in Ocular TB may lead to severe inflammatory damage due to the release of mycobacterial antigens.

title: Aniridia: The PAX6 Pan-Ocular Syndrome
summary: Aniridia is a complex, bilateral pan-ocular disorder caused by a haploinsufficiency of the PAX6 gene (11p13). Beyond the striking absence of the iris, it involves progressive keratopathy, glaucoma, cataracts, and foveal hypoplasia, requiring lifelong multidisciplinary management.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Aniridia is a congenital, bilateral condition characterized by the partial or complete absence of the iris. However, the term 'aniridia' is a misnomer as it is a global pan-ocular developmental defect affecting the cornea, anterior chamber angle, lens, retina, and optic nerve. It is most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion (85%) with high penetrance but variable expressivity.

rows: 30% of sporadic cases involve WT1 gene deletions

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Clinical Exam (Slit lamp for iris stump, Gonioscopy for angle)
Step 2: Pediatric Genetic Testing (PAX6 sequencing & FISH for 11p13 deletion)
Step 3: Imaging (OCT of macula for foveal hypoplasia; UBM for iris stump)
Step 4: Systemic Screening (Renal Ultrasound for Wilms Tumor)
Step 5: Functional Assessment (Visual acuity, Nystagmus evaluation)

sections.title: Critical: WAGR Screening Protocol
content: MANDATORY: Renal Ultrasound every 3 months until age 8 in sporadic cases.
Risk of Wilms Tumor is 50% in WAGR (deletion of 11p13 including WT1).
Monitor for Nephropathy and Gonadoblastoma.
Developmental delays require early intervention services.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Optical: Tinted lenses/CL for photophobia.
Corneal: Preservative-free lubricants; Autologous serum.
LSCD: Limbal Stem Cell Transplant (KLAL or Cincinatti technique).
Glaucoma: Prostaglandins/Beta-blockers; Gonio-surgery early; GDD/Tube shunts for refractory cases.
Cataract: Careful MICS; specialized iris-prosthetic IOLs (e.g., Morcher/Ophtec).

content.explanation: W: Wilms Tumor, A: Aniridia, G: Genitourinary anomalies (cryptorchidism), R: Range of developmental delays (formerly Mental Retardation).

sections.title: Surgical Pearls: Cataract & Iris Prosthesis
content: Zonular instability is common; use Capsule Tension Rings (CTR).
Artificial Iris Implants (HumanOptics) can be sutured or placed in-the-bag.
Avoid iris implants if glaucoma is uncontrolled.
High risk of Aniridic Fibrosis Syndrome (AFS) post-surgery.

sections.title: Prognosis & Red Flags
content: Sudden vision loss: Rule out retinal detachment or acute glaucoma.
Progressive corneal whitening: Indicative of AAK progression.
Avoid routine use of Pilocarpine (may worsen angle crowding).
Guarded prognosis for penetrating keratoplasty (PK) due to LSC deficiency.

sections.title: Landmark Insights & Recent Advances
content: Nonsense Suppression Therapy: Ataluren (PTC124) shows promise in restoring PAX6 function in PTC mutations.
Boston Keratoprosthesis (Type 1): Often preferred over standard PK for end-stage AAK.
Gene Therapy: Research into CRISPR/Cas9 to correct PAX6 haploinsufficiency is ongoing.
Epidemiology Note: Gillespie Syndrome is NOT associated with Wilms Tumor risk.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome (AWS) is a hyper-excitable state of the central nervous system that occurs when a chronic, heavy drinker suddenly ceases or significantly reduces ethanol intake. It ranges from mild tremulousness to life-threatening Delirium Tremens (DTs). In the ophthalmic context, AWS is critical due to its association with Wernicke Encephalopathy, characterized by ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, and ataxia.

branches: Chronic Alcohol: Potentiates GABA (Inhibitory), Inhibits NMDA (Excitatory)
Adaptation: Down-regulation of GABA receptors, Up-regulation of NMDA receptors
Withdrawal: Massive loss of GABAergic inhibition + NMDA-mediated glutamate surge

sections.title: Chronological Progression of Symptoms
content: 6-12 Hours: Mild symptoms (Insomnia, tremulousness, mild anxiety, GI upset, headache, diaphoresis, palpitations).
12-24 Hours: Alcoholic Hallucinosis (Visual, auditory, or tactile hallucinations; sensorium is clear).
24-48 Hours: Withdrawal Seizures (Generalized tonic-clonic; usually singular or in short bursts).
48-96 Hours: Delirium Tremens (Clouded consciousness, extreme autonomic hyperactivity, severe tremors, fever).

sections.title: The Ocular Examination: Wernicke’s Focus
content: Horizontal Gaze-Evoked Nystagmus (Most common ocular sign)
Abducens (CN VI) Nerve Palsy: Often bilateral, but can be asymmetrical
Conjugate Gaze Palsy: Inability to move eyes in tandem vertically or horizontally
Sluggish Pupillary Light Response or Miosis
Papilledema (Rare, but indicates severe encephalopathy)
Retinal Hemorrhages (Usually secondary to associated thrombocytopenia or trauma)

content.explanation: C: Confusion (Encephalopathy); A: Ataxia (Gait instability); N: Nystagmus (and Ophthalmoplegia). If untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff Psychosis (Anterograde/Retrograde amnesia + Confabulation).

rows: 0 (None) to 7 (Severe, even with arms not extended)
Goiter, exophthalmos, elevated T4/T3, suppressed TSH
High anion gap metabolic acidosis, 'snowfield' vision, optic disc hyperemia
Similar to AWS but typically longer duration/delayed onset
Fever, leukocytosis, focal neurological deficits, abnormal CSF
Oxalate crystals in urine, acute renal failure, cranial nerve palsies

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Delirium Tremens (DTs)
content: Severe autonomic instability (Tachycardia >120, BP >160/100)
Profound hyperthermia (Fever >38.5°C / 101.3°F)
Fluctuating level of consciousness and severe disorientation
Vivid, often terrifying 'zoopsia' (hallucinations of small animals/insects)
DANGER: High risk of cardiovascular collapse or status epilepticus

sections.title: Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Laboratory: CBC (Macrocytosis, Thrombocytopenia), BMP (Electrolytes, Anion gap), LFTs (AST:ALT > 2:1), Blood Alcohol Level (BAL).
2. Nutritional Screen: Serum B1 (Thiamine) level (often low), Mg2+ (critical to correct for B1 response).
3. Imaging: CT Head if first-time seizure or trauma; MRI Brain (T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in mammillary bodies for Wernicke's).
4. ECG: Evaluate for QTc prolongation (risk of Torsades de Pointes).

sections.title: Management Strategy: Step-by-Step
content: 1. Stabilization: Airway protection and IV access.
2. Thiamine Replacement: 500mg IV TID for 2 days, then 250mg daily. GIVE BEFORE GLUCOSE.
3. Symptom-Triggered BZDs: Diazepam or Lorazepam based on CIWA-Ar scores.
4. Fluid/Electrolyte Correction: Replace Magnesium (target >2.0 mg/dL) and Potassium.
5. Supportive Care: Quiet, dimly lit room; frequent reorientation.

rows: Preferred in liver failure or elderly (short half-life).
Commonly used for outpatient/mild withdrawal tapers.
Used for BZD-refractory AWS or status epilepticus.
Adjunct for autonomic control; does not treat underlying GABA deficit.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Thiamine deficiency causes mitochondrial dysfunction; glucose infusion without Thiamine exacerbates pyruvate accumulation, worsening Wernicke's.
Abducens palsy in AWS is often the most responsive sign to Thiamine, resolving within hours to days.
Ataxia may take weeks to improve, and 50% of patients have permanent gait deficits.
Kindling Effect: Each subsequent withdrawal episode is more severe and carries a higher risk of seizures/DTs.

sections.title: Landmark Evidence: The ASAM Guidelines
sections.content: The American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Clinical Practice Guideline recommends 'Symptom-Triggered' therapy over 'Fixed-Schedule' therapy for BZDs in AWS. This approach reduces the total dose of medication used and the duration of treatment, provided the patient can be monitored frequently using the CIWA-Ar scale.

sections.title: Red Flag: Refractory AWS
content: Requirement of >50mg Diazepam or >10mg Lorazepam in first hour
Failure to respond to high-dose BZDs suggests need for Phenobarbital or Propofol
Escalate to ICU level care immediately

title: LHON: The Mitochondrial Silent Thief of Sight
summary: Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON) is the most common primary mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) disorder, characterized by subacute, painless, bilateral central vision loss primarily affecting young males. It represents a paradigm of mitochondrial genetics and selective retinal ganglion cell (RGC) vulnerability.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: LHON is a maternally inherited mitochondrial disease resulting from mutations in the ND genes (encoding subunits of Complex I of the respiratory chain). It causes selective apoptosis of Retinal Ganglion Cells (RGCs), specifically the parvocellular pathway, leading to severe optic atrophy and permanent central scotoma.

sections.title: Clinical Progression Stages
content: Step 1: Asymptomatic Carrier (Normal acuity, subclinical RNFL thickening)
Step 2: Subacute Phase (Weeks 0-6): Rapid painless vision loss, dyschromatopsia
Step 3: Dynamic Phase (Months 1-6): Fellow eye involved (sequential > simultaneous)
Step 4: Chronic Phase (>6-12 Months): Progressive RNFL loss, optic atrophy

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Peripapillary telangiectatic microangiopathy
Pseudo-edema: Swelling of the nerve fiber layer (NFL) without leakage
Absence of Optic Disc Cupping (unlike glaucoma)
Tortuosity of retinal arterioles
Centrocecal scotoma on Visual Field testing
Pupillary light reflex is often DISPROPORTIONATELY spared

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: Genetic Testing: Targeted screening for the 3 primary mutations
OCT RNFL/GCL: Shows temporal thinning followed by global atrophy
Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): CRITICAL to show NO disc leakage
Visual Field (Goldmann or HVF): Demonstrates central/centrocecal scotomas
Neuroimaging (MRI): To rule out compressive or demyelinating lesions

sections.title: Red Flags & Contraindications
content: Smoking: Strongest environmental trigger for conversion
Excessive Alcohol: Synergistic effect with tobacco
Ethambutol/Linezolid: Avoid mitochondrial toxins
Rapid, Painful loss: Consider inflammatory etiology instead
Extraocular Signs: 'LHON Plus' (Dystonia, tremors, MS-like symptoms)

content.explanation: S: SYMMETRIC (eventually), S: SUBACUTE (painless), S: SMOKING (must stop!)

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Lifestyle Modification: Immediate cessation of smoking and limited alcohol consumption.
Step 2: Idebenone (Raxone): 900mg/day (300mg TID). Start early for best results, continue for at least 1 year.
Step 3: Gene Therapy (Lumevoq/GS010): Intravitreal injection of rAAV2/2-ND4. Recent studies show bilateral benefit after unilateral injection.
Step 4: Supportive Care: Low vision aids and genetic counseling for maternal relatives.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: LHON is often misdiagnosed as 'Retrobulbar Optic Neuritis' in the early phase.
Fenestration of the optic nerve sheath is CONTRAINDICATED.
The pseudo-edema corresponds to stasis of axoplasmic transport, NOT fluid.
Melanopsin-containing RGCs are spared, explaining the preserved pupillary reflex.
Wait at least 12-18 months before declaring no chance of spontaneous recovery.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
content: RESCUE & REVERSE Trials: Evaluated Lumevoq gene therapy for ND4 mutations.
REFLECT Trial: Confirmed the efficacy of bilateral IVT gene therapy injections.
RHODOS Trial: Provided the evidence base for high-dose Idebenone (900mg/day).
The 'Bilateral Benefit' Phenomenon: Discovery of viral vector transfer via the optic chiasm.

summary: High-Risk PDR represents a critical threshold in diabetic eye disease where the risk of severe vision loss (SVL) increases exponentially. This guide covers the landmark DRS criteria, multimodal imaging, and the evolving paradigm of PRP vs. Anti-VEGF therapy.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Significance
sections.content: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) is characterized by the presence of extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation. 'High-Risk' PDR is a specific subset defined by the Diabetic Retinopathy Study (DRS) as having a high risk of developing severe visual loss (defined as visual acuity <5/200 on two consecutive visits) within 2 years if left untreated.

rows: Neovascularization at or within 1DD of the optic disc.
Any NVD associated with Vitreous Hemorrhage (VH) or Preretinal Hemorrhage (PRH).
Neovascularization elsewhere ≥ 0.5 disc area AND VH or PRH.
Large area of ischemia and active bleeding.
Vitreous or Preretinal hemorrhage associated with NVD or NVE.
The hallmark of proliferative activity and risk.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Ischemic Cascade
content: 1. Chronic Hyperglycemia: Leads to polyol pathway activation and AGE accumulation.
2. Capillary Non-perfusion: Pericyte loss and basement membrane thickening cause microvascular occlusion.
3. Retinal Hypoxia: Triggered by extensive capillary dropout.
4. Cytokine Release: Upregulation of VEGF (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor) and Erythropoietin.
5. Neovascularization: New vessels lack tight junctions, leading to leakage and tractional membranes.

rows: Hemisheaths, sudden onset, optic disc swelling in CRVO.
Pain, mid-peripheral blot hemes, narrowed arteries.
History of plaque or external beam radiation.

branches: FFA: Identifying areas of capillary non-perfusion (CNP) and leakage at NVD/NVE
OCT-Macula: Evaluate for concomitant DME (Diabetic Macular Edema)
OCT-A: Non-invasive detection of FVP and foveal avascular zone (FAZ) enlargement
B-Scan USG: Critical if VH obscures fundus; rule out Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD)
Wide-field Imaging: Captures peripheral ischemia and NVE outside standard 7-fields

sections.title: Management Algorithm: Treatment of Choice
content: Step 1: Systemic Optimization (HbA1c < 7.0%, BP < 130/80, Lipid control).
Step 2: Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) - Gold Standard. 1200-1500 burns, 200-500um spot, 0.1s duration.
Step 3: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab/Aflibercept) - Non-inferior to PRP for VA (Protocol S), but requires high compliance.
Step 4: Combination Therapy - Anti-VEGF prior to PRP to reduce DME risk and facilitate NV regression.
Step 5: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) - Indicated for non-clearing VH, TRD, or combined RRD/TRD.

sections.title: Surgical Indications & Red Flags
content: Non-clearing Vitreous Hemorrhage (>1 month in T1DM, >3 months in T2DM)
Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD) involving or threatening the macula
Combined Tractional and Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment
Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) with media opacity preventing PRP
Ghost Cell Glaucoma

content.explanation: High risk of PDR progression: 4 quadrants of severe hemorrhages, 2 quadrants of venous beading, or 1 quadrant of IRMA.

rows: PRP reduces risk of SVL by >50%.
Established PRP as standard of care.
PRP not recommended for mild/mod NPDR; consider in severe NPDR/early PDR.
Ranibizumab non-inferior to PRP through 5 years for visual acuity.
Alternative to laser in compliant patients.
Aflibercept superior to PRP for VA outcomes at 1 year.
Anti-VEGF prevents PDR in high-risk NPDR.

sections.title: PRP Technical Pearls
content: Burn intensity: Dull white/grey (Level II-III).
Spacing: One burn width apart.
Extent: From vascular arches to the periphery.
Avoid: Direct treatment of the macula, major vessels, or optic disc.
Retrobulbar block: Consider if patient is sensitive or for extensive supplementation.

sections.title: Vitreoretinal Surgery Steps
content: 1. 23G or 25G Valved Trocar Placement.
2. Core Vitrectomy and induction of PVD (if not present).
3. Segmentation/Delamination of fibrovascular membranes.
4. Hemostasis using endodiathermy.
5. Endolaser Photocoagulation (Filling in PRP gaps).
6. Fluid-Air Exchange and optional Silicone Oil/Gas Tamponade.

branches: PRP: Constriction of visual field, night blindness, choroidal effusion
Surgery: Iatrogenic breaks, recurrence of VH, cataract progression

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always rule out Neovascular Glaucoma; perform gonioscopy on all HR-PDR patients.
Treat DME before or concurrent with PRP to prevent laser-induced maculopathy.
Falsely low HbA1c: Check for sickle cell, anemia, or recent transfusions.
Pregnancy can cause rapid acceleration of PDR; requires monthly screening.
Post-PRP VH: Doesn't always mean failure; may be 'washout' of old heme.

title: Band Keratopathy: The Calcific Bridge
summary: A chronic corneal degeneration characterized by the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite in the subepithelial space, Bowman's layer, and anterior stroma. This textbook-grade guide covers its metabolic, inflammatory, and surgical management pathways.

data.title: Band Keratopathy: The Calcific Bridge
data.summary: A chronic corneal degeneration characterized by the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite in the subepithelial space, Bowman's layer, and anterior stroma. This textbook-grade guide covers its metabolic, inflammatory, and surgical management pathways.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Band Keratopathy (BK) is a chronic, degenerative condition involving the deposition of grey-to-white calcium hydroxyapatite crystals in the anterior cornea. Deposits typically begin at the peripheral 3 and 9 o'clock positions, separated from the limbus by a 'lucid interval' of clear cornea, eventually progressing centrally to form a horizontal band across the interpalpebral fissure.

branches: Evaporation of tears increases local pH
Loss of CO2 at the interpalpebral fissure
Primary site: Bowman's Layer & Subepithelial space

rows: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) - most common in kids, Chronic Uveitis, Phthisis Bulbi, Interstitial Keratitis.
Hypercalcemia, Hyperphosphatemia, Chronic Renal Failure, Hyperparathyroidism, Sarcoidosis, Vitamin D Toxicity, Milk-Alkali Syndrome.
Chronic exposure to Mercury (preservatives), Silicone Oil in the Anterior Chamber, Phosphate-containing eye drops.
Primary calcific band keratopathy (rare), Familial forms.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Peripheral inception at 3 and 9 o'clock limbus.
Lucid Interval: A clear zone between the limbus and the calcium deposit (due to lack of Bowman's layer at the extreme periphery).
'Swiss Cheese' appearance: Small holes in the band representing where corneal nerves pierce the Bowman’s layer.
Surface irregularity: Leading to foreign body sensation and secondary epithelial erosions.
Advanced progression: Centripetal growth across the visual axis leading to vision loss.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Laboratory Panels
content: Step 1: Serum Calcium and Phosphate levels (rule out hyperparathyroidism/renal issues).
Step 2: Serum Albumin (to calculate corrected calcium).
Step 3: BUN and Creatinine (assess renal function).
Step 4: Serum ACE and Chest X-ray (if sarcoidosis suspected).
Step 5: Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) levels.

sections.title: Surgical Management: EDTA Chelation
content: 1. Anesthesia: Topical Proparacaine/Tetracaine +/- peribulbar block for long cases.
2. Epithelial Debridement: Use a #15 Bard-Parker blade or alcohol (20%) to remove epithelium overlying the calcium.
3. Chemical Chelation: Apply Disodium EDTA (1.5% to 4%) using a cellulose sponge or a well (e.g., a 6-8mm trephine ring).
4. Mechanical Scraping: Use a blade or diamond burr as the calcium softens/dissolves.
5. Irrigation: Copious rinsing with Balanced Salt Solution (BSS) to remove residual EDTA and debris.
6. Post-Op: Bandage Contact Lens (BCL), topical antibiotics, and NSAIDs/Steroids.

rows: White/Yellow line at 3/9 o'clock; no clear lucid interval.
Amber-colored oily droplets; collagenous, not calcific.
Lipid deposition; involves the entire circumference; has lucid interval.

content.explanation: C: Chronic Uveitis; A: Age-related/Alkali (Milk-Alkali); L: Local (Silicone oil); C: Chronic Renal Failure; I: Increased Serum Ca2+; U: Under-treated Sarcoidosis; M: Mercury exposure.

sections.title: Advanced Treatment Options
content: PTK (Phototherapeutic Keratectomy): Excimer laser ablation for smoother surface but risks hyperopic shift.
Diamond Burr Polishing: Often combined with EDTA for faster results.
Amniotic Membrane Grafting: For persistent epithelial defects post-chelation.
Lamellar Keratoplasty: Reserved for cases with deep stromal involvement.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: When to worry
content: Bilateral BK in a child: High suspicion for Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA).
Rapidly progressive BK: Likely systemic hypercalcemia or renal crisis.
Stromal Melting: Can occur if EDTA is used for excessive durations or high concentrations.
Non-healing epithelial defect post-op: Risk of secondary infection/keratitis.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Recurrence: High risk if the underlying cause (e.g., uveitis, hypercalcemia) is not controlled.
Induced Astigmatism: Resulting from irregular corneal surface.
Hyperopic Shift: Especially after deep scraping or PTK laser treatment.
Prognosis: Generally excellent for vision if the visual axis is cleared and the macula is healthy.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the 'Lucid Interval'; its presence is hallmark for BK vs. Arcus/Limbal Girdle.
EDTA 0.05M (1.5% to 3.0%) is the standard concentration; higher concentrations risk toxicity.
The 'Swiss Cheese' holes are technically called 'Nerve Canals of Bowman’s Layer'.
Silicone oil-induced BK is more common in aphakic eyes where oil contacts the corneal endothelium.

sections.title: Landmark Insights: Phosphate-Free Drops
sections.content: Recent studies and the AAO BCSC emphasize avoiding phosphate-buffered eye drops (e.g., certain Prednisolone or Dexamethasone formulations) in patients with corneal surface compromise, as they can accelerate the precipitation of calcium phosphate on the cornea, worsening BK.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations: JIA Focus
content: JIA is the most common systemic association in children.
BK may be the presenting sign of asymptomatic uveitis.
Requires collaborative care with Pediatric Rheumatology.
Aggressive treatment of the underlying uveitis is mandatory to prevent recurrence.

title: Mastering Lens Subluxation: From Etiology to Surgical Management
summary: Lens subluxation (ectopia lentis) represents a complex zonular pathology requiring precise diagnostic evaluation and tailored surgical intervention. This guide synthesizes clinical classification, management algorithms, and emergency protocols for the modern ophthalmologist.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Ectopia lentis is defined as the displacement of the crystalline lens from its physiological position due to zonular dehiscence. Subluxation is partial displacement; Luxation (dislocation) is total displacement. Prevalence is highly variable, often secondary to ocular trauma (most common) or systemic connective tissue disorders (Marfan syndrome, Homocystinuria).

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Iridodonesis (tremulous iris)
Phacodonesis (lens movement)
Monocular diplopia
Refractive shift (induced astigmatism/myopia)
Secondary glaucoma (pupillary block or phacolytic)
Vitreous prolapse into anterior chamber

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Assess zonular integrity (Slit lamp/Gonioscopy).
Step 2: Manage intraocular pressure (IOP).
Step 3: Determine need for surgery (Visual acuity, glaucoma, uveitis).
Step 4: Surgical planning (Capsular tension rings (CTR), Ahmed segment, pars plana vitrectomy).
Step 5: Post-op rehabilitation.

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Referral
content: Acute Angle Closure Glaucoma from pupillary block.
Phacolytic glaucoma (lens proteins in trabecular meshwork).
Evidence of open globe injury if traumatic.
Progressive worsening of vision in children (Amblyopia risk).

sections.title: Surgical Nuances
content: Use of Trypan Blue (0.06%) to visualize capsule.
Stabilize capsule early with CTR or hook system.
Avoid over-inflation of anterior chamber.
Consider pars plana lensectomy in severe displacement.
Scleral fixation of IOL (Yamane technique) if zonules are insufficient.

content.explanation: Homocystinuria = Inferior displacement; Marfan = upward (supero-temporal) displacement.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Femtosecond laser-assisted phacoemulsification (FLACS) helps reduce zonular stress during capsulotomy.
Development of adjustable suture-less scleral-fixated IOLs (Yamane technique).
Genetic counseling and systemic evaluation protocols have shifted toward early metabolic screening for Homocystinuria in suspected cases.

title: Clinical Mastery: Exposure Keratopathy
summary: Exposure keratopathy is a sight-threatening condition resulting from incomplete eyelid closure (lagophthalmos), leading to ocular surface desiccation, epithelial breakdown, and potential stromal ulceration. Prompt identification and aggressive lubrication are mandatory to prevent visual morbidity.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Exposure keratopathy results from a failure of the eyelid to provide adequate coverage of the globe. This disrupts the tear film, causing increased evaporation and hyperosmolarity. Without the blink-induced distribution of mucins and lipids, the corneal epithelium undergoes desiccation, shedding, and keratinization. In severe cases, secondary microbial keratitis occurs due to breach of the ocular surface barrier.

rows: Lax upper lids, chronic papillary conjunctivitis

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Status
content: Infiltrate or stromal thinning (risk of perforation)
Hypopyon (secondary infectious keratitis)
Decreased visual acuity (involvement of visual axis)
Ocular pain disproportionate to findings (risk of globe integrity loss)

sections.title: Clinical Examination Sequence
content: Step 1: Assess Bell's phenomenon (upward globe rotation on closure).
Step 2: Measure lagophthalmos gap in mm using a millimeter ruler.
Step 3: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with Fluorescein staining to evaluate interpalpebral epithelial defects.
Step 4: Check corneal sensation with a cotton-wisp test (r/o neurotrophic component).
Step 5: Exophthalmometry (Hertel) to rule out underlying proptosis.

sections.title: Management Protocol
content: Conservative: Preservative-free artificial tears (Q1H).
Nighttime: Preservative-free lubricating ointment.
Barrier: Moisture chambers / Hydrogel patches.
Mechanical: Taping eyelids closed during sleep.
Surgical: Temporary tarsorrhaphy, gold weight implants, or lower lid tightening.

content.explanation: S: Severity of gap, T: Tear film evaluation, A: Antibiotic prophylaxis, R: Rest/Nocturnal protection, E: Eyelid position repair.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the 'Bell's Phenomenon'. Patients lacking this are at extreme risk for corneal perforation.
Preservative-free preparations are mandatory if frequency exceeds 4x/day to prevent toxic epitheliopathy.
In ICU patients, consider the 'Vaseline technique' or clear plastic occlusive dressings to maintain moisture.
Gold weight implant (e.g., 0.8g to 1.6g) is the gold standard for facial nerve palsy-induced lagophthalmos.
Surgical correction should not be delayed if medical management fails to show epithelial healing within 48-72 hours.

title: Ptosis Surgery in Poor Bell's Phenomenon: A Surgical Imperative
summary: Managing ptosis in patients with poor or absent Bell’s phenomenon is a high-stakes clinical challenge, requiring precise surgical planning to prevent exposure keratopathy. This guide outlines the evidence-based assessment and modified surgical strategies essential for safeguarding ocular surface integrity.

sections.title: Clinical Significance of Bell's Phenomenon
sections.content: Bell’s phenomenon is the reflexive superior and outward rotation of the globe upon eyelid closure. In patients with poor Bell's, the cornea remains exposed during sleep (lagophthalmos). Performing standard ptosis surgery (e.g., Fasanella-Servat or maximal levator advancement) in these patients can lead to severe exposure keratopathy, corneal ulceration, and vision loss.

sections.title: Risk Factors for Poor Bell's
content: Neurotrophic keratopathy
CN VII palsy (Facial nerve dysfunction)
Severe dry eye (Aqueous deficient)
History of chronic orbital/eyelid surgery
Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles (CFEOM)
Senile orbicularis weakness

sections.title: Red Flags: Pre-Surgical Assessment
content: Incomplete lid closure at rest
Positive Schirmer I test < 5mm
Corneal staining patterns in the inferior third
Decreased corneal sensitivity
Current history of filamentary keratitis

sections.title: Pre-operative Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Perform complete ocular surface exam including slit-lamp with fluorescein/lissamine green.
Step 2: Assess Bell's phenomenon: Ask patient to close eyes tightly while you manually elevate the upper lid.
Step 3: Measure Marginal Reflex Distance 1 (MRD1) and Levator Function (LF).
Step 4: Conduct Schirmer's I test (without anesthesia) and TBUT (Tear Break-Up Time).
Step 5: Perform the 'Phenylephrine Test' to simulate eyelid height and observe for induced lagophthalmos.

content.explanation: B: Break-up time (TBUT), E: Examination of cornea, L: Lubrication status, L: Levator function, S: Schirmer test.

sections.title: Post-Operative Management
content: Aggressive lubrication: Preservative-free artificial tears hourly
Nocturnal protection: Lacri-Lube or heavy ointment at night
Eyelid taping if persistent lagophthalmos is noted
Follow-up at Day 1, Week 1, Month 1, and Month 3
Immediate assessment if pain or photophobia occurs

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Always under-correct in doubtful cases; it is easier to revise a ptosis than to treat a melting cornea.
A small lateral tarsorrhaphy can be combined with ptosis repair if the ocular surface is borderline.
Check corneal sensitivity: diminished sensitivity is a major risk factor for surgical complication.
The presence of a Bell’s phenomenon is a neuro-muscular integrity indicator; its absence suggests a higher risk of lagophthalmos.

sections.title: Definition & Surgical Principles
sections.content: Evisceration involves removing intraocular contents while preserving the scleral shell, extraocular muscles, and optic nerve. Enucleation involves removal of the entire globe. The 'prosthetic shell' serves to restore volume and mimic natural appearance. Clinical goal: Maintain a healthy, well-formed conjunctival sac capable of retaining a customized ocular prosthesis.

sections.title: Socket Evaluation Components
content: Superior and inferior fornix depth (crucial for prosthesis retention)
Conjunctival health (look for discharge, keratinization, or chronic inflammation)
Volume assessment (check for superior sulcus deformity)
Implant motility (assessing the coupling between the orbital implant and the prosthesis)
Palpebral fissure width and eyelid position (ptosis vs. retraction)

sections.title: Prosthesis Maintenance Protocol
content: Step 1: Annual polish by Ocularist to remove biofilm and surface scratches.
Step 2: Daily cleaning with mild, non-abrasive soap and warm water.
Step 3: Lubrication with preservative-free artificial tears if dry eye symptoms persist.
Step 4: Periodic socket irrigation if mucopurulent discharge is noted.
Step 5: Replace prosthesis every 5-7 years to account for volume loss in the orbit.

sections.title: Red Flags (Emergency Signs)
content: Implant exposure through the conjunctiva
Signs of orbital cellulitis (fever, erythema, extreme pain)
Sudden inability to retain the prosthesis
New onset socket mass/suspicion of recurrence (in cases of melanoma/R-B)

content.explanation: Socket (regular assessment), Surface (polish for smooth finish), Size (adjust for volume loss), Sanitation (daily cleaning).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always evaluate the socket without the prosthesis to grade baseline conjunctival health.
GPC in anophthalmic sockets is frequently caused by biofilm buildup on the prosthesis surface.
Use of a silicone sphere implant in evisceration provides better motility than simple scleral closure.
Secondary implants or dermis-fat grafts are gold standards for correcting post-enucleation volume deficits.

title: Mastering the Contracted Socket: A Clinical Reconstruction Guide
summary: The contracted socket represents a complex sequela of enucleation or evisceration, characterized by insufficient conjunctival volume and fornix depth. This guide provides a systematic approach to diagnosis, classification, and advanced reconstruction strategies for the reconstructive ocularist and surgeon.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: A contracted socket is a clinical state where the conjunctival sac lacks the necessary volume, surface area, and fornix depth to support a prosthetic eye. Pathophysiology involves myofibroblastic proliferation, chronic inflammation, and fibrosis of the subconjunctival connective tissue, leading to scar contracture and loss of the inferior/superior fornices.

rows: Severe: Significant contracture, no fornix depth
Total: Obliteration of the conjunctival sac

sections.title: Clinical Examination Checklist
content: Assessment of superior and inferior fornix depth.
Evaluation of eyelid margin position (entropion/ectropion).
Assessment of orbital implant volume (implant exposure/migration).
Examination of conjunctival mucosa for keratinization or symblepharon.
Palpation of the orbit for orbital floor fractures or implant mobility.
Measurement of the 'prosthetic eye retention' capacity.

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Referral
content: Exposed hydroxyapatite or porous polyethylene implant.
Socket pain suggestive of orbital cellulitis.
Rapidly progressive volume loss.
Signs of orbital implant extrusion.
Severe pyogenic granuloma formation.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Treat underlying inflammation (Topical antibiotics/steroids).
Step 2: Conservative management (Prosthetic resizing/expansion).
Step 3: Mild cases: Fornix reconstruction with mucosal grafting.
Step 4: Severe cases: Dermis-fat graft or orbital implant exchange.
Step 5: Total obliteration: Ocular surface reconstruction/orbital prosthesis.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques: Key Pearls
content: Mucosal Grafting: Buccal mucosa is the gold standard for donor tissue.
Dermis-Fat Graft: Excellent for secondary implant volume correction.
Tissue Expanders: Used in severely scarred, contracted sockets prior to reconstruction.
Symblepharon Lysis: Release of cicatricial bands with spacer placement.
Anterior Orbitotomy: Necessary for complete implant exchange or removal.

content.explanation: V: Vertical fornix depth, O: Orbital implant position, L: Lid margin stability, U: Underlying cicatrization, M: Mucosa integrity, E: External orbital bony support.

sections.title: Recent Advances
sections.content: Recent studies suggest the use of amniotic membrane transplantation (AMT) in conjunction with mitomycin-C to inhibit fibroblastic activity and recurrence. Advanced 3D-printed patient-specific orbital implants are currently under clinical investigation to restore superior socket volume.

title: Mastering Bull's-Eye Maculopathy: Pathophysiology & Clinical Management
summary: Bull's-eye maculopathy is a distinct phenotypic presentation characterized by a central area of RPE preservation surrounded by a ring of RPE atrophy. This pattern is pathognomonic for several hereditary and toxic retinal dystrophies requiring precise multimodal diagnostic differentiation.

sections.title: Definition & Etiology
sections.content: Bull's-eye maculopathy describes a specific fundus appearance: a central island of preserved RPE/foveal tissue, a ring of depigmentation/atrophy, and an outer ring of hyperpigmentation. Etiologically, it stems from metabolic disruption of the RPE/photoreceptor complex, often secondary to drug toxicity or genetic mutations (e.g., ABCA4, PROM1).

rows: ABCA4 mutation; early onset; dark choroid

sections.title: Red Flags for HCQ Toxicity
content: Parafoveal thinning on SD-OCT
Loss of ellipsoid zone integrity
Visual field defects (10-2 test)
Multifocal ERG amplitude reduction
Autofluorescence ring

sections.title: Diagnostic Protocol
content: Step 1: Baseline Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF) for baseline mapping.
Step 2: SD-OCT (horizontal/vertical macular scans) to check for EZ/OS layer attenuation.
Step 3: 10-2 Humphrey Visual Field (HVF) for pericentral scotomas.
Step 4: mfERG for functional assessment of central retinal health.
Step 5: Fundus photography (Color) to document the classic ring appearance.

content.explanation: H-Hydroxychloroquine, C-Cumulative dose check, Q-Quantitative 10-2 VF, S-Scanning OCT (parafoveal), T-Tamoxifen interaction, O-Observation of RPE, P-Periodic screening.

branches: Stargardt: ABCA4, Early Onset, Dark Choroid on FFA
Pattern: PRPH2, Adult Onset, Lipofuscin Deposits

sections.title: Recent Advances: The AAO 2016 Recommendations
content: Shifted screening paradigm from 'dosage' to 'functional imaging' (OCT/FAF/mfERG).
Maximal daily dose capped at 5.0 mg/kg of real weight.
Emphasis on early detection before the 'Bull's-eye' becomes visible on color fundus exam.
High-risk patients (Asian descent, kidney disease) require more frequent, rigorous screening.

sections.title: Definition & Molecular Pathogenesis
sections.content: Stargardt Disease (STGD1) is an autosomal recessive retinal dystrophy caused by mutations in the ABCA4 gene. The ABCA4 protein is an ATP-binding cassette transporter located on the disc membranes of rod and cone outer segments. Failure of this transporter leads to the accumulation of N-retinylidene-phosphatidylethanolamine (N-retinylidene-PE), which spontaneously condenses into toxic A2E (a major component of lipofuscin) within the Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE), leading to secondary photoreceptor death.

rows: Yellow-white sub-RPE deposits at the posterior pole
RPE atrophy centered at the fovea
A hallmark of FFA showing choroidal masking by RPE lipofuscin
Preservation of central vision in some advanced cases

sections.title: Red Flags: When to refer/suspect
content: Rapid vision loss in a teenager
Bilateral symmetric macular atrophy
Presence of pisciform yellow flecks beyond the arcades
Family history of childhood blindness

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: Step 1: BCVA and Color Vision (Ishihara/HRR) testing.
Step 2: Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF) - essential for visualizing hypo/hyper-autofluorescent flecks.
Step 3: Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) - Classic 'Dark Choroid' sign.
Step 4: SD-OCT - Quantifying ellipsoid zone (EZ) loss and outer retinal atrophy.
Step 5: ERG/EOG - To assess global rod/cone function.
Step 6: Molecular genetic testing (ABCA4 gene panel).

content.explanation: S: Symmetric atrophy; T: Toxic lipofuscin accumulation; G: Genetic (ABCA4); D: Dark choroid on FFA.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Dark Choroid' occurs because lipofuscin in the RPE absorbs the background choroidal fluorescence.
Avoid high-dose Vitamin A supplementation, which may accelerate lipofuscin accumulation.
Recent advances focus on gene therapy (AAV-mediated) and sub-retinal transplantation.
Prognosis is generally favorable for central vision until the atrophy involves the foveal center.

title: Silicone Oil in Vitreoretinal Surgery: A Comprehensive Clinical Compendium
summary: Silicone oil is a long-term endotamponade agent utilized for complex retinal detachments. Mastering its indications, ocular complications, and precise removal techniques is essential for the modern vitreoretinal surgeon.

data.title: Silicone Oil in Vitreoretinal Surgery: A Comprehensive Clinical Compendium
data.summary: Silicone oil is a long-term endotamponade agent utilized for complex retinal detachments. Mastering its indications, ocular complications, and precise removal techniques is essential for the modern vitreoretinal surgeon.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='none' stroke='#1e88e5' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M30 50 Q50 20 70 50 T30 50' fill='#bbdefb'/><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='10' fill='#1e88e5'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Indications
content: Definition: High-viscosity, clear, polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) used as an internal tamponade.
Indications: Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR), Giant Retinal Tears (GRT), CMV Retinitis-related detachments, and trauma.
Physical Properties: Hydrophobic, non-absorbable, chemically inert, and refractive index of 1.40.

sections.title: Ocular Complications
content: Secondary Glaucoma: Pupillary block or emulsification-induced trabecular meshwork obstruction.
Band Keratopathy: Prolonged corneal contact in phakic or aphakic eyes.
Cataract Formation: Inevitable in phakic eyes due to metabolic isolation of the lens.
Emulsification: Formation of micro-droplets leading to oil migration into the anterior chamber.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (check for oil droplets/pupillary block).
2. Intraocular pressure (Goldmann/Tonopen, watch for rapid spikes).
3. Gonioscopy (evaluate for emulsified oil in the angle).
4. B-Scan Ultrasonography (detect retro-oil or posterior staphyloma).
5. OCT (assess macular status through oil).

sections.title: Removal Protocol
content: Step 1: Perform complete vitrectomy and membrane peeling.
Step 2: Utilize a passive aspiration cannula or active pump at low suction (e.g., 200-300 mmHg).
Step 3: Consider use of viscous fluid injector (VFI) if oil is highly viscous (5000 cSt).
Step 4: Perform final fluid-air exchange to clear residual micro-droplets.

content.explanation: P: Pressure check (glaucoma?), R: Retinal integrity (attachment confirmed?), E: Emulsification check (angle evaluation), P: Patience (avoid rapid aspiration to prevent iatrogenic tears).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a peripheral iridectomy (PI) in inferior position for aphakic eyes to prevent pupillary block.
Avoid using silicone oil if the patient requires frequent MRI imaging (though some are safe, check protocols).
Oil emulsification is correlated with the duration of time left in the eye and eye movement frequency.
Silicone oil is not a substitute for complete relief of vitreous traction.

summary: Postoperative upper gastrointestinal (UGI) bleeding is a life-threatening complication necessitating rapid stabilization, multispecialty coordination, and precise endoscopic intervention. This guide outlines the evidence-based approach to the unstable surgical patient.

data.title: Postoperative Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Critical Management Guide
data.summary: Postoperative upper gastrointestinal (UGI) bleeding is a life-threatening complication necessitating rapid stabilization, multispecialty coordination, and precise endoscopic intervention. This guide outlines the evidence-based approach to the unstable surgical patient.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Postoperative UGI bleeding refers to hemorrhage originating from the esophagus, stomach, or duodenum occurring within 30 days post-surgery. It is distinct from pre-existing conditions, often exacerbated by systemic stress, coagulopathy, and pharmacological factors.

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Stabilization
content: Hemodynamic instability (Tachycardia > 100bpm, Hypotension < 90mmHg systolic)
Hematemesis (bright red blood) or Coffee-ground emesis
Melena (tarry, black stools indicating >50mL blood loss)
Syncope or altered mental status
Signs of hypovolemic shock (cool/clammy skin, oliguria)

rows: Anastomotic bleeding, Dieulafoy’s lesion, Aorto-enteric fistula

sections.title: Initial Resuscitation Protocol
content: Step 1: Secure two large-bore (16-18G) IV lines.
Step 2: Crystalloid fluid resuscitation (Goal: MAP > 65 mmHg).
Step 3: Transfuse PRBCs if Hb < 7 g/dL (or < 9 g/dL in high-risk cardiac patients).
Step 4: Reverse coagulopathy (FFP, Platelets, Vitamin K as indicated).
Step 5: Initiate IV PPI bolus (80mg) followed by infusion (8mg/hr).

sections.title: Endoscopic Intervention Modalities
content: Thermal: Heater probe, Bipolar electrocoagulation.
Injection: Epinephrine (1:10,000 dilution) to induce vasoconstriction.
Mechanical: Endoclips for visible vessels or active spurting.
Topical: Hemospray (hemostatic powder) for diffuse oozing.

content.mnemonic: IA, IB, IIA, IIB, IIC, III
content.explanation: IA: Spurting, IB: Oozing (High risk). IIA: Visible vessel, IIB: Adherent clot. IIC: Hematin-covered base, III: Clean base (Low risk).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: PPIs reduce the need for surgery but do not improve mortality directly.
Early endoscopy (within 24 hours) is mandatory for hemodynamically stabilized patients.
Always check INR/PT/PTT; surgical patients are often on prophylactic anticoagulation.
Consult Interventional Radiology (IR) early if endoscopic attempts fail.

title: Anaphylactic Shock: Clinical Mastery & Emergency Protocol
summary: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by rapid onset and multisystem involvement. Immediate recognition and administration of intramuscular epinephrine are the cornerstones of survival.

data.title: Anaphylactic Shock: Clinical Mastery & Emergency Protocol
data.summary: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by rapid onset and multisystem involvement. Immediate recognition and administration of intramuscular epinephrine are the cornerstones of survival.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='80' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' opacity='0.1'/><path d='M100 40 L100 160 M40 100 L160 100' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='8' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M100 60 L140 100 L100 140 L60 100 Z' fill='none' stroke='white' stroke-width='4'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Anaphylaxis is an acute, systemic IgE-mediated (or non-IgE-mediated) reaction involving mast cell and basophil activation. Pathophysiology involves the rapid release of mediators: Histamine, Tryptase, Prostaglandin D2, and Leukotrienes, leading to vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and bronchoconstriction.

rows: Acute onset (min to hrs) with skin/mucosal involvement PLUS respiratory or CV compromise.
2+ of: skin, respiratory, CV, or GI involvement after exposure to likely allergen.
Reduced BP after exposure to known allergen (e.g., <90mmHg systolic or 30% drop).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Actions
content: Airway obstruction (stridor, laryngeal edema)
Hypotension/Shock (end-organ hypoperfusion)
Cardiac arrest/Arrhythmia
Refractory bronchospasm
Loss of consciousness

content.explanation: E: Epinephrine (First line!) | P: Position (Supine) | I: IV Fluids | N: Nebulizers | E: Electrolytes | P: Pressors | H: H1/H2 Blockers | R: Refractory checks | I: Intubation if needed | N: Notify team | E: Evaluate vitals

sections.title: Emergency Treatment Algorithm
content: 1. Remove inciting agent immediately.
2. Administer IM Epinephrine (1mg/mL): 0.01 mg/kg (Max 0.5mg in adults) into mid-outer thigh.
3. Position patient supine with legs elevated.
4. High-flow Oxygen (10-15 L/min).
5. Volume expansion with Crystalloids (1-2L isotonic saline).
6. Adjuncts: Albuterol, H1-antagonists (Diphenhydramine 50mg), H2-antagonists (Famotidine), Corticosteroids (Methylprednisolone 125mg).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Do not wait for cutaneous signs (skin symptoms absent in 20% of anaphylaxis).
IM injection in the thigh is superior to SC or subcutaneous injection for rapid absorption.
Biphasic reactions occur in 1-20% of cases; keep patients observed for 4-6 hours.
Beta-blockers can render epinephrine ineffective; consider Glucagon (1-5mg IV) in such patients.
Serum tryptase levels (peak at 60-90 min post-onset) can confirm the diagnosis retrospectively.

title: Pulmonary Embolism: The Silent Architect of Hemodynamic Collapse
summary: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) represents a critical medical emergency involving the occlusion of the pulmonary arterial system, typically by a thrombus originating from the deep venous system. Rapid recognition and risk-stratification are the cornerstones of preventing fatal outcomes.

data.title: Pulmonary Embolism: The Silent Architect of Hemodynamic Collapse
data.summary: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) represents a critical medical emergency involving the occlusion of the pulmonary arterial system, typically by a thrombus originating from the deep venous system. Rapid recognition and risk-stratification are the cornerstones of preventing fatal outcomes.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M20 20 L50 80 L80 20 Z' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' opacity='0.7'/><circle cx='50' cy='40' r='10' fill='white'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: PE is a mechanical obstruction of the pulmonary vasculature. Epidemiology: Incidence is approx. 60–120 per 100,000 population. It is the third most common cause of cardiovascular death after myocardial infarction and stroke. Mortality rate of untreated PE is up to 30%.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: The Classic Triad
content: Dyspnea (Sudden onset)
Pleuritic chest pain
Tachypnea (>20 breaths/min)
Tachycardia (>100 bpm)
Hemoptysis (suggests pulmonary infarction)
Signs of DVT (unilateral leg swelling)

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Intervention
content: Hypotension (Systolic BP <90 mmHg)
Syncope (Hemodynamic instability)
Obstructive shock signs (pallor, sweating)
Hypoxemia refractory to oxygen
Right heart strain on ECG/Echo

sections.title: Investigations: The Gold Standard
content: Step 1: D-dimer assay (High negative predictive value if low probability).
Step 2: CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) — Test of choice.
Step 3: V/Q Scan (If renal failure or contrast allergy exists).
Step 4: Bedside Echocardiography (Assess RV function).
Step 5: Venous Compression Ultrasound (If DVT suspected).

content.explanation: C: Chest pain, H: Hemoptysis, E: ECG changes (S1Q3T3), S: SOB (Dyspnea), T: Tachycardia.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: 1. Stabilize: Supplemental O2, IV fluids, vasopressors (Norepinephrine).
2. Anticoagulation: LMWH (Enoxaparin 1mg/kg) or UFH (if renal failure).
3. Thrombolysis: rTPA (Alteplase) in massive PE (hemodynamic instability).
4. Embolectomy: Surgical or catheter-directed for absolute contraindications to lysis.
5. Long-term: DOACs (Apixaban/Rivaroxaban) for 3-6 months minimum.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The S1Q3T3 sign on ECG is classic but only present in ~20% of patients.
D-dimer increases with age; use age-adjusted cut-offs (Age x 10 for >50 yrs).
RV dilation (McConnell's sign) on Echo is a hallmark of severe PE.
Early mobilization reduces the risk of post-thrombotic syndrome.

title: TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX: The Lethal Breath-Stealer
summary: A life-threatening, time-sensitive emergency characterized by progressive accumulation of air in the pleural space, leading to hemodynamic collapse via obstructive shock. Immediate clinical diagnosis and decompression are mandatory.

data.title: TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX: The Lethal Breath-Stealer
data.summary: A life-threatening, time-sensitive emergency characterized by progressive accumulation of air in the pleural space, leading to hemodynamic collapse via obstructive shock. Immediate clinical diagnosis and decompression are mandatory.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='none' stroke='#1e40af' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M50 20 L50 80 M20 50 L80 50' stroke='#ef4444' stroke-width='6'/><path d='M30 30 L70 70 M70 30 L30 70' stroke='#1e40af' stroke-width='4'/></svg>

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Mechanism
sections.content: Tension pneumothorax is the presence of air in the pleural space with a 'one-way valve' mechanism. Air enters during inspiration but cannot exit during expiration. This results in positive intrapleural pressure, mediastinal shift, compression of the contralateral lung, and decreased venous return to the heart (obstructive shock).

sections.title: Pathophysiology Flow
content: Step 1: Pleural defect allows unidirectional airflow (valvular mechanism).
Step 2: Progressive intrapleural pressure elevation exceeds atmospheric pressure.
Step 3: Mediastinal deviation to the contralateral side.
Step 4: Mechanical obstruction of the Superior/Inferior Vena Cava.
Step 5: Drop in Preload -> Reduced Cardiac Output -> Obstructive Shock -> Cardiac Arrest.

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Action Required
content: Unilateral absent breath sounds
Tracheal deviation (Late sign!)
Distended neck veins (JVD)
Hypotension/Hemodynamic instability
Severe, rapid-onset dyspnea
Cyanosis and altered mental status

sections.title: Emergency Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Clinical Diagnosis ONLY (Do not wait for CXR!)
Step 2: Immediate Needle Decompression (14-16G needle)
Step 3: Location: 2nd Intercostal Space (Mid-clavicular) OR 4th/5th ICS (Mid-axillary)
Step 4: Emergent Tube Thoracostomy (Chest Tube, 28-32 French)
Step 5: Connect to underwater seal suction (-20 cm H2O)

sections.title: Diagnostic Pearls
content: Percussion: Hyper-resonance to percussion
Auscultation: Silent hemithorax
Imaging: If stable, CXR shows deep sulcus sign/mediastinal shift
POCUS: Lung point and absent lung sliding are diagnostic

content.explanation: P: Pleural air (trapped), D: Distended veins (JVD), T: Tracheal shift, H: Hypotension/Hypoxia
