sections.title: Clinical Definition & Urgency
sections.content: Bilateral corneal haze (congenital corneal opacity) refers to a loss of corneal transparency present at birth or within the first few months of life. It acts as a physical barrier to the visual axis, often leading to stimulus-deprivation amblyopia. Immediate referral for an Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA) is mandatory.

content.explanation: S: Sclerocornea; T: Tears in Descemet’s (Trauma/Glaucoma); U: Ulcers; M: Metabolic (MPS); P: Peters Anomaly; E: Edema (CHED); D: Dermoid.

sections.title: Primary Congenital Glaucoma (PCG)
content: Epidemiology: 1 in 10,000 live births; 65% male.
Classic Triad: Epiphora, Photophobia, Blepharospasm.
Pathophysiology: Maldevelopment of the trabecular meshwork (Barkan's Membrane).
Signs: Buphthalmos (large eye), Haab striae, increased C:D ratio (>0.3).

sections.title: Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED)
content: CHED Type 1: Autosomal Dominant (Rare). Progresses after 1-2 years.
CHED Type 2: Autosomal Recessive (Common). Present at birth.
Genetics: SLC4A11 gene mutations (sodium borate cotransporter).
Features: Significant corneal thickening (up to 1000+ microns) without inflammation.

sections.title: Urgent Ocular Examination (EUA)
content: Step 1: Intraocular Pressure (IOP) measurement using Tonopen or Perkins tonometer (before general anesthesia deepens).
Step 2: Corneal Diameter (Horizontal/Vertical) using calipers. >11mm in newborn is suspicious.
Step 3: Pachymetry to measure central corneal thickness (CCT).
Step 4: Gonioscopy using a Koeppe lens to visualize angle structures.
Step 5: Fundoscopy (if view permits) or B-Scan Ultrasound to assess C:D ratio and axial length.

branches: Imaging: UBM (for iridocorneal adhesions), B-Scan (Axial length)
Labs: Urinary Mucopolysaccharides, Serum Cystine levels
Microbiology: Corneal scrapings if ulcer is suspected (TORCH titers)

sections.title: Red Flags: The 'Big Eye' Danger
content: Corneal diameter >12 mm before age 1
Asymmetric corneal diameters (>0.5mm difference)
New onset of clouding with irritability
Rapidly increasing axial length
Vague red reflex on Bruckner test

sections.title: Management of PCG
content: 1. Medical: Topical CAIs (Dorzolamide) or Beta-blockers (Caution: Timolol can cause apnea in neonates).
2. Surgical: Primary treatment is always surgical. Goniotomy (if cornea is clear enough).
3. Surgical: Trabeculotomy (if cornea is too hazy for goniotomy).
4. Refractory: Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDD) or Diode Laser Cyclophotocoagulation.

rows: High risk of rejection in infants
Technically difficult but better survival than PK
Stable central opacity with clear periphery

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: CIGTS/AGIS principles: Aggressive early IOP control prevents 10-year blindness.
Endo-illuminated Trabeculotomy: Uses a micro-catheter (iTrack) to ensure 360-degree cannulation.
AAV Gene Therapy: Emerging research for SLC4A11 (CHED) correction.
Anterior Segment OCT: Now used intraoperatively to guide Peters anomaly dissection.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Normal newborn corneal diameter is 9.5-10.5 mm.
Horizontal Descemet's tears = Glaucoma; Vertical = Birth Trauma (Forceps).
CHED is often mistaken for glaucoma, but IOP and corneal diameter are usually normal.
Amblyopia management (patching) is as important as the surgery itself.

author: dodi

title: Carotid Cavernous Fistula (CCF): The Clinical Masterclass
summary: A comprehensive guide to the abnormal communication between the carotid arterial system and the cavernous sinus. This high-yield infographic covers everything from the Barrow classification to advanced endovascular management for ophthalmology residents and fellows.

data.title: Carotid Cavernous Fistula (CCF): The Clinical Masterclass
data.summary: A comprehensive guide to the abnormal communication between the carotid arterial system and the cavernous sinus. This high-yield infographic covers everything from the Barrow classification to advanced endovascular management for ophthalmology residents and fellows.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='80' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M60,100 Q80,60 140,100 T140,140' fill='none' stroke='red' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M60,105 Q80,65 140,105' fill='none' stroke='blue' stroke-width='4' stroke-dasharray='4'/><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='30' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' opacity='0.2'/><text x='75' y='170' font-family='Arial' font-size='10' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)'>HIGH-FLOW SHUNT</text></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: A Carotid Cavernous Fistula (CCF) is an acquired or congenital communication between the carotid artery (or its dural branches) and the cavernous sinus. This creates a high-pressure arterial flow into a low-pressure venous system, leading to venous congestion, ocular hypertension, and potential vision loss.

rows: Meningeal branches of the External Carotid (ECA)
Meningeal branches of BOTH ICA and ECA

sections.title: Pathophysiology & Hemodynamics
content: 1. Arterial-Venous Communication: High-pressure blood bypasses capillary bed.
2. Venous Arterialization: Episcleral and orbital veins become engorged and tortuous.
3. Reduced Outflow: Elevated episcleral venous pressure (EVP) impairs aqueous humor drainage.
4. Orbital Congestion: Leads to proptosis, chemosis, and extraocular muscle edema.
5. Ischemic Cascade: Decreased ocular perfusion pressure (OPP) leads to retinal and optic nerve ischemia.

sections.title: Clinical Features: The Classic Triad
content: Pulsatile Proptosis: Often associated with a palpable thrill.
Conjunctival Chemosis: Significant 'corkscrew' epibulbar vessel arterialization.
Orbital Bruit: Subjective (whooshing heard by patient) or objective (audible via stethoscope over the temple).

branches: Anterior: Arterialized 'corkscrew' vessels, Chemosis, Raised IOP (EVP > 10mmHg)
Extraocular: CN III, IV, VI palsies (VI most common due to position in CS)
Fundus: Venous tortuosity, Retinal hemorrhages, Disc edema, Choroidal effusions
Vision: Decreased VA due to Glaucoma, Exposure Keratopathy, or ON Ischemia

rows: Lid retraction, no bruit, no corkscrew vessels
Fever, elevated WBC, pain on movement
Sinusitis on CT; orbital fat stranding
Involvement of EOM tendons and fat

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Non-Invasive Screening: B-Scan USG (demonstrates dilated Superior Ophthalmic Vein [SOV]).
2. CT/MRI: Shows enlarged EOMs, dilated SOV, and bowing of the cavernous sinus wall.
3. MRA/CTA: Useful for visualizing the shunt, but may miss low-flow indirect CCFs.
4. Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): THE GOLD STANDARD. Required for definitive diagnosis and planning treatment.
5. Tonometry: Tonopen/Goldmann to assess EVP-related ocular hypertension.

sections.title: Medical & Conservative Management
content: Observation: Appropriate for low-flow (Type B-D) shunts as up to 70% may spontaneously close.
IOP Control: Topical Beta-blockers, Alpha-agonists, or CAIs (Avoid Miotics).
Lubrication: Intensive artificial tears/ointments for exposure keratopathy.
Carotid Massage: Intermittent compression of the carotid artery to induce thrombosis (Use with caution!).

branches: Transvenous Embolization: Preferred for Indirect shunts (via Inferior Petrosal Sinus)
Transarterial Embolization: Usually for Direct Type A (Detachable coils/Onyx)
Direct SOV Access: Surgical cut-down to SOV when venous routes are occluded
Stereotactic Radiosurgery: Reserved for refractory low-flow dural shunts

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Neurosurgical Emergencies
content: Rapidly progressive vision loss (Ischemic Optic Neuropathy or Glaucoma)
Intractable retro-orbital pain
Evidence of cortical venous reflux on angiography (High risk of Intracranial Hemorrhage)
Rapidly expanding proptosis with exposure-related corneal melt

content.explanation: P: Pulsatile proptosis; U: Unilateral (usually); L: Loud bruit; S: Shunt (A-V); E: Elevated IOP/Episcleral venous pressure.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Secondary Glaucoma: Most common cause of permanent vision loss.
Venous Stasis Retinopathy: Mimics CRVO but with high EVP.
Intracranial Hemorrhage: Risk associated with dural shunts and cortical venous drainage.
Prognosis: Excellent if treated timely; Indirect shunts often resolve with minimal intervention.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Board Exam
content: The 6th Nerve (Abducens) is the most commonly affected CN because it lies centrally within the cavernous sinus.
Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome Type IV (Vascular type) is a major risk factor for spontaneous direct CCF.
Gold Standard for diagnosis is always Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA).
Post-traumatic CCF (Type A) is usually high-flow and requires urgent endovascular intervention.
Indirect shunts in post-menopausal women are often mistaken for chronic conjunctivitis or thyroid eye disease.

sections.title: Recent Advances
sections.content: The shift from surgical ligation to endovascular techniques has revolutionized CCF management. The use of liquid embolic agents like Onyx and sophisticated microcatheters has increased the success rate of transvenous approaches to >90% for complex dural shunts. Recent studies emphasize the importance of identifying 'cortical venous reflux' as a primary indicator for aggressive treatment to prevent stroke.

title: The Constricted Field: Clinical Mastery
summary: A comprehensive guide to 'tunnel vision' and peripheral field loss, ranging from end-stage glaucoma and tapetoretinal degenerations to neurological and functional etiologies. Essential for board-prep and advanced ophthalmic practice.

data.title: The Constricted Field: Clinical Mastery
data.summary: A comprehensive guide to 'tunnel vision' and peripheral field loss, ranging from end-stage glaucoma and tapetoretinal degenerations to neurological and functional etiologies. Essential for board-prep and advanced ophthalmic practice.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='80' fill='#2c3e50' opacity='0.8'/><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='15' fill='#ffffff'/><path d='M100 20 L100 180 M20 100 L180 100' stroke='#3498db' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='4'/><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='15' fill='none' stroke='#e74c3c' stroke-width='2'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Constricted visual fields, colloquially termed 'tunnel vision', involve the loss of peripheral vision while retaining a small central island (typically <10–20°). This can result from end-stage optic neuropathies, retinal dystrophies, or cortical insults. Clinically, it significantly impacts mobility and orientation, while central visual acuity often remains remarkably preserved (20/20) until the terminal stages.

sections.title: Pathophysiology Mechanisms
content: Step 1: Peripheral Photoreceptor or Ganglion Cell death (Retrograde/Anterograde degeneration).
Step 2: Microvascular compromise in the watershed zones of the peripheral retina.
Step 3: Glial proliferation (gliosis) and RPE migration (Bone Spicules).
Step 4: Optic nerve remodeling and axonal loss at the Lamina Cribrosa.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Optic Disc: Cupping (Glaucoma), Waxy Pallor (RP), or Chronic Swelling/Atrophy (Papilledema).
Vessels: Arteriolar attenuation (characteristic of RP and long-standing atrophy).
Retina: Bone-spicule pigmentation in the mid-periphery (RP), or sector-based atrophy.
Macula: Often spared until late stages; check for Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) in RP.
Gonioscopy: Assess for Angle-Closure (synechiae) as a cause of rapid field loss.

sections.title: CRITICAL EMERGENCY SIGNS
content: Sudden onset peripheral loss (Vascular Occlusion/Retinal Detachment)
New onset headache and disc edema (Intracranial Hypertension)
Temporal artery tenderness (GCA - can cause ischemic optic neuropathy)
Rapidly progressive field loss in an only eye
Presence of neurological deficits (Hemiparesis/Ataxia)

sections.title: Investigations & Workup
content: 1. Static Perimetry (HVF 24-2/30-2): Initial assessment of depth and pattern.
2. Kinetic Perimetry (Goldmann): Gold standard for peripheral constriction and 'tubular' testing.
3. 10-2 Perimetry: Crucial for monitoring the remaining central island.
4. OCT (RNFL and GCL): Quantify structural loss; follow-up for progression.
5. Electroretinogram (fERG/mfERG): Differentiate retinal (RP) from neural (Optic Nerve) causes.
6. Neuro-imaging (MRI Brain/Orbits): Mandatory if field loss does not match clinical exam or is neurological.

content.explanation: P: Papilledema (Chronic Stage); U: Uveitis (Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada late); R: Retinitis Pigmentosa; G: Glaucoma (End-stage); E: Embolus (CRAO with cilioretinal sparing).

sections.title: Surgical & Medical Management
content: Medical (Glaucoma): PG Analogs (Latanoprost 0.005% QHS), Beta-blockers (Timolol 0.5% BID).
Surgical (Glaucoma): Trabeculectomy with Mitomycin-C or GDD (Ahmed/Baerveldt) to stabilize field.
Gene Therapy: Voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna) for RPE65-mediated RP.
Systemic: Acetazolamide for chronic papilledema; weight loss (IIH).
Vitamins: Vitamin A Palmitate (15,000 IU/day) for RP (consult specialist first).

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Trabeculectomy
content: 1. Conjunctival peritomy (limbal or fornix based).
2. Partial thickness scleral flap creation.
3. Application of Mitomycin-C (0.2-0.4 mg/ml) for 2-3 minutes.
4. Sclerostomy and peripheral iridectomy.
5. Flap closure with 10-0 Nylon (releasable or fixed).

content.explanation: Sudden loss of the remaining central island after glaucoma surgery. Occurs in end-stage patients with <10 degrees of field.

rows: Tubes vs. Trab for previous failure.

sections.title: Toxic & Nutritional Causes
content: Quinine Toxicity: Can lead to profound peripheral constriction.
Vigabatrin: Anti-epileptic causing irreversible peripheral VF loss (requires baseline perimetry).
Ethambutol: Usually central/cecocentral but can cause generalized depression.
Methanol: Severe optic atrophy and field constriction.

sections.title: Pediatric & Special Populations
sections.content: In children, constricted fields often point towards Leber Congenital Amaurosis (LCA) or syndromes like Usher's (sensorineural hearing loss + RP). Testing is difficult; utilize FPL (Formatted Preferential Looking) and objective electrophysiology (ERG) early to assess potential for low vision rehabilitation.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Eyelid retraction is defined as the abnormal elevation of the upper eyelid (superior limbus exposure) or depression of the lower eyelid (inferior limbus exposure) in primary gaze. In unilateral cases, the Margin Reflex Distance (MRD1 for upper, MRD2 for lower) exceeds the contralateral eye, often indicating underlying orbital, neurological, or systemic pathology. The most common cause in adults is Thyroid Eye Disease (TED).

sections.title: Pathophysiological Mechanisms
content: 1. Sympathetic Overactivity: Müller's muscle stimulation (e.g., stress, hyperthyroidism).
2. Myopathic Contracture: Fibrosis and shortening of the Levator Palpebrae Superioris (LPS).
3. Neurogenic Overaction: Increased neural output to LPS (e.g., Hering's Law in contralateral ptosis).
4. Mechanical Tethering: Scarring or adhesion of the eyelid retractors to orbital structures.
5. Structural/Positional: Proptosis pushing the eyelid forward and upward.

rows: Most common; associated with lid lag, proptosis, and motility restriction.
Collier’s sign (bilateral but can be asymmetric), upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation.
Synkinetic retraction upon moving the jaw/pterygoid muscles (pediatric focus).
Retraction occurs on adduction or infraduction (pseudo-Graefe sign).
Present from birth, non-progressive, often isolated.
Hering’s Law of equal innervation; the 'normal' eye retracts to compensate for ptotic eye.
History of blepharoplasty or squint surgery (recession of superior rectus).
Chemical burns, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, or orbital trauma.

sections.title: Clinical Signs & Eponyms
content: Dalrymple Sign: Widening of the palpebral fissure in primary gaze.
Von Graefe Sign: Delayed descent of the upper lid on slow downward gaze (Lid Lag).
Kocher Sign: Staring and frightened appearance on attentive fixation.
Collier's Sign: Retraction associated with midbrain lesions (Dorsal Midbrain Syndrome).
Boston Sign: Jerky movement of the lid on downgaze.
Grove Sign: Resistance to pulling the retracted lid down.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Compressive Optic Neuropathy: Decreased vision, RAPD, color vision loss.
Exposure Keratopathy: Persistent staining, corneal thinning, or ulceration.
Parinaud Syndrome: New-onset upgaze palsy (rule out pineal gland tumor).
Rapidly Progressive Proptosis: Rule out orbital cellulitis or malignancy.
New onset diplopia in primary gaze.

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination
content: 1. Measure MRD1 & MRD2: Document the amount of scleral show in millimeters.
2. Palpebral Fissure Height: Vertical distance between upper and lower lid margins.
3. Evaluate Lid Lag: Observe the lid during slow downward pursuit.
4. Assess Hering's Law: Manually lift the contralateral (ptotic) lid; observe if retraction resolves.
5. Exophthalmometry: Measure proptosis using a Hertel exophthalmometer.
6. Extraocular Motility: Check for restrictions (especially IR and MR in TED).
7. Forced Duction Test: Differentiate restrictive (TED) from paretic causes.
8. Slit Lamp Exam: Check for 'flare-up' signs like caruncle edema, chemosis, and corneal staining.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Labs
content: Thyroid Function Tests: TSH, Free T3, Free T4.
Antibody Testing: TSH-Receptor Antibodies (TRAb/TSI) - highly specific for Graves'.
Orbital Imaging: CT or MRI (Corals sign on MRI; muscle belly enlargement sparing tendons).
Neuro-Imaging: MRI Brain/Orbit if Parinaud's or CN III signs are suspected.
Ice Pack/Tensilon Test: If Myasthenia Gravis is a remote possibility (though usually causes ptosis).

sections.title: Management Strategy: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Observation & Lubrication (Artificial tears, ointments for mild cases).
Step 2: Medical Management (Teprotumumab for active TED; Selenium supplements).
Step 3: Botulinum Toxin Injection (Temporary relief for LPS/Müller's overaction).
Step 4: Surgical Rehabilitation (Once stable for 6-12 months).

sections.title: Surgical Techniques for Lid Retraction
content: Müllerectomy: Excision of Müller’s muscle (internal approach) for 1-2mm retraction.
Levator Recession: Weakening the LPS via anterior or posterior approach (for >2mm).
Spacer Grafts: Use of ear cartilage, donor sclera, or acellular dermal matrix for severe retraction.
Lateral Tarsorrhaphy: To reduce palpebral fissure width and protect the cornea.
Lower Lid Spacers: For inferior scleral show (often combined with midface lift).

content.explanation: T: Thyroid (TED), H: Hering's Law (Contralateral ptosis), E: Eye Surgery (Post-op), M: Midbrain (Parinaud's), A: Aberrant Regeneration (CN III), N: Neurogenic (Marcus Gunn).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always rule out TED first: It is the most frequent cause of unilateral and bilateral retraction.
Stability is Key: Do not perform eyelid surgery in TED until the inflammatory phase is over (Stable for 6 months).
The Sequence Matters: In TED rehab, perform Orbital Decompression first, then Strabismus surgery, then Lid surgery.
Check for 'Pseudo-retraction': Always lift the ptotic lid of the other eye to see if the retraction disappears.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
sections.content: In children, unilateral lid retraction is rarely thyroid-related. The most common cause is Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking phenomenon (synkinetic CN V3 to CN III). Other causes include neonatal Graves' (transient) and congenital abnormalities of the levator muscle. Management is usually conservative unless there is significant amblyopia risk or cosmetic distress.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Teprotumumab (Tepezza): IGF-1R inhibitor, the first FDA-approved medical treatment to reduce proptosis and lid retraction in active TED.
MMP-9 Testing: Point-of-care testing for ocular surface inflammation in TED patients.
Small-incisional Müllerectomy: Minimally invasive techniques providing faster recovery and predictable outcomes.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Syncope is defined as a transient loss of consciousness (TLOC) due to global cerebral hypoperfusion, characterized by rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous, complete recovery. It must be differentiated from other causes of TLOC such as seizures or metabolic disturbances where blood flow to the brain is maintained.

branches: 5-10 seconds of cessation of blood flow
Decreased Cardiac Output (CO = SV x HR)

rows: AV Block, Brugada, Aortic Stenosis, HOCM, Long QT

sections.title: Ophthalmic-Specific Triggers
content: Intravitreal Injections: Anxiety and pain trigger reflex syncope.
Oculocardiac Reflex (Aschner Reflex): Pressure on globe or traction on extraocular muscles.
Applanation Tonometry: Contact-induced vasovagal response in sensitive patients.
Retrobulbar/Peribulbar Blocks: Sudden increase in orbital pressure.
Laser Procedures: Strong visual stimuli or pain during PRP.

sections.title: The Oculocardiac Reflex (OCR)
content: Step 1: Afferent stimulus via Long and Short Ciliary Nerves.
Step 2: Signal travels to Ciliary Ganglion and Ophthalmic Division of Trigeminal Nerve (V1).
Step 3: Synapse at Sensory Nucleus of Trigeminal Nerve near the Floor of 4th Ventricle.
Step 4: Efferent signal via Vagus Nerve (X) to Sinoatrial (SA) node.
Step 5: Clinical Result: Bradycardia, Arrhythmia, or Cardiac Arrest.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: High-Risk Features
content: Syncope while supine or during exercise
Family history of sudden cardiac death at young age (<40 yrs)
New onset chest pain or dyspnea preceding TLOC
Palpitations immediately followed by syncope
Presence of structural heart disease (HF, low EF)
ECG findings: Brugada pattern, QT prolongation (>450ms), Bifascicular block

sections.title: The Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Thorough History: Prodrome (nausea/warmth) suggests vasovagal; sudden onset suggests cardiac.
2. Physical Exam: Orthostatic vitals (3-min stand test) and cardiac auscultation.
3. 12-Lead ECG: Mandatory for ALL patients to rule out conduction delay.
4. Carotid Sinus Massage: If >40 years and etiology unknown (Caution: check for bruits first).
5. Echocardiogram: If structural heart disease is suspected.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Not All TLOC is Syncope

branches: Cataplexy (Triggered by emotion, no loss of consciousness)

sections.title: Risk Stratification: San Francisco Syncope Rule

content.explanation: C: Congestive Heart Failure; H: Hematocrit < 30%; E: ECG abnormalities; S: Shortness of breath; S: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg. Any positive = High risk for serious outcome.

sections.title: Acute Management Protocol (In-Clinic)
content: 1. Safety: Lay patient supine, elevate legs (Trendelenburg position).
2. Assessment: Check ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) and Glucose.
3. Ocular Check: If OCR suspected, stop ocular manipulation immediately.
4. Recovery: Monitor for 15-30 mins; if cardiac features present, activate EMS.
5. Fluid Resuscitation: Oral fluids if conscious; IV Saline if hypotensive.

sections.title: Pharmacological Considerations
content: Midodrine: Alpha-1 agonist for refractory orthostatic hypotension (2.5-10mg TID).
Fludrocortisone: Mineralocorticoid to expand plasma volume (0.1-0.2mg QD).
Beta-Blockers: Controversial; may help in hyperadrenergic vasovagal syncope.
Atropine: 0.5mg IV for symptomatic bradycardia during Oculocardiac Reflex.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Ophthalmologists
content: Always check a glucose level in diabetic patients who faint in the waiting room.
Patients with 'graying out' of vision (Amaurosis Fugax) may be pre-syncopal due to orthostatic drop.
If a patient faints during a slit-lamp exam, be careful of head trauma against the frame.
Documentation: Note the presence/absence of a prodrome, duration of TLOC, and vitals upon recovery.
The 'Eyes Open' sign: During true syncope, eyes are usually open; closed eyes strongly suggest psychogenic causes.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: Evidence Base
sections.content: The POST (Prevention of Syncope Trial) series demonstrated that fludrocortisone and physical counter-maneuvers (leg crossing, limb tensing) significantly reduce recurrence in reflex syncope. The ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 Guidelines emphasize that a 12-lead ECG is the single most important initial test with the highest diagnostic yield.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Breath-holding spells: Common TLOC mimic in toddlers (6mo - 2yrs).
Long QT Syndrome: May first manifest as 'seizure' during exercise or startle.
Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS): Common in adolescents; HR increase >40bpm without BP drop.

This clinical picture primarily points toward Behçet’s Disease or Sarcoidosis, requiring a rigorous multidisciplinary workup to prevent irreversible ocular and systemic morbidity.

sections.title: Clinical Case Synthesis & Overview
sections.content: The constellation of recurrent uveitis, aphthous stomatitis (oral ulcers), polyarthritis, and erythema nodosum (skin nodules) in a young adult is a classic presentation for Behçet’s Disease (BD). However, the presence of a cough necessitates the exclusion of Sarcoidosis, Tuberculosis, and Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA). In ophthalmology, these systemic diseases manifest as sight-threatening panuveitis or retinal vasculitis.

sections.title: International Criteria for Behçet's (ICBD)
content: Oral Aphthosis (Mandatory in older criteria): 2 points
Genital Aphthosis: 2 points
Ocular Lesions (Uveitis/Vasculitis): 2 points
Skin Lesions (Pseudofolliculitis/Nodules): 1 point
Neurological Manifestations: 1 point
Vascular Manifestations: 1 point
Positive Pathergy Test: 1 point (optional)
Diagnosis: Score ≥ 4 points is diagnostic.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Neutrophilic Blitz
sections.content: Behçet's is an autoinflammatory vasculitis. It is characterized by hyperactive neutrophils and Th1/Th17 mediated response. Unlike Sarcoidosis, which is granulomatous, Behçet's features a sterile, neutrophilic infiltration leading to tissue necrosis and vascular occlusion.

sections.title: Red Flags: Ocular Emergencies
content: Sudden, painless vision loss (Central Retinal Artery Occlusion)
Thunderclap headache (Dural Sinus Thrombosis)
Severe hemoptysis (Pulmonary Artery Aneurysm Rupture)
Numbness/Weakness (Neuro-Behçet's)
Hypopyon with severe pain (Endophthalmitis Mimic)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Baseline Labs - CBC (Leukocytosis), ESR/CRP (Elevated), ANA/RF (Exclude SLE/RA).
Step 2: Pathergy Test - Prick forearm with 20G needle; read at 48h for sterile pustule.
Step 3: Imaging - Chest X-Ray or HRCT Chest (Look for Hilar Adenopathy for Sarcoid).
Step 4: Ocular Imaging - Fluorescein Angiography (FA) to detect 'fern-like' leakage and capillary non-perfusion.
Step 5: Ancillary Ocular - OCT for Macular Edema; ICG for choroidal involvement.
Step 6: Multidisciplinary Consult - Rheumatology and Pulmonology referral.

rows: Anti-TNF alpha agents are highly effective for BD

sections.title: Surgical Considerations
content: Cataract Surgery: Delay until 3 months of complete quiescence.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): Indicated for non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage or tractional RD.
Glaucoma: Often secondary to steroids or synechiae; may require tube shunts.
Intravitreal Implants: Ozurdex (Dexamethasone) can be used but risk of IOP spike.

content.explanation: B: Blood clots (Vasculitis); E: Erythema nodosum; H: Hypopyon (Shifting); C: CNS involvement; E: Eye (Panuveitis); T: Triad (Oral, Genital, Eye); S: Skin pathergy.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Landmark Evidence
content: Pearl: The Behçet's hypopyon is 'cold' and moves with head position, unlike the 'sticky' hypopyon of HLA-B27.
Evidence: The VISUAL I & II trials established Adalimumab as a steroid-sparing agent for non-infectious uveitis.
Pearl: Always check for genital ulcers; patients are often embarrassed to report them.
Observation: Retinal veins in Behçet's often show 'perivascular cuffing' and 'sheathing' early in the disease.

title: Intumescent Cataract: Clinical Mastery & Surgical Management
summary: An intumescent cataract represents a lens in the rapid, advanced stages of maturation, characterized by cortical liquefaction and increased lens volume. Understanding the 'intumescent crisis' is critical to avoiding devastating surgical complications like the 'Argentinian Flag Sign'.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Intumescent cataract occurs when the lens protein undergoes osmotic degradation, creating high-molecular-weight protein aggregates that exert significant oncotic pressure. This draws aqueous humor into the lens, causing cortical swelling (intumescence), anterior capsular stretching, and shallowing of the anterior chamber.

sections.title: Clinical Features
content: Markedly reduced visual acuity (often CF or HM)
Shallow anterior chamber depth
Increased lens thickness (anteroposterior diameter)
Lens-induced angle-closure glaucoma
Phacomorphic glaucoma symptoms (pain, nausea, haloes)

rows: Acute angle closure with swollen lens
Nucleus settles inferiorly in liquefied cortex

sections.title: Surgical Hazards: The Argentinian Flag Sign
content: High Intralenticular Pressure: Leads to uncontrolled radial tears of the anterior capsule.
Argentinian Flag Sign: Radial tears extend to the lens equator; the anterior capsule retracts, creating a 'flag' appearance.
Zonular Instability: Resulting from prolonged lens swelling.
Posterior Capsule Rupture: High risk during hydrodissection.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Step 1: Perform preoperative IOP lowering (Mannitol IV, topical anti-glaucoma meds).
Step 2: Create a small initial capsulorhexis (or use high-viscosity OVD).
Step 3: Puncture the capsule to aspirate liquefied cortex, decompressing the lens.
Step 4: Once decompressed, extend the capsulorhexis to the desired diameter.
Step 5: Utilize 'bimanual' or 'femtosecond laser-assisted' capsulotomy (FLACS) if available.

content.explanation: S: Stabilize IOP, W: Withdraw fluid (cortex), E: Endothelial protection (OVD), L: Laser-assisted or micro-incision preferred, L: Lens removal (phacoemulsification).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the fellow eye: Intumescence is frequently bilateral.
Use heavy-molecular-weight viscoelastic (e.g., Healon5) to maintain anterior chamber depth.
Avoid hydrodissection in the intumescent phase—hydrodelineation is preferred once decompressed.
Consider pars plana vitrectomy for lens aspiration if zonular support is severely compromised.

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Referral Needed
content: Painful eye (ciliary injection, photophobia)
Hypopyon (even if small)
Dense vitreous debris/haze
RAPD (Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect)
IOP > 30 mmHg unresponsive to topical therapy

sections.title: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) Diagnostic Protocol
content: Step 1: Perform dilated fundoscopy to assess macular contour.
Step 2: Obtain Spectral-Domain OCT (look for intraretinal fluid pockets).
Step 3: Consider FFA (Fundus Fluorescein Angiography) for late-phase petaloid staining.
Step 4: Initiate topical NSAIDs (Bromfenac 0.09% or Nepafenac 0.3%) + topical steroids.
Step 5: Follow-up at 2 weeks post-initiation.

sections.title: P. acnes Endophthalmitis: Clinical Pearls
content: Often misdiagnosed as chronic uveitis.
Classic 'White Plaque' located in the lens capsular bag.
Fluctuating vision is characteristic.
Requires pars plana vitrectomy with capsular bag lavage.
Intravitreal vancomycin is the gold standard treatment.

sections.title: Mnemonic: Why is the vision dropping?

content.explanation: C: Cystoid Macular Edema, L: Lens/Capsule (PCO/IOL tilt), E: Endophthalmitis (Delayed), A: Ametropia (Residual refractive error), R: Retinal (RD or ERM).

sections.title: Management of PCO
sections.content: Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy is the definitive treatment for symptomatic PCO. Ensure the IOL is stable and no active inflammation is present. Typical energy levels: 0.8–2.0 mJ per shot. Complications include IOL pitting, transient IOP spikes, and retinal detachment (rare). Check IOP 1 hour post-procedure.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: SCCa is a rare, aggressive malignancy arising from the meibomian glands, glands of Zeis, or caruncular sebaceous glands. It accounts for 1-5% of all eyelid malignancies in Caucasians but up to 20-30% in Asian populations. It typically presents in the 6th to 7th decade of life, with a slight female predilection.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: The Great Masquerader
content: Unilateral chronic blepharoconjunctivitis
Persistent chalazion (recurrent in the same location)
Diffuse eyelid thickening
Loss of cilia (madarosis)
Eyelid margin nodule
Ulceration and keratinization

sections.title: Red Flags: High-Risk Features
content: Unilateral, persistent inflammation unresponsive to topical steroids/antibiotics
Recurrent chalazion after surgical excision
Pagetoid spread (intraepithelial spread of tumor cells)
Orbital invasion or palpable preauricular/submandibular lymphadenopathy

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: The 'Map' Biopsy
content: Step 1: Clinical suspicion (Any chronic eyelid mass > 6 weeks)
Step 2: Full-thickness wedge biopsy of the tumor
Step 3: Conjunctival mapping biopsies (Random 4-quadrant biopsies to rule out pagetoid spread)
Step 4: Histopathology with Oil Red O (fresh tissue) or adipophilin/EMA immunostaining
Step 5: Staging via orbital MRI or CT if orbital extension is suspected

rows: Bilateral, crusting at lashes, responsive to hygiene
Resolves with excision or intralesional steroid

sections.title: Management Protocol
content: Primary Treatment: Wide surgical excision with frozen section control (Mohs micrographic surgery or margin-controlled excision).
Adjuvant Therapy: Topical Mitomycin C (0.04%) for pagetoid involvement of the ocular surface.
Systemic: Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) for high-risk tumors (>10mm).
Orbital Exenteration: Indicated for extensive orbital invasion.

content.explanation: P: Persistent blepharoconjunctivitis, P: Pagetoid spread, P: Poor response to standard therapy.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always send all chalazion specimens for histopathology, especially in middle-aged/elderly patients.
SCCa has a high mortality rate; systemic metastasis can occur in 10-20% of cases.
If pagetoid spread is present, the entire conjunctival surface is at risk (field cancerization).
The risk of skip lesions necessitates wide margins in surgical planning.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Evidence
sections.content: Recent studies underscore the efficacy of immunohistochemical markers such as Adipophilin and Perilipin 2, which demonstrate high sensitivity and specificity for sebaceous differentiation. Management has shifted toward more organ-sparing techniques, with topical Mitomycin C playing a pivotal role in managing extensive surface ocular involvement, reducing the need for destructive procedures like exenteration.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Intraoperative miotics are parasympathomimetic agents injected directly into the anterior chamber (AC) to induce rapid constriction of the iris sphincter muscle. They are primarily utilized to stabilize Intraocular Lenses (IOLs), protect the crystalline lens or IOL during surgical maneuvers, and lower immediate postoperative intraocular pressure (IOP).

sections.title: Primary Indications
content: Phacoemulsification: To ensure IOL centration and prevent iris incarceration.
Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): To protect the host iris and the underlying lens/IOL.
Glaucoma Surgery: To pull iris tissue away from the angle during trabeculectomy.
Anterior Vitrectomy: To constrict the pupil and sequester vitreous in the posterior segment.
Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI): Pre-treatment to thin the peripheral iris (topical).

sections.title: Miochol-E Reconstitution Process
content: Step 1: Inspect the Univial dual-chamber container for clarity.
Step 2: Press the plastic plunger to dislodge the rubber stopper between chambers.
Step 3: Shake gently to mix the lyophilized Acetylcholine powder with the electrolyte diluent.
Step 4: Draw the 1:100 solution into a sterile syringe using a filtered needle.
Step 5: Administer into the AC within 6 hours of preparation.

sections.title: Surgical Administration Technique
content: Step 1: Evacuate Ophthalmic Viscosurgical Device (OVD) from the AC.
Step 2: Introduce a 27G or 30G blunt-tipped cannula through the side-port incision.
Step 3: Gently irrigate the miotic agent over the iris surface or behind the IOL.
Step 4: Wait for pupillary response; if slow, ensure no residual OVD is blocking receptors.
Step 5: Verify the pupil is round and central without iris incarceration in the wound.

content.explanation: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis. Though rare with intraocular use, systemic absorption can occur through the nasolacrimal duct.

sections.title: CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATIONS
content: Active Anterior Uveitis: Risk of synechiae formation and increased inflammation.
Neovascular Glaucoma: Risk of bleeding from fragile iris vessels.
Malignant Glaucoma: May worsen the anterior displacement of the lens-iris diaphragm.
Known Hypersensitivity to Acetylcholine or Carbachol.
Asthma/COPD: Extreme caution due to risk of bronchospasm from systemic absorption.

sections.title: Differential: Causes of Poor Pupillary Response

rows: Physical barrier prevents drug reaching M3 receptors
Damage to sphincter muscle (e.g., prior acute glaucoma)

sections.title: Ocular Complications & Side Effects
content: Postoperative 'Brow Ache': Ciliary muscle spasm (common with Carbachol).
Corneal Edema: Rare, linked to preservatives or pH imbalance in non-buffered solutions.
Retinal Detachment: Historically debated link due to peripheral retinal traction from ciliary body contraction.
Anterior Chamber Inflammation: Increased protein flare due to breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier.
Induced Myopia: Temporary shift due to ciliary contraction (accommodative spasm).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the dual-chamber vial for Miochol-E; ensure the center stopper has fallen and the drug is fully dissolved.
Carbachol (Miostat) is significantly more potent and is the drug of choice for lowering IOP after a complicated case.
During PKP, miosis is vital to avoid 'cheese-wiring' the donor tissue with the iris during suturing.
Avoid miotics if you suspect you will need to re-enter the eye for a posterior segment complication (miosis obscures the view).

sections.title: The Role of Carbachol in Glaucoma
sections.content: Carbachol is often preferred in glaucoma filtration surgery or complex cataract cases with high risk of postoperative IOP spikes. Unlike Acetylcholine, which is rapidly degraded, Carbachol provides sustained miosis and trabecular meshwork tension for up to 24 hours, effectively blunting the 4-6 hour post-op pressure rise.

sections.title: Management of Miotic-Induced Spasm
content: Step 1: Patient complains of severe headache or ocular pain post-op.
Step 2: Assess IOP to rule out pressure spike.
Step 3: If IOP is normal, diagnose ciliary spasm.
Step 4: Use mild cycloplegics (e.g., Cyclopentolate) if severe.
Step 5: Counsel patient on the transient nature of the symptoms.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Preservative-Free Formulations
content: Move toward single-dose, preservative-free (PF) formulations to eliminate TASS (Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome) risk.
Studies comparing intracameral miotics vs. topical instillations show 30% faster onset with the intracameral route.
Development of sustained-release miosis/mydriasis combinations for complex vitreoretinal-anterior segment combined cases.

author: dodi

title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (AACG): The Ophthalmological Emergency
summary: AACG represents a true ocular emergency characterized by a rapid, sustained elevation of intraocular pressure due to mechanical obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris. Immediate recognition and intervention are critical to prevent permanent optic nerve damage and blindness.

data.title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (AACG): The Ophthalmological Emergency
data.summary: AACG represents a true ocular emergency characterized by a rapid, sustained elevation of intraocular pressure due to mechanical obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris. Immediate recognition and intervention are critical to prevent permanent optic nerve damage and blindness.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='8'/><path d='M50 10 L50 90 M10 50 L90 50' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='10' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: AACG is defined by the sudden apposition of the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork (TM), causing acute outflow obstruction. The primary mechanism is pupillary block (relative resistance to aqueous flow between the lens and iris), leading to iris bombe and angle closure. Secondary causes include plateau iris, phacomorphic glaucoma, or tractional mechanisms.

sections.title: Clinical Features (The 5 'P's)
content: Pain: Severe, boring ocular/periorbital pain.
Pupil: Mid-dilated, non-reactive.
Pressure: Often > 50 mmHg.
Prostration: Nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis.
Perception: Blurred vision with halos around lights.

sections.title: Red Flags (Emergency Signs)
content: Corneal Edema (hazy view)
Fixed mid-dilated pupil
Shallow anterior chamber (Van Herick Grade 1)
Glaukomflecken (anterior subcapsular lens opacities)
Nausea/Vomiting (often misdiagnosed as GI event)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (Assess AC depth, corneal edema, iris position).
Step 2: Tonometry (Goldmann Applanation or Tono-Pen).
Step 3: Gonioscopy (The Gold Standard - assess TM pigmentation and synechiae).
Step 4: Fundoscopy (Evaluate C/D ratio if view allows; check for disc edema).
Step 5: UBM or Anterior Segment OCT (Assess angle anatomy).

sections.title: Management Protocol
content: Immediate: Topical Beta-blockers, Alpha-agonists, Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors.
Systemic: Oral or IV Acetazolamide (500mg), Hyperosmotic agents (Mannitol/Glycerol).
Miotics: Pilocarpine 1-2% (once pressure < 40 mmHg).
Definitive: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) or surgical peripheral iridectomy.

content.explanation: C: Corneal edema, A: A-chamber shallow, M: Mid-dilated pupil, P: Pressure high.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never perform LPI on a hazy cornea; use topical glycerin to clear it.
Always examine the fellow eye; 50% risk of closure in 5 years.
Avoid pilocarpine in high pressure as it is ineffective due to iris ischemia.

summary: Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency (LSCD) is a profound ocular surface pathology resulting from the loss or dysfunction of the limbal stem cell niche, leading to conjunctivalization, chronic inflammation, and vision loss. sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: LSCD occurs when the limbal stem cell population (located in the Palisades of Vogt) is depleted, exhausted, or rendered dysfunctional. The primary barrier to conjunctival cell migration is lost, allowing conjunctival epithelium (goblet cells) to migrate onto the corneal surface, resulting in vascularization, scarring, and persistent epithelial defects.

sections.title: Clinical Features Checklist
content: Chronic ocular surface pain/photophobia
Decreased visual acuity
Recurrent epithelial breakdown
Loss of limbal palisades of Vogt
Conjunctivalization (pannus)
Tear film instability (MGD, aqueous deficiency)
Chronic conjunctival inflammation

sections.title: Red Flags: When to refer for Surgery
content: Persistent epithelial defect > 2 weeks
Secondary microbial keratitis
Intractable ocular pain (glaucoma or surface nerve exposure)
Rapid centripetal progression of conjunctival pannus
Vision loss preventing daily function

sections.title: Investigations Workup
content: 1. Slit-lamp exam: Look for loss of Palisades of Vogt
2. Impression Cytology: Gold standard (look for goblet cells)
3. In-vivo Confocal Microscopy (IVCM): Identify basal cell density
4. Fluorescein staining: Map epithelial defects
5. Anterior Segment OCT: Measure corneal epithelial thickness

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: 1. Optimize surface: Preservative-free ATs + Scleral lenses
2. Address Ocular Surface inflammation: Topical steroids/CsA
3. Conjunctival Limbal Autograft (CLAU): Unilateral cases
4. Cultivated Limbal Epithelial Transplantation (CLET): Bilateral
5. Keratoprosthesis (Boston KPro): End-stage salvage

content.explanation: L: Loss of palisades, S: Staining/fluorescein, C: Conjunctivalization, D: Defects (epithelial), Eyes: Examine for goblet cells via cytology.

title: LSCD Mastery & The SLET Revolution
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency (LSCD) and the Simple Limbal Epithelial Transplantation (SLET) technique—the gold standard for ocular surface reconstruction. This poster covers everything from molecular pathophysiology to the nuances of surgical execution.

data.title: LSCD Mastery & The SLET Revolution
data.summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency (LSCD) and the Simple Limbal Epithelial Transplantation (SLET) technique—the gold standard for ocular surface reconstruction. This poster covers everything from molecular pathophysiology to the nuances of surgical execution.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency (LSCD) is a pathological condition characterized by the loss or dysfunction of the limbal epithelial stem cells (LESCs) located in the Palisades of Vogt. This leads to the failure of corneal epithelial maintenance, resulting in 'conjunctivalization' (invasion of conjunctival epithelium onto the cornea), chronic inflammation, neovascularization, and significant visual morbidity. SLET (Simple Limbal Epithelial Transplantation) is a modern, single-stage surgical technique using a small donor biopsy to treat unilateral or asymmetric bilateral LSCD.

sections.title: Etiology: Why do the Stem Cells Fail?

rows: Total LSCD of the visual axis (central)
Total LSCD of the visual axis (central)

sections.title: Classic Ocular Examination Findings
content: Loss of Palisades of Vogt (visible on high-mag slit lamp)
Vortex-like Keratopathy (early sign)
Dull, irregular corneal reflex (epithelial instability)
Stippled Fluorescein staining (late/delayed uptake)
Superficial Neovascularization (pannus)
Persistent Epithelial Defects (PEDs)
Symblepharon or Fornix shortening (in SJS/Chemical)

sections.title: The SLET Surgical Protocol
content: Step 1: Donor Biopsy - 2x2mm strip of limbal tissue from the healthy eye (superior preferred).
Step 2: Recipient Preparation - 360-degree peritomy and excision of the pannus (kerato-epitheliectomy) to reveal bare stroma.
Step 3: Amniotic Membrane (AMT) - Secured over the bare stroma using fibrin glue (epithelial side up).
Step 4: Fragmenting - The 2x2mm donor biopsy is divided into 8 to 15 tiny 'seeds' using Vannas scissors.
Step 5: Seeding - Fragments are placed on the AMT, avoiding the visual axis, and secured with Fibrin Glue (Tisseel).
Step 6: Protection - A large-diameter bandage contact lens (BCL) is applied.

rows: Presence of Goblet cells on cornea (PAS positive)
Thinning of epithelium, loss of limbal crypts
Absence of basal cells/Palisades; presence of goblet cells
Horner-Trantas dots, not total epithelial loss
Decreased sensation, distinct rolled edges of PED

sections.title: Medical Management (Pre-op/Mild)
content: Preservative-free artificial tears (lubrication is vital)
Autologous Serum Eye Drops (20% or 50% concentration)
Therapeutic Scleral Lenses (PROSE/Scleral) to hydrate surface
Topical Cyclosporine/Tacrolimus for inflammation control
Punctal Occlusion

sections.title: RED FLAGS: When to Suspect Total LSCD
content: Chronic Fluorescein staining that never resolves with lubricants
Loss of corneal transparency with recurrent sterile melts
Progression of vascularization toward the visual axis
Failure of standard epithelial healing post-cataract surgery

rows: Simple, low cost, no lab needed
Risk of LSCD in donor eye due to large biopsy

content.explanation: P: Palisades loss; A: Abnormal staining; N: Neovascularization; N: Night/Day photophobia; U: Uneven surface; S: Sight loss.

sections.title: Complications of SLET
content: Hemorrhage under the AMT (affects graft take)
Graft displacement (seed loss)
Recurrent Conjunctivalization (incomplete pannus removal)
Secondary Glaucoma (often steroid-induced)
Pyogenic Granuloma at the biopsy site

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The success of SLET depends on a 'clean' recipient bed—meticulous pannus removal is mandatory.
Always check the donor eye carefully for subclinical LSCD (especially in CL wearers) before taking a biopsy.
SLET is primarily for unilateral cases; for bilateral cases, consider Allo-SLET with systemic immunosuppression.
Recent studies show SLET success rates of >75-80% for long-term corneal stability.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The Sangwan Series
sections.content: SLET was first described by Dr. Virender Sangwan and colleagues at LV Prasad Eye Institute in 2012. Their multi-center trials demonstrated that SLET is more cost-effective than CLET and safer for the donor eye than CLAU, revolutionizing the treatment of chemical burns in developing nations.

sections.title: Surgical Instrument Checklist
content: 0.12 or Colibri Forceps
Vannas Scissors (sharp for micro-fragmenting)
Crescent blade/64 Beaver blade (for kerato-epitheliectomy)
Tisseel / Fibrin Glue kit
Cryopreserved or Dehydrated Amniotic Membrane
20mm Bandage Contact Lens

title: Corneal Collagen Cross-Linking (CXL): Clinical Mastery
summary: CXL is the gold-standard therapeutic intervention for halting the progression of keratoconus and other corneal ectasias by increasing biomechanical rigidity via riboflavin-UVA photopolymerization. This guide outlines the comprehensive clinical protocols, patient selection criteria, and landmark evidence-based management strategies.

data.title: Corneal Collagen Cross-Linking (CXL): Clinical Mastery
data.summary: CXL is the gold-standard therapeutic intervention for halting the progression of keratoconus and other corneal ectasias by increasing biomechanical rigidity via riboflavin-UVA photopolymerization. This guide outlines the comprehensive clinical protocols, patient selection criteria, and landmark evidence-based management strategies.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M50 10 A40 40 0 0 1 90 50' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='8'/><path d='M30 50 Q50 30 70 50' fill='none' stroke='black' stroke-width='2'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: CXL utilizes exogenous Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) as a photosensitizer and Ultraviolet A (UVA, 370 nm) light to induce the formation of covalent bonds (cross-links) between collagen fibrils in the corneal stroma. The reaction is driven by the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), specifically singlet oxygen, which creates stable bridges between collagen type I molecules. This results in a permanent increase in the biomechanical stiffness of the cornea by approximately 300-450%.

sections.title: Indications & Candidacy
content: Documented progressive keratoconus (e.g., Kmax increase >1.0D over 12 months).
Pellucid marginal degeneration (PMD).
Post-LASIK/PRK ectasia.
Corneal melting (keratomalacia/infectious adjunct).
Young age (<18 years) often mandates immediate prophylactic CXL due to aggressive progression.

sections.title: The Dresden Protocol (Standard)
content: Step 1: Corneal epithelial debridement (8-9 mm diameter).
Step 2: Riboflavin 0.1% drops (Isotonic) instilled every 2-3 minutes for 30 minutes (soaking phase).
Step 3: Slit-lamp check for complete stromal saturation (yellow flare in the AC).
Step 4: UVA irradiation (370 nm) at 3 mW/cm² for 30 minutes (total energy 5.4 J/cm²).

rows: Inferior steepening, central thinning, Vogt striae.

sections.title: Red Flags & Contraindications
content: Corneal thickness <400 microns (thinner corneas require hypo-osmolar riboflavin or custom treatment).
Advanced corneal scarring (limits UVA penetration).
Active infectious keratitis (non-collagenolytic).
Severe dry eye disease/neurotrophic keratopathy.

content.explanation: S: Soak Riboflavin, T: Thickness check, I: Irradiation (UVA), F: Follow-up frequent, F: Fixate (patient compliance).

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Accelerated CXL: Higher intensity (9mW/cm² for 10 min) maintains efficacy with reduced chair time.
Transepithelial (Epi-on) CXL: Utilizing riboflavin enhancers (e.g., BAC) to bypass debridement and reduce pain.
Iontophoresis-assisted Riboflavin delivery: Improves stromal saturation speed.
Combined CXL+PRK (Athens Protocol): Used for visual rehabilitation in stable/stabilized ectatic eyes.

rows: Increase steroid frequency, rule out infection.
Bandage contact lens, lubrication, halt steroids.

title: Mastering Scleritis: The Anterior vs. Posterior Paradigm
summary: An inflammatory, potentially vision-threatening condition affecting the scleral tissue, characterized by severe pain and complex systemic associations. Differential diagnosis remains paramount to distinguish scleritis from episcleritis and orbital pseudotumor.

data.title: Mastering Scleritis: The Anterior vs. Posterior Paradigm
data.summary: An inflammatory, potentially vision-threatening condition affecting the scleral tissue, characterized by severe pain and complex systemic associations. Differential diagnosis remains paramount to distinguish scleritis from episcleritis and orbital pseudotumor.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M30 50 Q50 20 70 50 T50 80' fill='hsl(0, 80%, 60%)'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Scleritis is a chronic, painful, inflammatory disorder of the sclera. It is characterized by edema and cellular infiltration of the collagenous scleral framework. Unlike episcleritis, it is frequently associated with life-threatening systemic autoimmune diseases, notably rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Panic
content: Severe 'boring' pain radiating to the temple or jaw.
Avascular areas in necrotizing scleritis (high risk of perforation).
Decreased visual acuity (posterior involvement).
Presence of systemic vasculitis symptoms (hematuria, dyspnea).
Poor response to topical NSAIDs.

rows: Disc edema, choroidal folds, exudative RD

sections.title: Pathophysiology & Etiology
content: Type III/IV Hypersensitivity reactions causing collagen degradation.
Immune-complex deposition in scleral vessels.
Systemic Associations: Rheumatoid Arthritis (most common), GPA (Wegener's), Relapsing Polychondritis, Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN).
Infectious etiology: Herpes Zoster, Pseudomonas, Syphilis, Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Thorough history (rheumatologic/infectious review).
Step 2: Slit-lamp exam (diffuse light vs. red-free light).
Step 3: Phenylephrine 2.5% test to distinguish from episcleritis.
Step 4: B-Scan Ultrasound (looking for retrobulbar edema).
Step 5: Systemic blood work (CBC, ESR, CRP, RF, ANCA, ACE, QuantiFERON).

content.explanation: T for 'Tenon's Capsule' fluid. In Posterior Scleritis, the T-sign on B-scan represents fluid in the sub-Tenon space creating a perpendicular appearance to the optic nerve.

rows: Involvement of extraocular muscles, usually unilateral pain.

sections.title: Treatment Protocol
content: 1st Line: Oral NSAIDs (Indomethacin 25mg TID or Naproxen 500mg BID).
2nd Line: Systemic Corticosteroids (Prednisone 1mg/kg/day).
3rd Line: Immunomodulatory therapy (Methotrexate, Mycophenolate Mofetil, or Rituximab for refractory GPA).
Surgical: Scleral patch graft for impending perforation (tectonic support).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a fundus examination to rule out subclinical posterior involvement.
Necrotizing scleritis without inflammation ('scleromalacia perforans') is highly characteristic of RA.
Always investigate the underlying systemic cause; the eye may be the 'window' to a life-threatening systemic vasculitis.
Avoid subconjunctival steroid injections in scleritis; they increase the risk of scleral melting.

title: Orbital Compartment Syndrome: The Surgical Emergency
summary: Orbital Compartment Syndrome (OCS) is a sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency characterized by increased intraorbital pressure leading to vascular compromise. Immediate recognition and decompression are the only definitive treatments to prevent irreversible optic nerve ischemia.

data.title: Orbital Compartment Syndrome: The Surgical Emergency
data.summary: Orbital Compartment Syndrome (OCS) is a sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency characterized by increased intraorbital pressure leading to vascular compromise. Immediate recognition and decompression are the only definitive treatments to prevent irreversible optic nerve ischemia.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='80' fill='none' stroke='#1e88e5' stroke-width='8'/><path d='M60 100 Q100 40 140 100 T100 160' fill='#bbdefb' stroke='#1e88e5' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='15' fill='#1e88e5'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: OCS occurs when intraorbital pressure exceeds ocular perfusion pressure, leading to ischemia of the optic nerve and retina. The orbit is a closed fibro-osseous compartment; any increase in volume (hematoma, edema, emphysema) results in an exponential rise in orbital pressure (IOP + orbital venous pressure), culminating in venous stasis and rapid infarction.

sections.title: Red Flags (Immediate Action Required)
content: Tense, firm globe (rock-hard eyelids)
Afferent pupillary defect (APD)
Proptosis (exophthalmos)
Ophthalmoplegia (restricted motility)
Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) appearance
Loss of light perception (LP)

content.explanation: P: Proptosis, R: Resistance to retropulsion, E: Elevated IOP (>40mmHg), S: Sight loss (APD/Decreased VA), S: Stretched/Tense lids.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Lateral Canthotomy & Cantholysis
content: Step 1: Instill proparacaine and prepare sterile field.
Step 2: Clamp lateral canthus with hemostat for 30s to crush tissue (hemostasis).
Step 3: Cut lateral canthal tendon using Stevens scissors.
Step 4: Perform superior and inferior crural cantholysis—the 'snap' confirms release.
Step 5: Re-assess IOP and visual status immediately.

rows: Fever, elevated WBC, pain on motility
Rapid onset but usually responds to steroids

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations
content: Goldmann Applanation Tonometer: IOP > 40mmHg is highly suspicious.
Exophthalmometry: Quantify displacement.
Urgent CT Orbit/Brain: Only if it does not delay immediate decompression.
Pupil Exam: Critical indicator of optic nerve compromise.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Do not wait for CT imaging if clinical signs are definitive.
The lateral canthal tendon consists of superior and inferior crura; both must be severed.
OCS is a 'clinical diagnosis'—eyes do not wait for imaging studies.
If IOP remains elevated post-cantholysis, consider medical adjuncts (IV Mannitol 1g/kg or Acetazolamide).

sections.title: Recent Landmark Considerations
sections.content: Recent literature emphasizes that the 'time-to-decompression' is the single most important predictor of visual recovery. Studies show that optic nerve ischemia occurs within 60-100 minutes of sustained orbital pressure elevation, suggesting that bedside lateral cantholysis is superior to any medical therapy or imaging-based delay.

title: Clinical Management of Abnormal Head Posture (AHP)
summary: Abnormal head posture (AHP) is a compensatory mechanism employed by patients to optimize binocularity or visual acuity in the setting of strabismus or nystagmus. Understanding the biomechanics of AHP is essential for diagnostic stratification and surgical planning.

data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='80' fill='#e3f2fd'/><path d='M70 120 Q100 140 130 120' stroke='#1565c0' stroke-width='5' fill='none'/><circle cx='80' cy='80' r='10' fill='#1565c0'/><circle cx='120' cy='80' r='10' fill='#1565c0'/><line x1='100' y1='100' x2='100' y2='60' stroke='#1565c0' stroke-width='2'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Purpose
sections.content: AHP is a patient-driven compensatory mechanism to achieve fusion, avoid diplopia, or reach a 'null zone' in nystagmus. It represents the 'path of least resistance' for the oculomotor system to maintain stable binocular vision.

sections.title: Nystagmus 'Null Zone' Considerations
content: Null zone: Angle of gaze where oscillation amplitude is minimal.
Patient turns head to move the target into the null gaze position.
Evaluation: Measure visual acuity in primary gaze vs. preferred head posture.
Clinical Pearl: Do not perform recession/resection to 'fix' AHP if it eliminates the only position of stable vision.

sections.title: RED FLAGS
content: Sudden onset AHP in adults (rule out cranial nerve palsy/decompensated phoria).
Associated torticollis vs. ocular torticollis (check sternocleidomastoid spasm).
AHP masking severe amblyopia.
Underlying neurological lesions (e.g., posterior fossa tumor).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Thorough history (congenital vs. acquired).
Step 2: Prism adaptation test to verify fusional compensation.
Step 3: Hess-Lancaster screen or Lees screen for paretic identification.
Step 4: Cover-uncover test in different gazes to map the binocular field.
Step 5: Document AC/A ratio and presence of A-V patterns.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: 1. Optical: Fresnel prisms to move image to null zone.
2. Medical: Treat underlying causes (myasthenia, thyroid eye disease).
3. Surgical (Strabismus): Recess/Resect based on paretic muscles.
4. Surgical (Nystagmus): Anderson or Kestenbaum procedure to shift null zone to primary position.

content.explanation: To treat horizontal AHP: Recess the agonist (the muscle in the direction of the turn) and resect the antagonist in both eyes to shift the null zone by 45 degrees.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Argyll Robertson Pupil (ARP) is classically defined by 'light-near dissociation' (LND). The pupils exhibit: 1) Failure to constrict to direct light, 2) Preservation of constriction during accommodation, 3) Miosis, and 4) Poor dilation in response to mydriatics due to iris atrophy/fibrosis.

rows: Lesions in the pretectal nuclei of the midbrain
Disruption of the light reflex arc; sparing of the accommodation-convergence pathway
Historically associated with chronic untreated Treponema pallidum infection

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Unilateral presentation (ARP is classically bilateral/asymmetrical)
Presence of optic atrophy or severe vision loss (requires rule-out of syphilitic optic neuropathy)
Complete lack of iris movement (consider mechanical synechiae)
Acute onset (ARP is usually chronic)

sections.title: Clinical Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp exam to evaluate for iris atrophy and synechiae.
Step 2: Compare reaction to light vs. near stimulus (e.g., accommodative target).
Step 3: Serology (RPR/VDRL + Treponemal-specific FTA-ABS/TP-PA).
Step 4: Lumbar puncture for CSF VDRL and protein/cell count analysis.

content.explanation: A: Accommodation present; R: Reflex (light) absent; P: Pupil small (miotic).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The pupils are often irregular and asymmetric, not just small.
They show poor dilation to hydroxyamphetamine because the postganglionic sympathetic fibers are typically intact in pure neurosyphilis.
Always perform a full neurological exam for signs of Tabes Dorsalis (loss of proprioception/vibration).
Even with modern antibiotics, clinicians must maintain a high index of suspicion in immunocompromised populations.

summary: Supranuclear gaze palsies involve disruption of the supranuclear pathways controlling eye movements, manifesting as loss of voluntary gaze while preserving the Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR). This guide bridges the neuro-anatomical pathways from the frontal eye fields to the brainstem PPRF.

sections.title: Clinical Definition
sections.content: Supranuclear gaze palsy is a clinical condition characterized by the inability to move the eyes in one or more directions of gaze, despite intact cranial nerves (III, IV, VI) and extraocular muscles. It is defined by the integrity of the VOR (doll's head maneuver), which confirms the lesion is superior to the ocular motor nuclei in the brainstem.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Image
content: Acute onset (Stroke/Hemorrhage)
Papilledema (Raised ICP)
Contralateral hemiparesis
Ataxia/Vertigo (Brainstem syndrome)
Rapidly progressive cognitive decline

sections.title: Epidemiology & Etiology
content: PSP (Progressive Supranuclear Palsy): Most common cause, prevalence ~5/100,000
Corticobasal Degeneration (CBD)
Niemann-Pick Type C
Whipple's Disease (Oculomasticatory myorhythmia)
Brainstem Stroke (Midbrain/Pontine)
Parinaud's Syndrome (Dorsal midbrain)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: Step 1: Bedside VOR assessment (Oculocephalic reflex).
Step 2: Smooth pursuit and Saccadic velocity testing.
Step 3: MRI Brain (High resolution T1/T2, focus on midbrain/pons).
Step 4: Lumbar puncture if neuro-infectious/inflammatory suspected.
Step 5: Genetic testing (MAPT gene for PSP).

content.explanation: S: Supranuclear gaze palsy; T: Tall (often), E: Early falls; E: Extension (posture); L: Limb rigidity; E: Emotional lability.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Vertical gaze palsy often precedes horizontal involvement in PSP.
Square wave jerks are classic findings in supranuclear palsy.
Always assess for convergence insufficiency.
Hummingbird sign (MRI midbrain atrophy) is diagnostic for PSP.

sections.title: Recent Advances
sections.content: Recent research focuses on Tau-pathology mitigation. Landmark studies (e.g., PASSPORT trial) highlight the use of monoclonal antibodies targeting extracellular Tau protein. Digital eye-tracking metrics are now being used as biomarkers for disease progression in clinical trials.

summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to differentiating Trochlear Nerve (CN IV) Palsy from Skew Deviation, featuring diagnostic algorithms, the Parks Three-Step test, and the critical Upright-Supine differentiator.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Overview
sections.content: The Trochlear Nerve (CN IV) innervates the Superior Oblique (SO) muscle, which depresses, abducts, and incyclotorts the eye. A palsy results in hypertropia and excyclotorsion. Conversely, Skew Deviation is a vertical misalignment caused by an imbalance in gravity-sensing vestibular pathways (otolith-ocular reflex), often mimicking a 4th nerve palsy but originating from brainstem or cerebellar pathology.

sections.title: Anatomical Path of CN IV
content: 1. Nucleus: Level of inferior colliculus in midbrain
2. Decussation: ALL fibers cross in the Superior Medullary Velum
3. Exit: Only CN to exit DORSALLY from the brainstem
4. Course: Longest intracranial course (7.5cm) around brainstem
5. Entry: Cavernous sinus (lateral wall) to Superior Orbital Fissure

sections.title: The Parks Three-Step Test (for CN IV)
content: Step 1: Identify which eye is higher (hypertropic) in primary gaze.
Step 2: Determine if the hypertropia increases on right or left gaze (Maximized when the affected SO is trying to act as a pure depressor).
Step 3: Determine if the hypertropia increases on right or left head tilt (Bielschowsky Head Tilt Test). Ipsilateral tilt increases hypertropia in 4th NP.

rows: Alternating (RHT on L-tilt, LHT on R-tilt)
Severe (> 10 degrees on Double Maddox Rod)
Patient sees images as tilted 'V' shape

sections.title: Ocular Tilt Reaction (OTR) Triad
content: Skew Deviation (Vertical misalignment)
Ocular Torsion (Incyclotorsion of the higher eye, excyclotorsion of the lower eye)
Head Tilt (Towards the side of the lower eye)

content.explanation: If the vertical deviation decreases by 50% or more when the patient moves from an upright to a supine (laying down) position, it is SKEW DEVIATION. CN IV palsies remain stable regardless of position.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Image Neuro?
content: Associated neurologic deficits (ataxia, weakness)
Papilledema or signs of increased ICP
Patient < 40 years old with no trauma history
History of malignancy
Positive Upright-Supine test result
Presence of Ocular Tilt Reaction (OTR)

sections.title: Bilateral 4th NP Signs (The Traumatic Check)
content: 1. Reversal of hypertropia on side-to-side head tilt.
2. Excyclotorsion >10 degrees on Double Maddox Rod.
3. V-pattern Esotropia (narrower in upgaze).
4. Chin-down head position (compensating for lack of depression).
5. Fundus torsion visible on indirect ophthalmoscopy.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Prism Cover Test: Primary, 8 cardinal gazes.
2. Parks 3-Step Test: Essential for verticality.
3. Double Maddox Rod: Quantify torsion (Subjective).
4. Fundus Photos: Quantify torsion (Objective).
5. Upright-Supine Test: Rule out Skew.
6. MRI Brain/Orbit: If neuro-signs or atypical.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Congenital 4th NP: Check old family photos for a head tilt ('FAT' scan: Family Album Tomography) and look for increased vertical fusion amplitudes (>3 prism diopters).
Ischemic CN IV: Typically recovers within 3-4 months. Watch and wait with a Fresnel prism.
Bilateral Surgery: Often requires Harada-Ito procedure for symptomatic excyclotorsion (moving the anterior SO tendon laterally).
Differential: Don't forget Myasthenia Gravis and Thyroid Eye Disease for any vertical diplopia!

content.explanation: Superiors are IN-torters (Superior Oblique and Superior Rectus). Superior Oblique is the primary in-torter.

sections.title: Landmark Study: Wong et al. (2011)
sections.content: The Upright-Supine test was validated as highly sensitive and specific for differentiating skew deviation from CN IV palsy. A reduction of vertical deviation by >50% in the supine position had 92% sensitivity and 100% specificity for Skew Deviation in their cohort.

data.summary: A textbook-grade overview of PSS, a rare inflammatory hypertensive condition characterized by unilateral, recurrent bouts of markedly elevated IOP and mild anterior uveitis. Essential for differentiating from acute angle-closure and managing CMV-related trabeculitis.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Posner-Schlossman Syndrome (PSS), or Glaucomatocyclitic Crisis, is a clinical entity characterized by recurrent, unilateral episodes of mild non-granulomatous anterior chamber inflammation associated with disproportionately high intraocular pressure (often 40-60 mmHg). Between attacks, the IOP and the eye typically return to normal, though chronic damage can occur with frequent recurrences.

branches: Viral Trigger: CMV (most common DNA found in aqueous), HSV, VZV
Trabeculitis: Acute inflammation of the trabecular meshwork reducing outflow
Prostaglandin Release: High levels of PGE2 in aqueous during crises
Allergic/Vascular: History of migraine or vasomotor instability
Autoimmune: Association with HLA-Bw54 and HLA-Cw1

sections.title: Clinical Features: Symptoms
content: Mild ocular discomfort or 'fullness'
Blurred vision (due to corneal edema/Sattler's veil)
Colored halos around lights
Surprisingly white eye (despite high IOP)
Minimal photophobia compared to other uveitides
Self-limiting nature (hours to weeks)

rows: Acute elevation (40–60 mmHg); significantly higher than expected for AC reaction
Fine, white, 'stellate' KPs on the inferior endothelium; localized edema
Mild cells (1-2+), minimal flare; No synechiae (PAS or PS)
Open on gonioscopy; No neovascularization or debris
May be slightly dilated or sluggish compared to contralateral eye
Rare heterochromia; mild iris atrophy in long-standing cases

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (Essential)
2. Gonioscopy (Mandatory to rule out angle closure)
3. Slit Lamp with dilated fundus exam (C:D ratio)
4. Aqueous humor PCR (Testing for CMV/HSV/VZV DNA)
5. Visual Fields (SITA-Standard 24-2) for chronic monitoring
6. OCT-RNFL to assess for glaucomatous damage

sections.title: Acute Management Protocol
content: 1. Topical Beta-Blockers (Timolol 0.5% BID)
2. Alpha-Agonists (Brimonidine 0.2% TID)
3. Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (Dorzolamide 2% TID)
4. Topical Steroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1% QID for inflammation)
5. Oral Acetazolamide (Diamox 250mg) for refractory high IOP
6. Cycloplegics (rarely needed unless photophobia is significant)

sections.title: CMV-Specific Therapy (Advanced)
content: Consider in recurrent/refractory cases with PCR+ results
Topical Ganciclovir 0.15% gel (5-6 times daily)
Oral Valganciclovir 900mg BID (loading) then 450-900mg QD
Long-term prophylaxis may be required to prevent recurrence
Monitor CBC and LFTs for systemic antiviral toxicity

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Concerns
content: Developing Posterior Synechiae (Suggests a different diagnosis)
Progressive Optic Nerve Cupping (Requires aggressive IOP control)
Ciliary Flush (Suggests more severe anterior uveitis or AACG)
Constricted Angles on Gonioscopy
Poor response to aqueous suppressants

content.explanation: P: Pressure is sky-high; S: Stellate KPs (minimal); S: Self-limiting & Solitary (unilateral).

sections.title: Surgical & Laser Considerations
content: Surgical intervention is rarely needed for acute crisis
Trabeculectomy with Mitomycin-C: If optic nerve damage progresses despite meds
Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDD): Secondary option if trabeculectomy fails
Note: LPI (Laser Peripheral Iridotomy) is NOT indicated as the angle is open

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Chronic Secondary Open-Angle Glaucoma (25% of long-term cases)
Optic nerve atrophy/cupping from cumulative pressure spikes
Corneal endothelial cell loss over time
Prognosis is generally excellent if IOP is managed during spikes

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The IOP elevation in PSS is out of proportion to the mild AC reaction (1+ cell).
Avoid Pilocarpine: It can exacerbate inflammation and break the blood-aqueous barrier.
Prostaglandin Analogs (PGAs): Use with caution as they might theoretically worsen uveitis, though evidence in PSS is mixed.
Always check the fellow eye: While unilateral, patients may have asymmetric optic nerve susceptibility.
In between attacks, the KPs disappear completely, unlike Fuchs Uveitis Syndrome where they persist.

sections.title: Recent Advances: The CMV Connection
sections.content: Recent landmark studies using PCR analysis of aqueous humor have revolutionized our understanding of PSS. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is now identified as the primary etiologic agent in many PSS cases. This has shifted the treatment paradigm for chronic or recurrent PSS toward the use of topical and systemic anti-virals (Ganciclovir/Valganciclovir), which have been shown to reduce the frequency of attacks and the need for glaucoma surgery.

summary: Biometry error is the leading cause of surprise in modern cataract surgery. This guide provides a systematic approach to identifying, quantifying, and mitigating axial length and keratometry inaccuracies to achieve emmetropic outcomes.

data.title: Mastering Biometry: The Architecture of Refractive Precision
data.summary: Biometry error is the leading cause of surprise in modern cataract surgery. This guide provides a systematic approach to identifying, quantifying, and mitigating axial length and keratometry inaccuracies to achieve emmetropic outcomes.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Impact
sections.content: Biometry error refers to any inaccuracy in the measurement of the axial length (AL), corneal curvature (K), or anterior chamber depth (ACD) that leads to a discrepancy between the predicted and achieved postoperative refractive outcome. A 1 mm error in AL corresponds to approximately 2.5 to 3.0 D of refractive surprise. Achieving refractive targets within ±0.50 D in >90% of eyes is the current gold standard.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Error
content: Difference in AL > 0.1 mm between eyes
Inconsistent keratometry across multiple readings
Steep K > 47.0 D or Flat K < 40.0 D
Short AL (< 22.0 mm) or Long AL (> 25.0 mm)
Staphyloma indicated on A-scan trace
History of prior corneal refractive surgery (LASIK/PRK)

sections.title: Systematic Troubleshooting Process
content: Step 1: Check signal quality (SNR) on Optical Biometry (e.g., IOLMaster 700).
Step 2: Validate K-values via Topography or Tomography (Pentacam).
Step 3: Perform contact or immersion ultrasound if optical biometry fails (e.g., dense cataract).
Step 4: Recalculate using Barrett Universal II or Kane formula for extreme axial lengths.
Step 5: Verify IOL power constants (User-specific constants).

content.explanation: P: Precision (Check SNR), A: Axial Length (Verify with USG), K: Keratometry (Check for dry eye/topography), S: Selection (Choose modern formulas).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always dry the ocular surface before keratometry to avoid tear film instability.
In post-LASIK eyes, utilize Barrett True-K or ASCRS Online Calculator.
A signal-to-noise ratio < 2.0 on optical biometry necessitates manual verification.
When in doubt, use Immersion A-scan; never rely solely on contact A-scan.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The introduction of Swept-Source OCT-based biometry (e.g., IOLMaster 700) has significantly reduced errors in eyes with dense media. Landmark studies (e.g., Melles et al.) demonstrate that the Barrett Universal II formula consistently outperforms older generation formulas (Hoffer Q, SRK/T) in eyes with extreme axial lengths.

summary: Corneal astigmatism, defined by non-spherical corneal curvature, necessitates precise diagnostic mapping and evidence-based surgical intervention. This guide navigates the path from topometric analysis to advanced refractive correction techniques.
