sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Corneal astigmatism occurs when the corneal surface is toroidal rather than spherical. It is defined as a refractive state where the eye's refractive power varies across different meridians, resulting in two focal lines instead of a single point (Sturm's Conoid). Pathophysiology typically relates to the anterior corneal surface curvature, though posterior corneal surface contribution (PCC) is critical in modern surgical planning.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Ectasia
content: Inferior steepening on topography (Klyce/Maeda)
High Scissoring reflex on retinoscopy
KISA% index > 60
I-S ratio > 1.4 D
Unexplained refractive shifts in adolescents

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: Step 1: Manifest Refraction (Subjective)
Step 2: Placido-disk Topography (Curvature)
Step 3: Scheimpflug Imaging (Pentacam - Elevation/Pachymetry)
Step 4: Optical Coherence Tomography (Epithelial mapping)
Step 5: Wavefront Analysis (Total ocular aberration)

content.explanation: Topography check, Orientation alignment (0-180), Rotation risks, IOL stability, Capsular bag integrity.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always account for Posterior Corneal Astigmatism (PCA) using the Barrett Toric Calculator.
Surgically Induced Astigmatism (SIA) at the incision site should be calculated via vector analysis.
For cataract surgery: Consider LRI for < 1.0D and Toric IOL for > 1.0D of corneal astigmatism.
Epithelial thickness mapping is the 'gold standard' for detecting early Keratoconus.

summary: Mastering the shift from acoustic to optical biometry is fundamental for modern refractive cataract surgery. This guide compares gold-standard optical coherence interferometry with immersion A-scan ultrasound to optimize IOL power calculations.

sections.title: Indications for A-Scan Ultrasound
content: Dense mature cataracts (White/Black/Brown cataracts)
Advanced posterior subcapsular cataracts
Vitreous hemorrhage or dense asteroid hyalosis
Corneal scarring preventing light penetration
Phthisis bulbi or microphthalmos
Fixation difficulties or nystagmus

sections.title: The IOL Master Process
content: Step 1: Patient alignment to the chinrest; fixate on the internal target.
Step 2: Dual-beam emission to measure axial length (AL) from tear film to RPE.
Step 3: Automated keratometry using 6 spots in a hexagonal pattern.
Step 4: White-to-White (WTW) measurement for anterior segment evaluation.
Step 5: Automated calculation using SRK/T, Holladay 2, or Barrett Universal II formulas.

sections.title: Gold Standard: Immersion vs. Contact
content: Immersion Technique: Use a Prager shell filled with BSS; avoids direct pressure on the globe, decreasing error by ~0.15mm.
Contact Technique: Risk of corneal indentation leading to artifactual shortening of the AL by up to 0.5mm, causing hyperopic shift.
Standardized Velocity: Always confirm 1550 m/s in phakic eyes. Use 1532 m/s for aphakic and 1532 m/s for pseudophakic eyes.
Signal Quality: Ensure clear retinal spike with 80-100% gain.

content.explanation: O: Optical is best (IOL Master); I: Immersion is second; L: Least precise is contact (Log/Applanation).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A 1mm error in AL measurement results in a ~2.5D error in IOL power calculation.
Always compare eyes: AL difference between two eyes should typically be <0.3mm.
Refractive Surprise: Always re-verify biometry if the calculated IOL power differs by >1.0D from the predicted emmetropic power.
Modern Formula Evolution: Shift from regression formulas (SRK II) to vergence-based formulas (Barrett, Hill-RBF, Haigis) to account for effective lens position (ELP).

summary: Navigating the 'Double Error' of keratometry and ELP prediction to achieve emmetropia in the post-LASIK, PRK, and RK era. A comprehensive guide for high-precision surgical planning.

sections.title: The Fundamental Challenge: The 'Double Error'
sections.content: Standard IOL calculation formulas fail post-refractive surgery due to two primary errors: 1. Keratometric Error (Incorrectly assuming the ratio of anterior-to-posterior corneal curvature is 1.21 after the anterior surface is altered) and 2. ELP Error (Standard formulas use K-values to predict the Effective Lens Position; flattened corneas lead the formula to predict a more shallow ACD, resulting in an underpowered IOL and a hyperopic surprise).

rows: Standard keratometers measure 3.2mm zone, missing the central effective power.
Keratometers use n=1.3375 based on virgin corneas; surgery changes the n-ratio.
Formula assumes flat cornea = shallow AC; erroneously places IOL too far anterior.

sections.title: Pre-Operative Diagnostic Workup
content: Obtain prior surgical records (Pre-op K, Manifest Refraction, Surgically Induced Refractive Change).
Perform Scheimpflug Tomography (Pentacam) or OCT-based Pachymetry.
Measure 'True Net Power' or 'Total Corneal Refractive Power' (TCRP).
Axial Length (AL) measurement via Optical Biometry (Lenstar/IOLMaster 700).
Assess for corneal ectasia or irregular astigmatism.
Dry eye management (aggressive treatment before measurements).

branches: Methods based on Clinical History (e.g., Clinical History Method)
Methods based on Adjusted K (e.g., Masket, Modified Masket)
Methods based on No Prior Data (e.g., Barrett True-K, Haigis-L, Shammas)
Direct Measurement (e.g., OCT-based, Ray Tracing, Pentacam TNP)

sections.title: The Gold Standard: Barrett True-K
sections.content: The Barrett True-K formula is a universal formula that accommodates both myopic and hyperopic LASIK/PRK, as well as Radial Keratotomy (RK). It uses a modified Universal II formula and incorporates a predicted posterior corneal curvature and a proprietary ELP adjustment to correct the double-error phenomenon. It is currently the most validated method in literature.

sections.title: Red Flags: Critical Errors to Avoid
content: NEVER use standard formulas (SRK/T, Hoffer Q, Holladay 1) without specific adjustments.
Do not rely on a single calculation method; use the ASCRS online calculator for consensus.
Avoid multifocal IOLs in patients with significant corneal higher-order aberrations (>0.4 μm).
Watch for RK patients with fluctuating vision (diurnal variation).

sections.title: Radial Keratotomy (RK) Considerations
content: RK corneas are extremely unstable and often hyperfocal centrally.
Target a myopic outcome (-0.75D to -1.25D) to account for potential hyperopic shifts.
Calculate using the Barrett True-K (RK) or the Double-K modified formulas.
Avoid large incisions that intersect RK scars.
Incisions should be placed between RK scars to prevent 'fish-mouthing'.

content.explanation: Flat corneas Lead to Anterior Targeting (formula thinks IOL is too far forward), resulting in Low-power IOL selection and a Troublesome hyperopic surprise.

sections.title: Management Workflow (The ASCRS Algorithm)
content: Step 1: Determine the type of prior surgery (Myopic LASIK, Hyperopic LASIK, or RK).
Step 2: Collect data (Historical records, Biometry, Tomography).
Step 3: Enter data into the ASCRS Online Post-Refractive Calculator.
Step 4: Compare results from Barrett True-K, Haigis-L, and Shammas-PL.
Step 5: Select the IOL power based on the 'Average' or 'Min' value depending on surgeon preference.
Step 6: Adjust target to -0.50D for LASIK/PRK and -1.00D for RK.

sections.title: IOL Selection Pearls
content: Use aspheric Monofocal IOLs with negative spherical aberration (e.g., Tecnis, AcrySof IQ) to counteract positive corneal aberration in post-myopic LASIK.
Use neutral aspheric IOLs (e.g., enVista, SofPort LI61AO) for post-hyperopic LASIK.
Small-aperture IOLs (IC-8) are excellent for irregular corneas/RK.
Toric IOLs should be used with extreme caution (ensure axis stability and regularity).

sections.title: Intraoperative Aberrometry (ORA)
sections.content: Intraoperative wavefront aberrometry (e.g., Alcon ORA) provides real-time refractive data after the cataract is removed (aphakic state). It is a powerful adjunct that bypasses corneal measurement errors by measuring the whole eye's refractive power, though it can be influenced by speculum pressure and corneal hydration.

content.explanation: Calculates central power from topography: (Central Power x 1.114) - 6.1. Useful when no prior history is available but topography is accessible.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: Always warn the patient about the high possibility of a 'refractive surprise' and potential for IOL exchange.
Check the 'Corneal Sphericity' — if highly irregular, avoid complex optics.
If using ORA, ensure the eye is at physiologic IOP before the measurement.
The 'Clinical History Method' is now considered less reliable than modern formula-based approaches.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Functional Visual Loss (FVL) is the report of reduced visual acuity or visual field deficit in the absence of an identifiable organic ocular or neurological substrate. It encompasses two primary categories: Malingering (conscious fabrication for secondary gain) and Conversion Disorder/Psychogenic Visual Loss (unconscious manifestation of psychological distress).

sections.title: Diagnostic Verification: The 'Must-Do' Tests
content: Step 1: Check Pupils (RAPD absent in pure FVL).
Step 2: Formal Refraction (Rule out uncorrected refractive error).
Step 3: Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN) drum (Positive response confirms vision is present).
Step 4: Mirror Test (Follows movements, confirming peripheral processing).
Step 5: Visual Evoked Potentials (VEP) to assess retrobulbar pathway integrity.
Step 6: Goldmann/Automated perimetry (Look for tunnel vision or spiraling fields).

rows: Preserved pupils, intact OKN, CT/MRI findings
Optic nerve cupping, characteristic VF defects

sections.title: Red Flags: Non-Organic Indicators
content: Tubular visual fields (field size remains constant regardless of distance to tangent screen).
Inconsistency between objective findings (VEP/ERG) and subjective reports.
Rapid 'flickering' of acuity on E-chart (e.g., seeing 20/200 then 20/20).
Monocular 'blindness' with binocular vision intact (Polaroid test).
Resistance to confrontation testing or extreme visual hesitation.

content.explanation: S-pacing of field, P-eripheral constriction, I-nconsistency, R-elation to distance (Tubular), A-lternating responses, L-acking organic cause.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Use the 4-diopter prism test: A patient claiming monocular blindness who tracks the prism is seeing with that eye.
The patient's visual acuity on a near chart should correlate with the distance chart; ask the patient to read inverted charts to confuse memory.
Always document objectively: 'Visual acuity is inconsistent' rather than 'Patient is malingering'.
Collaborate: Early referral to psychology/psychiatry is vital for conversion cases.
Avoid confrontational language; maintain a supportive, diagnostic-focused bedside manner.

sections.title: Anatomy: The Angle Landmarks (Schwalbe to Ciliary Body)
content: 1. Schwalbe's Line: Termination of Descemet's membrane.
2. Non-pigmented Trabecular Meshwork: Posterior to Schwalbe's.
3. Pigmented Trabecular Meshwork: Primary site of aqueous outflow.
4. Scleral Spur: The most anterior projection of the sclera; attachment site of the ciliary muscle.
5. Ciliary Body Band: The vascularized, darker, most posterior structure visible.

sections.title: Gonioscopy Red Flags
content: Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS)
Iris processes masking the angle
Neovascularization of the angle (NVA)
Blood in Schlemm's Canal (high episcleral venous pressure)
Exfoliation material on the trabecular meshwork

content.mnemonic: I Can See The Scleral Spur
content.explanation: I (Iris) - C (Ciliary Body) - S (Scleral Spur) - T (Trabecular Meshwork) - S (Schwalbe's Line). Posterior to Anterior.

sections.title: Technique: Dynamic Gonioscopy
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic; ensure patient is upright or supine.
Step 2: Apply gonioscopy lens (e.g., Goldmann 3-mirror or Posner 4-mirror) with viscoelastic coupling agent.
Step 3: Keep the beam narrow and vertical (1-2mm width) to avoid light-induced pupil constriction.
Step 4: Use indentation (compression) gonioscopy to differentiate appositional from synechial closure.
Step 5: If angle opens under compression, the closure is appositional (potential for LPI).

sections.title: Recent Advances: Imaging vs. Gonioscopy
content: AS-OCT (Anterior Segment OCT): Non-contact, high resolution (5-10 microns). Useful for objectively measuring AOD500 (Angle Opening Distance at 500 microns).
UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy): 35-50 MHz frequency. The gold standard for visualizing structures behind the iris (e.g., ciliary cysts, ciliary body position).
Note: Gonioscopy remains the clinical gold standard as it allows for direct observation of pigment and PAS that OCT may miss.

summary: Rupture of the globe is a vision-threatening emergency defined by a full-thickness wound of the eye wall caused by blunt trauma. Rapid diagnosis, protective measures, and primary surgical closure are the cornerstones of management to prevent irreversible blindness and sympathetic ophthalmia.

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Rupture occurs when blunt force causes a sudden increase in intraocular pressure (IOP). The eye wall gives way at its weakest points: the limbus, the insertion of the rectus muscles (where the sclera is thinnest at ~0.3mm), and prior surgical incisions (e.g., old ECCE scars). This is an 'inside-out' injury mechanism compared to the 'outside-in' nature of sharp lacerations.

rows: High risk of RD and severe vision loss

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Marked vision loss (often NLP to HM)
Severe subconjunctival hemorrhage (often bullous/360°)
Shallow or extremely deep Anterior Chamber
Peaked or 'teardrop' pupil pointing toward the wound
Iris prolapse (brown uveal tissue at wound)
Hyphema (often total/8-ball)
Vitreous hemorrhage
Commotio retinae or retinal detachment

sections.title: The 'Occult' Rupture Red Flags
content: 360-degree Bullous Subconjunctival Hemorrhage (high suspicion for scleral rupture)
Persistent hypotony (IOP < 5 mmHg) after blunt trauma
Abnormally deep anterior chamber (posterior rupture)
Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
Limitation of ocular motility (muscle involvement or incarceration)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: History (time, mechanism, last meal for NPO)
Step 2: Visual Acuity (crucial for OTS scoring)
Step 3: External exam (DO NOT perform tonometry or push on globe)
Step 4: Non-contrast CT Orbits (1mm thin cuts) to look for 'Flat Tire Sign'
Step 5: B-Scan Ultrasound (ONLY if globe is closed/repaired; contraindicated in open globe)

rows: IOP may be high, globe intact

sections.title: Immediate Management Protocol
content: 1. Apply rigid Fox Shield (no pressure patches)
2. Bed rest with head elevated 30 degrees
3. NPO status for urgent surgical repair
4. IV Antibiotics: Vancomycin (1g Q12h) + Ceftazidime (1g Q12h) or Ciprofloxacin
5. Update Tetanus prophylaxis
6. Analgesics and Anti-emetics (Ondansetron) to prevent Valsalva

sections.title: Surgical Repair Principles
content: General Anesthesia (avoid succinylcholine - increases IOP)
360-degree peritomy to explore all quadrants
Primary goal: Restore globe integrity (water-tight closure)
Minimize tissue excision (repose viable uveal tissue)
Corneal Scleral wounds: Suture limbus first as anatomical landmark
'Close-as-you-go' technique for long scleral wounds

content.explanation: Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis following trauma to one eye (exciting eye). Occurs 2 weeks to many years later. Dalen-Fuchs nodules are characteristic.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Endophthalmitis
content: Increasing pain out of proportion to injury
Rapidly decreasing vision post-repair
Increasing hypopyon or vitritis
Fibrinous anterior chamber reaction
Eyelid edema and chemosis worsening

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Always examine the fellow eye thoroughly; trauma is often the focus, but pre-existing conditions or bilateral trauma can be missed.
If the wound is posterior to the rectus insertions, do not attempt to excise prolapsed vitreous aggressively as it may cause more traction.
Low IOP is the most reliable sign of occult rupture, but a normal IOP does NOT rule it out.
The 'Flat Tire Sign' on CT refers to the loss of the globe's spherical contour.
Siderosis bulbi: Retained iron foreign bodies can cause irreversible retinal toxicity within weeks.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: An Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB) is any exogenous object that penetrates the ocular tunics and resides within the globe. It represents a subset of open-globe injuries (OGI) and requires urgent ophthalmic intervention. The severity is determined by the mechanism of injury, size, composition, and location of the object, as well as the presence of associated endophthalmitis or retinal detachment.

rows: Glass may be difficult on CT
Low density on CT; mimics air

sections.title: The Siderosis Bulbi Cascade
content: 1. Iron IOFB undergoes oxidation in ocular fluids.
2. Ferrous ions (Fe2+) release and diffuse through tissues.
3. Free radical production via Fenton reaction leads to lipid peroxidation.
4. Selective damage to RPE, photoreceptors, and ganglion cells.
5. Progressive ERG changes (Initial supernormal A-wave, then b-wave depression).
6. End-stage Ocular Siderosis: Glaucoma, retinal pigmentary degeneration, and blindness.

sections.title: Pathognomonic Signs of Siderosis
content: Iris Heterochromia (affected eye becomes darker/rust-colored)
Fixed, dilated pupil (mydriasis due to iris sphincter damage)
Rusty anterior subcapsular lens opacities (Siderotic Cataract)
Pigmentary retinopathy (mimics Retinitis Pigmentosa)
Secondary Glaucoma (Iron deposition in Trabecular Meshwork)

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging Protocol
content: Step 1: Non-contrast Thin-Cut CT (1mm) of the Orbit - Gold Standard.
Step 2: X-Ray Orbits (Caldwell and Lateral views) - If CT is unavailable.
Step 3: B-Scan Ultrasonography - ONLY if globe is closed or intraoperatively; detects RD/VH.
Step 4: MRI - STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED unless metallic IOFB is 100% ruled out.

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Rapidly worsening pain or hypopyon (Endophthalmitis)
Projecting metallic object (Do NOT remove in clinic)
Extruding intraocular contents (Uveal tissue/Vitreous)
Afferent Pupillary Defect (Optic nerve damage or massive RD)
Low Intraocular Pressure (Seidel positive or occult rupture)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis of Post-Traumatic Vision Loss
Immediate Medical Management
content: NPO (Nothing by Mouth) for surgery.
Place a Rigid Fox Shield (No pressure on globe).
Update Tetanus prophylaxis.
Systemic Antibiotics: IV Vancomycin (1g Q12H) + Ceftazidime (2g Q8H) OR Oral Moxifloxacin (400mg Daily).
Antiemetics to prevent Valsalva (Ondansetron).

content.explanation: S: Shield eye immediately; T: Tetanus & Toxins (Siderosis); E: Endophthalmitis prophylaxis; E: Imaging (CT); L: Localization & Laser/Ligation.

rows: Limbal incision, use of viscoelastic, forceps removal.
Rarely used now due to risk of uncontrolled retinal traction.
3-port PPV, induce PVD, stabilize retina, use IOFB forceps.
PPV performed, then IOFB brought through pupillary space/limbal wound.

sections.title: Intravitreal Antibiotic Dosing
content: Vancomycin: 1.0 mg in 0.1 mL (Gram-positive coverage)
Ceftazidime: 2.25 mg in 0.1 mL (Gram-negative coverage)
Amikacin: 0.4 mg in 0.1 mL (Alternative for Ceftazidime)
Amphotericin B: 0.005 mg in 0.1 mL (If fungal/organic suspected)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Always look for an 'Entry Wound' — a self-sealing corneal track can be easily missed.
A 'Hole in the Iris' + 'Focal Lens Opacity' = IOFB until proven otherwise.
Siderosis can occur years after a forgotten injury; always ask about a history of metal-working.
If the IOFB is organic (wood), the risk of fungal endophthalmitis (Aspergillus/Fusarium) is extremely high.
In cases of multiple IOFBs (e.g., blast injury), prioritize the largest or most reactive ones.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Evidence
sections.content: The National Eye Trauma System (NETS) and the United States Eye Injury Registry (USEIR) provide the largest datasets on IOFB. Key findings include: 1) Early vitrectomy (within 24 hours) significantly reduces endophthalmitis risk. 2) Zone I injuries have better visual outcomes than Zone III. 3) The presence of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is the strongest negative predictor of final visual acuity.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Temporal Triage
sections.content: Sudden Vision Loss (SLOV) describes a subjective decrease in vision reaching its peak within 24 hours. The primary clinical bifurcation is based on the presence or absence of PAIN. Painless loss suggests vascular, retinal, or neuro-ophthalmic causes, while painful loss often points to the anterior segment, glaucoma, or inflammatory processes.

branches: Painless: Retinal (RD, Vitreous Heme, Wet AMD)

rows: Mid-dilated pupil, high IOP, hazy cornea

sections.title: Critical Red Flags (GCA & Vascular)
content: Scalp tenderness or Jaw claudication (GCA Emergency)
Profound vision loss (NPL/PL) in a white eye (CRAO/GCA)
Bilateral sudden loss (Cortical blindness or GCA)
New onset flashes and floaters (RD/Tear)
Third Nerve Palsy with pupillary involvement (Aneurysm)

sections.title: RAPD Logic: Localizing the Lesion
content: 1. RAPD Present + Clear Media: Optic Nerve (ON) lesion or extensive RD.
2. RAPD Present + Opaque Media: Large RD or Vitreous Heme.
3. RAPD Absent + Dense Vision Loss: Macular pathology or Functional loss.
4. RAPD Absent + Mild Loss: Refractive error or mild Maculopathy.

content.explanation: V: Vascular (CRAO/CRVO/GCA); I: Inflammatory (Optic Neuritis/Uveitis); S: Structural (RD/Heme); I: IOP (AACG); O: Optical (Cornea/Lens changes); N: Neurological (Stroke/Cortex).

sections.title: Immediate Management: CRAO (The 90-Min Window)
content: 1. Digital Massage: Dislodge embolus.
2. IOP Lowering: IV Acetazolamide (500mg) or Paracentesis.
3. Carbogen/Paper Bag: Induce hypercapnia (vasodilation).
4. Immediate Neurology/Stroke Team consultation.
5. Rule out GCA: Stat ESR/CRP if age > 50.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: Step 1: VA, IOP, and Pupil exam (Check for RAPD).
Step 2: Slit lamp exam (Corneal clarity, AC cells/hypopyon, Gonioscopy).
Step 3: Dilated fundus exam (Look for disc edema, cherry red spot, blood, or RD).
Step 4: If media is hazy (dense cataract/heme), perform B-Scan Ultrasound.
Step 5: Ancillary Imaging: OCT for macula/ONH, FFA for vascular occlusion.
Step 6: Systemic screen: BP, Pulse (A-fib), Carotid auscultation, ESR/CRP.

sections.title: The 'Disc at Risk' (NAION vs AAION)
content: NAION: Painless, sectoral edema, small C/D ratio in fellow eye (disc at risk).
AAION (GCA): Painful (headache), chalky-white edema, systemic malaise.
Clinical Pearl: Every patient >55 with sudden vision loss and disc edema is GCA until proven otherwise.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The Evidence Base
content: ONTT (Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial): IV methylprednisolone speeds recovery but doesn't change final VA outcome vs placebo.
SCORE/BRAVO/CRUISE: Established anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab/Aflibercept) as gold standard for RVO macular edema.
EAGLE Study: Early lens extraction is superior to LPI for primary angle closure with high IOP.
CVOS (Central Vein Occlusion Study): PRP indicated only when neovascularization develops (360-degree).

sections.title: Surgical Intervention Triggers
content: Rhegmatogenous RD: Immediate surgery (Pars Plana Vitrectomy or Scleral Buckle).
Vitreous Heme with RD: Urgent Vitrectomy.
Non-clearing Vitreous Heme: Elective Vitrectomy after 1-3 months.
Endophthalmitis: Tap and Inject (EVS Study protocols).

sections.title: Recent Advances: The Future of SLOV
content: Tenecteplase for CRAO: Ongoing trials for intra-arterial vs intravenous thrombolysis within 4.5h.
AI-Driven Fundus Screening: Immediate diagnosis of CRVO/CRAO via smartphone imaging.
Neuroprotection: Investigational agents for RGC survival in ischemic events.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Femtosecond Lenticule Extraction (FLEX) and Small Incision Lenticule Extraction (SMILE) are keratorefractive procedures utilizing a femtosecond laser to create an intrastromal lenticule, which is then removed to correct refractive errors. FLEX, a precursor to SMILE, involved creating a corneal flap similar to LASIK. SMILE refined this by eliminating the need for a full flap, instead creating a small incision for lenticule extraction, aiming for enhanced corneal biomechanical stability and reduced dry eye symptoms.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Demographics
content: **Prevalence:** Myopia affects 30-40% of adults in developed countries, driving demand for refractive surgery.
**SMILE Growth:** Rapidly gaining popularity globally, especially in Asia, due to flapless nature.
**Ideal Candidates:** Typically adults 18-45 years old with stable myopia (-0.5 to -10.0 D) or myopic astigmatism (up to -5.0 D).
**Global Reach:** Over 10 million SMILE procedures performed worldwide since its introduction.

sections.title: Risk Factors / Contraindications
content: Unstable Refraction: Change >0.5 D/year.
Keratoconus/Pellucid Marginal Degeneration (PMD): Any corneal ectasia.
Thin Cornea: Residual stromal bed <250 µm after ablation.
Severe Dry Eye Syndrome: Pre-existing ocular surface disease.
Collagen Vascular Disease: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE (impaired healing).
Immunosuppression: Increased risk of infection/poor healing.
Pregnancy/Lactation: Hormonal fluctuations affect corneal hydration and refraction.
Glaucoma/Ocular Hypertension: IOP spikes during suction.
Severe Blepharitis/Meibomian Gland Dysfunction: Increased infection risk.
Monocular Patients: Relative contraindication.

sections.title: 3. Etiology & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Both FLEX and SMILE correct refractive error by precisely removing an intrastromal lenticule of corneal tissue. The femtosecond laser (e.g., Carl Zeiss VisuMax) creates micro-cavitation bubbles through photodisruption, separating corneal tissue layers. The shape and thickness of the lenticule are customized based on the patient's refractive error, determined by pre-operative topography and wavefront analysis. Removing this lenticule alters the anterior corneal curvature, thus changing its refractive power. SMILE's key advantage lies in preserving the anterior corneal lamellae and Bowman's layer integrity outside the small incision, leading to superior biomechanical stability compared to flap-based procedures like LASIK and FLEX. This preservation minimizes nerve severance, potentially reducing post-operative dry eye.

branches: **FLEX (Femtosecond Lenticule Extraction)**: Flap-based removal of intrastromal lenticule.
**SMILE (Small Incision Lenticule Extraction)**: Flapless, cap-based removal via small incision.
**ReLEX (Refractive Lenticule Extraction)**: Term encompasses both FLEX and SMILE, though often used synonymously with SMILE due to its prevalence.
**Contoura Vision SMILE (Next-gen)**: Combines topography-guided ablation with SMILE for enhanced precision.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms (Post-Op)
content: **Visual Recovery**: Good functional vision by day 1, stabilizes over weeks.
**Mild Discomfort**: Foreign body sensation, tearing, photophobia (12-24 hrs post-SMILE, similar to LASIK post-FLEX).
**Halo/Glare**: Transient, especially at night, improving over months.
**Dry Eye Symptoms**: Less severe and shorter duration with SMILE vs. FLEX/LASIK.
**Fluctuating Vision**: Common in early post-op period due to corneal hydration/healing.
**Subconjunctival Hemorrhage**: Due to suction, resolves in 1-2 weeks.

rows: Anterior segment health, tear film assessment
Corneal clarity, interface (FLEX: flap edge, SMILE: cap & incision), lenticule residue, IOP
Rule out keratoconus/ectasia, central corneal thickness (CCT), pachymetry maps
Corneal curvature changes, assess for decentration, induced astigmatism
Rule out retinal pathology (e.g., lattice degeneration)

sections.title: 6. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic History & Examination** - Refractive stability, systemic health, ocular history, current medications.
**Step 2: Manifest & Cycloplegic Refraction** - Accurate measure of refractive error, particularly for hyperopes and young patients.
**Step 3: Best Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA) Assessment** - Rule out underlying ocular pathology.
**Step 4: Slit-lamp Biomicroscopy** - Anterior segment health, tear film evaluation (Schirmer test, TBUT, OSDI questionnaire).
**Step 5: Intraocular Pressure (IOP) Measurement** - Baseline check for glaucoma.
**Step 6: Dilated Fundus Examination** - Rule out peripheral retinal pathology (e.g., tears, lattice degeneration).

**Step 7: Corneal Topography & Tomography (e.g., Pentacam HR, Orbscan IIz, Sirius)** - Essential for ruling out ectatic disorders (keratoconus, PMD), assessing CCT, anterior/posterior corneal elevation, pachymetry progression maps, epithelial maps (for subtle ectasia).
**Step 8: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)** - Anterior segment OCT (AS-OCT) for detailed corneal layer assessment, epithelial thickness mapping, residual stromal bed estimation.
**Step 9: Wavefront Aberrometry** - Measures higher-order aberrations (HOAs) to predict potential night vision issues (less critical for SMILE/FLEX vs. wavefront-guided LASIK).
**Step 10: Specular Microscopy (Endothelial Cell Count)** - Important for patients with previous ocular surgery or suspected endothelial compromise.

sections.title: 9. Management & Treatment (Post-operative)
content: **Immediate Post-op (Day 0-7):**
**Topical Steroids:** e.g., Prednisolone Acetate 1% QID for 1-2 weeks (e.g., FML 0.1% for 3-4 weeks for SMILE) to reduce inflammation and prevent haze.
**Topical Antibiotics:** e.g., Moxifloxacin 0.5% QID for 1 week to prevent infection.
**Artificial Tears (Preservative-free):** QID to hourly as needed for dry eye relief.
**NSAID Drops:** (Optional) for pain relief, e.g., Ketorolac 0.4% BID-TID for a few days.
**Protective Eyewear:** Eye shields at night, sunglasses outdoors for 1 week.
**Subsequent Weeks/Months:**
**Steroid Taper:** Gradually taper steroids based on inflammation.
**Continued Lubrication:** As needed, may continue for several months post-SMILE.
**Refractive Enhancement:** If significant residual refractive error after 3-6 months, consider PRK (most common for SMILE/FLEX) or relift (FLEX/LASIK).
**Management of Complications:**
**DLK:** Aggressive topical steroids (e.g., Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h), consider oral steroids. Interface irrigation for Grade 3/4.
**Infection:** Immediate culture, broad-spectrum fortified antibiotics (e.g., Vancomycin + Ceftazidime), potentially corneal scrape/biopsy.
**Epithelial Ingrowth:** Observation for Grade 1. Surgical debridement with flap lift, scraping, polishing, +/- fibrin glue, +/- alcohol for Grade 2/3 (FLEX/LASIK).
**Corneal Ectasia:** Cross-linking (CXL) to stabilize the cornea.

sections.title: 12. Red Flags / Emergency Signs (Post-Op)
content: Sudden, severe decrease in vision.
Intense or worsening eye pain not relieved by OTC analgesics.

content.explanation: Helps remember SMILE's key benefits: superior biomechanical stability due to flapless nature (stronger mechanics) and its core principle (lenticule extraction).

sections.title: 14. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **SMILE's Biomechanical Advantage:** Preserves more anterior stromal lamellae and Bowman's layer integrity compared to LASIK/FLEX, leading to better corneal biomechanical strength.
**Dry Eye Mitigation:** SMILE severs fewer corneal nerves, resulting in a significantly lower incidence and severity of post-operative dry eye symptoms compared to LASIK/FLEX.
**Learning Curve:** SMILE has a steeper learning curve for surgeons, particularly in lenticule dissection and extraction.

**Visual Recovery:** While SMILE patients often report feeling better sooner, initial visual acuity may be slightly slower to achieve optimal levels compared to LASIK/FLEX in some studies, but rapidly catches up.
**Enhancements:** For residual refractive error post-SMILE, surface ablation (PRK) is the preferred enhancement method, as creating a secondary lenticule or converting to LASIK is more complex.
**Myopia Range:** SMILE is currently FDA approved for myopia up to -10.0 D and astigmatism up to -3.0 D (varies by region/device).
**Hyperopia:** SMILE for hyperopia is still in clinical trials and not yet widely available or approved.
**Suction Loss:** A critical intraoperative event, requiring immediate re-docking or conversion to PRK. Prevention through proper patient selection and docking technique is paramount.

sections.title: 15. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Carl Zeiss Meditec VisuMax Laser:** The pioneering femtosecond laser platform for SMILE technology.
**ReLEx SMILE (Refractive Lenticule Extraction, Small Incision Lenticule Extraction):** Introduced in 2011, it revolutionized flapless refractive surgery.
**FDA Approval:** SMILE received FDA approval in the U.S. in 2016 for myopia and in 2018 for myopic astigmatism, expanding its global adoption.
**VisuMax 800:** Next-generation VisuMax laser with faster repetition rates (2 MHz) for reduced suction time and potential for even faster visual recovery.
**SMILE Pro:** Latest advancement, further optimizing the procedure with faster laser pulse, reducing treatment time to ~10 seconds.
**Topography-guided SMILE (e.g., Contoura Vision SMILE):** Emerging technology aiming to integrate topography data for personalized, even more precise lenticule creation.

sections.title: 16. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Age Limit:** Refractive surgery is generally not recommended for individuals under 18-21 years due to unstable refraction.
**Pregnancy/Lactation:** Contraindicated due to hormonal shifts affecting corneal hydration and refraction, and potential medication effects.
**Diabetics:** Well-controlled diabetes is generally acceptable, but uncontrolled diabetes is a contraindication due to impaired healing and increased infection risk.
**Immuno-compromised:** Systemic immunosuppression (e.g., HIV, organ transplant patients on high-dose steroids) is a contraindication due to increased infection risk and poor wound healing.
**Mental Health:** Patients with unrealistic expectations or psychiatric disorders (e.g., Body Dysmorphic Disorder) are poor candidates.
**Occupational Considerations:** Specific visual requirements for pilots, military personnel may influence procedure choice.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Blebitis is defined as a localized infection involving the filtering bleb, but notably lacking vitreous involvement. It is a precursor to Bleb-Associated Endophthalmitis (BAE). It occurs post-trabeculectomy or post-GDD, often months to years after the initial surgery (late-onset). The hallmark is a 'milky' appearance of the bleb contents due to purulent material (hypopyon within the bleb).

Seidel Test: Critical to check for active bleb leaks
Conjunctival hyperemia (localized or diffuse)

Fundoscopy: Must rule out vitreous involvement (critical distinction)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Immediate clinical assessment and slit-lamp photography.
Step 2: Conjunctival and bleb surface swabs for Culture (Blood agar, Chocolate, Thioglycollate).
Step 3: If AC reaction present, consider AC tap (though controversial in isolated blebitis).
Step 4: Dilated fundus exam with indirect ophthalmoscopy to assess vitreous.
Step 5: B-scan ultrasonography to rule out posterior segment involvement if view is obscured.

sections.title: Medical Management Strategy
content: Intensive Topical Therapy: Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin) every 30-60 mins.
Fortified Antibiotics: Vancomycin (50mg/mL) + Tobramycin (14mg/mL) or Ceftazidime (50mg/mL).
Cycloplegics: Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1% BID to prevent synechiae.
Oral Antibiotics: Moxifloxacin 400mg QD (good ocular penetration).
Topical Steroids: DELAY 24-48 hours until clinical improvement is noted.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention Indicators
content: Progression to Stage III (Endophthalmitis) requires Vitrectomy + Intravitreal antibiotics.
Persistent Bleb Leak: Requires surgical revision once infection clears.
Bleb Excision: Reserved for recurrent infection or intractable leaks.
Patch Grafting: Using sclera, cornea, or pericardium for structural reinforcement.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A 'white' bleb is not always infected, but a 'milky' bleb always is.
Streptococcal blebitis can blind an eye within 24 hours—act aggressively.
Avoid inferior trabeculectomies whenever possible to reduce lifelong risk.
Lifelong education: Patients must report any 'red eye' immediately.
Ischemic, thin-walled blebs have a 5-10% lifetime risk of infection.

sections.title: Landmark Insights: CIGTS & Beyond
sections.content: The CIGTS (Collaborative Initial Glaucoma Treatment Study) and other long-term trabeculectomy cohorts highlighted that the risk of blebitis does not diminish over time; it is a cumulative lifetime risk. Modern surgical trends have shifted toward GDDs or MIGS in high-risk patients (like contact lens wearers or those with ocular surface disease) to avoid the vulnerable filtration bleb.

content: Step 1: Clinical Assessment - Rule out internal ostium blockage via gonioscopy.
Step 2: Digital Pressure (Buratto's Maneuver) - Apply pressure through lower lid to force aqueous through flap.
Step 3: Laser Suture Lysis (LSL) - Use Hoskins lens to cut 10-0 nylon flap sutures (typically days 3-14).
Step 4: Pharmacological Modulation - Subconjunctival 5-FU (5mg in 0.1ml) to inhibit fibroblast proliferation.
Step 5: Bleb Needling - Break episcleral adhesions using a 27G or 30G needle, often with MMC (0.02%).

sections.title: Surgical Landmarks for Trabeculectomy
content: Scleral Flap: 3x4mm rectangular or triangular, 50% depth.
Internal Ostium: 1.5x2mm block removed with Kelly Punch.
Iridectomy: Basal, wider than the ostium to prevent blockage.
Suture Tension: Titrated to allow 1 drop/5 seconds of flow at 20mmHg.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: Never perform digital pressure if you suspect a wound leak.
Always use Atropine 1% BID in 'shallow AC' cases until the cause is confirmed.
A 'Large, Low' bleb is usually better than a 'Small, High' bleb.
If IOP is high on Day 1, check the ostium with a Gonio lens immediately.

sections.title: Landmark Studies
sections.content: The Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (TVT) study and the Primary Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (PTVT) study have provided critical insights. The PTVT study showed that at 3 years, trabeculectomy with MMC had a higher success rate compared to tube shunts in primary surgical eyes, though complications like hypotony were more frequent in the trabeculectomy group.

summary: Hyphema, the presence of red blood cells within the anterior chamber, is a common consequence of ocular trauma and systemic disease. This guide provides a high-yield, resident-level overview of classification, management protocols, and critical complications.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A hyphema is the accumulation of red blood cells (RBCs) in the anterior chamber, typically settling inferiorly due to gravity. While most cases are traumatic, resulting from the rupture of iris or ciliary body vessels (e.g., the Major Arterial Circle), spontaneous cases must prompt investigation into iris neovascularization, uveitis, or hematological dyscrasias.

sections.title: Critical Pathophysiology
content: 1. Blunt force causes anteroposterior compression and equatorial expansion.
2. Rapid increase in intraocular pressure (IOP).
3. Posterior displacement of the iris-lens diaphragm.
4. Shearing of vessels at the Iris Root or Ciliary Body (Angle Recession).
5. Hemorrhage into the Aqueous Humor.

sections.title: The Sickle Cell Emergency
content: MANDATORY screening for Sickle Cell Trait/Disease (SCD) in all African American/Mediterranean patients.
AVOID Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs) - Methazolamide/Acetazolamide increase sickling via acidosis.
AVOID Hyperosmotic agents (Mannitol) - can cause hemoconcentration and sickling.
IOP Threshold for surgery is lower (>24 mmHg for >24 hours) due to risk of CRAO/Optic Atrophy.

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination
content: Visual Acuity (initial and daily monitoring).
Slit-lamp exam: Assess Grade, Clot status (Red vs. Black), and Corneal Staining.
IOP measurement: Goldmann applanation is preferred (unless ruptured globe).
Deferred Gonioscopy: Perform at 2-4 weeks to assess for angle recession/PAS.
Dilated Fundoscopy: Rule out retinal tears, dialysis, or Berlin's edema (Commotio Retinae).
B-Scan Ultrasonography: If view is obscured to rule out RD or vitreous hemorrhage.

sections.title: Standard Medical Management
content: 1. Bed rest with Head of Bed elevated to 30-45 degrees (promotes settling).
2. Rigid Fox Shield at all times (prevent further trauma).
3. Cycloplegia (Atropine 1% BID/TID) to reduce iris movement and spasm.
4. Topical Steroids (Pred Forte 1% QID) to reduce inflammation.
5. Antifibrinolytics (Aminocaproic Acid 50mg/kg q4h) - Consider in high-risk/pediatric cases to prevent rebleed.
6. IOP control: Beta-blockers or Alpha-agonists first-line.

sections.title: Indications for Surgical Intervention
content: Uncontrolled IOP: >50 mmHg for 2 days or >35 mmHg for 7 days.
Early Corneal Blood Staining: Any sign of endothelial pigment/haze.
Total Hyphema (8-Ball): If IOP > 35 mmHg for 5 days.
Persistence: Large clot remaining for >10 days (risk of PAS).
Sickle Cell: IOP >24 mmHg for >24 hours.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: 1. Simple Paracentesis: Burping the wound to lower IOP.
2. AC Washout: Two-port irrigation/aspiration of liquid blood.
3. Clot Express: Manual expression through a larger limbal incision (less common).
4. Automated Vitrectomy: Using a vitrector probe to remove organized clot (highest safety).

rows: IOL haptic rubbing iris; chronic inflammation/IOP/blood.
Diffuse stellate KPs, iris atrophy, fine NVI (Amsler sign).
NVI at pupillary margin, fibrous membrane in angle.
High IOP, sector iris atrophy, corneal scarring.

content.explanation: R: Risk peaks at day 2-5; E: Elevate head; B: Beta-blockers (avoid CAIs in Sickle); L: Look for corneal staining; E: Every day VA/IOP; E: Evaluate for SCD; D: Defer gonioscopy.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Aspirin and NSAIDs are STRICTLY contraindicated as they increase the risk of rebleeding.
An 8-ball hyphema is black because the blood is deoxygenated and trapped; it is not necessarily older than red blood.
Corneal blood staining begins in the deep stroma and can take years to clear, often from the periphery inward.
Angle recession is found in 70-100% of traumatic hyphema cases; long-term glaucoma follow-up is mandatory.

sections.title: Recent Evidence & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The 'Aminocaproic Acid vs. Placebo' trials demonstrated a significant reduction in rebleed rates (from 25-30% down to 3-4%) in high-risk populations. Recent Cochrane reviews emphasize that while systemic antifibrinolytics reduce rebleeds, they do not necessarily improve final visual acuity compared to standard conservative management. Current standard of care focuses on outpatient management for Grade I-II unless social factors or SCD are present.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: A 'Refractive Surprise' is defined as a postoperative spherical equivalent (SE) deviation of >0.50D or >1.00D from the intended target. While modern biometry aims for >90% of patients within ±0.50D, real-world data often shows 75-80% success, leaving a significant cohort with unexpected outcomes.

Patient Factors: Previous Refractive Surgery & Ocular Surface

sections.title: Pre-operative Biometry Pitfalls
content: Axial Length (AL) Error: 1mm error = ~2.5D to 3.0D refractive error.
Keratometry (K) Error: 1D error in K = ~1D refractive error.
Ocular Surface Disease: Dry eye causes inconsistent K-readings; MUST treat before biometry.
Posterior Staphyloma: Optical biometry (IOLMaster/Lenstar) is superior to A-scan ultrasound (measures to fovea, not anatomical pole).
Data Entry Errors: 'Transcription errors' remain a leading cause of extreme surprises (Wrong IOL power transcribed).

sections.title: The ELP Challenge
sections.content: Effective Lens Position (ELP) is the estimated distance from the corneal vertex to the IOL plane. 1mm of axial displacement leads to ~1.5D change. Factors affecting ELP include: Anterior Chamber Depth (ACD), Lens Thickness (LT), and white-to-white (WTW) diameter. Modern 5th-gen formulas (Kane, Barrett, Hill-RBF) better predict ELP than older 2-variable formulas (SRK/T, Holladay 1).

rows: Use Barrett True-K or ASCRS calculator
Avoid standard formulas; use RK-specific algorithms

sections.title: Investigation & Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Manifest Refraction (Wait at least 2-3 weeks for corneal stability).
Step 2: Dilated Exam (Check IOL centration, tilt, and capsular bag status).
Step 3: Repeat Biometry (Compare with pre-op data; check for AL/K discrepancies).
Step 4: Topography/Tomography (Rule out irregular astigmatism or keratoconus).
Step 5: OCT Macula (Rule out Cystoid Macular Edema - CME can mask/cause shift).
Step 6: Chart Review (Confirm IOL model, power, and serial number implanted matches calculation).

sections.title: Critical Management Timeline
content: Week 1: Identify the surprise; rule out surgical complications (TASS, Endophthalmitis).
Week 2-4: Treat ocular surface; allow refraction to stabilize.
Week 4-6: Finalize plan (IOL Exchange vs. Laser vs. Piggyback).
Month 3+: Perform enhancement if IOL exchange is not feasible.

Cost; dry eye risk; requires another surgery

sections.title: Surgical Pearl: Piggyback Calculations
sections.content: Gills' Rule for Sulcus Piggyback: For Hyperopic surprise, multiply the refractive error by 1.5. For Myopic surprise, multiply by 1.0 to 1.3 (depending on lens material). Always use a silicone IOL (e.g., Staar AQ2010V) in the sulcus over an acrylic IOL in the bag to prevent ILO.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Action Needed
content: Shallow AC with High IOP (Capsular Bag Distension Syndrome)
Iris Transillumination Defects (IOL-Iris Chafing/UGH)
Variable Refraction (Worsening Ocular Surface or Diurnal RK shifts)
Decreased Vision with Normal Refraction (Rule out Maculopathy)

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
content: The Barrett Universal II: Consistently ranked top for all axial lengths in various meta-analyses.
Hill-RBF 3.0: Uses Big Data/AI to predict outcomes; warns 'out of bound' when data is insufficient.
Light Adjustable Lens (LAL): Allows post-operative UV-light adjustment of IOL power, virtually eliminating refractive surprise.
Intraoperative Aberrometry (Optiwave): Real-time aphakic refraction to confirm IOL power choice mid-surgery.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always measure BOTH eyes; if AL difference >0.3mm, re-measure.
Verify the IOL constant (A-constant) used in the calculator matches the IOL model.
In post-refractive eyes, the 'double-K' method is essential to avoid ELP prediction errors.
Never perform YAG capsulotomy until the refraction is final and management is decided (YAG makes IOL exchange much harder).

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
sections.content: With modern enhancement techniques (IOL exchange or LVC), >95% of patients with refractive surprise can be successfully corrected to within 0.5D of their target. Patient counseling is key—frame it as an 'enhancement phase' rather than a 'surgical failure'.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular coloboma is a congenital defect characterized by a localized absence of one or more ocular tissues (iris, ciliary body, lens, retina, choroid, or optic nerve). It results from the failure of the embryonic (optic) fissure to close during the 5th to 7th week of gestation. Typically located in the inferonasal quadrant, it represents a spectrum from a small iris notch to a large defect involving the entire posterior pole and microphthalmos.

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: Step 1: Embryonic fissure forms on the ventral aspect of the optic vesicle during the 4th week.
Step 2: Fissure closure normally begins at the equator and proceeds anteriorly (ciliary body) and posteriorly (optic nerve).
Step 3: Closure failure occurs between the 5th and 7th week of gestation.
Step 4: Persistence of the gap leads to absence of neuroectoderm-derived tissues.
Step 5: Secondary defects in the mesoderm (choroid and sclera) occur due to the absence of the inductive influence of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).

rows: Keyhole pupil appearance; typical (inferonasal) or atypical.
Photophobia; usually minimal effect on acuity.
Notch in lens periphery; zonular absence; often associated with CB coloboma.
Visible ciliary processes in the gap.
White/yellow area with pigmented borders; bare sclera visible.
Enlarged, excavated disc; peripapillary pigment changes.
Reduced VA; visual field defects; risk of serous RD.

content.explanation: C: Coloboma (Ocular); H: Heart defects (Tetralogy of Fallot/PDA); A: Atresia choanae; R: Retardation of growth/development; G: Genitourinary anomalies; E: Ear anomalies/deafness. Associated with CHD7 gene mutation.

rows: Coloboma limited to the optic disc only.
Coloboma extending above the level of the disc.
Coloboma extending below the level of the disc.
Total coloboma involving the disc and the macula.
Coloboma involving the disc but sparing the macula.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Checklist
content: Measurement of Corneal Diameter (Check for microcornea/microphthalmos).
Slit-lamp: Assess for Iris/Lens notch and zonular integrity.
Gonioscopy: Check for angle anomalies or dysgenesis.
Indirect Ophthalmoscopy: Scleral depression to find 'Intercalary Membrane' (ICM) breaks.
B-Scan Ultrasonography: Assess axial length and posterior staphyloma/excavation.
Refraction: Look for high refractive errors or anisometropia.

sections.title: Red Flags: Risk of Retinal Detachment
content: New onset of floaters or flashes (photopsia).
Sudden decrease in visual field or acuity.
Presence of Intercalary Membrane (ICM) breaks.
Associated Microphthalmos (increased risk of complex RD).
Optic nerve coloboma (risk of serous maculopathy).

rows: Funnel-shaped excavation; central glial tuft; radial vessels; not truly inferonasal.
Deep excavation; normal disc appearance inside the staphyloma.
Small, gray/white depression usually on the temporal disc; not a full closure defect.
Optic disc dysplasia; enlarged disc with peripapillary pigment.
Usually post-inflammatory; random location; not typically following the embryonic fissure.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Refraction: Early and aggressive correction of refractive errors and anisometropia.
2. Amblyopia Therapy: Patching of the better eye if acuity is asymmetric.
3. Photophobia Management: Cosmetic contact lenses or iris prostheses for iris defects.
4. RD Prophylaxis: Regular fundus exams (6-12 months). Laser photocoagulation along the coloboma margin (controversial, but used for ICM breaks).
5. Surgical Intervention: Cataract extraction (Malyugin ring often needed); Vitrectomy + Endolaser + Silicon Oil for coloboma-related RD.
6. Systemic Referral: Pediatrician/Genetics for CHARGE or other syndromic screening.

sections.title: Surgical Nuances: The Cataract Challenge
content: Poor pupillary dilation due to iris coloboma (requires iris hooks).
Localized zonular weakness/absence (requires Capsule Tension Ring - CTR).
Increased risk of posterior capsule rupture.
Potential for 'Sunset Syndrome' (IOL decentration into the colobomatous gap).
Consider Iris Reconstruction/Suturing during the same procedure.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Intercalary Membrane' (ICM) is the thin, transparent tissue covering the coloboma. It is extremely fragile and prone to breaks.
Retinal detachments in coloboma are often rhegmatogenous, caused by breaks in the ICM or at the margin between normal retina and the coloboma.
Optic nerve coloboma can lead to a 'Serous Macular Detachment' similar to optic pit maculopathy.
Atypical coloboma (e.g., temporal or superior) is NOT caused by embryonic fissure failure and suggests other developmental insults.
Visual prognosis depends entirely on the involvement of the fovea and the optic nerve head (Gopal Grade IV has the poorest prognosis).

sections.title: Recent Advances & Research
sections.content: Recent studies in 'Deep Phenotyping' use OCT-Angiography to map the peripapillary capillary density in colobomatous eyes, revealing significant reduction in flow even in areas that appear clinically normal. Furthermore, Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) is now identifying causative mutations in up to 30% of previously 'sporadic' cases, highlighting a more complex genetic architecture than previously understood (e.g., dual molecular diagnoses).
