sections.title: Graves' Ophthalmopathy: Pathophysiology & Management
sections.content:
Pathophysiology: Autoimmune disorder where antibodies (TRAb) stimulate TSH receptors on orbital fibroblasts, leading to increased GAG production, fat accumulation, and inflammation of extraocular muscles (EOMs) and orbital fat. This causes muscle swelling, proptosis, and restricted eye movements.

Systemic Signs (other than ocular): Thyroid gland enlargement (goiter), hyperthyroidism symptoms (tachycardia, weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance), pretibial myxedema (skin thickening on shins), thyroid acropachy (clubbing of fingers/toes).

Treatment Options: Depends on severity and activity (CAS score). Lubricants for dry eye, prisms for diplopia, orbital decompression (for optic neuropathy or severe proptosis), strabismus surgery (for stable diplopia), eyelid surgery (for lid retraction). Systemic: high-dose steroids (IV preferred for active disease), orbital radiotherapy, teprotumumab (new targeted therapy).

sections.title: Red Flag: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) with Papilledema
content: Hallmark: Papilledema, often bilateral, due to elevated CSF pressure. Can lead to irreversible vision loss.
Investigations: Neuroimaging (MRI brain with venography to rule out structural causes/CVT), Lumbar Puncture (elevated opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults, normal CSF composition).

Management: Weight loss (crucial), Acetazolamide (first-line), close monitoring of vision/fields/papilledema. Surgical options for progressive vision loss despite maximal medical therapy: Optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF) or CSF shunting (VP or LP shunt). Referral to neurology and neurosurgeon is essential.

sections.title: Grand Mal Seizures: Causes and Ophthalmic Relevance

branches.label: Causes
branches: Structural Brain Lesions (tumors, stroke, trauma, malformations)

branches.label: Management
branches: Acute: Protect patient from injury, position on side, administer benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam IV) if prolonged.
Long-term: Antiepileptic drugs, address underlying cause.

branches.label: Ophthalmic Relevance
branches: Drug-induced ocular side effects (e.g., phenytoin toxicity, topiramate glaucoma)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Swollen Optic Disc with Pain on Eye Movements

rows: Unilateral vision loss (acute), dyschromatopsia, afferent pupillary defect
Often associated with MS (MRI brain for plaques)
Sudden, painless vision loss (altitudinal defect), disc edema (pallid or hyperemic)
Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) is critical DDx (ESR/CRP, temporal artery biopsy)
Severe, bilateral optic neuritis, often recurrent, spinal cord involvement
Variable vision loss, disc edema, vitreous cells
Syphilis, Lyme disease, viral infections (e.g., VZV)
Systemic inflammatory signs, chest imaging, serum ACE
Slow, progressive vision loss, mild edema (early), later atrophy

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Unilateral Ptosis with Double Vision and Headache (3rd Nerve vs. Horner's)

rows: Severe (complete eyelid closure), often with eyelid retraction on attempted upgaze
Mild (1-2mm), often with inverse ptosis (lower lid elevation)
Dilated (mydriasis), often fixed to light if pupil-involving
Constricted (miosis), anisocoria worse in dark, reacts to light
Limitation of adduction, elevation, depression (down-and-out position)
Common (especially with compressive lesions like aneurysm)
Variable, can be associated with pain (e.g., carotid dissection)
Absent Bell's phenomenon, potential for aberrant regeneration

sections.title: Management Protocol: Intermittent Exotropia
content: 1. Initial Assessment: Confirm diagnosis, measure deviation (distance/near, with/without correction), assess fusion, stereoacuity, amblyopia, convergence.
2. Refractive Correction: Prescribe full refractive correction, especially hyperopia/astigmatism. Correct any anisometropia.
3. Amblyopia Treatment: Patching or atropine penalization if present.
4. Non-Surgical Options: Observation (if well-controlled), prismatic correction (temporary for diplopia, rarely for long-term), orthoptic exercises (convergence insufficiency type).

5. Surgical Management: Indicated if control worsens, deviation increases, or symptoms (diplopia, asthenopia, cosmetic concern) persist despite conservative measures. Recess lateral rectus muscles (uni- or bilateral) or resect medial rectus (often combined). Consider adjustable sutures in adults.

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Complications of Silicone Oil (IOFB/RRD cases)
content: Glaucoma (most common, due to inflammation, pupillary block, silicone oil migration)
Cataract (nuclear sclerosis, often rapid progression)
Band keratopathy (due to silicone oil emulsification)
Corneal edema/decompensation (if oil emulsifies into AC)
Retinal redetachment after oil removal
Diplopia, phthisis bulbi (rare)

branches: Sixth Nerve Palsy (rare in infancy, usually incomitant)
Duane's Retraction Syndrome (often with retraction on adduction)
Mobius Syndrome (facial nerve palsy + abducens palsy)
Sensory Esotropia (due to poor vision in one eye)

content.center: Anisocoria (larger pupil in dark) & Large Discs

branches.label: Anisocoria (worse in dark - impaired sympathetic)
branches: Physiological Anisocoria (rarely more noticeable in dark)

branches.label: Large Optic Discs (often with large C/D ratio)
branches: Myopic Optic Neuropathy (myopic tilt, temporal crescent)
Glaucoma (progressive thinning of NRR, asymmetry, hemorrhage, RNFL defects)
Combined Presentation: May suggest a complex neuro-ophthalmic or structural issue requiring comprehensive evaluation (e.g., prior trauma, congenital anomalies affecting both).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Ptosis in a Young Girl

rows: Unilateral/bilateral, present at birth, poor LF, possible amblyopia
Variable, fatigable, worse late day, often bilateral asymmetric
Diplopia, orbicularis weakness (Bell's poor), generalized weakness
High lid crease, thin lid skin
Due to lid mass, scar, edema

branches: Sebaceous Gland Carcinoma (must rule out for sebaceous lesions, biopsy is crucial)

sections.title: Management Protocol: Trichiasis & Symblepharon
content: Trichiasis: Epilation (temporary), Electrolysis, Cryotherapy, Argon Laser, Surgical excision with lid margin reconstruction.
Symblepharon: Prevention (early management of chemical burns with symblepharon rings/AMT), Surgical lysis with conjunctival graft/AMT, Amniotic membrane transplantation.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Chronic Anterior Uveitis (CAU) with Band Keratopathy

branches: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) / Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis (JRA)
Herpetic Uveitis (less common to cause BK)
Metabolic Causes of Band Keratopathy (non-inflammatory, non-ocular): Hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, vitamin D toxicity), chronic renal failure, gout, chronic mercury exposure.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Failed Keratoplasty Graft & Corneal Vascularization
content: 1. Confirm Graft Failure: Rule out rejection (epithelial, stromal, endothelial), infection, persistent inflammation, recurrent disease, chronic endothelial decompensation.
2. History: Time of surgery (primary vs. late graft failure), previous rejections, underlying corneal pathology.

3. Management of Graft Failure: Depends on cause. For rejection, intensive topical/systemic steroids. For infection, appropriate antimicrobials. For endothelial failure, repeat keratoplasty (PKP, DMEK, DSAEK).

4. Corneal Vascularization Treatment: Topical steroids (to suppress inflammation), Anti-VEGF (subconjunctival, intrastromal, topical - off-label), Laser photocoagulation (argon laser to feeder vessels), Cauterization of feeder vessels (intraoperative or transconjunctival).

sections.title: Perioperative Management: Atrial Fibrillation for Cataract Surgery
content: Determine if acute vs. chronic AF.
Rate Control: Beta-blockers (e.g., Esmolol), calcium channel blockers (e.g., diltiazem), digoxin.
Rhythm Control: Antiarrhythmic drugs (e.g., amiodarone), cardioversion (electrical or pharmacological) if unstable or recent onset.
Anticoagulation: Warfarin, DOACs (direct oral anticoagulants like rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban). CHADS2-VASc score guides long-term anticoagulation.
Coordination: Consult with cardiologist/internist for optimization before surgery.
Red Flag: Uncontrolled AF increases risk of stroke and myocardial infarction perioperatively. Postpone elective surgery until stable.

sections.title: Perioperative Management: Cataract Surgery on Warfarin
content: Risk of retrobulbar hemorrhage with regional anesthesia (retrobulbar, peribulbar block).
Anesthesia Options: Topical anesthesia, subconjunctival, or subtenon anesthesia (with careful technique) are safer choices.
Surgical Approach: Clear corneal incision is preferred over scleral tunnel incisions to minimize bleeding.

Anticoagulation Management: Generally, for routine cataract surgery, warfarin does not need to be stopped if INR is in therapeutic range (e.g., 2.0-3.0). Discontinuation carries higher thrombotic risk than bleeding risk in this context.
Bridging therapy is usually NOT recommended for cataract surgery. Always consult with the prescribing physician/hematologist to assess individual thrombotic risk vs. bleeding risk.

sections.title: Investigation & Management: Pituitary Adenoma (Prolactinoma)
sections.content:
Examination: Anterior segment, posterior segment (optic disc), pupillary reaction, confrontation visual field, automated perimetry (for bitemporal hemianopia, usually starting superiorly).

Neuroimaging: Brain MRI with pituitary protocol is essential.

Hormonal Assay: Prolactin level (significantly elevated), other pituitary hormones (TSH, free T4, cortisol, GH, IGF-1, LH, FSH, estradiol/testosterone).

Medical Treatment: Dopamine agonists (Bromocriptine, Cabergoline) are first-line for prolactinomas, often normalizing prolactin and reducing tumor size.

Surgical Treatment: Transsphenoidal hypophysectomy for progressive visual field loss, macroadenomas unresponsive to medical therapy, or apoplexy. Stereotactic radiotherapy is an alternative for residual tumor or recurrence.

Post-Surgery Complication: Polyuria (problem: Diabetes Insipidus due to damage to posterior pituitary or hypothalamus, leading to ADH deficiency).

sections.title: Diagnosis & Tests: Myasthenia Gravis (MG)
content: Clinical Tests: Fatigability (sustained upgaze, repeated blinking), Ice pack test (improves ptosis temporarily), Sleep test (improves ptosis after rest).
Pharmacological Tests: Tensilon (Edrophonium) test (rapid but transient improvement in muscle weakness after IV edrophonium). Must be done with atropine available for cholinergic crisis.
Electrophysiological Tests: Repetitive nerve stimulation (decremental response), Single-fiber EMG (increased jitter and blocking).
Antibody Tests: Acetylcholine Receptor (AChR) antibodies (most common), Muscle-Specific Kinase (MuSK) antibodies (for seronegative MG), LRP4 antibodies.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Amblyopia
content: 1. Correct Refractive Error: Prescribe appropriate glasses for significant refractive error or anisometropia (full cycloplegic refraction).
2. Amblyopia Therapy: Initiate immediately after refractive correction if amblyopia persists. Modalities include:
a. Patching: Occlusion of the good eye for several hours daily (e.g., 4-5 hours for moderate amblyopia).
b. Atropine Penalization: Atropine drops in the good eye to blur vision, forcing use of the amblyopic eye.
c. Filters (e.g., Bangerter filters): Applied to glasses over the good eye.
d. Binocular therapy (new approaches): Dichoptic games and virtual reality systems.
3. Follow-up: Regular monitoring to assess visual acuity, compliance, and adjust therapy. Treatment can continue up to 10-12 years of age or even older in some cases.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Acute Convergent Strabismus in a 3-year-old

branches: Accommodative Esotropia (most common cause in this age group, typically with hyperopia)
Acute Esotropia (sudden onset, often with underlying systemic or neurological cause)
Sixth Cranial Nerve Palsy (incomitant esotropia, abduction deficit)
Brainstem Tumor (e.g., pontine glioma) - Red Flag!
Hydrocephalus (rare, but can cause 6th nerve palsy)
Dissociated Vertical Deviation (DVD - often associated with infantile ET)

sections.title: Management Protocol: Lateral Rectus Paralysis (6th Nerve Palsy)
content: 1. History & Examination: Onset, progression, duration, systemic diseases (diabetes, HTN, vasculitis), measure angle (prism cover test), check other cranial nerves, AS/PS/pupillary exam.

2. Investigations: Blood sugar, lipid profile. Neuroimaging (MRI brain with contrast) to rule out compressive lesions (tumors, aneurysm) or inflammation/demyelination, especially in younger patients or atypical presentations. If suspected GCA, ESR/CRP.

3. Management (Acute): Observation for 3-6 months (many vasculopathic palsies resolve spontaneously). Patching one eye (to relieve diplopia), prism glasses (Fresnel prisms for temporary, ground-in for stable). Botulinum toxin injection (into ipsilateral medial rectus) to prevent contracture of antagonist and reduce deviation.

4. Management (Chronic/Stable after 6 months): Strabismus surgery (lateral rectus recession + medial rectus resection; vertical muscle transposition if severe) if deviation is stable and non-resolving.

sections.title: Pre-operative Assessment for Cataract Surgery under Local Anesthesia
content: Systemic Diseases: Diabetes, hypertension, cardiac disease, respiratory disease (COPD, asthma), rheumatoid arthritis, bleeding disorders, neurological disorders (Parkinson's, seizures).
Ocular History: Onset, progression, duration of cataract, previous ocular surgery/trauma, any pain/other complaints.
Ocular Examination: Visual acuity, intraocular pressure, anterior segment (cornea, iris, lens), posterior segment (fundus, optic nerve). Check the other eye.
Pupils: Size, shape, reactivity, presence of RAPD.
Extraocular Motility: Assess for strabismus or diplopia.

Fitness for Local Anesthesia: Evaluate patient's ability to lie flat, cooperate, remain still (e.g., not suitable for severe tremors, claustrophobia, active cough). Consider general anesthesia for these cases.

sections.title: Red Flag: Leukocoria in a Child
content: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) is a pediatric ophthalmologic emergency.
Most critical differential diagnosis: Retinoblastoma (life-threatening).
Investigations: Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA), B-scan ultrasonography (to assess posterior segment, rule out mass), CT/MRI orbit (for retinoblastoma staging).

Differential Diagnosis for Leukocoria: Retinoblastoma, Persistent Hyperplastic Primary Vitreous (PHPV), Congenital Cataract, Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP), Coats' Disease, Toxocariasis, Familial Exudative Vitreoretinopathy (FEVR), Retinal Detachment (especially exudative/tractional).

sections.title: Management of PHPV (Persistent Hyperplastic Primary Vitreous)
content: Anterior PHPV: May present with leukocoria, microphthalmia, shallow AC, cataract, ciliary body processes. Management: Lensectomy/cataract surgery (visual prognosis guarded), amblyopia therapy, watchful for glaucoma.
Posterior PHPV: Retinal fold, tractional RD, optic disc hypoplasia. Management: Vitrectomy to remove fibrotic tissue and prevent RD. Prognosis often poor.
Counseling: Parents need to understand guarded visual prognosis, risk of amblyopia, glaucoma, and retinal detachment, and need for long-term follow-up and amblyopia therapy.

sections.title: Informed Consent: Cataract Surgery Risks
content: Intraoperative: Posterior capsule rupture (PCR), vitreous loss, suprachoroidal hemorrhage, dropped nucleus, iris damage, zonular dialysis.

Postoperative: Endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, cystoid macular edema (CME), bullous keratopathy, glaucoma (e.g., pigment dispersion, steroid-induced), persistent uveitis, refractive error, IOL dislocation, secondary membrane formation.

sections.title: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) of the Eyelid: Rodent Ulcer
sections.content:
Description: A classic 'rodent ulcer' presents as a raised, pearly nodule with rolled borders, telangiectatic vessels, and often a central ulceration. It is slow-growing but locally invasive.

Most Probable Diagnosis: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), the most common eyelid malignancy.

Treatment: Surgical excision with clear margins (Mohs micrographic surgery is ideal for margin control, especially near critical structures). Reconstruction of the eyelid defect depends on size and location (e.g., direct closure, skin graft, Tenzel flap, Hughes flap, Mustarde flap).

sections.title: Dry Eye Disease: Diagnosis and Management
sections.content:
Stains: Rose Bengal (stains devitalized cells, mucus), Lissamine Green (similar to Rose Bengal, less irritating), Fluorescein (stains corneal epithelial defects).

Other Tests: Tear break-up time (TBUT - measure time from blink to first dry spot), Schirmer test 1 & 2 (tear production), Tear Meniscus Height (TMH - inferior meniscus height at slit lamp), Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI) questionnaire.

Treatment Steps:
1. Address Underlying Cause: Systemic diseases (e.g., Sjogren's, thyroid eye disease, rheumatoid arthritis), medications.
2. Environmental Changes: Avoid dry/windy conditions, use humidifiers, frequent blinking, eyelid hygiene (warm compresses, lid scrubs).
3. Artificial Tears: Start with preservative-containing, then shift to preservative-free if needed. Gels/ointments at night.
4. Anti-inflammatory: Topical steroids (short course), Cyclosporine A or Lifitegrast (long-term immunomodulation).
5. Punctal Plugs: To retain natural tears.
6. Systemic Treatment: Doxycycline (for meibomian gland dysfunction - MGD, anti-inflammatory effect), Omega-3 fatty acids.
7. Surgical Options: Tarsorrhaphy (for severe lagophthalmos), correction of entropion/ectropion/trichiasis if contributing.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Facial Nerve Palsy with Lagophthalmos
content: 1. Diagnosis: Confirm facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy, trauma, tumor, infection, stroke). Refer to neurologist for workup.
2. Eye Protection (Temporary Measures): Lubricant eye drops (frequent), lubricant ointments (especially at night), eyelid taping/patching at night, moisture chambers (goggles).
3. Surgical Options (Permanent Measures for prolonged palsy):
a. Medial Canthoplasty: Narrows the palpebral fissure.
b. Lateral Tarsorrhaphy: Temporarily or permanently sutures lateral eyelids together to narrow fissure.
c. Gold Weight Implant: Placed in upper eyelid to aid gravity-assisted lid closure.
d. Lower eyelid tightening procedures (e.g., lateral tarsal strip) for ectropion.
e. Transposition of temporalis muscle for active lid closure.

4. Botulinum Toxin: Can be used in the contralateral orbicularis oculi for symmetry in severe cases or to manage associated tearing due to punctal eversion and reflex tearing (not to treat the palsy itself).
5. Referral: Oculoplastic surgeon for surgical management, neurologist for etiology and systemic management.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis & Management: Child with Lid Swelling and Redness

rows: Eyelid swelling/redness, tenderness. NO proptosis, NO ophthalmoplegia, NO pain on eye movements, NO vision change.
Oral antibiotics (outpatient if mild, no systemic signs). Close monitoring.
Severe eyelid swelling/redness, pain, FEVER, PROPTOSIS, OPHTHALMOPLEGIA, pain on eye movements, decreased vision, RAPD.

URGENT admission, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, CT orbit & sinuses (to check for abscess, differentiate from preseptal), ENT consultation for sinus drainage if needed. Look for optic nerve affection and pupils.
Redness, discharge, lid swelling (mild), usually bilateral. Itching (allergic).
Sudden, bilateral, often itchy, resolves quickly with antihistamines. No pain/fever.
Localized tender lump. Stye (acute infection), Chalazion (chronic inflammation).
Warm compresses, lid hygiene. Incision & drainage if refractory.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Post-Trabeculectomy Hypotony (Shallow AC, Low IOP)
content: 1. Assess: AC depth (grade 1,2,3 - iridocorneal, pupillo-corneal, lenticulo-corneal), Seidel test (bleb leak?), bleb height, fundus (choroidal detachment?). IOP.
2. Differential Diagnosis: Overfiltration (diffuse, flat bleb), Bleb leak (positive Seidel), Ciliary body shutdown (decreased aqueous production), Choroidal detachment (serous or hemorrhagic).
3. Management:
a. Bleb Leak: Aqueous suppressants (if no choroidals), bandage contact lens, patching, ocular lubricants, bleb compression sutures, blood patch, surgical repair.

b. Overfiltration/Ciliary Shutdown (without leak): Cycloplegics (to deepen AC, reduce aqueous flow across ciliary body), viscoelastic injection (to deepen AC), decrease topical steroids, increase antibiotics (prophylactically). Choroidal drainage (only for 'kissing' choroidals threatening macula/optic nerve or chronic effusion, usually avoided for acute serous choroidals).

sections.title: Management Protocol: Malignant Glaucoma (Aqueous Misdirection)
content: 1. Diagnosis: Elevated IOP, shallow/flat AC (often peripheral iridocorneal touch), normal bleb, no pupillary block, no suprachoroidal hemorrhage (confirmed by B-scan).

2. Medical Management: Cycloplegic eye drops (e.g., Atropine 1%), aqueous suppressants (beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors), hyperosmotic agents (oral glycerol/isosorbide, IV mannitol). Intensive medical therapy is first-line.

3. Laser Management: If pseudophakic: YAG laser posterior capsulotomy and hyaloidotomy (disrupt anterior vitreous face). If phakic: YAG laser through peripheral iridotomy (to disrupt anterior hyaloid face).

4. Surgical Management: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) with anterior hyaloidectomy (often with lensectomy in phakic eyes) to disrupt vitreous integrity and redirect aqueous flow. This is the definitive treatment.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Primary Open Angle Glaucoma (POAG) - Medication Intolerance
content: 1. Initial Treatment: First-line is prostaglandin analog (Latanoprost, Travoprost, Bimatoprost once daily) or beta-blocker (Timolol 0.5% twice daily) if no contraindications.

2. Patient Counseling (Prostaglandin Analogs): Inform about complications (red eye, trichomegaly, iris hyperpigmentation, periocular fat atrophy). Emphasize compliance for a progressive, chronic disease.
3. If Intolerant to Medications:
a. Switch to another class of eye drops (e.g., different prostaglandin, alpha-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor).
b. Consider Preservative-Free (PF) formulations: Often better tolerated for patients with ocular surface disease or irritation.
c. Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT/ALT): Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT) is a safe and effective option, can be repeated. Reduces IOP by enhancing aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork.
d. Surgical Intervention: If all else fails, consider trabeculectomy or glaucoma drainage device (GDD). Especially important for monocular patients or those with advanced disease.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) with Cilioretinal Artery Sparing
content: CRAO is an ocular emergency. Vision loss is sudden and profound. Cilioretinal artery sparing indicates a better prognosis for central vision.
1. Emergency Treatment (within 90-120 minutes of onset):
a. Ocular Massage: Firm digital pressure (10-15s) then rapid release (5-10s) for 5-10 minutes, to dislodge embolus.
b. Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: Rapidly lowers IOP, potentially dislodging embolus.
c. Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy: Limited availability, but can improve oxygenation.
d. Carbogen (95% O2, 5% CO2) or breathing into a paper bag: To induce vasodilation (controversial effectiveness).
e. IOP-lowering drugs: Topical (Timolol), IV (Acetazolamide, Mannitol).
2. Systemic Workup & Referral: URGENT referral to internist/neurologist/cardiologist.
a. Carotid Doppler Ultrasound: To detect carotid artery stenosis (common embolic source).
b. Echocardiogram: To look for cardiac emboli (e.g., atrial fibrillation, valvular disease).
c. Blood tests: ESR/CRP (rule out GCA), coagulation profile, fasting glucose, lipid profile.
d. Check other eye for any signs of vascular disease.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Vitreomacular Traction (VMT)
content: Diagnosis: Confirmed by OCT showing vitreous adherence to the macula.
Treatment Options:
1. Observation: If good vision and no metamorphopsia. Many cases resolve spontaneously.
2. Pharmacological Vitreolysis: Ocriplasmin injection (for focal VMT <1500µm, no epiretinal membrane, phakic eyes).

3. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): If vision is worsening, severe metamorphopsia, or VMT-related macular complications (e.g., macular hole, cystoid macular edema). May include membrane removal and ILM peeling.

sections.title: Ocular Side Effects of Systemic Medications (Rheumatoid Arthritis)

rows: Posterior Subcapsular Cataract, Glaucoma (steroid-responder), increased infection risk

Baseline exam, annual screening after 5 years or cumulative dose >1000g, or if high risk (renal disease, tamoxifen use). Includes fundus exam, OCT, automated visual fields (10-2), fundus autofluorescence.
Baseline eye exam, monitor for dry eye
Baseline eye exam, monitor for symptoms

sections.title: Glaucomatous Optic Disc Evaluation & CCT
content: Features of Glaucomatous Optic Disc: Large vertical cupping, peripapillary atrophy (alpha and beta zones), nasalization of vessels, bayonetting of vessels, disc hemorrhage, localized or diffuse retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) defects, asymmetry between eyes.

Central Corneal Thickness (CCT) Importance: Thin CCT (<555µm) can lead to underestimation of IOP by Goldmann applanation tonometry, increasing glaucoma risk. Thick CCT (>588µm) can lead to overestimation. Normal CCT is ~550µm.

Investigations: Full glaucoma evaluation includes IOP measurement, gonioscopy, optic disc evaluation (clinical + stereo photos), visual field testing (HVF), OCT of RNFL and optic disc, pachymetry (CCT).

sections.title: Management Protocol: Myasthenia Gravis (MG)
content: 1. Pharmacological: Pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) for symptomatic relief. Oral steroids (e.g., prednisone) for immunosuppression. Other immunosuppressants (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil).
2. Thymectomy: Often considered for generalized MG, especially with thymoma.
3. Crisis Management: Plasmapheresis or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) for myasthenic crisis.
4. Referral: Neurologist for diagnosis, workup (AChR antibodies, EMG, Tensilon test, CT chest for thymoma), and long-term systemic management.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Causes of DCR Tube Indications

branches: Secondary Acquired Lacrimal Obstruction (SALDO - e.g., trauma, inflammation, tumors)
Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (persistent after probing/balloon dilation)

sections.title: Complications of DCR (Dacryocystorhinostomy)
content: Bleeding (intra- or post-operative)
Infection
Failure of lacrimal drainage (most common, due to fibrosis/scarring)
Nasal synechiae
CSF leak (rare with external DCR)
Diplopia (rare)
Dislodgement of tube (if intubation performed)

sections.title: Management of Phthisis Bulbi (Cosmetic Options)
content: Colored Contact Lenses (if globe integrity allows and some vision remains)
Prosthetic Shell (scleral shell) for cosmesis over a phthisical eye.

Evisceration with Orbital Implant: Removes contents of the globe, leaving scleral shell, then implant placed to restore orbital volume, followed by a prosthetic eye shell. Preferred over enucleation for phthisis due to better motility and volume.

sections.title: Complications of Scleral Fixation IOL (SFIOL)
content: Intraocular Hemorrhage (hyphema, vitreous hemorrhage)
IOP elevation/Glaucoma (due to trauma, inflammation, cyclodialysis, PAS)
Infection (endophthalmitis)
IOL Decentration/Tilt/Dislocation
Suture-related complications (suture erosion, breakage, knot exposure, inflammation)
Retinal Detachment
Cystoid Macular Edema
Corneal Edema
Diplopia

sections.title: Management Protocol: IOL Subluxation
content: 1. Assessment: Visual acuity, IOP, type of IOL, degree of subluxation, presence of vitreous in AC.
2. Conservative Management: If vision is good and minimal symptoms: observation, glasses, contact lenses.
3. Surgical Management: If vision is poor, diplopia, or IOL rubbing iris/cornea (causing inflammation/glaucoma):
a. Repositioning (if possible, e.g., with iris hooks or viscodissection).
b. Exchange for a new IOL (ACIOL, iris-fixated, scleral-fixated).
c. Removal of IOL and leave aphakic (then secondary IOL later).

branches: Endothelial Cell Loss (from complicated cataract surgery)
Trauma (e.g., intra-capsular cataract extraction (ICCE) or complicated extra-capsular cataract extraction (ECCCE) with extensive iris loss)
IOL rubbing on endothelium (e.g., ACIOL, misplaced PCIOL)
Pre-existing endothelial dystrophy (e.g., Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy)

sections.title: Corneal Graft Options for PBK
content: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): Full-thickness corneal replacement. Indicated if stromal scarring is significant.
Endothelial Keratoplasty (DMEK/DSAEK): Partial-thickness replacement of endothelium. Preferred if stroma is clear.
Combined Procedure: Graft + IOL implantation (if aphakic or IOL malpositioned).
Staged Procedure: Graft first, then IOL implantation later.
Aphakic Contact Lens: For correction if no IOL is placed and surgery is deferred.

sections.title: Complications of Endothelial Keratoplasty (EK)
content: Graft Detachment (most common, requires rebubbling)
Primary Graft Failure
Graft Rejection
IOP elevation/Glaucoma
Infection
Pupillary block
Retinal detachment (rare)

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Full Thickness Macular Hole
content: Grading (Gass classification): Stage 1 (foveal cyst/split), Stage 2 (partial break), Stage 3 (full thickness with operculum), Stage 4 (full thickness with PVD).
Causes: Vitreomacular traction (most common), trauma, high myopia, inflammation.
Surgery: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) with Internal Limiting Membrane (ILM) peeling and gas tamponade.
Gas Injection: Types (SF6, C2F6, C3F8), complications (pupillary block glaucoma, cataract), precautions (face-down positioning, no air travel).

sections.title: Management Protocol: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) with Macular Edema
content: Diagnosis: Fundus exam (NVD, NVE, vitreous hemorrhage), FA, OCT (for macular edema, VMT).
1. Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) Laser: First-line for PDR (neovascularization), settings typically 500µm spot size, 0.1s duration, 200-500mW power, 1200-1600 spots over multiple sessions.
2. Vitrectomy Indications for Diabetes: Persistent vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment (TRD) involving or threatening the macula, combined rhegmatogenous and tractional RD.
3. Silicone Oil in Vitrectomy: Complications (glaucoma, band keratopathy, cataract), duration (ideally 3-6 months, but longer for complex cases).
4. Macular Edema (CME) Management:
a. Intravitreal Injections: Anti-VEGF (Bevacizumab, Ranibizumab, Aflibercept) are first-line, or steroid implants (Dexamethasone, Fluocinolone).

b. Vitreomacular Traction (VMT) with Macular Edema: Intravitreal injections are CONTRAINDICATED or less effective. Laser may increase traction. Vitrectomy to remove membrane and relieve traction is preferred.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Congenital Optic Disc Anomalies

branches: Glaucomatous Optic Disc (can be congenital or developmental glaucoma)

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Alternating Exotropia & Inferior Oblique Overaction
content: Alternating Exotropia: Deviation of one eye outwards, then the other. Indicates good vision in both eyes and alternation of fixation.
Inferior Oblique Overaction (IOOA): Eye elevates and abducts excessively on attempted adduction. Often associated with V-pattern strabismus.
Management: Refractive correction, amblyopia treatment if unilateral, then surgical correction (bilateral lateral rectus recession, +/- inferior oblique weakening procedures for IOOA).

sections.title: Investigation Workup: Optic Neuropathy (RAPD, Cupped Disc, Pallor)
content: Visual Acuity, Color Vision (dyschromatopsia), Visual Fields (e.g., automated perimetry for specific defects).
Pupil Exam: RAPD (afferent pupillary defect) indicates asymmetric optic nerve damage.
Fundus Exam: Optic disc for pallor, cupping, swelling, atrophy. Assess RNFL.
OCT of Optic Nerve Head (ONH) and RNFL: Quantifies nerve fiber layer thickness and disc changes, useful for monitoring progression.

Systemic Workup: Depending on suspected cause – ESR/CRP (GCA), MRI Brain/Orbit (compressive, inflammatory, demyelinating lesions), autoantibodies (NMO, sarcoidosis), infectious workup (syphilis, Lyme).
Types of Optic Atrophy: Primary (e.g., hereditary, compressive), Secondary (e.g., post-papilledema), Consecutive (e.g., post-retinal disease), Glaucomatous (distinct cupping pattern).

sections.title: Management Protocol: Dislocated IOL with Pupillary Block and Iris Bombe
content: 1. Diagnosis: Slit lamp exam (IOL optic in AC, iris bombe, peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS), pigments on IOL), IOP measurement.
2. Effects: High IOP (due to pupillary block, PAS), corneal endothelial damage (from IOL contact), inflammation.
3. Emergency Management: Topical aqueous suppressants (beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, CAIs), cycloplegics (to dilate pupil and break block), hyperosmotic agents (oral glycerol/IV mannitol).
4. Definitive Management:
a. Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI): To relieve pupillary block if the block is between iris and lens.
b. Surgical Repositioning/Exchange: If LPI fails or IOL causing endothelial damage. Repositioning or exchange to ACIOL, iris-fixated IOL, or scleral-fixated IOL.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Corneal Decompensation Post-Cataract Surgery

branches: Pre-existing endothelial dystrophy (e.g., Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy)
Endothelial cell loss during complicated surgery
IOL trauma to endothelium (e.g., ACIOL, IOL subluxation)
Cystoid macular edema (indirectly affecting vision, but not corneal decompensation)

sections.title: Management Protocol: Macular Edema (General)
content: 1. Confirm Diagnosis: OCT (gold standard), fundus exam, FA.
2. Treat Underlying Cause: Diabetes (control blood sugar, BP, lipids), RVO (laser, anti-VEGF), inflammation (steroids).
3. Intravitreal Injections: Anti-VEGF agents (Bevacizumab, Ranibizumab, Aflibercept) for DME, RVO, nAMD. Steroid implants (Dexamethasone, Fluocinolone) for refractory or non-VEGF driven edema.
4. Laser: Focal/grid laser for non-center-involving DME or some RVOs (less common now).
5. Vitrectomy: For macular edema with significant vitreomacular traction (VMT) or epiretinal membrane (ERM).

sections.title: Red Flag: Unilateral Large Peripheral Visual Field Defect
content: Cause: Needs urgent neuro-ophthalmic evaluation.
Differential Diagnosis:
1. Optic Neuropathy (e.g., AION, compressive lesion): Severe damage to optic nerve head, can cause altitudinal or diffuse defects.
2. Retinal Detachment: Peripheral RD can cause a dense, sharp-bordered field defect corresponding to the detached area.
3. Retinoschisis: Can cause absolute or relative field defects, typically stable.
4. Chorioretinal Scars/Lesions: Large lesions (e.g., choroidal melanoma, toxoplasmosis scar) can cause corresponding field loss.
5. Stroke/Tumor in Optic Radiations or Occipital Cortex: Typically respecting vertical or horizontal meridians (e.g., homonymous hemianopia).

sections.title: Cosmetic Options for Phthisis Bulbi with Enophthalmic Deep Sulcus
content: Prosthetic Shell (scleral shell): Worn over the existing phthisical globe.
Evisceration with Orbital Implant: Removes globe contents, replaces with implant to restore volume, then custom prosthetic eye.
Enucleation with Orbital Implant: Removes entire globe. Often necessary if phthisis is painful or risk of sympathetic ophthalmia.
Volume Augmentation: Injectable fillers (fat, hyaluronic acid) or implants (dermofat graft) into the anophthalmic socket or deep superior sulcus to improve appearance.

sections.title: Keratoconus: Vogt Striae and Management
content: Vogt Striae: Fine, vertical, whitish lines in the deep stroma/Descemet's membrane, parallel to the cone axis. Disappear with digital pressure.
Other signs: Munson's sign, Rizzuti's sign, Fleischer's ring, irregular astigmatism, corneal thinning, apical scarring.
Management of Keratoconus:
1. Optical Correction: Glasses, then rigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lenses (gold standard for visual rehabilitation). Scleral lenses for advanced cases or intolerance to RGP.
2. Corneal Collagen Cross-linking (CXL): To halt progression in early to moderate disease.
3. Intracorneal Ring Segments (ICRS/Intacs): To reduce corneal steepness and improve vision.
4. Keratoplasty: Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) or Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) for advanced cases with significant scarring or poor vision with contact lenses.

Management of Acute Hydrops: Cycloplegics, topical steroids, topical hyperosmotic agents (e.g., Muro 128), aqueous suppressants (if IOP elevated). May inject gas (SF6) into AC to tamponade Descemet's tear. Requires close follow-up.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) with Ahmed Valve
content: 1. Diagnosis: History of ischemic vascular disease (e.g., PDR, CRVO), rubeosis iridis, elevated IOP, gonioscopy shows neovascularization of angle.

2. Initial Management: Treat underlying cause (PRP, anti-VEGF injections - for rapid NVI regression and to reduce surgical inflammation), topical anti-glaucoma medications (avoid miotics), topical steroids.
3. Ahmed Valve Implantation: Often necessary for refractory NVG. It's a glaucoma drainage device that shunts aqueous from AC to a subconjunctival reservoir.
4. Post-Ahmed Valve: Continue anti-VEGF if rubeosis persists, topical steroids, aqueous suppressants until IOP stabilizes.

5. Next Eye NVG: If one eye has NVG, the other eye is at high risk. Close monitoring of the fellow eye (fundus exam, IOP, gonioscopy) is crucial. Prophylactic PRP may be considered if signs of severe ischemia.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Corneal Trauma with Anterior Synechiae
content: 1. Initial Assessment: Rule out ruptured globe (Seidel test), assess vision, IOP, AC depth, extent of synechiae.

2. Medical Management: Cycloplegics (e.g., atropine, cyclopentolate) to prevent further synechiae formation and reduce inflammation. Topical steroids (to reduce inflammation). Topical antibiotics (prophylactically if epithelial defect). IOP lowering agents if elevated.
3. Surgical Management: If synechiae are extensive, causing pupillary distortion, glaucoma, or corneal endothelial damage:
a. Synechiolysis: Surgical separation of adhesions (e.g., using a cyclodialysis spatula, fine instrument).
b. Reconstructive surgery: If iris damage is severe.
c. Glaucoma surgery: If secondary glaucoma persists despite synechiolysis and medical therapy.

sections.title: Investigation Workup: Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO)
content: Fundus Exam: Retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, dilated tortuous veins in a sector.
OCT: Macular edema, intraretinal fluid, subretinal fluid, epiretinal membrane, retinal thickening.
Fluorescein Angiography (FA): Shows non-perfusion (ischemia), macular edema, leakage from vessels, neovascularization.
Systemic Workup: Hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, glaucoma, hypercoagulable states (less common for BRVO than CRVO). Refer to internist.

sections.title: Follow-up for PDR with PRP Scars and Neovascularization (Stable)
content: Frequency: Typically every 3-6 months if stable (no active neovascularization, no significant vitreous hemorrhage, well-controlled macular edema).
Closer Follow-up: Every 1-3 months if any signs of progression (new NV, recurrent VH, worsening ME), or if systemic control is poor.
Monitoring: Fundus exam (check for new NV, re-evaluate PRP completeness), OCT (for ME, VMT), IOP (secondary glaucoma).

sections.title: Clinical Examination & OSCE Performance
content: Candidates MUST maintain composure: OSCE/VIVA is a 'mind game'—treat it as a professional discussion with a senior colleague.
Always perform a systematic examination: Anterior to posterior approach is standard.
Clinical pearls: When performing Hertel exophthalmometry on patients with unilateral proptosis/exotropia, ensure the eye takes fixation correctly.
Be systematic for Oculoplasty: Always assess Bell’s phenomenon, corneal sensation, and lid lag in ptosis cases.
The 'Wait' Factor: You are not required to answer every question to pass; demonstrate clinical reasoning and safe practice.

rows: PHPV, Retinoblastoma, Coats disease, Congenital Cataract
Bleb leak, Over-filtration, Choroidal detachment, Ciliary shutdown
Pupillary block, Suprachoroidal hemorrhage, Malignant glaucoma (aqueous misdirection)
IIH, Papilledema, Optic Neuritis, Infiltrative/Compressive lesions

sections.title: Oculoplastic & Orbital Emergencies
content: Orbital vs. Preseptal Cellulitis: MUST rule out orbital signs (proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, RAPD).
Facial Nerve Palsy: Assess for CP angle tumor (Schwannoma/Acoustic Neuroma) as a life-threatening cause.
Ruptured Globe: Explore posterior extent of tear; apply first suture at the limbus.
Bell's Phenomenon: Assess strictly before proceeding with aggressive ptosis surgery.

content.explanation: When evaluating Ptosis: P-Position of lid, T-Torsion (intorsion/extorsion), O-Ocular motility, S-Sensory (cornea), I-IOP, S-Systemic associations (Myasthenia: Edrophonium, Acetylcholine receptor antibodies).

sections.title: Posterior Segment: Clinical Protocol
content: Step 1: Media clarity and Disc assessment (look for pallor, cup/disc ratio, peripapillary atrophy).
Step 2: Macular evaluation (dull reflex, fibrous bands, hard exudates, or macular hole).
Step 3: Peripheral retina (look for endolaser marks, tears, or retinal detachment).
Step 4: Complications of Silicone Oil (Glaucoma, Band keratopathy, emulsification).

sections.title: Exam-Day Strategy: 'The Fellow Mindset'
content: Take a breath: Take 3–5 seconds before answering any scenario to frame your thoughts.
Precision: Keep answers concise, structured, and to the point. Avoid blabbering.
Eye Contact: Professionalism is key. Maintain eye contact and stay polite, even if challenged.
Resilience: Do not be preoccupied with a previous bad station. Treat every station as a fresh start.
Technique Mastery: Perform routine OPD-style examinations (Confrontation fields, Motility, Pupillary reflexes) with standard protocols.
Simulation: Practice with study partners to verbalize your clinical reasoning.

rows: Myasthenia Gravis, Aponeurotic, Horner's, 3rd Nerve Palsy (Aneurysm/Ischemic)
Bleb leak (Seidel+), Over-filtration, Choroidal detachment, Aqueous misdirection

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Red Flags
content: Sudden Ptosis + Intermittent Diplopia: Always rule out Myasthenia Gravis (Fatigability test).
Pupillary Abnormalities: Anisocoria must be checked in both light and dark. Rule out 3rd Nerve Palsy if associated with motor deficits.
Chemical Injury: The 'Time' factor is critical—lavage until pH neutral (7.0).
Orbital Cellulitis: Differentiate from Preseptal via proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and pupillary involvement. Immediate imaging required.
Endophthalmitis: Post-op 5 days of CF vision is a medical emergency.

sections.title: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): Clinical Case Analysis
sections.content: Case Presentation: A limited Anterior Segment photo showing normal lids and conjunctiva, a linear central horizontal scar in the cornea with multiple small vertical scars of old approximating sutures. The possible etiology here is a full thickness corneal laceration. Management: As it is a full thickness corneal scar, patient will need an Optical Penetrating Keratoplasty. In my opinion we should try glasses, CL (soft/rigid), if vision still poor we may go for PKP.

rows: 1. Scleral perforation (bridal/scleral ring placement). 2. Donor damage – Trephine reversal: causes hyperopia/wound closure difficulty. 3. Retained Descemet’s (double AC postop day 1 - needs re-grafting). 4. Iris-lens damage. 5. AC hemorrhage. 6. Suprachoroidal expulsive hemorrhage.

1. Wound leaks (Seidel +): BCL or resuturing. 2. Epithelial defect: Lubricants, antibiotics, BCL, tarsorrhaphy, reduce steroids. 3. Filamentary keratitis. 4. Suture issues: Infection, Immune infiltrates (recipient side, treat with steroids/removal), Endophthalmitis, Kaye dots (non-pathologic donor side dots). 5. Glaucoma. 6. Anterior synechiae. 7. Pupillary block. 8. Urrets-Zavalia pupil (irregular pupil, iris atrophy, ectropion uvea). 9. Subcapsular opacities.
1. Graft failure: Rejection, poor donor quality, trauma, flat AC, HSV reactivation. 2. Post-operative astigmatism.

sections.title: Immunologic Graft Rejection: Differential Patterns
content: Epithelial Rejection: Elevated line staining with fluorescein; responds to topical steroids.
Subepithelial Infiltrates: Immune reaction in donor tissue ONLY; no conjunctivitis; responds to steroids.
Endothelial Rejection (Khodadoust line): KPs at leading edge, hazy stroma, DM folds. Does not cross graft-host junction. Treat with intensive topical/IV steroids.
Diffuse Endothelial Rejection: Scattered KPs limited to donor endothelium + AC reaction. Treat with intensive steroids.

branches: Vascular (ROP, OIS, Coats, PDR, Sickle Cell)
Congenital (PHPV, Peters' Anomaly Type 2, Norrie, FEVR)

sections.title: Pre-PKP Assessment & Prognosis
content: History: Past BCVA, Age of Insult, Ocular Alignment, Projection of rays.
Lids & Surface: Blepharitis, Ectropion, Entropion, Trichiasis, Dry eye (TBUT/Schirmer), Inflammation.
Cornea & AC: Scar size/depth, Vascularization, PAC, lens status, vitreous presence.
Posterior: IOP measurement, DFE.
Investigations: ASOCT, UBM.
Favorable Prognosis: Keratoconus, localized scars, dystrophies.

sections.title: High Risk Factors for Graft Rejection
Phthisis Bulbi: Pathology & Identification
content: Identification: End-stage response to injury, shrunk, non-functional eye.
Characteristic Changes: Small, soft, collapsed globe; Opaque/thickened cornea.
Internal Changes: Iris neovascularization, cataract, cyclitic membrane, ciliochoroidal/retinal detachment.
Late Stage: Osseous metaplasia (intraocular bone).
Mechanism: Hypotony, deranged blood-ocular barrier, cytokines/angiogenic factors.
Management: Alleviating pain; Enucleation/Evisceration + Prosthesis (No vision restoration).

rows: 1. Primary Intraocular Malignancy (RB, Melanoma). 2. Painful Blind Eye (Glaucoma). 3. Severe Trauma (Sympathetic Ophthalmia risk). 4. Unsightly blind eye. 5. Phthisis/Microphthalmia. 6. Endophthalmitis/Panophthalmitis.

Non-integrated: Silicone/Acrylic spheres (may migrate/extrude). Integrated: Hydroxyapatite, Porous polyethylene (Medpor), Bioceramic, Baseball, Dermis fat graft. Historical: Arruga (exposed integrated).

sections.title: Post-Enucleation Socket Syndrome (PESS)
content: Clinical Signs: Deep upper lid sulcus, Ptosis, Enophthalmos (confirm with Hertel/Birds-eye view).
Prosthesis Signs: Posterior displacement, superior rotation, backward tilting, ectropion.
Lid/Socket: Horizontal laxity, forniceal shortening, Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis (GPC) from friction.
Diagnosis: Confirmed by inspection of motility and examination of conjunctiva/implant under prosthesis.

sections.title: Stepwise Management of PESS
content: Step 1: Treat infection with topical antibiotics and irrigation.
Step 2: Address Orbital Volume. Replace with larger implant or Dermis Fat Graft (DFG).
Step 3: Manage Exposure/Extrusion. Small: Direct closure. Large: Buccal mucosa patch. Very large: DFG.
Step 4: Correct Conjunctival Deficiency with transplant (Buccal/Conjunctival).
Step 5: Correct Lid Abnormalities (Entropion, Ectropion, Ptosis) and Prosthetic fitting.

rows: Fornix-forming sutures, Weiss procedure for entropion
Full-thickness Mucous Membrane Graft (MMG) or Amniotic Membrane
Secondary orbital implant or Dermis Fat Graft (DFG)

sections.title: Prosthesis & Socket Red Flags
content: Implant Exposure or Extrusion (Risk increased by irradiation, trauma, infection)
Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis (GPC) from friction
Contracture of fornices (Conjunctival deficiency)
Pyogenic granuloma formation (associated with integrated motility pegs)
Dermis Fat Graft (DFG) complications: Necrosis, fat atrophy, deep cysts, donor site dehiscence
Sympathetic Ophthalmia risk in traumatized fellow eye

sections.title: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK) Diagnostics
sections.content: Description: Slit lamp anterior segment coloured photo showing peripheral thinning and ulceration extending from 1 to 5 o'clock with limbal injection, with scleral thinning, I can see scleral hue otherwise rest of cornea clear. There is no kps. AC looks formed and hence no perforation, however I should assess the depth using focal slit beam. Patient is phakic, upper and lower lid show MGD. All of this picture consistent with peripheral ulcerative keratitis.

branches: Systemic: RA, SLE, Wegener’s, PAN, Relapsing Polychondritis, Sarcoidosis, Leukemia
Non-Infective: Mooren’s, Terrien’s, Marginal keratitis, Pellucid, Rosacea, Exposure, Neurotrophic, Trauma

sections.title: PUK Management Strategy
content: 1. Collaboration with rheumatologist for systemic immunosuppression
2. Systemic steroids (pulsed IV for acute phase)
3. Preservative-free topical lubricants
4. Prophylactic topical antibiotics (if epithelial defect)
5. Oral tetracycline (Doxycycline 100mg) for anti-collagenase effect
6. Avoid topical steroids (except possibly in Relapsing Polychondritis)
7. Surgical: Conjunctival excision or tectonic keratoplasty

rows: GAG deposits, stains with colloidal iron
Cone protrusion, Fleischer ring, Vogt striae

content: Seidel sign positive: Indicates perforation
C-ANCA positive: Suggests Wegener’s granulomatosis (requires cyclophosphamide)
Graft rejection signs in post-PKP cases
Acute hydrops: Requires cycloplegics, aqueous suppressants, and NaCL 5% ointment

sections.title: Keratoconus Management (Dresden Protocol)
content: 1. Topical anaesthesia application.
2. Central 9 mm corneal epithelium removal.
3. 0.1% riboflavin administration every 1–5 min for 30 min.
4. UVA light exposure (3 mW/cm2, 365 nm) for 30 min (Total energy: 5.4 J/cm2).

content.explanation: Diagnostic indices for Keratoconus: Central K > 47.2D, I-S value > 1.2, Sim-K > 1.5D, SRAX > 21°.

sections.title: Pentacam Interpretation (Advanced Keratoconus)
content: K-Max front > 47.2D (Severe: >58D)
Thinnest location < 470 microns (Severe: <433 microns)
Elevation maps: Abnormal tongue shape, >15-20 micron deviation
ART-Max: Significantly low (<400 microns)
CTSP: Red line shows steep downward slope before 6mm zone

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: The Fungal Index
sections.content: A 30-year-old presents to the clinic with complaints of decreased vision and mild pain in his right eye. He vaguely recalls being hit in the right eye with a tree branch while pruning his garden around 3 weeks back. He had mild discomfort in his eye since then and his vision has been gradually worsening. Clinical signs include: pale whitish paracentral infiltration involving the visual axis, fuzzy margins, and surrounding wispy satellite lesions. A pale whitish hypopyon filling approximately one-fifth of the Anterior Chamber. Severe conjunctival congestion. (Note: Fungal hypopyon typically features a convex upper border, low mobility with head posture, and yellow color, whereas bacterial hypopyon is concave, mobile, and whitish.)

rows: Vegetative trauma, fuzzy margins, satellite lesions, slow course.
Rapid onset, concave hypopyon, purulent discharge.
Pain out of proportion, ring infiltrate, neural involvement.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: Direct Microscopy: KOH preparation for rapid evaluation.
Staining: Gram, Giemsa, PAS, Calcofluor white, Methenamine Silver, ZN stain (if Mycobacterial suspected).
Culture Media: Blood agar (General), Chocolate agar (Fastidious), Sabouraud dextrose agar (Fungi), Non-nutrient agar with E. coli (Acanthamoeba).
Advanced: PCR analysis, Corneal biopsy, Anterior chamber tap, In vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM).

sections.title: Evidence-Based Studies (MUTT)
content: MUTT 1: Topical Natamycin 5% vs. Voriconazole 1%. Natamycin is superior for filamentous fungi.

sections.title: Phthisis Bulbi: Identification & Pathogenesis
sections.content:
Identification: End-stage ocular response to severe eye injury or disease damage; characterized by a shrunk and non-functional eye.

Pathological Changes: Small, soft, and collapsed eye, opaque and thickened cornea, neovascularization of the iris, cataract, cyclitic membrane, ciliochoroidal detachment, and retinal detachment. In late stages: intraocular calcifications (osseus metaplasia: intraocular bone). Occurs due to hypotony, deranged blood–ocular barrier, and release of cytokines and angiogenic factors.

sections.title: Enucleation: Indications & Complications

Post-Enucleation Complications: Post-enucleation socket syndrome (PESS), Orbital implant exposure/extrusion/displacement, Oversized implant, Orbital Hematoma, Conjunctival prolapse, Infection/Pyogenic granuloma, Socket/fornix contracture, Dissemination of intraocular neoplasm, Giant Papillary conjunctivitis.

Management: 1. Treat infection (antibiotics/irrigation). 2. Treat volume/implant issues (Dermal fat graft/larger implant). 3. Correct conjunctival deficiency (mucosa transplant). 4. Correct lid abnormalities (entropion/ectropion/ptosis). 5. Adjust prosthetic.

sections.title: Management Strategy for Malignant Eyelid Lesions
content: Diagnostic Workup: Confirmatory incisional biopsy with adequate margin for histopathology.
Primary Treatment: Surgical excision is first-line.
Alternative Treatments: Radiation therapy is the second-best treatment. Topical imiquimod and topical/injectable interferon for non-surgical elderly patients.
Systemic/Regional Workup: Referral to oncologist/internist. SCC/SGC/Melanoma: CT/MRI of brain/orbit (check infiltration of lacrimal gland or perineural invasion). Check sentinel lymph nodes.
Surgical Clearance: Conventional paraffin-embedded, standard frozen section, or Mohs micrographic surgery (lowest recurrence 1%).
Margins: Small BCC (2-4 mm). Large BCC, SCC, SGC, Melanoma (5 mm wide margins).

Imaging: CT orbits/MRI with contrast for infraorbital/intracranial spread in SCC, SGC, and malignant melanoma. For BCC, only if medial canthal lesion.
Medial Canthal BCC: Higher risk of lacrimal sac/orbital involvement. If extended: Radiotherapy or Hedgehog pathway inhibitors (vismodegib).

sections.content: Exotropia is a binocular vision anomaly where the visual axes diverge. Prevalence is roughly 1-2% of the general population. Early surgery is preferred in patients losing stereopsis.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular biometry is the measurement of specific anatomical dimensions of the eye, primarily axial length (AL), keratometry (K), anterior chamber depth (ACD), and lens thickness (LT), for the calculation of intraocular lens (IOL) power. This ensures precise refractive outcomes post-cataract surgery. Two main methods dominate: A-scan ultrasonography and Optical Biometry.

sections.title: 2. A-scan Ultrasonography: Fundamentals
sections.content: A-scan uses high-frequency sound waves (typically 10-12 MHz) generated by a piezoelectric crystal to measure ocular structures. Sound waves travel through the eye, reflecting off tissue interfaces. The time taken for echoes to return is converted into distance using a known speed of sound (e.g., 1532 m/s for phakic eye, 1550 m/s for general ocular tissue, 1641 m/s for silicone oil). It's a contact method, either direct corneal contact or immersion.

sections.title: 3. Optical Biometry: Fundamentals
sections.content: Optical biometry employs light, typically infrared, to measure ocular distances. It relies on interferometry, specifically Partial Coherence Interferometry (PCI) or Optical Low Coherence Reflectometry (OLCR), to achieve sub-micron precision. Light is emitted, reflected off ocular surfaces, and recombination creates interference patterns used to calculate distances. It's a non-contact method.

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup (Biometry Protocol)
content: **A. A-scan Protocol (Immersion)**
1. **Anesthesia**: Topical anesthetic (e.g., proparacaine 0.5%) applied.
2. **Coupling**: Eye cup (e.g., Prager shell, Staar surgical shell) filled with saline/methylcellulose and placed on globe.
3. **Probe Placement**: Transducer immersed in saline, aligned coaxially with visual axis, avoiding corneal contact.
4. **Image Acquisition**: Multiple measurements (e.g., 5-10) taken, ensuring high spike amplitude for retina and clear, steep spikes for lens capsules.
5. **Validation**: Waveform evaluated for on-axis alignment (steep, high spikes for cornea, anterior & posterior lens, retina), average AL, and standard deviation.
**B. Optical Biometry Protocol (e.g., IOLMaster 700)**
1. **Patient Positioning**: Chin on chin rest, forehead against headrest.
2. **Fixation**: Patient instructed to fixate on internal target. Auto-alignment system engages.
3. **Measurement**: Device automatically measures AL, K (corneal curvature), ACD, LT, WTW, pupil diameter, and often 'Total Keratometry' (TK) using swept-source OCT for the posterior cornea.

4. **Quality Assessment**: Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and reliability scores are evaluated. Repeat measurements until acceptable quality achieved (e.g., 5-10 measurements with low standard deviation <0.02 mm for AL).
5. **Data Export**: Data automatically populated into IOL calculation formulae.

Poor patient fixation → off-axis measurement. Media opacities (dense cataract, PCO, vit heme) → signal loss, no measurement.
Manual K readings subject to operator error and poor tear film. Peripheral measurements only.
Dry eye or corneal surface irregularities → unreliable K readings. Device may struggle with irregular astigmatism.
Misidentification of corneal or lens peaks. Relatively less accurate.
Often measured by OCT-based methods, but severe corneal edema or irregularity can interfere.
Difficult to accurately delineate anterior/posterior lens surfaces, especially in dense cataracts. Limited clinical utility.
Measured directly by some optical biometers (e.g., Lenstar, IOLMaster 700) using OCT, improving formula accuracy (e.g., Haigis).

2nd Gen (Hoffer Q, Holladay 1, SRK/T) - Theoretical, 2-variable (AL, K)
3rd Gen (Haigis, Holladay 2, SRK/T) - Theoretical, 3-variable (AL, K, ACD/LT), **Enhanced by Optical Biometry**
4th Gen (Barrett Universal II, Kane, EVO) - Ray-tracing, AI-enhanced, posterior corneal astigmatism, **Leverage Optical Biometry for high precision**
Post-Refractive Surgery Formulae (Barrett True-K, Haigis-L, Shammas, Masket) - Compensate for altered K/AL relationship

sections.title: 10. Advantages of Optical Biometry (Key Differences)
content: **Non-Contact**: Hygienic, comfortable for patient, reduces risk of corneal abrasion/infection.
**Superior Accuracy & Precision**: Sub-micron resolution for AL (vs. 0.1 mm for A-scan), leading to more predictable refractive outcomes.
**Reduced Operator Dependence**: Automated alignment and measurement minimizes inter-operator variability seen with A-scan.
**Simultaneous Multiple Parameters**: Measures AL, K, ACD, LT, WTW in a single scan, streamlining workflow.
**Integrated Advanced Formulae**: Optimized for modern formulae (e.g., Barrett, Kane, Haigis) directly within the software.
**Objective Measurement**: Less subjective interpretation compared to A-scan spike identification.
**Faster Acquisition**: Quicker measurement time, improving patient flow.
**Better for Toric IOLs**: Precise K readings and often integrated axis marking guidance.
**Total Keratometry (TK)**: Newer SS-OCT biometers measure anterior and posterior corneal curvature for more accurate total K.

sections.title: 11. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Complication**: Post-operative refractive surprise (PORS) due to inaccurate biometry, leading to dissatisfaction, need for refractive enhancement, or IOL exchange.

**Prognosis**: With accurate biometry (especially optical) and appropriate formula selection, >90% of patients achieve refraction within ±0.5 D of target. Optical biometry has significantly improved predictability of outcomes compared to older A-scan methods.

sections.title: 12. Red Flags / Emergency Signs in Biometry
content: **Inter-eye AL difference >0.3 mm** without clear anatomical explanation (e.g., microphthalmia, unilateral trauma).
**Significant discrepancy between A-scan and Optical Biometry** (e.g., AL difference >0.15 mm) in the same eye – requires re-evaluation and careful review of both scans.
**Low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)** or poor quality indicators on optical biometry (e.g., IOLMaster Signal-to-Noise Ratio <2.0).
**Erratic or widely varying K readings** (e.g., difference >0.5 D between readings or significant astigmatism inconsistent with topography).
**Missing key data points** required by chosen IOL formula (e.g., ACD, LT, WTW).

content.explanation:
P: Precision (Sub-micron)
R: Reduced operator variability
I: Integrated formulae
S: Speedy & Simultaneous (multiple params)
M: Multi-modal (AL, K, ACD, LT, WTW)
S: Sterile (Non-contact)

sections.title: 14. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Immersion A-scan > Contact A-scan** for accuracy in cases where optical biometry fails.
Always **cross-reference biometry results** with clinical findings (e.g., corneal topography, anterior segment OCT, patient history).
For **post-refractive surgery eyes**, always use specific formulae (e.g., Barrett True-K, Haigis-L) and consider using average of multiple K-sources if available.
**Be cautious with dense PCO** as it can lead to inaccurate optical biometry; consider A-scan or repeat measurement after YAG capsulotomy.
For **toric IOLs**, precise K readings and axis of astigmatism are critical; optical biometry is superior.

sections.title: 15. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content:
**Swept-Source OCT (SS-OCT) Biometry**: Devices like the IOLMaster 700 have revolutionized biometry. They utilize a longer wavelength (1050 nm) enabling deeper penetration through denser cataracts, making optical biometry feasible in more challenging cases. SS-OCT also provides 'Total Keratometry' (TK), which measures both anterior and posterior corneal surfaces directly, eliminating assumptions about the posterior cornea and significantly improving toric IOL and post-refractive surgery outcomes. 

**AI-based IOL Formulae**: Formulas like the Kane and PEARL-D use artificial intelligence and large datasets to predict IOL power with unprecedented accuracy, further leveraging the precise data provided by optical biometry. These models often consider more input parameters and complex interactions than traditional theoretical formulas. 

**Integration with Surgical Planning Systems**: Optical biometers increasingly integrate with surgical planning software (e.g., Verion, Callisto eye) for seamless data transfer, digital marking for toric IOLs, and intraoperative guidance, minimizing transcription errors and improving surgical efficiency.

sections.title: 16. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Pediatric Cataracts**: Optical biometry is often challenging due to lack of cooperation. A-scan, particularly immersion A-scan under general anesthesia, is frequently necessary. Growth factor considerations are crucial for IOL power calculation in growing eyes.

**Dense Media Opacities**: If optical biometry fails due to dense cataracts or vitreal opacities, an immersion A-scan is the essential fallback. Adjusting sound velocities for silicone oil-filled eyes is critical.
**Post-Vitrectomy Eyes**: While some optical biometers can work, especially SS-OCT, A-scan may be necessary due to residual vitreous or gas/oil presence, with appropriate velocity adjustments.
**Amblyopia**: Accurate biometry is even more critical in amblyogenic cataracts to ensure clear visual axis and facilitate visual rehabilitation.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Scleromalacia perforans is a rare, severe, painless form of scleritis characterized by necrotizing scleral thinning without overt inflammation. It is pathognomonic for long-standing, seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). The underlying mechanism involves occlusive vasculitis of the episcleral/scleral vessels leading to tissue infarction and sequestration.

sections.title: 3. Clinical Features & Exam Findings
content: Painless "sequestration" of scleral tissue.
Absence of injection (white eye).
Visible underlying uveal tissue (dark brown/blue).
Intact overlying conjunctiva until rupture.
Thinning progressing to actual staphyloma formation.

sections.title: 4. Red Flags: Impending Rupture
content: Increase in size of the necrotic plaque.
Development of a localized staphyloma.
A sudden drop in intraocular pressure (IOP) suggesting occult leak.
New onset of pain (indicates transition to active inflammatory scleritis).
Presence of overlying conjunctival epithelial defect.

content.explanation: S: Systemic Control (DMARDs/Biologics), T: Tissue Support (Grafts), A: Avoid Steroid Drops (can worsen melt), B: Biologics (Rituximab/Infliximab).

sections.title: 6. Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Serology (RF, Anti-CCP, ANA, ANCA, ESR/CRP).
Step 2: Slit-lamp exam with scleral transillumination.
Step 3: B-scan Ultrasound to assess posterior staphyloma size.
Step 4: OCT (Anterior Segment) to measure exact scleral thickness.
Step 5: Rheumatology consult for immediate systemic escalation.

sections.title: 7. Surgical Intervention Steps
content: 1. Debridement: Remove necrotic tissue (if loose/sequestrated).
2. Patch Grafting: Use scleral patch graft (donor sclera or pericardium).
3. Tectonic Support: Suture graft using 8-0 or 9-0 Vicryl/Nylon.
4. Conjunctival Flap: Cover the area with a vascularized conjunctival pedicle flap to promote healing.
5. Tissue Glue: Use Histoacryl (Cyanoacrylate) only for micro-perforations.

rows: Blue sclera is diffuse, not patchy

sections.title: 9. Key Clinical Pearls
content: NEVER perform cataract surgery in an eye with active scleromalacia; wait for systemic stability.
Topical corticosteroids are generally CONTRAINDICATED as they inhibit collagen synthesis and exacerbate scleral melting.
The risk of globe perforation is highest during minor eye rubbing or sudden IOP spikes.
Rituximab (anti-CD20) is currently the gold-standard systemic therapy for refractory RA-associated scleromalacia.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD) is a chronic, progressive disease of the macula characterized by the presence of drusen and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) abnormalities. It is classified into 'Dry' (non-exudative), involving geographic atrophy (GA), and 'Wet' (exudative/neovascular), characterized by Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV). It remains the primary cause of legal blindness in individuals aged 65 and older in industrialized nations.

rows: Multiple small drusen, few intermediate (63-124μm), or RPE changes
At least one large drusen (>125μm), extensive intermediate drusen, or non-central GA
Central GA or Neovascular AMD in one eye

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Metamorphopsia (distortion on Amsler Grid)
Central Scotoma (relative or absolute)
Decreased Contrast Sensitivity
Slow Dark Adaptation (early sign)
Micropsia/Macropsia in exudative stages
Painless, progressive decline in visual acuity

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Hard Drusen: Small, yellow, well-defined (hyaline deposits)
Soft Drusen: Large, fuzzy-edged (signify RPE detachment risk)
RPE Hyper/Hypopigmentation (mottling)
Geographic Atrophy: Sharply demarcated areas of RPE loss showing choroidal vessels
Subretinal fluid, hemorrhage, or lipid exudation (CNV)
Disciform Scar: End-stage subretinal fibrosis

rows: Active exudation, often worse prognosis than SRF
Sign of active CNV; better tolerated than IRF
High risk of RPE tear if serous
Fibrin, blood, or CNV; correlates with poor VA
Shallow elevation of RPE from Bruch's
Vitelliform lesion, abnormal EOG, normal ERG
Yellow-orange pigment at macula, younger onset
High myopia, lacquer cracks, smaller CNV

sections.title: Management: Dry AMD & GA
content: 1. Smoking Cessation (Critical step)
2. AREDS2 Supplementation (for Category 3 or 4)
3. Home Monitoring: Amsler Grid or ForeseeHome PHP
4. Low Vision Rehabilitation: For advanced GA
5. Complement Inhibitors: Pegcetacoplan or Avacincaptad pegol (IVT injections)

sections.title: Management: Wet AMD (Anti-VEGF)
content: 1. Diagnosis: Confirm activity via OCT/FFA/OCTA
2. Loading Phase: 3-5 Monthly injections
3. Maintenance: Treat-and-Extend (T&E) or Pro-re-nata (PRN)
4. Monitoring: Monthly or extended intervals with OCT
5. Switching: Consider agent change if poor response

rows: Fab fragment, binds all VEGF-A isoforms

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS
content: Sudden onset of Metamorphopsia (Signifies fluid/CNV conversion)
Submacular Hemorrhage (Requires urgent pneumatic displacement or TPA)
RPE Tear (Sudden vision drop, usually after IVT in large serous PED)
Endophthalmitis post-injection (Pain, hypopyon, rapid vision loss)
Intraocular Inflammation (IOI) / Vasculitis (Especially associated with Brolucizumab)

content.explanation: C (500mg), E (400 IU), Zinc (80mg), Lutein (10mg), Zeaxanthin (2mg). Copper (2mg) is added to prevent zinc-induced anemia.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Trials
content: MARINA/ANCHOR: Established Ranibizumab superiority over PDT/Sham.
CATT: Bevacizumab is non-inferior to Ranibizumab.
AREDS/AREDS2: Antioxidants reduce risk of progression by 25%.
VIEW 1/2: Aflibercept q8w is non-inferior to Ranibizumab q4w.
GATHER/OAKS: New treatments for GA (geographic atrophy).

sections.title: Advanced Surgical & Laser Interventions
content: Photodynamic Therapy (PDT): Cold laser with Verteporfin; mainly for PCV now.
Submacular Surgery: Clot displacement with gas + TPA.
Port Delivery System (Susvimo): Permanent refillable implant for Ranibizumab.
Telescopic Implants (Samsara): For end-stage bilateral GA/Disciform scars.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: Classic CNV (Type 2) shows early bright lacy hyperfluorescence on FFA.
Occult CNV (Type 1) shows late stippled leakage.
RAP (Type 3) often starts with intraretinal hemorrhages and edema.
PCV (Type 4) is more common in Asian populations; use ICG to see polyps.
Geographic Atrophy expansion is faster in 'hyperautofluorescent' borders on FAF.

Management requires immediate identification of risk factors, grading of severity, and aggressive, broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy to prevent perforation and permanent scarring.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Microbial (bacterial) keratitis is a serious infection of the corneal stroma. Unlike viral or sterile keratitis, it often presents with an epithelial defect overlying a dense, necrotic stromal infiltrate, often accompanied by significant anterior chamber inflammation (hypopyon). Most bacteria (except N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis, C. diphtheriae, and H. influenzae) require a breach in the corneal epithelium to initiate infection.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Cascade of Destruction
content: 1. Epithelial Breach: Trauma or contact lens-induced hypoxia creates an entry point.
2. Adherence: Bacteria utilize fimbriae or pili to bind to the exposed corneal stroma/extracellular matrix.
3. Invasion & Multiplication: Organisms replicate and release exotoxins (e.g., Exotoxin A in Pseudomonas).
4. Host Response: Neutrophil infiltration (chemotaxis) releases matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).
5. Stromal Melting: Combination of bacterial toxins and host enzymes leads to keratomalacia (liquefactive necrosis).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Scraping Protocol
content: 1. Topical Anesthesia: Proparacaine is preferred (Benoxinate may be more bacteriostatic).
2. Sample Collection: Use a Kimura spatula, 25G needle, or sterile blade to scrape the leading edge and base.
3. C-Streaks: Transfer directly to agar plates using 'C-streaks' for semi-quantitative assessment.
4. Slide Prep: Gram and Giemsa/Diff-Quik stains for immediate visualization.
5. Culture: Blood Agar (aerobes), Chocolate Agar (fastidious), Sabouraud (fungi), Thioglycollate (anaerobes).

sections.title: Primary Medical Management
content: Loading Dose: 1 drop every 5–15 minutes for the first hour, then every 30–60 minutes around the clock.
Monotherapy (Mild/Mod): 4th Generation Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin 0.5%, Gatifloxacin 0.5%, Besifloxacin 0.6%).
Duo-therapy (Severe/Central): Fortified Tobramycin (14 mg/mL) AND Fortified Vancomycin (25-50 mg/mL).
Cycloplegia: Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1% TID to reduce ciliary spasm and prevent synechiae.
Systemic Rx: Consider if scleral involvement (e.g., Ciprofloxacin 500mg BID) or N. gonorrhoeae (Ceftriaxone 1g IM/IV).

sections.title: Steroid Use: The SCUT Trial (2011)
sections.content: The Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT) found no significant difference in 3-month visual outcomes between topical corticosteroids and placebo. However, a subgroup analysis showed benefit in vision for central, deep, and severe ulcers (excluding Nocardia). RULE: Start steroids only AFTER 48-72 hours of clinical improvement and negative cultures, and NEVER if fungus or Acanthamoeba is suspected.

branches: Marginal Keratitis (Sterile, lucid interval at limbus)

sections.title: CRITICAL: Red Flags for Worsening
content: Enlarging Infiltrate or Epithelial Defect despite 48h therapy.
Progressive Stromal Thinning (Descemetocele or Perforation).
Scleral involvement (Scleritis/Scleral melting).
Rise in Intraocular Pressure (Secondary Glaucoma).
Signs of Endophthalmitis (hypopyon increase, vitreous cells, loss of red reflex).

content.explanation: P: Pain (is it increasing?); E: Epithelial defect size; D: Discharge (purulent?); A: Anterior chamber reaction/hypopyon; L: Location and Size of infiltrate.

sections.title: Surgical Interventions
content: Cyanoacrylate Tissue Adhesive: For small perforations (<2mm) or impending perforation.
Tectonic Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): For large perforations or uncontrolled infection.
Amniotic Membrane Graft (AMG): Promotes re-epithelialization in neurotrophic cases.
PACK-CXL: Photoactivated Chromophore for Keratitis (Cross-linking) as adjuvant therapy for resistant organisms.

rows: Enriched with Factor V and X
Low pH, contains antibiotics to inhibit bacteria

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: Contact lens wearers with ulcers have Pseudomonas until proven otherwise.
Wessely Ring: An immune ring (antigen-antibody complex) often seen in Gram-negative infections.
Fortified drops are generally stable for 7-14 days if refrigerated.
Never use a 'taper' on antibiotics until the infection is sterilized; maintain 'therapeutic' levels.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Corneal Scarring/Leucoma (Permanent vision loss if central).
Irregular Astigmatism (Secondary to scarring).
Anterior Synechiae and Secondary Glaucoma.
Infectious Endophthalmitis (Rare unless perforation occurs).
Phthisis Bulbi (In severe, untreated cases).
