sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) is a premotor ocular motility disorder resulting from a lesion in the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) in the pons or midbrain. The MLF is a heavily myelinated pathway that coordinates conjugate horizontal gaze by connecting the abducens nucleus (VI) on one side to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus of the oculomotor nerve (III). The hallmark is an adduction deficit on the ipsilateral side of the lesion during horizontal version, accompanied by dissociated nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye.

sections.title: The MLF Circuitry (Pathophysiology)
content: 1. Horizontal Gaze Command: Initiated in the Frontal Eye Fields (FEF) or Superior Colliculus.
2. PPRF Activation: The Parapontine Reticular Formation (PPRF) triggers the ipsilateral Abducens (VI) Nucleus.
3. VI Nucleus Split: Some neurons exit as the VI Nerve to the Lateral Rectus; others (interneurons) cross the midline.
4. MLF Ascent: These interneurons travel upward via the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF).
5. III Nucleus Synapse: The MLF fibers reach the contralateral Oculomotor (III) Nucleus (Medial Rectus subnucleus).
6. Medial Rectus Contraction: Resulting in coordinated adduction synchronous with the other eye's abduction.

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Ipsilateral Adduction Deficit: Ranges from total paralysis to a mild 'adduction lag' (slower saccades).
Contralateral Abducting Nystagmus: Fast phase directed away from the lesion; thought to be Hering's Law compensation for weak adduction.
Diplopia: Horizontal diplopia, most pronounced when looking away from the side of the lesion.
Skew Deviation: Often present; the eye on the side of the lesion is typically hypertropic.
Preserved Convergence: Usually maintained if the lesion is in the pons (Posterior INO).

rows: Adduction deficit in one eye; abduction nystagmus in the other.
Adduction deficit in BOTH eyes; large exotropia (sometimes).
Wall-Eyed Bilateral INO: Both eyes are exotropic in primary position.
Only movement possible is abduction of one eye; all other horizontal movements gone.
MLF + PPRF (or VI Nucleus) on one side
C-INO (Anterior/Midbrain) lacks convergence; P-INO (Posterior/Pons) has convergence.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Neuro-Ophthalmic Exam: Confirm adduction lag via OKN tape or saccadic assessment.
2. MRI Brain + Brainstem: T2, FLAIR, and DWI sequences to identify MS plaques or small infarcts.
3. Lab Testing: If MS is suspected, consider CSF (Oligoclonal bands) and Serum (Neuromyelitis Optica IgG).
4. Rule out MG: Ice pack test, Tensilon (historical), or Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies.
5. Syphilis/Lyme Serology: In atypical or chronic cases.

sections.title: One-and-a-Half Syndrome
sections.content: A specific variant where the lesion involves the PPRF (or VI nucleus) AND the ipsilateral MLF. This results in an absolute paralysis of all horizontal movements in the ipsilateral eye and an adduction deficit in the contralateral eye. The ONLY preserved horizontal movement is the abduction of the contralateral eye (often with nystagmus). This is the 'Half' that remains.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Sudden onset INO with headache (Suspect Stroke/Dissection)
Associated Hemiparesis or Aphasia
Progressive worsening (Suspect Glioma or Tumor)
Presence of systemic signs of vasculitis or SLE
Bilateral INO in an older patient (Basilar Artery Ischemia)

content.explanation:
L: Left Medial Rectus (MR) doesn't move. 
I: Ipsilateral to the lesion side. 
N: Nystagmus in the opposite (Right) eye during abduction. 
O: Often MS (Young) or Stroke (Old).

sections.title: Management & Treatment
content: Treat Underlying Cause: Corticosteroids for MS flares; antiplatelets/risk factor control for stroke.
Diplopia Management: Fresnel Prisms (temporary) or patching one eye (alternate eyes to prevent suppression).
Observation: Ischemic INO often resolves spontaneously within 3-6 months.
Botulinum Toxin: Injection of the antagonist Lateral Rectus for transient relief of exotropia.
Surgical Options: If stable for >12 months, Medial Rectus resection or transposition procedures may be considered.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: The OKN Tape Trick: If adduction looks normal, use an OKN tape. The adduction saccades in INO will look 'slower' than the abduction saccades.
C-INO vs P-INO: If convergence is lost, the lesion is in the Midbrain (Ciliary/Anterior). If preserved, it's in the Pons (Posterior).
Skew Deviation: The eye on the side of the MLF lesion is usually the higher one (Hypertropic).
MS is the most common cause of BILATERAL INO in adults under 50.

sections.title: Landmark Concept: Hering's Law in INO
sections.content: Why the abducting nystagmus? According to Hering's Law of Equal Innervation, when the brain sends a strong signal to the weak adductor (to overcome the MLF block), an equal signal is sent to its yoked muscle (the contralateral lateral rectus). This results in 'overshoot' and compensatory nystagmus in the abducting eye.

title: Monofixation Syndrome: The Subnormal Binocularity Guide
summary: Monofixation Syndrome (MFS) is a state of subnormal binocular vision characterized by a central suppression scotoma in one eye despite peripheral fusion. Often presenting as a 'stable' endpoint of strabismus surgery, it requires precise diagnostic testing to differentiate from bifoveal fixation.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Monofixation Syndrome (MFS), first described by Marshall Parks in 1969, is a condition where binocularity exists without bifoveal fixation. It is characterized by a small-angle strabismus (usually <8-10 prism diopters), a central suppression scotoma (1° to 3°) in the non-fixing eye, and preserved peripheral fusion. It serves as a clinically stable 'functional cure' in many strabismus cases.

rows: Post-operative result of infantile esotropia repair
Blurred foveal image leads to suppression

sections.title: The 4-Diopter Base-Out Prism Test
content: Step 1: Patient fixates on a distant target.
Step 2: Place a 4PD Base-Out prism over the suspected monofixating eye.
Step 3: Observe for an 'adjustment' movement. In MFS, the eye will NOT move because the image remains within the central scotoma.
Step 4: Place prism over the FIXING eye; both eyes will shift (Version), but the monofixating eye will not perform a secondary 'vergence' movement.

rows: Target image falls entirely within the small central scotoma

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Stereopsis: Gross only (60 to 3000 arcsec); never fine (<40 arcsec).
Cover Test: May show a small manifest tropia (Microtropia) or only a phoria (Monofixation Phoria).
Visual Acuity: Usually 20/20 to 20/50 in the non-dominant eye (mild amblyopia).
Bagolini Lenses: Symmetrical cross but with a central gap in one line (scotoma).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & High-Yield Facts
content: MFS is the 'ideal' outcome for infantile esotropia surgery (Stability).
Patients rarely complain of diplopia due to the suppression scotoma.
The scotoma size is typically 1 to 3 degrees (2 to 6 prism diopters).
If stereopsis is better than 40 arc-seconds, MFS is excluded.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Correct Refractive Error: Full cycloplegic refraction.
2. Amblyopia Therapy: Patching or Atropine if acuity is asymmetric.
3. Observe Stability: Monitor for increases in deviation size.
4. Surgery: NOT indicated for the micro-angle; only if the latent component breaks down into a large manifest tropia.

sections.title: Red Flags: When it's NOT MFS
content: Presence of Fine Stereopsis (<40 arcsec)
Diplopia (Suggests lack of suppression scotoma)
Large Angle Strabismus (>10 PD)
Rapidly worsening visual acuity (Look for organic maculopathy)

content.explanation: S: Scotoma (Central); C: Cover test (Small or no shift); A: Anisometropia (Common); L: Low Stereopsis (Gross); P: Peripheral Fusion (Present).

branches: MFS: X-pattern with a central gap in one line
Diplopia: Two separate lines, no crossing

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: ELIS (Early Lens Insertion Study): Highlighted the role of early correction in preventing MFS.
Bifoveal Fixation Recovery: Recent studies suggest limited plasticity to regain bifoveal fixation in adults with MFS.
OCT Imaging: Used to ensure 'Organic MFS' is not present by ruling out subtle epiretinal membranes or macular holes.

sections.title: Prognosis & Long-term Stability
sections.content: MFS is considered one of the most stable forms of binocular alignment. Patients with secondary MFS after esotropia surgery have a significantly lower rate of recurrence (re-operation) compared to those who achieve no binocularity. It is a functional success even if it is not an anatomical 'perfect' alignment.

title: Mastering OCT: The Retina & Optic Nerve Blueprint

Designed for the advanced clinician to navigate the nuances between 'Red Disease' and true pathology.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Physics
sections.content: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a non-invasive, non-contact imaging modality employing low-coherence interferometry (usually near-infrared light ~840nm) to produce high-resolution cross-sectional 'optical biopsies'. Time-Domain (TD) is obsolete; Spectral-Domain (SD) uses a spectrometer to achieve 5µm resolution, while Swept-Source (SS-OCT) uses a tunable laser at ~1050nm for deeper penetration into the choroid.

rows: Thickest at poles; thins in glaucoma
Disrupted in AMD, CNV, or CSR

sections.title: Systematic Macular Interpretation
content: Step 1: Check Signal Strength (Must be >6/10 for reliability).
Step 2: Evaluate Foveal Contour (Normal dip vs. flattening vs. elevation).
Step 3: Analyze Intra-retinal Space (Check for cysts, exudates, hemorrhage).
Step 4: Inspect the EZ & RPE line (Look for 'shagginess' or pigment epithelial detachments).
Step 5: Review Quantitative Maps (Compare Central Subfield Thickness to normative data).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Sub-retinal Fluid (SRF): Indicator of active CNV, CSR, or VKH.
Intra-retinal Cysts (IRC): Hallmarks of DME, RVO, or post-cataract Irvine-Gass.
Hyper-reflective Foci: Migratory RPE cells or hard exudates; indicates chronicity and inflammation.
Full Thickness Macular Hole (FTMH): Immediate surgical referral if symptomatic.
Nasal Stepping on RNFL: High specificity for early glaucomatous damage.
Bilateral Diffuse Thinning: Consider neuro-ophthalmic causes (e.g., toxic, nutritional, or compressive optic neuropathy).

sections.title: The Pitfalls: Why Your Scan is 'Red'
content: Segmentation Error: Software misidentifies layers due to high myopia or dense media.
Decentration: The scan is not centered on the fovea/disc, mimicking focal loss.
Media Opacities: Cataracts or vitreous hemorrhage reduce signal, causing false thinning.
Axial Length: High myopes often show 'Red Disease' due to temporal shift of the bundles.
Vitreous Floaters: Casting shadows (signal drop-off) interpreted as RNFL loss.

content.explanation: Normal Neuroretinal Rim thickness order: Inferior (thickest) > Superior > Nasal > Temporal (thinnest). Reversal often indicates glaucoma.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workflow: Glaucoma
content: 1. Clinical Correlate: Look at the Disc first.
2. Check RNFL Thickness: Look for focal 'V-shaped' defects.
3. Ganglion Cell Analysis: Check the Macula (parafoveal thinning).
4. Functional Correlation: Match OCT defects to Humphrey Visual Field (HVF).
5. Progression Analysis: Guided Progression Analysis (GPA) over 3+ scans.

rows: Splitting of layers, often in RNFL/OPL

sections.title: Ancillary Testing Integration
content: OCT-Angiography (OCT-A): Visualize flow without dye; detects CNV membranes.
Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Gold standard for 'leakage' vs 'pooling'.
Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): Detects metabolic stress (RPE health) in GA or dystrophies.
Enhanced Depth Imaging (EDI): Specifically used to measure choroidal thickness.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: The 'Bruch's Membrane Opening' (BMO) is the true anatomic edge of the optic nerve.
A 'Floor Effect' occurs when RNFL reaches ~50µm; OCT cannot measure further loss accurately.
Temporal thinning is common in non-glaucomatous optic atrophy (e.g., Toxic/Nutritional).
Always look at the 'En Face' image to ensure the scan line crossed the lesion of interest.

sections.title: Recent Advances: AI & Deep Learning
sections.content: Artificial Intelligence algorithms (like Google Health and various FDA-approved platforms) are now capable of autonomous screening for Diabetic Retinopathy and predicting CNV conversion in AMD. Future OCT systems will likely integrate 'Fluid Volume' quantification as a routine metric for treatment intervals (Treat-and-Extend).

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The OCT Impact
content: OHTS: Demonstrated that thinner corneas (CCT) are risk factors, but OCT provides the structural proof of damage.
CATT/HARBOR: Established OCT as the primary tool for monitoring anti-VEGF response.
ALTS: Highlights the importance of structural vs. functional discordance in early glaucoma.

title: Advanced Diabetic Eye Disease: Mastering TRD & End-Stage PDR
summary: Advanced Diabetic Eye Disease (ADED) represents the sight-threatening zenith of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, characterized by Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD), persistent vitreous hemorrhage, and fibrovascular proliferation. This guide provides a residency-level deep dive into its surgical and clinical management.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Ischemic Cascade
content: 1. Chronic Hyperglycemia → Capillary non-perfusion
2. Retinal Ischemia → Upregulation of VEGF & PEDF imbalance
3. Neovascularization at Disk (NVD) or Elsewhere (NVE)
4. Fibrous scaffolding grows along posterior hyaloid face
5. Vitreous contraction → Tangential & Anteroposterior traction
6. Retinal elevation → Tractional Retinal Detachment

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: NVI/NVA: Check undilated gonioscopy for angle vessels.
Vitreous: Shafer sign (uncommon in pure TRD), vitreous heme.
Membranes: Opaque white fibrovascular fronds along arcades.
Macula: Tractional macular edema or heterotopia.
Periphery: Signs of prior incomplete PRP (skip areas).

sections.title: Urgent Red Flags
content: Rapid vision drop in one eye (Combined TRD/RRD)
Sudden 'curtain' with flashes (New break)
Painful red eye with high IOP (NVG)
Macula-threatening TRD (Urgent surgery indication)
B-scan showing 'kissing choroidals' or total RD

branches: B-Scan Ultrasonography (Critical if VH is dense)
Wide-field FFA: Identify areas of non-perfusion
B-Scan: Look for 'V' or 'X' shaped configuration

rows: Early vs late vitrectomy had similar 2-year outcomes.
Early PPV leads to better VA in very severe cases.

content.explanation: T: TRD involving macula; R: RRD (Combined); A: Acute premacular heme; C: Chronic VH (>3 mo); T: Tight hyaloid; I: Iris neovasc (NVG prophylaxis); O: Opacity preventing PRP; N: Neovascularization progression despite laser.

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol (PPV)
content: 1. Port Placement: 23G, 25G, or 27G Pars Plana Vitrectomy.
2. Core Vitrectomy: Clear central vitreous hemorrhage.
3. Induction of PVD: Often difficult due to tight adhesions; use Triesence/TA.
4. Segmentation: Cutting membranes into small islands to relieve tangential traction.
5. Delamination: Peeling membranes off the retinal surface using shears or forceps.
6. Hemostasis: Endodiathermy for bleeding fronds; increase IOP temporarily.
7. Endolaser: Complete 360-degree Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP).
8. Tamponade: Air, Gas (SF6/C3F8), or Silicone Oil if breaks are present.

sections.title: Key Surgical Techniques & Tools
content: Bimanual Technique: Using a chandelier light and two instruments.
Viscodissection: Injecting Healon GV to separate membranes.
Foldback Technique: Starting delamination at the edge of a membrane.
Vertical Scissors: Crucial for cutting tight bridges between retina and hyaloid.
Valved Cannulas: Maintain stable IOP during instrument exchange.

sections.title: Post-operative Management
content: Steroid-Antibiotic drops (Pred Forte/Vigamox) QID.
Atropine 1% BD if significant inflammation/gas.
Prone positioning if gas/oil tamponade used.
Monitor IOP closely (risk of steroid response or gas expansion).
Early Anti-VEGF (Avastin) injection if recurrent VH occurs.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: Don't 'chase' every peripheral membrane; focus on relieving macular traction.
Pre-op Anti-VEGF (2-7 days prior) significantly reduces intra-op bleeding.
Always check the renal status; ADED patients often have diabetic nephropathy.
In cases of NVG, perform PRP/PPV early to save the optic nerve.
TRD fluid is slowly absorbed; don't expect immediate flattening post-op.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED), also known as Graves' Orbitopathy (GO), is an organ-specific autoimmune inflammatory disorder characterized by remodeling of orbital tissues. It is the most common cause of unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults, primarily associated with Graves' hyperthyroidism, though patients may be euthyroid or hypothyroid.

branches: TSHR & IGF-1R Crosstalk: Synergistic signaling on CD34+ fibroblasts
Glycosaminoglycan (GAG) Production: Hyaluronic acid causes osmotic edema
Adipogenesis: Differentiation of fibroblasts into adipocytes (fat expansion)
Cytokine Storm: IL-1, TNF-alpha, and IF-gamma drive inflammation
Muscle Fibrosis: End-stage cicatricial changes leading to restrictive strabismus

rows: Widened palpebral fissures due to upper lid retraction in primary gaze.
Lid lag: The upper eyelid fails to follow the globe downward on downgaze.
Inability to maintain convergence of the eyes.
Absence of forehead wrinkling on upward gaze.
Staring or frightened expression on active fixation.

sections.title: Clinical Activity Score (CAS)
content: 1. Spontaneous retrobulbar pain
2. Pain on upward or downward gaze
3. Eyelid erythema
4. Conjunctival injection
5. Chemosis (conjunctival edema)
6. Swelling of the caruncle or plica
7. Eyelid edema
Note: Score ≥ 3/7 indicates Active TED.

content.explanation: N: No signs/symptoms; O: Only signs (lid retraction); S: Soft tissue involvement; P: Proptosis; E: Extraocular muscle involvement; C: Corneal involvement; S: Sight loss (Optic Neuropathy).

rows: Minor impact on daily life; lid retraction <2mm; mild soft tissue signs.
Observation, Selenium (100mcg BID), Lubricants, Smoking cessation.
Lid retraction ≥2mm; Proptosis ≥3mm above normal; Diplopia.
Dysthyroid Optic Neuropathy (DON) or Corneal Breakdown.
Emergency IV Steroids or Orbital Decompression Surgery.

sections.title: Imaging Findings: CT and MRI
content: Coke-Bottle Sign: Characteristic spindle-shaped enlargement of muscle bellies.
Tendon Sparing: Unlike orbital myositis, TED spares the muscle tendons.
Increased Orbital Fat: Proliferation and herniation of fat.
Apical Crowding: Compression of the optic nerve at the orbital apex.
MRI T2 Signal: High signal in muscles indicates active inflammatory phase (edema).

content.explanation: Order of muscle involvement: 1. Inferior Rectus (most common); 2. Medial Rectus; 3. Superior Rectus; 4. Lateral Rectus; 5. Obliques (least common).

rows: Painful; involves the muscle tendon; rapid onset.
Diffuse involvement (lacrimal gland, fat, muscle); rapid response to oral steroids.
Pulsatile proptosis; corkscrew epibulbar vessels; orbital bruit.
Molding to globe shape; 'salmon-patch' conjunctival lesions; slow progression.
Bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement; infraorbital nerve enlargement.

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Achieve Euthyroidism (Antithyroid drugs, RAI, or Surgery).
Step 2: Smoking Cessation (Absolute requirement to reduce progression).
Step 3: Selenium Supplementation (100mcg twice daily for 6 months for mild GO).
Step 4: IV Methylprednisolone (EUGOGO Protocol: 0.5g weekly for 6 wks, then 0.25g for 6 wks; Max 6-8g).
Step 5: Biologicals - Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor) for significant proptosis/diplopia.
Step 6: Second-line - Mycophenolate Mofetil or Orbital Radiotherapy (20 Gy in 10 fractions).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Dysthyroid Optic Neuropathy (DON)
content: Decreased Visual Acuity (unexplained by surface)
Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
New-onset Dyschromatopsia (loss of color vision)
Visual Field defects (Central or Arcuate)
Optic Disc edema or pallor

sections.title: Rehabilitative Surgical Sequence
content: 1. Orbital Decompression: Must be done first (may change alignment/lids).
2. Strabismus Surgery: Performed once alignment is stable for 6 months.
3. Eyelid Recession: To address lid retraction (Müller's muscle/levator).
4. Blepharoplasty: Final aesthetic touch for fat prolapse and skin excess.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Teprotumumab
content: Mechanism: Fully human monoclonal antibody inhibitor of IGF-1R.
Dosing: 10mg/kg first dose, then 20mg/kg every 3 weeks for 7 additional doses.
Evidence: OPTIC trials showed significant reduction in proptosis (mean ~3mm).
Side Effects: Muscle cramps, hyperglycemia, and hearing loss (audiometry monitoring required).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: The Rundle Curve: TED has an active phase (6-18 months) followed by a stable burnt-out phase.
Never perform elective surgery in the active phase; only for emergencies like DON.
Radioiodine (RAI) can worsen TED; cover with oral Prednisone (0.5mg/kg/day) if needed.
Superior Limbic Keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) is frequently associated with TED.

title: Exposed Orbital Implant: Management Unveiled
summary: Orbital implant exposure, a challenging complication following enucleation or evisceration, threatens socket integrity, cosmesis, and patient comfort. This comprehensive guide delves into its etiology, diagnosis, and a spectrum of management strategies, from conservative measures to intricate surgical repairs, providing ophthalmologists with a robust framework for optimal patient care.

data.title: Exposed Orbital Implant: Management Unveiled
data.summary: Orbital implant exposure, a challenging complication following enucleation or evisceration, threatens socket integrity, cosmesis, and patient comfort. This comprehensive guide delves into its etiology, diagnosis, and a spectrum of management strategies, from conservative measures to intricate surgical repairs, providing ophthalmologists with a robust framework for optimal patient care.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content:
**Anophthalmic Socket:** Refers to the orbit and adnexa following surgical removal (enucleation or evisceration) or congenital absence of the globe.

**Orbital Implant:** A spherical or ovoid device (e.g., hydroxyapatite, porous polyethylene, PMMA) placed within Tenon's capsule at the time of globe removal to restore orbital volume and maintain motility for the overlying prosthetic eye.

**Implant Exposure:** A significant complication where the orbital implant becomes visible through a defect in the overlying conjunctiva and Tenon's capsule. This breakdown of the anatomical barrier leads to potential infection, extrusion, discomfort, and poor cosmetic outcomes, necessitating meticulous management.

sections.title: 2. Risk Factors for Exposure
content: **Surgical Factors:** Inadequate Tenon's closure, thin conjunctival flaps, excessive cautery, oversized implant, anterior malposition, rough implant edges, omission of patch graft (for porous implants).
**Patient Factors:** Prior orbital radiation (up to 30% risk), diabetes mellitus, autoimmune disorders (e.g., cicatricial pemphigoid), malnutrition, smoking, poor wound healing.
**Post-operative Factors:** Early prosthesis fitting (<6 weeks), ill-fitting prosthesis (friction/pressure), trauma, chronic infection/inflammation, poor socket hygiene, suture erosion.
**Implant Factors:** Material (non-porous PMMA > porous), infection, migration, excessive post-operative inflammation.

branches: Ischemic Necrosis (most common): Thin/compromised tissue (post-radiation, cautery) loses blood supply.
Infection: Bacterial colonization (Staph, Pseudomonas), biofilm, inflammation, tissue destruction.
Mechanical Erosion: Chronic friction from prosthesis, direct implant pressure.
Foreign Body Reaction: Chronic inflammation/granuloma around implant/sutures.
Trauma: Direct injury to the socket.
Suture Dehiscence: Early breakdown of surgical closure.

rows: Superior, Inferior, Medial, Lateral Fornix, Central
Sterile (no active infection), Infected (purulent discharge, inflammation)

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Symptoms:**
- Mucoid/mucopurulent discharge
- Foreign body sensation, gritty feeling
- Pain or discomfort (especially with infection)
- Difficulty wearing/retaining ocular prosthesis
- Prosthesis discoloration or malposition
- Decreased cosmetic appearance
- Often asymptomatic, discovered incidentally
**Signs:**
- Visible implant surface (white PMMA, integrated vascularized porous implant)
- Conjunctival thinning, erosion, or ulceration
- Gaping wound/dehiscence
- Inflammation, hyperemia, edema of surrounding conjunctiva
- Granuloma formation (pyogenic granuloma) at exposure site
- Lid edema, ptosis, or retraction
- Prosthesis instability or malposition

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **External Exam:** Assess lid abnormalities, proptosis/enophthalmos, preauricular nodes (if infectious).
**Prosthesis Removal:** MANDATORY for full socket visualization.
**Inspection:**
- **Location & Size:** Precisely document with measurements.
- **Implant Character:** Note exposed surface (porous, smooth, clean, or covered with biofilm/granulation tissue).
- **Discharge:** Quantity, character (serous, mucoid, purulent).
- **Conjunctiva:** Hyperemia, chemosis, thinning, cicatrization.
- **Fornices:** Depth, presence of synechiae.
**Palpation:** Assess for tenderness, fluctuation (abscess), implant mobility.

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Clinical Assessment & Documentation** - Detailed history, comprehensive socket exam, photographic documentation of size and characteristics.

**Step 2: Microbiology** - If infection suspected (purulent discharge, significant inflammation): Obtain conjunctival swab for Gram stain, aerobic & anaerobic cultures, and sensitivity testing. Common pathogens: *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus spp.*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*.
**Step 3: Imaging (Selected Cases)** -
- **Orbital CT Scan:** To rule out orbital abscess, assess implant position/integrity, bony erosion, or retained foreign bodies. Especially useful for deeper involvement.
- **Orbital MRI:** Better soft tissue contrast for inflammation, abscess, or extent of granuloma/infection.
**Step 4: Biopsy (Rarely)** - If atypical lesion or malignancy suspected, biopsy of granuloma or surrounding tissue.

rows: Exposed white/tan scleral tissue, not the underlying implant itself. Management similar.
Separation of conjunctiva, but Tenon's capsule remains intact, protecting the implant. Less severe.
Reactive vascular proliferation, often obscuring the implant. Bleeds easily. Not true exposure unless ulcerated.
Inflammation and discharge, but implant remains fully covered by intact conjunctiva/Tenon's.
Small (<5mm), asymptomatic, sterile, chronic, stable exposure.
Conservative: Topical antibiotics/lubricants, prosthesis modification/removal, close observation.
Medium (5-10mm), mild symptoms (discharge, discomfort), low-grade inflammation, or acute small exposure.
Surgical: Local flap/graft (conjunctival advancement, amniotic membrane, small autogenous graft).
Large (>10mm), significant pain/purulent discharge, acute infection (cellulitis), implant instability, or previous repair failure, radiated socket.
Complex Surgical: Autogenous robust graft (fascia lata, dermis-fat), regional flap, or implant removal/replacement.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Principles
content: **Primary Goal:** Eliminate infection, provide viable vascularized tissue cover, restore socket integrity, preserve orbital volume, and maintain cosmesis/comfort.
**Conservative Management (Stage 1):**
- **Topical Antibiotics:** Broad-spectrum, e.g., Moxifloxacin 0.5% QID or Tobramycin 0.3% ointment BID. Culture-directed if possible.
- **Topical Steroids:** Cautious use for inflammation without infection, e.g., Dexamethasone 0.1% BID-TID (risk of delayed healing/infection).
- **Lubricants:** Artificial tears/ointments (e.g., Refresh P.M.) to reduce friction.
- **Lid Hygiene:** Warm compresses, gentle cleaning.
- **Prosthesis Management:** Temporarily remove prosthesis or modify to relieve pressure. Delay refitting until stable.
- **Close Observation:** Monitor for progression every 1-2 weeks.
**Surgical Management (Stage 2/3 or failed conservative):**
- **Debridement:** Remove unhealthy tissue, biofilm, pyogenic granuloma.
- **Grafting/Flaps:** Provide robust, vascularized tissue coverage. Choice depends on size, location, tissue availability, and patient history (esp. radiation).

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Detail Guide
content: **1. Direct Primary Closure:** For <5mm, acute, non-infected defects. Debride edges, undermine conjunctiva/Tenon's, layered closure (6-0 Vicryl for Tenon's, 7-0 Vicryl/Chromic for conjunctiva). Ensure tension-free.

**2. Conjunctival Advancement Flaps:** For small-medium defects with healthy surrounding conjunctiva. Incise conjunctiva 3-5mm from limbus, mobilize a broad flap of conjunctiva and Tenon's, advance over defect, suture to opposing edge (e.g., 6-0 Vicryl/Chromic).

**3. Amniotic Membrane Graft (AMG):** Adjunct for small, superficial defects or to promote healing after flap. Suture single/multi-layered AMG over exposure, often with an overlying temporary tarsorrhaphy or conformer.
**4. Autogenous Grafts (Preferred for Robust Repair):**

- **Fascia Lata Graft:** Gold standard for medium-large defects. Harvested from lateral thigh (e.g., 3x2 cm ellipse). Excised exposed tissue, suture graft over implant to Tenon's/periosteum (e.g., 6-0 Vicryl), then close conjunctiva over graft.
- **Dermis-Fat Graft:** Harvested from abdomen/buttock. Excellent for volume replacement, especially in contracted sockets or after implant removal. Can be used as primary implant/volume restorer.
- **Temporalis Fascia Graft:** Thinner, well-vascularized, harvested from temporal fossa.
**5. Allogeneic Grafts (Donor Sclera):** Less common now due to higher re-exposure rates and disease transmission concerns. Can be used as a patch graft but requires careful follow-up.
**6. Regional Flaps (for extensive/recurrent defects):**
- **Tarsoconjunctival Flap (e.g., Modified Hughes):** Utilizes eyelid tissue (tarsus and conjunctiva) for robust, vascularized cover. Requires temporary eyelid closure and two-stage procedure.
- **Periosteal Flap:** Mobilized from orbital rim, offers vascularized tissue for specific defects.

**7. Implant Removal and Replacement:** Last resort for persistent infection, repeated failure of repair, complete extrusion, intractable pain. Remove infected implant, debride thoroughly, irrigate with antibiotics. Consider delayed placement of a new, often smaller, porous and wrapped implant (3-6 months later) or immediate dermis-fat graft.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Complications:**
- Recurrence of exposure (especially in radiated sockets or with inadequate repair).
- Infection: Orbital cellulitis, osteomyelitis, implant abscess.
- Implant extrusion: Complete loss of the implant, leading to severe volume deficit.
- Socket contraction, fornix foreshortening, ptosis.
- Chronic discharge/inflammation, granuloma formation.
- Prosthetic intolerance (pain, instability).
- Cosmetic dissatisfaction.
- Donor site morbidity (for autogenous grafts).

**Prognosis:** Variable. Small, uninfected exposures may respond to conservative/simple repair (success rate ~80-90%). Large, infected, or recurrent exposures (especially post-radiation) have poorer prognosis, higher recurrence rates, and often require complex, multi-stage procedures. Early, aggressive management improves outcomes. Success rates for complex repairs range from 50-70%.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Rapidly increasing pain, swelling, or redness around the anophthalmic socket.
Fever, chills, malaise (suggesting systemic infection).
Copious, purulent, or foul-smelling discharge.
Proptosis or significant displacement of the implant (indicates orbital involvement or abscess).
Signs of orbital cellulitis: painful ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, vision loss (if infection spreads posteriorly into orbit – requires immediate intervention).
Sudden loss or complete extrusion of the orbital implant.

content.mnemonic: COVER UP for Implant Exposure Management
content.explanation:
**C**onsider infection first (culture & antibiotics).
**O**bserve small, sterile defects.
**V**ascularized tissue is key for repair (autogenous fascia lata/dermis-fat).
**E**xamine prosthesis fit and modify.
**R**emove implant as last resort.
**U**nderlying risk factors (radiation, poor closure) must be addressed.
**P**revention is paramount (meticulous surgery, patch grafts).

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Prevention is superior to cure:** Meticulous surgical technique during primary surgery (tension-free layered closure, appropriate implant size, patch graft for porous implants) significantly reduces exposure risk.
**Always identify the 'why':** Understanding the underlying cause (e.g., poor closure, infection, radiation) guides appropriate management and prevents recurrence.
**Infection first, then repair:** If active infection is present, treat aggressively with appropriate antibiotics (topical, systemic) before or concurrently with surgical repair.

**Autogenous tissue offers the best chance:** Fascia lata and dermis-fat grafts provide robust, vascularized coverage with lower recurrence rates than allografts or simple conjunctival flaps for larger defects.

**Radiation changes everything:** Sockets with prior orbital radiation are highly prone to exposure and re-exposure due to poor vascularity. Dermis-fat grafts or vascularized regional flaps are often preferred.
**Manage the prosthesis:** Ensure proper fit, temporarily remove or modify during healing to minimize mechanical stress.
**Document meticulously:** Use photographs and precise measurements to track progression and response to treatment.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Biomaterials:** Ongoing research into new implant materials (e.g., bioceramics, polymers) and antimicrobial coatings to reduce infection and improve tissue integration.
**Customized Implants:** 3D printing allows for custom-sized implants, potentially reducing tension and improving fit within the anophthalmic socket.

**Enhanced Patch Grafts:** Continued refinement of tissue bank processing for allografts and growing use of autogenous fascia lata due to superior vascularization. Landmark studies (e.g., Jordan et al. Ophthalmology 1999; Custer et al. OPRS 2005) solidified the role of patch grafts over porous implants.

**Role of Dermis-Fat Grafting:** Renewed interest as a primary implant or for complex socket reconstruction, especially in severely compromised or radiated sockets, providing both volume and a vascularized surface.
**Microvascular Flaps:** Advances in reconstructive microsurgery offer highly specialized options for severe, recurrent exposures with extensive tissue loss, utilizing distant vascularized tissue.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric & Special Populations
content: **Pediatric Sockets:**
- Rapid orbital growth requires careful monitoring; relative implant size changes can increase exposure risk.
- Managing exposure in children is challenging due to smaller structures and potential for lack of cooperation.
- Growth stimulation often involves serial enlargement of conformers/prostheses or custom implants.
**Systemic Conditions:**
- Patients with diabetes, autoimmune diseases (e.g., cicatricial pemphigoid, granulomatosis with polyangiitis), or on immunosuppression have impaired wound healing and higher infection risk.
- Require aggressive infection control and often more robust surgical repair techniques.
**Radiated Sockets:**
- As noted, compromised vascularity and tissue quality make these sockets high risk for primary and recurrent exposure.
- Autogenous vascularized tissue (fascia lata, dermis-fat, or complex regional flaps) is often the preferred initial approach; simple conjunctival flaps are prone to failure.

sections.title: 18. Prevention Strategies
content: **Meticulous Surgical Technique (Primary Enucleation/Evisceration):**
- Maintain excellent hemostasis.
- Preserve maximum viable Tenon's capsule and conjunctiva.
- Perform robust, tension-free, layered closure of Tenon's (e.g., 5-0 or 6-0 Vicryl) and conjunctiva (e.g., 7-0 Vicryl).
- Select appropriate implant size (avoiding oversized implants that create tension).
- Ensure smooth implant edges, especially with PMMA.

**Patch Grafting:** Routinely consider wrapping porous implants (hydroxyapatite, porous polyethylene) with autogenous (fascia lata) or allogeneic (donor sclera) patch grafts to enhance tissue coverage and vascularization. Autogenous fascia lata is preferred.
**Optimized Post-operative Care:**
- Delay fitting of ocular prosthesis (typically 6-8 weeks, sometimes longer).
- Ensure precise prosthesis fit to avoid pressure points or friction.
- Patient education on meticulous socket hygiene and avoiding trauma.
- Prompt assessment and management of any signs of inflammation or infection.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Entropion is the inversion of the eyelid margin towards the globe. This results in the eyelashes and outer skin rubbing against the ocular surface, leading to mechanical irritation, trichiasis, and potential corneal scarring or ulceration. Unlike ectropion, it is frequently symptomatic from the onset.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Involutional Triad
content: Horizontal Eyelid Laxity: Stretching of the medial/lateral canthal tendons.
Vertical Instability: Disinsertion or attenuation of the lower lid retractors (capsulopalpebral fascia).
Orbicularis Override: Preseptal orbicularis moves superiorly over the pretarsal orbicularis during blinking.
Tarsal Plate Atrophy: Loss of structural rigidity in the tarsus.

rows: Type II hypersensitivity; symblepharon; linear IgA/IgG
Post-prodromal mucocutaneous sloughing; severe dry eye
Arlt's line; Herbert's pits; SAFE strategy
Acute limbal ischemia followed by symblepharon
Chronic use of Pilocarpine, Timolol, or IDU
Severe meibomian gland loss; lacrimal fibrosis

sections.title: Foster Staging of OCP
content: Stage I: Chronic conjunctivitis and subepithelial fibrosis.
Stage II: Fornix shortening (especially inferior).
Stage III: Symblepharon formation.
Stage IV: Ankyloblepharon and surface keratinization.

sections.title: Clinical Examination Checklist
content: Snap-back Test: Assess horizontal laxity.
Distraction Test: Lid pulled >10mm from globe indicates laxity.
Excursion of Lower Lid: Check for retractor disinsertion (decreased movement on downgaze).
Slit Lamp: Look for Arlt's line (superior tarsal scarring) and trichiasis.
Fluorescein Staining: Check for PEEs or corneal ulcers.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Ocular Emergencies
content: Corneal Opacification or Perforation due to persistent lash abrasion.
Rapidly progressive Symblepharon indicating active OCP/Autoimmune flare.
Lid Margin Keratinization causing irreversible corneal surface damage.
Microbial Keratitis secondary to epithelial defects.

rows: Transverse lid blepharotomy with marginal rotation
Shortening of the lid at the lateral canthus

sections.title: Managing Cicatricial Entropion (Upper Lid)
content: 1. Address underlying inflammation (e.g., Dapsone/Cyclophosphamide for OCP).
2. Tarsal Grooving (Streatfeild-Snellen): Wedge excision of tarsus.
3. Posterior Lamella Grafting: Mucous membrane (buccal), hard palate, or amniotic membrane.
4. Terminal Tarsal Rotation (Ballen): For severe upper lid cases.

content.explanation: C: Chemical burns; I: Infections (Trachoma, HSV); D: Drugs (Pilocarpine); E: Erythema Multiforme (SJS); R: Radiation; S: Systemic disease (OCP, Sarcoid).

sections.title: Landmark Study: The SAFE Strategy
content: S: Surgery for Trichiasis.
A: Antibiotics (Azithromycin) for active infection.
F: Facial cleanliness.
E: Environmental improvement (water/sanitation).
WHO target: Global elimination of trachoma as a public health problem.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Differentiate Trichiasis (misdirected lashes) from Distichiasis (extra row from Meibomian glands).
Always check for a 'hidden' upper lid entropion in cases of unexplained corneal staining.
In OCP, never perform surgery during an active inflammatory flare if possible.
Dermatochalasis can coexist but usually masks the severity of the entropion.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup for Scarring
content: Conjunctival Biopsy: Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF) to look for linear basement membrane zone deposits.
Microbiology: Swabs for Chlamydia PCR or bacterial cultures.
Systemic Screen: HLA-B12 (SJS), skin biopsy for Pemphigoid.
Schirmer's Test: Assess associated aqueous tear deficiency.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
sections.content: Surgical success for involutional entropion is high (>90% with combined horizontal/vertical tightening). Cicatricial cases have a guarded prognosis and often require multiple interventions. Complications include recurrence, overcorrection (ectropion), and lid margin notch formation.

title: Hashimoto’s & Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to Hashimoto's Thyroiditis and its ophthalmic manifestation. While typically associated with hypothyroidism, Hashimoto's accounts for up to 10% of Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) cases, requiring vigilant monitoring for orbitopathy.

data.title: Hashimoto’s & Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)
data.summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to Hashimoto's Thyroiditis and its ophthalmic manifestation. While typically associated with hypothyroidism, Hashimoto's accounts for up to 10% of Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) cases, requiring vigilant monitoring for orbitopathy.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Hashimoto’s Thyroiditis (Chronic Lymphocytic Thyroiditis) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the destruction of the thyroid gland by cell- and antibody-mediated immune processes. In ophthalmology, it is the second most common cause of Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) after Graves' disease. TED in Hashimoto's often presents in euthyroid or hypothyroid states and may have a more subtle but equally progressive course.

branches: Antibodies: TPO-Ab, Tg-Ab, and TSH-R Ab (Blocking/Stimulating)
Orbital Fibroblasts: Expression of TSH-R and IGF-1R
Glycosaminoglycan (GAG): Hyaluronic acid accumulation leads to osmotic edema
Adipogenesis: Expansion of orbital fat volume
Myocyte Inflammation: T-cell infiltration (CD4+ and CD8+) into EOMs

sections.title: Clinical Activity Score (CAS)
content: Spontaneous retrobulbar pain
Pain on attempted upgaze or sidegaze
Eyelid erythema
Eyelid edema/swelling
Conjunctival injection
Chemosis (conjunctival edema)
Inflammation of the caruncle or plica
Score ≥ 3/7 indicates active disease.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Von Graefe’s Sign: Lid lag on downgaze
Dalrymple Sign: Widened palpebral fissures
Kocher Sign: Staring/frightened appearance
Stellwag Sign: Infrequent or incomplete blinking
Hertel measurement: Typically >20mm or >2mm asymmetry
IOP: May increase >2mmHg on upgaze (EOM restriction)

content.explanation: Inferior Rectus (most common) → Medial Rectus → Superior Rectus → Lateral Rectus → Obliques (least common).

sections.title: Red Flags: Sight-Threatening TED
content: Dysthyroid Optic Neuropathy (DON): Decreased VA, RAPD (+)
Dyschromatopsia: Faded colors (red desaturation)
Corneal Ulceration: From severe lagophthalmos
Significant Choroidal Folds: Suggesting high orbital pressure

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: Serology (TSH, Free T4, T3, TPO antibodies, TR-Ab/TSI)
Step 2: Formal Visual Fields (Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2) to check for DON
Step 3: Color Vision testing (Ishihara plates)
Step 4: CT Orbit (Non-contrast): Look for 'Coca-Cola Bottle' sign (tendon sparing muscle enlargement)
Step 5: MRI Orbit: T2-weighted sequences to assess active inflammation/edema

rows: Acute onset; unilateral; prompt response to steroids
Fever, leukocytosis, proptosis, history of sinusitis
Pulsatile proptosis, bruit, corkscrew episcleral vessels
Painless, 'salmon-patch' subconjunctival lesion, molded to globe

sections.title: Management of Active Phase
content: 1. Smoking Cessation (Mandatory)
2. Selenium Supplementation (100mcg BID) for mild cases
3. IV Methylprednisolone (EUGOGO protocol: 500mg weekly x 6, then 250mg x 6)
4. Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor): 8 infusions every 3 weeks
5. Orbital Radiotherapy (20 Gray over 10 fractions)

sections.title: Surgical Intervention Sequence
content: Step 1: Orbital Decompression (Fat or Bone) - Perform ONLY when stable (except for emergency DON)
Step 2: Strabismus Surgery (Recessions, adjustable sutures preferred)
Step 3: Eyelid Recession (To address lid retraction)
Step 4: Blepharoplasty (Removal of prolapsed orbital fat)

sections.title: Landmark Study: OPTIC Trial
content: Intervention: Teprotumumab vs Placebo
Result: 83% of patients had ≥2mm reduction in proptosis
Significant improvement in diplopia and CAS scores
Adverse Effects: Muscle cramps, hyperglycemia, hearing loss (ototoxicity)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: Always check IOP in upgaze; a rise >2mmHg suggests IR restriction.
TED can occur in hypothyroidism; check antibodies even if TSH is high.
Eyelid retraction is the most common sign of TED (90% of cases).
Smoking is the single most important modifiable risk factor for progression.

sections.title: Prognosis & Rundle's Curve
sections.content: Rundle's Curve describes the natural history of TED: an initial 'Active Phase' of worsening inflammation (6–18 months) followed by a 'Plateau' and a slow 'Fibrotic Phase' of improvement. Surgery for cosmesis and function (except in emergencies) should be delayed until the patient has reached the stable, inactive phase for at least 6 months.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK) is a crescent-shaped destructive inflammation of the juxtalimbal corneal stroma associated with an epithelial defect, stromal thinning, and inflammatory cell infiltration. Mooren's Ulcer is a specific, idiopathic form of PUK that occurs in the absence of any detectable systemic autoimmune or infectious disease, characterized by an overhanging leading edge of deep stromal melting.

sections.title: The Great Comparison: PUK vs. Mooren’s

rows: Spares the limbus (usually starts near it)
Vessels grow into the ulcer base
Unilateral, older patients, slow progression, responds well to surgery/medical Rx.
Bilateral, younger patients (often African/Asian), rapid progression, poor prognosis.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Cascade of Melt
content: Step 1: Immune complex deposition (Type III Hypersensitivity) in the limbal vascular network.
Step 2: Recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages to the limbus.
Step 3: Release of Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMP-1, MMP-2, MMP-9) and Collagenases.
Step 4: Destruction of corneal stromal lamellae and epithelial basement membrane.
Step 5: Stromal melting proceeds circumferentially and then centrally.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Mandatory Labs
content: Complete Blood Count (CBC) with differential
ESR and C-Reactive Protein (CRP)
Rheumatoid Factor (RF) & Anti-CCP
ANCA (c-ANCA for GPA, p-ANCA for PAN/MPA)
ANA (Antinuclear Antibody) profile
BUN/Creatinine & Urinalysis (check for renal involvement)
Chest X-Ray or CT (rule out GPA/Sarcoid)
Syphilis Serology (RPR/FTA-ABS)

sections.title: The 'Red Flag' Symptoms
content: Extreme pain disproportionate to clinical findings (suggests Scleritis/GPA)
Sudden decrease in vision (threatened perforation)
Positive Seidel test over the area of thinning
Hematuria or hemoptysis (indicates systemic vasculitis emergency)
Scleral involvement (Sclerokeratitis indicates high systemic mortality risk)

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: 1. Lubrication: Preservative-free tears and ointments.
2. Systemic Steroids: Oral Prednisolone (1mg/kg/day) for acute control.
3. Immunomodulators: Methotrexate, Azathioprine, or Mycophenolate.
4. Biologics: Rituximab (highly effective for GPA/refractory RA) or Infliximab.
5. Collagenase Inhibitors: Oral Doxycycline (100mg BID) and topical Medroxyprogesterone.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention Techniques
content: Conjunctival Resection: Removes the source of collagenases and antibodies (Primary for Mooren's).
Cyanoacrylate Tissue Adhesive: For small perforations (<1mm) or extreme thinning.
Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT): Multilayered to promote epithelialization.
Tectonic Lamellar Keratoplasty: Crescentic grafts to restore globe integrity.
Gundersen Flap: If visual potential is poor but globe needs stabilization.

content.explanation: M: Marginal melt, O: Overhanging edge, O: Orphan (Idiopathic), R: Relentless progression, E: Exclude systemic disease, N: No scleritis.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: PUK may be the presenting sign of a lethal systemic vasculitis (e.g., GPA).
A patient with RA who develops PUK has a 50% mortality rate at 10 years if not treated systemically.
Mooren's ulcer is a diagnosis of EXCLUSION. Always run the full vasculitis panel first.
Topical steroids can sometimes ACCELERATE melting in PUK by inhibiting collagen synthesis.

sections.title: Recent Advances: The Rituximab Revolution
sections.content: Landmark studies have shown that B-cell depletion therapy with Rituximab is superior to traditional cyclophosphamide for induction of remission in ANCA-associated vasculitis (RAVE and RITUXVAS trials). In PUK associated with Wegener's (GPA), Rituximab has become a first-line agent, showing rapid stabilization of the corneal stroma and better safety profiles than older alkylating agents.

branches: Afferent: Retinal Ganglion Cells -> Optic Nerve -> Chiasm -> Optic Tract
Pretectal: Fibers exit tract before LGN -> Pretectal Nuclei (Midbrain)
Interneuron: Pretectal nuclei to bilateral Edinger-Westphal (EW) Nuclei
Efferent: EW Nucleus -> CN III -> Ciliary Ganglion -> Short Ciliary Nerves -> Sphincter Pupillae

sections.title: Defining the RAPD (Marcus Gunn Pupil)
sections.content: A Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) occurs when there is an asymmetric response to a light stimulus between the two eyes. It indicates a lesion in the pre-chiasmal afferent pathway (optic nerve or severe retinal disease). Note: A dense cataract does NOT cause an RAPD.

sections.title: The Swinging Flashlight Test Protocol
content: 1. Dim room lighting; patient fixes on a distant target to negate accommodation.
2. Use a bright, focal light source (transilluminator).
3. Shine light in Eye A for 2-3 seconds, then quickly swing to Eye B.
4. Observe the initial movement of the pupil in Eye B.
5. Repeat the swing rhythmically to confirm the 'escape' or dilation.

rows: Weak initial constriction followed by greater escape/redilation.
Initial stall/no movement followed by immediate dilation.
No response in the affected eye; consensual only in the fellow eye.

branches: Optic Nerve: Optic Neuritis (MS), NAION, AION (GCA), Glaucoma (asymmetric), Trauma, Compression
Retinal: Massive Retinal Detachment, Ischemic CRVO, Severe Macular Degeneration (extensive)
Pre-Chiasmal: Optic Tract lesions (contralateral RAPD), Chiasmal compression (asymmetric)

sections.title: 2017 McDonald Criteria for MS
content: Dissemination in Space (DIS): ≥1 T2-hyperintense lesion in ≥2 of 4 MS-typical CNS areas (Periventricular, Cortical/Juxtacortical, Infratentorial, Spinal Cord).
Dissemination in Time (DIT): Simultaneous presence of gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions OR a new T2/Gd+ lesion on follow-up.
CSF Oligoclonal Bands: Can substitute for DIT in some cases.
No better clinical explanation for the neurological deficits.

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations of MS
content: Optic Neuritis: Pain with eye movement (92%), sudden vision loss, dyschromatopsia (red desaturation).
Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO): Lesion in MLF; ipsilateral adduction deficit, contralateral abducting nystagmus.
Intermediate Uveitis: Pars planitis and 'snowbanking' are significantly associated with MS.
Periphlebitis Retinae: Venous sheathing found in up to 10% of cases.
Nystagmus: Pendular or jerk nystagmus (often vestibular or cerebellar involvement).

sections.title: Acute Treatment of Optic Neuritis (ONTT Protocol)
content: Step 1: IV Methylprednisolone (1,000 mg/day) for 3 days.
Step 2: Follow with Oral Prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) for 11 days.
Step 3: Rapid taper over 3-4 days (e.g., 20mg day 1, 10mg day 2/3).
CONTRAINDICATION: Do NOT use low-dose oral steroids alone (increased recurrence rate per Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial).

rows: First-line for RRMS; high safety profile, modest efficacy.
Fingolimod requires monitoring for FAME (Fingolimod Associated Macular Edema).
High efficacy. Natalizumab risk: PML (JC virus screening required).
B-cell depletion and S1P receptor modulation.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags: Atypical Optic Neuritis
content: Absence of pain (consider NAION or compression).
Severe disc edema with hemorrhages or macular star (Neuroretinitis).
Failure to recover vision after 4-6 weeks.
Bilateral involvement or rapid sequential involvement (Think NMO/MOGAD).
Systemic symptoms (Weight loss, cough, skin lesions).

content.explanation: P: Pulfrich Effect (altered depth perception), H: Hyperacusis, E: Eye Pain (ON), N: Nystagmus (INO), O: Optic Atrophy, M: Marcus Gunn Pupil (RAPD), E: Uhthoff's (Heat sensitivity), N: Neuralgia (Trigeminal), A: Ataxia.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearl: The Pulfrich Effect
content: Occurs due to delayed conduction in the affected optic nerve.
An object moving in a straight line appears to move in an elliptical path.
Can be neutralized by placing a neutral density filter over the fellow (good) eye.
Highly specific for previous optic neuritis.

sections.title: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) Key Findings
content: IV Steroids speed up the rate of recovery but do not affect long-term visual outcome (at 1 year).
Low-dose oral steroids (1mg/kg) doubled the risk of recurrence.
Steroids provide a temporary protective effect (2 years) against the development of clinically definite MS.
Baseline MRI is the strongest predictor of MS risk (72% if ≥1 lesion vs 25% if 0 lesions at 15 years).

sections.title: Advanced Diagnostic Workup Flow
content: 1. Neuro-Ophthalmic Exam (RAPD, Color, Visual Fields, Motility).
2. MRI Brain & Orbits with/without Gadolinium (Standard of care).
3. OCT: Quantify RNFL and GCL loss (thinning starts ~3-6 months post-ON).
4. Serology: AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG (rule out NMO/MOGAD if atypical).
5. VEP (Visual Evoked Potentials): Shows prolonged latency in demyelination.
6. Lumbar Puncture: Only if MRI is inconclusive or atypical features present.

data.label: Risk of MS if MRI shows 0 lesions
Risk of MS if MRI shows ≥1 lesion

data.summary: A complex strabismus condition, historically termed 'Double Levator Palsy,' characterized by a unilateral limitation of elevation in all positions of horizontal gaze. It requires a precise distinction between restrictive and paretic etiologies for successful management.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Monocular Elevation Deficiency (MED) is defined as the deficiency of elevation of one eye from any position of horizontal gaze (abduction, adduction, and primary position). While the term 'Double Levator Palsy' suggests a combined palsy of the Superior Rectus (SR) and Inferior Oblique (IO), the pathophysiology is often supranuclear (near the pretectal nucleus) or restrictive (Inferior Rectus tightness). It is primarily a congenital condition but can be acquired.

rows: Superior Rectus (SR) and Inferior Oblique (IO) weakness

sections.title: Clinical Features Checklist
content: Hypotropia of the affected eye in primary gaze.
Limited elevation in abduction, adduction, and midline.
Chin-up head posture to maintain binocularity.
Ptosis or Pseudo-ptosis (check if lid follows eye down).
Bell's Phenomenon: Usually absent in supranuclear cases.
Normal horizontal excursions.
Potential amblyopia in the hypotropic eye.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Sensorimotor exam (9-position photos and prism measurements).
Step 2: Evaluate for Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking phenomenon.
Step 3: Differentiate Ptosis vs. Pseudo-ptosis (cover the non-paretic eye).
Step 4: Forced Duction Test (FDT) - Crucial for surgical planning.
Step 5: Force Generation Test (FGT) to assess SR power.
Step 6: Neuro-imaging if acquired (MRI Brain/Orbit).

rows: Elevation deficit worse in adduction; V-pattern; positive FDT in adduction.
History of trauma; positive FDT; 'trapdoor' signs on CT.
Eyelid retraction; IR thickening on imaging; positive FDT.
Usually bilateral; severe restriction in all directions; autosomal dominant.
Involves depression, adduction, and pupil involvement; severe ptosis.

sections.title: Surgical Management Algorithm
content: Perform FDT under anesthesia.
If FDT Positive (Tight IR): Perform IR Recession (standard 4-5mm) first.
Wait 3-6 months; if elevation deficit persists, proceed to paretic correction.
If FDT Negative (Paretic): Perform Knapp Procedure (Full tendon transposition).
Knapp Procedure: MR and LR shifted to the SR insertion.
Address Ptosis ONLY after the ocular alignment is stabilized.

sections.title: The Knapp Procedure Details
content: Indication: Negative FDT (paretic SR/IO).
Technique: Full-tendon transposition of Medial Rectus and Lateral Rectus to the Superior Rectus insertion.
Goal: Convert horizontal recti into elevators.
Modification: Scott and Wood recommend moving the tendons 2mm posterior to the SR insertion for better vector.
Success: Best for primary position hypotropia < 25-30 prism diopters.

sections.title: URGENT: Red Flags
content: Sudden onset MED in an adult: Rule out midbrain stroke or Parinaud syndrome.
Presence of pupillary abnormalities: Suggests CN III involvement or midbrain lesion.
Proptosis or chemosis: Suggests orbital inflammatory disease or TED.
Pain on eye movement: Rule out orbital cellulitis or myositis.

content.explanation: F: Forced duction test (Primary step); L: Lid position (Ptosis vs Pseudo); A: Amblyopia check; T: Traumatic hx (exclude fracture); S: Supranuclear vs Infranuclear signs (Bell's phenomenon).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: Pseudo-ptosis occurs because the upper lid follows the hypotropic eye. Always check lid height with the paretic eye fixing.
Never perform a Knapp procedure if the IR is tight; you must recess the IR first.
Knapp procedure can induce a 'rectus muscle' slackening effect, reducing horizontal range slightly.
A positive Bell's phenomenon in a patient with no elevation indicates a supranuclear lesion (Infranuclear/Nuclear pathways are intact).

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Anterior Segment Ischemia (ASI): Risk increased if 3 or more rectus muscles are operated on (caution during Knapp).
Persistent Diplopia: Especially in acquired adult cases.
Induced Astigmatism: Changes in corneal contour post-transposition.
Prognosis: Generally good for primary position alignment; full elevation recovery is rare.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
sections.content: Recent literature highlights the use of 'Augmented Knapp' procedures using posterior fixation sutures (Faden) to enhance the elevation effect. Studies on the use of Botulinum Toxin in the IR as a temporary measure for acquired MED have shown utility in stroke-related cases to prevent contracture while waiting for spontaneous recovery.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Trabeculectomy remains the 'gold standard' for surgical glaucoma management. A 'fresh' trabeculectomy (Days 1–14) requires meticulous monitoring. Failure to achieve the target IOP in this phase often indicates a mechanical or physiological blockage of the newly created drainage pathway. Early intervention is paramount to prevent bleb failure and irreversible glaucomatous damage.

sections.title: The Post-Op Exam Checklist
content: Visual Acuity: Rule out 'wipe-out' syndrome or macular serous detachment.
IOP Measurement: Goldmann Applanation (avoid excessive pressure) or Tonopen.
Bleb Morphology: Assess height (elevated vs. flat), extent (diffuse vs. localized), and vascularity (corkscrew vessels).
Seidel Test: Use 2% Fluorescein to check for wound or bleb leaks.
Anterior Chamber Depth: Grade using Van Herick or Shaffer (Peripheral vs. Central depth).
Internal Ostium: Gonioscopic view of the sclerostomy site (if safe/view allows).
Fundoscopy: Rule out choroidal effusions or suprachoroidal hemorrhage.

branches: Obstruction of Internal Ostium (Blood, Fibrin, Iris, Vitreous)

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags (High IOP + Shallow AC)
content: Malignant Glaucoma (Ciliary Block): High IOP, Shallow AC, no choroidals.
Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage: Sudden pain, loss of vision, high IOP, dark fundus mass.
Pupillary Block: High IOP, iris bombe, usually due to absent/blocked iridectomy.
Incarceration of Vitreous: Blockage of the ostium by vitreous wick.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Gonioscopy: Vital to see if iris or blood is plugging the ostium.
2. B-Scan Ultrasound: Crucial if the media is hazy to rule out Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage.
3. AS-OCT: Visualizes the scleral flap, subconjunctival space, and ostium patency.
4. UBM: Detailed view of the ciliary body position in suspected Malignant Glaucoma.

sections.title: Management: The Step-by-Step Protocol
content: Step 1: Digital Ocular Massage (Allen-Burian Maneuver) to force fluid through the flap.
Step 2: Laser Suture Lysis (LSL) if sutures are too tight (use Hoskins lens).
Step 3: Medical Therapy (Aqueous suppressants, but avoid miotics if malignant glaucoma is suspected).
Step 4: Atropine 1% for Malignant Glaucoma or Pupillary Block.
Step 5: AC Reformation or Surgical Revision if mechanical blockage persists.

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: The Scleral Flap
content: Suture tension is a balance: Too tight = High IOP; Too loose = Hypotony/Flat AC.
Always place adjustable or releasable sutures if you anticipate a high risk of failure.
Check for 'Overhang' of the bleb, which may indicate posterior flow.

content.explanation: B: Bleb (Height/Vascularity), I: Inflammation (AC cells), G: Gonioscopy (Ostium), H: Hemorrhage (Choroidal), E: Effusion, L: Leak (Seidel), P: Pressure (IOP).

sections.title: Specific Surgical Obstructions
content: Blood/Fibrin: Can be cleared with Intracameral TPA (25 micrograms).
Iris Incarceration: Requires surgical repositioning or YAG PI if localized.
Vitreous: Requires anterior vitrectomy to clear the ostium.
Tenon's Cyst: Requires needling with MMC or 5-FU.

sections.title: Malignant Glaucoma Management
content: 1. Cycloplegia: Immediate Atropine 1% TID to pull the ciliary body back.
2. Aqueous Suppressants: IV Mannitol, Oral Acetazolamide, Timolol.
3. YAG Capsulotomy/Hyaloidotomy: To break the aqueous misdirection.
4. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): With 'Zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy' if medical therapy fails.

rows: Monitor for steroid-induced IOP spike (weeks later)
Avoid in very wide angles unless necessary

sections.title: Prognosis & Landmarks
content: TVT Study (Tube vs Trab): Trabeculectomy with MMC remains effective but has higher early complication rates than tubes.
Early high IOP is a significant predictor of long-term surgical failure if not addressed within the first 14 days.
Encapsulated blebs (Tenon's cyst) often respond well to needling with an 80% success rate if performed early.

title: Behçet's Disease: A Multisystemic Inflammatory Odyssey
summary: Behçet's Disease is a chronic, relapsing, multisystemic inflammatory vasculitis of unknown etiology, predominantly affecting young adults. Characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, skin lesions, and frequently, vision-threatening ocular inflammation, it presents a complex diagnostic and management challenge for ophthalmologists and rheumatologists alike.

data.title: Behçet's Disease: A Multisystemic Inflammatory Odyssey
data.summary: Behçet's Disease is a chronic, relapsing, multisystemic inflammatory vasculitis of unknown etiology, predominantly affecting young adults. Characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, skin lesions, and frequently, vision-threatening ocular inflammation, it presents a complex diagnostic and management challenge for ophthalmologists and rheumatologists alike.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Behçet's Disease (BD), also known as Behçet's Syndrome, is a chronic, relapsing, multisystemic inflammatory disorder characterized by vasculitis affecting arteries and veins of all sizes, leading to tissue damage in various organs. While its etiology remains unknown, it is considered an autoimmune disease with a strong genetic predisposition, particularly associated with HLA-B51. The cardinal features include recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, skin lesions, and ocular inflammation. Ocular involvement, particularly posterior segment disease, is a major cause of severe vision loss and blindness.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Risk Factors
content: **Geographic Distribution (Silk Road Disease)**: Highest prevalence along the ancient Silk Road (East Asia, Middle East, Mediterranean basin).
**Prevalence**:
- Turkey: 80-420 cases per 100,000 (highest worldwide)
- Japan: 10-15 cases per 100,000
- Europe/USA: 0.1-7.5 cases per 100,000
**Incidence**: Varies geographically, generally low in Western countries.
**Age of Onset**: Typically young adults, 20-40 years (peak 3rd decade). Rarely seen in children or elderly.
**Gender**: Overall incidence similar, but males tend to have more severe disease, especially ocular involvement, and a worse prognosis in endemic areas.
**Risk Factors**: Genetic predisposition (HLA-B51, MICA, ERAP1 alleles), environmental triggers (e.g., infections like Streptococcus sanguis, Herpes Simplex Virus), smoking.

branches: - **HLA-B51**: Strongest genetic association (relative risk ~5-6). Involved in antigen presentation.
- **MICA (MHC class I chain-related gene A)**: Also associated, involved in NK cell activation.
- **ERAP1 (Endoplasmic Reticulum Aminopeptidase 1)**: Modifies peptides presented by HLA-B51.
- Systemic pan-vasculitis affecting arteries and veins of all sizes, leading to thrombosis and aneurysms.
- Predominantly T-cell mediated (Th1 and Th17 cells) inflammatory response.
- Neutrophil hyperfunction: Enhanced chemotaxis, phagocytosis, oxidative burst.
- Endothelial dysfunction: Increased adhesion molecule expression (VCAM-1, ICAM-1).
- Pro-inflammatory cytokines: Elevated TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, IL-17, IL-21, IL-23.
- Infectious agents (e.g., Streptococcus sanguis, HSV-1) may trigger immune response via molecular mimicry in genetically predisposed individuals.
- Heat shock proteins (HSPs): Cross-reactivity between microbial HSPs and human HSPs may initiate autoimmunity.

rows: Minor or major aphthous ulcers or herpetiform ulcers, observed by physician or patient, recurring at least 3 times in 12 months.
Aphthous ulcers or scarring, observed by physician or patient.
Anterior uveitis, posterior uveitis, or retinal vasculitis, observed by ophthalmologist.
Erythema nodosum (past or present), pseudofolliculitis, papulopustular lesions, or acneiform nodules (not attributable to other causes).
Physician-read papule >2mm 24-48 hours after sterile needle prick (often on forearm).

branches: **Oral Ulcers** (nearly universal, 98-100%): Recurrent, painful, round/oval with erythematous halo, shallow/deep, on lips, tongue, buccal mucosa, palate, pharynx. Heals in 1-3 weeks, may scar.
**Genital Ulcers** (60-80%): Painful, similar to oral ulcers, on scrotum, penis, labia majora/minora, vagina, perineum. Often scar.
- Erythema Nodosum-like lesions: Tender red nodules, mainly on legs, but can be anywhere.
- Pseudofolliculitis/Papulopustular lesions: Sterile pustules, acneiform nodules.
- Pathergy Phenomenon: Hyperreactivity of skin to trauma (sterile needle prick).
**Arthritis** (50-60%): Non-erosive, asymmetric, oligoarticular, affecting large joints (knees, ankles, elbows, wrists). Self-limiting.
- Venous thrombosis: DVT, Budd-Chiari syndrome, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, superior/inferior vena cava occlusion.
- Arterial lesions: Aneurysms (pulmonary artery most common), occlusions.
- Parenchymal: Brainstem lesions, meningoencephalitis, pyramidal signs, ataxia, cognitive dysfunction.
- Non-parenchymal: Cerebral venous thrombosis, intracranial hypertension.
**Gastrointestinal (GI) Involvement** (5-15%): Ulcers (ileocecal region most common), abdominal pain, diarrhea, bleeding, perforation.

sections.title: 6. Ocular Features & Examination Findings
content: **Prevalence**: 50-90% of patients, often bilateral.
**Anterior Uveitis (AU)**: Recurrent, non-granulomatous, severe.
- Cells and flare in anterior chamber (AC), keratic precipitates (KPs).
- **Hypopyon**: Classic sign, often transient and shifting (in 1/3 of cases).
- Fibrinous exudates, posterior synechiae, iris nodules.
- Secondary glaucoma, complicated cataract are common.
**Posterior Uveitis (PU)**:
- **Retinal Vasculitis**: Obliterative and non-obliterative. Perivascular sheathing (white cuffing), retinal hemorrhages, exudates, branch retinal artery/vein occlusions.
- **Vitritis**: Inflammatory cells in vitreous.
- **Macular Edema**: Cystoid macular edema (CME) is a major cause of vision loss.
- **Optic Neuropathy**: Optic disc edema, hyperemia, followed by secondary optic atrophy.
- Neuroretinitis.
**Panuveitis**: Coexistence of AU and PU is common.
**Less common ocular findings**: Scleritis, episcleritis, orbital inflammation, extraocular muscle paresis.

**Ocular Examination Findings**: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (AC reaction, KPs, hypopyon, synechiae), fundoscopy (vitreous haze, vasculitis, hemorrhages, CME, optic disc appearance), gonioscopy (anterior synechiae, angle neovascularization).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **1. Clinical Assessment**: Detailed history of recurrent oral/genital ulcers, skin lesions, ocular symptoms, and systemic features.
**2. Ophthalmic Examination**: Full dilated eye exam including slit-lamp, gonioscopy, and indirect ophthalmoscopy to assess for characteristic uveitis, vasculitis, and their complications.

**3. Pathergy Test**: Intradermal sterile needle prick (20-gauge) into the forearm. Positive if a papule or pustule ≥2mm forms within 24-48 hours. Highly specific (90-98%) but sensitivity varies geographically (60-70% in Turkey, lower in Europe/USA).
**4. Laboratory Tests (Non-specific)**:
- **Inflammatory Markers**: ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate), CRP (C-reactive protein) may be elevated during flares but are non-specific.
- **HLA-B51 Typing**: Performed by PCR. Presence supports diagnosis but is not diagnostic (present in 15-20% of general population). Negative HLA-B51 does not rule out BD.
- **Autoantibody Screening**: ANA, RF, ANCA, anti-dsDNA usually negative (to rule out other autoimmune conditions).
- **Infection Screening**: Syphilis serology (VDRL/RPR, FTA-ABS), TB skin test/IGRA, Lyme serology to rule out masquerade syndromes.
**5. Ocular Imaging**:
- **Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA)**: Crucial for evaluating retinal vasculitis (leakage, non-perfusion, vessel occlusion), optic disc leakage, and macular edema.
- **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**: Detects and quantifies macular edema (CME), epiretinal membranes, and neuroretinal thinning (indicating optic atrophy).
- **Ocular Ultrasound (B-scan)**: Useful in cases of dense vitreous hemorrhage or opacities precluding fundus view to assess for retinal detachment or other posterior segment pathology.
**6. Systemic Imaging (if indicated)**:
- **Brain MRI**: For suspected Neuro-Behçet's (parenchymal lesions, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis).
- **Vascular Imaging (CT/MR Angiography, Doppler Ultrasound)**: For suspected arterial aneurysms or venous thrombosis.
