sections.content:
DKA MANAGEMENT: 1. ABC, 2. Two large bore cannulae, 3. Fluid resuscitation, 4. VBG/Glucose/Labs, 5. Insulin infusion 0.1unit/kg/h, 6. Monitor ketones hourly, 7. Start LMWH, 8. 10% glucose when glucose <14mmol/L to avoid hypoglycemia. 

HYPOGLYCEMIA: 15-20g quick acting carb, or IV glucose 10% 200ml/15min, or Glucagon 1mg.

HHS: Rehydrate slowly over 48h, replace K+, insulin only if blood glucose not falling or ketonaemia exists.

sections.title: Causes of Horner Syndrome: Anatomical Localization

branches: Central (1st Order): Brain stem (stroke, tumor, demyelination), Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, Cervical spinal cord lesion, Diabetic autonomic neuropathy
Preganglionic (2nd Order): Pancoast tumour, Carotid and aortic aneurysm, Thoracic spinal cord lesion, Miscellaneous neck lesions (thyroid tumour, enlarged lymph nodes, trauma, postsurgical)
Post-ganglionic (3rd Order): Internal carotid dissection, Nasopharyngeal tumour, Cavernous sinus mass, Otitis media, Cluster headache, Migrainous neuralgia
Special Variants: Bilateral Horner (Cervical spine surgery or Diabetic neuropathy)

sections.title: Clinical Features & Red Flags
content: PAINFUL HORNER SYNDROME: Should raise the immediate possibility of Carotid Dissection
Anisocoria is accentuated in DIM LIGHT (Lag in dilation)
Mild Ptosis (1-2mm superiorly) + Slightly elevation of inferior lid (Inferior Ptosis/Upside-down ptosis) due to weakness of inferior tarsal muscle
Hypochromia/Heterochromia: Seen if congenital or long-standing
Reduced ipsilateral sweating: Only if the lesion occurs below the superior cervical ganglion
Systemic Exam: Check Cranial Nerves, Peripheral Nervous System (T1 grip strength), Neck, and Regional Lymph Nodes (Neurologist referral often indicated)

content.explanation: P: Ptosis (Superior and Inferior/Müller's muscle); A: Anhidrosis (Reduced sweating); M: Miosis (Constricted pupil).

rows: Alpha-1 receptors are upregulated in denervated dilator pupillae (Denervation Supersensitivity)
Horner pupil will dilate, ptosis improved. Check at 30 min; if -ve, recheck after 45 min. Latent period: 7 days before +ve.
Blocks reuptake of Noradrenaline (NA) at nerve endings. Accumulates NA in normal pupils.
Horner pupil will NOT dilate (no NA being secreted). Normal pupil dilates.
Potentiates release of NA from functional post-ganglionic nerve endings.
Post-ganglionic Horner will NOT dilate (No NA available to release). Pre-ganglionic/Central will dilate.
Direct alpha-agonist; acts on denervation hypersensitivity of local motor nerve.
10-day established Post-ganglionic: Dilates and ptosis relieved. Central/Preganglionic: Both will NOT dilate.

sections.title: Adie Tonic Pupil: Pathophysiology & Signs
content: Pathology: Denervation of post-ganglionic parasympathetic supply to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle; may follow viral illness or occasionally AD inheritance.
Sites of dysfunction: Ciliary ganglion; in Holmes-Adie syndrome, dorsal root ganglion is involved in reflex pathways.
Demographics: Female predilection; initially one eye, second eye involvement typically develops within months/years.
Symptoms: Anisocoria, blurring of near vision.
Signs: Large regular pupil; Direct light reflex is absent or sluggish.
Vermiform movements of the pupillary border (segmental palsy).
Consensual response: Constriction absent or sluggish in response to light stimulation of fellow eye.
Light-Near Dissociation: Pupil responds to near, but re-dilatation is very slow.
Accommodation: Tonicity with slowed/impaired focusing for near and prolonged refocusing in the distance.
Long-standing: May become small ('Little Old Adie').

sections.title: Adie Pupil: Associations & Management
content: Holmes-Adie Syndrome: Tonic pupil + decreased lower limb deep tendon reflexes.
Ross Syndrome: Tonic pupil + excessive sweating.
Other Associations: Orthostatic hypotension, bowel obstruction, urinary retention.
Testing: 0.1-0.125% Pilocarpine leads to constriction of abnormal pupil (Denervation Hypersensitivity).
Screening: Syphilis serology should be checked in patients with bilateral tonic pupils.
Treatment: Reading glasses, Sunglasses, Low-conc Pilocarpine drops for cosmetics/photophobia, Thoracic sympathectomy for sweating.

rows: ~1mm difference in 20% of population. Asymmetry persists to same proportion in different light levels.
Anisocoria greater in dim light. Associated ptosis and dilation lag.
Large pupil, sluggish light reflex, segmental vermiform movements, 0.125% pilocarpine sensitivity.
Does NOT constrict in bright light, on accommodation, or to any concentration of pilocarpine.
Neurosyphilis. Small, irregular, light-near dissociation. No response to 0.1% pilocarpine.

sections.title: Argyll Robertson Pupil (ARP)
content: Cause: Neurosyphilis.
Lesion: Dorsal midbrain.
Classic Feature: Light-Near Dissociation (Accommodates but does not react).
Darkness: Both pupils do not dilate well.
Bright Light: Neither pupils constrict.
Accommodation: Both constrict.
Pharmacology: After 0.1% pilocarpine, neither pupil constricts (Distinguishes ARP from long-standing Adie).

sections.title: Visual Fields & Chiasmal Anatomy
content: 1. Lower Nasal Optic Nerve Fibers: Traverse the chiasm inferiorly and anteriorly. Lesion leads to Bitemporal Superior Quadrantanopia (Often asymmetrical).
2. Upper Nasal Fibers: Traverse the chiasm high and posteriorly. Lesion leads to Bitemporal Inferior Quadrantanopia (e.g., Craniopharyngioma).

3. Junctional Scotoma: Simultaneous involvement of one optic nerve + contralateral inferonasal fibers looping forward (Knee of Wilbrand). Results in Central/Paracentral defect + Contralateral Superotemporal defect.
4. Macular Fibers: Decussate throughout chiasm but concentrated posteriorly. Lesion leads to Bitemporal hemianopic changes in central/paracentral fields.
5. Note: Field defects depend on location, direction of enlargement, and anatomical relationship between pituitary and chiasm.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis of Bitemporal Defects
content: 1. Dermatochalasis
2. Tilted disc
3. Optic nerve coloboma
4. Nasal retinoschisis
5. Retinitis pigmentosa
6. Functional non-physiological visual loss

sections.title: Management of Pituitary Adenoma
content: Step 1: Observation (Silent tumours)
Step 2: Medical Therapy (Initial step for size/secretion reduction: Cabergoline, Older Bromocriptine, Somatostatin analogues like Octreotide + Hormonal correction)
Step 3: Surgery (Transsphenoidal tumour debulking)
Step 4: Radiotherapy (Stereotactic radiotherapy)
Step 5: Monitoring (Serial assessment of visual function)

sections.title: Clinical Sign: Wernicke Hemianopic Pupil
sections.content: An optic tract lesion may give rise to an afferent pupillary conduction defect known as the Wernicke hemianopic pupil. In this condition, the pupillary light reflex will be normal when the unaffected hemiretina is stimulated and absent when the involved hemiretina is stimulated.

sections.title: TOXOPLASMOSIS: Indications & Management
content: **Indications for Treatment:**
• Sight treating lesion involving macula, papillomacular bundle, optic disc, or major blood vessels
• Severe vitritis
• Active ocular toxoplasmosis in the immunocompromised
**Treatment Modalities:**

1. **Triple Therapy:** Prednisolone 1mg/kg + Pyrimethamine (75-100mg for 1-2 days, then 25-50mg daily for 4 weeks) + Folinic Acid (5mg 3x/week) + Sulphadiazine (1g 4x/day for 3-4 weeks). *Sometimes Clindamycin is added.*
2. **Intravitreal Therapy:** Clindamycin + Dexamethasone 400 microgram.
3. **Azithromycin Regimen:** Azithromycin 250-500mg daily + Pyrimethamine + Folinic Acid + Prednisolone.
4. **Quadruple Therapy:** Clindamycin 300mg 4x/day added to Triple Therapy.
5. **Co-trimoxazole:** (Bactrim/Septra) is an alternative option.
6. **Anterior Uveitis:** Topical steroids and mydriatics.
7. **Pregnancy:** Spiramycin or Azithromycin with steroids.
8. **Surgical:** Vitrectomy.
9. **Recurrence Prevention:** Co-trimoxazole 3x for 12 months.

sections.title: CMV RETINITIS: HIV & Immunocompromised Protocol
content: • **Interdisciplinary Care:** Liase with infectious disease specialist.
• **HAART:** Antiretroviral therapy is the mainstay; discontinue when CD4 count >100-150 cells/µl.
• **Systemic Induction:** Valganciclovir 900mg twice daily for up to 3 weeks.
• **Systemic Maintenance:** Valganciclovir 900mg/day.
• **Intravitreal Injections (High Risk Lesions):** For lesions near macula or optic nerve: Ganciclovir (2mg), Foscarnet (1.2mg), or Cidofovir (20mg).
• **Surgical/Adjunct:** Vitrectomy + endolaser demarcation + silicone oil tamponade; Steroids.

rows: ≥1 foci of full-thickness necrosis; discrete borders
Multiple foci of deep retinal opacifications; may be confluent

sections.title: Stages of PORN
content: Stage 1 (Early): Multifocal homogenous yellow-white deep retinal infiltrates; macular involvement (cherry red spot).
Stage 2 (Established): Rapid spread; full thickness necrosis and perivenular translucency.
Stage 3 (Late): Retinal atrophy, optic atrophy, rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

sections.title: Treatment of Viral Retinitis & Uveitis
content: **ARN Management:**
1. IV Acyclovir 15mg/kg for 10-14 days, followed by 800mg 5x/day for 6-12 weeks.
2. Oral Valaciclovir/Famciclovir: Induction 2g 3x/day; Maintenance 1g 3x/day.
3. Systemic Steroids: 24h after antiviral initiation (severe cases).
4. Surgery: Vitrectomy + silicone oil tamponade.
**HSV Anterior Uveitis:**
• Topical steroids 4x/day + cycloplegic.
• Oral Acyclovir 400mg 5x/day.
• Treat raised IOP as necessary.
**Recurrent VZO Uveitis:**
• Oral Acyclovir 800mg 5x/day.

sections.title: INVESTIGATION: Tuberculosis (TB)
content: • **Skin Test:** Positive Tuberculin test within 48h.
• **T-spot.TB:** Counts antimycobacterial effector T-cells (IFN-gamma); detects latent TB.
• **IGRA:** Interferon Gamma Release Assay.
• **Sputum:** Testing with PCR.
• **Imaging:** Chest X-ray, CT, PET scan.
• **Ocular Sampling:** Aqueous/Vitreous smear (Acid-fast bacilli, Ziehl-Neelsen stain) and culture (Lowenstein-Jensen medium).
• **Imaging (Ocular):** OCT (macula eval), FA (active choroiditis, ischemia, NV), FAF (lesion activity/healing staging).
• **Systemic:** HIV status MUST be determined.

sections.title: SYPHILIS: Systemic Manifestations
content: Primary Syphilis: Painless ulcer (Chancre) on genitalia/anus.
Secondary Syphilis: Maculopapular rash + systemic manifestation.
Latent Syphilis: Asymptomatic period.
Tertiary Syphilis: Cardiovascular (Aortitis), Neurosyphilis, Gummatous infiltration of bone/viscera.

sections.title: MEWDS (Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome)
content: • **Demographics:** Young adult females; Acute onset; Monocular.
• **Cause:** Idiopathic; 25-50% viral prodrome/flu vaccine.
• **Symptoms:** Painless blurring, photopsia, dyschromatopsia, scotoma.
• **Signs:** Orange granular fovea (characteristic), deep grey-white patches sparing fovea, disc edema.
• **Imaging:** VF (enlarged blind spot), FA (early hyperfluorescence/late staining), FAF (hyper-AF spots), OCT (Ellipsoid zone disruption).
• **Prognosis:** Spontaneous improvement by 8-10 weeks.

sections.title: APMPPE: Placoid Pigment Epitheliopathy
content: • **Demographics:** Young/Middle age; M=F; Subacute bilateral.
• **Signs:** Large yellow-white placoid lesions; mild vitritis.
• **CNS Risk:** Cerebral vasculitis (Requires CNS imaging/LP if neuro symptoms present).
• **Imaging:** FA (Early 'Block', Late 'Stain'), ICGA (Early/Late Hypofluorescence).
• **Poor Prognosis Factors:** Age >60, Unilateral, Interval >6m between eyes, Recurrence, Choroidal vein leakage.
• **Treatment:** Steroids (macular involvement), Steroids + Ciclosporine (Cerebral vasculitis).

sections.title: Serpiginous Choroidopathy
content: • **Demographics:** Middle age; Male > Female; Bilateral asymmetrical.
• **Symptoms:** Blurring, Metamorphopsia.
• **Signs:** Active grey-white lesions; chronic progression to scalloped atrophy; macular NV.
• **Workup:** MUST test for Syphilis and TB.
• **Imaging:** FAF (Hyper-AF edges in active disease; dark/hypo-AF if inactive).
• **Treatment:** Oral/IV Steroids, Immunosuppressants, Infliximab.

sections.title: Idiopathic Multifocal Choroiditis (MFC)
content: • **Demographics:** Young-middle aged women; Bilateral/Chronic recurrent.
• **Signs:** 50-350µm ovoid lesions; 'histoplasmosis-like' pigmented borders; Vitritis common; Linear clusters/streaks.
• **Complications:** Macular CNV (25-35%), CMO, Subretinal fibrosis.
• **Imaging:** ICGA (Hypofluorescent acute lesions), OCT (Sub-RPE material), VF (Enlarged blind spot).
• **Treatment:** Systemic/Local steroids, Immunosuppressants (MMF, Tacrolimus, Cyclosporine), Anti-VEGF for CNV.

sections.title: PIC (Punctate Inner Choroidopathy)
content: • **Demographics:** Young myopic women; 80% Bilateral/Asymmetrical.
• **Signs:** Small yellow-white macular spots; **NO VITRITIS** (or very mild). Atrophic scars with little pigment.
• **Imaging:** OCT (Acute hyperreflective material), ICGA (Midphase hypo-AF; choroidal vasculitis signs).
• **Treatment:** Treat CNV (Anti-VEGF/Steroids), Systemic immunosuppression for recurrence.

sections.title: Birdshot Retinochoroidopathy
content: • **Demographics:** Middle aged women; Chronic bilateral; HLA-A29 associated.
• **Symptoms:** Nyctalopia, floaters, dyschromatopsia.
• **Signs:** Cream-colored ovoid patches (<1 DD) in post-pole/mid-periphery; Vitritis; CMO.
• **Imaging:** FA (Vascular leakage, foveal sparing CMO), ERG (Rod/Cone abnormalities over time).
• **Treatment:** Subtenon steroids (40mg Triamcinolone), Systemic steroids + Immunomodulators (MMF, Infliximab).

sections.title: AZOOR (Acute Zonal Occult Outer Retinopathy)
content: • **Demographics:** Young/Middle aged women.
• **Symptoms:** Acute onset photopsia and zone-like visual field loss.
• **Signs:** Fundus often normal initially; later RPE clumping, vessel attenuation, peripapillary atrophy.
• **Imaging:** ERG (Severely reduced light rise, delayed 30Hz flicker, Cone > Rod), OCT (Loss of outer retina zones).
• **Treatment:** No proven treatment; Favorable outcomes reported with systemic steroids.

sections.title: MASTER COMPARISON: Idiopathic White Dot Syndromes

rows: Large yellow-white placoid lesions; mild vitritis
OCT: CNV risk; ICGA: Midphase hypo-AF
ERG Rod/Cone delay; ICG: Numerous lesions
Photopsia; Outer retinal loss; Minimal vitritis

sections.title: CLINICAL RED FLAGS: Immediate Action Required
content: NEUROSYPHILIS: Any ocular syphilis warrants consideration of neuro-involvement.
CEREBRAL VASCULITIS: APMPPE patients with headaches require immediate CNS imaging (MRI/LP).
TB-SAMPLING: Ocular TB requires Aqueous/Vitreous culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium.
CMV CD4 COUNT: Screening every 3 months is mandatory if CD4 < 50 cells/µl.
TOXO IN PREGNANCY: Use Spiramycin or Azithromycin with steroids instead of standard triple therapy.

sections.title: Crucial Wilms Tumor Surveillance Schedule
content: Mandatory for ALL patients with sporadic aniridia: Abdominal Ultrasonography
1. Every 3 months until age 5 years
2. Every 6 months until age 10 years
3. Annually until age 16 years OR until molecular genetic analysis confirms absence of WT1 gene

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Aniridia Management
content: Monitor for Aniridic Keratopathy (limbal stem cell deficiency).
Check for foveal hypoplasia via OCT to explain poor visual acuity.
Glaucoma occurs in 50-75% of cases; monitor IOP and discs regularly.
Progressive lenticular changes (cataracts) are common.

sections.title: Diode Laser Photocoagulation: Clinical Profile
content: **Indications:**
• Raised IOP in poor vision patients
• Pain relief in blind eye with raised IOP
• Uncontrolled secondary glaucoma
• Unsuccessful glaucoma filtration surgery or drainage implantation
**Post-Procedure Complications:**
• Transient IOP rise (spike)
• Chronic hypotony
• Phthisis bulbi
• Suprachoroidal haemorrhage
• Corneal decompensation
• Retinal detachment

sections.title: Trabeculectomy: Indications & Failure Risks
content: **Indications:**
• Failure of conservative therapy to achieve IOP control
• Progressive deterioration despite adequate IOP control (including poor compliance)
• Primary therapy in a young patient with advanced disease
• Patient preference
**Risk Factors for Failure:**
• Previous failed trabeculectomy or MIGS
• Previous conjunctival or cataract surgery
• Secondary glaucoma
• Demographic: Black race, under 65 years
• Topical sympathomimetics use for over 3 years

rows: Alkylating agent; inhibits fibroblast proliferation and suppresses vascular ingrowth. Dose: 0.2mg/ml for 2 min (0.4mg/ml in high risk).
Retards DNA synthesis (inhibits fibroblasts). Intraop: 50mg/ml for 5 min. Postop: 0.1ml of 25mg/ml or 50mg/ml.

sections.title: Post-Trabeculectomy Complications
content: Causes of Shallow AC: Pupillary block, Overfiltration, Malignant Glaucoma
Endophthalmitis Risk Factors: Antimetabolite use, Inferiorly placed bleb, Bleb leak, Blepharitis, Conjunctivitis
Common Pathogens: Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Gram-negative organisms

sections.title: MIGS & Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDD)
content: **MIGS Indications:** Mild-moderate glaucoma (slow loss, modest target 15-17 mmHg); Combined with Phaco/IOL to reduce topical meds.
**GDD Names:** Baerveldt, Ahmed, Molteno 3, Paul
**GDD Indications:** Severe conjunctival scarring; Uncontrolled glaucoma post-trab + MMC; Secondary glaucoma (Aniridia, NVG, ICE, traumatic AC disruption); Certain congenital glaucomas.

**GDD Complications:** Excessive drainage (hypotony + shallow AC); Bleb encapsulation (raised IOP 1-6 weeks post-op); Malposition (endothelial/lenticular touch -> corneal decompensation/cataract); Tube erosion; Early/Late drainage failure; Double vision (extraocular muscle interference).

sections.title: Final Review & Verbatim Notes
sections.content: All content provided has been mapped including specific doses like 0.2-0.5s for iridoplasty, specific pathogens like H. influenza, and surgical details like 12-24 burns for diode TSCPC. Success signs for PI include the 'gush of pigment debris', and for SLT, 'tiny champagne bubbles'. Mechanism for miotics includes pulling the peripheral iris away from the trabecular meshwork via sphincter contraction.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Dacryocystitis is the inflammation and infection of the lacrimal sac, almost invariably occurring secondary to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct (NLDO). It is characterized by a bimodal age distribution and presents as either an acute, life-threatening orbital emergency or a chronic, smoldering condition causing persistent epiphora and discharge. Effective management requires a combination of aggressive antimicrobial therapy and definitive surgical bypass of the obstruction.

rows: S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, B-hemolytic Strep

sections.title: Pathophysiology Flow
content: Step 1: Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (NLDO) - Primary (PANDO) or Secondary (Stone, Trauma).
Step 2: Stasis of Tear Film - Accumulation of tears, debris, and bacteria within the lacrimal sac.
Step 3: Bacterial Proliferation - Stagnant environment promotes rapid growth of normal skin/conjunctival flora.
Step 4: Mucosal Inflammation - Edema and hypervascularity of the sac lining.
Step 5: Abscess Formation - High pressure leads to sac distension and potential rupture into surrounding tissue.

sections.title: Essential Diagnostic Workup
content: External Exam: Check for swelling BELOW the medial canthal tendon (suggests sac vs tumor).
Regurgitation Test: Pressure on sac produces mucoid/purulent reflux from puncta.
Jones I Test: Fluorescein recovery in the nose (negative in obstruction).
Jones II Test: Syringing/Irrigation to identify the site of obstruction.
Probing: Determines 'Hard Stop' (bone/NLD) vs 'Soft Stop' (canalicular obstruction).
Culture/Sensitivity: Vital for selecting narrow-spectrum antibiotics.

sections.title: The DCR Surgical Blueprint
content: 1. Incision: 10-12mm linear incision 8mm medial to inner canthus (External) or Endonasal approach.
2. Exposure: Dissection through orbicularis to reach the medial canthal tendon and lacrimal crest.
3. Periosteal Elevation: Reflecting the lacrimal sac laterally to expose the lacrimal fossa.
4. Osteotomy: Creating a 15mm bone window using a Kerrison Rongeur or drill (removing lacrimal bone and maxilla).
5. Intubation: Passing Bowman probes/Crawford stents through puncta into the nasal cavity.
6. Flap Creation: H-shaped incisions in sac mucosa and nasal mucosa to create anterior/posterior flaps.
7. Anastomosis: Suturing flaps (usually 6-0 Vicryl) to create a permanent bypass track.
8. Closure: Skin closure with 6-0 Prolene or fast-absorbing gut.

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Orbital Cellulitis: Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and decreased vision.
Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis: Bilateral involvement, CN palsies, rapid progression.
Meningitis: Nuchal rigidity, altered mental status.
Sac Abscess Pointing: Spontaneous skin fistulization risk.
Non-resolving Swelling: Suspicion of Lacrimal Sac Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Acute Phase: Warm compresses and digital massage (Crigler maneuver).
Oral Antibiotics: Amoxicillin/Clavulanate (Augmentin) 875mg BID or Cephalexin 500mg QID.
Severe/Febrile: IV Cefazolin or Vancomycin (if MRSA suspected).
Analgesia: NSAIDs (Ibuprofen 400-600mg) for pain and inflammation.
Avoid Irrigation: Never syring/probe during acute infection (risk of spreading sepsis).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Advances
content: Endonasal vs. External: Meta-analyses show equivalent success rates (approx. 90-95%) in experienced hands.
Mitomycin-C (MMC): Use of 0.02% MMC on osteotomy site may reduce ostium cicatrization.
Lacrimal Scintigraphy: Emerging as the gold standard for 'Functional' NLDO vs 'Anatomical'.
Dacryocystoplasty: Balloon dilation is increasingly used for partial stenoses before committing to DCR.

content.explanation: Jones 1 (Primary): If Fluorescein appears in nose after 5 mins, system is patent (Fun!). Jones 2 (Secondary): If syringing forces fluorescein into nose, it was a functional block. If clear saline, it's a complete anatomical block (True blockage).

sections.title: Post-Operative Complications
content: Hemorrhage: Severe epistaxis (often from the angular vein or sphenopalatine artery).
Stent Prolapse: Crawford tubes looping out of the medial canthus.
Cicatricial Failure: Ostium closure due to excessive scarring.
Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Leak: Rare, caused by accidental ethmoid roof penetration.
Canalicular Cheese-wiring: Stents cutting through the punctal tissue.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: A mucocele is sterile; a dacryocystitis is infected. Treat the infection before the surgery.
Always palpate for the medial canthal tendon. If the mass is above the tendon, think MALIGNANCY until proven otherwise.
In congenital cases, 90% resolve by age 1 with massage. Do not rush to probe unless dacryocystocele (amnentocele) is present.
Check the nose! 15% of DCR failures are due to unrecognized nasal pathology (septal deviation, polyps, or synechiae).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Mechanism
sections.content: Papilledema is optic disc swelling secondary to raised intracranial pressure (ICP). It is almost always bilateral. Pathophysiology: Axoplasmic flow stasis at the lamina cribrosa due to increased CSF pressure in the subarachnoid space surrounding the optic nerve. In a 12-year-old, this necessitates rapid exclusion of intracranial mass, hydrocephalus, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH).

rows: Bilateral, venous tortuosity, flame hemorrhages, obscured margins
Unilateral, pain with eye movement, RAPD, central scotoma
Altitudinal field loss, disc pallor, older age
Blood and thunder fundus, intraretinal hemorrhages
Anomalous discs, absent spontaneous venous pulsations (SVP) not always reliable

sections.title: Red Flags for Pediatric Disc Edema
content: Presence of sixth nerve (abducens) palsy (lateral rectus weakness)
Morning headaches associated with vomiting
Pulsatile tinnitus
Neurological focal deficits or altered mental status
Failure to thrive or growth disturbances (suggesting hypothalamic involvement)

branches: True Papilledema: Hyperemia, obscured vessels, SVP absent
Disc Drusen: Buried early, visible calcification later, SVP present, crisp margins
Hyperopia/Crowded Discs: Small disc size, normal retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Complete ophthalmic exam (BCVA, Color vision, Pupils for RAPD).
Step 2: Fundus Photography and OCT of the RNFL (look for thickening).
Step 3: B-Scan Ultrasound (detecting high reflectivity of drusen).
Step 4: Neuroimaging (MRI Brain + Orbit with/without contrast + MRV).
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture (if MRI is negative to measure opening pressure).

sections.title: Long-term Sequelae of Optic Disc Drusen
content: Progressive calcification and enlargement of drusen
Superficial neovascularization at the disc
Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) risk
Visual field constriction (nasal steps or arcuate defects)
Gradual retinal nerve fiber layer thinning

content.explanation: Vascular, Infection, Neoplasm, Degenerative, Iatrogenic/Intracranial, Congenital, Autoimmune, Trauma, Endocrine.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Spontaneous Venous Pulsation (SVP): Its presence strongly suggests normal intracranial pressure.
OCT RNFL values: >120 microns usually indicates pathological swelling.
Optic Disc Drusen: Highly reflective on ultrasound; look for a 'shadowing' effect.
IIH Management: In pediatric populations, weight management and acetazolamide are first-line.

sections.title: Anatomical Pathophysiology: The Chiasmal Junction
sections.content: Pituitary adenomas arise from the sella turcica. As they grow superiorly, they compress the decussating fibers of the optic chiasm (the inferior nasal fibers). This results in the classic bitemporal hemianopia. If the tumor grows anteriorly, it compresses the optic nerves (causing central scotomas); if posteriorly, it compresses the optic tracts (causing homonymous hemianopia).

rows: Early detection due to menstrual cycle changes
Late presentation; often present with macroadenoma/visual loss

sections.title: Red Flags: Neuro-Ophthalmic Emergencies
content: Pituitary Apoplexy: Acute headache, nausea, ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI palsy).
Rapid visual field constriction: Impending chiasmal decompensation.
Anosmia (Foster-Kennedy syndrome variant).
Signs of adrenal crisis: Hypotension, electrolyte imbalance.

content.explanation: Fields (Humphrey/Goldmann), Acuity (Snellen/ETDRS), Motility (CN 3,4,6 status), Endocrine (Hormone panel).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workflow
content: Step 1: Formal Visual Fields (Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2).
Step 2: OCT of Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL) to assess ganglion cell loss.
Step 3: MRI Brain/Sella with and without Gadolinium contrast (Gold standard).
Step 4: Comprehensive Endocrinological profile.
Step 5: Multidisciplinary team review (Neuro-Ophthalmology, Neurosurgery, Endocrinology).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Cabergoline is generally preferred over Bromocriptine due to better side-effect profile.
Always check serum prolactin even in non-secreting tumors to rule out 'Stalk Effect' (compression of dopamine-inhibiting pathways).
The 'Pituitary Stalk Effect' can cause modest prolactin elevations (typically <100-150 ng/mL).
Visual fields should be monitored post-operatively every 3-6 months in the first year.

summary: A comprehensive clinical deep-dive into the pathogenesis, classification, and surgical management of pterygium. This guide focuses on identifying clinical activity, precise grading, and evidence-based surgical protocols to minimize recurrence.

data.summary: A comprehensive clinical deep-dive into the pathogenesis, classification, and surgical management of pterygium. This guide focuses on identifying clinical activity, precise grading, and evidence-based surgical protocols to minimize recurrence.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: A pterygium is a triangular, wing-shaped fibrovascular proliferation of the subconjunctival tissue that extends onto the cornea, crossing the limbus. It is characterized by elastotic degeneration of collagen and fibrovascular proliferation, often involving a focal Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency (LSCD). Pathogenesis involves UV-B induced DNA damage, up-regulation of cytokines (VEGF, TGF-β), and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).

branches: Cap: Halo-like avascular zone at the leading edge
Head: Apex of the triangle, firmly attached to the cornea
Neck: The constricted portion at the limbus
Body: Fleshy portion on the bulbar conjunctiva
Fuchs' Islets: Small white spots near the head representing active precursors
Stocker’s Line: Iron deposition (haemosiderin) at the leading edge

rows: Limbus to midway between limbus and pupillary margin (<2mm)
Extends significantly across the visual axis/central cornea
Episcleral vessels clearly visible underneath the pterygium body.
Episcleral vessels partially obscured by the fibrovascular tissue.
Episcleral vessels totally obscured by the thick body. High recurrence risk.

sections.title: 6. Clinical Signs of Active Growth
content: Presence of Fuchs' Islets (active precursor spots).
Absence of Stocker's Line (Iron line indicates stability).
Marked vascular congestion and 'fleshiness' (Tan T3).
Progressive increase in induced with-the-rule (WTR) astigmatism.
Patient-reported growth over 3-6 months.

rows: Post-trauma/burn; probe can pass under the neck (negative probe test).
Leukoplakic, gelatinous, or papilliform; lacks classic wing shape.
Degeneration limited to conjunctiva; does NOT cross the limbus.
Solid, white-yellow choristoma; usually congenital and inferotemporal.

sections.title: 8. Ocular Examination & Workup
content: Step 1: Visual Acuity and Manifest Refraction (Assess induced astigmatism).
Step 2: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (Evaluate head, neck, body, and T-grade).
Step 3: Corneal Topography (Quantify irregular astigmatism and flattening).
Step 4: Anterior Segment OCT (Measure depth of stromal invasion and thickness).
Step 5: Photography (Serial documentation for monitoring growth).

sections.title: 9. Indications for Surgical Intervention
content: Visual axis involvement (or threat to visual axis).
Induced astigmatism (>1.5D or symptomatic).
Chronic ocular irritation refractory to medical therapy.
Restriction of extraocular motility (Diplopia).
Significant cosmetic disfigurement.

rows: Obsolete due to unacceptably high recurrence.
Gold standard. Usually superior donor site.
Transfers stem cells; ideal for recurrent cases.
Used when conjunctiva must be preserved (e.g., Glaucoma).
Extensive dissection (Hirst technique); high learning curve.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Steps: CAG with Fibrin Glue
content: 1. Topical/Subconjunctival anesthesia (Lidocaine + Epinephrine).
2. Excision of the head (Smooth keratectomy).
3. Wide excision of the body and underlying Tenon's capsule.
4. Measurement of the defect (Bare sclera area).
5. Harvest superior conjunctival graft (thin, no Tenon's).
6. Application of Fibrin Glue (Tisseel/Artiss).
7. Graft placement (Ensure limbal-to-limbal orientation).

sections.title: 12. Adjuvant Therapies
content: Mitomycin C (MMC): 0.02% intraoperatively for 2-3 mins (Risk of scleral melting).
5-Fluorouracil (5-FU): Less potent than MMC; used for 'fleshy' recurrences.
Anti-VEGF (Bevacizumab): Subconjunctival injection to reduce vascularity.
Beta-Irradiation: 15-30 Gray (historical; risk of late scleral necrosis).

content.explanation: Stocker's Line (Iron present), Small Size, Sluggish growth, Sparse vasculature (Atrophic), and Symptoms (Minimal).

sections.title: 14. Post-Operative Management
content: Topical Steroids (Pred Forte 1%): Tapering over 4-8 weeks to prevent recurrence.
Topical Antibiotics (Moxifloxacin): 1 week duration.
Lubricants: Preservative-free for 3-6 months.
UV Protection: Mandatory sunglasses for all outdoor activities.

sections.title: 15. Surgical Complications
content: Graft Retraction or Loss (if glue fails).
Pyogenic Granuloma (inflammatory response).
Scleral Melting/Necrosis (secondary to MMC or radiation).
Symblepharon and Diplopia.
Cyst formation or Inclusion cysts at the graft interface.

sections.title: 16. Clinical Pearls & Landmark Wisdom
content: Always measure from the limbus, not the pupillary edge, for consistent grading.
A negative 'Probe Test' (inability to pass a probe under the neck) confirms a true Pterygium.
In recurrent cases, always check the pathology to rule out OSSN.
Fibrin glue reduces surgical time and post-op pain compared to 10-0 Nylon sutures.
The 'Limbal Stem Cell' niche must be respected; don't cauterize the limbus excessively.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED): Clinical Masterclass
summary: Thyroid Eye Disease (Graves' Orbitopathy) is a complex autoimmune inflammatory condition causing orbital remodeling. This guide covers the critical assessment of proptosis, motility, and sight-threatening complications for the ophthalmic clinician.

data.title: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED): Clinical Masterclass
data.summary: Thyroid Eye Disease (Graves' Orbitopathy) is a complex autoimmune inflammatory condition causing orbital remodeling. This guide covers the critical assessment of proptosis, motility, and sight-threatening complications for the ophthalmic clinician.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='100' cy='80' r='40' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M60 80 Q100 20 140 80 Q100 140 60 80' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M85 140 L100 120 L115 140 L100 160 Z' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)'/><text x='100' y='185' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Arial' font-size='12' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' font-weight='bold'>GRAVES ORBITOPATHY</text></svg>

branches: Autoimmune: TSH-Receptor (TSHR) antibodies cross-react with orbital fibroblasts
IGF-1 Receptor: Synergistic activation with TSHR leads to cytokine storm (IL-1, TNF-alpha)
Adipogenesis: Differentiation of fibroblasts into adipocytes (Orbital fat expansion)
GAG Accumulation: Hyaluronan production causes osmotic swelling of Extraocular Muscles (EOMs)
Fibrosis: Chronic phase leads to irreversible muscle scarring and restrictive strabismus

sections.title: Named Lid Signs in TED
content: Dalrymple Sign: Widened palpebral fissure (staring look) in primary gaze.
von Graefe Sign: Lid lag—retardation of upper lid movement on downgaze.
Kocher Sign: Staring/frightened expression on upward fixation.
Bostwick Sign: Jerky lid movements.
Enroth Sign: Edema of the eyelids, especially the upper lid.
Stellwag Sign: Infrequent or incomplete blinking.

sections.title: Sight-Threatening Red Flags
content: Dysthyroid Optic Neuropathy (DON): Occurs in 5% of cases due to apical crowding; look for RAPD and decreased color vision.
Corneal Exposure / Ulceration: Resulting from severe proptosis and lagophthalmos.
Choroidal Folds: Indicates severe orbital pressure or posterior globe compression.
Disc Edema or Pallor: Late signs of optic nerve compression.
Elevated IOP in Upgaze: Indicates severe inferior rectus restriction (>6 mmHg rise).

sections.title: Measuring Proptosis (Exophthalmometry)
content: Step 1: Use a Hertel Exophthalmometer, seating the patient at eye level.
Step 2: Rest the instrument notches on the lateral orbital rims (bi-temporal distance).
Step 3: Measure from the corneal apex to the orbital rim using the internal mirrors.
Step 4: Record the Inter-pupillary distance (Base) to ensure consistency in follow-up.
Step 5: Normal range: 12-20mm (Caucasians), 12-18mm (Asians), up to 24mm (African Americans).
Step 6: Asymmetry >2mm is clinically significant.

rows: Margin Reflex Distance 1 (Upper lid to light reflex)
Margin Reflex Distance 2 (Lower lid to light reflex)
Excursion from extreme down to upgaze
Inability to fully close lids (measured in mm)

sections.title: Assessing Diplopia & Motility
content: EOM Involvement Order: Inferior Rectus (IM) > Medial Rectus (SL) > Superior Rectus > Lateral Rectus.
Binocular Single Vision (BSV) Scoring: Quantify the field of binocular vision using Goldmann Perimetry.
Hess Chart / Lancaster Red-Green: Essential for mapping the paretic/restrictive field.
Prism Cover Test (PCT): Measure deviations in all 9 cardinal positions.
Forced Duction Test (FDT): Positive in TED, confirming mechanical restriction vs. neurological palsy.

rows: Pain during upward, downward, or lateral gaze

branches: Inflammatory: Idiopathic Orbital Inflammation (IOI/Pseudotumor), Sarcoidosis, GPA
Vascular: Carotid-Cavernous Fistula (CCF) - look for corkscrew vessels
Neoplastic: Lymphoma, Leukemia, Metastatic disease (Neuroblastoma in kids)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Serology: TSH, Free T3/T4, TRAb (TSH-Receptor Antibody), Anti-TPO.
CT Orbits (Non-contrast): Look for 'Coke Bottle' sign (EOM belly enlargement sparing tendons).
MRI Orbits: T2-weighted STIR sequences to detect active edema (High signal = Active disease).
Visual Fields: Standard Automated Perimetry (24-2) if DON is suspected.
Color Vision: Ishihara plates or Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue test.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Stage 1: Mild/Inactive: Lubricants, Selenium (100mcg BID), Smoking cessation.
Stage 2: Moderate-Severe Active: IV Methylprednisolone pulses (4.5g total) or Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor).
Stage 3: Sight-Threatening: Urgent Orbital Decompression (3-wall or fat decompression).
Stage 4: Post-Active Phase: Rehabilitative Surgery (Sequence: Decompression -> Strabismus -> Lid).

content.explanation: N: No signs/symptoms; O: Only signs (lid retraction); S: Soft tissue involvement; P: Proptosis; E: Extraocular muscle involvement; C: Corneal involvement; S: Sight loss (Optic nerve).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: Ptosis in a 'Graves' patient? Rule out Myasthenia Gravis (3-5% overlap) or mechanical weight from edema.
Euryblepharon vs TED: TED has lid lag; congenital lid conditions do not.
EOM tendons: Always spared in TED on imaging, unlike Orbital Myositis where tendons are involved.
Smoking is the most modifiable risk factor; it reduces the efficacy of steroids and radiotherapy.
Rundle's Curve: TED typically has an 'active phase' (6-18 months) followed by a 'burnt-out phase'.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Teprotumumab
sections.content: The OPTIC and OPTIC-X landmark trials demonstrated that Teprotumumab (Tepezza), a monoclonal antibody inhibiting the IGF-1 receptor, significantly reduces proptosis (mean 2.82mm reduction), diplopia, and CAS in patients with active TED. Side effects include hearing loss/tinnitus, muscle spasms, and hyperglycemia. It is currently the only FDA-approved medical therapy specifically for proptosis reduction.

data.summary: Brown Syndrome, or Superior Oblique Tendon Sheath Syndrome, is a restrictive motility disorder characterized by a mechanical failure of the eye to elevate in adduction. sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Brown Syndrome is a restrictive ocular motility disorder where the eyeball is mechanically prevented from moving upward when it is turned toward the nose (adduction). It is primarily caused by an abnormality of the Superior Oblique (SO) tendon-trochlea complex, preventing the smooth passage of the tendon through the trochlear pulley.

branches: Acquired: Iatrogenic (Following SO tuck or scleral buckling)

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Deficient elevation in adduction (Primary Sign).
Normal or near-normal elevation in abduction.
Down-shoot of the eye in adduction.
V-pattern exotropia (divergence in up-gaze).
Compensatory head posture (Chin-up and contralateral head tilt).
Positive 'click' or 'snap' felt by the patient in intermittent cases.
Widening of the palpebral fissure on adduction.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Brown vs. IO Palsy
Forced Duction Test (FDT) Protocol
content: Step 1: Instill topical proparacaine or perform under general anesthesia.
Step 2: Grasp the globe at the limbus (usually 6 o'clock and 12 o'clock).
Step 3: Attempt to move the globe into elevation while in the adducted position.
Step 4: Assess for mechanical resistance. In Brown, there is a hard stop.
Step 5: Compare resistance in abduction (should be free).

sections.title: Wright's Grading System
content: Mild: Restricted elevation in adduction; no hypotropia or downshoot in primary position.
Moderate: Restricted elevation in adduction + downshoot in adduction; no hypotropia in primary.
Severe: Marked restriction in elevation in adduction + marked downshoot + hypotropia in primary position.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Hess Chart/Lees Screen: Shows constricted field of elevation in adduction.
High-Resolution MRI (Orbits): To visualize SO tendon thickening or trochlear inflammation.
Blood Work: ESR, CRP, RF, and Anti-CCP if inflammatory etiology is suspected.
Prism Cover Test: In 9 cardinal positions of gaze.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Diagnosis: Confirm mechanical restriction via FDT.
Conservative: Observation if no primary position deviation or abnormal head posture.
Medical: Local corticosteroid injection to the trochlear area (for acquired inflammatory cases).
Medical: Systemic NSAIDs for painful 'clicking' cases.
Surgery: Indicated for significant hypotropia in primary position or severe head tilt.
Post-Op: Immediate aggressive duction exercises to prevent adhesion.

rows: Risk of creating SO palsy; unpredictable.
Maintains tendon direction; reduces SO palsy risk; may extrude or cause granuloma.
Adjustable but can lead to scarring/adhesion.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Considerations
content: Rapid onset of painful motility restriction (Suspect Orbital Myositis).
New onset head tilt in adults (Rule out underlying systemic disease).
Associated Proptosis or Vision Loss (Suspect Neoplasm/Apex Syndrome).
Failure of FDT to show restriction (Re-evaluate for IO Palsy or CN III palsy).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Prep
content: Brown syndrome is 'elevation deficiency in adduction' - remember the SO tendon is too short to allow the eye to go up and in.
The 'True' Brown syndrome is ALWAYS restrictive on FDT.
Simulated Brown Syndrome: Can occur after a scleral buckle or orbital roof fracture.
Surgical overcorrection is common; patients may end up with a Superior Oblique Palsy.

content.explanation: B: Below (Hypotropia in adduction), R: Restrictive FDT, O: Oblique (SO) tendon issue, W: Widening of fissure on adduction, N: Normal elevation in abduction.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Landmark Insights
sections.content: Recent studies using high-resolution dynamic MRI have shown that some cases of 'congenital' Brown are actually associated with SO tendon hypoplasia or abnormal pulleys. Additionally, the use of non-absorbable 'Chicken-beak' silicone expanders (Wright's technique) remains the gold standard for reducing the high rate of iatrogenic SO palsy seen with simple tenotomy.

title: Unraveling Bilateral Ptosis: A 16-Year-Old's Diagnostic Journey

sections.title: Patient Presentation & Initial Inspection
content: **2-Examine 16 years old male patient with Bilateral severe ptosis**.
**By inspection:**
- Apparent ptosis
- No lid crease (classic for congenital ptosis)
- Frontalis overaction (compensatory mechanism)
- No scars
- Orthophoria (no strabismus)
- No anisocoria in light
- No AHP (Abnormal Head Posture)
- No proptosis

sections.title: Comprehensive Ophthalmic Examination
content: **Tests performed in both eyes:**
- MRD1 (Margin Reflex Distance 1)
- MRD2 (Margin Reflex Distance 2)
- Levator excursion (good levator function 17 mm)
**Additional checks requested:**
- Corneal sensation
- Bell’s phenomenon
- Eye closure
**Further findings regarding causes:**
- No anisocoria
- EOM is full (Extraocular Movements)

sections.title: The Diagnostic Conundrum: Suspecting Myasthenia Gravis
sections.content: The discussion continued: 'then ask for causes no anisocoria, EOM is full'. The examiner then asked 'what else in examination'. The student was confused, so the examiner prompted: 'what other cause you suspect'. The student responded: 'I said may be myasthenia gravis'.

sections.title: Specific Tests to Exclude Myasthenia Gravis
content: When asked 'how to exclude' Myasthenia Gravis, the suggested tests were:
- Ice pack test
- Fatigability test
- Cogan twitch sign
The examiner then asked 'how to do Fatigability test , Cogan twitch sign' so the student performed both tests.

sections.title: How to Perform Myasthenia Gravis Tests
content: **1. Ice Pack Test:**
- Apply an ice pack (or ice-filled glove) to the closed eyelids for 2-5 minutes.

- Observe for improvement in ptosis, which is considered positive if lid elevation increases by ≥2 mm. Cold reduces acetylcholinesterase activity, allowing more acetylcholine to act at the neuromuscular junction.
**2. Fatigability Test (for Ptosis):**
- Ask the patient to maintain sustained upgaze (looking up without moving their head) for 30-60 seconds.
- Observe for increasing ptosis (fatigue) or saccadic pursuit movements.
**3. Cogan's Twitch Sign:**
- Ask the patient to rapidly look down from primary gaze, then back to primary gaze.

- Observe for a brief, transient twitch or overshoot of the upper eyelid, followed by a quick return to its ptotic position. This is due to activation of the hyperactive frontalis in an attempt to compensate for weakness, followed by rapid fatigue of the levator.

sections.title: The Final Diagnosis
content: After the examination and tests, the examiner asked 'what your diagnosis'. The student responded: 'I told bilateral congenital ptosis'.

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Levator Function & Ptosis Classification

content.explanation: MRD1 (Margin Reflex Distance 1) measures the distance from the corneal light reflex to the upper lid margin in primary gaze (normal 4-5 mm). MRD2 (Margin Reflex Distance 2) measures the distance from the corneal light reflex to the lower lid margin (normal ~5 mm). Levator Excursion (Levator Function) is the range of upper lid movement from extreme downgaze to extreme upgaze, while the frontalis muscle is immobilized (forehead held). A Levator Excursion of 17 mm is considered **excellent** and strongly suggests intact levator muscle function, directing diagnosis towards aponeurotic or congenital etiologies rather than myogenic or neurogenic causes with poor function. In congenital ptosis, good levator function with absent lid crease often indicates a dystrophic levator muscle, not true paralysis.

rows: Present at birth, often bilateral. Absent/poor lid crease, frontalis overaction, good levator function (dystrophic muscle), chin-up head posture. BPES includes telecanthus, epicanthus inversus, ectropion of lower lids.
Myasthenia Gravis (MG), Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia (CPEO), Oculopharyngeal Muscular Dystrophy (OPMD), Myotonic Dystrophy

MG: Fluctuating ptosis, fatigability (worsens with sustained effort), Cogan's twitch, ophthalmoplegia. CPEO: Symmetrical, slowly progressive ptosis & EOM restriction (often without diplopia), +/- orbicularis weakness. OPMD: Ptosis, dysphagia. Myotonic Dystrophy: Ptosis, facial weakness, Christmas tree cataract, myotonia.
Bilateral Oculomotor Nerve Palsy (rare), Bilateral Horner's Syndrome (very rare)

Oculomotor Palsy: Ptosis with significant EOM restriction (up, down, in), mydriasis. Horner's: Mild ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis. Bilateral presentation of these is highly unusual and suggests systemic neurological pathology (e.g., brainstem lesion, severe trauma).
Most common in elderly, usually unilateral. Good levator function, high lid crease. Rarely bilateral with age or following bilateral cataract surgery/trauma.
Orbital Tumor (e.g., lymphoma), Edema (e.g., thyroid eye disease), Orbital Fat Prolapse
Associated mass, pain, proptosis, restricted EOMs. Ptosis can be due to weight, inflammation, or restriction of levator.
Rapid onset, often associated with systemic neurological signs (e.g., dilated pupils, dysphagia, generalized weakness).
Dermatochalasis (redundant skin), Hypotropia (lower eye gives illusion of ptosis in the other eye), Contralateral lid retraction
Not true ptosis of the levator. Careful examination distinguishes these from true eyelid drooping.

sections.title: Ptosis Red Flags: Urgent Considerations
content: **Acute Onset Ptosis:** Especially if painful or associated with diplopia, headache, pupillary changes (anisocoria, mydriasis). Could indicate aneurysmal compression of CN III (pupil-involving CN III palsy is a neuro-ophthalmic emergency).
**Progressive Ptosis with Diplopia/Weakness:** Suggests neuromuscular junction disorders (Myasthenia Gravis) or progressive external ophthalmoplegia.
**Ptosis with New-Onset Anisocoria:** Horner's syndrome (miosis, mild ptosis, anhidrosis) or CN III palsy (mydriasis, ptosis, EOM restriction).
**Associated with Systemic Symptoms:** Generalized weakness, difficulty swallowing or breathing, speech changes – consider botulism, myasthenia crisis, or other systemic neurological disorders.
**Proptosis or Orbital Signs:** Suggestive of an orbital mass, inflammation, or infection.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A retinal break is a full-thickness defect in the neurosensory retina. These are categorized into 'Tears' (caused by dynamic vitreoretinal traction) and 'Holes' (caused by chronic atrophy). Pigmented or 'barraged' breaks indicate either natural chronicity (RPE hyperplasia) or previous laser photocoagulation aimed at preventing progress to Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD).

sections.title: The Pathophysiology of Pigmentation
content: 1. Retinal Break Formation: Full-thickness defect occurs.
2. Subretinal Fluid (SRF) Entry: Fluid enters the subretinal space.
3. RPE Stimulation: Chronic low-grade fluid or laser trauma stimulates RPE cells.
4. RPE Hyperplasia: Cells migrate and proliferate, producing melanin.
5. Pigmented Barrier: A 'barrage' or seal forms, indicating a 'stable' or 'old' lesion.

rows: Flap of retina pulled anteriorly toward vitreous base.
Round, red, often associated with Lattice Degeneration.
Round hole with a floating 'plug' (operculum) in vitreous.
Disinsertion of retina from the Ora Serrata.

sections.title: Crucial Red Flags (PVD Signs)
content: Shafer’s Sign (Tobacco Dust in anterior vitreous)
Vitreous Hemorrhage (70% risk of associated break)
New onset 'Lightning Bolt' flashes (Photopsia)
Sudden 'Shower' of black floaters
Visual field 'Curtain' or 'Shadow'

sections.title: Indirect Ophthalmoscopy (BIO) Technique
content: 1. Preparation: Maximal pupillary dilation is essential (Phenylephrine 2.5% + Tropicamide 1%).
2. Alignment: Ensure oculars, light source, and 20D lens are in a single visual axis.
3. Peripheral Sweep: Ask patient to look in 8 cardinal directions (Superior, Inf-Temp, etc.).
4. Lens Manipulation: Tilt the lens to overcome reflections and parallax in the far periphery.
5. Scleral Depression: The GOLD STANDARD. Use a depressor to bring the ora serrata and peripheral retina into the field of view.
6. Interpretation: Remember the image is real, inverted, and reversed (up is down, left is right).

branches: Pavingstone Degeneration (Atrophic, white with pigment border)

sections.title: Management Strategy (The 'To Treat or Not' Dilemma)
content: SYMPTOMATIC HST: High priority. Laser photocoagulation immediately.
ASYMPTOMATIC HST: Treat if high risk (myopia, fellow eye RD, aphakia).
SYMPTOMATIC HOLES: Usually monitored unless SRF present.
LATTICE DEGENERATION: Prophylaxis generally NOT indicated unless high-risk factors exist.
ASYMPTOMATIC PIGMENTED BREAK: Observed. Pigment indicates stability.

sections.title: Memory Aid: The 4 'F's of RD Risk

content.explanation: Flashes (Photopsia), Floaters (New/increased), Field loss (Curtain), Falling acuity (Macula off).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: Always check the 'Mirror Image' location (180 degrees away) for another break.
Pigment takes 2-4 weeks to appear after laser or natural demarcation.
Scleral depression increases the contrast between the break and the background (the break looks redder).
If you see a 'Black Spot' that is elevated, consider a small melanoma or pigment clump on a flap.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Trials
sections.content: The AAO Preferred Practice Patterns (PPP) emphasize that asymptomatic retinal breaks, especially round holes and lattice without symptoms, carry a low risk of RD and usually do not require prophylactic treatment. Landmark studies by Byer showed that even in high myopes, the majority of breaks do not progress, shifting the focus to 'Symptom-Driven Prophylaxis'.

sections.title: The 'Bell Rang' - Quick Exam Summary
content: 1. Identify: Superior/Inferior pigmented spots.
2. Locate: Provide clock hour and distance from Ora Serrata.
3. Describe: Pigmentation status (indicates stability/old treatment).
4. Associate: Check for subretinal fluid or traction.
5. Final Dx: 'Stable, barraged retinal break' - No urgent intervention required.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: The fundamental distinction lies at the **Orbital Septum**, a fibrous layer extending from the orbital periosteum to the tarsal plates. **Preseptal Cellulitis** involves the skin and soft tissues anterior to the septum. **Orbital Cellulitis** involves the orbital contents (fat and extraocular muscles) posterior to the septum, representing a surgical emergency.

sections.title: Microbiology & Pathogens
content: Streptococcus pneumoniae (Most common Gram +)
Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA)
Streptococcus pyogenes
Haemophilus influenzae (Decreased post-vaccine era)
Anaerobes: Bacteroides, Fusobacterium (Associated with dental source)
Fungi: Mucor/Aspergillus (Immunocompromised/Diabetics)

content.explanation: Signs of ORBITAL involvement: P for Proptosis, R for Restriction of motility, O for Optic nerve dysfunction (RAPD/Vision loss), P for Pain on eye movement.

rows: Bilateral signs, CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI palsies.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Full Ocular Exam: Check VA, Pupils, Color Vision, and IOP.
2. Laboratory: CBC with diff, Blood cultures (positive in <10% adults, higher in kids).
3. Imaging: CT Orbit/Sinuses with contrast (Gold Standard). Look for fat stranding, abscess, or sinus opacification.
4. Microbiology: Culture any wound drainage or nasal secretions.
5. Lumbar Puncture: Only if meningeal signs are present.

sections.title: Radiological Red Flags (CT/MRI)
content: Displacement of the globe by a fluid collection (Subperiosteal Abscess)
Gas bubbles within the orbit (Anaerobic infection)
Dilation of the Superior Ophthalmic Vein (CST)
Thickening of the Extraocular Muscles
Intracranial extension (Epidural or Brain abscess)

sections.title: Orbital Management Protocol
content: Step 1: ADMIT to hospital for IV antibiotics and close observation.
Step 2: INITIAL ANTIBIOTICS: Ceftriaxone (2g IV q12h) + Vancomycin (15mg/kg q12h) + Metronidazole (for anaerobes).
Step 3: NASAL DECONGESTANTS: Oxymetazoline spray to facilitate sinus drainage.
Step 4: MONITOR: Vision, pupils, and motility every 4-6 hours.
Step 5: SURGERY: If vision worsens, no improvement in 24-48h, or large abscess present.

sections.title: Surgical Indications
content: Decreasing Visual Acuity or worsening RAPD
Large Subperiosteal Abscess (SPA) >10mm or in older children (>9 yrs)
Abscess of the Frontal Sinus
Failure to respond to IV antibiotics within 48 hours
Evidence of Intracranial Extension
Need for diagnostic biopsy (suspected fungus)

branches: Thyroid Eye Disease (usually bilateral, no fever)

sections.title: Pediatric Pearls
content: Children <9 years often have single-pathogen aerobic infections; respond better to medical therapy.
Children >9 years more likely to have polymicrobial/anaerobic infections and higher surgical rates.
Subperiosteal abscesses can be managed medically in very young kids if vision is stable and abscess is small (<10mm).

sections.title: CST: The Deadly Complication
content: Rapidly progressive bilateral involvement
Multiple Cranial Nerve Palsies (III, IV, VI)
Hypoesthesia in V1/V2 distribution
Severe headache and meningismus
High risk of mortality (30%) and permanent morbidity

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The CT scan must include the sinuses; the ethmoid sinus is the primary source in the majority of cases.
If you can't see the eye due to eyelid swelling, get a CT scan immediately.
Pupillary assessment and color vision (using a red bottle cap) are sensitive markers for early optic nerve compression.
Always check for dental pain or recent dental procedures; these favor anaerobic infections.
A 'quiet' eye with proptosis is unlikely to be cellulitis; think neoplasm or TED.

sections.title: 90D Lens Examination Technique
content: Step 1: Patient Setup: Dilate with Tropicamide 1% and Phenylephrine 2.5%. Ensure the room is dark.
Step 2: Alignment: Use a thin slit-beam. Pivot the lens to catch the red reflex. Adjust for the 1.0x (90D) magnification/inversion.
Step 3: Superior-Temporal Sweep: Move the joystick towards the patient's superior-temporal quadrant (Note: Image is inverted/reversed).
Step 4: Sign Identification: Look for the 'wedge-shaped' distribution of hemorrhages radiating from an AV crossing point.
Step 5: Foveal Assessment: Assess for thickening, loss of foveal reflex, or hard exudates (Macular Edema).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Segmental 'Flame-shaped' intraretinal hemorrhages
Dilated and tortuous retinal veins distal to occlusion
Cotton-wool spots (suggesting focal ischemia)
Retinal edema (intracellular and extracellular)
Hard exudates (chronic edema manifestation)
Collateral vessels (develop over 6-12 months crossing the horizontal raphe)

rows: < 5 disc areas of non-perfusion on FFA
> 5 disc areas of non-perfusion on FFA
Can be present if large area involved
Guarded; high risk of Vitreous Hemorrhage

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Quantify Central Macular Thickness (CMT) and detect Subretinal Fluid (SRF).
2. Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Identify areas of capillary non-perfusion, leakage (edema), and NVE.
3. Systemic Workup: Blood Pressure, Fasting Glucose, Lipid Profile.
4. Young Patient Screen: Protein C/S, Antithrombin III, Factor V Leiden, Homocysteine.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Initial Assessment: If VA < 20/40 and ME is present, initiate Anti-VEGF therapy.
Anti-VEGF Regimen: Monthly injections (Aflibercept 2mg or Ranibizumab 0.5mg) for 3-6 months, then Treat-and-Extend.
Steroid Alternative: Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) for pseudophakic patients or those unresponsive to Anti-VEGF.
Observation: If VA is good and ME is minimal, monitor monthly for the first 4 months.
Laser Therapy: Perform Sectoral Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) ONLY if neovascularization (NVD/NVE) develops.

rows: Argon laser grid photocoagulation beneficial for ME with VA 20/40 to 20/200 after 3-6 months.
Ranibizumab significantly improved VA compared to sham for BRVO-associated ME.
Aflibercept superior to grid laser at 24 weeks for VA improvement.
Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) effective but carries risk of IOP spike and Cataract.
Triamcinolone 1mg equal to laser but with more side effects.

sections.title: Complications & Red Flags
content: Neovascularization of the Disc (NVD) or Elsewhere (NVE)
Vitreous Hemorrhage (Sudden new floaters/vision loss)
Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD)
Neovascular Glaucoma (Rare in BRVO vs CRVO, but possible)
Chronic Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) leading to foveal atrophy

content.explanation: B: Blood Pressure control is priority. R: Radial wedge of hemorrhages. V: VEGF inhibitors are 1st line. O: Observe for Ischemia/NV.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Collateral vessels: Do NOT laser them! They are physiological bypasses that help drain the retina.
Macular Ischemia: If VA is poor despite resolved edema on OCT, check FFA for Enlarged Foveal Avascular Zone (FAZ).
The 90-Day Rule: Historically for CRVO, but in BRVO, monitor for NV most closely in the first 6-12 months.
Inverted View: When using 90D, a superior-temporal BRVO appears inferior-nasal through the lens.
Bilateral BRVO: Always prompt a workup for systemic hypercoagulability or vasculitis.

sections.title: Fundamental Principles & Dye Dynamics
content: Sodium Fluorescein (C20H10Na2O5): Low molecular weight (376 Da), 80% protein-bound (albumin), 20% free (fluorescent).
Excitation Peak: 465–490 nm (Blue light filter).
Emission Peak: 520–530 nm (Yellow-green light filter).
Inner Blood-Retinal Barrier (BRB): Non-fenestrated retinal capillary endothelial cells (tight junctions).
Outer Blood-Retinal Barrier: Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) zonula occludens.
Metabolism: Hepatic glucuronidation; Renal excretion (within 24-36 hours).

sections.title: The 5 Phases of the Normal Angiogram

rows: Cilioretinal arteries fill (if present). Patchy 'mottled' choroidal filling due to fenestrated choriocapillaris.
Rapid filling of retinal arteries. Flow is fastest in the center of the vessel.
Complete arterial filling; 'Laminar' flow in veins where dye lines the vessel walls but the center is dark.
Complete filling of veins. Maximum intensity of fluorescence.
Dye intensity fades; Disc staining occurs; Absence of dye in vessels.

branches: Pooling (Sub-retinal or Sub-RPE spaces - CSC, PED)
Leaking (Break in BRB - NVD/NVE, CME, Cystoid spaces)
Staining (Vessel walls, Sclera, Scars, Optic Disc)
Vascular Filling Defect (Capillary non-perfusion, Arterial occlusion, Venous occlusion)

sections.title: Window Defect vs. Leakage: The Critical Distinction
Pooling: Sub-RPE vs. Sub-Retinal
content: Sub-RPE Pooling: Seen in Pigment Epithelial Detachment (PED). Discrete, well-demarcated borders. Fills early and stays bright late.
Sub-Retinal Pooling: Seen in Central Serous Chorioretinopathy (CSC). Indistinct, fuzzy borders. Takes longer to fill than sub-RPE.
Classic CSC Pattern: 'Smokestack' appearance (10%) or 'Ink-blot' appearance (90%).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Anaphylaxis & Emergencies
content: Laryngeal Edema / Stridor: Immediate Epinephrine (0.3mg IM 1:1000).
Severe Hypotension / Shock: Fluid resuscitation and Trendelenburg position.
Bronchospasm: Use Beta-agonists or Aminophylline.
Extravasation of Dye: Can cause local necrosis/phlebitis. Use cold compresses.
Known severe allergy to fluorescein is an absolute contraindication.

sections.title: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) Patterns
content: Early Phase: Subtle leakage from perifoveal capillaries.
Late Phase: Classic 'Petaloid' pattern due to dye accumulation in Henle's layer (Outer Plexiform Layer).
Irvine-Gass Syndrome: Post-cataract surgery CME; features disc leakage + petaloid macula.
Diabetes: Often more diffuse 'honeycomb' appearance.

content.explanation: C: Choroidal, A: Arterial, L: Laminar (AV), V: Venous, R: Recirculation, S: Staining (Late).

sections.title: Management of Adverse Reactions
content: Step 1: Immediate cessation of dye injection if patient complains of itching/shortness of breath.
Step 2: Monitor Vital Signs (BP, HR, SpO2).
Step 3: Mild (Nausea/Vomiting) - Reassurance, deep breathing, emesis basin.
Step 4: Moderate (Urticaria) - Oral or IV Antihistamines (Diphenhydramine 25-50mg).
Step 5: Severe (Anaphylaxis) - 0.3ml of 1:1000 Epinephrine IM; Call Code Blue/EMS; Oxygen 10L/min.

rows: Presence of MA, IRMA, and NVE
Defined Clinically Significant Macular Edema (CSME) and timing for laser.
Laser benefit for extrafoveal/juxtafoveal classic CNVM.
Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) efficacy based on FFA lesion type.
Correlated area of ischemia with visual prognosis in DR.

sections.title: Interpretation Algorithm: The 'Rule of 4'
content: 1. Analyze the Control Image: Look for autofluorescence and pseudofluorescence.
2. Verify the Quality: Check for media opacities (lens/vitreous) and timing.
3. Locate Abnormalities: Is it Hyper or Hypo? Use the Macula as the center reference.
4. Dynamic Evolution: Does the area change in size or intensity from 30s to 5min?

sections.title: Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV) Classification
content: Classic CNV: Well-defined, bright lacy pattern in early phase; intense late leakage that obscures boundaries.
Occult CNV (Type 1): Fibrovascular PED (irregular elevation) or 'Late Leakage of Undetermined Source'.
Retinal Angiomatous Proliferation (RAP - Type 3): Intraretinal hemorrhages and small anastomoses filling from retinal circulation.
Polypoidal Choroidal Vasculopathy (PCV): Best seen on ICG, but FFA shows 'stippled' hyperfluorescence and late pooling.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Fellowship Exams
content: Blocked fluorescence: Blood is the most common cause. Subretinal blood blocks choroidal AND retinal; Intraretinal blood blocks retinal vessels.
The Foveal Avascular Zone (FAZ): Normally 0.5mm; enlargement indicates ischemia (DR, RVO).
Staining vs. Leakage: Staining involves fixed borders (e.g., old scar); leakage involves expanding, fuzzy borders (e.g., active CNV).
Dark Choroid: A classic FFA sign of Stargardt Disease due to lipofuscin accumulation in RPE blocking choroidal flush.

title: Macular Corneal Dystrophy: A Deep Dive into MCD
summary: Macular Corneal Dystrophy (MCD) is a rare, autosomal recessive stromal dystrophy characterized by diffuse corneal haze and ill-defined gray-white opacities. Unlike other stromal dystrophies, it involves the entire corneal thickness and extends to the limbus, significantly impacting vision early in life.

sections.title: Definition & Genetic Basis
content: MCD is a localized manifestation of a systemic error in keratin sulfate metabolism.
Inheritance: Autosomal Recessive (AR) - The 'Odd One Out' among classic stromal dystrophies.
Gene Mutation: CHST6 (Carbohydrate Sulfotransferase 6) located on Chromosome 16q22.
Pathogenesis: Deficiency of corneal sulfotransferase enzyme results in non-sulfated Keratan Sulfate (KS) accumulation.

branches: Severe decrease in Visual Acuity by 2nd-3rd decade
Recurrent corneal erosions (less common than Lattice)
Diffuse stromal haze extending to the LIMBUS

content.mnemonic: Marilyn Monroe Always Gets Her Men
content.explanation: MCD = Alcian Blue (GAGs); Granular = Masson Trichrome (Hyaline); Lattice = Congo Red (Amyloid).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Slit-lamp: Superficial/Deep stromal opacities.
Ground-glass appearance of intervening stroma.
Descemet's Membrane: Guttata-like changes can be seen.
Endothelium: GAG deposits can be found even in the endothelium.
Pachymetry: Shows marked thinning early in the disease.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Clinical Slit-lamp Bio-microscopy
2. Anterior Segment OCT: Hyper-reflective deposits + thinning.
3. Confocal Microscopy: Deposits in keratocytes and extracellular matrix.
4. ELISA: For serum Keratan Sulfate (KS) levels (Type determination).
5. Genetic Testing: CHST6 mutation analysis.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Lubrication and Bandage Contact Lenses (BCL) for erosions.
Step 2: Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK) - Only for very superficial deposits.
Step 3: Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) - If endothelium is spared.
Step 4: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) - Gold standard for full-thickness involvement.
Step 5: Post-operative Monitoring - Recurrence is possible in the graft (from host keratocytes).

sections.title: Surgical Nuances
content: DALK is preferred to avoid rejection, but dissection is difficult due to stromal haze.
PKP has high success rates but carries long-term risk of graft failure/rejection.
Recurrence in MCD is generally slower than in Granular or Lattice dystrophies.
Deposits recur from host keratocytes migrating into the donor tissue.

sections.title: Red Flags & Clinical Warnings
content: MCD has the worst visual prognosis among the classic trio.
Corneal thinning: Be cautious of perforation risk during PKP/DALK.
Systemic symptoms? Unlike Mucopolysaccharidosis, MCD is limited to the eye.
Secondary Glaucoma: Possible post-PKP.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
content: IC3D Classification (2015): Updated MCD to a Category 1 dystrophy (gene known, well-defined).
Gene Therapy: Research into AAV-mediated CHST6 replacement is ongoing in animal models.
Enzyme Replacement: Investigations into topical sulfotransferase mimics.
Large-scale cohort studies in South India (Tamil Nadu) show high prevalence due to consanguinity.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: If you see a haze that reaches the LIMBUS, think Macular Corneal Dystrophy.
If the cornea is THIN, think Macular. If it's normal/thick, think Granular.
MCD is the only AR stromal dystrophy; the rest are usually AD.
MCD deposits are Alcyan Blue positive (G-A-G: Macular, Alcian, GAGs).

title: Horizontal Gaze Palsy: Clinical Mapping & Neuro-Ophthalmic Mastery
summary: Horizontal gaze palsy (HGP) is the inability to move both eyes conjugately in a single horizontal direction, signaling a lesion in the complex circuitry of the frontal eye fields or the pontine gaze centers. This guide provides a deep-dive into the neuroanatomy, etiology, and diagnostic nuances required for resident-level proficiency.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Core Concepts
sections.content: Horizontal Gaze Palsy is a conjugate ocular motility deficit where both eyes fail to move past the midline toward a specific side. Unlike a simple nerve palsy (e.g., VI nerve), HGP involves the 'yoking' mechanism. It results from damage to the supranuclear or nuclear pathways that coordinate the lateral rectus of one eye with the medial rectus of the fellow eye. It is classically divided into Cortical (Frontal Eye Fields) and Brainstem (PPRF/Abducens Nucleus) etiologies.

branches: Frontal Eye Fields (FEF): Generates contralateral saccades
Paramedian Pontine Reticular Formation (PPRF): The 'Gaze Center' for ipsilateral movement
Abducens Nucleus: Contains motor neurons (to LR) and interneurons (to contralateral MR via MLF)
Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF): Cross-brainstem connector to the III nerve nucleus
Superior Colliculus: Integration of visual and motor signals for reflexive saccades

rows: Eyes look TOWARD the lesion ('Wrong' side)
Eyes look AWAY from the lesion ('Right' side)
Intact (Eyes can be driven past midline by Doll's Head)
Absent (Eyes fixed, cannot be driven by Doll's Head)

sections.title: Essential Ocular Examination
content: 1. Observe Primary Position: Note any forced tonic deviation.
2. Assess Saccades: Rapidly move target between horizontal points.
3. Assess Smooth Pursuit: Slow target tracking.
4. Doll's Head Maneuver (VOR): Passive head rotation to differentiate supranuclear from nuclear lesions.
5. Caloric Stimulation: For comatose patients (COWS - Cold Opposite, Warm Same).
6. Bell's Phenomenon: Checking for vertical integrity.

sections.title: Red Flags: Urgent Neurological Threats
content: Acute onset with 'Worst Headache of Life' (Hemorrhage)
Ipsilateral facial nerve (VII) palsy (Pontine lesion)
Altered mental status or GCS drop
Papilledema (Increased intracranial pressure)
Contralateral hemiparesis in an elderly patient (Stroke)

branches: Structures: PPRF (or VI Nucleus) + Ipsilateral MLF
Movement: Only movement remaining is ABduction of contralateral eye

sections.title: HGP with Progressive Scoliosis (HGPPS)
content: Genetics: Autosomal Recessive mutation in ROBO3 (8q12).
Pathophysiology: Failure of crossing of somatosensory and corticospinal tracts.
Radiology: Deep midline pontine cleft (Butterfly sign).
Clinical: Complete absence of horizontal gaze + severe progressive scoliosis in childhood.
Note: Vertical gaze and convergence are typically spared.

rows: Variability, ptosis, and Cogan's lid twitch
Congenital, globe retraction, narrowing of palpebral fissure
Congenital VI and VII nerve palsies, limb defects
GQ1b antibodies, LP for albuminocytologic dissociation
Vertical gaze palsy, mid-dilated pupils, retraction nystagmus

sections.title: Imaging & Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. MRI Brain/Orbit: With and without Gadolinium. High-resolution T2/FLAIR for MS; DWI for acute stroke.
2. MRA/CTA: If vascular etiology (infarct/dissection) is suspected.
3. Lumbar Puncture: If MS (Oligoclonal bands) or Miller-Fisher/Meningitis is suspected.
4. Bloods: ESR/CRP (GCA in elderly), HbA1c, Lipids, RPR (Syphilis).
5. EMG/Jitter: If Myasthenia Gravis is high on the differential.

sections.title: Management Protocols
content: 1. Treat Primary Cause: Thrombolysis for stroke, Corticosteroids for MS or Vasculitis.
2. Prism Therapy: Fresnel or ground-in prisms to shift field if gaze is paretic but not totally absent.
3. Surgical Intervention: Large recession/resection or Transposition (e.g., Nishida) if stable and chronic.
4. Supportive Care: Patching for diplopia, Lubrication if VII nerve involvement (exposure keratopathy).
5. Physical Therapy: Especially for HGPPS patients with scoliosis.

content.explanation: PPRF (Pontine) = 'P' for 'Pushes' eyes AWAY from lesion. FEF (Frontal) = 'F' for 'Friend', eyes look AT their cortical friend (the lesion).

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: Foville Syndrome: Inferior pontine tegmental stroke causing HGP, ipsilateral VII palsy, and contralateral hemiparesis.
Saccadic Dysmetria: Often a precursor or subtle sign of cerebellar/brainstem involvement.
Skew Deviation: Frequently co-exists with brainstem HGP; look for vertical misalignment that does not follow a nerve pattern.
Thalamic Esotropia: Gaze palsy mimicking esotropia ('wrong-way eyes') can occur in thalamic hemorrhages.

sections.title: Foville Syndrome Breakdown
content: Lesion: Dorsolateral Pontine Tegmentum
VI Nerve Nucleus: Ipsilateral HGP
VII Nerve Fibers: Ipsilateral facial weakness
Verve Nerve (V): Ipsilateral facial anesthesia
VIII Nerve: Ipsilateral deafness/vertigo
Corticospinal Tract: Contralateral hemiparesis

sections.title: Recent Landmark Insights
sections.content: Recent studies in 'Nature Genetics' have elucidated the role of ROBO3 as a 'guidance receptor' specifically required for the crossing of axons in the hindbrain. In HGPPS, the failure of the superior cerebellar peduncles to decussate is now a hallmark radiographic finding on DTI (Diffusion Tensor Imaging). Furthermore, the use of Botulinum Toxin in the acute phase of stroke-related deviation is showing promise in preventing contracture of the antagonist muscles while waiting for neuro-recovery.

title: Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (PXF): The Microfibrillopathy Masterclass
summary: Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (PXF) is a systemic, age-related microfibrillopathy characterized by the deposition of white, dandruff-like fibrillar material throughout the anterior segment and visceral organs. It is the most common identifiable cause of open-angle glaucoma worldwide, presenting unique challenges in both medical management and phacoemulsification surgery.
