sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pseudoexfoliation (PXF) is a generalized ordered proteolysis disorder. It involves the production and progressive accumulation of an abnormal fibrillar extracellular material. While visually most prominent on the anterior lens capsule, it is a systemic condition affecting the heart, lungs, liver, and kidneys. Clinically, it manifests as white flaky material on the pupillary margin and lens, leading to secondary open-angle glaucoma (PXG) and significant zonular instability.

sections.title: The Ocular 'Bull's Eye' Anatomy
content: Central Disk: Translucent zone on the anterior lens capsule.
Intermediate Clear Zone: Created by the mechanical rubbing of the iris during miosis/mydriasis.
Peripheral Granular Zone: Often only visible after maximal pupillary dilation; shows a 'hoarfrost' appearance.
Pupillary Margin: White flakes resembling dandruff ('moth-eaten' appearance).
Iris Sphincter: Atrophy leading to 'moth-eaten' transillumination defects at the ruff.

sections.title: Gonioscopy Findings
content: Sampaolesi Line: Pigment deposition anterior to Schwalbe's line.
Hyperpigmentation: Dense, dark, 'tobacco-dust' pigment in the trabecular meshwork.
Narrow Angles: Occurs in ~15% due to anterior lens displacement (zonular laxity).
Dandruff-like flecks in the angle.

sections.title: Pseudoexfoliative Glaucoma (PXG) Profile
content: More aggressive than POAG with higher mean IOP and larger diurnal fluctuations.
Faster rate of progression and greater optic nerve damage at presentation.
Poorer response to medical therapy compared to POAG.
High risk of unilateral presentation initially, with high conversion rate of the fellow eye.

sections.title: Surgical Red Flags: The 'Phaco Nightmare'
content: Poor Pupillary Dilation (Miosis) due to iris stromal fibrosis.
Zonular Dehiscence and Phacodonesis (Lens wobbling).
Spontaneous Lens Subluxation.
Increased risk of Vitreous Loss and Dropped Nucleus.
Capsular Phimosis and IOL Decentration post-operatively.
Corneal Endothelial Vulnerability.

sections.title: Intraoperative Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Mechanical Pupil Expansion (Iris hooks or Malyugin Ring).
Step 2: Liberal use of Cohesive OVD to stabilize the lens and expand the pupil.
Step 3: Carefully sized Capsulorhexis (Not too small, to prevent phimosis).
Step 4: Gentle Hydrodissection (Avoid over-pressurizing the bag).
Step 5: Capsular Tension Ring (CTR) insertion early if zonular instability is noted.
Step 6: Slow-motion Phacoemulsification with reduced parameters.
Step 7: Consider 3-piece IOL if sulcus fixation is required due to posterior capsule rupture.

rows: Mid-peripheral transillumination, younger myopes, Krukenberg spindle.
No PXF material, lower IOP spikes, normal zonules.
Glass wool vitreous opacities, systemic amyloid signs.

content.explanation: S: Sampaolesi line, A: Age-related, M: Miosis (Poor dilation), P: Pigment in angle, A: Aggressive IOP, O: Open angle, L: LOXL1 gene, E: Exfoliation material, S: Subluxation risk, I: Instability of zonules.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Medical: Prostaglandins are 1st line; Aqueous suppressants (Beta-blockers/CAIs) for spikes.
Laser: SLT (Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty) is highly effective due to heavy pigmentation but carries higher risk of post-laser IOP spikes.
Surgical: Trabeculectomy or Tube Shunts have higher failure rates than in POAG; MIGS is an emerging option.

sections.title: Investigation & Workup
content: 1. Dilated Slit Lamp Exam (Gold Standard).
2. Gonioscopy (Vital for grading angle and pigment).
3. Pachymetry (CCT often thinner or normal).
4. Optic Nerve Imaging (OCT RNFL/GCC).
5. Visual Field (24-2 SITA Standard).
6. UBM (if zonular dialysis is suspected).

sections.title: Landmark Study: EMGT
sections.content: The Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT) sub-analysis revealed that PXF is a strong independent risk factor for progression. Patients with PXF progressed twice as fast as those with POAG. Each 1 mmHg of IOP reduction reduced the risk of progression by approximately 10%.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Late IOL-Capsular bag complex dislocation (can occur 5-15 years post-op).
Corneal decompensation due to endothelial PXF deposition.
Higher incidence of Posterior Capsule Opacification (PCO).
Prognosis: Guarded for PXG; requires frequent monitoring of IOP and Visual Fields (every 3-4 months).

title: VKH Syndrome: The Definitive Clinical Guide
summary: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is a multisystemic autoimmune disorder characterized by bilateral granulomatous panuveitis involving the eyes, ears, meninges, and skin. It is driven by T-cell mediated destruction of melanocytes in genetically susceptible individuals.

data.title: VKH Syndrome: The Definitive Clinical Guide
data.summary: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is a multisystemic autoimmune disorder characterized by bilateral granulomatous panuveitis involving the eyes, ears, meninges, and skin. It is driven by T-cell mediated destruction of melanocytes in genetically susceptible individuals.

sections.title: 1. Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is an idiopathic multisystem autoimmune disease directed against melanocyte-associated antigens (tyrosinase, TRP1, TRP2). It manifests as a bilateral, diffuse, granulomatous panuveitis often associated with exudative retinal detachments, neurological (meningismus), auditory (tinnitus/dysacusis), and integumentary (vitiligo/poliosis) signs.

sections.title: 4. The Four Clinical Stages
content: Step 1: Prodromal Stage (Days) — Mimics viral illness; headache, meningismus, tinnitus, CSF pleocytosis.
Step 2: Acute Uveitic Stage (Weeks) — Sudden bilateral vision loss; multifocal exudative RD, optic disc edema, thickened choroid.
Step 3: Convalescent Stage (Months) — Depigmentation; 'Sunset Glow Fundus', Sugiura sign (perilimbal vitiligo), integumentary vitiligo.
Step 4: Chronic Recurrent Stage — Smoldering granulomatous anterior uveitis; Mutton-fat KPs, Busacca nodules, Iris bombe/Glaucoma.

sections.title: 5. Extraocular Manifestations
content: Neurological: Headache, stiff neck, meningeal signs, CSF pleocytosis (>90% in acute stage).
Auditory: Tinnitus, dysacusis, vertigo, high-frequency hearing loss.
Integumentary: Vitiligo (patchy depigmentation), Poliosis (whitening of lashes/hair), Alopecia.

rows: No hx trauma/surgery + Bilateral ocular involvement + Neurological/Auditory signs + Integumentary signs.
No hx trauma/surgery + Bilateral ocular involvement + EITHER Neurological/Auditory OR Integumentary signs.
No hx trauma/surgery + Bilateral ocular involvement ONLY (Isolated Ocular Disease).

sections.title: 8. Multimodal Imaging Pearls
content: FFA: Early pinpoint 'starry sky' leakage, late pooling in subretinal spaces (flower-petal pattern).
ICGA: Hypofluorescent dark spots (HDLs) representing granulomas; delayed choroidal filling.
EDI-OCT: Massive diffuse choroidal thickening (>600-800 microns) in acute stage.
B-Scan: Low-to-medium internal reflectivity choroidal thickening; absence of posterior scleritis signs.

sections.title: 10. Management Protocol
content: Phase 1: Induction — IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day for 3 days) or high-dose oral Prednisone (1.0–1.5 mg/kg).
Phase 2: Slow Taper — Very gradual oral steroid reduction over 6-9 months; do NOT taper faster than 5-10mg/month.
Phase 3: IMT — Early introduction of Mycophenolate Mofetil (1g BID) or Azathioprine to reduce recurrence.
Phase 4: Biologics — Adalimumab or Infliximab for refractory cases failing traditional IMT.

sections.title: 11. Red Flags & Emergencies
content: Rapid tapering of steroids (Primary cause of recurrence)
Development of CNVM (Requires Anti-VEGF)
Secondary Glaucoma (Pupillary block or steroid-induced)
Neurological deterioration despite therapy

content.explanation: S: Sunset glow fundus, K: KPs (mutton-fat), I: Integumentary (Vitiligo/Poliosis), N: Neurological/Noise (Tinnitus).

sections.title: 13. Ocular Complications
content: Cataract: Most common complication (40-50%).
Glaucoma: Angle-closure (ciliary body edema) or Steroid-response.
Subretinal Fibrosis: Occurs in chronic phase; poor visual prognosis.
CNVM: Juxtafoveal choroidal neovascular membranes.

sections.title: 14. Landmark Study: Steroids vs. IMT
sections.content: Recent evidence (e.g., studies by Abu El-Asrar et al.) suggests that early aggressive combined therapy (Steroids + Mycophenolate Mofetil) leads to better long-term visual outcomes and a lower rate of progression to the 'Sunset Glow' stage compared to steroid monotherapy.

sections.title: 15. Clinical Pearls for Rounds
content: Sugiura Sign: Perilimbal vitiligo, the earliest depigmentation sign (often within 1 month).
The 3-Month Rule: Most recurrences happen when Prednisone is tapered below 20mg within the first 3 months.
CSF Pleocytosis: May be present even if the patient has no meningeal symptoms.
Dalen-Fuchs Nodules: Not pathognomonic; seen in VKH, Sarcoid, and Sympathetic Ophthalmia.

title: Stargardt Disease: The ABCA4 Retinopathy Masterclass
summary: Stargardt Disease (STGD1) is the most common inherited juvenile macular dystrophy, characterized by the accumulation of lipofuscin (A2E) within the RPE due to mutations in the ABCA4 gene. This guide provides a deep dive into the clinical findings, the pathognomonic 'dark choroid' on FFA, and current management protocols for residents and fellows.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Retinoid Cycle Failure
content: Step 1: Defective ABCA4 protein fails to transport all-trans-retinal out of the photoreceptor disc.
Step 2: Accumulation of N-retinylidene-phosphatidylethanolamine (PE).
Step 3: Conversion into toxic bis-retinoid A2E within the RPE lysosomal system.
Step 4: RPE cell death due to lysosomal membrane rupture and oxidative stress.
Step 5: Secondary secondary degeneration of overlying photoreceptors (Macular Atrophy).

rows: Pigmentary changes at fovea; No flecks within 1 DD of fovea
Pisciform (fish-tail) flecks beyond 1 DD; may reach nasal to disc
Extensive flecks and RPE atrophy; Beaten-bronze macula
Diffusely resorbed flecks; Extensive chorioretinal atrophy

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Beaten-Bronze Macula: Snail-slime appearance of the fovea.
Pisciform Flecks: Yellow-white, fish-tail shaped subretinal deposits at the level of RPE.
Sparing of the Peripapillary RPE: Often seen in ABCA4-related STGD1.
Bull’s Eye Maculopathy: Late stage appearance of RPE atrophy.
Salt and Pepper Pigmentary Changes: In the peripheral retina of advanced cases.

rows: Normal FFA (No dark choroid), adult onset
History of drug intake, no pisciform flecks
Static night blindness, distinct white dots
Earlier color vision loss, severe photophobia

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging Workup
content: Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): Hyper-AF flecks (active) and Hypo-AF areas (RPE atrophy).
Fluorescein Angiogram (FFA): Look for 'Silent/Dark Choroid' (80% sensitive) due to lipofuscin blocking choroidal flush.
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Loss of Ellipsoid Zone (EZ), RPE thinning, and 'outer retinal tubulations' in late stages.
Electrophysiology: Full-field ERG to determine prognostic category (Group I, II, or III).
Genetic Testing: Confirmation of biallelic ABCA4 mutations.

sections.title: CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATION
content: DO NOT supplement with Vitamin A / Beta-carotene.
Vitamin A fuels the visual cycle and accelerates A2E accumulation/toxicity.
Avoid AREDS formulations containing Vitamin A in these patients.

content.explanation: S: Silent Choroid on FFA; T: Toxic A2E accumulation; A: ABCA4 Mutation (Recessive); R: RPE Flecks (Pisciform); G: Genetics (1p22).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Boards
content: The 'Silent Choroid' occurs because lipofuscin absorbs the blue light of the FFA, preventing visualization of the choroidal flush.
Stargardt is the most common cause of a childhood macular dystrophy.
Vision loss often precedes visible ophthalmoscopic findings ('Phenotype-Genotype lag').
Peripapillary sparing is a hallmark that differentiates STGD1 from other dystrophies.

sections.title: Management & Low Vision Strategy
content: 1. Confirm diagnosis via genetic testing (ABCA4) and multimodal imaging.
2. Counseling: Explain the recessive inheritance (25% risk for siblings).
3. Protection: Prescribe UV-blocking and Blue-light blocking sunglasses (may slow A2E formation).
4. Nutrition: Advise against Vitamin A; emphasize lutein/zeaxanthin and Omega-3s.
5. Low Vision: Refer early for magnifiers, telescopic lenses, and school/workplace accommodations.
6. Clinical Trials: Monitor for Gene Therapy (SAR422451) or pharmacological trials (e.g., Emixustat).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
sections.content: The ProgStar Study (Natural History of the Progression of Stargardt Disease) provided critical longitudinal data on lesion growth (atrophy) using FAF. Recent research focuses on 'Visual Cycle Modulators' (like ALK-001, a deuterated Vitamin A) which aim to slow down the dimerization of Vitamin A into toxic A2E without causing night blindness. Gene therapy trials using Lentiviral vectors are ongoing due to the large size of the ABCA4 gene (cDNA ~6.8kb), which exceeds standard AAV capacity.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Rapid Progression
content: Rapid expansion of scotoma on Goldmann visual fields.
Development of Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV) - Rare but possible.
Significant reduction in scotopic ERG amplitudes (indicates rod involvement).
Sudden metamorphopsia (requires immediate OCT to rule out CNV).

title: Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy (BVMD)
summary: A progressive, autosomal dominant macular dystrophy caused by mutations in the BEST1 gene, characterized by the accumulation of subretinal lipofuscin in a classic 'egg-yolk' appearance. It is uniquely identified by a pathognomonic reduction in the EOG Arden ratio despite a normal ERG.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy (BVMD), or 'Best Disease', is an autosomal dominant generalized tapetoretinal dystrophy. It primarily affects the Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) and secondarily involves the photoreceptors. The hallmark is the bilateral, symmetrical accumulation of yellowish, 'egg-yolk' like material (lipofuscin) within the subretinal space, typically appearing in the first or second decade of life.

sections.title: Epidemiology & Genetics
content: Inheritance: Autosomal Dominant with variable expressivity and high penetrance.
Gene: BEST1 (formerly VMD2) located on chromosome 11q12.3.
Protein: Bestrophin-1, a transmembrane protein acting as a calcium-sensitive chloride channel in the RPE basolateral membrane.
Prevalence: Estimated at 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 15,000.
Age of Onset: Usually 3–15 years, though often asymptomatic until later stages.

sections.title: Pathophysiology Flow
content: Mutation in BEST1 gene → Defective Bestrophin-1 protein.
Impaired chloride ion transport across RPE basolateral membrane.
Failure of fluid regulation and phagocytosis in the subretinal space.
Accumulation of lipofuscin/vitelliform material (A2E) between RPE and photoreceptors.
Secondary RPE atrophy and photoreceptor degeneration.

rows: Normal fundus; abnormal EOG is the only finding.
Subtle RPE pigmentary changes or tiny yellow flecks.
Partial absorption of material; layer of yellow fluid settles inferiorly.
'Scrambled Egg' appearance as material breaks up.
Central RPE and chorioretinal atrophy; looks like GA.

content.explanation: In Best Disease, the EOG (Electro-oculogram) is ALWAYS abnormal. The Arden Ratio (Light peak / Dark trough) is typically < 1.5 (Normal > 1.85). CRITICALLY: The Full-field ERG remains NORMAL because the global photoreceptor function is preserved.

branches: OCT: Hyperreflective material between RPE and Ellipsoid Zone
FAF: Intense hyper-autofluorescence of vitelliform material
FFA: Early blockage (masking) by material; late staining
OCT-A: Used to rule out CNV in stage 6

rows: Smaller lesions, older age (40-60), minimal progression.
Pisciform flecks, 'dark choroid' on FFA, early vision loss.
Serous detachment without yellow material; 'smoke stack' FFA.
History of sun gazing, small foveal hole/defect.
Pigment at RPE level, various patterns (butterfly, etc.).

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Step 1: Baseline EOG and Genetic testing (BEST1).
Step 2: Annual monitoring with OCT and Amsler Grid.
Step 3: Screen family members (even if asymptomatic) with EOG.
Step 4: Treat CNV (Stage 6) with intravitreal Anti-VEGF (e.g., Ranibizumab, Aflibercept).
Step 5: Low vision rehabilitation for atrophic stages.

sections.title: Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Sudden drop in vision or new metamorphopsia (Suggests CNV).
Subretinal hemorrhage or hard exudates on fundoscopy.
Rapidly expanding subretinal fluid on OCT.
Development of Macular Hole (Rare complication of stage 4/5).

content.explanation: Pre-vitelliform, Vitelliform (Yolk), Pseudohypopyon, Vitelliruptive (Scrambled), Atrophic, Cicatricial.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Vision often remains surprisingly good despite a dramatic 'egg-yolk' appearance.
An abnormal EOG in a parent with a normal fundus confirms they are a carrier.
The vitelliform material is located between the RPE and the photoreceptors (subretinal).
Anti-VEGF response for CNV in Best disease is generally very good.

sections.title: Recent Advances
sections.content: Gene therapy is the most promising frontier for BVMD. Ongoing research focuses on adeno-associated virus (AAV) mediated delivery of a functional BEST1 gene to the RPE. Recent studies using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have successfully modeled the chloride channel defect and tested potential small-molecule therapies to enhance RPE function.

data.summary: A comprehensive comparison of Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (von Recklinghausen) and Type 2 (MISME Syndrome), focusing on genetic foundations, clinical diagnostic criteria, and pathognomonic ocular findings for the ophthalmic specialist.

rows: MISME Syndrome (Multiple Inherited Schwannomas, Meningiomas, and Ependymomas)
Neuroectodermal hamartomas affecting skin, nervous system, and skeleton.
Tumor suppressor syndrome characterized by bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
Lisch Nodules, Optic Nerve Glioma, Plexiform Neurofibromas.
PSC Cataracts, Combined Hamartoma of Retina and RPE (CHRRPE).

branches: NF1: Negative regulator of RAS/MAPK pathway
NF2: Linker between cytoskeleton and membrane proteins
Inheritance: Both Autosomal Dominant (50% de novo)

sections.title: Revised NIH Diagnostic Criteria for NF1
content: 6 or more Café-au-lait macules (>5mm prepubertal, >15mm postpubertal)
2 or more neurofibromas of any type OR 1 plexiform neurofibroma
Freckling in the axillary or inguinal regions (Crowe sign)
Optic pathway glioma (OPG)
2 or more Lisch nodules (examined by slit lamp) OR 2 or more choroidal abnormalities
A distinctive osseous lesion (sphenoid dysplasia, anterolateral bowing of tibia)
A heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant with a variant allele fraction of 50%
A first-degree relative (parent, sibling, or offspring) who meets the above criteria

sections.title: Diagnostic Criteria for NF2 (Manchester Criteria)
content: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (VS) <70 years
Unilateral VS AND 1st degree relative with NF2
Any 2 of: Meningioma, Schwannoma, Glioma, Neurofibroma, Posterior subcapsular opacities
Multiple meningiomas AND (Unilateral VS OR any 2 of: Schwannoma, Glioma, Neurofibroma, Cataract)
Pathogenic NF2 variant in blood or tumor

branches: Plexiform Neurofibroma (S-shaped lid deformity, 'bag of worms')
Optic Pathway Gliomas (15-25% of patients, usually low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma)
Pulsating Proptosis (Secondary to sphenoid wing dysplasia)
PSC Cataracts (60-80% of patients, often early onset)
Combined Hamartoma of Retina and RPE (CHRRPE)

sections.title: Optic Pathway Gliomas (OPG) in NF1
sections.content: OPGs are the most common CNS tumor in NF1, typically appearing before age 6. They are usually pilocytic astrocytomas (WHO Grade I). Unlike sporadic gliomas, NF1-associated gliomas often have a more indolent course but can cause profound vision loss, precocious puberty (if chiasmal), and proptosis. Screening via annual eye exams is mandatory until age 10. Treatment with chemotherapy (Vincristine/Carboplatin) is reserved for progressive vision loss or significant neuroradiological growth; radiotherapy is strictly avoided due to the risk of secondary malignancies and Moyamoya syndrome.

rows: CALS and freckling present, but NO Lisch nodules or neurofibromas.
Large 'Coast of Maine' CALS, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, precocious puberty.
Multiple schwannomas without vestibular involvement or NF2 criteria.
Webbed neck, pulmonary stenosis, similar facial features to NF1.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: Complete Ophthalmic Exam (Visual acuity, color vision, Slit-lamp for Lisch nodules, Dilated Fundus Exam).
Step 2: Imaging - MRI of Brain and Orbits with Contrast (Identify OPG, sphenoid dysplasia, or Vestibular Schwannomas).
Step 3: Near-Infrared Reflectance (NIR) or EDI-OCT to detect Choroidal Nodules (High sensitivity for NF1).
Step 4: Formal Audiometry and ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response) for NF2 screening.
Step 5: Genetic Testing for NF1/NF2 variants (Multigene panels).

rows: Surgical debulking for visual axis clearance

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Urgent Referral Needed
content: Rapidly progressive proptosis or vision loss (Optic Glioma growth)
New onset seizures or focal neurological deficits
Rapid growth or pain in a pre-existing neurofibroma (Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor - MPNST)
Bilateral hearing loss or balance issues in a young patient (NF2 Vestibular Schwannomas)
Severe hypertension in NF1 (Possible Pheochromocytoma or Renal Artery Stenosis)

content.explanation: NF1 is on Chromosome 17 (17 letters in 'Neurofibromatosis'). NF2 is on Chromosome 22 (2 acoustic neuromas, 2 eyes with cataracts, 2 ears affected).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Recent Advances
content: Choroidal hamartomas are now a recognized diagnostic criterion for NF1.
Selumetinib is the first FDA-approved systemic therapy for symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas.
Lisch nodules do not affect vision but are diagnostic gold; they are absent in NF2.
Always check for a 'Sentinel' CHRRPE in children; it may be the presenting sign of NF2.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: SPRINT Trial
sections.content: The SPRINT Phase 2 Trial (NEJM 2020) demonstrated that the MEK 1/2 inhibitor Selumetinib induced partial responses in 70% of children with inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, leading to significant improvements in pain and physical function. This shifted the paradigm from purely surgical 'watch and wait' to medical intervention in NF1.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Stickler Syndrome is a group of genetic disorders affecting connective tissue, specifically collagen types II, IX, and XI. It is characterized by a distinctive 'optically empty' vitreous, high myopia, and a high risk of giant retinal tears (GRT). Systemically, it manifests as orofacial abnormalities (Pierre Robin sequence), sensorineural/conductive hearing loss, and premature osteoarthritis.

branches: Type 1: Membranous (Plicated membranes in retrolental space)
Early PVD: Spontaneous and often complete

sections.title: Diagnostic Red Flags (Emergency Signs)
content: Sudden shower of floaters or flashes in a myopic child
Giant Retinal Tear (GRT) > 90 degrees
Stridor or feeding difficulties in neonates (Pierre Robin)
Acute onset of high IOP (Secondary Glaucoma)
Rapidly progressing nuclear sclerotic cataract (presenile)

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Refraction: High Myopia (usually > -6.00D), non-progressive
Slit Lamp: Retrolental membranes or beads; cortical/nuclear cataracts
Gonioscopy: Prominent iris processes and angle anomalies in 10%
Fundoscopy: Radial perivascular pigmentary degeneration (RPPD)
Lattice-like degeneration: Often circumferential or atypical
Vitreous: Syneresis and liquefaction

branches: Craniofacial: Flat midface, saddle nose, micrognathia
Palate: Cleft palate, Bifid uvula, Pierre Robin Sequence

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Step 1: Comprehensive dilated fundus exam with scleral depression
Step 2: Expert Slit Lamp biomicroscopy of the vitreous (Goldmann lens)
Step 3: Audiometry (high-frequency SNHL) and Speech/Language evaluation
Step 4: Skeletal surveys (X-rays of hips, spine, and knees)
Step 5: Genetic testing (Multigene panels for COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2)
Step 6: Echocardiogram (minor association with MVP)

rows: More severe hearing loss, short stature, thickened skull bones, more pronounced facial features.
Isolated Ocular findings; VCAN gene; NO systemic features; Low risk of RD.
COL18A1; Encephalocele, severe high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration.
COL2A1; Severe dwarfism, 'dumbbell' shaped long bones, prominent joints.
Severe short-trunk dwarfism, coxa vara, possible RD.

sections.title: Surgical Management: Retinal Detachment
content: 1. Pre-operative stabilization and marking of all breaks
2. Scleral Buckling: Primary choice for simple RRD in kids
3. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): Often required for Giant Retinal Tears (GRT)
4. Heavy Liquid (PFCL): Crucial for stabilizing the retina during GRT repair
5. Long-acting Tamponade: Silicone oil is frequently preferred due to PVR risk

sections.title: The Cambridge Prophylaxis Protocol
sections.content: The Cambridge Protocol involves 360-degree cryotherapy (or laser) to the ora serrata and vitreous base. Landmark studies by Fincham et al. demonstrated a massive reduction in RD risk: from 73% in untreated eyes to 8% in treated eyes. This is now considered the standard of care for Stickler Type 1 patients.

content.explanation: S: Skeletal (Arthritis/Hypermobility), T: Tongue (Pierre Robin), I: Inherited (AD), C: Cataracts/Cleft Palate, K: Knee/Joint pain, L: Liquefied Vitreous, E: Empty Vitreous, R: Retinal Detachment.

sections.title: Surgical Complications & Challenges
content: Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR) is highly prevalent (over 50% in some series)
Post-operative glaucoma (steroid-induced or angle-related)
Multiple breaks and posterior extension of lattice
Poor surgical visibility due to early cataracts
Choroidal effusions post-cryotherapy

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: Cambridge Prophylaxis Trial: Confirmed 360° cryotherapy reduces RD risk by 10-fold in Type 1 Stickler.
AI Vitreous Analysis: Utilizing deep learning on OCT to differentiate Type 1 vs Type 2 vitreous phenotypes.
Gene Therapy: Early-stage research into COL2A1 mRNA modulation to prevent collagen cross-linking failure.
Ultra-widefield Imaging: Essential for early detection of radial perivascular pigmentary changes in the periphery.

content.explanation: If a child has high myopia and you see NO vitreous structure on slit lamp, it's not a 'good view'—it's Stickler until proven otherwise. Check the palate and ask about joint pain!

sections.title: Prognosis and Follow-up
content: Lifelong 6-12 month follow-up with widefield imaging
Genetic counseling is mandatory (50% risk to offspring)
Visual prognosis is good if RD is prevented/treated early
Hearing aids significantly improve quality of life
Avoid contact sports to minimize trauma-induced RD risk

title: COPD: The Ophthalmologist's Guide to Systemic Care & Ocular Impact
summary: A comprehensive review of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) through the lens of a board-certified ophthalmologist. This poster bridges systemic pathophysiology with critical perioperative considerations and ocular manifestations for the eye care specialist.

data.title: COPD: The Ophthalmologist's Guide to Systemic Care & Ocular Impact
data.summary: A comprehensive review of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) through the lens of a board-certified ophthalmologist. This poster bridges systemic pathophysiology with critical perioperative considerations and ocular manifestations for the eye care specialist.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: COPD is a common, preventable, and treatable disease characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation. It is caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases. The chronic airflow limitation is caused by a mixture of small airways disease (obstructive bronchiolitis) and parenchymal destruction (emphysema), the relative contributions of which vary between individuals.

rows: Destruction of alveolar walls; capillary loss

sections.title: Diagnosis: The Gold Standard
content: Post-Bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70 is mandatory for diagnosis.
FEV1: Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second.
FVC: Forced Vital Capacity.
Spirometry is required to differentiate from asthma (irreversible vs. reversible).
Screening: Perform in any patient with dyspnea, chronic cough, or sputum production.

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations & Concerns
content: Hypoxic Retinopathy: Chronic CO2 retention and low O2 can cause retinal venous tortuosity and dilation.
Dry Eye Disease (DED): Increased prevalence due to smoking and oxygen mask airflow ('wind' over the ocular surface).
Steroid-Induced Glaucoma: Chronic systemic or inhaled steroid use increases IOP risk (Ocular Hypertension).
Posterior Subcapsular Cataract (PSC): Higher incidence in patients on long-term corticosteroids for exacerbations.
Normal Tension Glaucoma (NTG): Potential link due to chronic vascular dysregulation and nocturnal hypoxia.
Floppy Eyelid Syndrome: Strongly associated with OSA, which frequently co-exists with COPD (Overlap Syndrome).

sections.title: Perioperative Ophthalmic Considerations
content: Step 1: Assess Positioning - Can the patient lie flat (orthopnea)? Consider 'Incline' surgery for cataracts.
Step 2: Cough Control - Intense coughing during intraocular surgery (e.g., Phaco) risks expulsive choroidal hemorrhage.
Step 3: Anesthesia Choice - Avoid retrobulbar blocks if the patient cannot hold their breath or is highly anxious.
Step 4: Oxygenation - Ensure nasal cannula flow doesn't create 'wind' across the cornea during surgery (DED/Infection risk).
Step 5: Drug Interactions - Topical Beta-blockers (Timolol) are CONTRAINDICATED or must be used with extreme caution (risk of bronchospasm).

sections.title: CRITICAL: Ophthalmic Red Flags
content: Use of Topical Timolol/Beta-blockers in COPD (Potential for fatal bronchospasm).
Sudden vision loss during a coughing fit (Valsalva Retinopathy).
Acute Angle Closure triggered by nebulized anticholinergics (Ipratropium) leaking into the eyes via poorly fitted masks.
Chronic high-dose steroids resulting in IOP > 30 mmHg.

content.explanation: A: Albuterol (SABA); B: Bromides (LAMA/Anticholinergics); C: Corticosteroids (Inhaled); D: Diet/Delivery (Oxygen); E: Exercise/Education (Rehab).

sections.title: Surgical Management & Advanced Care
content: Lung Volume Reduction Surgery (LVRS) for upper-lobe emphysema.
Endobronchial Valves (EBV): One-way valves to collapse hyperinflated segments.
Lung Transplantation: For GOLD 4 patients with high BODE scores.
Pulmonary Rehabilitation: Proven to improve QoL and exercise tolerance.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: BODE Index: Predictive of mortality (BMI, Obstruction, Dyspnea, Exercise capacity).
Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) Screening: Every patient with COPD should be tested at least once.
Oxygen Therapy: The only intervention (besides smoking cessation) shown to improve survival in COPD with severe resting hypoxemia.
The 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT): A simple, reproducible marker of functional capacity and prognosis.
ECLIPSE Study: Confirmed that frequent exacerbators (≥2/year) remain frequent exacerbators, regardless of GOLD grade.

title: Bronchial Asthma: Systemic & Ocular Perspectives
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to bronchial asthma, focusing on the GINA-aligned management protocols, underlying pathophysiology, and the critical ocular associations including atopic disease and steroid-induced complications.

data.title: Bronchial Asthma: Systemic & Ocular Perspectives
data.summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to bronchial asthma, focusing on the GINA-aligned management protocols, underlying pathophysiology, and the critical ocular associations including atopic disease and steroid-induced complications.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Bronchial asthma is a heterogeneous chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by a history of respiratory symptoms such as wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough that vary over time and in intensity, together with variable expiratory airflow limitation. From an ophthalmic perspective, it is frequently associated with atopic ocular surface diseases (AKC/VKC).

content.explanation: Aspirin Exacerbated Respiratory Disease consists of: 1. Asthma, 2. Sinusitis/Nasal Polyps, 3. Aspirin/NSAID Sensitivity.

sections.title: Ocular Associations & Manifestations
content: Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis (AKC): Chronic, bilateral, potentially blinding inflammation.
Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC): Seasonal, giant papillae (cobblestones), Horner-Trantas dots.
Keratoconus: High association due to chronic eye rubbing (itch-scratch cycle).
Steroid-Induced Glaucoma: Secondary to chronic systemic or inhaled corticosteroid use.
Posterior Subcapsular Cataracts (PSC): Common side effect of long-term ICS or systemic prednisone.
Allergic Conjunctivitis: Frequently co-exists with allergic asthma and rhinitis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Spirometry: Demonstrate reversible airflow obstruction (FEV1 increase >12% and >200mL).
2. Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) Monitoring: Diurnal variability >10%.
3. Bronchial Provocation: Methacholine or Histamine challenge (PC20 < 8mg/mL).
4. Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO): Marker of eosinophilic inflammation.
5. Allergy Testing: Skin prick tests or Specific IgE.

rows: Inspiratory stridor; flattened inspiratory loop on spirometry
Basal crackles; orthopnea; B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) elevated
Acute onset; pleuritic chest pain; normal spirometry
Add LAMA; Add Biologic (Anti-IgE, Anti-IL5, Anti-IL4R); Consider OCS

sections.title: Red Flags: Status Asthmaticus
content: Silent Chest (Ominous sign of minimal air movement)
Cyanosis or SpO2 < 90% on room air
Altered Mental Status (Confusion or exhaustion)
Inability to speak in full sentences
Paradoxical Thoraco-abdominal breathing
Normal or elevated PaCO2 (Indicates impending respiratory failure)

sections.title: Biologic Therapies (Precision Medicine)
content: Omalizumab: Anti-IgE (For severe allergic asthma).
Mepolizumab/Reslizumab: Anti-IL5 (For eosinophilic asthma).
Benralizumab: Anti-IL5 Receptor α.
Dupilumab: Anti-IL4/IL13 (Also used for severe Atopic Dermatitis).
Tezepelumab: Anti-TSLP (Targets upstream epithelial cytokines).

sections.title: Ocular Side Effects of Asthma Tx
content: Inhaled Corticosteroids (ICS): Risk of Ocular Hypertension/Glaucoma if technique is poor (facial deposition).
Systemic Corticosteroids: Highest risk for PSC Cataracts and Glaucoma.
Antimuscarinic agents (LAMA/SAMA): May trigger Acute Angle Closure in susceptible narrow angles.
Dupilumab: Frequently causes Conjunctivitis and Blepharitis as a side effect (10-25%).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: A normal CXR does not rule out asthma; it is usually normal or shows hyperinflation.
Avoid Beta-Blockers (even topical Timolol) in asthmatics as they can trigger fatal bronchospasm.
The 'Asthmatic Eye': Always check IOP and lens clarity in patients on long-term steroid therapy.
Charcot-Leyden crystals and Curschmann spirals are classic pathology findings in sputum.
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) peaks 5-10 minutes after stopping exercise.

rows: PRN ICS-formoterol is superior to SABA alone for symptom control and exacerbation reduction.
Addition of LAMA to ICS/LABA improves lung function in uncontrolled asthma.
ICS improves airway hyperresponsiveness but does not prevent lung function decline over time.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Atrial Fibrillation (AFib) is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia characterized by uncoordinated atrial activation and subsequent deterioration of atrial mechanical function. On ECG, it is defined by the replacement of consistent P waves by rapid oscillations or fibrillatory waves (f-waves) and an 'irregularly irregular' ventricular response.

content.explanation: P: Pulmonary disease (PE, COPD); I: Ischemia (MI); R: Rheumatic heart disease (Mitral Stenosis); A: Anemia/Atrial Myxoma; T: Thyrotoxicosis; E: Ethanol (Holiday Heart)/Electrolytes; S: Sepsis/Surgery (Post-CABG).

rows: Terminates spontaneously or with intervention < 7 days.
Often triggered by pulmonary vein foci.
Focus shifts to rate control and anticoagulation.

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations & Examination
content: CRAO/BRAO: Sudden, painless vision loss; AFib is a leading cause of cardioembolic retinal artery occlusion.
Calcific Emboli: Large, dull, white/yellow plaques at the disc or proximal vessels; highly suggestive of cardiac origin.
Amaurosis Fugax: Transient monocular vision loss (fleeting curtain).
Ocular Ischemic Syndrome: Chronic hypoperfusion; mid-peripheral hemorrhages.
Anticoagulation Side Effects: Subconjunctival or vitreous hemorrhages.

sections.title: HAS-BLED: Bleeding Risk Assessment
content: H: Hypertension (SBP > 160 mmHg)
A: Abnormal Renal/Liver Function (1 pt each)
S: Stroke history
B: Bleeding predisposition/anemia
L: Labile INRs (if on Warfarin)
E: Elderly (Age > 65)
D: Drugs (NSAIDs/Antiplatelets) or Alcohol

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 12-Lead ECG: Absence of P waves; irregular RR intervals.
Transthoracic Echogram (TTE): Assess chamber size and valvular function.
Transesophageal Echogram (TEE): Gold standard to rule out LAA thrombus before cardioversion.
Holter/Event Monitor: 24h-30d monitoring for paroxysmal AFib.
Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs): Rule out thyrotoxicosis.
Renal Function (CrCl): Necessary for DOAC dosing.

rows: Reduce AF burden or eliminate anticoagulation needs

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Trials
content: AFFIRM: Found no survival advantage of rhythm control over rate control.
RE-LY: Dabigatran non-inferior/superior to Warfarin for stroke prevention.
ARISTOTLE: Apixaban superior to Warfarin in stroke prevention and lower bleeding.
ROCKET-AF: Rivaroxaban non-inferior to Warfarin in high-risk patients.

sections.title: Surgical & Procedural Steps
content: Pulmonary Vein Isolation (PVI): Circumferential ablation around PV ostia.
Cox-Maze Procedure: Surgical creation of 'maze' scars to direct electrical signals.
Direct Current Cardioversion (DCCV): Synchronized shock; requires 3-4 weeks anticoagulation prior (or TEE rule-out).
AV Node Ablation: 'Pace and Ablate'—permanent pacemaker followed by AV node destruction.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Ocular & Systemic Emergencies
content: Sudden monocular vision loss (CRAO/BRAO) — Needs immediate neurology consult.
Acute-onset focal neurologic deficits (FAST: Face, Arms, Speech, Time).
Hemodynamic instability: Hypotension, altered mentation, or acute HF in new-onset AFib.
New onset chest pain or severe shortness of breath.
Signs of internal hemorrhage in patients on anticoagulants (e.g., melena, hematuria).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Ophthalmologist
content: Calcific emboli are heart valves until proven otherwise—order an Urgent Echo.
Ophthalmologists are often the first to diagnose AFib via retinal embolic events.
Pre-op: Aspirin can usually be continued; Warfarin/DOACs require surgeon-specific bridging protocols.
Hollenhorst plaques are usually carotid (cholesterol), but AFib is the primary source of 'white' emboli.

sections.title: Recent Advances: AI & Wearables
sections.content: Smartwatch technology (Apple/Fitbit) utilizing photoplethysmography (PPG) has revolutionized the detection of paroxysmal AFib, allowing for earlier intervention and stroke prevention in 'silent' cases. AI algorithms can now predict AFib development from 12-lead ECGs even when the patient is in sinus rhythm.

title: Anaphylactic Shock: Ophthalmic Emergency Protocol
summary: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic Type I hypersensitivity reaction. In the ophthalmic setting, it is most commonly triggered by intravenous dyes (FFA/ICG), local anesthetics, or latex, requiring immediate recognition and IM Epinephrine administration.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Anaphylaxis is a rapidly developing, multi-systemic immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. It results from the sudden systemic release of mediators (histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes) from mast cells and basophils. In ophthalmology, it represents the most critical office-based emergency, often occurring within minutes of diagnostic dye injection or anesthetic block.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Type I Cascade
content: 1. Sensitization: Initial exposure leads to IgE production by B-cells.
2. Priming: IgE binds to FcεRI receptors on Mast cells and Basophils.
3. Re-exposure: Allergen cross-links IgE on cell surfaces.
4. Degranulation: Massive release of Histamine, Prostaglandin D2, and Leukotrienes.
5. Systemic Effect: Vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and smooth muscle contraction.

rows: Generalized urticaria, pruritus, flushing, angioedema (lips, tongue, uvula).
Hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmia, chest pain, cardiac arrest.
Anxiety, 'sense of impending doom', altered mental status, syncope.

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations
content: Severe conjunctival chemosis (often immediate).
Periorbital edema and erythema.
Profuse lacrimation and conjunctival injection.
Sudden vision blurring (due to corneal edema or hypotension).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Threats
content: Stridor or hoarseness (Laryngeal edema)
Silent chest on auscultation (Severe bronchospasm)
Systolic BP < 90 mmHg
Rapidly spreading urticaria after IV dye injection
Cyanosis or SpO2 < 92%

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup (Post-Stabilization)
content: 1. Serum Tryptase: Drawn 0.5–3 hours after onset (peak at 1hr).
2. Repeat Tryptase: At 24 hours to establish baseline.
3. Allergy Referral: For skin prick or IgE testing (after 4-6 weeks).
4. Review FFA/ICG logs for lot numbers and dosages.

rows: Bradycardia, pallor, no urticaria, rapid recovery when supine.
Normal BP/O2, tachypnea, carpopedal spasm, no angioedema.
Chest pain, ECG changes, elevated troponins.
No skin changes, history of triggers, slow onset.

sections.title: Management Step-by-Step
content: 1. STOP the offending agent (Disconnect FFA infusion immediately).
2. CALL for help / Activate Emergency Medical Services (EMS).
3. POSITION: Supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress predominates).
4. ADRENALINE (Epinephrine): 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1:1000) in the mid-outer thigh.
5. AIRWAY: High-flow Oxygen (15L/min via non-rebreather mask).
6. FLUIDS: Rapid IV bolus of Normal Saline (1-2 Liters).
7. ADJUNCTS: Antihistamines (H1/H2 blockers) and Corticosteroids.

content.explanation: A: Airway, D: Dye Stop, R: Recline/Raise legs, E: Epinephrine IM, N: Normal Saline, A: Antihistamines, L: Lungs (Oxygen/Albuterol), I: IV Access, N: Next dose of Epi if needed.

rows: Skin & subcutaneous tissues only (generalized erythema, urticaria).
Respiratory, cardiovascular, or GI involvement (dyspnea, stridor, nausea).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Ophthalmologist
content: IM Epinephrine is safer and easier than IV Epinephrine for non-coding patients; use the mid-thigh (Vastus Lateralis).
Patients on Beta-blockers may be resistant to Epinephrine; consider Glucagon (1-5mg IV over 5 mins).
Biphasic reactions occur in up to 20% of cases; observe patients for at least 4-12 hours post-event.
Always have a 'Crash Cart' in the FFA suite with up-to-date medications and a portable oxygen tank.
ICG contains Iodine; check for shellfish or iodine allergy before administration.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Consensus
sections.content: The 2020 World Allergy Organization (WAO) Anaphylaxis Guidance emphasizes that there are no absolute contraindications to Epinephrine in anaphylaxis. Recent studies in 'Ophthalmology' (AAO) suggest that pre-filled auto-injectors (EpiPens) should be accessible in every retina clinic due to their ease of use during high-stress FFA reactions.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (due to prolonged shock).
Myocardial Ischemia / Stress-induced Cardiomyopathy.
Biphasic Reaction (recurrence of symptoms without re-exposure).
Prognosis is excellent if Epinephrine is administered early.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Spectrum
sections.content: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) represents a spectrum of clinical conditions ranging from unstable angina (UA) to non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). It is characterized by a sudden reduction in blood flow to the heart, typically due to plaque rupture or erosion and subsequent thrombus formation.

branches: Plaque Rupture/Erosion: Most common; exposes prothrombotic core
Thrombosis: Platelet aggregation and fibrin mesh formation
Inflammation: Cytokine-mediated weakening of the fibrous cap
Coronary Vasospasm: Prinzmetal angina or cocaine-induced
Supply-Demand Mismatch: Type 2 MI (Tachycardia, Anemia, Sepsis)
Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection (SCAD): Non-atherosclerotic tear

sections.title: Emergency RED FLAGS
content: New onset S3 gallop or pulmonary rales (Acute Heart Failure)
New systolic murmur (Papillary Muscle Rupture or VSD)
Persistent hypotension (Cardiogenic Shock)
Dynamic ST-segment changes despite therapy
Ventricular Tachycardia or Fibrillation
Chest pain refractory to nitrates

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Not All Chest Pain is ACS

branches: GI: GERD, Esophageal Spasm, Boerhaave Syndrome

content.explanation: M: Morphine (if pain refractory), O: Oxygen (if Sat <90%), N: Nitrates (Vasodilation), A: Aspirin (325mg chewable), B: Beta-blockers (if no HF), A: ACE Inhibitors, S: Statins (High-intensity), H: Heparin/Anticoagulation.

sections.title: Step-by-Step STEMI Protocol
content: Step 1: Immediate 12-Lead ECG (within 10 minutes of arrival)
Step 2: Loading doses of ASA (325mg) and P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g., Ticagrelor 180mg)
Step 3: Assess for Primary PCI (Door-to-balloon time < 90 mins)
Step 4: If PCI not available within 120 mins, consider Fibrinolytics (Door-to-needle < 30 mins)
Step 5: Anticoagulation (UFH or Bivalirudin)
Step 6: Post-procedure Statins and Beta-blockers

sections.title: The Ophthalmic Connection
content: Hollenhorst Plaques: Cholesterol emboli seen on fundoscopy suggest carotid or aortic atherosclerosis, risk markers for future ACS.
Hypertensive Retinopathy: Grades III-IV indicate severe systemic end-organ damage and higher risk for MI.
Perioperative Management: Ophthalmic surgery is low risk, but ACS in the last 6 months requires cardiology clearance.
Antiplatelet Strategy: DAPT (Aspirin + P2Y12) should generally not be stopped for intravitreal injections or cataract surgery.

branches: LV Free Wall Rupture: Leads to Cardiac Tamponade (Days 3-5)
Papillary Muscle Rupture: Acute Mitral Regurgitation & Pulmonary Edema
Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD): New harsh systolic murmur; L-to-R shunt
Dressler Syndrome: Post-MI Pericarditis (Weeks later; autoimmune)
Ventricular Aneurysm: Persistent ST elevation weeks after MI

rows: PLATO Trial: Superior to Clopidogrel in ACS
PROVE IT-TIMI 22: High dose better post-ACS

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: High-Sensitivity Troponins (hs-cTn): Can rule out MI in 1-3 hours if initial levels are low and repeat levels are stable.
Type 2 Myocardial Infarction: Ischemia due to supply-demand mismatch (e.g., severe anemia) rather than plaque rupture; treatment involves correcting the underlying cause.
Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT) Duration: Standard is 12 months post-PCI, but can be shortened to 1-6 months for high-bleeding risk patients.
Cocaine-Induced MI: Avoid non-selective beta-blockers due to risk of unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation/vasospasm.
The 'Widow Maker': Proximal LAD occlusion, leading to massive anterior wall infarction and high mortality.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of a thrombus within a deep vein, most commonly in the lower extremities. While primarily a systemic condition, it serves as a critical marker for hypercoagulable states that also manifest in the eye as Retinal Vein Occlusions (RVO) and poses significant perioperative risks during ophthalmic surgery.

branches: Hypercoagulability (Factor V Leiden, Cancer, Pregnancy, OCPs)

sections.title: The Wells Criteria for DVT Probability

rows: Bedridden >3 days or major surgery <12 wks
Alternative diagnosis at least as likely

content.explanation: T: Trauma/Travel; H: Hormones (OCP/HRT); R: Relatives (Genetics); O: Old age; M: Malignancy; B: Blood disorders; O: Obesity; S: Surgery; I: Immobilization; S: Sickness (CHF/Nephrotic).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Pulmonary Embolism
content: Sudden onset Dyspnea (Shortness of breath)
Pleuritic Chest Pain
Hemoptysis (Coughing up blood)
Tachycardia (>100 bpm) and Tachypnea
Syncope or Sudden Collapse

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Flow
content: Step 1: Clinical Assessment (Wells Score calculation).
Step 2: D-dimer Assay (High sensitivity, low specificity; use to rule out in low-risk).
Step 3: Compression Ultrasonography (CUS) - Gold standard imaging.
Step 4: Venography (Rarely used now; gold standard if CUS is inconclusive).
Step 5: CT Pulmonary Angiogram (If PE is suspected).

sections.title: Perioperative Management for Ophthalmic Surgeons
content: Cataract Surgery: Continue anticoagulants (Warfarin/DOACs); risk of retrobulbar hemorrhage is minimal with topical anesthesia.
Glaucoma Surgery (Trabeculectomy): High risk of hyphema/suprachoroidal hemorrhage; consider stopping 3-5 days pre-op if systemic risk is low.
Vitreoretinal Surgery: Generally continue anticoagulation for small-gauge (23/25/27g) surgery unless extensive dissection is needed.
Orbital Surgery: High risk for sight-threatening hematoma; must coordinate with Hematology to bridge/stop anticoagulation.
DVT Prophylaxis: Use sequential compression devices (SCDs) for long orbital or plastic procedures (>90 mins).

rows: Inhibits Vit K dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X)

sections.title: Ocular Complications of Anticoagulants
content: Subconjunctival Hemorrhage (Benign but alarming to patients).
Spontaneous Hyphema (Rare, usually associated with underlying rubeosis).
Increased risk of vitreous hemorrhage in exudative AMD.
Progression of Sub-retinal hemorrhage in neovascular membranes.

sections.title: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (CST)
content: The Ocular Equivalent of DVT: Often septic (Staph aureus).
Signs: Proptosis, Chemosis, Cranial Nerve Palsies (III, IV, V1, V2, VI).
Key Finding: Rapid progression to bilateral involvement.
Treatment: High-dose IV antibiotics + Anticoagulation (controversial but often used).

branches: Baker's Cyst Rupture (Sudden pain, fluid in popliteal fossa)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens: A surgical emergency where massive DVT causes arterial compromise (blue, painful leg).
Post-Thrombotic Syndrome (PTS): Chronic venous hypertension causing leg heaviness and ulcers in 20-50% of DVT patients.
D-dimer Caveat: Elevated in pregnancy, cancer, and inflammation; only useful for its Negative Predictive Value.
Pre-op: Always document a baseline INR for patients on Warfarin before performing any needle-based anesthesia (e.g., retrobulbar block).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
sections.content: The **EINSTEIN** and **AMPLIFY** trials revolutionized management by proving DOACs (Rivaroxaban and Apixaban) are non-inferior to Warfarin for DVT/PE treatment with a lower risk of major bleeding. In ophthalmology, recent retrospective series suggest that stopping DOACs for cataract surgery may actually increase the risk of systemic thromboembolism without significantly reducing surgical complications.

title: Pulmonary Embolism: A Comprehensive Clinical Blueprint
summary: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is a life-threatening occlusion of the pulmonary arterial system, most commonly secondary to Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). Rapid identification via risk stratification (Wells Score) and definitive imaging (CTPA) is vital for reducing the high mortality associated with right ventricular failure.

data.title: Pulmonary Embolism: A Comprehensive Clinical Blueprint
data.summary: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is a life-threatening occlusion of the pulmonary arterial system, most commonly secondary to Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). Rapid identification via risk stratification (Wells Score) and definitive imaging (CTPA) is vital for reducing the high mortality associated with right ventricular failure.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is the most serious clinical manifestation of Venous Thromboembolism (VTE). It occurs when a thrombus (or occasionally fat, air, or amniotic fluid) migrates from the systemic venous circulation to the pulmonary arterial tree. This leads to a ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch, increased pulmonary vascular resistance, and potential right ventricular (RV) failure.

branches: Hypercoagulability (Factor V Leiden, Cancer, OCP, Protein C/S Deficiency)

rows: Alternative diagnosis less likely than PE

sections.title: Clinical Presentation & Physical Signs
content: Sudden onset dyspnea (85% of cases)
Pleuritic chest pain (Inflammation of the pleura)
Tachycardia (HR > 100 bpm) and Tachypnea (RR > 20/min)
Cough and Hemoptysis (indicative of pulmonary infarction)
Syncope (signifies massive PE and reduced cardiac output)
Accentuated P2 (Loud second heart sound component)
Distended jugular veins (JVD)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: Step 1: Clinical Assessment & Wells Score calculation
Step 2: D-Dimer test (if low clinical probability) to rule out
Step 3: CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) - Gold Standard
Step 4: V/Q Scan (if CTPA is contraindicated, e.g., renal failure)
Step 5: Lower limb Doppler USG if DVT is suspected
Step 6: Bedside Echo to assess RV strain in unstable patients

content.explanation: S-wave in Lead I, Q-wave in Lead III, and Inverted T-wave in Lead III. Note: Sinus Tachycardia is actually the most common finding; S1Q3T3 is specific for RV strain but rare.

sections.title: Ocular Connection: Fat Embolism Syndrome
content: Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES) can present as a subtype of PE
Triad: Respiratory distress, petechial rash, and confusion
Ocular Findings: Purtscher-like Retinopathy
Cotton-wool spots and Purtscher flecken (ischaemic retinal whitening)
Caused by occlusion of precapillary arterioles by fat globules

sections.title: Acute Management Protocol
content: 1. Oxygen Supplementation (Maintain SpO2 >90%)
2. Fluid Resuscitation (Cautious, to avoid RV over-distention)
3. Anticoagulation: UFH (bolus then infusion) or LMWH (Enoxaparin 1mg/kg BID)
4. Thrombolysis (Alteplase 100mg over 2h) for Massive PE
5. IVC Filter: Only if anticoagulation is contraindicated or fails

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Hemodynamic Instability
content: Systolic Blood Pressure < 90 mmHg for > 15 minutes
Refractory hypoxia despite 100% FiO2
Altered Mental Status / Impending Doom
New-onset Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB) on ECG
Evidence of Right Ventricular Dilation on Echo (RV > LV size)

sections.title: Long-Term Anticoagulation Options
content: DOACs (First line): Apixaban, Rivaroxaban (no bridging needed)
Warfarin (Vitamin K Antagonist): Requires Heparin bridge (INR 2.0-3.0)
Duration: 3 months for provoked PE (surgery/trauma)
Duration: Extended/Indefinite for unprovoked or recurrent VTE
Special consideration: LMWH is preferred in pregnancy and active cancer

sections.title: Landmark Studies in PE
sections.content: PEITHO Trial: Demonstrated that while thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE prevents hemodynamic collapse, it significantly increases the risk of major hemorrhage and stroke. MOPETT Trial: Suggested that 'Safe Dose' (half-dose) thrombolysis may be effective with fewer bleeding complications for submassive PE.

sections.title: Surgical & Interventional Techniques
content: Surgical Embolectomy: Indicated for massive PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated
Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis (CDT): Lower dose of Alteplase delivered via ultrasound-assisted catheter
Mechanical Thrombectomy: Fragmenting and aspirating the clot via percutaneous route
ECMO: Veno-arterial (VA) ECMO for circulatory support in extreme shock

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: A normal Chest X-ray in a setting of severe hypoxia is a strong hint for PE (Westermark sign and Hampton’s hump are classic but rare).
D-dimer has high negative predictive value but low specificity; it is useless in post-operative or pregnant patients.

In the Ophthalmic Perioperative setting: If a patient on anticoagulants requires urgent surgery (e.g., ruptured globe), discuss reversing with Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) vs. Heparin bridging.
Tachycardia is often the only sign in the early stages—never ignore it in a post-surgical patient.

summary: A life-threatening accumulation of extravascular fluid in the lung parenchyma and alveoli, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory failure. This guide covers the critical pathophysiology, classification, and rapid-response protocols required for stabilization.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pulmonary Edema is the pathological accumulation of fluid in the extravascular spaces of the lungs. It occurs when the rate of fluid filtration from the pulmonary capillaries into the interstitium exceeds the lymphatic drainage capacity. Broadly categorized into Cardiogenic (High Hydrostatic Pressure) and Non-Cardiogenic (Increased Permeability), it represents a medical emergency often encountered in patients with decompensated heart failure or acute systemic insults.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation & Symptoms
content: Dyspnea: Sudden onset, progressive worsening at rest.
Orthopnea: Difficulty breathing while lying flat; relieved by sitting.
Paroxysmal Nocturnal Dyspnea (PND): Sudden awakening with air hunger.
Cough: Often productive of 'pink, frothy sputum'.
Diaphoresis: Excessive sweating due to sympathetic surge.
Agitation: Feeling of 'impending doom'.

sections.title: Physical Examination Findings
content: Auscultation: Fine inspiratory crackles (rales), often bilateral.
Wheezing: 'Cardiac asthma' due to peribronchial edema.
Cardiac: S3/S4 gallop, jugular venous distention (JVD).
Periphery: Lower extremity pitting edema, cyanosis.
Vitals: Tachypnea, Tachycardia, Hypertension (initial) or Hypotension (shock).

sections.title: Radiological Landmarks (CXR)
content: Stage 1: Cephalization - Dilation of upper lobe pulmonary veins.
Stage 2: Interstitial Edema - Kerley B lines (short horizontal lines at lung periphery).
Stage 3: Alveolar Edema - 'Bat-wing' or butterfly perihilar opacities.
Stage 4: Pleural Effusions - Often bilateral with blunting of costophrenic angles.

sections.title: The MAD DOG Mnemonic: Immediate Tx

content.explanation: M: Morphine (decreases preload/anxiety); A: Aminophylline (bronchodilation); D: Digitalis/Diuretics (Furosemide); D: Dopamine/Dobutamine (inotropes); O: Oxygen (NIV/CPAP); G: Gases (Monitor ABGs).

sections.title: LMNP: Standard Pharmacological Protocol
content: L: Lasix (Furosemide) 40-80mg IV stat.
M: Morphine 2-5mg IV (Vasodilates, reduces work of breathing).
N: Nitrates (Nitroglycerin SL or IV) to reduce preload.
P: Position (Sit patient upright with legs hanging).

sections.title: Ocular Considerations for the Ophthalmologist
content: Hypertensive Emergency: Pulmonary edema often co-exists with Grade IV Hypertensive Retinopathy (Papilledema).
Pre-eclampsia: High risk of pulmonary edema; look for Elschnig spots and serous retinal detachments.
Surgical Risk: Patients with underlying CHF/Pulmonary Edema risk require cardiac clearance before elective ophthalmic surgery.
Medication Side Effects: High-dose systemic Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (Acetazolamide) can exacerbate metabolic acidosis in respiratory failure.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg): Suggests cardiogenic shock.
Silent Chest: No air movement on auscultation (Impending failure).
Altered Mental Status: Signs of hypercapnia or cerebral hypoxia.
Asymmetrical Edema: Consider pulmonary embolism or focal infection.
Refractory Hypoxemia: Failure to improve with high-flow O2.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Early NIV: BiPAP/CPAP reduces the need for intubation by 50% in CPE.
Preload vs Afterload: Nitroglycerin is more effective than Furosemide in the first 15 mins for preload reduction.
The 'Dry Lung': Non-cardiogenic edema (ARDS) requires low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg).
Ophthalmic Exam: Fundoscopy can be a 'window' to the severity of systemic hypertensive damage.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent evidence from the DOSE trial suggests that high-dose bolus Furosemide is safe and more effective for symptom relief than low-dose continuous infusion in acute decompensation. Furthermore, the use of SGLT2 inhibitors (EMPEROR-Reduced study) has shown significant long-term reduction in re-hospitalization for patients prone to pulmonary edema episodes. In ophthalmology, the management of systemic fluid status remains critical for preventing postoperative complications like venous stasis or IOP spikes during prone-positioning surgeries.

title: Status Epilepticus: Clinical Essentials & Ocular Signatures
summary: Status Epilepticus (SE) is a life-threatening neurological emergency characterized by prolonged or rapidly recurring seizures without recovery. For the ophthalmologist, recognizing ictal eye movements and managing neuro-critical care pathways is paramount to preventing irreversible neuronal damage.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Temporal Thresholds
sections.content: Status Epilepticus (SE) is defined as a seizure with 5 minutes or more of continuous clinical and/or electrographic seizure activity, or recurrent seizure activity without recovery between seizures. While the traditional definition was 30 minutes, the 't1' operational threshold (5 mins) is when treatment must start to prevent the 't2' point (30 mins), after which permanent neuronal injury or system failure occurs.

branches: Acute Insults (Stroke, TBI, Hypoxia, CNS Infection)
Toxic/Withdrawal (AED Non-compliance, Alcohol, Cocaine, Benzo withdrawal)

rows: Rhythmic limb jerking, mental status impairment, tonic-clonic activity
Comatose or 'wandering confused' state, subtle twitching
Continuous rhythmic discharges, often focal or generalized
Recurrent focal motor seizures (e.g., finger/face) with preserved consciousness
Brief, shock-like jerks; common in post-anoxic brain injury

sections.title: Ophthalmic Manifestations in SE
content: Versive Gaze Deviation: Eyes look AWAY from the cortical seizure focus (contraversive) during ictus.
Nystagmoid Eye Movements: Repetitive, rhythmic, slow/fast phase movements, often horizontal.
Hippus: Paradoxical pupillary cycling (dilation/constriction) independent of light.
Mydriasis: Sympathetic surge leading to dilated, sluggishly reactive pupils.
Optic Disc Edema: Rarely seen in prolonged SE due to increased ICP or venous congestion.
Blindsidedness: Post-ictal cortical blindness (transient).

rows: Closed eyes, pelvic thrusting, out-of-phase limb movements
Rapid recovery, preceded by prodrome (tunnel vision, pallor)
Response to pain, not rhythmic; suggests brainstem herniation

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Point-of-Care Glucose (Rule out hypoglycemia immediately).
Step 2: Continuous EEG (cEEG) - Gold standard for diagnosis and monitoring of NCSE.
Step 3: Laboratory Panel (CBC, CMP, Tox Screen, AED levels, ABG/Lactate).
Step 4: Neuroimaging (CT Head non-contrast first; MRI Brain with DWI later to assess for cytotoxic edema).
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture (If CNS infection suspected, after stabilizing and ruling out mass effect).

rows: Preferred if no IV access established

sections.title: Phase 3: Refractory SE (40-60+ min)
content: Definition: Failure of initial Benzodiazepine + one Second-line AED.
Intubation Required: Proceed to general anesthesia for burst-suppression.
Midazolam Drip: 0.2 mg/kg bolus, then 0.05-2.0 mg/kg/hr infusion.
Propofol: 1-2 mg/kg bolus, then 20-200 mcg/kg/min (Watch for PRIS).
Ketamine: 0.5-3 mg/kg bolus, then 0.3-5 mg/kg/hr (NMDA antagonism).

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS): Metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia.
Valproate-Induced Hyperammonemic Encephalopathy.
Phenytoin-induced cardiac arrhythmias or hypotension (Purple Glove Syndrome).
NCSE in the elderly: Presents as subtle 'altered mental status'—often missed.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: GABA Exhaustion
sections.content: As seizures persist, GABA-A receptors are internalized (endocytosis), reducing the inhibitory response to Benzodiazepines. Simultaneously, NMDA and AMPA (excitatory) receptors are upregulated and trafficked to the synaptic membrane. This 'pharmacoresistance' explains why delayed treatment of SE is significantly less effective.

sections.title: Memory Aid: The 5 'S's of SE Management

content.explanation: S: Stabilize (ABCDEs). T: Termination (Benzos). A: Anti-seizure meds (IV Load). B: Brain imaging/EEG. S: Search for etiology.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Neuronal Death: Excitotoxicity leading to hippocampal sclerosis.
Systemic: Lactic acidosis, aspiration pneumonia, neurogenic pulmonary edema.
Rhabdomyolysis: Leading to acute tubular necrosis and renal failure.
Prognosis: Poor in elderly, post-anoxic etiology, and long durations (>1 hour).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: If the patient is 'shaking' but the eyes are tightly closed, suspect psychogenic seizures.
Never wait for an EEG to start treatment in convulsive SE—time is brain.
Always check a finger-stick glucose; hypoglycemia is the most treatable cause of SE.
In refractory SE, the goal is often 'burst suppression' on EEG for 24-48 hours.
Fosphenytoin is preferred over Phenytoin because it can be infused faster and has less risk of tissue necrosis.

title: Hereditary Angioedema (HAE): A Comprehensive Clinical Overview
summary: Hereditary Angioedema is a rare but potentially life-threatening genetic condition characterized by recurrent episodes of severe, non-pitting swelling. Unlike common allergies, HAE is mediated by bradykinin and does not respond to antihistamines or corticosteroids.

branches: Unregulated Activation of the Kallikrein-Kinin System

rows: Normal C1-INH; often Factor XII mutations

sections.title: Clinical Presentation & Symptoms
content: Recurrent episodes of non-pitting, non-pruritic skin swelling.
Commonly affects hands, feet, face, and genitalia.
Severe abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal wall edema (often mimicking surgical abdomen).
Periorbital edema and facial swelling (Ophthalmic relevance).
Laryngeal edema (High risk of asphyxiation).
Absence of urticaria (hives) or itching.
Erythema marginatum (non-itchy, serpiginous rash) may act as a prodrome.

sections.title: CRITICAL: Life-Threatening Warnings
content: Laryngeal Edema: Can lead to fatal airway obstruction within minutes to hours.
Ineffective Treatments: Epinephrine, Antihistamines, and Steroids generally DO NOT work for HAE.
ACE Inhibitors: Strictly contraindicated as they prevent bradykinin breakdown.
Estrogen-containing medications: Known to exacerbate or trigger attacks.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Screen with Serum C4 levels (almost always low during and between attacks).
Step 2: Measure C1-INH Quantitative Antigen levels.
Step 3: Measure C1-INH Functional levels if antigen is normal.
Step 4: C1q levels (to differentiate from Acquired Angioedema; C1q is low in AAE but normal in HAE).
Step 5: Genetic testing for SERPING1 or Factor XII mutations.

sections.title: Common Attack Triggers
content: Physical trauma or minor injury.
Dental procedures and oral surgery.
Emotional stress or fatigue.
Infections (Viral or Bacterial).
Menstruation or Pregnancy.
Certain medications (ACE Inhibitors, Oral Contraceptives).

sections.title: Management: Acute Attacks
content: C1-Inhibitor Concentrates (Berinert, Ruconest, Cinryze).
Icatibant (Firazyr): Bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist.
Ecallantide (Kalbitor): Plasma kallikrein inhibitor.
Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP): Used only if specific HAE therapies are unavailable.

sections.title: Management: Long-term Prophylaxis
content: Lanadelumab (Takhzyro): Monoclonal antibody against plasma kallikrein.
Berotralstat (Orladeyo): Oral kallikrein inhibitor.
Routine C1-INH Replacement Therapy.
Attenuated Androgens (Danazol, Stanozolol): Increase C1-INH production (limited by side effects).

sections.title: Genetic Context
sections.content: Hereditary Angioedema is primarily an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in the SERPING1 gene, which encodes the C1-esterase inhibitor protein. However, approximately 25% of cases result from de novo mutations with no prior family history. Understanding the genetic basis is crucial for family screening and early intervention, particularly since symptoms often manifest in late childhood or adolescence and may worsen after puberty.

content.explanation: NO Hives (Urticaria), NO Itching (Pruritus), NO response to Antihistamines, NO response to Epinephrine.

summary: Marfan syndrome is a systemic, autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene. It is characterized by specific ocular, cardiovascular, and skeletal manifestations that require lifelong monitoring.

sections.title: Ocular Hallmarks
content: Ectopia Lentis: Classic Upward and Superotemporal subluxation of the crystalline lens.
Zonular Integrity: Stretched or broken zonules (fibrillin-rich fibers).
Cornea Plana: Characteristically flat corneal curvature.
Increased Axial Length: Leading to high axial myopia.
Iris Hypoplasia: Resulting in transillumination defects and poor pupillary dilation.
Ciliary Body Hypoplasia: Often observed on ultrasound biomicroscopy.
Vitreous Liquefaction: Premature vitreous syneresis.

sections.title: Major Systemic Involvement
content: Cardiovascular: Aortic root aneurysm, Aortic dissection, Mitral valve prolapse (MVP).
Skeletal: Arachnodactyly (spider fingers), Pectus excavatum or carinatum, Scoliosis.
Integumentary: Striae atrophicae (stretch marks) without weight change.
Pulmonary: Spontaneous pneumothorax, apical blebs.
Dural Ectasia: Widening of the dural sac in the lumbosacral spine.

sections.title: Red Flag Complications
content: Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (High Risk due to axial length and vitreous changes)
Aortic Dissection (Life-threatening emergency)
Secondary Glaucoma (Angle-closure due to lens subluxation or pupillary block)
Presenile Cataracts (Nuclear sclerosis)
Endophthalmitis (Increased risk if lens surgery is required)

content.explanation: M: Mitral valve prolapse; A: Aortic Aneurysm; R: Retinal detachment; F: Fibrillin-1 mutation; A: Arachnodactyly; N: Near-sightedness (Myopia); S: Subluxated lens.

sections.title: Diagnostic Pathway: Ghent Criteria
content: Step 1: Clinical Evaluation of Systemic Score (>7 points).
Step 2: Slit-lamp exam to confirm Ectopia Lentis.
Step 3: Echocardiography to measure Aortic Root Z-score.
Step 4: Molecular Genetic Testing for FBN1 mutation.
Step 5: Review Family History of Marfan Syndrome.

sections.title: Exhaustive Overview of Marfan
sections.content: Marfan syndrome (MFS) is a pervasive multi-system genetic disorder. In the eye, the classic finding of ectopia lentis occurs because the zonular fibers, composed of fibrillin-1, are weak or absent. This leads to the lens being pulled toward the strongest remaining zonules, typically in a superior-temporal direction. Beyond the eye, the cardiovascular implications are the most life-threatening, particularly aortic root dilation which can lead to rupture. Skeletal features like a high-arched palate and joint hypermobility are common. Management requires a multidisciplinary team including ophthalmologists, cardiologists, and geneticists. Regular dilated fundus exams are mandatory to monitor for retinal tears and detachments, which occur at a higher frequency in this population due to increased axial length and collagen defects.

title: REACTIVE ARTHRITIS: The Triple Threat
summary: A systemic inflammatory condition emerging as a sterile joint response to a distant infection, primarily in the gastrointestinal or urogenital tracts. It is classically recognized by a triad of symptoms affecting the eyes, joints, and urinary system.

sections.title: Clinical Definition
sections.content: Reactive Arthritis (formerly known as Reiter’s Syndrome) is a multi-systemic inflammatory disorder that follows an infection. It belongs to the family of seronegative spondyloarthropathies, meaning Rheumatoid Factor (RF) is typically negative. The condition is characterized by an asymmetric inflammatory arthritis that develops days to weeks after a primary extra-articular infection.

content.mnemonic: Can't See, Can't Pee, Can't Climb a Tree
content.explanation: This represents the classic triad: Conjunctivitis (Can't See), Urethritis/Cervicitis (Can't Pee), and Arthritis (Can't Climb a Tree).

rows: Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter jejuni, Clostridium difficile

sections.title: Ophthalmic Manifestations
content: Bilateral Conjunctivitis: The most common ocular finding, often mucopurulent.
Acute Anterior Uveitis: Typically unilateral, recurrent, and characterized by pain, redness, and photophobia.
Episcleritis and Scleritis: Less common but documented.
Keratitis: Punctate epithelial erosions or subepithelial opacities.
Cystoid Macular Edema: Possible complication of severe chronic uveitis.

rows: Psoriatic skin plaques, nail pitting, DIP joint involvement.
Positive cultures for N. gonorrhoeae, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis.
Symmetric small joint involvement, RF/Anti-CCP positive.
Association with Crohn's or Ulcerative Colitis symptoms.

sections.title: Pathogenesis Process
content: 1. Initial Infection: Mucosal infection (GI or GU) occurs.
2. Immune Activation: Pathogen-derived antigens interact with HLA-B27.
3. Cross-Reactivity: Molecular mimicry leads to T-cell activation against host tissues.
4. Localized Inflammation: Sterile inflammation manifests in joints, eyes, and skin.

sections.title: Red Flags & Complications
content: Severe Vision Loss from uncontrolled Acute Anterior Uveitis.
Permanent Joint Deformity or chronic disability.
Aortic Regurgitation (rare cardiac complication).
Cardiac Conduction Abnormalities.
Development of secondary amyloidosis.

branches: The 'Little Brain': Regulates precision and timing

rows: Downbeat (often Craniocervical junction), Upbeat, Gaze-evoked, or Rebound.
Overshoot (hypermetria) or undershoot (hypometria) when shifting gaze.
Broken, 'cogwheel' or saccadic pursuit instead of smooth tracking.
Spontaneous, back-to-back horizontal saccades without an intersaccadic interval.
Vertical misalignment of the eyes due to asymmetric vestibular input.

content.explanation: D: Dysdiadochokinesia (Impaired rapid alternating movements); A: Ataxia (Gait and limb incoordination); N: Nystagmus (Rhythmic eye oscillation); I: Intention Tremor (Tremor increases near target); S: Slurred Speech (Dysarthria); H: Hypotonia (Reduced muscle tone).

sections.title: Localization of Lesions
content: Vermal Lesions: Result in truncal ataxia, head tilting, and bilateral ocular motor deficits.
Hemispheric Lesions: Result in ipsilateral limb ataxia and dysmetria.
Flocculonodular Lesions: Primarily affect balance and vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) suppression.

sections.title: Urgent Red Flags
content: Sudden Onset Ataxia: Potential cerebellar stroke or hemorrhage.
Papilledema: Signs of increased intracranial pressure (e.g., posterior fossa tumor).
Rapidly Progressive Opsoclonus: May indicate Paraneoplastic Syndrome (e.g., Neuroblastoma in children, Small Cell Lung Cancer in adults).
Acute Vertigo with 'HINTS' positive findings: Differentiating central from peripheral causes.

branches: Toxic: Alcohol, Phenytoin, Chemotherapy, Heavy Metals
Inflammatory/Autoimmune: Multiple Sclerosis, Post-viral Cerebellitis, Gluten Ataxia
Degenerative: Spinocerebellar Ataxias (SCA), Multiple System Atrophy (MSA-C)

sections.title: The Diagnostic Process
content: Step 1: Detailed History (Onset, Duration, Toxic exposure, Family history).
Step 2: Neuro-Ophthalmic Exam (Nystagmus, Saccades, Pursuit, Cover Test).
Step 3: Motor Exam (Finger-to-nose, Heel-to-shin, Rapid alternating movements).
Step 4: Gait Analysis (Tandem gait, Romberg test).
Step 5: Neuroimaging (MRI Brain/Posterior Fossa is the Gold Standard).
Step 6: Laboratory Testing (Genetic panels, Paraneoplastic markers, Vitamin levels).

sections.title: Verbatim Clinical Context
sections.content: Cerebellar disease represents a broad spectrum of disorders where the primary deficit is the loss of motor control and coordination. While the cerebellum does not initiate movement, it acts as a critical 'comparator'—adjusting motor output by comparing intended movement with actual sensory feedback. In ophthalmology, this manifest as 'dysmetria of thought' and eye movement, where the brain cannot accurately calibrate the magnitude of saccades or the smoothness of tracking, leading to visual instability and vertigo.

title: Mastering the Gap: Full Thickness Macular Hole (FTMH)
summary: A full-thickness macular hole (FTMH) is a definitive anatomical defect in the fovea, extending from the internal limiting membrane to the outer segments of the photoreceptors. This condition results in a significant loss of central vision and requires precise surgical intervention.

data.title: Mastering the Gap: Full Thickness Macular Hole (FTMH)
data.summary: A full-thickness macular hole (FTMH) is a definitive anatomical defect in the fovea, extending from the internal limiting membrane to the outer segments of the photoreceptors. This condition results in a significant loss of central vision and requires precise surgical intervention.
