sections.title: Defining the Defect
sections.content: A Full Thickness Macular Hole (FTMH) is a primary foveal break that involves all layers of the neurosensory retina. It is most commonly idiopathic and occurs frequently in women over the age of 60. The condition is characterized by the sudden or progressive loss of central vision and the presence of metamorphopsia (distorted vision).

rows: Foveal detachment; loss of foveal depression.
Eccentric or central break in neurosensory retina.
Complete defect; no posterior vitreous detachment (PVD).
FTMH with complete Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD).
Full thickness defect; cystic edges; cuff of subretinal fluid.
Partial thickness; intact outer retinal layers; 'scooped out' look.
Steep foveal edges caused by ERM; no loss of tissue.
History of sun gazing; small outer retinal defect.
Petaloid pattern on FA; intraretinal fluid but no break.

sections.title: Diagnostic Bedside Tests
content: Watzke-Allen Test: Patient perceives a break/thinning in a narrow slit beam over the fovea.
Laser Aim Beam Test: 50μm laser spot is not seen when directed into the center of the hole.
Amsler Grid: Central scotoma and significant metamorphopsia.
OCT (Gold Standard): Confirms full-thickness loss, measures hole diameter, and identifies VMT status.

sections.title: Surgical Management Process
content: 1. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) to remove vitreous traction.
2. Induction of Posterior Vitreous Detachment (if not present).
3. Internal Limiting Membrane (ILM) Peeling to relieve tangential traction.
4. Gas Tamponade (SF6 or C3F8) to seal the hole edges.
5. Post-operative face-down positioning (5-7 days typically).

sections.title: Critical Post-Op Red Flags
content: Sudden increase in pain or redness (Endophthalmitis)
New onset of 'curtain' or 'shadow' in vision (Retinal Detachment)
Elevated Intraocular Pressure (IOP) due to gas expansion
Progression of Nuclear Sclerotic Cataracts (Commonly post-vitrectomy)

content.explanation: P: Pars Plana Vitrectomy; E: Excision of the ILM; E: Exchange of fluid for gas; L: Low-head positioning (Face-down).

summary: Angioid streaks are irregular, jagged, tapering lines radiating from the peripapillary region, resulting from dehiscences in a calcified and brittle Bruch's membrane. This visual guide explores their systemic associations, clinical presentation, and management.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Irregular, jagged, reddish-brown to dark gray lines
Tapering appearance away from the optic disc
Peau d'orange: Mottled RPE appearance (often precedes streaks)
Optic Disc Drusen: Frequently seen in PXE patients
Focal chorioretinal scars (Salmon spots)

rows: Grönblad-Strandberg syndrome; 'plucked chicken skin' appearance; most common cause.
Type VI (Ocular-scoliotic form); joint hypermobility; skin hyperextensibility.
Increased bone turnover; 1-2% of patients develop angioid streaks.
HbSS, HbSC, and Thalassemia; vascular occlusions.
Pituitary tumors, Lead poisoning, Hyperphosphatemia, Hypercalcinosis.

sections.title: Major Complications
content: Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV): Leading cause of vision loss
Subretinal Hemorrhage: Can occur after trivial blunt trauma
Foveal Involvement: Direct extension of a streak into the macula
Disciform Scarring: Resulting from untreated CNV

rows: High myopia; usually horizontal; no peripapillary radiating pattern.
History of trauma; concentric to the optic disc; usually white/yellow.
Atrophic scars with pigmented borders; inflammatory history.
Posterior staphyloma; tilted disc; lacquer cracks.

sections.title: Diagnostic Evaluation
content: Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Streaks show 'window defects' (hyperfluorescence) or staining.
Indocyanine Green Angiography (ICGA): May reveal more extensive streaks than clinical exam.
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Detects intraretinal or subretinal fluid (CNV).
Autofluorescence: Streaks often appear hypo-autofluorescent with hyper-autofluorescent borders.

sections.title: Management & Patient Education
content: Step 1: Baseline documentation with fundus photography and OCT.
Step 2: Home monitoring with Amsler grid to detect early CNV.
Step 3: Strict use of safety glasses (polycarbonate) during sports to prevent trauma-induced hemorrhage.
Step 4: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF therapy if CNV develops.
Step 5: Systemic workup for associated diseases (Cardiology, Dermatology, Genetics).

sections.title: Verbatim Clinical Summary
sections.content: Angioid streaks are characterized by a crack-like appearance of the fundus due to changes in Bruch's membrane. While the streaks themselves are often asymptomatic, they predispose the eye to choroidal neovascularization and extreme sensitivity to trauma. Clinical management focuses on the early detection of neovascular complications and the identification of potentially serious systemic underlying conditions such as Pseudoxanthoma Elasticum or Paget's Disease.

title: AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION (AMD): A Comprehensive Visual Guide
summary: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a degenerative disorder in which the structure and function of the macula deteriorates. It is the leading cause of irreversible visual loss in industrialized countries, characterized by drusen and RPE changes.

data.title: AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION (AMD): A Comprehensive Visual Guide
data.summary: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a degenerative disorder in which the structure and function of the macula deteriorates. It is the leading cause of irreversible visual loss in industrialized countries, characterized by drusen and RPE changes.

sections.title: Introduction & Basic Definition
sections.content: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a degenerative disorder in which the structure and function of the macula deteriorates. It is characterized by the presence of specific clinical findings, including drusen and RPE changes, in the absence of another disorder. Later stages of the disease are associated with impairment of vision secondary to neovascularization or atrophy.

headers: Definition (Presence of lesions within two disc diameters of the fovea)
rows: No drusen; No AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Only drupelets; No AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Medium drusen (>63 μm but <125 μm); No AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Large drusen (>125 μm); Any AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Neovascular AMD and/or Any geographic atrophy

sections.title: Nomenclature & Main Types
content: A consensus committee provided the clinical classification and standardized nomenclature for neovascular AMD.
Dry (non-exudative, non-neovascular) AMD: Most common form (90%). Geographic atrophy (GA) is the advanced stage. Note: It's suggested 'dry AMD' should describe GA rather than early stages.
Wet (exudative, neovascular) AMD: Less common but rapid progression to sight loss. Main entities: MNV, PED, RAP, and PCV.
TIP: The term 'choroidal neovascularization' (CNV) is no longer appropriate because neovascularization may start in the outer retina. Macular neovascularization (MNV) should be used instead.

sections.title: Epidemiological Context
content: Most common cause of irreversible visual loss in industrialized countries.
In USA: Severe sight loss = better eye worse than 6/60.
Symptoms rare in patients under 50 years of age.
UK: 1.6% of those over 75 have binocular acuity of less than 6/60.
Fellow Eye Risk: Patients with late AMD in one eye (or moderate loss in non-advanced AMD) have a 50% chance of developing advanced AMD in the fellow eye within 5 years.

branches: Genetic Susceptibility (CFH gene 1q31 - 7x risk; ARMS2 gene 10q26 - 8x risk)
Aspirin (Weak statistical association; benefits outweigh risk)
Other factors (Cataract surgery, Blue iris, Sunlight, Female gender)

sections.title: Drusen: Histopathology
sections.content: Drusen are extracellular deposits located at the interface between the RPE and Bruch membrane. Composed of constituents from immune-mediated and metabolic processes in the RPE. Role in pathogenesis is unclear but associated with lesion size and pigmentary abnormalities. Rare before age 40; common by the sixth decade. Distribution: Variable (fovea, encircling fovea, band around macular periphery, or mid-peripheral fundus).

sections.title: Drusen: Clinical Features & Sizes
content: Small Drusen (Drupelets): ≤63 μm (half width of retinal vein at disc). Well-defined, white-yellow. Little visual loss risk alone.
Intermediate Drusen: 63–125 μm. Yellow-white focal deposits. <10% 5-year progression risk unless bilateral pigmentary changes present (>10%).
Large Drusen ('Soft'): >125 μm. Less well delineated. May coalesce into 'drusenoid RPE detachment'. 13% bilateral progression risk; 50% with bilateral pigmentary changes.
Dystrophic Calcification: May develop in all types.
Pigmentary Abnormalities: Hyper- and hypopigmentation (not due to other disease) significantly increases visual loss risk.

branches: Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy (malattia leventinese): Autosomal dominant radial drusen; appears 2nd-3rd decades.
Cuticular drusen (Basal laminar drusen): Small (25–75 μm) yellowish nodules; clustering; FA shows 'stars in the sky'; linked to CFH variant.
Type 2 membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis: Chronic renal disease; bilateral diffuse drusen-like lesions; CFH gene implicated.

sections.title: Drusen Imaging & Diagnostic Tools
content: TIP: Strong association between risk of advanced AMD, drusen size, and macular pigmentary change.
Size Estimation: Retinal vein diameter at optic disc margin is approx 125 μm.
OCT: Medium/Large drusen seen as hyper-reflective irregular nodules beneath RPE, on or within Bruch membrane.
FA: Hyperfluorescence (window defect from atrophy or late staining). Hypofluorescence (hydrophobic, high lipid content masking fluorescence).

sections.title: Antioxidant Supplementation (AREDS)
content: AREDS1/AREDS2 Evidence: High-dose antioxidants/minerals decrease risk of advanced AMD.
Recommendation (Age >55 with high-risk signs): Extensive intermediate drusen, One or more large drusen, GA in one or both eyes, or Late AMD in one eye.
Risk Reduction: 25–30% reduction in 10-year progression risk for advanced baseline signs. No reduction seen in early or no AMD.
AREDS1 Regimen: Vitamin C, E, Beta-carotene, Zinc (80mg), Copper.

content.explanation: Vitamin E (400 IU), Vitamin C (500 mg), Lutein (10 mg), Zeaxanthin (2 mg), Zinc (25–80 mg; lower may be equally effective), Copper (2 mg; not required with low-dose zinc).

sections.title: AREDS2 Key Findings
content: Lutein/Zeaxanthin: Safe and superior alternative to Beta-carotene (18% risk reduction).
Beta-carotene Warning: Increases lung cancer incidence in current/former smokers.
Zinc: 25 mg is maximal absorbed; lower dose reduces genitourinary/GI side effects.
Omega-3: Adding omega-3 fatty acids did not enhance outcomes.
Competition: Carotenoids may compete for absorption.
Cataract Benefit: One-third reduction in likelihood of cataract surgery in specific groups.

sections.title: Lifestyle Considerations
content: Green leafy vegetables: Lower risk (prudent for family history/early AMD).
Smoking cessation: Strongly advised.
Sun protection: Consider protective measures.
Oily fish: Consumption supported by some authorities.
TIP: Regular antioxidant dietary supplementation can reduce advanced AMD risk in high-risk dry AMD patients.

sections.title: Non-Exudative (Dry) AMD Overview
sections.content: A common condition threatening vision in up to 5 million people worldwide. Loss of photoreceptors and RPE cells results in Geographic Atrophy (GA). Process is slow but GA results in significant acuity loss and is an inevitable long-term outcome for many wet AMD patients. Lesion size is measured by FAF. Pathogenesis involves complement factors C3 and C5 activation.

sections.title: Dry AMD Diagnosis & Symptoms
content: Symptoms: Gradual vision impairment (months/years); usually bilateral but asymmetric. Vision fluctuates and may be better in bright light.

Sign Sequence: 1. Numerous intermediate-large soft drusen (may coalesce). 2. Focal hyper- or hypopigmentation. 3. Circumscribed RPE atrophy (loss of retina/choriocapillaris). 4. Geographic Atrophy (GA) with visible larger choroidal vessels and disappearing drusen. 5. Drusenoid RPE detachment.

sections.title: Advanced Imaging for Dry AMD
content: OCT: Loss of RPE and morphologic retinal alterations. Increased hyper-reflectivity in outer layers.
Outer Retinal Tubulations (OCT): Roundish hyporeflective spaces (degenerating photoreceptors) often at GA margins.
Outer Retinal Corrugations (OCT): Undulating hyper-reflective layer; Histological Basal Laminar Deposit (between RPE and basement membrane).
Basal Linear Deposit: Membranous debris between RPE basement membrane and Bruch membrane (may form drusen).
Microperimetry: Accurate method of testing central vision.
FAF: Visualizes atrophy; Hyperautofluorescence in junctional zone indicates higher progression risk.
FA: Window defect due to unmasked background fluorescence (if choriocapillaris intact); scleral late staining.

sections.title: Management of Dry AMD
content: 1. Prophylaxis: AREDS supplementation + address risk factors (smoking, sun, CV, diet).
2. Home Monitoring: Provide Amsler grid with advice for regular self-testing.
3. Visual Support: Provision of low vision aids and visually impaired certification.
4. Future: Complement inhibitors (Avacincaptad pegol [C5] or Pegcetacoplan [C3]) reduce GA growth in short term.

sections.title: Ineffective or Experimental Treatments
content: Emixustat (Visual cycle modulation): Not helpful in slowing atrophy growth.
Photocoagulation of drusen: Reduces extent but does not reduce progression risk.
Saffron (20 mg/day): Short-term improvement in retinal function.

Experimental Surgery: Miniature intraocular telescope; RPE stem cell implants (improved vision in some); Macular translocation (unsuccessful/high complication rate); Visual prostheses (under investigation).

sections.title: Indications for Urgent Surgery
content: Acutely symptomatic RD: Should be surgically repaired as soon as possible, particularly if the macula is not involved (Fig. 16.22A).
Superior or large break: Increases urgency as Subretinal Fluid (SRF) is likely to spread more rapidly.
Advanced syneresis: Found in high myopia, increasing the urgency of intervention.
Impossible visualization: Patients with dense fresh vitreous haemorrhage where fundus visualization is impossible require surgery ASAP if B-scan ultrasonography shows an underlying RD.
Macular Threat: Urgent surgery is needed in an acute progressive RD if the macula is threatened.
Macula-off timing: Visual results are better if surgery is performed within 72 hours, even if the macula is already off.

sections.title: Pre-Operative Preparation
content: Step 1: NPO Status - The patient should not eat or drink if urgent surgery is contemplated.
Step 2: Activity Modification - Minimizing activity may be helpful.
Step 3: Posturing - Bed-rest with the head turned so the retinal break is in the most dependent position.
Benefit: Reduces the amount of SRF and facilitates surgery.

rows: Outpatient procedure using intravitreal gas bubble + cryotherapy or laser to seal break without scleral buckling.
Success rates are worse than those achievable with conventional scleral buckling.
Uncomplicated RD, small retinal break, or cluster of breaks < 2 clock hours in the upper 2/3 of peripheral retina.

sections.title: Pneumatic Retinopexy: Visual Sequence
content: A: Cryotherapy is applied.
B: Gas injection into the vitreous cavity.
C: Gas seals the retinal break and the retina becomes flat.
D: Gas is eventually absorbed.
Observation: Gas bubble breakup can lead to 'fish eggs' appearance.

sections.title: Principles of Scleral Buckling
sections.content: Scleral buckling (conventional/external RD surgery) involves suturing material (explant) onto the sclera to create an inward indentation (buckle). The purpose is to close retinal breaks by opposing the RPE to the sensory retina and to reduce dynamic vitreoretinal traction at sites of local vitreoretinal adhesion. This technique should ALWAYS be used for patients with detachment secondary to post-traumatic dialysis.

sections.title: Scleral Buckling Explant & Configuration
content: Materials: Soft or hard silicone.
Sizing: Entire break should be surrounded by approx 2 mm of buckle.
Anterior Extension: Buckle must involve the area of the vitreous base anterior to the tear to prevent reopening/leakage.
Measurement: Break dimensions are assessed by comparing them with the optic disc diameter.
Configurations: Radial, segmental, circumferential, or encircling (depending on size/position/number of breaks).

sections.title: Buckling Surgical Technique
content: 1. Peritomy: Conjunctiva is incised to facilitate access.
2. Localization: Retinal breaks are localized (Fig 16.30A).
3. Cryotherapy: Applied to the localized break.
4. Explant Placement: Appropriate dimensions/orientation sutured to sclera (mattress sutures common).
5. Verification: Position of buckle checked in relation to the break.

rows: Drainage-Air-Cryotherapy-Explant; advocates cite rapid reattachment in deep or longstanding viscous SRF.
Retinal perforation, retinal incarceration in the drainage site, or choroidal haemorrhage.
Some practitioners prefer Pars Plana Vitrectomy as a primary option to avoid external drainage complications.

sections.title: Complications of Scleral Buckling
content: Diplopia: Due to mechanical effect; common; early spontaneous resolution typical, but intervention may be needed.
Cystoid Macular Oedema (CMO): Occurs in up to 25%; usually responds to treatment.
Epiretinal Membrane (ERM): Occurs in around 15%.
Foveal Complications: Persistent subfoveal fluid and structural disruption (usually in macula-off detachments).
Anterior Segment Ischaemia: Vascular compromise risk; higher with encircling bands and sickle haemoglobinopathies.
Buckle-Related: Extrusion, intrusion, or infection (requires removal and antibiotics).
Intraocular Pressure (IOP): Early spikes (usually resolve) or persistent elevation; potential angle closure.
Choroidal Detachment: Usually resolves spontaneously as oedema settles and vortex vein function improves.

branches: Missed Breaks (requires thorough search if RD configuration doesn't match primary break)
Buckle Failure (Inadequate size, incorrect positioning, or inadequate height)
Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR) - Most common late failure; traction opens old/new breaks; occurs weeks post-op
Fish-mouthing (Large superior equatorial U-tear in bullous RD opens widely post-buckling)
Reopening of Break (Inadequate cryo/buckling, or decrease in buckle height over time/removal)

sections.title: Managing Buckle Failure
content: Incorrect size/position: Requires replacement or repositioning of explant.
Inadequate height: May be addressed by SRF drainage, intravitreal gas injection, or Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) as a definitive measure.

sections.title: CRITICAL RECALL: The Three Commonest Causes of Failure

content.explanation: P: Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR). C: failure to Close all breaks. N: development of New breaks.

sections.title: Pathogenesis of Diabetic TRD
content: 1. Progressive contraction of fibrovascular membranes occurs over large areas of vitreoretinal adhesion.
2. Gradual and frequently incomplete PVD (unlike acute PVD in rhegmatogenous RD).
3. Leakage of plasma constituents into the vitreous gel from fibrovascular networks adherent to the posterior vitreous surface.
4. Cortical vitreous remains strongly adherent to areas of fibrovascular proliferation.
5. Rare Event: If a subsequent complete PVD occurs, new blood vessels are avulsed and RD does not develop.

sections.title: The Mechanics of Vitreoretinal Traction
content: Tangential Traction: Caused by contraction of epiretinal fibrovascular membranes; results in puckering of the retina and distortion of blood vessels.
Anteroposterior Traction: Due to contraction of fibrovascular membranes extending from the posterior retina (usually major arcades) to the vitreous base anteriorly and/or bridging (trampoline).
Bridge Traction: Contraction of fibrovascular membranes stretching from one part of the retina to another or between vascular arcades, pulling the two involved points together.

rows: Convex configuration; surface is smooth and not corrugated.
No photopsia (no traction). Floaters if vitritis present.
Defect progresses slowly; may be stable for months/years.
Defect may develop suddenly and progress rapidly.
Shallower; seldom extends to ora serrata; shifting fluid absent.
Exhibits 'shifting fluid' phenomenon; fluid collects based on gravity.
Occurs at sites of vitreoretinal traction.

sections.title: TRD Clinical Indicators & B-Scan
content: B-scan ultrasonography shows incomplete PVD and a relatively immobile retina (Fig. 16.34B).
Signs (Fig. 16.34A): Localized tractional detachment secondary to preretinal fibrosis.
Combined Tractional–Rhegmatogenous RD: If a break occurs, it assumes rhegmatogenous characteristics and progresses rapidly.

sections.title: Exudative Retinal Detachment (ERD) Pathogenesis
sections.content: Exudative RD is characterized by the accumulation of SRF in the absence of retinal breaks or traction. It occurs in vascular, inflammatory, and neoplastic diseases involving the retina, RPE, and choroid. Fluid leaks outside vessels and accumulates under the retina. While the RPE can normally pump leaking fluid into choroidal circulation, RD occurs when this mechanism is overwhelmed or functions sub-normally.

sections.title: Etiology of Exudative Retinal Detachment
content: Choroidal tumours: Melanoma, haemangioma, and metastases.
Inflammation: Harada disease and posterior scleritis.
Bullous central serous chorioretinopathy (rare cause).
Iatrogenic: RD surgery and panretinal photocoagulation.
Choroidal neovascularization: Extensive subretinal fluid at the posterior pole.
Hypertensive choroidopathy: E.g., toxaemia of pregnancy (very rare).
Idiopathic: Uveal effusion syndrome.

sections.title: CRITICAL TIP: Tumor Warning
content: An intraocular tumour should be considered the cause of an exudative RD until proved otherwise.
Exudative RD is characterized by 'shifting' subretinal fluid.

sections.title: The 'Shifting Fluid' Phenomenon
content: 1. Gravity-Dependent: SRF detaches the area of retina under which it accumulates (Fig. 16.35A/B).
2. Upright Position: SRF collects under the inferior retina.
3. Supine Position: After several minutes, the inferior retina flattens.
4. Posterior Shift: SRF shifts posteriorly, detaching the superior retina.

sections.title: Additional ERD Signs & Diagnostics
content: Bilateral Involvement: Depending on the cause, both eyes may be involved simultaneously.
Systemic Association: Patients may have systemic disease responsible (e.g., Harada disease, toxaemia of pregnancy).
Leopard Spots: Consist of scattered areas of subretinal pigment clumping seen after the detachment has flattened (Fig. 16.36B).
Visual Evidence: Choroidal tumours may be apparent on fundus exam or B-scan (Fig. 16.36A).

sections.title: Treatment Strategies for ERD
content: Cause-Dependent: Treatment is tailored to the specific underlying etiology.
Spontaneous Resolution: Some cases resolve without intervention.
Systemic Corticosteroids: Used for inflammatory causes like Harada disease and posterior scleritis.
Laser Photocoagulation: Used to seal the leak in the RPE in some eyes with bullous central serous chorioretinopathy.

rows: Buckle extrusion complication (Courtesy of S Chen).
Fresh upper temporal retinal detachment prior to surgery.
Failure: Tear is still open because the plomb is undersized.
Failure: Tear is still open because the plomb is incorrectly positioned.
Failure: 'Fish-mouthing' of a U-tear communicating with a radial fold.
Flat retina following insertion of a radial buckle.

Retinal Detachment Chapter 16, Pages 691-693. Exudative Retinal Detachment section notes that SRF accumulates without breaks or traction.

branches: Normally myelinated nerve fibres lose insulating myelin layer
Myelin is phagocytosed by microglia and macrophages
Astrocytes lay down fibrous tissue in plaques
Disrupts nervous conduction within white matter tracts (brain, brainstem, spinal cord)

sections.title: Major Demyelinating Conditions
content: Isolated optic neuritis: No initial clinical evidence of generalized demyelination (though high proportion subsequently develop it).
Multiple sclerosis (MS): By far the most common demyelinating disease.
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD): Previously Devic disease; rare autoimmune disease.
MOG antibody disorder (MOGAD): Recently identified rare autoimmune disease.
Schilder disease: Very rare relentlessly progressive generalized disease.

sections.title: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)
sections.content: NMOSD involves antibodies against aquaporin 4 protein in astrocyte cell membranes. It typically affects middle-aged women but can occur at any age. Characterized by bilateral optic neuritis and long-segment transverse myelitis (spinal cord demyelination) within a few weeks. Most patients have repeated attacks separated by remission. The NMO-IgG blood test is highly specific and positive in 70% of patients. Acute treatment: high-dose IV steroids, followed by oral steroids; if ineffective, plasmapheresis. Long-term: immunosuppressive drugs. Recently approved for anti-aquaporin positive adults: Eculizumab, inebilizumab, and satralizumab.

sections.title: MOGAD & Schilder Disease
content: MOGAD: Antibodies form against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG); results in inflammation of optic nerve and spinal cord; bilateral simultaneous optic neuropathy is common.
Schilder Disease: Onset prior to age 10; death within 1–2 years; bilateral optic neuritis without improvement may occur.

sections.title: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) Overview
content: Idiopathic demyelinating disease of CNS white matter.
Infection with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) significantly increases risk (though not sufficient alone).
More common in women than men.
Presentation: Typically 3rd–4th decades; usually relapsing/remitting pattern (may switch to unremitting later); less commonly progressive from outset.

sections.title: Clinical Features of Demyelinating Optic Neuritis
content: Symptoms: Subacute monocular visual impairment; usual age 20–50 years (mean ~30).
Phosphenes: Tiny white or coloured flashes or sparkles.
Pain: Present in >90%; exacerbated by ocular movement; may precede/accompany visual loss; lasts a few days.
Other Symptoms: Frontal headache and tenderness of the globe.
Signs: VA usually 6/18–6/60 (rarely worse); impaired colour vision; Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD).
Disc Appearance: Normal in 2/3 (retrobulbar neuritis); 1/3 show papillitis (Fig 19.8).
Fellow Eye: Temporal disc pallor may indicate previous optic neuritis.

rows: Vision worsens over several days to 3 weeks
Initial recovery rapid; then slower over 6-12 months
TIP: MS-related ON usually improves without treatment over months
Weakness, stiffness, sphincter disturbance, sensory loss
Lhermitte sign (neck flexion shock), Uhthoff phenomenon (heat/exercise worsening)
Common: Retrobulbar ON, Internuclear ophthalmoplegia, Nystagmus. Uncommon: Skew deviation, Ocular motor nerve palsies. Rare: Uveitis, Periphlebitis

sections.title: Investigations in Multiple Sclerosis
content: Lumbar Puncture: Oligoclonal bands on CSF protein electrophoresis in 90–95%.
MRI: Changes in optic nerve (STIR imaging) and characteristic white matter plaques (supratentorial/corpus callosum).
VEPs: Abnormal (conduction delay, reduced amplitude) in up to 100% of clinically definite MS.

sections.title: Risk of Developing MS Post-Optic Neuritis
Predictors of Lower MS Risk
content: Male gender
Absence of preceding viral syndrome
Negative test for EBV
Presence of optic disc swelling, disc/peripapillary haemorrhages, or macular exudates
Vision reduced to No Light Perception (NLP)
Absence of periocular pain

sections.title: MS Statistics & Genetics
content: Optic neuritis is the presenting feature of MS in up to 30%.
ON occurs in 50% of established MS patients.
Not hereditary, but higher probability in close relatives.
Association with HLA DR15 and DQ6.

sections.title: Indications for Steroid Treatment in ON
content: Start treatment within 48 hours for potential axon preservation and VA improvement.
If VA is worse than 6/12 in week 1: speeds recovery by 2–3 weeks and delays clinical MS short-term.
IV Regimen: Methylprednisolone sodium succinate 1g daily (250mg 6-hourly) for 3 days.
Oral Regimen: Prednisolone (1mg/kg daily) for 11 days, followed by 3-day taper.
Warning: Oral prednisolone alone may increase recurrence risk if used without prior IV steroids.

rows: 1a/1b variants; early stage use; subcutaneous/intramuscular; flu-like symptoms; good long-term safety.
Subcutaneous; reduces relapse/progression; 'decoy' action; injection site reaction in 1/3.
Monoclonal antibody for highly active relapsing-remitting MS; reduces relapses by 2/3; systemic side effects.
Helpful for highly active and primary progressive disease; rare risk of fatal PML (leukoencephalopathy).
Potentially most cost-effective due to dosing strategy; used in difficult cases.
Cladribine, fingolimod, mitoxantrone (used for active/highly active relapsing MS).

sections.title: Prognosis & Management Strategy
content: Prognosis: >90% recover VA to 6/9 or better. Colour vision/RAPD may stay abnormal. Temporal pallor or atrophy may ensue.
Chronic ON: ~10% develop stepwise/progressive loss.
Relapse: 80-85% of MS patients experience relapses.
Approach: Multidisciplinary. First attack = Steroids + IFNβ/Glatiramer. Progressive MS = Ocrelizumab.

rows: Post-viral (measles, mumps, rubella, etc.) or post-immunization. Common in children. Bilateral papillitis/neuroretinitis. Good prognosis.
Unilateral loss, severe headache, spheno-ethmoidal sinusitis. Spread of infection/vasculitis. Rx: Antibiotics/Drainage.
Bartonella henselae; cat scratch/bite; causes neuroretinitis.
Borrelia burgdorferi (tick bite); neuroretinitis or retrobulbar neuritis; mimics MS.
Associated with AIDS and meningitis; can be bilateral.
Spread from retinitis (ARN/PORN) or HZO; common in immunocompromised.

content.explanation: Bilateral severe visual loss 1-3 weeks after viral infection is common in children; however, the prognosis for visual recovery is good.

branches: Failure of LR innervation by hypoplastic 6th nerve nucleus
Anomalous LR innervation by 3rd nerve fibers
Approximately 10% familial; associated with gene mutations
Up to 50% have systemic defects (Deafness, External ear abnormalities, Speech disorder, Skeletal abnormalities)

sections.title: DRS Clinical Features
content: Typical face turn: Confers Binocular Single Vision (BSV) and avoids amblyopia
Abduction: Complete or partial restriction
Adduction: Restricted (usually partial)
Globe Retraction on adduction: Result of co-contraction of medial and lateral recti
Narrowing of palpebral fissure on adduction
Up-shoot or Down-shoot in adduction: Tight LR muscle slipping over/under the globe
Convergence Deficiency: Affected eye remains fixed in primary position while unaffected eye converges

sections.title: Management of Duane Syndrome
content: Non-Surgical: Majority do not need intervention. Children maintain BSV via Compensatory Head Posture (CHP).
Surgical Indications: Loss of binocular function (failure to use CHP), psychosocially unacceptable head posture, neck discomfort, severe up-shoots/down-shoots, or severe globe retraction.
Amblyopia: Usually results from anisometropia rather than strabismus.
Procedures: Unilateral/bilateral medial or lateral rectus recession. Transposition of SR and IR (or SR only) to LR to improve abduction.
Contraindication: Lateral rectus of the involved side should NOT be resected (increases retraction).

branches: Congenital non-progressive bilateral 6th and 7th cranial nerve palsies
Limb anomalies and mild mental handicap

sections.title: CFEOM & Strabismus Fixus
sections.content: Congenital Fibrosis of the Extraocular Muscles (CFEOM) is a rare non-progressive, autosomal dominant disorder (most commonly CFEOM1 via KIF21A mutation) featuring bilateral ptosis and restrictive external ophthalmoplegia. Pathologically, the superior division of the oculomotor nerve is hypoplastic. Eyes are typically fixed 10° below horizontal with compensatory chin elevation. Strabismus Fixus involves eyes fixed by fibrous tightening of the medial recti (convergent) or lateral recti (divergent), in both congenital and acquired forms.

rows: Inability to elevate eye from abduction to adduction; tight IR or hypoplastic SR
Limited elevation in adduction; can be congenital or acquired
Congenital ptosis, horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, congenital 4th/7th palsy
Chin-up; Face-turn away from affected eye

sections.title: Brown Syndrome Management
content: Congenital: Usually no treatment if BSV/posture are maintained. Spontaneous improvement often by end of 1st decade.
Congenital Surgery: Recommended if significant hypotropia or deteriorating control. Procedure: Lengthening of superior oblique tendon.
Acquired Causes: Trauma to trochlea, inflammation (RA, pansinusitis, scleritis).
Acquired Treatment: Address specific etiology; steroids (oral or peritrochlear injection).

branches: Causes: IO overaction (4th palsy), SO underaction, SR underaction, Brown syndrome
Treatment (Oblique): IO weakening or SO strengthening
V-Eso Treatment: MR recession + downward transposition
V-Exo Treatment: LR recession + upward transposition
Causes: Primary SO overaction, IO underaction/palsy, IR underaction
Treatment (Oblique): SO posterior tenotomy (20Δ) or total tenotomy (50Δ)
A-Eso Treatment: MR recession + upward transposition
A-Exo Treatment: LR recession + downward transposition

content.explanation: Before surgical realignment, any significant refractive error and/or underlying amblyopia MUST be corrected.

sections.title: Strengthening Procedures
content: Resection: Muscle exposed, absorbable sutures inserted at measured distance, muscle excised anteriorly, reattached to original insertion.
Plication (Tucking): Fold muscle; less traumatic, preserves anterior ciliary vessels, reversible. Used for recti or lax SO.
Advancement: Moving previously recessed muscle closer to the limbus.

sections.title: Weakening Procedures
content: Rectus Recession: Suture outer quarters, disinsert, measure/mark sclera, resuture at measured distance (or hang-back).
Inferior Oblique Recession: Exposed via inferotemporal fornix, disinserted, sutured 3mm posterior/temporal to temporal IR insertion edge.
Disinsertion (Myectomy): Detaching without reattachment (commonly for overacting IO).
Posterior Fixation (Faden): Suture muscle belly to sclera (or pulley) 12mm posteriorly to decrease pull in field of action without affecting primary position.

sections.title: Transposition & Specialized Surgery
sections.content: Transposition relocates muscles to substitute for absent/deficient action, most commonly for severe LR weakness in 6th nerve palsy, Duane syndrome, alphabet patterns, and MED. Techniques involve recti and oblique muscles. Vector adjustment procedures primarily aim to alter the direction of muscle action.

sections.title: Adjustable Suture Techniques
content: Step 1: Indications - Precise outcome needed (Restrictive strabismus, trauma, previous surgery, Duane/Möbius/Myasthenia, complex deviations).
Step 2: Operative - Muscle sutures passed through stump; Noose knot tied; Ends tied in a loop; Conjunctiva left open.
Step 3: Adjustment (Post-Op) - Perform under topical anesthesia when patient is awake.
Step 4: More Recession - Pull noose knot anteriorly to provide slack; patient looks towards field of action.
Step 5: Less Recession - Pull muscle suture anteriorly and tighten knot against stump.
Step 6: Completion - Once aligned, secure main knot, remove loop, close conjunctiva.

sections.title: Complications of Strabismus Surgery
content: Operative: Lost or 'slipped' muscle (especially Medial Rectus).
Operative: Globe perforation by misplaced suture (risk high in thin-sclera high myopia).
Operative: Opening posterior Tenon capsule leading to fat/muscle fibrosis (risk in IO surgery).
Postoperative: Over-correction and Under-correction (may require reoperation).
Postoperative: Anterior segment ischaemia (Avoid removing >2 rectus muscles at once; more common in elderly).
Postoperative: Stretched scar (can occur years later, causing malalignment).

title: THYROID EYE DISEASE: THE DEFINITIVE CLINICAL COMPENDIUM
summary: Thyroid eye disease (TED), or Graves ophthalmopathy, is the most common cause of adult proptosis and stems from a complex organ-specific autoimmune reaction. This guide covers the pathogenesis, EUGOGO classification, clinical manifestations from lid retraction to sight-threatening optic neuropathy, and the multi-staged medical and surgical management protocols.

This guide covers the pathogenesis, EUGOGO classification, clinical manifestations from lid retraction to sight-threatening optic neuropathy, and the multi-staged medical and surgical management protocols.

sections.title: Introduction & Thyrotoxicosis
sections.content: Thyroid eye disease (TED), also known as thyroid-associated orbitopathy and Graves ophthalmopathy, is a common orbital disorder and is the most common cause of both bilateral and unilateral proptosis in an adult. Thyrotoxicosis (hyperthyroidism) is a condition involving excessive secretion of thyroid hormones. Graves disease, the most common form of hyperthyroidism, is an autoimmune disorder in which IgG antibodies bind to receptors in the thyroid gland and stimulate secretion of thyroid hormones. It is more common in females and may be associated with other autoimmune disorders.

rows: Presentation often in the fourth or fifth decades; more common in females.
Weight loss despite good appetite, increased bowel frequency, sweating, heat intolerance, nervousness, irritability, palpitations, weakness and fatigue.
Enlargement of the thyroid gland (goitre), tremor, palmar erythema and warm and sweaty skin.
Thyroid acropachy: Similar to clubbing of the fingers (1%). Pretibial myxoedema (1–5%): Indurated thickening of the skin of the shins.
Other autoimmune disorders can be associated.

sections.title: Thyroid Function & Management
content: 1. Initial Testing: TSH level (Commonly tested initially).
2. Secondary Investigation: If TSH is low, or normal but disease is suspected, carry out additional investigations.
3. Treatment Options: Carbimazole, propylthiouracil, propranolol, thyroid ablation with radioactive iodine, and partial thyroidectomy.

sections.title: Risk Factors - Extended Detail
sections.content: Once a patient has Graves disease, the major clinical risk factor for developing TED is smoking. The greater the number of cigarettes smoked per day, the greater the risk and giving up smoking seems to reduce the risk. Women are five times more likely to be affected by TED than men, but this largely reflects the increased incidence of Graves disease in women. Radioactive iodine used to treat hyperthyroidism can worsen TED. This condition can also, though less commonly, occur in euthyroid and hypothyroid (including treated hyperthyroid) patients. It can sometimes be the presenting manifestation of thyroid-related disease.

branches: Autoimmune: Anti-thyrotropin-receptor antibody reacts against thyroid cells and orbital fibroblasts.
Receptors: Upregulation of Insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R) and TSH receptor (TSHR) in orbital/brow fat.
Inflammation: Extraocular muscles, interstitial tissues, orbital fat, and lacrimal glands affected.
Muscle Swelling: Muscles can swell up to eight times normal size due to glycosaminoglycan secretion and osmotic water imbibition.
Lipogenesis: Induced by fibroblasts and preadipocytes causing fat enlargement.
Fibrosis: Degeneration leads to fibrosis, causing restrictive myopathy and diplopia.

rows: Eyes are red and painful. Tends to remit within 1–3 years.
Eyes are white; painless motility defects may be present.
(1) Soft tissue involvement, (2) Lid retraction, (3) Proptosis, (4) Optic neuropathy, (5) Restrictive myopathy.
Only about 10% of patients develop serious long-term ocular problems.

sections.title: EUGOGO Classification (2021)
content: ACTIVITY ASSESSMENT:
• Spontaneous retrobulbar pain.
• Pain on attempted upward or downward gaze.
• Redness of eyelids.
• Redness of conjunctiva.
• Swelling of conjunctiva or plica.
• Swelling of eyelids.
• Chemosis.
SEVERITY ASSESSMENT:
• Mild: Minor impact on daily life.
• Moderate–severe: Moderate–severe soft tissue involvement, lid retraction ≥ 2 mm, diplopia, and proptosis ≥ 3 mm.
• Sight-threatening: Due to optic neuropathy or corneal breakdown.

sections.title: Soft Tissue Involvement
content: Symptoms: Grittiness, red eyes, lacrimation, photophobia, puffy lids, and retrobulbar discomfort.
Epibulbar hyperaemia: Sensitive sign of activity; focal hyperaemia outlines horizontal recti insertions.
Periorbital swelling: Caused by oedema and infiltration; associated with chemosis and fat prolapse.
Tear insufficiency: Common instability of the tear film.
Corneal signs: Punctate epithelial erosions, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis, bacterial keratitis, thinning, and scarring.

sections.title: Lid Retraction Signs
content: Prevalence: Occurs in 50% of Graves patients.
Mechanism: Müller muscle overstimulation, levator/inferior rectus fibrosis, and secondary overaction.
Dalrymple sign: Lid retraction/spasm in primary gaze (widened palpebral opening).
Kocher sign: Staring and frightened appearance on attentive fixation.
von Graefe sign: Retarded descent of the upper lid on downgaze (lid lag).
Scleral Show: Margin is level with or above superior limbus; lower margin is below inferior limbus.

sections.title: Proptosis & Restrictive Myopathy
content: PROPTOSIS: Axial, unilateral/bilateral, symmetrical/asymmetrical, and frequently permanent. Severe cases lead to exposure keratopathy and corneal ulceration.
MYOPATHY: 30–50% develop ophthalmoplegia. Restricted by inflammatory oedema then fibrosis. Causes double vision and discomfort.
Order of Rectus Involvement (Approximate):
1. Inferior Rectus (Elevation defect) - Most common motility deficit.
2. Medial Rectus (Abduction defect) - May simulate sixth nerve palsy.
3. Superior Rectus (Depression defect).
4. Lateral Rectus (Adduction defect).

sections.title: Optic Neuropathy: SIGHT THREATENING
content: Occurs in up to 6% of patients.
Caused by compression of optic nerve or blood supply at the orbital apex by enlarged recti.
Scleral show/proptosis may be ABSENT while nerve compression is present.
Symptom: Impairment of central vision. Patients should self-monitor by occluding eyes and assessing color intensity (e.g., TV screen).
Signs: Reduced Visual Acuity (VA), Colour desaturation, diminished light brightness appreciation.
Critical Sign: Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) gives cause for marked concern.
Field Defects: Central or paracentral, may be combined with nerve fibre bundle defects (confusable with glaucoma).
Optic Disc: Normal, swollen, or rarely atrophic.

sections.title: Investigations & Imaging
content: Visual field testing: For suspected optic nerve compromise or baseline.
Imaging (MRI, CT, Ultrasound): Indicated for equivocal diagnosis or pre-surgery.
Radiological Pattern: Muscle belly enlargement with tendon sparing.
Visual Evoked Potentials (VEP): Utilized in some optic neuropathy cases.

sections.title: Treatment Choice Factors
content: Treatment depends on: (a) Clinical activity, (b) Severity, (c) Duration.
Anti-inflammatory efficacy: Significantly less effective after 18 months duration.
Cessation of smoking: The first measure in ALL cases.
Radioiodine precaution: Give short course oral steroids if TED is pre-existing.

sections.title: Management of Mild & Active Disease
content: Lubricants: For SLK, corneal exposure, and dryness.
Topical Agents: Steroids, NSAIDs, or ciclosporin.
Selenium: Sodium selenite 200 μg daily for 6 months (in deficient areas).
Postural adjustment: Head elevation with three pillows during sleep.
Eyelid taping: During sleep to alleviate mild exposure keratopathy.

sections.title: Moderate–Severe Active Disease: Steroids
content: 1. Clinical Activity Score (CAS): Calculate based on EUGOGO; Treat if score ≥ 3/7.
2. Oral Steroids: Prednisolone 60–80 mg/day initially, then tapered.
3. IV Methylprednisolone: Better tolerability and superior outcomes vs oral. Regimen: 0.5 g once weekly for 6 weeks, then 0.25 g once weekly for 6 weeks.
4. Monitoring: Max response in 2–8 weeks; discontinue oral therapy after several months if possible.
5. Contraindications (IV): Hepatic dysfunction, significant CVD, uncontrolled hypertension, or diabetes.

sections.title: Advanced Medical Therapies
content: Combined Therapy: IV corticosteroids weekly + Mycophenolate sodium (0.72 g/day for 24 weeks) is the regimen of choice.
Orbital steroid injections: Triamcinolone acetate (less effective than systemic).
Low-dose fractionated radiotherapy: Second-line. 40% non-response rate. Risks: cataract, radiation retinopathy, local cancer.
Combined Irradiation: Radiotherapy + Azathioprine + Low-dose prednisolone.
Second-line Monoclonals: Rituximab, Tocilizumab.
Teprotumumab: IGF-1R inhibitor; effective for proptosis/CAS in acute and chronic TED; risk of hearing loss.

sections.title: Management of Acute Sight-Threatening TED
content: Aggressive Treatment: Pulsed IV methylprednisolone (0.5–1 g for 3 days or alternate days).
Dose Limit: Keep cumulative dose below 8 g to reduce liver risk.
Surgical Intervention: Orbital wall/apex decompression if steroids are ineffective (20%) or contraindicated.
Adjuvants: Orbital radiotherapy.
Mandatory Monitoring: Liver function tests, gastric protection, and osteoporosis prophylaxis.

rows: 1. Orbital Decompression → 2. Strabismus Surgery → 3. Eyelid Surgery.

One-wall (lateral): 4-5 mm reduction. Two-wall (medial/lateral): Balanced but risk of diplopia. Three-wall (+floor): 6-10 mm reduction; risk of hypoglobus/nerve damage. Four-wall (+roof): For very severe cases.
Requires stable deviation for 6–12 months. Goal: Binocular vision in primary/reading gaze. RECESSION ONLY (never resect). Adjustable sutures preferred.
Mild: Müllerotomy. Severe: Recession/disinsertion of levator aponeurosis/suspensory ligament. Lower lid: Recession of retractors +/- hard palate graft.
Temporary measure for lid retraction (levator/Müller) or diplopia while awaiting surgery.

content.explanation: T: Tendon Sparing (in imaging). E: EUGOGO (score for activity). D: Decompression (for sight-threat). P: Pulsed Steroids (first line for neuropathy). R: Recession only (no resection in muscles). I: Immunosuppression (prevent long-term complications). N: No Smoking (first measure). C: Cumulative Steroids (stay < 8g). I: IGF-1R Inhibitors (Teprotumumab). P: Pillows (3 for head elevation). L: Lid lag (von Graefe sign). E: Elevation defect (most common myopathy). S: Scleral show (sign of retraction).

content: Fig. 22.4 (A): Small upper lid laceration in a child showing the tip of a coloured pencil.
Fig. 22.4 (B): Axial CT scan showing the broken tips (arrows) of a coloured pencil.
Fig. 22.4 (C): Penetrating injury to the left upper lid with an intact globe.
Fig. 22.4 (D): Axial CT scan showing a retrobulbar glass shard.
Fig. 22.5 (B): Marked periocular ecchymosis, oedema, and subconjunctival haemorrhage.

sections.title: Introduction to Orbital Floor Blow-out Fractures

branches: Mechanism: Sudden increase in orbital pressure from an impacting object (e.g., fist, tennis ball) > 5 cm (orbital aperture diameter).
Impact Dynamics: Eyeball is displaced and transmits rather than absorbs the impact (Fig. 22.5A).
Location: Most frequently involves the floor along the thin bone covering the infraorbital canal; medial wall occasionally involved.
Resistance: Lateral wall and roof are usually able to withstand such trauma.
Systemic Care: Ensure full evaluation for head and systemic injury; initiate necessary interspecialty referrals.

rows: Visual acuity should be recorded and monitored.
Variable ecchymosis, oedema, and occasionally subcutaneous emphysema (crackling sensation on palpation due to air in subcutaneous tissues).
Infraorbital nerve anaesthesia: involves lower lid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, upper teeth, and gums (common due to infraorbital canal involvement).
Exclude hyphaema, angle recession, and retinal dialysis (relatively uncommon in blow-out fractures).
Manifests after oedema resolves (a few days). Late enophthalmos is uncommon; only 20% of large fractures have >2mm enophthalmos at 6 months (Fig. 22.6B).

sections.title: Mechanisms of Diplopia
content: 1. Haemorrhage and Oedema: Tightening of septa connecting inferior rectus/oblique to periorbita restricts movement. Usually improves as swelling resolves.

2. Mechanical Entrapment: Entrapment of inferior rectus, inferior oblique, or adjacent connective tissue/fat within the fracture (Fig. 22.6D). Causes diplopia in both upgaze (Fig. 22.6A & C) and downgaze.
3. Direct Muscle Injury: Associated with a negative forced duction test. Muscle fibres usually regenerate with normal function returning within ~2 months.

sections.title: Diagnostic Tests for Restricted Motility
content: Forced Duction Test: Positive in mechanical entrapment.
Differential Intraocular Pressure Test: Positive (IOP increases as a restricted muscle presses on the globe).
Hess Chart Testing: Useful to map eye movements, assess, and monitor (Fig. 22.7).
Hess Chart (Fig. 22.7): Shows restriction of left upgaze (SR and IO) and downgaze (IR) with secondary overaction of the right eye.

sections.title: Imaging & Evaluation (CT Scan)
content: CT Coronal Sections: Essential for evaluating fracture extent (Fig. 22.8, Fig. 22.6D).
Tear Drop Sign: Soft tissue prolapse into the maxillary antrum (Fig. 22.8).
Antral Densities: May represent prolapsed orbital fat, extraocular muscles, haematoma, or unrelated antral polyps.

sections.title: Initial Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Observation and prescription of oral antibiotics.
Step 2: Application of ice packs and use of nasal decongestants.
Step 3: Patient Instruction: Do NOT blow nose (prevents forcing infected sinus contents into the orbit).
Step 4: Systemic Steroids: Occasionally required for severe orbital oedema, especially if compromising the optic nerve.

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAG: ‘White-eyed’ Fracture
content: Subgroup requiring URGENT repair to avoid permanent neuromuscular damage.
Patient Demographic: Generally < 18 years of age due to greater bone elasticity.
Clinical Presentation: Little visible external soft tissue injury (Fig. 22.6C).
Mechanism: 'Trap-door' effect causing acute incarceration of herniated tissue.
Systemic Symptoms: Acute nausea, vomiting, headache.
Risk: Persistent activation of the oculo-cardiac reflex.
CT Imaging: Features may be subtle.

rows: No treatment required (risk of permanent complications is small).
Fracture < 1/2 floor, no herniation/enophthalmos, improving diplopia
May develop enophthalmos if left untreated.
Entrapment, Enophthalmos > 2mm, or persistent diplopia in primary position
No difference in outcome between surgery at 2 weeks vs 6 months.
Often improves without surgery; delayed surgery still effective (except in extreme upgaze).

sections.title: Surgical Repair Methods
content: 1. Incision Approach: Transconjunctival, subciliary, or via the maxillary sinus.
2. Periosteal Elevation: Elevation of the periosteum from the orbital floor.
3. Freeing Contents: Freeing of trapped orbital contents.
4. Reconstruction: Repair of the bony defect with a synthetic implant.

sections.title: Exhaustive Text Preservation Bloc
sections.content: CHAPTER 22 Trauma. Orbital Trauma (p. 911-912). Fig. 22.4 (A) Small upper lid laceration in a child showing the tip of a coloured pencil; (B) axial CT scan showing the broken tips (arrows); (C) penetrating injury to the left upper lid with an intact globe; (D) axial CT scan showing a retrobulbar glass shard. Diagnosis: Visual function, especially acuity, should be recorded and monitored. Orbital floor fracture Introduction: A blow-out fracture of the orbital floor is typically caused by a sudden increase in the orbital pressure from an impacting object that is greater in diameter than the orbital aperture (about 5 cm), such as a fist or tennis ball, so that the eyeball itself is displaced and transmits rather than absorbs the impact (Fig. 22.5A). Since the bones of the lateral wall and the roof are usually able to withstand such trauma, the fracture most frequently involves the floor of the orbit along the thin bone covering the infraorbital canal. Occasionally, the medial orbital wall may also be fractured. Fractures of the orbital rim and adjacent facial bones require appropriately tailored management. Clinical features vary with the severity of trauma and the interval between injury and examination. Care should be taken to ensure that a full evaluation for head and systemic injury has been performed and any necessary interspecialty referrals initiated. Periocular signs include variable ecchymosis, oedema (Fig. 22.5B) and occasionally subcutaneous emphysema (a crackling sensation on palpation due to air in the subcutaneous tissues). Infraorbital nerve anaesthesia involving the lower lid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, upper teeth and gums is common as the fracture frequently involves the infraorbital canal. Diplopia may be caused by: Haemorrhage and oedema causing tightening of septa connecting inferior rectus/oblique to periorbita; mechanical entrapment within the fracture (Fig. 22.6D); direct injury to muscle (negative forced duction). Forced duction and differential IOP tests are positive in entrapment. Enophthalmos manifests as oedema resolves; 20% of large fractures show >2mm at 6 months. Hess chart (Fig 22.7) maps eye movements. CT coronal sections (Fig 22.8) evaluate fracture extent and 'tear drop' sign. Initial Treatment: Observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, nasal decongestants. No nose blowing. Steroids for severe oedema. Subsequent Treatment aims to prevent permanent vertical diplopia/enophthalmos. Small cracks/minimal herniation do not require treatment. Fractures > 1/2 floor or with >2mm enophthalmos/persistent primary diplopia should be repaired within 2 weeks. 'White-eyed' fracture (under 18 years) requires urgent repair for tissue incarceration/trap-door effect; presents with nausea/vomiting. Surgical repair via transconjunctival, subciliary, or maxillary sinus with synthetic implant.

sections.title: Diagnosis and Initial Presentation
content: Symptoms are often absent, with a tumour detected by chance on routine fundus examination.
A range of visual disturbance can occur depending on tumour characteristics.
Signs: A solitary elevated subretinal grey-brown (Fig. 20.26A) or rarely amelanotic (Fig. 20.26B) dome-shaped mass.
Diffuse infiltration is uncommon.
About 60% are located within 3 mm of the optic disc (Fig. 20.26C) or fovea.
Clumps of overlying orange pigment are common (Fig. 20.26D).

sections.title: Advanced Clinical Signs
content: Breakthrough: If the tumour breaks through Bruch membrane it acquires a ‘collar stud’ appearance (see Fig. 20.25C and Fig. 20.28C).
Associated haemorrhage and subretinal fluid (Fig. 20.26E) are common.
Exudative retinal detachment (Fig. 20.26F) may result from subretinal fluid, which can mask the underlying lesion.
Other signs: Sentinel vessels (Fig. 20.27), choroidal folds, inflammation, rubeosis iridis, secondary glaucoma and cataract.

rows: Usually exhibits numerous surface drusen, without serous retinal detachment and little if any orange pigment.
Deeply pigmented and usually located at the optic disc.
Flat, often grey-black; has a well-defined margin with lacunae.
In subretinal or suprachoroidal space (e.g., from choroidal neovascularization or retinal artery macroaneurysm).
Smooth surface, light brown colour, indistinct margins, extensive retinal detachment; often a past history of malignancy.
Typically posterior, pink, dome-shaped with a smooth surface.
Often associated with exudative retinal detachment.
Presents with large elevated lesion; unlike melanoma, pain is a common feature.
Eccentrically located (temporal pre-equatorial), associated with exudate and fresh haemorrhage (rare in melanoma).
Small, smooth, brown, dome-shaped lesion that disappears with pressure on the eye.
Tightly arranged fusiform cells with indistinct cell membranes and slender or plump oval nuclei.
Large pleomorphic cells with distinct cell membranes, large vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations (Imaging)
content: Examination: Sufficient for diagnosis in the majority of cases.

Fluorescein Angiography (FA): Limited diagnostic value; no pathognomonic pattern. Shows intrinsic ‘dual’ circulation (Fig. 20.28A), mottled fluorescence (arteriovenous phase), late diffuse leakage and staining.

Ultrasound: Measures dimensions and detects tumours through opaque media/exudative detachment. Shows internal homogeneity, low to medium reflectivity, choroidal excavation (Fig. 20.28B), and orbital shadowing.
Acoustic Hollowing: A basal acoustically quiet zone due to greater tissue homogeneity in this region.
Collar Stud (US): Configuration (Fig. 20.28C) is almost pathognomonic when present.
FAF: Intense diffuse or confluent hyperautofluorescence is a useful indicator of melanoma.
OCT: Measures dimensions and demonstrates subretinal fluid/secondary retinal changes overlying the lesion.
ICGA: Usually shows hypofluorescence throughout; provides more information than FA about tumour extent due to lower RPE interference.
MRI: Useful for extraocular extension (Fig. 20.28D) and differential diagnosis.

sections.title: Biopsy and Advanced Pathology
content: Biopsy: Used when diagnosis is not established by non-invasive methods. Performed via fine needle or 25-gauge vitrectomy system (larger sample).
Immunocytochemistry (PAX8): Distinguishes tumours. Melanoma and melanocytoma are PAX8-negative; pigmented adenocarcinomas are PAX8-positive.

content.explanation: Loss of one copy of chromosome 3 (M3) and changes in chromosome 8 (i8q) strongly correlate with poor outcome, especially when occurring together. Metastasis occurs almost exclusively with certain genetic profiles.

sections.title: Prognostic Resources
content: The Liverpool Uveal Melanoma Prognosticator is an online resource combining anatomic, genetic, and histopathological data to determine prognosis for life.
Reduced surveillance can be adopted for patients with a low-risk genetic profile.

sections.title: Systemic Investigation Protocol
content: Step 1: Detect metastatic spread (primary focus on liver).
Step 2: Liver function testing and ultrasonography (mainstays).
Step 3: Chest radiography (rarely shows lung secondaries without liver disease).
Step 4: Consider whole-body PET/CT (Greater sensitivity for extrahepatic lesions, but high ionizing radiation dose).

sections.title: Treatment Principles
content: Objective: Avoid a painful/unsightly eye while conserving useful vision.
Survival: Influence of ocular treatment on survival is not yet defined, though smaller earlier tumours may have lower risk of metastasis.
Management: Individualized based on tumour characteristics (apical height, basal diameter) and patient factors (health, age, preferences, fellow eye).

rows: Tumours < 20mm basal diameter and < 10mm thick. Plaque sutured to sclera for several days. Regression starts 1–2 months post-treatment.
Cataract, papillopathy, disc neovascularization, radiation retinopathy, 'toxic tumour syndrome'.
Used for large or posterior tumours unsuitable for brachytherapy. Targeting aided by tantalum markers. Survival comparable to brachytherapy.
Lashes loss, eyelid depigmentation, keratitis, and intraocular complications similar to brachytherapy.
Multiple collimated beams (concurrent or sequential) delivering high dose only to the tumour.
Effective, but may have a comparatively high complication rate.

sections.title: Laser and Surgical Therapies
content: Transpupillary thermotherapy (TTT): Uses infrared laser for hyperthermia (not coagulation). For small tumours when radiotherapy is inappropriate or for vision-threatening exudation. Tumour disappears to leave bare sclera.
TTT Complications: Retinal traction, tears, rhegmatogenous detachment, vascular occlusion, neovascularization. Local recurrence common in thick, amelanotic, or disc-margin tumours.
Trans-scleral choroidectomy: Technically difficult. For tumours > 16mm in diameter too thick for radiotherapy. Complications: Detachment, hypotony, wound dehiscence, recurrence.
Light-activated AU-011: Novel treatment for small melanomas (2–3.4 mm). Nano-particles from HPV + infrared dye injected into vitreous; activated by infrared light to cause necrosis.

sections.title: Enucleation: Removal of the Eye
content: Large tumour size
Optic disc invasion
Extensive involvement of ciliary body or angle
Irreversible loss of useful vision
Poor motivation to keep the eye
Critical: Must perform ophthalmoscopy after surgical draping to ensure correct eye is removed.

sections.title: Metastatic Disease Management
content: No standard treatment for metastatic disease exists.
Tebentafusc: Immunotherapy drug that can modestly increase survival in some patients.
Note: Cutaneous melanoma checkpoint inhibitors are NOT effective against uveal melanoma.
Systemic chemotherapy has NOT been shown to benefit cases without evidence of metastatic spread.

sections.title: Introduction & Demographics
content: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood.
40% develop in the head and neck.
It is the most common primary orbital malignancy in children but is still a rare condition.
Approximately 90% occur in children under 16 years.
The average age of onset is 7 years.
CHAPTER 4: Orbit | Page 149

branches: Potential to differentiate into striated muscle
Variants of the RB1 gene (responsible for retinoblastoma)
Evidence supports role of epigenetic dysregulation

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: The Mimicker
content: TIP: Rhabdomyosarcoma can mimic an orbital infection in a child.
May mimic an inflammatory condition such as orbital cellulitis.
Differential Concern: Rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis.
Differential Concern: Swelling and redness of overlying skin (Note: the skin is NOT warm).

rows: Cells show light microscopic features of striated muscle differentiation (Fig. 4.42A).
Most of the balance of orbital RMS
Fewer cells show skeletal muscle differentiation; particular chromosomal translocations characteristic on cytogenetics.
Much less common in the orbit.
Much less common in the orbit.

sections.title: Clinical Diagnosis: Signs & Symptoms
content: Symptoms: Rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis is usual.
Tumour Location: Most commonly superonasal or superior (Fig. 4.42B).
Alternative Locations: May arise anywhere in the orbit, including inferiorly (Fig. 4.42C), conjunctiva, and uvea.
Skin Signs: Swelling and redness develop (not warm).
Sensory: Diplopia is frequent.
Sensory: Pain is less common.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations
content: MRI: Shows a poorly defined mass.
CT: Shows a poorly defined mass of homogeneous density, often with adjacent bony destruction (Fig. 4.42D).
Incisional Biopsy: Performed to confirm diagnosis, establish histopathological subtype, and cytogenetic characteristics.
Systemic Investigation: Should be performed for metastasis (most common sites: lung and bone).

sections.title: Treatment Protocols
sections.content: Commonly used guidelines for staging and a corresponding treatment protocol were produced by the Intergroup Rhabdomyosarcoma Study Group (IRSG). Treatment encompasses a combination of radiotherapy, chemotherapy and sometimes surgical debulking. A single oncogenic fusion gene is associated with treatment resistance and a 40–45% decrease in overall survival. Entinostat with chemotherapy may improve the prognosis in selected cases of rhabdomyosarcoma, but has not yet been approved for clinical use.

content.explanation: The prognosis for patients with disease confined to the orbit is good.

data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='45' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M30 40 L50 20 L70 40 M50 20 V80' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='5' stroke-linecap='round' fill='none'/><path d='M35 60 Q50 75 65 60' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/></svg>

branches: Immediate coughing reaction to expel foreign body
Most events occur during play or eating
Risk: Rapid asphyxiation if cough is absent/ineffective

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Suspect Foreign Body IF:
content: 1. The onset was very sudden
2. There are no other signs of illness
3. Clues present: History of eating or playing with small items immediately prior to symptoms
Note: Similar signs/symptoms can be laryngitis or epiglottitis (require different management)

rows: No external manoeuvre. Encourage coughing and monitor continuously.
Shout for help immediately. Determine conscious level. Active intervention required.

sections.title: Conscious Child: Back Blows (Infant vs. Child)
content: Determine conscious level: If still conscious but cough is absent/ineffective, give back blows.
INFANT: Support head-downwards, prone position across rescuer's lap.
INFANT: Support head by thumb at angle of lower jaw and fingers at the other side. Do NOT compress soft tissues under jaw.
CHILD > 1 YR: Position head down (across lap or forward-leaning position supported from behind).
ACTION: Deliver up to 5 sharp back blows with the heel of one hand between shoulder blades.
GOAL: Relieve obstruction with each blow rather than giving all 5.

sections.title: Conscious Child: Thrusts (When Back Blows Fail)

rows: Head-downwards supine position on arm/thigh; encircle occiput with hand.
Stand or kneel behind; arms under child's arms; encircle torso.
Sharp chest compressions delivered at a slower rate.
Clench fist, grasp with other hand; pull sharply inwards and upwards.
Up to 5 thrusts (relieve with each thrust).
Do NOT use Abdominal Thrusts (Heimlich) for infants.
Do NOT apply pressure to xiphoid process or lower rib cage.

sections.title: Following Thrusts: Reassessment
content: If object not expelled and victim conscious: Continue sequence of back blows and chest/abdominal thrusts.
Call or send for help if not available. Do not leave the child.
If object expelled: Assess clinical condition. Part may remain in respiratory tract.
If doubt: Seek medical assistance.

sections.title: Unconscious Child Management
content: Place on firm, flat surface.
Call/send for help (Do not leave child).
Airway: Open mouth and look for object.
Remove ONLY if visible with a single finger sweep.
Attempt 5 rescue breaths (Reposition head if chest doesn't rise).
Proceed to CPR immediately after breaths if no response.

sections.title: DANGER: Airway Opening Warning
content: Do NOT attempt blind or repeated finger sweeps.
These can impact the object more deeply into the pharynx and cause injury.

content.explanation: Rate: 100-120 min-1. Ratio: 15 compressions to 2 breaths. Depth: 1/3 of chest depth.

sections.title: CPR Execution Protocol (Step 7B)
content: Check pulse: If no signs of life (unless pulse >60 min-1 is certain within 10s), start chest compression.
Combine rescue breathing and chest compression.
Compress lower half of sternum (avoiding upper abdomen).
Locate xiphisternum: compress sternum one finger’s breadth above the angle where ribs join.
Release pressure completely between compressions.
Perform for ~1 min before summoning EMS (if alone).
If obstruction relieved: Check airway, deliver rescue breaths if not breathing, assess for life, continue CPR if needed.
If breathing/conscious: Place in safe side-lying (recovery) position and monitor.

rows: Compress sternum with tips of two fingers.
Encircling technique: Thumbs side-by-side on sternum; fingers encircle rib cage supporting the back.
Heel of one hand over lower sternum; lift fingers off ribs. Arm straight, position vertically above chest.
For larger children/small rescuers: Use both hands with fingers interlocked.

branches: Definition: Characterized by increased serum creatinine & urea, often with oliguria or anuria
Prerenal/Systemic: Hypovolaemia, low COP, Hepatorenal syndrome

sections.title: ARF Initial Management & Monitoring
content: 1. Catheterize: Assess hourly urine output & establish fluid charts.
2. Assess Intravascular Volume: BP, JVP, skin turgor, fluid balance sheet, weight, CVP.
3. Cardiac Monitoring: Attach to cardiac monitor.
4. Access: Consider inserting a central venous cannula.

sections.title: Comprehensive ARF Investigations
content: Blood: U&E, Ca2+, PO4-3, FBC, ESR, CRP, INR, LFT, CK, LDH, protein electrophoresis, hepatitis serology
Autoantibodies: ANA, ANCA, complement, anti-GBM, ASOT
Cultures: Blood cultures, Urgent urine microscopy & cultures
Urine WBCs: Infection & interstitial nephritis
Urine RBCs: Inflammatory glomerular condition
Imaging: USS of renal tract (exclude obstruction), ECG, CXR

sections.title: Hyperkalaemia: Red Alert (K+ > 6mmol/L)
content: Causes: Oliguric renal failure, metabolic acidosis (DM) & K+ sparing diuretics
ECG Sign 1: Tall T waves ± flat P waves ± increased PR interval
ECG Sign 2: Widening of QRS complex leads to VF/VT
TREATMENT: 10 mL Ca gluconate (10%) IV over 2min (Cardioprotection/threshold potential; NO change to K+ levels)
TREATMENT: Insulin (10U) + 50% glucose (50mL) IV over 30 mins (Moves K+ into cells)
TREATMENT: Nebulized salbutamol (2.5 mg) (Moves K+ into cells)
TREATMENT: Polystyrene sulfonate resin (Ca Resonium 15g/6-8h PO or 30g enema) to remove K+ from colon
TREATMENT: Dialysis

rows: 20 mL + previous hour’s urine output per hour
Urgent dialysis. Nitrate infusion, furosemide, 'renal dose' dopamine

sections.title: Urgent Dialysis Indications & Nephrotoxins
content: AVOID: Nephrotoxic drugs e.g., NSAIDS & aminoglycosides
DIALYSE IF: Persistent hyperkalaemia (> 6 mmol/L)
DIALYSE IF: Acidosis (pH < 7.2)
DIALYSE IF: Hypercatabolic renal failure
DIALYSE IF: Pulmonary edema & no substantial diuresis
DIALYSE IF: Pericarditis (in tamponade, dialyse after pressure relief)

sections.title: Acute Poisoning: General Management
content: A: Adequate ventilation
B: Oxygenation
C: Circulation -> IV line
D: Level of consciousness (Naloxone if decreased)
Monitor: Vital signs monitoring
Assess: History (patient/friends/family) + Physical examination
Investigate: Glucose, U&E, FBC, LFT, INR, ABG, ECG, Paracetamol/Salicylate levels, Toxicology

rows: Rarely used; Worse after 30-60m; Contraindicated: Petroleum/corrosives, unconscious, unable to protect airway. NEVER induce vomiting.
50g with water. Use for: Salicylates, paracetamol. Don't use: Petroleum, corrosives, alcohols, metal salts.

sections.title: Salicylate Poisoning
content: Dose: Mild (150 mg/kg), Moderate (250 mg/kg), Severe (>500 mg/kg)
Symptoms: Vomiting, dehydration, hyperventilation, tinnitus, vertigo, sweating
Rare/Severe: Coma, seizures, decreased BP, Heart block, pulmonary oedema, hyperthermia
Acid-Base: Respiratory alkalosis (central stimulation) then metabolic acidosis
Management: Gastric lavage (within 1h) + charcoal; Correct metabolic acidosis with HCO3 (Aim urine pH 7.5-8.5)
Dialysis: If salicylate level > 700 mg/L

sections.title: Paracetamol Poisoning & NAC Protocol
content: Threshold: 150 mg/kg or 12g (fatal). Symptoms: RUQ pain, jaundice, encephalopathy, renal failure.
NAC Step 1: 150 mg/kg IVI in 200 mL 5% dextrose over 15 min.
NAC Step 2: 50 mg/kg in 500 mL 5% dextrose over 4h.
NAC Step 3: 100 mg/kg every 16h in 1L 5% dextrose.
Alternative: Methionine 2.5g/4h PO for 16h (if NAC unavailable).
Specialist Transfer: INR > 2 (<48h) or > 3.5 (<72h), Encephalopathy, Creatinine > 200 umol/L, Blood pH < 7.3, Systolic BP < 80mmHg.

rows: Partial: Blisters, erythema, wet, VERY painful (epidermis/superficial dermis)
Full: White/black eschar, dry, PAINLESS (loss of nerve endings)
Serious Sites: Face/Neck (Oedema of glottis), Perineum (nursing difficulty)

content.explanation: 4 X weight (kg) X % burn = mL crystalloid solution in 24h (Half given in first 8h). Muir & Barclay Formula (Colloid/Albumin): [weight (kg) X % burn] / 2 per time period.

sections.title: Burns Management Process
content: Airway: Intubate if airway obstruction or smoke inhalation.
Breathing: 100% O2; exclude tension pneumothorax & CO poisoning (cherry-red skin).
Circulation: 2 large-bore (14 or 16G) IV lines.
Target Output: 0.5mL/kg/h (1mL/kg/h in children).
Cooling: Use saline/tap water but warm the patient to prevent shock.
Meds: Antitetanic/Anti-gas gangrene serum, antibiotics, morphine 10mg.
Dressings: Biological/Synthetic for Partial; Tangential excision/grafts for Full.

sections.title: Hypothermia Management
content: Definition: Core (rectal) temperature < 35º C.
Causes Young: Exposure, near-drowning, alcohol/drug overdose.
Causes Elderly: Impaired homeostasis, immobility, hypothyroidism, DM, confusion, drugs (tranquilizers, diuretics).
Investigations: U&E, glucose, TFTs, FBC, ECG (J-waves).
Management: ABCs, warm IVI, Urinary catheter, Antibiotics (if >65y and T<32C).
Rewarming: Slowly (Aim 0.5ºC/h). Rapid warming = decreased BP/shock.
Complications: Arrhythmias, pneumonia, pancreatitis, ARF, intravascular coagulation.
Prognosis: Age > 70y & T < 32C = Mortality > 50%.

sections.title: Needle-stick: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)
content: Immediate: Encourage bleeding, wash under running water; eyes: irrigate copiously.
Reporting: Within 1h to Occupational Health or A&E.
PEP Initiation: Within 1h for High Risk (sharps injury from known/suspected HIV donor).
PEP Regimen: Zidovudine 250mg 2x/d + Lamivudine 150mg 2x/d + Indinavir 800mg 3x/d.
Duration: Continue PEP for 4 weeks if donor is HIV+.
Testing: Recipient tested at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months.

sections.title: Perioperative Contraindications (Ophthalmic)
content: Uncontrolled BP (>180/100 mmHg)
Myocardial Ischemia/MI within last 3 months
Uncontrolled Hyperglycemia
Uncontrolled Arrhythmias
Excessive INR
Acute Systemic Illness

rows: Continue antihypertensives (including day of surgery); Postpone if BP >180/100.
Continue antianginals; ensure sublingual nitro is available; postpone if MI < 3 months.
Antibiotic prophylaxis NOT required for intraocular procedures.
Continue for intraocular/strabismus; discontinue 2 weeks for orbital/oculoplastic (discuss with PCP).
INR < 3 for intraocular/strabismus; INR < 2 for orbital/oculoplastic. Check within 48h.

sections.title: Diabetic Surgery: Type 1 IDDM
content: Priority: Place first on the surgery list.
Insulin: Stop all long-acting insulin the night before. Morning of surgery: Stop all SC insulin.
Infusion: Start IV 1L 5% dextrose + 20mmol KCl/8h.
Pump: 50U short-acting insulin in 50mL 0.9% saline per sliding scale.
Monitoring: Check blood glucose hourly; aim for 7-11mmol/L during surgery.
Post-op: Continue IV insulin/dextrose until tolerating food.

sections.title: Diabetic Surgery: Type 2 NIDDM
content: Control: If fasting glucose > 10mmol/L, treat as Type 1.
Sulphonylureas: Do not give long-acting (e.g., glibenclamide) on morning of surgery (risk of prolonged hypoglycemia).
Metformin: Beware lactic acidosis, especially with IV contrast or poor renal function (Creatinine > 150 umol/L).
Major Surgery: Check fasting glucose; start IV/SC insulin sliding scale if NBM post-op.

sections.title: Local Anaesthetic (LA) Toxicity
content: Signs: Sudden LOC ± tonic-clonic convulsions; Cardiovascular collapse (Bradycardia, conduction blocks, asystole, VT).
Immediate: STOP injection, call for help, maintain airway/100% O2, confirm IV access.
Seizures: Small incremental doses of benzodiazepine, thiopental, or propofol.
Cardiac Arrest CPR: Start standard CPR; manage arrhythmias; consider bypass.
LIPID EMULSION (70kg patient): IV Bolus Intralipid 20% 1.5 ml/kg (100ml) over 1 min.
INFUSION: Start Intralipid at 0.25 ml/kg/min (400ml over 20 min).
REFRACTORY: Repeat bolus twice at 5 min intervals; increase rate to 0.5 ml/kg/min if no recovery.
NOTE: Recovery may take > 1 hour. Propofol is NOT a substitute for Intralipid.
