title: NEURO-OPHTHALMIC & MEDICAL EMERGENCIES: INTERNAL MEDICINE FOR FRCS
summary: An exhaustive clinical guide for the FRCS (Glasg) Exam covering life-threatening headaches, coma management, meningitis, encephalitis, and status epilepticus. This poster provides a critical diagnostic framework for distinguishing ophthalmic presentations from systemic neurological emergencies.

data.title: NEURO-OPHTHALMIC & MEDICAL EMERGENCIES: INTERNAL MEDICINE FOR FRCS
data.summary: An exhaustive clinical guide for the FRCS (Glasg) Exam covering life-threatening headaches, coma management, meningitis, encephalitis, and status epilepticus. This poster provides a critical diagnostic framework for distinguishing ophthalmic presentations from systemic neurological emergencies.

sections.title: A. Life- or Vision-Threatening Headache D.D.
content: 1. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Extremely severe headache, stiff neck,  conscious level; rarely, subhyaloid hemorrhages seen on fundus examination, usually from a ruptured aneurysm.
2. Structural abnormality of the brain e.g tumor, aneurysm, AV malformation ( conscious level, signs of  ICT, or neurologic signs during, and often after, the headache episode).
3. Epidural or subdural hematoma (follows head trauma; altered level of consciousness; may produce anisocoria.).
4. Infectious CNS disorder e.g meningitis, encephalitis, brain abscess (fever, stiff neck,  conscious level, photophobia, neurologic signs).
5. Giant cell arteritis (GCA): Age >50 years,  ESR & CRP, scalp tenderness, …..etc.
6. Acute angle-closure glaucoma.
7. Ocular ischemic syndrome.
8. Malignant hypertension.
9.  ICT e.g Papilloedema & ICH (headaches usually worse in the morning & worsened by Valsalva).

sections.title: B. Other Headache Etiologies
content: Migraine
Cluster headache
Tension headache
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: headache or periocular pain may precede the herpetic vesicles.
Sinus headache: may be a serious headache in diabetic patients and immunocompromised hosts because mucormycosis may be responsible.
Vertebral artery dissection (neck pain & cerebellar/medullary signs).
Cervical spine disease.
Paget’s disease ( Alk phos).
Tolosa-Hunt syndrome.
Convergence insufficiency & Accomodative spasm.
Drugs e.g nitrates, CCB & Carbon monoxide poisoning.

rows: Brief attacks of severe paroxysmal & sharp pain (like an electric shock) lasting a few seconds; starts in distribution of one division of trigeminal nerve; Normal facial sensation.

Occurs in middle aged men; Severe unilateral headache with periocular pain in 1st division of trigeminal nerve; Lasts hours to weeks before spontaneous resolution; Associated with ipsilateral postganglionic Horner syndrome.

branches: Metabolic: Drugs, poisoning (CO, alcohol), Hypoglycaemia, Hyperglycaemia, Hypoxia, CO2 narcosis (COPD), Septicaemia, Hypothermia, Myxoedema, Addisonian crisis, Hepatic/uraemic encephalopathy
Neurological: Trauma, Infection (meningitis, encephalitis), Tumours, Stroke, Epilepsy

sections.title: Management of Coma
content: 1. Call for help.
2. ABC.
3. Consider intubation if GCS < 8.
4. Stabilize cervical spine.
5. Vital signs monitoring.
6. Level of consciousness (document).
7. Blood glucose in all patients; give 50 mL 50% dextrose IV immediately if presumed hypoglycemia.
8. Control seizures.
9. Consider IV glucose, IV thiamine (alcohol, Wernicke’s encephalopathy), IV naloxone (opiate intoxication) and IV flumazenil (benzodiazepine intoxication if airway compromised).

10. Brief examination: Signs of trauma (haematoma, laceration, fracture); Signs of other diseases (liver disease, DM); Skin (needle marks, cyanosis, pallor); Smell breath (alcohol, hepatic fetor, ketosis, uremia); Meningism, heart/lung, abdomen/rectum; Eye examination; Foci of infection (abscesses); Examine for CNS asymmetry (tone, spontaneous movements, reflexes).

sections.title: Eye Examination in Coma (Critical Ophthalmic Signs)

headers: Findings and Clinical Significance (Do Not Dilate)
rows: In light coma, test fields with visual threat. No blink in 1 field suggests hemianopia & contralateral hemisphere lesion.
Vestibulo-ocular reflex (doll’s head maneuver or ice water calorics).

a) Fixed, dilated: Unilateral (3rd nerve palsy with transtentorial herniation); Bilateral (atropine or barbiturate poisoning). b) Marcus Gunn pupil: ON or chiasm damage, Pituitary Apoplexy. c) Pin point: Unilateral (Horner’s syndrome); Bilateral (pontine haemorrhage, opiate poisoning).
Papilloedma (↑ ICT). Hemorrhage: subhyaloid & subarachnoid in Terson’s syndrome. Signs of other disease e.g HTN and DM.

sections.title: Advanced Coma Care & Investigations
content: Quick history from family, ambulance staff and bystanders.
Investigations: ABG, FBC, CXR, U&E, LFT, toxin screen, ethanol and drug levels, CT and lumbar puncture.
Urine analysis: save first few for drug levels, monitor outflow, check for glucose and ketones.
Mannitol 20% ± hydrocortisone in case of cerebral edema.
Monitor neurological signs and coma scale.
General care of comatosed patients.
Reference: Waleed Badr, FRCS INTERNAL & EMERGENCY MEDICINE FOR FRCS (GLASG) EXAM 2016 (Page 52-53).

rows: Obeying(6), Localizing(5), Withdrawal*(4), Flexor (decorticate)**(3), Extensor (decerebrate)***(2), None(1). *Omitted in some centers.
Spontaneous(4), To speech(3), To pain(2), None(1).
A: Alert, V: Vocal stimuli, P: Pain, U: Unresponsive.

content.explanation: ** Damage ABOVE the level of red nucleus in midbrain = Flexor response (decorticate); *** Damage BELOW the level of red nucleus in midbrain = Extensor response (decerebrate).

sections.title: Meningitis: Organisms & Features
content: Organisms: Meningococcus, pneumococcus. Less commonly: H. influenza; listeria; CMV; cryptococcus or TB.
Early Features: headache, leg pains, cold hands/feet, abnormal skin colour.
Signs of Meningism: neck stiffness, photophobia, Kernig’s sign (pain + resistance on passive knee extension with hip flexed).
Later Features:  conscious level & coma, Seizures ± focal CNS signs ± opisthotonus, Petechial rash (non blanching), Signs of septicaemia ( capillary refill; DIC; BP ).

sections.title: Meningitis Management Protocol
content: 1. ABC: Adequate ventilation, Oxygenation, Circulation (IV line).
2. Start antibiotics immediately: < 55Y: Cefotaxime 2g/6h slow IV; > 55Y: Cefotaxime + ampicillin 2g/4h IV (for listeria); Aciclovir (if viral encephalitis suspected).
3. If septicaemic signs: Don’t attempt LP; Get help from critical care; Treat shock & monitoring.
4. If meningitic signs: Dexamethasone 4-10 mg/6h IV (avoid if immunocompromised).
5. If signs of  ICP: Take to ITU & don’t do LP. If no shock/ICP signs: do LP.
6. Subsequent therapy: Cefotaxime 2g/8h IVI for 10 days ( dose in renal failure); Maintenance fluids; Isolation for 1st 24h.
7. Investigations: U&E, FBC, LFT, glucose, coagulation, Blood culture, LP (opening pressure , CSF microscopy), CSF PCR, CXR (TB).

sections.title: Encephalitis: A High-Mortality Emergency
content: Organisms: Viral (HSV-1&2, arboviruses, CMV, EBV, VZV, HIV, measles, mumps, rabies, West Nile, etc.); Non-viral (Bacteria, TB, malaria, lyme, aspergillosis).
Signs: Confusion, coma, seizures, fever, headache, focal neurological signs ± history of travel/bite.
Investigations: CT/MRI (Focal bilateral temporal lobe = HSV; Meningeal enhancement = meningoencephalitis); LP & CSF PCR ( protein/lymphocytes,  glucose); EEG.
Management: Mortality in untreated viral encephalitis is 70%. Symptomatic (phenytoin for seizure); Aciclovir 10 mg/kg/8h IV over 1h for 14 days.

sections.title: Cerebral Abscess
content: Causes: Follows ear, sinus, dental infection; skull fracture; heart disease; endocarditis; bronchiectasis.
Signs: seizures, fever, signs of  ICP & sepsis elsewhere.
Investigations: CT/MRI,  WBC,  ESR.
Management: Referral to neurosurgery; treat source infection + treat  ICP.

content.center: Status Epilepticus (>30min or no intervening consciousness)
branches: Metabolic: Hyper/hypoglycaemia, Hyponatraemia, Hypocalcaemia, Liver/Renal failure

sections.title: Status Epilepticus: Management Steps
content: 1. ABC: Maintain airway (remove false teeth, oral/nasal airway, intubate if needed), 100% O2.
2. Circulation: IV access, take blood (U&E, LFT, glucose, ABG, ECG, calcium, toxicology, anticonvulsant levels).
3. Immediate Treatment: Thiamine 250 mg IV (if alcoholism); Glucose 50% 50 mL (if low); IVI Saline (if hypotensive).
4. Control Seizures (Aim < 20min): Lorazepam 2-4 mg slow bolus (repeat in 10min if needed); OR Diazepam 10 mg IV over 2min (repeat 5 mg/min to max 20mg).
5. If fits continue: Phenytoin infusion (18mg/Kg at ≤ 50mg/min) - Monitor BP/ECG (Beware hypotension/bradycardia).
6. If fits continue: Diazepam infusion (100mg in 500mL 5% dextrose at 40 mL/h); Dexamethasone 10 mg IV (if edema/vasculitis).
7. Final Tier: General anesthesia.
8. Post-control: Start oral drugs & Search for cause.

sections.title: Asthma Investigations & Initial Treatment (ABC)
content: Investigations: Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR)
Investigations: ABG (high CO2, low O2 [<90%] + low pH)
Investigations: CXR, FBC & U&E
Call for help
Sit patient up & do not sedate
ABC: Ensure patent airway
Give oxygen 100% & secure IV line

sections.title: First-Line Asthma Pharmacotherapy
content: Step 1: Salbutamol (B2-agonist) 5 mg (or terbutaline 10 mg) plus ipratropium bromide 0.5 mg nebulized with oxygen
Step 2: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or prednisolone 30 mg PO or both if very ill
Step 3: Monitor oxygen saturation (pulse oximeter), heart rate and respiratory rate
Step 4: CXR to exclude pneumothorax

sections.title: If Asthma Not Improving: Escalation Protocol
content: After 30 min: Repeat salbutamol every 15min or 10mg continuously per hour
Give Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or prednisolone 30 mg PO if not already given
Next Step: Consider aminophylline (5 mg/kg IVI over 20 min) OR give salbutamol IVI (3 – 20 ug/min)
Final Escalation: Consider transfer to ICU to intubate, give adrenaline and 500 mL colloid IVI

sections.title: Asthma Recovery & Weaning Protocol
content: Wean and stop aminophylline over 12 – 24h
Switch to inhaled B-agonist bronchodilator and steroids
Continue to monitor PEFR for 24h: Aim for rate > 75% of predicted or best with diurnal variability < 25%
Warning: Beware of early morning dips in PEFR
Look for cause of acute exacerbation

sections.title: Acute Exacerbation of COPD
content: Common in winter & triggered by viral or bacterial infections
Presentations: Increased cough, breathlessness or wheeze with decreased exercise capacity
History: Ask about usual treatment (home oxygen), smoking and exercise capacity
Investigations: PEFR, ABG, CXR, ECG
Lab Tests: Blood culture (if pyrexial) & sputum culture
Management Step 1: Look for the cause e.g. infection or pneumothorax

sections.title: COPD: Controlled Oxygen Therapy
content: Don’t leave patients hypoxic
Risk: Patients relying on hypoxic drive; too much oxygen may lead to reduced respiratory rate, hypercapnia, and fall in conscious level
If CO2 retention: Start with 24 – 28% O2. Reassess after 30 min
Aim: Raise O2 above 8.0KPa with a rise in CO2 < 1.5KPa
If no retention: Use 28-40% O2 but still monitor and repeat ABG

sections.title: COPD Medical Management Steps
content: 1. Nebulized bronchodilator (salbutamol 5mg/4h & ipratropium 500ug/6h)
2. Hydrocortisone 200mg IV & oral prednisolone 30-40mg
3. Antibiotics if evidence of infection
4. Physiotherapy to aid sputum expectoration
5. If no response: consider IV aminophylline
6. If still no response: consider nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV)
7. Intubation and ventilation: Consider if pH decreases and CO2 increases
8. Respiratory stimulant: Doxapram (short term only, for patients not suitable for mechanical ventilation)

sections.title: Long-Term Management of Stable COPD
content: Stop smoking, encourage exercise, proper nutrition, weight reduction
Influenza vaccination
Medications: Short acting B2-agonist, ipratropium and corticosteroid inhalations (according to severity)
Consider long term oxygen therapy
Surgery: Indicated for recurrent pneumothorax or isolated bullous disease
Social/Psych: Assess social circumstances/support; Identify and treat depression
Travel: Air travel is hazardous if O2 saturation is low; check availability of O2

sections.title: Pneumonia: Definition & Incidence
content: Definition: An infection of the lung parenchyma
Incidence: 12 per 1000 adults
Mortality rate: 10%

sections.title: Pneumonia Organisms: The Full List
sections.content: Strept. pneumoniae (commonest 60-75%); Mycoplasma pneumoniae (5-18%); Others: Staph. aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Legionella & Chlamydia psittaci, G-ve bacilli e.g. Pseudomonas (often hospital-acquired or immunocompromised).

rows: Signs of consolidation: diminished expansion, dull percussion note
Increased tactile vocal fremitus/vocal resonance, bronchial breathing

content.explanation: C: Confusion; U: Urea > 7mmol/L; R: Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min; B: BP < 90/60; 65: Age ≥ 65

sections.title: CURB-65 Scoring Actions
content: Score 0-1: Home treatment if possible
Score 2: Hospital therapy
Score ≥ 3: Severe pneumonia

sections.title: Pneumonia Management: ABC & Investigations
content: A: Adequate ventilation (may need intubation)
B: Oxygenation
C: Circulation (IV line, treat hypotension & shock)
Investigations: CXR, ABG, FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, blood culture
Advanced Investigations: Aspiration of pleural fluid for culture & bronchoscopy (if immunocompromised)

rows: Pericarditis, Myocarditis, Cholestatic jaundice, Renal failure

sections.title: Tension Pneumothorax: EMERGENCY
content: MEDICAL EMERGENCY: Requires immediate relief
CRITICAL: Do not delay management for obtaining a CXR
Pathophysiology: Air inside pleural space has no route to escape, pushing mediastinum to opposite side, kinking/compressing great veins
Risk: Unless air is rapidly removed, cardio respiratory arrest will occur

sections.title: Causes of Pneumothorax
content: Primary (Spontaneous): Especially in young thin men
Secondary: Underlying disease (Asthma, COPD, TB, Pneumonia, Lung abscess, Fibrosis, Carcinoma)
Trauma
Iatrogenic: Subclavian CVP line insertion, Pleural aspiration/biopsy, Percutaneous liver biopsy, +ve pressure ventilation

rows: Trachea deviated away from affected side

sections.title: Management Step 1: Aspiration
content: 1. Infilterative anaesthesia
2. Insert large bore (14-16 G) cannula (venflon) into 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
3. Connect to 3-way tap and 50mL 0.9% saline
4. Aspirate up to 2.5 litres of air
5. Request CXR to confirm resolution
6. If successful: Repeat CXR after 24h to exclude recurrence

sections.title: Management Step 2: Chest (Intercostal) Drain
content: Insert in 4th – 6th intercostal space, anterior to mid-axillary line
Use small tube unless blood/pus present
Removal: 24h after lung re-expanded & air leak stopped (bubbling stops)
Removal technique: Done during expiration or a Valsalva manoeuvre
Failed expansion: If failed within 48h, suction or surgery required

sections.title: Surgical Consultation & Long-term Advice
content: Request surgical advice if: Bilateral pneumothorax
Request surgical advice if: Lung fails to expand after drain insertion
Request surgical advice if: 2 or more previous episodes on same side
Request surgical advice if: History of pneumothorax on opposite side
Travel Advice: Avoid air travel for 6 weeks after normal CXR
Activity Advice: Diving should be permanently avoided

sections.title: Document Information
sections.content: Waleed Badr, FRCS INTERNAL & EMERGENCY MEDICINE FOR FRCS (GLASG) EXAM, 2016. Pages 42-47.

sections.title: Venous Thromboembolic Disease (VTE) Overview
content: The most common presentation is Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the leg and/or pulmonary embolism (PE).
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) occurs in 25-50% of surgical patients, and many non-surgical patients.

branches: Patient factors: Increased Age, obesity, varicose veins, previous DVT/PE, family history, pregnancy, oestrogen-containing oral contraceptives & HRT.
Immobility: Especially long flights (> 4 hours) or associated with illness / hospital admission.
Surgical conditions: Recent major surgery (especially pelvic or orthopaedic).
Medical conditions: MI/heart failure, inflammatory bowel disease, pneumonia & malignancy.
Haematological disorders: Thrombophilic states, hyperviscosity syndromes & Myeloproliferative disease.

sections.title: Clinical Signs of DVT
content: Calf warmth, tenderness, swelling, and erythema.
Pitting oedema.
Mild fever.

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNING: Homans' Sign
content: Homans' sign: Increased resistance/pain on forced foot dorsiflexion.
SHOULD NOT BE TESTED: It may dislodge the thrombus.

rows: Usually occurs in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
Usually distinguished by marked skin erythema & heat localized within a well-demarcated area; may have an entry source (insect bite/ulcer).
Both Ruptured Baker's Cyst and Cellulitis may coexist with a DVT.

sections.title: VTE Investigations
content: 1. FBC: WCC for infection; Hb for polycythaemia; Platelet count for thrombocytosis.
2. D-dimer blood tests: High sensitivity, low specificity (increased in thrombosis, infection, malignancy, and post-op).
3. Compression U/S of calf & leg (Doppler): If negative, repeat at 1 week to catch early propagating DVTs; rules out ruptured knee.
4. Pulmonary Concern: ECG, CXR, ABG, V/Q scan & CT pulmonary angiography.
5. Thrombophilia tests: Before starting anticoagulants if no predisposing factors exist, in recurrent DVT, or strong family history.

sections.title: Complications of VTE
content: 1. Pulmonary embolism: Severity ranges from asymptomatic to sudden death.
2. Chronic post-phlebitic leg problems (10-30%): Due to valve damage; causes pain, swelling, eczema, itch & ulceration.
3. Stroke/Arterial embolus: Paradoxical embolus via cardiac defect.
4. Anticoagulant complications: Haemorrhage (intra-cranial, ocular, GI & other).

sections.title: Prophylaxis against DVT/PE
content: Early post-op mobilization (simplest method).
Compression stockings.
Low M.W heparin (e.g., enoxaparin 20 mg/24h SC).
Aspirin.
Avoid contraceptive pill in high-risk (major/orthopedic surgery).
Vena caval filters (limited use).

sections.title: DVT Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Graded support stockings and treatment of underlying risk factors.
Step 2: Assess risk factors for haemorrhage.
Step 3: Start Heparin (e.g., LMWH enoxaparin 1.5mg/kg/24h SC).
Step 4: Start Warfarin simultaneously with LMWH (prothrombotic for first 48h).
Step 5: Stop heparin when INR reaches 2-3.
Duration: 3 months if post-op; 6 months if no cause found, malignancy, or recurrent DVT.
Vena caval filters: Use in active bleeding or anticoagulant failure to minimize PE risk.

sections.title: WELLS Score: High Probability DVT
content: Calf swelling > 3cm (measured 10cm below tibial tuberosity).
Immobile (bed, plaster, or paralysed).
Local tenderness over deep venous system.
Active malignancy.
Family history of DVT (≥ 2 close relatives).
Others: Pitting edema & dilated superficial veins.

sections.title: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) Essentials
content: Always suspect PE in sudden collapse 1-2 wks after surgery.
Mechanism: Venous thrombi pass into pulmonary circulation and block blood flow.
Signs/Symptoms: Acute dyspnea, tachypnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypotension, tachycardia, gallop rhythm, loud P2, increased JVP, haemoptysis, syncope, Cyanosis, AF, and DVT signs.

rows: Normal/Sinus Tachycardia (commonest). Right ventricular strain (V1-3), Rt Axis deviation, RBBB, AF. Rarely: SI, QIII, TIII (Deep S in I, path. Q in III, inverted T in III).
Often normal. Decreased vascular markings, small pleural effusion, wedge-shaped area of infarction.
Decreased O2, Decreased CO2, Increased pH.
Increased if thrombosis present; helps exclude PE if Normal (High sens/Low spec).
Sensitive & specific for emboli in pulmonary artery. Helical/Spiral CT preferred.
U&E, FBC, baseline clotting. V/Q scan if CTPA unavailable. Pulmonary angiography/venograms if equivocal. Doppler U/S for legs.

sections.title: Immediate PE Management
content: 1. Oxygen 100%.
2. Morphine 10 mg IV (if pain) + antiemetic.
3. If critically ill: Consider immediate thrombolysis or surgery.
4. Start LMWH or Unfractioned Heparin (10,000 U IV bolus then 15–25 U/Kg/h IVI guided by APTT).
5. If Systolic BP > 90 mmHg: Start Warfarin 10 mg/24h PO and confirm diagnosis.
6. If Systolic BP < 90 mmHg: Start rapid colloid infusion (500 mL).
7. Persistent Low BP: Give dobutamine 2.5–10 ug/kg/min IV (Aim BP >90). Consider noradrenaline.
8. Thrombolysis: Consider streptokinase if no improvement after 30–60 min (250,000 U IVI over 30 min, then 100,000 U/h for 12–72 h).

sections.title: Beta-Blocker Clinical Profile
content: Mechanism: Block B-adrenoceptors; B1-blocking is negatively inotropic/chronotropic; B2-blocking induces peripheral vasoconstriction and bronchoconstriction.
Indications: Hypertension (2nd line), IHD (Angina, Post-MI), Cardiac arrhythmias, Hyperthyroidism, Prophylaxis of migraine, Anxiety & tremors, Glaucoma.

Side Effects: Bronchospasm, Hypotension, Bradycardia, Peripheral ischaemia/Cold extremities, Decreased metabolism of other drugs, Potentiation of insulin hypoglycaemia & masking symptoms, Hyperkalaemia (diabetic/uraemic), Nightmares, depression, headache, nausea, vomiting, impotence, possible decreased HDL.

sections.title: BB Bradycardia Antidote & Contraindications
content: Bradycardia Antidote: Atropine up to 3mg IV. If fails, Glucagon 2-10mg IV bolus + 5% dextrose (or 50µg/kg/h infusion). Pacing/Balloon pump if unresponsive.
Contraindications: Congestive heart failure, Heart block, Asthma/COPD, Hypotension & Bradycardia, Prinzmetal's angina, Peripheral vascular disease.

rows: Ascending limb Loop of Henle. Inhibits Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransport.
Acute pulmonary edema, Hypertensive emergencies, Hyper Ca2+ & Hyper K+.
Hypokalaemia, Hypomagnesaemia, Hyponatraemia, Hypocalcaemia, Hyperuricaemia, Ototoxicity.
Proximal part of DCT. Inhibits NaCl cotransport.
Congestive heart failure, Essential hypertension, Diabetes insipidus.
Distal DCT & upper collecting tubules. Competitive inhibition with aldosterone.
Given with other diuretics to balance K+ loss, Hyperaldosteronism.
Hyperkalaemia, Gynecomastia & impotence in males, Menstrual disorders & hirsutism in females.
Nifedipine, Amlodipine, Lacidipine, Nimodipine, Nicardipine, Felodipine
Peripheral V.D, Coronary V.D, Tachycardia (safe with BB), BP lowering.
A-V & S-A conduction delay, Bradycardia (NO BB - risk of LVF), Peripheral & Coronary V.D, BP lowering.

sections.title: CCB Mechanism & Side Effects
content: Mechanism: Block voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in cardiac muscle & vessels. Decreased intracellular Ca2+ reduces muscle contraction, promoting V.D and reducing myocardial oxygen consumption.
Side Effects: CHF aggravation, A-V block, Dizziness, fatigue, headache, flushing, Ankle oedema, Gingival hyperplasia, Nausea, vomiting, constipation.
Contraindications: Heart failure & Heart block.

sections.title: Digitalis (Digoxin) Profile
content: Mechanism: +ve inotropic (blocks Na+/K+ pump), slows HR (control ventricular rate in AF <100), conduction velocity increased in small dose/decreased in large dose.
Indications: CHF with AF (major), heart failure non-responsive to diuretics, atrial flutter, paroxysmal atrial tachycardia.
Dosage: PO loading 0.5mg BID (AF total 1.25-1.5mg in 3-4 doses). Maintenance 0.125-0.25mg daily. IV 0.75-1mg in 0.9% NaCl over 2h.
CI: Digitalis toxicity, Heart block, HOCM, WPW syndrome, Paroxysmal VT.

sections.title: Digitalis Toxicity & Management
content: Precautions: Check K+ levels; lower dose for elderly; halved dose with amiodarone; avoid cardioversion; verify no digitalis in previous 14 days before IV load.
Cardiac SE: Any arrhythmia (AV block, VT/VF).
Ocular SE: White halos, yellow/green chromatopsia, diplopia.
Other SE: Nausea/Vomiting/Anorexia, Hypokalaemia, Digitalis Delirium (Confusion/hallucinations), Gynaecomastia/Galactorrhea.
Management: Stop Digoxin, correct hypokalaemia, treat arrhythmias. Use Digibind® (Digoxin-specific antibody fragments IVI).

rows: Ia: Quinidine, Disopyramide, Procainamide; Ib: Lidocaine; Ic: Flecainide

sections.title: Amiodarone Side Effects
content: Vortex keratopathy
Cataract
Optic neuropathy
Peripheral neuropathy
Myopathy
Alteration of thyroid function
Hepatotoxicity

sections.title: Clinical Definition
sections.content: Shock: Circulatory failure resulting in inadequate organ perfusion. (Source: Waleed Badr, FRCS INTERNAL & EMERGENCY MEDICINE FOR FRCS (GLASG) EXAM 2016)

sections.title: The Seven Primary Etiologies of Shock

branches: 1) Cardiogenic: Pump failure or 2ry to PE, tension pneumothorax & cardiac tamponade (Obstructive Shock).
2) Hypovolaemic: Loss of blood volume (Trauma, Ruptured Aneurysm, Ectopic Pregnancy, Vomiting/GIT obstruction, Diarrhea/Cholera, Burns, Heat Exhaustion).
4) Neurogenic: Nervous system injury (e.g., post spinal surgery).
7) Endocrine Failure: Addison’s disease or Hypothyroidism.

rows: Temp: Commonly hypothermia. Heart Rate: Commonly tachycardia >100 bpm. BP: Early rise (COP increase), then rapid fall (hypotension). Resp Rate: Increase (compensatory tachypnea to remove CO2/acid).
Early: Personality change, restlessness. Late: Confusion, ultimately coma.
Chest pain. Profound acidosis and abnormal heart rhythms (cardiac dysrhythmias) are prevalent and potentially fatal.
Due to blood shunting. Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, GIT bleeding with black/tarry stool (melena).
Cold, pale, clammy & cyanosed (if extreme low blood O2 content).

sections.title: General Management Protocol
content: CRITICAL: If BP unrecordable, call the cardiac arrest team.
1. Call for help + Position patient on hard surface with raised legs.
2. A (Airway): Ensure patent airway (remove obstruction, chin elevation, head tilt) & adequate ventilation.
3. B (Breathing): Administer O2 100%.
4. C (Circulation): IV access x2 wide bore (get help if this takes > 2 min).
5. Identify & treat underlying cause: Check abdomen for trauma/aneurysm, GIT bleeding/melena. If unclear, treat as Hypovolaemic (most common).
6. Consider: Arterial line, central venous line & Foley's catheter.
7. Fluids: Infuse crystalloids fast to raise BP (unless cardiogenic). Aim for urine flow > 30 mL/h. Titrate by BP, CVP & output.
8. NB: Do not overload fluids in Cardiogenic shock (exclude PE & RV infarct first).
9. Monitor: Pulse, BP, temp, respiration, and peripheral perfusion.
10. Investigations: FBC, U&E, ABG, glucose, cross matching, ECG.

sections.title: Cardiogenic Shock Management
content: Characterized by cold & clammy patient; High mortality.
Can occur suddenly or after worsening heart failure.
Requires senior physician help for diagnosis & treatment.
Causes: MI, myocarditis, myocardial depression (drugs, hypoxia, acidosis, sepsis), endocarditis, arrhythmias, or 2ry to tamponade/pneumothorax/PE.
MI Management: Prompt thrombolysis or acute angioplasty. Manage in CCU/ICU.
Medication: Morphine (2.5 – 5 mg IV) for pain/anxiety.
Monitoring: ECG (hourly until diagnosed), enzymes/troponins, U&E, CXR, Echo, ABG, CVP, urine output.
Swan-Ganz Catheter: Assess PCWP and cardiac output.
PCWP < 15 mm Hg: Plasma expanders (100 mL every 15 min IV); aim for 15 – 20 mm Hg.
PCWP > 15 mm Hg: +ve inotropes (Dopamine or Dobutamine 2.5 – 10 ug/kg/min IVI); aim for systolic BP > 80 mm Hg.
Surgical: Consider surgery for valvular lesions; treat reversible causes like MI/PE.

sections.title: Cardiac Tamponade Essentials
content: Definition: Pericardial fluid collection -> High intrapericardial pressure -> Heart cannot fill -> Pumping stops.
Causes: Trauma, Lung/Breast Cancer, Pericarditis, MI.
Beck’s Triad: Low BP, High JVP, Muffled heart sounds.
Kussmaul’s sign: JVP increases on inspiration.
Pulsus paradoxus: Pulse fades on inspiration.
ECG: Electrical alternans.
CXR: Globular heart, Lt. heart border convex/straight, Rt. costophrenic angle < 90°.
Echo: Diagnostic.
Treatment: Prompt pericardiocentesis (requires senior help/luck).
Await surgery/procedure: O2, ECG monitor, IVI, Group & Save blood.
Surgical roles: CABG, ventricular repair, or pericardial window.

rows: Treat underlying cause (control hemorrhage, urgent laparotomy/thoracotomy). Fluid: Saline 0.9% or colloid initially. If bleeding: Cross matched blood or Group O Rh -ve via large bore cannula. Titrate against BP, CVP, urine. Correct electrolytes/acidosis.

Endotoxin-induced vasodilatation. Presentation: Warm and well-perfused with bounding pulse (may lack fever/high WCC). Treatment: Antibiotics after blood culture (e.g., IV Cefuroxime 1.5g/8h or Gentamycin + Antipseudomonal). Fluids: Colloid/Crystalloid IVI. Monitor: ICU (CVP and PAWP).

content.explanation: Type 1 IgE-mediated hypersensitivity. Histamine/mediator release from mast cells -> increased vascular permeability, vasodilatation & respiratory smooth muscle contraction.

sections.title: Anaphylaxis: Clinical Features & Causes
content: Causes: Penicillin, Radiology contrast (FA), Stings, Foods (strawberries, eggs, fish).
Anaphylactoid: Direct mediator release without antibodies (drug-related).
Features: Allergy history, Itching, Sweating, Erythema, Urticaria.
Systemic Signs: Tachycardia, Hypotension, Wheezing, Laryngeal obstruction (edema), Apnea, Cyanosis.
Other: Vomiting, Diarrhea, Urinary incontinence, Syncope.

sections.title: Anaphylaxis Emergency Treatment
content: 1. Remove cause, raise feet, call for help.
2. ABC: Airway, 100% O2, Secure IV access.
3. Adrenaline: 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) IM. Repeat every 5 min guided by BP/Pulse/Respiration until better.
4. Antihistamine: Chlorpheniramine 10 mg IV (repeat every 6h if urticaria persists).
5. Hydrocortisone: 200 mg IV.
6. If Hypotensive: IVI 0.9% saline 500 ml over 15 min (up to 2L may be needed).
7. If Bronchospasm: Aminophylline & nebulized Salbutamol 2.5 mg.
8. If Laryngeal Edema Worsens (Stridor): Refer to ICU, Intubation/Ventilation.
9. Severe/No Pulse Case: IV Adrenaline (1 mL of 1:10,000 solution per minute). Stop at response.
10. Discharge: Only after 48hrs due to risk of Biphasic Reaction.

sections.title: Prophylaxis & Prevention
content: Detailed history of atopy, drug allergy, or stings.
Identify Family H/O anaphylaxis (AD inheritance).
Skin-prick tests for specific IgE to identify allergens.
Emergency tray: Ambu bag, mask, laryngoscope, ET tube, O2, Meds (Adrenaline, hydrocortisone, antihistaminics, aminophylline, IV glucose).
Staff training for emergencies.
Suggest Medic-alert bracelet.
Teach self-injected adrenaline techniques.

rows: Cause: Generalized vasodilatation. Picture: Bradycardia & hypotension. Treatment: Raise legs, IVI fluids, Atropine 1mg IV & Hydrocortisone 200mg IV.
Treatment: Tepid sponging and fanning. Avoid ice/immersion. IVI 0.9% saline ± Hydrocortisone 100mg IV. Chlorpromazine 25mg IM (stops shivering). Stop cooling at core temp < 39°C.

title: Comprehensive Acute GIT Bleeding & Haemostasis Management
summary: An exhaustive clinical guide covering the classification, emergency management, and prognostic scoring of Upper and Lower GI bleeding, alongside an in-depth approach to coagulation disorders, anticoagulant therapies, and surgical considerations.

data.title: Comprehensive Acute GIT Bleeding & Haemostasis Management
data.summary: An exhaustive clinical guide covering the classification, emergency management, and prognostic scoring of Upper and Lower GI bleeding, alongside an in-depth approach to coagulation disorders, anticoagulant therapies, and surgical considerations.

branches: Upper GI bleeding (above the ligament of Treitz)
Lower GI bleeding (below the ligament of Treitz)

sections.title: Upper GIT Bleeding: Causes
content: Esophagus: Esophagitis, Esophageal varices, Esophageal cancer
Stomach: Gastric ulcer (40%), Gastritis, Gastric cancer
Duodenum: Duodenal ulcer, Aortoenteric fistula (if previous aortic graft)
Mallory Weiss tear: mucosal tear at gastro-esophageal junction due to retching
Coagulopathy
Drugs: alcohol, aspirin, NSAIDS, thrombolytics & anticoagulants
Renal disease
Liver disease

rows: Vomiting of blood: frequency, volume of blood
Black tarry stool: usually due to upper GI bleeding. Occurs when blood comes in contact with hydrochloric acid in the gut. Only need > 50 ml of blood loss.
Bright red or maroon rectal bleeding: Usually a sign of a lower GI bleed & rarely seen unless the patient is having a very large, brisk upper GI bleed ( > 1000 ml).
Postural dizziness, fainting, abdominal pain, dysphagia, Chest pain, dyspnea & syncope.
Cool & clammy skin. Vital signs: Pulse (tachycardia), Bl.P (hypotension & postural changes). Urine output & JVP: decreased. Jaundice: biliary colic + jaundice + melaena suggests haemobilia.

sections.title: Emergency Shock Assessment
content: Cool and clammy skin
Pulse > 100 bpm
Systolic BP < 100mm Hg
JVP < 1cm H2O
Urine output < 30mL/h

sections.title: Management Strategy: Shocked vs. Not Shocked
content: If Not Shocked: Insert 2 big cannulae (14-16G), start slow saline IVI (to keep lines patent), check bloods & monitor vital signs + urine output.
If Shocked Step 1: Protect airway (endotracheal intubation to prevent aspiration in massive bleeding or mental status change) and give high flow oxygen.
If Shocked Step 2: Insert 2 big cannulae. Draw bloods for laboratory investigations & Cross match 6 units.
If Shocked Step 3: Rapid IV crystalloid infusion (normal saline or ringer lactate) up to 1L.
If Shocked Step 4: If still shocked, give group specific blood or group O Rh –ve until cross matching is done (transfuse as dictated by haemodynamics).
NB: Avoid saline in patients with decompensated liver disease (ascites, peripheral oedema).

sections.title: Ongoing Management & Monitoring
content: Correct clotting abnormalities (Vit k, FFP, platelet concentrates)
Set up CVP line to guide fluid replacement
Catheterize and monitor urine output (aim for > 30 mL/h)
Vital signs monitoring every 15min until stable, then every 1h
Notify surgeons of all severe bleeds
Keep NPO
Nasogastric tube placement (Sengstaken-Blakemore tube): if massive or continuous bleeding for aspiration & lavage
ECG: looking for signs of ischemia or infarct (inferior MI)
Proton pump inhibitors: e.g omeprazole 40 mg PO to prevent stress ulcers
Eradicate Helicobacter pylori if +ve

sections.title: The Role of Endoscopy
sections.content: Endoscopy can identify the source of bleeding, estimate the risk of rebleeding +/- therapeutic intervention (e.g varices ligation/injection therapy, injection therapy for ulcer, heat probe thermocoagulation, hemoclip or laser). It should be performed early after volume resuscitation. Risks for rebleeding include spurting or oozing, visible vessel or fibrin clot. NB: If site not identified; bleeding site healed; nose bleed (swallowed blood); site distal to 3rd part of duodenum. NB: UGI barium studies are contraindicated in acute bleed as they interfere with endoscopy/surgery.

content.explanation: Age > 60; Signs of shock (pulse > 100 bpm, SBP < 100 mmhg); Significant co-morbidity (renal/liver failure or malignancy); Bleeding diathesis.

branches: Small Bowel: Neoplasm, Meckel’s diverticulum, Crohn’s, Aortoenteric fistula, Vascular problems
Colon: Diverticuli, Angiodysplasia, IBD (UC/Crohn's), Ischemic gut, Neoplasm, Infectious
Coagulopathy: Drugs, renal disease, liver disease

rows: Site distal to the pylorus; Must rule out massive UGIB!
Likely diverticulosis, angiodysplasia, or aortoenteric fistula
Recent ingestion of poorly cooked meat

sections.title: Lower GI Management & Diagnostics
content: ABC Management: Priority volume resuscitation.
Stable Patients: Clinical follow-up with volume/blood as needed; prep for colonoscopy once settled.
Tagged RBC Scan (TRBC): 99mTc labels RBCs (last 48h); accurate to 80%; detects rates as low as 0.1 ml/min. Screening for arteriography.
Angiography: Rapid localization/therapy when rates > 0.5 ml/min; identifies site in 60%; therapeutic vasopressin or embolization.
Colonoscopy: Not useful in ongoing bleeding; best for stabilized patients with bowel purge. Barium enemas contraindicated in acute setting.
Surgery: For ongoing bleeding, hemodynamic instability, or failure of other therapeutic maneuvers.

sections.title: 3 Sets of Questions for Bleeding Disorders

content.explanation: 1. Is there an emergency (exsanguination, hypovolaemia, CNS bleeding)? 2. Why is the patient bleeding (Normal context, secondary cause like drugs/alcohol, pattern indicative of vascular/platelet/coagulation, family history)? 3. What is the mechanism (Clotting screen results)?

sections.title: Coagulation Test Definitions
sections.content: 1. Prothrombin Time (PT) & INR: Measures extrinsic and common pathways (Factors I, II, V, VII, X). PT normal: 11-16s. INR standardizes results (Normal: 0.9–1.3; Warfarin target: 2.0–3.0). Prolonged by Vitamin K deficiency, warfarin, liver disease, or DIC. 2. aPTT: Measures intrinsic and common pathways (Factors I, II, V, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII). Normal: 35-45s. Prolonged by Heparin, haemophilia, DIC, liver disease. 3. Thrombin Time (TT): Measures fibrinogen to fibrin conversion. Normal: 10-15s. Prolonged by Heparin, DIC, dysfibrinogenaemia. 4. D-dimers: Fibrin degradation product. Increased in DIC, DVT, PE, infection, or malignancy. 5. Bleeding Time: Assesses platelet function (Platelet count N: 150k-400k). Normal <7 mins. Prolonged in thrombocytopenia, DIC, or antiplatelet use. Seldom performed now.

sections.title: Management of Bleeding Disorders
sections.content: Resuscitate if shocked. Discuss need for FFP/Platelets with a haematologist for massive transfusion or clotting disorders. ITP: Steroids +/- IV immunoglobulin. Pregnancy: Consult expert. Haemophilia: Factor replacement; Never give IM injections. Drugs Categories: 1. Coagulants (Vit. K, Ethamsylate). 2. Anticoagulants (Heparin/Warfarin). 3. Antiplatelets (Aspirin/Clopidogrel). 4. Fibrinolytics (Streptokinase/tPA). 5. Antifibrinolytics (Tranexamic acid).

rows: Binds Antithrombin III; inhibits IIa, Xa, IXa

sections.title: Heparin Details & Warnings
content: S/E: Bleeding, Heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), Osteoporosis
HIT/Osteoporosis less common with LMWH; Beware hyperkalaemia
Contraindications: Bleeding disorders, previous HIT, peptic ulcer, cerebral haemorrhage, severe hypertension, neurosurgery

rows: Inhibits Vit K regeneration; analogous to deficiency
Peptic ulcer, bleeding disorders, hypertension, pregnancy
Vit K 5-10mg IV; PCC (50u/kg) or FFP

sections.title: Initiating Therapeutic Anticoagulation
content: Step 1: Use LMWH or UFH initially; give Warfarin in combination from Day 1.
Step 2: Continue Heparin until INR reached and until Day 5 (Warfarin has initial prothrombotic effect).
Step 3 (UFH Bolus): 5000iu IV over 30min (10,000iu if severe PE).
Step 4 (UFH Infusion): 25,000iu in 50mL saline; start 1000-2000iu/h. Aim for aPTT ratio 1-2.
Step 5 (Warfarin Start): 10mg PO Day 1; Lower dose (5-10mg) if >60yrs, liver disease, or cardiac failure.

sections.title: Surgery & Antiplatelets
content: Minor Surgery: May proceed if INR within 24h is < 3.5.
Major Surgery: Stop drugs 2-5 days pre-op; Individual risk/benefit assessment.
Emergency Surgery: Vitamin K (10mg IV) +/- FFP may be required.
Elective Conversion: Conversion to heparin (stop 6h prior to surgery); Monitor aPTT.
Antiplatelet Mechanism: Aspirin irreversibly inactivates cyclo-oxygenase (Thromboxane A2/Prostacyclin inhibition).
Aspirin Reversal: Effects reversed by 5 days after stopping.
Clopidogrel: Less gastric irritation; used for aspirin intolerance or post-coronary stent.

sections.title: Hyperviscosity Syndrome
content: Definition: Viscosity rise impairs microcirculation due to high RBC, WBC, or plasma components (immunoglobulins).
Causes: Polycythaemia rubra vera, Leukaemia, Multiple myeloma (IgG 55%, IgA 25%), Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia (IgM).
Presentation: Lethargy & confusion, Spontaneous bleeding (GU/GI), Retinopathy (venous dilatation, segmentation, tortuosity, haemorrhages, exudates).
Treatment: Venesection (Polycythaemia), Leucopheresis (Leukaemias), Plasmapheresis (Myeloma/Waldenstrom's).

title: ECG Mastery & Acute Respiratory Assessment
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to methodical ECG interpretation, ventricular conduction disorders, and the emergency management of the acutely breathless patient. Designed for FRCS Internal and Emergency Medicine examination preparation.

data.title: ECG Mastery & Acute Respiratory Assessment
data.summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to methodical ECG interpretation, ventricular conduction disorders, and the emergency management of the acutely breathless patient. Designed for FRCS Internal and Emergency Medicine examination preparation.

sections.title: ECG: A Methodical Preliminary Approach
content: First confirm the patient's name and age, and the ECG date.
Calculate Rate: At usual speed (25mm/s) each 'big square' is 0.2s; each 'small square' is 0.04s. Divide 300 by the number of big squares per R-R interval.

Assess Rhythm: If not regular, use the 'card method': lay a card along ECG, marking positions of 3 successive R waves. Slide to check equality. Note if rates are multiples (varying block) or 100% irregular (AF or VF).

rows: P wave (upright in II, III, & aVF; inverted in aVR) followed by a QRS complex.
No discernible P waves; QRS complexes are irregularly irregular.
'Sawtooth' baseline of atrial depolarization (~300/min) and regular QRS complexes.
Normal QRS complex; P waves absent or occur just before or within the QRS.
QRS complexes >0.12s with P waves following them.

branches: Sum of ventricular forces during depolarization
Lies at 90° to the isoelectric complex
Normal: -30° to +90° (Leads I and II both positive)
LAD (-30° to -90°): Left anterior hemiblock, Inferior MI, VT (LV focus), WPW
RAD (+90° to +180°): RVH, PE, Anterolateral MI, Left posterior hemiblock, WPW

sections.title: P Wave & P-R Interval
content: P Wave: Normally precedes each QRS.
Absent P: AF, sinoatrial block, junctional rhythm.
Dissociation: Complete heart block.
P mitrale: Bifid; indicates left atrial hypertrophy.
P pulmonale: Peaked; indicates right atrial hypertrophy (Pseudo-P-pulmonale if K+ ↓).
P-R Interval: Start of P to start of QRS. Normal: 0.12-0.2s (3-5 small squares).
Prolonged P-R: Delayed AV conduction (1st degree heart block).
Short P-R: Fast AV conduction (accessory pathway e.g., WPW).

rows: >0.12s: Ventricular conduction defects (BBB). Large: Ventricular hypertrophy.
Prolonged: Ischaemia, Myocarditis, Bradycardia, Head injury, Hypothermia, K+/Ca2+/Mg2+ ↓, Drugs (Quinidine, Macrolides, Amiodarone, TCAs).
Abnormal: Inverted in I, II, V4-V6. Peaked: Hyperkalaemia. Flattened: Hypokalaemia.

content.explanation: V1: R sternal edge, 4th IC space; V2: L sternal edge, 4th IC space; V3: Mid-way V2/V4; V4: Apex beat; V5: Anterior axillary line; V6: Mid-axillary line (V7: Posterior axillary line). Finish with long rhythm strip in Lead II.

sections.title: Bundle Branch Blocks
content: General: Prolongation of QRS >0.12s. Incomplete blocks <0.12s.
RBBB: QRS >0.12s, 'RSR' in V1, Dominant R in V1, Inverted T in V1-V3/V4, Deep wide S in V6. (Normal variant, PE, Cor Pulmonale).
LBBB: QRS >0.12s, 'M pattern' in V5, No septal Q, Inverted T in I, aVL, V5-V6. (IHD, HTN, Cardiomyopathy, Fibrosis). NB: Cannot comment on ST/T if LBBB present.
Bifascicular: RBBB + Left bundle hemiblock (e.g., LAD).
Trifascicular: Bifascicular block + 1st degree heart block.

sections.title: Ventricular Hypertrophy
content: LVH Criteria: R wave in V6 >25mm OR (S in V1 + R in V6) >35mm.
RVH Criteria: Dominant R wave in V1, T wave inversion V1-V3/V4, Deep S in V6, RAD.
Dominant R in V1 Causes: RVH, RBBB, Posterior MI, WPW types.
Low Voltage QRS (<5mm limb leads): Hypothyroidism, COPD, ↑ Haematocrit, Chest wall impedance (Renal failure, Emphysema), PE, BBB, Amyloid, Pericardial effusion/pericarditis.

sections.title: Heart Blocks (A-V Block)
content: 1st Degree: PR >0.20s. Rarely symptomatic.
2nd Degree Mobitz I: Progressive lengthening of PR until a dropped beat occurs.
2nd Degree Mobitz II: Constant PR for conducted beats; some P waves not conducted (2:1/3:1). High asystole risk.
3rd Degree (Complete): Atria and ventricles beat independently (AV dissociation). Narrow QRS if escape is AV node/His; Broad if distal Purkinje.

branches: MI Localisation: Inferior (II, III, aVF), Anteroseptal (V1-4), Anterolateral (V4-6, I, aVL), Posterior (Tall R/ST-down in V1-2)
MI Timeline: Hours (Peaked T, ST rise) -> 24h (T inverts, ST resolves) -> Days (Pathological Q waves form)
ST Elevation: Acute MI, Normal Variant (high take-off), Prinzmetal's, Pericarditis (Saddle-shaped), LV Aneurysm
ST Depression: Ischaemic (Horizontal), Digoxin (Downward sloping/reversed tick), Normal (Upward sloping)
T Inversion: Ischaemia, LVH, PE, RBBB, Subarachnoid hemorrhage, Lithium, HOCM

sections.title: Exercise ECG Testing
content: Indications: Confirm IHD, cardiac function/tolerance, post-MI prognosis, treatment evaluation, exercise arrhythmias.
Contraindications: Unstable angina, Recent Q wave MI (<5 days), Severe AS, Uncontrolled HTN/HF/arrhythmia.
Cautions: LBBB, Pacemakers, COPD, Stroke/OA.
Interpretation: 75% sensitivity for CAD. 5% false positive (higher in middle-aged women). Down-sloping ST 1mm J-point depression = 99% predictive of 2-3 vessel disease.

sections.title: STOP THE EXERCISE TEST IF:
content: Chest pain or dyspnoea occurs.
Patient feels faint, exhausted, or may fall.
ST segment elevation/depression >2mm.
Atrial or ventricular arrhythmia (not just ectopics).
BP fall or failure of HR/BP to rise.
BP excessive rise (systolic >230mmHg).
Development of AV block or LBBB.
90% maximal heart rate achieved.

sections.title: Bedside Chest Medicine & ABGs
content: PEFR: Correlates with FEV1; estimates airway calibre. Used to monitor asthmatics.
Pulse Oximetry: Assessment of SaO2. Alarm at 90%. PaO2 ≤ 80% is abnormal.
ABG Normal pH: 7.40 ± 0.05. Acidosis < 7.35; Alkalosis > 7.45.
Simple Rules: CO2 is acidic gas (4.5-6.0 kPa). HCO3- is alkaline (22-28 mmol/L).
Respiratory changes follow CO2; Metabolic follows HCO3-.

sections.title: Acid-Base Analysis Example
sections.content:
Example: pH 7.05, CO2 2.0 kPa, HCO3- 8.0 mmol/L.
Step 1: Acidosis (pH low).
Step 2: CO2 low (Opposite of acidosis = compensatory).
Step 3: HCO3- low (In keeping with acidosis = primary cause).
Result: Metabolic Acidosis.

branches: Wheezy: Asthma, COPD Exac, Heart Failure, Anaphylaxis
Clear Chest: PE, Metabolic Acidosis (DKA), Anemia, Shock, CNS, Salicylates

rows: Cyanosis, frothy sputum, JVP↑, basal crackles
Pleurisy, syncope, shock, signs absent in lung

sections.title: Pulmonary Embolism & Metabolic Metabolic Summary
content: PE: Sinus tachycardia commonest. RAD, RBBB, RV strain (T inversion/ST dep in V1-V2). Rare: S1Q3T3.
Digoxin: ST depression/T inversion V5-6 (reversed tick). Toxicity causes any arrhythmia.
Hyperkalaemia: Tall tented T, wide QRS, absent P, 'sine wave'.
Hypokalaemia: Small T waves, prominent U waves.
Hypercalcaemia: Short QT interval.
Hypocalcaemia: Long QT interval, small T waves.

sections.title: Reference Source
sections.content: Waleed Badr, FRCS INTERNAL & EMERGENCY MEDICINE FOR FRCS (GLASG) EXAM, 2016.

title: Emergency Medicine & Acute Chest Pain for FRCS
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide covering the differential diagnosis, workup, and management of acute chest pain, coronary syndromes, pulmonary edema, and tachycardias as required for the FRCS (Glasg) Exam.

branches: Others: Musculoskeletal (muscular, rib fractures, bony metastasis, costochondritis)

sections.title: Immediate Management Protocol
content: 1. Call for help
2. ABC (Airway, Breathing, Circulation)
3. Assess Level of consciousness
4. Vital sign monitoring

sections.title: Workup of Chest Pain: Comparison Table

rows: Dull, constricting, choking, squeezing, crushing or pressure
Exercise, emotion, cold, after a large meal
Autonomic disturbance e.g. sweating, nausea & vomiting; Breathlessness
Can mimic anginal pain i.e. constricting
Food, lying flat, hot drinks, alcohol
Local tenderness over a rib or costal cartilage

sections.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) Definitions
content: Unstable angina
Non ST elevation MI (NSTEMI) = non Q wave or subendocardial MI
ST elevation MI (STEMI) = acute MI

sections.title: STEMI (Acute MI): Risk & Clinical Picture
content: Risk factors: DM, HTN, atherosclerosis & smoking.
Clinical picture: Heavy chest pain > 15min, radiating to the arm, neck and shoulder.
Dyspnea, sweating, palpitations, nausea, dizziness, collapse and shock.
Epigastric pain & vomiting (inferior MI).
Silent MI: May present without chest pain in elderly or diabetics.

sections.title: STEMI Investigations & Cardiac Enzymes
content: Bloods: FBC, U&Es, glucose, lipids and cardiac enzymes.
CK (Creatine Kinase): ↑ 8 – 12 h till 72 h.
Lactate dehydrogenase (mentioned in text as 'Lactate dehy').

sections.title: STEMI: Reperfusion Strategies
content: B-blocker: e.g. atenolol 5 mg IV (unless asthma or Lt. ventricular failure).
Primary PCI (Angioplasty): Treatment of choice if ongoing ischaemia & presentation < 12h. More effective than thrombolysis in reducing death, recurrence, or stroke.
Thrombolysis: Greatest benefit if given < 12 h of onset, up to 24 h. Contraindicated beyond 24h.

content.explanation: 1. ST elevation > 1 mm in 2+ limb leads OR > 2 mm in 2+ chest leads. 2. LBBB (unless known previously). 3. Posterior changes: deep ST depression & tall R waves in V1 to V3. NB: Don't thrombolyze ST depression alone, T-wave inversion alone or normal ECG.

sections.title: Thrombolysis: Contraindications & Agents
content: CONTRAINDICATIONS: Internal bleeding, suspected aortic dissection, esophageal varices, active peptic ulcer, recent surgery, trauma or hemorrhagic stroke, severe hypertension, pregnancy.
Streptokinase (SK): 1.5 million units in 100 mL 0.9 % saline IVI over 1h.
Allergy to SK: Tissue plasminogen activator (Alteplase, Tenecteplase, Reteplase).
COMPLICATIONS: Recurrent ischaemia, Failure to reperfuse (consider re-thrombolysis/rescue angioplasty), Stroke, Pericarditis, cardiogenic shock & heart failure.

sections.title: NSTEMI Management
content: Admit to CCU and monitor closely.
High flow O2.
Analgesia: Morphine (5 – 10 mg IV) + metoclopramide (10 mg IV).
Nitrates: GTN spray or sublingual tablets as required; IV GTN 50 mg in 50mL saline if pain continues.
Aspirin 300 mg PO followed by 75mg/d.
B–Blockers: e.g. metoprolol 50-100 mg/8h (If contraindicated, give verapamil 80-120 mg/8h).
Low molecular weight (LMW) heparin SC with monitoring APTT.
Failure to improve: Urgent angiography ± angioplasty or CABG.
If improving: Treat medically, address risk factors (DM, HTN, smoking), mobilize, arrange stress test/angiogram.

sections.title: NSTEMI: Assessment & Investigations
content: Assessment: History (previous attack, relief with rest/nitrates, IHD risk factors), Examination (vitals, signs of HF).
Investigations: ECG (ST depression, flat/inverted T or normal), cardiac enzymes, CXR, glucose, lipids, U&E, FBC.
Troponin (T and I): Measurement helps predict risk and discharge timing.

sections.title: Severe Pulmonary Edema
content: Causes: Cardiovascular (LV failure, MI, IHD, MS, arrhythmias, malignant HTN), ARDS (trauma, post-op, sepsis), Fluid overload, Neurogenic (head trauma).
Symptoms: Dyspnea, orthopnea, pink frothy sputum.
Signs: Distressed, pale, sweaty, ↑pulse, tachypnea, fine lung basal crackles & wheeze (usually sitting up/leaning forward).
DD: Asthma/COPD, Pneumonia (often co-exist in elderly; treat all three simultaneously).
Investigations: CXR (cardiomegaly, bilateral shadowing, small effusions, Kerley B lines), ECG, U&E, enzymes, ABG, Echo.

sections.title: Pulmonary Edema Treatment
content: Sit the patient upright.
Oxygen 100%.
IV access, monitor ECG, treat arrhythmias (AF).
Diamorphine (2.5 – 5 mg IV slowly).
Diuretics: frusemide 40-80 mg IV slowly.
GTN spray/SL or nitrate infusion (Isosorbide dinitrate 2-10 mg/h) if SBP ≥ 100 mmHg.
If worsening: repeat frusemide, consider ventilation or venesection.
If SBP < 100 mmHg: treat as cardiogenic shock with inotropes.

sections.title: Broad Complex Tachycardia
content: ECG: Rate > 100bpm, QRS > 120 ms (> 3 small squares).
Management: If in doubt, treat as Ventricular Tachycardia (VT).
No pulse: Treat as arrest.
VT Treatment: Oxygen, IV, correct hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia. Unstable: Sedation, DC shock, amiodarone/lidocaine. Stable: Drugs, then DC shock.
Ventricular Fibrillation (VF): Use non-synchronized DC shock.
Ventricular extrasystoles (ectopics): common post-MI, usually no treatment needed.

sections.title: Narrow Complex Tachycardia & AF
content: ECG: Rate > 100 bpm, QRS < 120 ms.
DD: Sinus tachycardia (normal P), AF (absent P, irregular QRS), Atrial flutter (300bpm, sawtooth, 150bpm vent rate), Multifocal Atrial tachycardia, Junctional tachycardia.
AF Symptoms: Asymptomatic, chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea.
AF Signs: Irregularly irregular pulse (apical > radial rate), variable 1st heart sound intensity.
AF Complications: Embolic stroke, CRAO.

sections.title: Atrial Fibrillation (AF) Causes & Tests
content: Cardiac: CAD, MI, Valvular disease (Mitral), Hypertension.
Non-cardiac: Pneumonia, PE, Hyperthyroidism.
Idiopathic: Lone AF.
Investigations: U&E, enzymes, TFTs, D-dimer, ECG, ECHO (LA size, mitral disease, LV function).

sections.title: Treatment of Acute AF (< 72h)
content: 1. Hemodynamic stabilization & Rate Control.
2. Rate Control: B-blocker (Esmolol) or Digoxin (PO loading 0.5mg 6-hourly x2 then 0.125-0.25mg/d; IV 0.75-1mg over 1h).
3. Cardioversion: Amiodarone IVI (5 mg/kg over 1h) OR DC cardioversion (200J, 360J, 360J - Do Echo first).
4. Prevention of embolics: Aspirin 300mg (recent onset/normal echo) OR Warfarin (3 wks before and 4 wks after DC cardioversion).

sections.title: Stroke: Definition & Clinical Manifestation
sections.content: Definition: ischemic infarction (or bleeding into) any part of the brain. It manifests by rapid onset (over minutes) of focal CNS signs and symptoms (contralateral hemiplegia & sensory loss + homonymous hemianopia).

branches: CNS bleed (hypertension, trauma and aneurysm rupture)

sections.title: Risk Factors
content: Hypertension
Hypercholesterolemia
Smoking
DM
Heart disease (AF, valvular, ischaemic)

sections.title: Immediate Management Protocol
content: 1. Call for help.
2. A → Adequate ventilation.
3. B → Oxygenation.
4. C → Circulation → IV line.
5. Document Level of consciousness.
6. Vital sign monitoring: For hypertension, admit and control over days not hours.
7. Admission to stroke units for nursing/physio (saves lives and provides motivation).

rows: Within a few days to differentiate hemorrhagic from ischemic if considering anticoagulation.
Meningism, severe headache, and coma within hours.
Carotid bruit, AF, and past TIA.

content.explanation: NB1. TIA: sudden onset of focal CNS signs (resolve within few minutes) due to temporary occlusion, usually by emboli, of part of cerebral circulation. NB2: carotid bruit may signify stenosis (>30%), often near internal carotid origin. Best heard behind the angle of the jaw.

sections.title: Comprehensive Investigations List
content: FBC
CXR
ECG
ESR
U&E
Lipids
Blood glucose
Clotting tests
Echo
Carotid doppler
Carotid angiography

sections.title: Stroke Treatment Strategy
content: Aspirin: 300mg/24h PO (unless strong suspicion of CNS bleeding).
Nil by mouth if swallowing is a problem.
Maintain hydration: Do not over-hydrate (cerebral edema).
Monitor and treat ↑ BP.
Immediate evacuation: Refer if cerebellar hemorrhage is possible.
Nursing care: Turn regularly and keep dry (consider catheterization) to stop bed sores.
DVT Prophylaxis: Passive limb movements, subcutaneous heparin, and compressing stockings.
Support: Emotional support and rehabilitation.

sections.title: Thrombolysis & Prevention
content: NB Thrombolysis: Alteplase within 3h of onset may decrease adverse outcomes (trials). Requires dedicated 24h CNS thrombolysis teams. Note: Not yet recommended in the UK in 2016.
Prevention 1: Control risk factors.
Prevention 2: Exercise (↑ HDL).
Prevention 3: Life long anticoagulants for rheumatic/prosthetic heart valves on left side.
Prevention 4: Aspirin 75 mg/day for life.

sections.title: Increased Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
content: Normal ICT: 0-10 mmHg.
Causes: Tumours (1ry or metastatic), Head injury, Brain haemorrhage (any type).
Causes: Infection (meningitis, encephalitis, brain abscess), Hydrocephalus, Cerebral oedema, Status epilepticus.

sections.title: Signs & Symptoms of ICP
content: Headache, vomiting ± nausea.
Deterioration of consciousness: drowsiness, irritability, seizures, coma.
Cushing’s response: ↓ pulse, ↑ BP & Cheyne-Stokes respiration.
Ophthalmic: ↓ VA & peripheral visual field loss.
Ophthalmic: Pupil changes (constriction 1st, later dilatation). DON’T DILATE.
Papilloedema: Loss of previous spontaneous venous pulsation. (If preserved, exclude papilloedema).

sections.title: ICP Management
content: 1. ABC (Intubate if needed).
2. Correct hypotension & treat seizures.
3. Brief history & examination.
4. Elevate head of bed 30º- 40º.
5. Mannitol 20%: 1-2g/kg IV over 10-20 min (5mL/kg). Clinical effect after 20 min, lasts 2-6h. Aim for serum osmolarity 300 mosmol/kg.
6. Dexamethasone: 10 mg IV then 4 mg/6h IV/PO (if cerebral oedema).
7. Fluid restriction to < 1.5L/d.
8. Close monitoring of ICP & vitals.
9. Search for cause & treat factors like hyperglycaemia, hyponatraemia.
10. Refer to neurosurgeon for definitive treatment.

sections.title: Hypoglycemia Treatment
content: Give 200–300 mL of 10% dextrose IV (20-30g).
OR Glucagon 1mg IM (if no IV access; will not work in drunk patients).
Once conscious: give sugary drinks & a meal.
Thiamine 1-2 mg/kg IV: if malnutrition or alcohol suspicion.
If oral hypoglycemic history: Admission for 10% glucose over 1-2 hours.

sections.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
sections.content: DKA coma only occurs in type I D.M (IDDM); it may be the mode of presentation. Diagnosis requires: hyperglycaemia + ketosis + metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.3).

sections.title: DKA: Signs & Precipitants
content: Signs: Gradual drowsiness, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, polydipsia, lethargy, anorexia, polyuria, ketotic breath, coma.
Precipitants: Infection, surgery, MI, chemotherapy, non-compliance, or wrong insulin dose.

sections.title: DKA Fluid Replacement Protocol
content: 1. IV 0.9% saline immediately (Dehydration correction is priority).
2. 1L stat.
3. 1L over next 1 hour.
4. 1L over next 2 hours.
5. 1L over next 4 hours.
6. 1L over next 6 hours.
7. Use Dextrose 5% when blood glucose is < 10 mmol/L.
8. Caution in elderly/heart failure; monitor CVP.

sections.title: DKA Insulin & Potassium Management
content: Insulin Pump: 50U soluble insulin in 50ml saline (1U/ml). Give 4-8 U/h if glucose > 20mmol/L. Aim for fall of 5 mmol/L per h.
If No Pump: Load 20U IM, then 4-6 U/h IM while glucose > 10mmol/L.
K+ Replacement: Add 20-40mmol/L to IV fluid (Normal K+: 3.5-5).
K+ Shifting: Serum K+ is high in DKA due to lack of insulin, but total body K+ is low. Insulin shifts K+ into cells; must monitor to prevent hypokalaemia/arrhythmias.
K+ Timing: Don't add to 1st bag. Start when urine flow > 30ml/h.

rows: Longer history (1 wk), glucose > 35 mmol/L, marked dehydration.
Focal CNS signs, DIC, DVT (fully heparinize).
Rehydration with 0.9% saline (1/2 DKA rate) over 48h. Heparinize.

sections.title: Hyperthyroid Crisis (Thyrotoxic Storm)
content: Signs: Hyperpyrexia (>41°C), Tachycardia (>140bpm), AF, CHF, Diarrhea, Vomiting, Agitation, Coma.
Precipitated by: Infection, trauma, MI, stroke, stopping antithyroid meds, surgery, radioiodine.
Propranolol: 40 mg/8h PO or 1 mg IV over 1min (unless asthma/heart failure).
Carbimazole: 15-25 mg/6h PO; followed by Lugol’s solution 0.3 mL/8h after 4h.
Hydrocortisone: 100 mg/6h IV or Dexamethasone 4 mg/6h PO (blocks T4 to T3 conversion).
Aspirin Warning: Avoid Aspirin as it can ↑ T4.

sections.title: Myxoedema Coma
content: Signs: Hypothyroid, >65yrs, hypothermia, hyporeflexia, ↓ glucose, bradycardia, goitre, cyanosis.
Management: High flow O2, Correct hypoglycaemia.
T3: 5-20 ug/12h IV slowly (Caution: may precipitate ischaemia).
Hydrocortisone: 100 mg/8h IV if pituitary cause suspected.
Avoid precipitating LVF with saline.

sections.title: Addisonian & Hypopituitary Crisis
content: Addisonian: Endocrinal shock, hypoglycemia. Treat with Hydrocortisone 100mg/6h IV and IV fluids.
Hypopituitary: Refractory hypotension, short stature, loss of axillary/pubic hair, hypoglycaemia.
Hypopituitary Management: Hydrocortisone IV first, then Liothyronine (T3) 10 ug/12h PO. Surgery if pituitary apoplexy.

sections.title: Pheochromocytoma
content: Definition: Rare catecholamine-producing tumour of adrenal medulla.
Signs: Pallor, pulsating headache, malignant hypertension, VT, cardiogenic shock.
Emergency Management: Phentolamine 2-5 mg IV (repeat to maintain safe BP).
Follow-up: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg/24h PO (titrate up to 30 mg).
Elective surgery usually performed after 4-6 weeks.

data.title: Aids to Diagnosis: Diplopia, Anisocoria & Nystagmus
data.summary: An exhaustive clinical framework for the differential diagnosis of visual ghosting, pupillary asymmetry, and involuntary ocular oscillations. This guide covers monocular vs. binocular diplopia, light-dependent anisocoria, and early- vs. late-onset nystagmus patterns.

branches: Abnormal refraction: High ametropia, astigmatism, or edge effect from corrective lenses: usually correctable with appropriate refraction; Cl may be more effective than glasses.

Abnormal cornea: Opacity: associated with scarring (e.g. trauma, infection), oedema (e.g. iIOp, decompensation), deposition (e.g. corneal dystrophies). Shape: peripheral thinning associated with ectasias (e.g. keratoconus), puK, and other marginal disease.
Abnormal lens: Opacity: cataract. Shape: lenticonus. Position: subluxation of lens (ectopia lentis) or implant (especially if complicated surgery).
Abnormal iris: Defect: polycoria due to trauma (e.g. IOFB), pI (laser or surgical), or disease (e.g. ICe syndrome).
Normal examination: Not diplopia: ‘double vision’ may be used by the patient to describe other visual anomalies (e.g. ghosting or blurring). Functional: this is a diagnosis of exclusion.

sections.title: Binocular Diplopia: Intermittent or Variable
content: Decompensating phoria: intermittent, but usually predictable (e.g. when fatigued) with a constant pattern (e.g. only for distance, only horizontal); underlying phoria with variable/poor recovery.
MG: intermittent diplopia of variable orientation and severity which worsens with fatigue; may be associated with ptosis ± generalized muscular fatigue.
INO: diplopia may only be noticed during saccades when the adducting eye is slower to refixate.
GCA: intermittent diplopia may occur due to ischaemia; may progress to become permanent.

sections.title: Binocular Diplopia: Persistent Neurogenic Lesions
sections.content:
In neurogenic lesions, the diplopia is worst when looking in the direction of the paretic muscle(s); saccades are slowed in this direction; full sequelae will evolve with time. Forced duction test shows normal passive movements.

• Horizontal only: typically VIn palsy | underaction of lr | ipsilateral reduced abduction ± convergent eye, head turn to same side.

• Vertical/torsional only: typically IVn palsy | underaction of SO, with ipsilateral hypertropia, extorsion, and reduced depression in adducted position, head tilt to opposite side.

• Mixed ± ptosis/pupillary abnormalities: typically IIIn palsy | underaction of any/all of lpS, Sr, Mr, Ir, IO, and sphincter pupillae, resulting in anything from single muscle involvement (rare) to complete ptosis obscuring a hypotropic divergent eye.

• Complex: unusual patterns may be due to brainstem lesions, causing nuclear or supranuclear gaze palsies (often associated with other neurological signs), orbital pathology, or disorders of the neuromuscular junction (e.g. MG).

sections.title: Binocular Diplopia: Persistent Mechanical Lesions
sections.content:
In mechanical lesions, the diplopia is worst when looking away from the restricted muscle(s); signs of restriction may include IOp increase, globe retraction, and pain when looking away from the restricted muscle(s); ductions and versions are equally reduced, but saccades are of normal speed; sequelae are limited to underaction of contralateral synergist. Forced duction test shows restriction of passive movements.

• Congenital: these rarely give rise to diplopia unless progressive or decompensating.

• Acquired: associated with inflammation (e.g. TeD, myositis, idiopathic orbital inflammatory disease), trauma (orbital wall/floor fracture), or infiltration.

rows: Vermiform movements; pupil initially dilated, later abnormally constricted; response to light is poor, response to near is initially poor, later tonic (exaggerated but slow), i.e. there is light-near dissociation; will constrict with 0.1% pilocarpine due to denervation hypersensitivity.
Dilated pupil (often irregular) due to a torn sphincter with associated anterior segment damage (e.g. transillumination defects).
Dilated pupil (often irregular) due to sectoral iris atrophy (typically with herpes group of viruses) or stuck down by pS.
Constricts to pilocarpine 1%; dilated pupil associated with other features of IIIn palsy (e.g. ptosis, oculomotor abnormality).
Does not constrict to pilocarpine 1%; dilated pupil resulting from anticholinergic mydriatics such as atropine (rather than adrenergics).
Does not constrict to pilocarpine 1%; dilated pupil occurring after angle-closure glaucoma or intraocular surgery (e.g. urrets–Zavalia syndrome).

branches: Abnormal iris appearance (Structural damage): Iris inflammation: constricted pupil (may be irregular) stuck down by pS.

Normal iris appearance (Dilates at normal speed): Physiological anisocoria: anisocoria is usually mild (≤1mm) and only marginally worse in dim, rather than bright, light; responses to light and near are normal; degree of anisocoria varies from day to day and may reverse; will not dilate with 1% apraclonidine (cf. Horner’s syndrome).

Normal iris appearance (Dilates slowly - ‘dilatation lag’): Horner’s syndrome: constricted pupil, with mild ptosis; iris hypochromia suggests congenital or very long-standing lesion; confirm with 1% apraclonidine (a Horner’s pupil will dilate) or 4% cocaine (a Horner’s pupil will not dilate).

Horner's (Dilates with hydroxyamfetamine 1%): Central or preganglionic Horner’s syndrome: constricted pupil, mild ptosis, facial anhydrosis; may have other features related to level of lesion (brainstem, spinal cord, lung apex, neck).

Horner's (Does NOT dilate with hydroxyamfetamine 1%): Post-ganglionic Horner’s syndrome: constricted pupil, mild ptosis; may have other features related to level of lesion (neck, cavernous sinus, orbit).
Normal iris appearance (Does not dilate in dim light): Pharmacological: constricted pupil may be due to cholinergic miotics such as pilocarpine.

sections.title: Early Onset Nystagmus
content: Stable head position: Infantile nystagmus syndrome (Conjugate horizontal jerk).
Idiopathic infantile nystagmus: very early onset (usually by 2mo of age); worsens with fixation; improves within ‘null zone’ and on convergence; mild dVA.

Fusion maldevelopment nystagmus (syn MLN): fast phase towards fixing eye; worsens with occlusion of non-fixing eye, and with gaze towards fast phase; alternates if opposite eye takes up fixation; often associated with infantile esotropia.
Erratic: Sensory deprivation: erratic waveform ± roving eye movements; moderate/severe dVA due to ocular or anterior visual pathway disease.
Unstable head position: Head-bobbing and torticollis in Spasmus nutans: rare idiopathic benign condition, but which requires exclusion of other more serious pathology.

sections.title: Late Onset Nystagmus: Conjugate & Sustained
content: Peripheral vestibular: conjugate horizontal jerk nystagmus, improves with fixation and with time since injury, worsens with gaze towards fast phase (Alexander’s law) or change in head position.
Cerebellar/central vestibular/brainstem (Does not improve with fixation):
Horizontal type: lesions of the vestibular nuclei, cerebellum, or their connections.
Upbeat type: usually cerebellar/lower brainstem lesions, e.g. demyelination, infarction, tumour, encephalitis, Wernicke’s syndrome.
Downbeat type: usually craniocervical junction lesions, e.g. Arnold-Chiari malformation, spinocerebellar degenerations, infarction, tumour, demyelination.
Periodic alternating: conjugate horizontal jerk nystagmus with waxing–waning nystagmus; 90s in each direction with a 10s ‘null’ period; usually associated with vestibulocerebellar lesions.

rows: Conjugate horizontal jerk nystagmus on eccentric gaze, fast phase towards gaze direction; failure of ipsilateral neural integrator/cerebellar dysfunction.
Due to CNS depression (e.g. fatigue, alcohol, anticonvulsants, barbiturates) or structural pathology (e.g. brainstem, cerebellum).
INO: nystagmus of the abducting (and occasionally adducting) eye. SO myokymia: unilateral high-frequency, low-amplitude torsional nystagmus.
See-saw nystagmus: vertical/torsional components; one eye elevates/intorts, other depresses/extorts; slow pendular or jerk waveform.
Acquired pendular nystagmus: usually disconjugate (horizontal, vertical, torsional); may be associated with involuntary repetitive movement of palate, pharynx, and face.

sections.title: Increased Tear Production: Basal
content: Basal increase • i parasympathetic drive: from pro-secretory drugs (e.g. pilocarpine) or autonomic disturbance.

sections.title: Increased Tear Production: Reflex
content: Reflex increase
• Local irritants, e.g. FB, trichiasis.
• Chronic ocular disease, e.g. blepharitis, KCS.

rows:
• Lid laxity: common involutional change in the elderly.
• Orbicularis weakness: associated with VIIn palsy.
• Ectropion: most commonly an involutional change in the elderly but may also be cicatricial, mechanical, or congenital.

sections.title: Decreased Drainage: Punctal Obstruction
content: Congenital: punctal atresia.
Acquired: punctal stenosis is most commonly idiopathic but may arise 2° to punctal eversion, post-HSV infection, or any scarring process (e.g. post-irradiation, trachoma, cicatricial conjunctivitis).

sections.title: Decreased Drainage: Canalicular Obstruction
content: Acquired: canalicular fibrosis is most commonly idiopathic but may arise 2° to HSV infection, chronic canaliculitis (usually actinomycosis), chronic dacrocystitis, cicatricial conjunctivitis, and 5-Fu administration.

sections.title: Decreased Drainage: Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction
content: Congenital: delayed canalization.

Acquired: stenosis is most commonly idiopathic but may arise 2° to trauma (nasal/orbital fracture), post-irradiation, GpA, tumours (e.g. nasopharyngeal carcinoma), and other nasal pathology (chronic inflammation/polyps).

sections.content: The watery eye. Increased tear production. Basal increase • i parasympathetic drive: from pro-secretory drugs (e.g. pilocarpine) or autonomic disturbance. Reflex increase • Local irritants, e.g. FB, trichiasis. • Chronic ocular disease, e.g. blepharitis, KCS. • Systemic disease, e.g. TeD. Lacrimal pump failure. Lid tone • Lid laxity: common involutional change in the elderly. • Orbicularis weakness: associated with VIIn palsy. Lid position • Ectropion: most commonly an involutional change in the elderly but may also be cicatricial, mechanical, or congenital. Decreased drainage. Punctal obstruction • Congenital: punctal atresia. • Acquired: punctal stenosis is most commonly idiopathic but may arise 2° to punctal eversion, post-HSV infection, or any scarring process (e.g. post-irradiation, trachoma, cicatricial conjunctivitis). Canalicular obstruction • Acquired: canalicular fibrosis is most commonly idiopathic but may arise 2° to HSV infection, chronic canaliculitis (usually actinomycosis), chronic dacrocystitis, cicatricial conjunctivitis, and 5-Fu administration. rows: Conjunctivitis: infective, allergic, or chemical; gritty/itchy; watery, mucoid, mucopurulent, or purulent exudate; papillae or follicles.
Anterior scleritis: severe pain; diffuse deep injection which does not blanch with vasoconstrictors (e.g. phenylephrine 10%), oedema; globe tender.

• Keratitis: photophobia, watering, circumlimbal injection, corneal infiltrate ± epithelial defect ± AC activity.
• Anterior uveitis: photophobia, watering, Kps, AC activity ± pS.
• Corneal FB: appropriate history, FB sensation, visible FB.

• Episcleritis: mild discomfort; may be recurrent; sectoral (occasionally diffuse) redness which blanches with topical vasoconstrictor (e.g. phenylephrine 10%); globe non-tender.
• Marginal keratitis: photophobia, watering, marginal corneal infiltrate ± epithelial defect.

sections.title: Normal/Near Normal Vision: Painless
content: Subconjunctival haemorrhage: well-defined, confluent area of haemorrhage.

rows:
• Corneal abrasion: photophobia, watering, sectoral/circumlimbal injection, epithelial defect.
• Keratitis: photophobia, watering, circumlimbal injection, corneal infiltrate ± epithelial defect ± AC activity ± mucopurulent discharge.

• Anterior uveitis: photophobia, watering, Kps, AC activity ± pS.
• Endophthalmitis: pain, floaters, watering, diffuse deep injection, inflammation (vitreous > AC), chorioretinitis.

sections.title: Reduced Vision: Increased IOP (Critical)
content: Acute glaucoma: usually due to angle closure; photophobia, watering, corneal oedema, fixed mid-dilated pupil ± anterior segment/angle abnormalities such as rubeosis.
Hypertensive uveitis: AC cells and flare ± corneal involvement; often due to herpes group of viruses.

content.explanation: Used to differentiate redness: Episcleritis (blanches with topical vasoconstrictor) vs. Anterior Scleritis (does NOT blanch).

sections.title: PRP Red Flags & Complications
content: Pain
Transient visual loss
Permanent loss of peripheral field (driving implications)
Decreased dark adaptation (night vision effect)
Permanent scotomas
Worsened acuity (macular decompensation or inadvertent macular laser)
Choroidal or retinal detachment
Vitreous haemorrhage

sections.title: Macular Laser (Focal or Grid)
content: Indication: Clinically significant macular oedema.
Consent: Explain reduction of sight loss, need for retreatment, pain, scotomas, worsened acuity, retinal/choroidal detachment.
Prep: Topical anaesthetic + fundus CL (e.g. area centralis) with coupling agent.
Settings: 532nm/green; 50-200 micron spot; 0.08–0.1s; very gentle blanching burn. Smaller/shorter for central burns.
Focal Technique: Burns to microaneurysms 500-3000 microns from foveal centre (min 300 if outside FAZ).
Grid Technique: Burns ≥1 burn-width apart around fovea; min 500 microns from foveal centre and disc margin.
Review: 3 months or sooner.

sections.title: Macular Laser Complications
content: Pain and Scotomas
Worsened acuity (decompensation or scar 'creep')
Choroidal or retinal detachment
Choroidal neovascular membrane
Vitreous haemorrhage

branches: Indications: Retinal break with RD risk (usually U-tears) without excessive SRF
Slit-lamp: For equatorial and post-equatorial lesions
Indirect: For anterior lesions (with indentation) or cryotherapy

sections.title: Nd-YAG Peripheral Iridotomy (PI)
content: Indications: Angle closure with pupil block (Acute/Subacute/Chronic/1°/2°) & Prophylaxis for occludable angles.
Consent: Explain purpose, bilateral treatment, failure risk, bleeding, inflammation, corneal burns, monocular diplopia.
Pre-Medication: Pilocarpine 2% (iris tension) + Apraclonidine 1% (IOP spike/bleeding prevention) + Anaesthetic.
Laser Setup: 2-3 pulse bursts of 3–6mJ (higher for thick/pigmented irides); Angle the beam (not perpendicular).
Positioning: Abraham lens + coupling agent.
Site Selection: Superior (under lid), peripheral, ideally in iris crypt.
Execution: Focus and fire; success shown by forward gush of pigment-loaded aqueous (usually 2–4 shots).
Post-op: Topical steroid (dexamethasone 0.1% 6x/d for 1wk); IOP check at 30-60min; Review within 10d.

sections.title: Nd-YAG PI Complications
content: Bleeding (stop with lens pressure)
Inflammation (increase steroids)
Raised IOP
Corneal burns (caution in shallow AC)
Glare and optical aberrations (avoid interpalpebral area/tear meniscus)

rows: OAG with pigmented TM (POAG/PXF/PDS); Medical/Surg ineffective.
As for ALT, but more targeted, utilizes less energy.
50 equally spaced shots over 180° on anterior border of pigmented TM.
50 non-overlapping spots over inferior 180° centered on TM.
Adjust power 0.1mJ below bubble formation level.

sections.title: Argon Laser Peripheral Iridoplasty (ALPI)
content: Indications: Plateau iris syndrome (common), APAC (rare).
Method: Ring of burns to peripheral iris stroma (Abraham/Goldmann lens).
Applications: 20–50 burns over 360° (≥2 spot sizes apart).
Settings: 200-500um spot, 0.2-0.5s duration, 200-400mW power.
Complications: Inflammation (mild), IOP spike, corneal burns.

rows: Intractable IOP (rubeotic/synechial); unwell patients; temporizing pre-trab.
Refractory IOP; easier in pseudophakic eyes; can combine with Phaco.
Contact probe 0.5–2mm from limbus; 5–10 shots per quadrant.
Limbal or pars plana; laser process until shrinkage/whitening.
Avoid 3/9 o’clock and superior quadrant; avoid audible 'pops'.
Fill AC with viscoelastic; avoid treating 'valleys'; avoid 'pops'.
Antibiotics, Steroids, continue glaucoma meds; oral acetazolamide stat.

sections.title: Nd-YAG Posterior Capsulotomy
content: Indication: Visually significant PCO.
Caution: Assess for uveitis, glaucoma, macular oedema, retinal degeneration (high-risk).
Prep: Mydriatics (Tropicamide 1% ± Phenylephrine 2.5%); Capsulotomy lens + coupling agent.
Settings: 1–1.5mJ (higher for thicker PCO); Angle the beam.
Technique 1 (Full Ring): Posterior capsulorhexis (detached capsule free-floating).
Technique 2 (Partial Ring): Inferior hinge (capsule drops but stays attached).
Technique 3 (Cross): Peripheral start in each axis.
Post-op: Topical steroid 4x/d 2wk; Review 4–6 weeks for visual axis clarity and inflammation check.

sections.title: YAG Capsulotomy Risks
content: Lens damage (pitting, dislocation)
Inflammation (severe in uveitics)
Floaters
Retinal damage (tears, detachment)
Corneal oedema
Increased IOP
Cystoid Macular Oedema (CMO)
Failure/need for retreatment

rows: Cataract: Clear corneal incisions, LRIs, capsulorhexis, lens fragmentation. Refractive: LASIK flaps, ICRS channels, keratoplasty cuts.
Ablative reshaping of the cornea for PRK, LASIK, and LASEK.
