sections.title: Understanding Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis
sections.content: Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) is the formation of a blood clot within the cavernous sinus, a large dural venous sinus located at the base of the skull. This condition is most commonly caused by the retrograde spread of infection from the 'danger triangle' of the face, the paranasal sinuses, or the teeth. Because the veins of the face lack valves, bacteria can travel backward into the cavernous sinus, leading to inflammation, thrombus formation, and potential damage to the vital cranial nerves that pass through it.

sections.title: Anatomical Contents of the Cavernous Sinus
Clinical Signs & Symptoms
content: Abrupt onset of unilateral periorbital edema and chemosis
Proptosis (bulging of the eye) due to venous congestion
Ophthalmoplegia: Paralysis of eye muscles (CN III, IV, VI)
Severe headache or retro-orbital pain
Decreased corneal sensation (CN V1 involvement)
Fever, chills, and altered mental status (Systemic involvement)
Bilateral progression: Signs usually spread to the other eye within 24-48 hours

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Act Immediately
content: Rapidly progressing bilateral proptosis
Complete external ophthalmoplegia (frozen eye)
Papilledema or retinal vein engorgement
Signs of meningitis (nuchal rigidity, Kernig's sign)
Sepsis or septic shock indicators

sections.title: Diagnostic & Management Pathway
content: Step 1: Clinical Suspicion - Immediate neurological and ophthalmic exam.
Step 2: Imaging - MRI with MRV (preferred) or Contrast-enhanced CT to visualize filling defects.
Step 3: Laboratory Work - Blood cultures, CBC, and Lumbar Puncture if meningitis is suspected.
Step 4: Aggressive Antibiotics - High-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone/Metronidazole).
Step 5: Anticoagulation - Consider Heparin to prevent thrombus propagation.
Step 6: Surgical Intervention - Drainage of the primary infection source (e.g., sinus surgery).

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Mortality rate: Reduced to <20% with modern antibiotics
Vision loss (30% of survivors)
Persistent CN palsies
Pituitary insufficiency
Brain abscess or Meningitis

content.explanation: CN 6 is inside (with ICA), while CN 3, 4, 5 (V1/V2) are in the lateral wall. If CN 6 goes first, suspect CST early!

sections.title: The Mechanism of Action
content: Step 1: Argon laser creates thermal burns in the peripheral retina.
Step 2: Destruction of metabolic high-demand ischemic tissue.
Step 3: Reduction in Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) production.
Step 4: Regression of abnormal, fragile new blood vessels.

content.explanation: N: Night vision reduction; P: Peripheral visual field constriction; C: Color vision alterations.

sections.title: Verbatim Procedural Summary
sections.content: Argon laser PRP is performed to stabilize the retina by sacrificing peripheral vision to preserve central vision. The Argon laser's specific wavelength is highly absorbed by the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and hemoglobin, making it an effective tool for thermal photocoagulation in the treatment of proliferative vascular diseases.

sections.title: Compiled Notes
content:
📝 Note 1 (Bilateral Disc Swelling: Clinical Emergency & Diagnostic Framework - 17/02/2026):
Clinical Signs of True Swelling

Blurring of the peripapillary nerve fiber layer
Obscuration of major retinal vessels as they leave the disc
Paton’s lines (circumferential retinal folds)
Flame-shaped hemorrhages at or near the disc margin
Cotton wool spots (indicative of axonal ischemia)
Absence of Spontaneous Venous Pulsation (SVP)
Hyperemic appearance of the optic nerve head

📝 Note 2 (NEOVASCULAR GLAUCOMA (NVG): A Comprehensive Guide - 14/02/2026):
Key Causes & Risk Factors

Ischaemic CrVO (common); risk of progression to NVG is 50%.
Diabetic retinopathy (common); risk of NVG highest in PDr.
Other vascular disorders: OIS, CrAO, BrVO.
Other retinal disease: chronic retinal detachment, sickle cell retinopathy.
Retinal or choroidal tumours.

📝 Note 3 (SEVENTH NERVE DISORDERS: THE OPHTHALMIC PERSPECTIVE - 14/02/2026):
Differential: Isolated vs Complex?

1. Check for involvement of all other cranial nerves.
2. Check Vn (cerebellopontine lesions).
3. Check VIn (lesion in pons).
4. Check VIIn (cerebellopontine angle lesions).
5. Check for alteration of taste.
6. Check for alteration of salivation.
7. Check for alteration of lacrimation.

📝 Note 4 (Uveal Emergencies: VKH Disease & Sympathetic Ophthalmia - 14/02/2026):
Management of VKH

Step 1: Liaise with physician.
Step 2: Start high-dose systemic corticosteroids (e.g. 1–2mg/kg/d prednisolone PO or IVMP 1g/d for 3d).
Step 3: For resistant or recurrent disease, add corticosteroid-sparing agents (immunosuppressants).
Immunosuppressants include: Methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and ciclosporin.

branches: Anophthalmia: Absence of an eye within the orbit
1° Anophthalmia: Complete failure of any ocular tissue to develop
2° Anophthalmia: Partial development which then halts, leaving a very small microphthalmic eye
Degenerative Anophthalmia: Partially developed eye regresses

sections.title: Developmental Treatment Strategy
content: Early treatment: Use of conformers and orbit expanders (Normal development of orbit and lids depends on globe presence)
Age < 2 years: Hydrophilic orbital expanders (must be replaced every few weeks)
Subsequent Phase: Replace with painted prostheses
Long-term: Continue treatment until the face has fully developed

sections.title: Specialized Management Needs
content: Special conformers: Available for microphthalmic eyes where limited vision is preserved; improves cosmesis without obstructing vision
Surgery: Used to reduce orbital asymmetry
Multidisciplinary Team: Paediatric ophthalmologist, orbital surgeon, and orbital prosthesist (among others)

sections.title: Surgical Classifications
content: Enucleation: Eye removal, leaving extraocular muscles (eOMs) intact
Evisceration: Eye content removal, leaving sclera and eOMs
Exenteration: Removal of eye and parts of the orbit (lids, orbital tissue, bone)

sections.title: Orbital Implant Principles
sections.content: Placement of an orbital implant (acrylic or hydroxyapatite) is almost always performed in conjunction with enucleation/evisceration. The principal of implant placement is to choose the largest possible for that patient’s socket.

branches: Definition: Features resulting from deficient, shrunken volume of orbital tissues surrounding a socket
Superior sulcus deformity (hollowing above the upper eyelid)

sections.title: PESS Treatment: Inadequate Volume
content: Prosthetist to modify or replace existing prosthesis
Exchange orbital implant for one of a larger volume
Subperiosteal orbital floor implant
Orbital injection of filler material (i.e. hyaluronic acid-based)
Dermis fat graft: Autogenous dermis and subdermal fat (e.g. from abdomen, left inguinal region, or buttocks)

sections.title: PESS Treatment: Abnormal Lid Position
content: Lateral or medial tarsal strip
Levator resection

sections.title: The Discharging Socket
content: Small amount of discharge is common and needs differentiation from socket infection or Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis (GPC)
Causes: Socket dryness, presence of prosthesis, resulting abrasion of socket conjunctiva
Infection Hallmark: Recurrent discharge resistant to multiple drops
Infection Hallmark: Implant discomfort (to touch)
Infection Hallmark: Recurrent pyogenic granuloma

sections.title: Management of Infection and Discharge
content: Ensure regular cleaning and polishing of prosthesis (e.g. annual)
Advise patient not to remove prosthesis too frequently
Ensure no exposed sutures or implant exposure
Short course of topical lubricants, antibiotics, and steroids
Deep socket infection: Requires implant removal (responds poorly to topical/PO/IV antibiotics)

rows: Inadequate surgical closure (wound closure under tension, poor technique)
Hydroxyapatite debridement and grafting (donor sclera, fascia lata)
Dermis fat graft if orbital implant exchange fails

sections.title: Prosthesis Mobility Challenges
content: Commoner for horizontal gaze than vertical (shorter fornices)
Less common after evisceration than enucleation
Movement issue may relate to prosthesis rather than implant
Pegged implants: Higher complication rates
Treatment: Prosthetist review of fitting
Treatment: Increase size of orbital implant

sections.title: Shortening of the Fornices
content: Causes: Recurring socket infection and/or scarring 2° to trauma
Anatomy: Lower fornix shortening > Upper fornix shortening
Associations: Lower lid retraction, difficulty fitting prosthesis, prosthesis falling out
Treatment (Fornix-deepening sutures): Generally do not work
Treatment (Grafts): Amniotic Membrane Graft (AMG), hard palate, ear cartilage, or donor sclera graft

sections.title: Ophthalmic Importance of the VII Nerve
sections.content: The seventh or facial nerve has a number of important motor, sensory, and secretory functions. Of these, it is the facial nerve’s ability to close the eyelids (i.e. innervation of orbicularis oculi) that make it so important to the ophthalmologist. Facial nerve palsy should not be underestimated. Do not automatically assume that every facial nerve palsy is a ‘Bell’s palsy’, and be alert to its capacity to cause blinding exposure keratopathy (see Box 16.15). Anatomy: See E Anatomy and physiology (3), p. 732.

branches: Motor: muscles of facial expression and movement
Motor: superficial platysma muscles of the neck
Sensory/Secretory: lacrimal gland (via greater superficial petrosal nerve)
Sensory: taste for anterior two-thirds of tongue (via chorda tympani)

rows: Weakness of one side of the face/facial asymmetry (if unilateral).
Lagophthalmos, with or without lower lid ectropion.
Check for alteration of taste, salivation, and lacrimation.

sections.title: Differential: UMN vs. LMN Lesions
content: Upper Motor Neurone (UMN): Upper facial muscles still function (e.g. can still raise eyebrows) due to bilateral innervation (see E Anatomy and physiology (3), p. 732).
Lower Motor Neurone (LMN): Both upper and lower facial muscles are involved.

sections.title: Complex Palsy: Cranial Nerve Check
content: Check Vn: Cerebel-lopontine lesions
Check VIn: Lesion in pons
Check VIIn: Cerebellopontine angle lesions

sections.title: Box 16.15: Causes of VIIn Palsy
content: • Bell’s palsy (idiopathic).
• Ramsay–hunt syndrome (varicella-zoster infection).
• Cerebellopontine angle lesions.
• Trauma.
• Otitis.
• Neurofibroma (NF-2).
• Parotid gland mass.
• Congenital (e.g. Moebius’ syndrome).
• Guillain–Barré syndrome (Commonly present with bilateral VIIn weakness).
• Lyme disease (Commonly present with bilateral VIIn weakness).
• Sarcoidosis (Commonly present with bilateral VIIn weakness).
• Meningitis (Commonly present with bilateral VIIn weakness).

sections.title: Bell's Palsy Clinical Data
sections.content: Bell’s palsy (idiopathic facial paralysis) is a diagnosis of exclusion. It can affect any age group (peak 40y), with males and females equally affected. Associations include diabetes and pregnancy. Symptoms reach their peak at 48h; most start recovery at 3wk.

sections.title: Management Strategy: New & Recurrent Palsy
content: Step 1: ENT or neurology referral for all new-onset facial nerve palsies to establish cause.
Step 2: Neuroimaging for all recurrent facial nerve palsy to exclude inflammatory or neoplastic causes.
Step 3: Immediate ocular surface protection with lubricants (preservative-free tears day/ointment night).
Step 4: Assess need for lid closure (taping at night or temporary tarsorrhaphy).

sections.title: Surgical & Chronic Management
content: Insertion of gold weights to the upper lid for chronic cases.
Late surgical options: Facial nerve repair.
Late surgical options: Nerve substitution.
Late surgical options: Muscle transposition.
Crocodile tears (gustatory hyperlacrimation 2° aberrant regeneration): Transcutaneous injection of botulinum toxin to the lacrimal gland.

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNINGS
content: Do not automatically assume every palsy is Bell's Palsy.
Blinding exposure keratopathy risk is high.
Recurrent palsy requires neuroimaging to exclude neoplastic causes.
Anti-herpes simplex antivirals alone confer no recovery benefit compared to placebo.

sections.title: At-Risk Populations & Etiology
sections.content: Sarcoidosis is a relatively common granulomatous multisystem disorder that may be life-threatening. It affects up to 0.1% of the population, being higher in ♀ and with peaks in the third and sixth decades. It is commoner in African-Caribbeans, Irish, and Scandinavians. The cause is unknown; there is PCR evidence for several agents (including atypical mycobacteria) that may trigger the disease in susceptible individuals. The Th1 response predominates in typical sarcoidosis granulomata, although it appears that a transition to the Th2 response underlies progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

rows: Erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL)
Better prognosis; tends to be self-limiting

branches: Anterior Uveitis: 2/3 persistent, 1/3 acute; unilateral or bilateral; 'granulomatous'; circumlimbal injection, mutton fat KPs, AC flare/cells, PS, vitreous cells; iris granulomas and nodules.
Intermediate Uveitis: Vitreous cells, snowballs, snowbanking.

Posterior Uveitis: CMO (commonest cause of dVA), periphlebitis (± patchy sheathing ± 'candle wax dripping'), occluded vessels (especially BRVO), neovascularization, choroidal/retinal/preretinal nodules (probably granulomata), pigment epithelial changes, disc swelling (from inflammatory papillitis, optic nerve granuloma, or papilloedema 2° to CNS disease).
Diagnostic Sign: Peripheral multifocal chorioretinitis (small punched-out atrophic spots) are highly suggestive of sarcoidosis.
Complications: Cataract, glaucoma (↑ risk with duration of active disease), CNV.

sections.title: Systemic Clinical Features
content: Respiratory (RS): Often asymptomatic despite CXR changes, dry cough, dyspnoea; BHL, parenchymal disease.
Cardiovascular (CVS): Pericarditis, cardiomyopathy, conduction defects, cardiac failure, cor pulmonale.

Skin: Erythema nodosum (red, tender, elevated lesions typically on shins; commonest in younger ♀); cutaneous granulomata (non-tender nodules/papules/macules, almost anywhere including lids); lupus pernio (uncommon bluish plaque on face/ears).
Joints: Arthritis (commoner in acute sarcoidosis); bone cysts (usually in digits).
Glands: Swelling of lacrimal, salivary, parotid, and submaxillary glands; lymphadenopathy; hepatosplenomegaly.

CNS (Neurosarcoidosis): Commoner in patients with posterior uveitis; cranial nerve palsies (most commonly VIIn; can be bilateral), peripheral neuropathy, myopathy, aseptic meningoencephalitis (typically basal leptomeninges); CNS granuloma may mimic a tumour; optic nerve involvement may present as an atypical optic neuritis.

sections.title: Primary Investigations
content: Diagnosis: Essentially clinical but supported by ACE, imaging, and histology. Difficult to distinguish neurosarcoidosis from MS in some cases.
Serum ACE: Commonly elevated in active disease due to activated macrophages; synthesis. False negatives in patients on ACE inhibitors.
Serum Ca2+: Less commonly elevated.
CXR: Abnormal in >90% with ocular sarcoid.
HRCT Thorax: High sensitivity and specificity; useful if CXR is normal.
MRI Brain/Optic Nerves: Fat-suppressed, gadolinium-enhanced T1 and LP for suspected neurosarcoid.

sections.title: CXR Staging
content: Stage 0: Normal
Stage 1: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) only
Stage 2: BHL + parenchymal disease
Stage 3: Parenchymal disease only

sections.title: Advanced Diagnostic Imaging
content: Gallium-67 scan: Typical uptake pattern is lacrimal and parotid glands (panda appearance) or mediastinum (lambda sign).

PET-CT scan: PET captures images of minuscule changes in metabolism caused by growth of abnormal cells; CT allows exact location, size, and shape pinpointing. Small lesions (e.g. lymph nodes) detected with PET and located with CT.
FFA (Fundus Fluorescein Angiography): Includes ischaemia (hypofluorescence), leakage from periphlebitis, new vessels, CMO (hyperfluorescence).
ICG (Indocyanine Green): Choroidal stromal vasculitis, early lobular hypofluorescence, late hyperfluorescence (focal or diffuse).

sections.title: Biopsy and Histology
sections.content: Biopsy (transbronchial, endobronchial, or conjunctival) may reveal the typical non-caseating granulomata of whorls of epithelioid cells surrounding multinucleate giant cells. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) may show lymphocytosis with high CD4+/CD8+ ratio, but has low specificity.

sections.title: Box 11.3: Differential Diagnosis of Elevated Serum ACE
content: Child (peaks at 13y of age, adult level by 18y)
Sarcoidosis
Mycobacterial infection (including leprosy and TB)
Chronic lung diseases (berylliosis, silicosis, farmer’s lung, histoplasmosis, lymphangiomyomatosis)
Gaucher’s disease

sections.title: Treatment of Ophthalmic Disease
content: Anterior Segment: Treated as for idiopathic AAU (Acute Anterior Uveitis).
Posterior Segment: Treated as for intermediate uveitis.
Cataract: Conventional surgery with tight control of inflammation.
Glaucoma: Medical ± surgical (augmented trabeculectomy/tube).
CNV: Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy or intravitreal corticosteroid.

content.explanation: Heerfordt’s syndrome (uveoparotid fever): Parotid/submandibular gland enlargement, VIIn palsy, uveitis. Löfgren’s syndrome: Fever, erythema nodosum, BHL. Mickulicz’s syndrome: Diffuse swelling of lacrimal/salivary glands (most commonly due to sarcoidosis).

sections.title: CMV: Anterior Uveitis & Endotheliitis
content: Anterior Uveitis (Immunocompetent): Occurs in healthy individuals; increasingly recognized as a cause of unilateral, hypertensive uveitis.
Clinical Features: Unilateral, usually with increased Intraocular Pressure (iIOP). Note: There may be no obvious iris atrophy, distinguishing it from HSV or VZV.
Corneal Endotheliitis (Commoner in Far East): Focal (coin-shaped) to diffuse bullous keratopathy.
Endotheliitis Signs: Stromal corneal oedema, Keratic Precipitates (KPs) of variable appearance.
Anterior Chamber (AC) Inflammation: Usually mild with no Posterior Synechiae (PS); ± diffuse iris atrophy and iIOP.
Treatment: Often challenging; may respond to oral valganciclovir. IOP control can be difficult.

sections.title: HIV: Global Epidemiology & Stats (2015-2016)
sections.content: HIV (HIV-1 and 2) is an RNA retrovirus infecting CD4+ T-cells. Statistics: 736.7 million people living with HIV end of 2015. ART expansion reduced deaths to 1.1 million in 2015 (45% fewer than 2005). Over 18 million were on ART by mid-2016. Most cases are in developing countries (sub-Saharan Africa) linked to socio-economic deprivation. Transmission: blood, bodily fluids, unprotected sex, IV drug abuse, transfusions, and vertical transmission.

rows: Viral (VZV, HSV), Bacterial (S. aureus, S. epidermidis, P. aeruginosa), Protozoan (microsporidia) keratitis
Conjunctival microvasculopathy, Vortex keratopathy (antivirals, atovaquone), dry eye, Anterior uveitis
CMV, VZV (PORN, ARN), HSV (ARN), Toxoplasma, Syphilis, Pneumocystis, Cryptococcus, TB
Retinal microvasculopathy, Ischaemic maculopathy, Immune recovery uveitis
Cerebral toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcal meningitis, Neurosyphilis, PML
Optic neuritis, Optic atrophy, Ocular motility disorders

sections.title: CD4 Levels and Typical Ocular Disease
Disease Markers & Management
content: Markers: CD4 level (immunocompromise/susceptibility indicator) and Viral Load (RNA copies/mL, risk of progression).
ART Regimen: At least 3 drugs—usually 2 nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors + 1 protease inhibitor or non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor.
Coordination: Care must be shared between an experienced HIV ophthalmologist and an HIV physician.

sections.title: HIV Anterior Segment Conditions
content: Conjunctival Microvasculopathy: Common; irregular-calibre vessels, often in a corkscrew pattern; may associate with retinal microvasculopathy.
VZV Keratouveitis: Common; may lack HZO rash. Features: moderate anterior uveitis, iIOP, iris atrophy. Rx: Systemic aciclovir/famciclovir.
HSV Keratouveitis: Equal prevalence to general population but more severe in HIV; limbal, more recurrences, larger/less defined dendrites. Rx: Topical ± systemic antiviral.
Microsporidial Keratouveitis: Bilateral irritation, photophobia, punctate keratopathy, follicular conjunctivitis, and/or anterior uveitis.
Anterior Uveitis: Seen in >50% of HIV patients. VZV/HSV cause mild inflammation with iIOP. Posterior uveitis (Toxo/Syphilis) also causes AC inflammation.
Drug-Induced Uveitis: Caused by Rifabutin (anti-atypical mycobacteria) and Cidofovir (anti-CMV).

branches: Granular Retinitis: Indolent, minimal haemorrhage, no vascular sheathing
Perivascular Retinitis: 'Frosted branch angiitis' following retinal vessels

sections.title: Specific Anti-CMV Treatment Protocols
content: Prophylaxis: Sustain CD4 count >50/mm3 via ART.
Induction Therapy: Initial high-dose treatment to control active infection.
Maintenance Therapy: Lifelong treatment if immune recovery does not occur.
Drug Options: PO Valganciclovir; IV Ganciclovir (Neutropenia risk); IV Foscarnet (Renal toxicity risk); IV Cidofovir (Renal toxicity, uveitis risk).
Local Therapy: Intravitreal injections of ganciclovir and/or foscarnet.

sections.title: Posterior Segment: Toxoplasma & Fungal Infections
content: Toxoplasma Retinochoroiditis: More severe in HIV; often multifocal/bilateral. Moderate/severe vitritis/uveitis. Common neuro-toxo association. Always requires treatment; corticosteroids usually avoided.
Pneumocystis carinii Choroiditis: Bilateral yellow patches (1/4 to 2DD) around posterior pole. Minimal vitritis. Rx: systemic co-trimoxazole or pentamidine.
Cryptococcus Choroiditis: Associated with meningitis. Multifocal off-white lesions ± retinitis/endophthalmitis. Rx: Systemic amphotericin or fluconazole.

sections.title: Immune Recovery & Microvasculopathy
content: Immune Recovery Uveitis (IRU): Paradoxical worsening of inflammation in inactive CMV retinitis as T-cells recover. Features: severe vitritis, TRD, CMO, neovascularization.
Syphilis Choroiditis: Co-infection due to sexual transmission; protean manifestations.
HIV Microvasculopathy: Affects 75%; mechanism unclear (thrombotic vs immune vs direct infection).
Retinal Microvasculopathy signs: Vessel tortuosity, Cotton Wool Spots (CWS), telangiectasia, intraretinal haemorrhages, venous/arterial occlusions.

sections.title: Treatment Safety Warning
content: Neutropenia Risk: Associated with Valganciclovir and IV Ganciclovir.
Renal Toxicity: Major side effect of IV Foscarnet and IV Cidofovir.
Drug-Induced Uveitis: Specifically linked to Cidofovir and Rifabutin therapy.
Steroid Contraindication: Ocular toxoplasmosis in HIV is not normally given with corticosteroids.

sections.title: Pleomorphic Adenoma (Benign Mixed Cell Tumour)
content: Commonest lacrimal neoplasm: Accounts for up to 20% of all lacrimal fossa lesions.
Origin: Derived from epithelial and mesenchymal tissue.
Lobe Involvement: May arise from either lobe, most commonly the orbital lobe.
Demographics: Occurs in middle age; slight ♂ bias (♂:♀ 1.5:1).
Malignant Transformation: Occurs in <3% in 10y and 10–20% in 20y.
Clinical Features: Gradual painless proptosis (inferonasal), upper lid swelling, diplopia, palpable mass (orbital lobe tumours may not be palpable).
Globe Effects: Indentation may cause choroidal folds ± hypermetropic shift.

rows: Round, lobulated lesion, typically medium/high reflectivity.
Expansion of lacrimal fossa, indentation of globe, well-circumscribed and slightly nodular tumour, calcification in 3%.
Surgical removal of whole tumour with intact pseudocapsule by anterior (palpebral lobe) or lateral (orbital lobe) orbitotomy.
Excellent with complete excision; needs prolonged follow-up for malignant transformation even if clearance is complete.

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNING: Pleomorphic Adenoma
content: DO NOT PERFORM PRIOR BIOPSY: Risk of seeding.
Patient must be warned regarding subsequent KCS (Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca).

sections.title: Lacrimal Carcinomas
content: Commonest malignant lacrimal tumour: Adenoid cystic carcinoma.
Other types: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma and pleomorphic adenocarcinoma.
Clinical: Rapid proptosis, ophthalmoparesis, and orbital pain.
Spread: Sensory disturbance from perineural spread is common.
Imaging: Irregular poorly defined lesion; bony destruction and calcification (20–30%).
Treatment: Seldom curative; exenteration ± radiotherapy.
Prognosis: Very poor with high mortality.

branches: Slow-growing tumour of glial tissue (Children focus)
Presentation: Gradual dVA (often stabilizes), disc swelling/atrophy, proptosis
Imaging: Fusiform enlargement of optic nerve ± chiasmal mass
Management: Observation (good vision), MRI monitoring, Surgery (reduced vision/pain/chiasm threat), Chemo/Radio (chiasmal/midbrain involvement)

sections.title: Optic Nerve Sheath Meningioma
content: Rare benign tumour of meningothelial cells; middle age focus.
Gender: Slight ♀ bias (♀:♂ 1.5:1).
Association: Neurofibromatosis-2.
Presentation: Gradual dVA, disc swelling/atrophy, optic disc collateral vessels (30%), proptosis, ophthalmoparesis.
Imaging Hallmark: Tubular enlargement with ‘tram-track’ enhancement of the sheath ± calcification.
Management: Observation if VA is good. Surgery for blind eyes, severe proptosis, or chiasm threat.
Prognosis: Good for life.

rows: Childhood; NF-1; ‘bag-of-worms’ mass; S-shaped lid deformity; Poorly defined/unencapsulated; Hard to excise (debulking needed).
Adulthood; Gradual proptosis; Well circumscribed; Straightforward surgical excision.
Slow-growing/Benign (rarely malignant); NF association; Adulthood; Superior orbit; Cystic non-tender mass; Good prognosis with excision.

sections.title: Vascular Tumours: Cavernous Haemangioma
content: Commonest benign orbital neoplasm in adults.
Pathology: Hamartoma of dilated large vascular spaces lined by endothelial cells.
Presentation: Young adulthood; accelerated growth during pregnancy.
Location: 80% Intraconal.
Features: Axial proptosis, restricted motility, globe indentation (choroidal folds/hypermetropic shift), dVA.
Rare Sign: Gaze-evoked amaurosis (apical retrobulbar lesions).
US: Well-defined, round intraconal lesion with high internal reflectivity.
CT/MRI: Well-circumscribed intraconal lesion; mild/moderate enhancement; possible thrombosis.
Treatment: Observation (most); excision (symptomatic).

rows: Hamartoma; Kasabach–Merritt syndrome (dplatelets, dHb, dclotting factors) or cardiac failure in large tumours. Treatment: Corticosteroids (topical/intralesional/systemic), Propranolol, Surgery.
‘Strawberry naevus’ (dermis); appears <2mo, full size at 1y, involutes by 6y. Risk: Amblyopia/astigmatism.
Posterior to septum; proptosis worsens with Valsalva/crying; partial involution.

Rare hamartoma (childhood); size increases with Valsalva/head-down posture. Superficial: Transilluminable cystic lid/conjunctival spaces. Deep: 'Chocolate cyst' (haemorrhage). Treatment: Observation, sclerosing agents, Bleomycin, Onyx®, drainage, or surgery (difficult/friable).

sections.title: Lymphoproliferative Disorders
content: Spectrum: Benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas (85% B-lymphocytes). Classified by WHO system.
Benign Reactive Lymphoid Hyperplasia: Polyclonal; superolateral orbit/lacrimal gland; firm rubbery mass. 25% progress to lymphoma by 5y. Rx: Steroids, Radio, Rituximab.
Atypical Lymphoid Hyperplasia: Intermediate; homogeneous pattern with larger nuclei.
Malignant Orbital Lymphoma: Low-grade B-cell (Non-Hodgkin); commonest is Marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of MALT (40–70%).
Lymphoma Stats: 50% are primary tumours; 25% bilateral; up to 60% systemic involvement within 5y. Rx: Systemic work-up mandatory; Radio/Chemo/Antibody.

sections.title: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis
content: Rare proliferative disorder of childhood.
Spectrum: Eosinophilic granuloma (benign/unifocal) to Letterer–Siwe form (disseminated).
Presentation: Rapid proptosis with superotemporal swelling.
Bilateral involvement occurs in disseminated forms.
Treatment: Surgical excision is usually curative.

sections.title: Rhabdomyosarcoma: The Pediatric Emergency
content: Commonest primary orbital malignancy in children; 87% present <15y.
Types: Embryonal (commonest), Alveolar, Pleomorphic.
Clinical: Acute/subacute proptosis, ptosis, and inflammation (mimics orbital cellulitis).
Investigations: US (high internal flow on Doppler); CT/MRI (mass ± bony erosion).
Mandatory: Biopsy + Systemic work-up.
Rx: Surgery (localized) or Combined Radio/Chemo (extensive).

rows: Commonest adult mesenchymal tumour; superonasal location; benign or malignant.
Complete surgical excision; recurrences common; metastases rare.
Aggressive; rapid proptosis, restricted motility, CN involvement. Scirrhous (Breast/Gastric) may cause enophthalmos.
Half of cases precede primary tumour diagnosis.

sections.title: Vascular Lesions: Varices & AV Fistulae
content: Orbital Varices: Congenital; intermittent proptosis (worse with Valsalva/coughing); phleboliths on imaging. Rx: Surgery (difficult) or sclerosant/coil.

Carotid–Cavernous Fistula (Direct): High-flow; Trauma/Spontaneous; Pulsatile proptosis + audible bruit, chemosis, iIOP, ophthalmoparesis, RAPD, disc swelling. Rx: Catheter embolization (>85% success).
Dural Shunt (Indirect CCF): Low-flow; Spontaneous (Hypertension); Episcleral venous arterialization, chemosis. Rx: 40% spontaneously thrombose; intervention for glaucoma/pain/dVA.
AV Fistula Investigations: US/CT/MRI show dilated superior ophthalmic vein and thick EOMs.

sections.title: Prognosis Summary
content: Pleomorphic Adenoma: Excellent with complete excision.
Lacrimal Carcinoma: Very poor; high mortality.
Optic Nerve Glioma: Good for life (if restricted to nerve).
Schwannoma: Good with excision.
Langerhans (Eosinophilic): Curative with excision.
Dural Shunt: 40% Spontaneous resolution.

branches: Retinal traction: Vitreoretinal traction, pDr, sickle-cell retinopathy, rOp.
CNS: Papilloedema, Migraine, Occipital lobe lesions, Visual hallucinations.

sections.title: Pseudoflashes & CNS Visual Phenomena
content: • Photophobia: discomfort commonly associated with anterior segment inflammation or retinal hypersensitivity.
• Glare: dazzle commonly associated with media opacities.
• Haloes: ring effect associated with corneal oedema and some media opacities.
• Papilloedema: transient, associated with straining or change in posture.
• Migraine: classic enlarging zigzag fortification spectra moving central to peripheral, usually followed by headache.
• Occipital lobe lesions (tumours, AVMs): coloured shapes/blobs.
• Other visual hallucinations: bilateral severe visual loss may result in more complex visual hallucinations (Charles Bonnet syndrome).

sections.title: Floaters Only: Differential Diagnosis
content: • PVD: partial/complete Weiss ring overlying the optic disc ± visible posterior vitreous face.
• Vitreous condensations: degenerative changes within the vitreous lead to translucent opacities.

• Vitreous haemorrhage: red cells in the vitreous, varies from minor bleed (‘spots’ in vision, fundus easily visualized) to severe (severe dVA, no fundal view); may be followed by synchysis scintillans (golden particles which settle with gravity).
• Vitritis: white cells in the vitreous, may be bilateral and associated with features of intermediate or posterior uveitis.
• Asteroid hyalosis: small, yellow-white particles that move with the vitreous (rather than settling with gravity), usually innocuous.
• Amyloidosis: sheet-like opacities, usually bilateral; most commonly seen with familial systemic amyloidosis.
• Tumours (e.g. choroidal melanoma, lymphoma): vitritis of inflammatory and/or tumour cells may be seen.

sections.title: Flashes and Floaters Combined
content: • PVD: partial/complete Weiss ring overlying the optic disc ± visible posterior vitreous face.
• Retinal tear: usually u-shaped tear and pigment in the vitreous; may be associated with vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment.
• Retinal detachment: usually rhegmatogenous (associated with a tear), resulting in elevated retina with SrF.
• Tumours: visual phenomena include ‘slow-moving ball of light’ and floaters 2° to tumour cells/inflammation associated with a choroidal or retinal mass.

sections.title: He ADACH e: Swollen Optic Discs (Bilateral)
content: Raised ICP: worsening headache on lying flat, coughing/sneezing/ Valsalva, visual obscurations, diplopia, disc swelling with loss of SVp, blind spot enlargement, VIn palsy.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage: ‘thunderclap headache’, meningism, altered consciousness.
Accelerated hypertension: iBp, hypertensive retinopathy, including CWS, haemorrhages, and exudates.

sections.title: Causes of Raised ICP
content: Cerebral tumour
IIH (Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension)
Venous sinus thrombosis
Meningitis
Encephalitis
Brain abscess
Congenital ventricular abnormalities
Cerebral oedema

sections.title: Unilateral Serious Headache: GCA
content: GCA (Giant Cell Arteritis): usually age >55y.
Visual loss/transient obscurations, scalp tenderness (± necrosis), jaw/tongue claudication.
Limb girdle pain/ weakness, fevers, weight loss.
Non-pulsatile, tender, thickened temporal arteries.
AION results in unilateral or, less commonly, bilateral disc swelling.

sections.title: Serious Headaches: No Optic Disc Swelling
content: • Raised ICP: may occur in the presence of non-swollen discs (e.g. myopic discs, atrophic discs, anomalies of the optic nerve sheath).
• GCA: (Giant Cell Arteritis features as noted above).
• Pituitary mass: endocrine dysfunction (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, infertility, acromegaly, Cushing’s disease; optic atrophy; bitemporal field loss).
• Pituitary apoplexy: recent major hypotensive episode, e.g. surgery, postpartum haemorrhage; acute dVA, meningism, ± loss of consciousness (lOC).

rows: Common; dull, non-pulsatile, diffuse, band-like (or vice-like) pain; mild to moderate intensity.
Pain in the head, scalp or neck.
Common; headache (usually hemicranial). Scintillating visual aura (starts paracentral and expands peripherally).
Prodrome, nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, transient visual loss (unilateral or homonymous), occasionally ophthalmoplegia.
Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalgias: unilateral severe pain involving face and eye; lasts < 4 hours.
Autonomic features: conjunctival hyperemia, lacrimation, nasal stuffiness.

sections.title: Facial and Sinus Pain
content: • Trigeminal neuralgia: sudden stabbing pains in trigeminal branch distribution; precipitants include touch, cold, and eating.
• Ophthalmic shingles: hyperaesthesia in acute phase followed by neuralgic-type pain.
• Acute sinusitis: coryzal/urTI symptoms, tender over paranasal sinuses; proptosis, diplopia, or optic neuropathy warrant urgent exclusion of orbital involvement.

sections.title: Ocular Pain and Asthenopia
content: • Generalized Ocular Pain: includes ApAC, anterior uveitis, keratitis, scleritis, and ocular ischaemia.
• Retrobulbar Ocular Pain: includes optic neuritis, orbital pathology (e.g. infection, infiltration, neoplasm, TeD).
• Pain on eye movement: includes optic neuritis.
• Asthenopia (eye strain): usually worsens with reading/fatigue; ametropia (especially hypermetropia), astigmatism, anisometropia, decompensating phoria, convergence insufficiency, etc.

summary: An exhaustive diagnostic framework for Ophthalmic assessment, categorizing vision loss by onset (sudden vs. gradual), presence of pain, duration, and anatomical findings. This guide ensures high-fidelity clinical differentiation across all major ocular pathologies.

branches: Few seconds’ duration (Unilateral): GCA (age >55y, weight loss, fatigue, jaw/tongue claudication, pulseless/tender/thickened temporal artery, ieSr/Crp); Papilloedema (bilateral disc swelling, loss of SVp, peripapillary haemorrhages, features of raised ICp); Impending CRVO (dilated, tortuous retinal veins, haemorrhages); OIS (veins dilated and irregular but not tortuous, mid-peripheral haemorrhages; ± NVD, iIOp, carotid bruits).
Few seconds’ duration (Bilateral): Papilloedema: see described previously.
Few minutes’ duration (Unilateral): Amaurosis fugax (complete or partial monocular blindness ± evidence of emboli, AF, carotid bruits); GCA (see described previously).
Few minutes’ duration (Bilateral): Vertebrobasilar artery insufficiency (recurrent episodes ± ataxia, dysphasia, dysarthria, hemiparesis, hemisensory disturbance).

Up to 1h duration (Bilateral): Migraine: aura—fortification spectra, transient VF defects; followed by unilateral headache, associated nausea/vomiting, photophobia, phonopohobia, exercise aggravation, and often FH.

sections.title: Persistent Painless Loss: Cornea & Vitreous
content: Abnormal cornea - Hydrops: acute corneal oedema associated with underlying disease such as keratoconus.
Abnormal vitreous - Vitreous haemorrhage: varies from microscopic level to completely obscuring the fundus.

sections.title: Persistent Painless Loss: Abnormal Fundus (Vascular & Retinal)

rows: rApD, attenuated arterioles, pale fundus, cherry-red spot.
dilated tortuous veins, haemorrhages in all four quadrants ± macular oedema ± CWS, rApD; BrVO may give symptomatic altitudinal defects, particularly if on temporal arcade.
flashes/floaters, tobacco dust, convex elevated retina with (multiple) break(s).
convex elevated retina with shifting fluid, no break.
concave elevated retina with tractional membranes.
floaters, vitritis, snow balls/banking ± macular oedema.
floaters, significantly reduced vision; vitritis, retinal/ choroidal infiltrates, macular oedema, vascular sheathing/occlusion, haemorrhages.

sections.title: Persistent Painless Loss: Disc, Macula & Normal Fundus
content: Abnormal disc - AION: rApD, pale oedematous disc ± flame-shaped haemorrhages; may have altitudinal field defect; may be arteritic (with symptoms of GCA) or non-arteritic (usually sectoral disc swelling).
Abnormal macula - Choroidal neovascular membrane: distortion ± positive scotoma, drusen, subretinal membrane ± haemorrhage, exudate.
Abnormal macula - CSC: colour desaturation, micropsia, serous detachment of neurosensory retina.
Normal fundus - Cortical blindness: ± denial, small residual field; normal pupil reactions; abnormal CT/MrI head.

Normal fundus - Functional: inconsistent acuity between different tests and at different times, normal ophthalmic examination, normal eDTs, spiralling and/or crossing of isopters on kinetic perimetry.

sections.title: Sudden/Recent Loss of Vision: Painful
content: Abnormal cornea - APAC: usually hypermetropic, haloes, frontal headache, vomiting; injected, corneal oedema, fixed semi-dilated pupil, shallow AC with closed angle, raised IOp.
Abnormal cornea - Bullous keratopathy: thickened, hazy cornea, stromal/subepithelial oedema, bullae, evidence of underlying pathology, e.g. ACIOl, Fuchs’ endothelial dystrophy, etc.
Abnormal cornea - Keratitis: photophobia, watering, circumlimbal injection, corneal infiltrate ± epithelial defect ± AC activity.

Abnormal disc - Optic neuritis: usually age 18–45y, with retro-orbital pain, especially on eye movement, rApD, reduced colour vision, VF defects, swollen disc ± peripapillary flame-shaped haemorrhages; may also be painless.
Abnormal uvea - Anterior uveitis: anterior pain, photophobia, mildly reduced vision, circumlimbal injection, AC cells and flare, Kps.
Normal fundus - Retrobulbar neuritis: as for optic neuritis, but with a normal disc; may also be painless.

sections.title: Gradual Loss of Vision: Generalized
content: Abnormal cornea - Corneal dystrophies: corneal clouding (deposition/oedema); usually bilateral but may be asymmetric; common types include Fuchs’ endothelial dystrophy in the elderly and reis–Bucklers dystrophy in young adults.
Abnormal cornea - Keratoconus: refractive error from progressive astigmatism; corneal oedema from acute hydrops; usually bilateral but may be asymmetric.
Abnormal lens - Cataract: uni- or bilateral opacification of the lens; cloudy, misty; glare; commonest in the elderly.

sections.title: Gradual Loss of Vision: Central (Macula)
content: Note: Macular disease usually leads to distortion ± micropsia and early dVA; pupillary responses and colour vision are relatively preserved.
AMD: very common bilateral disease of the elderly; the commonest type is ‘dry’ changes which are associated with gradual, patchy central loss.
Macular dystrophies: group of diseases with specific patterns occurring in younger age group; bilateral disease; may have FH, and genetic testing is sometimes possible.
Diabetic maculopathy: ischaemia may lead to gradual dVA; oedema may lead to more acute distortion/dVA; associated with other diabetic changes.
CMO: oedema resulting in distortion/dVA; may be associated with surgery, inflammation, or vascular disease.

sections.title: Gradual Loss: Central (Optic Disc/Nerve)
content: Note: Optic nerve disease usually leads to dimness and darkening of colours; although commonly central, it may lead to peripheral or generalized loss of vision; pupillary responses, colour vision, and brightness testing are all reduced.
Compressive optic neuropathy: progressive dVA, disc pallor ± pain, involvement of other local structures.
LHON: severe sequential dVA over weeks/months, telangiectatic vessels around disc (acutely); usually young adult ♂; FH.
Toxic or nutritional optic neuropathies: slowly progressive, symmetrical dVA with central scotomata; relevant nutritional, therapeutic, or toxic history.
Inflammatory optic neuropathies: associated with systemic disease (e.g. sarcoid, vasculitis, and syphilis); often very steroid-sensitive.
Chronic papilloedema: sustained disc swelling due to raised ICp may cause permanent optic nerve dysfunction, including dVA and field defects, and optic disc pallor.

sections.title: Gradual Loss: Peripheral or Patchy
content: Abnormal choroid/retina - Posterior uveitis: floaters, patchy loss of vision ± central distortion/dVA from CMO; may include chorioretinitis, vitritis, and retinal vasculitis.
Abnormal choroid/retina - RP: bilateral concentric field loss, peripheral ‘bone spicule’ pigmentation, retinal arteriole attenuation, and optic disc pallor.
Abnormal optic disc - Glaucoma: asymptomatic peripheral field loss; usually bilateral, but often asymmetric; characteristic cupping and other disc changes; often associated with iIOp.

sections.title: Ocular Injection Routes & Applications
sections.content: In addition to their use in ocular anaesthesia (see E Ocular anaesthesia, pp. 1040–1 to pp. 1044–5), the sub-Tenon’s and peribulbar routes may be used to deliver drugs, such as corticosteroids, to the posterior aspect of the globe. Although primarily used for ocular anaesthesia (e.g. lidocaine, bupivacaine), these routes may be used for delivering corticosteroids (e.g. triamcinolone, methylprednisolone) in posterior segment inflammation, exudation, or macular oedema.

sections.title: Sub-Tenon’s Cannula Technique (Box 25.1)
content: 1. Apply Topical anaesthetic to conjunctiva (e.g. proxymetacaine 0.5%).
2. Wash hands, and don sterile gloves.
3. Instil 5% povidone iodine onto the ocular surface; drape (optional), and insert lid speculum (optional).
4. Ask patient to look in opposite direction to intended injection site (e.g. inferonasally).
5. Open conjunctiva around 8mm from the limbus (e.g. superotemporally).
6. Dissect down to bare sclera with blunt curved scissors.
7. Insert sub-Tenon’s cannula (19G, 25mm, blunt, curved), and slide posteriorly along the globe.
8. Inject medication.
9. Carefully withdraw cannula; forceps or a cotton-tipped applicator can be used to provide countertraction and to hold the conjunctival opening closed (which may help reduce regurgitation).

rows: Relatively safe (blunt needle, appropriately curved for globe shape).
Significant regurgitation along track may result in poor drug delivery.
Less regurgitation and improved drug delivery.
Relatively safe (blunt, flexible, moulds to globe). Less regurgitation than Sub-Tenon's cannula.
Can be difficult to direct the flexible cannula.

sections.title: Step-by-Step: IV Cannula Technique
content: Enter sub-Tenon’s space using the trocar of a 22G or 23G, 0.9/25mm PTFE IV cannula.
Advance cannula (trocar engaged, bevel-up) for about 3mm within space.
Slightly withdraw trocar (sharp end no longer exposed); advance cannula further 3mm.
Completely withdraw trocar.
Direct cannula posteriorly for further 12–15mm using gentle rotatory movements.
Attach syringe to cannula and inject medication.

sections.title: Peribulbar Injection Protocol
content: Definition: Sharp needle technique for extraconal space delivery.
Anesthesia preference: Medial compartment block via medial canthal injection (p. 930).
Safety Note: For corticosteroids, the safer sub-Tenon’s route is recommended.
Method: Inferolateral injection using 25G sharp-bevel needle.
Entry: Through lid or conjunctiva.
Direction: Inferolateral to globe, just above orbital floor.

sections.title: Corticosteroid Licensing Notes
sections.content: These are non-licensed uses of commercial IM/intra-articular preparations. Kenalog® is preserved with benzyl alcohol and is not licensed for intraocular use. Triesence® and Trivaris® are preservative-free and licensed for intravitreal use (UK via importers). *Depo-Medrone contains polyethylene glycol and myristyl-γ-picolinium chloride.

branches: Principles: Isotonic, neutral pH, no preservatives
Vascular/Exudative: Anti-VEGF or Corticosteroids for AMD, CMO, etc.
Setting: Theatre or dedicated clean room (enclosed, free from interruptions, good illumination, washable floor, non-particulate ceiling)

sections.title: Intravitreal Procedure: Preparation
content: Confirm consent and correct eye.
Measure IOP.
Ensure adequate dilation.
Instil topical anaesthesia.
Set up trolley; ensure all treatments (including post-injection antibiotics) are available.
Hands washed and sterile gloves worn (Full gowning not necessary).

sections.title: Intravitreal Technique (RCOphth Guidelines)
content: 1. Wash hands, don sterile gloves.
2. 5% Povidone iodine to ocular surface (allow 3min).
3. Clean periocular area with 5–10% povidone iodine.
4. Drape and insert lid speculum.
5. Consider supplemental anaesthesia (subconjunctival/sub-Tenon’s lidocaine 1%).
6. Prepare syringe immediately; expel air; maintain asepsis.
7. Identify site: Inferotemporal quadrant (Avoid horizontal meridians).
8. Site Distance: 3.0–3.5mm (aphakic/pseudophakic) or 3.5–4mm (phakic) from limbus.
9. Insert needle (27–30G; 1/2–5/8in) perpendicularly toward globe centre.
10. Inject therapeutic agent (Max 0.1mL).
11. Remove needle; use sterile cotton-tip for counterpressure/reflux prevention.

sections.title: Critical Post-Injection Care
content: Test gross VA and check central retinal artery patency.
URGENT: If non-perfusion occurs (often no perception of light), perform AC paracentesis immediately.
Check injection site at slit-lamp and IOP (not mandatory).
Topical antibiotics (e.g. chloramphenicol 0.5% 4x/d for ≥3d) are at clinician discretion.
RCOphth & SPC (Ranibizumab/Aflibercept) Note: Routine post-injection antibiotics are not recommended due to lack of evidence.

sections.title: Corticosteroid Footnotes (NICE & Licensing)
sections.content:
* Dexamethasone (Ozurdex®): NICE-approved for macular oedema post-RVO (TA229), DMO (TA349), and non-infectious posterior uveitis in adults (ID763).
† Fluocinolone (Iluvien®): NICE-approved for DMO insufficiently responsive to other therapies in pseudophakic patients (TA301).
‡ Triamcinolone: Kenalog® contains benzyl alcohol (not licensed for intraocular use). Triesence® and Trivaris® are alcohol-free and licensed for intravitreal use.

title: Disc Edema: Clinical Diagnostics & Management
summary: Disc edema is the clinical swelling of the optic nerve head, signaling potential vision-threatening or life-threatening conditions. Precise identification and differentiation between unilateral and bilateral presentations are critical for urgent care.

data.title: Disc Edema: Clinical Diagnostics & Management
data.summary: Disc edema is the clinical swelling of the optic nerve head, signaling potential vision-threatening or life-threatening conditions. Precise identification and differentiation between unilateral and bilateral presentations are critical for urgent care.

sections.title: Core Ophthalmoscopic Signs
content: Blurred or indistinct disc margins
Elevation of the optic nerve head
Hyperemia of the disc tissue
Obscuration of peripapillary retinal vessels
Absence of Spontaneous Venous Pulsation (SVP)
Paton’s Lines (circumferential retinal folds)
Splinter (Drance) or flame-shaped hemorrhages

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: New-onset, severe, or 'thunderclap' headache
Nausea and projectile vomiting
Pulsatile tinnitus (whooshing sound in ears)
Sudden, painless vision loss
Diplopia (suggestive of 6th Nerve Palsy)
Transient Visual Obscurations (TVOs) triggered by posture

branches: Unilateral: NAION, Optic Neuritis, CRVO, Orbital Mass
Bilateral: Papilledema (↑ ICP), Malignant HTN, Diabetic Papillopathy
Pseudo-edema: Optic Disc Drusen, Tilted Discs, High Hyperopia

sections.title: Diagnostic Workflow
content: Step 1: Perform comprehensive Dilated Fundus Exam
Step 2: Immediate Blood Pressure Measurement (Rule out HTN Crisis)
Step 3: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) to quantify RNFL thickness
Step 4: Neuroimaging (MRI Brain/Orbits with Gadolinium + MRV)
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture (LP) to assess Opening Pressure (if imaging clear)

content.explanation: V: Vascular (AION, CRVO); I: Inflammation (Neuritis); T: Tumor (Orbital/Brain); A: Autoimmune (Sarcoid); M: Metabolic (Diabetic); I: Infection (Syphilis, Cat-scratch); N: Nutrition/Toxic (B12 deficiency, Methanol).

sections.title: Strategic Pathophysiology Note
sections.content: Disc edema occurs when axoplasmic flow is interrupted within the optic nerve. This stasis leads to cellular swelling and secondary extracellular fluid accumulation. Whether caused by mechanical compression (mass), vascular insufficiency (ischemia), or increased subarachnoid pressure (papilledema), the end result is a visible expansion of the optic disc that requires immediate localization of the blockage point to prevent permanent axonal loss.

title: The Science of IOL Power Calculation
summary: Achieving the 'Refractive Bullseye' in cataract surgery requires high-precision biometry and the application of sophisticated mathematical formulas. This guide explores the variables, equations, and clinical considerations essential for selecting the perfect intraocular lens.

Keratometry (K): Corneal curvature and refractive power
Anterior Chamber Depth (ACD): Distance from cornea to lens

sections.title: Red Flags: Risk of Refractive Surprise
content: Post-Refractive Surgery (LASIK/PRK/RK) - standard formulas will fail.
Extreme Axial Lengths: High Myopia (>26.0 mm) or High Hyperopia (<22.0 mm).
History of Silicone Oil tamponade (requires AL correction).
Dense Brunescent Cataracts interfering with optical biometry.
Keratoconus or irregular corneal astigmatism.

sections.title: Formula Selection Guide
content: Short Eyes (<22mm): Hoffer Q is traditionally favored.
Medium Eyes (22-26mm): Barrett Universal II or SRK/T.
Long Eyes (>26mm): Barrett Universal II or Wang-Koch adjusted SRK/T.
Universal Choice: Barrett Universal II performs well across all ranges.

sections.title: The Calculation Workflow
content: 1. Perform Optical Biometry (Gold Standard).
2. Review K-values for regularity and astigmatism.
3. Select IOL Model (Monofocal, Toric, or Multifocal).
4. Choose formula based on AL and anterior segment data.
5. Optimize A-Constant based on surgeon personal outcomes.

sections.title: Verbatim Clinical Context
sections.content: IOL power calculation is a critical step in cataract surgery that determines the postoperative refractive state. The accuracy of the calculation depends heavily on the precision of biometry (axial length and corneal power) and the mathematical formula used to predict the Effective Lens Position (ELP). Modern biometers use partial coherence interferometry or optical low-coherence reflectometry to provide measurements with micron-level precision, significantly reducing the errors associated with older ultrasound-based immersion or applanation techniques.

sections.title: Mechanism of Action
content: Step 1: Light emission in the blue-green spectrum.
Step 2: Absorption by ocular chromophores (Melanin and Hemoglobin).
Step 3: Conversion of radiant energy into thermal energy.
Step 4: Protein denaturation and tissue coagulation.

sections.title: Contraindications & Red Flags
content: Opaque Media (e.g., dense cataract or vitreous hemorrhage) preventing beam focus.
Tractional Retinal Detachment involving the macula.
Severe Foveal Ischemia (caution with focal treatment).
Patient inability to maintain fixation during delivery.

sections.title: Treatment Parameters (Example: ALT)
content: Spot Size: 50 microns
Exposure Duration: 0.1 seconds
Power: Adjusted to achieve 'champagne bubble' reaction
Location: Junction of pigmented and non-pigmented trabecular meshwork

sections.title: Laser Definitions
sections.content: The term LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. The Argon laser specifically uses ionized argon gas as its active medium, requiring high-voltage electricity to achieve population inversion and generate its characteristic coherent beam.

sections.title: Defining Bilateral Disc Swelling
sections.content: Bilateral disc swelling refers to the objective elevation and blurring of the optic nerve head margins in both eyes. This clinical finding is a medical priority. It may represent true papilledema (swelling specifically due to increased intracranial pressure) or pseudopapilledema (mimics of swelling). Because of the potential for vision loss and the association with life-threatening conditions like intracranial tumors or malignant hypertension, a systematic and rapid evaluation is mandatory.

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: New-onset, severe, or 'worst ever' headache
Nausea and projectile vomiting (often worse in the morning)
Pulsatile tinnitus (whooshing sound in ears)
Transient Visual Obscurations (TVOs) - brief graying out of vision
Diplopia (usually horizontal, suggesting a Sixth Nerve Palsy)
Blood pressure readings exceeding 180/120 mmHg

sections.title: Clinical Signs of True Swelling
content: Blurring of the peripapillary nerve fiber layer
Obscuration of major retinal vessels as they leave the disc
Paton’s lines (circumferential retinal folds)
Flame-shaped hemorrhages at or near the disc margin
Cotton wool spots (indicative of axonal ischemia)
Absence of Spontaneous Venous Pulsation (SVP)
Hyperemic appearance of the optic nerve head

sections.title: Urgent Diagnostic Process
content: Step 1: Immediate Blood Pressure Measurement - Exclude Malignant Hypertension.
Step 2: Comprehensive Eye Exam - Confirm bilateral involvement and assess for pseudopapilledema vs. true swelling.
Step 3: Multi-modal Imaging - Utilize Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) and B-scan ultrasonography.
Step 4: Neuroimaging - Urgent MRI of the brain with contrast and MRV (Magnetic Resonance Venography) to check for masses or venous sinus thrombosis.
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture - If imaging is negative, perform LP to determine opening pressure and analyze CSF composition.

content.explanation: P: Pressure (check ICP/BP); A: Axonal stasis; P: Pulsation loss (SVP); I: Imaging (MRI/MRV); L: Lumbar puncture.

branches: DALK: Keratoconus, Corneal Scars, Corneal Dystrophies (Anterior)
DSAEK: Fuchs' Dystrophy, Bullous Keratopathy, ICE Syndrome
DMEK: Fuchs' Dystrophy, Failed DSAEK, Posterior Polymorphous Dystrophy

sections.title: Key Advantages of Each Technique
content: DALK: Eliminates endothelial rejection risk and maintains the integrity of the host's inner cornea.
DSAEK: Technically easier graft handling than DMEK; automated microtome creates predictable graft thickness.
DMEK: Superior visual acuity (often 20/20 or 20/25); minimal stromal interface interference.
Both Endothelial (DMEK/DSAEK): Small incision surgery, no suture-related astigmatism, rapid recovery compared to PKP.

sections.title: The Surgical Process: Lamellar Steps
content: 1. Donor Preparation (Pre-cut or Manual)
2. Recipient Bed Preparation (Stripping or Bubble)
3. Graft Insertion (Glide or Injector)
4. Graft Centration & Positioning
5. Air/Gas Tamponade for Attachment

content.explanation: A for Air bubble positioning (supine post-op); B for Bubbling (re-bubbling for detachments); C for Check intraocular pressure (pupillary block risk).

sections.title: Critical Red Flags & Complications
content: Graft Detachment (High risk in DMEK, requires re-bubbling)
Pupillary Block Glaucoma (from air/gas bubble migration)
Interface Haze or Scarring (Specific to DALK and DSAEK)
Inadvertent Descemet's Membrane Perforation (During DALK dissection)
Primary Graft Failure (Non-clearing cornea within 4 weeks)

sections.title: Note on Technical Execution
sections.content: Lamellar surgery represents a paradigm shift from full-thickness Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP). DALK focuses on stromal replacement while sparing the healthy endothelium. In contrast, DSAEK and DMEK focus solely on the posterior layers, replacing the diseased endothelium while preserving the anterior structure of the host cornea. Choice of procedure depends on the patient's specific layer of disease and the surgeon's expertise with ultrathin tissues.

data.title: Uveal Emergencies: VKH Disease & Sympathetic Ophthalmia
data.summary: An exhaustive clinical guide to Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease and Sympathetic Ophthalmia—two profound multisystem inflammatory conditions characterized by bilateral granulomatous panuveitis and autoimmune-mediated melanocyte targeting.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='60' cy='50' r='30' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='140' cy='50' r='30' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M50 50 Q60 40 70 50 Q60 60 50 50' fill='hsl(0, 80%, 60%)' opacity='0.6'/><path d='M130 50 Q140 40 150 50 Q140 60 130 50' fill='hsl(0, 80%, 60%)' opacity='0.6'/><circle cx='60' cy='50' r='5' fill='black'/><circle cx='140' cy='50' r='5' fill='black'/><path d='M90 20 L110 20 M100 10 L100 30' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='2'/></svg>

branches: Multisystem inflammatory disease: Affects eyes (bilateral granulomatous panuveitis), ears, brain, skin, and hair.
Mechanism: T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease directed against melanocyte antigen(s).
Risk Factors: Higher prevalence in darker-skinned races (Asians, Native Americans, Hispanics, Middle and Far East).
Demographics: Commonest in women in their 3rd and 4th decades; can occur in either sex at any age.
Genetic Association: HLA-DR4, notably HLA-DRB1*0405 (recognizes various melanocyte proteins).
Triggers: May arise after cutaneous injury, presumably via liberation of melanocyte antigens.

sections.title: Clinical Features: Systemic & Prodrome
content: Prodrome: Fever, meningism, and auditory symptoms for a few days before blurring/profound visual loss.
Neurological: Sterile meningitis (headache, neck stiffness), encephalitis (convulsions, altered consciousness), cranial neuropathies (including ocular motility disturbance).
Auditory: Tinnitus, deafness, vertigo.
Cutaneous (Late features): Vitiligo, alopecia, poliosis.

sections.title: Clinical Features: Ophthalmic & Complications
content: Anterior Uveitis: Bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis, PS (Posterior Synechiae), iris nodules, AC (Anterior Chamber) shallowing.

Posterior Uveitis: Multifocal choroiditis, multifocal detachments of sensory retina, ERD (Exudative Retinal Detachment), choroidal depigmentation ('sunset glow fundus'), Dalen–Fuchs’ nodules (peripheral yellow-white choroidal granulomas), subretinal fibrosis.
Complications: Cataract, glaucoma, CNV (Choroidal Neovascular) membrane.

sections.title: VKH Investigations
content: OCT: Used to monitor extent and height of serous detachments.
FFA: Focal areas of delay in choroidal perfusion, multifocal areas of pinpoint leakage, large placoid areas of hyperfluorescence, pooling within subretinal fluid (SRF), and optic nerve staining.
US: Low to medium reflective diffuse choroidal thickening.
LP (Not always required): Lymphocytic pleocytosis.

sections.title: Management of VKH
content: Step 1: Liaise with physician.
Step 2: Start high-dose systemic corticosteroids (e.g. 1–2mg/kg/d prednisolone PO or IVMP 1g/d for 3d).
Step 3: For resistant or recurrent disease, add corticosteroid-sparing agents (immunosuppressants).
Immunosuppressants include: Methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and ciclosporin.

sections.title: Table 11.15: Revised Diagnostic Criteria for VKH (AUS Criteria)

rows: No history of penetrating ocular trauma or surgery preceding initial onset of uveitis.
No clinical or laboratory evidence suggestive of other ocular disease entities.
(1) Diffuse choroiditis (focal SRF or bullous serous retinal detachments). (2) If equivocal: Characteristic FFA findings AND diffuse choroidal thickening (no posterior scleritis on US).

(1) History of early features AND (2) Two or more of: Ocular depigmentation (sunset glow fundus or Sugiura sign), Nummular chorioretinal depigmented scars, RPE clumping/migration, Recurrent or chronic anterior uveitis.
(a) Meningismus (malaise, fever, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, neck/back stiffness), (b) Tinnitus, (c) CSF pleocytosis.
Findings not preceding ocular/CNS disease: (a) Alopecia, (b) Poliosis, (c) Vitiligo.

branches: Definition: Rare bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with remarkable parallels to VKH.
Causality: Related to antecedent trauma or surgery.
Timing: Can occur within a few days or over 60y later; usually arises between 1 and 12mo after injury.
Pathogenesis: T-cell-mediated response to ocular antigen liberated during initial insult.
BOSU Study findings: Commonest cause was ocular (vitreoretinal) surgery.

sections.title: Verbatim Statistics & Risk
sections.content: It occurs in 0.1% of cases of penetrating ocular trauma and in 0.01% of cases of routine vitrectomy. In one prospective study (BOSU), the commonest cause of sympathetic ophthalmia was ocular (particularly vitreoretinal) surgery.

sections.title: SO Clinical Features
content: Anterior: Bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis with mutton fat KPs, PS.
Posterior: Vitritis, choroidal infiltration, Dalen–Fuchs nodules, macular oedema, ERD; the exciting eye may be phthsical.
Complications: Cataract, 2° glaucoma, end-stage disease (optic atrophy, chorioretinal scarring).
Systemic: As for VKH, but systemic involvement less common.

sections.title: SO Prevention: The Window of Opportunity
content: 7-10 Days: Short window after trauma where enucleation almost certainly prevents sympathetic ophthalmia.
Patient Selection: Best option for blind, painful eyes with no hope of useful vision.
Modern Trend: Preserve the eye where possible for many traumatized eyes with visual potential.

sections.title: SO Treatment & Prognosis
content: Enucleation role: Controversial once inflammation develops; may modify disease if performed within 2wk of symptoms.
Immunosuppression: Start high-dose systemic corticosteroids (1–2mg/kg/d prednisolone PO or IVMP 1g/d for 3d).
Corticosteroid-sparing agents: Consider Methotrexate, azathioprine, ciclosporin, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus for resistant/recurrent disease or side effects.
Outcome: With aggressive treatment, around 60% may achieve >6/15 in the sympathizing eye.

sections.title: EYELID TRAUMA: PERIOCULAR HAEMATOMA
content: Definition: A ‘black eye’ consists of a haematoma (focal collection of blood) and/or periocular ecchymosis (diffuse bruising) and oedema (Fig. 22.1A).
Most common blunt injury to the eyelid or forehead; generally innocuous.
Critical Exclusion 1: Trauma to the globe or orbit. Examine before oedema sets in. Use gentle sustained pressure to open lids; never apply force to the globe.
Critical Exclusion 2: Orbital roof fracture. Suspect if associated with subconjunctival haemorrhage without a visible posterior limit (Fig. 22.1B).
Critical Exclusion 3: Basal skull fracture. Characterized by bilateral ring haematomas (‘panda eyes’ – Fig. 22.1C).
Imaging: Consider CT, MRI, or bedside ultrasonography (with meticulous care) if clinical visualization is impossible.

sections.title: LID LACERATIONS: MANAGEMENT & REPAIR
sections.content: The presence of a lid laceration, however insignificant, mandates careful exploration of the wound and examination of the globe and adnexal structures. Any lid defect should be repaired by direct closure whenever possible, even under tension, since this affords the best functional and cosmetic result (Fig. 22.2A and B). Superficial lacerations parallel to the lid margin without gaping can be sutured with 6-0 black silk or nylon; sutures removed after 5–6 days. Infection is always a risk, even from a small laceration (Fig. 22.2C). Lacerations with mild tissue loss just sufficient to prevent direct primary closure can usually be managed by performing a lateral cantholysis. Extensive tissue loss may require major reconstructive procedures similar to malignant tumour resection.

sections.title: STEP-BY-STEP: LID MARGIN SUTURING
content: Step 1: Vertical Mattress Suture. Insert a 5-0 silk suture in line with meibomian gland orifices, 2 mm from edges and 2 mm deep; leave untied.
Step 2: Tarsal Plate Alignment. Bring edges together with partial-thickness lamellar 5-0 absorbable (e.g., polyglactin) sutures tied anteriorly.
Step 3: Tie Margin Suture. Tie the 5-0 silk so cut edges slightly pucker; leave ends long (~2 cm).
Step 4: Skin Closure. Use interrupted 6-0 or 7-0 nylon or absorbable sutures.
Step 5: Knot Security. Secure the silk suture ends to direct them and knots away from the cornea.

sections.title: CANALICULAR & AUXILIARY MANAGEMENT
content: Canalicular Lacerations: Repair within 24 hours (Fig. 22.3A).
Bridging: Use silicone tubing (Crawford tube) tied in the nose or a monocanalicular stent (Mini Monoka – Fig. 22.3B).
Fixation: Suture footplate to lid with 8-0 material; leave tubing in situ for 3–6 months.
Tetanus Status: Satisfactory status is mandatory. No prior immunization: 250 units human tetanus immunoglobulin (IM). Previously immunized (>10 years): subcutaneous tetanus toxoid booster.
Foreign Bodies: CT scan required for any suspicion in soft tissues or orbit (Fig. 22.4A-D).

sections.title: CRITICAL TRAUMA WARNINGS
content: Bilateral ‘panda’ eyes = Possible skull-base fracture.
Orbital cellulitis risk exists for any penetrating lid laceration, especially with retained foreign bodies.
NEVER apply force on the globe until integrity is confirmed.
Low IOP with a full hyphaema = Suspect occult posterior scleral rupture.
NO MRI if a ferrous metallic foreign body is suspected.
Avoid nose blowing in orbital floor/medial wall fractures.

branches: Mechanism: Sudden pressure increase from object >5cm (fist/tennis ball)
Signs: Ecchymosis, oedema, subcutaneous emphysema, infraorbital nerve anaesthesia
Diplopia: From haemorrhage/oedema (tightening septa) or mechanical entrapment (Inf. Rectus/Oblique)
Enophthalmos: Manifests after days; 20% have >2mm at 6 months
Diagnosis: Visual acuity, CT (coronal sections), Hess Chart, Forced Duction Test
Treatment: Observation, antibiotics, ice, nasal decongestants, steroids for nerve compromise
Surgery: Required within 2 weeks for persistent diplopia, >50% floor involvement, or enophthalmos >2mm

content.explanation: Typically seen in patients <18 years due to bone elasticity. Minimal external signs but acute tissue incarceration. Symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, headache, persistent oculocardiac reflex. Requires URGENT repair to avoid permanent damage.

rows: Common in children (sharp object/minor blow). Adults (major trauma). Signs: Upper lid haematoma, CSF leak risk (meningitis), globe pulsation.
Usually associated with floor fractures. Signs: Subcutaneous emphysema (on nose blowing), defective abduction/adduction (medial rectus entrapment).
Rare. Solid bone; usually associated with extensive facial damage.

sections.title: ORBITAL (RETROBULBAR) HAEMORRHAGE
content: Risk: Acute orbital compartment syndrome and irreversible blindness.
Signs: Proptosis, haemorrhagic chemosis, high IOP, APD, optic disc swelling.
Canthotomy: 1-2 cm horizontal full-thickness incision at lateral canthus angle under local anaesthesia.
Cantholysis: Retract lower lid, cut inferior crus of lateral canthal tendon directed inferiorly/parallel to rim.
Extension: If necessary, cut superior limb of tendon (caution: adnexal damage risk).

rows: Full-thickness wound where globe gives way at weakest point.
Single full-thickness wound; no exit wound.

sections.title: IMAGING MODALITIES IN GLOBE TRAUMA
content: Plain Radiographs: Detect foreign bodies; metallic ones move during upgaze/downgaze.
Ultrasonography: Useful for IOFBs, globe rupture, retinal detachment. Use gentle technique.
CT Scan: Superior for detecting and localizing IOFBs (Fig. 22.11B-D) and evaluating bony structures.
MRI: Superior for injuries of the globe (e.g., occult posterior rupture) but contraindicated for ferrous IOFBs.
Electrodiagnostics: Assess optic nerve and retinal integrity, especially with retained IOFB.

branches: Cornea: Abrasion (fluorescein stain), Acute oedema, Descemet tears (vertical/birth trauma)
Hyphaema: Blood in AC settling inferiorly. High IOP risk leads to ischaemic optic neuropathy/blood staining
Iris: Vossius ring (pigment on lens), Traumatic mydriasis, radial tears, Iridodialysis (D-shaped)
Lens: Rosette cataract, Subluxation (iridodonesis), Dislocation (into vitreous or AC)
IOP: Angle recession (6-9% late glaucoma risk), Hypotony (suspect occult injury)
Globe Rupture: Usually anterior at Schlemm canal; prolapse of iris/lens/vitreous

sections.title: BLUNT TRAUMA: POSTERIOR COMPLICATIONS
content: Vitreous Haemorrhage: Often associated with PVD and 'tobacco dust' (pigment cells).
Commotio Retinae: Concussion-induced cloudy swelling (grey appearance). Temporal fundus typical. 'Cherry-red spot' if macula involved. Resolves in ~6 weeks.
Chorioretinitis Sclopetaria: High-velocity projectile splits chorioretinal layers exposing intact sclera. 15% achieve 6/6 vision.
Choroidal Rupture: Involves Bruch membrane/RPE. Fresh rupture obscured by blood; old rupture appears as white crescentic streak. Late CNVM risk.
Retinal Dialysis: Break at ora serrata from traction. Most common superonasal/inferotemporal. Can lead to slow-progressing RD.
Macular Hole: Occurs at time of injury or after commotio resolution.
Choroidal Detachment: Occurs in soft eyes; must distinguish from RD.

sections.title: TRAUMATIC OPTIC NEUROPATHY (TON)
sections.content: Occurs in up to 5% of facial fractures. Classification: Direct (bone fragments/projectile) or Indirect (force transmission, shearing, vasospasm). Presentation: Sudden visual loss (50% light perception only), APD, initially normal fundus with pallor developing over weeks. Management: Individualized imaging (CT for bone, MRI for soft tissue). Treatment: Spontaneous improvement in ~50% of indirect cases. Steroids (IV methylprednisolone) within 8 hours remain controversial (CRASH study notes death risk in brain injury). Decompression considered for visual decline despite steroids or bony compression. Optic Nerve Avulsion: Striking cavity where nerve head retracted; no treatment.

sections.title: ABUSIVE HEAD TRAUMA (SHAKEN BABY)
content: Demographics: Children < 2 years. Mortality > 25%; responsible for 50% of child abuse deaths.
Mechanism: Rotational acceleration/deceleration. Hypoxia, raised ICP, and ischaemia.
Systemic Signs: Irritability, lethargy, vomiting, skull/rib/long bone fractures, subdural haemorrhage.
Ocular Features: Retinal haemorrhages (80% bilateral) involving multiple layers from posterior pole to periphery. APD, poor visual response.
Visual Outcome: Visual loss in 20% (largely from cerebral damage).

sections.title: PENETRATING TRAUMA PROTOCOLS
sections.content: Penetrating injuries are 3x more common in males (50% aged 15–34). High risk of endophthalmitis/panophthalmitis. Prophylactic intravitreal antibiotics (vancomycin) recommended. Ascertain tetanus status. Most need URGENT surgical repair under general anaesthesia. TECHNIQUE: Small corneal wounds may heal with bandage contact lens. Medium wounds: 10-0 nylon (shorter stitches near visual axis). Iris involvement: Reposition if possible; excise if necrotic/contaminated. Lens damage: Suturing followed by phacoemulsification/vitrectomy. Scleral: Anterior wounds have better prognosis than posterior. Use 8-0 nylon or 7-0 polyglactin. Reposit viable uveal tissue; cut prolapsed vitreous flush.

sections.title: TRAUMATIC RETINAL DETACHMENT (RD)
content: Trauma accounts for ~10% of all RD cases; most common cause in children.
Mechanism: Vitreous incarceration in penetrating wounds leads to fibroblastic proliferation.
Progression: Contraction of epiretinal fibrosis causes anterior tractional RD.
Delayed Risk: Retinal breaks may develop weeks later, leading to rapid rhegmatogenous RD.
Prognosis Factors: Initial VA, APD, IOFB presence, infection, and extent of retinal injury.

title: GATT vs Goniotomy vs Ab Externo Trabeculotomy
summary: An exhaustive comparative analysis of surgical trabeculotomy techniques. This poster distinguishes between the minimally invasive GATT approach, the focal goniotomy, and the traditional ab externo trabeculotomy procedure.

data.title: GATT vs Goniotomy vs Ab Externo Trabeculotomy

sections.title: GATT: Gonioscopy-Assisted Transluminal Trabeculotomy
content: Ab interno approach utilizing a gonioscopic lens for visualization.
Cannulation of Schlemm's canal is performed via a clear corneal incision.
Uses a 5-0 or 6-0 prolene suture or a specialized microcatheter (e.g., iTrack).
Achieves a circumferential (360-degree) opening of the trabecular meshwork.
Considered a 'MIGS' (Minimally Invasive Glaucoma Surgery) procedure.

sections.title: Goniotomy: The Focal Approach
content: Traditional ab interno procedure often used in pediatric glaucoma.
Direct incision into the trabecular meshwork to reach Schlemm's canal.
Limited by the direct line-of-sight across the anterior chamber.
Does not involve cannulating the canal circumferentially.
Requires a clear cornea for adequate visualization of the angle.

sections.title: Ab Externo Trabeculotomy: The Classic Route
content: Traditional 'outside-in' approach to the trabecular meshwork.
Requires conjunctival peritomy and the creation of a partial-thickness scleral flap.
Schlemm's canal is located and unroofed from the external surface.
A metal trabeculotome is inserted into the canal and rotated into the anterior chamber.
Typically used when corneal clarity is insufficient for ab interno visualization.

sections.title: Surgical Process: Ab Interno (GATT/Goniotomy)
content: Step 1: Corneal incision and viscoelastic injection.
Step 2: Head tilt and microscope adjustment for gonioscopic view.
Step 3: Incision through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal.
Step 4: (GATT) Cannulation 360 degrees using a suture or catheter.
Step 5: Pulling the tool through to rupture the meshwork into the chamber.

sections.title: Critical Warnings & Contraindications
content: Poor visualization of the angle precludes ab interno approaches (GATT/Goniotomy).
Active neovascular glaucoma is a contraindication for these procedures.
Post-operative hyphema is a common risk across all trabeculotomy types.
Previous failed glaucoma surgeries may distort the anatomy of Schlemm's canal.

content.explanation: GATT = 360° Internal, Goniotomy = Focal Internal, Ab Externo = External Scleral Flap.
