sections.title: Definition & Visual Presentation
sections.content: Definition: A white pupillary reflex (see Figure 8.1.1). Figure 8.1.1 Leukocoria.

sections.title: Primary Etiology: Retinoblastoma
content: A malignant tumor of the retina.
Presentation: White, nodular mass.
Endophytic: Breaks through internal limiting membrane into vitreous.
Exophytic: Subretinal mass lesion often underlying a serous retinal detachment.
Diffuse infiltrating: Diffusely spreading lesion simulating uveitis.
Associated Findings: Iris neovascularization (common with large tumors), Aqueous and vitreous seeding.
Eye Characteristics: Cataract is uncommon; eye is normal in size.
Distribution: May be bilateral, unilateral, or multifocal.
Epidemiology: Diagnosis usually made in patients under years of age (mean age: 18 months).
Genetics: Family history elicited in about 10% of cases.

sections.title: Infectious Etiology: Toxocariasis
content: Nematode infection.
Appearance: Localized, white, elevated granuloma in retina OR diffuse endophthalmitis.
Complications: Localized inflammation, vitreous traction bands, macular dragging, traction retinal detachment, and cataract.
Demographics: Rarely bilateral; usually diagnosed between 6 months and 10 years (may present in adults).
Clinical Clues: History of contact with puppies or eating dirt.
Transmission: Can be acquired prenatally/congenital infection.
Diagnostics: Paracentesis may reveal eosinophils; serum ELISA for Toxocara is positive.

rows: Retinal vascular abnormality (micro/macroaneurysms) usually inferotemporal periphery.
Failure of regression of fetal hyaloid complex; fibrovascular stalk from optic nerve to lens.
Xanthocoria; yellow-colored lipid-rich subretinal fluid/exudate; bullous retinal detachment.
Membrane behind lens placing inward traction on elongated ciliary processes.
Usually associated with a small eye; usually unilateral.
Usually boys in first decade; severe cases in early childhood.
Cataract noted at birth or early in life; no family history/risk factors.
Shallowing of anterior chamber, secondary glaucoma, traction retinal detachment.

sections.title: Other Significant Etiologies
content: Pediatric cataract: Opacity present at birth or first months; unilateral/bilateral; family history or systemic disorder common.
Retinal astrocytoma: Sessile to slightly elevated yellow-white mass; may be calcified; associated with tuberous sclerosis complex or neurofibromatosis; giant drusen on optic nerve.
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP): Predominantly premature children; leukocoria usually from retinal detachment.

sections.title: Comprehensive Differential List
sections.content: Others: Retinal detachment, retinochoroidal coloboma, high myopia or anisometropia, familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR), myelinated nerve fibers, uveitis, toxoplasmosis, trauma, cytomegalovirus retinitis, endophthalmitis, retinal dysplasia, incontinentia pigmenti, Norrie disease, and medulloepithelioma.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: History & Exam
content: Step 1: History - Check Age at onset, Family history, Prematurity, contact with puppies, or eating dirt.
Step 2: Ocular Exam - Measure corneal diameters (small eye?), Iris check (neovascularization), Lens inspection (cataract).
Step 3: Essential Screens - Dilated fundus examination and anterior vitreous examination.
Step 4: Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA) - Needed for young/uncooperative children, especially if retinoblastoma is suspected.
Step 5: Early Screening - If heritable retinoblastoma is a concern, perform office exam within 1 to 2 weeks of birth.

rows: Used when no view of fundus; looks for calcification (tumor), persistent stalk (optic disc to lens), or RD.
Useful for evaluating Coats disease, ROP, and retinoblastoma.
For bilateral/familial retinoblastoma or advanced Coats. MRI preferred for RB to reduce radiation.
Positive at 1:8 in the vast majority of infected patients.
By pediatrician; specifically for retinal astrocytic hamartoma, RB, or systemic cataracts.

sections.title: CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATION
content: NOTE: Anterior chamber paracentesis in a patient with a retinoblastoma should be avoided as it could lead to tumor cell dissemination.

branches: Retinoblastoma: Chemoreduction, Intra-arterial/Intravitreal/Intracameral chemotherapy, Cryotherapy, Thermotherapy, Laser, Plaque radiotherapy, Enucleation (advanced/refractory), Systemic chemo (metastatic).
Toxocariasis: Topical/Periocular/Systemic Steroids, Vitrectomy (traction/non-improvement), Laser photocoagulation of nematode, Albendazole (only for systemic disease).

sections.title: Treatment: Vascular & Developmental
content: Coats Disease: FA-guided laser to leaking vessels/aneurysms; consider Intravitreal anti-VEGF; External drainage for severe RD; Enucleation for neovascular glaucoma.
PFV: Cataract removal, Retrolental stalk resection, Posterior vitrectomy. Amblyopia treatment (Outcome often poor due to foveal/optic nerve hypoplasia, anisometropia, and deprivation).
Retinal Astrocytoma: Observation.
Pediatric Cataract & ROP: See specific sections (8.12 and 8.2).

content.explanation: Timing depends on diagnosis. If heritable disorders are suspected, refer to Ophthalmic Genetics and screen family members. For RB, frequency depends on tumor type, severity, and germline mutations. External irradiation for RB is rarely used due to secondary tumor risk.

sections.title: Disease Hallmarks & Critical Warnings
content: Cicatrizing conjunctivitis: rare, usually bilateral, sight-threatening group of disorders.
Hallmarks: loss of goblet cells, ocular surface failure (from chronic limbitis, limbal epithelial stem cell (lesC) failure | blinding keratopathy), and progressive conjunctival scarring.
Onset may be insidious, delaying diagnosis.
CRITICAL: Get expert help early—it is very easy to underestimate these conditions.

branches: Chronic inflammatory subepithelial blistering disease of mucous membranes
Age: >60y usually; may occur in adolescents (more severe disease)
Markers: Linear deposition of Ig and complement at BM zone of mucosal surfaces
Targets: Antibodies specific to components of BM and hemidesmosomes (triggers unclear)
Associations: Rheumatoid arthritis (rA) and pernicious anaemia
Locations: Oral mucosa and conjunctiva (most common); skin and other membranes; Trachea/Oesophagus (life-threatening)

sections.title: MMP: Diagnosis & Clinical Features
content: International Consensus Diagnosis: Requires direct immunopathological confirmation + typical clinical features.
OcMMP Specific Diagnosis: Primarily clinical; immunopathology provides supporting evidence only.
Symptom: Irritation.
Conjunctival Signs: Acute/chronic papillary conjunctivitis, subconjunctival bulla ± ulceration.
Progressive Cicatrization: Loss of plica semilunaris and fornices, symblepharon/ankyloblepharon formation.
Lid/Surface Signs: Trichiasis, cicatricial entropion, dry eye, 2° microbial keratitis, corneal neovascularization, ulcerative keratitis, perforation, lesC failure, keratinization.

sections.title: MMP Treatment Strategy
content: 1. Early Diagnosis & Specialist Referral: Refer early for help to improve outcome.
2. Adnexa Management: Ensure lids/lashes don't cause inflammation; use early conjunctiva-sparing surgery.
3. Maximize Tear Film: Punctal occlusion, tear substitutes; treat MgD and blepharitis.
4. Exclude Infection: Must rule out infection before attributing inflammation to disease; risk factors include poor surface and lid trauma.
5. Define Residual Inflammation: Any inflammation remaining after 2° causes are treated is disease-related.

rows: Use with caution; may mask disease.
'Step-down strategy'; continuous dosing/taper or IV pulses.

sections.title: MMP Management Notes & Complications
content: Immunosuppression generally required for >1y.
NB: Clinically quiescent eyes may have occult inflammation resulting in progression.
Monitoring: Photography and measurements (e.g., fornix depth measurer).
Surgery: Entropion/trichiasis repair, oral mucosal grafting for fornix reconstruction.
Corneal Issues: Persistent epithelial defects, lesC failure, perforations.
Mechanical: Botulinum toxin (limited use due to restriction but can be effective).
End-stage: May require osteo-odonto-keratoprosthesis.

branches: Acute, severe dermatosis: epidermal loss + multisite mucositis + systemic disturbance
Incidence: 1–2 cases per million per year
Initiators: Drugs (sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, allopurinol) or Infection (Mycoplasma, HSV)
Pathophysiology: MHC Class I drug presentation -> CD8+ CTL expansion -> Granulysin mediator
Molecules: TNF-α, interferon (IFN), inducible nitric oxide synthase
Prognosis: Systemic disease severity predictors do NOT predict acute or chronic ocular disease

sections.title: SCORTEN Parameters
content: Age >40y
Presence of malignancy
Heart rate >120 bpm
Epidermal detachment >10% BSA at admission
Serum urea >10mmol
Serum glucose >14mmol
Bicarbonate <20mmol

sections.title: SJS/TEN Ocular Classification
content: Mild: Eyelid oedema, mild conjunctival injection, chemosis.
Moderate: Membranous conjunctivitis ± corneal epithelial defects (>30% healing with med therapy) ± corneal ulceration ± corneal infiltrates.
Severe: Symblepharon formation ± non-healing corneal epithelial defects ± visual loss ± conjunctival fornix foreshortening (as for OcMMP).

sections.title: SJS/TEN Acute Ocular Treatment
content: Multidisciplinary care; regional burns unit preferred.
Lubricant: Non-preserved hyaluronate/carmellose every 2h.
Hygiene: Daily by ophthalmologist/trained nurse.
Corticosteroids: Non-preserved dexamethasone 0.1% 2×/d.
Antibiotics: Broad-spectrum (e.g., moxifloxacin 4×/d) if staining/ulceration present.
Exposure Prevention: Essential in unconscious patients.
Surgery: Adhesion division; symblepharon rings (controversial); gas-permeable scleral Cl; conformers.
Amniotic Membrane Grafting (AMG): To protect surfaces/lids (John’s procedure); ProKera®; Omnilenz™; amnion-wrapped conformer ± subtarsal triamcinolone 20mg.

sections.title: SJS/TEN Systemic & Chronic Phases
sections.content: Systemic Immunosuppression: Controversy surrounds systemic steroids (role in ocular disease vs negative systemic effect). Usually given for acute scleritis. Possible role for IVIG and IV ciclosporin. Chronic Phase: Sequelae include persistent inflammation, scleritis, ocular surface failure, and cicatrizing changes with OcMMP phenotype. Management follows OcMMP or scleritis protocols. Progression can occur years after acute illness.

rows: Thermal, radiation, chemical (alkali), surgical (e.g., glaucoma surgery).
Anterior (Staphylococcal): limited cicatrization/keratinization of lid margin.
Most common with C. trachomatis; also membranous/pseudomembranous conjunctivitis.
Ectodermal dysplasia (hair/teeth abnormalities); Epidermolysis bullosa (hemidesmosome disease).
Unilateral: sebaceous cell carcinoma, conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia, or SCC; lymphoma.

sections.title: Drug-Induced Cicatrization
content: Clinically indistinguishable from OcMMP.
Systemic: Practolol (discontinued), penicillamine.
Topical: Propine (discontinued), pilocarpine, timolol, idoxuridine, gentamicin (especially 1.5%), guanethidine.

branches: Occurs in allogeneic bone marrow transplant (donor leucocytes attack recipient)
Acute Response: TEN-like response; pseudomembranous conjunctivitis
Chronic Response: Scleroderma-like skin changes; Sjögren’s-like gland changes
Posterior Segment (Rare): Posterior scleritis, choroidal thickening during acute stage

rows: Pseudomembranous conjunctivitis with corneal epithelial sloughing

title: Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV): The Resident's Masterclass
summary: Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV) involves the proliferation of abnormal blood vessels from the choriocapillaris through Bruch's membrane. This masterclass covers the pathophysiology, multimodal imaging, and the evolving landscape of anti-VEGF therapies.

data.title: Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV): The Resident's Masterclass
data.summary: Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV) involves the proliferation of abnormal blood vessels from the choriocapillaris through Bruch's membrane. This masterclass covers the pathophysiology, multimodal imaging, and the evolving landscape of anti-VEGF therapies.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: CNV is the growth of new, fragile blood vessels from the choriocapillaris through defects in Bruch’s membrane into the sub-RPE or sub-retinal space. Pathogenesis is driven by an imbalance between pro-angiogenic factors (VEGF, bFGF) and anti-angiogenic factors (PEDF, Angiostatin). Chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and hypoxia (HIF-1α) are key triggers in conditions like AMD.

branches: Type 1: Sub-RPE (Occult on FFA, most common in AMD)
Type 2: Sub-retinal (Classic on FFA, above RPE)
Type 3: RAP (Retinal Angiomatous Proliferation - originates from retina)
Type 4: Mixed (Components of both Type 1 and 2)
Polypoidal Choroidal Vasculopathy (PCV): Variant with aneurysmal dilations

content.explanation: Causes of CNV: C: Choroidal Rupture, H: Histoplasmosis (POHS), A: Angioid Streaks, M: Myopia (Pathologic), P: Post-inflammatory/PIC, S: Senile (AMD).

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Metamorphopsia (Amsler Grid distortion)
Sudden or gradual central scotoma
Micropsia (due to photoreceptor spreading)
Decreased contrast sensitivity
Subretinal fluid or hemorrhage on fundoscopy
Sub-RPE 'Gray-Green' membrane appearance

rows: Polyps on ICG; Notch on OCT

sections.title: OCT Biomarkers of Activity
content: Intraretinal Fluid (IRF) - Cystoid spaces
Subretinal Fluid (SRF) - Hyporeflective space below retina
Sub-RPE Fluid - Pigment Epithelial Detachment (PED)
SHRM - Subretinal Hyper-reflective Material
Foveal Tubulations - Sign of chronic degeneration

sections.title: Management Protocols
content: 1. Loading Phase: 3 monthly injections
2. Assessment: OCT/VA stability
3. Treat-and-Extend (T&E): Extend interval by 1-2 weeks if dry
4. Pro Re Nata (PRN): Inject only when fluid recurs
5. Fixed Interval: Injection every 4-8 weeks regardless of fluid

sections.title: Red Flags & Emergency Signs
content: Massive Submacular Hemorrhage
RPE Rip (Tear) - sudden vision drop during treatment
Signs of Endophthalmitis (Pain, Hypopyon)
Retinal Vasculitis (esp. with Brolucizumab)
Acute Intraocular Pressure Spike post-injection

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Trials
content: MARINA/ANCHOR: Established Ranibizumab superiority over PDT/Sham.
CATT: Bevacizumab is non-inferior to Ranibizumab.
VIEW 1/2: Aflibercept q8w equal to Ranibizumab q4w.
TENAYA/LUCERNE: Faricimab durability up to 16 weeks.
FLUID Study: Tolerate some SRF vs zero-tolerance (T&E).

sections.title: Surgical & Alternative Options
content: Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) - Vertoporfin for PCV or refractory CNV
Submacular Hemorrhage Displacement - tPA + Gas (C3F8/SF6)
Macular Translocation (Historical)
Susvimo (Port Delivery System) - Continuous Ranibizumab release

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for a 'double-layer sign' on OCT, which may indicate Type 1 CNV or PCV.
Type 2 CNV is more common in inflammatory conditions like PIC or myopia.
Myopic CNV requires fewer injections (often 1-3) compared to AMD.
Persistent Sub-Retinal Fluid (SRF) may sometimes be tolerated if the macula is stable, but IRF must always be treated.
The presence of 'SHRM' is a high-risk factor for poor visual outcome and fibrosis.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Disciform Scar formation (End-stage)
Geographic Atrophy (can develop during Anti-VEGF therapy)
Epiretinal Membrane (ERM) formation
RPE Tear (Highest risk in large PEDs)
Vitreous Hemorrhage

sections.title: Diagnostic Workflow
content: 1. BCVA and Amsler Grid
2. Dilated Fundus Exam
3. Structural OCT (look for IRF/SRF/PED)
4. OCT-Angiography (Non-invasive vessel visualization)
5. FFA/ICG (If diagnosis is uncertain or suspect PCV)

summary: A comprehensive guide to the evaluation and surgical management of blepharoptosis and entropion, emphasizing clinical examination techniques, ocular protective mechanisms, and levator-based surgical interventions.

data.summary: A comprehensive guide to the evaluation and surgical management of blepharoptosis and entropion, emphasizing clinical examination techniques, ocular protective mechanisms, and levator-based surgical interventions.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Blepharoptosis (Ptosis) is the abnormally low position of the upper eyelid margin in primary gaze. Entropion is the inward turning of the eyelid margin towards the globe, potentially causing trichiasis and corneal scarring.

sections.title: The Comprehensive Ptosis Exam (Right Eye Focus)

rows: Distance from pupillary light reflex to upper lid margin
Distance from pupillary light reflex to lower lid margin
Vertical distance between upper and lower lid margins
Excursion of lid from extreme downgaze to upgaze (negating frontalis)
Distance from lid margin to the skin crease

sections.title: Red Flags in Ptosis
content: New-onset Ptosis + Pupil Involvement (R/O Aneurysm/CN III)
Ptosis + Miosis + Anhydrosis (Horner Syndrome - R/O Carotid Dissection/Pancoast)
Variability/Fatigability (R/O Myasthenia Gravis)
Proptosis + Ptosis (R/O Orbital mass)
Poor Bell's Phenomenon (High risk for exposure keratopathy post-op)

sections.title: Entropion: Clinical Evaluation
content: Snap-back Test: Pull lid down; slow return without blink indicates laxity.
Distraction Test: Pull lid away from globe; >10mm indicates horizontal laxity.
White Line Sign: Visualization of disinserted lower lid retractors through conjunctiva.
Orbicularis Overriding: Eyelid margin rotates inward upon forceful lid closure.
Cicatricial Check: Eversion of lid to look for tarsal scarring or symblepharon.

sections.title: Management of Involutional Entropion
content: 1. Horizontal Lid Shortening (Lateral Tarsal Strip)
2. Retractor Reattachment (Jones/Jones-Wies procedure)
3. Everting Sutures (Quickert sutures for temporary/spastic)
4. Transverse Tarsotomy (Wies procedure for cicatricial components)

sections.title: Surgery: Levator Resection (For Good LF)
content: 1. Skin Incision: Mark the desired lid crease and incise through skin and orbicularis.
2. Orbital Septum Entry: Open the septum to expose pre-aponeurotic fat pads.
3. Levator Identification: Identify the white, glistening levator aponeurosis beneath fat.
4. Dissection: Free levator from underlying Muller's muscle and conjunctiva (optional) or tarsus.
5. Resection: Measure the amount of levator to be excised based on ptosis severity.
6. Suture Attachment: Fixate the shortened levator to the upper third of the tarsal plate.
7. Intraoperative Adjustment: Check lid height and contour with patient sitting upright (if local).
8. Skin Closure: Incorporate levator fibers into skin sutures to reform the lid crease.

content.explanation: High Effort Results In Negative Gains for the 'normal' lid. Lifting the more ptotic lid may cause the contralateral lid to drop due to decreased equal innervation (Law of Equal Innervation).

rows: Massage, suture release, or spacer graft

sections.title: Clinical Pearls: Ptosis & Entropion
content: Always perform a Phenylephrine test to assess Muller muscle contribution.
Check for Lagophthalmos pre-operatively to avoid post-op corneal disasters.
Congenital ptosis often shows lid lag in downgaze; involutional ptosis does not.
In entropion, check for symblepharon to rule out Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid (OCP) before surgery.
The 'Lid Distraction' test is the gold standard for measuring horizontal laxity.

sections.title: Common Surgical Dosages & Tools
content: Local: Lidocaine 2% with Epinephrine 1:100,000 (minimizes bleeding).
Sutures: 5-0 or 6-0 Vicryl for levator-tarsal fixation; 6-0 Prolene or Silk for skin.
Instruments: Desmarres lid retractor, Westcott scissors, Bishop-Harmon forceps.
Hemostasis: Bipolar cautery is essential to avoid thermal damage to the levator.

title: Mastering Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD) & Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD) is the second most common type of retinal detachment. It occurs when neurosensory retina is pulled away from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) by contracting vitreoretinal membranes. Unlike Rhegmatogenous RD, TRD is typically associated with a concave surface and lacks a causative retinal break in its pure form.

sections.title: Etiology: Causes of TRD in Both Eyes
Pathophysiology: The Ischemic Cascade
content: Step 1: Capillary non-perfusion leads to chronic retinal ischemia.
Step 2: Upregulation of Pro-angiogenic factors (VEGF, bFGF).
Step 3: Neovascularization (NVD/NVE) grows along the posterior hyaloid face.
Step 4: Fibroglial proliferation accompanies the vessels, forming contractile membranes.
Step 5: Vitreous contraction exerts tangential and anteroposterior traction on the retina.
Step 6: Progressive elevation of the retina (TRD) ± Vitreous Hemorrhage from fragile vessels.

sections.title: Symptomatology & Features
content: Painless, progressive visual field loss.
Sudden vision drop if Vitreous Hemorrhage occurs.
Photopsia (flashing lights) is less common than in RRD.
Metamorphopsia if the macula is distorted by tractional bands.
History of poorly controlled Diabetes Mellitus or prior laser treatment.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Imaging & Exams
content: B-Scan Ultrasonography: Essential if media is opaque (VH). Shows 'tenting' or 'table-top' configuration.
Wide-field Fundus Photography (Optos): To document PRP status and NVE locations.
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Assess for Macular Edema or subclinical macular detachment.
Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Identify areas of active leakage (NVD/NVE) and ischemia.
Gonioscopy: To rule out Neovascularization of the Angle (NVA).

sections.title: Management: The Affected Eye (TRD + VH)
content: Step 1: Pre-operative Anti-VEGF (e.g., Bevacizumab) 3-7 days prior to surgery to reduce intraoperative bleeding.
Step 2: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) - 23, 25, or 27 Gauge.
Step 3: Core Vitrectomy and induction of Posterior Vitreous Detachment (if not present).
Step 4: Membrane Peeling: Segmentation (cutting bridges) and Delamination (stripping membranes from retinal surface).
Step 5: Control of Hemorrhage using endodiathermy or increasing infusion pressure.
Step 6: Completion of Panretinal Photocoagulation (Endolaser) to all ischemic peripheral retina.
Step 7: Internal Tamponade (Air, Gas, or Silicone Oil) if iatrogenic breaks or significant traction remain.

sections.title: Management: The Fellow Eye (Post-PRP)
content: Monitor for 'PRP Creep' or regression of NVE.
Supplementary PRP (Fill-in laser) if new NVE or NVD appears.
Anti-VEGF injections if Center-Involving Diabetic Macular Edema (CI-DME) is present.
Strict Glycemic and Blood Pressure control (HbA1c target <7.0%).
Regular follow-up every 3-4 months depending on stability.

sections.title: Red Flags: Surgical Emergencies
content: Macula-threatening TRD (Rapidly progressing towards the fovea).
Combined Tractional-Rhegmatogenous RD (TRRD) - requires urgent repair.
Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) with elevated IOP.
Dense Vitreous Hemorrhage obscuring retinal view for >1 month.
Sudden 'Crunch Syndrome' (rapid TRD progression) after Anti-VEGF injection.

content.explanation: V: Vitreous Hemorrhage; I: Ischemia; T: Tractional RD; R: Rubeosis Iridis; E: Edema (Macular); O: Oil/Gas Tamponade; U: Upregulated VEGF; S: Segmentation/Delamination.

rows: PRP reduces the risk of severe vision loss by >50% in high-risk PDR.
Defined 'High-Risk PDR' and timing for laser intervention.
Ranibizumab is non-inferior to PRP for proliferative disease over 2 years.
Vitrectomy vs. Anti-VEGF for VH: Similar visual outcomes at 2 years; surgery faster for recovery.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Resident Tips
content: Always check for NVI before dilating a patient with dense VH.
In TRD, the 'peak' of the tent is usually the site of strongest vitreoretinal adhesion.
Avoid giving Anti-VEGF too early (e.g., >10 days before surgery) in eyes with severe traction to prevent 'The Crunch'.
B-scan 'V' shape: If the apex is at the disc, suspect TRD; if the apex is at the optic nerve head but mobile, suspect PVD.
Endolaser should be applied 360 degrees to the periphery, not just the area of detachment.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Graft Rejection is an immunological response of the host against the donor corneal tissue, most commonly a Type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. It is potentially reversible if treated promptly. Graft Failure is a permanent loss of graft clarity due to endothelial pump dysfunction, which can be 'Primary' (failure to clear from day 1) or 'Late' (gradual exhaustion of endothelial cells over years). Failure is generally irreversible without repeat keratoplasty.

branches: Afferent Loop: Host APCs (Langerhans) recognize donor HLA
Sensitization: T-cells in regional lymph nodes
Efferent Loop: Cytotoxic T-cells travel to graft
Destruction: Endothelial cell lysis via perforins/granzymes

rows: Poor donor quality / Cold chain issues

sections.title: Classification of Rejection Types
content: Epithelial Rejection: Elevated epithelial line (fluorescein stains edge). Often asymptomatic or mild irritation.
Subepithelial Rejection: 'Krachmer Spots' (resemble EKC nummular infiltrates). Indicates stromal involvement.
Stromal Rejection: Peripheral localized haze/edema with deep vascularization.
Endothelial Rejection: The most severe. Characterized by Khodadoust line, KPs, and diffuse corneal edema.

sections.title: The Endothelial Hallmarks
content: Khodadoust Line: A linear 'front' of Keratic Precipitates (KPs) moving across the endothelium.
Ciliary Flush: Perilimbal injection.
Anterior Chamber Reaction: Cells and flare (Tyndall effect).
Graft Edema: Sudden onset localized or diffuse thickening (pachymetry > 650μm).

rows: Elevated IOP, hazy cornea but no KPs
Localized injection, mucus at suture site
Hypopyon, vitritis, severe pain, decreased vision

sections.title: Emergency Warning Signs (RSVP)
content: REDNESS: Sudden increase in circumcorneal injection.
SWELLING: Visible cloudiness or 'steamy' appearance of the cornea.
VISION LOSS: Sudden drop in acuity or increased glare/halos.
PAIN: New onset ache, grittiness, or photophobia.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Slit Lamp: Assess KPs, Khodadoust line, and AC reaction.
2. Pachymetry: Measure corneal thickness (compare to baseline).
3. IOP Check: Rule out steroid-induced or inflammatory glaucoma.
4. Specular Microscopy: Assess endothelial cell count and morphology.
5. Anterior Segment OCT: Quantify edema and visualize Descemet's attachment.

sections.title: Acute Rejection Protocol
content: 1. Topical: Prednisolone Acetate 1% or Dexamethasone 0.1% every hour (day and night).
2. Subconjunctival: Dexamethasone 2-4mg injection for severe cases.
3. Systemic: Oral Prednisolone (1mg/kg/day) or IV Methylprednisolone pulse for multi-vessel vascularized high-risk grafts.
4. Taper: Very slow taper over months; never stop abruptly.
5. Long-term: Consider Cyclosporine A or Tacrolimus drops.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: DMEK/DSAEK Rejection: Often presents as isolated 'spots' or sudden localized edema without a classic Khodadoust line.
The 'Window of Opportunity': Treatment started within 24-48 hours has a significantly higher salvage rate.
Steroid Responders: Always monitor IOP; high IOP can mimic graft failure (pseudofailure).
Epithelial rejection is a warning shot; it doesn't cause failure but signals an immune system 'awakening'.

content.explanation: P for Pain, E for Epithelial rejection line, D for Diffuse/Deep Stromal Edema, A for AC Reaction/Cells, L for Line of Khodadoust.

sections.title: Landmark Evidence: CCTS & HEDS
content: Collaborative Corneal Transplantation Study (CCTS): HLA matching does not significantly improve outcomes in high-risk grafts, but ABO compatibility might.
HEDS (Herpetic Eye Disease Study): Prophylactic Acyclovir (400mg BID) significantly reduces the risk of recurrent HSK-induced graft failure.
Corneal Donor Study (CDS): Donor age (up to 75) does not affect 10-year success rates for most routine cases.

sections.title: Surgical Nuances for Success
content: Suture Management: Remove loose or vascularized sutures immediately as they act as a 'highway' for vessels/APC influx.
Graft Size: Stay between 7.0mm and 8.0mm if possible to avoid the limbal 'immune ring'.
DALK vs. PKP: Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) eliminates endothelial rejection risk entirely.

title: DACRYOPS: Unveiling the Lacrimal Gland Cyst

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Dacryops (from Greek 'dakryon' - tear, 'ops' - eye) refers to a true cyst of the lacrimal gland duct. It results from obstruction of one or more lacrimal gland ducts, leading to cystic dilation. It is lined by lacrimal ductal epithelium, distinguishing it from other pseudocysts or inflammatory lesions. Dacryops can occur in either the palpebral or orbital lobe of the lacrimal gland, with palpebral lobe dacryops being more common and typically visible through the conjunctiva.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology
content: **Rarity:** Relatively uncommon, precise incidence/prevalence unknown due to benign nature and frequent asymptomatic presentation.
**Age:** Can occur at any age, but most commonly diagnosed in young to middle-aged adults (20-50 years). Congenital cases are rare but reported.
**Sex:** No significant sex predilection has been consistently reported.

**Associations:** May be rarely associated with chronic inflammation (e.g., dacryoadenitis), trauma, cicatricial changes affecting the lacrimal ducts, or systemic conditions like Sjögren's syndrome or sarcoidosis.

branches: **Ductal Obstruction:** Primary mechanism, leading to retained lacrimal gland secretions and subsequent cystic dilation of the duct lumen.
**Inflammation:** Chronic dacryoadenitis or other inflammatory processes causing stenosis and occlusion of lacrimal gland excretory ducts.
**Trauma/Scarring:** Direct injury to the conjunctiva or previous surgical procedures leading to cicatricial closure of duct orifices.
**Congenital Anomalies:** Rare cases due to aberrant development or malformation of lacrimal gland ducts.
**Idiopathic:** A significant number of cases have no clear identifiable cause, suggesting spontaneous ductal occlusion.
**Secondary Obstruction:** Rarely, extrinsic compression from adjacent lesions or systemic conditions affecting duct patency.

rows: Palpebral lobe of the lacrimal gland (accessible via superior fornix)
Visible through the everted superior fornix as a translucent, bluish-gray or yellowish mass, often causing mild discomfort or epiphora.
Typically visible on slit-lamp examination with upper eyelid eversion.
Orbital lobe of the lacrimal gland (deeper, within the bony orbit)
Less common. May present with painless proptosis, globe displacement (inferonasal), or a palpable mass in the superotemporal orbit, but not directly visible.
Requires advanced imaging (CT/MRI) for definitive diagnosis.
Either lobe, present at birth or early childhood
Manifests as a visible mass or proptosis in infancy/childhood. May be associated with other craniofacial anomalies.
Variable, depending on location and size. Imaging is crucial.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Painless Swelling/Mass:** The hallmark symptom, often slow-growing and noticed incidentally in the superotemporal orbit or upper eyelid.
**Palpable Mass:** Soft, rubbery, fluctuant, non-tender, and typically mobile, felt in the superotemporal quadrant.
**Epiphora (Watery Eyes):** Due to mass effect on lacrimal drainage system or irritation from the cyst itself.
**Foreign Body Sensation/Discomfort:** Especially with larger palpebral lobe cysts that rub against the globe.
**Proptosis:** Rare, occurring with larger orbital lobe dacryops, leading to downward and nasal globe displacement.
**Diplopia:** Extremely uncommon, usually only if a very large orbital cyst interferes with extraocular muscle function.
**Vision Changes:** Generally absent unless severe proptosis induces secondary astigmatism or optic nerve compression (very rare).

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Eyelid Eversion (Superior Fornix):** Essential for palpebral lobe dacryops, revealing a smooth, translucent, bluish-gray or yellowish cyst.
**Palpation:** Confirm a soft, fluctuant, non-tender, and sometimes compressible mass in the superotemporal orbit.
**Globe Position:** Normal, or mild inferior/nasal displacement with orbital lobe dacryops.
**Conjunctiva:** Overlying conjunctiva is typically normal, non-inflamed, unless secondary irritation or infection is present.
**Visual Acuity & Refraction:** Usually normal; astigmatism may be induced by large cysts causing globe distortion.
**Ocular Motility & Pupils:** Typically normal; restricted motility or relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) are rare and suggest significant orbital compression by other lesions.
**Fundoscopy:** Normal. Papilledema or optic atrophy are extremely rare and indicate severe, chronic orbital involvement, prompting re-evaluation for malignancy.

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Thorough Clinical Examination & History** - Detailed review of onset, duration, associated symptoms. Comprehensive ophthalmic exam including careful lid eversion and orbital palpation.
**Step 2: Imaging Studies** - Crucial to confirm cystic nature, delineate extent, and differentiate from other orbital masses. Generally non-invasive and highly informative.

**Step 2a: Orbital Ultrasound (USG)** - Useful for initial assessment. Shows an anechoic, well-defined, thin-walled cystic lesion with good sound transmission within the lacrimal gland. Can differentiate cystic from solid components.

**Step 2b: Computed Tomography (CT) Orbit** - Preferred for bony detail and defining extent. Demonstrates a well-circumscribed, homogenously hypodense (water-density, 0-15 Hounsfield Units), non-enhancing cystic mass within the lacrimal fossa/gland. May show chronic bone remodeling in long-standing cases.

**Step 2c: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Orbit** - Provides superior soft tissue contrast. Characteristically shows a T1-hypointense, T2-hyperintense, well-demarcated lesion. No enhancement post-gadolinium administration, confirming its simple cystic nature and differentiating from inflammatory or neoplastic lesions.

**Step 3: Biopsy (Rarely Indicated)** - Typically not required for clear dacryops diagnosed by imaging and clinical exam. Reserved for atypical presentations (e.g., rapid growth, pain, ill-defined margins), suspicion of malignancy (e.g., adenoid cystic carcinoma), or inflammatory conditions (e.g., dacryoadenitis or lymphoproliferative disorder).

rows: Painless, slow-growing, firm, rubbery, usually non-tender. May cause bone remodeling but typically no erosion.
Well-defined, lobulated, often heterogeneous signal. May show calcifications on CT. Variable enhancement on MRI.
Rapid, painful progression. Often associated with bone erosion, nerve involvement (pain, numbness), vision loss, and aggressive proptosis.
Irregular, infiltrative margins. Bone destruction/erosion on CT. Heterogeneous signal with strong, irregular enhancement on MRI.
Congenital, often firm, non-tender, fixed mass near orbital rim. May cause inflammation if ruptured.
Well-defined, bone remodeling. Heterogeneous density on CT (fat, keratin, fluid). MRI signal varies with contents, typically T1 hyperintense (fat).
Acute onset, pain, redness, proptosis, often with restricted motility. Responds to systemic corticosteroids.
Diffuse lacrimal gland enlargement (dacryoadenitis). Inflammation of surrounding orbital tissues (fat, muscles). Strong, diffuse enhancement on imaging.
Typically arises from an obstructed paranasal sinus (e.g., frontal, ethmoid). More medial orbital location.
Originates within a sinus, causing bone erosion/expansion. Thin-walled, homogenous fluid density/signal within the sinus and orbit.
Painless, slowly progressive proptosis or palpable mass. Can be bilateral. May have systemic B symptoms.
Homogeneous, well-defined mass conforming to orbital structures. Mild to moderate enhancement. Characteristic restricted diffusion on DWI MRI.
Acute onset of pain, redness, swelling, fever, vision loss, restricted motility. Often with systemic signs of infection.
Diffuse orbital inflammation. Abscess appears as a rim-enhancing collection on CT/MRI.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Grading
sections.content: Dacryops, being a benign cystic lesion, does not have a formal staging or grading system analogous to malignant tumors (e.g., TNM staging). Its clinical characterization is primarily based on anatomical location (palpebral vs. orbital lobe), size, and etiology (e.g., simple vs. congenital). Monitoring for growth is typically done by serial clinical examination and imaging in cases managed conservatively.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment
content: **Step 1: Observation & Monitoring** - Recommended for small, asymptomatic palpebral lobe dacryops. Regular clinical monitoring (e.g., every 6-12 months) for any change in size, symptoms, or cosmetic concerns.

**Step 2: Surgical Intervention** - Indicated for symptomatic cysts (discomfort, epiphora, vision changes), cosmetic deformity, significant proptosis (orbital lobe dacryops), or suspicion of malignancy (though rare for dacryops).

**Step 2a: Marsupialization (for Palpebral Lobe Dacryops)** - The preferred surgical approach for accessible cysts. Involves incising the anterior cyst wall and suturing the edges to the conjunctiva, creating a permanent opening for drainage into the superior fornix. This prevents recurrence by maintaining an open communication.

**Step 2b: Excision (for Orbital Lobe Dacryops or Recurrent Palpebral Cysts)** - Complete surgical removal of the cyst. Often requires an orbitotomy approach (e.g., lateral orbitotomy, transcranial) for orbital lobe cysts. Careful dissection is critical to minimize damage to surrounding lacrimal gland parenchyma and orbital structures, preserving tear production.

**Step 3: Aspiration (Generally Discouraged)** - Simple needle aspiration of the cyst fluid can provide temporary relief but is associated with a very high recurrence rate due to re-accumulation of secretions. It is not considered a definitive treatment and should generally be avoided unless for diagnostic fluid analysis in atypical cases.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques
content: **Marsupialization (Palpebral Lobe Dacryops):**
1. **Anesthesia:** Topical anesthetic (e.g., proparacaine 0.5%) followed by subconjunctival infiltration of 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine.
2. **Exposure:** Evert the upper eyelid to fully expose the cyst in the superior fornix.

3. **Incision:** Using a fine blade (e.g., Bard-Parker No. 15 or radiosurgical unit), make an elliptical incision along the anterior wall of the cyst, carefully excising a portion of the anterior wall.
4. **Drainage:** Evacuate the clear, mucinous, or yellowish fluid contents.

5. **Suturing:** Suture the remaining cyst edges to the surrounding conjunctiva with fine absorbable sutures (e.g., 6-0 or 7-0 Vicryl) in an interrupted fashion, creating a permanent epithelialized opening for drainage.
**Excision (Orbital Lobe Dacryops):**
1. **Anesthesia:** General anesthesia is typically required.
2. **Approach:** A lateral orbitotomy is commonly used for masses in the superotemporal orbit. Other approaches like superior orbitotomy via eyelid crease incision may be considered.
3. **Dissection:** Carefully dissect through orbital tissues to expose the lacrimal gland. Identify the dacryops, which appears as a well-encapsulated cystic structure.
4. **Removal:** Meticulously dissect the entire cyst from surrounding orbital structures and lacrimal gland parenchyma, aiming for complete removal while preserving normal lacrimal tissue.
5. **Closure:** Close the orbital and eyelid tissues in layers.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Recurrence:** The most common complication, especially after simple aspiration or incomplete marsupialization. Proper marsupialization or complete excision significantly reduces this risk.
**Infection:** Rare, but can occur post-operatively or if the cyst ruptures spontaneously, leading to acute dacryoadenitis or orbital cellulitis.
**Dry Eye Syndrome:** A potential complication after extensive surgical excision of normal lacrimal gland tissue, particularly with orbital lobe dacryops. Less common with marsupialization.
**Scarring:** Minimal conjunctival scarring may occur after marsupialization, generally without functional impairment.

**Prognosis:** Excellent. Dacryops is a benign condition with a very favorable prognosis following appropriate surgical management. Symptom resolution is the norm with low rates of long-term complications.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Rapid Increase in Size:** Suggests an aggressive inflammatory process, hemorrhage into the cyst, or underlying malignancy.
**New Onset or Worsening Pain/Tenderness:** While dacryops is typically painless, pain can indicate acute inflammation (dacryoadenitis), infection, or a malignant transformation (very rare).

**New Onset Diplopia (Double Vision) or Vision Changes:** Suggests optic nerve compression, extraocular muscle involvement, or significant mass effect, warranting urgent investigation for more aggressive lesions.
**Rapidly Progressive Proptosis:** A concerning sign that mandates immediate workup to rule out malignancy (e.g., adenoid cystic carcinoma) or severe orbital inflammation.
**Signs of Acute Inflammation:** Conjunctival injection, erythema, warmth, or discharge around the cyst could indicate infection.
**Evidence of Bone Erosion on Imaging:** Highly suspicious for malignancy and requires urgent biopsy to exclude aggressive lacrimal gland carcinoma.

content.explanation: **M**arsupialization (for accessible palpebral cysts), **E**xcision (for orbital or recurrent cysts), **S**ymptomatic care (for discomfort/epiphora), **S**urveillance (for small, asymptomatic cysts).

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always remember to thoroughly evert the upper eyelid to visualize the superior fornix; many palpebral lobe dacryops are missed on routine exam.
Dacryops is a true epithelium-lined cyst, distinguishing it from inflammatory pseudocysts or lymphangiectasias.
Orbital imaging (CT or MRI) is mandatory for any suspected orbital lobe dacryops or any atypical presentation to accurately define its extent and rule out malignancy.
Marsupialization is the definitive and preferred surgical treatment for accessible palpebral lobe dacryops due to its simplicity and low recurrence rate.
Simple aspiration offers only temporary relief and has a very high recurrence rate; it is not a curative treatment.
Painless, slow growth is characteristic. Any rapid change in size, new pain, or vision alteration should prompt urgent and thorough re-evaluation for more aggressive pathology.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: While the core understanding and surgical management of dacryops have remained consistent for decades due to its benign nature, recent advances primarily focus on imaging. High-resolution orbital imaging techniques (e.g., 3T MRI with advanced sequences like Diffusion-Weighted Imaging) have improved pre-operative diagnostic certainty, allowing for better differentiation from other orbital cystic or solid lesions. Additionally, refinements in minimally invasive endoscopic surgical approaches, though not yet standard for dacryops, are continually being explored in orbital surgery. There have been no specific landmark studies that have significantly altered the fundamental diagnostic or therapeutic protocols for dacryops, reflecting its well-established clinical profile.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Congenital Dacryops:** Though rare, dacryops can present at birth or in early childhood, often detected due to a visible mass or subtle proptosis. These cases warrant a thorough workup to exclude other congenital orbital anomalies.

**Management in Children:** Principles of management are similar to adults, but considerations for general anesthesia are paramount. Marsupialization is generally favored for accessible palpebral cysts due to its less invasive nature.

**Differential Diagnosis in Children:** It is critical to differentiate dacryops from other pediatric orbital lesions such as dermoid cysts, orbital cellulitis, rhabdomyosarcoma (a highly malignant tumor), capillary hemangioma, or lymphangioma, which are more common in this age group.

**Syndromic Associations:** Extremely rare reports exist of dacryops occurring in association with certain systemic syndromes, necessitating a comprehensive systemic evaluation in any atypical pediatric presentation.

title: Mastering the Squint Case: Your FRCS Exam Blueprint
summary: Navigate complex strabismus cases with confidence for your FRCS exam. sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview of Strabismus
sections.content: Strabismus, commonly known as squint or 'crossed eyes,' is a misalignment of the visual axes of the two eyes, preventing them from simultaneously fixating on the same object. This can be constant or intermittent, affecting binocular vision, depth perception (stereoacuity), and potentially leading to amblyopia in children. For the FRCS exam, a structured approach is paramount, focusing on meticulous history taking, comprehensive examination, differential diagnosis, and management planning for both comitant and incomitant deviations.

sections.title: Epidemiology - Key Risk Factors
content: Family History: Strong genetic predisposition (e.g., accommodative esotropia).
Refractive Errors: Hyperopia (accommodative esotropia), high myopia (exotropia).
Prematurity/Low Birth Weight: Increased risk for all types of strabismus.
Neurological Disorders: Cerebral Palsy, Down Syndrome, hydrocephalus, brain tumors.
Systemic Syndromes: Craniosynostoses, ocular motor apraxia.
Ocular Conditions: Amblyopia, cataracts, retinoblastoma, optic nerve hypoplasia, severe anisometropia.

branches: Sensory Factors (Poor Vision in one eye: Amblyopia, Cataract, Ptosis, Anisometropia)
Motor Factors (Intrinsic EOM issues: Restrictive myopathy, Palsy, Anomalous insertion, Trauma)
Innervational Factors (Cranial nerve palsies: III, IV, VI; Supranuclear lesions: internuclear ophthalmoplegia, gaze palsies)
Central Control Issues (Disruption of vergence, fusion, or ocular motor pathways in the brainstem/cortex)

rows: Inward, Outward, Upward, Downward, Torsional deviation respectively.
Deviation always present vs. present only at times (e.g., fatigue, distance fixation).
Deviation magnitude consistent in all gaze positions (comitant) vs. varying with gaze direction (incomitant).
Presence from birth/early infancy vs. later onset.
Paretic (e.g., CN III palsy), Restrictive (e.g., TED, orbital fracture), Sensory (e.g., amblyopia), Accommodative
Weak muscle, mechanically restricted muscle, poor vision, excessive accommodation leading to convergence.
Duane's Retraction Syndrome, Brown's Syndrome, Mobius Syndrome, Duane's, INO
Specific syndromes with characteristic ocular motor limitations and findings.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Diplopia (double vision): Especially in acquired strabismus.
Amblyopia ('lazy eye'): Reduced visual acuity not correctable by refraction, common in childhood strabismus.
Asthenopia (eye strain): Headaches, fatigue, especially with intermittent deviations.
Abnormal Head Posture (AHP): Head tilt, turn, or chin up/down to maintain single binocular vision or minimize diplopia (e.g., torticollis).
Cosmetic Concern: Misalignment evident to patient/family.
Reduced Stereoacuity: Impaired 3D vision.
Photophobia: Less common, but can occur.
Confusion: Superimposition of two different images in the same visual space (less common than diplopia).

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: 1. Visual Acuity (VA) & Refraction: Cycloplegic refraction is crucial. Check for amblyopia (Crowding phenomenon, preferential looking for infants).
2. Ocular Motility: Ductions (monocular) & Versions (binocular) in 9 cardinal positions. Look for underaction, overaction, limitations, saccadic abnormalities. Note smooth pursuits.
3. Cover-Uncover Test: For manifest deviation (tropia). Fixate distant & near. Observe movement of uncovered eye.
4. Alternate Cover Test (ACT): For total deviation (phoria + tropia). Break fusion. Observe magnitude and direction of refixation movement.
5. Prism Bar Cover Test: Quantifies deviation (e.g., Prism Diopters, PD) in primary, secondary, and tertiary positions, distant and near. Hirschberg/Krimsky for infants/poor fixation.
6. Stereoacuity: Randot, Titmus, Lang tests. Important for assessing binocular function.
7. Assessment of Abnormal Head Posture (AHP): Observe, measure range of motion. Determine if compensatory.

8. Bielschowsky Head Tilt Test: For vertical deviations, particularly superior oblique palsy (CN IV). Tilt head to shoulder; hypertropia increases in the paretic eye when tilting towards the paretic side.
9. Parks 3-Step Test: Systematic approach for isolating a paretic cyclovertical muscle (e.g., for CN IV palsy).
10. Forced Duction Test (FDT): Differentiates paretic (no restriction) from restrictive (mechanical restriction) strabismus. Performed under topical anesthesia with forceps.
11. Forced Generation Test (FGT): Assesses muscle strength; used if FDT is negative for restriction.
12. Synoptophore/Maddox Rod: Objective measurement of deviation, fusion range, subjective angle.
13. Fundoscopy: Look for cyclotorsion, optic nerve hypoplasia, macular abnormalities (causes of sensory strabismus).
14. Anterior Segment Exam: Rule out ptosis, congenital anomalies, lens opacities.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Grading (Amblyopia Severity)
sections.content:
While strabismus itself doesn't have a universal staging system, the associated amblyopia is graded by severity based on best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA):

*   **Mild Amblyopia**: BCVA 20/25 (6/9) to 20/40 (6/12)
*   **Moderate Amblyopia**: BCVA 20/50 (6/15) to 20/80 (6/24)
*   **Severe Amblyopia**: BCVA 20/100 (6/30) or worse

This grading guides treatment intensity and duration (e.g., patching hours).

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Algorithm
content: 1. Refractive Correction: Prescribe full cycloplegic correction (especially for hyperopia in accommodative esotropia). Re-evaluate deviation after 6-8 weeks.
2. Amblyopia Management (if present): Patching (occlusion therapy) of the good eye for 2-6+ hours/day, atropine penalization. Critical in pediatric cases.
3. Prisms: For small, comitant deviations causing diplopia in adults, or to provide single binocular vision in specific gaze positions. Can be temporary Fresnel or permanent ground-in.

4. Botulinum Toxin Injection (Botox): Temporarily weakens specific EOMs (e.g., medial rectus for small esotropia, or lateral rectus for VI nerve palsy). Lasts 3-4 months. Useful diagnostically, for small angle strabismus, or prior to surgery.
5. Orthoptic Exercises: Convergence exercises for convergence insufficiency exotropia. Limited role for other deviations.

6. Surgical Intervention: Indicated for significant primary gaze deviation, large angle, persistent diplopia not managed by prisms, significant AHP, or cosmetic reasons. Aims to realign eyes, restore binocularity, eliminate diplopia, or improve AHP. Timing is crucial for children (e.g., congenital esotropia at 6-12 months).

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques for Strabismus
content: 1. Recession: Weakens a muscle by detaching it from its original insertion and reattaching it further posteriorly. Common for medial rectus (esotropia) or lateral rectus (exotropia). Instruments: muscle hook, calipers, non-absorbable sutures (e.g., 6-0 Vicryl/Mersilene).

2. Resection: Strengthens a muscle by shortening it. A segment of the muscle is resected, and the remaining muscle is reattached to the original insertion. Common for lateral rectus (esotropia) or medial rectus (exotropia).

3. Fadenoperation (Posterior Fixation Suture): Limits muscle action in a specific field of gaze without altering primary position. A suture is placed on the muscle belly and fixed to the sclera posteriorly. Used for large angle deviations that increase in certain gazes (e.g., high myopia with XT).

4. Adjustable Sutures: Allows post-operative fine-tuning of eye alignment. Muscle is secured with a slip knot, adjusted hours/days after surgery, then permanently tied. Excellent for adults with diplopia, re-operations, or complex cases.
5. Transposition Procedures: Moves muscle from one quadrant to another to compensate for palsied muscles (e.g., Hummelsheim, Jensen, Knapp procedures for CN VI palsy).
6. Sling Procedures: For severe ptosis or hypotropia (e.g., using fascia lata or Gore-Tex for superior rectus weakness).

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: Surgical Complications:
- Under/Overcorrection: Most common (up to 20-30% may require re-op).
- Diplopia: New onset or persistent.
- Infection (orbital cellulitis, endophthalmitis): Rare but serious.
- Scleral Perforation: Can lead to retinal detachment, endophthalmitis.
- Lost/Slipped Muscle: Requires urgent re-exploration.
- Anterior Segment Ischemia: Rare, especially with multiple muscle surgery.
Prognosis:
- Amblyopia: Excellent if treated early. Prognosis decreases with age.
- Binocular Vision: Can be restored/improved, especially with early surgical correction.
- Cosmetic Outcome: Generally good, but some residual deviation or asymmetry may persist.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Acute Onset Strabismus: Especially in adults, suggestive of neurological cause (e.g., CN palsy, intracranial lesion).
Associated Neurological Symptoms: Headaches, vomiting, weakness, sensory deficits, papilledema (suggests raised ICP).
Pupil Involvement: Anisocoria with CN III palsy (PCOM aneurysm until proven otherwise).
Proptosis/Lid Retraction: Suggests orbital pathology (e.g., TED, tumor).
Rapidly Progressive Deviation: Or worsening symptoms.
Painful Ocular Motility: Suggests inflammation or compression.

content.explanation:
1. Identify which eye is hypertropic in primary gaze.
2. Determine if hypertropia increases in Right Gaze or Left Gaze.
3. Determine if hypertropia increases on Right Head Tilt or Left Head Tilt.
This helps isolate the paretic cyclovertical muscle (e.g., CN IV palsy = Superior Oblique).

Superior Oblique (SO) is innervated by CN IV (4). Lateral Rectus (LR) is innervated by CN VI (6). All Other (AO) Extraocular Muscles (EOMs) are innervated by CN III (3). 'LIRAD' helps remember actions: Lateral Rectus Abducts, Medial Rectus Adducts.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls for FRCS
content: Always perform cycloplegic refraction in children with strabismus.
For acute onset CN III palsy with pupil involvement, assume posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise – urgent neuroimaging (MRA/CTA) is mandatory.
Incomitant strabismus needs thorough investigation to rule out neurological or restrictive causes.
Amblyopia treatment should *always* precede strabismus surgery in children, unless the strabismus prevents proper amblyopia therapy (e.g., severe ptosis).
The aim of strabismus surgery is typically to achieve alignment in primary gaze and improve binocularity, not necessarily to restore full range of motion in all gazes.
Adjustable sutures are a game-changer for precise alignment, especially in adults and re-operations.
Convergence insufficiency is a common cause of exotropia symptoms (asthenopia, intermittent diplopia) and responds well to exercises.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent advances include improved surgical techniques, wider adoption of adjustable sutures for better post-operative alignment, and advancements in neuroimaging for diagnosing underlying causes. The Amblyopia Treatment Studies (ATS) have provided evidence-based guidelines for patching and atropine penalization, defining optimal treatment durations and showing effectiveness even in older children. Botulinum toxin has gained acceptance for specific indications, offering a less invasive alternative in selected cases.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric & Special Population Considerations
content: Infantile Esotropia: Often large angle, non-accommodative. Surgical correction typically between 6-12 months to maximize chances of rudimentary binocular vision.
Accommodative Esotropia: Managed with full hyperopic correction. Bifocals may be needed if significant accommodative convergence/accommodation ratio (AC/A).
Sensory Strabismus: Deviation secondary to severe unilateral visual impairment. Surgical alignment is often for cosmetic reasons or to improve field of vision, binocularity is rarely regained.
Nystagmus: Can be associated with strabismus (e.g., latent nystagmus, manifest latent nystagmus). Surgery can shift null point to primary gaze.
Down Syndrome: High prevalence of strabismus (especially esotropia), nystagmus, and significant refractive errors. Requires careful, individualized management.

content: 1. Choroidal tumour (Melanoma, haemangioma, metastasis)
2. Inflammation (Harada disease, posterior scleritis)
3. Bullous CSR (rare)
4. Iatrogenic (RD surgery, PRP)
5. Choroidal neovascularization
6. Hypertensive choroidopathy (toxaemia of pregnancy)
7. Idiopathic (choroidal effusion syndrome)

sections.title: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV)
content: Indications: Masked breaks (VH, debris, PCO, IOL edge), Giant tears, PVR, Tractional RD (foveal), Combined TRD/RRD, Penetrating trauma.
Intraoperative Complications: Posterior/Peripheral retinal breaks, Choroidal haemorrhage.

Postoperative Complications: RRD, Retinal folds, Inflammation (diabetics), Raised IOP (gas expansion, oil glaucoma, ghost cell, steroid-induced), Cataract (feathering/nucleosclerosis), Band keratopathy.
Pneumatic Retinopexy Indications: Uncomplicated RD with small breaks, clusters < 2 clock hours in upper 2/3 of retina.

sections.title: Vitreous Haemorrhage Etiology
content: Acute PVD
Proliferative retinopathy (DM, RVO, Sickle cell, Eales disease, Vasculitis)
Macroaneurysm, Telangiectasia, Capillary haemangioma
Trauma
Systemic bleeding disorder, Terson syndrome

sections.title: Motility: Basic Measurements
sections.content: Near Point of Convergence (NPC): The nearest point on which the eye can maintain binocular fixation (normally nearer than 10cm without undue effort). Near Point of Accommodation (NPA): The nearest point on which the eyes can maintain clear focus.

sections.title: Brown Syndrome: Classification & Care
content: Mild: No hypotropia in primary position; No downshoot in adduction.
Moderate: No hypotropia in primary position; Downshoot in adduction.
Severe: Hypotropia in primary position; Downshoot in adduction; Chin-up head posture.
Congenital Treatment: Observation if binocular function holds. Indications for surgery: Primary hypotropia or head posture. Procedure: Lengthening of Superior Oblique (SO) tendon.
Acquired Treatment: Steroids (oral or injection near trochlea).

sections.title: Differential: Brown Syndrome vs. Inferior Oblique (IO) Palsy
V-Pattern & A-Pattern Strabismus
sections.content: V-Pattern: Significant if difference between upgaze and downgaze >= 15 prism. Causes: IOOA with 4th nerve palsy, SO underaction + IOOA (infantile ET), SR underaction, Brown syndrome, Craniofacial anomalies. Treatment: Oblique weakening/strengthening. If no oblique dysfunction: Bilateral MR recession with downward transposition or LR recession with upward transposition. A-Pattern: Significant if difference >= 10 prism. Face turn away from affected eye. Causes: Primary SO overaction (Exo in primary), IO underaction, IR underaction. Treatment: SO posterior tenotomy (corrects 20PD) or total tenotomy (50PD). If no oblique dysfunction: Bilateral MR recession with upward transposition (ET) or LR recession with downward transposition (XT).

sections.title: Strabismus Surgery: Complications & Botox
content: Operative Risks: Lost/slipped muscle (Medial Rectus), Globe perforation (High myopia), Posterior Tenon capsule opening (fibrosis/fat involvement).
Postoperative Risks: Over/under correction, Anterior segment ischaemia, Stretched scar (years later).

Botulinum Toxin Indications: Small angle residual squint, Infantile esotropia, Active thyroid orbitopathy, Determining diplopia risk, Assessing BSV potential, Lateral rectus palsy, Psychosocial unacceptable deviation after multiple surgeries.

content: Nondominant lobe lesions: May cause dressing apraxia, constitutional apraxia, and spatial neglect.
Cortical blindness: Formed visual hallucinations.
Anton Syndrome: Denial of blindness.
Riddoch Phenomenon: Only moving visual targets are perceived.

Fasciculus as it passes through the red nucleus

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS: 3rd Nerve Palsy
content: Pupillary involvement may be the only sign of 3rd N palsy (Basal meningitis, Uncal herniation)
Painful 3rd nerve palsy: Rule out PCoA Aneurysm immediately
Uncal herniation: Secondary to subdural haematoma

sections.title: 4th Nerve Palsy: Clinical Features & Compensations
content: Idiopathic: Often congenital
Trauma: Most common cause of bilateral 4th N palsy
Microvascular / Aneurysm / Tumor: Less common causes
Contralateral Head Tilt: To the right (if left palsy) to compensate for weakness of intorsion
Chin Depression: To alleviate weakened depression of the eye
Face Turn: Slightly to the right (if left palsy) as weakness is most marked in adduction

sections.title: Diagnosis of Bilateral 4th Nerve Palsy
content: Right hypertropia in left gaze
Left hypertropia in right gaze
Cyclodeviation > 10 degrees (measured via Double Maddox Rods or Synoptophore)
V-pattern Esotropia
Bilateral positive Bielschowsky head tilt test

sections.title: Park's Three-Step Test
content: Step 1: Identify the hypertropic eye in primary position. This implicates either the depressors of the elevated eye (SO/IR) or elevators of the hypotropic eye (SR/IO).
Step 2: Determine if deviation is worse in right or left gaze. This assigns weakness to the two muscles having the greatest vertical action in that position.
Step 3: Hypertropia in head tilt. Assess muscle responsible for cyclotorsion when the patient is fixed on a target at 3m with head tilt to either side.

rows: Symmetrical recession of both Inferior Rectus muscles

branches: Foville Syndrome: Inferior medial pontine. Ipsilateral 5th, 8th, central sympathetic (Horner), horizontal gaze palsy.
Millard-Gubler Syndrome: Ventral pontine. Ipsilateral 6th N palsy (fasciculus), LMNL facial N palsy, contralateral hemiplegia (pyramidal tract).
Raymond Syndrome: Ipsilateral 6th N palsy, contralateral hemiplegia (pyramidal tract involvement).
Gradenigo Syndrome: Mastoiditis/acute petrositis. Damage to 6th N at petrous tip. Symptoms: 6th N palsy, 7th N weakness, pain, hearing difficulty.
Intracavernous 6th N Palsy: Damage to 6th N and paracarotid sympathetic plexus (Horner syndrome).
Parkinson Syndrome: (Listed in input context of base of skull/pontine)

sections.title: Facial Nerve (CN VII) Disorders
content: Ramsay Hunt Syndrome: Reactivation of Herpes Zoster in geniculate ganglion. Ear pain, vesicles on face/ear.
Causes: Bell's palsy, Trauma, Viral infection, Lyme disease, Neoplastic, Diabetes, Sarcoidosis.
Stroke Mimics: Hemiparesis/facial drooping caused by hypoglycaemia (elderly), migraine, sepsis, transient focal neuro signs.

sections.title: Management of Facial Nerve Palsy
content: 1. Corneal protection (Essential)
2. Corticosteroids: Prednisolone 60-80mg daily for 1 week (started within 48-72h), then taper over 1 week.
3. Antivirals: Acyclovir or Valaciclovir.
4. Neuroimaging: MRI scan of the brain.
5. If Bilateral: Chest X-ray and ACE levels to exclude Sarcoidosis.
6. Surgery (if indicated).

sections.title: Supranuclear Control of Eye Movements
sections.content: Saccades are initiated in the premotor cortex frontal eye fields; each lobe initiates contralateral saccades. Impulses for horizontal movement pass to the contralateral PPRF. Smooth pursuits pathway is complex, involving the cortex, PPRF, and superior colliculus. Pursuit palsy results from damage/hyperactivity in the parietoccipital lobe, causing unilateral pursuit palsy in the ipsilateral direction.

sections.title: Parinaud (Dorsal Midbrain) Syndrome
content: Signs: Straight eye in primary position.
Supranuclear upgaze/downgaze palsy in saccadic movement.
Defective convergence.
Normal downgaze using doll’s head manoeuvre.
Large pupils with light-near dissociation.
Collier Sign: Lid retraction.
Convergence-retraction nystagmus.
Causes (Children): Aqueduct stenosis, meningitis, pinealoma.
Causes (Young Adults): Demyelination, trauma, AVM.
Causes (Elderly): Midbrain vascular accidents, mass lesions, periaqueductal grey matter, posterior fossa aneurysms.

rows: Horizontal/Vertical/Torsional; Fine amplitude; Damped by fixation; Intensity increases with gaze in fast phase direction.
Pendular or Jerk; Horizontal uniplanar; No oscillopsia; Dampened by convergence; Null point present; Absent in sleep.
X-linked; Low amplitude pendular converting to jerk on side gaze; VA > Sensory deficit nystagmus.
Small amplitude, high frequency horizontal; Head nodding; Asymmetrical; Increases in abduction.
Idiopathic (resolves by 3y), Glioma, Empty Sella, Porencephalic cyst.
Congenital, Cerebellar disease, Ataxic telangiectasia, Phenytoin.
Arnold Chiari, Syringobulbia, Lithium, Phenytoin, Wernicke's, Demyelination, Hydrocephalus.
Posterior fossa lesions, Drugs, Wernicke encephalopathy.
One eye elevates/intorts while other depresses/extorts.
Parasellar tumor, Brain stem stroke, Syringobulbia.

sections.title: Myasthenia Gravis (MG): Workup & Management
content: Investigations: Ice pack test, Edrophonium (Tensilon) test, Electromyography, Muscle biopsy.
Antibody Testing: AChR antibodies, MuSK protein antibodies, Striational antibodies (severe marker), Voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies (Lambert-Eaton).
Imaging: Thoracic CT/MRI/PET (Thymoma/Lung tumor), Thyroid function testing.
Treatment: Pyridostigmine + Steroids/Azathioprine.
Acute/Short-term: Plasmapheresis and IVIG.
Surgical: Thymectomy.
Emergency: Respiratory support.

content.explanation: 1. CPEO & Ptosis, 2. Cardiac conduction abnormalities, 3. Pigmentary retinopathy (Salt and pepper affecting macula).

sections.title: Kearns-Sayre Syndrome: Clinical Details
content: Etiology: Mitochondrial DNA deletion; Cerebral folate deficiency.
Onset: 1st-2nd decades (Sporadic).
Systemic: Fatigue, proximal muscle weakness, deafness, diabetes, cerebellar ataxia, short stature, renal disease, dementia.
Histology: Ragged red fibres (intramuscular accumulation of abnormal mitochondria).
Screening: Genetic testing, ECG, Endocrine screening.

sections.title: Ocular Surface Oncology: Conjunctival & Iris Lesions
content: Malignant Conjunctival Nevus signs: Unusual site (palpebral/forniceal), prominent feeder vessels, sudden growth, increased pigmentation, development after 2nd decade.
Conjunctival Melanoma Poor Prognosis: Caruncle/forniceal/lid margin location, thickness >= 2mm.
Iris Nevus Risk Factors: Age <40y, inferior location, bleeding, diffuse involvement, feathery margin, ectropion uvae.

sections.title: Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN)
content: Risk Factors: UV light, pale complexion, Ciclosporin, Smoking, Petroleum exposure, AIDS, Xeroderma pigmentosum, HPV Type 16.
Investigations: UBM, AS-OCT, Exfoliative/Impression cytology.
Treatment: Excision with 2-4mm margins (do not cut below Bowman's).
Adjunctive: Cryotherapy, Brachytherapy, Topical Chemo, Subconjunctival Interferon.
Limbal Dermoid Associations: Goldenhar, Treacher Collins, Linear naevus sebaceous of Jadassohn.

sections.title: Role of Topical Chemotherapy in OSSN
content: A. Avoid recurrence & stem cell damage.
B. Reduce tumour size prior to excision.
C. Treat recurrence.
Regimen: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) 4x daily for 1 week, followed by 3 weeks rest.
Other agents: Topical Interferon Alfa-2b, Mitomycin C.

sections.title: Management of Orbital Blow Out Fractures

branches: 1. Observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, nasal decongestants, patient is instructed not to blow out nose
2. Systemic steroids for sever orbital edema compromising optic n
3. Prevention of permanent vertical diplopia and cosemetically unacceptable enophthalmos

sections.title: Clinical Decision Matrix: Blowout Fractures
content: Small cracks without herniation —> observation
Fractures involving one half of orbital floor with little or no herniation no enophthalmos, no diplopia do not require treatment
Fractures > 1/2 of the orbital floor may develop enophthalmos if left untreated
Fractures with entrapment of orbital contents enophthalmos >2mm and persistent diplopia in primary position should be repaired within 2 weeks
Patient with diplopia and tissue incarceration but without muscle entrapment improvement often occur without surgery
White eyed fracture is a subgroup for which urgent repair is required to avoid permanent vertical diplopia neuromuscular damage

sections.title: Supplemental: Differential Diagnosis of Orbital Trauma

rows: Rock hard lids, afferent pupillary defect (APD)
Decreased vision, APD, normal appearing orbit

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Lateral Canthotomy & Cantholysis
content: Indication: Treatment of retrobulbar hge (hemorrhage)
Step 1: Clamping the incision site for 60 seconds
Step 2: 1-2 cm horizontal full thickness incision under local anaesthesia (1-2ml lidocaine 1-2% with adrenaline) at the angle of lateral canthus

Step 3: The lower lid is retracted downwards and the inferior crust of lateral canthal tendon is cut using blunt tipped scissors directed inferiorly and inserted adjacent and parallel to lateral orbital rim between conjunctiva and skin angled away from eyeball
Step 4: Blood gently encouraged to drain
Step 5: If necessary the superior limb of tendon can also cut but carry risk of damage to adnex structures.

sections.title: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED): Activity & Severity
sections.content: Treatment of thyroid eye disease depends on clinical activity, severity, and duration of orbitopathy. Essential first steps include: Patient counselling on aim, expectations, benefits and risk of different therapy, and absolute cessation of smoking in all cases.

rows: Lubricants, Topical anti-inflammatory agents, Selenium daily for 6 months, Head elevation (3 pillows) to reduce periorbital edema, Eyelid tapping during sleep

Consider treatment for 3/7 activity or more. Systemic steroids 60-80mg/day initially then tapering; long term low dose may be needed. Low dose fractionated radiotherapy (2nd line). Combined therapy: steroids+azathioprine+low dose prednisolone

sections.title: TED: Optic Neuropathy & Post-Inflammatory Complications
content: C. Optic Neuropathy: Pulsed methyl prednisolone IV 0.5-1g on three successive days
C. Optic Neuropathy: Conversion to oral 40mg/day + liver function monitoring + gastric & osteoporosis prophylaxis
C. Optic Neuropathy: Second line (steroid resistance/persistent disease): monoclonal antibody (teprotumumab)
D. Post-Inflammatory Complications: Orbital decompression

D. Strabismus Surgery: For persistent diplopia in primary or reading position after 6-12m from inflammation; until then use prisms or botulinum toxin (recession of inferior and medial rectus) with adjustable sutures
D. Lid Surgery (Mild): Improve by control of hyperthyroidism
D. Lid Surgery (Moderate): Botulinum toxin injection levator aponeurosis and muller muscle, prisms
D. Lid Surgery (Severe): Recession/disinsertion of muller muscle in severe lid retraction

sections.title: Senile Entropion Treatment
content: Temporary: Lubricant, taping, bandage soft contact lens
Chemodenervation: Orbicularis botulinum toxin
Surgical (Overriding/Disinsertion): Transverse everting sutures
Surgical (Durable): Wies procedure (full thickness horizontal lid splitting + insertion of everting sutures)
Lower lid retraction reinsertion: Reserved for recurrence
Horizontal lid laxity: Lateral tarsal sling, full thickness lateral pentagon excision, Tightening

branches: Main Features: Enophthalmos, Upper lid ptosis, Superior sulcus hollowing, Sagging of lower lid
Surgical: Silicon block in inferior orbit (if implant present)
Non-Surgical: Intermittent injection of filler (hyaluronic acid) into orbital apex
Lower Lid: Correction of laxity by lateral tarsal sling (strip)

Upper and lower half of same side face
Lower half of face on opposite side (upper spared)

Lagophthalmos and exposure keratitis
Infection

sections.title: Surgical Process: Levator Advancement
content: 1. Mark level of desired post-op lid crease and peak position
2. Subcutaneous local anesthesia
3. Skin incision at predetermined skin crease level
4. Divide orbicularis/septum; retract fat pads to expose LPS
5. Free LPS from tarsus and underlying Muller muscle
6. Dissect to expose superior tarsus
7. Advance aponeurosis and suture to tarsus (6/0 vicryl); check lid eversion
8. Observe and adjust position in awake patient
9. Lid crease formation (orbicularis-levator-orbicularis suture)
10. Close skin incision (6/0 or 7/0 vicryl), remove at 1 week

Lid shortening laterally and tightened canthus
Everting sutures and full thickness + wedge excision to shorten lid

title: Sickle Cell Retinopathy: From Hemoglobinopathy to Sea Fans
summary: Sickle Cell Retinopathy (SCR) is a sight-threatening manifestation of systemic sickling hemoglobinopathies. While HbSS causes severe systemic disease, the ocular manifestations are paradoxically more frequent and severe in HbSC and S-Thal variants due to higher blood viscosity.

data.title: Sickle Cell Retinopathy: From Hemoglobinopathy to Sea Fans
data.summary: Sickle Cell Retinopathy (SCR) is a sight-threatening manifestation of systemic sickling hemoglobinopathies. While HbSS causes severe systemic disease, the ocular manifestations are paradoxically more frequent and severe in HbSC and S-Thal variants due to higher blood viscosity.

sections.title: Clinical Overview & Definition
sections.content: Sickle Cell Retinopathy (SCR) encompasses the ocular changes resulting from vaso-occlusive events in the retinal and choroidal circulation. It is caused by the inheritance of abnormal hemoglobin (HbS), where valine is substituted for glutamic acid at the sixth position of the β-globin chain. This leads to RBC sickling under hypoxic, acidotic, or hyperosmolar conditions.

sections.title: The Pathophysiological Cascade
content: 1. HbS Polymerization: Triggered by hypoxia or acidosis.
2. RBC Sickling: Erythrocytes become rigid and crescent-shaped.
3. Vaso-occlusion: Stasis in peripheral retinal arterioles.
4. Retinal Ischemia: Release of pro-angiogenic factors (VEGF).
5. Proliferative Retinopathy: Neovascular 'Sea Fan' formation.

rows: A-V shunts at the junction of perfused and non-perfused retina.
The 'Sea Fan' stage; often at the border of ischemia.
Bleeding from fragile sea fan vessels into the vitreous cavity.
Tractional or rhegmatogenous (secondary to breaks near traction).

sections.title: Anterior Segment & Unique Findings
content: Conjunctival Comma Sign: Isolated vascular segments on the bulbar conjunctiva.
Iris Ischemia: Can present as sectoral atrophy or even rubeosis iridis.
Hyphema Danger: Sickled cells clog the trabecular meshwork rapidly, raising IOP.
Angioid Streaks: Occur in up to 6% of patients (calcification of Bruch's membrane).

sections.title: Macular Manifestations
content: Sickle Maculopathy: Chronic ischemia leads to thinning of the inner retinal layers.
Vascular Changes: Enlarged Foveal Avascular Zone (FAZ) on OCT-A.
Macular Depression Sign: Oval depression due to focal atrophy.
Peripheral-to-Central Progression: Macula is usually spared until late stages.

rows: Idiopathic peripheral perivasculitis, usually bilateral, male predominance.
History of prematurity, bilateral, lack of 'salmon patches'.
Microaneurysms, hard exudates, posterior pole involvement initially.
Massive exudation, telangiectatic 'light bulb' vessels, usually unilateral.

sections.title: Investigation & Imaging Workup
content: 1. DFE: Wide-field fundus examination is mandatory.
2. Hemoglobin Electrophoresis: To confirm Hb variant (SS, SC, S-Thal).
3. Wide-field FFA: Gold standard to identify 'Sea Fans' and peripheral non-perfusion.
4. OCT-A: Non-invasive detection of macular and peripheral capillary drop-out.
5. B-scan USG: Indicated if Vitreous Hemorrhage obscures the view.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Observation: For Stages I and II, and small Stage III fans (high autoinfarction rate).
Scatter Laser Photocoagulation: Target the peripheral ischemic zone (not the fans directly).
Feeder Vessel Treatment: Historically used but high risk of VH and retinal breaks.
Anti-VEGF: Temporary regression of sea fans; used as adjunct to surgery/laser.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy: Reserved for non-clearing VH or TRD.

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Hyphema Management
content: Avoid Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs): They increase acidity, promoting sickling.
Avoid Hyperosmotics (Mannitol): Increases hemoconcentration and sickling.
Aggressive IOP Control: Lower threshold for surgical washout (IOP > 24 mmHg for 24h).
Use Beta-Blockers and Alpha-Agonists: Safest options for IOP reduction.

sections.title: Surgical Considerations (PPV)
content: Pre-op Exchange Transfusion: Consider to reduce HbS levels below 30%.
Avoid Scleral Buckling: High risk of anterior segment ischemia (ASI).
Intraoperative Hydration: Vital to prevent sickling crises.
Monitor for Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) post-operatively.

content.explanation: Occlusion (1), Anastomoses (2), Neovascularization (3), Vitreous Heme (4), Detachment (5).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Autoinfarction: Sea fans may spontaneously regress (withered sea fan) in up to 25% of cases.
Peripheral Predominance: SCR is primarily a disease of the temporal periphery.
Higher Hematocrit = Higher Risk: This is why HbSC (higher Hct than HbSS) is more ocularly dangerous.
Systemic Screening: All patients with sickle cell disease should have annual dilated exams starting at age 10.

sections.title: Landmark Insights
sections.content: Evidence from the Sickle Cell Retinopathy Study group suggests that while laser photocoagulation effectively regresses neovascularization and reduces the incidence of vitreous hemorrhage, it does not significantly change the long-term visual acuity outcome compared to observation for most patients, unless advanced proliferative disease is present.

title: Decoding the Cornea: Mastering Suspicious Topography Indices
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to identifying early keratoconus and corneal ectasia. This poster integrates Placido-disk indices, elevation-based tomography, and biomechanical parameters for refractive surgery screening.
