sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Corneal topography/tomography indices are quantitative values derived from the mathematical analysis of corneal shape. Suspicious indices represent the 'subclinical' or 'fruste' phase of corneal ectasia, where the cornea appears normal on slit-lamp examination but demonstrates biomechanical instability or morphological irregularities. Identifying these is the 'Holy Grail' of pre-operative refractive screening to prevent post-LASIK ectasia.

sections.title: Placido-Based Global Indices
content: SRI (Surface Regularity Index): High values (>1.0) suggest irregular astigmatism.
SAI (Surface Asymmetry Index): Measures centrally weighted asymmetry (Normal <0.5).
KISA% Index: Combines K, I-S, Astigmatism, and SRAX. >100% is diagnostic; 60-100% is suspect.
CIM (Corneal Irregularity Measure): Derived from WaveLight; indicates wavefront irregularity.

sections.title: Red Flags: Topographic Warning Signs
content: Localized steepening (Inferior or Central)
Abnormal Skewing of the steepest radial axes
Vertical Asymmetry (I-S ratio > 1.4D)
Disparity between manifest refraction and topography axes
Maximum K > 48.0 D (relative)
Pellucid-like 'Crab Claw' pattern

sections.title: Elevation-Based Tomography (Scheimpflug)
content: Posterior Elevation: Most sensitive early marker. Use BFS (Best Fit Sphere).
Pentacam Thresholds: >15μm (Suspicious), >20μm (Abnormal).
Enhanced BFS: Subtracts the 3.5mm central zone to highlight ectatic areas.
Elevation Difference: Comparing BFS vs. BFS-enhanced; difference >5μm is suspect.

sections.title: Pachymetric Progression Indices
content: Step 1: Locate Thinnest Point (TP) — Normal TP is ~530-550μm.
Step 2: Calculate TP Displacement — Distance from center. >1.0mm is suspicious.
Step 3: Analyze PPI (Pachymetric Progression Index) — Normal slope is gradual.
Step 4: Assess ART (Ambrósio Relational Thickness) — TP / PPI. Suspicious if < 339μm.

rows: Regresses after lens cessation; No posterior steepening.
Irregular Placido mires; Improves with lubrication.
History of RK or PRK; Flattened center.
Inferior thinning 1-2mm from limbus; 'Kissing birds' pattern.

content.explanation: P: Posterior Elevation (>15μm), A: Asymmetry (I-S > 1.4), C: Central K (>47.2), H: Height of BAD-D (>1.6), Y: Young Age (<25 years is higher risk).

sections.title: Biomechanical Indices (Corvis ST)
content: CBI (Corvis Biomechanical Index): Uses dynamic Scheimpflug to assess stiffness.
TBI (Tomographic Biomechanical Index): Combines Pentacam + Corvis. Most sensitive (AUC 0.99).
SPA1 (Stiffness Parameter at First Applanation): Lower in early ectasia.

sections.title: Landmark Study: CLEK Study
sections.content: The Collaborative Longitudinal Evaluation of Keratoconus (CLEK) study demonstrated that steepening of >1.19D in one year is a sign of rapid progression. It also noted that scarring is common in eyes with K > 52D or in those with poor fitting contact lenses.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Identify Suspicious Indices in Refractive Candidate.
Step 2: Rule out CL warpage (repeat topography in 2-3 weeks).
Step 3: If still suspicious, monitor for 6 months (pachymetry/Kmax change).
Step 4: If progressive, perform CXL (Corneal Cross-Linking).
Step 5: Visual rehabilitation via Scleral lenses, INTACS, or Topo-guided PRK (carefully).

sections.title: Recent Advances: Epithelial Mapping
content: The 'Donut' Sign: Thickened epithelium surrounding a thin center (seen in manifest KC).
Epithelial Masking: Epithelium thins over a steep 'cone' to smooth the surface.
Early Sign: Focal thinning of the epithelium over the point of maximum elevation is a high-yield 'suspect' sign.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: Never rely on a single index; look for 'concordance' between elevation and pachy.
A posterior elevation 'hot spot' that doesn't coincide with thinnest pachy is often an artifact.
In PMD, the 'crab-claw' pattern is usually accompanied by a very thin peripheral cornea.
Check the quality factor (QS) on the Pentacam; low quality can mimic suspicious indices.

title: Acute Corneal Hydrops: Clinical Crisis & Management Strategy
summary: Acute corneal hydrops is a sight-threatening complication of corneal ectasia where a rupture in Descemet's membrane allows aqueous humor to flood the corneal stroma. This masterclass poster details the pathophysiology, diagnostic nuances, and the shift from conservative to interventional management.

sections.title: Primary Etiologies
content: Keratoconus (Most common: usually stage 3-4 Amsler-Krumeich)
Pellucid Marginal Degeneration (PMD)
Keratoglobus (Higher risk due to generalized thinning)
Post-LASIK Ectasia
Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (Associated with vigorous eye rubbing)

sections.title: Pathophysiological Sequence
content: 1. Progressive corneal thinning and mechanical stress
2. Rupture of Descemet's Membrane (DM)
3. Influx of Aqueous Humor into the corneal stroma
4. Massive stromal edema and epithelial bullae formation
5. Endothelial migration to bridge the DM gap

sections.title: Clinical Presentation (Symptoms)
content: Sudden, painless (initially) or painful drop in vision
Severe photophobia and epiphora
A visible 'white spot' or clouding on the eye
Foreign body sensation due to epithelial bullae
Blepharospasm

sections.title: Slit-Lamp Examination Findings
content: Localized or generalized corneal edema (ground-glass appearance)
Large stromal fluid clefts (intrastromal cysts)
Epithelial bullae (risk of rupture/infection)
Retracted DM scrolls (visible at the edges of the break)
Conjunctival hyperemia (ciliary flush)
Pseudopseudophakia appearance (extreme corneal convexity)

rows: Mid-dilated pupil, high IOP, shallow AC
Vertical DM breaks (Haab striae), history of birth trauma
Bilateral, guttae, central edema, slow onset

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT): GOLD STANDARD to visualize DM break size and intrastromal clefts.
Pachymetry: Will show massive increase (often >1000 microns).
Slit-lamp Photography: For monitoring resolution progress.
Seidel's Test: Usually negative (the rupture is internal, not a full-thickness perforation).

sections.title: First-Line Medical Management
content: Hypertonic Saline (5% NaCl drops/ointment): Reduces epithelial edema (Muro 128).
Cycloplegics (Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate): For ciliary spasm pain.
Topical NSAIDs/Steroids: To control secondary inflammation (use with caution).
Bandage Contact Lens (BCL): If epithelial bullae are causing significant pain.
Aqueous Suppressants: If IOP is elevated or to reduce pressure on the DM break.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention: Gas Tamponade
content: 1. Topical or peribulbar anesthesia in a sterile setting.
2. Paracentesis at the limbus.
3. Injection of Iso-expansile gas (SF6 20% or C3F8 14%).
4. Position the patient supine to allow the bubble to tamponade the DM break.
5. Monitor IOP closely for 24-48 hours (risk of pupillary block).
6. Gas facilitates faster endothelial migration and DM apposition.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Secondary Microbial Keratitis (Infection of bullae)
Full-thickness corneal perforation (rare)
Neovascularization of the cornea (high risk for future graft failure)
Persistent Flat Anterior Chamber after gas injection
Uncontrolled IOP (Pupillary block glaucoma)

content.explanation: H: Hypertonics, Y: Yield to time (often self-resolves), D: Descemet's repair, R: Rubbing cessation, O: OCT monitoring, P: Pain control, S: Surgical gas (SF6/C3F8).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Evidence
sections.content: Basu et al. (2014) demonstrated that intracameral C3F8 reduces resolution time from ~100 days to ~20 days. Grewal et al. highlighted the utility of AS-OCT in identifying the exact location of DM scrolls, which determines the success rate of gas tamponade. Recent studies suggest pre-emptive cross-linking (CXL) in the fellow eye is vital as rubbing behavior is often bilateral.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (Fellow Level)
content: The 'Silver Lining': Hydrops often leads to significant apical scarring and flattening, which can actually make contact lens fitting easier after resolution.
Wait before Grafting: Never perform PKP/DALK in the acute phase; wait at least 3-6 months for edema to clear and inflammation to subside.
The DM Break size: If the DM break is >1.5mm on OCT, medical management alone will take significantly longer; prioritize gas.
Steroid use: Use only mild steroids (Fluorometholone) to prevent slowing of endothelial migration while controlling discomfort.
Pediatric Alert: Children with Down Syndrome and VKC are high-risk; they require aggressive counseling against eye rubbing and early CXL.

title: Corneal Iron Lines: The Ferritin Fingerprints of Ocular Surface Dynamics
summary: Corneal iron lines represent localized epithelial ferritin deposits within basal cells, occurring at sites of tear film stagnation or structural irregularity. They serve as critical clinical signposts for diagnosing conditions ranging from keratoconus to glaucoma filtering bleb function.

branches: Basal Epithelial Layer: Primary site of intracellular ferritin storage
Mechanism: Tear film stagnation + Localized drying
Source: Plasma-derived ferritin from the precorneal tear film
Structural Association: Occur at sites of abrupt corneal contour change
Composition: 450kDa globular protein (Ferritin) with Fe3+ core

rows: Junction of middle and lower 1/3 of cornea
At the base of the surgical bleb

sections.title: Clinical Examination Techniques
content: 1. High-Magnification Slit Lamp: Use a broad beam to scan the corneal surface.
2. Sclerotic Scatter: Decenter the beam to highlight subtle pigment shifts.
3. Cobalt Blue Filter: Iron lines appear dark/black (attenuation of fluorescence).
4. Specular Reflection: Evaluates the regularity of the overlying epithelium.
5. Anterior Segment OCT: May show hyper-reflective basal epithelial layer.

sections.title: The Fleischer Ring: Keratoconus Hallmark
content: Found in approximately 50% of Keratoconus eyes.
Encircles the base of the cone where curvature changes most rapidly.
Thickness and density correlate with the chronicity of the disease.
Best visualized using a Cobalt Blue filter at the slit lamp.
Often fades or disappears following successful corneal cross-linking (CXL).

sections.title: Secondary Ocular Iron Lines
content: Salzmann Nodular Degeneration: Iron lines often encircle the base of the nodules.
Post-LASIK: Central iron lines may form due to the 'steep-to-flat' transition zone.
Intracorneal Ring Segments (ICRS): Iron deposits commonly form over the segments.
Filtering Blebs: Ferry's line indicates the mechanical barrier to the tear meniscus.
Radial Keratotomy (RK): Stellated iron lines can follow the incisional scars.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Sudden appearance of a Fleischer Ring in a previously stable eye (Progression!).
Pigment at Descemet's level (Suspect Wilson's Disease/Kayser-Fleischer).
Rust ring surrounding a foreign body (Requires surgical debridement).
Unilateral Hudson-Stahli line (Consider localized surface irregularity or trauma).
Iron line associated with epithelial breakdown or persistent defect.

content.explanation: F-leischer (Cone), S-tocker (Pterygium), H-udson (History/Age), F-erry (Filter/Bleb), L-iesegang (Lens/Ortho-K).

sections.title: Management & Clinical Pearls
content: Observation: Ocular iron lines themselves are asymptomatic and require no direct treatment.
Diagnostic Clue: Their presence helps confirm the location of corneal ectasia or the stability of a pterygium.
Corneal Topography: Always perform topography if a Fleischer ring is suspected to rule out subclinical keratoconus.
Surgical Note: During pterygium excision, Stocker's line does not need to be specifically removed; it usually resolves post-op.
Contact Lens Fitting: Iron lines can guide the placement of RGP lenses by identifying the 'base' of the corneal steepening.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Insights
sections.content: Recent studies using In-Vivo Confocal Microscopy (IVCM) have localized these deposits specifically to the cytoplasm of basal epithelial cells. Research into AI-driven slit lamp imaging is now focusing on the automated detection of the Fleischer ring as an early screening biomarker for keratoconus in pediatric populations, where topography may be difficult to obtain.

title: TOXOPLASMOSIS: THE FOCAL RETINITIS MASTERCLASS
summary: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular protozoan and the most common identifiable cause of focal retinitis worldwide. This comprehensive guide covers the lifecycle, clinical manifestations, and the 'classic' vs. modern management protocols for ocular toxoplasmosis.

data.title: TOXOPLASMOSIS: THE FOCAL RETINITIS MASTERCLASS
data.summary: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular protozoan and the most common identifiable cause of focal retinitis worldwide. This comprehensive guide covers the lifecycle, clinical manifestations, and the 'classic' vs. modern management protocols for ocular toxoplasmosis.

sections.title: The Pathogen & Global Burden
content: Causative Agent: Toxoplasma gondii (obligate intracellular protozoan).
Northern Temperate Countries: Estimated 10% adult infestation.
Mediterranean & Tropical Countries: Over 50% adult infestation.
Brazil: Responsible for up to 85% of posterior uveitis cases.
Global Posterior Uveitis: Accounts for 20–60% of all cases.
Primary Ocular Presentation: Average age of 29 years (likely due to decreasing immunity).

branches: Definitive Host: Cats (Oocysts excreted in faeces)
Intermediate Hosts: Humans, livestock, birds, rodents
Inactive Stage: Bradyzoite (Dormant in tissue cysts: eye, brain, skeletal muscle)
Active Form: Tachyzoite (Proliferating form released upon cyst rupture)
Transmission: Ingestion of contaminated water/soil, cat litter disposal, undercooked meat/eggs
Medical Transmission: Organ transplantation, Blood transfusion, Transplacental spread

rows: Often subclinical; 10% result in fetal death. 75%+ have retinochoroiditis. Severity depends on gestation duration (worse in early pregnancy).
Accounts for >50% of childhood cases. Usually subclinical. Ocular lesions may develop years later.
80–90% subclinical. Symptomatic: Cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise, pharyngitis. Retinitis in up to 20%.
Reactivation or acquired. Risks: Meningoencephalitis, pneumonitis, fulminant retinochoroiditis.

sections.title: Ocular Presentation & Symptoms
content: Symptoms: Unilateral acute/subacute floaters, blurring, and photophobia.
Spill-over Anterior Uveitis: Common; can be granulomatous or resemble FUS. Elevated IOP may occur.
Typical Lesion: Fluffy white retinitis associated with a pigmented 'satellite' scar.
Vitritis: Often severe. 'Headlight in the fog' appearance (inflammatory nidus viewed through vitreous haze).
Vasculitis: More commonly venous than arterial.
Optic Disc: Oedema is common.
Punctate Outer Retinal Toxoplasmosis: Small (25–75 μm) grey-white lesions in younger patients.
Neuroretinitis: Rare; marker of acutely acquired infection (mimics cat-scratch).

rows: More rapid progression, peripheral location, lack of adjacent pigmented scars (usually).
Can mimic any uveitis; 'ground glass' vitritis, positive treponemal serology.
Neuroretinitis with macular star; history of cat scratch/bite; negative Toxo serology.
Granulomatous uveitis, but usually lacks the focal necrotizing retinitis and satellite scar.
Multifocal 'fluff-balls' in vitreous; history of IV access/candidemia.

sections.title: Complications Leading to Vision Loss
content: Overall Risk: Permanent vision reduction in 25% of eyes.
Macular Pathology: Inflammatory lesions, oedema, and late secondary neovascularization.
Vascular: Retinal vascular occlusion (periarteritis).
Structural: Serous, rhegmatogenous, or tractional retinal detachment.
Optic Nerve: Involvement leading to atrophy.
Healing: Spontaneous resolution in 6–8 weeks (immunocompetent); vitreous takes longer.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: 1. Clinical Exam: Primary method of diagnosis.
2. Serology (IgG): Indicates past exposure; 1/3 community seroprevalence.
3. Serology (IgM): Indicates infection within 1 year; critical in pregnancy.
4. Goldmann–Witmer Coefficient: Ratio of specific IgG in aqueous vs. serum (48–90% sensitivity).
5. PCR Testing: Intraocular fluid; highly specific, variable sensitivity (16–67%).
6. Imaging (OCT/B-Scan): Monitor macular oedema or exclude RD in severe vitritis.
7. Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): Facilitates monitoring of inflammatory activity.

sections.title: Treatment Indications & Duration
content: General: Treatment is not always needed as spontaneous resolution occurs.
Sight-Threatening Lesion: Involving macula, papillomacular bundle, optic nerve, or major vessel.
Severe vitritis: Clear indication for therapy.
Immunocompromised Status: Always requires treatment.
Duration: Typically 4–6 weeks for antibiotics.
Healing Time: Active lesions take 4–6 months to heal completely.

content.explanation: Pyrimethamine (75-100mg load, then 25-50mg daily) + Sulfadiazine (1g QID) + Prednisolone (1mg/kg). ALWAYS add Folinic Acid (5mg 3x/week) to prevent marrow toxicity.

rows: Clindamycin (1mg) + Dexamethasone (400µg). 2-3 injections 2 weeks apart. Effective as triple therapy.
Trimethoprim 160mg / Sulfamethoxazole 800mg BID. Low cost, better tolerated.
250–500 mg daily. Shows promise in reducing recurrence rates.
300 mg QID. Risk of pseudomembranous colitis.
750 mg 2–4 times daily. Attacks encysted bradyzoites (theoretically).

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNINGS & CONTRAINDICATIONS
content: NEVER use depot steroids (e.g., triamcinolone) intra- or periocularly (uncontrolled progression reported).
Systemic steroids should be used with extreme caution in immunocompromised patients.
Pyrimethamine: Perform weekly blood counts (risk of thrombocytopenia/leukopenia).
Sulfonamides: Risk of Stevens–Johnson syndrome and renal stones.
AIDS Patients: Avoid or reduce pyrimethamine due to marrow suppression and zidovudine antagonism.
Pregnancy: Avoid pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine (fetal harm). Use Spiramycin or Intravitreal therapy.

sections.title: Recurrence & Long-term Management
content: Average Recurrences: 2.7 attacks per patient.
2-Year Risk: 12–15% recurrence rate.
5-Year Risk: Over 50% experience a further episode.
Prophylaxis Regimen: Co-trimoxazole (160/800) three times daily for 12 months.
Prophylaxis Benefit: Reduces recurrence from 22% to 3% for up to 3 years.
Neonatal Care: 1 year of antimicrobials in congenital cases may reduce future scarring.

content.explanation: Start steroids 24–48 hours AFTER starting antimicrobial therapy to ensure parasitic cover before dampening the immune response.

sections.title: Verbatim Figure Descriptions & Notes
sections.content: Fig 12.29 Life cycle includes oocysts in faeces, contaminated food/water/soil, transfusion, transplantation, and vertical transmission. Fig 12.30 identifies scars at the macula, peripapillary, upper temporal, and inferonasal periphery. Fig 12.31 illustrates 'satellite' lesions and 'headlight in the fog'. Fig 12.32 notes uncommon complications: Branch retinal artery occlusion, non-perfusion on FA, serous macular detachment, and macular neovascularization. Healing results in a sharply demarcated atrophic scar with a pigmented border (Fig 12.33). Children should undergo varicella zoster vaccination if they have not had chickenpox before starting steroids.

title: Behçet’s Disease: The Silk Road Vasculitis
summary: An idiopathic, chronic multisystem inflammatory disorder characterized by occlusive vasculitis of both arteries and veins. It is a sight-threatening condition requiring a multidisciplinary approach, most prevalent along the historic Silk Road.

data.title: Behçet’s Disease: The Silk Road Vasculitis
data.summary: An idiopathic, chronic multisystem inflammatory disorder characterized by occlusive vasculitis of both arteries and veins. It is a sight-threatening condition requiring a multidisciplinary approach, most prevalent along the historic Silk Road.

sections.title: Historical Context & Epidemiology
content: Possibly first recognized by Hippocrates.
Modern description: Adamantiades (Greek) and Behçet (Turkish).
Prevalence: Highest along the traditional 'Silk Road' route.
Turkey: Peaking at up to 0.4% of the population.
Demographics: Typically affects young adults (peak onset: third decade).
Geography: Lower prevalence in Europe and North America; high in Middle and Far East.
Mortality: Around 5% at 5–10 years, typically due to cardiovascular or CNS complications.
UK Care: Three National Centres of Excellence (Birmingham, Liverpool, London) established in 2012 for multidisciplinary care.

content.explanation: A transient, mobile hypopyon in a relatively 'white' eye is characteristic of Behçet disease and JIA-associated uveitis. Unlike HLA-B27, the eye is often not as injection-heavy during a hypopyon flare.

branches: Anterior: Acute non-granulomatous AAU, transient mobile hypopyon.
Vitreous: Severe vitritis (universal in active posterior disease), inflammatory deposits on inferior peripheral retina.
Retina: Transient superficial white infiltrates (no scarring), deep retinitis (viral-like), exudative detachments.
Vasculitis: Occlusive periphlebitis & arteritis (contrast to Sarcoid), sheathing, hemorrhages, CMO.
Optic Nerve: Hyperaemia, oedema (secondary to inflammation or raised ICP), atrophy.
End-Stage: Retinal/optic atrophy, attenuated 'ghost' vessels, gliosis, phthisis.

sections.title: Systemic Multi-Organ Involvement
content: Oral: Recurrent aphthous ulceration (scarring or non-scarring).
Genital: GU (Genital Ulceration).
Skin: Erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopustules, acneiform rash/nodules, Dermatographia.
Joints: Arthritis (mono or poly), though arthralgia is more common.
Vascular: Thromboses (Venous > Arterial), SVC/IVC obstruction, superficial thrombophlebitis, Aneurysms (pulmonary/coronary).
GI: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea (especially ileocecal).
CNS: Meningoencephalitis (brainstem), sinus thrombosis, intracranial hypertension, neuropathies.
Renal/Hepatic: Relatively uncommon.

rows: Recurrent Oral Ulceration (at least 3x in 12 months)
Usually unilateral, very red eye (not white), non-transient hypopyon.
Purely venous involvement (periphlebitis), granulomatous KPs (Behçet is non-granulomatous).
Rapidly progressive necrotizing herpetic retinitis; Behçet retinitis infiltrates may heal without scarring.
The 'Great Mimicker'; requires serology to rule out.
Also presents with hypopyon in a white eye, but usually in children/females with positive ANA.

sections.title: Investigation Workup
content: 1. Clinical Assessment: No specific diagnostic lab test exists.
2. Pathergy Test: Oblique 20g needle insertion; check for sterile pustule at 24–48h (>95% specific).
3. Lab Markers: ESR, CRP, Complement levels, WBC (often elevated).
4. Genetic Testing: HLA-B51 association.
5. Ocular Imaging: FA (delineates ischaemia/leakage), Laser Flare Photometry (correlates with activity).
6. Systemic Imaging: MRI/MRV Brain (Neuro), CT/CTA or MRA for aneurysms/thrombosis.
7. Screenings: Thrombophilia screening, TB screening (prior to biologics).

sections.title: Ophthalmic Complications
content: Cataract & Glaucoma (Steroid-induced or inflammatory)
Neovascularization (NVD/NVE) responding to ischemia
Vitreous Haemorrhage & Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD)
Cystoid Macular Oedema (CMO) and diffuse leakage
Optic Atrophy and Retinal Atrophy (End-stage)
Severe Vision Loss: 2/3 of males at 10 years (historical data)

sections.title: Management Protocols (EULAR/AUS)
sections.content: Liaise with a physician. Referral to National Centres is advised. SYSTEMIC STEROIDS: Initial Prednisolone 1–2mg/kg/d PO; Pulsed IV Methylprednisolone (1g/d for 3d) for acute flares. STEROID-SPARING AGENTS: Azathioprine (2.5 mg/kg daily), Ciclosporin (2–5 mg/kg daily), Mycophenolate Mofetil, Methotrexate, Tacrolimus. BIOLOGICS: Infliximab or Adalimumab (Anti-TNF) considered early for vision-threatening disease. INTERFERON-ALFA: Alternative for severe disease (do not combine with Azathioprine due to myelosuppression). NOTE: Topical steroids alone are rarely adequate. Intravitreal steroids carry a high risk of ocular hypertension.

sections.title: Critical Warnings
content: ANTICOAGULANTS ARE NOT RECOMMENDED.
Ciclosporine should be avoided in patients with CNS involvement (neurotoxicity risk).
Infliximab requires TB screening (risk of reactivation).
Visual loss rate in women is roughly half that in men.
Arterioles are affected later than veins in the retina.

title: Clinical Mastery: Congenital Eyelid Coloboma
summary: An in-depth guide to the identification, associations, and surgical management of congenital eyelid colobomas, focusing on ocular safety and functional restoration. This guide bridges core clinical questions with surgical pearls for the practicing ophthalmologist.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation & Diagnosis
sections.content: Scenario 1: 1. What does the picture show? The picture shows a coloboma of the upper eyelid where the eyelid is fused to the globe. 2. What is the diagnosis? Congenital Coloboma of the Eyelid (eyelid cleft or notch). Scenario 2: Q1: Describe the picture. (Note: Clinical diagnosis is consistent with Congenital Eyelid Coloboma, characterized by a full-thickness defect of the eyelid margin).

sections.title: Management & Monitoring
content: Step 1: Monitor infant for exposure keratopathy due to the eyelid defect.
Step 2: Perform surgical closure of the eyelid defect (required in most cases).
Step 3: For defects < 1/3 eyelid: Create raw vertical margins and slide flaps along the eyelid crease.
Step 4: Use lateral cantholysis if additional horizontal relaxation is needed.
Step 5: For large defects: Utilize a variation of the lateral canthal semicircular flap technique.
Step 6: Avoid eyelid-sharing procedures that occlude the visual axis to prevent amblyopia.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Red Flags
content: Exposure Keratopathy: High risk in infants with eyelid coloboma.
Amblyopia: Significant risk if visual axis is occluded.
True Coloboma Definition: Must involve a defect in the eyelid margin.
Surgical Priority: Protect the visual axis at all costs during reconstruction.

sections.title: Investigation Workup & Assessment
content: Complete ocular examination to rule out co-existing ocular colobomas.
Systemic assessment for facial clefts and syndrome screening (Goldenhar).
Assessment of lacrimal system patency, especially in lower lid defects.
Baseline corneal assessment for signs of drying or epithelial defects.

title: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK): The Limbal Battleground
summary: A crescent-shaped, destructive inflammation of the peripheral corneal stroma characterized by epithelial defect, stromal thinning, and inflammatory cell infiltration. Often a precursor to lethal systemic vasculitis, PUK requires urgent multidisciplinary intervention to prevent both ocular perforation and systemic morbidity.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK) is a serious inflammatory condition of the peripheral cornea. It is characterized by a crescentic 'juxtalimbal' ulceration with an overlying epithelial defect and stromal melting (lysis). Unlike simple marginal keratitis, PUK involves the destruction of the corneal collagen matrix and is frequently driven by an underlying systemic autoimmune process.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Limbal Microenvironment
content: Step 1: Systemic circulating immune complexes (Type III Hypersensitivity) or Autoantibodies (Type II) reach the limbal vasculature.
Step 2: Pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1) upregulate adhesion molecules on limbal vessel endothelium.
Step 3: Massive recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages to the peripheral corneal stroma.
Step 4: Release of Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMP-1, MMP-2, MMP-9) and collagenases from the limbal conjunctiva and inflammatory cells.
Step 5: Rapid degradation of corneal Type 1 Collagen, leading to stromal melting and crescentic thinning.

rows: Vasculitis of the episcleral and limbal vessels.
Necrotizing vasculitis of small and medium-sized arteries.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Intense ocular pain (often deep and boring, radiating to forehead).
Severe photophobia and lacrimation.
Decreased visual acuity (if visual axis involved or high astigmatism).
Crescent-shaped peripheral stromal thinning.
Active epithelial defect at the leading edge of the ulcer.
Associated scleritis or episcleritis (in 30-40% of cases).
Significant conjunctival and limbal injection.

branches: Type I: Benign, Unilateral, Elderly, Responds to local therapy
Type II: Malignant, Bilateral, Young (esp. African/Asian), Progressive
Diagnosis of Exclusion: NO systemic autoimmune disease

sections.title: Ocular Examination Checklist
content: Slit-Lamp: Assess depth of thinning (Descemetocele check).
Fluorescein: Map size of epithelial defect and undermining edges.
Scleral Exam: Check for 'bluish' hue (thinning) or necrotizing scleritis.
Gonioscopy: Evaluate for iris incarceration if perforation is suspected.
Imaging: AS-OCT to quantify residual stromal thickness precisely.

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Full Physical Exam: Check skin, joints, nose/throat, and lungs.
2. Blood Panel: CBC, ESR, CRP, RF, Anti-CCP.
3. Autoimmune Serology: ANA, ANCA (c-ANCA and p-ANCA).
4. Renal/Heme: Urinalysis (hematuria/proteinuria), Creatinine.
5. Imaging: Chest X-ray or CT Chest (look for GPA cavities).

rows: SLE or other connective tissue diseases

sections.title: Systemic Management Protocol
content: Induction: Oral Prednisone (1mg/kg/day) or IV Methylprednisolone pulse if impending perforation.
Steroid-Sparing Agents: Methotrexate (15-25mg/week), Azathioprine, or Mycophenolate Mofetil.
Biologic Therapy: Rituximab (anti-CD20) is now 1st line for GPA-associated PUK.
TNF Inhibitors: Infliximab or Adalimumab for refractory RA cases.
Monitoring: Co-management with Rheumatology for bone protection and marrow suppression.

sections.title: Ocular Management & Surgery
content: Preservative-free lubricants and topical antibiotics (prophylaxis).
Topical Medroxyprogesterone or Acetylcysteine (Collagenase inhibitors).
Avoid topical steroids (can accelerate melting/perforation).
Cyanoacrylate Tissue Adhesive: For microperforations < 2mm.
Amniotic Membrane Grafting (AMT): Multilayer for tectonic support.
Crescentic Lamellar Keratoplasty: For severe thinning/structural loss.

sections.title: Red Flags & Critical Signs
content: Descemetocele: Imminent perforation (looks like a clear bubble in the ulcer).
Positive Seidel Test: Indicates full-thickness corneal perforation.
Necrotizing Scleritis: Severe associated scleral thinning and 'melting'.
Sudden loss of pain: Can paradoxically indicate total corneal anesthesia or perforation.
Unexplained Weight Loss/Hemoptysis: Suggests systemic vasculitis mortality risk.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Corneal Perforation & Endophthalmitis.
Secondary Glaucoma (inflammatory or steroid-induced).
Severe irregular astigmatism and corneal scarring.
Systemic Mortality: Untreated PUK in GPA has a 5-year mortality rate > 50%.
Cataract formation (due to chronic inflammation/steroids).

content.explanation: L: Limbal involvement, I: Inflammatory (Severe), M: Melting (Stromal), I: Immune-mediated (Systemic), T: Tectonic compromise.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Topical steroids are usually 'The Enemy' in PUK—they inhibit collagen synthesis and promote melting.
The limbal conjunctiva is the source of collagenases; surgical recession of the conjunctiva can sometimes slow the melt.
PUK may be the very first sign of a fatal systemic disease—treat the 'Eye as a Window' to the patient's survival.
Always check the nose and ears! GPA and Relapsing Polychondritis have distinct extraocular signs.

title: Bilateral Disc Swelling: A Comprehensive Clinical Masterclass
summary: Bilateral optic disc edema is a critical clinical finding requiring urgent differentiation between life-threatening papilledema (elevated ICP) and sight-threatening inflammatory or vascular etiologies. This guide provides an evidence-based framework for diagnosis, grading, and management according to AAO BCSC and Kanski standards.

branches: Mechanical: High ICP transmitted via CSF in the optic nerve sheath
Vascular: Microvascular ischemia and capillary leakage at the nerve head
Orthograde Stasis: Accumulation of mitochondria and organelles in the pre-laminar space
True Papilledema: ONLY used for swelling secondary to increased Intracranial Pressure (ICP)

rows: Clear margins; physiological cup visible; no NFL blurring.
C-shaped halo of blurring (temporal gap); disruption of NFL bundles.
Circumferential (360°) halo; no obscuration of major retinal vessels.
Obscuration of one or more major retinal vessels as they leave the disc.
Total obscuration of the central cup and major vessels on the disc.
Dome-shaped protrusion; narrow/missing vessels; Paton's lines (circumferential folds).

content.explanation: C: Contraceptives/Corticosteroids (withdrawal); A: All-trans retinoic acid (Vitamin A); N: Nitrofurantoin/Nalidixic acid; T: Tetracyclines (Minocycline/Doxycycline).

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Headache (90%): Often worse in morning or with Valsalva.
Transient Visual Obscurations (TVOs): Seconds-long graying out, often postural.
Pulsatile Tinnitus: Whooshing sound synchronous with heartbeat.
Diplopia: Horizontal, usually due to CN VI (Abducens) palsy (false localizing sign).
Photopsias: Flashing lights even without retinal traction.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Disc Hyperemia: Capillary dilation on the disc surface.
Splinter (SVP) Hemorrhages: Located at or near the disc margin.
Cotton Wool Spots: Indicative of acute nerve fiber layer ischemia.
Paton's Lines: Circumferential retinal folds temporal to the disc.
Loss of Spontaneous Venous Pulsation (SVP): Present in 20% of normal pop, but absence + swelling suggests high ICP (>200 mmH2O).

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Rapid, progressive visual field loss or declining visual acuity.
Presence of focal neurological deficits (e.g., hemiparesis, ataxia).
New-onset seizure activity.
Macular star formation (Neuroretinitis) - though usually unilateral, can be bilateral.
Severe 'Thunderclap' headache (R/O Subarachnoid Hemorrhage).

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Urgent Neuroimaging (MRI Brain + MRV) to R/O mass or Venous Sinus Thrombosis.
Step 2: Lumbar Puncture (LP) in lateral decubitus position (ONLY after imaging).
Step 3: Measure Opening Pressure (Normal <250 mmH2O in adults).
Step 4: CSF Analysis (Protein, Glucose, Cytology, Culture) to R/O meningitis/sarcoid.
Step 5: Automated Perimetry (SITA-Standard 24-2) to baseline visual field loss.

sections.title: Evidence-Based Management (IIHTT)
content: Weight Loss: 6-10% of total body weight is often curative.
Acetazolamide (Diamox): Start 500mg BID; max 4g/day. Side effects: Paresthesia, dysgeusia (metallic carbonated drinks).
Topiramate: Second-line; provides migraine prophylaxis and mild carbonic anhydrase inhibition.
Furosemide: Adjunctive diuretic if Acetazolamide is not tolerated.
Serial Visual Fields: Monthly follow-up in active phase.

branches: Optic Nerve Sheath Decompression (ONSD): Best for progressive vision loss despite meds.
CSF Shunting (VP or LP Shunt): Best for refractory headache + vision loss.
Venous Sinus Stenting: For patients with significant transverse sinus stenosis.
Bariatric Surgery: Highly effective for long-term IIH remission.

sections.title: Landmark Study: The IIHTT
sections.content: The Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Treatment Trial (IIHTT) confirmed that for mild visual loss, the combination of Acetazolamide and a low-sodium weight-reduction diet resulted in greater improvement in visual field function and quality of life compared to diet alone. It standardized the starting dose at 1g/day, titrating up to 4g/day as tolerated.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Pitfalls
content: Always check Blood Pressure: Malignant Hypertension is a common mimic of papilledema.
OCT GCL Analysis: Ganglion Cell Layer thinning is a better predictor of permanent axonal loss than RNFL in chronic cases.
Pregnancy: Acetazolamide is generally avoided in the 1st trimester but can be used after 20 weeks if vision is threatened.
Foster-Kennedy Syndrome: Unilateral disc edema with contralateral optic atrophy (Frontal lobe tumor).

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Pre-pubertal IIH: No strong gender predilection and less correlation with obesity.
Common Triggers: Recombinant growth hormone, tetracycline, or Vitamin A therapy.
Opening Pressure: Normal limit is slightly higher (up to 280 mmH2O) in children.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Secondary Optic Atrophy: Results from chronic untreated swelling; irreversible vision loss.
Subretinal Neovascular Membranes: Rare complication of chronic disc edema.
Recurrence: 10-20% risk, especially with weight regain.
Macular Pigmentary Changes: Can occur after resolution of severe swelling.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis & The Eye: A Comprehensive Ophthalmic Perspective
summary: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease primarily affecting joints, but its ocular manifestations are diverse and vision-threatening, ranging from common dry eye to severe necrotizing scleritis and peripheral ulcerative keratitis. Ophthalmologists play a critical role in diagnosis, monitoring, and management to prevent irreversible vision loss.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic inflammatory autoimmune disease primarily characterized by symmetrical polyarthritis, leading to progressive joint destruction, deformity, and functional impairment. It predominantly affects small joints of the hands and feet. Beyond articular involvement, RA frequently manifests with extra-articular features, including significant ocular involvement, which can range from benign conditions like dry eye to severe, vision-threatening scleritis or peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK).

sections.title: 2.1 Epidemiological Details
content: **Prevalence:** ~0.5-1% of the adult population worldwide.
**Incidence:** Varies geographically, typically 20-50 cases per 100,000 adults per year.
**Demographics:** Predominantly affects women (female:male ratio 2-3:1).
**Age of Onset:** Most common between 40-60 years.
**Risk Factors:** Genetic predisposition (HLA-DRB1 alleles, especially shared epitope), smoking, obesity, periodontal disease, certain infections (e.g., Porphyromonas gingivalis), silica exposure.

rows: Most common. Aqueous tear deficiency (secondary Sjögren's Syndrome) or evaporative dry eye (MGD).
Mild to Moderate; can cause corneal complications if severe.
Benign, self-limiting inflammation of the episclera. Sectoral or diffuse redness, mild discomfort.
Severe, painful inflammation of the sclera. Can be anterior (diffuse, nodular, necrotizing) or posterior.
Crescentic stromal thinning and ulceration at the limbus, often associated with active scleritis. Can lead to corneal perforation.
Severe; high risk of perforation and vision loss.
Less common than in other spondyloarthropathies, but can occur.
Mild to Moderate; can lead to synechiae, glaucoma.
Inflammation of retinal or choroidal vessels, leading to occlusions, ischemia.
Severe; high risk of vision loss.
Macular toxicity (bull's eye maculopathy) from long-term hydroxychloroquine use.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms (Ocular Focus)
content: **KCS:** Foreign body sensation, burning, stinging, gritty feeling, photophobia, blurred vision (fluctuating), increased reflex tearing followed by dryness.
**Episcleritis:** Acute onset mild redness, localized tenderness, mild discomfort (not severe pain), no significant vision change. Vessels blanch with phenylephrine.

**Scleritis (Anterior):** Severe, deep, boring pain radiating to brow/temple/jaw, tenderness to palpation, intense violaceous redness (non-blanching with phenylephrine), photophobia, lacrimation, decreased vision. Nodular type shows elevated, immobile nodule. Necrotizing type shows avascular patches, scleral thinning, potentially globe perforation.
**Scleritis (Posterior):** Often painless or vague orbital pain, proptosis, diplopia, reduced vision, serous retinal detachment, choroidal folds, disc edema, macular edema.
**PUK:** Severe pain, redness, photophobia, rapid decrease in vision, crescentic ulceration at the limbus, often with an epithelial defect and stromal melt. Can be sterile or secondarily infected.
**Anterior Uveitis:** Pain, photophobia, redness (circumlimbal flush), blurred vision, floaters.
**Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy:** Asymptomatic early, paracentral scotomas, eventually central vision loss. Visual field defects (10-2), color vision changes.

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **KCS:** Decreased tear meniscus height, conjunctival injection, punctate epithelial erosions (fluorescein stain), positive Rose Bengal or Lissamine Green staining (conjunctival/corneal epithelial damage), reduced tear break-up time (TBUT <10s).
**Episcleritis:** Sectoral or diffuse redness, engorged episcleral vessels (move with conjunctival manipulation), easily blanch with 2.5% topical phenylephrine.

**Scleritis (Anterior):** Violaceous hue of sclera (non-blanching with phenylephrine), edema, vessel engorgement. Nodular: firm, tender, immobile scleral nodule. Necrotizing: areas of scleral thinning (blueish discoloration of underlying choroid), avascular patches, potentially exposed uvea, impending perforation.

**Scleritis (Posterior):** Normal anterior segment. Fundoscopy: disc edema, choroidal folds, serous retinal detachment, macular edema. B-scan ultrasonography is diagnostic: 'T-sign' (fluid in Tenon's capsule, thickening of choroid/sclera).
**PUK:** Ciliary injection, perilimbal crescentic corneal thinning/ulceration, epithelial defect, underlying stromal infiltrate. May see exposed Descemet's membrane, iris prolapse if perforated.
**Anterior Uveitis:** Keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cell and flare, posterior synechiae, iris nodules, band keratopathy, raised intraocular pressure.
**Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy:** Early: subtle RPE mottling. Late: classic 'bull's eye' maculopathy (ring of RPE atrophy surrounding a relatively spared fovea).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **1. Systemic Evaluation (Rheumatologist Referral):** Confirm RA diagnosis. Obtain detailed history of joint symptoms, systemic involvement.

**2. Serological Tests:**
    - Rheumatoid Factor (RF): Positive in 70-80% (non-specific).
    - Anti-cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (Anti-CCP) antibodies: Highly specific for RA (95-98%), prognostically significant.
    - Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) & C-Reactive Protein (CRP): Elevated during active inflammation.

**3. Ocular Surface Tests (for KCS):**
    - Schirmer's Test: <10mm wetting in 5 minutes (without anesthesia for basal secretion, with for reflex).
    - Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT): <10 seconds.
    - Ocular Surface Staining: Fluorescein (corneal epithelial defects), Lissamine Green/Rose Bengal (conjunctival & corneal devitalized cells).

**4. Imaging for Scleritis/PUK:**
    - B-scan Ultrasonography: Essential for posterior scleritis ('T-sign', choroidal thickening, fluid in Tenon's).
    - UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy): High-resolution imaging of anterior segment, useful for anterior scleritis extent.
    - OCT: Retinal/choroidal changes in posterior scleritis, early HCQ retinopathy (parafoveal RPE/photoreceptor atrophy).
**5. Visual Field Testing:** 10-2 visual field for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy screening (early paracentral scotomas).
**6. Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF):** Used in HCQ screening, shows RPE atrophy.
**7. Angiography (FFA/ICG):** In rare cases of retinal vasculitis.

sections.title: 8. Differential Diagnosis of Ocular Inflammation in RA Patients

rows: Primary Sjögren's, age-related, meibomian gland dysfunction, contact lens wear, medications, environmental factors.
Often idiopathic, but can be associated with RA
Idiopathic, other systemic inflammatory diseases (IBD, lupus), infection.
Strong association with severe RA (necrotizing type)
Systemic vasculitides (GPA, PAN), Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus, syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, post-surgical.
Other systemic vasculitides (GPA), Mooren's ulcer, infection (Herpes Simplex/Zoster, bacterial/fungal), trauma.
Less common than in other SpA, but can occur
Ankylosing Spondylitis, Psoriatic Arthritis, JIA, sarcoidosis, Behcet's, infection, idiopathic.
Lupus, Behcet's, sarcoidosis, multiple sclerosis, infections (CMV, syphilis).

sections.title: 9. Staging/Grading (Ocular Specificity)
content: **RA Disease Activity:** Assessed by rheumatologist using tools like DAS28 (Disease Activity Score 28), CDAI (Clinical Disease Activity Index) which guide systemic therapy.
**KCS Severity:** Graded by symptoms (OSDI), Schirmer's, staining patterns.

**Scleritis Grading:** 
    - **Anatomical:** Anterior (diffuse, nodular, necrotizing), Posterior.
    - **Inflammatory:** Active, quiescent.
    - **Severity:** Mild (diffuse/nodular anterior), Severe (necrotizing, posterior, PUK).

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment (Ocular RA)
content:
**1. Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca (KCS):**
    - **Initial:** Preservative-free artificial tears (e.g., Refresh Optive, Systane Ultra) q2-4h.
    - **Moderate:** Topical cyclosporine 0.05% (Restasis) BID or 0.09% (Cequa) BID; topical lifitegrast 5% (Xiidra) BID.
    - **Severe:** Punctal plugs (silicone or collagen), topical corticosteroids (e.g., loteprednol 0.2% BID for short courses), amniotic membranes, autologous serum tears, oral omega-3 fatty acids.

**2. Episcleritis:**
    - **Mild:** Usually self-limiting. Cool compresses, topical NSAIDs (e.g., Ketorolac 0.4% QID).
    - **Persistent:** Mild topical corticosteroids (e.g., Loteprednol 0.2% BID-QID) for short duration, oral NSAIDs (e.g., Ibuprofen 400-600mg TID).

**3. Scleritis (Anterior Diffuse/Nodular):**
    - **Systemic NSAIDs:** First-line. Indomethacin 25-50mg TID-QID, Naproxen 250-500mg BID, Flurbiprofen 100mg TID. Full trial for 2-3 weeks.
    - **Systemic Corticosteroids:** If NSAIDs fail or severe. Prednisone 1mg/kg/day (max 60-80mg/day), then slowly taper.

**4. Scleritis (Necrotizing / Posterior) & PUK:**
    - **Urgent Immunosuppression:** This is an ocular emergency.
        - **High-dose Systemic Corticosteroids:** Prednisone 1mg/kg/day (up to 80mg/day) for several weeks, then taper.
        - **Immunomodulatory Therapy (DMARDs):** Often initiated concurrently. Methotrexate (7.5-25mg/week), Azathioprine (1-3mg/kg/day), Mycophenolate Mofetil (1-2g/day), Cyclosporine (2.5-5mg/kg/day).
        - **Biologics:** If refractory to conventional DMARDs. TNF-α inhibitors (e.g., Infliximab, Adalimumab, Etanercept), Rituximab (anti-CD20), Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R), Abatacept (CTLA-4-Ig). Selection based on systemic RA control and specific ocular manifestation.
    - **Topical Corticosteroids:** *Cautious use for PUK.* May worsen corneal melt unless combined with strong systemic immunosuppression. Prednisolone acetate 1% (QID-hourly) can be used, but risks must be weighed.

**5. Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy:**
    - **Discontinuation of HCQ:** If retinopathy is confirmed, stop medication immediately to prevent progression.
    - **Regular Screening:** Annual screening after 5 years of use (or earlier if high risk - >5mg/kg/day, renal disease, concomitant tamoxifen use). Includes SD-OCT (parafoveal outer retinal thinning), 10-2 visual fields, FAF.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques (Ocular RA)
content:
**1. Corneal Perforation (PUK):**
    - **Cyanoacrylate Glue Application:** For small perforations (<3mm) to seal the defect and allow healing.
    - **Lamellar or Penetrating Keratoplasty:** For larger perforations or extensive corneal melt. May require tectonic patch graft (donor sclera, cornea, fascia lata) to restore structural integrity.
    - **Amniotic Membrane Transplant:** Can aid in surface healing and reduce inflammation.
**2. Punctal Occlusion:** Punctal plugs (silicone or dissolvable collagen) for severe KCS.
**3. Cataract Surgery:** For steroid-induced cataracts, typically phacoemulsification with IOL implantation.
**4. Glaucoma Surgery:** For steroid-induced or uveitic glaucoma (trabeculectomy, glaucoma drainage device) if medically uncontrolled.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Scleritis:** Scleral thinning, staphyloma formation, anterior uveitis, glaucoma, cataract, globe perforation (especially necrotizing type). Vision loss is a significant risk.
**PUK:** Corneal perforation, secondary infection, irregular astigmatism, permanent vision loss, globe loss (rare).
**KCS:** Chronic discomfort, recurrent corneal erosions, infectious keratitis, corneal scarring, vision impairment.
**Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy:** Irreversible central vision loss if not detected and medication stopped early.
**General:** Poorly controlled systemic RA increases risk of severe ocular complications. Early diagnosis and aggressive systemic immunosuppression improve ocular prognosis.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Severe, Deep Boring Ocular Pain:** Highly suggestive of scleritis, especially if unresponsive to topical analgesics.
**Violaceous Redness of the Sclera (Non-blanching):** Pathognomonic for scleritis.
**Scleral Thinning / Avascular Patches:** Indicates necrotizing scleritis, high risk of perforation.
**Crescentic Perilimbal Corneal Ulceration (PUK):** Imminent risk of corneal perforation and globe loss.
**Sudden Decrease in Vision, Diplopia, Proptosis (without anterior segment inflammation):** Suggests posterior scleritis, requiring urgent investigation.
**New or Worsening Visual Field Defects (especially paracentral):** May indicate hydroxychloroquine retinopathy progression, necessitating drug cessation.

content.explanation: **S**cleritis, **C**orneal involvement (PUK), **R**etinal involvement, **A**queous tear deficiency (KCS), **P**osterior Scleritis, **D**rug toxicity. This helps remember the key ocular manifestations.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Scleritis pain is often worse at night and wakes patients from sleep.
Differentiating episcleritis (blanches with phenylephrine) from scleritis (does not blanch) is crucial.
Necrotizing scleritis and PUK are true ocular emergencies requiring prompt and aggressive systemic immunosuppression, often with a rheumatologist.
Always inquire about systemic symptoms (joint pain, stiffness, fatigue) in patients presenting with unexplained recurrent or severe ocular inflammation.
Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy is irreversible; emphasize meticulous screening and patient education.
B-scan ultrasonography is indispensable for diagnosing posterior scleritis and orbital inflammation.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent advances in RA management, particularly the development of biologics (e.g., TNF-α inhibitors like Infliximab, Adalimumab; IL-6 receptor blockers like Tocilizumab; B-cell inhibitors like Rituximab), have significantly improved systemic disease control and, consequently, reduced the incidence and severity of severe ocular complications like scleritis and PUK. The **AAO guidelines for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy screening (2016, updated 2021)** have standardized surveillance, emphasizing SD-OCT and 10-2 visual fields as primary screening tools, leading to earlier detection and prevention of severe vision loss. Ongoing research focuses on personalized medicine approaches, including identifying biomarkers for predicting ocular involvement and response to specific therapies.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA):** The most common systemic rheumatic disease in children, with significant ocular involvement.

**Chronic Anterior Uveitis:** Most frequent ocular manifestation in JIA, often asymptomatic, bilateral, and non-granulomatous. Can lead to irreversible vision loss from band keratopathy, posterior synechiae, cataract, glaucoma, and macular edema.

**Screening for Uveitis in JIA:** All children with JIA require regular ophthalmic screening (slit-lamp examination) by an ophthalmologist, even in the absence of symptoms. Frequency depends on age of onset, specific JIA subtype (oligoarticular is highest risk), and presence of ANA antibodies.
**Treatment in JIA:** Topical corticosteroids are first-line for uveitis flares. Systemic immunosuppression (methotrexate, biologics) is often required for persistent or severe uveitis.

sections.title: Sclerotic Scatter: Step-by-Step Technique
content: Step 1: Darken the exam room completely.
Step 2: Decouple the slit-lamp beam from the microscope.
Step 3: Direct a bright, narrow slit beam (2-3mm wide) onto the limbus.
Step 4: Ensure the light undergoes Total Internal Reflection through the cornea.
Step 5: Observe the cornea from the side (naked eye) or through the oculars at low magnification.
Step 6: Look for a 'Glow' or 'Halo' at the opposite limbus (indicating a clear cornea).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Sclerotic Scatter: Reveals subtle microcystic edema often missed by direct focal illumination.
Sclerotic Scatter: Identifies 'Sattler’s Veil' (epithelial edema due to hypoxia or high IOP).
Specular Microscopy: Visualizes 'Guttata' (dark non-reflective spots on the mosaic).
Specular Microscopy: Detects 'Intracellular vacuoles' or 'Snail tracks' in trauma/inflammation.
Both: Crucial for pre-operative assessment of Fuchs' Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD).

rows: Usually normal mosaic adjacent to scar
Often impossible to image due to scattering

sections.title: Red Flags: Endothelial Decompensation Signs
content: ECD < 500 cells/mm²: High risk for permanent corneal edema (Bullous Keratopathy).
CV > 0.40: Significant instability of the endothelial pump.
Pachymetry > 640 μm: High suspicion of clinical edema regardless of clarity.
Sclerotic Scatter: Visualization of 'striae' (Descemet's folds) indicates deep stromal edema.
Epithelial Bullae: End-stage endothelial failure.

sections.title: Surgical Decision Algorithm
content: 1. Perform Sclerotic Scatter: If haze is present, quantify with Specular Microscopy.
2. Assess ECD: If >1500, proceed with routine phacoemulsification.
3. Assess ECD: If 1000-1500, use 'soft-shell' viscoelastic technique and low ultrasound energy.
4. Assess ECD: If <800 OR CCT >620um, consider combined Phaco-DMEK/DSAEK (Triple Procedure).

content.explanation: P: Polymegethism (CV < 0.30); H: Hexagonality (> 60%); D: Density (> 2000 cells/mm²).

sections.title: Recent Advances: AI & Cell Imaging
content: Automated AI segmentation: Reduces manual marking errors in low-density counts.
Wide-field Specular Microscopy: Images larger areas to detect peripheral cell loss.
NICE Study Insights: Endothelial cell loss is highest in the first 3 months post-op.
Cell-Injection Therapy: Potential future replacement for DMEK/DSAEK.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Sclerotic scatter is the most sensitive 'quick' clinical screen for early Fuch's dystrophy.
If you see a 'black hole' on specular microscopy that isn't a guttata, consider a leukocyte or pigment clump.
Specular microscopy requires a clear cornea; if the cornea is too edematous, use Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT) instead.
Always adjust the patient's fixation to image the central, superior, and inferior endothelium separately.
A 'Hard' cataract requires more energy; if ECD is low, prioritize laser-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS) to protect the endothelium.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
sections.content: In children, ECD is significantly higher (often >3500 cells/mm²). Sclerotic scatter is vital in pediatric glaucoma cases to monitor for 'Haab Striae' or corneal enlargement (buphthalmos). Specular microscopy in children often requires hand-held units or sedation due to fixation requirements.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Corneal Macular Dystrophy (CMD, Groenouw type II) is a rare, bilateral, slowly progressive, autosomal recessive inherited disorder of the cornea. It is characterized by the accumulation of mucopolysaccharide (specifically keratan sulfate) deposits within the corneal stromal keratocytes, Bowman's layer, Descemet's membrane, and endothelium. This leads to diffuse grey-white opacification of the central and then peripheral cornea, significantly impairing visual acuity and often necessitating corneal transplantation.

sections.title: Epidemiology Details
content: **Incidence:** Extremely rare, estimated to be <1 per 100,000.
**Prevalence:** No specific racial or geographic predilection, found worldwide.
**Age of Onset:** Typically presents in the first decade of life (often by age 3-5), with progressive vision loss throughout childhood and adolescence.
**Risk Factors:** Exclusively genetic (autosomal recessive inheritance).

sections.title: 3. Etiology & Pathophysiology
sections.content: CMD is caused by mutations in the *carbohydrate sulfotransferase 6* (*CHST6*) gene, located on chromosome 16q22. Mutations in *CHST6* lead to a deficiency of corneal N-acetylglucosamine-6-sulfotransferase, an enzyme critical for the sulfation of keratan sulfate (a major corneal glycosaminoglycan). This enzymatic defect results in the production of abnormally sulfated or unsulfated keratan sulfate. These altered GAGs cannot be properly secreted by corneal keratocytes and accumulate intracellularly, forming characteristic electron-dense deposits throughout the corneal stroma, Bowman's layer, and even within endothelial cells. The accumulation of these insoluble GAGs disrupts corneal transparency and leads to progressive opacification and vision loss.

branches: Historically: Type I (systemic keratan sulfate not excreted)
Historically: Type II (systemic keratan sulfate excreted)

sections.title: Historical Classification Note
content: Historically, CMD was classified into Type I and Type II based on the absence or presence of sulfated keratan sulfate in serum and urine.
**Type I:** No detectable keratan sulfate in serum/urine. More severe phenotype.
**Type II:** Detectable keratan sulfate in serum/urine. Often a milder phenotype.

This distinction is less clinically relevant now due to direct *CHST6* genetic testing, which identifies the underlying cause regardless of systemic keratan sulfate levels. All forms are now understood to be allelic variants of *CHST6*.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Progressive Vision Loss:** Typically noticed in early childhood (ages 3-9), worsening over time.
**Photophobia:** Sensitivity to light, often severe.
**Glare:** Significant visual discomfort in bright light conditions.
**Blurred Vision:** Constant and worsening visual acuity impairment.
**Tearing (Epiphora):** Due to corneal irritation and irregular surface.
**Foreign Body Sensation:** Can occur due to epithelial irregularities.
**Pain:** Less common in early stages, but can develop with secondary epithelial breakdown or erosions.

rows: **Stromal Opacities:** Diffuse, grey-white, poorly demarcated, granular opacities scattered throughout the entire corneal stroma from limbus to limbus, though often more concentrated centrally initially. In contrast to granular dystrophy, the cornea between the opacities is NOT clear. Opacities extend full-thickness.
**Corneal Thinning:** Progressive, often severe thinning, especially noticeable in later stages. Mean central corneal thickness (CCT) can be significantly reduced (e.g., <450 µm).
**Bowman's Layer:** Deposits present, can be irregular.
**Descemet's Membrane & Endothelium:** Accumulation of GAGs in Descemet's membrane and within endothelial cells, leading to endothelial dysfunction and secondary edema in advanced stages.
Reduced central and peripheral corneal thickness.
Hyper-reflective deposits throughout the stroma, visible thinning, epithelial irregularities.
Highly reflective intracellular deposits within keratocytes, visible changes in endothelial cells.
Typically unremarkable, as CMD is purely a corneal disorder.

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic Examination:** Detailed history of vision loss, photophobia, glare; slit-lamp biomicroscopy to observe characteristic diffuse stromal opacities.
**Step 2: Corneal Pachymetry:** Measure central and peripheral corneal thickness (often thinned).
**Step 3: Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT):** Visualize corneal layers, extent of opacification, and confirm thinning.
**Step 4: Confocal Microscopy:** Identify highly reflective intracellular deposits in keratocytes and endothelial cells, aiding in differentiating from other dystrophies.
**Step 5: Genetic Testing (Confirmatory):** Analysis of the *CHST6* gene for known pathogenic mutations. This is the definitive diagnostic test.

**Step 6: Histopathology (if corneal tissue available, e.g., post-keratoplasty):** Light microscopy reveals numerous electron-dense inclusions within keratocytes. Alcian blue staining confirms GAG accumulation. Electron microscopy shows vacuolar degeneration and intracellular deposits.

rows: Autosomal dominant, discrete 'crumb-like' opacities with clear intervening stroma, usually superficial to mid-stroma. Deposits are hyaline, not GAGs. TGFBI gene.
Autosomal dominant, 'lattice-like' branching linear amyloid deposits, often associated with recurrent epithelial erosions. Deposits are amyloid, not GAGs. TGFBI gene.
Autosomal dominant, central crystalline (cholesterol) deposits, arcus lipoides, often associated with systemic hyperlipidemia. UBIAD1 gene.
Congenital flattening of cornea, not progressive opacification. Associated with other anterior segment anomalies.
Systemic involvement (skeletal, neurological, cardiac). Corneal clouding is diffuse but often less dense than CMD and is a part of a multi-system disorder. Different gene mutations.
Diffuse corneal edema and clouding from birth or early infancy, primarily affecting the endothelium. No discrete stromal deposits like CMD. SLC4A11 gene.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Grading
sections.content:
While there is no formal universally adopted staging system like TNM for cancer, CMD progression can be clinically described:

*   **Early Stage:** Mild central stromal opacities, good visual acuity, minimal symptoms. Detected in early childhood.
*   **Intermediate Stage:** Increasing density and extent of opacities, moderate vision loss (e.g., 20/50 to 20/200), photophobia, glare. Corneal thinning may be present.
*   **Advanced Stage:** Severe, diffuse corneal opacification extending to the limbus, significant vision loss (<20/200, often count fingers or hand motion), pronounced corneal thinning, potential for recurrent erosions or secondary edema. Often requires corneal transplantation.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Algorithm
content: **Step 1: Conservative Management (Early/Mild Disease):**
*   **Spectacle Correction:** For refractive error.
*   **Lubricating Eye Drops/Ointments:** To alleviate dryness and surface irritation (e.g., sodium hyaluronate 0.1-0.3%, carboxymethylcellulose 0.5-1%).
*   **Glare Control:** Tinted spectacles or sunglasses to manage photophobia and glare.
*   **Low Vision Aids:** As vision deteriorates.
**Step 2: Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK) (Limited Role):**
*   **Indication:** Superficial opacities *only* where visual axis is significantly affected, and corneal thickness allows adequate residual stroma.
*   **Procedure:** Excimer laser (e.g., 193 nm ArF) ablation of anterior corneal opacities.
*   **Limitations:** High recurrence rate as deposits are stromal and diffuse; often temporary improvement; risk of haze.
**Step 3: Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) (Preferred for Deeper Stromal Disease):**
*   **Indication:** Opacities primarily confined to the stroma with a healthy Descemet's membrane and endothelium.
*   **Procedure:** Selective transplantation of donor stroma, preserving recipient Descemet's membrane and endothelium. 'Big Bubble' technique (Melles, Anwar) often used.
*   **Advantages:** Lower risk of endothelial graft rejection, faster visual recovery, better long-term survival compared to PKP.
**Step 4: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) (Full-Thickness Disease/Endothelial Involvement):**
*   **Indication:** Advanced disease with full-thickness corneal involvement, significant thinning, or endothelial dysfunction.
*   **Procedure:** Full-thickness replacement of the host cornea with a donor cornea.
*   **Limitations:** Higher risk of endothelial rejection, suture-related complications, astigmatism.
**Step 5: Post-Operative Management (All Surgical):**
*   **Topical Corticosteroids:** To prevent graft rejection (e.g., Prednisolone acetate 1% q.i.d. tapered over months to years).
*   **Antibiotics:** Prophylactic (e.g., fluoroquinolones) post-surgery.
*   **Close Monitoring:** For graft clarity, rejection, infection, glaucoma, astigmatism.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Graft Rejection:** Endothelial rejection (for PKP) or stromal rejection (less common in DALK).

**Recurrence in Graft:** A hallmark of CMD; the most significant long-term complication. Deposits can recur in the transplanted donor cornea (especially in PKP and DALK, though typically later than in GCD). This can necessitate repeat transplantation.
**Secondary Glaucoma:** Post-keratoplasty complication.
**Cataract Formation:** Accelerated by steroid use post-keratoplasty.
**High Astigmatism:** Post-surgical complication impacting visual outcome.
**Infection:** Post-operative endophthalmitis or microbial keratitis.

**Prognosis:** Overall visual prognosis is fair to good with successful corneal transplantation (DALK or PKP). However, the high recurrence rate of CMD in the graft remains a significant challenge, often requiring multiple procedures over a patient's lifetime.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Sudden, acute decrease in vision (could indicate graft rejection, infection, or other complication).
Severe ocular pain, redness, and discharge (suggests infection, especially post-surgical).
Rapid onset of severe photophobia or glare in a previously stable patient.
Any signs of graft rejection (epithelial or stromal edema, KPs, anterior chamber reaction) post-keratoplasty.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: CMD is the **only** corneal dystrophy associated with diffuse, non-distinct stromal opacities and *no clear intervening stroma*.
**Autosomal recessive** inheritance, making genetic counseling crucial for affected families.
Caused by mutations in the **CHST6 gene** on chromosome 16q22.
Involves abnormal metabolism and accumulation of **keratan sulfate (a GAG)** within keratocytes.
Typically presents in **early childhood** with progressive vision loss, photophobia, and glare.
Corneal thinning is a common feature, progressing with disease severity.
DALK is generally preferred over PKP due to the lower risk of endothelial rejection, provided the Descemet's membrane and endothelium are healthy.
**Recurrence of deposits in the donor graft** is a significant long-term challenge after both DALK and PKP, requiring vigilant follow-up.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The identification of the *CHST6* gene in 1999 by the Klintworth group was a landmark discovery, elucidating the molecular basis of CMD. Advances in imaging like AS-OCT and confocal microscopy have improved in-vivo diagnosis. While gene therapy remains investigational for CMD, current research is exploring strategies to modify the *CHST6* gene or deliver functional enzyme. Studies continue to refine DALK techniques, aiming for even lower complication rates and improved visual outcomes, such as advancements in visco-dissection and automated lamellar dissection systems.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Early Onset:** CMD often presents in early childhood, impacting visual development and education.
**Amblyopia Risk:** Profound vision loss can lead to amblyopia if not managed promptly.
**Genetic Counseling:** Essential for parents and affected individuals, given the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
**Surgical Timing:** Balancing disease progression with the child's age and ability to cooperate with post-operative care.
**Lifelong Management:** Children with CMD require lifelong ophthalmological care, often involving multiple surgical interventions over their lifetime due to disease recurrence.

sections.title: Definition & Mechanism
sections.content: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) uses a Neodymium:Yttrium-Aluminum-Garnet (Nd:YAG) laser (1064 nm) to create a full-thickness opening in the peripheral iris. This equalizes the pressure gradient between the posterior and anterior chambers, eliminating pupillary block and allowing the iris to fall away from the trabecular meshwork.

branches: Prophylaxis in fellow eye of AACC

sections.title: The 'Ando' Iridotomy (Inferior PI)
content: Definition: A specific LPI performed at the 6 o'clock position (inferiorly).
Indication: Aphakic or pseudophakic eyes filled with Silicone Oil.
Pathophysiology: Because silicone oil is lighter than aqueous (buoyant), it floats upward and can block the pupil and any superior iridotomies.
Mechanism: An inferior opening (Ando) allows aqueous to flow into the anterior chamber from below, preventing pupillary block by the buoyant oil.
Critical Pearl: Always perform before or during silicone oil injection in aphakic eyes.

sections.title: Pre-Procedure Workup
content: 1. Gonioscopy: Confirm presence of appositional/synechial closure.
2. Van Herick: Slit-lamp estimation of peripheral AC depth.
3. IOP Measurement: Baseline pressure is critical.
4. Medical Prep: 1 drop Pilocarpine 2% (stretch iris) and 1 drop Apraclonidine 1% or Brimonidine (prevent spike).

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Superior PI
content: 1. Anesthesia: Topical Proparacaine/Tetracaine.
2. Contact Lens: Use Abraham or Wise Iridotomy lens with coupling gel (magnifies and concentrates energy).
3. Site Selection: 11 or 1 o'clock (avoid 12 o'clock to prevent air bubble entrapment). Target iris crypt or thinnest area.
4. Firing: Aim for peripheral 1/3 of iris. Apply laser bursts until a 'plume' of pigment and gush of aqueous is seen.
5. Confirmation: Transillumination defect and visualization of lens capsule/zonules through the hole (minimum 0.5mm size).

sections.title: Contraindications & Barriers
content: Corneal Edema (poor visualization/scattering)
Flat Anterior Chamber (risk of corneal endothelial damage)
Neovascularization of the Iris (High risk of massive hyphema)
Severe Intraocular Inflammation (Fibrinous closure risk)
Patient Inability to Cooperate/Stay still

rows: Used for Plateau Iris Syndrome (iris thinning).
Superior for PACG with cataract (EAGLE Study).
Reserved for failed LPI or during other surgery.

sections.title: Post-Operative Regimen
content: Check IOP 30-60 minutes post-procedure.
Topical Steroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1%) QID for 4-7 days.
Continue previous glaucoma drops unless instructed otherwise.
Repeat Gonioscopy in 1-2 weeks to assess angle opening.

content.explanation: Pigment release confirms penetration; Look for the lens capsule; Use a lens for focus; Monitor IOP post-op; Edge of iris (peripheral) is the target.

rows: Prophylactic LPI in PACS patients significantly reduces risk of PAC conversion but has low overall incidence of PAC without treatment.
Clear lens extraction showed better IOP control and quality of life than LPI for PACG and high-IOP PAC.
Established the necessity of the 6 o'clock PI to prevent silicone oil-induced glaucoma in aphakic eyes.

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Pressure > 40 mmHg post-op (requires immediate therapy)
Full-thickness Hyphema
Fibrinoid reaction in the anterior chamber
Lens capsule strike (Laser-induced cataract)
Corneal 'pit' or burn

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Success
content: Always treat the fellow eye of a patient with Acute Angle Closure; risk of attack is 50-75% over 5 years.
If the iris is thick/brown, consider 'pre-treating' with Argon laser to thin it before using YAG.
Dysphotopsias (Ting's phenomenon) occur most when the LPI is partially covered by the lid; fully covered or fully exposed is preferred.
The 'plume' of pigment is the most reliable sign of success.

title: PRP: Pan-Retinal Photocoagulation Mastery
summary: The definitive surgical laser intervention for ischemic retinal diseases, primarily Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR). By selectively destroying peripheral photoreceptors, PRP reduces metabolic demand and suppresses the production of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pan-Retinal Photocoagulation (PRP) is a thermal laser procedure applied to the peripheral retina. Its primary goal is to induce the regression of neovascularization (NV) by ablating ischemic retinal tissue, thereby reducing the drive for vasoproliferative factors like VEGF and improving the oxygenation of the remaining viable retina.

sections.title: DRS High-Risk Characteristics (HRCs)
content: NVD > 1/4 to 1/3 disc area
Any NVD associated with Vitreous Hemorrhage (VH) or Preretinal Hemorrhage
NVE > 1/2 disc area associated with Vitreous Hemorrhage
Presence of Neovascularization of the Iris (NVI) or Angle (NVA)

branches: Reduction of Oxygen Consumption: Destroys high-metabolic-rate photoreceptors
Improved Inner Retinal Oxygenation: Allows oxygen from choroid to reach inner retina
Downregulation of Cytokines: Significant drop in intraocular VEGF levels
RPE Stimulation: Production of anti-angiogenic factors (e.g., PEDF)

rows: Higher power needed due to short duration

sections.title: Treatment Anatomy & Zones
content: Step 1: Posterior Border - 2 disc diameters from the foveal center.
Step 2: Nasal Border - 1 disc diameter from the optic disc margin.
Step 3: Superior/Inferior Borders - Beyond the vascular arcades.
Step 4: Peripheral Extent - To the equator or beyond (ora serrata in severe cases).

sections.title: Indications Beyond Diabetes
content: Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) - Ischemic type (10 DD non-perfusion)
Hemicentral Retinal Vein Occlusion
Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO) with NV
Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (OIS)
Sickle Cell Retinopathy (Stage 3+)
Eales Disease

content.explanation: 3 sessions (if manual), 2 disc diameters from fovea, 1 disc diameter from optic nerve.

sections.title: Immediate Post-Op Complications
content: Choroidal Effusion / Ciliary Body Detachment
Acute Angle Closure (anterior displacement of lens-iris diaphragm)
Exacerbation of Macular Edema (CME)
Transient IOP Spike
Accidental Foveal Burn (Visual Disaster)

rows: Minimal to no leakage (stays within vessel)

sections.title: Surgical Pearl: The 'Filler' Technique
content: Always treat the inferior retina first; if a VH occurs during the session, superior burns are still achievable.
Use a Goldmann 3-mirror or Mainster PRP lens for optimal visualization of the periphery.
Avoid visible retinal vessels to prevent hemorrhage.
Ensure retrobulbar or sub-Tenon's anesthesia if patient is unable to tolerate laser or if long sessions are planned.

sections.title: Modern Advances: DRCR.net Protocol S
sections.content: Protocol S compared PRP vs. Ranibizumab (0.5mg) for PDR. Findings: Anti-VEGF is non-inferior to PRP for visual acuity through 5 years. Anti-VEGF resulted in less peripheral field loss and fewer vitrectomies but requires high patient compliance for repeated injections.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to STOP Laser
content: Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD) involving or threatening the macula (PRP can worsen traction via 'crunch' syndrome)
Dense Vitreous Hemorrhage obscuring view (requires Vitrectomy/Endo-laser)
Patient Vasovagal Response
Poor pupillary dilation (requires indirect ophthalmoscope laser delivery)

sections.title: Pre-Procedure Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. BCVA and IOP measurement.
2. Dilated Fundus Exam (DFE) with Scleral Depression.
3. Wide-field Fundus Photography.
4. Fluorescein Angiography (FA) to identify areas of NVE and non-perfusion.
5. OCT Macula to check for co-existing DME (determines if Anti-VEGF is needed first).

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-up
content: Regression of NV typically occurs within 4-6 weeks.
Follow-up: Every 4-8 weeks initially to assess regression.
Supplemental (Fill-in) Laser: Needed in up to 25% of cases with persistent NV.
If NV progresses despite maximal PRP: Consider Anti-VEGF or Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV).

title: Mastering the Oculomotor Nerve: A Comprehensive Guide to 3rd Nerve Palsy
summary: The Oculomotor Nerve (CN III) is the workhorse of ocular motility. Understanding its palsy is critical for distinguishing benign microvascular events from life-threatening aneurysms of the Posterior Communicating Artery.
