sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Third Nerve Palsy (Oculomotor Nerve Palsy) is a clinical condition resulting from damage to the third cranial nerve. It typically presents with a combination of ptosis, a 'down and out' eye position, and potentially pupillary involvement. It is a 'rule-out-emergency' condition due to its association with intracranial aneurysms.

branches: Nucleus: Midbrain at level of Superior Colliculus
Fascicular: Passes through Red Nucleus & Substantia Nigra
Subarachnoid: Passes between PCA and SCA; travels near PComm
Cavernous Sinus: Lateral wall, above CN IV
Superior Orbital Fissure: Splits into Superior and Inferior divisions
Orbit: Superior (SR, LPS) & Inferior (MR, IR, IO, Ciliary Ganglion)

rows: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + Contralateral Hemiparesis
Ipsilateral CN III palsy + Contralateral Tremor/Chorea
Ipsilateral CN III palsy + Contralateral Ataxia
Ipsilateral CN III palsy + Cerebellar Ataxia (usually bilateral)
Up-gaze palsy, Convergence-retraction nystagmus, Light-near dissociation

sections.title: The Pathophysiology of the Pupil
sections.content: The 'Rule of the Pupil' relies on the peripheral location of parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor fibers. In microvascular disease (diabetes), ischemia affects the deep vasa nervorum (central nerve trunk), sparing the superficial pupil fibers. In compressive lesions (aneurysm), the external parasympathetic fibers are compressed first, leading to a blown pupil.

sections.title: CRITICAL EMERGENCY: The Blown Pupil
content: PComm Aneurysm: Must be ruled out in ANY pupil-involved palsy.
Uncal Herniation: Rapidly decreasing GCS + CN III palsy.
Sudden 'Thunderclap' Headache: Suggests SAH from ruptured aneurysm.
New onset ptosis with miosis: Consider Horner Syndrome (Differential).
Nuchal Rigidity: Sign of meningeal irritation.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation Checklist
content: Ptosis: Severe, due to LPS weakness.
Exotropia: 'Out' position due to unopposed CN VI (LR).
Hypotropia: 'Down' position due to unopposed CN IV (SO).
Mydriasis: Dilated pupil (if parasympathetic involved).
Accommodation Loss: Blurred near vision.
Diplopia: Horizontal, vertical, or torsional; often resolves when eye shuts (ptosis).

sections.title: Investigation & Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Check Pupils. Involved? Urgent CTA/MRA/DSA.
Step 2: Check Age. >55? Check ESR, CRP, Platelets for GCA.
Step 3: History of DM/HTN? Check HbA1c and Blood Pressure.
Step 4: Neuroimaging (MRI Brain/Orbit) if non-vasculopathic or no improvement in 3 months.
Step 5: Tensilon or Ice Pack Test if Myasthenia is suspected.

rows: Variable ptosis, Cogan lid twitch, no pupil involvement
Involvement of CN II, IV, VI, and V1

sections.title: Management & Treatment
content: Step 1: Acute Phase (0-6 months): Observation for microvascular recovery.
Step 2: Symptomatic relief: Patching (occlusion) or Fresnel Prisms for diplopia.
Step 3: Botulinum Toxin to the Lateral Rectus (optional in acute phase).
Step 4: Surgical Intervention: Only after stability for 6-12 months.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: Large Recession-Resection: Maximize LR recession and MR resection.
Transposition Procedures: Superior Oblique tendon transposition to the Medial Rectus.
Foster Modification: Vertical rectus transposition with augmentation sutures.
Ptosis Repair: Frontalis sling (preferred as LPS function is usually poor).

content.explanation: P: Pressure (Aneurysm) = Pupil Involved; U: Urgency needed; P: Parasympathetic fibers are external; I: Ischemia (DM) = Pupil Sparing; L: Localization is key.

sections.title: Aberrant Regeneration
content: Pseudo-Graefe Sign: Lid elevation on downgaze.
Pupillary Dyskinesia: Pupil constricts on adduction or downgaze.
Cause: Misdirection of axons during healing (never seen in microvascular).
Significance: Suggests chronic compression (Tumor/Aneurysm) or Trauma.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A 'partial' pupil-sparing palsy is still an emergency—treat it as pupil-involved.
CN III palsy with spared pupils in patients <50 years old ALWAYS warrants imaging.
Complete recovery of microvascular palsy usually occurs within 12-16 weeks.
If the 4th nerve is also out, the eye will fail to intort on attempted downgaze.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
sections.content: Congenital CN III palsy is rare and often associated with aberrant regeneration at birth. It carries a high risk of amblyopia. Neuroimaging is mandatory to rule out structural lesions or birth trauma. Ophthalmoplegic Migraine is a rare pediatric diagnosis of exclusion involving recurrent CN III palsy after headache.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: High-resolution 3T MRI/MRA: Sensitivity for aneurysms >3mm is nearly 95-98%.
Endovascular Coiling vs. Clipping: Faster recovery of CN III function often seen with surgical clipping if done early.
AI-Driven Triage: Algorithms are being developed to detect CN III palsy patterns via smartphone photos.

title: Mastering Brown Syndrome: The Superior Oblique Tendon Restriction
summary: Brown syndrome is a restrictive motility disorder characterized by the inability to elevate the eye in adduction. This comprehensive guide covers the mechanical pathophysiology of the trochlear-tendon complex, diagnostic pearls, and the surgical nuances of tendon lengthening.

data.summary: Brown syndrome is a restrictive motility disorder characterized by the inability to elevate the eye in adduction. This comprehensive guide covers the mechanical pathophysiology of the trochlear-tendon complex, diagnostic pearls, and the surgical nuances of tendon lengthening.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Brown syndrome (Superior Oblique Tendon Sheath Syndrome) is a mechanical restriction of the superior oblique (SO) tendon's movement through the trochlea. Pathophysiology involves a short or inelastic SO tendon, or an inflammatory thickening (nodule) that prevents the tendon from sliding through the pulley mechanism when the eye attempts to elevate in an adducted position.

sections.title: Clinical Hallmarks: The Diagnostic Triad
content: Severe limitation of elevation in ADDUCTION.
Minimal or no limitation of elevation in ABDUCTION.
Minimal or no Superior Oblique Overaction (SOOA) — helps distinguish from IO Palsy.
Positive Forced Duction Test (FDT) on attempt to elevate the eye in adduction.
V-pattern strabismus (divergence in upgaze).
Downshoot in adduction (pseudo-overaction of the SO).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Brown vs. IO Palsy

rows: Limited elevation in adduction; No downshoot; Ortho in primary.
Limited elevation in adduction; Downshoot in adduction; Ortho in primary.
Severe limitation in adduction; Marked downshoot; Hypotropia in primary.

sections.title: The Forced Duction Test (FDT) Protocol
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic (proparacaine) or perform under general anesthesia.
Step 2: Grasp the limbus at 3 and 9 o'clock with toothed forceps.
Step 3: Move the globe into an adducted position.
Step 4: Attempt to rotate the globe upward (elevation).
Step 5: Feel for mechanical resistance (positive result if eye cannot be elevated).

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Observation for asymptomatic patients with good binocular vision/no head tilt.
Step 2: Treat underlying inflammation (Steroids/NSAIDS) for acquired/inflammatory cases.
Step 3: Steroid injection (Triamcinolone 40mg) near the trochlea for 'Click Syndrome'.
Step 4: Surgical Intervention if there is hypotropia in primary position or significant abnormal head tilt.
Step 5: Post-operative monitoring for Inferior Oblique Overaction (consecutive palsy).

sections.title: Surgical Techniques & Options
content: SO Tenotomy or Tenectomy: Simple but high risk of SO palsy.
SO Tendon Lengthening: Using a silicone spacer (Wright's technique).
SO Tendon Suture Spacers (Non-absorbable): Graduated lengthening.
Split-Tendon Lengthening: Z-plasty of the tendon.
Superior Oblique Recession: Less effective due to anatomical constraints.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Acquired Brown
content: Sudden onset in adulthood
Pain upon eye movement or palpation of the trochlea
History of Rheumatoid Arthritis or Autoimmune disease
Recent orbital trauma or sinus surgery
Intermittent 'locking' and 'unlocking' with an audible click

content.explanation: B: Below (Hypotropia in primary if severe); R: Restriction on FDT; O: Outward (V-pattern divergence); W: Worse in adduction; N: No SO overaction.

sections.title: Canine Tooth Syndrome
sections.content: A specific subset of traumatic Brown syndrome caused by penetrating injury to the trochlea (classically a dog bite to the superior medial orbit). It results in a combined Brown syndrome and Superior Oblique palsy due to damage to both the trochlea and the nerve/muscle fibers.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Acquired Brown syndrome is more likely to resolve spontaneously than congenital.
The 'Click' in intermittent Brown syndrome represents the nodule snapping through the trochlea.
A compensatory chin-up and contralateral head tilt are common to maintain binocularity.
In surgical spacers, the standard length of silicone used is 6mm to 7mm.
Always check for IO palsy in the DDx using the Parks 3-step test (though 3-step is for paretic, not restrictive).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
content: The Wright Silicone Spacer Study: Established the use of medical-grade silicone for controlled tendon lengthening to prevent consecutive SO palsy.
MRI Studies: Demonstrated that in some 'True' Brown cases, the SO muscle belly is actually hypoplastic.
Bupivacaine Injection: Emerging research into chemodenervation/activation, though not yet standard of care.
Botulinum Toxin: Limited utility in Brown, but occasionally used in the SO for acute inflammatory phases.

sections.title: Complications of Surgery
content: Consecutive Superior Oblique Palsy (Most common)
Extrusion of the silicone spacer (Foreign body reaction)
Persistence of restriction (Under-correction)
Fat Adherence Syndrome
Post-operative scarring/Adhesions

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging Workup
content: Thin-cut MRI of the Orbits (Coronal & Sagittal views).
Focus on the trochlea and SO tendon complex.
Look for: Tendon thickening, enhancement (inflammatory), or trochlear masses.
Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM): Can sometimes visualize the anterior tendon dynamics.

This poster covers clinical classification, surgical management, and the underlying neuro-anatomical anomalies.

sections.title: Definition & Neuro-Etiology
sections.content: Duane Retraction Syndrome (DRS) is a congenital motility disorder resulting from the failure of the abducens nerve (CN VI) nucleus and nerve to develop normally. The lateral rectus (LR) muscle is instead innervated by a branch of the oculomotor nerve (CN III), leading to anomalous co-contraction of the medial and lateral recti on attempted adduction.

rows: Absent CN VI; LR innervated by CN III only on adduction.
Limited adduction; normal or slightly limited abduction.
CN VI present; LR innervated by both CN VI and CN III branches.
Co-contraction of MR and LR in both directions of horizontal gaze.

sections.title: The Pathophysiological Cascade
content: Step 1: Failure of CN VI nucleus/nerve development in the first trimester.
Step 2: Aberrant axonal sprouting from CN III (inferior division).
Step 3: Synaptic connection to the Lateral Rectus (LR) muscle.
Step 4: Attempted adduction triggers both MR and LR (Co-contraction).
Step 5: Globe is pulled posteriorly into the orbit (Retraction).

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Globe Retraction: Occurs on attempted adduction.
Palpebral Fissure Narrowing: Secondary to globe retraction.
Upshoots & Downshoots: 'Leash effect' or 'Sling effect' during adduction.
Compensatory Abnormal Head Position (AHP): Usually a face turn to maintain binocularity.
Secondary Strabismus: Esotropia (Type I) or Exotropia (Type II) in primary position.

content.explanation: 60% are Female, 60% are Left Eye, 60% of cases are Type I (actually 70-80%, but 60 is a helpful anchor for the other stats).

sections.title: Critical Surgical Contraindications
content: NEVER perform a Lateral Rectus Resection: This severely worsens globe retraction.
Avoid large bimedial recessions if globe retraction is the primary concern.
Do not operate if the patient is orthophoric with no AHP and good stereopsis.
Watch for post-operative 'Pseudo-6th nerve palsy' after large recessions.

rows: No globe retraction; acquired onset; secondary deviation > primary.
Large angle ET; cross-fixation; no retraction.
Positive FDT for superior oblique tendon.
Result of trauma or medial wall fracture (MR entrapment).

sections.title: Surgical Management Goals
content: Eliminate AHP (Abnormal Head Position).
Align the eyes in primary position.
Reduce cosmetically significant globe retraction.
Minimize severe upshoots/downshoots (Leash Effect).
Expand the binocular single vision (BSV) field.

rows: Reduce primary position esotropia and face turn.
Reduce primary position exotropia and face turn.
Decrease the co-contraction pull on the globe.
Prevents the LR from slipping over the globe (Sling effect).
Improve abduction (Warning: risk of worsening retraction).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: 1. Measurement of deviation in all 9 cardinal gazes.
2. Assessment of AHP and palpebral fissure width.
3. Forced Duction Test (FDT) to differentiate from 6th nerve palsy.
4. Cycloplegic refraction (Rule out accommodative component).
5. MRI Brain/Orbit (Only if atypical or part of research).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Board Exam
content: FDT is usually positive (tight) for the MR in chronic Type I.
Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking is rarely associated.
Bilateral DRS: Always rule out Möbius Syndrome.
Stereopsis is usually excellent within the field of the head turn.
V-pattern esotropia is the most common pattern found in Type I.

sections.title: Genetic Considerations
sections.content: While 90% are sporadic, familial cases (10%) often show Autosomal Dominant inheritance. Mutations in the CHN1 gene (coding for α-chimerin) have been identified in familial Duane Syndrome, which is involved in pathfinding of ocular motor axons during development.

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
content: Surgical success (alignment in PP) is achieved in >80% of cases.
Amblyopia occurs in 10-20% (often anisometropic, not strabismic).
Full restoration of normal motility is never possible.
Long-term stability is generally high following surgery.

sections.title: Modern Trends in Glaucoma Therapy
content: Increasing awareness of ocular side effects of preserved glaucoma drugs.
Focus on using preservative-free drop therapy.
Reducing polypharmacy by the use of fixed combination preparations.
Major drug groups summarized in table 10.6.

sections.title: Prostaglandin Analogues (PGAs)
sections.content:
These analogues of PGF2α increase uveoscleral outflow. 

• Ocular side effects: common—conjunctival hyperaemia, i pigmentation of iris (and sometimes lid skin), thickening and lengthening of lashes, loss of orbital fat; rare—uveitis, CMO, reactivation of herpetic kerato-uveitis.

sections.title: PGA Contraindications
content: May be associated with CMO after complicated cataract surgery (possibly active uveitis).

sections.title: Beta-blockers
sections.content:
These reduce aqueous production, probably by acting on β -receptors on the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium and vasoconstriction of the arterioles supplying ciliary processes. 

• Ocular side effects: uncommon; allergic blepharoconjunctivitis, punctate keratitis.

sections.title: Beta-blocker Red Flags
content: Asthma/COPD (bronchospasm may occur, even with selective β 1 agents)
Heart block
Bradycardia
Cardiac failure
Try to avoid in nursing mothers (secreted in breast milk)
Interaction: concurrent use of cardiac-directed Ca 2+ antagonists (e.g. verapamil) may compound bradycardia, heart block, and hypotension.

sections.title: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs)
sections.content:
These reduce aqueous production by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase isoenzyme II (and hence bicarbonate production) in the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium. 

• Ocular side effects: common—burning, tearing, allergic blepharoconjunctivitis (up to 10%); rare—intraocular inflammation.

sections.title: CAI Contraindications & Interactions
content: Sulfonamide sensitivity
Renal failure
Liver failure (systemic acetazolamide)
Interaction: K+ -losing diuretics (e.g. thiazide) may cause profound hypokalaemia with acetazolamide.
Note: K+ supplementation is not usually required for acetazolamide used alone.

sections.title: Sympathomimetics
sections.content: The highly α2-selective brimonidine is well tolerated, and apraclonidine (α1 + α2) is useful for short-term use, e.g. after laser iridotomy. Non-selective sympathomimetics (adrenaline/epinephrine, dipivefrine, guanethidine) are now seldom used due to frequent side effects.

sections.title: Sympathomimetic Side Effects & Risks
content: Common: allergic blepharoconjunctivitis (15% brimonidine, 30% apraclonidine)
Older agents: scarring, mydriasis, adrenochrome deposits
Uncommon: CMO in aphakia (possibly pseudophakia)
Acute hypersensitivity: Intraocular inflammation and iIOP
Contraindications: heart block, bradycardia
Drug interactions: monoamine oxidase inhibitors

sections.title: Miotics (Parasympathomimetics)
sections.content:
Muscarinic receptor agonism leads to ciliary muscle contraction, which pulls on the scleral spur to open the trabecular meshwork. 

• Ocular side effects: fluctuating myopia, miosis (constricted VF, reduced night vision).

sections.title: Miotics: Clinical Use & Warnings
content: Pilocarpine: first line in narrow-angle glaucoma; sometimes in POAG.
Useful in: pigmentary glaucomas, aphakic glaucoma, some 2° glaucomas (e.g. post-PK).
Contraindications: inflammatory or aqueous misdirection/malignant glaucoma.
Systemic concern: GI disturbance.

sections.title: Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG): Pathophysiology
sections.content: Posterior segment ischaemia drives neovascularization of the iris and drainage angle, leading to a fibrovascular membrane. Initially, this overlies the trabecular meshwork so that the angle appears open, but with time, PAS form and the membrane contracts to cause complete synechial angle closure. Ischaemic CrVO and diabetes each account for about a third of the cases of neovascular glaucoma (NVG). The advent of intravitreal anti-VEGF therapies have significantly helped in the management of early and refractory NVG. (Page 405)

sections.title: Comprehensive Etiology List
content: Ischaemic CrVO (common); risk of progression to NVG is 50%.
Diabetic retinopathy (common); risk of NVG highest in PDR.
Other vascular disorders: OIS, CrAO, BrVO.
Other retinal disease: chronic retinal detachment, sickle cell retinopathy.
Retinal or choroidal tumours.

branches: Pain: often severe; history of sudden vision loss months prior (e.g., CrVO)
Iris rubeosis: abnormal/non-radial vessels at pupil sphincter margin
High IOP; AC flare/cells; hyphaema; ectropion uvea
Conjunctival injection and corneal oedema (acute iIOP/decompensation)
Disc changes and field loss (as for POAG, pp. 390–1)
Gonioscopy: Abnormal vessels; fibrovascular membrane; PAS; synechial closure

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations
content: Dilated fundoscopy in all cases ± FFA to determine cause.
Carotid Doppler US: if no retinal pathology or asymmetric diabetic retinopathy.
B-scan US: if poor fundal view (cataract associated with tumours, detachment, inflammation).
Haematological/biochemical factors: factors increasing hypoxic drive, e.g., anaemia.

sections.title: NVG Treatment: Underlying Cause
content: PRP for retinal ischaemia.
Retinal reattachment for retinal detachment.
Carotid endarterectomy for suitable carotid artery stenosis.
Treat exacerbating factors: e.g., anaemia, hyperviscosity.

sections.title: Management of Neovascularization
sections.content:
Treatment is undergoing a positive transformation with anti-VEGF. Note: anti-VEGF alone will not control NVG unless posterior hypoxic drive is addressed (PRP, etc). PRP decreases long-term drive. If no fundal view, anti-VEGF temporizes. Consider Vitrectomy/endolaser ± cataract extraction based on prognosis. Anti-VEGF improves drainage surgery survival. Intravitreal bevacizumab shows regression of NV and decreased IOP alone [6] or with PRP [7].

6: Wakabayashi t et al. Ophthalmology. 2008;115:1571–80.
7: Ehlers JP et al. Retina. 2008;28:696–702.

rows: Cycloplegic (Atropine 1% 2x/d); Topical steroids (Pred acetate 1% 1-4hrly); Ocular hypotensives (as for POAG). Surgical: Augmented trabeculectomy, tube-shunt, or cyclodiode.
Cycloplegia (atropine) and topical corticosteroids; Lubricants for sick epithelium (suspicion for microbial keratitis); Full surface regime for dry eyes/blepharitis/toxicity.
Retrobulbar alcohol or chlorpromazine; Evisceration or enucleation.

sections.title: Inflammatory Glaucoma: General Principles
sections.content: Raised IOP in intraocular inflammation is common. Challenges: elucidating time course (acute vs chronic iIOP), angle state (open vs appositional vs synechial), and mechanism. Therapy is difficult due to IOP fluctuations (ciliary body shutdown lowers IOP; trabeculitis increases IOP) and concerns regarding steroid-induced glaucoma. (Page 406-407)

rows: iIOP; open angle; signs of uveitis ± keratitis; IOP returns to normal after episode.
Inflammatory process: Topical steroids/cycloplegics (as for AAU, pp. 460-1). IOP: if >27mmHg, sustained, or vulnerable disc, use topical (β-blocker, CAI) or systemic (acetazolamide).
iIOP; open angle; no active inflammation but signs of previous episodes; ± disc/field defects (p. 384); Sectorial iris atrophy.
Medical: as for POAG. Avoid PGAs (risk of herpetic reactivation). Surgical: Augmented trabeculectomy (tight inflammation control first) or tube. Cyclodestruction risk: Phthisis.

sections.title: Steroid-Induced Glaucoma
content: Important differential for inflammatory glaucoma.
If due to steroids: reduce potency/frequency ± steroid-sparing agents.
If due to inflammation: steroid dose may need to be increased.
IOP elevation may be dose-dependent.

rows: 360° PS blocks aqueous flow; iris bombé; appositional closure.
Features: Iris bombé; shallow AC. Tx: Minimize PS (subconjunctival Betnesol®/mydricaine). Nd:YAG PI (large/multiple); surgical PI if needed. Topical/systemic IOP meds.
PAS lead to closure; risk increases in granulomatous inflammation/narrow angles.
Features: PAS; signs of previous inflammation. Tx: Medical (caution with PGAs); Augmented trabeculectomy or tube (risk of hypotony); Cyclodiode (risk of phthisis). Ensure patent PI.

content.explanation: Painless unilateral recurrent high IOP episodes in a 'white' eye. Typically young males. Postulated HSV trabeculitis.

sections.title: PSS Clinical & Treatment
content: Features: Blurring, haloes, high IOP (40–80mmHg), minimal flare, white eye, occasional cells/KPs, NO synechiae, open angle.
Treatment: Topical steroid (dexamethasone 0.1% 4x/d); Topical IOP meds (β-blocker, α2-agonist, CAI) or systemic acetazolamide.
NB: Recurrent episodes may lead to severe angle damage.

sections.title: Fuchs’ Heterochromic Uveitis
content: Syndrome of mild chronic anterior uveitis, iris heterochromia, and cataract.
Glaucoma occurs in 10–30% of cases. Typically affects young adults; unilateral in >90%.
Strong association with the rubella virus.
Symptoms: dVA (cataract), floaters; often asymptomatic.

Signs: White eye, white stellate KPs (whole endothelium), mild flare/few cells, iris atrophy (moth-eaten), transillumination defects, abnormal iris vessels, iris heterochromia (becomes bluer), iris nodules, vitritis, iIOP.
Gonioscopy: Open angle; ± twig-like neovascularization of the angle (NVA).
Treatment: Inflammatory process tx usually unnecessary. iIOP treated as for POAG (pp. 390–1).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Infantile Esotropia (IE), also known as Essential Infantile Esotropia, is a large-angle, constant convergent strabismus with onset within the first 6 months of life. It is distinct from accommodative types as it typically presents with minimal refractive error and is associated with a specific constellation of oculomotor findings including DVD and latent nystagmus.

rows: Innate, irreversible defect in the fusion faculty of the brain.
Primary motor misalignment preventing development of normal binocular reflexes.
Esotropia associated with nystagmus in abduction and head turn.

sections.title: MANDATORY: Rule out Life-Threatening Etiology
content: Retinoblastoma: MUST perform dilated fundus exam on ALL new ET cases.
CN VI Palsy: Suspect if abduction is limited beyond cross-fixation/doll's head.
Hydrocephalus: Increased ICP can present as sudden onset esotropia.
Sensory Esotropia: Corneal scarring, congenital cataract, or optic nerve hypoplasia.

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination Findings
content: Motor: Constant, large-angle ET (usually 40-60 PD). Measured via Hirschberg/Krimsky or Prism Cover Test.
Fixation: Cross-fixation is common; the infant uses the ADducted eye to view the opposite field.
Pseudo-Abducens Palsy: Apparent abduction deficit due to cross-fixation. Resolved by Doll's Head Maneuver or Monocular Patching for 1 hour.
Refraction: Cycloplegic refraction usually shows low hyperopia (+1.00 to +2.00 D), which is normal for age.
Asymmetric OKN: Stronger response in the temporonasal direction than nasotemporal direction.
DVD: Upward drifting of the eye when covered or inattentive, without a corresponding downward movement of the other eye.

rows: Wide nasal bridge, epicanthal folds; positive corneal light reflex.
Onset later (2-3 years), high hyperopia (>+3.00D), corrected by glasses.
Limited abduction, globe retraction, and palpebral fissure narrowing on adduction.
Observation or surgery if head turn.
Mask-like facies, inability to abduct, multiple cranial nerve palsies.
Nystagmus decreases or stops when the eye is in adduction.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. History: Confirm onset < 6 months and rule out neurological delays.
2. Visual Assessment: CSM (Central, Steady, Maintained) or Fix & Follow.
3. Motor Evaluation: Angle measurement at distance/near (Hirschberg/Krimsky).
4. Ductions/Versions: Check for abduction capability and IOOA.
5. Cycloplegic Refraction: Use 1% Cyclopentolate (or Atropine for dark irides).
6. Fundus Exam: Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy to rule out posterior pole pathology.

sections.title: Surgical Dosing: Bilateral Medial Rectus (BMR) Recession

content.explanation: C: Cross-fixation / Constant large angle; L: Latent nystagmus; A: Asymmetric OKN; S: Small refractive error (Normal for age); S: Stereopsis is usually absent/poor.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: 1. Treat Amblyopia First: Patching of the dominant eye if fixation is not alternating.
2. Correct Significant Refractive Error: If >+2.50D or significant astigmatism.
3. Timing: Goal is surgical alignment between 6 and 12 months of age.
4. Primary Surgery: Usually Bilateral Medial Rectus Recession (BMR).
5. Secondary Surgery: Address IOOA (Inferior Oblique Myectomy/Recession) or DVD if they emerge.

sections.title: Post-Operative Complications & Risks
content: Consecutive Exotropia: Over-correction (common in children with neurological issues).
Residual Esotropia: Under-correction requiring further recession or resection of lateral recti.
Scleral Perforation: Rare but serious surgical complication.
Lost Muscle: Surgical emergency requiring immediate retrieval.
Recurrent Amblyopia: Requires long-term follow-up and monitoring.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: ELIS (Early vs Late Infantile Strabismus)
sections.content: The ELIS study and various multicenter trials have demonstrated that alignment achieved before age 2 (ideally by age 1) provides the best chance for 'subnormal' binocular vision (peripheral fusion) and gross stereopsis (200-400 arc sec). Fine stereopsis is rarely achieved in IE.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls for the Boards
content: Initial management is ALWAYS medical (patching/glasses) until vision is equalized.
BMR is the gold standard; however, in massive angles (>70PD), some surgeons combine BMR with Lateral Rectus resection (3-4 muscle surgery).
IOOA and DVD often don't appear until age 2 or 3, even if the primary ET is successfully corrected early.
Ciancia Syndrome features esotropia with head turn towards the side of the fixating eye to dampen nystagmus.
Botulinum Toxin: An alternative to surgery in select cases, though effect may be temporary or require multiple injections.

data.title: Mastering the Macular Hole: From Pathogenesis to Post-Op
data.summary: A comprehensive clinical deep-dive into Full-Thickness Macular Holes (FTMH), covering the evolution of staging from Gass to IVTS, gold-standard diagnostic maneuvers, and the nuances of vitreoretinal surgical management.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A Full-Thickness Macular Hole (FTMH) is a primary neurosensory retinal defect involving all layers from the internal limiting membrane (ILM) to the outer segments of the photoreceptors. It typically occurs at the fovea centralis, leading to a significant loss of central visual acuity and metamorphopsia. While most are idiopathic and related to age-related vitreoretinal interface changes, they can also be secondary to trauma or high myopia.

sections.title: The Gass Staging System (Historical Gold Standard)

rows: Central yellow spot; loss of foveal reflex.
Central yellow ring; further elevation of the foveola.
Small eccentric break in the foveal floor; 'can-opener' tear.
Large hole with cuff of subretinal fluid; No Weiss Ring.
Large hole; Weiss ring present on biomicroscopy.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Gass Theory
content: 1. Perifoveal Vitreous Detachment begins.
2. Focal tangential traction at the fovea by the posterior hyaloid.
3. Cystic changes occur in the foveolar layers (Stage 1).
4. Centrifugal migration of photoreceptors.
5. Full-thickness dehiscence and centripetal retraction of retinal edges.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Progressive decrease in central vision (usually 20/80 to 20/400).
Metamorphopsia: Distorted lines on Amsler Grid.
Central Scotoma: A 'hole' in the center of vision.
Micropsia: Objects appearing smaller.
Typically painless and unilateral onset.

sections.title: Diagnostic Ocular Examination
content: Watzke-Allen Sign: Slit beam over hole is perceived as thinned or broken.
Laser Beam Test: 50um spot disappears into the hole.
Biomicroscopy: Round, red lesion with yellow-white deposits (drusen-like) at the base.
Cuff of Subretinal Fluid: Surrounding the hole edges.
Pseudo-operculum: Suspended tissue over the hole (condensed vitreous).

rows: Verticalized foveal edges; no tissue loss.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Spectral Domain OCT (SD-OCT): The gold standard for sizing and staging.
2. Amsler Grid: To document the area of metamorphopsia.
3. Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Shows 'window defect' early, but rarely necessary.
4. Microperimetry: Maps the depth and extent of the central scotoma.
5. Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): Increased autofluorescence in the hole due to RPE unmasking.

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol
content: 1. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (23G, 25G, or 27G).
2. Induction of Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD) if not present.
3. ILM Peeling: Often aided by Brilliant Blue G (BBG) or Indocyanine Green (ICG).
4. Fluid-Air Exchange (FAX).
5. Gas Tamponade: Long-acting (C3F8) or short-acting (SF6).
6. Post-operative positioning: Face-down for 3-7 days (surgeon dependent).

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Considerations
content: Acute vision drop in the fellow eye (15% risk).
Signs of Endophthalmitis post-op (pain, hypopyon).
Iatrogenic retinal breaks during surgery.
Rapidly progressive cataract (common after vitrectomy).
Elevated Intraocular Pressure (IOP) from gas expansion.

content.explanation: Beam broken = Macular hole; Ray is bent = Pseudohole; Entirely normal = Malingering/Functional; All light seen = Lamellar hole; Kinked beam = Epiretinal membrane.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Cataract formation (occurs in >75% within 2 years).
Retinal Detachment (1-2% risk).
Visual field defects (often related to air-fluid exchange).
RPE Toxicity (if ICG dye is used for ILM peeling).
Success Rate: >90% closure for Stage 2 holes.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Small holes (<250μm) have a higher chance of spontaneous closure (rare but documented).
Inverted ILM flap technique is superior for large holes (>400μm) and high myopia.
The presence of a Weiss ring confirms Stage 4 and reduces risk to the fellow eye.
OCT 'Base Diameter' is always larger than 'Minimum Linear Diameter' (MLD).

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: MIVS (Micro-Incision Vitrectomy Surgery): Reducing surgical trauma and recovery time.
Ocrplasmin (Jetrea): Pharmacologic vitreolysis for VMT, though use has declined due to limited efficacy in FTMH.
Autologous Retinal Flaps: For refractory or ultra-large holes.
Valved Cannulas: Maintaining stable IOP during ILM peeling.
Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) adjuvants: Exploring biological 'glue' for closure.

sections.title: Long-Term Monitoring Protocol
content: 1. Week 1: Check IOP and wound integrity.
2. Month 1: Monitor gas bubble resolution and OCT for closure.
3. Month 3: Assess visual acuity and metamorphopsia improvement.
4. Ongoing: Annual Amsler Grid monitoring of the fellow eye.

title: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): The Clinician’s Masterclass
summary: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) represents the final common pathway for diverse retinal pathologies, characterized by fluid accumulation in the Henle layer. Mastering its diagnosis and multi-modal treatment is fundamental to preserving central visual acuity in the clinical setting.

data.title: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): The Clinician’s Masterclass
data.summary: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) represents the final common pathway for diverse retinal pathologies, characterized by fluid accumulation in the Henle layer. Mastering its diagnosis and multi-modal treatment is fundamental to preserving central visual acuity in the clinical setting.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: CME is a distinct retinal condition characterized by fluid accumulation within the outer plexiform layer (Henle's layer). Pathophysiologically, it results from the breakdown of the Inner Blood-Retinal Barrier (iBRB) at the level of the retinal vascular endothelium or the Outer Blood-Retinal Barrier (oBRB) at the RPE. This leads to increased permeability, secondary to inflammatory mediators (Prostaglandins, VEGF, IL-6), surgical trauma, or venous stasis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Hierarchy
content: Step 1: Dilated Fundus Exam: Evaluate for foveal thickening and loss of foveal reflex.
Step 2: SD-OCT: Gold standard to quantify Central Subfield Thickness (CST) and map intraretinal cystic spaces.
Step 3: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Demonstrates late-phase 'petaloid' hyperfluorescence.
Step 4: Ancillary: Indocyanine Green (ICG) angiography for occult choroidal pathology if suspecting inflammatory etiology.

rows: Subretinal fluid vs Intraretinal cystoid fluid

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: First-line: Topical NSAIDs (e.g., Nepafenac 0.1%, Bromfenac 0.09%) for 4-8 weeks.
Second-line: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab, Aflibercept) for chronic cases.
Third-line: Intravitreal Steroids (Dexamethasone implant, Triamcinolone) for uveitic CME.
Surgical: Pars Plana Vitrectomy if vitreous traction or residual membrane is present.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Refer/Escalate
content: Significant decrease in VA (worse than 20/40)
Evidence of underlying infectious uveitis
Neovascularization present on FFA
Acute pain or signs of endophthalmitis post-op

content.explanation: P: Post-surgical (Irvine-Gass); E: Edema (Diabetic); T: Thrombosis (RVO); A: Autoimmune/Uveitis; L: Latrogenic (Drugs).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a 360-degree scleral depression or fundus exam to rule out peripheral pathology in unexplained CME.
Irvine-Gass syndrome typically presents 4-6 weeks post-cataract surgery.
CST on OCT is more reliable than clinical exam for monitoring treatment response.
Topical steroids and NSAIDs exhibit synergy; consider combination therapy for refractory cases.

sections.title: Primary Open Angle Glaucoma (POAG) Risk Factors

branches: Race: Black people 4 times > white people

sections.title: Anderson's Criteria & AGIS Insights
content: Minimal criteria for glaucoma damage on SAP (Anderson’s criteria):
1. GHT (Glaucoma Hemifield Test): Outside normal level at least 2 occasions.
2. Cluster of three or more non-edge points in a location typical for glaucoma, all of which are depressed on PSD at <5% and one which is depressed at p<1% level on two consecutive occasions.
3. Corrected PSD that occurs in less than 5% of normal individuals on two consecutive occasions.
AGIS (Advanced Glaucoma Interventional Study): Significant visual field progression is unlikely to occur in most patients in the medium term if IOP can be kept below 18mmHg at all times.

branches: Systemic hypotension: Nocturnal dip in BP >20% (especially on oral hypotensives)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis of Normal Tension Glaucoma

rows: Angle closure glaucoma; Falsely low IOP (ectasia, LASIK); Myopic degeneration; Optic disc drusen; Congenital disc anomalies
POAG + normal IOP due to diurnal fluctuation; Previous episodes of raised IOP (trauma, uveitis, steroid therapy); Masked by systemic beta-blockers
Neurological lesion; Previous AION secondary to Temporal Arteritis; Previous acute optic nerve insult; Miscellaneous optic nerve neuropathy

sections.title: Primary Angle Closure (PAC) Classification
content: 1. Primary Angle Closure Suspect (PACS): ACD < normal. Gonioscopy: ITC in >= 3 quadrants, no PAS. OR 2 quadrants of ITC + signs of intermittent closure (pigment smudging). Normal IOP, optic disc, and visual field.
2. Primary Angle Closure (PAC): Gonioscopy: >= 3 quadrants of ITC + raised IOP and/or PAS. Normal optic disc and field. Ischaemic PAC shows iris changes and Glaukomflecken.
3. Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma (PACG): Gonioscopy: ITC in >= 3 quadrants + Glaucomatous Optic Neuropathy.

sections.title: PACG Risk Factors & Definitions
content: Lens Vault Definition: The distance between the anterior pole of the lens and a horizontal line joining scleral spurs at diametrically opposite locations.
Age: Pupillary block (~62y); Non-pupillary block (younger).
Gender: Female predominance.
Race: Non-pupillary block prevalent in Far Eastern and Indian Asians.
Family History: Poorly defined but increased prevalence in family members.
Refraction: Pupillary block (Hypermetropes); Non-pupillary block (can occur in Myopes).
Axial Length: Short eyes tend to have a shallow AC (Anterior Chamber).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Acute IOP Elevation
content: Lens-induced angle closure (swollen/subluxated lens)
Malignant glaucoma (aqueous misdirection - post-op)
Secondary angle closure (with/without pupillary block)
Neovascular glaucoma (sudden pain/congestion)
Hypertensive uveitis (Iridocyclitis, Trabeculitis, CMV, Posner-Schlossman)
Scleritis (with/without angle closure)
Pigment dispersion
Pseudoexfoliation
Orbital/Retrobulbar lesions (Inflammation, Hemorrhage, CC-Fistula)

sections.title: Pseudoexfoliation (PXS) & Systemic Health
sections.content: Pseudoexfoliation material is a grey-white fibrillary substance derived from abnormal extracellular matrix metabolism in ocular and other tissues. Systemic manifestations include: 1. High-tone hearing loss. 2. Ischaemic cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease. 3. Increased risk of pelvic organ prolapse in older women.

sections.title: Investigations for Choroidal Melanoma
content: Photographic documentation: Essential for serial monitoring.
FAF (Fundus Autofluorescence): Nevus = patchy increase. Melanoma = intense or diffuse increase.
OCT: Measures lesion thickness and detects subretinal fluid.

U/S (B-scan): Localized flat or slightly elevated lesion with internal homogeneity, low to medium reflectivity. Measures dimensions, detects extraocular extension, choroidal excavation, orbital shadowing. 'Collar stud' configuration is pathognomonic.
FA (Fluorescein Angiography): Shows intrinsic tumour 'dual circulation', mottled fluorescence (AV phase), late diffuse leakage and staining.
ICGA: Hypofluorescence throughout the study.
MRI: To demonstrate extraocular extension.
Biopsy & Immunocytochemistry: PAX8 expression helps differentiate. Melanoma and melanocytoma are PAX8 negative; pigmented adenocarcinoma is PAX8 positive.
Genetic Analysis: Loss of chromosome 3 (M3) and changes in chromosome 8 (8q) correlate with poor prognosis.
Systemic Investigation: Liver function tests, U/S, and chest radiography to detect metastatic spread.

rows: Prominent vortex vein ampulla (disappears with pressure)

sections.title: Melanoma: Prognosis & Treatment Options
content: Adverse Features: Large no. of epithelioid cells, mitotic activity, large dimensions, somatic BAP1 mutation (50% risk of metastasis), extrascleral extension, anterior location.
Brachytherapy: Tumour <20mm basal diameter, up to 10mm thick, vision salvage possible.
External Beam Radiotherapy: For large/posterior tumours unsuitable for brachy.
Stereotactic Radiotherapy: Targeted radiation.
Transpupillary Thermotherapy (TTT): Small tumours or adjunct to radiotherapy.
Transscleral Choroidectomy: Tumour <16mm diameter but too thick for radiation.
Light activation AU-011: Small melanomas (2-3.4mm).
Enucleation Criteria: Large size, optic disc invasion, extensive ciliary body/angle involvement, irreversible loss of vision, or poor patient motivation.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Keratoconus is a bilateral, asymmetric, progressive, non-inflammatory corneal ectasia characterized by focal stromal thinning, apical protrusion, and subsequent irregular astigmatism. This leads to reduced visual acuity that cannot be fully corrected with conventional spectacles. It typically manifests in adolescence or early adulthood and progresses over 10-20 years before stabilizing, though it can continue to progress in older age.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Risk Factors
content: **Prevalence:** Highly variable, ranging from 1:500 to 1:2000 in the general population, with higher rates in certain populations (e.g., Middle East, Asia).
**Onset:** Typically during puberty, progressing over the next 10-20 years. Can occur earlier in childhood.
**Gender:** No significant predilection.
**Genetics:** Familial history in 6-10% of cases. Specific gene loci identified (e.g., VSX1, ZEB1, SOD1, DOCK9). Often autosomal dominant with variable penetrance.

**Associated Conditions (Systemic):** Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), Leber congenital amaurosis, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Osteogenesis imperfecta, Atopic conditions (asthma, eczema, allergic conjunctivitis).
**Environmental/Behavioral Factors:** Vigorous eye rubbing is a significant risk factor, chronic allergic conjunctivitis.

branches: Genetic Predisposition (VSX1, ZEB1, SOD1, DOCK9, FOXO1)
Enzymatic Degradation (Increased Proteases: MMP-1, MMP-3, MMP-9)
Oxidative Stress & Apoptosis (Increased ROS, Keratocyte Loss)
Inflammation & Allergic Response (Mast Cell Activation, Cytokines)
Environmental Factors (Chronic Eye Rubbing, UV Exposure)

rows: Traditional staging based on steepest keratometry (Kmax), central corneal thickness (CCT), presence of scarring, and best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA).
Anterior Curvature, Posterior Curvature, Thinnest Pachymetry, BCVA

Modern, tomography-based classification. A: Anterior curvature. B: Posterior curvature. C: Corneal Thickness (thinnest point). D: Best corrected distance visual acuity. Each rated 0-4, providing a comprehensive index.
Global Consensus on Keratoconus & Ectatic Diseases
Confocal microscopy, Genetic testing, Progression criteria
Combines clinical, topographic, and tomographic features. Defines suspected KC, forme fruste KC, and clinical KC. Emphasizes progression criteria for intervention.
Common patterns include 'Nipple cone' (small, central steepening), 'Oval cone' (larger, inferior/inferotemporal steepening), and 'Globus' (generalized steepening).

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Progressive Myopia & Irregular Astigmatism:** Most common initial presentation, requiring frequent spectacle changes.
**Blurred Vision:** Cannot be fully corrected with conventional spectacles.
**Monocular Diplopia/Polyopia:** Double or multiple images in one eye due0 to irregular astigmatism.
**Glare & Halos:** Especially noticeable at night, due to scattering of light.
**Photophobia:** Increased sensitivity to light.
**Reduced Best-Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA):** Even with optimal correction.
**Eye Strain & Headaches:** Due to constant visual effort.

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Retinoscopy:** Scissor reflex (dark shadow splitting into two moving against each other).
**Slit Lamp Examination:**
- **Fleischer's Ring:** Iron deposition in the basal epithelial cells at the base of the cone, best seen with cobalt blue filter.
- **Vogt's Striae:** Fine, vertical stress lines in the deep posterior stroma/Descemet's membrane, disappearing with external pressure.
- **Corneal Thinning:** Especially at the apex of the cone.
- **Apical Scarring:** Develops in advanced stages from chronic microtrauma or hydrops.
- **Prominent Corneal Nerves:** Less specific, but can be seen.
**External Observation:**
- **Munson's Sign:** V-shaped indentation of the lower eyelid on downgaze.
- **Rizzuti's Sign:** Conical reflection of light on the nasal cornea when a penlight is shone from the temporal side.

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Ophthalmic History & Best-Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA):** Assess for progressive vision changes, frequent spectacle changes, monocular diplopia, history of eye rubbing/atopy.
**Step 2: Manifest & Cycloplegic Refraction:** Reveal progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism, often with cylinder axes that are difficult to refine.
**Step 3: Slit Lamp Examination:** Look for Fleischer's ring, Vogt's striae, Munson's/Rizzuti's signs, apical thinning/scarring.
**Step 4: Keratometry:** Reveal central or inferior steepening and high astigmatism.
**Step 5: Corneal Topography (Placido-disc based):** Gold standard for diagnosis. Shows classic 'bow-tie with skewed axes' pattern, central/inferior steepening, localized power abnormalities.

**Step 6: Corneal Tomography (Scheimpflug imaging - e.g., Pentacam, Galilei; or Anterior Segment OCT):** Provides anterior and posterior corneal elevation maps, pachymetry maps (thinnest point, percentage thickness increase). Essential for early diagnosis (forme fruste KC) and monitoring progression. Measures total corneal refractive power.
**Step 7: Pachymetry:** Measures corneal thickness, identifies the thinnest point, crucial for CXL candidacy and progression monitoring.
**Step 8: Wavefront Aberrometry:** Quantifies higher-order aberrations, particularly coma, which is a hallmark of keratoconus.
**Step 9: Genetic Testing (Optional/Research):** Rarely performed routinely, but can be relevant in familial cases or for research.

rows: Inferior peripheral corneal thinning (0.5-2mm from limbus), often with normal central cornea. No Fleischer's ring or Vogt's striae.
'Kissing Doves' or 'Crab Claw' pattern, with inferior steepening and a relatively flat central cornea. Band of thinning visible in pachymetry map.
Generalized global corneal thinning and protrusion, usually congenital. Entire cornea involved, not just apex.
Diffuse, global steepening and thinning across the entire cornea.
Progressive steepening and thinning occurring after refractive surgery (LASIK). History of prior refractive surgery is key.
Similar topographic patterns to KC but often centered at the flap margin or within the ablation zone.
Subclinical keratoconus, asymptomatic, normal slit lamp. Diagnosed only by advanced imaging.
Subtle abnormalities on posterior elevation maps, mild asymmetry, or small areas of localized thinning on pachymetry maps. Clinically insignificant without progression.
Peripheral, usually superior, stromal thinning with lipid deposition, vascularization, and an intact epithelium. Associated with inflammation.
Asymmetric flattening with peripheral thinning, distinct from the central/paracentral steepening of KC.
Mild topographic distortion, often no obvious signs.
Fleischer's ring, early Vogt's striae, minimal thinning.
Prominent Fleischer's ring, Vogt's striae, moderate thinning, early apical scarring.
Dense apical scarring, acute hydrops (or history of), severe thinning.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Algorithm
content: **Initial Diagnosis & Monitoring:** Confirm diagnosis with topography/tomography. Monitor for progression every 3-6 months in active disease, annually if stable.
**Step 1: Optical Correction (Early to Moderate KC):**
- **Spectacles:** For mild, regular astigmatism.
- **Rigid Gas Permeable (RGP) Lenses:** Primary optical management. Create a new refractive surface over the irregular cornea, masking irregularities. Requires expert fitting.
- **Piggyback Lenses:** RGP over a soft contact lens for improved comfort.
- **Hybrid Lenses:** Soft skirt with a rigid center, offering comfort of soft lenses and visual acuity of RGPs.

- **Scleral Lenses:** Vault the entire cornea, resting on the sclera. Ideal for advanced KC, highly irregular corneas, or patients intolerant to RGPs. Provides excellent vision and comfort, can help with ocular surface disease.
**Step 2: Corneal Collagen Cross-linking (CXL) (Progressive KC):**
- **Purpose:** To halt disease progression by strengthening corneal collagen fibers.
- **Indication:** Documented progression (increase in Kmax > 1D, increase in astigmatism > 1D, or decrease in CCT > 20µm) in patients with minimum CCT (usually >400µm post-epithelial debridement).
- **Procedure:** Dresden Protocol (Epi-off) is standard. Accelerated and Transepithelial (Epi-on) variations exist.
**Step 3: Intracorneal Ring Segments (ICRS) / Intacs / Kerarings (Moderate KC with intolerance to CL):**
- **Purpose:** To flatten the central cornea, reduce astigmatism, improve visual acuity, and potentially delay keratoplasty.
- **Indication:** Moderate KC (Amsler-Krumeich Stage II-III) with good BCVA with contact lenses but intolerance, or significant irregular astigmatism.
- **Procedure:** Femtosecond laser-assisted channel creation for segment insertion into mid-stroma.
**Step 4: Keratoplasty (Advanced KC):**
- **Purpose:** Restore vision in cases of severe scarring, extreme thinning, or contact lens intolerance.
- **Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK):** Preferred for advanced KC if Descemet's membrane is intact. Replaces only the diseased stroma. Lower risk of endothelial rejection.
- **Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP):** Full-thickness corneal transplant. Reserved for severe cases with dense scarring, acute hydrops, or failed DALK.

sections.title: 11. Corneal Collagen Cross-linking (CXL) Techniques
content: **1. Standard 'Dresden Protocol' (Epithelium-Off CXL):**
- **Anesthesia:** Topical anesthetic (e.g., Proparacaine, Tetracaine).
- **Epithelial Debridement:** Removal of central 8-9 mm of corneal epithelium (e.g., with blunt spatula or alcohol-assisted).

- **Riboflavin Application:** Iso-osmolar 0.1% Riboflavin-5-phosphate in 20% Dextran solution (e.g., Ricrolin) applied every 2-5 minutes for 30 minutes, ensuring stromal saturation (observed with yellow flare in anterior chamber). CCT must be ≥ 400µm after debridement; if less, hypo-osmolar riboflavin can be used.
- **UVA Irradiation:** 370 nm UVA light at 3 mW/cm² for 30 minutes (total energy 5.4 J/cm²). Riboflavin drops continued every 2-5 minutes during irradiation.

- **Post-op:** Bandage contact lens (BCL), topical antibiotics (e.g., Moxifloxacin QID x 1 week), topical steroids (e.g., Prednisolone Acetate QID, tapered over 4-6 weeks), topical NSAIDs for pain, artificial tears.
**2. Accelerated CXL:**
- **Principle:** Higher irradiance for shorter duration (e.g., 9 mW/cm² for 10 min, 18 mW/cm² for 5 min) to maintain total energy (5.4 J/cm²).
- **Advantages:** Shorter procedure time, similar efficacy to standard protocol.
**3. Transepithelial (Epi-On) CXL:**
- **Principle:** Intact epithelium. Enhanced riboflavin formulations (e.g., with EDTA, BAC, TRIS) or iontophoresis to improve stromal penetration.
- **Advantages:** Less pain, faster visual recovery, lower risk of infection/haze. Efficacy is still debated, generally considered less effective than epi-off but improving.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Keratoconus (Disease Related):**

- **Acute Hydrops:** Rupture of Descemet's membrane, allowing aqueous humor into stroma, leading to sudden pain, severe vision loss, and corneal edema. Usually resolves over weeks/months, often with scarring.
- **Corneal Scarring:** From chronic microtrauma, hydrops, or prolonged contact lens wear.
**Corneal Collagen Cross-linking (CXL):**
- **Corneal Haze:** Temporary or permanent, typically peaks at 1-3 months, usually clears.
- **Sterile Infiltrates/Infection:** Rare but serious, can lead to scarring or vision loss.
- **Persistent Epithelial Defect:** Prolonged healing time.
- **Treatment Failure/Progression:** 5-10% of cases may still progress.
**Intracorneal Ring Segments (ICRS):**
- Segment extrusion, infection, stromal melting, glare, poor refractive outcome.
**Keratoplasty (DALK/PKP):**
- **Graft Rejection:** Higher in PKP than DALK. Requires lifelong immunosuppression.
- **Infection:** Endophthalmitis, keratitis.
- **Astigmatism:** Post-operative irregular astigmatism is common.
- **Glaucoma:** Steroid-induced or angle closure.
- **Cataract:** Especially in PKP, due to intraocular surgery.
- **Graft Failure/Recurrence.**

**Prognosis:** With modern management, most patients maintain good functional vision. CXL has revolutionized management, preventing the need for keratoplasty in many cases. Visual outcomes depend on the stage at diagnosis and timely intervention.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Sudden onset of severe eye pain, photophobia, and marked decrease in vision in a patient with keratoconus:** This is highly suggestive of **Acute Hydrops** (Descemet's membrane rupture). Immediate ophthalmic evaluation is required.
**New onset discharge, increasing pain, or worsening vision after CXL:** May indicate **Post-CXL Infection** and requires urgent assessment and culture.
**Sudden, unexplained vision loss or excruciating pain after keratoplasty:** Could indicate **Endophthalmitis** or **Acute Graft Rejection**, needing immediate attention.

content.explanation:
Remember the classic slit-lamp and external signs of Keratoconus:

*   **F**leischer's ring (iron ring)
*   **V**ogt's striae (stromal lines)
*   **M**unson's sign (lower lid indentation)
*   **R**izzuti's sign (conical reflection)

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always suspect keratoconus in young patients (adolescents/young adults) presenting with **progressive, unexplained astigmatism**, especially if it's irregular or rapidly changing.
**Corneal topography/tomography** is paramount for early diagnosis and monitoring, often detecting subclinical disease (forme fruste KC) before slit-lamp signs are evident.
**Eye rubbing** is a major modifiable risk factor; educate patients to avoid it vigorously.
**CXL is a disease-modifying treatment:** It halts progression, but does not reverse existing ectasia. Timely intervention is crucial, especially in younger, more aggressive cases.
**Scleral contact lenses** are a game-changer for visual rehabilitation in moderate to severe keratoconus, offering superior vision and comfort compared to RGPs for many patients.
**Acute hydrops** is a significant complication. Manage with cycloplegics, topical steroids, and hypertonic agents; often resolves spontaneously but leaves scarring.
Be vigilant for keratoconus in patients with **Down syndrome** or other connective tissue disorders, as it can be rapidly progressive.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Personalized/Topography-Guided CXL:** Utilizing pre-operative topography to guide UVA application, aiming for a more uniform stiffening or targeted flattening of the cone, potentially improving refractive outcomes.
**Iontophoretic CXL:** A transepithelial CXL technique using an electric current to enhance riboflavin penetration, aiming for better efficacy than passive epi-on methods with reduced discomfort.

**Combination Procedures:** CXL combined with ICRS (Corneal Cross-linking with Intacs - CACXL) or CXL with photorefractive keratectomy (CXL-PRK, 'Athens Protocol') for both stabilization and visual improvement in suitable cases.

**AI and Machine Learning in Diagnosis:** Development of algorithms for early detection and progression prediction using vast topographic and tomographic datasets, enhancing diagnostic accuracy for forme fruste KC.
**Genetic Research:** Ongoing identification of new genetic loci and pathways involved in keratoconus, paving the way for potential future gene therapies or targeted pharmacological interventions.
**Landmark Studies:** The **Dresden Study** established the safety and efficacy of the standard CXL protocol (epithelium-off, 3 mW/cm² for 30 min), providing the foundation for widespread adoption.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric & Special Population Considerations
content: **Faster Progression:** Keratoconus in children and adolescents tends to be more aggressive and progresses faster than in adults.
**Early Intervention:** CXL is often indicated earlier in pediatric cases due to rapid progression and higher risk of severe visual impairment if untreated.
**Anesthesia:** CXL in younger children may require general anesthesia or conscious sedation for cooperation.
**Monitoring:** More frequent monitoring (every 3 months) is essential for pediatric patients to detect progression promptly.
**Associated Conditions:** Higher incidence of systemic associations (e.g., Down Syndrome, Leber Congenital Amaurosis, Atopy) which can influence disease severity and management.
**Contact Lens Wear:** Challenges in fitting and compliance with RGP or scleral lenses in younger children, requiring careful parent/guardian education and support.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Etiology
sections.content: Ocular toxoplasmosis is a retinochoroiditis caused by Toxoplasma gondii. Humans are accidental intermediate hosts. The parasite exists in three forms: Oocysts (excreted by cats), Tachyzoites (active, proliferative form causing tissue damage), and Bradyzoites (inactive, encysted form in chronic infection).

content.explanation: Chorioretinitis (often bilateral/macular), Convulsions (CNS involvement), and Cerebral Calcifications.

rows: Responsible for acute inflammation and tissue destruction.
Latent stage; rupture causes recurrent retinochoroiditis.
Product of sexual cycle in cat gut
Environmental contaminant; highly resistant to disinfection.

sections.title: Primary Ocular Findings
content: Focus of fluffy white retinitis (satellite lesion) adjacent to a pigmented scar.
Moderate to severe vitritis ('Headlight in the Fog').
Kyrieleis Arteritis (periarterial immune deposits).
Anterior uveitis (Granulomatous or non-granulomatous).
Elevated Intraocular Pressure (secondary inflammatory glaucoma).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Clinical Examination: Dilated fundoscopy to identify active vs scarred lesions.
2. Serology: Serum IgG (exposure) and IgM (acute infection).
3. Multimodal Imaging: OCT (identifies focal thickening), FFA (early hypofluorescence, late leakage).
4. Anterior Chamber Tap: PCR for T. gondii DNA or Goldmann-Witmer Coefficient (GWC) for local antibody production.
5. Systemic Screening: Evaluate for immunosuppression (HIV/AIDS).

rows: Typically unilateral, peripheral/macular granuloma with tractional bands.
Rapidly progressing peripheral necrosis, significant vitritis, viral etiology (HSV/VZV).

sections.title: Indications for Systemic Treatment
content: Lesion within 1 disc diameter of Fovea or Optic Nerve.
Lesion threatening a major retinal vessel.
Significant vitritis causing 2+ drop in visual acuity.
Immunocompromised patients (MANDATORY treatment).
Congenital toxoplasmosis in the first year of life.
Only seeing eye or bilateral involvement.

sections.title: Classic 'Triple Therapy' Regimen
content: 1. Pyrimethamine: 50-100mg loading dose, then 25-50mg daily.
2. Sulfadiazine: 1g four times daily.
3. Folinic Acid (Leucovorin): 5-15mg 3x weekly (prevents bone marrow suppression).
4. Systemic Prednisone: 0.5-1.0mg/kg daily (start 48h AFTER antibiotics).

sections.title: Alternative Treatment Options
content: Bactrim DS (Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole): 160/800mg BID. Increasingly popular due to cost and safety.
Clindamycin: 300mg QID (Risk of Pseudomembranous colitis).
Azithromycin: 500mg daily (Used in pregnancy or sulfa allergy).
Intravitreal Injection: Clindamycin (1mg/0.1ml) + Dexamethasone (400µg/0.1ml).

content.explanation: Pyrimethamine can cause thrombocytopenia and leukopenia. Check Weekly Complete Blood Count (CBC)!

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: NEVER give systemic steroids without antibiotic coverage (risk of fulminant retinal necrosis).
The 'satellite lesion' is the most characteristic finding.
Toxoplasmosis is the most common cause of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent patients.
Recurrence risk is highest in the first year after an active episode.
In HIV patients, lesions may be large, multifocal, and lack pigmentary scarring.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: A landmark study by Silveira et al. demonstrated that prophylactic treatment with Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole (one tablet every other day) significantly reduced the rate of recurrent retinochoroiditis in high-risk patients. Recent trends show a shift toward intravitreal therapy to minimize systemic side effects, especially in pregnant patients or those with contraindications to systemic sulfa drugs.

title: Mastering the 4 Prism Diopter Base Out Test
summary: A sophisticated objective clinical tool used to detect microstrabismus and small central suppression scotomas (monofixation syndrome) by observing the biphasic ocular motor response to prism displacement.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: The 4 Prism Diopter (4Δ) Base Out Test, originally described by Irvine and later popularized by Jampolsky, is an objective method to identify microtropia (microstrabismus) when subjective tests like stereopsis or Bagolini lenses are inconclusive. It relies on the Hering’s Law of equal innervation and the presence or absence of a central suppression scotoma (typically 1° to 3° in size).

branches: Hering's Law: Equal innervation to yolk muscles
Fusional Vergence: Corrective adduction for binocularity
Panum's Area: Limits of sensory fusion
Suppression Scotoma: Cortical inhibition of central macula

sections.title: Core Indications
content: Suspected Microstrabismus (Microtropia)
Subnormal stereopsis (60-200 arcsec) with no apparent deviation
Monofixation Syndrome (Primary or Secondary)
Anisometropic Amblyopia screening
Unexplained mild reduction in visual acuity

sections.title: Standard Operating Procedure
content: Step 1: Patient fixates on a small accommodative target (e.g., a single 6/9 letter) at distance (6m) or near (33cm).
Step 2: Ensure the patient is wearing their full refractive correction.
Step 3: Quickly place a 4Δ prism Base Out over the right eye while observing the movements of both eyes.
Step 4: Remove the prism and allow fusion to recover.
Step 5: Repeat the process by placing the 4Δ prism Base Out over the left eye.
Step 6: Carefully document the biphasic movement (Version followed by Vergence).

sections.title: The Normal (Bifoveal) Response
content: Phase 1 (Version): The prism shifts the image onto the temporal retina. Both eyes move towards the apex of the prism (conjugate movement) to refixate.
Phase 2 (Vergence): The fellow eye (without prism) performs a slow fusional adduction (vergence) to eliminate diplopia, as the image is now on its nasal retina.

rows: NO movement of either eye (Image remains within scotoma).
Both eyes move (Version), but NO fusional adduction occurs (Image falls on scotoma of fellow eye).

branches: Atypical: No movement at all (Prism over scotoma eye)
Inconclusive: Poor cooperation or large scotoma (>4Δ)

sections.title: Critical Red Flags & Pitfalls
content: Poor fixation: Can mimic an abnormal test result.
Large scotomas: If scotoma > 4 prism diopters, test is invalid.
Atypical Microtropia: Some patients with microtropia lack a scotoma (rare).
Over-interpretation: Normal patients can occasionally show delayed vergence due to fatigue.

content.explanation: 4 Diopters, Small Scotoma, Search for Symmetry, Stereopsis Correlation.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform the test at distance AND near to check for consistency.
Ensure the target is small enough to require foveal fixation.
Wait at least 5 seconds between eyes for fusional recovery.
A 'negative' test (normal response) effectively rules out microtropia with central scotoma.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Parks (1969) established the 'Monofixation Syndrome' concept, highlighting that the 4Δ BO test is a primary diagnostic criterion. Recent studies using high-speed eye tracking have validated the biphasic nature of the 4Δ BO test, showing that the initial saccade (version) occurs within 200ms, while the vergence component follows at a significantly higher latency and lower velocity.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Test is difficult in children under 4 years old due to fixation stability.
Use a flickering toy or video for distance fixation to maintain interest.
Useful in differentiating refractive amblyopia from microtropic amblyopia.

sections.title: Management of Findings
content: 1. Full Cycloplegic Refraction.
2. Correct Anisometropia.
3. Patching therapy if amblyopia is present (note: microtropia usually limits VA to 6/9-6/12).
4. Surgery is rarely indicated for the micro-deviation itself unless a large manifest component co-exists.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Intracameral silicone oil (ISO) refers to the migration of silicone oil droplets from the posterior segment into the anterior chamber, typically through a patent or surgically created peripheral iridotomy/iridectomy, or secondary to pupillary block. It is most commonly associated with heavy silicone oil or high-viscosity oil tamponades. Prevalence ranges from 2% to 20% post-vitrectomy, depending on the indication (PVR, giant retinal tears).

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Blurred vision or visual fluctuations
Photophobia or halos
Corneal edema (oil-endothelium contact)
Secondary open-angle glaucoma (oil emulsification in the trabecular meshwork)
Band keratopathy (long-term)
Pupillary block

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Operate
content: Corneal decompensation (edema, bullous keratopathy)
Uncontrolled secondary glaucoma (IOP > 30 mmHg)
Signs of endotheliitis
Patient intolerance to visual obstruction

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Observation if small, asymptomatic, and stable IOP.
Step 2: Medical management (topical hypotensives) if IOP elevated.
Step 3: Surgical washout via limbal paracentesis using irrigation/aspiration.
Step 4: Mechanical removal using bent 27G needle or cannula.
Step 5: Peripheral iridotomy management if blockage is suspected.

content.explanation: Observe if stable, Irrigated if corneal touch, Lower pressure (glaucoma meds), Surgical removal if refractory.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Silicone oil in the AC can cause silent corneal endothelial cell loss (endotheliopathy).
Perform specular microscopy if possible to assess endothelial count before major interventions.
When removing oil via paracentesis, consider using a viscoelastic (OVD) to protect the endothelium during aspiration.
Always check the posterior segment; ensure the retina is attached, as oil in the AC may be a sign of posterior migration issues or failure of tamponade.
