sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular Myasthenia Gravis (OMG) is a localized form of Myasthenia Gravis (MG) affecting only the levator palpebrae superioris, orbicularis oculi, and extraocular muscles. It is an autoimmune Type II hypersensitivity reaction where antibodies block or destroy post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the motor end-plate.

branches: AChR Antibodies (80-90% in gMG; 50% in OMG)
MuSK Antibodies (Muscle-Specific Kinase) - Rare in pure OMG

sections.title: Clinical Hallmarks
content: Fatigability: Symptoms worse toward the end of the day or after prolonged use.
Variability: Symptoms change from hour to hour or day to day.
Ptosis: Often asymmetric; may shift from one eye to the other.
Diplopia: Does not follow a single cranial nerve pattern (Pseudo-internuclear ophthalmoplegia).
Orbicularis Weakness: Difficulty keeping eyes tightly closed against resistance.
Pupillary Sparing: The pupil is NEVER involved in MG.

sections.title: The Bedside Diagnostic Toolkit
content: 1. Ice Pack Test: Apply ice to ptotic lid for 2 mins. Improvement of >2mm is (+) due to inhibited acetylcholinesterase.
2. Cogan's Lid Twitch: Overshoot of the upper lid when shifting gaze from down to primary position.
3. Curtain Sign: Manually lifting the more ptotic lid causes the contralateral lid to droop (Hering's Law).
4. Sleep Test: 30 minutes of sleep in a dark room leads to transient resolution of ptosis/diplopia.
5. Enhanced Ptosis: Maintaining upgaze for 60 seconds triggers or worsens lid droop.

rows: Highly specific; risk of generalization if positive.
More common in females; often severe bulbar/respiratory involvement.
High association with Thymoma, especially in older patients.
Progressive, symmetric, lack of variability, 'Frozen Globe'.
Strength improves with exercise; associated with SCLC.

sections.title: Investigations & Workup
content: 1. Serology: AChR-Ab (Binding, Blocking, Modulating), MuSK-Ab.
2. Electrophysiology: Single-fiber EMG (SFEMG) is the gold standard (95%+ sensitivity).
3. Repetitive Nerve Stimulation (RNS): >10% decrement in amplitude.
4. Imaging: Chest CT or MRI to rule out Thymoma (Mandatory in all MG patients).
5. Thyroid Panel: Check TSH/T4 due to high co-occurrence of TED.

sections.title: Management Ladder
content: 1. First Line: Pyridostigmine (Mestinon) 60mg TID-QID. Adjust for symptoms.
2. Second Line: Corticosteroids (Prednisone). Start low/slow to avoid transient worsening.
3. Steroid Sparing: Azathioprine, Mycophenolate Mofetil, or Cyclosporine.
4. Crisis/Severe: IVIG or Plasmapheresis (PLEX).
5. Thymectomy: If thymoma present or in non-thymomatous gMG (MGTX trial).

sections.title: Red Flags & Contraindicated Drugs
content: MYASTHENIC CRISIS: Respiratory failure or severe dysphagia (Emergency!).
Avoid Fluoroquinolones (Ciprofloxacin/Levofloxacin) - can precipitate crisis.
Avoid Aminoglycosides (Gentamicin/Tobramycin).
Avoid Beta-blockers (Systemic and Topical Timolol).
Avoid Magnesium Sulfate.
Neuromuscular blockers (Succinylcholine/Vecuronium) require extreme caution in surgery.

rows: Mild generalized MG; slow progression; no crisis.
Moderate generalized MG; severe skeletal/bulbar involvement.
Acute fulminating MG; rapid onset; respiratory crisis.
Late severe MG; progression from Grade I/II.

content.explanation: S: Simpson's test (upgaze fatigue), T: Tensilon test (Edrophonium), A: Antibodies (AChR/MuSK), R: Rest (Ice pack/Sleep test), E: EMG (Single-fiber).

sections.title: Surgical Nuances
content: Ptosis Surgery: Generally avoided unless MG is medically stable for >1 year.
Sling vs. Levator Resection: Frontalis sling is often preferred due to poor levator function and risk of lagophthalmos.
Strabismus Surgery: Rarely performed due to the shifting nature of the deviation; prisms are first-line.
Pre-op Warning: Always notify anesthesiology about MG status due to sensitivity to paralytics.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: OMG patients with positive AChR antibodies are more likely to generalize.
The 'pseudointernuclear ophthalmoplegia' of MG can be distinguished from a true INO because MG lacks the nystagmus of the abducting eye.
Tensilon (Edrophonium) test is rarely used now due to risks of bradycardia/asystole; keep Atropine at bedside if performing.
Prednisone can cause a transient 'dip' in muscle strength during the first 7-10 days of therapy.

sections.title: Landmark Study: EPITOME & MGTX
sections.content: The MGTX Trial (2016) demonstrated that thymectomy plus prednisone was superior to prednisone alone in non-thymomatous gMG patients (ages 18-65) regarding symptom control and steroid-sparing. For pure OMG, the EPITOME trial explored low-dose steroids, suggesting earlier intervention may reduce the rate of generalization, though this remains a topic of clinical debate.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: 90% of those who generalize will do so within the first 2 years of onset.
If MG remains purely ocular for 3 years, the chance of generalization is <10%.
Exposure keratopathy: A common complication of ptosis surgery or severe orbicularis weakness.
Steroid side effects: Cataracts, Glaucoma, and Weight Gain must be monitored.

title: Aniridia: Unveiling the PAX6 Spectrum
summary: Aniridia is a rare, bilateral congenital panocular disorder primarily caused by PAX6 gene mutations, characterized by incomplete iris development and a constellation of ocular abnormalities. It leads to severe visual impairment and can be associated with systemic conditions like WAGR syndrome, requiring a comprehensive, lifelong multidisciplinary approach.

data.title: Aniridia: Unveiling the PAX6 Spectrum
data.summary: Aniridia is a rare, bilateral congenital panocular disorder primarily caused by PAX6 gene mutations, characterized by incomplete iris development and a constellation of ocular abnormalities. It leads to severe visual impairment and can be associated with systemic conditions like WAGR syndrome, requiring a comprehensive, lifelong multidisciplinary approach.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Aniridia is a rare, bilateral congenital panocular disorder characterized by partial or complete hypoplasia of the iris, often appearing as a 'missing' iris. It is part of a developmental spectrum of ocular abnormalities, including foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, glaucoma, cataracts, and aniridia-associated keratopathy (AAK). It is primarily caused by mutations in the *PAX6* gene, a master control gene for eye development, and can manifest as isolated ocular disease or as part of a systemic syndrome.

sections.title: Incidence & Demographics
content: **Incidence**: Estimated at 1 in 60,000 to 1 in 100,000 live births worldwide.
**Prevalence**: Consistent with incidence due to its congenital nature.
**Demographics**: No reported gender or ethnic predilection.
**Risk Factors**: Family history (autosomal dominant inheritance, ~60-70% cases) or *de novo* *PAX6* mutation (~30-40% cases).

sections.title: 3. Etiology & Pathophysiology: The PAX6 Gene
sections.content: The primary cause of aniridia is a heterozygous mutation in the *PAX6* gene, located on chromosome 11p13. *PAX6* is a highly conserved paired box transcription factor essential for the development of the eye, brain, olfactory system, and pancreas. Haploinsufficiency of *PAX6* (one functional copy) leads to the spectrum of aniridia phenotypes. Pathologically, it results from arrested development of anterior segment structures and other ocular components during embryogenesis, specifically affecting neuroectodermal and mesenchymal precursors.

sections.title: Pathophysiology Breakdown
content: **Iris**: Failure of appropriate neuroectodermal and mesenchymal cell migration and differentiation, leading to variable degrees of iris hypoplasia, typically appearing as a rudimentary stump.

**Cornea**: *PAX6* is crucial for limbal stem cell development and maintenance. Deficiency results in limbal stem cell deficiency (LSD), leading to conjunctivalization, vascularization, chronic epithelial defects, and opacification (Aniridia-Associated Keratopathy, AAK).
**Lens**: Abnormal lens vesicle formation and differentiation, predisposing to early onset polar or subcapsular cataracts.
**Retina/Fovea**: Impaired foveal development (foveal hypoplasia) due to PAX6's role in retinal patterning and differentiation. This is a primary cause of reduced vision.

**Glaucoma**: Anomalous angle development, including anterior displacement of Schwalbe's line and hypoplasia/dysgenesis of the trabecular meshwork, leading to compromised aqueous outflow and elevated IOP, often later in life.
**Nystagmus**: Typically a sensory nystagmus, secondary to the poor visual acuity caused by foveal hypoplasia and other ocular anomalies.

branches: WAGR Syndrome (Wilms Tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary Anomalies, Intellectual Disability)
Gillespie Syndrome (Aniridia, Cerebellar Ataxia, Intellectual Disability)
Isolated Foveal Hypoplasia (Mildest spectrum of PAX6 defect)

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Photophobia**: Universal due to the absence of a functional iris.
**Decreased Visual Acuity**: Variable, typically 20/100 to 20/400, present from infancy due to foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, and other progressive complications (cataract, glaucoma, AAK).
**Nystagmus**: Congenital, pendular, often manifest early due to foveal hypoplasia and poor central fixation.
**Strabismus**: Common, secondary to poor vision and nystagmus.
**Epiphora/Irritation**: Due to severe dry eye and corneal epithelial defects from AAK.
**Pain/Redness**: Can indicate acute glaucoma or severe corneal inflammation/infection.
**Amblyopia**: Can develop, especially if significant anisometropia or strabismus.

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Visual Acuity**: Severely reduced, often non-correctable beyond 20/100-20/400.
**Slit Lamp Exam**:
- **Iris**: Apparent partial or total absence of iris. A small rudimentary iris stump usually visible, especially on gonioscopy or AS-OCT.
- **Cornea**: Limbal stem cell deficiency (LSD) leading to corneal pannus, vascularization, opacification, recurrent epithelial defects (AAK).
- **Lens**: Polar cataracts (anterior/posterior) are common; subcapsular or complete cataracts can occur. Subluxation is possible.
- **Anterior Chamber**: May show peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) or angle dysgenesis.
**Gonioscopy**: Crucial for assessing angle configuration, visualizing iris stumps, and identifying malformed trabecular meshwork and anteriorly displaced Schwalbe's line.
**Fundoscopy**: Foveal hypoplasia (absence of foveal reflex, normal foveal contour, visible underlying choroidal vessels). Optic nerve hypoplasia or dysplastic changes can also be seen.
**Refraction**: Often high myopia and astigmatism.

**IOP**: Can be difficult to measure accurately due to nystagmus and corneal irregularities. Tono-Pen or Icare tonometry may be preferred. IOP elevation often manifests later in childhood or adulthood.

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **1. Comprehensive Ophthalmic Exam**: Visual acuity, refraction, slit lamp, gonioscopy, fundoscopy, IOP measurement.
**2. Ocular Imaging**:
- **Macular OCT**: Confirm and quantify foveal hypoplasia, assess retinal architecture.
- **Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT) / UBM**: Detailed visualization of iris remnants, angle structures, ciliary body, corneal layers (especially for AAK).
**3. Genetic Testing**:
- **PAX6 Gene Sequencing**: Identify point mutations, small deletions/insertions (gold standard).
- **Chromosomal Microarray / FISH**: Detect larger deletions involving 11p13, crucial for WAGR syndrome diagnosis.
**4. Systemic Workup (especially for sporadic cases or suspected WAGR)**:
- **Renal Ultrasound**: Screening for Wilms tumor (every 3 months until age 8, then annually).
- **Urinalysis & Renal Function Tests**.
- **Pediatric Consultation**: General health assessment, developmental screening.
- **Neurological Assessment**: Evaluate for developmental delay or cerebellar ataxia.
**5. Genetic Counseling**: Essential for families, discussing inheritance, recurrence risk, and systemic implications.

rows: Sectoral iris defect (often inferonasal), typically with underlying choroidal/retinal coloboma. Pupil is keyhole-shaped. Often unilateral or asymmetrical.
History of trauma, focal detachment of iris root, typically unilateral. Often associated with other signs of trauma.
Diffuse iris transillumination (stroma present but hypopigmented), foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, reduced acuity. Often associated with skin/hair hypopigmentation.
Acquired inflammatory iris atrophy, synechiae, often with signs of inflammation (cells/flare, KPs). History of recurrent inflammation.
Progressive, typically unilateral, pupil distortion, peripheral anterior synechiae, corneal decompensation (Chandler's syndrome variant). Often involves corectopia.
Small pupils (miotic) unresponsive to dilating agents, often without significant iris hypoplasia, associated with glaucoma.
Often normal, or mutations in other genes (e.g., FOXC1)

sections.title: 9. Staging: Aniridia-Associated Keratopathy (AAK)
content: AAK is a progressive condition leading to corneal blindness. The Holland & Mannis classification (simplified):
**Stage 1**: Epithelial defects, punctate keratopathy, mild dry eye.
**Stage 2**: Persistent epithelial defects, chronic inflammation, early peripheral corneal neovascularization.
**Stage 3**: Stromal opacification, central neovascularization, goblet cell metaplasia, conjunctivalization.
**Stage 4**: Complete corneal opacification, severe limbal stem cell deficiency, total vision loss from corneal pathology.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment: A Lifelong Journey
content: **1. Diagnosis & Systemic Screening**: Confirm aniridia, perform genetic testing, screen for WAGR syndrome (renal ultrasound, pediatric consult).
**2. Low Vision Rehabilitation**: Early referral for visual aids, magnifiers, occupational therapy to maximize residual vision.

**3. Photophobia Management**: Dark tinted glasses/contact lenses (e.g., opaque iris pattern), iris diaphragm contact lenses. Surgical options include artificial iris implants (e.g., HumanOptics CustomFlex, Ophtec Artificial Iris).
**4. Ocular Surface Management (AAK)**:

- **Conservative**: Preservative-free artificial tears (e.g., Systane Ultra UD, Refresh Plus UD), lubricating gels/ointments, topical cyclosporine 0.05-0.09% (Restasis, Cequa) or lifitegrast 5% (Xiidra) for inflammation.
- **Advanced**: Autologous serum tears, scleral lenses for comfort and epithelial healing, topical corticosteroids (short-term for acute inflammation).

- **Surgical**: Limbal Stem Cell Transplantation (LSCT - autologous, allogeneic, or cultivated), often followed by Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) or Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) once ocular surface is stable.
**5. Glaucoma Management**:

- **Medical**: Topical beta-blockers (Timolol 0.25-0.5% BID), prostaglandin analogs (Latanoprost 0.005% QD), alpha-agonists (Brimonidine 0.1-0.2% BID/TID), topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (Dorzolamide 2% TID, Brinzolamide 1% TID). Oral CAIs (Acetazolamide) for acute pressure spikes.
- **Surgical**: Trabeculectomy with antimetabolites (Mitomycin C 0.2-0.4mg/ml for 1-3 min, 5-FU), Glaucoma Drainage Devices (Ahmed, Baerveldt). Cyclophotocoagulation (CPC) as a last resort.
**6. Cataract Management**: Phacoemulsification with extreme caution. May require special IOLs (e.g., iris diaphragm IOLs like HumanOptics CustomFlex) to reduce glare and improve cosmesis.

**7. Nystagmus/Strabismus**: Vision therapy, prism correction. Surgical correction for strabismus may be considered for cosmetic or functional benefits, but does not address the underlying nystagmus or foveal hypoplasia.
**8. Genetic Counseling**: Ongoing support for family planning and understanding the condition.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Key Considerations
content: **Cataract Surgery**: Challenging due to zonular weakness, corneal issues, and poor visualization. Careful capsulorhexis (often larger than normal), use of capsular tension rings, and meticulous IOL selection are vital. Consider an iris diaphragm IOL.
**Limbal Stem Cell Transplantation (LSCT)**:
- **Autologous**: Harvest from contralateral healthy eye (rare in bilateral aniridia).

- **Allogeneic**: From living related donor or cadaveric. Requires systemic immunosuppression (e.g., oral cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil). Cultivated autologous/allogeneic limbal epithelial transplantation (CALET/CALELT) is an evolving technique.
- Often combined with keratoplasty (PKP/DALK) for severe opacification.

**Glaucoma Surgery**: Trabeculectomy has variable success due to abnormal anatomy. Use of antimetabolites (MMC) is crucial. Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDDs) are often considered for refractory cases. Minimize conjunctival scarring for future LSCT.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Ocular Complications**:
- **Glaucoma**: Most common blinding complication, affecting 50-75% of patients.
- **Aniridia-Associated Keratopathy (AAK)**: Leading cause of corneal blindness.
- **Cataracts**: Present in 50-80% of patients.
- **Foveal Hypoplasia**: Universal, primary cause of baseline reduced vision.
- **Nystagmus**: Universal, usually congenital sensory.
- **Retinal Detachment**: Increased risk, though rare.
**Systemic Complications (WAGR Syndrome)**:
- **Wilms Tumor**: Occurs in ~50% of WAGR patients.
- **Genitourinary Anomalies**: Undescended testes, hypospadias, renal anomalies.
- **Intellectual Disability/Developmental Delay**.

**Prognosis**: Variable. Lifelong management required. Visual acuity typically remains poor (20/100 to 20/400) even with intervention. Early detection and aggressive management of complications are key to preserving vision.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Acute, Severe Eye Pain with Redness/Halos**: Suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma or high IOP, requiring immediate evaluation.
**Sudden Drop in Vision**: Could indicate retinal detachment, severe corneal decompensation, or acute glaucoma.
**Rapid Progression of Corneal Opacification/Vascularization**: Worsening AAK requiring urgent intervention to prevent irreversible vision loss.
**Any Signs of Wilms Tumor (in WAGR patients)**: Abdominal mass, hematuria, hypertension – requires immediate pediatric and oncologic evaluation.

content.explanation:
**W**: **W**ilms Tumor
**A**: **A**niridia
**G**: **G**enitourinary Anomalies
**R**: Intellectual **R**etardation (Developmental Delay)

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Sporadic Aniridia = WAGR Risk**: ALWAYS screen for WAGR syndrome in patients with sporadic aniridia and 11p13 deletion.
**Foveal Hypoplasia is Primary**: It's the intrinsic cause of baseline poor vision, not correctable by optical means.
**Glaucoma & AAK are Progressive**: These are the main causes of progressive vision loss and require aggressive, proactive management.
**Early Intervention is Key**: Especially for AAK and glaucoma, to optimize outcomes and prevent irreversible damage.
**Multidisciplinary Care**: Essential for managing the ocular and potential systemic complexities.
**Genetic Counseling**: Crucial for informed family decisions and understanding disease implications.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent research focuses on understanding the diverse roles of *PAX6* beyond eye development, and developing novel therapeutic strategies. Gene therapy approaches, including CRISPR/Cas9 editing to correct *PAX6* mutations or enhance residual gene expression, are under investigation. Advances in cultivated limbal epithelial stem cell transplantation (C-LEST) are improving outcomes for severe AAK. The development of advanced artificial iris prostheses has enhanced cosmetic and functional rehabilitation for photophobia. Landmark studies continue to refine the understanding of PAX6-related developmental pathways and risk stratification for associated syndromes.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Early Diagnosis & Genetic Testing**: Critical for timely initiation of WAGR screening and genetic counseling.
**Aggressive WAGR Surveillance**: Regular renal ultrasounds are paramount for early detection of Wilms tumor in at-risk children.
**Refractive Correction**: Optimize vision with spectacles/contact lenses, even if visual potential is limited, to prevent amblyopia and aid development.
**Low Vision Aids & Rehabilitation**: Early referral for specialized services to support visual development and daily living skills.
**Glaucoma Management in Children**: Particularly challenging; often requires early surgical intervention with careful consideration of long-term outcomes and potential need for repeat surgeries.
**Ocular Surface Protection**: Lifelong management of AAK with lubricants, anti-inflammatory drops, and potentially scleral lenses from a young age.
**Psychosocial Support**: For children and families coping with a lifelong condition, reduced vision, and potential systemic complications.

summary: Diabetic Macular Edema (DME) is the leading cause of moderate vision loss in the working-age population. This poster provides a deep-dive into its pathophysiology, evidence-based management, and the latest landmark clinical trials.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: DME is defined as retinal thickening or hard exudate accumulation within 1 disc diameter of the center of the macula. It results from the breakdown of the inner Blood-Retinal Barrier (BRB), leading to the leakage of fluid and plasma constituents into the intraretinal layers, specifically the Outer Plexiform Layer (Henle's layer) and Inner Nuclear Layer.

branches: VEGF Pathway: Upregulation due to hypoxia
Angiopoietin-2: Competes with Ang-1 for Tie2 receptor
Leukostasis: Neutrophil adhesion to capillary endothelium
Oxidative Stress: PKC pathway & Polyol pathway activation
Pericyte Loss: Leading to microaneurysm formation

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Microaneurysms (MAs): Earliest sign, focal leakage points.
Hard Exudates (HE): Lipid deposits, often in circinate patterns.
Retinal Edema: Thickening/clouding of the macula.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Fluid pockets in a petaloid pattern.
Ischemic Maculopathy: Enlarged Foveal Avascular Zone (FAZ).
Vitreomacular Interface issues: Epiretinal membranes (ERM).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: BCVA & Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (90D lens) for baseline.
Step 2: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) to measure CST and identify IRF/SRF.
Step 3: Fluorescein Angiography (FA) to differentiate Focal vs. Diffuse leakage.
Step 4: OCT-Angiography (OCT-A) to assess FAZ and capillary non-perfusion.
Step 5: Fundus Photography for longitudinal tracking of hard exudates.

Widespread flame hemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins.

sections.title: Medical Management: The Systemic 'Big Three'
content: Glycemic Control: Target HbA1c < 7.0% (DCCT/UKPDS).
Blood Pressure Control: Target < 130/80 mmHg.
Lipid Management: Statins to reduce hard exudate accumulation (FIELD study).
Renal Function: Monitoring GFR and albuminuria.

rows: 2mg (VIVID/VISTA) - VEGF Trap, binds VEGF-A, B, PlGF

sections.title: Corticosteroid Implants
content: Ozurdex (Dexamethasone 0.7mg): 3-6 month duration, biodegradable.
Iluvien (Fluocinolone 0.19mg): 36 month duration, non-biodegradable.
Indications: Chronic DME, pseudophakic patients, anti-VEGF non-responders.
Side Effects: Cataract progression (near 100%), IOP elevation (approx 30%).

sections.title: Laser & Surgery
content: Focal Laser: Target MAs 50-100µm size, 0.1s duration, 'light gray' burn.
Grid Laser: Applied to areas of diffuse thickening.
Subthreshold Micropulse: Minimizes collateral RPE damage.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): Reserved for tractional DME (VMT/ERM) or refractory cases.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Endophthalmitis: Post-injection pain, redness, hypopyon.
IOP Spike: Post-steroid injection glaucoma.
Retinal Detachment: Floaters/flashes post-injection or surgery.
Ischemic Maculopathy: BCVA < 20/200 with normal CST on OCT.
Pregnancy: Caution with anti-VEGF (potential systemic absorption).

content.explanation: If vision is 20/50 or worse, Aflibercept was superior to Bevacizumab/Ranibizumab at 1 year. If 20/40 or better, all drugs performed similarly.

rows: Focal laser reduced risk of moderate vision loss by 50%.
Ranibizumab significantly improved VA vs Sham.
Observation is viable for DME with 20/25 or better vision.
Aflibercept can improve DR severity scale (DRSS) score.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for 'Disorganization of Retinal Inner Layers' (DRIL) on OCT as a prognostic marker.
DME can be 'Tractional' or 'Non-tractional'—vitrectomy only helps the former.
Hard exudates at the fovea often leave permanent scarring/subfoveal fibrosis.
NSAID drops (e.g., Nepafenac) may be an adjunct in mild, non-CI DME.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Future Trends
sections.content: Port Delivery Systems (PDS) for continuous ranibizumab release and Gene Therapy (RGX-314) aiming for 'one-and-done' treatment are currently in advanced clinical trials. Dual inhibition of Ang-2 and VEGF-A (Faricimab) represents the new standard for extending treatment intervals up to Q16 weeks.

summary: Esotropia is the most common form of childhood strabismus, characterized by an inward deviation of one or both eyes. This guide covers the spectrum from infantile onset and accommodative types to surgical management and landmark clinical evidence.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Esotropia (ET) is a form of strabismus where the visual axes intersect in front of the object of regard. It is categorized by onset (congenital vs. acquired), frequency (constant vs. intermittent), and mechanism (accommodative vs. non-accommodative). Precise diagnosis is critical as it may be the presenting sign of life-threatening pathology such as retinoblastoma or intracranial tumors.

sections.title: Infantile Esotropia Syndrome (IES)
content: Onset: Within the first 6 months of life.
Angle: Usually large (>30 Prism Diopters) and stable.
Refraction: Usually normal for age (approx +1.50D).
Cross-fixation: Patient looks left with right eye and right with left eye.
Latent Nystagmus: Jerk nystagmus appearing when one eye is covered.
Dissociated Vertical Deviation (DVD): Upward drift of the non-fixing eye (found in 50-90%).
Inferior Oblique Overaction (IOOA): Frequent late finding.

rows: ET greater at near than distance
Significant ET at both, worse at near
Residual ET remains after full correction

sections.title: Ocular Examination Protocol
content: Step 1: History (Onset, frequency, family history).
Step 2: Visual Acuity (Fix and Follow, CSM, or Snellen/LEA).
Step 3: Cover/Uncover and Alternate Cover Test (Prism neutralization).
Step 4: Ocular Motility (Versions/Ductions, look for IOOA or A/V patterns).
Step 5: Cycloplegic Refraction (1% Atropine or 1% Cyclopentolate mandatory).
Step 6: Dilated Fundus Exam (Rule out sensory causes like Retinoblastoma).

sections.title: Sensory Esotropia Red Flags
content: Leukocoria (White pupillary reflex)
Optic Atrophy or Hypoplasia
Macular Scars (e.g., Toxoplasmosis)
Retinoblastoma (Must exclude in ALL new cases)
Dense Cataract

rows: Prominent epicanthal folds; symmetrical Hirschberg reflex.
Limited abduction, globe retraction/narrowing of palpebral fissure on adduction.
Recent onset, limited abduction, diplopia (if old enough), head turn.
Large angle ET with limited abduction and jerk nystagmus.

content.explanation: AC/A = (Δ1 - Δ2) / D. Where Δ1 is original deviation, Δ2 is deviation with lens, and D is power of lens used.

sections.title: Surgical Management: Infantile ET
content: 1. Stabilization: Ensure amblyopia is treated first.
2. Procedure Selection: Bilateral Medial Rectus (BMR) Recession is gold standard.
3. Dosing: 5mm for 20-25PD; 6mm for 30-35PD; 7mm for 45-50PD.
4. Associated Patterns: Address Inferior Oblique (Myectomy) if OAIO is present.
5. Timing: Ideally before 2 years of age to maximize binocular potential.

sections.title: Post-Operative Complications
content: Slipped or Lost Muscle (Surgical emergency)
Consecutive Exotropia (Overcorrection)
Globe Perforation
Anterior Segment Ischemia (Risk if >2 muscles/eye)
Suture Granuloma or Tenon's Prolapse

sections.title: Special Form: Acute Acquired Comitant ET
content: Swan Type: Following occlusion/loss of vision.
Burian-Franceschetti Type: Idiopathic, large angle, no refractive error.
Bielschowsky Type: Found in uncorrected myopes due to near work.
NEURO ALERT: Acute ET can be a sign of cerebellar tumor (Chiari Malformation).

sections.title: The ELIS Trial & Timing of Surgery
sections.content: The Early vs. Late Infantile Strabismus (ELIS) study suggests that surgery performed before age 2, specifically between 6 months and 2 years, results in better stereopsis and gross binocularity compared to delayed surgery, though re-operation rates may be higher.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Board Exam
content: Always check for a 'V' or 'A' pattern; 'V' is often IOOA, 'A' is often SOOA.
Prism Adaptation Test (PAT): Used to identify patients who 'eat' prism before surgery.
Monofixation Syndrome: A common 'success' state after ET surgery (small angle, central scotoma, peripheral fusion).
Sensory ET in adults: If sudden onset, think intracranial pressure.

content.explanation: D: Diminished Abduction, U: Up/Down shoots, A: Adduction causes globe retraction, N: Narrowing of fissure, E: Esotropia in primary position.

sections.title: Investigations: Ancillary Testing
content: Worth 4-Dot Test: Assess for suppression or diplopia.
Stereopsis Testing: Titmus Fly or Randot (IES usually has no stereopsis).
Hess Screen / Lancaster Red-Green: Useful for paralytic ET.
Neuroimaging (MRI/CT): Mandatory if ET is associated with neurological signs, ataxia, or papilledema.

sections.title: Summary of Success Criteria
content: Primary Success: Orthotropia within 10 PD of central alignment.
Functional Success: Restoration of gross stereopsis (e.g., 200-400 arc sec).
Cosmetic Success: Deviation not noticeable by casual observers.

title: NON-PENETRATING & MICRO-INVASIVE GLAUCOMA SURGERY

sections.title: Non-penetrating Glaucoma Surgery (NPGS) Overview
sections.content: Non-penetrating glaucoma surgery (NPGS) describes a group of techniques in which improved aqueous drainage is achieved surgically without penetrating into the AC at the time of initial surgery. Controversy continues regarding their long-term success rate, partly due to the long learning curve associated with these challenging techniques. It is likely that, in experienced hands, NPGS with augmentation can achieve similar long-term success to that seen with penetrating glaucoma surgery, but final IOPs are often higher than after augmented trabeculectomy surgery.

sections.title: Early Risks vs. Serious Complications
content: Although NPGS has a lower rate of early hypotony after surgery, serious complications have been described:
Severe hypotony
Endophthalmitis
Suprachoroidal haemorrhage

branches: Mechanism: Guarded filtration (like trabeculectomy); drainage rate controlled at TM/Descemet's membrane instead of scleral flap.
Outline: Formation of conjunctival and superficial scleral flaps.
Deep (90% depth) scleral flap to expose Schlemm's canal.
Schlemm's canal deroofed; endothelium and juxtacanalicular TM peeled off to improve drainage.
Deep scleral flap part excised to form deep sclerectomy space.
Final: Antifibrotics may be applied, implant may be inserted; conjunctival flap closed.

sections.title: Deep Sclerectomy Variations
content: Antifibrotics: Used in high-risk cases to reduce intrascleral scarring. No benefit demonstrated with 5-FU; small studies show improved IOP control with MMC.14
Implants: Inserted into deep scleral space to maintain space during healing and form 'intrascleral bleb'.
Absorbable Implants: e.g. Aquaflow or SKGel.
Non-absorbable Implants: e.g. t Flux.

Goniopuncture: Nd-yAG goniopuncture used as 2° procedure if IOP control is insufficient; effectively converts it to a penetrating procedure. performed in about half of cases in one study. Sight-threatening complications (hypotony) reported.

rows: Expected (with deep AC); may transiently affect vision.
Inadequate dissection of TM/Descemet's membrane (treated with Nd-yAG goniopuncture).
Rupture of TM/Descemet's membrane by mild trauma (rubbing, Valsalva), causing iris prolapse and drainage blockage (requires revision/conversion to trabeculectomy).
PAS formation blocking drainage site (reversible with laser iridoplasty).
Detachment of Descemet's membrane (very rare). All complications of penetrating surgery have been reported.

sections.title: Viscocanalostomy Details
content: Mechanism: Proposed to increase aqueous flow into Schlemm's canal (little evidence to support).
Procedure: Creation of conjunctival, superficial, and deep scleral flaps; deroofing of Schlemm's canal.
Key Feature: Schlemm's canal is opened with a viscoelastic to improve drainage.
Closure: Superficial scleral flap tightly sutured to minimize sub-Tenon's filtration, encouraging canal drainage.
Variations: Both antifibrotics and implants may be used.
Complications: Similar to deep sclerectomy. Detachment of Descemet's membrane (at time of viscoelastic injection) is more common but still uncommon.

sections.title: Micro-invasive Glaucoma Surgery (MIGS) Landscape
sections.content: Over the past decade, there has been a proliferation in the number of MIGS devices developed, in an attempt to improve the safety and ease of glaucoma surgery. these devices target Schlemm’s canal, the suprachoroidal space, and the sub-tenon’s space. MIGS devices can be used alone or in combination with phaco cataract surgery. however, IOP reduction achieved with the use of these devices are less than IOP reduction achieved with trabeculectomy. therefore, at present, their role is in the management of early to moderate glaucoma, and their role in advanced disease has not been defined.

sections.title: Schlemm's Canal Procedures (Part 1)
content: iStent: Small transtrabecular titanium stent (1mm x 0.3mm). Drains aqueous from AC into Schlemm's canal. Placed through 2.8mm clear corneal incision with gonioscopy lens. Inserted in inferonasal quadrant via introducer. Positive sign: Immediate blood reflux from Schlemm's canal through/around snorkel. For phaco, pseudophakic, or phakic eyes. Advanced glaucoma role under evaluation.
Hydrus stent: 8mm nitinol (nickel-titanium alloy) stent. Functions as intracanalicular scaffold in Schlemm's canal and dilates the canal. Early data are promising.
Trabectome: Thermal cautery device ablating 2- to 4-clock-hour segment of TM and Schlemm's canal under direct gonioscopy. Connects AC directly with collector channels. Phaco/phakic/pseudophakic use.

sections.title: Schlemm's Canal Procedures (Part 2)
content: Kahook dual blade: Microblade designed to strip a section of TM and anterior wall of Schlemm's canal (similar principle to Trabectome).
Ab interno canaloplasty (ABiC): Microcatheter threaded 360° around Schlemm's canal under gonioscopic view; viscoelastic used to mechanically dilate canal.
Ab externo canaloplasty: Uses 9-0 or 10-0 prolene suture through 360° of Schlemm's canal with microcatheter and viscoelastic. Involves construction of a deep sclerectomy-type flap for access.

sections.title: Suprachoroidal Procedures
content: CyPass Micro-Stent: Supraciliary microstent implanted through 1.5mm clear corneal incision. Increases uveoscleral outflow (AC to suprachoroidal space). Inserted over micro-guidewire creating small cyclodialysis cleft.
Solx Gold Shunt: Small shunt placed into supraciliary space through 3mm incision to increase uveoscleral outflow. Direct access from AC to suprachoroidal space.
Failure Risk: All current supraciliary microstents may develop fibrosis around the device.

sections.title: Sub-Tenon's Microshunt Procedures
content: Xen and Innfocus: Connect AC to sub-Tenon's space for traditional filtering bleb. Xen uses a gelatin implant.
Adjuvant MMC: Anti-scarring MMC may be injected subconjunctivally at surgery.
PI: Peripheral iridectomy is NOT performed in these procedures.
Maintenance: Bleb needling revision may be required if fibrosis occurs.
Ex-Press: Small stainless steel minishunt. Drains AC to sub-Tenon's space. Used with standard trabeculectomy. PI is NOT performed.

summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis, pathophysiology, and surgical management of infantile nystagmus variants. This poster contrasts the passive induction of Latent Nystagmus (LN) with the active dampening mechanism of Nystagmus Blockage Syndrome (NBS).

data.summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis, pathophysiology, and surgical management of infantile nystagmus variants. This poster contrasts the passive induction of Latent Nystagmus (LN) with the active dampening mechanism of Nystagmus Blockage Syndrome (NBS).

branches: Latent Nystagmus (LN): Conjugate horizontal jerky nystagmus evoked only by monocular occlusion.
Manifest Latent Nystagmus (MLN): LN present with both eyes open but one eye is functionally suppressed (e.g., amblyopia).
Nystagmus Blockage Syndrome (NBS): A strategy where esotropia is used to dampen nystagmus intensity.

content.explanation: In Latent Nystagmus, the fast phase ALWAYS beats TOWARD the FIXATING (uncovered) eye. If you cover the Left Eye, the nystagmus beats Right.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: Why it Happens
sections.content: Latent Nystagmus arises from a failure of binocular development in infancy. It is linked to the subcortical visual pathway (nucleus of the optic tract) where monocular input dominates. In NBS, the adduction of the eye places the eye in a 'null zone' or uses the mechanical restriction of the medial rectus to physically stabilize the globe, thereby improving visual acuity.

branches: Type I: Nystagmus present in primary, disappears in adduction.
Type II: Nystagmus appears when the fixating eye moves from adduction to primary.
Type III: Manifest nystagmus in all positions, dampened by ET.

sections.title: Red Flags: Pseudo-NBS
content: Sixth Nerve Palsy (Abducens): Rule out if abduction is limited without nystagmus.
Duane Retraction Syndrome: Look for globe retraction and palpebral fissure narrowing.
Ciancia Syndrome: Large angle ET with apparent abduction deficit, but full abduction on doll's head maneuver.
Mobius Syndrome: If associated with facial nerve palsy.

sections.title: Clinical Examination Steps
content: Step 1: Observe primary position with both eyes open (Check for MLN).
Step 2: Cover one eye and observe the onset and direction of jerky oscillations (LN).
Step 3: Perform 'Translucent Cover' test to maintain light input while dissociating.
Step 4: Assess head posture (Face turn toward fixating eye in LN).
Step 5: Check 'Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex' (VOR) to rule out true paretic abduction deficits.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Electronystagmography (ENG) or Video-oculography (VOG) showing 'decelerating slow phase' characteristic of INS/LN.
Cycloplegic Refraction: Hyperopia is common in infantile ET/NBS.
Stereopsis Testing: Usually absent or severely reduced.
Visual Acuity: Test monocularly using high plus lenses (+5.00D) rather than an opaque occluder to prevent inducing LN.

sections.title: Surgical Management of NBS
content: Step 1: Determine the 'Blocking' eye and the preferred adducted position.
Step 2: Large Recessions of Medial Recti (often exceeding standard tables).
Step 3: Posterior Fixation Sutures (Cüppers Faden procedure) to weaken the muscle in its field of action without changing primary position.
Step 4: Combined Recession + Faden if esotropia is massive and nystagmus is severe.

sections.title: Surgical Management of LN/MLN
content: Step 1: Address underlying Strabismus (ET/DVD) first.
Step 2: If significant head turn exists, perform Kestenbaum-type procedure.
Step 3: Move the eyes in the direction of the head turn (opposite the null point).
Step 4: Consider Faden procedure on the fixating eye to dampen the MLN.

sections.title: Alexander's Law in LN
content: Nystagmus intensity increases when the eye moves in the direction of the fast phase.
In LN, abduction of the fixating eye increases the fast-phase intensity.
In LN, adduction of the fixating eye decreases the fast-phase intensity.
This explains the head turn: the patient turns their face toward the fixating eye to keep it in adduction.

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
content: Visual Acuity: Often good binocularly, but monocular testing is misleadingly poor.
Motor Alignment: Surgical success rate for NBS is approximately 60-70% for achieving <10PD.
Sensory: True 3D stereopsis is rarely achieved, but peripheral fusion is possible.
Stability: LN usually persists throughout life but may dampen with age.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always suspect NBS in a child with a large-angle esotropia who cross-fixes and appears to have bilaterally limited abduction.
The 'translucent occluder' is your best friend: it allows enough light to prevent the 'darkness-induced' component of LN during VA testing.
Differentiating NBS from 'Ciancia Syndrome': Ciancia is a constellation of findings (Large ET, LN, DVD, Limited Abduction) where NBS is specifically the dampening mechanism.
Surgical overcorrection is a risk in NBS; however, under-correction usually results in a return of the compensatory head posture.

sections.title: Lens-Related Glaucoma Overview
sections.content: Lens-related glaucoma may result from abnormalities of lens size, lens position, release of lens protein (mature cataract/trauma/surgery), and/or the consequent inflammatory response.

branches: Normal eye: 2° to intumescent cataractous lens
Short eye: 2° to normal increase in lens size with age

sections.title: Phacomorphic: Clinical & Treatment
content: Clinical Features: iIOP, shallow AC, fixed semi-dilated pupil, swollen cataractous lens.
Ipsilateral: Closed angle (appositional; sigma sign may be seen on indentation gonioscopy).
Contralateral: Angle may be open with deep AC (contrast to PACG); sign may be absent if contralateral eye has significant cataract.
Treatment Medical: Topical and systemic (as for PACG).
Treatment Laser: Nd-yAG PI to reverse pupillary block component.
Definitive Treatment: Early cataract extraction (needs an experienced surgeon).

rows: Hypermature cataract loses soluble lens proteins through the anterior capsule, causing trabecular obstruction and subsequent 2° open-angle glaucoma.
iIOP, lens protein in a deep AC (may form a pseudohypopyon), hypermature/mature cataract, open angle (with lens protein); AC tap reveals lens protein and foamy macrophages.
Topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents; consider topical steroids for associated inflammation.

sections.title: Phacoanaphylactic Uveitis
sections.content: Mechanism: This is an inflammatory reaction to lens protein, usually following traumatic capsular rupture or post-operative retention of lens material (when it must be distinguished from endophthalmitis). This insult may also cause sensitization such that lens protein exposure in the contralateral eye (surgery, hyper-/mature cataract) may be associated with an aggressive response.

sections.title: Phacoanaphylactic Clinical & Management
content: Clinical Features: Recent trauma/surgery, exposed lens protein, AC flare + cells ± hypopyon, KPs, synechiae (PS + PAS), angle usually open (but ± PAS); IOP may be high, normal, or low.
Treatment of Inflammatory Process: Topical steroid (e.g. dexamethasone 0.1% hourly) and surgical removal of any retained lens fragments.
Treatment of iIOP: Medical—topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents, as required.
Contralateral Eye: Consider removal by intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCe) to reduce lens protein exposure.

sections.title: Lens Subluxation / Dislocation
content: Mechanism: Pupillary block by anterior lens subluxation or complete dislocation into the AC; possible coincident angle abnormality (e.g. Marfan’s syndrome).
Clinical: iIOP, subluxed/dislocated lens ± corneal oedema (if acute or lenticulocorneal touch); lenticular astigmatism and variable refraction.
Positional Management: Dilate and lie patient supine (encourage posterior movement), then constrict (keep lens behind pupil).
Surgical: Early lens extraction if positional measures fail, complete dislocation to AC, cataract, or recurrence. Often requires vitreoretinal approach.

sections.title: Steroid-Induced: Mechanisms & Rx
sections.content: Exogenous/endogenous steroids decrease outflow facility. POAG patients are particularly sensitive. Mechanisms include prostaglandin inhibition (e.g. PGF2A) and structural changes in ECM (glycosaminoglycans) and trabecular meshwork (cross-linking of actins). Always check for steroid use (anabolics, skin/hemorrhoid creams, inhaled, oral courses for asthma/COPD). Treatment: Decrease frequency/potency or stop steroid (± steroid-sparing agent); if essential, treat as POAG. SLT may be helpful.

rows: Hyphaema (traumatic) blocks TM. Rebleed 10% risk at ~5d. Sickle-cell patients harder to treat (acidosis from CAIs worsens sickling).
Strict bed rest, topical steroid, mydriatic/cycloplegic, topical/systemic IOP agents. Surgical: AC paracentesis ± washout. Refractory: Trabeculectomy.
Vitreous hemorrhage leads to TM blockage by degenerate RBCs (tan-colored) usually 2–4wk post-hemorrhage.
Medical treatment (as for POAG) usually sufficient. If failure: AC washout + vitrectomy.

sections.title: Other Open-Angle Varieties
content: Angle Recession: Blunt trauma risk; 10% glaucoma risk at 10y. Look for asymmetry of AC depth, pupil, and angle. Screen 3mo, 6mo, yearly. Treat as POAG.

Raised Episcleral Venous Pressure: From vascular abnormalities (Sturge–Weber, orbital varices, AV fistulae, SVC obstruction). Signs: Engorged veins, chemosis, proptosis, blood in Schlemm's canal. Surgery is hazardous (refractory uveal effusion).

Tumours: iIOP via TM clogging/infiltration, rubeosis, or 2° angle closure. 20% of malignant melanoma associated with iIOP. Suspect in atypical unilateral glaucoma. B-scan essential if posterior view poor.
Schwartz–Matsuo Syndrome: Mild AC inflammation + iIOP from RRD. Photoreceptor outer segments obstruct TM. Resolves rapidly with retinal detachment surgical repair.

sections.title: Iridocorneal Endothelial (ICE) Syndrome
content: General: Unilateral condition; abnormal endothelium migrates across angle/TM/iris. Rare, typically 20–40y old females. 50% glaucoma risk. HSV possible cause.
Variants: Chandler syndrome (corneal focus), Essential iris atrophy (iris focus), Iris naevus (Cogan–Reese) syndrome (pigmented nodules).
Clinical: Unilateral pain, blurred vision, fine corneal guttata ('beaten metal'), corneal oedema, corectopia, pseudopolycoria.
Gonioscopy: Broad-based PAS inserting anterior to Schwalbe’s line.
Management: Specular microscopy for diagnosis. Treatment: Medical (β-blocker, α2-agonist, CAI, PGA), Surgery (trabeculectomy ± augmented/tube), or cyclodestruction.

rows: Bilateral splitting/atrophy of anterior iris leaf. Elderly. Associated with nanophthalmos.
Angle-closure: Nd-YAG PI. Open-angle: As for POAG.
Bilateral, dominantly inherited, childhood detection. Iridocorneal adhesions. 15% glaucoma risk.
Trauma/surgery allows epithelium to proliferate on endothelium/angle. Poor prognosis.
Difficult. Lower IOP (POAG style), intracameral 5-FU, extensive surgical excision.
Peripheral corneal oedema causes 2° angle closure, especially in at-risk eyes with shallow AC.
Refer to primary corneal dystrophy management.

content.explanation: Mechanism: Posterior misdirection of aqueous into vitreous causing anterior displacement of vitreous, ciliary processes, and lens/PCIOL.

sections.title: Aqueous Misdirection Management
content: Risk Factors: Short axial length, chronic angle closure, previous acute closure, nanophthalmos, uveal effusion, surgery (trab, tube, cataract), laser PI, miotics.
Diagnosis: Acute iIOP, shallow/flat AC, patent PI present (no pupillary block/bombé), no choroidal detachment/hemorrhage.

Initial Medical: Patent PI check (repeat if needed), Dilate (Atropine 1% 3x/d + Phenylephrine 2.5% 4x/d), Systemic (Acetazolamide IV stat then PO + mannitol/glycerol), Topical (β-blocker + Apraclonidine).
Laser Intervention: YAG anterior vitreous disruption (capsulotomy/hyaloidotomy); Argon laser to ciliary processes; Trans-scleral cyclodiode photocoagulation.
Surgery (Goal: Uni-chamber eye): Peripheral zonulo-hyaloidectomy is key.
Phakic Surgery: VPV procedure (vitrectomy–phacoemulsification–vitrectomy) or phaco/ECCE + capsulotomy + vitrectomy.
Aphakic/Pseudophakic Surgery: Pars plana vitrectomy and posterior capsulotomy.

sections.title: Post-Cataract & VR Surgery
content: Post-Cataract Spike: Retained viscoelastic, lens fragments, or inflammation. Prophylaxis: Acetazolamide SR 250mg stat.
Post-Cataract Rare Causes: Suprachoroidal hemorrhage, phacolysis, phacoanaphylaxis, Amsler hemorrhage (Fuchs’ heterochromic), epithelial downgrowth, aqueous misdirection, UGH syndrome.
Intraocular Gas (SF6, C3F8): iIOP from expansion/overfill. Rx: Short-term medical (Acetazolamide SR 250mg 2x/d for 5d) or gas removal.
Scleral Buckles: 2° angle closure from ciliary body swelling/choroidal detachment. Usually resolves; medical treatment interim.
Silicone Oil: Oil in AC blocks TM. Rx: Medical; cyclodestruction if persistent. Early removal (<6mo) helps; late removal (>6mo) less effective due to macrophage incorporation.
Vitrectomy: Increases risk of rubeosis in PDR and ghost cell glaucoma.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is the sudden occlusion of a pulmonary arterial vessel by an embolus (most commonly a thrombus from deep vein thrombosis, but also air, fat, or amniotic fluid). It is the third most common cause of cardiovascular death and a critical consideration in prolonged ophthalmic surgeries (e.g., orbital exenteration, complex retinal detachment repair).

branches: Stasis (Immobility, Obstructive Sleep Apnea, Ocular Surgery >2hrs)
Hypercoagulability (Factor V Leiden, Cancer, Pregnancy, OCP)

sections.title: Pathophysiological Sequence
content: 1. Embolus lodges in pulmonary artery
2. Increase in Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR)
3. Right Ventricular (RV) afterload increase
4. RV dilation and septal shift to the left
5. Decreased Left Ventricular filling & Cardiac Output
6. V/Q mismatch and profound hypoxemia

sections.title: The Ophthalmic Connection: Purtscher-like Retinopathy
content: Rare manifestation of systemic microembolization (Fat/Air/Thrombotic).
Clinical Signs: Multiple Cotton Wool Spots (CWS), Purtscher Flecken (areas of inner retinal whitening), and intraretinal hemorrhages.
Mechanism: Microvascular occlusion and complement-mediated (C5a) leukoembolization.
Differential: Diabetics or Hypertensives can mimic, but Purtscher's is typically acute and associated with recent trauma or systemic emboli.
Prognosis: Often resolves spontaneously; visual outcome depends on macular ischemia.

sections.title: Clinical Symptoms Profile
content: Sudden Onset Dyspnea (82%)
Pleuritic Chest Pain (49%)
Cough (20%)
Hemoptysis (7%)
Syncope (indicates massive PE)
Apprehension / Impending Doom

sections.title: Diagnostic Red Flags
content: Hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg)
Oxygen Saturation < 90% on Room Air
Tachycardia > 100 bpm in Ophthalmic Post-op
Unilateral Calf Swelling (DVT sign)
New onset Right Bundle Branch Block (ECG)

rows: Alternative Dx Less Likely than PE

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Strategy
content: 1. Risk Stratify: Use Wells Criteria or PERC rule.
2. Biomarkers: High-sensitivity D-dimer (only if Wells <= 4).
3. Imaging: CT Pulmonary Angiogram (CTPA) - Gold Standard.
4. Alternative Imaging: V/Q Scan if Renal Failure or Contrast Allergy.
5. Bedside Echo: Look for 'McConnell's Sign' (RV free wall akinesia).

sections.title: Management Protocol
content: 1. Stabilization: High-flow O2, fluid resuscitation (cautious).
2. Immediate Anticoagulation: LMWH (Enoxaparin 1mg/kg) or UFH.
3. Thrombolysis: Alteplase (tPA) reserved for Massive PE.
4. Long-term Anticoagulation: DOACs (Rivaroxaban, Apixaban) for 3-6 months.
5. Interventional: Catheter-directed thrombectomy for high-risk cases.

rows: ECG shows ST-elevation/depression; Troponin rise pattern.
Acute onset, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation.
Tearing back pain, unequal BP in arms, widened mediastinum.
Normal SpO2, circumoral tingling, normal D-dimer.

content.explanation: T: Tachycardia, H: Hemoptysis, R: Reduced SaO2, O: Orthopnea, M: Mid-line chest pain (Pleuritic), B: Breathlessness, I: Increased RR (Tachypnea).

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: S1Q3T3 is famous but only present in <20% of cases.
A normal CXR in a hypoxic patient should strongly raise suspicion of PE.
D-dimer has high sensitivity but poor specificity; it is for 'ruling out' only.
The PESI score (Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index) helps decide on home vs hospital care.
In Ophthalmic surgery, avoid retrobulbar blocks in patients on full anticoagulation.

sections.title: Surgical/Procedural Interventions
content: Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) Filters: Used if anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g., immediate post-op bleeding risk).
Surgical Embolectomy: Indicated for massive PE when thrombolysis fails or is contraindicated.
Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis (CDT): Lower doses of tPA delivered directly to the clot.

rows: Tenecteplase in submassive PE reduces decompensation but increases bleed risk.
Rivaroxaban is non-inferior to standard therapy (Enox/Warfarin).
Validated the use of D-dimer adjusted by clinical probability.

rows: Continuous activity >5 min or ≥2 seizures without recovery. t2 marks risk of long-term damage.
Focal awareness or impaired awareness seizures without recovery.
Prolonged altered consciousness with generalized spike-wave on EEG.
Rhythmic motor activity, tonic-clonic movements, impaired consciousness.
Altered mental status, 'Twilight state', mild eyelid myoclonus.
Automatisations, staring, focal EEG changes, aphasia.
Failure of 1st and 2nd line drugs; SE continuing >24 hrs despite anesthetics.

sections.title: Neuro-Ophthalmic Examination Findings
content: Ictal Eye Deviation: Eyes usually deviate AWAY from the focus in destructive lesions, but TOWARDS the focus during ictus.
Nystagmus-like movements: Rapid eye jerking (Epileptic nystagmus) can occur in focal SE.
Pupillary Changes: Mydriasis or sluggish reactivity is common during the ictal phase.
Post-ictal Findings: Transient Horner's Syndrome or gaze palsy (Todd's paralysis of eye movements).
Fundus: Look for papilledema (suggests raised ICP as etiology) or chorioretinal scars (suggests TORCH infections).

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Molecular Failure
content: 1. Failure of GABA-ergic Inhibition: GABA-A receptors are internalized (trafficked out of the synapse).
2. Over-activation of Glutamate: NMDA and AMPA receptors are mobilized to the synapse, increasing excitation.
3. Depletion of Neuropeptides: Depletion of inhibitory peptides like Substance P.
4. Neuronal Damage: Excessive Calcium influx leads to excitotoxicity and mitochondrial failure within 30-60 mins.

rows: Asynchronous movements, eye closure (forceful), side-to-side head shaking, no post-ictal period.
Prodromal 'dimming' of vision, brief duration, immediate recovery of consciousness.
Extensor response due to brainstem herniation, fixed/blown pupils (unlike most SE).
Visual 'scintillating scotomas' (positive symptoms), slow progression (minutes, not seconds).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Step 1: Point-of-Care Glucose (Rule out Hypoglycemia immediately).
Step 2: Stat Labs (CBC, BMP, LFTs, Calcium, Magnesium, Tox Screen).
Step 3: Emergent Neuroimaging (Non-contrast Head CT to rule out ICH/Mass).
Step 4: Continuous EEG (Essential for diagnosing Non-Convulsive SE).
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture (If febrile or immunosuppressed, after checking for mass effect).

content.explanation: Lorazepam (Ativan) 4mg IV (repeated once) is the drug of choice. If no IV access: Midazolam 10mg IM (RAMPART Trial).

rows: Excellent safety profile, few drug interactions.
Avoid in pregnancy or liver failure.

sections.title: Phase 3: Refractory SE (Anesthetic Phase)
content: Midazolam (Dormicum): Bolus 0.2mg/kg followed by infusion (0.05-2mg/kg/hr).
Propofol (Diprivan): Bolus 1-2mg/kg followed by infusion (2-10mg/kg/hr). Beware Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS).
Ketamine: NMDA antagonist (Bolus 1-2mg/kg). Useful as receptor profile changes in late SE.
Phenobarbital: Bolus 15-20mg/kg. Strong sedation, risk of respiratory depression.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Threats
content: Airway Obstruction / Hypoxia: Intubate early if Benzodiazepines cause respiratory drive failure.
Hyperthermia: Sustained SE can cause rhabdomyolysis and core temps >40°C.
Herniation Signs: Fixed dilated pupil or Cushing's Triad (Bradycardia, Hypertension, Irregular Breathing).
Propofol Infusion Syndrome: Metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac failure.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The Evidence Base
sections.content: The ESETT Trial (2019) demonstrated that Levetiracetam, Fosphenytoin, and Valproate are equally effective for benzodiazepine-refractory SE (approx. 50% success). The RAMPART Study (2012) proved that IM Midazolam is superior to IV Lorazepam in the pre-hospital setting due to faster administration times.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Don't wait for EEG to start treatment if clinical suspicion is high.
Pseudo-Status: If the patient is 'resistant' to eye opening, consider PNES.
Aggressive treatment is key: Every minute of seizure increases the risk of pharmacoresistance.
In patients with known epilepsy, the most common trigger is low AED levels/non-compliance.

sections.title: Long-Term Prognosis & Complications
content: Permanent Cognitive Deficits: Memory impairment (hippocampal sclerosis).
Systemic: Pulmonary edema, cardiac arrhythmias, and acute kidney injury (from rhabdo).
Mortality: Highest in the elderly and those with stroke or hypoxia as the etiology.
Recurrence: Approx. 15-20% chance of another SE episode.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Endophthalmitis is a severe form of ocular inflammation involving the inner coats of the eye (vitreous and aqueous humors), typically caused by infection. It is categorized into exogenous (introduced via surgery, trauma, or needle) and endogenous (hematogenous spread). It remains one of the most feared complications in ophthalmology due to its potential for rapid, irreversible vision loss and phthisis bulbi.

rows: P. acnes, C. albicans, S. epidermidis

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Referral Needed
content: Sudden decrease in vision (out of proportion to post-op day)
Severe, deep-seated ocular pain
Loss of Red Reflex or significant media haze
Rapidly progressing hypopyon
Proptosis and restricted motility (suggests Panophthalmitis)

sections.title: Clinical Features & Ocular Findings
content: Symptoms: Pain (75%), Vision Loss (95%), Redness, Photophobia.
Eyelids: Edema, Chemosis.
Anterior Segment: Ciliary congestion, Hypopyon, Fibrinous membrane.
Vitreous: Dense vitritis, 'snowball' opacities (fungal), loss of fundus view.
IOP: May be low (ciliary body shutdown) or high (inflammatory debris).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: 1. Immediate Clinical Exam & B-scan (if fundus obscured to check for RD).
2. Conjunctival Swabs (low yield but useful).
3. Aqueous Tap (0.1ml via limbal paracentesis).
4. Vitreous Tap/Biopsy (0.2ml via needle or vitrectomy cutter).
5. Culture (Blood/Chocolate/Thioglycolate) & PCR (for fastidious organisms).

sections.title: The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS) Summary
content: EVS Primary Finding: Immediate PPV is indicated if vision is Light Perception (LP) or worse.
EVS Primary Finding: If vision is Hand Motion (HM) or better, 'Tap and Inject' is equivalent to PPV.
Systemic Antibiotics: Ceftazidime and Amikacin did not improve outcomes in the EVS (Note: Modern agents like Moxifloxacin were not tested).
Diabetes: Diabetic patients trended toward better outcomes with PPV regardless of initial vision.

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV)
content: 1. 23G or 25G valved cannulas (maintain IOP).
2. Obtain undiluted vitreous sample (0.2-0.5ml) before turning on infusion.
3. Core vitrectomy to clear visual axis and reduce pathogen load.
4. Careful induction of PVD (risk of retinal tears is high).
5. Peripheral shave if view allows; avoid aggressive traction.
6. Intravitreal antibiotics injected at end of case.

sections.title: Prevention & Prophylaxis Protocols
content: Povidone-Iodine (5%): The most critical step for preoperative skin and conjunctival prep.
Intracameral Cefuroxime (1mg/0.1ml): ESCRS study showed 5x reduction in post-op infection.
Lid Hygiene: Treating blepharitis/meibomianitis before elective surgery.
Avoidance of Topical Antibiotics: No clear evidence that pre-op topical drops reduce incidence.
Surgical Technique: Ensure watertight wound closure (leaking wounds are portals for bacteria).

content.explanation: B: Blood Cultures; U: Urine Cultures / Ultrasound (Heart/Liver); G: Gallium scan (if source hidden); S: Swabs / Secretion cultures.

sections.title: Chronic/Delayed-Onset Endophthalmitis
content: Pathogen: Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes most common.
Signs: Chronic low-grade uveitis, white plaque on posterior capsule, granulomatous KPs.
Management: Intravitreal Vancomycin + Capsular bag washout. Total capsulectomy with IOL exchange may be required for recalcitrant cases.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Retinal Detachment (up to 10-20% of cases).
Hypotony and Phthisis Bulbi.
Secondary Glaucoma (inflammatory debris in TM).
Prognosis: Poor for Viridans Strep and Gram-negatives; Better for Coag-neg Staph.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (High-Yield)
content: Post-injection (IVT) endophthalmitis is more likely to be Streptococcal (aggressive) than post-cataract cases.
If a patient presents with 'sterile' hypopyon after IVT Steroids, consider if it is settling of the drug vs. infection.
B-Scan: Look for 'choroidal thickening' and 'vitreous membranes' as indicators of severity.
Always treat the underlying source in endogenous cases; ocular treatment alone will fail if bacteremia persists.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Pediatric cataracts are any lens opacities present at birth or developing within the first decade of life. Unlike adult cataracts, they pose an immediate threat to the development of the visual cortex (amblyopia) and require urgent intervention during the 'critical period' of visual development (birth to 7 years).

branches: Ocular: PFV, Aniridia, Peter's Anomaly, Trauma

rows: Central opacity in the embryonic/fetal nucleus
Shell-like opacity surrounding a clear nucleus
Located at the posterior capsule; risk of rupture
Small, white, central opacity on ant. capsule
High; reversible if diet changes early
Calcified mass on B-scan; LIFE THREATENING
Ciliary body mass; 'string of pearls' in vitreous

sections.title: The Surgical Protocol: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Two-port incision (Clear cornea or Limbal) using 20G or 23G MVR blades.
Step 2: Capsulorhexis (FCCC or Vitrectorhexis) - Children's capsules are highly elastic.
Step 3: Hydrodissection (Gentle! Avoid in posterior polar) and Aspiration of soft cortex.
Step 4: Primary Posterior Capsulotomy (PPC) - Essential in children <6 years to prevent VAO.
Step 5: Limited Anterior Vitrectomy - Prevents scaffold for LEC migration.
Step 6: IOL Implantation in the Bag (usually 3-piece or hydrophobic acrylic).
Step 7: Stromal Hydration and/or 10-0 Vicryl sutures (Mandatory in kids).
Step 8: Intracameral or Subconjunctival Antibiotics/Steroids.

sections.title: IOL Power Calculation: The 'Rule of Under-Correction'

content.explanation:
To account for the 'myopic shift' as the child grows: 
• <1 yr: Stay Aphakic (usually)
• 1-2 yrs: Undercorrect by 20%
• 2-3 yrs: Undercorrect by 10%
• >8 yrs: Target Emmetropia

T: Toxoplasmosis
O: Other (Syphilis, Varicella)
R: Rubella
C: CMV
H: Herpes Simplex
S: Screen for all in bilateral cases!

sections.title: Critical Timing Red Flags
content: Monocular Cataract: Must operate by 4-6 weeks of age to avoid irreversible amblyopia.
Binocular Cataract: Operate by 6-10 weeks of age.
Nystagmus: Develops by 3 months if surgery is delayed; sign of poor visual prognosis.
Signs of Endophthalmitis: Hypopyon is often late; look for sudden change in behavior/redness.

sections.title: Essential Pre-operative Workup
content: B-scan Ultrasonography: To rule out RD/RB if there is no view of the fundus.
A-scan Biometry: Axial length measurement (usually under GA).
Keratometry: Challenging; manual Javal-Schiotz or handheld auto-K.
Urine for Reducing Substances: Screen for Galactosemia.
Pediatric Clearance: Rule out cardiac/systemic issues for GA.

sections.title: Landmark Study: IATS
content: Infant Aphakia Treatment Study (IATS).
Conclusion: No difference in VA at age 1 and 5 between IOL and CL for unilateral infants <7 months.
IOL group: Had significantly higher rates of adverse events and re-operations.
Result: Aphakia with contact lens is often preferred for infants <6 months.

sections.title: Amblyopia Management
content: Refraction: Perform 1 week post-op and every 3 months thereafter.
Patching: Critical for monocular cases; usually 50% of waking hours.
Over-correction: Target +2.00D or +3.00D for near vision in young infants.

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: Sclerocorneal tunnels are preferred by some to avoid limbal bleeding and suture irritation.
Healon GV or Provisc are excellent for maintaining the anterior chamber against high posterior pressure.
Always perform a 'water-tight' closure; children rub their eyes, increasing the risk of wound dehiscence.
Lifelong glaucoma screening is mandatory; risk remains even 20 years post-op.
Bilateral surgery is often performed 1 week apart or during the same GA in specific settings.

sections.title: Clinical Overview: Advanced Keratoconus
sections.content: Advanced Keratoconus (Stage IV) is characterized by severe corneal thinning (<200μm), extreme steepening (>55D), and the presence of Vogt's striae, Fleischer rings, and potentially apical scarring. When one eye has progressed to surgical intervention (PKP), the fellow eye requires meticulous monitoring and often specialized contact lens fitting or lamellar surgery to maintain visual rehabilitation.

sections.title: The Vascularization Verdict: Deep vs. Superficial

rows: Bypasses the 'immune privilege' by providing direct access for T-lymphocytes and antibodies to the donor stroma and endothelium.
Significant drop; often <50% if >2 quadrants involved

sections.title: Treatment Algorithm: Advanced Keratoconus
content: Step 1: Scleral Lens Trial - Bypasses irregular cornea with a fluid reservoir.
Step 2: CXL (Cross-linking) - Only if cornea >400μm (or use riboflavin-soaked sponge/hypotonic drops).
Step 3: DALK (Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty) - Preferred if endothelium is healthy; eliminates rejection risk of endothelium.
Step 4: PKP (Penetrating Keratoplasty) - Reserved for full-thickness scars or Descemet's membrane ruptures.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup for Advanced KC
content: Tomography (Pentacam/Galilei): Posterior elevation is the earliest sign.
AS-OCT: Measure minimum corneal thickness and epithelial mapping.
Specular Microscopy: Assess endothelial health before considering DALK.
Retinoscopy: Scissor reflex is pathognomonic.
Slit Lamp: Fleischer ring (iron at base), Vogt's striae (vertical stress lines).

content.explanation: R: Redness (Perilimbal/Ciliary flush); S: Sensitivity to light (Photophobia); V: Vision decrease (Blurred vision); P: Pain.

sections.title: Red Flags: Acute Hydrops
content: Sudden onset of severe pain
Dramatic drop in vision
White, opaque corneal appearance
Break in Descemet's Membrane
Avoid PKP in acute phase (poor suture hold)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Graft Management
content: Suture removal is indicated for vascularization tracking toward the graft-host junction.
Deep vascularization requires aggressive topical steroids (e.g., Pred Forte q1h) and potentially subconjunctival injections.
In the KC eye, scleral lenses can delay the need for surgery by 5-10 years.
Always check for Khodadoust line: a linear precipitate of inflammatory cells on the endothelium.

sections.title: Landmark Study: CLEK
sections.content: The Collaborative Longitudinal Evaluation of Keratoconus (CLEK) study demonstrated that corneal scarring was associated with a higher risk of disease progression and that rigid contact lens wear does not 'stop' the progression of ectasia, though it provides the best visual correction.

sections.title: Recent Advances: CXL Plus
content: Athens Protocol: Simultaneous Topography-guided PRK + CXL.
KeraNatural: Use of gamma-irradiated sterile corneal tissue inlays.
CAIRS: Corneal Allogenic Intrastromal Ring Segments (using donor stroma instead of PMMA).

sections.title: Post-PKP Management Protocol
content: Week 1-4: Pred Forte q2h + Topical Antibiotic qid.
Month 3-6: Suture adjustment/removal based on topography and astigmatism.
Month 12+: Tapering to once-daily steroid (often lifelong in high-risk grafts).

sections.title: Signs of Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR)
content: Sudden deepening or shallowing of the Anterior Chamber (AC)
Momentary pupillary dilation
Nucleus falls away and cannot be approached by phaco tip
Marked slowing of aspiration due to clogged vitreous in phaco tip
Torn capsule may be directly visible
Vitreous gel may be directly visible

sections.title: Sequelae of Vitreous Loss after PCR
PCR Management: Core Principles
content: Management depends on the magnitude of the tear
Depends on the size and type of any residual lens material
Depends on the presence or absence of vitreous prolapse
CRITICAL: Do NOT pull out the phaco probe immediately (maintains AC pressure)

sections.title: PCR Surgical Protocol
content: Step 1: Inject dispersive viscoelastic before removing phaco probe
Step 2: If a complete or nearly complete nucleus remains, convert to ECCE
Step 3: If residual nuclear fragments, remove by phaco using low bottle height and low aspiration flow rate
Step 4: If large fragments, use visco-expression after extending the main wound
Step 5: Once remnants are removed, replug the tear with dispersive OVD
Step 6: Gently fill the AC with cohesive viscoelastic
Step 7: Use manual aspiration cannula with irrigation OFF to aspirate residual cortex
Step 8: Remove all vitreous from AC, wound, and capsular tear with a vitrector
Step 9: Infusion cannula of vitrector remains HIGH; Cutter remains LOW
Step 10: Visualize vitreous using 0.1 ml of 40mg/ml Triamcinolone

rows: Constrict pupil following PC IOL or prior to AC IOL

sections.title: Clinical Complications: Continuous List
sections.content: Additional complications noted include: Corneal decompensation, chronic endophthalmitis, and specific post-operative inflammation rates ranging from 2% to 6%. PCO remains a primary late complication at 10% within 2 years.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Acute Post-Op Vision Loss

rows: Immediate onset (12-24h), no pain, limbus-to-limbus edema
Elevated IOP, corneal edema, mid-dilated pupil
Loss of red reflex, sudden pain, AC shallowing

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Endophthalmitis (0.1%): Immediate referral if pain/hypopyon present
Choroidal Haemorrhage (0.1%): Intraoperative disaster requiring immediate wound closure
Loss of nuclear fragment posteriorly (0.3%): Requires vitreoretinal consultation
Wound leak (1%): Risk for hypotony and endophthalmitis
Iris Prolapse (0.7%): Requires surgical repair to prevent infection

content.explanation: D: Deepening/shallowing of AC. R: Red reflex change/loss. O: Out of reach nucleus (falls away). P: Pupil dilation (momentary).

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Vitreous Visualization
content: Always use preservative-free Triamcinolone (0.1ml of 40mg/ml) to stain vitreous strands.
Stained vitreous appears as white specks trapped in the gel, making clean-up far more precise.
Ensure AC is stable with OVD before starting the vitrectomy cutter.

sections.title: Treatment Protocols: Multiple Sclerosis
content: Steroid Regimen: 1g methy prednisolone Na succinate daily for 3 days
Followed by: Oral prednisolone 1mg/kg daily for 11 days
Conclusion: Subsequenty tapered over 3 days
Other Therapies: Interferon beta, Glatiramer acetate, Monoclonal antibodies
Specific mAbs: Natalizumab, Ocrelizumab, Alemtuzumab

sections.title: Steroid Tapering Regimen for AION
content: Step 1: IV methylprednisolone 500mg - 1g/day for 3 days
Step 2: Oral prednisolone 1-2mg/kg daily
Step 3: 3 days later, reduce dose to 50-60mg/4w or until symptoms resolve & ESR/CRP normalizes
Step 4: Reduce daily dose by 10mg/day every 2 weeks until 20mg/day is reached
Step 5: 2.5 mg reduction every 2-4 weeks until 10mg reached, then 1mg reduction every 1-2 months
Bone+GIT Protection: VitD, calcium, proton pump inhibitor
Vascular Prophylaxis: Aspirin 600mg then 100mg/day to reduce visual loss and stroke risk

sections.title: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) Management
sections.content: Treatment of gaint cell arteritis without AAION: Oral prednisolone 1mg/kg daily governed by symptoms, level of ESR, and CRP. CRP level is important in monitoring disease activity as it falls more rapidly than ESR in response to tratment.
