content: 1. Photoreceptors
2. Optic nerve
3. Optic chiasma
4. Optic tract
5. Pretectal nucleus (Midbrain/Superior Colliculi): Nasal fibers cross, Temporal fibers stay ipsilateral
6. Edinger Westphal nuclei (both sides receive bilateral input)
7. Oculomotor nerve (inferior division)
8. Ciliary ganglion (via nerve to inferior oblique)
9. Short ciliary nerves
10. Pupillary sphincter
NOTE ON NEURONS: Red = 1st order (sensory), Brown = 2nd order (internuncial), Baby blue = 3rd order (preganglionic motor), Dark blue = 4th order (postganglionic motor)

rows: Both pupils dilate instead of constrict (Swinging light)

content.explanation: Asymmetrical pupil diameter implies disease of the efferent motor nerve or the iris itself. Sensory lesions (like RAPD) do NOT cause anisocoria.

sections.title: Sympathetic Pathway (Pupillary Dilation)
content: 1st Order (Central): Posterior hypothalamus descends uncrossed to Ciliospinal Center of Budge (C8-T2).
2nd Order (Preganglionic): From Center of Budge to Superior Cervical Ganglion (neck).
3rd Order (Postganglionic): Ascends along Internal Carotid Artery to Cavernous Sinus; joins V1 (trigeminal); reaches Dilator Pupillae via Nasociliary and Long Ciliary nerves.

sections.title: Neuro-Ophthalmology Red Flags
content: Sudden VA loss with headache and jaw claudication (GCA)
Electrical sensation on neck flexion (Lhermitte sign)
Pupillary dilation on swinging flashlight test (RAPD)
Absent Spontaneous Venous Pulsation (SVP) in disc elevation
Sudden worsening of symptoms with heat/exercise (Uhthoff phenomenon)

title: Herpes Ophthalmicus: HSV vs. HZO & The HEDS Legacy
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to differentiating Herpes Simplex (HSV) and Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO), featuring deep-dive analysis of the Herpetic Eye Disease Studies (HEDS) for evidence-based management.

data.title: Herpes Ophthalmicus: HSV vs. HZO & The HEDS Legacy
data.summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to differentiating Herpes Simplex (HSV) and Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO), featuring deep-dive analysis of the Herpetic Eye Disease Studies (HEDS) for evidence-based management.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Overview
sections.content: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1, rarely HSV-2) and Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) are neurotropic DNA viruses. HSV Keratitis is the most common cause of infectious corneal blindness in the US. Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO) results from reactivation of latent VZV in the Trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion, specifically involving the Ophthalmic (V1) division.

sections.title: HZO Pathognomonic Signs
content: Hutchinson Sign: Vesicles on tip/side of nose (Nasociliary nerve involvement); 3x higher risk of intraocular involvement.
Dermatomal Rash: Respects the midline, V1 distribution (Frontal, Lacrimal, Nasociliary nerves).
Post-Herpetic Neuralgia (PHN): Pain persisting >3 months after rash resolution.
Sectoral Iris Atrophy: Suggests past or present herpetic uveitis (often seen in HZO and CMV).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Labs
content: 1. Clinical Exam: Slit-lamp exam and Corneal Sensitivity (Aesthesiometry - usually decreased).
2. Scraping/Swab: Viral culture (Gold standard but slow).
3. PCR: High sensitivity/specificity for HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV.
4. Giemsa Stain: Look for Multinucleated Giant Cells (Tzanck smear - non-specific).
5. In-Vivo Confocal Microscopy: Can visualize decreased sub-basal nerve plexus density.

branches: Stromal Keratitis: Topical steroids (Pred Phos) + Trifluridine faster resolution & less progression.
Iridocyclitis: Oral Acyclovir (400mg 5x/day) beneficial for treatment.
Epithelial Keratitis: Oral Acyclovir does NOT prevent progression to stromal disease/uveitis.
Recurrence: 400mg Acyclovir BID for 1 year reduced recurrence by 45%.
Stromal Keratitis: Prophylaxis particularly effective for those with prior stromal history.
Stress: No statistical correlation found between stress and HSV recurrence (counter-intuitive).

sections.title: Medical Management: HZO
content: Oral Acyclovir: 800mg 5x/day for 7-10 days (Must start within 72 hrs of rash).
Oral Valacyclovir: 1g TID for 7-10 days (Better bioavailability).
Oral Famciclovir: 500mg TID for 7-10 days.
Topical Steroids: Required for uveitis or stromal keratitis, often needs long-term taper.
PHN Management: Gabapentin, Pregabalin, or Amitriptyline.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Consults
content: Stromal Melting/Perforation: Imminent risk in Necrotizing Keratitis.
Acute Retinal Necrosis (ARN): Rapidly progressive peripheral necrotizing retinitis (HSV/VZV).
Secondary Glaucoma: Trabeculitis or PAS causing severe IOP spikes.
Immunocompromised Status: Disseminated VZV or bilateral involvement.

content.explanation: S: Steroids are needed, T: Trifluridine/Prophylaxis added, R: Red eye, O: Opacity (haze), M: Melting (if necrotizing), A: Acyclovir (HEDS proven), L: Long-term taper.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques & Interventions
content: 1. Debridement: Effective for epithelial HSV to reduce viral load.
2. Amniotic Membrane: Promotes healing in neurotrophic ulcers.
3. Tarsorrhaphy: Essential for severe neurotrophic keratopathy.
4. Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): Avoid in active disease; wait 1 year quiet.
5. Gundersen Flap: For chronic non-healing ulcers with low visual potential.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Prep
content: Acyclovir 400mg BID (HSV) vs. 800mg 5x/day (Acute HZO) vs. 800mg daily (HZO prophylaxis).
HZO dendrites are 'stuck on' plaques and don't involve the basement membrane (unlike HSV).
Never use topical steroids alone in HSV; always cover with an antiviral.
Disciform keratitis is a clinical diagnosis; it is an immune reaction to viral antigen in the endothelium.
Zostavax (Live) vs. Shingrix (Recombinant): Shingrix is preferred and >90% effective in seniors.

sections.title: Recent Advances: ZEDS Study
sections.content: The Zoster Eye Disease Study (ZEDS) is currently investigating whether long-term suppressive Valacyclovir (1g daily) reduces complications of HZO, similar to how HEDS II proved effectiveness for HSV. Results are highly anticipated to standardize HZO prophylaxis.

sections.title: CHAPTER 11: PRotoZoAN UVeItIS - Overview
sections.content: Toxoplasmosis: The protozoa Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular parasite which is estimated to infect up to 50% of the world’s population. Lifetime risk of ocular toxoplasmosis is around 18/100,000 in the UK, but up to 20 times this level in West Africa. (Source: Page 507-508)

sections.title: Geographic Pathogen Variation
content: Prevalence and incidence depend on socio-economic factors and circulating parasite genotypes.
Common locations: South America, Central America, Caribbean, tropical Africa.
Rare: China.
South America severity: More severe due to extremely virulent genotypes of the parasite.

branches: Definitive Host: The Cat (excretes oocysts in faeces)
Forms: Oocysts (faeces), Bradyzoite (encysted in tissue), Tachyzoite (actively proliferating)
Transmission: Cat faeces/contaminated soil, Raw/undercooked meat, Contaminated water, Transplacental

rows: Acquired infection now more important than congenital

content.explanation: Transmission rate increases from 15% (1st trimester) to 60% (3rd trimester); HOWEVER, disease severity is much greater if acquired in early pregnancy.

sections.title: Ophthalmic Clinical Features
content: Laterality: Affects both eyes in 40%.
Immunocompromise Sign: Suspect if both eyes are simultaneously active.
Symptoms: Asymptomatic finding, floaters, dVA (decreased Visual Acuity).
Vitritis: May have 'vitreous precipitates' (akin to KPs on posterior surface of PVD).
Retinitis: White, fluffy area when active; becomes circumscribed and pigmented as it heals.
Inactive State: Atrophic scar with pigmented border.
Satellite Lesions: Adjacent to old scars (commonly seen).
Retinal Vasculitis: Possibly four-quadrant periphlebitis.
'Headlamp in the fog': Indistinct pale lesion seen through 4+ vitreous haze.
Anterior Uveitis: Often with iIOP (increased Intraocular Pressure).

sections.title: Diverse Presentations & Complications
content: Scleritis
Punctate outer retinitis (quiet vitreous)
Punctate retinal lesions +/- vitreous activity
Large lesions (especially in the elderly)
Endophthalmitis-like presentation
Neuroretinitis
Serous retinal detachments
Pigmentary retinopathy
Complications: Cataract, Glaucoma, CNV (Choroidal Neovascularization) membrane

rows: Usually unilateral, large granuloma, no satellite scars.
Can mimic any uveitis; positive treponemal serology.
Pizza-pie appearance, minimal vitritis, HIV+ status.
Rapid progression, peripheral necrosis, prominent vasculitis.
Candle-wax drippings, systemic involvement, hilar adenopathy.
Hydrocephalus, cerebral calcification, hepatosplenomegaly, retinochoroiditis (bilateral, macula-affecting).
Usually asymptomatic; may have fever and lymphadenopathy.
Life-threatening: Encephalitis, intracerebral cysts, hepatitis, and myocarditis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations
content: Primarily a clinical diagnosis.
Serology: Interpret positive results with caution (many adults are IgG positive).
IgM Antibodies: Suggest acquired infection.
Negative Serology: Should exclude the diagnosis.
PCR: Identification of T. gondii DNA in aqueous or vitreous samples may be helpful.

sections.title: Box 11.6: Indications for Treatment
content: Lesions involving disc, macula, or papillomacular bundle.
Lesions threatening a major vessel.
Marked vitritis.
Any lesion in an immunocompromised patient.

sections.title: Treatment Evidence & Protocols
sections.content: A Cochrane systematic review showed no level 1 evidence to support the efficacy of routine antibiotic or corticosteroid treatment for acute Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis in immunocompetent patients. There is level 2 evidence suggesting that long-term prophylactic treatment may reduce recurrences in chronic relapsing disease. In immunocompetent patients, the disease is self-limiting (unless sight-threatening). Recurrence is common; mean number of recurrences is two (wide range seen).

sections.title: Systemic Medical Management
content: Step 1: Initiation of ≥4 weeks of antibiotic therapy.
Step 2: Options include Co-trimoxazole OR Clindamycin/Sulfadiazine OR Pyrimethamine/Sulfadiazine/Folinic acid (requires weekly FBC) OR Atovaquone.
Step 3: Corticosteroids (Prednisolone) - MUST NOT be used without effective anti-toxo therapy. Use caution/avoid if immunosuppressed.
Special Cases: Spiramycin for maternal infection to reduce transplacental spread. Azithromycin used in some centers. Atovaquone active against bradyzoites and tachyzoites.

sections.title: Intravitreal & Pregnancy Management
content: Intravitreal Option: 1 mg clindamycin plus 400 μg dexamethasone (in immunocompetent patients).
Maternal Infection: Treat with spiramycin (named-patient basis).
Screening: Some countries perform serial antenatal serological screening to permit early treatment.

rows: Wash all fruit/vegetables; Avoid unpasteurized goat’s milk; Cook all meat thoroughly; Avoid handling cat litter (or use rubber gloves).
15–60% risk if acquired during pregnancy. No risk otherwise (even if recurrence of active disease during pregnancy).

sections.title: Microsporidiosis (Bonus Section)
content: Etiology: Protozoan obligate intracellular parasites (4 genera cause human disease).
Patient Profile: Usually seen in immunosuppressed (notably AIDS).
Systemic Disease: Chronic diarrhoea, respiratory infection.
Ocular Presentation: Keratoconjunctivitis with bilateral irritation, photophobia, and punctate keratopathy.
Associated Signs: Follicular conjunctivitis and/or anterior uveitis.

This guide provides a high-yield, textbook-quality breakdown of its pathophysiology, clinical diagnosis, and surgical management.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Aponeurotic ptosis (involutional ptosis) is an acquired drooping of the upper eyelid caused by the thinning, stretching, or frank disinsertion of the levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) aponeurosis from its insertion site on the anterior surface of the tarsal plate. Unlike myogenic ptosis, the levator muscle itself remains healthy and functional; the 'pulley' system is simply detached or loose. This results in an eyelid that cannot be lifted effectively despite normal muscle contractility.

sections.title: The Pathognomonic Clinical Features
content: Excellent Levator Function (usually >12mm-15mm).
High or Absent Upper Eyelid Crease: The aponeurosis fibers that normally create the crease are retracted.
Deep Superior Sulcus: Caused by the posterior migration of the preaponeurotic fat pad along with the retracted levator.
Thinning of the Upper Eyelid: The iris may be visible through the eyelid skin in severe cases.
Worsening in Downgaze: The lid may actually drop further when looking down, unlike congenital ptosis.
Brow Ache/Frontalis Overaction: Patients use their forehead to compensate for the lid drop.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Ruling out the Mimics

rows: Poor LF, Lid Lag in downgaze
Contralateral lid drops upon manual elevation

sections.title: Red Flags: When NOT to assume Aponeurotic
content: New onset Diplopia (Think CN III palsy or Myasthenia)
Anisocoria (Think Horner's or CN III palsy)
Diurnal variation or fatigue (Think Myasthenia Gravis)
Poor Levator Function (Think Myogenic or Neurogenic origins)
Orbital signs: Proptosis or limited motility (Think Orbital Mass/TED)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Step 1: Phenylephrine 2.5% Test (Check response of Muller's muscle)
Step 2: External Photography (Documentation for insurance)
Step 3: Visual Field Testing (Goldmann or Humphrey with/without taping)
Step 4: If suspected MG: Ice pack test or Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies
Step 5: If suspected Horner: Apraclonidine test

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol
content: Pre-op: Assess Hering's Law and Corneal Sensation/Bell's Phenomenon.
Step 1: Local Anesthesia (Lidocaine + Epinephrine).
Step 2: Eyelid Crease Incision (Skin and Orbicularis).
Step 3: Identification of Orbital Septum and Preaponeurotic Fat.
Step 4: Levator Aponeurosis Advancement and Suture to Tarsal Plate.
Step 5: Intraoperative height and contour adjustment (Patient sitting up).

content.explanation: H: High Lid Crease; E: Excellent Levator Function; L: Lid Thinning (Iris visible); P: Posterior retraction of fat (Deep Sulcus).

rows: Gold Standard; any degree of ptosis with good LF
Mild ptosis (1-2mm) with positive Phenylephrine test
Minimal ptosis; rarely used due to tarsal sacrifice
NEVER for Aponeurotic ptosis; reserved for poor LF (<4mm)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for Hering’s Law pre-operatively to avoid a post-op 'surprise' in the fellow eye.
Rule out Dry Eye Disease: Surgery can worsen exposure and tear film evaporation.
If the LF is poor, reconsider the diagnosis; aponeurotic ptosis must have good LF.
Post-cataract ptosis is often aponeurotic due to the eyelid speculum or bridle suture.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Medical Management
sections.content: Upneeq (Oxymetazoline hydrochloride ophthalmic solution, 0.1%) was FDA-approved in 2020 as the first non-surgical treatment for acquired blepharoptosis. It is an alpha-adrenergic agonist that triggers the contraction of Muller's muscle, providing a temporary lift (approx. 1-1.5mm) in mild-to-moderate aponeurotic cases. While not a replacement for surgery in severe cases, it offers a viable 'medical' alternative for patients seeking temporary cosmetic improvement or those unfit for surgery.

sections.title: Landmark Concept: Hering's Law of Equal Innervation
sections.content: In many patients with bilateral asymmetric ptosis, the brain sends an increased signal to both levators to keep the droopier lid open. Because the signal is bilateral, the 'better' eye appears less ptotic than it actually is. When the more ptotic eye is surgically repaired, the brain reduces the neural drive, and the contralateral lid 'drops' post-operatively. This is why testing with a manual lift of the more ptotic lid is critical in pre-op assessment.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: PCO, or 'after-cataract,' is the opacification of the posterior lens capsule due to the proliferation and migration of residual lens epithelial cells (LECs). Incidence: Up to 20-40% of pseudophakic eyes within 2-5 years. Incidence is higher in younger patients and those with specific comorbidities like Uveitis or Retinitis Pigmentosa.

sections.title: Etiology: The Fibrotic vs. Elschnig Pathway
Clinical Features
content: Reduced visual acuity (gradual onset)
Increased glare and halos
Difficulty with contrast sensitivity
Monocular diplopia
Obscuration of fundus view during exam

sections.title: Indications & Contraindications
content: DO NOT perform if patient is symptomatic (glare/acuity loss) and visual function is not impaired.
Rule out other pathology (e.g., CME, ERM) before blaming PCO.
Caution in high myopes (retinal detachment risk).
Contraindicated in acute ocular inflammation/uveitis.
Corneal edema: Ensure clear view to avoid accidental IOL pitting.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Procedure
content: Step 1: Dilate pupil (Tropicamide 1%).
Step 2: Apply topical anesthesia (Proparacaine) and gel-coupled capsulotomy lens.
Step 3: Set focus. Align YAG laser aim beam on the posterior capsule.
Step 4: Start at 1.0–2.0 mJ energy. Use a circular or 'can-opener' pattern.
Step 5: Ensure IOL offset is set to 'posterior' to avoid IOL pitting.
Step 6: Post-procedure: Check IOP at 1-hour and prescribe NSAID/steroid drops for 3-5 days.

content.explanation: P: Power (start low), I: IOL protection (offset focus), T: Timing (ensure patient symptoms justify procedure), S: Safety (monitor IOP)

sections.title: Complications
content: IOP spikes (up to 30% of cases)
IOL damage (pitting/cracking)
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME)
Retinal Detachment (rare, 0.5-1%)
IOL dislocation

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Advanced IOL materials (hydrophobic acrylic) have significantly reduced PCO rates.
Laser-less prevention: Use of 'Capsule polishing' techniques during phacoemulsification.
Landmark Studies: Focus on the 'Posterior Capsule Opacification' meta-analyses confirming IOL edge design (square-edged) as the gold standard for prevention.

sections.title: Definition & Anatomical Peculiarities
content: The Trochlear Nerve (CN IV) is the thinnest cranial nerve (~2,400 axons).
Longest intracranial course (approx. 75mm) making it highly susceptible to trauma.
The only cranial nerve to exit the brainstem dorsally.
The only cranial nerve where all lower motor neuron fibers decussate (in the superior medullary velum).
Innervates the Superior Oblique (SO) muscle, which depresses, abducts, and incyclotorts the eye.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation & Symptoms
content: Vertical Diplopia: Worse on down-gaze (reading) and looking away from the side of the lesion.
Torsional Diplopia: Images appear tilted.
Compensatory Head Tilt: To the opposite shoulder to minimize diplopia (Bielschowsky's sign).
Aesthenopia: Vague eye strain during near work.
Facial Asymmetry: Often seen in long-standing congenital cases (hypoplasia of the affected side).

sections.title: Parks-Bielschowsky Three-Step Test
content: Step 1: Identify which eye is Hypertropic in primary position (e.g., Right Hypertropia).
Step 2: Determine if the Hypertropia increases in Right or Left Gaze (e.g., increases in Left Gaze).
Step 3: Determine if the Hypertropia increases on Right or Left Head Tilt (e.g., increases on Right Tilt).
Conclusion: If RHT is worse in Left Gaze and Right Tilt = Right SO Palsy.

rows: Shows head tilt (FAT Scan - Family Album Tomography)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Orthoptic measurements (Prism Cover Test) in 9 positions of gaze.
2. Double Maddox Rod test: Quantify excyclotorsion (usually >5-10° in bilateral).
3. Hess Chart / Lancaster Red-Green: Documentation of paretic field.
4. Neuroimaging (MRI Brain/Orbit): If non-vasculopathic, non-traumatic, or associated with other CN signs.
5. Systemic screen: BP, HbA1c, Myasthenia screen (Ice test/Tensilon) if mimicry suspected.

rows: Associated with brainstem signs, tilt is non-comitant

sections.title: Bilateral IV Nerve Palsy Red Flags
content: Excyclotorsion > 10 degrees on Double Maddox Rod.
Reversing Hypertropia (RHT in left gaze, LHT in right gaze).
Significant V-pattern Esotropia (>15PD difference).
Positive Bielschowsky tilt test to both sides.
Chin-down head position.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: Inferior Oblique (IO) Weakening: Recession, Myectomy, or Anteriorization. Used for Class I/III.
Superior Oblique (SO) Tuck: Tightening the tendon. Used for lax tendons or Class II.
Harada-Ito Procedure: Splitting the SO tendon and moving the anterior portion anteriorly/laterally to correct excyclotorsion.
Ipsilateral Superior Rectus (SR) Recession: For small deviations in primary gaze.
Contralateral Inferior Rectus (IR) Recession: For deviations larger in down-gaze.

content.explanation: IV Nerve, 4000 (actually 2.4k) fibers, 4th decade (ischemic), 4 types of surgery. Remember SO: Superior Oblique = SIN (Superior muscles are Incyclotortors).

sections.title: Key High-Yield Pearls
content: The 'Masked Bilateral' phenomenon: Operating on one eye reveals a palsy in the other that was previously hidden by suppression.
Superior Medullary Velum is the most common site of traumatic injury due to decussating fibers.
Non-traumatic, non-vasculopathic isolated IV palsy in adults should prompt neuroimaging to rule out schwannoma or meningioma.
Prism therapy (Base-down over the hypertropic eye) is excellent for stable, small-angle acquired palsies.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
sections.content: Most ischemic IV nerve palsies resolve spontaneously within 3 to 6 months. Surgical success rates are high, but patients must be warned about the possibility of 'iatrogenic Brown syndrome' following an over-zealous SO tuck. Recurrence is rare unless the underlying cause (e.g., tumor) progresses.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: CISS/FIESTA MRI sequences: High-resolution imaging now allows direct visualization of the trochlear nerve to detect atrophy or aplasia.
Botulinum Toxin: Used in the acute phase into the antagonist IO muscle to prevent contracture and alleviate symptoms while waiting for recovery.
Computerized Strabismus Mapping: Improved pre-operative planning for complex multi-muscle surgery.

sections.title: The Neuro-Ophthalmic Headache Landscape
sections.content: Headache is one of the most common complaints in ophthalmic practice [32, 785]. While many cases are benign primary syndromes, the ophthalmologist must identify secondary causes that are life- or vision-threatening, such as Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), intracranial mass lesions, and aneurysms [30, 567].

sections.title: Scenario 1: The Ophthalmic Emergency (GCA)
content: Scenario: 75-year-old female, 3-day history of severe right-sided temporal headache, malaise, and a 'shade' coming down over her vision for several minutes.
Diagnosis: Suspected Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) with amaurosis fugax [85, 760].
Red Flags: Scalp tenderness (pain when combing hair), jaw claudication (pain while chewing), and sudden visual loss [36, 85, 754].
Investigations: Immediate ESR, CRP, and Platelet count (Platelets are a strong predictor) [36, 757].
Gold standard: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) (specimen >2 cm to avoid skip lesions) [5, 586, 762].
Management: Do not wait for biopsy results. Immediate IV Methylprednisolone (g/day for 3 days) followed by oral Prednisone ( mg/kg/day) [5, 89, 762].

sections.title: Scenario 2: The Obese Young Patient (IIH)
content: 1. Identify: 28-year-old obese female, constant global headache (worse in morning/coughing), 'greying out' (TVOs) when standing.
2. Clinical Picture: Papilledema (bilateral disc swelling), transient visual obscurations (TVOs), pulsatile tinnitus, and possible CN VI palsy [38, 40, 182].
3. Workup: Blood pressure check (exclude malignant HTN) [183]. Emergent MRI and MRV (rule out mass/venous thrombosis) [39, 183, 769].
4. LP: Lumbar puncture (LP) showing opening pressure ≥ 250 mm H2O with normal CSF composition [4, 184, 770].
5. Management: Weight loss primary [185, 554]. Acetazolamide (250 mg QID to g BID). Surgery: Optic nerve sheath fenestration (vision) or CSF shunting (headache) [44, 45, 554].

sections.title: Scenario 3: 'Worst Headache of My Life'
content: Scenario: 50-year-old male, sudden explosive headache, 'droopy' eyelid, double vision, large non-reactive pupil.
Diagnosis: Ruptured intracranial aneurysm (typically PCoA) causing Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) [38, 199, 343].
Key Finding: Pupil-involving Third Nerve Palsy (fixed, dilated pupil) [0, 174, 198].
Action: Neurosurgical emergency. Urgent CTA preferred over MRA [202, 200, 346].
Treatment: Referral for endovascular coiling or surgical clipping [016, 346].

content.explanation: C: Conjunctival injection; L: Lacrimation; U: Unilateral (stabbing pain); S: Smoking history (35y male); T: Time-locked (2:00 AM); E: Eye/Ear autonomic signs (Rhinorrhea/Horner); R: Relief with 100% Oxygen (10–15 L/min) or Sumatriptan (6 mg SC). Prophylaxis: Verapamil or Lithium [157, 801, 1195].

sections.title: Scenario 5 & 6: Migraine & ICA Dissection
content: Scenario 5 (Migraine): 24-year-old female, 20-min shimmering zig-zag aura, followed by unilateral throbbing headache/nausea. Aura: 5–60 mins. Mgmt: Aspirin, Ibuprofen, Triptans. Avoid triggers [41, 795, 791].
Scenario 6 (ICA Dissection): 45-year-old male, acute temple/neck pain after car accident, small right pupil, 1 mm ptosis. Diagnosis: Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) Dissection [24, 180, 783].
Red Flag: A painful Horner syndrome is an ICA dissection until proven otherwise; high stroke risk. Mgmt: Urgent MRA/CTA head and neck; antiplatelet/anticoagulation [515, 784].

sections.title: Scenario 7 & 8: Pituitary & Trigeminal Pain
content: Scenario 7 (Pituitary Apoplexy): 40-year-old female, sudden severe headache, bilateral vision loss, total ophthalmoplegia. Red Flags: Bitemporal hemianopia, multiple CN palsies (III, IV, VI). Mgmt: Urgent MRI, immediate steroids to prevent Addisonian crisis [138, 802, 1532].

Scenario 8 (Trigeminal Neuralgia): 60-year-old male, 'electric shock-like' stabs in cheek triggered by shaving. Mgmt: Carbamazepine (100 mg BID up to 1200 mg/day) or Baclofen. Image to rule out MS or vascular compression [362, 805, 1197].

sections.title: Scenario 9: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
content: 1. Presentation: 65-year-old hyperope, sudden severe headache, eye pain, vomiting, hazy cornea.
2. Exam: IOP 50–80 mmHg, rock-hard eye, fixed mid-dilated vertically oval pupil, shallow anterior chamber [487, 681, 1235].
3. Acute Mgmt: Lie supine. Systemic Acetazolamide (500 mg IV) + topical suppressants.
4. Definitive: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (PI) in BOTH eyes [488, 686, 1236].

sections.title: Scenario 10, 11, & 12: Inflammation, Meds, & Ischemia
content: Scenario 10 (Tolosa-Hunt): 50-year-old, intense boring orbital pain, CN III, IV, VI palsies. MRI shows apex enhancement. DX of exclusion (rule out lymphoma/aneurysm). Rx: Systemic steroids [962, 1800].
Scenario 11 (Medication Overuse): Chronic migraineur, headache ≥15 days/month, daily paracetamol/triptans. Mgmt: Abruptly stop offending drug (withdrawal lasts ~3 weeks) [838, 1012].

Scenario 12 (Ocular Ischemic Syndrome): 70-year-old, carotid disease, dull aching 'ocular angina', vision improves in dark. Mid-peripheral dot-blot hemorrhages, iris neovascularization. Mgmt: Carotid endarterectomy; manage IOP/PRP [81, 1597].

sections.title: Scenario 13, 14, & 15: Tension, Meningitis, & Raeder
content: Scenario 13 (Tension): 30-year-old student, 'viselike' band, worse end of day. Bilateral, pressing, no physical aggravation. Rx: NSAIDs, Amitriptyline [153, 798].

Scenario 14 (Meningitis): 20-year-old, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia. Pearl: Pain on eye movement is common; normal ocular exam. Mgmt: LP (after CT if focal) + IV antibiotics [139, 1568].
Scenario 15 (Raeder Paratrigeminal): Middle-aged man, Horner syndrome + daily unilateral periorbital headaches (V1). Mgmt: Exclude parasellar/cavernous sinus pathology with MRI [126, 807].

branches: Life-Threatening Screening: Sudden (Aneurysm), Fever (Meningitis), Age >55 (GCA), High BP (Crisis)
Detailed History: Timing (Morning=ICP, Night=Cluster), Triggers (Touch=CN V, Food=Migraine)
Special Tests: Hertel (Proptosis), Corneal Sensation (CN V), LP (if imaging normal)
Labs: ESR/CRP/FBC for all patients >50 years

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination
content: Pupils: Check for RAPD (Optic nerve) and Anisocoria (Horner/CN III).
Fundus: Look for Disc edema (Papilledema/GCA) and Hemorrhages (HTN/CRVO).
IOP/Gonio: Crucial to exclude Acute Glaucoma.
Motility: Identify CN III, IV, or VI palsies indicating compressive lesions.

content.explanation: Pearl: SVP absence is common in papilledema, but presence strongly suggests normal ICP [1572]. Pitfall: Never LP before neuroimaging if mass suspected (herniation risk). Examiner's Pick: Headache + Adie-like pupil? Check for CN III aberrant regeneration. Precaution: Beta-blockers for glaucoma can mask migraine/systemic signs. High Yield: Pregnant + Headache + Vision Loss? Consider Preeclampsia/Eclampsia & PRES.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: The SNOOP Mnemonic
content: S: Systemic signs/symptoms (Fever, Weight Loss, Pregnancy)
N: Neurologic signs (Palsies, Papilledema, RAPD)
O: Onset (Sudden, Thunderbolt, Explosive)
O: Older age of onset (>50 years, GCA risk)
P: Progression or Pattern change (New type of headache)

Scenario: A 50-year-old male presents with a sudden, explosive headache and a "droopy" right eyelid. On lifting the lid, he has double vision and the right pupil is large and non-reactive.

Scenario 4: The "Suicide" Headache (Cluster Headache)
Scenario: A 35-year-old male smoker reports excruciating, stabbing pain behind his left eye occurring every night at 2:00 AM for the last two weeks. The eye is red and tearing.
Diagnosis: Cluster Headache [57, 80, 95].
Signs: Ipsilateral conjunctival injection, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, and miosis/ptosis (Horner syndrome) [58, 803, 95].

Scenario 6: Painful Horner Syndrome (ICA Dissection)

Mechanism: Infarction or hemorrhage of a pituitary adenoma [38, 532].

Scenario: A 60-year-old male describes "electric shock-like" stabs of pain in his right cheek triggered by shaving or light touch.

Scenario: A 65-year-old hyperopic female presents with sudden severe headache, eye pain, and vomiting. The eye is rock-hard and the cornea is hazy.
Diagnosis: Acute Primary Angle Closure (APAC) [487, 68, 235].
Examination Pick: High IOP (50–80 mmHg), fixed mid-dilated vertically oval pupil, and shallow anterior chamber [487, 68, 235].
Management: Lie supine. Systemic Acetazolamide (500 mg IV) and topical suppressants [685, 899, 478]. Definitive: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (PI) in both eyes [488, 686, 236].
Scenario 10: Tolosa-Hunt Syndrome
Scenario: A 50-year-old presents with intense boring orbital pain and multiple ocular motor nerve palsies (III, IV, VI). MRI shows enhancement at the orbital apex.
Diagnosis: Tolosa-Hunt Syndrome (idiopathic granulomatous inflammation) [249, 96, 533, 800].
Examiner's Pick: Diagnosis of exclusion; must rule out lymphoma, metastasis, and aneurysm [, 96, 458].

Scenario: A chronic migraineur reports a headache on ≥ 5 days per month for the last four months. She is taking paracetamol and triptans daily.
Diagnosis: Medication Overuse Headache [838, 02].
Management: Counsel patient to abruptly stop the offending drug (withdrawal may last 3 weeks) [800, 02].

Diagnosis: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome [8, 293, 597].

Management: Carotid endarterectomy; manage IOP and retinal ischemia (PRP) [82, 600].
Scenario 13: Tension-Type Headache
Scenario: A 30-year-old law student describes a "viselike" band of pain around her head, typically worse at the end of a long day of studying.
Diagnosis: Tension-type headache [53, 798].
Key Points: Bilateral, pressing quality, not aggravated by physical activity.
Management: Simple analgesics (NSAIDs); prophylactic tricyclic antidepressants (Amitriptyline) [55, 799].

Scenario: A 20-year-old presents with a severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia.
Diagnosis: Meningitis [39, 350, 568].

Diagnosis: Raeder Syndrome [26, 807, 80].
Management: Must exclude intracranial pathology in the parasellar or cavernous sinus regions with MRI [26, 807, 80].

Comparisons: Primary vs. Secondary Headaches
Feature
Primary (Migraine/Cluster/Tension)
Secondary (GCA/IIH/Aneurysm)
Onset
Often chronic/recurrent [40]
Can be sudden/new [3, 566]
Systemic Symptoms
Rare (except nausea) [4, 792]
Fever, weight loss, jaw pain [36, 85]
Neurological Signs
Transient aura only [42, 008]
Persistent palsies, disc edema [37, 82]
Urgency
Non-urgent treatment [54]
Immediate medical/surgical referral [30, 99]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Workup & Approach Mind Map
Life-Threatening Screening (Triage):
Sudden "Worst" headache? → Aneurysm/SAH [38].
Fever + Stiff neck? → Meningitis [39].
Age >55 + Scalp tenderness? → GCA [36].
Malignant BP? → Hypertensive Crisis [568].
Detailed History:
Timing: Morning (High ICP), Evening (Tension), Night (Cluster) [37, 53, 58].
Triggers: Touch (Trigeminal Neuralgia), Alcohol (Cluster), Foods (Migraine) [58, 03, 576].
Comprehensive Ocular Exam:
Pupils: RAPD (Optic nerve lesion), Anisocoria (Horner/CN III) [8, 22, 98].
Fundus: Disc edema (Papilledema/GCA), Hemorrhages (HTN/CRVO) [82, 548, 585].
IOP/Gonio: Exclude Acute Glaucoma [235, 475].
Special Tests:
Hertel Exophthalmometry (Proptosis) [429, 439].
Corneal Sensation (Exclude CN V involvement) [, 300].
Imaging & Labs:
ESR/CRP/FBC for all >50 years [79, 762].
MRI/MRV (Soft tissue/Sinuses) vs. CT/CTA (Bone/Blood/Vessels).
Lumbar Puncture (If imaging normal and ICP suspected) [37, 83].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Management Highlights: Pearls & Pitfalls
Pearl: The absence of Spontaneous Venous Pulsations (SVPs) is common in papilledema, but its presence strongly suggests normal ICP [572].
Pitfall: Do not perform an LP before neuroimaging if a mass lesion is suspected, as this can lead to brainstem herniation [64, 83].
Examiner's Pick: In a patient with headache and an "Adie-like" pupil, always check for aberrant regeneration of CN III, which could indicate an old compressive lesion [9, 74].
Precaution: Topical Beta-blockers for glaucoma can worsen migraine management or mask systemic signs [892, 53].
High Yield: In pregnant women with headaches and visual loss, always consider Preeclampsia/Eclampsia and Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) [403, 779, 9].

sections.title: Defining Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)
sections.content: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED), also known as Graves’ Orbitopathy, is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammation and swelling of the extraocular muscles (EOMs) and orbital fat. It is the most common cause of both unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults.

sections.title: Scenario 1: Interpreting Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs)
content: Scenario: A 45-year-old female presents with eyelid retraction. Labs: Suppressed TSH and elevated Free T4.
Definition: Hyperthyroidism (Thyrotoxicosis) – excessive secretion of thyroid hormones.
Examiner's Pick: Suppressed TSH with high T4/T3 is classic for Graves' disease.
High Yield: Severity of TED often does not parallel serum levels of T3 or T4.
Red Flag: TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) or Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI) are specific markers for Graves' and correlate with eye disease activity.

sections.title: Scenario 2: The Medical Emergency – Thyrotoxic Storm
content: Clinical Picture: Hyperpyrexia (>41°C), dehydration, tachycardia (>140 bpm), heart failure, and coma.
Scenario: Patient with known Graves’ presenting for surgery with Temp 41°C, HR 150 bpm, and extreme agitation.
TREATMENT DOSES:
Beta-blockers: Propranolol (40 mg PO or 1 mg slow IV) to control heart rate.
Antithyroid Drugs: Carbimazole (15–25 mg Q6H PO) or Propylthiouracil.
Iodine: Lugol’s solution (0.3 mL PO Q8H) to block hormone release.
Corticosteroids: Hydrocortisone (100 mg Q6H IV) to block T4-to-T3 conversion.

sections.title: Scenario 3: The Hypothyroid Emergency – Myxoedema Coma
content: Clinical Picture: Hypothermia (34°C), bradycardia (45 bpm), hypotension, seizures, and 'myxoedema madness'.
Management Step 1: Thyroid replacement with T3 (5–20 µg IV Q12H) or Levothyroxine.
Management Step 2: Steroids – Hydrocortisone (100 mg Q8H IV) if pituitary involvement is suspected.
Pitfall: Avoid rapid rewarming; treat infections and hypoglycemia concurrently.

sections.title: Scenario 4: Sight-Threatening TED (CON)
content: Diagnosis: Compressive Optic Neuropathy (CON).
Clinical Scenario: 'Washed out' colors, reduced vision, and positive RAPD.
Mechanism: Crowding of the orbital apex by enlarged EOMs.
Treatment: Pulse Steroids – IV Methylprednisolone (500 mg–1 g daily for 3 days).
Emergency Surgery: Urgent orbital decompression if steroids fail within 48–72 hours.

rows: Tachycardia, Tremor, Heat intolerance, Weight loss, Goiter
Bradycardia, Cold intolerance, Weight gain, Dry skin, Constipation

sections.title: Scenario 5: Exposure Keratopathy in TED
content: Clinical Picture: Incomplete blink (lagophthalmos), inferior punctate erosions, and possible bacterial keratitis.
Scenario: 26 mm proptosis with central corneal infiltrate.
Management: Intensive lubricants, nocturnal eyelid taping, or Moisture goggles.
Hazard: Permanent vision loss from corneal perforation.

sections.title: Smoking Key Points
sections.content: Smoking is the single most important modifiable risk factor for TED progression. Smokers are 7–10 times more likely to develop TED and have a longer active phase (2–3 years vs. 1 year in non-smokers).

rows: Parinaud syndrome (Collier sign), 3rd nerve misdirection, Myasthenia Gravis (Hering’s law), or orbital mass.
Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) - Rule out with Platelet count and ESR.

content.explanation: Order of Muscle Involvement: Inferior Rectus > Medial Rectus > Superior Rectus > Lateral Rectus > Obliques.

sections.title: Scenario 9 & 10: Signs & Management
content: Restrictive Myopathy: Persistent 20-prism diopter hypotropia in TED.
Strabismus Management: Recession only (avoid resection due to fibrosis). Delay until 6 months of stability.
Eyelid Signs: Dalrymple sign (retraction at rest), von Graefe sign (lid lag on downgaze).

branches: Diagnosis (2 of 3): Immune dysfunction, Ocular signs (Proptosis/CON), Imaging (Tendon-sparing EOM)
Assessment: CAS Score (Pain, redness, swelling). Score ≥ 3/7 = Active
Tiered Rx: Mild (Lubes, Selenium 100µg BD), Mod/Severe (Steroids), Sight-Threat (CON)

sections.title: Clinical Phases: Active vs. Quiescent (Rundle’s Curve)
content: Active Phase: Congestive stage, red/painful eyes, lasts 6–18 months. Requires immunosuppression.
Quiescent Phase: 'Burned-out' phase, white eyes but persistent fibrosis/motility defects.
Examiner's Pick: Clinical Activity Score (CAS) ≥ 3/7 indicates active disease.

sections.title: Systemic Hazards & Precautions
content: Radioactive Iodine (RAI): Can exacerbate/trigger TED. Precaution: Co-administer oral steroids (Prednisone).
Myasthenia Gravis (MG): Occurs in 5% of TED. Suspect MG if PTOSIS is present instead of lid retraction.
Timolol Glaucoma Meds: Can mask hyperthyroid tachycardia. Abrupt withdrawal can precipitate thyroid storm.
Surgical Pitfall: Do not perform strabismus or lid surgery until euthyroid and stable for 6–9 months.

rows: Best for bony resolution, planning decompression, and identifying 'apical crowding' in CON.
Best for identifying active muscle inflammation via increased water content.
Tendons are characteristically SPARED in TED (unlike orbital pseudotumor).

sections.title: Management Pearls & New Horizons
content: Pearl: Apraclonidine 0.5% acts as 'chemical sympathectomy' for temporary relief of lid retraction.

data.generationPrompt:
Thyroid Disorders in Ophthalmic Practice: Internal Medicine & Emergencies
Thyroid Eye Disease (TED), also known as Graves’ Orbitopathy, is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammation and swelling of the extraocular muscles (EOMs) and orbital fat. It is the most common cause of both unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
OSCE & VIVA Clinical Scenarios
Scenario 1: Interpreting Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs)
Scenario: A 45-year-old female presents with eyelid retraction. Her labs show a suppressed TSH and elevated Free T4.
Definition: Hyperthyroidism (Thyrotoxicosis) – excessive secretion of thyroid hormones.
Examiner's Pick: Suppressed TSH with high T4/T3 is classic for Graves' disease.
High Yield: Severity of TED often does not parallel serum levels of T3 or T4.
Red Flag: TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) or Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI) are specific markers for Graves' and correlate with eye disease activity.
Scenario 2: The Medical Emergency – Thyrotoxic Storm
Scenario: A patient with known Graves’ disease presents for surgery but is found to have a temperature of 41°C, tachycardia of 150 bpm, and extreme agitation.
Clinical Picture: Hyperpyrexia (>41°C), dehydration, tachycardia (>140 bpm), heart failure, and coma.
Treatment (Drug Doses):
Beta-blockers: Propranolol (40 mg PO or 1 mg slow IV) to control heart rate.
Antithyroid Drugs: Carbimazole (15–25 mg Q6H PO) or Propylthiouracil.
Iodine: Lugol’s solution (0.3 mL PO Q8H) to block hormone release.
Corticosteroids: Hydrocortisone (100 mg Q6H IV) to block T4-to-T3 conversion.
Scenario 3: The Hypothyroid Emergency – Myxoedema Coma
Scenario: An elderly patient is found unresponsive in the ward with a heart rate of 45 bpm and a core temperature of 34°C.
Clinical Picture: Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, seizures, and "myxoedema madness".
Management:
Thyroid replacement: T3 (5–20 µg IV Q12H) or Levothyroxine.
Steroids: Hydrocortisone (100 mg Q8H IV) if pituitary involvement is suspected.
Pitfall: Avoid rapid rewarming; treat infections and hypoglycemia concurrently.
Scenario 4: Sight-Threatening TED (Compressive Optic Neuropathy)
Scenario: A patient with severe TED reports "washed out" colors and reduced vision. You note a positive RAPD.
Diagnosis: Compressive Optic Neuropathy (CON).
Mechanism: Crowding of the orbital apex by enlarged EOMs.
Treatment:
Pulse Steroids: IV Methylprednisolone (500 mg–1 g daily for 3 days).
Emergency Surgery: Urgent orbital decompression if steroids fail within 48–72 hours.
Scenario 5: Exposure Keratopathy in TED
Scenario: A patient with 26 mm proptosis and severe eyelid retraction presents with a central corneal infiltrate.
Clinical Picture: Incomplete blink (lagophthalmos), inferior punctate erosions, and possible bacterial keratitis.
Management: Intensive lubricants, nocturnal eyelid taping, or Moisture goggles.
Hazard: Permanent vision loss from corneal perforation.
Scenario 6: The Smoking Risk Factor
Scenario: The examiner asks, "What is the single most important modifiable risk factor for TED progression?"
Answer: Smoking.
Key Point: Smokers are 7–10 times more likely to develop TED and have a longer active phase (2–3 years vs. 1 year in non-smokers).
Scenario 7: Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Hazard
Scenario: A patient with mild TED is scheduled for RAI for hyperthyroidism.
Hazard: RAI can exacerbate or trigger TED.
Precaution: Co-administer oral steroids (Prednisone) during treatment to prevent progression.
Scenario 8: Pediatric TED
Scenario: A 10-year-old presents with bilateral proptosis and hyperthyroidism.
Key Point: TED is rare in children; symptoms are usually milder, and vision loss is exceptional.
DDx: Rule out orbital cellulitis, rhabdomyosarcoma, or neuroblastoma.
Scenario 9: Restrictive Myopathy and Diplopia
Scenario: A patient with stable TED has a persistent 20-prism diopter hypotropia in the right eye.
Muscle Involvement Order (IMSLO): Inferior Rectus > Medial Rectus > Superior Rectus > Lateral Rectus > Obliques.
Management: Strabismus surgery (recession only, avoid resection due to fibrosis).
Precaution: Surgery must be delayed until measurements are stable for at least 6 months.
Scenario 10: Eyelid Retraction Differential Diagnosis
Scenario: A patient has a "staring look" but normal thyroid tests.
Ocular Signs: Dalrymple sign (retraction at rest), von Graefe sign (lid lag on downgaze).
DDx: Parinaud syndrome (Collier sign), 3rd nerve misdirection, Myasthenia Gravis (Hering’s law), or orbital mass.
Scenario 11: Active vs. Quiescent TED (Rundle’s Curve)
Scenario: Describe the clinical course of TED.
Active Phase: Congestive stage, red/painful eyes, lasts 6–18 months.
Quiescent Phase: "Burned-out" phase, white eyes but persistent fibrosis/motility defects.
Examiner's Pick: Clinical Activity Score (CAS) ≥ 3/7 indicates active disease requiring immunosuppression.
Scenario 12: Systemic Associations (Autoimmune)
Scenario: What other diseases should you screen for in a TED patient?
Answer: Myasthenia Gravis (MG) (occurs in up to 5% of TED patients).
Clinical Pearl: Suspect MG if the patient has ptosis instead of lid retraction.
Scenario 13: Order of Surgical Rehabilitation
Scenario: A patient needs several surgeries for TED. What is the correct sequence?
Sequence: 1. Orbital Decompression → 2. Strabismus Surgery → 3. Eyelid Surgery.
Rationale: Decompression changes orbital volume and can alter muscle alignment and lid position.
Scenario 14: Orbital Imaging in TED (CT vs. MRI)
Scenario: Which imaging modality is preferred for TED and why?
CT: Best for bony resolution and planning decompression.
MRI (T2/STIR): Best for identifying active muscle inflammation (water content).
Key Point: Tendons are characteristically spared in TED (unlike orbital pseudotumor).
Scenario 15: Complications of Glaucoma Meds in Thyroid Disease
Scenario: You prescribe Timolol for a patient with TED and hyperthyroidism.
Hazard: Topical beta-blockers can mask symptoms of hyperthyroidism (e.g., tachycardia).
Precaution: Abrupt withdrawal of beta-blockers can precipitate a thyroid storm.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Comparison: Hyperthyroidism vs. Hypothyroidism
Feature
Hyperthyroidism (Graves)
Hypothyroidism (Hashimoto)
TSH Level
Suppressed (Low)
Elevated (High)
Systemic Signs
Tachycardia, Tremor, Heat intolerance, Weight loss, Goiter
Bradycardia, Cold intolerance, Weight gain, Dry skin, Constipation
Ocular Relation
Associated with 90% of TED
Associated with 5-10% of TED
Red Flag
Thyroid Storm (Tachycardia/Fever)
Myxoedema Coma (Bradycardia/Hypothermia)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Workup & Approach Mind Map (The "TED Algorithm")
Diagnosis (2 of 3 signs):
Immune thyroid dysfunction (Graves/Hashimoto).
Ocular signs (Lid retraction, proptosis, CON).
Imaging findings (Tendon-sparing EOM enlargement).
Assessment of Activity:
CAS Score: Pain, redness, swelling (Score ≥ 3/7 = Active).
Tiered Management:
Mild: Lubricants, smoking cessation, Selenium (100 µg BD).
Moderate/Severe: Oral Prednisone or pulsed IV Methylprednisolone.
Sight-Threatening (CON): Urgent IV Steroids → Orbital Decompression.
Rehabilitation Sequence:
Decompress → Squint → Lids.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Management Pearls & Pitfalls
Pearl: Apraclonidine 0.5% can be used as a "chemical sympathectomy" for temporary relief of lid retraction while waiting for stabilization.
Pitfall: Do not perform strabismus or lid surgery until the patient has been euthyroid and measurements stable for 6–9 months.
Examiner's Pick: In CON, the orbital apex is the site of maximal compression; CT scans will show "apical crowding".
Highlight: Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor) is a new FDA-approved biologic that effectively reduces proptosis in active disease.
High Yield: Platelet count and ESR are important to rule out Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) in elderly patients presenting with AION-like vision loss.

sections.title: Definitions & Overview
content: In the context of Advanced Life Support (ALS) and emergency medicine, distinguishing between shockable and non-shockable rhythms is the critical first step in managing a cardiorespiratory arrest.
Shockable Rhythms: Rhythms that respond to electrical defibrillation, aimed at terminating chaotic electrical activity to allow the heart's natural pacemaker to resume a coordinated rhythm.

Non-Shockable Rhythms: Rhythms where electrical activity is either absent or organized but disconnected from mechanical contraction; these require high-quality CPR and the treatment of underlying causes rather than a DC shock.

sections.title: Scenario 1: Ventricular Fibrillation (VF) during FFA
content: Scenario: You are performing a Fundus Fluorescein Angiogram (FFA) when the patient suddenly collapses. You attach the monitor, and it shows rapid, bizarre, and irregular ventricular complexes. The patient has no carotid pulse.
Diagnosis: Shockable rhythm: Ventricular Fibrillation (VF).
Key Points: VF is the most common and easily treatable cardiac arrest rhythm. It represents ineffective, uncoordinated ventricular movement.
Management: Immediate defibrillation (360J monophasic or 150–360J biphasic) followed by immediate resumption of CPR (30:2) for 2 minutes without a pulse check.

sections.title: Scenario 2: The 'Organized' PEA Arrest
content: Scenario: During an ocular surgery, the anesthesiologist notes a sudden loss of blood pressure. The ECG monitor shows a normal-looking sinus rhythm at 60 bpm, but you cannot feel a carotid pulse.
Diagnosis: Non-shockable rhythm: Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA), also known as electromechanical dissociation (EMD).

Key Points: Organized electrical activity exists, but there is no effective cardiac output. It often carries a poor prognosis unless a catastrophic event like a massive pulmonary embolism (PE) is reversed.
Management: Immediate CPR (30:2) for 2 minutes. Do NOT shock. Search for and correct '4H and 4T' reversible causes.

sections.title: Scenario 3: Recognizing Asystole
content: Scenario: A patient is found unresponsive in the waiting room. The monitor shows a flat line.
Diagnosis: Non-shockable rhythm: Asystole.
Definition: Complete absence of electrical activity within the ventricles.
Pitfall: Ensure the leads are correctly attached to avoid 'false asystole.'
Management: CPR (30:2) for 2 minutes. Adrenaline 1mg IV every 3–5 minutes. Consider cardiac pacing if appropriate.

sections.title: Scenario 4: Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia (pVT)
content: Scenario: A patient with a history of myocardial infarction (MI) develops a very rapid, wide-complex regular rhythm on the monitor and loses consciousness.
Diagnosis: Shockable rhythm: Pulseless (sustained) Ventricular Tachycardia (VT).
Key Points: Mechanical contraction and relaxation cannot occur effectively due to the extreme rate. It may degenerate into VF.
Management: Treat identically to VF with immediate defibrillation.

branches: 4 Ts: Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Toxins, Thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary)

sections.title: Refractory VF & Pharmacology
content: Step 1: Administer Shock 1 and 2.
Step 2: Administer Shock 3.
Step 3: Drug Therapy: Administer Adrenaline 1mg IV.
Step 4: Amiodarone Dose: 300mg bolus.
Step 5: For resistant VF/VT, a further 150mg Amiodarone can be given.

sections.title: Scenario 7: Post-Operative Pulmonary Embolism
content: Context: 75-year-old patient 5 days post-vitrectomy develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and collapse.
Diagnosis: PE causing PEA.
Clinical triad: Acute dyspnea, tachypnea, and pleuritic chest pain.
Management: Aggressive CPR and consideration of immediate thrombolysis (Streptokinase) or surgical intervention.

content.explanation: Mechanism: Trigeminal-vagal reflex triggered by muscle traction (especially medial rectus) or pressure on the globe. Management: Immediately stop manipulating the eye. Start BLS/ALS and consider IV Atropine if rhythm does not recover.

sections.title: Scenario 9: Fluorescein Anaphylaxis
content: Diagnosis: Anaphylactic shock mimicking arrest.
Key Signs: Tachycardia, hypotension, wheeze, laryngeal edema.
Management: Secure airway, 100% O2, IV fluids, and IM Adrenaline (0.5mg of 1:1000).

sections.title: Scenario 10 & 11: Drugs and Defibrillation
content: Atropine: Indicated in Non-shockable rhythms (Asystole/PEA) and severe symptomatic bradycardia. Dose: 3mg IV once for asystole.
Biphasic Energy: 150–360 J.
Monophasic Energy: 360 J.
Pearl: Higher energy levels are used if the first shock is unsuccessful.

sections.title: Scenario 12: Stopping Resuscitation
content: Criteria: Stop after 20 minutes if there is refractory Asystole/PEA and no reversible cause is identified.
Physiological markers: Stop if core temperature is >33°C, pH and K+ are normal, and no rhythm return is noted.

sections.title: Scenario 13: Complications of CPR
content: Complications: Rib fractures, sternal fractures, pneumothorax, and gastric insufflation.
Key Performance Indicator: Ensure compressions are 4–5 cm deep at a rate of 100/min to maintain coronary perfusion.

sections.title: Scenario 14: The Unconscious Diabetic
content: Differentials for non-responsive state: Hypoglycemic coma, Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), HONK, or primary cardiac arrest.
Key Action: Check plasma glucose immediately if there is a pulse; if no pulse, prioritize BLS/CPR.

sections.title: Scenario 15: Post-Resuscitation Management
content: Step 1: Achieving Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC).
Step 2: Transfer to ICU/CCU.
Step 3: Monitor vital signs and obtain 12-lead ECG.
Step 4: Check ABGs/electrolytes.
Step 5: Seek cardiologist advice.

sections.title: Mind Map: Systematic Approach to Arrest

branches: Shout for Help: Call cardiac arrest team and get AED/Defibrillator.
Airway (A): Head tilt/chin lift or jaw thrust.
Breathing (B): Look, listen, feel for 10 seconds. Give 2 rescue breaths if not breathing.
Circulation (C): Check carotid pulse for 10 seconds. Start CPR 30:2 (100 bpm, 4-5cm).
Rhythm Analysis: Shockable? (Shock then 2 min CPR) vs Non-Shockable? (No Shock, 2 min CPR + Fix 4H/4T).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Critical Pitfalls
content: Pearl: 'Vocal Local' or 'Verbal Anesthesia' during surgery can help monitor patient consciousness and prevent sudden movements.
Examiner's Pick: In PEA, always consider Hypovolaemia (bleeding) if the patient has had recent surgery or trauma.
Pitfall: Do not interrupt CPR for pulse checks or rhythm analysis for more than 10 seconds.
High Yield: In the elderly, always prioritize Regional Anesthesia over General Anesthesia to reduce intraoperative hemodynamic fluctuations.
Red Flag: Sudden tachycardia and rising CO2 during anesthesia may indicate Malignant Hyperthermia, requiring Dantrolene and surgery termination.

Scenario: You are leading a code for a patient in PEA. The examiner asks, "What must you check to reverse this non-shockable rhythm?"

Criteria: Stop after 20 minutes if there is refractory Asystole/PEA and no reversible cause is identified. Also stop if core temperature is >33°C, pH and K+ are normal, and no rhythm return is noted.

Scenario: During chest compressions, you hear a "crack." What are the hazards?
Answer:

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Accommodative Esotropia (Acc ET) is defined as a convergent ocular deviation associated with the activation of the accommodation reflex. Early-onset cases typically manifest between 6 months and 3 years of age, though 'early-onset' specifically refers to those occurring before age 1. It is driven by the physiological link between accommodation and convergence (the AC/A ratio) and is the most common cause of childhood esotropia.

rows: Residual ET even with full correction

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Sudden or gradual onset of 'crossing'
Initial intermittency (worse with fatigue/near work)
Variable angle of deviation
Diplopia or suppression in older children
Risk of refractive or strabismic amblyopia
Closing one eye in bright light (occasional)

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Cycloplegic Refraction (Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1%)
Step 2: Measurement of Deviation (SPCT) at Distance & Near
Step 3: Determination of AC/A Ratio (Gradient or Heterophoria)
Step 4: Assessment of Sensory Status (Stereopsis/Worth 4-Dot)
Step 5: Dilated Fundus Exam to rule out sensory causes

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Is it truly Acc ET?

content.explanation: AC/A = (Deviation with lens - Deviation without lens) / Power of lens. Example: If +3.00 lens changes ET from 30 to 12, AC/A = (30-12)/3 = 6.

sections.title: Management Strategy: Refractive ET
content: 1. Prescribe FULL cycloplegic hyperopic correction
2. Re-evaluate in 4-6 weeks for adaptation
3. Check for residual amblyopia; treat with patching
4. Monitor every 3-6 months for stability
5. Gradual reduction of plus (weaning) only after age 7-8

sections.title: Management: Non-Refractive (High AC/A)
content: 1. Prescribe full distance correction
2. Add +2.50 or +3.00D Bifocals (Executive or Flat-top)
3. Ensure the bifocal line bisects the pupil (high line)
4. If residual ET remains at near, consider surgery
5. Miotics (Phospholine Iodide) rarely used due to side effects

sections.title: RED FLAGS: When it's NOT simple Acc ET
content: Acute onset with headache or vomiting (Intracranial Pressure)
Abduction deficit (6th Nerve Palsy/Duane's)
Leukocoria (Retinoblastoma causing sensory ET)
Incomitance in different gazes
Nystagmus with neurological features

sections.title: Surgical Indications
content: Partially Accommodative ET: Surgery for the NON-accommodative residual component
Decompensated ET: When glasses no longer control the deviation
High AC/A: Surgery (Bi-Medial Recession) if bifocals fail or are unacceptable
Recession is based on the residual angle with full correction

content.explanation: Accommodation (driving force), Amblyopia (primary risk), Anisometropia (frequent association).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Exam Room
content: Always use Atropine for the first refraction in early onset cases to ensure maximal cycloplegia.
Hyperopia in Acc ET is dynamic; it may increase until age 7.
Don't 'cut the plus' in children under 6 years old.
Stereopsis is the best indicator of successful management.

sections.title: Prognosis & Long-Term Outcomes
sections.content: Most children with pure refractive Acc ET achieve excellent binocularity and high-grade stereopsis if treated early. About 10-15% may eventually require surgery for decompensation. Spontaneous resolution occurs in some children as they outgrow hyperopia in their teens.

sections.title: Recent Advances: The PEDIG Evidence
content: PEDIG studies suggest that +2.50 bifocals are generally as effective as +3.00 for High AC/A.
Early full correction significantly reduces the incidence of permanent amblyopia.
Ongoing research into the genetic markers of high hyperopia and Acc ET linkage.

While TASS is a sterile inflammatory response to an intraocular insult, endophthalmitis is a vision-threatening infection requiring urgent antimicrobial intervention.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS) is an acute, sterile, non-infectious intraocular inflammation caused by a non-infectious substance entering the anterior segment, resulting in toxic damage to intraocular tissues. Acute Endophthalmitis is a severe intraocular infection (usually bacterial) involving the vitreous and aqueous humors, often occurring within 1 week of surgery.

sections.title: The Golden Clock: Time of Onset
content: TASS: 12–24 hours post-op (can occur as early as 6h).
Acute Virulent Endo: 24–48 hours (Streptococcus, Pseudomonas).
Typical Endo: 3–7 days post-op (Staph epidermidis).
Delayed-Onset Endo: Weeks to months (P. acnes, Fungal).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Think Endophthalmitis!
content: Profound, sudden loss of vision (Light Perception or worse)
Severe eye pain and periorbital headache
Marked chemosis and eyelid edema
Presence of vitreous membranes/cells on B-scan
Failure to respond to intensive topical steroids after 6 hours

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Clinical History (Onset time is critical)
Step 2: Slit Lamp (Look for limbus-to-limbus edema vs vitritis)
Step 3: B-Scan Ultrasonography (Assess vitreous status)
Step 4: If suspicious for Endo: AC & Vitreous Tap for culture/gram stain
Step 5: PCR Analysis (If available, for rapid pathogen ID)

content.explanation: T: Timeline (Acute <24h); A: Anterior focus (No Vitritis); S: Sterile (Culture Negative); S: Steroid response (Rapid improvement).

sections.title: Management: TASS Protocol
content: Intensive Topical Steroids (Pred Forte 1% every 30-60 mins)
Topical NSAIDs as adjunct
Aqueous Suppressants (if IOP > 30 mmHg)
Close follow-up (every 6-12 hours initially)
Rule out infection if no response in 24 hours

sections.title: Management: Endophthalmitis Protocol
content: Intravitreal Vancomycin (1mg/0.1mL) + Ceftazidime (2.25mg/0.1mL)
AC/Vitreous Tap & Gown (Before antibiotics)
Immediate Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) if Vision is Light Perception (LP) or worse
Intensive Topical Fortified Antibiotics (Vancomycin/Tobramycin)
Systemic Antibiotics (Controversial, except in specific cases)

sections.title: Evidence-Based Pearl: EVS Study
content: EVS (Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study) Findings:
Primary outcome: PPV is superior to Tap/Inject ONLY if presenting vision is Light Perception (LP).
If vision is Hand Motion (HM) or better, Tap/Inject is equivalent to PPV.
Systemic antibiotics (Amikacin/Ceftazidime) showed NO benefit for visual outcome.
Diabetes was a significant risk factor for worse outcomes.

rows: Secondary to massive endothelial cell loss

sections.title: Prevention Checklist
content: Strict instrument cleaning protocols (No enzymatic detergents)
Single-use cannulas preferred
Minimize volume of intracameral medications
Wait 20 mins after ETO sterilization for off-gassing
Regular autoclave maintenance & biological indicators

content.explanation: TASS often presents with a 'cold' hypopyon—one that shifts easily with head movement and is associated with a white, quiet conjunctiva—whereas infectious endophthalmitis presents with a 'hot' hypopyon, often fibrin-locked and associated with angry, injected conjunctiva/chemosis.

sections.title: Phases of VKH Syndrome
content: 1. Prodromal Phase: Neurological & Auditory manifestations, Cranial nerve palsies, Optic neuritis.

2. Acute Uveitic Phase: Bilateral granulomatous AU, Multifocal posterior uveitis, Diffuse choroidal infiltrate, Dalen-Fuchs nodules, Vitritis, Papillitis, Exudative retinal detachments, Ciliary effusion, Iris lens diaphragm rotation.
3. Convalescent Phase: Development of integumentary signs (Alopecia, Poliosis, Vitiligo, Sunset glow fundus).
4. Chronic Recurrent Phase: Smouldering anterior uveitis with exacerbations, recurrent posterior uveitis.

sections.title: Modified Diagnostic Criteria for VKH
content: 1. Absence of history of penetrating ocular trauma
2. Absence of other ocular diseases and entities
3. Bilateral uveitis
4. Neurological, auditory manifestations
5. Integumentary: Localized alopecia, poliosis, vitiligo, depigmented fundus (sunset glow), depigmented limbal lesions (Sugiura sign) in pigmented Japanese patients

sections.title: Advanced VKH Investigations
content: LP (Lumbar Puncture): Lymphocytic pleocytosis, melanin-containing macrophages
FAF: Hyperautofluorescence in areas of serous detachment
U/S: Diffuse choroidal thickness; use to exclude posterior scleritis
FA: Multifocal hyperfluorescent dots (RPE level); Chronic phase shows RPE window defect
OCT: Used to quantify subretinal fluid
ICGA: Monitoring acute phase; regularly distributed hypofluorescent spots (most remain hypo in late phase); diffuse hyperfluorescence over posterior pole

6. Optic disc nodules / Granuloma / Solitary choroidal nodule
7. Other: Conjunctival nodules, Lacrimal gland infiltrate, Dry eye, Eyelid nodules, Scleral lesions

sections.title: Investigations for Sarcoidosis
content: 1. Negative tuberculin skin test
2. Elevated ACE levels +/- elevated serum lysozyme
3. Chest X-ray: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL)
4. Chest High Resolution CT (HRCT) scan
5. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with biopsy
6. Thoracic endosonography
7. Biopsy sites: Lymph node, skin lesion, conjunctival nodules, lacrimal gland, vitreous biopsy (CD4/CD8 ratio)
8. MRI cardiac and CNS imaging, PET scan, whole body Gallium scan
9. Calcium, Vit D levels
10. Hypercalciuria
11. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): CD4/CD8 T-cell ratio is key indicator
12. Induced sputum analysis

sections.title: Behcet Disease Diagnostic Criteria
content: Recurrent oral ulceration (3 times in 12m) - MANDATORY
PLUS 2 OF THE FOLLOWING:
Genital ulceration
Ocular inflammation
Skin lesions (Erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, acneform nodules, papulopustular lesions)
Positive Pathergy reaction (Pustule 24-48h after sterile needle prick) - >95% specific

sections.title: Systemic Manifestations of Behcet's
content: Vascular: Aneurysm (pulmonary, coronary), venous thrombosis, thrombophlebitis
Arthritis: 30% arthralgia
Neurological: 5% meningoencephalocele of brainstem, dural sinus thrombosis, cerebral aneurysm
GIT: Ileocecal involvement
Hepatic & Renal: Relatively uncommon

sections.title: Ocular Behcet: Clinical Presentation
content: 1. Acute Anterior Uveitis: 'White eye', shifting hypopyon, non-granulomatous uveitis
2. Vitritis
3. Retinitis: Transient superficial white infiltrates (heal without scarring), deeper diffuse retinitis, exudative detachment, inflammatory deposits (KP-like) on inferior peripheral retina
4. Retinal Vasculitis: Artery and vein sheathing, perivascular hemorrhage, occlusion, CMO, diffuse retinal edema
5. Optic Disc: Hyperemia and edema (due to increased ICP), leading to optic atrophy
6. Other: Conjunctival ulcers, episcleritis, scleritis, ophthalmoplegia (from neuro involvement)

sections.title: End Stage Disease in Behcet
content: Optic atrophy
Retinal atrophy
Gliosis and sheathing
Attenuation and ghosting of affected vessels
Posterior synechia, Cataract, Glaucoma
Retinal detachment
Phthisis bulbi

sections.title: Behcet's: Investigations
content: HLA-B51 Association
Pathergy Test
ESR, CRP, WBC, Complement levels
Thrombophilia screening
Fluorescein Angiography (FA): Delineate ischemia, detect inflammation, monitor activity
Laser Flare Photometry: Correlate AC activity with inflammation levels
Biopsy: Superficial lesions, synovial fluid aspiration, lumbar puncture
Imaging: MRI, MRA, CT, CTA (identify ischemia)

sections.title: Behcet Disease Management Protocol
content: 1. Immunomodulatory therapy: The mainstay of treatment
2. Topical Steroids: Alone effective only if NO posterior segment involvement
3. Initial Management: Systemic steroids + Azathioprine (2.5mg/kg)
4. Severe Disease: Cyclosporine (2-5mg/kg) OR Infliximab + Azathioprine + Steroids
5. Posterior Uveitis: Single Infliximab infusion as initial treatment
6. TB Precaution: Infliximab may activate T.B; must give with Isoniazid if risk present
7. Vision Threatening: Infliximab or Adalimumab for early vision-threatening BD
8. Intravitreal Administration: Infliximab as an option
9. Interferon Alfa: 6 million IU per day subcutaneously

Yellowish discoloration (hyperbilirubinaemia), subconjunctival hge, keratoconjunctival sicca, pinguicula (Gaucher's)
Kayser-Fleischer ring (Wilson), posterior embryotoxon, central corneal clouding (Mucopolysaccharidosis)

This poster details the clinical progression from hearing loss to complex ocular motility and facial nerve deficits.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A Cerebellopontine Angle (CPA) tumor is a neoplasm located in the potential space between the cerebellum and the pons. While Vestibular Schwannomas (Acoustic Neuromas) are most common, the clinical hallmark of CPA syndrome is the progressive involvement of the V, VI, VII, and VIII cranial nerves as the tumor expands from the internal auditory canal (IAC) toward the brainstem.

sections.title: The 'Seven-Six-Five' Progression
content: Step 1: CN VIII - Tinnitus, high-frequency hearing loss, and vertigo.
Step 2: CN VII - Progressive Lower Motor Neuron facial weakness and gustatory changes.
Step 3: CN V - Reduced corneal sensation (an early, subtle sign of enlargement).
Step 4: CN VI - Lateral rectus palsy leading to esotropia and horizontal diplopia.
Step 5: Brainstem/Cerebellum - Ataxia, nystagmus, and signs of increased ICP.

rows: Eccentric to IAC, broad dural base
Slow hearing loss, NF2 if bilateral
Pearly white on surgery, slow growth

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: CN VI Palsy: Failure of abduction, esotropia worse at distance.
CN VII Palsy: Lagophthalmos, ectropion, and loss of the blink reflex.
CN V Involvement: Absent or diminished corneal sensation (test with cotton wisp).
Nystagmus: Bruns nystagmus (large-amplitude, slow-frequency toward lesion).
Papilledema: If the tumor causes obstructive hydrocephalus.
Exposure Keratopathy: Secondary to combined VII and V nerve dysfunction.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Sudden onset headache with nausea (Hydrocephalus)
Bilateral CPA tumors (Pathognomonic for NF2)
Rapidly progressive ophthalmoplegia
Profound corneal anesthesia with lagophthalmos (High risk for perforation)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Pure Tone Audiometry: To document sensorineural hearing loss and speech discrimination.
2. Gadolinium-Enhanced MRI (Gold Standard): Focus on IAC and posterior fossa.
3. CT Temporal Bone: If bony erosion or anatomy of the semi-circular canals is needed for surgery.
4. Corneal Esthesiometry: Objective measurement of V1 trigeminal involvement.
5. Automated Perimetry: If papilledema is suspected (blind spot enlargement).

rows: Tumor protrudes into CPA; no brainstem contact
Tumor displaces brainstem and cranial nerves

content.explanation: A: Acoustic Neuroma; M: Meningioma; E: Epidermoid / Ependymoma; N: Neuroma (Facial) or Nerve Metastasis.

rows: Best exposure for CN VII preservation
High risk of post-op headache and CN VI traction
Risk of temporal lobe traction seizures

sections.title: Ophthalmic Management Protocol
content: 1. Lubrication: Preservative-free tears every 1-2 hours.
2. Moisture Chambers: At night or for severe exposure.
3. Punctal Occlusion: For chronic dry eye management.
4. Upper Lid Gold Weight: To aid gravity-assisted closure.
5. Botulinum Toxin: Temporary protective ptosis.
6. Prism Therapy: For CN VI esotropia if stable.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Hitselberger's Sign: Hypesthesia of the posterior external auditory canal (early CN VII sign).
Crocodile Tears: Gustolacrimal reflex can occur during regeneration after CN VII palsy.
The 'Dangerous Combo': The combination of CN VII palsy and CN V anesthesia leads to rapid corneal melt.
NF2: Always check for posterior subcapsular cataracts (PSC) in suspected NF2 patients.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Bevacizumab in NF2
sections.content: Recent landmark studies have shown that Bevacizumab (Avastin), an anti-VEGF agent, can induce tumor shrinkage and improve hearing in patients with Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2) who have progressive vestibular schwannomas that are not amenable to surgery or radiation.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Permanent Facial Paralysis (10-30% depending on size).
CSF Leaks (Rhinorrhea or Otorrhea).
Tinnitus (Persistent in 50%).
Corneal Scarring/Perforation due to neurotrophic keratopathy.
Vascular stroke (AICA or PICA territory).

content.explanation: Afferent: Trigeminal Nerve (V1). Efferent: Facial Nerve (Orbicularis oculi). In CPA tumors, both can be damaged, abolishing the blink entirely.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Abducens (CN VI) nerve palsy is the most common isolated ocular motor paralysis. It results from dysfunction of the nerve innervating the lateral rectus (LR) muscle, leading to an inability to abduct the eye beyond the midline, resulting in binocular horizontal diplopia and an ipsilateral esotropia (ET) that is greater at distance than at near.

branches: Nucleus: Located in the lower pons; fibers wrap around CN VII (facial colliculus).
Fascicular: Passes through the pontine tegmentum near the medial lemniscus.
Subarachnoid: Exits at the pontomedullary junction; travels up the clivus.
Petrous: Crosses the petrous apex through Dorello’s Canal (under Gruber's ligament).
Cavernous Sinus: Located centrally (not in the lateral wall) adjacent to the ICA.
Orbital: Enters via the Superior Orbital Fissure (SOF) within the Annulus of Zinn.

rows: Rule out Gradenigo's Syndrome if otitis present.
Trauma, MS, Idiopathic, Raised ICP (Pseudo-localizing sign)
Restricted Medial Rectus on forced duction test.
Variable ptosis; fatigue; no pupil involvement.
Ice pack test positive; Cogan's lid twitch.
Narrowing of palpebral fissure on adduction.
Induced miosis and myopia during abduction effort.

sections.title: Diagnostic Clinical Features
content: Horizontal binocular diplopia (worse at distance).
Compensatory head turn toward the side of the palsy.
Primary position esotropia (Incomitant).
Secondary deviation > Primary deviation (fixing with paretic eye).
Limited abduction on the affected side.
Slowing of abducting saccades (early/mild sign).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: When to Image Immediately
content: Age < 45 without microvascular risk factors.
Multiple cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, V, VII).
History of malignancy (Breast, Lung, Prostate).
Presence of Papilledema (Raised ICP).
Associated Horner's Syndrome (Cavernous sinus lesion).
Severe headache or meningismus.
Failure to improve after 3 months.

sections.title: The Investigative Workup
content: Step 1: Vital Signs - Measure BP and screen for Diabetes (HbA1c/Fasting Glucose).
Step 2: Ophthalmic Exam - Check for papilledema and other CN deficits (especially V, VII).
Step 3: Laboratory Tests - CBC, ESR, CRP (if >55 yrs), RPR/FTA-ABS, and Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies.
Step 4: Neuro-imaging - MRI Brain/Orbits with Gadolinium + MRA/MRV if indicated.
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture - Indicated if MRI is normal but papilledema or meningeal signs are present.

rows: 25% reduction in abduction; eye crosses midline easily.
50% reduction; eye just reaches the midline.
75% reduction; eye cannot reach the midline.
Total palsy; eye fixed in adduction.

content.explanation: S: Side turn of head, T: Towards paretic muscle, 6: Sixth nerve, D: Distance diplopia worse, I: Incomitant esotropia, P: Primary deviation less than secondary.

sections.title: Management Strategy: Non-Surgical
content: Observation: Spontaneous recovery in 78% of microvascular cases within 3-6 months.
Patching: Alternate patching or patching paretic eye to eliminate diplopia.
Prism Therapy: Fresnel prisms (up to 20-30 PD) or ground-in prisms for small stable deviations.
Botulinum Toxin: Injection into the ipsilateral Medial Rectus (MR) to prevent contracture.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention Protocols
content: Step 1: Wait 6-12 months for stabilization or spontaneous recovery.
Step 2: Perform Forced Duction Test (FDT). If positive MR restriction, must recess MR first.
Step 3: If Force Generation Test (FGT) shows partial LR function, perform 'Recess-Resect' (R&R) procedure.
Step 4: If FGT shows NO LR function (Complete Palsy), perform a Transposition Procedure.
Step 5: Transposition types: Full-tendon (Hummelsheim, Schillinger) or Nishida Procedure (no tenotomy).

branches: Gradenigo’s: CN VI palsy + facial pain (V) + otitis media (Petrositis).
Foville’s: CN VI palsy + VII, V, VIII, and Horner's (Dorsal Pontine lesion).
Millard-Gubler: CN VI palsy + VII + contralateral hemiplegia (Ventral Pons).
Raymond's: CN VI palsy + contralateral hemiparesis.
Miller Fisher: Variant of GBS; Ataxia, Areflexia, Ophthalmoplegia.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the 5th nerve (corneal sensitivity) in every isolated 6th nerve palsy.
If an esotropia is greater at near than at distance, think Spasm of the Near Reflex or Divergence Insufficiency.
Bilateral 6th nerve palsy is a hallmark of raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise.
The 'Park's 3-step' is for Vertical palsies (CN IV), not CN VI.
Nishida transposition is preferred in older patients to avoid Anterior Segment Ischemia (ASI).

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The 6th Nerve
sections.content: A randomized clinical trial by the PEDIG group suggested that Botulinum Toxin was as effective as surgical transposition for chronic VI palsy in some cases, though surgical results are generally more predictable for large angle deviations. Microvascular recovery rates remain high, with the majority of patients recovering binocularity without surgery within 24 weeks.
