sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Endophthalmitis is defined as severe inflammation of the inner coats of the eye, specifically the vitreous and aqueous humors. It is categorized as Exogenous (inoculation from the environment, e.g., surgery, trauma) or Endogenous (hematogenous spread from a distant focus). It represents the most feared complication in ophthalmic surgery.

rows: S. epidermidis (70%), S. aureus, Strep spp.
High risk with intraocular foreign body

sections.title: Pathophysiology Process
content: 1. Microbial Inoculation: Pathogens enter the vitreous cavity (exogenous) or uveal tract (endogenous).
2. Proliferation: Microbes multiply rapidly in the nutrient-rich vitreous, escaping early immune detection.
3. Toxogenesis: Release of bacterial exotoxins and enzymes (proteases) that directly damage photoreceptors.
4. Host Response: Massive influx of neutrophils (PMNs) and release of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha).
5. Retinal Destruction: Bystander damage from host inflammatory mediators leads to irreversible retinal necrosis.
6. Organization: Chronic inflammation leads to cyclitic membrane formation and tractional retinal detachment.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Lid Edema and Chemosis: Significant soft tissue swelling.
Conjunctival Injection: Intense circumcorneal flush.
Corneal Edema: Due to toxic endothelial damage.
Hypopyon: Layered WBCs in the anterior chamber (present in 75-85%).
Fibrinous Membrane: Dense AC reaction often obscuring the pupil.
Vitritis: Dense vitreous cells and debris causing loss of red reflex.
Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD): Suggests advanced retinal or optic nerve damage.

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS
content: Pain that is out of proportion to clinical signs.
Sudden, profound loss of vision (Light Perception or worse).
Rapidly progressing hypopyon within hours.
Loss of Red Reflex or inability to visualize fundus.
Proptosis or limited motility (suggests panophthalmitis).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Clinical Suspicion: History of recent surgery or trauma + pain/vision loss.
2. B-Scan Ultrasonography: Essential if fundus is obscured. Look for vitreal opacities, membranes, or RD.
3. Vitreous Tap/Biopsy: Gold standard. Needle aspiration (0.1ml) or undiluted vitreous cutter sample.
4. Aqueous Tap: Lower yield than vitreous but easier to perform (0.1ml).
5. Microbiological Processing: Immediate Gram/Giemsa stain, culture on Blood, Chocolate, Sabouraud, and Thioglycolate.
6. Molecular Diagnosis: PCR for 16S rDNA (high sensitivity, especially if pre-treated).

sections.title: EVS Treatment Algorithm (Based on Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study)

branches: Vision Hand Motions (HM) or Better: Tap and Inject Antibiotics
Vision Light Perception (LP): Immediate Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) + Antibiotics
Systemic Antibiotics: Found not useful (Amikacin/Ceftazidime) in EVS

sections.title: Surgical Technique: PPV Steps
content: 1. Anesthesia: Retrobulbar or general (if severe pain/uncooperative).
2. Trocar Placement: Careful 23G/25G/27G entry; caution with hypotony.
3. Sample Collection: Obtain undiluted vitreous sample before turning on infusion.
4. Core Vitrectomy: Clear central opacities to improve antibiotic distribution.
5. Avoid PVD Induction: The retina is extremely necrotic/friable; do not induce PVD.
6. Antibiotic Injection: Controlled injection into the mid-vitreous cavity.

sections.title: Post-Traumatic Specifics
content: Bacillus cereus: Most common in soil-related trauma; causes rapid panophthalmitis in 24h.
IOFB: Retained foreign bodies increase risk by 10x.
Clostridium: Rare but causes 'Gas Gangrene' of the eye with rapid vision loss.
Immediate PPV: Often indicated earlier in trauma than in post-cataract cases.

content.explanation: Vision (LP vs HM), Vitreous (Tap vs Vitrectomy), Vancomycin (The cornerstone of therapy).

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: Povidone-Iodine 5%: Only proven prophylactic measure to reduce endophthalmitis risk.
Intracameral Cefuroxime (1mg/0.1ml): ESCRS study showed 5x reduction in post-op infection.
C. acnes: Suspect if there is a 'white plaque' on the posterior capsule months after surgery.
Klebsiella Endogenous: Often presents with a 'hypopyon of the posterior pole' (subretinal abscess).

sections.title: Complications & Sequelae
content: Retinal Detachment (Tractional or Rhegmatogenous).
Phthisis Bulbi: Hypotony and shrinkage of the globe.
Secondary Glaucoma: Due to inflammatory debris or PAS.
Cyclitic Membrane: Resulting in ciliary body detachment.
Evisceration/Enucleation: Required if panophthalmitis occurs or for intractable pain.

title: NEOVASCULAR GLAUCOMA (NVG): A Comprehensive Guide
summary: Neovascular glaucoma is a challenging condition driven by posterior segment ischaemia, leading to the formation of a fibrovascular membrane in the iris and drainage angle. This guide details the progression from open-angle to synechial closure, common causes like CrVO and diabetes, and the transformative role of anti-VEGF therapies.

sections.title: Pathophysiology & Progression
content: 1. Posterior segment ischaemia drives neovascularization of the iris and drainage angle.
2. This leads to the development of a fibrovascular membrane.
3. Initially, the membrane overlies the trabecular meshwork so that the angle appears open.
4. Over time, Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS) form.
5. The fibrovascular membrane contracts to cause complete synechial angle closure.

sections.title: Key Causes & Risk Factors
content: Ischaemic CrVO (common); risk of progression to NVG is 50%.
Diabetic retinopathy (common); risk of NVG highest in PDr.
Other vascular disorders: OIS, CrAO, BrVO.
Other retinal disease: chronic retinal detachment, sickle cell retinopathy.
Retinal or choroidal tumours.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Presentation
content: Pain is often a feature and may be severe.
The predisposing condition may be known or suggested by history (e.g. sudden loss of vision several months previously in cases of CrVO and NVG).
Iris rubeosis: abnormal/non-radial vessels at pupil sphincter margin.
Increased Intraocular Pressure (iIOP).
AC flare/cells and hyphaema.
Ectropion uvea.
Conjunctival injection and corneal oedema (if acute iIOP or decompensating).
Disc changes and field loss as for POAG (see E Primary open-angle glaucoma, pp. 390–1).

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations
content: Dilated fundoscopy in all cases ± FFA to determine cause.
Carotid Doppler US: performed if no retinal pathology or asymmetric diabetic retinopathy is found.
B-scan US: if there is a poor fundal view (cataract may be associated with chronic retinal pathology such as tumours, detachment, and inflammation).
Haematological/biochemical factors: looking for factors that increase the hypoxic drive, e.g. anaemia.

sections.title: Core Treatment Philosophy
sections.content: Treatment of NVG (see p. 405) has often been challenging and unsatisfactory but is undergoing a positive transformation with the advent of anti-VeGF therapies. It is important to remember that anti-VeGF therapy alone will not control NVG, unless the posterior segment hypoxic drive is also addressed through adequate PrP, etc.

sections.title: Managing Neovascularization
content: PrP to decrease retinal ischaemic drive long term.
If no fundal view exists, anti-VeGF therapy can be administered to temporize.
Vitrectomy/endolaser photocoagulation ± cataract extraction (depending on visual prognosis).
Anti-VeGF impact: Significant impact on neovascularization and improves survival of drainage surgery.
Bevacizumab Evidence: Small retrospective studies show regression of neovascularization and decreased IOP when used alone or with PrP.

sections.title: Managing IOP and Inflammation
content: Cycloplegic: e.g. atropine 1% 2×/d.
Frequent topical steroids: e.g. prednisolone acetate 1% 1- to 4-hourly.
Ocular hypotensive agents: as for POAG.
If medical treatment fails: Consider trabeculectomy (augmented), tubeshunt procedures, or cyclodestruction (e.g. cyclodiode), depending on visual prognosis.

sections.title: Pain Management & The Blind Eye
content: Use Cycloplegia (atropine) and topical corticosteroids for pain.
Lubricants for sick corneal epithelium (keep high index of suspicion for microbial keratitis).
Consider full ocular surface regime for dry eyes/blepharitis/drop toxicity.
If the eye is blind and painful: Consider retrobulbar alcohol or chlorpromazine, or evisceration/enucleation.

summary: Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, arising from melanocytes within the uveal tract. Early detection via clinical markers is essential for systemic prognosis and vision preservation.

sections.title: Disease Overview
sections.content: Choroidal melanoma is a malignant tumor arising from the melanocytes of the uveal tract. It represents approximately 80% of all uveal melanomas and is recognized as the most common primary intraocular cancer found in the adult population.

sections.title: Predisposing Risk Factors
content: Fair skin and light eye color (Blue/Green)
Oculodermal melanocytosis (Nevus of Ota)
Presence of pre-existing uveal nevi
BRCA1-associated protein 1 (BAP1) mutation
Congenital ocular melanocytosis

content.explanation: T: Thickness > 2 mm; F: Fluid (subretinal); S: Symptoms (blurred vision/flashes); O: Orange pigment (lipofuscin); M: Margin within 3 mm of optic disc; U: Ultrasound (acoustic hollowness); HH: Halo absence; D: Drusen absence.

rows: Acoustic hollowness, choroidal excavation, and 'collar-button' (mushroom) shape.
Double circulation pattern (simultaneous retinal and tumor vessel filling).
Documentation of pigmentation (melanotic vs. amelanotic) and borders.

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNING SIGNS
content: Rapid growth of a documented pre-existing nevus
Presence of Sentinel Vessels (dilated episcleral vessels)
Extraocular extension through the scleral emissary channels
Diffuse growth pattern (higher risk of delayed diagnosis)

sections.title: Management Pathway
content: Step 1: Observation for small, low-risk, dormant lesions.
Step 2: Radiation Therapy (Plaque Brachytherapy or Proton Beam).
Step 3: Surgical Enucleation for large tumors or blind/painful eyes.
Step 4: Systemic Surveillance for hepatic metastasis.

title: (Not oxford) MGD: Unmasking Meibomian Gland Dysfunction
summary: Meibomian Gland Dysfunction (MGD) is a chronic, diffuse abnormality of the meibomian glands, typically characterized by terminal duct obstruction and qualitative or quantitative changes in glandular secretion. It is the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease worldwide.

sections.title: What is MGD?
sections.content: MGD stands for Meibomian Gland Dysfunction. It occurs when the tiny oil glands in your eyelids (meibomian glands) are blocked or produce poor-quality oil (meibum). This oil is crucial because it forms the outer layer of your tear film, preventing your tears from evaporating too quickly. Without enough high-quality oil, your eyes become dry, irritated, and inflamed.

sections.title: The Vicious Cycle of MGD
content: Step 1: Hyperkeratinization of the gland duct leads to obstruction.
Step 2: Meibum (oil) becomes stagnant within the gland.
Step 3: Bacteria proliferate and release enzymes (lipases).
Step 4: Enzymes break down healthy oils into irritating free fatty acids.
Step 5: Tear film instability leads to rapid evaporation and surface inflammation.

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNING SIGNS
content: Burning or stinging sensations
Persistent redness of the lid margins
Blurred vision that improves with blinking
Feeling of 'sand' or 'grit' in the eyes
Excessive watering (Reflex Tearing)

content.explanation: L for Lid hygiene (cleaning margins), I for Inflammation control, D for Daily warm compresses, S for Secretion improvement (Omega-3s).

sections.title: Key Risk Factors
content: Aging: Increased risk as we get older.
Digital Use: Reduced blink rate while staring at screens.
Hormones: Especially estrogen/androgen imbalances.
Medications: Retinoids (Acne meds) and Antihistamines.
Environment: Low humidity or high wind exposure.

sections.title: Management & Treatment
content: Warm Compresses: Melts hardened oils (at least 104°F).
Lid Debridement: Clearing debris from gland openings.
Thermal Pulsation: In-office automated heat/massage.
Omega-3 Supplements: Improves meibum consistency.
Topical Azithromycin: Targets both bacteria and inflammation.

branches: Periocular involvement is rare but lethal

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Pain out of proportion to clinical findings
Dusky, purple, or 'dishwater' skin discoloration
Cutaneous anesthesia (loss of sensation)
Crepitus (gas in tissues)
Formation of bullae or blisters
Rapidly progressing necrosis

sections.title: Stages of Clinical Progression
content: Step 1: Early Erythema - Mimics preseptal cellulitis with warmth and swelling.
Step 2: Ischemic Phase - Skin becomes dusky/violaceous due to thrombosed vessels.
Step 3: Bullae Formation - Clear or hemorrhagic fluid blisters appear.
Step 4: Gangrene - Full-thickness skin and fascial necrosis occurs.
Step 5: Systemic Toxicity - Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and multi-organ failure.

content.explanation: F: Fever & Toxicity; A: Anesthesia of the skin; S: Surface necrosis; T: Tension/Swelling beyond margins.

sections.title: Immediate Management Protocol
content: URGENT Surgical Debridement: Removal of all necrotic tissue until healthy bleeding margins are reached.
Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics: High-dose triple therapy (e.g., Penicillin, Clindamycin, and an Aminoglycoside).
Hemodynamic Support: Fluid resuscitation and ICU admission.
Imaging: CT or MRI to detect gas in tissues and depth of spread (do not delay surgery for imaging).
Secondary Reconstruction: Skin grafting or ophthalmic plastic surgery once infection is controlled.

sections.title: Clinical Summary Note
sections.content: Necrotising fasciitis of the eyelids is a devastating condition where time is tissue. Because the eyelid skin is the thinnest in the body, the infection can penetrate the orbital septum rapidly. A high index of suspicion is required when an apparent 'cellulitis' does not respond to standard antibiotics or shows signs of systemic toxicity. Immediate multi-disciplinary involvement including ophthalmology, infectious disease, and intensive care is mandatory.

summary: Keratoconus is a progressive, non-inflammatory eye condition where the normally round cornea thins and begins to bulge into a cone-like shape. This structural change deflects light as it enters the eye, causing significant visual distortion and sensitivity.

sections.title: Common Symptoms
content: Blurred or distorted vision
Increased sensitivity to light and glare
Frequent changes in eyeglass prescriptions
Clouding or sudden worsening of vision
Monocular polyopia (ghosting/multiple images)

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNING: EYE RUBBING
content: Vigorous eye rubbing is strongly linked to disease progression.
Mechanical trauma can accelerate corneal thinning.
Chronic rubbing is often associated with atopic (allergic) eye disease.
Stopping the 'rubbing habit' is the first step in management.

rows: Iron deposits in the basal epithelium at the base of the cone.
Fine, vertical stress lines in the deep stroma/Descemet’s membrane.
V-shaped indentation of the lower lid on down-gaze.
A conical reflection on the nasal cornea when light is shone from the temporal side.
Sudden swelling caused by a rupture in Descemet’s membrane.

sections.title: The Treatment Ladder
content: Step 1: Spectacles or Soft Contact Lenses (Early stages)
Step 2: Rigid Gas Permeable (RGP) or Scleral Lenses
Step 3: Corneal Collagen Cross-linking (CXL) to halt progression
Step 4: Intracorneal Ring Segments (Intacs) to flatten the cone
Step 5: Topography-guided Laser (Partial/Combined treatments)
Step 6: Corneal Transplant (DALK or PKP for advanced cases)

content.explanation: T: Topography is gold standard, H: Hydrops (acute risk), I: Irregular astigmatism, N: Non-inflammatory, C: Cross-linking (CXL), O: Optical correction (Lenses), N: Nasal light reflex (Rizutti), E: Eye rubbing avoidance.

sections.title: Diagnostic Gold Standards
content: Corneal Topography/Tomography: Essential for mapping curvature.
Pachymetry: Measures corneal thickness (thinning at the apex).
Slit-lamp Biomicroscopy: Visualizing striae and rings.
Retinoscopy: Detection of the 'Scissor Reflex'.

sections.title: Disease Definition
sections.content: Keratoconus is characterized by the biomechanical failure of the corneal stroma. As the collagen matrix weakens, intraocular pressure causes the cornea to distend forward, usually beginning in puberty and progressing until the third or fourth decade of life. It is the most common primary ectasia.

summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis, classification, and management of pigmented lesions of the periocular region. Essential for distinguishing benign melanocytic proliferation from life-threatening malignancies like Lentigo Maligna Melanoma.

data.summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis, classification, and management of pigmented lesions of the periocular region. Essential for distinguishing benign melanocytic proliferation from life-threatening malignancies like Lentigo Maligna Melanoma.

sections.title: Overview & Clinical Significance
sections.content: Pigmented eyelid lesions encompass a broad spectrum ranging from common benign nevi to highly aggressive malignant melanomas. The eyelid is a unique anatomical site where skin thickness is minimal, and proximity to the globe and orbit makes early diagnosis critical. While basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common eyelid malignancy, pigmented variants can mimic melanoma, requiring high clinical suspicion and histopathological confirmation.

rows: Blue-grey nodule due to Tyndall effect

content.explanation: Asymmetry of shape; Border irregularity (notched/blurred); Color variegation (multiple shades); Diameter >6mm; Evolution (change in size, shape, or symptoms).

rows: Sun-damaged skin, flat, slow radial growth
Most common, irregular borders, varied color
Aggressive, vertical growth phase, dark blue-black

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Madarosis (loss of eyelashes) within the lesion area
Destruction of the Meibomian gland orifices
Ulceration or spontaneous bleeding
Acquired Melanosis with 'satellite' lesions
Change in pigment onto the palpebral conjunctiva
Rapid growth or increase in thickness (vertical growth phase)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Comprehensive History: UV exposure, family hx, rate of change.
2. Slit-Lamp Examination: High-mag assessment of lid margin and conjunctiva.
3. Dermoscopy: Evaluation of pigment network, dots, and vessels.
4. Photodocumentation: Baseline imaging for monitoring.
5. Biopsy: Full-thickness incisional (wedge) or excisional if small.
6. Histopathology: H&E staining + Immunohistochemistry (S100, MART-1, Mel-5, HMB-45).

sections.title: Surgical Management Margins
content: Melanoma in situ: 5mm surgical margin.
Breslow <1mm: 1cm surgical margin.
Breslow 1-2mm: 1-2cm surgical margin (difficult on eyelid).
Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Contested for melanoma but widely used for pigmented BCC.
Slow-Mohs (Permanent Sections): Often preferred for melanoma to ensure clearance.

sections.title: Ocular Melanocytosis (Nevus of Ota)
sections.content: A congenital dermal melanocytosis involving the distribution of the trigeminal nerve (V1, V2). It presents as slate-blue hyperpigmentation of the periocular skin and ipsilateral scleral blueing. These patients carry a higher risk of uveal melanoma (1 in 400) and glaucoma, requiring annual fundoscopy and IOP checks.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Lid margin nevi often 'kiss' the opposing lid (Kissing Nevus), suggesting origin before eyelid separation in utero.
Pigmented BCC often retains a pearly border and telangiectasia; look closely with the slit-lamp.
Biopsy is MANDATORY for any new pigmented lesion in an adult or any changing lesion in a child.
Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) should be considered for tumors >0.8mm thick or those with ulceration.
Map biopsies are essential if Primary Acquired Melanosis (PAM) of the conjunctiva is suspected alongside the lid lesion.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Targeted Therapy
content: BRAF Inhibitors: Vemurafenib/Dabrafenib for V600E mutations.
MEK Inhibitors: Trametinib often used in combination.
Checkpoint Inhibitors: Pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) for metastatic or unresectable melanoma.
Ipilimumab: Anti-CTLA-4 therapy.

sections.title: Prognostic Factors
content: Vertical growth phase (worst prognosis).
Mitotic rate (measured in mitoses/mm²).
Presence of ulceration.
Lymphovascular or perineural invasion.
Nodal involvement (most significant predictor of survival).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) accounts for approximately 90% of all malignant eyelid tumors. While it rarely metastasizes (less than 0.1%), it is characterized by significant local destruction and invasion if left untreated. It arises from the pluripotential cells in the basal layer of the epidermis and is particularly common in the periocular region due to chronic ultraviolet (UV) exposure.

sections.title: Etiology & Risk Factors
content: UVB Exposure: Primary environmental driver (DNA damage).
Phenotype: Fitzpatrick Type I & II (fair skin, blue eyes, red hair).
Genetics: PTCH1 gene mutations (Hedgehog signaling pathway).
Syndromes: Gorlin-Goltz (Basal Cell Nevus Syndrome), Bazex, Xeroderma Pigmentosum.
Previous Radiation: History of radiotherapy for other conditions.
Immunosuppression: Post-transplant or HIV patients.

branches: PTCH1 Mutation: Loss of inhibition on SMO
SMO Activation: Triggers GLI transcription factors
GLI1/GLI2: Upregulate genes for cell proliferation/survival
TP53 Mutations: Found in 50% of sporadic cases
Peripheral Palisading: Typical histopathologic cell arrangement

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Pearly Border: Rolled, translucent edges.
Telangiectasia: Fine, branching vessels on the surface.
Madarosis: Localized loss of eyelashes (highly suspicious).
Meibomian Gland Distortion: Notched lid margin.
Fixation: Tumor attachment to underlying periosteum.
Canthal Involvement: Check for orbital extension/motility.

sections.title: Red Flags: High-Risk Features
content: Medial Canthal Location: Higher risk of deep orbital invasion.
Morpheaform/Sclerosing Subtype: Invisible lateral spread.
Recurrent Lesions: Higher risk of perineural invasion.
Perineural Invasion: Patient reports pain or paresthesia.
Tumor Size >20mm: Increased risk of recurrence.
Immunocompromised State: Rapid growth and multiple lesions.

rows: Faster growth, more scaling, lacks pearly border
Yellowish hue, associated with blepharitis, pagetoid spread
Central keratin plug, rapid onset then regression
Lack of characteristic BCC features, rapid growth

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Biopsy
content: 1. Clinical Photography for documentation.
2. Incisional Biopsy (Punch or Shave): For large or suspicious lesions.
3. Histopathology: Look for peripheral palisading & retraction artifact.
4. Imaging (CT/MRI): Only if orbital or bone invasion is suspected.
5. Lymph Node Palpation: Check preauricular and submandibular nodes.

content.explanation: Pearly nodules, Pink color, Peripheral palisading (path), Persistent ulcer, and Pre-cancerous UV exposure.

rows: Tumor > 20mm OR involving tarsal plate/lid margin
Tumor involving full thickness eyelid OR ocular structures
Tumor involving orbit, sinuses, or brain

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocols
content: Step 1: Surgical Excision with Frozen Section: 3-4mm clear margins standard.
Step 2: Mohs Micrographic Surgery (MMS): Gold standard for medial canthal or morpheaform types.
Step 3: Reconstruction: Direct closure, Tenzel flap, or Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap.
Step 4: Non-Surgical (Small/Superficial): Imiquimod 5% cream or Cryotherapy.
Step 5: Advanced/Metastatic Case: Vismodegib (Hedgehog inhibitor) or Radiotherapy.

sections.title: Surgical Reconstruction Pearls
content: Primary Closure: Possible for <33% lid defect.
Tenzel Semicircular Flap: Best for 33-50% moderate defects.
Hughes Flap: For large (>50%) lower lid defects using upper lid tarsus.
Mustardé Flap: Large cheek rotation flap for total lower lid loss.
Cutler-Beard Flap: Full thickness upper lid reconstruction.

sections.title: Systemic Hedgehog Inhibitors
content: Drug Name: Vismodegib (Erivedge) or Sonidegib.
Indication: Metastatic BCC or locally advanced BCC not amenable to surgery.
Mechanism: SMO (Smoothened) protein antagonist.
Common Side Effects: Muscle cramps (71%), alopecia (61%), dysgeusia (loss of taste).
Pregnancy Warning: Category X (highly teratogenic).

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Recurrence Rate: <5% with Mohs; higher with standard excision.
Canalicular Involvement: Requires intubation or dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).
Orbital Invasion: May necessitate orbital exenteration in rare cases.
Cicatricial Ectropion: Potential post-operative complication.
Metastasis: Extremely rare, usually to regional lymph nodes or lungs.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Board Exam
content: Medial canthal BCCs have 'silent' deep invasion along the periosteum.
A 'recurrent chalazion' is SCC or Sebaceous Carcinoma until proven otherwise (BCC is less likely to mimic a chalazion).
Cryotherapy is contraindicated for morpheaform BCC.
In Gorlin Syndrome, lesions appear at a young age; avoid radiation due to risk of secondary tumors.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Keratoconus is a bilateral, typically asymmetric corneal ectasia. It involves progressive stromal thinning, Bowman’s layer fragmentation, and iron deposition in the basal epithelium (Fleischer ring), leading to irregular astigmatism, high myopia, and decreased best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA).

branches: Genetic: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21), Leber Congenital Amaurosis
Connective Tissue: Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan Syndrome, Osteogenesis Imperfecta
Environmental: Chronic UV exposure, Atopic dermatitis
Biochemical: Increased Lysosomal enzymes, decreased Protease inhibitors

sections.title: Clinical Signs: Slit-Lamp Findings
content: Fleischer Ring: Iron deposition at the base of the cone (best with cobalt blue filter).
Vogt Striae: Fine, vertical stress lines in deep stroma/Descemet membrane (disappear with digital pressure).
Munson Sign: V-shaped indentation of the lower lid on down-gaze.
Rizzuti Sign: Conical reflection on the nasal iris when light is shone from the temporal side.
Charleux Sign: Oil-droplet reflex on distant ophthalmoscopy.
Prominent Corneal Nerves: Visible in the stroma.

content.explanation: Vogt striae, Fleischer ring, Munson sign, Rizzuti sign.

rows: Crescent-shaped thinning 1-2mm from inferior limbus; 'Butterfly' pattern on topography.
Generalized, globular thinning from limbus to limbus; maximal peripherally.
Increased curvature of the posterior corneal surface only; usually non-progressive.
Superior thinning with lipid deposits and vascularization; usually older patients.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Corneal Topography: Placcido-based mapping of the anterior surface.
2. Corneal Tomography (Pentacam/Galilei): Elevation mapping of BOTH anterior and posterior surfaces.
3. Pachymetry: Measuring the thinnest point (crucial for CXL candidacy).
4. Epithelial Mapping (OCT): Characteristic epithelial thinning over the cone apex.
5. Biomechanics (Corvis ST/ORA): Measuring Corneal Hysteresis (CH) and Resistance Factor (CRF).

sections.title: Red Flags: Acute Hydrops
content: Sudden, painful vision loss.
Severe corneal edema (Descemet membrane rupture).
Intrastromal clefts on OCT.
Risk of perforation (rare but critical).
Management: Topical hypertonics, cycloplegics, and observation (Avoid emergency PKP).

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1 (Early): Spectacles or Soft Toric Contact Lenses.
Step 2 (Moderate): Rigid Gas Permeable (RGP) or Scleral Lenses for irregular astigmatism.
Step 3 (Progression): Corneal Collagen Cross-linking (CXL) to stabilize the cornea (Dresden Protocol).
Step 4 (Alternative): Intrastromal Corneal Ring Segments (ICRS) to flatten the cone and improve lens fit.
Step 5 (Late/Scarred): Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) - Preferred if endothelium is healthy.
Step 6 (End-stage): Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) if full-thickness scarring or previous hydrops exists.

sections.title: Corneal Cross-linking (CXL) Protocol
content: Standard (Dresden): 30 mins Riboflavin (0.1%) soaking + 30 mins UVA (3 mW/cm²).
Epi-Off: Gold standard; requires removal of central 8-9mm of epithelium.
Epi-On: Lower risk of infection/haze but potentially less effective.
Accelerated CXL: Higher intensity UVA for shorter duration (e.g., 9-30 mW/cm²).
Inclusion: Progressive KC with pachymetry > 400 µm (or 320 µm with hypotonic riboflavin).

sections.title: Contraindications for CXL
content: Corneal thickness < 400 µm (standard protocol).
Prior Herpes Simplex Keratitis (risk of reactivation).
Severe central corneal scarring.
Active ocular infection or severe ocular surface disease.
Pregnancy (hormonal changes affect ectasia).

rows: Radius of curvature in the thinnest 3mm zone (anterior).
Radius of curvature in the thinnest 3mm zone (posterior).

sections.title: Surgical Pearls
content: ICRS: Place at 70-80% depth; goal is 'arc-shortening' effect.
DALK: Big Bubble technique (Dua/Anwar) allows for bare Descemet exposure.
PKP in KC: Excellent prognosis (>90% graft survival at 10 years).
Post-Op: Watch for 'Urrets-Zavalia Syndrome' (permanent iris atrophy/mydriasis) after keratoplasty.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always screen family members of KC patients.
Stop contact lens wear (RGP 2 weeks, Soft 1 week) before topography.
Atopy must be controlled to prevent eye rubbing and progression.
Progressive KC in children is more aggressive; consider early CXL.

title: Behçet's Disease: A Multisystem Vasculitis with Ophthalmic Fury
summary: Behçet's disease (BD) is an idiopathic, chronic multisystem syndrome characterized by recurrent episodes of acute inflammation, particularly aphthous oral ulcers, genital ulceration, and uveitis. With a key pathogenetic component being vasculitis, it primarily affects young adults along the 'Silk Road' route, posing a significant threat to vision due to panuveitis and retinal vasculitis. Early diagnosis and aggressive immunosuppressive therapy are crucial for managing this complex condition and preventing severe complications.

sections.title: Introduction to Behçet's Disease (BD)
sections.content: Possibly first recognized by Hippocrates, the modern description of this disease dates from the greek Adamantiades and the turk Behçet. Behçet disease (BD) is an idiopathic, chronic multisystem syndrome characterized by recurrent episodes of acute inflammation, particularly recurrent aphthous oral ulcers, genital ulceration and uveitis. The commonest ophthalmic presentation is of a sight-threatening panuveitis and retinal vasculitis.

sections.title: Epidemiology & Pathogenesis
content: **Prevalence**: Highest along the traditional Silk Route (Turkey, Middle and Far East), peaking in Turkey where up to 0.4% of the population may be affected. Lower prevalence in Europe and North America.
**Affected Population**: Typically affects young adults (peak age of onset is the third decade).

**Risk Factors**: Geographical variation including gender (reported gender prevalence varies with ethnicity), FH (more significant in Middle Eastern countries), and the HLA-B51 allele (strongly associated, more significant in Japan, with a relative risk of 6.7; ethnic groups with higher prevalence of BD also have a higher rate of HLA-B51 positivity).

**Pathogenesis**: Vasculitis is a key pathogenetic component and may involve small, medium and large veins and arteries. The condition probably has an autoimmune basis and may be precipitated by exposure to an infectious agent with subsequent cross-reaction.
**Mortality**: Around 5% at 5–10 years, typically due to cardiovascular or CNS complications.

sections.title: National Centres of Excellence (England)
content: In 2012, three National Centres of excellence were set up in England (Birmingham, Liverpool, London) to provide a multidisciplinary approach to clinical care.

sections.title: Systemic Clinical Features
content: **Oral Ulceration**: Aphthous or scarring.
**GU (Genital Ulceration)**.

**Skin Lesions**: Erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopustules, acneiform rash. Dermatographia (Fig. 12.27B), similar to the pathergy reaction, indicates skin hypersensitivity and consists of the formation of erythematous lines following stroking or scratching.
**Joints**: Arthritis (mono/poly) occurs in 30%, though arthralgia is more common.
**Vascular**: Thromboses (venous > arterial), including superficial thrombophlebitis, SVC/IVC obstruction. Aneurysms, including pulmonary and coronary and venous thrombosis/thrombophlebitis.
**GI**: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea. Gastrointestinal inflammation, especially ileocecal.

**CNS**: Meningoencephalitis, sinus thrombosis ± intracranial hypertension, cranial or peripheral neuropathies, focal CNS signs. Neurological manifestations occur in 5% such as meningoencephalitis of the brainstem, dural sinus thrombosis and cerebral aneurysms.
**Hepatic and renal lesions**: Relatively uncommon.

sections.title: Ocular Clinical Features: Overview & Anterior Segment
sections.content: Ocular inflammation occurs in about 70%, tends to be more severe in men and is the presenting manifestation in about 10%. Signs are virtually always bilateral eventually. Relapsing/remitting acute onset panuveitis with retinal vasculitis and often spontaneous resolution even without treatment is the classical pattern of eye involvement. Retinal vascular disease (vasculitis and occlusion) is the main cause of visual impairment. Acute anterior non-granulomatous uveitis (AAU), often bilateral, is typical, typically with hypopyon (Fig. 12.28A). It is not granulomatous.

content.explanation: A transient mobile hypopyon in a relatively white eye (Fig. 12.28A) is characteristic of Behçet disease and JIA-associated uveitis.

sections.title: Ocular Clinical Features: Posterior Segment & Complications
content: **Vitritis**: May be severe and is universal in eyes with active posterior segment disease.

**Retinitis**: Transient superficial white infiltrates (Fig. 12.28B) that heal without scarring may be seen during acute systemic disease. There may be deeper more diffuse retinitis similar in appearance to viral inflammation. Exudative detachments can also occur. Inflammatory deposits analogous to KPs may be seen on the inferior peripheral retina.

**Retinal Vasculitis**: Arteritis as well as phlebitis, in contrast to pure venous involvement in sarcoidosis – can manifest with sheathing, perivascular haemorrhages and occlusion (Fig. 12.28C, FA showing periphlebitis (arrow heads) and arterial attenuation (arrow)). Vascular leakage may give rise to diffuse retinal oedema and CMO. This is the commonest ophthalmic presentation and is sight-threatening.
**Optic Disc Involvement**: Optic disc hyperaemia and oedema. Raised intracranial pressure can also cause optic disc swelling and optic atrophy in BD.
**Neovascularization**: Disc and retinal neovascularization may be seen as a response to inflammation and ischaemia (± vitreous haemorrhage/tRd).
**Diffuse Capillary Leakage**.
**Uncommon Manifestations**: Conjunctivitis, conjunctival ulcers, episcleritis, scleritis and ophthalmoplegia from neurological involvement.

**Complications**: Cataract, glaucoma, end-stage disease (optic atrophy, retinal atrophy with attenuated vessels (arterioles are affected later); can lead to blindness). Other complications include PS, retinal detachment and phthisis. Severe visual loss in males of up to two-thirds of patients at 10 years has been reported, but is probably much lower with aggressive management. The rate in women is about half that in men.
**End-stage disease**: Characterized by optic atrophy, retinal atrophy and gliosis and sheathing, attenuation and ghosting of affected vessels (Fig. 12.28D). The vitreous tends to clear.

sections.title: Investigations
content: There are no laboratory tests to diagnose Behçet’s disease, but there are classification criteria (see table 11.14 / ISGBD Diagnostic Criteria section).
**HLA-B51** (see above).
**Pathergy test**: Positive pathergy test – sterile pustule appearing 24–48h after oblique insertion of a 20g needle (see above).
**Inflammatory markers**: (e.g. ESR, CRP, complement levels, white cell count) may be elevated.
**Thrombophilia screening**: Appropriate in some patients to exclude other causes of thrombosis.
**Fluorescein Angiography (FA)**: Delineates ischaemic areas and aids detection of posterior segment inflammation and monitoring of disease activity.
**Laser flare photometry of the AC**: Correlates well with FA in determining the level of inflammatory activity.
**Biopsy/Aspiration**: Superficial lesion biopsy, synovial fluid aspiration and lumbar puncture may be used to help rule out alternative diagnoses.

**Systemic imaging**: May include brain MRI/MRV brain (if neurological features), magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), CT/computed tomography angiography (CTA) and conventional angiography to identify ischaemia.

sections.title: Treatment: General Principles & Agents
content: **Multidisciplinary Approach**: Liaise with physician. Refer to National Centre for advice.
**Mainstay of Treatment**: Immunosuppressants are the mainstay of treatment, but availability and expense may limit therapeutic options in many regions.
**Topical Steroids**: May be adequate if – rarely – there is no trace of posterior segment involvement.
**Systemic Corticosteroids**: e.g., initially 1–2mg/kg/d prednisolone PO; IV (e.g. pulsed methylprednisolone 1g/d IV for 3d); for an acute flare.
**Corticosteroid-Sparing Agents (Immunosuppressants)**: Consider adding these for an acute flare. Include azathioprine, ciclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate, tacrolimus.
**Anti-TNF Therapies**: e.g. infliximab or adalimumab.
**Interferon alfa**.

sections.title: EULAR 2008 BD Guidelines for Uveitis Management
content: **Step 1: Initial Management of Posterior Uveitis**

Systemic steroids and azathioprine (2.5 mg/kg daily) in combination are recommended. Steroids should be tapered slowly. Topical and/or regional steroids may also be used. Azathioprine may have a role in prophylaxis.
**Step 2: Management of Severe Eye Disease**

For severe eye disease (>2 lines reduction in visual acuity and/or retinal vasculitis or macular involvement): Cyclosporine (2–5 mg/kg daily) or infliximab, in combination with azathioprine and systemic steroids, is recommended.
A recent study recommended a single infliximab infusion as initial treatment of posterior uveitis.
**Step 3: Alternative for Severe Disease**

Interferon-alfa (6 million IU per day subcutaneously initially, gradually tapered) with or without steroids is a EULAR-recommended alternative to the ciclosporin/infliximab/azathioprine/steroid regimen above for severe disease.
**Step 4: American Uveitis Society Recommendation**
Infliximab or adalimumab should be considered early for vision-threatening BD.

sections.title: Important Treatment Considerations & Red Flags
content: **Ocular Hypertension with Intravitreal Steroids**: There may be a high rate of ocular hypertension with intravitreal steroid injection.

**Cyclosporine Concerns**: Hypertension, nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity are concerns. Cyclosporine should be avoided in patients with CNS involvement unless it is determined that severe eye disease warrants the risk.

**Infliximab and Tuberculosis**: Infliximab may lead to activation of tuberculosis. Screening-positive patients should receive prophylactic treatment (e.g. isoniazid). Intravitreal administration is a novel alternative route of administration for infliximab.
**Interferon-alfa and Azathioprine**: Interferon-alfa should not be used in combination with azathioprine (risk of myelosuppression).
**Anticoagulants**: Anticoagulants are not recommended.

sections.title: The Phenylephrine Blanch Test
content: Step 1: Observe the baseline congestion and vessel color in natural light.
Step 2: Instill one drop of Phenylephrine 2.5% into the affected eye.
Step 3: Wait 10-15 minutes for the vasoconstrictive effect.
Step 4: Re-evaluate: If vessels whiten, it's Episcleritis. If they remain dark/congested, suspect Scleritis.

sections.title: Scleritis Red Flags
content: Necrotizing Scleritis: The most severe form, often associated with systemic vasculitis.
Scleral Thinning: Appearance of the dark uvea through the thinned sclera (Scleromalacia Perforans).
Vision Loss: Potential for permanent damage due to uveitis, glaucoma, or keratitis.
Exudative Retinal Detachment: A serious complication of Posterior Scleritis.

content.explanation: D: Deep Boring Pain (Scleritis), E: Episcleral Blanching (Episcleritis), E: Edema of Sclera (Scleritis), P: Phenylephrine Test (Diagnostic)

sections.title: Vessel Mobility Details
content: In Episcleritis, the inflamed vessels can be moved over the underlying sclera with a cotton-tipped applicator.
In Scleritis, the inflammation is deep within the sclera; the vessels are fixed and do not move independently of the globe.
Episcleritis usually resolves within 1-3 weeks without treatment.
Scleritis requires urgent systemic workup and aggressive anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive therapy.

sections.title: Fitting Principles for Keratoconus
content: Aim for 'Three-point touch' in corneal RGP fitting: central apical touch and mid-peripheral bearing.
Scleral lenses vault the entire cornea and limbus, landing on the conjunctiva, eliminating corneal mechanical stress.
Piggyback: Place a thin high-Dk silicone hydrogel lens under the RGP to enhance comfort.
Calculate 'Vault' for scleral lenses: Ensure 100-200 microns of clearance after settling.
Topography-guided fitting is standard: Use E-map or Sagittal maps to predict base curve.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never dispense CLs to a patient with active blepharitis or MGD without prior treatment.
Always check oxygen transmissibility (Dk/t) for patients with history of hypoxic stress.
For scleral lenses, use preservative-free saline to prevent toxic epitheliopathy.
Hydrogel lenses are contraindicated in patients with extreme dry eye; recommend daily disposables with high water content or silicone hydrogel with low modulus.
In Keratoconus, regular topography is essential to monitor progression before fitting.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Cicatricial ectropion is a structural malposition where the eyelid margin turns outward, away from the globe, due to vertical cicatricial contraction of the anterior lamella (skin and orbicularis oculi). This results in exposure keratopathy, chronic epiphora, and conjunctival keratinization.

sections.title: Etiology: Causes of Cicatricial Ectropion
content: Mechanical Trauma: Full-thickness skin loss
Thermal/Chemical Burns
Chronic Actinic Damage: Solar elastosis
Dermatologic Conditions: Ichthyosis, Pemphigoid, SJS/TEN
Post-Surgical: Over-aggressive blepharoplasty
Infectious: Zoster, Necrotizing fasciitis

rows: Inability to move tears to puncta

sections.title: Ocular Examination Protocol
content: Step 1: Snap-back and Distraction tests to assess horizontal laxity.
Step 2: Assess vertical eyelid height (measurement of vertical shortening).
Step 3: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy to grade corneal exposure/keratitis.
Step 4: Palpate for masses or subcutaneous scar tissue.
Step 5: Fluorescein staining for detection of exposure keratopathy.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Phase 1: Lubrication (PF-AT, gels, nocturnal ointment) to protect the cornea.
Phase 2: Surgical lysis of bands for mild cases.
Phase 3: Z-plasty or V-Y advancement flaps for localized scars.
Phase 4: Full-thickness skin graft (FTSG) for severe/extensive cicatricial loss.
Phase 5: Mid-lamellar lysis with spacers (e.g., hard palate graft) if posterior lamella is also involved.

sections.title: Red Flags for Urgent Referral
content: Corneal thinning or impending perforation
Severe exposure keratopathy unresponsive to maximal lubrication
Eyelid involvement from aggressive malignancy (e.g., BCC/SCC)
Evidence of orbital cellulitis or necrotizing process

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always evaluate for horizontal laxity; often, cicatricial ectropion requires a lateral tarsal strip concurrently.
Donors for skin grafts: Retroauricular skin is gold standard due to color/texture match.
If a patient has severe cicatricial ectropion, look for systemic mucous membrane pemphigoid.

sections.content: A-AION is an ischemic infarction of the optic nerve head due to occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries (PCAs), typically caused by Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA). It is rare under age 50; incidence increases sharply with age, peaking between 70–80. Prevalence is approximately 15–25 per 100,000 in those over 50 years old.

Step 3: Perform Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) within 1-2 weeks; minimum 2cm length to avoid skip lesions.
Step 4: Ultrasound (USG) of temporal arteries (Halo sign).

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview: Intermittent Vision Loss
sections.content: Intermittent vision loss refers to transient episodes of diminished or absent vision, ranging from seconds to minutes, with full recovery between episodes. It can be monocular (affecting one eye, e.g., Amaurosis Fugax) or binocular (affecting both eyes). These episodes are critical red flags for underlying systemic conditions, particularly vascular or neurological, that may lead to permanent vision loss or stroke. Amaurosis Fugax (AF) specifically describes transient monocular vision loss due to retinal ischemia. Understanding the character, duration, and associated symptoms is key to differential diagnosis.

sections.title: 3.1 Pathophysiology - Atrial Fibrillation (AF)
sections.content: Atrial fibrillation is a common cardiac arrhythmia characterized by disorganized electrical activity in the atria, leading to ineffective atrial contraction. This stasis of blood within the atria, particularly the left atrial appendage (LAA), promotes thrombus formation. These thrombi can dislodge and embolize to systemic circulation, including the ophthalmic artery (causing TMVL/Amaurosis Fugax) or cerebral arteries (causing TIA/stroke). AF is responsible for approximately 15-20% of all ischemic strokes, often causing more severe and disabling strokes than other etiologies. Early detection and anticoagulation are paramount.

sections.title: 4. Classification / Subtypes of Intermittent Vision Loss

rows: Amaurosis Fugax (Carotid/Cardiac Emboli, Vasculitis), Ocular Ischemic Syndrome, Optic Disc Drusen
Migraine Aura, Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency (VBI), Papilledema (obscurations), Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES)
Scintillating scotomas, tunnel vision, grayouts, associated neurological symptoms (VBI)
Inconsistent, tunnel vision not related to organic causes, often situational

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Monocular:** 'Curtain-like' descent/ascent, 'graying out', altitudinal field defect, central scotoma. Duration typically 5-30 minutes (Amaurosis Fugax).
**Binocular:** Scintillating scotomas (migraine), tunnel vision, generalized dimming, diplopia, vertigo, dysphagia, ataxia (vertebrobasilar insufficiency).
**Associated Symptoms:** Headache (migraine, GCA), jaw claudication, scalp tenderness (GCA), dysarthria, hemiparesis, numbness (TIA), chest pain, palpitations (cardiac arrhythmia).
**Precipitating Factors:** Postural changes, bright light, exercise, stress (ocular ischemic syndrome, papilledema).
**AF-Related:** Often asymptomatic heart rhythm, but may present with palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue. Embolic events (TMVL, TIA, stroke) may be the first manifestation.

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Visual Acuity/Fields:** Normal between episodes. Subtle defects if permanent damage.
**Pupils:** Afferent pupillary defect (APD) if significant optic nerve or retinal ischemia.
**Slit Lamp:** Anterior segment usually normal. Rarely, signs of carotid artery disease (e.g., neovascularization of iris in OIS).

**Fundoscopy:** Retinal emboli (Hollenhorst plaques – cholesterol, calcific emboli – cardiac, fibrin-platelet – carotid), attenuated retinal arteries, retinal hemorrhages, cherry-red spot (if central retinal artery occlusion occurred), optic disc edema/pallor. Signs of Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (mid-peripheral retinal hemorrhages, dilated veins).
**Gonioscopy:** May show iris neovascularization extending into angle in OIS (neovascular glaucoma risk).
**Optic Nerve:** Optic disc edema (papilledema), optic atrophy (post-ischemic event).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Immediate Ophthalmic Evaluation & Visual Field Testing (if indicated):** Rule out acute ocular pathology. Humphrey Visual Field (HVF) for subtle defects.

**Step 2: Cardiovascular Assessment:** ECG (to detect AF, arrhythmias), 24-48hr Holter monitor (for paroxysmal AF), Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE) for valvular disease, PFO, wall motion abnormalities, left atrial appendage thrombus (if TEE not possible). Transesophageal Echocardiogram (TEE) is superior for LAA thrombus detection.
**Step 3: Carotid Artery Evaluation:** Carotid Doppler ultrasound (for stenosis), CTA/MRA of head and neck (for intracranial/extracranial vascular anatomy, dissections, vasculitis).
**Step 4: Neurological Imaging:** MRI Brain with DWI (diffusion-weighted imaging) to detect acute ischemic lesions (TIA/stroke). MRA Circle of Willis for intracranial vascular lesions.

**Step 5: Blood Tests:** CBC, ESR, CRP (inflammatory/vasculitic causes like GCA), Glucose, Lipid profile, Syphilis serology, Thrombophilia screen (Protein C/S, Factor V Leiden, Antiphospholipid antibodies) in young patients.
**Step 6: Specialized Tests (if indicated):** Temporal artery biopsy (GCA), Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) for retinal circulation, OCT-A for microvascular assessment.

content: **C**ongestive Heart Failure (1)
**H**ypertension (1)
**A**ge ≥75 years (2)
**D**iabetes Mellitus (1)
**S**troke/TIA/Thromboembolism (2)
**V**ascular Disease (MI, PAD, aortic plaque) (1)
**A**ge 65-74 years (1)
**S**ex category (Female) (1)
**Interpretation:** Score 0: Low risk (no anticoagulation); Score 1: Intermediate risk (consider anticoagulation based on clinical judgment); Score ≥2: High risk (anticoagulation recommended).

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment: General Principles
content: **Identify & Treat Underlying Cause:** Crucial for preventing permanent vision loss and stroke.
**Risk Factor Modification:** Aggressive management of hypertension (<130/80 mmHg), diabetes (HbA1c <7%), hyperlipidemia (LDL <70 mg/dL or <1.8 mmol/L), smoking cessation.
**Antiplatelet Therapy:** Aspirin 81 mg or Clopidogrel 75 mg daily, if stroke risk factors present and anticoagulation is contraindicated or not indicated.
**Emergency Referral:** Any new onset TMVL/TBVL should be evaluated urgently to rule out TIA/stroke.

sections.title: 10.1 Management & Treatment: Atrial Fibrillation (AF)
content: **Step 1: Confirm Diagnosis of AF:** ECG, Holter monitoring, event recorder. Distinguish paroxysmal, persistent, long-standing persistent, and permanent AF.
**Step 2: Stroke Risk Stratification:** Calculate CHA2DS2-VASc score.
**Step 3: Bleeding Risk Assessment:** Calculate HAS-BLED score to inform anticoagulation choice.
**Step 4: Anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2, or 1 with clinical judgment):**

- **NOACs (DOACs):** Apixaban (5 mg BID, 2.5 mg BID for specific criteria), Rivaroxaban (20 mg QD, 15 mg QD for specific criteria), Edoxaban (60 mg QD, 30 mg QD for specific criteria), Dabigatran (150 mg BID, 75 mg BID for specific criteria). Preferred over Warfarin in most non-valvular AF.
- **Warfarin:** Target INR 2.0-3.0. Requires regular monitoring. Used in mechanical heart valves, moderate-severe mitral stenosis, or if NOACs contraindicated/unavailable.
**Step 5: Rate Control (for symptomatic AF or prevention of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy):**
- **Beta-blockers:** Metoprolol, Carvedilol, Bisoprolol. First-line.
- **Non-dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers:** Diltiazem, Verapamil. Contraindicated in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
- **Digoxin:** For sedentary patients with heart failure.
**Step 6: Rhythm Control (for symptomatic AF despite rate control, or to maintain sinus rhythm):**

- **Antiarrhythmic Drugs:** Amiodarone (loading dose 800-1600 mg/day for 1-3 weeks, maintenance 100-400 mg/day - significant ocular/systemic side effects), Flecainide, Propafenone, Sotalol, Dofetilide. Requires careful monitoring.
- **Electrical Cardioversion:** For acute rhythm restoration.
- **Catheter Ablation:** For symptomatic, recurrent AF refractory to antiarrhythmic drugs.
**Step 7: Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion (LAAO):** For patients at high stroke risk with contraindications to long-term anticoagulation (e.g., Watchman, Amulet devices).

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques (Relevant to Embolic Causes)
content: **Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA):** Indicated for symptomatic carotid artery stenosis >70%, or 50-69% in selected patients, to prevent stroke. Removes atherosclerotic plaque.
**Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS):** Alternative to CEA for selected patients, especially those at high surgical risk, though higher periprocedural stroke risk.

**Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO) Closure:** For cryptogenic stroke/TIA, especially in younger patients with large right-to-left shunts, after thorough workup for other causes. Reduces risk of recurrent embolic events.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Stroke:** The most feared complication of TMVL/TBVL, especially if embolic origin. High risk immediately after first episode.
**Permanent Vision Loss:** Can occur if an episode of ischemia is prolonged or severe, leading to retinal artery/vein occlusion or optic neuropathy.
**Recurrence:** High risk of recurrence if underlying cause (e.g., AF, carotid stenosis) is not adequately managed.
**Prognosis:** Varies widely based on etiology. Excellent for migraine aura. Poor if underlying vascular disease progresses untreated. AF significantly increases stroke risk.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Sudden, painless, severe vision loss (consider CRAO, GCA, stroke)
Associated neurological deficits (hemiparesis, dysarthria, sensory loss) – HIGH SUSPICION FOR TIA/STROKE
Persistent vision loss > 20-30 minutes
Painful vision loss (GCA, acute glaucoma, optic neuritis)
Vision loss in older patients (>50 years) with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness (GCA – ophthalmic emergency)
Recurrent episodes of TMVL, especially with cardiovascular risk factors
New onset AF discovered during workup for vision loss

content.explanation: F: Face drooping, A: Arm weakness, S: Speech difficulty, T: Time to call emergency services. Applies to TIA/stroke, which can manifest with vision loss.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Any transient monocular vision loss (Amaurosis Fugax) is a TIA of the eye until proven otherwise; mandates urgent workup.
Hollenhorst plaques are pathognomonic for atherosclerotic emboli, usually from the carotid artery.

GCA is an ophthalmic emergency; treatment with high-dose steroids (e.g., IV methylprednisolone 1g daily for 3 days, then oral prednisone) should be started immediately if suspected, even before temporal artery biopsy.
AF is often asymptomatic; an embolic event (e.g., TMVL) may be the first clinical manifestation, prompting its diagnosis.
Always investigate the heart and carotids for any embolic source in TMVL; don't just focus on the eye.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **NOACs (Non-vitamin K antagonist Oral Anticoagulants):** Multiple trials (RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48) have shown NOACs to be superior or non-inferior to Warfarin for stroke prevention in non-valvular AF, with lower intracranial bleeding rates. They are now first-line.

**Extended Cardiac Monitoring:** Newer implantable loop recorders (ILRs) and wearable devices allow for prolonged rhythm monitoring, increasing detection rates of paroxysmal AF in cryptogenic stroke/TIA patients (e.g., CRYSTAL-AF trial).

**LAA Occlusion Devices:** WATCHMAN (PROTECT AF, PREVAIL trials) and Amulet (Amulet IDE trial) devices offer alternatives for AF patients unable to tolerate long-term anticoagulation, showing non-inferiority to Warfarin for stroke prevention.

**PFO Closure:** REDUCE and CLOSE trials demonstrated benefit of PFO closure in selected patients with cryptogenic stroke and PFO, showing reduction in recurrent stroke rates compared to antiplatelet therapy alone.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Pediatric:** Intermittent vision loss is rare. Causes include migraine, optic disc drusen, papilledema, optic neuritis, epilepsy, cerebral vasculitis. Thorough neurological workup is crucial. AF is rare but can occur in congenital heart disease, myocarditis, or channelopathies.

**Pregnancy:** Management of AF and anticoagulation in pregnancy requires careful consideration. Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is often preferred over Warfarin (teratogenic in 1st trimester) and NOACs (insufficient data). Risk of eclampsia-related vision changes (PRES) or migraine.
**Elderly:** Higher prevalence of AF, carotid artery disease, GCA. Requires aggressive risk factor management and careful consideration of polypharmacy and bleeding risk with anticoagulants.

title: Ocular Stroke: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)
summary: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is a true ocular emergency characterized by sudden, painless monocular vision loss. It represents the ocular equivalent of a cerebral stroke and requires immediate neuro-ophthalmic triage.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: CRAO is an infarction of the inner retinal layers due to blockage of the central retinal artery. The central retinal artery is an end-artery, meaning there is no collateral circulation. Retinal viability is lost after approximately 90-100 minutes of total occlusion.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Fundoscopy
content: Sudden, profound painless loss of vision (typically 'counting fingers' or 'hand motion').
Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD) — often profound.
Fundoscopy: 'Cherry-red spot' at the fovea (due to choroidal blood supply).
Retinal whitening: Edematous, necrotic inner retina.
Cattle-trucking (segmentation of blood flow in arterioles).

rows: Scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, ESR/CRP elevation

sections.title: Emergency Protocols
content: Rule out Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) with STAT ESR, CRP, and Platelet count.
Immediate stroke workup (Carotid Doppler, EKG, Echo, MRI Brain) is mandatory.
Irreversible retinal damage occurs after 90-100 minutes of occlusion.
Rule out hypercoagulable states in patients under 50 years of age.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Ocular massage (digital pressure to induce movement of embolus).
Step 2: Lower Intraocular Pressure (Topical timolol, acetazolamide 500mg IV).
Step 3: Paracentesis (if within 2-4 hours, though efficacy is debated).
Step 4: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (if available within 8-24 hours).
Step 5: Systemic anticoagulation/thrombolytics (if indicated by neuro-consult).

content.explanation: S: Sudden vision loss, T: Thinning of vessels, O: Ocular massage, K: Kidney function check (for contrast), E: ESR/CRP for GCA.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Cilioretinal artery sparing: Occurs in 15-30% of eyes, preserving central visual acuity.
Always listen for carotid bruits.
Follow-up for NVI/NVA (Neovascularization) at 4-6 weeks.
Prognosis is generally poor; no randomized trial has proven superiority of a single treatment.

title: Post-Operative Pulmonary Embolism: A Clinical Deep Dive
summary: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is a life-threatening post-surgical complication characterized by the occlusion of the pulmonary arterial tree. This guide provides an evidence-based framework for the rapid diagnosis, risk stratification, and management of PE in the post-operative setting.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is the obstruction of one or more pulmonary arteries by solid, liquid, or gaseous masses. In the post-operative ophthalmic patient, the most common etiology is a dislodged Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) from the lower extremities. While ophthalmic procedures are often perceived as 'low risk,' prolonged immobility, general anesthesia, and underlying patient comorbidities (e.g., malignancy, Factor V Leiden) can precipitate a fatal embolic event within 48–72 hours post-surgery.

branches: Stasis (Immobility, Bed rest, Obesity, Varicose veins)

rows: PE is #1 diagnosis or equally likely

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: The Classic Signs
content: Dyspnea (73%): Sudden onset shortness of breath.
Pleuritic Chest Pain (66%): Sharp pain on inspiration.
Cough (37%) and Hemoptysis (13%).
Tachypnea (RR > 20/min) and Tachycardia (HR > 100 bpm).
Signs of DVT: Unilateral leg swelling, calf tenderness, erythema.
Syncope: Suggests a massive PE with right heart strain.
Accentuated P2: Sign of pulmonary hypertension.

rows: Crushing pressure, radiation to jaw/arm, ST changes on ECG.
Sudden onset, hyper-resonance, diminished breath sounds.
Sharp pain, pleural rub, often viral or post-inflammatory.
Pain relieved by sitting forward, diffuse ST elevation.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: Step 1: Clinical Pre-test Probability (Wells Score or Geneva Score).
Step 2: D-Dimer (High sensitivity, low specificity). Only useful to rule out PE in low/moderate risk patients.
Step 3: Imaging - CT Pulmonary Angiogram (CTPA) is the GOLD STANDARD for diagnosis.
Step 4: V/Q Scan - Alternative if CTPA is contraindicated (e.g., Renal failure, severe contrast allergy).
Step 5: Lower Extremity Doppler US - To confirm DVT if PE imaging is inconclusive.
Step 6: Bedside Echocardiography - Check for McConnell's sign (RV free wall akinesia) in unstable patients.

content.explanation: S-wave in Lead I, Q-wave in Lead III, and T-wave inversion in Lead III. Note: Most common ECG finding is actually Sinus Tachycardia.

sections.title: ABG & Lab Findings
content: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG): Respiratory Alkalosis (due to hyperventilation) and Hypoxemia.
A-a Gradient: Usually widened.
Troponin & BNP: Elevated in submassive/massive PE (indicates Right Ventricular strain).
D-Dimer: > 500 ng/mL (using age-adjusted cutoffs if >50 yrs).

rows: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg or 40 mmHg drop from baseline.
Stable BP but evidence of RV dysfunction or Troponin rise.
Hemodynamically stable; no RV strain markers.

sections.title: Acute Management: Anticoagulation
content: LMWH (Enoxaparin): 1 mg/kg SC BID (standard therapeutic dose). Preferred in cancer patients.
Unfractionated Heparin (UFH): IV bolus 80 units/kg, then infusion 18 units/kg/hr. Preferred if thrombolysis or surgery is imminent (reversible).
Fondaparinux: Factor Xa inhibitor, SC daily.
DOACs (Apixaban/Rivaroxaban): Now first-line for stable patients. No bridge needed for Apixaban/Rivaroxaban.
Warfarin: Requires bridging with Heparin for at least 5 days until INR is 2.0-3.0.

sections.title: Emergency Interventions
content: Step 1: Supplemental Oxygen (Maintain Sat >90%).
Step 2: Fluid Resuscitation (Cautious: avoid overloading Right Ventricle).
Step 3: Vasopressors (Norepinephrine) if shock persists.
Step 4: Systemic Thrombolysis (Alteplase 100mg over 2h) for Massive PE.
Step 5: Surgical Embolectomy if thrombolysis is contraindicated or failed.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Crisis
content: Sudden onset Cardiovascular Collapse/Syncope.
Systolic Blood Pressure < 90 mmHg (Obstructive Shock).
New-onset Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB) on ECG.
Refractory Hypoxemia despite 100% FiO2.
Cyanosis of the upper body/neck.

content.explanation: If all 8 are 'NO', PE risk <1%. 1. Age <50, 2. HR <100, 3. O2 Sat >94%, 4. No unilateral leg swelling, 5. No Hemoptysis, 6. No recent surgery/trauma, 7. No prior PE/DVT, 8. No hormone use.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Surgeon
content: Prevention: Early ambulation is the most effective post-op strategy.
Chest X-Ray: Often normal in PE! Look for Westermark Sign (focal oligemia) or Hampton's Hump (wedge-shaped opacity).
PESI Score: Use the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index to decide if a patient can be managed at home.
IVC Filters: Indicated ONLY if there is an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite therapy.

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-up
sections.content: Untreated PE has a mortality rate of up to 30%. With proper anticoagulation, this drops to <8%. Patients with provoked PE (e.g., post-ophthalmic surgery) generally require 3 months of anticoagulation. Long-term complications include Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH), occurring in 2-4% of survivors; follow-up echocardiography is recommended if dyspnea persists at 3-6 months.

title: Valsalva Retinopathy: Understanding Acute Pre-Retinal Hemorrhage
summary: Valsalva Retinopathy (VR) is a condition characterized by acute pre-retinal hemorrhage, typically in the macula, triggered by a sudden increase in intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure. While often self-limiting, it causes abrupt vision loss and necessitates careful differential diagnosis to rule out more serious underlying pathologies. Management primarily involves observation, with laser or surgical intervention for persistent cases.
