sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Valsalva Retinopathy (VR) is an acute, typically unilateral, pre-retinal hemorrhage occurring as a consequence of a sudden, transient elevation in intrathoracic and/or intra-abdominal pressure. This pressure surge transmits to the choroidal and retinal venous systems, leading to a rupture of superficial retinal capillaries, most commonly in the macular region. It typically presents as sudden, painless vision loss.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Risk Factors
content: **Incidence:** Relatively uncommon, but often under-diagnosed due to spontaneous resolution.
**Demographics:** Predominantly affects young to middle-aged adults (20-40 years old) with no underlying systemic comorbidities, but can occur at any age.
**Sex:** No significant sex predilection.
**Risk Factors (Valsalva Maneuvers):**
• Intense physical exertion (e.g., weightlifting, vigorous exercise)
• Straining (e.g., defecation, coughing, vomiting, sneezing)
• Childbirth/Labor
• Blowing musical instruments (e.g., trumpet, saxophone)
• Scuba diving, flying
• Choking or strangulation
• Emesis (especially hyperemesis gravidarum)

sections.title: 3. Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: **Step 1: Valsalva Maneuver Initiation** – Patient performs an action that significantly increases intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., forced expiration against a closed glottis).
**Step 2: Venous Pressure Surge** – This pressure is transmitted to the superior vena cava and jugular veins, leading to a rapid and substantial rise in episcleral and intraocular venous pressure.
**Step 3: Retinal Capillary Stress** – The sudden elevation in retinal venous pressure, particularly in the perifoveal capillaries, overwhelms their structural integrity.
**Step 4: Capillary Rupture** – Fragile superficial retinal capillaries rupture due to the increased transmural pressure.

**Step 5: Hemorrhage Formation** – Blood extravasates into the potential spaces in front of the retina, most commonly in the sub-internal limiting membrane (sub-ILM) or sub-hyaloid space, forming a localized pre-retinal hemorrhage.

sections.title: 4. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Acute Onset:** Symptoms appear suddenly, often immediately after the Valsalva event.
**Painless Vision Loss:** The hallmark symptom, ranging from mild blurring to severe decrease in central visual acuity, depending on hemorrhage size and location.
**Floaters:** Patients often report numerous black or red 'floaters' corresponding to the blood cells in the vitreous or blood behind the ILM/hyaloid.
**Central Scotoma:** A blind spot in the central visual field.
**Metamorphopsia:** Less common, but can occur if there is underlying retinal distortion.
**Unilateral:** Typically affects one eye, though bilateral cases have been reported rarely.

sections.title: 5. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Visual Acuity (VA):** Variable, from 20/20 to hand motion, depending on the density and location of the hemorrhage (macular involvement causes significant drop).
**Anterior Segment:** Usually quiet, no signs of inflammation or hemorrhage.
**Pupils:** Normal, reactive.
**Fundoscopy (Dilated):**
• Well-demarcated, usually round or oval, bright red hemorrhage located anterior to the retina.
• Commonly observed in the macula or posterior pole.
• May appear 'boat-shaped' or 'dumbbell-shaped' if the hemorrhage is sub-hyaloid with fluid levels due to gravity.
• Retinal vessels appear normal, no signs of vasculitis or occlusion.
**Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):**

• Crucial for identifying the exact location of hemorrhage: either between the retina and the internal limiting membrane (sub-ILM hemorrhage) or between the ILM and the posterior hyaloid face (sub-hyaloid hemorrhage).
• Demonstrates an optically empty or moderately reflective space anterior to the retina, containing hyper-reflective material (blood).
• The ILM and hyaloid membrane can often be clearly visualized.

sections.title: 6. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic Examination**
• Best-corrected visual acuity, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, dilated fundus examination.
**Step 2: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) of the Macula**
• Essential for localizing the hemorrhage (sub-ILM vs. sub-hyaloid) and assessing underlying retinal structures. Also helps exclude choroidal neovascularization or other macular pathologies.
**Step 3: Fundus Photography**
• Documents the size, shape, and location of the hemorrhage for baseline and follow-up.
**Step 4: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) (If indicated)**
• Typically not required for classic VR, as retinal circulation is usually normal.

• May be performed to rule out other causes of hemorrhage (e.g., retinal macroaneurysm, CNVM, retinal vasculitis) if the diagnosis is uncertain. Usually shows blockage of choroidal and retinal fluorescence.
**Step 5: B-scan Ultrasonography (If view obscured)**
• If the hemorrhage is very dense or there's an associated vitreous hemorrhage obscuring fundus view, B-scan can evaluate for retinal detachment or other posterior segment pathologies.
**Step 6: Systemic Workup (If suspicion of underlying systemic cause)**
• Complete Blood Count (CBC) with platelet count (to rule out anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukemia).
• Coagulation Profile (PT/INR, aPTT) (if bleeding disorder or anticoagulant use suspected).
• Blood Pressure measurement (to rule out hypertensive retinopathy).

sections.title: 7. Differential Diagnosis of Acute Macular Hemorrhage

rows: No tortuosity/dilatation of retinal veins. No cotton wool spots, usually localized single hemorrhage.
Widespread retinal hemorrhages, tortuous and dilated veins, cotton wool spots, disc edema, often sectoral distribution (BRVO) or diffuse (CRVO).
Absence of other DR signs (microaneurysms, exudates, neovascularization).
Microaneurysms, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, intraretinal hemorrhages, neovascularization (PDR), macular edema.
Normal blood pressure, no other signs of hypertensive damage.
Arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, cotton wool spots, flame-shaped hemorrhages, optic disc edema in severe cases.
No saccular arterial dilatation. Hemorrhage usually single and localized to the macroaneurysm.
Saccular dilatation on an arteriole, often with surrounding lipid exudates, intraretinal/subretinal/vitreous hemorrhage. FFA confirms leakage.
No drusen, RPE changes, or underlying choroidal neovascularization (CNV).
Drusen, RPE atrophy/hyperplasia, subretinal fluid, subretinal hemorrhage, CNV complex visible on OCT/FFA.
No history of acute intracranial event (e.g., subarachnoid hemorrhage).
History of subarachnoid hemorrhage or other intracranial bleed, often bilateral intraocular hemorrhages (vitreous, sub-hyaloid, sub-ILM, intraretinal).
No history of significant ocular or systemic trauma.
Multiple cotton wool spots, retinal hemorrhages (often multi-layered), arterial narrowing after trauma or severe systemic insult (e.g., pancreatitis, fat embolism).
No high myopia, lacquer cracks, or CNV features on OCT/FFA.
High myopia, lacquer cracks, Fuchs spot, development of CNV, subretinal hemorrhage/fluid.
Roth spots (hemorrhages with white centers), scattered intraretinal hemorrhages, often bilateral. Systemic signs of anemia/thrombocytopenia.
No systemic signs of hematological malignancy.
White-centered hemorrhages (Roth spots), venous tortuosity, cotton wool spots, infiltrates. Systemic diagnosis of leukemia/lymphoma.
Retinal edema, exudates, serous retinal detachment, hemorrhages in pregnant patients with severe hypertension and proteinuria.

sections.title: 8. Management & Treatment Protocol
content: **Step 1: Observation (First Line)**
• The vast majority (80-90%) of Valsalva hemorrhages resolve spontaneously within 2-6 months, with good visual recovery.
• Hemoglobin breakdown products are absorbed, and the blood disperses or drains. Regular follow-up every 2-4 weeks is advised to monitor resolution and visual acuity.
**Step 2: Patient Education & Counseling**
• Explain the benign nature and favorable prognosis. Advise avoiding activities that induce Valsalva maneuvers (e.g., straining, heavy lifting) temporarily.
**Step 3: Nd:YAG Laser Membranotomy (Consider after 2-4 weeks if non-resolving)**
• **Indication:** Dense, non-resolving sub-hyaloid or sub-ILM hemorrhage significantly affecting central vision, typically after 2-4 weeks of observation.
• **Technique:** A small opening is created in the anterior limiting membrane (ILM or posterior hyaloid) to allow the blood to drain into the vitreous cavity, where it disperses more quickly.

• **Parameters:** Typically 1-3 mJ, 1-3 pulses per shot, targeting the superior-most edge of the hemorrhage (to allow gravity-assisted drainage and avoid direct foveal trauma). Use a contact lens (e.g., Abraham lens).

• **Risks:** Macular hole formation, retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) damage, iatrogenic retinal hemorrhage, vitreous hemorrhage (from drainage), epiretinal membrane (ERM) formation, increased intraocular pressure (IOP).
**Step 4: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) (Reserved for specific cases)**
• **Indications:**
• Very dense, non-resolving hemorrhage (especially vitreous hemorrhage) that fails to clear after extended observation or Nd:YAG laser.
• Associated complications like epiretinal membrane (ERM) or macular hole.
• Co-existing retinal detachment or other pathologies requiring surgical intervention.
• Chronic, organized sub-ILM hemorrhage that could induce ERM or traction.
• **Technique:** Standard 3-port vitrectomy to remove vitreous and hemorrhage, potentially peeling the ILM if necessary to prevent ERM. Gas or oil tamponade may be used.

sections.title: 9. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Complications (Rare):**
• **Macular hole:** Can occur spontaneously during resolution or as a complication of Nd:YAG laser.
• **Epiretinal Membrane (ERM):** May form secondary to inflammation or fibrous organization, leading to persistent metamorphopsia or vision loss.
• **Vitreous Hemorrhage:** If the hemorrhage breaks through the posterior hyaloid into the vitreous, causing significant vision loss and potentially requiring vitrectomy.
• **Iron-induced toxicity:** Rarely, hemosiderosis can cause retinal toxicity if hemorrhage persists for a very long time.
• **Persistent Scotoma/Vision Loss:** If damage to photoreceptors or RPE occurs, or if ERM/macular hole develops.
**Prognosis:**
• Generally excellent. Most patients achieve complete or near-complete visual recovery to baseline, especially with spontaneous resolution.
• Even with Nd:YAG laser, visual outcomes are typically good, with faster recovery compared to observation alone.

sections.title: 10. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Sudden vision loss accompanied by severe headache, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, or altered mental status:** Suggests possible intracranial hemorrhage (e.g., subarachnoid hemorrhage) with associated Terson's syndrome.
**Signs of systemic bleeding disorders:** Easy bruising, prolonged bleeding, or petechiae, necessitating urgent hematological evaluation.
**Rapidly worsening vision in both eyes:** Indicates a more widespread or severe systemic condition.
**Non-resolving dense hemorrhage with evidence of retinal toxicity (e.g., changes in RPE or photoreceptors on OCT):** May warrant earlier intervention.
**Associated retinal detachment or other acute intraocular pathology.**

content.explanation:
V: Vomiting/Valgus stress
A: Abdominal strain (constipation, labor)
L: Lifting (heavy weights)
S: Sneezing/Straining
A: Airway obstruction (coughing, choking)
V: Vasospasm (rarely linked, but can include other vascular stresses)
A: Alcohol excess (associated with vomiting)

sections.title: 12. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Valsalva Retinopathy typically affects young, otherwise healthy individuals.
A detailed history of recent strenuous activity is crucial for diagnosis.
OCT is indispensable for confirming the pre-retinal location (sub-ILM or sub-hyaloid) and ruling out other macular pathologies.
Most cases are self-limiting and resolve with excellent visual recovery without intervention.
Nd:YAG laser membranotomy can accelerate visual recovery in selected cases but carries risks.
Always consider and rule out Terson's syndrome if there's any suspicion of intracranial pathology.
A systemic workup is warranted if there are any atypical features or suspicion of underlying bleeding disorders.

sections.title: 13. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: While the fundamental understanding and management of Valsalva Retinopathy remain consistent, recent advances primarily lie in improved diagnostic imaging. High-resolution OCT has revolutionized the ability to precisely identify the layer of hemorrhage (sub-ILM vs. sub-hyaloid), which can influence the timing and approach to Nd:YAG laser treatment. Studies often focus on comparing visual outcomes and complication rates between observation, Nd:YAG laser, and vitrectomy, consistently affirming the generally favorable prognosis across management strategies. There are no recent landmark studies that have drastically altered the treatment paradigm, but continuous refinement of laser parameters and vitrectomy techniques for complications is ongoing.

sections.title: 14. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Children:** While less common, VR can occur in children due to severe coughing (e.g., pertussis), vomiting, or strenuous play. In infants, retinal hemorrhages, particularly multi-layered and bilateral, must raise suspicion for **Non-Accidental Trauma (Shaken Baby Syndrome)**.

**Pregnant Women:** Valsalva retinopathy can occur during labor. It is important to differentiate it from other causes of retinal hemorrhage in pregnancy, such as pre-eclampsia/eclampsia-related retinopathy, which has distinct features (e.g., serous detachments, exudates, severe hypertension).

**Elderly:** Although less frequent in this group, elderly patients may be on anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications, which can exacerbate the extent or duration of the hemorrhage. Careful medication history and systemic workup are crucial.

title: Apraclonidine: The Alpha-2 Powerhouse
summary: Apraclonidine (Iopidine) is a potent selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist primarily used for acute intraocular pressure (IOP) control, post-laser prophylaxis, and neuro-ophthalmic diagnosis. While highly effective for short-term use, its clinical utility is limited by rapid tachyphylaxis and high rates of follicular conjunctivitis.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Classification
sections.content: Apraclonidine is a synthetic sympathomimetic amine, a derivative of clonidine. It acts as a relatively selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist (though less selective than Brimonidine). It is classified as an ocular hypotensive agent that reduces IOP by decreasing aqueous humor production via the inhibition of adenylate cyclase in the ciliary body.

rows: 1 drop 1 hour pre-op; 1 drop immediately post-op
1 drop TID for up to 4 weeks

sections.title: The 'Reversal' Test: Horner's Syndrome
content: Step 1: Document baseline anisocoria in dim and bright light.
Step 2: Instill one drop of 0.5% or 1.0% Apraclonidine in both eyes.
Step 3: Wait 30 to 45 minutes (up to 60 mins).
Step 4: Pathophysiology: Denervation hypersensitivity causes Mueller's muscle (alpha-1 sensitive) to contract in the Horner's eye.
Step 5: Positive Result: Mydriasis and ptosis resolution (reversal) in the Horner's eye; no effect on the normal pupil.
Step 6: Interpretation: Confirms Horner's but does not localize the lesion (pre- vs. post-ganglionic).

sections.title: Prophylaxis of Post-Laser IOP Spikes
content: Nd:YAG Laser Capsulotomy (reduces risk of transient spikes >10mmHg)
Argon/Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (ALT/SLT)
Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI)
Laser Iridoplasty
Effectiveness: Reduces the incidence of post-laser spikes from 25-40% down to <2%.

sections.title: Contraindications & Absolute Restrictions
content: Concurrent use of Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs)
Hypersensitivity to Apraclonidine or Clonidine
Infants and children under age 6 (risk of severe CNS depression)
Severe Coronary Insufficiency or Recent MI
Nursing Mothers (systemic absorption risk)

rows: Loss of IOP lowering efficacy over 1-4 weeks

content.explanation: A: Acute use only (Post-laser); P: Ptosis reversal (Horner's); R: Redness goes away (Blanching); A: Allergy (Follicular reaction).

sections.title: Pediatric Warning: DO NOT USE
content: Risk of life-threatening CNS depression
Severe somnolence and bradycardia in neonates
Hypotension and respiratory distress reported in toddlers
Use alternative IOP lowering agents in pediatric populations

sections.title: Surgical & Perioperative Uses
content: Trabeculectomy: Used post-operatively for early IOP spikes.
Bleb Needling: Pre-treatment to prevent subconjunctival hemorrhage.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy: Acute post-operative pressure management.
Eyelid Surgery: Off-label use to assess Mueller muscle function pre-blepharoplasty.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for MAOI use before prescribing.
Warn patients about the 'washout' effect; it is not for chronic glaucoma management.
In Horner's testing, a negative result in the first week after injury may be a false negative due to lack of receptor upregulation.
Lid retraction can be used to differentiate Horner's from simple anisocoria.

sections.title: Landmark Research Context
sections.content: Early studies by Pollack et al. and Robin et al. (late 1980s) established Apraclonidine 1.0% as the gold standard for preventing the 30mmHg+ IOP spikes often seen after Argon Laser Trabeculoplasty. Its role evolved with the introduction of Brimonidine, which offered better selectivity and safety for chronic use, relegating Apraclonidine to its current 'acute and diagnostic' niche.

title: Coats Disease: Clinical Masterclass
summary: Coats disease is a rare, idiopathic, non-hereditary condition characterized by telangiectatic and aneurysmal retinal vessels with massive subretinal exudation. It is a leading mimic of retinoblastoma and requires aggressive management to prevent vision loss and phthisis.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Coats disease is an idiopathic condition (likely related to somatic mutations in the NDP gene) involving a breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier. Abnormal endothelial cells and 'leaky' pericytes lead to the formation of telangiectatic 'light-bulb' aneurysms. This results in massive plasma and lipid leakage into the intraretinal and subretinal spaces, forming cholesterol-rich exudates and exudative retinal detachments.

sections.title: Parental Presentation: How it's Noticed
content: Leukocoria: A 'white reflex' or 'cat's eye' noticed in flash photography or dim light.
Strabismus: New onset eye turn (esotropia or exotropia) due to poor central vision.
Vision Loss: Older children may complain of blurred vision or 'bumping into things' on one side.
Nystagmus: Rare, but possible if bilateral or very early onset.
Red Eye: Noticed in late stages due to secondary glaucoma (painful red eye).

rows: Phthisis Bulbi or blind painful eye

branches: Chronic Total RD with Subretinal Fibrosis

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Telangiectatic vessels: 'Light-bulb' appearance of aneurysms.
Massive Exudation: Deep, yellow, subretinal lipid deposits.
Retinal Crystals: Glistening cholesterol crystals within exudates.
Retinal Non-perfusion: Areas of peripheral ischemia.
Exudative RD: Shiftable subretinal fluid, often inferiorly.
Light-bulb Sign: Focal dilations on the retinal venules and arterioles.

sections.title: Treatment: Management of Exudative RD
content: Step 1: Indirect Laser Photocoagulation: Ablate the telangiectatic vessels directly ('double-tap' or 'triple-tap' technique).
Step 2: Cryotherapy: Used for peripheral lesions or when exudation is too thick for laser penetration.
Step 3: Subretinal Fluid Drainage: External drainage via sclerotomy if the RD is too bullous for laser/cryo to reach the vessels.
Step 4: Scleral Buckling or PPV: Reserved for complex cases with vitreoretinal traction or non-resolving RD.
Step 5: Anti-VEGF Adjunct: Intravitreal Bevacizumab/Ranibizumab to reduce leakage and facilitate fluid resorption.

sections.title: Treatment: Macular Edema in Coats
content: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF: Rapidly reduces vascular permeability and ME (e.g., Bevacizumab 1.25mg).
Corticosteroids: Intravitreal Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) or Triamcinolone (Kenalog) to stabilize the BRB.
Grid Laser: Rarely used today; replaced by pharmacotherapy.
Peripheral Ablation: Treating the primary peripheral telangiectasia is mandatory to stop the 'source' of the macular fluid.

rows: Calcification on USG/CT; solid endophytic/exophytic mass.
Genetic, usually bilateral, straightening of vessels/dragging.
Endophthalmitis or focal granuloma with tractional bands.
Persistent stalk from disc to lens; microphthalmos.

content.explanation: C: Child (young male); O: Out-of-place (Unilateral); A: Aneurysms (Light-bulb); T: Telangiectasia; S: Subretinal Exudates/Subretinal Fluid.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Pathognomonic 'light-bulb' aneurysms and early leakage.
2. B-Scan Ultrasound: Shows SRF; crucially lacks the high-spike calcification seen in Retinoblastoma.
3. OCT: Quantifies Macular Edema and SRF depth.
4. CT/MRI: Performed if Rb cannot be ruled out (Rb has calcification on CT and T2-darkness on MRI).

sections.title: Surgical Red Flags
content: IOP Elevation: High risk of neovascular glaucoma.
Vitreous Seedings: If seen, strongly suspect Retinoblastoma instead of Coats.
Rapidly Progressive RD: May require immediate surgical drainage to save the globe.
Corneal Edema: Sign of decompensated glaucoma or end-stage phthisis.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a dilated fundus exam on the 'good' eye; though rare, bilateral cases exist and are often more aggressive.
Exudates can migrate to the fovea even if the telangiectasia is in the far periphery (gravitational settling).
The 'Yellow Reflex' in Coats is due to lipid, whereas the 'White Reflex' in Rb is due to tumor mass.
Aggressive treatment of stage 2 and 3A can often preserve ambulatory vision.
Serial Wide-Field Imaging (Optos) is essential for monitoring treatment response.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), commercially known as Plaquenil, is a 4-aminoquinoline derivative used for Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). While safer than chloroquine, it carries a risk of irreversible, vision-threatening toxic maculopathy. The primary mechanism involves binding to melanin in the Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE), leading to metabolic disruption and subsequent loss of photoreceptors.

rows: The most important predictor; exceeds metabolic clearance.
Cumulative dose increases risk; risk is <1% before 5 years.
HCQ is cleared renally; reduced GFR doubles toxicity risk.
Synergistic toxicity; 5x increased risk of retinopathy.
Masks early toxicity signs and interferes with screening.

sections.title: The AAO Screening Schedule
content: Step 1: Baseline Exam (Within 1st year of starting HCQ) to rule out pre-existing maculopathy.
Step 2: Annual Screening begins after 5 years of treatment for low-risk patients.
Step 3: Immediate Annual Screening if 'High Risk' factors (e.g., Tamoxifen, Renal failure) are present.
Step 4: Frequent Monitoring if 'Borderline' findings are detected on OCT or VF.

content.explanation: D: Dose (>5mg/kg), D: Duration (>5yrs), R: Renal (Low GFR), T: Tamoxifen, M: Macular disease.

branches: SD-OCT: Look for 'Flying Saucer' sign (EZ loss)
mfERG: Objective mapping of paracentral cone function
Wide-field Imaging: Mandatory for Asian patients

sections.title: Subjective Screening: Visual Fields
content: Automated Perimetry is mandatory.
Standard: 10-2 SITA Standard/Fast protocol.
Look for 'Paracentral' or 'Ring' scotomas.
Pattern Deviation plot is more sensitive than Mean Deviation.
Asian Population Requirement: 30-2 or 24-2 (toxicity is often extramacular/peripheral).

sections.title: Pathognomonic OCT Findings
content: Loss of the Ellipsoid Zone (EZ) in the paracentral region.
Thinning of the Outer Nuclear Layer (ONL).
The 'Flying Saucer' Sign: Sparing of the foveal EZ creates a central 'island' appearance.
Late Stage: Total RPE and outer retinal atrophy.

sections.title: The Asian Phenotype Variation
content: Toxicity in Asian patients typically presents OUTSIDE the macula.
10-2 Visual Fields will MISS 50% of toxicity in this population.
Must perform 30-2 Visual Fields and Wide-field OCT/FAF.

sections.title: Ineffective Screening Methods (Do NOT Use)
content: Amsler Grid: Too insensitive for early detection.
Color Vision Testing: Non-specific and late-stage finding.
Fundus Photography: Misses early structural changes.
Full-field ERG: Only abnormal in end-stage disease.

rows: Presents earlier, 'Pisciform' flecks on FAF, dark choroid on FFA.
Progressive decrease in VA, abnormal Full-field ERG early.
Presence of Drusen, Pigmentary changes not confined to ring.
History of sun gazing, small foveal 'hole' on OCT.

sections.title: Management & Cessation Protocol
content: Step 1: Confirm findings with at least two different modalities (e.g., OCT + VF).
Step 2: Documentation: Detail the severity and risk of continued use.
Step 3: Multi-disciplinary Communication: Formally write to the Rheumatologist to advise cessation.
Step 4: Transition: Rheumatologist must switch to an alternative agent (e.g., Methotrexate, biologics).
Step 5: Follow-up: Continue monitoring for 1-2 years after stopping due to 'coasting'.

sections.title: The 'Coasting' Phenomenon
content: Retinopathy can continue to progress for 1-3 years AFTER drug cessation.
This is due to the extremely long half-life of HCQ in pigmented tissues.
Early detection is CRITICAL; if damage is foveal, it will likely worsen despite stopping.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Practice
content: Always use ACTUAL body weight for dosing (not Ideal weight).
Cumulative dose over 1000g is a major threshold for concern.
If the patient is on Tamoxifen, the risk is 'Extreme'.
Bull’s Eye Maculopathy is a LATE sign; the goal is to find sub-clinical change.

sections.title: Recent Landmark Studies
sections.content: The Melles & Marmor (2014) study in JAMA Ophthalmology revolutionized current dosing. It demonstrated that 5mg/kg actual weight was the most predictive safety threshold, significantly reducing the incidence of toxicity compared to previous dosing guidelines.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: The Glaucoma Assessment
content: Step 1: Precise Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (IOP check).
Step 2: Pachymetry (Correct IOP based on central corneal thickness).
Step 3: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (Evaluation of anterior chamber depth/Van Herick).
Step 4: Gonioscopy (Mandatory for classification of Open vs. Closed angle).
Step 5: Optic Nerve Head evaluation (Cup-to-disc ratio, neuroretinal rim thinning, NOTCHING).
Step 6: Perimetry (Humphrey Field Analyzer 24-2 or 30-2 SITA-Standard/Fast).
Step 7: Structural Imaging (OCT - RNFL thickness mapping and Ganglion Cell Complex analysis).

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Acute angle closure: IOP > 50mmHg, nausea, halos, fixed mid-dilated pupil.
Symptomatic progression: Sudden loss of central/peripheral vision.
Malignant Glaucoma (Aqueous misdirection) post-surgery.
Corneal edema obscuring view of the disc.
Inability to visualize the angle structure (gonioscopy).

sections.title: Beta-Blockers: Mechanism & Contraindications
content: Mechanism: Blocks beta-1 and beta-2 receptors in the ciliary body epithelium; reduces aqueous humor production by decreasing cAMP levels.
Efficacy: Lowers IOP by 20-30%.
Absolute Contraindications: Asthma, COPD, symptomatic bradycardia, second/third-degree heart block, overt heart failure.
Clinical Pearl: Non-selective (Timolol) has higher risk of systemic respiratory side effects compared to Beta-1 selective (Betaxolol).

content.explanation: G - Gonioscopy (Mandatory), R - Rim (Neuroretinal), I - IOP (Check), P - Perimetry (Fields).

summary: CRVO represents a spectrum of retinal venous outflow obstruction ranging from perfusion-stable to ischemic variants. This guide delineates the diagnostic workup, systemic associations by age, and the precise indications for anti-VEGF therapy versus panretinal photocoagulation (PRP).

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: CRVO is characterized by obstruction of the central retinal vein at or posterior to the lamina cribrosa. Pathophysiology follows 'Hayreh’s criteria' involving venous stasis, turbulent flow, and secondary endothelial damage. The resulting hydrostatic pressure elevation leads to intraretinal hemorrhage, macular edema, and ischemia.

rows: Factor V Leiden, Protein C/S deficiency

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup (The 10-Point Plan)
content: 1. Best Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA)
2. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (Iris neovascularization search)
3. Gonioscopy (Mandatory before treatment)
4. Fundus examination (7-field photography)
5. OCT (Macular thickness/Cystoid changes)
6. Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) - Gold Standard
7. IOP measurement
8. Blood Pressure check
9. CBC/ESR/CRP/HbA1c/Lipid profile
10. Thrombophilia screen (If <50y)

sections.title: When to perform PRP?
content: Perform panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) immediately upon detection of NVI (Neovascularization of the Iris) or NVA (Neovascularization of the Angle).
Prophylactic PRP is NOT indicated in non-ischemic CRVO, as conversion rates to ischemic CRVO are variable.
Follow up every 4 weeks for the first 6 months to detect the '100-day glaucoma' window.

sections.title: Role of Anti-VEGF Therapy
content: Indicated primarily for macular edema (ME) secondary to CRVO (BRAVO/CRUISE trials).
Anti-VEGF agents (Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, Bevacizumab) reduce VEGF-induced vascular permeability.
Pro-re-nata (PRN) or Treat-and-Extend (T&E) dosing is standard until BCVA stabilizes and OCT shows resolution of cystic edema.
Anti-VEGFs do not 'cure' the ischemia; they suppress the secondary effects of ischemia (edema and neovascularization).

content.explanation: C-Carotid artery stenosis (Ocular Ischemic Syndrome), R-Retinopathy (Diabetic), V-Venous stasis (Hemi-CRVO), O-Others (Hyperviscosity), D-Disc edema, I-Inflammation (Vasculitis), F-Fundus (Hemorrhagic glaucoma)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Landmarks
content: The '100-day glaucoma' (Neovascular glaucoma) typically appears within 3-4 months of onset.
CRUISE trial: Showed superiority of Ranibizumab vs Sham in improving BCVA.
Ischemic definition: >10 disc area of non-perfusion on FFA.
Always evaluate for POAG in the contralateral eye.

title: Double Vision Decoded: Monocular vs. Binocular Diplopia
summary: Diplopia, or double vision, is a critical symptom requiring thorough investigation. Differentiating between monocular (persists with one eye closed) and binocular (resolves with one eye closed) forms is the first crucial step in guiding the diagnostic and management pathway, with implications ranging from simple refractive errors to life-threatening neurological conditions.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Diplopia, commonly known as double vision, is the perception of two images of a single object. It is a critical ophthalmic symptom that demands thorough investigation due to its wide range of underlying causes, from benign refractive errors to life-threatening neurological conditions. The crucial first step in evaluation is determining if the diplopia is monocular or binocular.

rows: Persists when one eye is closed
Resolves when one eye is closed
Ghosting, overlapping, or split images in a single eye
Two distinct, separated images (horizontal, vertical, or oblique)
Often improves or resolves (due to reduction of optical aberrations)
Optical aberrations or retinal pathology within one eye
Misalignment of the visual axes between the two eyes (strabismus)

content.description: Diplopia affects a significant portion of the population at some point. Binocular diplopia is generally more common, often associated with decompensated phorias, cranial nerve palsies, or systemic conditions. Monocular diplopia frequency tends to increase with age due to common conditions like cataracts and dry eye.

branches: Corneal Irregularities (e.g., Keratoconus, Pterygium, Dry Eye, Corneal Scar, Post-LASIK Ectasia)
Lens Pathology (e.g., Cataract, Lenticular Opacities, Lens Subluxation/Dislocation, Polycoria, Aphakia)
Retinal Conditions (e.g., Macular Edema, Epiretinal Membrane, Foveal Schisis)
Intraocular Lens Issues (e.g., IOL Decentration/Tilt, Edge Glare, Multifocal IOL Aberrations)
Pupillary Abnormalities (e.g., Corectopia, Accessory Pupil, Iris Coloboma)
Neurological (Cranial Nerve Palsies: III, IV, VI)
Myogenic (e.g., Thyroid Eye Disease, Orbital Myositis, Restrictive Strabismus, Orbital Mass)
Supranuclear Disorders (e.g., Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia, Progressive Supranuclear Palsy)
Orbital Trauma (e.g., Blow-out Fracture with muscle entrapment)

sections.title: 6. Clinical Features & Associated Symptoms
content: Monocular: Often described as 'ghosting' or 'shimmering', stable in all gaze directions, no associated pain or neurological symptoms. Pinhole improves vision.

Binocular: Images separate in specific gaze directions (gaze-dependent). Often associated with pain (orbital, headache), ptosis, pupillary involvement, proptosis, or systemic symptoms. Patient may adopt a head turn/tilt to fuse images.

rows: May have uncorrected refractive error, astigmatism; Pinhole improves vision.
VA often normal, no improvement with pinhole.
Corneal irregularities (e.g., scarring, keratoconus striae), cataract (nuclear, PSC), IOL decentration.
Typically normal anterior segment, but may show proptosis (TED), chemosis, conjunctival injection.
May show anisocoria, relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) if optic nerve involved (rare with diplopia).
Restriction, underaction, or overaction in specific gazes (e.g., CN palsy, TED restriction, strabismus).
Manifest (tropia) or latent (phoria) strabismus detected; deviation angle varies with gaze.
Macular edema, epiretinal membrane, foveal schisis.
Usually normal, unless associated neurological or systemic condition affects the optic nerve.
Positive in restrictive myopathy (e.g., TED, orbital fracture).

sections.title: 8. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Thorough History & Ophthalmic Exam** (VA, refraction, pupils, motility, slit lamp, fundoscopy, forced duction, red-glass test).
**Step 2: Monocular Diplopia Specific Tests:** Corneal topography (for irregular astigmatism), OCT (macular pathology), B-scan (IOL position, retinal pathology).
**Step 3: Binocular Diplopia Specific Workup (Targeted based on clinical suspicion):**
- **Labs:** CBC, ESR, CRP (inflammation, GCA), TSH, free T4/T3 (TED), HbA1c (diabetes), Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies, MuSK antibodies (Myasthenia Gravis), Lyme serology, ANA (autoimmune).

- **Imaging:** CT Orbit (orbital fracture, tumor, TED muscle enlargement), MRI Brain/Orbit (cranial nerve palsies, aneurysm, tumor, demyelination, inflammation, brainstem lesions). Consider MRA/CTA for vascular pathology (aneurysm).
- **Electrophysiology:** Tensilon test (edrophonium) or Ice Pack Test for Myasthenia Gravis, Single-Fiber EMG.
- **Neurology/Endocrinology Consults:** For systemic or neurological causes.

sections.title: 10. Staging / Grading (of Underlying Causes)
sections.content:
While diplopia itself isn't staged, the underlying causes often have established classification systems. For example:
*   **Cataract:** Graded by LOCS III (Lens Opacities Classification System III) based on type (nuclear, cortical, posterior subcapsular) and severity.
*   **Thyroid Eye Disease (TED):** Classified by the NOSPECS classification (N=No signs/symptoms, O=Only signs, S=Soft tissue involvement, P=Proptosis, E=Extraocular muscle involvement, C=Corneal involvement, S=Sight loss). Diplopia falls under 'E' (Extraocular muscle involvement).
*   **Cranial Nerve Palsies:** Classified by etiology (e.g., microvascular, compressive, inflammatory). Severity can be graded by degree of motility restriction or deviation angle.

sections.title: 11. Management & Treatment Strategy
content: **Step 1: Treat the Underlying Cause:** This is paramount. E.g., Cataract extraction for cataract-induced monocular diplopia; Thyroid management for TED; Aneurysm clipping for CN III palsy.
**Step 2: Optical Management (for Residual/Stable Diplopia):**
- **Pinhole:** A temporary diagnostic aid, but can be a simple fix for mild monocular diplopia.

- **Prism Correction:** Fresnel prisms (temporary, stick-on) for changing deviations or diagnostic trials; Ground-in prisms (permanent) for stable deviations, often limited to ~10-15 prism diopters per eye.
- **Occlusion:** Patching one eye (full or partial/frosted lens) can eliminate diplopia but sacrifices peripheral vision/stereoacuity. Often used as a temporary measure or for intractable diplopia.
**Step 3: Pharmacological Management:**
- **Steroids:** Systemic (e.g., prednisone) for inflammatory conditions like orbital myositis or acute TED. Pulse methylprednisolone for severe cases.
- **Immunosuppressants:** For autoimmune conditions like Myasthenia Gravis (e.g., pyridostigmine, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil).
- **Botulinum Toxin Injection (Botox):** For selected cases of small-angle strabismus, partially paretic muscles, or ocular muscle spasms. Effective for 3-6 months.
- **Targeted Biologics:** Teprotumumab for moderate-to-severe active Thyroid Eye Disease.
**Step 4: Surgical Intervention:**
- **Strabismus Surgery:** Recession/resection of extraocular muscles to realign eyes. Adjustable sutures can be used for fine-tuning.
- **Cataract Surgery:** Phacoemulsification with IOL implantation.
- **Orbital Surgery:** Orbital decompression for severe TED proptosis or compressive optic neuropathy; Orbital tumor excision; Blow-out fracture repair.

sections.title: 12. Surgical Techniques for Diplopia Management
content: **Cataract Extraction (Phacoemulsification):** Standard procedure for lenticular monocular diplopia. Involves removing the clouded lens and implanting an intraocular lens (IOL).

**Strabismus Surgery:** Performed for binocular diplopia when deviation is stable. Procedures include recession (weakening) or resection (strengthening) of extraocular muscles (e.g., medial rectus recession for esotropia). Adjustable sutures allow for post-operative fine-tuning.

**Orbital Decompression:** Surgical removal of orbital bone or fat to increase orbital volume, primarily for severe proptosis and compressive optic neuropathy in Thyroid Eye Disease. This can indirectly improve diplopia by relieving muscle restriction.
**Ptosis Repair:** For significant ptosis associated with CN III palsy or Myasthenia Gravis, often combined with strabismus surgery, especially if vision is obstructed.

sections.title: 13. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Persistent Diplopia:** Even with treatment, some patients may have residual double vision, especially in complex neurological cases.
**Amblyopia (in children):** If strabismus is present from a young age, the child may suppress one image, leading to 'lazy eye' and permanent vision loss if not treated early.
**Abnormal Head Posture:** Patients may adopt a compensatory head turn or tilt to achieve single vision, leading to neck pain.
**Psychological Impact:** Diplopia can be debilitating, affecting reading, driving, work, and overall quality of life, leading to anxiety and depression.

**Prognosis:** Highly variable. Good for simple causes like cataract. Less predictable for chronic neurological conditions or progressive autoimmune diseases. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial for better outcomes.

sections.title: 14. RED FLAGS: Emergency Diplopia
content: **Acute onset binocular diplopia with severe headache & pain:** Suggests potential subarachnoid hemorrhage or aneurysm (especially if CN III palsy with pupil involvement).
**Diplopia with pupillary involvement:** (especially a dilated pupil) in CN III palsy is an oculomotor emergency (posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise).
**Diplopia with other neurological deficits:** (e.g., hemiparesis, dysarthria, ataxia, numbness, vision loss) indicates brainstem or widespread CNS involvement (stroke, tumor, demyelination).

**Diplopia with temporal headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, vision loss:** Suspect Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), requires immediate high-dose steroid treatment to prevent permanent blindness.
**Diplopia with rapidly progressive proptosis, vision loss, chemosis, pain:** Suggests orbital cellulitis or orbital inflammatory syndrome.
**Diplopia with sudden, severe, unexplained vision loss (monocular or binocular):** Always a red flag, requires urgent neuro-ophthalmological assessment.

sections.title: 16. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a pinhole test for any patient complaining of diplopia to quickly differentiate monocular from binocular.
In monocular diplopia, if the pinhole test doesn't resolve it, suspect retinal pathology (e.g., epiretinal membrane) or multiple pupillary apertures.
Vertical diplopia is often more bothersome and frequently points to CN IV palsy or restrictive thyroid eye disease.
A pupil-sparing CN III palsy in an elderly diabetic/hypertensive patient is often microvascular and may resolve spontaneously within 3-6 months.
Any acute, painful CN III palsy with pupil involvement is an emergency – immediate neuroimaging (CTA/MRA) to rule out aneurysm is crucial.
Variable diplopia that worsens with fatigue or sustained gaze strongly suggests Myasthenia Gravis.

sections.title: 17. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Teprotumumab for Thyroid Eye Disease (TED):** The OPTIC trial (2019) demonstrated significant improvement in proptosis and diplopia in active TED patients treated with teprotumumab, an IGF-1R inhibitor, revolutionizing TED management.

**Advanced Neuroimaging:** High-resolution MRI (e.g., 3T and 7T scanners) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) offer unprecedented detail for detecting subtle cranial nerve lesions, demyelination, and brainstem pathology.
**Customized Prism Design:** Sophisticated digital prism mapping and fabrication allow for more precise and comfortable prism correction, especially for complex or non-comitant deviations.

**AI in Diagnostic Imaging:** Emerging AI tools are assisting in automated detection of subtle macular pathology on OCT and early signs of neurological disease on MRI, potentially aiding earlier diagnosis of monocular and binocular diplopia causes.

sections.title: 18. Pediatric & Special Population Considerations
content: **Pediatrics:** Diplopia in children is rare; they often suppress one image, leading to amblyopia. Look for abnormal head posture, eye rubbing, or reduced vision. Causes include congenital strabismus, refractive errors, trauma, or rarely, brain tumors/hydrocephalus.
**Elderly:** More susceptible to microvascular cranial nerve palsies (due to diabetes, hypertension), Giant Cell Arteritis, cataracts, and decompensated phorias. GCA must always be considered.
**Pregnant Women:** Can experience transient diplopia due to hormonal changes, gestational hypertension, or rarely, pituitary apoplexy.

**Post-Surgical Patients:** Monocular diplopia post-cataract surgery (IOL decentration, edge glare, residual astigmatism) or binocular diplopia post-strabismus surgery (over/undercorrection, restrictive scarring).

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: FECD is a bilateral, slowly progressive, primary non-inflammatory dystrophy of the corneal endothelium characterized by the development of guttata (excrescences of Descemet membrane). Pathophysiologically, endothelial pump failure leads to stromal and epithelial edema. Surgical trauma in these eyes exacerbates the loss of endothelial cells (ECs), potentially triggering bullous keratopathy.

rows: Assess ECD (cells/mm²) and CV (coefficient of variation). <800 cells/mm² is high risk.
Baseline central corneal thickness (>640µm suggests decompensation).
Visualizing guttae severity and stromal edema depth.
Assess glare/haze severity (often worse in AM due to nocturnal lid closure).

sections.title: Surgical 'Red Flags'
content: Pre-existing stromal haze: Avoid phacoemulsification alone if >640µm thickness.
High endothelial cell loss during phaco: Excess fluid usage is dangerous.
Posterior synechiae: Increases risk of rupture during endothelial dissection.
Intraocular Pressure Spikes: Post-op IOP control is mandatory to prevent graft detachment.

sections.title: Intraoperative Precautions
content: Step 1: Use high-viscosity dispersive OVD (e.g., Viscoat) to coat the endothelium thoroughly.
Step 2: Maintain a deep anterior chamber; perform 'soft-shell' technique to protect the endothelium.
Step 3: Minimize phaco-time; utilize horizontal chop to reduce total ultrasound energy (CDE).
Step 4: Keep instruments away from the central 4-5mm zone of the endothelium.
Step 5: Perform aggressive irrigation/aspiration of OVD post-phaco to prevent IOP spikes.

content.explanation: S - Surrender the ultrasound energy (Minimize CDE); S - Shield the endothelium (Dispersive OVD); S - Steady the pressure (Post-op IOP management).

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: DMEK is now the gold standard over DSAEK due to lower rejection and better visual recovery.
Rho-kinase (ROCK) inhibitors (e.g., Ripasudil) are being investigated to promote endothelial survival.
DSAEK/DMEK in 'triple procedures' (Phaco + Keratoplasty) reduces surgical burden on the patient.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Bullous keratopathy (BK) refers to a chronic, progressive corneal edema caused by dysfunction or loss of corneal endothelial cells. This leads to a failure of the endothelial pump mechanism, resulting in excessive fluid accumulation within the corneal stroma and epithelium. Clinically, it manifests as epithelial microcysts, bullae, and eventual subepithelial fibrosis, causing significant vision impairment and ocular discomfort.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Risk Factors
content: Incidence: Varies globally; Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (PBK) is a leading indication for corneal transplantation worldwide, accounting for 20-30% of penetrating keratoplasties and 50-60% of endothelial keratoplasties.
Prevalence: Increases with age due to age-related endothelial cell loss and prevalence of cataract surgery.
Risk Factors:
Intraocular Surgery: Cataract extraction (especially complicated cases, prolonged phaco time, posterior capsular rupture, vitreous loss, anterior chamber IOLs, retained lens fragments).
Fuchs' Endothelial Dystrophy (FED): Pre-existing endothelial disease.
Intraocular Lens (IOL) Factors: Malpositioned IOLs, haptic-endothelium touch, IOL subluxation/dislocation.
Trauma: Direct endothelial damage, chemical injury.
Glaucoma: Chronic high intraocular pressure, glaucoma surgery (e.g., trabeculectomy with bleb-cornea touch), acute angle closure.
Uveitis: Chronic inflammation affecting endothelium.
Hereditary: Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED).

sections.title: 3. Etiology & Pathophysiology: The Endothelial Pump Failure

branches: Loss of Endothelial Cells (e.g., age, trauma, surgery)
Inflow > Outflow of Aqueous into Stroma
Result: Stromal & Epithelial Edema → Bullae Formation

rows: Corneal edema following cataract surgery with IOL implantation.
Surgical trauma, IOL-endothelium touch, pre-existing subclinical FED.
Corneal edema following cataract surgery without IOL implantation (historical, less common).
Surgical trauma, absence of protective IOL, pre-existing endothelial issues.

Genetic predisposition (e.g., TCF4 gene), age-related endothelial cell loss.

Trauma, uveitis, glaucoma, CHED, chemical injury.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Patient Symptoms
content: Gradual decline in vision (especially in mornings due to epithelial edema, clearing throughout day).
Ocular pain (due to bullae rupture, exposure of nerve endings).
Photophobia (light sensitivity).
Foreign body sensation.
Epiphora (tearing).
Halos around lights.
Redness (secondary inflammation or infection).

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings (Slit-Lamp)
content: Epithelium:
Microcystic edema (fine refractile dots).
Epithelial bullae (fluid-filled blisters), often rupturing to form erosions.
Subepithelial fibrosis (in chronic cases, grey-white opacities).
Stroma:
Stromal edema (thickened cornea, loss of transparency, stromal folds).
Descemet's folds (vertical or horizontal wrinkles).
Endothelium:
Cornea guttae (Fuchs' dystrophy, seen as 'beaten bronze' appearance).
Reduced endothelial cell density (difficult to appreciate clinically without specular microscopy).
Other:
Mild anterior chamber reaction (if associated with inflammation).
Stromal neovascularization (rare, in chronic cases with severe inflammation).
IOL position and integrity (for PBK).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic History & Exam: Assess visual acuity, pain, photophobia. Slit-lamp exam to evaluate corneal layers, IOP, IOL status.
Step 2: Corneal Pachymetry: Measures corneal thickness (CCT). Edematous corneas are significantly thicker (>600 µm, normal 500-550 µm).
Step 3: Specular Microscopy/Confocal Microscopy:
Specular Microscopy: Quantifies endothelial cell density (ECD) and analyzes cell morphology (polymegathism, pleomorphism). ECD <1000 cells/mm² is often a critical threshold for developing edema.
Confocal Microscopy: Provides in-vivo imaging of all corneal layers, including endothelial cells, to assess morphology and identify guttae.

Step 4: Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT): Visualizes corneal edema, epithelial and stromal thickening, presence of bullae, and Descemet's membrane abnormalities. Useful for pre-operative planning for endothelial keratoplasty.
Step 5: Fundus Examination: Rule out other posterior segment pathology, especially if vision loss is disproportionate.

rows: Sudden, painful vision loss in a known keratoconus patient; rupture of Descemet's, severe stromal edema, sometimes white scar. Usually unilateral and acute.
Tends to resolve over weeks-months with topical steroids, cycloplegics; often requires PKP later.
Pain, redness, discharge, epithelial defect with stromal infiltrate, sometimes hypopyon. Culture positive.
Aggressive antimicrobial therapy. May progress to perforation.
Posterior Polymorphous Dystrophy (PPMD), Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED). Characteristic slit-lamp signs (vesicles, band-like lesions in PPMD, diffuse haziness in CHED).
Specific genetic testing for CHED. Endothelial keratoplasty for advanced cases.
History of exposure, limbal ischemia, corneal opacification, inflammation.
Emergency irrigation, steroids, amniotic membrane, limbal stem cell transplant.
Presence of anterior chamber inflammation (cells, flare, keratic precipitates).
Treat underlying uveitis with steroids, cycloplegics.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Progression of Bullous Keratopathy
content: Stage 1: Mild Edema
Subclinical endothelial dysfunction.
Slight increase in corneal thickness (measured by pachymetry).
Early guttae formation (in FED).
Morning vision fluctuation.
Stage 2: Epithelial Microcysts & Bullae
Visible epithelial edema and microcysts.
Small, fragile epithelial bullae.
Moderate vision reduction, mild discomfort.
Stage 3: Ruptured Bullae & Persistent Epithelial Erosions
Recurrent episodes of bullae rupture leading to painful erosions.
Increased photophobia, foreign body sensation.
Risk of secondary infection.
Stage 4: Subepithelial Fibrosis & Scarring
Chronic inflammation and healing leads to subepithelial scarring.
Reduced transparency, irreversible vision loss.
Pain may lessen if nerve endings become scarred, but vision remains poor.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Algorithm
content: Step 1: Conservative/Medical Management (for mild-moderate symptoms or temporary relief):
Hypertonic Saline: Topical 5% NaCl drops (e.g., Muro 128) 4-6 times daily, ointment at night. Draws fluid from cornea by osmosis.
Bandage Contact Lens (BCL): Therapeutic BCLs provide pain relief by protecting exposed nerve endings from ruptured bullae; changed regularly (e.g., weekly or bi-weekly).
Topical Steroids: Low-dose prednisolone acetate 1% or fluorometholone 0.1% qid for short periods if significant inflammation is present, but judicious use due to steroid-induced IOP rise.
IOP Control: If secondary glaucoma, topical anti-glaucoma medications (e.g., timolol, brimonidine, prostaglandin analogues) as needed.
Pain Relief: Oral NSAIDs or topical diclofenac/ketorolac.
Step 2: Surgical Management (for severe symptoms, persistent pain, or significant vision loss):
Endothelial Keratoplasty (EK):

DMEK (Descemet's Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty): Preferred for Fuchs' and PBK due to superior visual outcomes, faster recovery, and lower rejection rates. Involves selective transplantation of Descemet's membrane and endothelium.

DSAEK/DSEK (Descemet's Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty): Involves transplantation of Descemet's membrane, endothelium, and a thin layer of posterior stroma. Easier technically than DMEK, good visual outcomes.

Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): Full-thickness corneal transplant. Reserved for cases with significant stromal scarring, peripheral involvement, or when EK is not suitable (e.g., very thin corneas, complex anterior segment).
Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT): Can be used for persistent epithelial defects or pain control in severe cases, but not a definitive treatment for edema.
Step 3: Advanced & Experimental Treatments:
Rho-kinase (ROCK) inhibitors (e.g., Netarsudil, Ripasudil) – promotes endothelial cell migration and proliferation.
Corneal endothelial cell injection therapy.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Endothelial Keratoplasty Focus
content: DMEK (Descemet's Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty):
Step 1: Donor Preparation: A very thin (10-15 µm) Descemet's membrane with endothelium is peeled from a cadaveric donor cornea. Often pre-stripped ('pre-DMEK').
Step 2: Recipient Preparation: The diseased Descemet's membrane is stripped from the recipient cornea (Descemetorhexis) through a small limbal incision (2.4-3.0mm).
Step 3: Graft Insertion: The scrolled donor graft is inserted into the anterior chamber via an injector.

Step 4: Graft Unfurling & Attachment: The graft is carefully unfurled and positioned centrally, then secured against the host stroma using an anterior chamber air bubble. Patient remains supine for a few hours post-op.
DSAEK/DSEK (Descemet's Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty):
Step 1: Donor Preparation: A microkeratome or femtosecond laser is used to create a posterior stromal lamellar graft (100-200 µm thick) from a donor cornea.
Step 2: Recipient Preparation: Recipient Descemet's membrane is stripped.
Step 3: Graft Insertion: The thicker donor lenticule is folded or inserted via an injector into the anterior chamber.
Step 4: Graft Attachment: An air bubble is used to secure the graft. Less prone to folding than DMEK.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: Complications of EK (DMEK/DSAEK):
Graft detachment (most common, requires re-bubbling: ~5-15%).
Graft rejection (lower with DMEK/DSAEK than PKP, ~1-5%).
Primary graft failure (due to poor donor quality or surgical trauma).
Infection (endophthalmitis, rare).
Pupillary block glaucoma (due to air bubble).
IOP spikes.
Cataract progression.
Complications of PKP:
Graft rejection (higher, ~10-20%).
Astigmatism (significant, often requiring rigid gas permeable lenses).
Infection, glaucoma, suture-related complications.

Prognosis: Excellent with successful EK; most patients achieve 20/40 or better vision. PKP also has good outcomes but longer visual recovery and higher complication rates. Untreated, BK leads to chronic pain and severe vision loss.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Sudden, severe increase in pain or vision loss post-operatively (suggests acute graft detachment, infection, or pupillary block).
Presence of purulent discharge or significant anterior chamber inflammation (suggests endophthalmitis or severe infection).
Progressive corneal opacification despite treatment (may indicate advanced disease or treatment failure).
Acute, painful red eye with reduced vision in a patient with a BCL (consider contact lens-related infection/ulcer).

content.explanation: Fuchs' Dystrophy, Aphakic/Pseudophakic Keratopathy, Trauma (surgical, chemical), Hydrops (acute), Endothelialitis (inflammatory), Raised IOP (glaucoma)

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls for Bullous Keratopathy
content: Morning blurry vision that improves during the day is a hallmark symptom due to overnight accumulation of epithelial edema.
Corneal pachymetry is a simple, non-invasive tool to objectively monitor corneal edema.
Specular microscopy is crucial for pre-operative assessment of endothelial cell health and guiding surgical decisions.
DMEK offers faster visual recovery and lower rejection rates compared to DSAEK and PKP, making it the preferred choice for suitable cases.
Persistent epithelial defects in BK are painful and increase the risk of infectious keratitis; BCLs and hypertonic saline are essential for management.
Always check IOL position in PBK to rule out haptic-endothelium touch or IOL subluxation.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Future Directions
content: Rho-Kinase (ROCK) Inhibitors: Topical Ripasudil (approved in Japan for FED) and Netarsudil (approved for glaucoma, shows promise in stimulating endothelial cell proliferation and adhesion, especially in FED). Currently off-label use for BK.

Corneal Endothelial Cell Injection Therapy: Cultured human corneal endothelial cells (HCECs) injected into the anterior chamber, often with a ROCK inhibitor, to repopulate the endothelium. Clinical trials underway (e.g., Shirasawa et al. in Japan). This represents a potential paradigm shift from transplantation to regeneration.
Ultrathin DSAEK (UT-DSAEK): Further reduction of graft thickness improves visual outcomes, bridging the gap towards DMEK.
Femtosecond Laser-Assisted EK: Potential for more precise and reproducible graft preparation.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
sections.content:
Bullous keratopathy is rare in the pediatric population. When present, it is typically associated with:

Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED): A bilateral, genetically inherited condition causing corneal clouding from birth or early infancy. Requires early PKP or EK (DMEK possible even in children) for visual rehabilitation.
Complicated Pediatric Cataract Surgery: Although rare, severe surgical trauma in an infant eye can lead to endothelial decompensation.
Trauma: Especially chemical injuries.
Glaucoma: Uncontrolled congenital glaucoma can lead to corneal edema.

Management in children requires careful consideration of amblyopia prevention and appropriate anesthetic and surgical techniques suitable for smaller eyes.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Bullous Keratopathy (BK) is a pathological condition characterized by the formation of epithelial bullae (blisters) resulting from chronic corneal edema. This occurs when the corneal endothelial cell density falls below a critical threshold (typically <500 cells/mm²), failing to maintain the cornea's relative state of dehydration (deturgescence). It is most commonly seen following cataract surgery (PBK) or as the end-stage of Fuchs' Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD).

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Pump vs. Leak Mechanism
content: Step 1: Endothelial cell loss due to surgical trauma, genetic dystrophy, or high IOP.
Step 2: Failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase 'pump' mechanism and breakdown of 'leaky' tight junctions.
Step 3: Aqueous humor enters the corneal stroma, causing significant swelling (Stromal Edema).
Step 4: Fluid migrates anteriorly through Bowman’s layer into the epithelium.
Step 5: Formation of subepithelial and intraepithelial bullae (blisters).
Step 6: Bullae rupture, exposing corneal nerves and causing intense pain and photophobia.

branches: Glaucoma: Acute high IOP, ICE Syndrome

rows: Very high IOP, mid-dilated pupil, shallow AC
Disciform edema, decreased sensation, keratic precipitates

sections.title: Clinical Features: Symptoms & Signs
content: Symptoms: Reduced visual acuity (worse in the morning), foreign body sensation.
Symptoms: Excruciating pain and tearing upon bullae rupture.
Signs: Epithelial microcystic edema and frank bullae.
Signs: Stromal thickening and Descemet’s folds (striate keratopathy).
Signs: Subepithelial haze/fibrosis in chronic cases.
Signs: Presence of AC-IOL or vitreous in the anterior chamber (in PBK).

rows: Epithelial separation, mapping of corneal thickness
Sclerotic scatter to view subtle microcystic edema

content.explanation: P: Pleomorphism (Shape change), U: Ultra-low cell count (<500), M: Morning blurring (classic sign), P: Pachymetry (>640 um).

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Hypertonic Saline: 5% NaCl (Muro 128) drops 4-6x daily and ointment at bedtime.
IOP Control: Beta-blockers or CAIs (Avoid Prostaglandins to minimize inflammation).
Bandage Contact Lens (BCL): For pain relief in cases of ruptured bullae.
Lubrication: Preservative-free artificial tears.
Hair Dryer Technique: Warm air (arm's length) to evaporate surface moisture in the morning.

branches: DMEK: Descemet Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty (Gold Standard)
DSAEK: Descemet Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (Thicker tissue)
PKP: Penetrating Keratoplasty (If significant stromal scarring is present)
Gundersen Flap: For pain relief in eyes with no visual potential
DSO: Descemet Stripping Only (For central Fuchs' with good peripheral cells)

sections.title: DMEK Surgical Steps
content: Step 1: Donor membrane preparation (8-9mm DM/Endothelium strip).
Step 2: Recipient Descemetorhexis under air or viscoelastic.
Step 3: Insertion of donor roll using a glass injector (e.g., Geuder).
Step 4: Centering and unrolling using 'tapping' techniques (Melles or Dirisamer).
Step 5: Air or SF6 gas tamponade to adhere the graft.
Step 6: Post-operative supine positioning for 24-72 hours.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Signs
content: Sudden vision loss and redness (Endophthalmitis or Graft Rejection)
Severe eye pain after BCL insertion (Possible infectious crystalline keratopathy)
IOP 'Spike' post-op (Pupillary block from air bubble)
Primary Graft Failure (Cornea remains thick and hazy after 2 weeks)

sections.title: Recent Advances: ROCK Inhibitors
content: Rho-kinase (ROCK) Inhibitors: Ripasudil/Netarsudil drops used to promote endothelial cell migration.
Endothelial Cell Injections: Cultured endothelial cells injected into the AC with the patient face-down (Kinoshita et al).
Descemet Stripping Only (DSO): Stripping central 4mm to allow peripheral cells to migrate inwards (no graft needed).
Synthetic Corneas: Evolution of keratoprosthesis (K-Pro) for multiple graft failures.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always rule out high IOP as a cause of corneal edema before diagnosing primary BK.
Specular microscopy is unreliable when the cornea is too thick (>650um) due to light scatter.
Avoid Prostaglandin Analogs (PGAs) in Fuchs' patients post-op as they may increase CME risk.
In PBK with a stable ACIOL, DSAEK is often preferred over DMEK due to easier graft manipulation.

sections.title: Definition & Overview: Mohs Micrographic Surgery (MMS)
sections.content: Mohs Micrographic Surgery (MMS) is a highly specialized, precise surgical technique used to remove skin cancer. It involves excising thin layers of cancerous tissue sequentially, with each layer immediately examined microscopically for cancer cells. The process continues until all margins are clear of cancer, allowing for maximum conservation of healthy tissue, particularly crucial in anatomically sensitive areas like the ocular adnexa. Developed by Dr. Frederic Mohs, it relies on complete circumferential peripheral and deep margin assessment (CCPDMA) through horizontal sectioning of excised tissue.

sections.title: Definition & Overview: Frozen Section (FS)
sections.content: Frozen section (FS) biopsy is a rapid intraoperative diagnostic method used to assess surgical margins during tumor excision. A tissue sample is rapidly frozen, sectioned using a cryostat, stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), and then immediately examined by a pathologist. While it provides quick feedback, standard frozen section typically involves vertical sectioning of selected margins, which offers less comprehensive margin control compared to MMS, especially for complex or infiltrating tumors. It's often used for initial diagnosis or confirmation of clear margins in less complex resections.

sections.title: Core Comparison: MMS vs. Standard Frozen Section

Smaller, low-risk tumors, initial diagnosis, confirmation of clear margins for benign lesions or low-risk malignancies.

Can be used on any site, but less suitable for complex/high-risk areas.
