sections.title: Epidemiology of Ocular Adnexal Malignancies
content: **Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC):** Accounts for ~90% of eyelid malignancies. Most common on lower eyelid, followed by medial canthus, upper eyelid, and lateral canthus. Incidence increases with age and UV exposure.
**Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC):** Second most common, ~5-10% of eyelid cancers. More aggressive than BCC, with higher metastatic potential (especially periorbital SCC).

**Sebaceous Gland Carcinoma (SGC):** Rare but highly malignant (1-5% of eyelid cancers), often mimicking chalazion or chronic blepharoconjunctivitis, leading to delayed diagnosis. High mortality if not completely excised.
**Melanoma:** Rare on eyelids (<1% of all skin melanomas), but highly aggressive with poor prognosis. Often arising from nevi or de novo.
The need for precise margin control techniques like MMS or FS is driven by the desire to minimize recurrence and preserve vital ocular function and aesthetics in these delicate areas.

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology: The Principle of Margin Control
sections.content: The fundamental principle underpinning both MMS and FS is the complete removal of malignant tissue while preserving as much surrounding healthy tissue as possible. Skin cancers, particularly those with aggressive subtypes or located in anatomically complex areas like the ocular adnexa, can have 'subclinical' extensions that are not visible to the naked eye. These extensions can spread laterally, deeply, or along nerves (perineural invasion). Failure to remove these extensions results in positive surgical margins and high rates of local recurrence. The objective is to achieve 'clear margins' – microscopic evidence that the tumor has been completely excised, thereby minimizing the risk of recurrence and potential metastasis.

sections.title: Mohs Surgery: The Procedure Step-by-Step
content: **Step 1: Clinical Assessment & Pre-operative Biopsy** — Confirm diagnosis of skin cancer (e.g., BCC, SCC, SGC) with a diagnostic punch or excisional biopsy. Mark tumor borders clinically.

**Step 2: Local Anesthesia & Initial Debulking** — Inject local anesthetic (e.g., 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine) around the tumor. Grossly visible tumor is often debulked with a curette or scalpel, without concern for margins at this stage.

**Step 3: First Excision (Mohs Layer)** — A thin, saucer-shaped layer of tissue is excised with a specialized Mohs scalpel, angling the blade to obtain a specimen with a 'beveled' edge. This excision typically extends 1-2mm beyond the clinical tumor margins.

**Step 4: Specimen Orientation & Mapping** — The excised tissue is marked with dyes (e.g., blue for superior, yellow for inferior) to orient it geographically to the patient and the wound bed. A precise map (drawing) of the tissue and wound is created.

**Step 5: Tissue Processing & Sectioning** — The specimen is rapidly frozen in a cryostat, then meticulously sectioned horizontally (parallel to the skin surface) by a Mohs histotechnician. This allows for 100% of the peripheral and deep margins to be visualized on one or more slides.

**Step 6: Staining & Microscopic Examination** — Slides are stained (typically with H&E, sometimes Toluidine Blue for rapid contrast) and immediately examined by the Mohs surgeon (who is also a trained dermatopathologist). The surgeon systematically checks all margins for residual cancer cells.

**Step 7: Re-excision (If Needed)** — If cancer cells are identified at any margin, the exact location is marked on the surgeon's map. The surgeon then returns to the patient and removes another layer of tissue *only* from the area where cancer was detected, preserving healthy tissue. Steps 3-7 are repeated.

**Step 8: Margin Clearance & Reconstruction** — Once all margins are confirmed clear, the surgical defect is closed. Reconstruction (primary closure, flap, graft) is performed, often by the Mohs surgeon or an oculoplastic surgeon, considering functional and aesthetic outcomes.

sections.title: Frozen Section: The Procedure Step-by-Step
content: **Step 1: Excision of Tumor** — The surgeon excises the tumor with a margin of clinically healthy tissue (often 3-5mm).
**Step 2: Specimen Orientation** — The excised tissue may be oriented with sutures or ink markings to indicate margins.
**Step 3: Sample Submission to Pathology** — The specimen is sent immediately to the pathology lab.

**Step 4: Rapid Freezing & Sectioning** — In the lab, the tissue is quickly frozen in a cryostat, then sectioned. Typically, vertical sections are taken from specific inked margins of the excised block.
**Step 5: Staining & Microscopic Examination** — The sections are stained with H&E and examined by a general pathologist.
**Step 6: Pathologist Report** — The pathologist reports whether the selected margins are clear or positive for tumor. This usually takes 15-30 minutes.

**Step 7: Surgical Decision** — Based on the pathologist's report, the surgeon decides whether to re-excise additional tissue if margins are positive, or to proceed with reconstruction if margins are clear.

rows: Horizontal (en face) sections, allowing for 100% margin evaluation.
Vertical sections from selected margins; tumor periphery often not entirely evaluated.
Multiple small blocks taken from a single layer, mapped precisely.
Usually one or few larger blocks of the excised tumor with margins.
Complete 3D visualization of peripheral and deep margins from the entire excised tissue layer.
Limited visualization of margins due to 'bread-loafing' effect, potentially missing tumor foci between sections.
Real-time, iterative process influencing surgical steps immediately.
Single assessment of submitted margins; delay in further excision if needed.

sections.title: Ocular Adnexal Applications of Frozen Section
Advantages of Mohs Micrographic Surgery
content: **Highest Cure Rates:** Reported cure rates up to 99% for primary BCC/SCC, and 94-96% for recurrent tumors, significantly outperforming other methods for high-risk lesions.
**Maximal Tissue Preservation:** Spares the maximum amount of healthy tissue, crucial for maintaining function (e.g., eyelid closure, tear drainage) and cosmesis in the periorbital region.
**Precision & Accuracy:** 100% microscopic margin control ensures all cancer roots are identified and removed.
**Cost-Effectiveness (Long-Term):** Higher initial cost but reduced recurrence rates mean fewer re-operations, potentially lower overall healthcare costs in the long run.
**Reduced Scarring:** Smaller defects due to tissue preservation often lead to better aesthetic outcomes.
**Single Visit Procedure:** Diagnosis, excision, and immediate reconstruction (often) completed in one visit.

sections.title: Disadvantages of Mohs Micrographic Surgery
content: **Time-Consuming:** Can take several hours or even a full day, depending on tumor size and number of stages.
**Costly (Initial):** Higher facility and professional fees compared to conventional excision or FS.
**Limited Availability:** Requires highly specialized Mohs surgeons and dedicated cryostat technicians, not universally available.
**Patient Anxiety:** Prolonged waiting between stages can be stressful for patients.
**Not Ideal for All Cancers:** Less suitable for diffuse tumors (e.g., Paget's disease, melanoma in situ) or tumors requiring deep, wide excisions where tissue preservation is not the primary goal.
**Potential for Artifacts:** Freezing artifacts can occasionally make microscopic interpretation challenging.

sections.title: Advantages of Standard Frozen Section
content: **Speed:** Rapid diagnosis and margin assessment, usually within 15-30 minutes.
**Wider Availability:** Most hospitals with pathology departments can perform frozen sections.
**Cost-Effective:** Generally less expensive than Mohs surgery for initial excisions.
**Confirms Diagnosis:** Can confirm the presence of malignancy or benignity intraoperatively.
**Surgical Flexibility:** Allows a general surgeon or oculoplastic surgeon to perform the excision with rapid pathological feedback.

sections.title: Disadvantages of Standard Frozen Section
content: **Less Comprehensive Margin Control:** Vertical sectioning of selected margins means only a fraction of the actual margin is evaluated, potentially missing skip lesions or microscopic extensions.
**Higher Recurrence Rates:** Due to less comprehensive margin control, recurrence rates for high-risk tumors are higher than MMS.
**Tissue Artifacts:** Freezing process can introduce artifacts (e.g., ice crystals, crush artifacts) that may hinder accurate diagnosis.
**Sampling Error:** The pathologist only examines the tissue submitted by the surgeon; if a positive margin isn't sampled, it won't be detected.
**Limitations for Certain Tumors:** Difficult for tumors with ill-defined borders, extensive perineural invasion, or multifocal growth patterns.
**Increased Tissue Excision:** To compensate for sampling error, surgeons may take larger initial margins, leading to greater tissue loss.

rows: Recurrent BCC/SCC, large (>2 cm) BCC/SCC, aggressive histologies (morpheaform, infiltrative, micronodular BCC; sclerosing, adenoid, desmoplastic SCC).
Eyelids (especially medial canthus), eyebrows, nose, lips, ears, digits, genitals – where tissue preservation is paramount.
Poorly defined clinical margins, rapid growth, perineural invasion, immunosuppressed patients, tumors arising in radiation-damaged skin or chronic ulcers.
Sebaceous gland carcinoma (especially ocular), Merkel cell carcinoma, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, extramammary Paget's disease (though controversial for diffuse disease).
Small (<1 cm), primary nodular BCC or well-differentiated SCC with clinically clear margins in non-critical areas.
To confirm malignancy or rule out benignity in suspicious lesions prior to definitive excision or complex reconstruction.
Excision of large benign lesions (e.g., papillomas, cysts) where complete removal is desired without extensive formal pathology.
Assessment of margins for orbital tumors or other deep structures where Mohs is not feasible.
Intraoperative assessment of sentinel lymph node status.

sections.title: Red Flags & Contraindications for MMS/FS
content: **MMS Not Ideal For:** Melanoma (standard treatment involves wide local excision with definitive paraffin-embedded sectioning, though controversial uses of modified Mohs for lentigo maligna exist). Lymphoma. Diffuse tumors like cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

**Frozen Section Limitations:** Not recommended for poorly differentiated tumors, tumors with significant desmoplasia, or those with very subtle cytological features (e.g., some spindle cell lesions, lymphoproliferative disorders), where freezing artifacts can obscure diagnosis.
**Patient Anticoagulation:** While not a contraindication, requires careful management of anticoagulants to minimize bleeding, especially in periorbital region.

**Inadequate Pathology Expertise:** Both techniques rely heavily on the expertise of the pathologist (Mohs surgeon or general pathologist). Inexperienced interpretation can lead to false negatives/positives.
**Active Infection:** Delay surgery until infection is controlled.
**Patient Factors:** Uncooperative patients, severe claustrophobia, or inability to tolerate prolonged supine position might preclude MMS.

sections.title: Complications of Ocular Adnexal Excision & Reconstruction
content: **Bleeding/Hematoma:** Common, especially in vascular areas like eyelids.
**Infection:** Risk with any surgical procedure; managed with antibiotics.
**Scarring/Deformity:** Ectropion, entropion, notching, web formation, especially after eyelid reconstruction.
**Tear Drainage Issues:** Damage to lacrimal system (puncta, canaliculi) can lead to epiphora (tearing).
**Visual Impairment:** Rare but possible if tumor extends to globe or optic nerve.
**Flap/Graft Necrosis:** Failure of reconstructive tissue.
**Recurrence:** Despite clear margins, local recurrence or metastasis can occur (lower with MMS).
**Neurological Deficits:** Damage to facial nerve branches (rare in superficial excision).

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-up After Margin-Controlled Excision
sections.content: With complete surgical excision (especially with MMS), the prognosis for most eyelid BCCs and SCCs is excellent. However, lifelong follow-up is essential due to the risk of local recurrence and the development of new primary skin cancers (field cancerization). Patients typically receive annual full-body skin exams by a dermatologist. For high-risk tumors (e.g., periorbital SCC with perineural invasion, SGC), more frequent follow-up (e.g., every 3-6 months for 2-5 years) with imaging (MRI) and regional lymph node examination may be warranted. Patient education on sun protection and self-skin exams is crucial.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls for Oculoplastic Surgeons
content: **Medial Canthus:** High recurrence rates and risk of orbital invasion, making MMS the preferred choice.

**Sebaceous Gland Carcinoma:** Often mimics benign lesions (chalazion, blepharitis). Consider biopsy of any chronic, recurrent, or suspicious eyelid lesion. FS is less reliable for SGC; MMS is often preferred due to its aggressive nature and pagetoid spread.

**Perineural Invasion (PNI):** Clinical signs include pain, numbness, motor deficits. PNI dramatically increases recurrence risk and mandates meticulous margin control, often favoring MMS or careful FS.
**Eyelid Reconstruction:** Always prioritize functional outcomes (protection of the globe, complete lid closure) over purely aesthetic ones. Maintain the lacrimal drainage system if possible.
**Immunosuppressed Patients:** Higher risk for multiple and more aggressive skin cancers; stricter indications for MMS and closer follow-up are needed.
**Biopsy Technique:** Incisional biopsy for larger lesions, shave or punch for smaller ones. Always ensure a representative sample for accurate diagnosis.

content.explanation:
R - Recurrent tumors
E - Esthetically/functionally critical areas (eyelids, nose, lips)
C - Large or high-risk Clinical features (indistinct borders, rapid growth)
L - Large tumors (>2 cm)
A - Aggressive histologies (morpheaform BCC, sclerosing SCC, desmoplastic SCC, SGC)
I - Immunosuppressed patients
M - Metastatic potential (SCC, Merkel cell carcinoma)

sections.title: Recent Advances & Future Directions
content: **Rapid Immunostaining:** Development of faster immunohistochemical stains for certain difficult-to-diagnose tumors (e.g., SGC, amelanotic melanoma) during MMS/FS.

**Non-Invasive Imaging:** Confocal microscopy and optical coherence tomography (OCT) are being explored for real-time, non-invasive margin assessment, potentially reducing the need for multiple surgical stages.
**Digital Pathology & AI:** Integration of digital pathology with artificial intelligence for enhanced and faster interpretation of slides, potentially aiding Mohs surgeons and pathologists.
**Improved Anesthesia & Pain Control:** Advancements in local anesthetic agents and techniques for patient comfort during prolonged procedures.

**Modified Mohs for Melanoma:** While controversial, modified slow Mohs or Mohs with immunostains (e.g., Melan-A, SOX10) is being explored for select cases of lentigo maligna with promising results in some centers.

sections.title: Pediatric & Special Population Considerations
sections.content: Skin cancers, though rare in children, can occur and often present with more aggressive features. Mohs surgery is generally safe and effective in pediatric patients, offering the same benefits of tissue preservation. Special considerations include managing anxiety, potential for general anesthesia for very young or uncooperative children, and long-term surveillance for syndromic associations (e.g., Gorlin syndrome). In immunosuppressed patients (e.g., organ transplant recipients, HIV+), skin cancers are more frequent, more aggressive, and have higher recurrence rates. For these individuals, MMS is often the preferred treatment for most non-melanoma skin cancers due to its superior margin control and lower recurrence rates, necessitating even more vigilant follow-up.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Neuroblastoma (NB) is the most common extracranial solid tumor in childhood, originating from neural crest cells of the sympathetic nervous system. It can manifest with paraneoplastic syndromes, notably Opsoclonus-Myoclonus Syndrome (OMS). Orbital Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common primary malignant orbital tumor in children, arising from primitive mesenchymal cells committed to skeletal muscle differentiation. Differentiation between these entities is crucial for timely and appropriate management.

sections.title: Epidemiology: Demographics & Incidence
content: **Neuroblastoma:** Accounts for 7-10% of all pediatric cancers. Median age at diagnosis is <2 years. 70-80% of children present with metastatic disease.
**Opsoclonus-Myoclonus Syndrome (OMS):** Very rare, affects 1 in 10,000,000 children. Associated with neuroblastoma in 2-3% of cases (most common paraneoplastic cause). 50% are idiopathic.

**Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS):** Accounts for 3-5% of all childhood cancers. Orbital RMS is the most common primary orbital malignancy in childhood (approx. 10% of all RMS). Median age at diagnosis 7-8 years, with a bimodal distribution (peaks at 1-5 years and 10-14 years). Slight male predominance.

branches.name: Neuroblastoma
sub_branches: Neural crest cell origin (sympathetic nervous system)
Genetic aberrations: MYCN amplification (poor prognosis, 20-25% of cases), 1p deletion, 17q gain

branches.name: Opsoclonus-Myoclonus Syndrome (OMS)
sub_branches: Paraneoplastic autoimmune response (most common in children: Neuroblastoma)
Antibody-mediated (anti-Ri/ANNA-2, anti-Hu, anti-CV2/CRMP5 - less specific for NB-OMS)
Cross-reactivity: Tumor antigens mimic neuronal antigens, causing immune attack on cerebellum/brainstem

branches.name: Rhabdomyosarcoma
sub_branches: Chromosomal translocations: t(2;13)(q35;q14) PAX3-FOXO1, t(1;13)(q25;q14) PAX7-FOXO1 (alveolar RMS)
Associations: NF1, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome

rows: **INSS (International Neuroblastoma Staging System):** Stage 1-4, 4S (special for infants). **INRGSS (International Neuroblastoma Risk Group Staging System):** Image-Defined Risk Factors (IDRFs), further refined into Low, Intermediate, High Risk groups based on stage, age, MYCN status, ploidy.
**Etiology-based:** Paraneoplastic (e.g., NB), Post-infectious, Post-vaccination, Toxic/Metabolic, Idiopathic. Often referred to as 'dancing eyes, dancing feet'.

**Histologic Subtypes:** 1. Embryonal RMS (60%, most common in orbit, better prognosis). 2. Alveolar RMS (20%, aggressive, PAX-FOXO1 fusion). 3. Pleomorphic RMS (rare in children, adults). 4. Spindle Cell/Sclerosing RMS (rare). **IRS Clinical Grouping:** Group I (completely resected), Group II (microscopic residual/regional nodes), Group III (gross residual), Group IV (metastatic).

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Neuroblastoma (Systemic):** Abdominal mass (most common), bone pain, fever, weight loss, constitutional symptoms. Paraneoplastic features: Diarrhea (VIPoma), Hypertension, Horner's syndrome (cervical sympathetic chain involvement).
**Neuroblastoma (Ocular/Orbital Metastasis):** Periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes') – pathognomonic, proptosis, lid edema, epibulbar mass, spontaneous orbital hemorrhage.

**Opsoclonus-Myoclonus Syndrome (OMS):** **Opsoclonus** (multidirectional, chaotic, conjugate, unpredictable, rapid saccades without intersaccadic pause – 'saccadomania'), Myoclonus (truncal, limb), Ataxia (cerebellar), Tremor, Encephalopathy (irritability, sleep disturbance, cognitive regression).

**Orbital Rhabdomyosarcoma:** Rapidly progressive, unilateral proptosis (weeks to months), ptosis, lid swelling, palpable mass (often superior-nasal), conjunctival injection/chemosis, globe displacement, ophthalmoplegia, pain (less common, suggests bony erosion).

rows: **Periorbital Ecchymosis:** Bruising around the eyes (classic for orbital metastasis). **Proptosis:** Usually unilateral, can be bilateral. **Horner's Syndrome:** (If cervical sympathetic chain involved) Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis (ipsilateral face). Fundoscopy typically normal unless optic nerve infiltration.

**Opsoclonus:** Involuntary, chaotic, multidirectional, high-amplitude, high-frequency, conjugate saccadic eye movements. Present during wakefulness and light sleep. Myoclonus of limbs/trunk. Ataxia on gait assessment. Nystagmus (less common, usually associated with intersaccadic oscillations).

**Rapid Onset Proptosis:** Hallmark feature. Unilateral, axial or non-axial globe displacement. **Palpable Mass:** Often firm, non-tender, in superior-nasal quadrant. **Lid Edema/Erythema:** Due to inflammation or tumor bulk. **Ophthalmoplegia:** Restricted ocular motility. **Vision Loss:** If optic nerve compressed/infiltrated. Slit-lamp exam usually normal anterior segment. Fundoscopy: Papilledema (rare), choroidal folds.

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Clinical Suspicion & Detailed History/Exam** (Age, onset, associated symptoms).

**Step 2: Initial Ocular Imaging** (For proptosis/orbital mass): Orbital CT with contrast (bony detail) and/or MRI with contrast (soft tissue detail, intracranial extension). Typical RMS: well-circumscribed, infiltrative mass, often enhancing. NB: more diffuse infiltration, sometimes lytic bone lesions.

**Step 3: Biopsy (For Orbital Mass):** Incisional biopsy for RMS (definitive diagnosis, histology, immunohistochemistry for desmin, myogenin, PAX3/7-FOXO1 fusion). Neuroblastoma orbital metastasis often diagnosed via primary tumor biopsy.

**Step 4: Neuroblastoma Workup (if suspected):**
    *   **Biochemical:** Urine catecholamines (VMA, HVA, dopamine) – elevated in >90% of NB.
    *   **Imaging:** MIBG scan (iodine-123 metaiodobenzylguanidine) for uptake in tumor cells; whole-body MRI; skeletal survey/bone scan.
    *   **Pathology:** Tumor biopsy (primary site or metastasis), bone marrow biopsy (iliac crest) for staging.
    *   **Molecular Genetics:** MYCN amplification, 1p deletion, 17q gain from tumor tissue.

**Step 5: OMS Workup (if suspected):**
    *   **Tumor Search:** Whole-body MRI, MIBG scan, abdominal ultrasound to rule out underlying neuroblastoma.
    *   **Neurological:** Brain MRI (may show cerebellar atrophy/inflammation, but often normal). CSF analysis (mild pleocytosis, increased protein, oligoclonal bands possible). Paraneoplastic antibody panel (anti-Ri, anti-Hu, anti-CV2/CRMP5, although often negative in NB-OMS).

rows: Acute to subacute (weeks-months), often with rapid progression of 'raccoon eyes'
Less common, but possible if large/invasive
Systemic: fevers, weight loss, abdominal mass, diarrhea (VIPoma), Horner's, Opsoclonus-Myoclonus (OMS)
Diffuse infiltration, bony erosions; MIBG+; primary tumor elsewhere
Well-circumscribed or infiltrative mass, iso/hyperdense on CT, enhances. No MIBG uptake.
Orbital cellulitis (diffuse inflammation), Hemangioma (flow voids), Lymphoma (molding)
Brain MRI (often normal in NB-OMS), tumor search
Neuroblastic cells (small round blue cells), Homer-Wright rosettes
Small round blue cells, rhabdomyoblasts, desmin/myogenin+
Orbital cellulitis, idiopathic orbital inflammation, pseudotumor

branches.name: Neuroblastoma
sub_branches: INRGSS (International Neuroblastoma Risk Group Staging System)

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment: Neuroblastoma
content: **Step 1: Risk Stratification:** Based on INRGSS (Low, Intermediate, High Risk).
**Step 2: Low-Risk Disease:** Observation, surgical resection (if amenable).
**Step 3: Intermediate-Risk Disease:** Chemotherapy (e.g., carboplatin, etoposide, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin) ± surgery ± radiation.

**Step 4: High-Risk Disease:** Intensive multimodal therapy.
    *   **Induction Chemotherapy:** High-dose (e.g., cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, cisplatin, etoposide) to shrink tumor.
    *   **Surgery:** Maximal safe resection of primary tumor.
    *   **Consolidation:** High-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell rescue.
    *   **Radiation Therapy:** To primary site and/or metastatic sites.
    *   **Maintenance Immunotherapy:** Dinutuximab (anti-GD2 monoclonal antibody) combined with GM-CSF, IL-2, and isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) for differentiation.

sections.title: 11. Management & Treatment: OMS
content: **Primary Goal:** Identify and treat the underlying neuroblastoma (tumor resection is crucial).

**Immunomodulation:**
    *   **Corticosteroids:** Prednisone (2 mg/kg/day initially, then taper). Often first-line.
    *   **Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG):** 1-2 g/kg/cycle, monthly.
    *   **Rituximab:** (Anti-CD20) for refractory cases.
    *   **Cyclophosphamide:** For severe, refractory cases.
    *   **ACTH:** Alternative to steroids.
**Symptomatic Management:** Physical therapy, occupational therapy for ataxia and myoclonus.

sections.title: 12. Management & Treatment: Rhabdomyosarcoma
content: **Step 1: Multimodal Approach:** Surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy.
**Step 2: Surgery:** Biopsy is essential for diagnosis. Debulking if technically feasible without significant morbidity. Complete resection is often difficult in orbital RMS.

**Step 3: Chemotherapy:** Primary treatment modality. Standard regimen includes Vincristine, Dactinomycin, Cyclophosphamide (VAC regimen) or Ifosfamide, Etoposide (IE regimen). Duration typically 6-12 months.

**Step 4: Radiation Therapy:** Essential for local control, especially for incompletely resected tumors (Group II/III) or alveolar subtype. Proton beam therapy preferred to minimize damage to ocular structures.

sections.title: 13. Complications & Prognosis
content:
**Neuroblastoma:**
    *   **Complications:** Metastasis (bone, bone marrow, liver, lymph nodes), spinal cord compression (neurological deficits), long-term effects of chemotherapy/radiation (cardiotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, secondary malignancies).
    *   **Prognosis:** Highly variable. Low-risk NB has excellent prognosis (>90%). High-risk NB (especially with MYCN amplification) has poor prognosis (3-year EFS ~50%). Age <18 months is a favorable prognostic factor.

**Opsoclonus-Myoclonus Syndrome (OMS):**
    *   **Complications:** Chronic neurological deficits (ataxia, cognitive impairment, developmental delay, behavioral problems) even after tumor resection and immunotherapy. Relapses are common (up to 50%).
    *   **Prognosis:** Good for tumor survival, but significant morbidity from the neurological syndrome.

**Orbital Rhabdomyosarcoma:**
    *   **Complications:** Local recurrence, metastasis (lungs, bone marrow, bone, brain), vision loss, strabismus, enophthalmos, ptosis, long-term effects of radiation (cataract, retinopathy, dry eye, optic neuropathy, bony hypoplasia).
    *   **Prognosis:** Excellent for localized orbital RMS (5-year survival >90%) due to localizing symptoms allowing early diagnosis. Poorer for alveolar subtype or metastatic disease.

sections.title: 14. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis in a child:** ALWAYS rule out rhabdomyosarcoma (requires urgent referral for imaging and biopsy).
**New-onset opsoclonus with myoclonus/ataxia in a child:** IMMEDIATELY search for an underlying neuroblastoma (whole-body MRI, MIBG scan, urine catecholamines).
**Periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes') without preceding trauma:** Highly suspicious for metastatic neuroblastoma.
**Signs of spinal cord compression** (weakness, sensory changes, bladder/bowel dysfunction) in a child with known or suspected neuroblastoma.
**Vision loss or optic nerve compression** due to orbital mass.

content.explanation: **R**apid Proptosis, **O**ften Unilateral, **C**hemotherapy is Key, **K**ids are affected, **S**urgery for Biopsy/Debulking

sections.title: 16. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Orbital RMS is a true ophthalmic emergency requiring rapid diagnosis and treatment.
Neuroblastoma is the most common tumor associated with OMS in children. A thorough tumor search is mandatory for new-onset OMS.
'Raccoon eyes' in a child is almost pathognomonic for metastatic neuroblastoma.
Horner's syndrome in an infant/child warrants investigation for neuroblastoma or other sympathetic chain pathology.
While orbital RMS has an excellent prognosis with modern therapy, long-term ocular sequelae from radiation are common.
OMS often requires long-term immunomodulatory therapy and can lead to persistent neurological deficits despite tumor control.

sections.title: 17. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content:
**Neuroblastoma:** The ANBL00P1 and ANBL0532 trials established the efficacy of anti-GD2 immunotherapy (dinutuximab) combined with GM-CSF, IL-2, and isotretinoin, significantly improving event-free survival and overall survival for high-risk neuroblastoma. Ongoing research explores MIBG-based radiation therapies and novel targeted agents (e.g., ALK inhibitors).

**Opsoclonus-Myoclonus Syndrome (OMS):** While the exact immunopathogenesis is still being elucidated, advances in antibody detection and understanding the role of tumor antigens (e.g., REM2) continue. Emphasis is shifting towards earlier and more aggressive immunotherapies to minimize long-term neurological sequelae, with trials exploring combinations of steroids, IVIG, and rituximab.

**Rhabdomyosarcoma:** The Intergroup Rhabdomyosarcoma Study (IRS) Group studies (I-V) have significantly advanced risk stratification and multimodal treatment protocols. Ongoing research focuses on identifying novel molecular targets (e.g., inhibitors of PAX-FOXO1 fusion proteins for alveolar RMS) and refining radiation techniques (e.g., proton therapy) to reduce long-term morbidity while maintaining efficacy.

sections.title: 18. Pediatric Considerations
content: **Age-Specific Presentation:** NB typically <2 years, RMS typically 7-8 years. This age difference is a key differentiator.
**Tolerance to Treatment:** Children tolerate chemotherapy and radiation differently than adults; dose modifications and monitoring for growth/developmental effects are critical.
**Long-term Sequelae:** High risk of neurocognitive, endocrine, cardiac, renal, and ocular complications from aggressive treatments. Long-term follow-up by multidisciplinary teams is essential.
**Family Support:** Diagnosis of a childhood malignancy is devastating for families. Comprehensive psychosocial support is crucial.
**Genetic Counseling:** For familial cases of NB (ALK mutations) or associations with RMS (NF1, Li-Fraumeni), genetic counseling is important.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Infectious uveitis accounts for 20-30% of uveitis cases in tertiary centers. It involves inflammation of the uveal tract (iris, ciliary body, choroid) caused by the direct invasion and multiplication of pathogens (viruses, bacteria, parasites, or fungi). Prompt recognition is critical to prevent irreversible vision loss from retinal necrosis, optic neuropathy, or secondary glaucoma.

sections.title: Herpetic Anterior Uveitis Features
content: Unilateral presentation (usually)
Elevated Intraocular Pressure (IOP) due to trabeculitis
Sectoral Iris Atrophy (highly suggestive of VZV)
Stellate Keratic Precipitates (KPs) distributed diffusely
Decreased corneal sensation (Cranial Nerve V involvement)

sections.title: Acute Retinal Necrosis (ARN) Criteria
content: 1. One or more foci of retinal necrosis with discrete borders in the peripheral retina.
2. Rapid progression in the absence of antiviral therapy.
3. Circumferential spread of the infection.
4. Occlusive vasculopathy with arteriolar involvement.
5. Prominent inflammatory response in the vitreous and anterior chamber.

rows: Monitor CBC for bone marrow suppression
Often used for prophylaxis or ease of use

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Red Flags
content: Rapidly expanding creamy-white peripheral retinal lesions (ARN)
Severely elevated IOP with minimal KPs in a painful eye
New onset 'string of pearls' vitreous opacities (Fungal)
Profound vision loss with cherry-red spot in Syphilis (Vascular occlusion)
Iris roseola (syphilitic nodules)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Hierarchy
content: Step 1: Clinical Exam (Slit lamp + Dilated Funduscopy)
Step 2: Multimodal Imaging (OCT Macula/RNFL, Fundus Autofluorescence)
Step 3: Serology (Quantiferon Gold, RPR/FTA-ABS, Toxoplasma IgG/IgM)
Step 4: Intraocular Sampling (AC Tap or Vitreous Tap for PCR)
Step 5: Goldmann-Witmer Coefficient (GWC) to compare antibody titers

content.explanation: H: Headlights in the fog (vitritis over lesion); O: Old scar adjacent to new lesion; G: Granulomatous inflammation; S: Satellite lesion.

sections.title: Viral Treatment Protocols
content: HSV/VZV Anterior: Acyclovir 400mg (HSV) or 800mg (VZV) 5x daily.
ARN: IV Acyclovir (10mg/kg q8h) for 10-14 days OR Valacyclovir 2g TID.
CMV: Intravitreal Ganciclovir (2mg/0.05mL) or Foscarnet injections.
Maintenance: Long-term oral antivirals to prevent recurrence in ARN.

sections.title: Surgical Considerations
content: Diagnostic Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) for PCR and Cytology.
Prophylactic Laser Retinopexy for ARN (to prevent RD).
Silicone Oil Tamponade in cases of necrotic Rhegmatogenous RD.
Glaucoma Drainage Devices for refractory herpetic glaucoma.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never start systemic steroids for uveitis without ruling out Syphilis or TB.
CMV Retinitis in HIV typically occurs when CD4+ count is < 50 cells/uL.
Aqueous PCR has a high sensitivity (>90%) for viral uveitis but lower for Toxo.
Kyrieleis Arteriolitis: Segmental periarterial exudates seen in Toxo or VZV.
Candida endophthalmitis often presents as 'fluff-ball' vitreous opacities.

sections.title: Recent Advances: mNGS
sections.content: Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing (mNGS) is an emerging tool for detecting 'unbiased' pathogens from intraocular fluids. Unlike PCR, which requires a primer for a specific suspected pathogen, mNGS sequences all DNA/RNA in a sample, making it invaluable for diagnosing rare or atypical infectious uveitis cases where standard cultures/PCR are negative.

summary: Ocular Tuberculosis is a complex, extrapulmonary manifestation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. It presents as a diverse range of uveitic entities, often requiring a high index of suspicion and a multi-disciplinary approach for diagnosis and management with Anti-Tubercular Therapy (ATT).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular Tuberculosis (OTB) refers to an infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb) in the eye, its adnexa, or the optic nerve. It can occur via direct invasion (primary) or, more commonly, via hematogenous spread from a distant site (secondary), often without clinically evident pulmonary involvement. It is a 'Master Mimicker' due to its ability to present as any form of intraocular inflammation.

sections.title: Posterior Segment Phenotypes
content: Tuberculoma: Large, solitary yellowish subretinal mass (2-10mm) with exudative RD.
Multifocal Choroiditis: Discrete yellowish-gray lesions at the RPE/Choriocapillaris level.
Serpiginous-like Choroiditis (SLC): Amoeboid, centrifugal progression, often sparing the fovea initially.
Endophthalmitis: Rare, seen in immunocompromised or miliary TB.
Subretinal Abscess: Rapidly enlarging yellowish lesion, may lead to perforation.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Slit-lamp: Mutton-fat Keratic Precipitates (KPs), Koeppe and Busacca iris nodules.
Gonioscopy: Broad-based peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) or angle nodules.
Fundus: Perivasculitis (Periphlebitis) with 'candle-wax' drippings (rare, mimic Sarcoid).
Vitreous: Vitreous seeds or string-of-pearls opacities.
Eales Disease: Peripheral periphlebitis and non-perfusion leading to vitreous hemorrhage.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Clinical Suspicion (Granulomatous inflammation or endemic background)
Step 2: Immunological Screening (TST/Mantoux >15mm or positive IGRA/QuantiFERON)
Step 3: Radiology (Chest X-ray or High-Resolution CT Chest to look for hilar adenopathy/calcifications)
Step 4: Ancillary Ocular Imaging (OCT for CME, FFA/ICGA for choroiditis and ischemia)
Step 5: Invasive Sampling (Aqueous/Vitreous tap for PCR for IS6110 gene and Culture)
Step 6: Multidisciplinary Consultation (Pulmonologist or Infectious Disease specialist)

sections.title: Management: The 4-Drug ATT Regimen
content: Intensive Phase (2 Months): Rifampin (10mg/kg), Isoniazid (5mg/kg), Pyrazinamide (25mg/kg), Ethambutol (15mg/kg).
Continuation Phase (4-7 Months): Rifampin and Isoniazid only.
Corticosteroid Integration: Start Prednisolone (1mg/kg) 48-72 hours AFTER initiating ATT to prevent Paradoxical Reaction (Jarisch-Herxheimer like).
Slow Steroid Taper: Over 6-12 weeks depending on clinical response.
Monitoring: Liver Function Tests (LFTs) and visual field/color vision for Ethambutol toxicity.

sections.title: Red Flags & Monitoring
content: Paradoxical Worsening (Upgrading reaction) after starting ATT.
Ethambutol Optic Neuropathy (Loss of color vision/central scotoma).
Rifampin-induced Hepatitis (Jaundice, elevated LFTs).
Non-response to ATT after 2 months (re-evaluate diagnosis).
Presence of CNVM in healing choroidal scars.

rows: M. tb cultured from ocular fluids or PCR positive.
Clinical signs + Positive TST/IGRA + CXR findings.

content.explanation: T: Tuberculoma, H: Hypersensitivity, E: Eales Disease, M: Multifocal Choroiditis, A: Anterior (Granulomatous), S: Serpiginous-like, K: Keratic Precipitates (Mutton-fat).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never start steroids alone if TB is suspected; it can lead to devastating bacillary multiplication.
Quantiferon-Gold is more specific than TST in BCG-vaccinated populations.
Serpiginous-like choroiditis in an Asian patient is Ocular TB until proven otherwise.
Ischemia in Eales disease is peripheral; management requires peripheral laser photocoagulation (PRP).

sections.title: Surgical Interventions
content: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): Indicated for non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage, tractional RD, or diagnostic biopsy.
Cataract Surgery: Delay until inflammation is quiet for at least 3 months.
Intravitreal Anti-VEGF: For secondary Choroidal Neovascular Membranes (CNVM).
Glaucoma Surgery: Required for refractory secondary OHT or PAS.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: COTS-1 & COTS-2
sections.content: The Collaborative Ocular Tuberculosis Study (COTS) provided evidence-based guidelines. COTS-1 highlighted that initiating ATT in 'Probable' cases significantly reduced the risk of recurrence compared to steroids alone. COTS-2 focuses on consensus-based management algorithms for diverse phenotypes like SLC and Tuberculoma, emphasizing that 6 months of ATT is often sufficient for most ocular manifestations.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Recurrence: Low if full course of ATT is completed.
Vision Loss: Most common due to Macular Scars, CME, or Optic Atrophy.
Phthisis Bulbi: Possible in end-stage, untreated panuveitis.
Prognosis: Generally good with early diagnosis and triple/quadruple therapy.

title: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB): The Gold Standard for GCA Diagnosis
summary: A definitive surgical diagnostic procedure for Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), involving the excision of a 2-3 cm segment of the superficial temporal artery. It remains the gold standard despite advances in non-invasive imaging, crucial for preventing irreversible vision loss from AAION.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) is a specialized surgical procedure to obtain a specimen of the superficial temporal artery (STA) for histopathological analysis. It is primarily indicated when Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA)—a systemic granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large-sized vessels—is suspected. Accurate diagnosis is vital to justify long-term, high-dose corticosteroid therapy and its associated morbidity.

branches: Contralateral biopsy if first side is negative (increases yield by 5-10%)
False negative risk (up to 9% due to skips)

rows: New onset or new type of localized pain in the head
Tenderness to palpation or decreased pulsation (not related to arteriosclerosis)
Artery showing vasculitis with mononuclear cell infiltration or granulomatous inflammation

sections.title: Surgical Anatomy: Temple Layers
content: 1. Skin and Subcutaneous Fat
2. Superficial Temporal Fascia (Temporoparietal Fascia - TPF)
3. Subaponeurotic Loose Areolar Tissue
4. Deep Temporal Fascia (Investing Temporalis Muscle)
Note: STA runs WITHIN the TPF/Superficial Fascia.

sections.title: Emergency 'Red Flags' for AAION
content: Sudden, painless, unilateral vision loss
Amaurosis fugax (Transient vision loss)
Chalky white disc edema on fundoscopy
Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
Cotton wool spots in a non-diabetic patient

sections.title: Pre-Operative Preparation
content: Palpate STA branches (Frontal vs. Parietal)
Use Doppler Ultrasound to mark the course of the vessel
Consent for facial nerve palsy, scarring, and bleeding
Ensure patient is NOT on anticoagulants if possible (though often continued)
Local anesthesia: Lidocaine 2% with Epinephrine (avoid direct intravascular injection)

sections.title: Step-by-Step Surgical Technique
content: 1. Incision: 3-5cm skin incision over marked vessel course.
2. Blunt Dissection: Through subcutaneous fat to the Superficial Temporal Fascia.
3. Isolation: Identify the pulsating artery; clear fascia using Stevens scissors.
4. Ligation: Proximal and distal ligation using 4-0 Silk or Prolene sutures.
5. Excision: Minimum 2-3 cm segment (account for 10-20% shrinkage).
6. Hemostasis: Meticulous cautery (bipolar preferred).
7. Closure: Two-layer closure (subcutaneous 4-0 Vicryl, skin 5-0 Prolene/Staples).

rows: Proximal muscle pain/stiffness, no vision loss
ANA positive, malar rash, multi-organ involvement
Weight loss, night sweats, localized findings

sections.title: Histopathological Hallmarks
content: Transmural inflammation (Mononuclear cells, macrophages)
Fragmentation of the Internal Elastic Lamina (IEL)
Multinucleated Giant Cells (present in ~50% of positive cases)
Intimal hyperplasia leading to luminal narrowing
Medial thinning and fibrosis

content.explanation: G: Granulomatous inflammation/Great ESR, I: Ischemic Optic Neuropathy, A: Age >50/Artery tenderness, N: Night sweats/New headache, T: Temporal artery biopsy (Gold Standard).

branches: Skin Necrosis (rare, collateral supply usually sufficient)

sections.title: Medical Management Algorithm
content: 1. Suspicion: Start Prednisone 1mg/kg (max 60-80mg) IMMEDIATELY.
2. Biopsy: Perform within 1-2 weeks (results valid even after steroids start).
3. Positive TAB: Taper steroids slowly over 12-24 months based on symptoms/ESR.
4. Steroid Sparing: Consider Tocilizumab (GiACTA trial) or Methotrexate.
5. Relapse: Increase to last effective dose.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A negative biopsy does NOT 100% rule out GCA; treat the patient, not the pathology if clinical suspicion is high.
Jaw claudication is the most specific symptom for GCA (Likelihood Ratio ~9.0).
Perform TAB as soon as possible, but do NOT delay steroids while waiting for the OR.
Always measure the specimen length BEFORE fixation in formalin to ensure adequacy.
The temporal branch of the facial nerve is most vulnerable as it crosses the zygomatic arch (stay superior/anterior).

sections.title: Recent Advances: The TABUL Study
sections.content: The TABUL study compared TAB with Ultrasound (US) for GCA diagnosis. Ultrasound showing the 'Halo Sign' (vessel wall edema) has high specificity but lower sensitivity than TAB. While US is increasingly used as a first-line screen in specialized 'Fast-track' clinics, TAB remains the definitive test for confirmation and for cases where US is indeterminate or negative despite high clinical suspicion.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) is a chronic vasculitis of large and medium-sized vessels, primarily involving the extracranial branches of the carotid artery. It is the most common primary systemic vasculitis in adults over 50. The ophthalmic hallmark is Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (A-AION), caused by occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries (SPCAs).

branches: Activation of adventitial dendritic cells via Toll-like receptors
Recruitment of CD4+ T-cells (Th1 and Th17 pathways)
Macrophage fusion into Multinucleated Giant Cells
Destruction of the Internal Elastic Lamina

rows: New onset or new type of localized pain in the head
Tenderness to palpation or decreased pulsation
Vasculitis with mononuclear cell infiltration or granulomatous inflammation

sections.title: Systemic Clinical Features
content: New-onset localized headache (often temporal)
Jaw Claudication (High specificity for GCA)
Scalp tenderness (pain when brushing hair)
Polymyalgia Rheumatica (stiffness in hips/shoulders)
Constitutional: Fever, weight loss, anorexia, malaise
Carotidynia or limb claudication

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations
content: Amaurosis Fugax: Transient vision loss (Warning sign!)
A-AION: Sudden, profound, painless vision loss
CRAO: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion
Cilio-retinal Artery Occlusion (Pathognomonic if combined with A-AION)
Diplopia: Due to cranial nerve palsies or EOM ischemia
Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (rare)

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Red Flags
content: Sudden vision loss in a patient >50 years old
New-onset headache with jaw claudication
Chalky-white disc edema on fundoscopy
Diplopia in an elderly patient with constitutional symptoms
Delayed choroidal filling on Fluorescein Angiography

sections.title: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) Protocol
content: Step 1: Perform within 1-2 weeks of starting steroids
Step 2: Obtain 2-3 cm length to minimize 'skip lesion' errors
Step 3: Incise skin over the frontal branch of the temporal artery
Step 4: Careful dissection to preserve facial nerve branches
Step 5: Ligation and excision of the segment
Step 6: Histopathological exam for Giant Cells and Intimal thickening

sections.title: The 'Halo Sign' on Ultrasound
sections.content: Color Doppler Ultrasound of the temporal arteries is an increasingly used non-invasive tool. A positive 'Halo Sign'—a hypoechoic area around the arterial lumen representing vessel wall edema—has high specificity. If bilateral halos are seen, sensitivity approaches 85%.

sections.title: Acute Management Protocol
content: 1. Immediate Start: DO NOT wait for biopsy if suspicion is high.
2. Vision Loss Present: IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day) for 3 days.
3. Oral Bridge: Transition to Oral Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (Max 60-80mg).
4. Tapering: Very slow taper (over 12-18 months) based on CRP/ESR and symptoms.
5. Steroid Sparing: Consider Tocilizumab (Actemra) - IL-6 Receptor Antagonist.
6. Protection: Add PPI, Calcium/Vitamin D, and Bisphosphonates for bone health.

sections.title: AION: Epidemiology & Vascular Supply
sections.content: Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is a significant cause of acute visual loss in the elderly population, affecting up to 10/ 100,000/ y of those over 50y. In 5– 10%, the aetiology is arteritic, in which the majority of these are caused by GCA, and in 90– 95%, the aetiology is non- arteritic (see Table 16.5). The vascular supply to the anterior optic nerve is from the short posterior ciliary artery and the choroidal circulation.

sections.title: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) Essentials
content: GCA or temporal arteritis is an ophthalmic emergency.
Requires immediate assessment and systemic corticosteroid treatment.
Mean onset is 70y; rare before 50y.
Commonly occurs in Caucasians; 3x more likely in ♀.
Pathology: Short posterior ciliary artery vasculitis leads to ischaemic necrosis of the optic nerve head.
Clinical judgement is required due to disease heterogeneity.

sections.title: GCA Clinical Features
content: Sudden dVA (<6/ 60 in 76%).
New- onset headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, weight loss, night sweats, myalgia (association with PMR).
Warning episode: Transient dVA (short obscurations or longer amaurosis fugax- like episodes).
Signs: RAPD, swollen disc (typically pale; rarely segmental) ± peripapillary haemorrhages and CWS.
Abnormal temporal arteries: Thickened, tender, non- pulsatile.
Associations: CRAO, BRAO, cilioretinal artery occlusion; III, IV, VIn palsy.

content.explanation: 3+ criteria = 93.5% sensitivity/91.2% specificity: 1. Age ≥50y. 2. New onset localized headache. 3. Temporal artery tenderness or dpulse. 4. ESR ≥50mm/ h (Westerngren). 5. Arterial biopsy showing necrotizing arteritis with mononuclear cell infiltrates or granulomatous process with multinuclear giant cells.

sections.title: Investigations Strategy
content: 1. Immediate Bloods: ESR, CRP, FBC (iESR, iCRP, and iPlt support GCA).
2. Prompt TAB: Recommended length ≥2cm, no <1cm. Aim within 1wk (positive up to 2– 6wk post-treatment).
3. Additional: U+E, LFTs, CXR, and urinalysis.
4. Long term: 2- yearly CXR for aneurysm detection (suspected large-vessel GCA).

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging & Specialized Tests
content: Duplex US: Hypoechoic ‘halo’ (vessel wall oedema) + stenosis/occlusion. User-dependent; positive >2wk post-steroids.
Fluoro- deoxyglucose PET: Assessing disease activity/extent, especially in large-vessel vasculitis.
High- resolution MRI: Superficial cranial/extracranial arteries (not routinely performed).

sections.title: Emergency Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Immediate systemic corticosteroids: e.g. 1g IVMP 1×/ d for 1– 3d.
2. Oral Follow-up: PO prednisolone 1– 2mg/ kg 1×/ d.
3. Patient Counseling: Mandatory explanation of side effects (gastric/bone protection required).
4. Titration: Once controlled, titrate by symptoms and markers (CRP responds faster than ESR).
5. Specialist Referral: Seek rheumatologist if comorbidities complicate therapy.
6. Emerging Agents: Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) inducing sustained remission at 1yr. Leflunomide under investigation.

sections.title: Management of Negative TAB
sections.content: If there is a typical clinical/laboratory picture and positive steroid response despite negative TAB, manage as GCA. If history and markers are atypical with negative TAB, consider alternative diagnoses and specialist referral. Steroids can be rapidly tapered within 2wk.

sections.title: Surgical Approach: Superficial TAB (Box 16.3)
content: Preoperative: Choose side of visual loss/abnormality. Map artery by palpation or US Doppler. Mark skin. Hair removal.
Procedure - Cleaning & LA: Clean skin. Infiltrate LA (27G). Adrenaline optional (helps haemostasis/visualization).
Procedure - Incision: Parallel to Langer's lines. Blunt dissection (do not breach superficial temporalis fascia).
Procedure - Ligation: Tie 4- 0 silk/Vicryl twice at distal/proximal ends. Pass needle backwards or double suture without needle. Ligate local tributaries.
Procedure - Specimen Care: Do not crush by regrasping specimen. Maximize biopsy length.
Procedure - Closure: Subcutaneous (5- 0 interrupted Vicryl). Skin (running 6- 0 Vicryl subcuticular).
Post-operative: Compression bandage for 24h. Optional antibiotic ointment for 3– 4d.

sections.content: A-AION is an ischemic infarction of the optic nerve head due to occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries (PCAs), typically caused by Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA). It is rare under age 50; incidence increases sharply with age, peaking between 70–80. Prevalence is approximately 15–25 per 100,000 in those over 50 years old.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Foster Kennedy Syndrome (FKS) is a constellation of neuro-ophthalmic findings caused by a mass lesion (typically a meningioma) in the anterior cranial fossa. The syndrome was first formally described by Robert Foster Kennedy in 1911. It highlights the dual effect of a single lesion: direct mechanical compression of one optic nerve and the systemic effect of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) on the other.

sections.title: Etiology: Primary Culprits
content: Olfactory Groove Meningioma (Most Common)
Sphenoid Wing Meningioma
Frontal Lobe Glioma / Astrocytoma
Craniopharyngioma
Esthesioneuroblastoma (Olfactory Neuroblastoma)
Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (Extension into cranium)
Large Aneurysms (Internal Carotid Artery)

sections.title: Pathophysiology: Dual Mechanisms
content: 1. Expanding mass in the anterior cranial fossa.
2. Direct pressure on the ipsilateral Optic Nerve (CN II) causes axonal death and atrophy.
3. Compression of the Olfactory Nerve (CN I) leads to loss of smell.
4. Large mass increases Intracranial Pressure (ICP).
5. Elevated ICP transmitted through subarachnoid space to the contralateral (uncompressed) optic nerve, causing papilledema.

content.explanation: Frontal lobe tumor, Optic atrophy (ipsilateral), Smelling loss (anosmia), Tumor-induced, Edema (contralateral papilledema), Raised ICP symptoms.

rows: Usually normal (early) or enlarged blind spot
New acute AION in fellow eye

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: 1. Comprehensive History: Inquire about headaches, personality changes, and smell.
2. Smell Testing: Use coffee/citrus (UPSIT test) to confirm anosmia.
3. Visual Field Testing: Automated Perimetry (HVF 24-2) and Goldmann.
4. OCT: Measure RNFL thickness and GCL (Ganglion Cell Layer) loss.
5. Emergent Neuroimaging: MRI Brain with/without Gadolinium (Gold Standard).
6. MRA/MRV: If vascular etiology or dural venous sinus involvement is suspected.
7. Neurology/Neurosurgery Consult: Immediate referral for surgical planning.

sections.title: Red Flags: Urgent Indicators
content: Sudden progressive vision loss in the 'good' eye.
Projectile vomiting (sign of severely raised ICP).
Altered mental status or coma.
Cushing Triad: Hypertension, Bradycardia, Irregular Respiration.
New onset seizures or focal neurological deficits.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Surgical Resection: Primary treatment for meningiomas or gliomas.
Corticosteroids: Dexamethasone (Decadron) to reduce peri-tumoral edema.
ICP Management: Acetazolamide or CSF shunting if papilledema is severe.
Radiation Therapy: Adjuvant therapy for malignant gliomas or subtotal resections.
Follow-up: Serial OCT, HVF, and MRI every 3-6 months post-op.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check smell! Anosmia is the 'forgotten' third sign of the triad.
Pseudo-FKS is far more common than true FKS in clinical practice.
The atrophic eye may develop secondary optic nerve head cupping, mimicking glaucoma.
Frontal lobe signs: Personality changes (apathy/disinhibition) are often missed.
The papilledema side is usually the side with BETTER visual function.

branches: Primary: No preceding edema (Compression in FKS)

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
sections.content: Prognosis is highly dependent on the tumor type and the duration of compression. The atrophic eye rarely recovers significant vision due to axonal death. However, the eye with papilledema usually has an excellent visual prognosis if ICP is lowered promptly before chronic changes (atrophy) occur in that eye. Survival rates for benign meningiomas are high (>90% at 5 years), whereas high-grade gliomas carry a poor survival prognosis.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) is a chronic vasculitis of large and medium-sized vessels, primarily involving the extracranial branches of the carotid artery. It is the most common primary systemic vasculitis in adults over 50. The ophthalmic hallmark is Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (A-AION), caused by occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries (SPCAs).

sections.title: Clinical Overview & Definitions
sections.content: Distinguishing between Orbital Cellulitis, Idiopathic Orbital Inflammatory Disease (IOID), and Rhabdomyosarcoma is a hallmark of ophthalmic emergency medicine. Orbital Cellulitis is a life-threatening infection posterior to the orbital septum. IOID (formerly Pseudotumor) is a non-specific, non-granulomatous inflammatory process. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary pediatric orbital malignancy, characterized by aggressive, rapid growth.

sections.title: Chandler Classification of Orbital Infection
content: Stage I: Preseptal Cellulitis (Eyelid edema only)
Stage II: Orbital Cellulitis (Proptosis, chemosis, motility loss)
Stage III: Subperiosteal Abscess (Displacement of globe)
Stage IV: Orbital Abscess (Intra-conal pus collection)
Stage V: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (Bilateral signs, CN palsies)

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) — Indicates Compressive Optic Neuropathy
Frozen Orbit (Total Ophthalmoplegia) — Suggests Cavernous Sinus involvement or Apex Syndrome
Rapidly Progressive Proptosis in a Child — Must rule out Rhabdomyosarcoma immediately
Bilateral Orbital Involvement — Consider Systemic Vasculitis, Lymphoma, or Metastasis
Meningismus or Altered Mental Status — Indicates intracranial extension of infection

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Urgent Contrast-Enhanced CT (Orbit/Brain/Sinuses)
2. CBC with Diff, ESR, CRP, Blood Cultures
3. Targeted Biopsy (Mandatory for suspected Rhabdo or non-responsive IOID)
4. Thyroid Function Tests (To rule out TED)
5. c-ANCA / p-ANCA / ACE levels (For GPA or Sarcoidosis)

sections.title: Management: Orbital Cellulitis
content: Admission for IV Antibiotics: Vancomycin (15-20mg/kg) + Ceftriaxone (2g QD)
Add Metronidazole if anaerobic infection suspected (dental origin)
Surgical Drainage if: Vision decreases, APD develops, or no improvement in 48h
Otolaryngology (ENT) consult for sinus debridement
Avoid steroids until 24-48h of antibiotic coverage (and only if improving)

sections.title: Management: IOID (NSOI)
content: High-dose Oral Prednisone: 1mg/kg/day with slow taper
IV Pulse Methylprednisolone for sight-threatening apex cases
Radiation Therapy (1000-3000 cGy) if steroid-resistant or contraindicated
Immunomodulatory Therapy (Steroid-sparing): Methotrexate, Ciclosporin, or Infliximab
Biopsy if atypical or recurrent to rule out Lymphoma

sections.title: Rhabdomyosarcoma Treatment (IRSG)
content: 1. Complete Surgical Excision (only if possible without mutilation)
2. Multi-agent Chemotherapy (VAC: Vincristine, Adriamycin/Actinomycin, Cyclophosphamide)
3. External Beam Radiotherapy (for residual disease)
4. Long-term surveillance for secondary malignancies

content.explanation: B-otryoid (Best), E-mbryonal (Excellent/Common), A-lveolar (Awful/Inferior orbit), M-etastatic (Most concerning)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: In IOID, 'The pain is out of proportion to the clinical signs' initially.
In Cellulitis, always check for 'Pain on eye movement' – it's the most sensitive sign to differentiate from preseptal.
Rhabdomyosarcoma is a 'Great Mimicker' and may present with bruising that looks like trauma.
Wait 24 hours after starting steroids in IOID; if no response, RE-THINK the diagnosis and biopsy.
Orbital Apex Syndrome = CN II, III, IV, V1, VI involvement; localized IOID or aggressive infection.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: IRSG
sections.content: The Intergroup Rhabdomyosarcoma Study Group (IRSG) trials established that orbital rhabdomyosarcoma has a significantly better prognosis than other sites. Modern protocols emphasize globe-sparing treatment with combined chemotherapy and radiation rather than primary exenteration.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Bowtie atrophy, also known as Band Atrophy, refers to a specific pattern of optic disc pallor occurring in the eye contralateral to a lesion of the optic tract. It is characterized by horizontal pallor (nasal and temporal) of the optic disc, reflecting the loss of retinal ganglion cell axons that subserve the contralateral hemifield.

branches: Contralateral Eye (Right): Loss of Nasal fibers (cross at chiasm) entering disc at 3 & 9 o'clock
Ipsilateral Eye (Left): Loss of Temporal fibers (uncrossed) entering disc at Sup/Inf poles
Result: 'Bowtie' Atrophy in the Right Eye
Result: Diffuse/Vertical Atrophy in the Left Eye

sections.title: The RAPD Paradox
sections.content: In an optic tract lesion, a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) is found in the eye CONTRALATERAL to the lesion (the eye with the bowtie atrophy). This occurs because the optic tract carries more fibers from the contralateral nasal retina (60% of total fibers) than from the ipsilateral temporal retina (40% of total fibers).

sections.title: Clinical Features Checklist
content: Contralateral Incongruous Homonymous Hemianopia
Horizontal 'Bowtie' pallor (Contralateral eye)
Diffuse/Generalized pallor (Ipsilateral eye)
Contralateral RAPD
Potential Wernicke’s Pupil (non-reactive to light when hemi-field is stimulated)
Hemianopic Saccades or Reading difficulties

rows: Cupping rather than just pallor; poles involved first.
Congenital; associated with situs inversus and myopia.
Hyperemic disc initially; central scotoma; mitochondrial DNA.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Perform Comprehensive Visual Field Testing (Goldmann or Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2).
Step 2: Dilated Fundus Exam to assess pattern of pallor (Bowtie vs Diffuse).
Step 3: Pupillary assessment for RAPD and light-near dissociation.
Step 4: OCT RNFL and Ganglion Cell Analysis (Look for nasal/temporal thinning).
Step 5: Urgent Neuro-imaging (MRI Brain & Orbits with/without Gadolinium) focusing on the Sellar and Supra-sellar regions.

sections.title: OCT RNFL Characteristics
content: Marked thinning in the Nasal quadrant (approx. 3 o'clock).
Marked thinning in the Temporal quadrant (approx. 9 o'clock).
Relative preservation of Superior and Inferior RNFL bundles.
Ganglion Cell Layer (GCL) thinning following a 'vertical step' pattern (Hemianopic GCL loss).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Urgent Referral Needed
content: Sudden onset visual field loss (Vascular event/Apoplexy)
New onset headaches or hormonal changes (Pituitary mass)
Bilateral rapid vision loss
Cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, VI) indicating cavernous sinus involvement

content.explanation: T: Temporal Macular fiber loss; R: RAPD (Contralateral); A: Atrophy (Bowtie); C: Contralateral Hemianopia; T: Tumors (most common cause).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Bowtie atrophy takes 4-6 weeks minimum to develop after an acute tract insult.
The 'Incongruity' of the field defect is key: The more posterior the lesion in the visual pathway, the more congruous the defect. Tract lesions are highly incongruous.
Wernicke's Pupil: Pupil reacts when light is shown on the functioning hemiretina, but not when shown on the non-functioning (hemianopic) hemiretina.
Always check for Pituitary symptoms (amenorrhea, acromegaly, galactorrhea) in these patients.

branches: Afferent Pupil Fibers (bypass LGN to Pretectal Nucleus)

sections.title: Management & Prognosis
sections.content: Management is etiologically driven (e.g., neurosurgical resection of a tumor or medical management of stroke risk factors). Prognosis for visual recovery is generally poor once pallor (atrophy) has manifested, as this represents irreversible axonal loss.

sections.title: Landmark Concept: Incongruity
content: Incongruous = The two eyes have differently shaped field defects.
Optic tract lesions are the most common cause of highly incongruous homonymous hemianopia.
This helps differentiate tract lesions from radiation or occipital cortex lesions.

title: See-Saw Nystagmus: Decoding the Torsio-Vertical Oscillation

This complex nystagmus serves as a critical localizing sign for lesions of the midbrain or the parasellar region.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: See-Saw Nystagmus (SSN) is a unique, cyclic, pendular ocular oscillation. One complete cycle consists of two phases: 1) Elevation and intorsion of one eye with simultaneous depression and extorsion of the fellow eye, followed by 2) The exact reversal of these movements. It is classically associated with parasellar lesions (e.g., craniopharyngioma) and midbrain pathology involving the interstitial nucleus of Cajal (INC).

branches: Dysfunction of Interstitial Nucleus of Cajal (INC)
Loss of Rostral Midbrain Vertical/Torsional Gaze Centers
Loss of visual input (Chiasm) causing disinhibition

rows: Jerk (slow phase followed by fast phase)
Bilateral INC involvement or Parasellar lesion
Unilateral lesion of INC or Vestibular Nuclei

sections.title: Top Etiological Factors
content: Parasellar Tumors: Craniopharyngioma (most common), Pituitary Adenoma.
Vascular: Thalamomesencephalic stroke, Medullary infarction.
Trauma: Severe head injury with midbrain shearing.
Degenerative: Multiple Sclerosis, Syringobulbia.
Visual Loss: Severe bilateral vision loss (Achromatopsia, Septo-optic dysplasia) can cause 'Pseudo-SSN'.
Pharmacological: High-dose benzodiazepines or barbiturate toxicity (rare).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Visual Acuity: Often decreased due to oscillopsia or underlying pathology.
Slit-lamp: Observation of subtle conjunctival vessel movement to confirm torsion.
Fundoscopy: Direct visualization of optic disc torsion (the 'gold standard' for diagnosis).
Visual Fields: Often reveals Bitemporal Hemianopsia (due to chiasmal involvement).
Pupils: Check for RAPD if chiasmal compression is suspected.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: Step 1: Neuro-Ophthalmic Exam (characterize waveform, frequency, and amplitude).
Step 2: Formal Visual Field Testing (Humphrey or Goldmann) to assess for chiasmal syndromes.
Step 3: High-Resolution MRI Brain with GAD (Focus on Sella, Parasellar region, and Rostral Midbrain).
Step 4: MRA/CTA if vascular etiology is suspected in the posterior circulation.
Step 5: Video-Nystagmography (VNG) for objective recording of the torsional-vertical components.

rows: Static vertical misalignment, no rhythmic oscillation.
Slow upward drift of an uncovered eye, usually associated with congenital esotropia.
Jerk waveform, usually indicates unilateral brainstem lesion.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocols
content: Address Underlying Cause: Neurosurgical resection of tumors (e.g., craniopharyngioma) may resolve nystagmus.
Medical Management: Gabapentin (300-900mg TID) or Memantine (10-40mg daily) can reduce oscillopsia.
Alternative Meds: Baclofen or Clonazepam (though often less effective).
Optical: Large base-out prisms (occasionally helpful to induce convergence).
Surgical: Kestenbaum-style procedures or vertical rectus recessions if a significant head tilt or null point is present (rarely curative).

sections.title: Red Flags: Urgent Neuro-Referral
content: Sudden onset of See-Saw Nystagmus (suspect acute stroke).
New-onset Bitemporal Hemianopsia (chiasmal compression).
Associated focal neurological deficits (ataxia, hemiparesis).
Obstructive Hydrocephalus signs (headache, vomiting, papilledema).

content.explanation: In classic See-Saw Nystagmus: One eye moves UP and IN (Elevation + Intorsion) while the other eye moves DOWN and OUT (Depression + Extorsion).

sections.title: Surgical Nuances: The INC
sections.content: The Interstitial Nucleus of Cajal (INC) is the neural integrator for vertical and torsional gaze. In SSN, the 'balance' between the two INC nuclei (one on each side) is lost. Stimulating the INC on one side produces the ipsilateral component of the Ocular Tilt Reaction (OTR); See-Saw Nystagmus is essentially a rhythmic, alternating OTR.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: SSN is often associated with bitemporal hemianopsia because the same lesions that damage the INC or its pathways often compress the optic chiasm.
Pseudo-See-Saw Nystagmus: Can occur in patients with severe congenital visual loss (e.g., Achromatopsia) but lacks the rhythmic 'teeter-totter' regularity of true SSN.
Null Points: Some patients may have a null point where nystagmus diminishes; identifying this is key for surgical planning.
Wait and Watch: In cases of traumatic brain injury, SSN can occasionally resolve spontaneously over several months.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Oscillopsia: The primary symptom, leading to significant functional impairment and reading difficulty.
Post-Surgical Outcome: SSN may persist even after successful removal of a parasellar tumor due to permanent damage to brainstem pathways.
Quality of Life: Chronic SSN is often disabling; low vision rehabilitation is frequently necessary.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Research
sections.content: Recent fMRI and high-resolution DTI (Diffusion Tensor Imaging) studies have confirmed that the disruption of the white matter tracts connecting the INC to the vestibular nuclei and the oculomotor complex is the primary driver of SSN. New trials are investigating the use of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) to stabilize these neural circuits, showing promise in jerk-type nystagmus variants.

title: Papilledema: The Ominous Optic Disc Swelling

Often associated with headache, it can lead to severe vision loss if the underlying cause isn't identified and managed promptly. This infographic provides a comprehensive overview for ophthalmology residents and fellows.
