sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview: The Foundation of IOL Calculation
sections.content: Ophthalmic biometry is the precise measurement of ocular dimensions, primarily axial length (AL), corneal curvature (K), anterior chamber depth (ACD), and lens thickness (LT), to calculate the appropriate intraocular lens (IOL) power for cataract and refractive lens exchange surgery. Accurate biometry is the single most critical factor for achieving predictable postoperative refractive outcomes. Two primary technologies dominate the field: optical biometry, utilizing light waves, and ultrasound biometry, employing sound waves. The choice of method profoundly impacts accuracy and patient satisfaction.

sections.title: 2. Principles of Measurement: Light vs. Sound

rows: Interferometry of coherent light (e.g., 830nm for IOLMaster 500, 1060nm for IOLMaster 700, 1310nm for Argos) or low-coherence reflectometry. Measures distance by analyzing interference patterns.
Acoustic pulses (e.g., 10-12 MHz) emitted and received by a piezoelectric transducer. Measures time-of-flight of sound waves reflected from ocular interfaces.
Light travels through all transparent ocular media (cornea, aqueous, lens, vitreous) to the retina.
Sound travels through ocular media, assuming a constant velocity of sound in different tissues. Velocity: Aqueous/Vitreous ≈ 1532 m/s, Lens ≈ 1641 m/s, PMMA ≈ 2718 m/s.
High (e.g., AL ±0.01mm). Non-contact, high repeatability. Measures to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
Lower (e.g., AL ±0.1mm). Contact method introduces variability. Measures to internal limiting membrane (ILM).
Non-contact, highly precise, automated, less operator-dependent, measures foveal AL.
Can measure through dense media opacities (e.g., mature cataract, corneal opacities, silicone oil).
Cannot penetrate dense media opacities (e.g., very dense cataracts, significant corneal edema/scarring, vitreous hemorrhage).
Contact method prone to corneal compression, operator-dependent, lower precision, requires trained personnel.

sections.title: 3. Epidemiology of Use: The Shift to Optical

branches.name: Optical Biometers
sub_branches: OLCR-based (Optical Low-Coherence Reflectometry): Haag-Streit Lenstar LS 900, Topcon OA-2000, Nidek AL-Scan
Swept-Source OCT-based: Zeiss IOLMaster 700, Alcon Argos

branches.name: Ultrasound Biometers
sub_branches: Immersion A-scan (Probe in scleral shell filled with saline)

rows: Most critical parameter. Optical AL is typically ~0.2mm longer than US AL due to foveal pit measurement vs. ILM.
Optical devices offer automated, often 9-point or Placido disc-based K. US typically 3.2mm or 2.5mm central K.
Distance from posterior corneal surface to anterior lens surface.
Many optical biometers (Lenstar, IOLMaster 700, Argos, OA-2000)
Useful for toric/multifocal IOLs, sulcus IOL sizing.
Mesopic/photopic pupil for multifocal IOL selection.
Can be important for corneal health assessment.

sections.title: 6. Clinical Indications for Biometry
content: Pre-operative evaluation for cataract surgery (standard)
Pre-operative evaluation for Refractive Lens Exchange (RLE)
Planning for Toric IOL implantation (requires precise keratometry and axis)
Planning for Multifocal/Extended Depth of Focus (EDOF) IOL implantation (requires high precision, patient selection parameters)
Monitoring of ocular growth in pediatric aphakia or pseudophakia

sections.title: 7. Ocular Examination Considerations Influencing Choice
content: **Dense Mature Cataract (posterior subcapsular, white, brunescent):** Optical often fails to penetrate, necessitating Immersion A-scan.
**Significant Corneal Opacities/Edema:** Can obstruct light for optical biometry; US may be required.
**Staphyloma/Posterior Segment Pathology:** Can cause false AL measurements with both, but US is more prone to off-axis measurements.
**Silicone Oil in Vitreous Cavity:** Requires adjustment of sound velocity for ultrasound (e.g., 980 m/s for silicone oil vs. 1532 m/s for vitreous) and specific optical biometers designed for this.
**Aphakia/Pseudophakia:** Requires specific IOL formulas and may necessitate US to confirm AL or detect silicone oil.
**Patient Inability to Fixate:** Optical biometry requires cooperation; US may be performed with topical anesthesia.

sections.title: 8. Diagnostic Workup / Biometry Protocol
content: **Step 1: Patient Preparation** - Explain procedure, ensure comfortable head/chin rest position, instill topical anesthetic if US (e.g., Proparacaine 0.5%)

**Step 2: Measurement Acquisition** - 
  *   **Optical:** Patient fixates target, alignment guides used, device automatically scans. Multiple scans taken (typically 5-10 per eye). Quality score/signal-to-noise ratio is critical.
  *   **Ultrasound (Immersion):** Topical anesthetic, scleral shell placed, filled with saline. Probe immersed perpendicular to cornea, gently touching water. Look for sharp, high-peaked retinal spike and choroidal spike.

**Step 3: Quality Control & Verification** - 
  *   Check signal quality, standard deviation of AL measurements (should be <0.05mm for optical). 
  *   Compare AL measurements between eyes (inter-eye difference >0.3mm without cause is suspicious). 
  *   Verify keratometry values against clinical observation (e.g., suspected astigmatism). 
  *   Ensure correct measurement mode (phakic, aphakic, pseudophakic) for US.
**Step 4: IOL Formula Selection & Calculation** - Input validated biometry data into appropriate IOL formulas (e.g., Barrett Universal II, SRK/T, Hoffer Q, Haigis-L, Kane Formula, Pearl DGS).
**Step 5: Documentation** - Record all measurements, selected IOL power, and any caveats or special considerations.

rows: Superior precision, non-contact, automated. Achieves best refractive outcomes.
Optical light cannot penetrate. Immersion avoids corneal compression of contact A-scan.
Optical biometers may struggle or provide inaccurate AL due to silicone oil refractive index. US velocity MUST be adjusted (e.g., 980 m/s).
Accurate K-values are critical. Optical devices with Total Keratometry (TK) are ideal. Specific formulas (Barrett True-K, Olsen, Haigis-L) are mandatory.
Patient cooperation issues for optical. Requires specific formulas (e.g., SRK/T with age-adjusted A-constant) or optical biometry in sedated children.
Optical biometers may have difficulty acquiring data due to extremely small eye size or irregular shape. Specialized probes may be needed.
Optical measurements can be unreliable or impossible. Immersion avoids contact with damaged cornea.

sections.title: 11. Red Flags / Critical Biometry Errors
content: **Inter-eye AL difference >0.3mm (unless known pathology):** Always re-measure and investigate.
**Low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) / Quality Score < 2 (Optical):** Indicates unreliable measurement. Re-scan.
**Flattened retinal spike (US):** Indicates off-axis measurement or poor probe contact.
**Absence of choroidal spike (US):** Possible retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage obscuring signal.
**Double peaks or spikes within the vitreous (US):** Indicative of fluid-filled spaces, vitreous hemorrhage, or probe artifact.
**Keratometry values outside typical range (38D-48D):** Re-verify, especially if not a known highly myopic/hyperopic eye.
**Patient eye movements causing significant measurement variability:** Re-position, re-instruct, or consider US if optical fails.

content.explanation:
**S**harp spikes: Clean, well-defined peaks.
**A**ligned: Perpendicular probe placement, spikes rise vertically from baseline.
**L**ong: High amplitude spikes (e.g., >90% for retinal spike).
**T**apered: Gradual decay of spikes (not abrupt drop-off), indicating good gain settings. Ensure retinal and choroidal spikes are distinct.

sections.title: 13. Key Clinical Pearls for Accurate Biometry
content: **Always perform biometry on both eyes, even if only one is planned for surgery.** Allows for inter-eye comparison and detection of anomalies.
**Check the quality metrics religiously.** Low signal quality is a direct indicator of unreliable data.
**Verify keratometry data.** Cross-reference with topography/tomography if available, especially for toric IOLs.
**Consider the patient's history.** Previous refractive surgery (LASIK/PRK) requires specific IOL formulas and often modern optical biometers with TK.
**Educate the patient.** Good fixation and cooperation are paramount for optical biometry.
**Understand the differences between optical and ultrasound AL measurements.** Optical typically measures to the foveal pit (0.2mm longer than US to ILM).
**Master immersion A-scan technique.** It's the gold standard when optical fails; corneal compression with contact A-scan is a major source of error.
**Beware of highly myopic eyes.** Staphylomas can lead to false AL measurements; consider B-scan ultrasound to confirm posterior segment anatomy.

sections.title: 14. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Swept-Source OCT Biometry:** Devices like IOLMaster 700 and Argos use a longer wavelength (1050-1310nm) and faster scanning, allowing for better penetration through denser cataracts and measurement of full-length scan images (B-scans).

**Total Keratometry (TK):** Introduced by IOLMaster 700, measures both anterior and posterior corneal surfaces directly, providing a more accurate total corneal power compared to estimated posterior corneal power. Shown to improve refractive predictability.

**New-Generation IOL Formulas:** Barrett Universal II, Kane, EVO 2.0, Pearl DGS – these formulas incorporate more biometry parameters (ACD, LT) and utilize advanced optical models, leading to greater accuracy, especially in challenging eyes (e.g., short/long AL, post-refractive surgery).
**Intraoperative Aberrometry (e.g., ORA System):** Provides real-time aphakic and pseudophakic refractive measurements during surgery, refining IOL power and toric IOL axis placement.
**AI Integration:** Artificial intelligence and machine learning are being explored to further refine IOL power calculations by recognizing patterns in large datasets and reducing prediction errors.

sections.title: 15. Management & Treatment: IOL Calculation Formulas
sections.content:
Accurate biometry feeds into sophisticated IOL calculation formulas, which have evolved significantly: 

**1st Generation (SRK-I):** Regression-based, less accurate for extreme axial lengths.
**2nd Generation (SRK-II):** Regression with AL-adjusted A-constant.
**3rd Generation (SRK/T, Hoffer Q, Haigis):** Theoretical/ray-tracing formulas, generally more accurate, especially SRK/T for average to long eyes, Hoffer Q for short eyes, and Haigis for wide AL range.
**4th Generation (Olsen, Holladay 2):** Incorporate more variables (ACD, LT, CCT, WTW) for greater personalization, often requiring more detailed biometry data.
**5th Generation & Beyond (Barrett Universal II, Kane, Pearl DGS, EVO 2.0):** Utilize advanced optical models, vector analysis for astigmatism, and often incorporate specific algorithms for post-refractive surgery eyes, offering the highest accuracy across all ALs. These formulas heavily benefit from comprehensive optical biometry data including TK.

sections.title: 16. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
sections.content:
**Pediatric Biometry:** Often performed under general anesthesia due to cooperation issues. Immersion A-scan is frequently used. Specialized biometers may have pediatric modes. Growth charts for AL are crucial for long-term IOL power planning, especially if IOL is implanted during infancy, often aiming for hyperopia to account for future growth.

**Post-Refractive Surgery Eyes:** This is a highly challenging group due to altered corneal curvature (oblate cornea after LASIK/PRK) and potential discrepancies between measured and effective K. Optical biometers with Total Keratometry (TK) are paramount. Specific formulas (e.g., Barrett True-K, Haigis-L, Kane) must be used. Access to pre-operative data (prior manifest refraction, surgical report) is invaluable.

title: Dissociated Vertical Deviation (DVD): A Clinical Masterclass
summary: Dissociated Vertical Deviation is a complex binocular motor anomaly characterized by upward drift, abduction, and excyclotorsion of the non-fixing eye. It is the signature of early-onset disrupted binocularity and follows neither Hering's nor Sherrington's laws.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: DVD is a slow, tonic, upward drift of an eye when it is covered or fusion is otherwise interrupted. Unlike most deviations, when the eye is uncovered, it moves downward to re-fixate, but the other eye does NOT move downward (violating Hering’s Law of equal innervation). It is almost always bilateral and asymmetric.

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: Disruption of binocular development in the 'critical period' (first 6 months).
Unmasking of primitive vestibular-ocular reflexes.
Damping Mechanism: The upward drift may be an evolutionary vestige to maintain gaze or damp latent nystagmus.
Non-Hering Deviation: The fixing eye remains stationary while the deviated eye drifts.

sections.title: Bielschowsky Phenomenon
content: 1. Place a neutral density filter bar in front of the fixing eye.
2. Observe the occluded (deviated/elevated) eye.
3. Gradually increase the filter density.
4. Result: The occluded eye will slowly move downward (sometimes below the midline) as light to the fixing eye is reduced.

rows: Elevation may improve or stay same

sections.title: Measurement Techniques
content: 1. Prism and Under Cover Test: Place base-down prism over the eye being covered until no upward movement is noted.
2. Modified Krimsky: Use prisms to center the light reflex in the deviated eye.
3. Synchronous Prism Cover: To neutralize the 'latent' component.
4. Note: Measurement is notoriously difficult due to the 'slow' and variable nature of the drift.

rows: Easily seen, occurs with short occlusion
Rapid drift, visible even without occlusion
Manifest drift, eye remains elevated most of the time

sections.title: Surgical Management Strategies
content: Superior Rectus (SR) Recession: Large recessions (7mm to 10mm) are standard. Most effective for primary position DVD.
SR Recession with Faden Procedure (Posterior Fixation): Adds a mechanical tether to limit elevation in the 'up' position.
Inferior Oblique Transposition (IOT): Effective if IOOA is also present. Moves the IO insertion anterior to the IR insertion.
Inferior Rectus (IR) Resection: Used if SR recession alone is insufficient or if there is associated pseudo-ptosis.
Important: Surgery is usually bilateral because unilateral surgery often 'unmasks' a hidden DVD in the other eye.

content.explanation: A: Abduction/Asymmetric, B: Bielschowsky/Bilateral, C: Cover test (slow upward drift) / Cyclotorsion.

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Do NOT perform unilateral surgery if the other eye shows any signs of latent DVD (will result in massive rebound).
Sudden onset vertical deviation in an adult (Suspect Skew Deviation/Neurological).
DVD is NEVER associated with a true hypotropia of the other eye (Distinguishes from SOP).
Avoid excessive SR recession if significant limitation of elevation would cause diplopia in up-gaze.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: DVD does not typically cause diplopia because the deviating eye is usually suppressed.
Bielschowsky Head Tilt test is usually negative (unlike 4th Nerve Palsy).
Latency is key: The drift is slow (tonic), unlike the fast (phasic) movement of a phoria.
Pseudo-ptosis: The upper lid may appear drooping in the non-fixing eye because the globe is elevated, making the lid look lower relative to the limbus.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent research into the 'Damping Hypothesis' suggests that DVD is a cortical adaptation to stabilize retinal images in patients with latent nystagmus. Landmark studies by von Noorden and Helveston established the standard for 'Large' SR recessions, demonstrating that standard 3-4mm recessions are ineffective for DVD and at least 7-9mm are required for lasting cosmetic correction.

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
content: Surgical success: 70-85% reduction in manifest drift.
Recurrence: Common (up to 20%) over 5-10 years.
Binocularity: True stereopsis is rare even after successful alignment due to early-onset suppression.

Early diagnosis via urgent biopsy and multi-modal treatment with chemotherapy and radiotherapy has transformed this once-fatal disease into one with a high survival rate.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Orbital Rhabdomyosarcoma is a highly malignant neoplasm of primitive mesenchymal cells that show a tendency toward rhabdomyoblastic differentiation. Despite its name, it does not typically arise from extraocular muscles but from undifferentiated pluripotent cells. It is a true ophthalmic emergency due to its potential for rapid orbital expansion and intracranial spread.

sections.title: Clinical Features: The Rapid Onset
content: Sudden, rapidly progressive proptosis (days to weeks)
Globe displacement (usually downward/outward for Embryonal)
Ptosis and lid edema with characteristic discoloration
Palpable, non-tender, firm orbital mass
Decreased ocular motility (ophthalmoplegia)
Pain is rare (only 10%), mimicking cellulitis
Late findings: Optic disc edema, choroidal folds

rows: Fever, leukocytosis, paranasal sinus opacification on CT, pain with movement.
Often bilateral, ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), adrenal primary on imaging.
Usually present at birth/infancy, blanches with pressure, Valsalva increase.
Acute onset only if hemorrhage occurs ('chocolate cyst'), slow growth otherwise.
Pain is a hallmark, dramatic response to corticosteroids.
Associated with AML, requires peripheral blood smear/marrow biopsy.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Urgent Imaging: CT (bone destruction) and MRI (soft tissue detail, T2 hyperintense).
2. Urgent Incisional Biopsy: Gold standard; avoid complete excision if it risks vital structures.
3. Immunohistochemistry: Test for Desmin, Myogenin, MyoD1, and Muscle-specific Actin.
4. Systemic Staging: Chest CT, Bone Scan, Bone Marrow Aspiration, and Lumbar Puncture (for parameningeal).
5. Pre-treatment Labs: CBC, LFTs, Renal function (baseline for chemotherapy).

rows: Incomplete resection or biopsy only (Most common)

sections.title: Management Strategy (IRS Protocols)
content: Step 1: Biopsy to confirm diagnosis and subtype.
Step 2: Debulking surgery only if vision/nerves are not compromised.
Step 3: Chemotherapy (VAC Regime) for 6–12 months.
Step 4: Radiotherapy (External Beam) for Groups II, III, and IV.
Step 5: Orbital Exenteration (Reserved for resistant or recurrent cases).

sections.title: The 'VAC' Chemotherapy Regimen
content: Vincristine: Mitotic inhibitor (microtubule disruption).
Actinomycin D (Dactinomycin): RNA synthesis inhibitor.
Cyclophosphamide: Alkylating agent (DNA cross-linking).
Orbital RMS is exquisitely chemosensitive.

sections.title: EMERGENCY: RED FLAGS
content: Rapidly increasing proptosis over 24-48 hours
New onset ophthalmoplegia in a child
Evidence of bony erosion on CT scan
Presence of 'raccoon eyes' (suggests metastatic neuroblastoma or RMS)
Distant metastases to lungs or bone (check for respiratory distress or bone pain)

content.explanation: To confirm RMS, remember the M's: Myogenin (most specific), MyoD1 (very sensitive), and Muscle-Specific Actin (MSA). These confirm the cell is trying to become a muscle cell.

sections.title: Surgical Principles
content: Primary goal: Tissue for diagnosis and IHC.
Avoid Exenteration as primary therapy (no survival benefit over chemo/RT).
Incisional biopsy is preferred over fine-needle aspiration (FNA) for architecture.
Lid-sparing approaches where possible.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Boards
content: Embryonal is 'Everyone' (most common) and occurs 'Everywhere' (but favors superonasal).
Alveolar is 'Awful' (worse prognosis) and occurs 'At the bottom' (inferior orbit).
RMS is the most common pediatric orbital primary, but Metastatic Neuroblastoma is the most common pediatric orbital secondary.
Cross-striations on H&E are found in only ~50-60% of cases; IHC is necessary.
Radiation doses are typically 40-50 Gy, but can cause late complications like cataract, dry eye, and orbital hypoplasia.

sections.title: Complications & Long-term Follow-up
content: Radiation-induced cataract (near 100% within years).
Radiation keratopathy and severe xerophthalmia.
Orbital bone growth arrest (facial asymmetry).
Secondary malignancies (Osteosarcoma) in the radiation field.
Infertility or secondary leukemia from alkylating agents (Cyclophosphamide).

sections.title: Landmark Studies: IRS I to IV
sections.content: The Intergroup Rhabdomyosarcoma Studies (IRS) have shown that orbital RMS has a 'favorable site' prognosis. IRS-IV established that pulsed VAC chemotherapy is highly effective and that local control is best achieved with 45-50.4 Gy radiation for residual disease. Current COG (Children's Oncology Group) trials aim to reduce toxicity by lowering radiation doses in specific 'low-risk' embryonal cohorts.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Transient Monocular Vision Loss (TMVL), traditionally termed 'Amaurosis Fugax,' is a sudden, temporary deficit in vision in one eye, typically lasting seconds to minutes, with complete recovery. It represents a Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) of the retina, optic nerve, or choroid and demands immediate systemic investigation to prevent cerebrovascular accidents (CVA).

sections.title: The GCA Red Flag Screen
content: New onset headache or scalp tenderness
Jaw claudication (highest predictive value)
Anorexia, weight loss, or night sweats
Proximal muscle aches (Polymyalgia Rheumatica)
Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD) with pale disc edema
Elevated ESR (>50 mm/hr), CRP, and Platelets

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: Step 1: Detailed History (Onset, duration, 'curtain' vs 'fog', triggers)
Step 2: Dilated Fundoscopy & BP measurement (urgent)
Step 3: Carotid Imaging (Duplex Ultrasound vs. CTA/MRA)
Step 4: Cardiac Workup (ECG, Holter monitor, Echocardiogram)
Step 5: Serology (CBC, PT/PTT, Lipid profile, A1c, ESR/CRP)
Step 6: Brain Imaging (MRI with DWI to rule out silent infarcts)

rows: Orbital tumors (cavernous hemangioma), Optic nerve sheath meningioma
Delayed photoreceptor recovery due to hypoperfusion
CEA beneficial (moderate reduction in stroke risk)

sections.title: Evidence-Based Medical Therapy
content: Antiplatelet Therapy: Aspirin (81-325mg) or Clopidogrel (Plavix) 75mg daily.
Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT): Often used for first 21-90 days post-symptom in high-risk patients.
High-Intensity Statins: Atorvastatin 80mg regardless of baseline LDL (SPARCL trial).
Blood Pressure Control: Target <130/80 mmHg (avoid aggressive drops in acute OIS).
Smoking Cessation: Essential to prevent plaque progression and rupture.

content.explanation: F: Flow (Carotid/Hemodynamic); U: Unusual (Vasospasm/Migraine); G: Giant Cell Arteritis (Must exclude!); A: Arrhythmia (Afib/Cardiac emboli); X: X-plore Hematological (Hypercoagulability).

sections.title: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (OIS)
content: Caused by severe (>90%) carotid occlusion.
Mid-peripheral 'blossom' hemorrhages (dot-and-blot).
Dilated, non-tortuous retinal veins (distinct from CRVO).
Iridocyclitis & Neovascularization of the Iris (NVI).
Ocular Angina: Dull periocular ache from ischemia.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Landmark Studies
sections.content: The **POINT** and **CHANCE** trials have revolutionized early TIA management, showing that short-term DAPT (Aspirin + Clopidogrel) significantly reduces early recurrent stroke risk compared to aspirin alone. In the ophthalmic world, OCT-Angiography is emerging as a non-invasive tool to detect focal areas of capillary non-perfusion in post-TMVL patients.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques: CEA vs. CAS
content: CEA (Carotid Endarterectomy): Gold standard for most surgical candidates; removes the plaque directly.
CAS (Carotid Artery Stenting): Preferred in high-risk surgical anatomy (previous neck radiation, recurrent stenosis).
Crest Trial: Showed parity in outcomes between CEA and CAS for symptomatic patients in terms of stroke/death rates.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Resident Exams
content: TMVL in a young patient? Think Retinal Migraine, Cardiac Shunts (PFO), or Hypercoagulable states.
Bright light-induced amaurosis is pathognomonic for Ocular Ischemic Syndrome.
Always check for a carotid bruit, but remember: its absence does NOT rule out significant stenosis.
Venous stasis retinopathy (early OIS) is often mistaken for a mild CRVO; check the venous pulsation and tortuosity.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Lattice Corneal Dystrophy (LCD) is the most common form of stromal corneal dystrophy characterized by the deposition of amyloid fibrils within the corneal stroma. It is primarily an autosomal dominant condition associated with mutations in the TGFBI gene (Transforming Growth Factor Beta Induced) on chromosome 5q31. Clinically, it presents with branching, refractile lattice lines, subepithelial white dots, and a progressive stromal haze, often leading to recurrent corneal erosions (RCE) and significant visual impairment by the fourth or fifth decade of life.

rows: Early onset (1st decade), fine lattice lines, severe RCE
Lattice lines start peripherally, late onset
Thick lattice lines, late onset (7th decade)
Thick lines, late onset, RCE common
Deep stromal lattice lines, late onset

sections.title: Clinical Features: The Slit-Lamp Exam
content: Fine, branching, refractile lines in the anterior/mid stroma.
Small, white subepithelial dots (amyloid deposits).
Diffuse stromal haze (ground-glass appearance) in later stages.
Lattice lines usually clear the peripheral 1-2mm (limbal sparing).
Recurrent Corneal Erosions (RCE) often precede lattice lines.
Decreased corneal sensitivity due to nerve involvement/amyloid.

sections.title: Red Flags: Meretoja Syndrome (LCD Type II)
content: Progressive Cranial Nerve Palsies (esp. Facial Nerve VII)
Mask-like facies (due to facial nerve involvement)
Cutis Laxa (loose, redundant skin)
Peripheral Neuropathy
Cardiac Arrhythmias or Amyloid Cardiomyopathy
Autonomic dysfunction (Postural hypotension)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. High-Magnification Slit-Lamp: Retroillumination is key for refractile lines.
2. Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT): Visualizes hyperreflective stromal deposits and epithelial irregularities.
3. In Vivo Confocal Microscopy (IVCM): Shows highly reflective, branching linear structures in the stroma.
4. Genetic Testing: TGFBI gene sequencing for definitive typing.
5. Corneal Sensitivity (Cochet-Bonnet): Often reduced early on.

rows: Diffuse haze to limbus, thinning, Autosomal Recessive
Central subepithelial crystals, arcus senilis early
Combination of granular dots and lattice lines

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Conservative management of RCE (Lubricants, Hypertonic saline, Bandage Contact Lens).
Step 2: Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK) for superficial deposits and RCE prevention.
Step 3: Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) if deposits are deep but endothelium is healthy.
Step 4: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) for full-thickness stromal haze.
Step 5: Post-operative monitoring for recurrence (Common in LCD).

rows: High success; risk of graft rejection

content.mnemonic: Marilyn Monroe Got Hers in Los Angeles
content.explanation: Macular = Mucopolysaccharide; Granular = Hyaline; Lattice = Amyloid.

sections.title: Prognosis & Recurrence
content: Lattice has the highest recurrence rate among stromal dystrophies.
Recurrence in graft usually occurs within 3-10 years post-op.
Recurrent deposits often start as a peripheral subepithelial haze.
Secondary RCE can occur even after successful keratoplasty.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: LCD Type I is almost always TGFBI Arg124Cys.
In retroillumination, lattice lines look like 'glass threads'.
Vision loss is dual-mode: chronic haze + acute RCE episodes.
Decreased corneal sensation is a helpful diagnostic sign for LCD.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Data
sections.content: Recent research focuses on siRNA (small interfering RNA) to silence the mutant TGFBI allele and gene editing via CRISPR/Cas9. Studies have shown that DALK may offer better long-term outcomes than PKP for LCD because the amyloid deposits do not involve the host endothelium, and maintaining the host's own endothelium reduces the long-term risk of rejection. However, recurrence in the donor stroma remains a significant hurdle across all keratoplasty techniques.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Pseudoexfoliation (PXF) is a systemic microfibrillopathy characterized by the production and progressive accumulation of an abnormal fibrillar material in ocular tissues and visceral organs. It involves a mutation in the LOXL1 gene. In the eye, this proteinaceous material deposits on the lens capsule, iris, and zonules, leading to zonular fragility and basement membrane dysfunction.

sections.title: The PXF Ocular Examination
content: Classic Three-Zone Lens Pattern: Central disc, peripheral granular zone, and clear intermediate zone.
Sampaolesi Line: Pigment deposition anterior to Schwalbe's line on gonioscopy.
Pupillary 'Moth-eaten' Atrophy: Transillumination defects at the sphincter.
Phacodonesis: Visible wobbling of the lens during rapid eye movements (indicates severe zonular loss).
Iridodonesis: Shaking of the iris upon eye movement due to lack of lens support.
Asymmetric Anterior Chamber Depth: May suggest subluxation or zonular laxity.

sections.title: Preoperative Red Flags
content: Frank Phacodonesis or Subluxation
History of ocular trauma (compounds PXF fragility)
Poor pupillary response to maximum mydriatics (< 4mm)
Angle closure or Very Shallow AC depth
Vitreous in the anterior chamber (spontaneous vitreous prolapse)

content.explanation: S: Sampaolesi Line; A: Asymmetric AC depth; F: Fibrillar material; E: Edge of lens visible on dilation; L: LOXL1 Genetics; E: Excessive Pigment; N: Narrow Angle; S: Shaking (Donesis).

rows: Expands capsular bag, redistributes tension to healthy zonules.
Allows for scleral suturing of the ring without violating the bag.
Segmental support; can be used in cases where a full ring cannot be threaded.
Mechanical expansion of the pupil to allow visualization.

sections.title: Surgical Strategy: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Maximizing Mydriasis - Use intracameral phenylephrine/lidocaine or mechanical dilators.
Step 2: Capsulorhexis (CCC) - Larger CCC (5.5mm-6.0mm) is safer to reduce later capsular phimosis.
Step 3: Hydrodissection - Perform 'Cortical Cleaving' hydrodissection to minimize zonular stress during rotation.
Step 4: Phacoemulsification - Use 'Slow Motion' settings; keep the nucleus central; avoid 'Push-Pull' maneuvers.
Step 5: CTR Insertion - Insert as LATE as possible (after cortex removal) unless necessary for stability during phaco.
Step 6: Cortex Removal - Use tangential stripping rather than radial pulling to protect remaining zonules.

sections.title: Postoperative Counseling & Warnings
content: Risk of Early IOP Spikes: PXF patients have compromised trabecular meshwork; monitor pressure 2-4 hours post-op.
Late IOL Dislocation: Explain that the entire 'bag' can dislocate years later, even if the surgery was perfect.
Chronic Inflammation: Higher risk of postoperative uveitis and fibrinous reactions.
Capsular Phimosis: The capsulorhexis opening may shrink over time; YAG laser capsulotomy may be needed.
Corneal Endothelial Fragility: PXF is associated with lower cell counts; recovery may be slower.

sections.title: Surgical Complication Management
content: Sudden deepening of AC: Suspect Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR).
Lens Tilt during Phaco: Indicates focal zonular dialysis.
Vitreous Prolapse: Perform early bimanual anterior vitrectomy; do NOT use sponge and scissors.
Dropped Nucleus: Do not chase! Level the eye and refer to a vitreoretinal surgeon.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Success
content: Use highly dispersive OVD (e.g., Viscoat) to protect the endothelium.
Try to avoid IOLs with high-angulation haptics if zonules are weak.
Always check for a Sampaolesi line in any 'glaucoma suspect'.
If the bag is extremely loose, consider 3-piece IOL in the sulcus with optic capture.

sections.title: Landmark Evidence
sections.content: The SCORPIO Study and various Nordic registries have highlighted that PXF is the leading identifiable cause of open-angle glaucoma and spontaneous IOL-capsular bag dislocation. Recent data suggests that early cataract intervention might be safer than waiting for the cataract to become 'hypermature' and zonules to further degrade.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Upbeat nystagmus (UBN) is a primary position vertical jerk nystagmus with the fast phase directed superiorly. It is an acquired ocular motor disorder that often violates Alexander's Law, typically increasing in intensity on upgaze. It results from an imbalance in the vertical vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) or a defect in the vertical neural integrator.

rows: Wallenberg Syndrome (Lateral Medullary Infarction), PICA or AICA stroke, Thalamic hemorrhage.
Medulloblastoma, Astrocytoma, Paraneoplastic syndromes (Anti-Yo, Anti-Hu antibodies).
Lithium toxicity, Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, Alcohol intoxication, Tobacco-alcohol amblyopia.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: Why does it happen?
content: Imbalance in Vertical VOR: Selective damage to the posterior semicircular canal pathways (which mediate downward slow phases).
Neural Integrator Failure: Damage to the Interstitial Nucleus of Cajal (INC) or the Nucleus Prepositus Hypoglossi (NPH) leads to a 'leaky' integrator.
Primary Position Instability: The slow phase drifts downward due to gravity or tonic imbalance, triggering a corrective upward fast phase.
Cerebellar Disinhibition: Loss of Purkinje cell inhibition from the flocculus/paraflocculus on the vestibular nuclei.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Fast phase directed UPWARD in primary position.
Amplitude increases in UPGaze (usually).
May decrease or convert to DBN in downgaze (occasionally).
Associated with Oscillopsia (visual blurring/shaking).
Often associated with other brainstem signs (ataxia, dysarthria, Horner's syndrome).

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Acute onset UBN with Ataxia & Confusion (Suspect Wernicke’s!)
Associated Papilledema (Suspect Midbrain tumor/Hydrocephalus)
Sudden 'Thunderclap' headache (Brainstem hemorrhage)
Progressive swallowing or breathing difficulties (Lower medullary compression)

content.explanation: U: Upper Medulla, P: Pons (paramedian), B: Brainstem (diffuse), E: Eye-movement Integrator (INC), A: Anterior Vermis (Cerebellum), T: Thiamine deficiency (Wernicke's).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Neuro-ophthalmologic Exam - Confirm UBN, check for internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) or skew deviation.
Step 2: Urgent Neuroimaging - MRI Brain with GAD + MRI Posterior Fossa (Focus on Craniocervical junction and Brainstem).
Step 3: Laboratory Testing - Serum Thiamine (B1) levels, CBC, BMP, Magnesium, Lithium levels.
Step 4: Paraneoplastic Panel - If imaging is negative and age/risk factors suggest occult malignancy.
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture - If MS or inflammatory/infectious etiology is suspected (check O-bands, cytology).

rows: NMDA receptor antagonist; helps suppress oscillation.
GABA-B agonist; particularly effective for periodic alternating or vertical nystagmus.
Calcium channel subunit ligand; reduces oscillopsia.
Potassium channel blocker; more commonly used for DBN but trial in UBN.
MANDATORY if Wernicke's suspected; give BEFORE glucose.

sections.title: Surgical & Optical Strategies
content: Base-down Prisms: Shift the image into a gaze position where the nystagmus is minimized (null zone).
Large-recess Kestenbaum: Surgical transposition of extraocular muscles to move the eyes toward the null zone (rarely used for acquired UBN).
Botulinum Toxin Injections: Retrobulbar injection can temporarily paretize muscles to reduce amplitude (last resort due to side effects).

content.explanation: If UBN is present in primary position and increases in upgaze, think Medulla. If UBN is present in primary position but increases in downgaze (or is associated with See-saw), think Midbrain.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
sections.content: Prognosis is entirely dependent on the underlying cause. Wernicke-related UBN can resolve rapidly with thiamine. MS-related UBN may fluctuate with relapses. Chronic UBN leads to severe reading difficulty and gait instability, significantly impacting quality of life and increasing fall risk.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Congenital UBN: Rare; often associated with ocular albinism or Leber Congenital Amaurosis.
Neuroblastoma: Always screen for opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome.
Leigh Syndrome: Mitochondrial disorder causing brainstem lesions and vertical nystagmus.

sections.title: GCD1 vs. GCD2: A Comparative Analysis

rows: Granular dots + Lattice-like lines + Star-shaped opacities
Gradual decline; severe in later life

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
sections.content: The TGFBI gene encodes keratoepithelin, a 68-kDa extracellular matrix protein. Mutations lead to misfolding and accumulation of insoluble mutant protein. In GCD1, the Arg555Trp mutation causes purely hyaline deposits. In GCD2 (Avellino), the Arg124His mutation results in a unique phenotypic mix of hyaline (granular) and amyloid (lattice-like) features. Deposits typically begin in the anterior stroma and progress posteriorly and peripherally.

sections.title: ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION
content: NEVER perform LASIK or PRK on patients with Granular/Avellino Dystrophy.
Laser refractive surgery triggers a massive wound-healing response.
Results in catastrophic, rapid deposition of mutant protein across the interface.
Genetic screening is mandatory in high-prevalence regions (e.g., Korea) before refractive surgery.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workflow
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (Sclerotic scatter is key).
Step 2: Anterior Segment OCT (Hyper-reflective stromal deposits).
Step 3: Genetic Testing (Confirms TGFBI mutation; Gold Standard).
Step 4: IVCM (In Vivo Confocal Microscopy) for deposit depth.
Step 5: Histopathology (Masson Trichrome and Congo Red stains).

content.mnemonic: Marilyn Monroe Always Gets Her Men in Sunny Cinema
content.explanation: M-Macular: M-Masson Trichrome/Acid-Schiff (False: Macular is Alcian Blue); G-Granular: H-Hyaline (Masson Trichrome); L-Lattice: A-Amyloid (Congo Red). Focus: Granular = Red (Masson); Lattice = Green (Congo Red bifringence).

sections.title: Management Ladder
content: 1. Conservative: Lubrication and bandage contact lenses (BCL) for RCEs.
2. PTK (Phototherapeutic Keratectomy): For superficial deposits and RCE management.
3. DALK (Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty): Preferred over PKP if endothelium is healthy.
4. PKP (Penetrating Keratoplasty): For full-thickness stromal involvement.
5. Post-Op: Monitor for recurrence in the graft (very common).

rows: Well-defined, mapped mutation; strong clinical evidence.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: GCD1: Clear spaces between 'crumbs' remain clear until late stages.
GCD2: Amyloid lines are typically fewer and thicker than in Lattice Dystrophy Type 1.
Recurrence: In GCD, recurrence in grafts often appears as a superficial subepithelial haze first.
Homozygotes: Rare, but present with much earlier and more aggressive disease than heterozygotes.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Gene Silencing: siRNA-based therapies aiming to reduce mutant TGFBI mRNA.
CRISPR/Cas9: Research into allele-specific gene editing to 'turn off' the mutant allele.
Autophagy Modulators: Investigating drugs that enhance the clearance of misfolded proteins.
Universal Pre-Refractive Genetic Screening: Becoming standard in high-risk populations.

sections.title: Surgical Complications
content: Graft Recurrence: Almost 100% over 15-20 years.
Iatrogenic Ectasia: Risk if PTK is too aggressive.
Interface Opacification: Unique to lamellar procedures.
Steroid-Induced Glaucoma: Post-keratoplasty risk.

sections.title: Investigation: OCT Interpretation
sections.content: Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT) is vital for surgical planning. Deposits in GCD appear as highly reflective 'shards' within the stroma. AS-OCT helps differentiate if deposits are limited to the anterior 100-150 microns (suitable for PTK) or extend deeper (requiring DALK/PKP).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Myasthenic Crisis is defined as an exacerbation of MG-related muscle weakness severe enough to necessitate intubation for airway protection or mechanical ventilation. It occurs in approximately 15-20% of patients with MG, usually within the first two years of diagnosis. It is a true neuro-ophthalmic and pulmonary emergency.

branches: AChR Antibodies (85%): Direct receptor blockade & complement-mediated destruction

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Impending Respiratory Failure
content: Weak cough and inability to clear secretions
Staccato speech (pausing for breath every few words)
Use of accessory respiratory muscles (sternocleidomastoid)
Paradoxical breathing (abdominal wall moves in during inspiration)
Difficulty swallowing saliva (pooling of secretions)
Rapidly progressive bulbar palsy

rows: Severe reduction in ventilatory reserve; elective intubation indicated.
Inability to generate enough force to expand lungs.
Inability to clear secretions; high risk of aspiration pneumonia.

sections.title: Ocular & Bulbar Clinical Findings
content: Cogan's Lid Twitch: Overshoot of the upper lid after looking down then rapidly back to primary.
Enhanced Ptosis: Manually lifting one lid causes the other to drop (Hering’s Law).
Variable Diplopia: Does not follow a single cranial nerve pattern; often mimics 3rd, 4th, or 6th nerve palsies.
Orbicularis Oculi Weakness: Pathognomonic 'peek sign' during sustained forceful closure.
Fatigability: Increasing ptosis during sustained upgaze for 60 seconds.

rows: Beta-blockers (even topical Timolol), Calcium Channel Blockers, Procainamide

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Hierarchy
content: Step 1: Clinical Assessment & Bedside Tests (Ice Pack Test: 2 mins on lid; improvement = positive).
Step 2: Pulmonary Function Tests (Bedside VC, MIP, MEP every 4-6 hours).
Step 3: Serology (AChR-Ab, MuSK-Ab, LRP4-Ab). Note: Crisis can occur in seronegative patients.
Step 4: Electrophysiology (Repetitive Nerve Stimulation showing >10% decrement; Single-fiber EMG for highest sensitivity).
Step 5: Imaging (Chest CT/MRI to evaluate for Thymoma or thymic hyperplasia).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: MG vs. The World

rows: Overdose of Pyridostigmine; SLUDGE syndrome (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, etc.), miosis, bradycardia.
Strength improves with exercise; associated with Small Cell Lung Cancer; autonomic dysfunction.
Triad of Ataxia, Areflexia, and Ophthalmoplegia; CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation.
Fixed dilated pupils (usually), descending paralysis, history of ingestion/wound.
Lid retraction (not ptosis), proptosis, restrictive strabismus, CT shows enlarged muscles.

sections.title: Acute Management Protocol
content: 1. ICU Admission: Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring.
2. Airway Management: Early elective intubation based on '20-30-40' rule.
3. Stop Anticholinesterases: Hold Pyridostigmine (Mestinon) during crisis to reduce bronchial secretions.
4. Targeted Therapy: Initiate Plasmapheresis (PLEX) 5-7 exchanges OR IVIG (2g/kg over 2-5 days). PLEX is often preferred for rapid response.
5. Corticosteroids: Start High-dose Prednisone (60-80mg) or IV Methylprednisolone. Caution: Steroids can cause transient worsening.
6. Complication Prophylaxis: VTE prophylaxis, stress ulcer prevention, and aggressive treatment of underlying infection.

content.explanation: C: Cholinesterase inhibitors (Hold them); R: Respiration (20/30/40 rule); I: Infection (Treat trigger); S: Steroids (Wait until PLEX/IVIG started); I: IVIG or PLEX; S: Secretion management.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Pyridostigmine has no role in the acute management of crisis and may worsen it by increasing secretions.
The Ice Pack Test has a sensitivity of ~80% for myasthenic ptosis; the cold decreases acetylcholinesterase activity.
MuSK-positive MG often involves more severe bulbar and respiratory weakness with less ocular involvement.
Up to 15% of MG patients have an underlying Thymoma; thymectomy is indicated after the patient is stabilized.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Targeted Biologics
content: Eculizumab (Soliris): Complement inhibitor (C5) for refractory AChR-positive MG.
Efgartigimod (Vyvgart): Neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) blocker; reduces circulating IgG levels.
Zilucoplan: Small peptide C5 inhibitor (subcutaneous delivery).
Rozanolixizumab: Another FcRn inhibitor specifically effective in both AChR+ and MuSK+ MG.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Significance
sections.content: A 'small pupil' in cataract surgery is typically defined as a diameter <4.0–5.0 mm after maximal pharmacological dilation. This significantly restricts the surgical field, increases the risk of iris trauma, posterior capsule rupture (PCR), and incomplete cortical cleanup. Proper management is essential for successful Phacoemulsification and IOL centration.

sections.title: IFIS: The Classic Triad
content: Billowing of a flaccid iris stroma in response to normal irrigation currents.
Propensity for the iris to prolapse toward the phaco or side-port incisions.
Progressive intraoperative miosis despite standard dilation protocols.

sections.title: Pre-operative Assessment Protocol
content: Medication Review: Specifically query Alpha-1 blockers (Flomax, Rapaflo) and Antipsychotics.
Dilation Check: Measure pupil size 30-45 mins post-dilation.
Slit Lamp: Check for PXE material on the lens capsule or pupillary margin.
Synechiae Check: Identify 360-degree adhesion via gonioscopy or high-mag slit lamp.
Zonular Integrity: Look for phacodonesis or iridodonesis (common in PXE).

rows: Potent dilation and iris anesthesia; pH balanced.
Maintains pupil size and reduces post-op pain/inflammation.
Relaxes iris sphincter and provides local analgesia.

content.explanation: S: Synechiolysis, T: Tamsulosin check, R: Ring (Malyugin), E: Epinephrine (Intracameral), T: Tissue stretching (Beehler), C: Capsulorhexis (Large enough!), H: Hooks (Iris).

sections.title: Viscoelastic Management (OVD)
content: Healon 5 (Super-viscoadaptive): High viscosity at rest to viscomydriate the pupil.
Healon GV: High molecular weight to maintain space and hold the iris back.
Soft-Shell Technique: Dispersive OVD (Viscoat) near the cornea, cohesive (Healon) for pupil management.

sections.title: Mechanical Expansion Hierarchy
content: Step 1: Pharmacological (Intracameral Shugarcaine/Epinephrine)
Step 2: Viscomydriasis (Healon 5 or GV)
Step 3: Manual Synechiolysis (using spatula or cyclodialysis hook)
Step 4: Pupillary Stretching (Two-instrument bimanual stretching)
Step 5: Iris Hooks (4-point or 5-point diamond configuration)
Step 6: Pupil Expansion Rings (Malyugin, Graether, or Diamond Ring)

rows: Local stress at hook points (risk of sphincter tears)
Can slip or rotate if not tightened properly

sections.title: Step-by-Step: Malyugin Ring Insertion
content: 1. Fill anterior chamber with cohesive OVD.
2. Insert injector through main incision (2.2mm or larger).
3. Engage the lead scroll on the distal iris margin.
4. Partially retract the injector to release side scrolls; engage iris.
5. Fully release the proximal scroll and use a Lester or Sinskey hook to seat it.
6. Verify all 4 scrolls are securely holding the pupillary margin.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Stop Dilation
content: Excessive Sphincter Bleeding (Hyphema risk).
Sudden Zonular Dehiscence during mechanical stretching.
Iris Prolapse through the main incision (classic IFIS).
Atonic Pupil (post-operative permanent mydriasis).

sections.title: Surgical Pearls for the Small Pupil
content: Create a larger Capsulorhexis (5.5mm-6.0mm) if possible, even if you have to go under the iris.
Lower your Fluidics: High flow and vacuum increase iris billowing in IFIS.
Bimanual Phaco: Use the second instrument to hold the iris back if hooks aren't available.
Cortical Cleanup: Use 'J-shaped' I/A tips to reach sub-incisional cortex hidden by the iris.
IOL Choice: Consider three-piece IOLs or those with high tactile feedback if zonules are weak.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Landmark Insights
sections.content: The 'BOLT' study (Chang et al.) emphasized that stopping Tamsulosin pre-operatively does not reliably prevent IFIS. Recent focus has shifted to the use of Femtosecond Laser-Assisted Cataract Surgery (FLACS) which can perform the capsulotomy and nuclear fragmentation before the pupil constricts due to prostaglandins.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Post-operative Atonic Pupil (Cosmetic and glare issues).
Micro-hyphema from sphincter tears.
Increased risk of Retained Lens Fragments.
Higher incidence of CME due to iris manipulation.
Prognosis is excellent (>95% success) with appropriate mechanical expansion.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Epithelial Basement Membrane Dystrophy (EBMD), also known as Cogan Microcystic Dystrophy or Map-Dot-Fingerprint Dystrophy, is an anterior corneal dystrophy characterized by an abnormal, redundant basement membrane that extends into the corneal epithelium. This lead to poor epithelial-stromal adhesion, causing recurrent corneal erosions (RCE) and visual disturbances due to irregular astigmatism.

branches: TGFBI Gene Mutation (Rarely associated; usually sporadic)

rows: Large, circumscribed areas of ground-glass opacification with clear borders.
Abnormal BM extending between epithelial layers.
Small, round, grayish-white intraepithelial opacities (Cogan cysts).
Trapped epithelial cells/debris and basement membrane.
Clusters of parallel, curvilinear lines mimicking a fingerprint.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Asymptomatic (vast majority of patients).
Recurrent Corneal Erosions (RCE): Sudden, severe pain, photophobia, and lacrimation upon waking.
Blurred Vision: Due to surface irregularity and secondary astigmatism.
Monocular Diplopia / Ghosting: From tear film instability.
Foreign Body Sensation (FBS): Chronic mild irritation.
Worse in the morning: Eyelids stick to poorly adhered epithelium.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Suspected Microbial Keratitis (Secondary to RCE)
Severe Vision Loss (Evaluate for irregular astigmatism)
Contact Lens Intolerance with sudden pain
Refractive Surgery Screening: EBMD is a relative contraindication for LASIK (risk of epithelial sloughing)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Slit-Lamp Bio: Use broad beam, retroillumination, and sclerotic scatter.
2. Fluorescein Staining: Look for 'negative staining' where maps/dots elevate the tear film.
3. AS-OCT: Visualizes duplicated basement membrane and intraepithelial cysts.
4. Corneal Topography: Displays irregular astigmatism and surface asphericity.
5. Epithelial Mapping: Highlights significant thickness variations.

rows: Stromal amyloid lines; deeper than EBMD.

sections.title: Management Strategy: Medical
content: 1. Intensive Lubrication: Preservative-free artificial tears (daytime).
2. Hypertonic Saline (Muro 128): 5% drops/ointment at bedtime to reduce epithelial edema.
3. Bandage Contact Lens (BCL): Extended wear for 4-12 weeks to allow hemidesmosome formation.
4. Doxycycline (50mg BID) + Topical Steroid: Inhibits Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs) involved in BM degradation.

sections.title: Management Strategy: Surgical
content: 1. Epithelial Debridement: Manual scraping to remove redundant BM (office procedure).
2. Diamond Burr Polishing (DBP): Polishing Bowman’s layer to encourage better adhesion (high success rate).
3. Anterior Stromal Puncture: For localized RCE; creates focal scarring to anchor epithelium.
4. PTK (Phototherapeutic Keratectomy): Excimer laser ablation of 5-10 microns of anterior stroma.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: Pearl 1: Always check for EBMD in patients with 'unexplained' vision loss or fluctuating refraction.
Pearl 2: Use the 'Dry Sponge' technique during debridement to identify loose, redundant epithelium.
Pearl 3: EBMD can mimic keratoconus on topography; always look at the physical cornea before diagnosing ectasia.
Pearl 4: In refractive surgery, PRK is preferred over LASIK if EBMD is present to avoid flap complications.
Pearl 5: Recurrence is common (up to 25%) even after surgical intervention; long-term lubrication is key.

sections.title: Memory Aid: The 3 M's of EBMD

content.explanation: M: Maps (Duplicated BM), A: Abnormal Adhesion (RCE risk), P: Polishing (Diamond Burr Treatment), S: Slit-lamp (Diagnosis key).

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Prognosis: Excellent for visual recovery after treatment.
Complication: Chronic RCE can lead to corneal scarring or secondary infection.
Complication: Post-surgical haze (after PTK).
Recurrence: Symptoms may return years after debridement due to ongoing BM production.

sections.title: Recent Advances
sections.content: Recent studies suggest that Matrix Metalloproteinase (MMP-9) levels are significantly elevated in the tear film of EBMD patients with active erosions. This has led to the use of MMP-9 inhibitors like topical Azithromycin and oral Doxycycline as primary adjunctive therapies. Furthermore, Epithelial Thickness Mapping (ETM) via OCT is becoming the gold standard for monitoring subclinical map and dot changes during treatment.

summary: A definitive clinical guide to differentiating mechanical ocular tethering from innervational failure. Mastery of the Forced Acton Test, saccadic velocities, and orbital imaging is essential for the strabismologist.

data.title: The Great Tug-of-War: Restrictive vs. Paralytic Strabismus
data.summary: A definitive clinical guide to differentiating mechanical ocular tethering from innervational failure. Mastery of the Forced Acton Test, saccadic velocities, and orbital imaging is essential for the strabismologist.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Core Concepts
sections.content: Restrictive Strabismus results from mechanical tethering or structural interference with the globe's rotation (e.g., fibrosis, entrapment, or orbital masses). Paralytic Strabismus (Paretic) results from a defect in the efferent pathway, including the cranial nerve nuclei, the nerves themselves (CN III, IV, VI), or the neuromuscular junction, leading to muscle weakness.

sections.title: The Deciding Factor: Forced Acton Test (FAT)
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic (Proparacaine 0.5%) and optional 4% Cocaine for vasoconstriction.
Step 2: Grasp the globe at the limbus with toothed forceps (0.5mm Castroviejo) opposite the direction of limited movement.
Step 3: Attempt to move the globe passively into the field of restricted gaze.
Step 4: POSITIVE result = Resistance felt (Restrictive etiology).
Step 5: NEGATIVE result = No resistance (Paralytic/Paretic etiology).

sections.title: Restrictive vs. Paralytic: The Clinical Duel

rows: Often more pronounced to minimize diplopia
Small plot in paretic field, large in overacting field

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls: Saccades & IOP
content: Saccadic Velocity: In 6th nerve palsy, the eye moves slowly toward abduction. In TED, the eye moves fast until it hits the 'tether'.
IOP Differential: Check IOP in primary position and upgaze. A rise of >4mmHg in upgaze suggests inferior rectus restriction (TED).
Secondary Deviations: In paralytic cases, the deviation is greater when the paretic eye is fixing.
Old Photos: Use the 'Krimsky' version of the 'Shoebox test' (looking at old photos) to determine chronicity.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Sudden onset painful 3rd nerve palsy (Aneurysm/SAH until proven otherwise).
Bilateral 6th nerve palsy (Raised intracranial pressure).
Variable ptosis and diplopia (Myasthenia Gravis - potential respiratory crisis).
Proptosis with restriction (Orbital Cellulitis or Malignancy).

content.explanation: Order of muscle involvement in Thyroid Eye Disease (most common restrictive): Inferior Rectus > Medial Rectus > Superior Rectus > Lateral Rectus > Obliques.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Step-by-Step
content: 1. Motor Exam: 9 positions of gaze, Prism Cover Test (distinguish comitant vs incomitant).
2. Sensory Exam: Worth 4-Dot, Bagolini lenses, Stereoacuity.
3. Forced Acton Test: Essential for confirming mechanical tethering.
4. Laboratory: TSH, TSI (for TED), Acetylcholine receptor antibodies (for MG).
5. Imaging: CT Orbit (axial/coronal) for bone/muscle bulk; MRI for nerves/brainstem.

rows: Large Recessions ONLY. Faden operation (Cüppers). Adjustable sutures recommended.
Resection/Recession (R&R) if some function remains. Transpositions (e.g., Nishida) if total palsy.

sections.title: Surgical Nuance: The 'Golden Rule'
content: NEVER perform a muscle RESECTION in a restrictive disease. It will worsen the restriction.
In complete 6th nerve palsy, a simple recession/resection is useless; a Transposition (e.g., Hummelsheim or Schillinger) is required.
In TED surgery: 'When in doubt, recess more.' Always use adjustable sutures to account for post-operative tissue creep.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The PEDIG Impact
sections.content: Recent Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group (PEDIG) studies emphasize that observation for 6 months is appropriate for isolated, non-traumatic 4th and 6th nerve palsies, as high rates of spontaneous recovery (up to 70-80%) are documented in microvascular cases.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Anesthesia Dolorosa (post-nerve injury).
Slipped or Lost Muscle (Surgical emergency).
Fat Adherence Syndrome (Common after repeated restrictive strabismus surgeries).
Prognosis: Restrictive cases are often stable but difficult to cure; Paralytic cases vary by etiology (vascular = good, traumatic = guarded).

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.content: Infantile Nystagmus Syndrome (INS) is a rhythmic, involuntary oscillation of the eyes present from early childhood. The 'Null Point' is the specific angle of gaze or distance where the nystagmus intensity is minimal and visual acuity is maximal. Patients often adopt an Anomalous Head Posture (AHP) to bring this null point into the primary position.

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: INS: Failed calibration of the ocular motor system (specifically the slow-eye-movement subsystem).
FRMD7 Mutations: Linked to X-linked idiopathic congenital nystagmus.
Sensory Defect Nystagmus: Occurs due to poor image quality (e.g., albinism, achromatopsia, Leber Congenital Amaurosis).
Spasmus Nutans: Pathophysiology remains idiopathic, but must be differentiated from optic pathway gliomas mimicking the triad.

sections.title: The Kestenbaum Procedure (Classical)
content: Objective: Rotate the eyes in the direction of the head turn to shift the null point to primary position.
Rule for Right Head Turn (Null Point in Left Gaze):
1. Right Eye: Recess Lateral Rectus 7mm, Resect Medial Rectus 6mm
2. Left Eye: Recess Medial Rectus 5mm, Resect Lateral Rectus 8mm
The '5-6-7-8' Rule (Millimeters of surgery).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: The Danger of Spasmus Nutans
content: Spasmus Nutans is a diagnosis of exclusion: Neuroimaging (MRI) is MANDATORY to rule out chiasmal/optic pathway gliomas.
Look for concurrent Optic Atrophy or Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD).
Differentiate from See-Saw Nystagmus (often associated with craniopharyngioma).
Nystagmus starting after age 2 should always be considered an emergency until imaging is clear.

sections.title: Surgical Principles: Anderson-Kestenbaum
content: Yoke Muscle Surgery: Always operate on the yoke muscles responsible for the direction of the null point.
For Chin Up posture: Recess superior recti, resect inferior recti.
For Chin Down posture: Recess inferior recti, resect superior recti.
For Torticollis (Head Tilt): Vertical muscle offsets or Kestenbaum-style transposition.

content.explanation: To correct a Head TURN, you must ROTATE the eyes toward the direction of the turn. (e.g., Right Head Turn = Rotate eyes Right = Recess RLR/LMR, Resect RMR/LLR).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Flow
content: 1. Measure Visual Acuity (Binocular, Monocular, and with AHP).
2. Identify Null Point angle using a goniometer.
3. Perform Slit Lamp exam (Iris transillumination for albinism).
4. Fundoscopy (Foveal hypoplasia, optic nerve hypoplasia).
5. Eye Movement Recordings (EMR) to identify foveation periods.
6. MRI Brain/Orbits if SN-like symptoms or neurologic signs.

sections.title: Non-Surgical Management
content: Prisms: Base-out prisms to induce convergence (dampens nystagmus).
Prisms for AHP: Base toward the direction of the head turn.
Pharmacology: Gabapentin (2400mg/d) or Memantine (40mg/d) for adult INS.
Contact Lenses: May improve VA by dampening nystagmus via tactile feedback on the cornea.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent research into FRMD7 gene therapy and the use of 'Tenotomy and Reattachment' (the Hertle-Dell'Osso procedure) suggests that simply cutting and re-sewing the extraocular muscles may dampen nystagmus by disrupting the peripheral feedback loop, even without shifting the null point.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: INS nystagmus *disappears* during sleep.
Paradoxical pupillary response (constriction in darkness) can be seen in CSNB or achromatopsia associated with nystagmus.
In latent nystagmus, the fast phase always beats toward the fixing eye.
Spasmus Nutans usually has a 'shimmering' frequency (>10 Hz).

sections.title: Post-Operative Complications
content: Under-correction: The most common outcome (requires augmentation).
Over-correction: Head turn shifts to the opposite side.
Induced Strabismus: Due to unequal muscle actions or pre-existing tropias.
Scleral perforation or Endophthalmitis (rare surgical risks).
