sections.title: Definition & Purpose
sections.content: Perimetry measures the sensitivity of the retina to light stimuli across the visual field. It maps the 'island of vision in a sea of darkness'. Static perimetry (automated) assesses threshold at fixed locations, while kinetic perimetry moves stimuli from non-seeing to seeing areas.

sections.title: The SITA Revolution
content: SITA (Swedish Interactive Thresholding Algorithm): Uses mathematical models to predict thresholds.
SITA Standard: Traditional 24-2 or 30-2 protocols.
SITA Fast: Reduces testing time by ~50% with minimal loss in sensitivity.
SITA Faster: Further reduces time, removes blind spot monitoring to optimize fixation.
SITA Faster 24-2C: Adds 10 peripheral points specifically to detect glaucomatous damage in the central 10 degrees.

sections.title: Red Flags in Reliability
content: False Positives > 15%: Suggests 'trigger happy' patient (invalid).
False Negatives > 20%: Suggests fatigue or inattention.
Fixation Losses > 20%: Unreliable gaze tracking.
Gaze Tracking Graph: Look for spikes, indicating frequent ocular movements.

sections.title: Clinical Workflow: The Perimetry Process
content: Step 1: Proper refraction for age and testing distance (add +3.25D for near for 30cm).
Step 2: Trial frame or bowl-mounted lens correction (prevent rim artifacts).
Step 3: Patient instruction and practice 'dummy' run.
Step 4: Real-time gaze monitoring during testing.
Step 5: Analysis of Global Indices (MD, PSD, VFI).

content.explanation: G (Global Indices: MD/PSD), L (Losses/Fixation), A (Artifacts: Rim/Ptosis), D (Defect morphology: Arcuate/Nasal Step).

sections.title: Landmark Studies
content: OHTS (Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study): Utilized SAP (Standard Automated Perimetry) to define conversion to glaucoma.
EMGT (Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial): Established the 'Mean Deviation' (MD) as a primary metric for progression.
Comparison Studies: Confirmed that SITA-Faster provides comparable clinical utility to SITA-Standard while increasing patient satisfaction.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Adie’s Tonic Pupil (ATP) is a benign clinical entity resulting from damage to the post-ganglionic parasympathetic innervation of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle (located in the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves). It is characterized by a mid-dilated pupil that reacts poorly to light but exhibits a slow, 'tonic' response to near effort and exhibits denervation supersensitivity to dilute miotics.

sections.title: Etiology: Why Does the Ganglion Fail?
Pathophysiology: The 97% Rule
sections.content: Normally, 97% of ciliary ganglion fibers serve the ciliary muscle (accommodation) and only 3% serve the iris sphincter (light reflex). After damage, fibers regrow randomly. Because there are so many more 'accommodation' fibers, they overwhelmingly re-innervate the iris sphincter. This 'Aberrant Regeneration' explains the Light-Near Dissociation: the pupil constricts during near effort because the ciliary muscle signal is misdirected to the iris.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Anisocoria: Greater in bright light (affected pupil is larger).
Sectoral Iris Palsy: Segmental paralysis of the iris sphincter.
Vermiform Movements: 'Worm-like' iris contractions visible under slit-lamp.
Tonic Near Response: Slow constriction followed by even slower redilation.
Decreased Accommodation: Transient blurred near vision in the acute phase.

content.explanation: 1. Tonic Pupil (unilateral or bilateral). 2. Tendon Reflexes absent or diminished (Deep Tendon Reflexes, particularly the Achilles and patellar). 3. Autonomic Dysfunction (e.g., localized segmental anhidrosis - Ross Syndrome).

sections.title: Pharmacological Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Measure resting pupil sizes in dark and light room conditions.
Step 2: Prepare Dilute Pilocarpine (0.1% or 0.125%). Standard 1% pilocarpine must be diluted with sterile saline.
Step 3: Instill one drop in both eyes (the normal eye acts as a control).
Step 4: Wait 30–45 minutes in a dimly lit room.
Step 5: Re-evaluate. A POSITIVE test shows constriction of the Adie's pupil (denervation supersensitivity) while the normal pupil remains unchanged.
Step 6: If no response, consider higher concentrations to R/O Pharmacological Blockade.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Rule out CN III Palsy!
content: Acute onset Ptosis or Diplopia (Suggests CN III)
Severe Headache or 'Worst Headache of Life' (Aneurysm risk)
Extraocular Muscle limitation (Down and Out)
Absence of Light-Near Dissociation
Sudden onset in patients with vascular risk factors

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Resident Exams
content: Long-standing Adie's pupils tend to become smaller over time ('Little Old Adie's').
Bilateral Adie's can mimic Argyll Robertson but ATP pupils are usually mid-dilated, not miotic.
Sectoral palsy is best seen using a slit-lamp with a narrow beam to stimulate specific iris segments.
The site of the lesion is the Ciliary Ganglion (Post-ganglionic).

sections.title: Management & Patient Counseling
content: Observation: The primary management for this benign condition.
Reassurance: Explain the non-neurological, non-life-threatening nature.
Reading Glasses: May help with unequal accommodation (unequal adds).
Cosmetic Miotics: Very dilute pilocarpine (0.05% - 0.1%) can be used for cosmesis or to reduce photophobia.
Sunglasses: For symptomatic glare in bright light.

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-up
sections.content: The prognosis is excellent. While the tonicity often persists, accommodation usually recovers through aberrant regeneration over several months. Patients should be warned that there is a 4% annual risk of the second eye becoming involved. Periodic follow-up is recommended to monitor for the development of bilateral involvement or associated autonomic features (Ross Syndrome).

content.explanation: A rare progression/variant of Holmes-Adie characterized by the Triad of: 1. Tonic Pupil, 2. Hyporeflexia, and 3. Segmental Anhidrosis (inability to sweat in certain areas). It represents a more widespread degeneration of the autonomic nervous system.

title: Acanthamoeba Keratitis: The Sight-Threatening Paradox
summary: Acanthamoeba keratitis (AK) is a severe, potentially blinding protozoan infection of the cornea, characterized by intense pain disproportionate to clinical findings. Early detection is the cornerstone of visual preservation, as delayed diagnosis often leads to ring infiltrate formation and scleritis.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Acanthamoeba is a free-living, ubiquitous protozoan (cysts and trophozoites) found in water, soil, and dust. AK is primarily associated with contact lens wear (85-90% of cases). Prevalence is rising due to increased soft contact lens (SCL) usage and improper hygiene, such as tap water rinsing or swimming in lenses.

branches: Trophozoite: Active, mobile, feeds on bacteria/corneal epithelial cells
Encystment: Dormant state, highly resistant to chlorine/anti-amoebic drugs
Adhesion: Mannose-binding protein facilitates corneal binding
Proteolysis: Secretion of collagenases/serine proteases inducing stromal necrosis

sections.title: Red Flags: Diagnostic Pitfalls
content: Pain disproportionate to slit-lamp signs (The 'Classic' mismatch)
Radial keratoneuritis (inflamed corneal nerves)
Failure to respond to antibiotic or antiviral therapy
Ring infiltrate (usually a sign of late-stage disease)
Diagnostic delay exceeding 2-3 weeks significantly worsens prognosis

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Corneal scraping (Gold standard) - Non-nutrient agar with E. coli overlay.
Step 2: In-vivo Confocal Microscopy (IVCM) - Visualizing double-walled cysts in vivo.
Step 3: PCR for Acanthamoeba DNA - Highly sensitive (up to 95%).
Step 4: Histopathology (if penetrating keratoplasty is performed) - Calcofluor white staining.

rows: Dendritic ulcers, positive history of recurrence

sections.title: Treatment Protocol
content: Biguanides: Polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) 0.02% or Chlorhexidine 0.02%.
Diamidines: Propamidine isethionate 0.1% (Brolene).
Adjuncts: Topical NSAIDs (for pain control), Cycloplegics (Atropine 1%).
Systemic: Oral Itraconazole may be considered in refractory cases.
Duration: Minimum 6-12 months of topical therapy to clear encysted forms.

sections.title: Memory Aid: The 3 R's of AK

content.explanation: Radiating pain (disproportionate), Radial keratoneuritis (nerve inflammation), Ring infiltrate (classic stromal ring).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always suspect AK in contact lens wearers with persistent red eye.
Stop all contact lens wear immediately.
Avoid topical steroids early in the disease; they promote trophozoite transformation and proliferation.
Surgical intervention (PKP) is only for non-responsive cases/perforation due to high recurrence rates in inflamed tissue.

title: Mastering the Perforated Corneal Ulcer: Clinical & Surgical Mastery

This guide provides a fellowship-level roadmap for diagnosis, medical stabilization, and tectonic reconstruction.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: A perforated corneal ulcer is defined as a full-thickness breach of the cornea. Pathophysiology involves the release of collagenases (MMPs) and proteolytic enzymes by infiltrated neutrophils and pathogens, exceeding the rate of stromal collagen synthesis. This leads to descemetocele formation, followed by rupture (Seidel positive) as intraocular pressure exceeds the resistance of the exposed Descemet’s membrane.

rows: History of alkali/acid exposure, limbal ischemia

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Action Required
content: Positive Seidel test (aqueous leakage)
Flat or shallow anterior chamber (AC)
Iris incarceration or prolapse (leukoma adherens)
Secondary endophthalmitis signs (vitritis, pain)
Intraocular foreign body presence

sections.title: Clinical Examination Checklist
content: Slit-lamp: Assess ulcer size, depth, and edge morphology.
Seidel test: Fluorescein strip on the suspected area + cobalt blue light.
Gonioscopy: Assess for peripheral anterior synechiae or angle closure.
Tonometry: Contraindicated if frank perforation is suspected.
Fundoscopy: B-scan USG is mandatory if media is opaque to rule out endophthalmitis.

sections.title: Management Algorithm: 'Seal and Heal'
content: Step 1: Immediate stabilization (Eye shield, topical broad-spectrum antibiotics).
Step 2: Microbiological workup (Corneal scrapings for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivity).
Step 3: Small perforation (<2mm) -> Cyanoacrylate glue + bandage contact lens.
Step 4: Medium/Large perforation -> Patch graft (corneal or scleral) or tectonic PKP.
Step 5: Control inflammation (Topical/Systemic immunosuppressants if autoimmune).

sections.title: Remember the Protocol: THE S.H.I.E.L.D. Mnemonic

content.explanation: S-Scrape (cultures); H-Hydrate/Shield; I-Intensive antibiotics; E-Evaluate depth; L-Lysis inhibition (e.g., Doxycycline); D-Definitive tectonic surgery.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Doxycycline (50-100mg BID) is critical as a non-antibiotic MMP inhibitor to prevent collagenolysis.
Topical steroids are ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in active infectious ulcers until the infection is under control.
Cyanoacrylate glue should be applied only to a dry stromal bed to ensure adequate adhesion.
In cases of peripheral perforation, consider tectonic lamellar grafts to spare the visual axis and lower rejection risks.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent research emphasizes the use of Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT) as a 'patch' for small/medium defects to promote epithelization and decrease inflammation. Clinical studies (e.g., The SCUT Trial for bacterial keratitis) continue to guide current evidence-based topical antibiotic regimens, favoring fourth-generation fluoroquinolones (Gatifloxacin/Moxifloxacin) for initial empiric therapy.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Fungal keratitis (FK) is a sight-threatening infection of the corneal stroma. Prevalence is highest in tropical climates and agricultural settings. Filamentous fungi (e.g., Fusarium, Aspergillus) account for ~70% of cases, while yeasts (e.g., Candida) are more common in temperate climates or compromised ocular surfaces.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Fungal Etiology
content: Infiltrate with feathery/indistinct borders
Satellite stromal lesions
Immune ring formation
Slow progression (indolent course)
Resistance to standard bacterial antibiotics
History of vegetative trauma or topical steroid use

sections.title: Investigation Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Corneal scraping from ulcer base and edge
Step 2: Immediate Gram stain (for bacteria) and KOH/Calcofluor White prep
Step 3: Inoculation onto Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (SDA) and Blood Agar
Step 4: Confocal Microscopy (In-vivo) if culture negative but suspicious
Step 5: PCR for fungal DNA if available (high sensitivity)

sections.title: Treatment Algorithm
content: Filamentous Fungi: Topical Natamycin 5% (First-line) or Voriconazole 1%
Yeast (Candida): Topical Amphotericin B 0.15% or Voriconazole 1%
Adjunctive Therapy: Oral Fluconazole 200mg BID or Voriconazole 200mg BID
Management Note: Avoid topical corticosteroids initially; taper only when fungal load is significantly reduced and re-epithelialization is observed.

content.explanation: F - Filamentous, E - Edge (Feathery), A - Agricultural trauma, T - Topical steroids, H - Hypopyon, E - Epithelial defect, R - Resistant to drops, S - Satellite lesions.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Study: Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial (MUTT)
content: MUTT-I: Natamycin 5% demonstrated superior efficacy over Voriconazole 1% for filamentous keratitis (Fusarium).
MUTT-II: Oral Voriconazole did not improve outcomes compared to placebo in cases already receiving topical Natamycin.

summary: Goldmann Applanation Tonometry remains the gold standard for intraocular pressure (IOP) measurement, relying on the Imbert-Fick principle. Precision is paramount in glaucoma screening, surgical planning, and long-term management.

data.title: Clinical Mastery: Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (GAT)
data.summary: Goldmann Applanation Tonometry remains the gold standard for intraocular pressure (IOP) measurement, relying on the Imbert-Fick principle. Precision is paramount in glaucoma screening, surgical planning, and long-term management.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M30 50 Q 50 30 70 50' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M30 50 Q 50 70 70 50' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='5' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Principle
sections.content: GAT is a contact method that measures the force required to flatten a fixed area (3.06 mm diameter) of the cornea. It is based on the Imbert-Fick Law: P = F / A, where Pressure (P) equals Force (F) applied over Area (A). For the cornea, when A is 3.06 mm, the capillary attraction of the tear film and corneal rigidity negate each other, allowing the force reading to directly approximate IOP in mmHg.

sections.title: Clinical Setup & Procedure
content: Step 1: Instill proparacaine and fluorescein sodium.
Step 2: Align the blue cobalt filter and set the biprism to 0 position.
Step 3: Advance the tonometer head until the biprism touches the apex.
Step 4: View through the slit lamp; align the inner edges of the two semi-circles.
Step 5: Record the reading when the edges are perfectly aligned (10x magnification).

sections.title: Red Flags: Procedural Errors
content: Do not apply excessive pressure (can induce vasovagal response or corneal abrasion).
Avoid contact with patients with active corneal ulcers (infectious transmission risk).
Disinfect biprism with 70% isopropyl alcohol for at least 5 minutes to prevent adenovirus transmission.
Ensure proper alignment (misalignment creates vertical shift of semi-circles).

content.explanation: T-ouch (Gentle contact), H-orizontal (Ensure semi-circles are level), E-dge (Align the inner margins perfectly).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Calibration check: Perform weekly using the standardized weight block (0, 2, and 6 g).
Astigmatism > 3.0D: Align the biprism mark with the patient's minus-cylinder axis.
Always dry the biprism after disinfection to prevent chemical keratitis.
IOP is typically highest in the morning; repeat measurements may be needed for diurnal curves.
Wait 10-15 minutes after topical anesthetic before performing Schirmer's testing.

sections.title: FFA: The Gold Standard for Vascularity
content: Phase 1: Pre-arterial (choroidal flush)
Phase 2: Arterial filling (approx 1-2s later)
Phase 3: Arteriovenous phase (laminar venous flow)
Phase 4: Venous phase (full filling)
Phase 5: Late phase (dye recirculation & staining)

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Immediate Action
content: FFA: History of anaphylaxis to fluorescein (Requires premedication/crash cart)
OCT: Sudden drop in RNFL thickness (Rule out acute compressive neuropathy)
FAF: 'Target' sign in hydroxychloroquine toxicity (Immediate cessation)
OCT Macula: Subfoveal fluid in wet AMD (Urgent Anti-VEGF)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Interpretation
content: FFA: Hyperfluorescence is caused by staining, pooling, or leakage; hypofluorescence by block or filling defect.
FAF: Hyper-AF implies metabolic stress (e.g., active atrophy border); Hypo-AF implies RPE cell death.
OCT: Always correlate the 'red' and 'green' maps in ONH analysis with the actual B-scan to rule out artifacts (segmentation errors).
OCT: EDI-OCT (Enhanced Depth Imaging) is mandatory for evaluating choroidal thickness.

content.explanation: Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal (The normal order of RNFL thickness thickness in a healthy eye).

sections.title: Evidence-Based Landmark Studies
sections.content: For macular edema, the DRCR.net protocols highlight OCT as the primary guide for anti-VEGF injection frequency. For ONH analysis, the OHTS (Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study) established the diagnostic baseline for early glaucoma detection using early versions of OCT/HRT.

data.title: Mastering The Filtering Bleb: Clinical Evaluation & Management
data.summary: A clinical guide to evaluating the post-trabeculectomy filtering bleb, balancing filtration efficiency with the prevention of sight-threatening complications. Proper assessment is the cornerstone of long-term IOP control.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='30' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' opacity='0.2'/><path d='M30 50 Q50 20 70 50 Q50 80 30 50' fill='white' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='2'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Purpose
sections.content: A filtering bleb is a surgically created conjunctival elevation resulting from the flow of aqueous humor through a partial-thickness scleral flap (trabeculectomy). Its goal is to provide controlled subconjunctival aqueous drainage to achieve target intraocular pressure (IOP) and stabilize glaucomatous damage.

sections.title: The INDIANA BLEB APPEARANCE GRADING SCALE (IBAGS)

content.explanation: P: Position (sup vs inf), O: Opacification/Cystic changes, W: Vascularity (Weight/Engorgement), E: Extent/Elevation, R: Rheology (Seidel sign/leakage).

sections.title: Clinical Red Flags
content: Positive Seidel test: Risk of endophthalmitis
Thin, 'cystic' bleb: High risk of bleb leak/infection
Encapsulated (Tenon's) cyst: Elevated IOP despite surgery
Hypervascularity: Indicator of imminent failure (fibrosis)
Flat, scarred bleb: 'Failed' bleb status

sections.title: Management Algorithm for Dysfunctional Blebs
content: Step 1: Digital ocular massage (if IOP high, no leak)
Step 2: Laser suture lysis (if flap is overtight)
Step 3: 5-FU/Mitomycin-C injections (if early fibrosis/engorgement)
Step 4: Needling revision with subconjunctival anti-metabolites
Step 5: Surgical revision (re-fashioning flap or excision of fibrosis)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Use fluorescein staining to detect occult leaks not visible under white light.
Superior blebs are generally more successful than inferior blebs due to lid-covered tear distribution.
Avoid excessive topical steroids early post-op to allow controlled fibrosis, unless intense inflammation is noted.
Always evaluate the bleb in primary gaze AND with the eyelid lifted to assess the full extent.

sections.title: Landmark Research Updates
sections.content: Recent evidence from the Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (TVT) study underscores that while bleb-based surgery offers superior pressure reduction, the longevity depends heavily on the 'bleb-maintenance' regimen. Newer studies focus on utilizing subconjunctival collagen matrix implants to modulate bleb scarring without the risks associated with intra-operative Mitomycin-C.

title: Blebitis and Infectious Endophthalmitis: A Comprehensive Clinical Management Protocol
summary: Blebitis represents an ocular emergency characterized by infection of the filtering bleb following trabeculectomy. Without immediate, aggressive intervention, it rapidly progresses to sight-threatening endophthalmitis.

data.title: Blebitis and Infectious Endophthalmitis: A Comprehensive Clinical Management Protocol
data.summary: Blebitis represents an ocular emergency characterized by infection of the filtering bleb following trabeculectomy. Without immediate, aggressive intervention, it rapidly progresses to sight-threatening endophthalmitis.
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 100 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M30 50 Q50 20 70 50 T30 50' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 90%)' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='10' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)'/></svg>

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Blebitis is a focal infection involving the filtering bleb post-trabeculectomy. It occurs when pathogens gain entry to the anterior chamber via a compromised bleb wall. Pathogenesis: 1. Bleb avascularity/thinning (leaky bleb). 2. Bacterial colonization (Staphylococcus epidermidis, Streptococcus spp.). 3. Penetration into the bleb and subsequently the vitreous cavity leading to endophthalmitis.

sections.title: Key Risk Factors
content: Inferior limbal site of trabeculectomy
Use of Mitomycin-C (MMC)
Thin, cystic, avascular blebs
Long-term topical antibiotic use
Contact lens wear
Blepharitis or ocular surface disease

rows: Minimal cells, less pain, usually self-limiting
Vitreous involvement, vision loss, severe pain
Anterior chamber cells but no bleb involvement

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Endophthalmitis
content: Presence of a hypopyon
Vitreous cells or haze on B-scan ultrasound
Significant visual acuity loss (worse than 20/200)
Severe, unrelenting ocular pain
Eyelid edema and chemosis

branches: Stage III: Overt Endophthalmitis (Heavy vitreous debris)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Perform Seidel test to confirm leak site.
Step 2: Slit-lamp examination: Assess bleb density, infiltration, and AC activity.
Step 3: B-scan Ultrasonography to evaluate for vitritis.
Step 4: Aqueous/Vitreous tap (if endophthalmitis is suspected) for culture and sensitivity.
Step 5: Cultures of the conjunctiva and the bleb area (swab).

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: 1. Hospitalization: Mandatory for blebitis/endophthalmitis.
2. Topical Antibiotics: Fortified Vancomycin (50mg/mL) & Fortified Ceftazidime (50mg/mL) every hour.
3. Systemic Coverage: Consider IV Fluoroquinolones (e.g., Moxifloxacin).
4. Cycloplegics: Atropine 1% BID for comfort and synechiae prevention.
5. Intravitreal Injection: If vitritis is present (Vancomycin 1mg/0.1ml + Ceftazidime 2.25mg/0.1ml).
6. Surgical Intervention: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) for dense vitritis.

content.explanation: B: Bacterial culture priority; L: Local antibiotic (fortified); E: Evaluate vitritis; B: Be aggressive with surgery.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never perform a bleb revision until the active infection is resolved.
Streptococcus species (esp. S. pneumoniae) carry the worst prognosis.
A clear view of the fundus is critical; if lost, treat as endophthalmitis.
Prophylactic antibiotic use post-trabeculectomy is highly controversial.

sections.title: Landmark Considerations
sections.content: Reference the 'Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study' (EVS) for surgical decision-making, acknowledging that bleb-associated endophthalmitis often requires earlier surgical intervention compared to post-cataract cases due to more virulent organisms.

data.title: Angle Surgery Showdown: Goniotomy vs. Trabeculotomy
data.summary: A comprehensive clinical comparison of ab interno goniotomy and ab externo trabeculotomy for the surgical management of childhood glaucoma. These procedures aim to bypass the pathologically high resistance of the trabecular meshwork in primary congenital glaucoma (PCG).
data.summary_illustration: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='80' fill='none' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M50 100 Q 100 50 150 100' stroke='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)' fill='none' stroke-width='6'/><circle cx='100' cy='100' r='10' fill='hsl(215, 90%, 45%)'/></svg>

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Both procedures are angle surgeries aimed at relieving obstruction in the trabecular meshwork (TM) for primary congenital glaucoma (PCG). Goniotomy involves an 'ab interno' approach, cutting the meshwork under direct visualization. Trabeculotomy involves an 'ab externo' approach, cannulating Schlemm's canal to rupture the TM.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Abandon Angle Surgery
content: Corneal opacification (Haab striae/edema) precluding visualization of the angle.
Uncontrolled IOP despite maximal angle intervention.
Evidence of secondary glaucoma (e.g., Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome or ICE).
Signs of angle closure or peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).

content.explanation: If the cornea is CLOUDY, choose Trabeculotomy (Ab externo). If the cornea is clear, Goniotomy is the 'Gold' standard.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Success of goniotomy is highly dependent on corneal clarity; if corneal edema is severe, use an ab externo approach.
In trabeculotomy, ensure the trabeculotome is correctly placed in Schlemm’s canal by noting the resistance change.
Both surgeries carry a risk of transient hyphema; maintain the anterior chamber with viscoelastic (e.g., Healon).
Success is defined as normalized IOP without need for topical anti-glaucoma medication.

sections.title: Step-by-Step: Goniotomy Procedure
content: Step 1: Administer retrobulbar or general anesthesia; position patient head.
Step 2: Place Barkan goniotomy lens on the cornea to visualize the angle.
Step 3: Create a paracentesis; inject cohesive OVD (e.g., Provisc).
Step 4: Advance goniotomy knife across the AC to the nasal angle.
Step 5: Incise the TM in the anterior 1/3, sweeping 60-90 degrees.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA) is mandatory for infants.
Measure horizontal corneal diameter (norm < 11mm in neonates; >12mm suspicious for buphthalmos).
Measure IOP (Tono-Pen or Perkins tonometer) - must be done quickly post-anesthesia induction.
Perform gonioscopy (critical to evaluate the insertion of the iris and presence of TM).
Axial length measurement (A-scan/IOLMaster) - compare to fellow eye or growth curves.

summary: A comprehensive clinical breakdown comparing the evolution, efficacy, and safety profiles of modern glaucoma filtration surgeries. Navigating the spectrum from the ultra-minimally invasive to the gold-standard 'filtering' procedures.

sections.title: Red Flags: When MIGS is Contraindicated
content: Advanced or end-stage visual field loss
High target IOP (needs < 10-12 mmHg)
Secondary glaucoma (neovascular/uveitic)
Closed-angle glaucoma (without synechiolysis)
Severe conjunctival scarring (precludes filtering)

sections.title: The Trabeculectomy Gold Standard
content: Step 1: Conjunctival peritomy (Fornix/Limbal base)
Step 2: Scleral flap creation (Partial thickness)
Step 3: MMC/5-FU application for antifibrosis
Step 4: Block excision (Trabeculectomy)
Step 5: Peripheral iridectomy (PI) to prevent iris incarceration
Step 6: Watertight closure of flap and conjunctiva

sections.title: Non-Penetrating Surgery (Deep Sclerectomy)
content: Preserves the integrity of the anterior chamber.
Avoids direct opening of the eyeball (no PI needed).
Decreased risk of shallow AC, hypotony, and endophthalmitis.
Requires highly skilled dissection of the juxtacanalicular tissue.
Often augmented with a collagen implant to maintain space.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Recent Evidence
content: Landmark Study: The 'LiGHT' Trial (Lancet 2019) suggests SLT as first-line, but in surgery, trabeculectomy remains superior to MIGS for absolute IOP lowering in advanced cases.
MIGS is best reserved for mild-to-moderate glaucoma in phakic patients who wish to reduce medication burden.
Bleb-related complications (leaks, blebitis) are unique to subconjunctival procedures (Trab/XEN).
GATT (Gonioscopy-Assisted Transluminal Trabeculotomy) is effectively a '360-degree' MIGS with potential for higher efficacy than stent-based procedures.

content.explanation: W - Watch for IOP spikes post-op; A - Antifibrotics (MMC) are critical for filtering success; T - Trabeculectomy is the gold standard for low targets; S - Stents (MIGS) are best for safety profiles.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Bacterial keratitis is a sight-threatening suppurative inflammation of the corneal stroma caused by bacterial invasion. It is characterized by the presence of a corneal epithelial defect with underlying stromal infiltration, often accompanied by significant anterior segment inflammation and pain. True emergencies require immediate culturing and intensive fortified antibiotic therapy.

branches: Gram (+) Cocci: S. aureus, S. epidermidis, S. pneumoniae
Gram (-) Rods: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CL wearers), Klebsiella, Proteus
Gram (-) Cocci: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Can penetrate intact epithelium)
Gram (+) Rods: Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Mycobacterium spp.

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: 1. Epithelial Breakdown: Disruption of the protective barrier due to trauma or hypoxia.
2. Adhesion: Bacteria utilize fimbriae or pili to bind to damaged cells and collagen.
3. Invasion: Secretion of enzymes (proteases, elastases) to digest the stroma.
4. Host Response: Influx of PMNs and cytokine release leads to stromal necrosis and edema.

sections.title: Specific Organism 'Clues'
content: Pseudomonas: Rapid progression, greenish mucopurulent discharge, soupy melt.
S. pneumoniae: Serpiginous ulcer, often with significant hypopyon.
S. aureus: Round, well-demarcated white-grey infiltrate, relatively dry.
Moraxella: Oval ulcer, typically in the inferior cornea, seen in debilitated patients.

sections.title: Microbiological Investigation Protocol
content: 1. Topical Anesthesia (Proparacaine preferred over Tetracaine).
2. Scrape leading edge and base of the ulcer using a Kimura spatula or 25G needle.
3. Direct Inoculation onto Blood, Chocolate, and Sabouraud Agar.
4. Slide Preparation: Gram stain and Giemsa stain for immediate microscopy.
5. Culture Enrichment: Place sample in Thioglycolate broth.

branches: Fungal Keratitis: Feathery borders, satellite lesions
Acanthamoeba: Ring infiltrate, radial keratoneuritis, extreme pain
Viral (HSV): Geographic ulcer, decreased corneal sensation
Sterile Infiltrates: Peripheral, clear space from limbus, minimal pain
Marginal Keratitis: Associated with blepharitis, hypersensitivity to Staph

rows: Reduces ciliary spasm and prevents synechiae

sections.title: Landmark Study: The SCUT Trial
content: Trial: Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT).
Finding 1: No overall difference in BCVA at 3 months with adjunctive steroids.
Finding 2: Significant benefit in VA for baseline severe ulcers (worst vision).
Finding 3: Nocardia ulcers worsened with steroids (contraindicated).
Conclusion: Steroids are safe after 48h of effective antibiotics, except in Nocardia.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Concern
content: Descemetocele (Imminent Perforation)
Scleral extension of the infiltrate
Worsening pain despite treatment
Limbal involvement (potential for stem cell loss)
Rapid stromal melting within 24 hours

content.explanation: P: Pain (Severe), E: Epithelial defect (Size/Shape), D: Discharge (Purulent), A: Anterior chamber reaction (Hypopyon), L: Location (Central vs. Peripheral).

sections.title: Surgical Interventions
content: 1. Cyanoacrylate Tissue Glue: For small perforations (<2mm) or thinning.
2. Conjunctival Flap (Gundersen): For chronic non-healing ulcers.
3. Amniotic Membrane Transplant: Promotes epithelialization.
4. Therapeutic Keratoplasty: PKP or LKP for uncontrolled infection or perforation.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Corneal Scarring/Leukoma: Results in irregular astigmatism and vision loss.
Endophthalmitis: Rare unless perforation occurs.
Secondary Glaucoma: Due to inflammatory debris in the trabecular meshwork.
Phthisis Bulbi: In severe, uncontrolled endophthalmitis cases.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: Never use a 'Steroid-Antibiotic' combo (e.g., Tobradex) for an undiagnosed ulcer.
Document the size of the epithelial defect AND the infiltrate separately.
Fungal keratitis should be suspected if the ulcer doesn't respond to broad-spectrum antibiotics within 48-72h.
A 'culture-negative' ulcer may be caused by fastidious organisms or prior antibiotic use.
In contact lens wearers, always culture the lens case and solution if available.

title: Microbial Keratitis: The Sight-Threatening Emergency
summary: An urgent, sight-threatening infection of the corneal stroma characterized by epithelial defect, infiltrate, and associated inflammation. Rapid diagnosis and targeted antimicrobial therapy are mandatory to prevent stromal melting and permanent vision loss.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Microbial keratitis is an infection involving the corneal stroma, often secondary to contact lens wear, ocular surface disease, or trauma. Globally, bacterial keratitis is the most common form, with Pseudomonas aeruginosa being the most frequent pathogen in contact lens wearers. Incidence is estimated at 2.5–799 per 100,000 person-years depending on geography and risk factor prevalence.

sections.title: Red Flags: Urgent Intervention Required
content: Corneal thinning or impending perforation (Seidel positive)
Involvement of the visual axis (central location)
Hypopyon exceeding 2mm
Scleral involvement (Sclerokeratitis)
Lack of response to initial therapy at 24-48 hours

rows: Peripheral, smaller, less pain, no hypopyon
Radial perineuritis, severe pain out of proportion to exam
Feathery edges, satellite lesions, slow progression

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Visual Acuity & Slit-lamp exam (map infiltrate size).
Step 2: Corneal scrapings using Kimura spatula or platinum blade.
Step 3: Inoculate onto Blood Agar, Chocolate Agar, Sabouraud Agar, and Thioglycolate broth.
Step 4: Perform Gram stain and initiate empiric fortified antibiotics.
Step 5: Perform in-vivo confocal microscopy if Acanthamoeba/Fungal suspected.

sections.title: Treatment Protocol: Fortified Antibiotics
content: Fortified Tobramycin (15mg/ml) q1h
Fortified Cefazolin (50mg/ml) q1h
Monotherapy: Gatifloxacin or Moxifloxacin 0.5% (for smaller lesions)
Cycloplegics (Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1%) for pain
Topical steroids: Only after epithelialization and reduced organism load

content.explanation: S: Staining (Fluorescein), T: Tincture (Stains like Gram), A: Acanthamoeba check, M: Microscopy (Confocal), P: Pathogen identification

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always evaluate for contact lens case contamination.
Avoid eye patching; it creates a warm, hypoxic environment for bacterial growth.
The 'SCUT trial' provided evidence that adjunctive topical corticosteroids do not improve visual outcomes at 3 months for bacterial ulcers.
If the patient is monocular, hospitalize for intensive monitoring.

title: TASS vs. Infectious Endophthalmitis: A Diagnostic Divide
summary: Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS) and postoperative endophthalmitis represent the two most feared acute inflammatory complications following intraocular surgery. Mastering their rapid differentiation is critical for sight-saving management.

sections.title: TASS vs. Endophthalmitis: Key Clinical Differentiators
TASS Red Flags
content: Inability to visualize the posterior pole (requires tap)
Presence of any vitreous haze/cells
Worsening pain 48h+ post-op
Decreasing visual acuity after initial stabilization

rows: Strands through wound; risk of endophthalmitis

content.explanation: P: Preservatives (e.g., BAC), I: Impurities (endotoxins), P: pH/Osmolality mismatch, E: Enzymatic residues, S: Sterilizing agents.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Clinical index of suspicion (Early vs Late onset).
Step 2: If vitritis exists: Emergent Vitreous Tap/Biopsy.
Step 3: Intravitreal antibiotics (Vancomycin 1mg/0.1ml + Ceftazidime 2.25mg/0.1ml).
Step 4: If TASS suspected: Aggressive topical Steroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h).
Step 5: Monitor IOP and repeat culture/Tap if no improvement at 24-48h.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: TASS is an inflammatory response to non-infectious substances; it is non-infectious by definition.
Any vitreous haze essentially rules out TASS and confirms Endophthalmitis until proven otherwise.
Always inspect the surgical logs/sterilization logs when a TASS cluster occurs.
The EVS (Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study) remains the gold standard for treatment guidelines regarding vitrectomy vs. tap/inject.
Post-operative pain is the patient's most reliable symptom for early infection.

title: TASS vs. Endophthalmitis: A Critical Ophthalmic Showdown
summary: Acute postoperative intraocular inflammation can rapidly threaten vision. Differentiating between sterile Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS) and infectious Endophthalmitis is paramount for optimal patient outcomes, as these conditions demand distinct diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. This guide meticulously compares their clinical profiles, etiologies, and management strategies.

Acute or chronic intraocular infection involving the vitreous cavity and/or anterior chamber.
Non-infectious: Toxic irritation from substances entering the anterior chamber during surgery.
Infectious: Microbial invasion (bacterial, fungal) into the eye, often post-surgical.
Presence of vitreous involvement (vitritis) is hallmark.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology
content: **TASS:** Incidence is variable, estimated between 0.01% and 0.2% post-cataract surgery. Often occurs in clusters linked to specific surgical batches, equipment, or sterilization protocols. Not linked to specific patient risk factors directly.
**Endophthalmitis:** Incidence typically 0.03% to 0.1% after cataract surgery. Rates vary by region and prophylactic strategies (e.g., intracameral antibiotics).

**Risk Factors for Endophthalmitis:** Posterior capsular rupture, vitreous loss, prolonged surgery, wound dehiscence, use of clear corneal incisions, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, blepharitis, use of non-preserved balanced salt solution (BSS).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **1. Clinical Assessment & History:** Thorough history, surgical details, symptom onset, progression.

**2. Ocular Examination:** Detailed slit-lamp exam, dilated fundus exam, IOP measurement, B-scan ultrasonography (essential if fundus view obscured, to rule out retinal detachment/vitreous abscesses).
**3. Anterior Chamber (AC) Tap (Paracentesis):** Collect 0.1-0.2 mL of aqueous fluid. Send for:
• Gram stain (rapid preliminary result, low sensitivity)
• Cultures (aerobic, anaerobic, fungal – on blood agar, chocolate agar, Sabouraud's dextrose agar)
• PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) for bacterial/fungal DNA (high sensitivity/specificity, rapid results for common pathogens).
• Cytology (if TASS suspected, to rule out infectious organisms and identify inflammatory cells).

**4. Vitreous Tap (Vitreous Biopsy):** Performed if AC tap is inconclusive or vitritis is dense. Collect 0.1-0.5 mL of undiluted vitreous. (Higher yield for culture than AC tap). Same lab tests as AC tap.

**5. Systemic Workup (for Endogenous Endophthalmitis):** Blood cultures, CBC, ESR/CRP, urine culture, chest X-ray, echocardiogram, referral to internal medicine/infectious disease if systemic source suspected.

rows: Less severe, gradual onset, usually responds well to topical steroids; typically NO vitritis; milder AC reaction.
Can cause chronic inflammation (often granulomatous), usually a history of complicated surgery, visible fragments on exam/US; may not have dense vitritis initially.
Bilateral granulomatous uveitis, history of penetrating trauma or intraocular surgery to one eye (2 weeks to years later); 'Dalén-Fuchs nodules'.
Severe vitritis, anterior uveitis, widespread necrotizing retinitis (often peripheral), occlusive vasculopathy. Viral etiology (HSV, VZV). Fundus involvement is primary.
High IOP, mature/hypermature cataract, visible lens material/macrophages in AC, ruptured lens capsule. Inflammation secondary to lens protein leakage.
Acute severe pain, rock-hard eye, shallow AC, fundus view obscured by hemorrhage. Usually intraoperative or immediate post-op. B-scan shows choroidal elevation.
History of trauma, visible IOFB, localized inflammation. Signs of siderosis/chalcosis if metallic.
History of uveitis, often milder flare-up, responds to usual uveitis treatment.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Grading
sections.content: Neither TASS nor Endophthalmitis have formal staging systems. Severity is generally assessed by initial visual acuity, density of AC reaction and vitritis, and extent of fibrin formation. The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS) uses initial visual acuity to stratify prognosis for acute postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis, specifically noting outcomes for patients presenting with light perception (LP) only vs. hand motions (HM) or better.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Algorithm
content: **STEP 1: Immediate Triage & Differentiation:** Based on clinical features (especially onset, pain, and presence/absence of vitritis). If doubt exists, treat as Endophthalmitis.
**STEP 2: TASS Management (Presumed Sterile):**
• **Topical Corticosteroids:** High-dose, frequent (e.g., Prednisolone acetate 1% q1h or Dexamethasone 0.1% q1h). Taper rapidly as inflammation subsides.
• **Cycloplegics:** (e.g., Cyclopentolate 1% bid-tid, Atropine 1% bid) to reduce pain and prevent posterior synechiae.
• **IOP Management:** If elevated, topical anti-glaucoma medications (e.g., topical beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors).
• **Systemic Steroids:** Reserved for severe, recalcitrant cases (e.g., oral Prednisone 40-60mg/day, tapered).
• **Anterior Chamber Wash:** If severe fibrin, hypopyon, or persistently high IOP (therapeutic and diagnostic by removing toxic substances).
**STEP 3: Endophthalmitis Management (Presumed Infectious):**
• **A. Obtain Samples:** Perform AC and/or vitreous tap for Gram stain, cultures, and PCR (as per 'Investigations' section).
• **B. Intravitreal Antibiotics:** IMMEDIATELY after samples are taken. Empirical broad-spectrum coverage:
• Vancomycin (Gram-positive): 1.0 mg in 0.1 mL.
• Ceftazidime (Gram-negative): 2.25 mg in 0.1 mL.
• OR Amikacin (if severe penicillin allergy or suspected atypical Gram-negatives): 0.4 mg in 0.1 mL (use with caution due to retinal toxicity).
• **C. Intravitreal Dexamethasone:** 0.4 mg in 0.1 mL (controversial, typically given concurrent with antibiotics to reduce inflammation, but potential to mask infection).

• **D. Systemic Antibiotics:** Oral Fluoroquinolones (e.g., Moxifloxacin 400mg PO daily) or IV antibiotics may be considered, but intravitreal agents are primary due to poor blood-retina barrier penetration.

• **E. Topical Medications:** Topical fortified antibiotics (e.g., Vancomycin 50mg/mL, Ceftazidime 100mg/mL) and topical corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisolone acetate 1% q1h) to control surface inflammation.
• **F. Vitrectomy:** Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) is indicated for:
• Patients presenting with initial visual acuity of Light Perception (LP) or worse (EVS criteria).
• Cases with dense vitritis, retinal detachment, or non-resolving infection/abscesses.
• Fungal endophthalmitis (often requires vitrectomy and intravitreal antifungals like Amphotericin B 0.005-0.01mg/0.1mL or Voriconazole 0.1mg/0.1mL).

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Vitrectomy
content: **1. Pre-op:** Topical povidone-iodine, peribulbar/retrobulbar anesthesia, sterile field.
**2. Incisions:** Typically 23, 25, or 27-gauge pars plana vitrectomy. Sclerotomies placed 3-4 mm posterior to the limbus (depending on phakic/aphakic status).
**3. Vitreous Sample:** Collect initial vitreous for cultures/PCR.
**4. Core Vitrectomy:** Remove as much infected vitreous gel as possible to reduce microbial load and inflammatory mediators. Use high cut rates and low aspiration.
**5. Peripheral Vitrectomy:** Careful removal of peripheral vitreous (may require scleral depression).
**6. Inspection:** Inspect retina for infiltrates, detachment, tears.
**7. Intravitreal Injections:** Administer intravitreal antibiotics (Vancomycin, Ceftazidime) and often dexamethasone at the end of the procedure.
**8. Closure:** Sclerotomy sites are hydrated or sutured as needed. Topical antibiotics.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **TASS:**
• Permanent corneal decompensation/edema (bullous keratopathy).
• Secondary glaucoma (due to trabeculitis, pigment dispersion).
• Iris atrophy, pupillary distortion/fixation, pigment dispersion glaucoma.
• Cystoid macular edema (CME).
• Prognosis generally good with prompt, appropriate treatment. Visual recovery often excellent.
**Endophthalmitis:**
• Permanent severe vision loss, blindness.
• Retinal detachment.
• Hypotony, phthisis bulbi (end-stage eye with severe shrinkage).
• Secondary glaucoma.
• Corneal decompensation/scarring.
• Choroidal detachment, suprachoroidal hemorrhage.

• Prognosis is guarded, dependent on organism virulence, initial visual acuity, and rapidity of treatment. Staphylococcal infections generally have better outcomes than Streptococcal or Gram-negative.

• EVS showed 53% of patients with VA of LP or worse achieved 20/40 or better with vitrectomy + antibiotics; 33% of patients with VA HM or better achieved 20/40 or better with tap/biopsy + antibiotics.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Severe, rapidly worsening ocular pain and profound vision loss post-op.**
**Any evidence of vitreous inflammation (vitritis) on dilated fundus exam or B-scan.**
**Absent red reflex.**
**Creamy, layered hypopyon.**
**Unilateral and progressively severe inflammation.**
**Any doubt regarding diagnosis: Treat aggressively as Endophthalmitis until proven otherwise. Delay is vision lost.**
**Failure of inflammation to respond to high-dose topical steroids within 24-48 hours.**

content.mnemonic: TASS vs. ENDO: 3 P's and V
content.explanation:
**TASS:** **P**resumed sterile, **P**ainless (relatively), **P**rompt onset (hours), NO **V**itritis. 
**ENDO:** **P**erilous (infectious), **P**ainful (severely), **P**ostponed onset (days), YES **V**itritis.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Vitritis is THE critical differentiating factor.** If you see vitritis, it's endophthalmitis until proven otherwise.
**Timing of onset is crucial:** TASS typically 12-48 hours, Endophthalmitis 2-7 days (acute).
**Corneal Edema:** Limbus-to-limbus edema suggests TASS; focal/patchy edema is less specific but can be seen in endophthalmitis.
**Hypopyon:** TASS hypopyon is often uniform, white, and 'fluffy'; endophthalmitis hypopyon can be layered, creamy, and denser.
**IOP:** Often high in TASS due to trabeculitis; variable in endophthalmitis (high from inflammation, low from ciliary body shutdown).
**Clusters of cases strongly suggest TASS,** indicating a breach in sterilization or surgical material contamination.
**Never delay treatment for endophthalmitis to await culture results.** Treat empirically with broad-spectrum intravitreal antibiotics immediately after obtaining samples.
**Intracameral antibiotics (e.g., cefuroxime 1mg/0.1mL) at the end of cataract surgery have significantly reduced the incidence of postoperative endophthalmitis.**

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content:
The **Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS)** (1995) remains the cornerstone for management of acute postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis. It demonstrated the benefit of immediate vitrectomy for patients with initial visual acuity of light perception or worse, compared to tap/biopsy alone. For those with better vision, tap/biopsy with intravitreal antibiotics yielded similar results to vitrectomy. 

Recent advances include the widespread adoption of **intracameral antibiotics** (e.g., cefuroxime, moxifloxacin) for prophylaxis, significantly reducing post-cataract endophthalmitis rates. **PCR-based diagnostics** offer faster and more sensitive identification of causative organisms, even with small sample sizes, guiding targeted antibiotic therapy sooner.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
sections.content:
**Pediatric Patients:** Diagnosis can be challenging in non-verbal children. Signs like irritability, eyelid swelling, and extreme photophobia may be more prominent. Pediatric eyes may have a more robust inflammatory response, potentially leading to faster disease progression and more severe complications like amblyopia. High index of suspicion is crucial.

**Immunocompromised Patients:** (e.g., HIV/AIDS, diabetics, organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressants) are at higher risk for opportunistic infections and more virulent courses of endophthalmitis. Fungal or atypical bacterial infections should be considered more readily. Systemic workup for endogenous sources is particularly important in this group.

title: UBM vs. AS-OCT: Unveiling the Anterior Segment with Precision
summary: A comprehensive comparison of two indispensable ophthalmic imaging modalities, Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM) and Anterior Segment Optical Coherence Tomography (AS-OCT). This guide dissects their underlying principles, technical specifications, diverse clinical applications, and unique advantages to empower ophthalmologists in selecting the optimal tool for precise anterior segment diagnosis and management. Understand their strengths, limitations, and synergistic utility.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content:
**Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM):** A high-frequency (typically 35-100 MHz) ultrasound technique providing real-time, cross-sectional images of the anterior segment and anterior vitreous. It excels in visualizing structures obscured by opaque media (e.g., corneal edema, hyphema, mature cataract) due to its use of sound waves, and penetrates deeper into the ciliary body, zonules, and retro-iridian space than AS-OCT. Requires a water bath or coupling gel for imaging.

**Anterior Segment Optical Coherence Tomography (AS-OCT):** A non-contact, high-resolution imaging modality utilizing low-coherence interferometry to generate cross-sectional images of the anterior segment. It uses near-infrared light (typically 800-1310 nm, commonly 840 nm for time-domain or 1310 nm for swept-source) to produce exquisitely detailed images of anterior ocular structures, offering superior resolution for superficial structures but with limited penetration through opaque tissues or deep into the ciliary body.

sections.title: 6. Patient & Operator Considerations
content: **UBM:** Requires patient supine position, use of a water-bath immersion shell (e.g., Prager shell) or coupling gel. The procedure is contact-based and highly operator-dependent, requiring skill for optimal probe alignment and image acquisition. Time-consuming.

**AS-OCT:** Non-contact, rapid acquisition (seconds per scan). Patient is typically seated at the instrument. Less operator-dependent and easier for most patients, including those who are less cooperative or pediatric, as it does not require direct eye contact or specific positioning for extended periods. Often integrated into standard clinic flow.

sections.title: 8. Limitations & Artifacts
content: **UBM:** Requires operator skill and training. Contact procedure can be uncomfortable for some patients or those with recent surgery/trauma. Image quality degradation from air bubbles in water bath or poor coupling. Acoustic shadowing from dense structures (e.g., dense calcification, gas). Cannot image posterior segment structures.

**AS-OCT:** Limited penetration through opaque media (e.g., severe corneal edema, hyphema, dense hypopyon, mature cataract). Motion artifacts from blinking or eye movement can degrade image quality. Cannot image deep ciliary body, zonules, or retro-iridian space. 'Mirror' artifacts can occur with highly reflective surfaces.

branches.label: Glaucoma Management
sub_branches: AS-OCT: Initial angle assessment, PAS detection.
UBM: Confirm plateau iris, assess ciliary body morphology in complex angle closure, cyclodialysis.

branches.label: Trauma & Foreign Bodies
sub_branches: AS-OCT: Superficial corneal/scleral injury, anterior chamber assessment.
UBM: Occult deeper foreign bodies, cyclodialysis, ciliary body damage, scleral rupture.

branches.label: Tumor Evaluation
sub_branches: AS-OCT: Surface characteristics, superficial iris lesions.

UBM: Sulcus-to-sulcus diameter for phakic IOLs, assessment of ciliary body for drainage devices.

sections.title: 10. Recent Advances & Future Directions
sections.content:
**AS-OCT:** The advent of **Swept-Source AS-OCT (SS-AS-OCT)** has significantly improved acquisition speed (up to 100,000-200,000 A-scans/sec), reduced motion artifacts, and increased penetration depth (with longer wavelengths, e.g., 1050-1310 nm) allowing for better visualization through cataractous lenses and deeper into the angle. **Enhanced Depth Imaging (EDI)** techniques allow for improved visualization of sclera and ciliary body. **Angiography-OCT** is exploring anterior segment vascularity. Integration with **Artificial Intelligence (AI)** is emerging for automated angle assessment, PAS detection, and glaucoma risk prediction.

**UBM:** While the core technology has been stable, advances focus on **higher frequency probes** (up to 100 MHz for ultra-high resolution), **3D UBM imaging** for volumetric analysis, and improved image processing algorithms. Research into combining UBM and OCT data for a more comprehensive 'fusion imaging' approach is also underway to leverage the strengths of both modalities.

sections.title: 11. Mnemonics: UBM vs. AS-OCT Core Differences

content.explanation:
**UBM: D**eep **E**valuation, **P**enetrates **T**hrough **H**aze. (Focuses on depth and ability to image through opaque media).

**AS-OCT: D**etail for **E**very **T**issue, **A**ngle **I**maging, **L**ight-based. (Focuses on high resolution for superficial structures and quantitative analysis).

sections.title: 12. Key Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: **UBM is your go-to for anything 'behind the iris' or if media opacity prevents light-based imaging.** Think ciliary body, zonules, or foreign bodies when the cornea is hazy.
**AS-OCT excels at quantifying angle parameters and providing exquisite detail of superficial structures.** Ideal for monitoring angle closure, corneal diseases, and bleb morphology.
**They are complementary, not competitive.** Often, using both provides a complete picture, especially in complex cases (e.g., trauma, tumors).

**For pediatric or uncooperative patients, AS-OCT is generally preferred** due to its non-contact and rapid acquisition nature, reducing the need for sedation or extensive restraint often required for UBM.
**Always evaluate the entire image** for artifacts (e.g., acoustic shadowing in UBM, mirror images in AS-OCT) that can lead to misinterpretation.
**A 'flat iris plane' on AS-OCT with a narrow angle is suspicious for plateau iris, but UBM provides definitive confirmation** by directly visualizing the ciliary body's anterior displacement.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview: Non-Penetrating Glaucoma Surgery (NPGS)
sections.content: Non-Penetrating Glaucoma Surgery (NPGS) refers to a group of filtering surgeries designed to reduce intraocular pressure (IOP) by enhancing aqueous humor outflow through a surgically thinned or modified scleral bed, without direct entry into the anterior chamber. Unlike trabeculectomy, NPGS avoids full-thickness fistula creation, thereby minimizing risks such as hypotony, endophthalmitis, and choroidal hemorrhage. The primary goal is to create a controlled filtration pathway.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Indications for NPGS
content: **Incidence/Prevalence**: Lower than trabeculectomy, but growing due to favorable safety profile for specific patient groups.
**Primary Indications**: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG), Ocular Hypertension (OHT) with documented progression, intolerance/refractory to maximal medical therapy.

**Specific Considerations**: Preferred in patients with higher risk for hypotony (e.g., high myopia, thin sclera), those with a history of choroidal detachment, or single-eyed patients where risk reduction is paramount.
**Contraindications to Trabeculectomy**: History of previous trabeculectomy failure with extensive scarring, active ocular inflammation, neovascular glaucoma (NPGS generally avoided).

sections.title: 3. Etiology & Pathophysiology (Relevant to NPGS)
sections.content: NPGS targets the conventional outflow pathway, where increased resistance in the juxtacanalicular trabecular meshwork (JCTM) and inner wall of Schlemm's canal (SC) is the primary cause of elevated IOP in POAG. NPGS aims to bypass or enhance aqueous flow through the JCTM and into Schlemm's canal or directly into a subscleral lake, ultimately draining into the episcleral venous system, without a direct communication with the anterior chamber.

sections.title: 5. Deep Sclerectomy (DS) - Overview
sections.content: Deep Sclerectomy involves creating a deep scleral flap that exposes the anterior chamber angle structures, including the Descemet's membrane and a thin layer of trabecular meshwork (the 'trabeculo-Descemet's window'). Aqueous filters into a subscleral lake, then diffuses into the subconjunctival space and through the uveoscleral outflow. Adjuncts like collagen implants (e.g., Aquaflow, SK-Gel) or anti-metabolites (Mitomycin C 0.02% for 1-2 min) are often used to prevent fibrosis and maintain the intrascleral lake.

sections.title: 6. Viscocanalostomy (VC) - Overview
sections.content: Viscocanalostomy creates a deep scleral flap and unroofs the outer wall of Schlemm's canal. High-molecular-weight viscoelastic (e.g., sodium hyaluronate like Healon GV, Provisc) is injected into Schlemm's canal to dilate it and its collector channels. This enhances aqueous outflow into an intrascleral lake and the episcleral venous system. VC typically avoids direct anterior chamber entry and cyclodialysis. Anti-metabolites are less commonly used compared to DS.

sections.title: 7. Canaloplasty (CP) - Overview
sections.content: Canaloplasty is a modification of viscocanalostomy, aiming to restore natural outflow by circumferentially dilating Schlemm's canal. A deep scleral flap is created, Schlemm's canal is unroofed, and a microcatheter (e.g., iScience iTrack 250 microcatheter) is advanced 360 degrees. Viscoelastic is injected as the catheter is withdrawn, followed by placement of a tensioned prolene suture (e.g., 10-0 prolene) within the canal to expand it and its collector channels. This procedure generally aims for internal filtration with minimal bleb formation.

sections.title: 8. Key Surgical Steps: Deep Sclerectomy (DS)
content: **1. Conjunctival/Tenon's Flap**: Limbal-based or fornix-based, dissection to bare sclera.
**2. Superficial Scleral Flap**: Half-thickness, rectangular (e.g., 5x5mm), base at limbus. Dissect 1-2mm into clear cornea.

**3. Deep Scleral Flap**: Dissected from within the superficial flap, exposing bluish underlying structures (choroid/ciliary body). Meticulous dissection to leave Descemet's membrane and a thin layer of trabecular meshwork intact.
**4. Trabeculo-Descemet's Window**: The deep flap is excised or retracted to create the window. Micro-perforation of Descemet's membrane is acceptable if small.
**5. Adjuncts (Optional)**: Collagen implant (e.g., Aquaflow) or Mitomycin C (0.02% for 1-2 min) application in the deep scleral bed.
**6. Scleral Flap Closure**: Superficial scleral flap sutured watertight (e.g., 10-0 nylon).
**7. Conjunctival Closure**: Watertight closure of conjunctival/Tenon's flap.

sections.title: 9. Key Surgical Steps: Viscocanalostomy (VC)
content: **1. Conjunctival/Tenon's Flap**: Limbal-based or fornix-based.
**2. Superficial Scleral Flap**: Half-thickness, rectangular (e.g., 5x5mm).
**3. Deep Scleral Flap**: Created within the superficial flap, extending to reveal Schlemm's canal (thin bluish line).
**4. Unroofing Schlemm's Canal**: Two radial incisions into the outer wall of Schlemm's canal (anterior & posterior) to unroof a segment.
**5. Viscoelastic Injection**: High-molecular-weight viscoelastic (e.g., Healon GV, Provisc) injected into the cut ends of Schlemm's canal to dilate the canal and collector channels.
**6. Deep Flap Excision/Retraction**: Deep scleral flap often excised or tucked back.
**7. Scleral Flap Closure**: Superficial scleral flap sutured watertight.
**8. Conjunctival Closure**: Watertight closure.

sections.title: 10. Key Surgical Steps: Canaloplasty (CP)
content: **1. Conjunctival/Tenon's Flap**: Limbal-based, dissection to bare sclera.
**2. Superficial Scleral Flap**: Half-thickness, trapezoidal or rectangular (e.g., 5x5mm), base at limbus.
**3. Deep Scleral Flap**: Created within the superficial flap, exposing Schlemm's canal.
**4. Unroofing Schlemm's Canal**: Small anterior incision into the outer wall of Schlemm's canal.
**5. Microcatheter Insertion**: Microcatheter (e.g., iTrack 250) inserted into Schlemm's canal and advanced 360 degrees, guided by an illuminated tip.
**6. Viscoelastic Injection**: Viscoelastic injected through the microcatheter as it is withdrawn, dilating Schlemm's canal and collector channels.
**7. Suture Placement**: A 10-0 prolene suture is threaded through the microcatheter lumen and left in place within Schlemm's canal.
**8. Suture Tensioning**: The ends of the prolene suture are tied over the superficial scleral flap to expand the canal.
**9. Deep Flap Closure**: Deep scleral flap reapproximated or excised (surgeon's preference).
**10. Superficial Flap Closure**: Watertight closure of the superficial scleral flap.
**11. Conjunctival Closure**: Watertight closure.

sections.title: 13. Advantages & Disadvantages of NPGS (General)
content: **Advantages**:
- Lower risk of hypotony, choroidal detachment, and suprachoroidal hemorrhage compared to trabeculectomy.
- Reduced risk of endophthalmitis and bleb-related infections due to intact conjunctiva.
- Less restrictive post-operative activity limitations.
- Maintains structural integrity of the globe.
- No peripheral iridectomy typically needed.
**Disadvantages**:
- Less predictable or potent IOP lowering compared to trabeculectomy, especially in advanced glaucoma.
- Higher risk of failure requiring conversion to trabeculectomy or secondary penetrating surgery.
- Longer learning curve for some techniques (e.g., Canaloplasty).
- May require post-operative laser goniopuncture (e.g., YAG laser goniopuncture for DS/VC).
- Higher cost for devices (e.g., microcatheter for CP).

sections.title: 14. Investigations & Pre-operative Workup
content: **Comprehensive Ocular History**: Glaucoma type, prior surgeries, current medications.
**Best Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA)**.
**Intraocular Pressure (IOP)**: Baseline, diurnal curve if indicated.
**Gonioscopy**: Essential for angle assessment (open, synechiae, pigment).
**Optic Nerve Head (ONH) & Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL) Assessment**: Stereo photography, Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT).
**Visual Field Testing**: Humphrey Visual Field (HVF) 24-2 or 10-2.
**Central Corneal Thickness (CCT)**.
**Slit-lamp examination**: Anterior chamber depth, corneal health, conjunctival status.
**Fundoscopy**: Macula and periphery.
**Systemic Review**: Co-morbidities, anticoagulation status (may need temporary cessation).

sections.title: 15. Post-operative Management
content: **1. Topical Steroids**: e.g., Prednisolone acetate 1% or Dexamethasone 0.1%, q2h-q4h initially, tapered over 6-8 weeks based on inflammation.
**2. Topical Antibiotics**: e.g., Moxifloxacin 0.5% or Gatifloxacin 0.5%, qid for 1-2 weeks.
**3. Cycloplegic (Optional)**: e.g., Cyclopentolate 1% bid or Atropine 1% daily for severe inflammation/pain.
**4. IOP Monitoring**: Daily initially, then weekly, then monthly. Target IOP achievement.
**5. Bleb Assessment**: Monitor for diffuse, low-lying bleb formation (for DS/VC).
**6. Laser Goniopuncture (for DS/VC)**: If IOP remains high 4-8 weeks post-op, YAG laser goniopuncture to create micro-perforations through Descemet's membrane/trabecular meshwork (from AC).
**7. Anti-glaucoma medications**: Reintroduce or adjust if target IOP not achieved.

sections.title: 16. Potential Complications (General NPGS)
content: **Intraoperative**:
- Perforation of Descemet's membrane (micro-perforation).
- Subconjunctival hemorrhage.
- Scleral flap tear.
**Early Postoperative**:
- Hyphema (usually resolves spontaneously).
- Transient IOP spike (due to inflammation, viscoelastic).
- Significant inflammation (manage with topical steroids).
- Shallow AC (rare, indicates larger inadvertent perforation).
- Choroidal detachment (less common than trabeculectomy).
**Late Postoperative**:
- IOP elevation/Failure (most common, due to fibrosis). May require laser goniopuncture, additional medications, or conversion to trabeculectomy.
- Bleb encapsulation/failure (less common with NPGS diffuse blebs).
- Cataract progression.
- Refractive shift/astigmatism (due to sutures).

sections.title: 17. Red Flags / Emergency Signs Post-NPGS
content: **Sudden, severe pain or vision loss**: May indicate intraocular hemorrhage, acute IOP spike, or endophthalmitis.
**Purulent discharge, severe redness, eyelid swelling**: Classic signs of infection (endophthalmitis/blebitis).
**Markedly shallow or flat anterior chamber with hypotony**: Suggests a large accidental perforation into the AC or overfiltration (rare for NPGS).
**Fixed dilated pupil**: Possible posterior synechiae, severe inflammation, or iris incarceration.
**Sudden drop in vision or 'curtain' effect**: Suggests retinal detachment or choroidal hemorrhage.

branches: Secondary Open-Angle Glaucomas (e.g., Pigmentary, Pseudoexfoliation) - *if angle open*
Patients with high risk of hypotony/complications from trabeculectomy
Patients with prior failed trabeculectomy (may still favor trab for robust IOP lowering)

sections.title: 19. Prognosis & Outcomes
sections.content: NPGS generally achieves lower mean IOP reduction compared to trabeculectomy but with a significantly better safety profile. Target IOPs are often in the mid-teens (e.g., 14-18 mmHg) with or without medications. Success rates (complete vs. qualified) vary: 1-year rates typically 70-90%, decreasing to 50-70% at 5 years. Canaloplasty, in particular, has demonstrated excellent long-term stability and success rates (up to 70% at 5 years without medication in some studies) by preserving physiological outflow without a bleb.

content.mnemonic: NPGS: 'No Punctures, Gentle Surgeries, Schlemm's Saved!'
content.explanation:
• **N**o direct AC **P**unctures: Significantly lowers risk of hypotony, hemorrhage, endophthalmitis.
  • **G**entle **S**urgeries: Preserves globe integrity, less invasive profile.
  • **S**chlemm's **C**anal: The primary target for outflow enhancement across all NPGS techniques.
  • **S**afety: The hallmark advantage of NPGS over trabeculectomy.

sections.title: 21. Key Clinical Pearls
content: NPGS is ideal for patients needing moderate IOP reduction with a lower risk profile (e.g., high myopes, thin sclera, single-eyed patients).
Canaloplasty offers internal filtration, minimizing bleb-related issues and having excellent long-term IOP stability.
YAG laser goniopuncture is a critical post-operative intervention for DS/VC to reactivate filtration if IOP is elevated.
Meticulous scleral flap dissection is paramount for success in all NPGS techniques; avoid perforating Descemet's membrane.
Patient selection is crucial: NPGS may not be suitable for very high IOPs or advanced glaucoma requiring very low target IOPs (<12 mmHg).

sections.title: 22. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The landscape of glaucoma surgery is rapidly evolving. While NPGS predates the modern Minimally Invasive Glaucoma Surgery (MIGS) era, it shares the philosophy of enhancing physiological outflow with a better safety profile. Advances include improved microcatheter designs for Canaloplasty (e.g., iTrack 250A), leading to more consistent results. The **STAR Study** provided important long-term data on Canaloplasty's safety and efficacy. Research continues into bio-compatible implants and drug delivery systems to augment NPGS procedures, blurring the lines between traditional NPGS and emerging MIGS technologies (e.g., some canal-based MIGS procedures share similar mechanisms to Canaloplasty).

sections.title: 23. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
sections.content: NPGS procedures are generally **not indicated for pediatric glaucoma**, such as primary congenital glaucoma. In these cases, the pathology involves developmental anomalies of the angle that typically require direct angle surgery (goniotomy or trabeculotomy) or more potent filtration surgery like trabeculectomy or tube shunts. For **uveitic glaucoma**, NPGS outcomes are often less favorable due to increased inflammation and higher risk of fibrosis. **Neovascular glaucoma** is a contraindication due to high risk of hemorrhage and aggressive scarring, necessitating anti-VEGF therapy followed by conventional filtration or cyclodestructive procedures.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Non-penetrating glaucoma surgeries (NPGS) are a group of ab externo filtering procedures designed to lower intraocular pressure (IOP) by enhancing aqueous outflow into a subconjunctival space, often referred to as a 'scleral lake.' Crucially, these surgeries avoid direct communication with the anterior chamber, preserving the intact trabeculo-Descemet membrane (TDM) or a fenestrated Schlemm's canal wall. This significantly reduces the risk of hypotony, shallow anterior chamber, and endophthalmitis compared to conventional trabeculectomy.

Patients at high risk for hypotony (e.g., high myopia, single-eye patients, aphakia/pseudophakia, previous vitrectomy, thin sclera), patients preferring lower risk profile.

2. Enhanced Schlemm's Canal Outflow: Particularly in Viscocanalostomy, where Schlemm's canal is unroofed and distended, improving physiological outflow.
3. Juxtacanalicular Bypass: The external scleral dissection exposes the conventional outflow pathway, reducing resistance.
4. Formation of Sub-Scleral Lake: Provides a reservoir for aqueous before it's absorbed by episcleral veins/lymphatics or through the conjunctiva.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Candidate Selection
content: Progressive optic neuropathy and/or visual field loss despite maximal tolerated medical therapy.
Target IOP reduction typically in the mid-teens (e.g., from 25 mmHg to 15 mmHg), less aggressive than trabeculectomy targets.
Patients who are pseudophakic or require combined cataract surgery (NPGS can be safely combined).
Patients with a history of vitrectomy or retinal detachment repair, where hypotony risks are higher.
Absence of significant conjunctival scarring or inflammation in the surgical quadrant.

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings (Pre-Op Assessment)
content: **Gonioscopy:** Essential to confirm open angles (e.g., Shaffer Grade > III) and rule out significant peripheral anterior synechiae.
**Slit-lamp Biomicroscopy:** Assess conjunctival health (no prior scarring, inflammation), corneal clarity, anterior chamber depth and activity.
**Pachymetry:** Central Corneal Thickness (CCT) for IOP correlation.
**Fundoscopy:** Detailed optic nerve head assessment for cup-to-disc ratio, rim thinning, nerve fiber layer defects.
**Visual Acuity & Refraction:** Baseline measurements.
**IOP Measurement:** Baseline IOP with various tonometers (Goldmann, Pascal).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic Exam** - Including baseline VA, refraction, IOP, anterior chamber assessment, gonioscopy, and dilated fundus exam.
**Step 2: Visual Field Testing** - Automated perimetry (e.g., SITA-Standard 24-2 or 30-2) to establish baseline damage and monitor progression.
**Step 3: Optic Nerve & RNFL Imaging** - Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) of the optic nerve head, retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL), and macular ganglion cell complex.
**Step 4: Central Corneal Thickness (CCT)** - Pachymetry for accurate IOP interpretation.
**Step 5: Axial Length Measurement** - A-scan biometry, particularly if concurrent cataract surgery is planned or for high myopes.
**Step 6: Systemic Workup** - Standard pre-operative blood tests (CBC, electrolytes, coagulation profile), ECG, and medical clearance for general or local anesthesia suitability.

branches: **Mild Glaucoma:** (VFI > 80%, MD < -6 dB) – NPGS is often suitable, especially for patients desiring minimal risk.
**Moderate Glaucoma:** (VFI 50-80%, MD -6 to -12 dB) – NPGS with augmentation is frequently a good option, balancing efficacy and safety.
**Severe Glaucoma:** (VFI < 50%, MD < -12 dB) – Trabeculectomy is generally preferred due to the need for aggressive IOP reduction and a very low target IOP. NPGS may be insufficient alone.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment (General Algorithm)
content: **Step 1: Maximize Medical Therapy** – Topical prostaglandin analogs, beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Oral CAIs if needed.
**Step 2: Consider Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT/ALT)** – If indicated and not previously successful or contraindicated.
**Step 3: Surgical Consideration** – Evaluate target IOP, patient comorbidities, risks of penetrating surgery vs. NPGS.
**Step 4: Choice of Surgery** – NPGS (DS/VC) vs. Trabeculectomy vs. MIGS vs. Tube Shunt based on severity, target IOP, and risk tolerance.
**Step 5: Pre-operative Workup & Counseling** – Detailed examination, diagnostic tests, and thorough discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives.
**Step 6: Surgical Procedure** – Perform chosen NPGS technique (Deep Sclerectomy or Viscocanalostomy).
**Step 7: Post-operative Care & Follow-up** – Topical steroids, antibiotics, IOP monitoring, and management of complications.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Deep Sclerectomy (DS)
content: **Step 1: Conjunctival & Tenon's Flap** – Creation of a limbal or fornix-based conjunctival flap.
**Step 2: Superficial Scleral Flap** – Dissection of a half-thickness, roughly 5x5 mm trapezoidal or rectangular superficial scleral flap. Base typically at the limbus.

**Step 3: Deep Scleral Flap Dissection** – Creation of a second, smaller deep scleral flap beneath the superficial flap. This flap is dissected down to the TDM, carefully leaving the TDM and the internal wall of Schlemm's canal intact. This forms the roof of the future subscleral lake.
**Step 4: Excision of Deep Scleral Block** – The deep scleral flap is excised, exposing the TDM and unroofing Schlemm's canal partially.

**Step 5: Space Maintainer Implantation** – Placement of a visco-elastic material or a non-resorbable implant (e.g., Ologen, Aquaflow Collagen Implant, SK-Gel) into the scleral bed to prevent collapse and promote filtration.
**Step 6: Superficial Scleral Flap Closure** – The superficial scleral flap is sutured watertight (e.g., with 10-0 nylon sutures), typically with 2-3 sutures.
**Step 7: Conjunctival Closure** – Re-approximation of the conjunctival flap with absorbable sutures (e.g., 8-0 or 9-0 Vicryl).

sections.title: 12. Surgical Techniques: Viscocanalostomy (VC)
content: **Step 1: Conjunctival & Tenon's Flap** – Similar to DS, a limbal or fornix-based conjunctival flap is created.
**Step 2: Superficial Scleral Flap** – Dissection of a half-thickness, typically 5x5 mm superficial scleral flap.
**Step 3: Deep Scleral Flap Creation** – A deep scleral flap is dissected, exposing Schlemm's canal and the TDM.
**Step 4: Unroofing of Schlemm's Canal** – The outer wall of Schlemm's canal within the deep scleral bed is excised, revealing the lumen of Schlemm's canal and its inner wall (TDM).

**Step 5: Cannulation & Viscodilation** – Microcannulae (e.g., 30-gauge) are inserted into the open ends of Schlemm's canal, and a high-molecular-weight viscoelastic (e.g., Healon GV, Provisc) is injected circumferentially to dilate the canal and collector channels.
**Step 6: Descemet's Window (Optional)** – Some surgeons create one or more microperforations or a small tear in the TDM to facilitate aqueous flow into the subscleral lake. Others leave it intact.
**Step 7: Superficial Scleral Flap Closure** – The superficial scleral flap is carefully re-approximated and sutured (e.g., with 10-0 nylon) to ensure a watertight seal.
**Step 8: Conjunctival Closure** – The conjunctival flap is closed with absorbable sutures.
