Elaboration:

Anisocoria with Ptosis:This combination strongly points to either aHorner's syndromeor athird cranial nerve (CN III) palsy.Adie tonic pupilcan cause anisocoria but typically not ptosis [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed., Review of Ophthalmology 4th Ed., Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition].Aberrant regeneration of CN IIIrefers to misdirection of regenerating nerve fibers after injury, leading to atypical movements and pupillary abnormalities [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Differential Diagnosis and Clinical/Pharmacological Tests:

Horner's Syndrome:

Clinical Presentation:Miosis(small pupil, worse in the dark),mild ptosis(due to denervation of Müller's muscle), andanhidrosis(lack of sweating on the affected side) [merged_2022experiences.txt, Review of Ophthalmology 4th Ed.].

Pharmacological Tests:

Cocaine (4-10%):Blocks norepinephrine reuptake. A normal pupil dilates, but a Horner's pupil does not.

Apraclonidine (0.5-1%):A weak alpha-agonist. In Horner's, the denervated pupil becomes hypersensitive and dilates, while the normal pupil has minimal change. Useful for acute diagnosis.

Hydroxyamphetamine (1%):Releases stored norepinephrine. Helps localize the lesion: if the pupil dilates, the lesion is preganglionic; if it does not, the lesion is postganglionic [merged_2022experiences.txt, Review of Ophthalmology 4th Ed.].

Causes (Life-threatening):Carotid artery dissection, apical lung tumors (Pancoast tumor), cavernous sinus lesions [Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Third Cranial Nerve (CN III) Palsy:

Clinical Presentation:Severe ptosis,dilated pupil(if pupil-involving), and the eye is typically deviated"down and out"(due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles) [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Surgical vs. Medical:Pupil involvement often indicates a surgical cause (e.g., aneurysm compressing the nerve), whereas pupil-sparing palsies are more commonly medical (e.g., microvascular ischemia) [The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Investigations:Urgent neuroimaging (MRI/MRA brain)is mandatory to rule out life-threatening causes like intracranial aneurysm [The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Adie Tonic Pupil:

Clinical Presentation:Primarily adilated pupilthat reacts poorly to light but constricts slowly to near vision (light-near dissociation). May have segmental iris constriction and vermiform iris movements. Deep tendon reflexes are often absent [merged_2022experiences.txt, Review of Ophthalmology 4th Ed.]. The pupil dilates slowly [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Pharmacological Test:Pilocarpine (0.125%): The denervated Adie's pupil demonstrates denervation hypersensitivity and will constrict, while a normal pupil will not [Review of Ophthalmology 4th Ed.].

General Investigations for Anisocoria:

Detailed History:Crucial to ascertain onset, associated ocular or neurological symptoms, and any relevant past medical history [Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Complete Ophthalmic Examination:Includes pupillary size measurement in both light and dark conditions, assessment of extraocular motility, visual acuity, and fundus examination [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed., Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition].

Neuroimaging (MRI brain and neck, MRA):Indicated for suspected Horner's syndrome (especially to evaluate carotid dissection or apical lung tumors) or CN III palsy (to rule out aneurysm or mass) [merged_2022experiences.txt, Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Head Question:Causes- early onset/infantile/sensory/accommodative [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Partially accommodative/ fully [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Why check posterior pole- rule out sensory eso [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Elaboration:

Esotropia:An ocular misalignment where one or both eyes turn inward (convergent strabismus) [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Clinical Presentation:Inward deviation of the eye(s), often noticed by parents. Can be constant or intermittent, alternating or unilateral. May be associated with amblyopia or an abnormal head posture (e.g., face turn) [merged_2022experiences.txt, Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Causes/Types:

Infantile (Congenital/Early Onset) Esotropia:Manifests within the first 6 months of life, usually with a large-angle deviation.

Accommodative Esotropia:Develops in young children with moderate to high uncorrected hyperopia. Can be:

Fully Accommodative:Deviation resolves completely with the appropriate hyperopic spectacle correction.

Partially Accommodative:A residual esotropia remains even with full spectacle correction [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Sensory Esotropia:Occurs when significant vision loss in one eye (e.g., from cataract, optic atrophy, retinoblastoma) prevents fusion, leading to the eye turning inward [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Other:Duane's retraction syndrome, 6th cranial nerve palsy (though typically causes abduction deficit) [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Differential Diagnosis:Pseudostrabismus (due to prominent epicanthal folds giving the illusion of esotropia) [The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Investigations:

Ocular Examination:Visual acuity assessment (including age-appropriate methods), Hirschberg test, cover-uncover test, alternate cover test, versions, ductions, convergence [merged_2022experiences.txt, 06-Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus.pdf, KANSAKI'S_Clinical_Ophthalmology_A_Systematic_Approach_10th_Ed_].

Refraction:Cycloplegic (wet) refractionis crucial to reveal the full extent of hyperopia (latent hypermetropia) that may be driving accommodative esotropia [merged_2022experiences.txt, 06-Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus.pdf].

Posterior Pole Examination:Adilated fundus examinationis essential to rule out posterior segment pathology (e.g., retinoblastoma, optic nerve hypoplasia) that could cause sensory esotropia [merged_2022experiences.txt]. B-scan ultrasonography may be used if media opacity [KANSAKI'S_Clinical_Ophthalmology_A_Systematic_Approach_10th_Ed_].

Management:

Refractive Correction:Spectacle correctionfor hyperopia is the primary treatment for accommodative esotropia [merged_2022experiences.txt]. Bifocal glasses may be used for high accommodative convergence [Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Amblyopia Treatment:If amblyopia (reduced vision in one eye) is present, it must be treated with patching or atropine penalization [06-Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus.pdf].

Surgical Intervention:Strabismus surgery (e.g., bilateral medial rectus recession, or recess-resect procedure) is performed for infantile esotropia or the non-accommodative component of partially accommodative esotropia [merged_2022experiences.txt, Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P]. Botulinum toxin (Botox) injections can also be used [Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Elaboration:

Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1, von Recklinghausen Disease):A genetic neurocutaneous disorder (phacomatosis) with multi-system involvement, including characteristic ocular and systemic features [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Systemic Manifestations:

Café-au-lait spots:Multiple hyperpigmented skin macules [merged_2022experiences.txt, Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Cutaneous Neurofibromas:Benign nerve sheath tumors on the skin [Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Bone Abnormalities:Scoliosis, pseudarthrosis, sphenoid wing dysplasia [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

CNS Tumors:Optic pathway gliomas, other brain tumors [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Other:Learning disabilities, increased risk of certain malignancies (e.g., pheochromocytoma) [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Ocular Features/Complications:

Lisch Nodules:Tan-colored iris hamartomas, pathognomonic for NF1, increasing in number with age [merged_2022experiences.txt, Postgraduate Ophthalmology Exam Success, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Optic Pathway Gliomas:Tumors affecting the optic nerve, chiasm, or optic tracts. Can present withvision loss (progressive), proptosis, optic disc swelling or atrophy, dyschromatopsia, and afferent pupillary defect[merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed., Postgraduate Ophthalmology Exam Success, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Eyelid Features (Plexiform Neurofibromas):Diffuse, infiltrative neurofibromas can involve the eyelids, causing a characteristicS-shaped ptosis, proptosis, or facial asymmetry [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed., Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Glaucoma:Can be primary congenital glaucoma or secondary to angle neurofibromas [Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Cranial Nerve Palsies:May occur due to compression by tumors or other CNS involvement [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Investigations:

Neuroimaging (MRI Brain and Orbits with contrast):Essential to detect optic pathway gliomas and other CNS involvement [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Slit Lamp Examination:For Lisch nodules, eyelid lesions, and to assess for glaucoma [The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Comprehensive Ophthalmic Examination:Visual acuity, color vision, pupillary assessment, visual fields, fundus examination.

Management:Requires amultidisciplinary approach. Regular ophthalmological and neurological monitoring. Surgical intervention for symptomatic proptosis, vision-threatening optic gliomas, or for cosmetic reasons [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed., Postgraduate Ophthalmology Exam Success].

Case 1: Rose Bengal stain in exposed cornea

Head Question:Describe [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Elaboration:

Dry Eye Disease (DED):A multifactorial disease of the ocular surface, characterized by a loss of tear film homeostasis. It leads to various ocular symptoms and may be etiologically driven by tear film instability, hyperosmolarity, ocular surface inflammation/damage, and neurosensory abnormalities [AAO 2024 Cornea Subspecialty Day.pdf, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Clinical Presentation:Symptoms include burning, foreign body sensation (FBS), itching, redness, and fluctuating vision [merged_2022experiences.txt, Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition]. Signs include punctate epitheliopathy, filaments, mucus strands, small/absent tear meniscus [Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition].Rose Bengalor lissamine green stains devitalized epithelial cells and mucus on the exposed cornea and conjunctiva [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Types:Broadly classified into:

Aqueous-Deficient Dry Eye (ADDE):Reduced tear production (e.g., Sjögren syndrome, non-Sjögren causes like age, systemic medications, lacrimal gland dysfunction) [AAO 2024 Cornea Subspecialty Day.pdf, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Evaporative Dry Eye (EDE):Excessive tear evaporation (e.g., Meibomian Gland Dysfunction (MGD), blepharitis, rosacea, low blink rate, exposure from lid malposition) [merged_2022experiences.txt, AAO 2024 Cornea Subspecialty Day.pdf, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Investigations (TFOS DEWS II recommended order):

Clinical History/Symptom Questionnaires:(e.g., Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI), Dry Eye Questionnaire 5 (DEQ-5)) to assess symptom severity [AAO 2024 Cornea Subspecialty Day.pdf, Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition].

Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT):Measured after fluorescein instillation. ATBUT of <10 secondsis indicative of tear film instability [merged_2022experiences.txt, AAO 2024 Cornea Subspecialty Day.pdf, Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition].

Ocular Surface Staining (Fluorescein, Rose Bengal, Lissamine Green):Grades epithelial damage [merged_2022experiences.txt, AAO 2024 Cornea Subspecialty Day.pdf, Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition].

Schirmer I/II Test:Measures tear production. ASchirmer I test (without anesthetic) of <5 mm over 5 minutesis generally considered abnormal [merged_2022experiences.txt, AAO 2024 Cornea Subspecialty Day.pdf, Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition].

Tear Osmolarity:Elevated osmolarity is a hallmark of DED [08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Management (Staged Approach - TFOS DEWS II):

Step 1:Patient education, environmental modifications (e.g., humidifiers, avoiding fans), lifestyle changes (e.g., screen breaks), use ofpreservative-free (BAK-free) artificial tears[merged_2022experiences.txt, Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition].

Step 2:Addition ofanti-inflammatory agents(e.g., topical corticosteroids (short-term), cyclosporine, lifitegrast), tear secretagogues, punctal plugs (temporary or permanent to retain tears) [merged_2022experiences.txt, Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition].

Step 3/4 (for severe/refractory cases):Therapeuticbandage contact lenses (BCL),autologous serum drops (AMG), oral immunomodulators (e.g., doxycycline for MGD), lid hygiene for blepharitis/MGD, surgical interventions liketarsorrhaphyfor severe exposure, or scleral shells [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed., Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition].

Elaboration:

Band Keratopathy:A corneal degeneration characterized by the deposition ofcalcium phosphate saltsin the superficial cornea (Bowman's layer and anterior stroma), typically in the interpalpebral zone [merged_2022experiences.txt, Basic Principles of Ophthalmic Surgery 4th Ed., The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.]. It appears as a gray-white, Swiss-cheese-like opacity.

Causes/Risk Factors:

Chronic Ocular Inflammation:Most common cause, seen in conditions likeJuvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis (JRA)(now Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis - JIA), chronic uveitis, chronic corneal edema, phthisis bulbi [merged_2022experiences.txt, Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Systemic Hypercalcemia:Hyperparathyroidism, renal failure, sarcoidosis [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Intraocular Silicone Oil:Eyes with silicone oil (e.g., after retinal detachment surgery) can develop band keratopathy [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Age:Can be idiopathic and age-related (senile band keratopathy) [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Topical Medications:Certain phosphate-containing eye drops [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Differential Diagnosis:Urates, iron deposits, other corneal degenerations [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Investigations:Clinical examination with a slit lamp. If a pathological specimen is obtained, Von Kossa stain confirms calcium deposits [Basic Principles of Ophthalmic Surgery 4th Ed.].

Management:

Chelation:Superficial corneal debridementcombined with application ofethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA)(1.5-3.0% solution) to chelate and remove the calcium deposits [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Laser:Excimer laser phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK)can be used to ablate the superficial calcium deposits [merged_2022experiences.txt]. Femtosecond laser is not typically used for this purpose.

Treatment of Underlying Cause:If a systemic condition (e.g., hypercalcemia) or chronic inflammation is present, managing that condition is important [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Surgical:In severe, recurrent, or visually significant cases unresponsive to chelation,Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP)may be required [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Supportive:Bandage contact lens (BCL)for comfort during healing [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Complications:Recurrence of calcium deposits, corneal scarring, vision loss [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Elaboration:

Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN):An umbrella term encompassing a spectrum of precancerous and cancerous epithelial lesions of the conjunctiva and cornea, ranging from dysplasia to invasive squamous cell carcinoma [08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Clinical Presentation:Highly variable; can appear as a fleshy, gelatinous, leukoplakic (white plaque), orpapillomatous growth[merged_2022experiences.txt, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf]. Often located at the limbus (nasal or temporal) but can spread onto the cornea or conjunctiva. May have prominent feeder vessels [08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Causes/Risk Factors:Ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure,Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection,HIV/AIDS(immunocompromised state), chronic irritation, petroleum exposure [merged_2022experiences.txt, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Differential Diagnosis:Pterygium, pseudopterygium, papilloma (benign), chronic conjunctivitis [08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf, Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Investigations:

Slit Lamp Examination with Vital Stains:Fluoresceinor Rose Bengal staining can delineate the often indistinct margins of the lesion, as dysplastic epithelium stains more readily than normal epithelium [merged_2022experiences.txt, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT):Can show characteristicgross thickening of the epitheliumin OSSN, differentiating it from other lesions like pterygium [08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Biopsy:Essential for definitive diagnosis.Excisional biopsywith wide margins is often preferred.Pathologyconfirms squamous cell changes (dysplasia or carcinoma) [merged_2022experiences.txt, Basic Principles of Ophthalmic Surgery 4th Ed.].

Management:

Surgical Excision:"No-touch" technique(to avoid seeding tumor cells) with wide excisional margins. Intraoperative adjuncts includedouble freeze-thaw cryotherapyto the margins and placement of aconjunctival autograftoramniotic membraneto cover the bare sclera [merged_2022experiences.txt, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf, Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P]. Drawing the lesion on filter paper can help map the extent [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Topical Chemotherapy/Immunotherapy:Mitomycin C (MMC), 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), or Interferon-alpha2b (IFN-α2b)can be used as primary treatment for small lesions, or as adjuvant therapy after excision to reduce recurrence [merged_2022experiences.txt, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Elaboration:

Chemical Injury:Ocular trauma caused by contact with chemical substances.Alkali burns(e.g., from lye, cement, ammonia, sodium hydroxide (hydroxide)) are generally more severe than acid burns because they rapidly penetrate ocular tissues and cause ongoing damage through saponification [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Emergency Treatment:

Immediate and Copious Irrigation:This is the most critical first step. Irrigate the eye continuously with saline, Ringer's lactate, or even tap water for at least 30 minutes to an hour [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Fornix Sweep:Use a cotton-tipped applicator to sweep the conjunctival fornices to remove any retained particulate matter [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

pH Measurement:Check conjunctival pH usinglitmus paper. Continue irrigation until the pH normalizes to 7.0-7.5 and remains stable for several minutes [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.]. A pH greater than 7 (alkaline) indicates ongoing damage [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Roper Hall Classification:A grading system used to assess the severity of chemical burns based on corneal clarity and the extent oflimbal ischemia. It helps predict visual prognosis and guide further management [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Slit Lamp Examination:Critical for assessing corneal opacity, conjunctival chemosis, and especially the extent oflimbal ischemia(blanching of limbal vessels), which is a key prognostic indicator [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Long-Term Complications:Corneal scarring, corneal vascularization, persistent epithelial defects,dry eye,symblepharon(adhesions between conjunctiva and globe), glaucoma, cataract, and ultimatelyperforation[merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Treatment (Post-Emergency):

Topical Medications:Corticosteroids(to reduce inflammation, but with caution due to risk of corneal melt),antibiotics(to prevent secondary infection),cycloplegics(to reduce pain and synechiae), andvitamin C (ascorbate)(thought to aid collagen synthesis) [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Amniotic Membrane Grafts (AMG):To promote epithelial healing and reduce inflammation and scarring [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Autologous Serum Drops:To provide growth factors and promote healing [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Lid Procedures:Tarsorrhaphy(temporary or permanent partial eyelid closure) for severe exposure, andscleral shells/symblepharon ringsto prevent adhesions [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Limbal Stem Cell Transplantation:For severe limbal stem cell deficiency [AAO 2024 Cornea Subspecialty Day.pdf].

Elaboration:

Conjunctival/Eyelid Papilloma:Benign epithelial tumors of the conjunctiva or eyelids [08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Clinical Presentation:Often appear as araspberry-like or sessile lesion, sometimes with a stalk (pedunculated). They can occur on the eyelid margin or conjunctiva, including the nasal quadrant [merged_2022experiences.txt, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf]. Vascularity may be present [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Causes/Risk Factors:Associated withHuman Papillomavirus (HPV) infectionand UV exposure [merged_2022experiences.txt, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Differential Diagnosis (Malignant vs. Benign):It is crucial to differentiate papillomas from malignant lesions such asBasal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)orOcular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN)[merged_2022experiences.txt].

Features Suggesting Malignancy (BCC/SCC):Irregular margins, ulceration, loss of lashes (madarosis), pearly rolled edges (classic for BCC), deeper infiltration, surrounding tissue damage, involvement of meibomian gland orifices, rapid growth [merged_2022experiences.txt, Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Investigations:

Biopsy:Excisional biopsyis performed for definitive diagnosis and to rule out malignancy. Pathological examination confirms the benign nature or identifies malignancy [merged_2022experiences.txt, Basic Principles of Ophthalmic Surgery 4th Ed.].

Management:

Surgical Excision:Excisionis the primary treatment for papillomas. For eyelid lesions,direct reconstructionof the defect is often performed after excision [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Adjuvant Therapy:For conjunctival papillomas, topical interferon-α2b or cryotherapy may be used to reduce recurrence risk [08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Case 6: Ectropion

Head Question:Types- involutonal, cicatricial, mechanical [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Cause of involutional- laxity [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:S/s- fbs, watering, inferior corneal ulcer [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Management- LTS, lid shortening [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:7th nerve palsy- observe [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Will epiphora resolve- no if orbicularis pump fails [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Bcl if required, lubricants, [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Elaboration:

Ectropion:An outward turning of the eyelid margin, most commonly affecting the lower eyelid [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Clinical Presentation (Signs & Symptoms):Exposed palpebral conjunctiva (often red and thickened),foreign body sensation (FBS), chronicepiphora(watering of the eye due to malposition of the punctum and disruption of the tear pump mechanism), and potential forexposure keratopathy(dryness, irritation, and eveninferior corneal ulceration) [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed., The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Types and Causes:

Involutional (Senile) Ectropion:The most common type, caused byage-related horizontal laxityof the eyelid (weakening of the medial and lateral canthal tendons and orbicularis oculi muscle tone) [merged_2022experiences.txt, 07-Oculofacial Plastic and Orbital Surgery.pdf, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Cicatricial Ectropion:Results from scarring and contraction of the skin or underlying tissues of the eyelid (e.g., from trauma, burns, chronic inflammation, skin cancers, previous surgery) [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed., The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Paralytic Ectropion:Caused byfacial nerve (CN VII) palsy, leading to paralysis of the orbicularis oculi muscle and subsequent loss of lid tone and outward sagging [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Mechanical Ectropion:Occurs when a tumor or mass on the eyelid mechanically pulls it away from the globe [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Investigations:Clinical examination, including gross inspection, assessment of lid laxity (e.g., snap-back test), and evaluation of orbicularis oculi function [07-Oculofacial Plastic and Orbital Surgery.pdf, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Management:

Conservative:Lubricating eye drops and ointments, temporary taping of the lid, orbandage contact lens (BCL)for corneal protection [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Surgical:

Involutional Ectropion:Lateral Tarsal Strip (LTS)procedure (tightens the lower eyelid horizontally) often combined with lid shortening procedures [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed., Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Cicatricial Ectropion:Release of scar tissue, often requiring a skin graft (full-thickness or split-thickness) [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Paralytic Ectropion (Facial Nerve Palsy):Initiallyobservationfor spontaneous recovery (e.g., Bell's palsy). If persistent, surgical interventions to correct laxity (e.g., lid-tightening procedures, canthoplasty). Theepiphora may not resolvecompletely if the orbicularis pump mechanism is permanently dysfunctional [merged_2022experiences.txt].

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Day 2 Clinical Exam: Neuro and Motility

Case 1: Right eye esotropia. 5-8 year old girl.

Instruction:Candidate performed Hirschberg test, versions, convergences, saccades, pursuits, cover-uncover tests, and found right esotropia with mild restriction in the right eye. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Head Question:Examiner asked candidate to summarize findings and demonstrate restriction. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Asked differentials- ? DRS, right 6 the nerve palsy, congenital/ infantile esotropia. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Elaboration:

Esotropia:(See OSCE Station 2, Case 4 for full elaboration).

Differential Diagnosis for Esotropia with Restriction in a Child:

Duane Retraction Syndrome (DRS):A congenital eye movement disorder characterized byabduction deficit(most common, Type I), globe retraction, and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on attempted adduction. It can mimic a 6th nerve palsy [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Right 6th Cranial Nerve (CN VI) Palsy:Weakness or paralysis of the right lateral rectus muscle, leading to anabduction deficit(inability to move the eye outward) and esotropia that is worse on gaze to the right [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Congenital/Infantile Esotropia:(See OSCE Station 2, Case 4 for full elaboration). This is a primary esotropia usually without restriction.

Accommodative Esotropia:(See OSCE Station 2, Case 4 for full elaboration). Also typically without restriction.

Other considerations for restriction:Orbital masses, restrictive myopathies, prior trauma.

Case 2: Examine face and eyelid.

Instruction:Candidate observed decreased blink rate on left, flat and expressionless left face, rounded angle of mouth on left. Performed VPH, MRD1, eye closure, forehead wrinkles, whistle, smile tests. Diagnosed left facial palsy (Lower Motor Neuron) in a young patient. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Head Question:Asked why you did vph and mrd. Cause of retratction- answered due to decreased orbicularis tone. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Causes- bells, ramsay hunt. Asked to look for cause. Candidate checked neck- found a large vertical scar. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Elaboration:

Facial Nerve (CN VII) Palsy:(See OSCE Station 2, Case 2 for full elaboration).

Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) Palsy:Affects all facial muscles on one side, including the forehead. This causes inability to raise the eyebrow, close the eye, or smile on the affected side [merged_2022experiences.txt, Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Eyelid Retraction with Decreased Orbicularis Tone:The candidate correctly identified that decreased orbicularis oculi tone from facial nerve palsy can lead tomild eyelid retraction(widening of the palpebral fissure) and lagophthalmos, which necessitates checking VPH (vertical palpebral fissure height) and MRD1 (margin reflex distance 1) to assess the degree of exposure and for baseline [merged_2022experiences.txt, 07-Oculofacial Plastic and Orbital Surgery.pdf, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Causes:

Bell's Palsy:Idiopathic LMN facial palsy [merged_2022experiences.txt, Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Ramsay Hunt Syndrome:Herpes zoster virus reactivation in the geniculate ganglion, causing facial palsy with a painful vesicular rash in the ear [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Trauma/Surgery:Alarge vertical neck scarcould indicate prior surgery (e.g., parotidectomy, neck dissection) that potentially injured the facial nerve, leading to iatrogenic palsy [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Other:Tumors (e.g., cerebellopontine angle tumors), infections (e.g., Lyme disease).

Case 3: Young boy with congenital ptosis both eyes

Instruction:Candidate performed face position observation, checked for scars/drooping/eyebrow elevation, Hirschberg, MRD, VPH, lagophthalmos. Noted no lid crease, checked LPS action, corneal sensation (absent), Bells phenomenon. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Head Question:How will you counsel this patient- surgery with risk of exposure [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Management plan- discussed frontalis sling- silicone vs facia lata [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Complications of sling surgery- mentioned all [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:How would you prevent exposure, mentioned frost suture, lubricants and eye gels at night and can tape at night [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:What are advantages of silicone sling- easy, no need for second surgery [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:How would you manage Marcus gun jaw- quantify eyelid synkinesis- mild, mod severe if mild the direct surgery, if severe then levator disinsertion then sling [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Elaboration:

Congenital Ptosis:(See OSCE Station 2, Case 3 for full elaboration).

Examination:Candidate performed a thorough ptosis examination, including observation for compensatory mechanisms, key measurements (MRD, VPH, levator function), and assessment of Bell's phenomenon and corneal sensation, which are crucial for surgical planning and risk assessment [merged_2022experiences.txt, 07-Oculofacial Plastic and Orbital Surgery.pdf, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Counseling:Essential to discuss the surgical plan, potential for improvement, and risks, especiallyexposure keratopathydue to lagophthalmos post-surgery [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Management (Frontalis Sling):

Indication:For poor levator function (<4-5 mm), which is common in significant congenital ptosis [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Materials:Siliconerods (advantages: easy to insert, adjustable, no need for a second surgical site) orautogenous fascia lata(harvested from the thigh, typically for older children) [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Complications of Sling Surgery:Exposure keratopathy/lagophthalmos, infection, granuloma formation, recurrence, asymmetry, under/over-correction [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Prevention of Exposure:Frost suture(a temporary tarsorrhaphy for immediate postoperative protection), frequent lubricants (drops andeye gels at night), and taping the eyelids closed at night [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking Syndrome Management:(See OSCE Station 2, Case 3 for full elaboration). If mild, direct ptosis repair; if severe, levator disinsertion followed by a frontalis sling [merged_2022experiences.txt].

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Day 2 Clinical Exam: Anterior Segment

Case 1: Slit lamp examination Old lady – examine the anterior segment of the left eye

Instruction:Candidate adjusted slit lamp, performed diffuse exam, assessed lids, conjunctiva, AC depth (by von Herick's), and identified a tube in the anterior chamber superiorly, an IOL in place with a non-reacting pupil, posterior synechiae, IOL pitting, and prior YAG capsulotomy. Commented on the tube and drainage implant in the superior temporal quadrant. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Head Question:What are the potential complications? Mentioned immediate post op ac shallowing, tube corneal touch and endothelial damage, tube migration, exposure and scleral necrosis, tube blockage by iris or vitreous. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:What will you do to prevent the exposure? And is the implant exposed in this? [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Elaboration:

Glaucoma Drainage Device (Tube Implant):Surgical device (e.g., Baerveldt, Ahmed valve) implanted to lower intraocular pressure (IOP) by diverting aqueous humor from the anterior chamber to a subconjunctival plate [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Clinical Findings:A tube visible in the anterior chamber, often leading to a drainage plate in the superior temporal quadrant. Associated findings like posterior synechiae (adhesions between iris and lens), IOL pitting, and prior YAG capsulotomy suggest a history of complicated intraocular inflammation or surgery [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Potential Complications (Tube-Related):

Early Postoperative:Shallow anterior chamber (AC), hypotony, choroidal detachment, hyphema, tube obstruction.

Late Postoperative:

Corneal Endothelial Damage:Fromtube-corneal touch(the tube rubbing against the corneal endothelium), which can lead to corneal edema and decompensation [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Tube Migration:The tube can shift from its intended position.

Exposure:Exposure of the tube or platethrough the conjunctiva, posing a significant risk for infection (endophthalmitis/blebitis) and scleral necrosis [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Tube Blockage:By iris, vitreous, fibrin, or scar tissue [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Infection:Endophthalmitis, blebitis.

Prevention of Exposure:Meticulous surgical technique, including covering the tube with a scleral patch graft (e.g., donor sclera, pericardium) and ensuring secure, tension-free conjunctival closure over the implant [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Case 2: Anterior segment slit lamp evaluation of the left eye of the patient

Instruction:Candidate noted normal lids/conjunctiva, a central, deep, leucomatous corneal scar (nothing visible through it), VH grade 4 AC depth, normal iris, no cataract. Measured scar size. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Head Question:Discuss differential diagnosis- told post corneal ulcer, trauma, corneal dystrophy [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:What else? I said I would like to examine the other eye. What do you want to see- transplant, corneal opacities in the other eye. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:What else this could be? I asked to examine again, did examination in high magnification Answered this is post corneal hydrops patient- diagnosed keratoconus [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:What else would you find? Did munson sign Mentioned prominent corneal nerves and stromal folds [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:How would you manage- pkp vs dalk [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:When dalk? If dm has healed high chances of pkp [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Other eye management- if progressive keratoconus- then I would advise c3r If other eye non progressive- then refraction, glasses, rigid lenses, pkp [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Elaboration:

Corneal Scar / Keratoconus / Acute Corneal Hydrops:

Corneal Scar:A permanent opacification of the cornea resulting from prior injury, infection (e.g., corneal ulcer), or disease. A"leucomatous" scaris dense and white, completely obscuring vision [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Keratoconus:A progressive, non-inflammatory corneal ectatic disease where the cornea thins and protrudes into a conical shape, causing irregular astigmatism and vision loss [merged_2022experiences.txt, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Acute Corneal Hydrops:A sudden, vision-threatening complication of advanced keratoconus, occurring when Descemet's membrane ruptures, allowing aqueous humor to acutely enter and opacify the corneal stroma [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.]. This eventually resolves, leaving a dense corneal scar.

Clinical Presentation (Keratoconus):Progressive vision reduction, irregular astigmatism. Signs includeMunson's sign(indentation of the lower eyelid by the conical cornea on downgaze), Fleischer ring (iron deposition at the base of the cone), prominent corneal nerves, and Vogt's striae (vertical stromal folds) [merged_2022experiences.txt, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Differential Diagnosis of Corneal Scarring:Post-corneal ulcer, trauma, corneal dystrophy (e.g., Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy, lattice dystrophy) [merged_2022experiences.txt, 08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Investigations:

Slit Lamp Examination:For direct visualization of the scar, Munson's sign, prominent nerves, stromal folds. History of corneal hydrops would explain a dense scar with keratoconus [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Examine the Other Eye:Keratoconus is typically bilateral, though often asymmetrical. Look for signs of keratoconus or previous corneal surgery (e.g., transplant) in the fellow eye [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Corneal Topography/Tomography:Essential for diagnosing and monitoring keratoconus, showing characteristic steepening and thinning [08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

OCT Corneal Epithelial Mapping:Can detect subtle changes in early keratoconus [08-External Disease and Cornea.pdf].

Management:

Early/Non-Progressive:Refractive correctionwith glasses orrigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lenses[merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Progressive Keratoconus:Corneal Cross-Linking (CXL or C3R)is advised to halt disease progression by strengthening corneal collagen [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Advanced Disease/Severe Scarring/Uncorrectable Vision:

Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK):Replaces the anterior corneal stroma, preserving the patient's own Descemet's membrane and endothelium. This is preferred if the endothelium is healthy (e.g., after healed hydrops) [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP):A full-thickness corneal transplant, used if Descemet's membrane is compromised or with severe scarring [merged_2022experiences.txt].

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Day 2 Clinical Exam: Posterior Segment

Case 1: Examine the posterior segment of the right eye with 90d. asked to use my own lens. Said that’s great

Instruction:Candidate noted vertically oval and tilted disc, a whitish lesion sparing the disc and fovea, inferior to the disc, with vessels dipping inside the defect. Diagnosed choroidal coloboma. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Head Question:Can you comment on the type? I said 2 (Incorrect) [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:What would be the visual status of the patient? I said that the macula is not involved so visual acuity will be good, but I would like to exainte the anterior segment also [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:What could be the type of refractive error in this patient> I answered myopia? Not sure about this [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:What else could be cause of poor visual acuity in this patient? Answered- strabismus and amblyopia either refractive of strabismic [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Elaboration:

Choroidal Coloboma (Coloboma of the Optic Disc/Choroid):A congenital anomaly resulting from incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure during development. It manifests as a defect in the optic disc, retina, or choroid [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed., Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Clinical Presentation:A characteristicwhitish, excavated lesion, typically locatedinferior to the optic discand sometimes involving the disc itself (optic disc coloboma) [merged_2022experiences.txt]. Retinal vessels may appear to "dip into" or disappear within the colobomatous defect [merged_2022experiences.txt]. The optic disc itself can be vertically oval or tilted [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Classification:Not extensively detailed in the provided sources, but it's a developmental defect.

Associated Conditions/Complications:

Refractive Error:Commonly associated withmyopiaand astigmatism [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Visual Acuity:Depends on the involvement of the macula. If the macula is spared, good visual acuity is possible [merged_2022experiences.txt]. However, associatedstrabismus(eye misalignment) andamblyopia(reduced vision due to abnormal visual experience during development, either refractive or strabismic) can cause significant vision loss [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Other Ocular Anomalies:Can be part of syndromes (e.g., CHARGE syndrome) and associated with iris coloboma, microphthalmos, aniridia, or anterior segment dysgenesis [Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P, The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed., The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Retinal Detachment:Serous retinal detachment can occur at the margins of the coloboma [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Investigations:

Dilated Fundus Examination (using 90D lens or indirect ophthalmoscopy):To visualize and characterize the coloboma [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Refraction:To identify and correct any refractive errors [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Anterior Segment Examination:To look for other associated ocular anomalies [merged_2022experiences.txt].

B-scan Ultrasonography:If media opacities preclude direct visualization or to evaluate for retinal detachment [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Management:

Refractive Correction:Prescribe glasses for any myopia or astigmatism [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Amblyopia Therapy:Essential if present, involving patching or atropine penalization [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Monitoring:Regular follow-up to monitor for complications like retinal detachment [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Case 2: middle aged lady- asked to examine with the IDO

Instruction:Candidate noted optic disc pallor, sharp margins, attenuation of vessels in all quadrants, pigments in all quadrants, and macular involvement. Checked other eye and saw disc pallor and macular pigmentation. Diagnosed Retinitis Pigmentosa. [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Head Question:What test will you do- mentioned visual acuity, refraction [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:How can you help the patient- do refraction, can plan cataract surgery [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:What ophthalmological tests will you do- slit lamp, oct [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:Why oct- if cme then Diamox and reduce cme [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Sub-Header Question:What else? [merged_2022experiences.txt]

Elaboration:

Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP):A group of inherited progressive retinal dystrophies characterized by primary degeneration of photoreceptors (initially rods, then cones) and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Clinical Presentation:

Symptoms:Earliest symptom is oftennight blindness (nyctalopia), followed by progressiveperipheral visual field loss(leading to "tunnel vision"), and eventually central vision loss [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed., Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Signs (Fundus):Classic triad includeswaxy pallor of the optic disc,attenuation of retinal vessels(especially arterioles), and characteristicbone-spicule-shaped retinal pigmentation(pigmented cells aggregating in the mid-periphery and later extending to the macula) [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed., Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P]. Macular involvement with pigmentation and pallor is a late sign [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Causes/Risk Factors:Predominantlygenetic, with various inheritance patterns (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, mitochondrial) [merged_2022experiences.txt, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Complications:Cystoid Macular Edema (CME), posterior subcapsular cataract, epiretinal membrane, vitreous cells/syneresis [merged_2022experiences.txt, 09-Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation.pdf, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed.].

Investigations:

Visual Acuity and Refraction:To assess current vision and correct refractive errors [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Visual Fields:To map and monitor progressive peripheral and central vision loss [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Electroretinogram (ERG):A definitive diagnostic test, showingreduced or extinguished a- and b-waves, reflecting photoreceptor dysfunction [merged_2022experiences.txt, Oxford Handbook of Ophthalmology 4th edition, The Ophthalmology Examinations Review Tien Yin WONG 3rd Ed., Past cadidate Exp-All chua + missing in chua - 429P].

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):To detect and monitorCMEand evaluate the structural integrity of the outer retina and RPE [merged_2022experiences.txt, 09-Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation.pdf].

Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF):To visualize areas of RPE atrophy and lipofuscin accumulation [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Genetic Testing:Can identify the specific gene mutation, aiding in diagnosis and genetic counseling [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Management:

Supportive Care:

Refractive correction:Glasses for any refractive errors [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Cataract Surgery:If a visually significant cataract (common complication) is present [merged_2022experiences.txt].

CME Treatment:Oral acetazolamide (Diamox)or topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors can reduce CME and improve vision in some cases [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Low Vision Aids:For significant vision impairment [The Wills Eye Manual 8th Ed.].

Genetic Counseling:To inform patients about inheritance patterns, prognosis, and potential for future therapies [merged_2022experiences.txt].

Experimental Treatments:Gene therapies and retinal prostheses are actively being investigated [12-Retina and Vitreous.pdf].

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

sections.title: Pediatric Case: Limbal Dermoid
content: Case: An 8-year-old patient presented with the this finding.
Q1: Describe what you are seeing.
Q2: How would you manage this patient?
Clinical Pearl: Limbal dermoids are choristomas. If associated with preauricular skin tags or vertebral anomalies, consider Goldenhar Syndrome.
Management options: Observation (if asymptomatic), or surgical excision with lamellar keratoplasty if causing significant astigmatism or visual axis obstruction.

sections.title: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) Clinical Presentation
sections.content: A1: This an image of an old man/ lady showing left temporal upper lid swelling with hyperemia and ulceration with temporal mild lower lid hyperemia and swelling associated with temporal upper lid ptosis. In addition, there is temporal eyebrow hair loss with temporal periocular skin hyperpigmentation.

rows: Acute inflammation of tissues anterior to the orbital septum.
Painful, focal inflammatory lesion of meibomian glands.
May arise from actinic keratosis; carries risk of perineural invasion.
Most common; pearly borders; telangiectasia; rarely metastasizes.
The 'Great Masquerader'; high mortality; skip lesions.
Violaceous nodule; highly aggressive; associated with polyomavirus.

sections.title: Malignant Eyelid Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Q1: Describe the photo? Q2: What is your ddx? Q3: If I told you that this photo represents a biopsy taken that confirm squamous cell carcinoma. What will you do next?
Step 2: Diagnosis: Perform incisional biopsy with adequate margin for histopathology.
Step 3: Surgical Planning: First-line treatment is surgical excision. Radiation therapy is the second-best treatment.
Step 4: Non-Surgical Options: Topical imiquimod and topical or injectable interferon (for elderly non-surgical candidates).
Step 5: Education: Inform patients about the etiologic role of the sun.
Step 6: Systemic Referral: Refer to oncologist or internist for regional/systemic workup and surveillance.
Step 7: Imaging: SCC requires CT of the brain and orbit to check infiltration (lacrimal gland) or perineural invasion (PNI).
Step 8: Nodes: Check sentinel lymph nodes (LNs) and local LNs for lymphadenopathy with metastasis.
Step 9: Distance Check: PET scan for distant metastasis.

rows: Wide margins necessary due to 'Skip Lesions'.

sections.title: Special Focus: Sebaceous Gland Carcinoma (SGC)
content: NB for Sebaceous cell CA: Wide excision (5mm) is MANDATORY due to skip lesions.
Send fresh tissue specifically for Oil Red O stain (to identify lipid).
Perform Conjunctival Map Biopsies: From at least 4 bulbar quadrants + medial and lateral tarsal conjunctiva (upper & lower lids).
If map biopsy is positive: Adjunctive cryotherapy is required.
Regional Management: Sentinel LN biopsy; KIV neck dissection for regional adenopathy.
Reconstruction: Repair lid defect depending on size and margin involvement.

branches: CT Orbits/MRI with Contrast: SCC, SGC, Malignant Melanoma
MRI Brain/Orbit: Check for Orbital/Intracranial extension
BCC Medial Canthal: Check Lacrimal sac or Orbital involvement
PET Scan: Evaluation for distant metastasis

sections.title: Management of Incomplete Margins
content: Q4: After excision, the edge of the excised sample is infiltrated with tumor cells. What to do next?
A4: If the excisional biopsy showed incomplete excision with unsafety margin, re-excise more of the margin to confirm clearance.
Following confirmed clearance via frozen section or Mohs, proceed with eyelid reconstruction.

content.explanation: For BCC with orbital/intracranial extension not amenable to surgery/radiation, use targeted therapy with Hedgehog pathway inhibitors (e.g., Vismodegib).

sections.title: Disc Coloboma: Embryonic Fissure Defects
sections.content: The embryonic fissure of the developing eye is located inferiorly and slightly nasally and extends from the optic nerve to the margin of the pupil. A coloboma is a defect in one or more ocular structures due to the fissure’s incomplete closure. The defect may be unilateral or bilateral and usually occurs sporadically in otherwise normal individuals (Fig. 19.26), though numerous systemic associations have been described, e.g. chromosomal abnormalities, CHARGE syndrome, Goldenhar syndrome and central nervous system abnormalities. An AD variety is caused by a mutation in the gene PAX6.

sections.title: Clinical Signs of Disc Coloboma
content: VA is often decreased; amblyopia and refractive error may be present. 19.25F).
A disc pit is sometimes associated (Fig. 19.27A). Pit-like excavations are sometimes seen with a disc coloboma.
A disc coloboma may be associated with, or even continuous with, a large chorioretinal coloboma (Fig. 19.27B).

A focal, glistening white, bowl-shaped excavation, decentred inferiorly so that the inferior neuroretinal rim is thin or absent and normal disc tissue is confined to a superior wedge of variable size depending on severity (Fig. 19.27C and D).
Perimetry shows a superior defect.
Ocular associations include microphthalmos, microcornea and coloboma of other structures such as the iris or lens.

sections.title: Coloboma Complications & Tips
content: Rare: Serous retinal detachment
Rare: Progressive neuroretinal rim thinning
Rare: Choroidal neovascularization
TIP: Buried optic disc drusen in children can mimic papilloedema.

branches: Rare, usually unilateral and sporadic condition
Bilateral cases: Rarer still, may be hereditary
Genetics: PAX6 gene mutation can be responsible
Systemic: Frontonasal dysplasia (midfacial anomalies, basal encephalocele, midline brain malformations, pituitary insufficiency)
Visual Acuity: May be normal or impaired to a variable extent

sections.title: Morning Glory: Physical Signs
content: Large disc with a funnel-shaped excavation surrounded by a ring-shaped chorioretinal disturbance (Fig. 19.28B and C).
White tuft of glial tissue overlies the central portion (persistent hyaloid vascular remnants).
Blood vessels emerge from the rim of the excavation in a radial pattern like the spokes of a wheel.
Vessels are increased in number; difficult to distinguish arteries from veins.

sections.title: Optic Nerve Hypoplasia (ONH)
sections.content: The hypoplastic optic nerve, unilateral or bilateral, carries a diminished number of nerve fibres. Its frequency seems to be increasing, though it remains relatively rare. Young maternal age, primiparity and maternal exposure to various agents have been linked. It may occur as an isolated anomaly in an otherwise normal eye, but systemic associations are common.

rows: Severe bilateral: blindness in early infancy, roving eye movements, nystagmus. Unilateral/less severe: squint. Mild: easily overlooked.
Ranges from normal to severely impaired.
RAPD may be present. Bilateral cases: both pupils may have sluggish light responses.
Mild: smaller than normal disc. Spectrum: small grey disc, central cupping-like deficiency, radial vessels (sometimes tortuous).
Foveola disc-centre distance ≥ 3x disc diameter suggests hypoplasia.
Characteristic: white ring of visible sclera surrounding a pigmented band (migrated pigment epithelium). Thin outer pigmented line possible (Fig. 19.29A).

sections.title: ONH: Associations & Investigation
content: Ocular: astigmatism, amblyopia, field defects, foveal hypoplasia, aniridia and microphthalmos.
Systemic: Developmental midline brain defects; pituitary and hypothalamic deficits are common.

Historical Association: 'Septo-optic dysplasia' (de Morsier syndrome) – bilateral ONH, absent septum pellucidum, corpus callosum agenesis (Fig. 19.29B–D) and hypopituitarism (Note: now believed not to exist as a specific entity).
Investigation: Screen all children for systemic associations, especially hormonal deficiencies and developmental delay.

sections.title: Myelinated Nerve Fibres (MNF)
content: Occurrence: ~1% of the population. Usually congenital and stable.
Variations: Progression and acquired forms reported. Occasionally familial. Systemic associations rare.
Signs: Whitish striated patches with feathery borders. Size variable (Fig. 19.30A–D). 2/3 are not contiguous with the disc (Fig. 19.30B).
Vision: Reduced VA if central macula involved. Absolute scotoma on perimetry corresponding to the area. Retinal vessels obscured.
Imaging: FAF (hypoautofluorescence), FA (masking), OCT (hyperreflective RNFL).
Treatment: Addressing refractive error, amblyopia and squint if present.
Differential: Between 5% and 10% are bilateral. Can be mimicked by neoplastic infiltration.
Ocular Associations: Myopia, anisometropia, strabismus and amblyopia.

sections.title: Aicardi Syndrome
content: Range of CNS malformations + multiple bilateral depigmented chorioretinal lacunae clustered around a hypoplastic, colobomatous or pigmented optic disc (Fig. 19.31).
Other Ocular Features: cataract and coloboma.
Inheritance: X-linked dominant.
Prognosis: Lethal in utero for males. Affected girls usually die within the first few years of life.

sections.title: Bergmeister Papilla
content: Relatively common anomaly.
Consists of remnants of the hyaloid vessels (Fig. 19.32).
Includes: Prepapillary loop and remnant of hyaloid vessel.

rows: Veno-venular shunts to bypass closure. Distended flat vessels starting and ending on the disc (Fig. 19.33A).
Unilateral retinal-choroidal circulation anastomoses. Large tortuous channels disappearing at disc margin (Fig. 19.33B).
Fine, lace-like vessels, flat or elevated. May extend to retina; associated with gliosis (Fig. 19.33C).
Non-hereditary, usually unilateral. Normal disc sits in deep excavation with atrophic walls (RPE/choroid) (Fig. 19.34A).
VA markedly reduced. Local RD possible. Rarely associated with systemic disease.
AD condition (PAX2 mutation). Renal and optic disc dysplasia. Failure of angiogenesis.
Normal size disc, central excavation, cilioretinal vessels replace central retinal vasculature (Fig. 19.34B).
Descriptive term for a markedly deformed disc.
Does not conform to any recognizable category (Fig. 19.34C).
Typically bilateral. Diameters ≥ 2.1 mm or area > 2.5 mm².
High C/D ratio but normal configuration. No focal rim loss. Normal macular GCC imaging.
Disc absent or rudimentary. Vessels absent or few/abnormal. Retinal pigmentary disturbance at site. Ocular/systemic defects present.

sections.title: The GATT Process
content: Step 1: Create temporal paracentesis and tilt microscope/head for gonioscopic view.
Step 2: Inject viscoelastic to maintain the anterior chamber and open the angle.
Step 3: Create a small goniotomy incision to access Schlemm's canal.
Step 4: Thread a microcatheter or blunted suture 360 degrees around the canal.
Step 5: Externalize the distal end and pull to rupture the trabecular meshwork circumferentially.

sections.title: The Goniotomy Process
content: Step 1: Position the patient and microscope for optimal gonioscopic visualization.
Step 2: Enter the eye through a clear corneal incision temporal to the target site.
Step 3: Advance the blade (e.g., Kahook Dual Blade) across the AC to the nasal angle.
Step 4: Engage the trabecular meshwork and create a focal incision (scoring).
Step 5: If using a dual-blade, remove a strip of TM tissue to prevent leaflets from closing.

sections.title: Surgical Red Flags
content: Poor visualization of the angle (Corneal edema/opacity)
Neovascular Glaucoma (Risk of massive hyphema)
Extensive Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS)
Active Uveitis or inflammatory glaucoma flare
Uncontrolled episcleral venous pressure

sections.title: Key Advantages: GATT
content: Maximizes outflow facility by treating the entire 360 circumference.
Effective in both primary and secondary open-angle glaucomas.
Can be performed as a standalone or combined with cataract surgery.
Cost-effective if using a 5-0 Prolene suture technique.

sections.title: Key Advantages: Goniotomy
content: Significantly shorter learning curve compared to GATT.
Reduced intraoperative time; less manipulation of the canal.
Lower risk of 'losing' the catheter/suture within the canal.
Proven track record in pediatric/congenital glaucoma cases.

content.explanation: C is for Catheter (The 360 threading tool); C is for Circular (The complete rupture of the TM); C is for Clear-View (The requirement for perfect gonioscopy).

sections.title: Post-Operative Considerations
sections.content: In both GATT and Goniotomy, the most common post-operative finding is a transient hyphema, which usually resolves within 1-2 weeks. Patients are typically started on a regimen of topical steroids and antibiotics. Pilocarpine may be used in some cases to keep the angle open and prevent the formation of synechiae. Success is defined by the reduction of intraocular pressure and the decrease in the number of required glaucoma medications.

content: Foreign body sensation (grittiness)
Ocular pain or irritation
Photophobia (sensitivity to light)
Excessive tearing (epiphora)
Blurred or fluctuating vision
Redness of the conjunctiva

content.explanation: S: Superior (SLK); T: Toxic (Medicamentosa); A: Aqueous Deficiency (Dry Eye); I: Inferior (Blepharitis); N: Neurotrophic Keratopathy.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Step 1: Identify and treat the primary underlying cause.
Step 2: Initiate intensive lubrication with preservative-free artificial tears.
Step 3: Apply nocturnal lubricating ointments for exposure-related cases.
Step 4: Discontinue any offending toxic topical medications.
Step 5: Consider a bandage contact lens for severe epithelial compromise.
Step 6: Monitor for secondary bacterial infection and provide prophylactic coverage if needed.

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS
content: Sudden, significant drop in Visual Acuity
Presence of a Hypopyon (white blood cells in anterior chamber)
Rapid corneal thinning or ulceration
Intense pain that is non-responsive to lubricants
Associated purulent discharge

sections.title: Clinical Summary Verbatim
sections.content: Punctate epithelial erosions are not a disease in themselves but a manifestation of ocular surface disease. They represent areas where the corneal epithelium has been shed. When viewed under a slit lamp with a cobalt blue filter after fluorescein instillation, they appear as bright green dots because the dye pools in the spaces where cells are missing. Management focuses on restoring the tear film and protecting the corneal surface to allow for re-epithelialization.

sections.title: Introduction to AMD
sections.content: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a degenerative disorder in which the structure and function of the macula deteriorates. It is characterized by the presence of specific clinical findings, including drusen and RPE changes, in the absence of another disorder. Later stages of the disease are associated with impairment of vision secondary to neovascularization or atrophy.

headers: Definition (Lesions within 2 disc diameters of fovea)
rows: No drusen; No AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Only drupelets (small drusen <63 μm); No AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Medium drusen (>63 μm but <125 μm); No AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Large drusen (>125 μm); Any AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Neovascular AMD and/or Any geographic atrophy

sections.title: Key Definitions & Terminology
content: Pigmentary abnormalities: definite hyper- or hypopigmentary abnormalities associated with medium/large drusen (not due to other disease).
Drupelets: Proposed term for small drusen (<63 μm).
Drusen sizing: Estimated by comparison with a retinal vein at the optic disc margin (~125 μm).
The consensus committee has standardized nomenclature for reporting neovascular AMD.

sections.title: The Two Main Types of AMD

branches: Dry (Non-exudative/Non-neovascular): 90% of cases; Advanced stage is Geographic Atrophy (GA).
Wet (Exudative/Neovascular): Less common; Rapid progression; Includes MNV, PED, RAP, and PCV.

content.explanation: TIP: The term ‘choroidal neovascularization’ (CNV) is no longer appropriate because neovascularization may start in the outer retina. Macular neovascularization (MNV) should be used instead.

sections.title: Global & Regional Epidemiology
content: Most common cause of irreversible visual loss in industrialized countries.
Symptoms are rare in patients under 50 years of age; prevalence increases with age.
UK: 4% of population over 75 and 14% of those over 90 have significant visual impairment (6/18 or worse).
UK: 1.6% of those over 75 have binocular acuity < 6/60.
Fellow Eye Risk: 50% chance of developing advanced AMD within 5 years if late AMD or moderate loss is present in the first eye.

sections.title: USA Visual Loss Statistics by Race
Multi-factorial Risk Factors
content: Age: The major risk factor.
Race: Late AMD is more common in White individuals.
Heredity: 3x risk if a first-degree relative is affected. Variants in 50+ genes implicated.
Smoking: Roughly doubles the risk of AMD.
Hypertension: Associated with other cardiovascular risk factors.
Dietary: High fat intake and obesity promote AMD; high antioxidants are protective.
Aspirin: Weak statistically significant association, but benefits (stroke/heart attack prevention) outweigh the risk of exacerbating wet AMD.
Uncertain Factors: Cataract surgery, blue iris colour, high sunlight exposure, and female gender.

rows: Complement factor H; protects cells from complement-mediated damage
Encodes protein in choroidal extracellular matrix

content.explanation: There is no advantage in undertaking genetic testing until studies confirm its value for determining prognosis or treatment response.

sections.title: Drusen: Histopathology & Distribution
sections.content: Drusen are extracellular deposits at the interface between the RPE and Bruch membrane. They consist of constituents from immune-mediated and metabolic RPE processes. Rare before age 40, common by the 60s. Distribution: foveal, encircling the fovea, band-like around the macular periphery, or in mid-peripheral fundus.

sections.title: Clinical Features of Drusen
content: Small Drusen (Drupelets/Hard): ≤63 μm. Well-defined, white-yellow. Little risk unless with pigmentary changes.
Intermediate Drusen: 63–125 μm. Focal yellow-white deposits. Risk to late AMD >10% if bilateral pigmentary abnormalities exist.
Large Drusen (Soft): >125 μm. Less delineated. Can coalesce into 'drusenoid RPE detachment'. Risk to late AMD is 13% (rises to 50% with bilateral pigmentary changes).
Dystrophic calcification: May develop in all drusen types.
Pigmentary abnormalities: Hyper- and hypopigmentation significantly increase late AMD likelihood.

content.explanation: TIP: There is a strong association between the risk of developing advanced AMD, drusen size, and macular pigmentary change.

sections.title: Imaging Findings for Drusen
content: OCT: Medium/large drusen appear as hyper-reflective irregular nodules beneath the RPE on/within Bruch membrane.
FA (Hyperfluorescence): Caused by window defects (RPE atrophy) or late staining.
FA (Hypofluorescence): Hydrophobic drusen with high lipid content mask background fluorescence and do not stain.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis of Drusen-like Lesions
content: Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy: Autosomal dominant; appears in 2nd/3rd decades.
Cuticular drusen: Grouped early adult-onset (25–75 μm). 'Stars in the sky' appearance on FA. Linked to CFH gene variant.
Type 2 membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis: Chronic renal disease; bilateral drusen-like lesions; CFH gene implicated.

sections.title: Antioxidant Supplementation: AREDS Findings
content: High-dose antioxidants/minerals decrease risk of advanced AMD development.
AREDS1 Risk Reduction: 25–30% at 10 years for advanced signs at baseline.
No benefit seen in those with early or no AMD at baseline.
AREDS1 High-Risk Characteristics for Age >55: Extensive intermediate drusen, One+ large drusen, GA in one/both eyes, or late AMD in one eye.

sections.title: AREDS2 Study Breakthroughs
content: Lutein/Zeaxanthin: Safe and likely superior alternative to beta-carotene (18% additional risk reduction).
Beta-carotene Warning: Increases lung cancer in smokers/former smokers.
Zinc: 25 mg likely maximal absorbed; lower dose (25 mg) reduces GI/urinary side effects vs 80 mg.
Omega-3 fatty acids: Did not enhance outcomes.
Competition: Carotenoid absorption competition may affect results in some patients.

sections.title: Recommended Daily Supplementation (AREDS2)
content: Vitamin C: 500 mg
Vitamin E: 400 IU
Lutein: 10 mg
Zeaxanthin: 2 mg
Zinc: 25–80 mg
Copper: 2 mg (may not be required with lower zinc dose)

sections.title: Lifestyle & Prevention Tips
content: Green leafy vegetables: Prudent choice for early AMD/family history.
Oily fish: Regular consumption supported by some authorities.
Smoking: Cessation is mandatory advice.
Sunlight: Protective measures against excessive exposure.
Home Monitoring: Provide Amsler grid for regular self-testing.
TIP: Risk of severe AMD in patients with high-risk dry characteristics can be reduced with regular supplementation.

sections.title: Non-exudative (Dry) AMD: Overview
sections.content: Common condition; GA threatens central vision in 5 million people worldwide. Involves loss of photoreceptors and RPE. Pathogenesis: Activation of complement factors C3 and C5 is vital. Lesion size measured via FAF is the primary trial outcome.

sections.title: Dry AMD Diagnostic Signs
content: Step 1: Gradual vision impairment (months/years); vision better in bright light.
Step 2: Numerous soft drusen (may become confluent).
Step 3: Focal RPE hyper- and/or hypopigmentation.
Step 4: Geographic Atrophy (GA) - sharply circumscribed areas of RPE atrophy; visible choroidal vessels.
Step 5: Severe impairment if fovea involved; rare MNV development in GA area.

sections.title: Advanced Imaging for Dry AMD
content: OCT - Outer Retinal Tubulations: Roundish hyporeflective spaces (degenerating photoreceptors) around GA margins.
OCT - Outer Retinal Corrugations: Undulating hyper-reflective layer (basal laminar deposit) between RPE and basement membrane.
Basal Linear Deposit: Membranous debris between RPE basement membrane and Bruch membrane inner layer.
Microperimetry: Accurate central vision testing method.
FAF: Shows hyperautofluorescence in junctional zones at high risk of GA progression.
FA: Window defects in atrophic areas; late staining of exposed sclera.

sections.title: Dry AMD Management & Social Support
content: Prophylaxis: Address smoking, sun, cardiovascular, and dietary factors.
Amsler Grid: Urgent professional advice needed if vision changes.
Support: Low vision aids and visually impaired certification to access social/financial support.

sections.title: Potential New & Experimental Therapies
content: Complement Inhibitors: Avacincaptad pegol (C5) or Pegcetacoplan (C3) intravitreal injections reduce GA growth.
Saffron: 20 mg/day may improve retinal function short-term.
Photocoagulation: Reduces drusen extent but not AMD progression risk.
Visual Cycle Modulation: Emixustat (vitamin A processing reduction) has not proved helpful.
Failed/Ineffective: Many of the 13 complement inhibitors studied were ineffective.

sections.title: Experimental Surgical Interventions
content: Patients must be informed of high risks and slender likelihood of long-term vision improvement.
Miniature Intraocular Telescope: Benefit in selected cases.
RPE Stem Cells: Implanted behind macula; improved vision in some patients.
Macular Translocation Surgery: High complication rate; not successful in improving vision.
Visual Prostheses: Various types currently under investigation.
